## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with several manuscripts; most carefully corrected; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.**

**A most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, but gathered together for the first time in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

The *Patrology* has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the Graeco-Latin edition is given as “eight hundred and one thousand three hundred” in the supplied text [the precise omitted unit is uncertain]. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# The complete works of St. Anselm

## Prolegomena to the works of St. Anselm

[Col. 0009]

### To the most illustrious and most noble lord, Dom James-Nicholas Colbert, Abbot of Bec, Prior and Lord of La Charité-sur-Loire, and also of Ambert

The one who surpasses all teachers of sacred doctrine, most illustrious lord, presents himself to you so that you may hasten into his embrace—the one whom you venerate as a father—and listen attentively to him whom you revere as a teacher, since you are most devoted to the study of purer theology.

He offers you his own readings, and indeed corrected ones, in which alone you may possess everything that you have read elsewhere, so that what you learn from him as he explains it, all may one day learn from you as their teacher.

This is Anselm, formerly abbot of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury. Restored at last to his original splendor, he now rejoices in illuminating the abbot of Bec with his own light, so that, in return for your favor, he himself may become more illustrious through your name; and so that you, illuminated by him, may shine together with the radiant Anselm.

Until now, whether mutilated or disfigured by errors, he had fallen into such disrepute that he could scarcely be read at all, since he could scarcely even be understood. We have now restored him to his native integrity and purity, consulting very many manuscripts gathered from every quarter, so that what previously offended the reader at every point now proceeds intact with an unobstructed step, and whoever had stumbled over the words may easily reach their meaning.

Now, therefore, so that the works of St. Anselm may become objects of love and study for everyone, what remains except that they should shine under your name? For under whose name could the works of that holy doctor emerge more happily than yours? Whatever is profound in the sciences, whatever is marvelous in the arts, rightly celebrates the name of Colbert while seeking his protection. Who would not seek the patronage of one who, while serving as the king’s and kingdom’s confidential counselor, advances or protects everyone’s studies so effectively that students of the sciences find in him a Maecenas and all men of letters a patron?

Therefore, most illustrious lord, Anselm, restored to his original splendor, desires to be marked with your name, so that for us he may have as patron one whom not France alone, but Europe and the entire world, glory in possessing as a father—Anselm, who was once the glory and adornment of France, England, and, even more, the Christian world.

He, taken from the abbacy of Bec, whose place you occupy, and raised to the episcopal insignia—which it is already the prayer of all that you may soon obtain by merit of learning and piety—does not submit his works to your examination for correction, as once to Lanfranc’s judgment; rather, corrected as they are, he entrusts them to your studies and protection.

Perhaps you alone will wonder that the acknowledged prince of theologians should seek to have you, a student of sacred doctrine, as his guardian. This is the one thing everyone wonders at in you: that you are not so much a student of your father as his agent and defender, more than his disciple. The works of this holy doctor certainly breathe a lofty understanding; yet the spirit with which you are aflame is not unequal even to loftier matters.

St. Anselm alone explored the majesty of the supreme essence with a humility that was not crushed by glory, and reached it with a wisdom that understood what he had believed by faith. He alone expounded the economy of the divine Word in such a way that what no one could grasp, everyone may apprehend who, together with him, has advanced from faith to understanding. He alone explained the fall of the angel and of man, and the transmission of original stain, in such a way that what had remained hidden from others now becomes manifest to all who believe in order to understand. He alone arranged the harmony of divine foreknowledge, predestination, and grace with human freedom—an harmony that few can penetrate—according to a principle by which anyone must perish who so defends one that he denies the other.

These are the things, most illustrious lord, that St. Anselm understood; these are the things that St. Anselm taught. They are lofty and supreme, but for that very reason worthy of your studies, which strive toward this one goal: to understand what is worthy of God. Who, then, is more worthy than you to receive the treasures of divine wisdom hidden in the works of this holy doctor—or what is more worthy of you? Receive them, therefore, in the spirit in which the man who dedicates them to your name, in homage to his reverence for you, prays eternally that you may always understand with Anselm nothing but what is right and holy, and may always prosper in God.

Your most devoted servant,

**Fr. Gabriel Gerberon**, priest and monk of the Congregation of St. Maur.

[Col. 0013]

# Preface to all the works of St. Anselm

[Col. 0013A]

Whatever we have been taught by the word of God and believe, we understand by being instructed through the volumes of the Holy Fathers; and no one who thinks as a Catholic doubts that richer and purer streams of our faith must be drawn from these public fountains of the Church. Hence all who have truly been learned have not merely devoted themselves entirely to reading these books of sacred doctrine, but also expended all the effort that was fitting in carefully cleansing them of the stains and impurities that, through the passage of time and the ignorance or negligence of copyists, they had acquired. This was the labor of all who watched over truth not only to learn it but also to transmit it to posterity.

Such are the studies of the monks—never sufficiently praised—and, above all, if we believe Eadmer, of Anselm himself: a pious as well as useful labor, by which they went before us as examples of learning and virtue, growing pale not only over the reading but also over the correction of the writings of the saints.

Several emulators of this ancestral piety and ancestral labor have already published certain works of holy doctors corrected by more purifying types, and more ascetics of the Congregation of St. Maur are still preparing others for printing. We encountered St. Anselm, formerly abbot of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury. Although his writings sparkled here and there with the splendors of loftier doctrine, we found them so corrupted that scarcely a single complete sentence remained in them.

To restore them to their native purity, we consulted several manuscript codices, which distinguished libraries freely supplied to us—namely, the Royal, Victorine, Thuana, Cistercian, and Cotton libraries in England; the Tournai Martinian Library; those of the distinguished gentleman Joly, precentor of Paris, and of the distinguished gentleman Bigot of Rouen. Nor did we omit the manuscript copies belonging to the libraries of Bec, Jumièges, St. Michael’s on the Mount, Corbie, and Saint-Germain.

We also consulted various editions of St. Anselm’s works: two Gothic editions without place or year; one Nuremberg edition of 1491; two Paris editions, one of 1544 and the other of 1549; the Venetian edition of 1549; two Cologne editions, one of 1573 and the other of 1612; and the Lyon edition, the latest, of 1630.

On the authority both of these printed editions and of the manuscripts, we restored whatever had been deleted or omitted in St. Anselm’s works; we cut away what had been wrongly inserted; and whatever had been diverted into other words or other meanings, we brought back, as far as we could, to the author’s words and intention, with the sincerity that was required of us.

We also separated, with equal judgment, works known not to be St. Anselm’s from those rightly attributed to him. We placed the former either in an Appendix or among Eadmer’s works, since Eadmer undoubtedly wrote some of the works circulated among those of St. Anselm—namely, the *Book on the Excellence of the Blessed Virgin*, the *Book on Heavenly Blessedness*, and the *Book on Similitudes*.

To have these works appear in some order, we divided them into four parts. The first contains didactic or dogmatic works—that is, treatises expounding theological or philosophical doctrines. The second contains exhortatory writings, namely homilies and exhortations. The third includes ascetic writings, that is, meditations and prayers. The fourth contains letters.

We arranged the dogmatic works not according to chronological order but according to the dignity of their subject or argument, and according to the requirements of method. Thus the works dealing with the one God—namely the *Monologion*, the *Proslogion*, and the *Book against the Respondent on behalf of the Fool*—come first; then those concerning the triune God, the *Book on the Faith of the Trinity*, and so forth, together with the *Book on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. Next come the works concerning the incarnation of the Word, namely the books *Why God Became Man* and *The Book on Virginal Conception*, and so forth. These are preceded by the little book *On the Will of God* and the *Book on the Fall of the Devil*, since they contribute to an understanding of the divine incarnation.

Next comes the *Book on the Agreement of Foreknowledge with Free Choice*. According to the requirements of proper method, the dialogues *On Truth* and *On Free Choice*, as well as the little book *On the Will*, ought likewise to have preceded it. After these come the books or letters that treat something concerning the sacraments, such as the letters *On Unleavened Bread*, *On the Diversity of the Sacraments*, *On Priests Living with Concubines*, and *On the Marriages of Blood Relatives*. This first part concludes with the dialectical question that is the subject of the dialogue *On the Grammarian*.

[Col. 0014C]

We properly arranged the exhortatory writings, namely the homilies, according to the sequence of the books and chapters of Scripture that they explain. We distinguished the ascetic writings—that is, the meditations and prayers—in such a way that we presented separately, first, the meditations in which the mind contemplates God, and then the prayers in which the faithful soul invokes God and implores the intercession of the saints.

In making these distinctions, we observed the following order. First come the meditations or prayers by which the mind is brought to compunction; then follow those by which the soul is inflamed with love of the virtues.

Furthermore, to the three books of letters first published by Dom Picard we have added a fourth, containing all the others found in the manuscripts of the Cotton Library. The distinguished Mr. Cotton, with his customary kindness toward students of truth, communicated to us more than one hundred letters that had hitherto remained unpublished, at the urging of the distinguished Mr. Joly, counselor to the king, who was then residing in England. We also drew several letters from the manuscripts of the Royal, Gislenian, and Martinian libraries of Tournai, and from the Remigian Library of Rheims, where there is more a fragment than a letter. We attached some of them to the third book, some to the fourth, and published others in the Supplement after the index, since they did not come to our attention until all the other works of this holy doctor had already been printed.

We have added an Appendix in which we have set aside works that, although they falsely bear Anselm’s name, we nevertheless judged should not be wholly excluded because they have not been published elsewhere. We have not printed here works already printed in other volumes. Thus we excluded entirely the *Book on the Members and Acts Attributed to God*, which is found among the works of St. Jerome and St. Augustine; likewise the *Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which begins, “I read and reread,” and which has been published among the works of William, abbot of St. Thierry, in the Cistercian Library; and finally the books *On the Image of the World*, which in the Library of the Fathers is attributed to Honorius of Autun.

The *Disputation of a Jew with a Christian*, however, which Gilbert, abbot of Westminster, wrote, has been given a place here because its author addressed it to St. Anselm and it has not previously been published.

By reason of similarity of subject we have also added another *Dialogue of a Jew and a Christian*, composed not long afterward by Rupert of Deutz. He himself calls it the *Ring of Faith*; I have discussed it at greater length in several places in my *Apology for Rupert*. Since I had long searched for it, knowing that this work was absent from the published writings of the abbot of Deutz, I finally obtained it fortunately. Through the diligence of the Very Reverend Father Dom Martin de Busch, prior of the monastery of Laeties, it was transcribed from a manuscript and sent to us in friendship. We have therefore made it public, most suitably attaching it to the other abbot’s dialogue against the Jews.

[Col. 0016A]

We have not thought it appropriate to print here the commentaries on Matthew, the Song of Songs, the Apocalypse, and Paul’s Epistles, since we are certain that they are not Anselm’s but chiefly those of Hervaeus, a monk of Bourg-Dieu. It is our intention to publish in another edition all his commentaries on Sacred Scripture that we possess in manuscript codices, when circumstances permit.

Finally, it is necessary to note here: first, that several exhortations and prayers, or other little works, may perhaps be listed here among St. Anselm’s books even though it is by no means certain that they are his; but a stricter judgment, to be presented below, will demonstrate what may rightly be assigned to him; second, that all the individual corrections and variant readings have been collected and reprinted more carefully and scrupulously at the end of the works. [We have placed them at the foot of the pages, as is our custom. *Editor of the Patrology*.] Thus anyone who wishes to attend to these matters will know how variously the manuscripts read in comparison with the Lyon edition of 1630, with which we collated them.

Moreover, so that nothing should be lacking from this small work of ours in this edition, we shall append a judgment on each of the works contained in this volume. From it anyone will easily distinguish spurious works from the legitimate works of St. Anselm, and will recognize without difficulty, insofar as the evidence permits conjecture, in what period and by which author each work appeared. Meanwhile, may the reader enjoy our work.

[Col. 0015B]

# Judgment on the works of St. Anselm

[Col. 0015C]

## Judgment on the *Monologion*

All editions contain this book, and all printed and manuscript authorities attribute it to Anselm. He himself mentions it in several places cited below.

It is not so certain in what order or at what time this work was written. Eadmer seems to suggest that it was written after the four dialogues discussed below (*Life of St. Anselm*, book I, col. 63); on his authority, all the others assign this work fifth place. Yet this book is mentioned several times in the first chapter of the first of those dialogues, namely the dialogue *On Truth*. It therefore appears that the book cannot be later than those dialogues.

Father Théophile Raynaud believes that the passages from the *Monologion* were later inserted or attached to this dialogue. His conjecture seems to be supported by the fact that the name *Monologion*, by which the book is called in that chapter, was not prefixed to it until long after such dialogues had been published, as will be explained below.

Nevertheless, this conjecture is mistaken. For what the disciple had quoted from the *Monologion* in the first chapter, the teacher deliberately takes up again for explanation in the tenth chapter of the same dialogue, and demonstrates it so well that the disciple replies that nothing can be objected to the teacher’s reasoning. Anyone who attends to the whole sequence of this dialogue can therefore see that these passages from the *Monologion* were not added to it. Moreover, all the manuscripts read in this way.

Nor does Eadmer assert that this work was published after the dialogues. After saying that these dialogues had been written by Anselm, he adds: “He also composed a little book which he called the *Monologion*.” These words do not prove that the book appeared only after the dialogues. As for the fact that the book is called the *Monologion* in chapters 1 and 10 [elsewhere 11] of the dialogue, I would readily judge that this title was added after Anselm changed the title of the work and wished it to be called *Monologion*. It is therefore established that Anselm composed this work before writing the dialogue *On Truth*.

In truth, it is first not only in the order of composition but also in the dignity of its subject. In it St. Anselm, speaking as one reasoning with himself, proves by many necessary arguments, without the authority of Scripture, everything that we believe by faith concerning God’s existence and essence. For this reason he had entitled the work *An Example of Meditating on the Rational Basis of Faith*, without the author’s name prefixed, as the Sagien manuscript presents it; we therefore regard that manuscript as older than the others. He later called it the *Monologion*.

When Hugh, Archbishop of Lyon, ordered him to place his name on it, Anselm, then already abbot of Bec, called it *Monologion*, that is, “Soliloquy.” These facts may be learned from his prologue to the *Proslogion*, from chapters 4 and 9 of the *Book on the Faith of the Trinity and the Incarnation of the Word*, from his letter to Hugh, which is letter 17 of book II, from his letter to Lanfranc, letter 63 of book I, and from his letter to Maurice, letter 65 of that same first book.

Anselm wrote this book at the insistence of his monks, especially Maurice, while he was prior of Bec. Before publishing it, he sent it to Lanfranc, already archbishop, for correction, as he himself testifies in his letters to him. See book IV, letter 102, and book I, letter 63.

When St. Anselm had said in this book that it was not properly said that there are three persons in God in the same way as there are three substances, and so forth, certain people criticized him. He defended himself against their judgment by the authority of Blessed Augustine, as he himself, while still prior, writes to Rainald, abbot, in letter 74 of book I, and to Lanfranc, archbishop, in letter 68 of book I.

## Judgment on the *Proslogion*

Anyone may learn the subject and title of this book from Eadmer, book I of the *Life of St. Anselm* (col. 63), from the prologue of the book itself, and from letters 11 and 17 of book II. This work of St. Anselm appears in all printed editions and manuscripts.

In printed editions it is entitled *Prosologion*, but this is an error. The book should be entitled *Proslogion*, as the manuscripts 464 and 2267 of the Royal Library and other older manuscripts have it, as may be seen in the corrections that we placed at the end of the works.

That Anselm composed it while still prior of Bec, and indeed after the *Monologion*—between 1063 and 1077—is clear from Eadmer at the place cited. St. Anselm himself commends what he explained in this little work concerning the divine nature and its persons in chapter 4 of the *Book on the Faith of the Trinity and the Incarnation of the Word*. As for what he expressed in it concerning the fullness of the joy of blessedness, he advises that it be read to Hugh the recluse in letter 22 of book II.

Although, as William of Jumièges says (*History of the Normans*, book VI, chapter 9), this little book was great in the weight of its arguments and in the subtlety of its contemplation, someone nevertheless undertook to refute its reasoning. We shall speak of him in the judgment of the following little work.

One point remains to be observed: since St. Anselm is unquestionably the author of this little work, from which a large part of the *Manual* attributed to St. Augustine was compiled, it is plainly established that the *Manual* is not Augustine’s but is, for the most part, Anselm’s production. We shall demonstrate this below in the judgment of Meditation 21, which begins “Come now,” and which is excerpted entirely from this little work.

[Col. 0018A]

## Judgment on the *Reply on Behalf of the Fool*

When the *Proslogion* came into the hands of someone who thought Anselm’s argument—that “that than which nothing greater can be conceived” exists at least in the understanding, and therefore necessarily exists in reality—was invalid, he wished to refute it and published a written reply, as Eadmer relates in book I of the *Life of St. Anselm*, at the place cited.

This work has various titles, which may be seen in the various readings of the little book placed at the end of the works. At the end of the reply, the *Proslogion* is highly commended.

Anselm was so determined to conceal who the author of this reply was that, in the prologue to his *Apologetic*, page 37, he thought it sufficient to say that the author was not a fool but a Catholic. Hence, until now, the name of the respondent had not been heard. We have established it from the testimony of manuscripts, which proclaim Gaunilo, a monk of Marmoutier, the author of this reply. See the variant readings of this and the following little work.

Let the opinion of Francesco Pico, therefore, assigning this work to Robert Olkot, be dismissed far away; Olkot is known to have lived two hundred years after Anselm. He and others with him rejected St. Anselm’s reasoning as though it violated logic; but I would dare say that they did not understand it. Perhaps another opportunity will arise for discussing it.

## Judgment of the book against Gaunilo, the respondent on behalf of the Fool

A certain friend of St. Anselm sent him Gaunilo’s reply. When the holy doctor examined it, he was pleased, and sent it back to the same friend together with a refutation, as Eadmer testifies in book I of the *Life of St. Anselm*, at the place cited.

This refutation is found in all printed and manuscript copies of St. Anselm’s works. In manuscript 142 of the library of the House of St. Peter, tract 3, it appears under the title *Against Fools*. In manuscript tract 8 of the library of Pembroke Hall it bears the title *Against the Foolish Respondent*.

Anselm’s modesty is remarkable in it. As Eadmer reports at the place cited, he thanks his critic, whom he himself declares not to be a fool but a Catholic in the prologue to his reply. He judged that the critic had undertaken his refutation not out of malice but out of goodwill, to refute what seemed weak to him, as Anselm says at the conclusion of this *Apologetic*.

We learn from Eadmer at the place cited that St. Anselm wrote this while he was prior of Bec, around the year 1070.

## Judgment of the book or letter *On the Faith of the Trinity and the Incarnation of the Word*

This book exists in all manuscript and printed copies of St. Anselm’s works. It was found with the following title: *A Book or Letter on Faith*, or *A Book on the Incarnation of the Word against the Jews*. This is confirmed by the preface to the little work in the Gothic editions, which give neither year nor place. In one of them the words “against the Jews” are omitted; these words were rightly deleted from subsequent editions.

As I conjecture, they had entered from Trithemius, who in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers* judged that St. Anselm had written a *Book on the Trinity* against the Jews, distinct from this work. This error arose from the various titles given to the little work. For in manuscript 336 of the Royal Library the book is entitled *Anselm on the Trinity*. Not without reason, since the faith of the Trinity is chiefly explained in it.

Accordingly, we have restored the complete title, *On the Faith of the Trinity*, and so forth; for we did not think that part should be omitted which more clearly indicates the subject of the work.

In chapter 4 of this work St. Anselm commends the *Monologion* and the *Proslogion*, and therefore this book is later than they. In chapter 17 of the *Book on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, however, he mentions this letter, and therefore that book is later than it.

[Col. 0019B]

Eadmer, in book II of the *Life of St. Anselm* (col. 84), and in book II of the *History of Recent Events*, writes that Anselm composed this work at the beginning of his archbishopric, in epistolary style, and intended it for Pope Urban II. He says that the holy pontiff used it at the Council of Bari to refute the error of the Greeks more firmly.

Nevertheless, it is certain, first, that Anselm began this work while he was still abbot, namely in 1092. In his letter to Baldwin, letter 51 of book II, he indicates that he began this book before crossing over to England.

He came to Canterbury on the day before the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, and in the following year, which Eadmer dates to 1093, he was elected archbishop, according to Eadmer’s own history, book II of the *Life of St. Anselm*. “On the day before the Nativity of the Blessed Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary,” he says, “he came to Canterbury … He was seized and carried by force into the neighboring church amid hymns. These events took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, on the day before the Nones of March.”

This is further proved by Anselm’s indication in chapter 1 of this work that it had been begun before the Council of Soissons, held under the presidency of Raynald, Archbishop of Rheims, in the closing months of 1092 or the beginning of 1093.

Second, it is certain that St. Anselm gave this work its final form in 1094, namely after his consecration in 1093, on the day before the Nones of December, when, after the king had crossed into Normandy, Anselm devoted himself to heavenly studies, as Eadmer relates in book II of the *Life of St. Anselm*. According to the same witness at the place cited, these events occurred in 1094.

The saint wrote this book against a certain cleric who asserted that the three persons in God were three things, just as there are three angels or three souls. When Anselm heard that the man had repented, he set aside his own work and did not complete it until he learned that the man had falsely renounced his error. He says this himself in the prologue to chapter 1 of the book.

This cleric, against whose blasphemies St. Anselm sharpened his pen, is called Roscelin or Ruzelin in manuscript 3 of the Thuana Library, as the variant readings note; and in the manuscript of the monastery of Longpont, where this book appears under the title *On the Incarnation of the Word against the Blasphemies of Rucelin of Compiègne*.

This Rucelin was Abelard’s teacher, as Horst observes in his notes to St. Bernard’s letters, volume V, page 37, column 1. His errors are also noted by St. Anselm in book II, letters 35, 41, and 51; by Abelard in letter 21; by Ivo of Chartres in letter 7; and by the writers of the annals under the years 1092 and 1094. Many people were troubled by this difficulty in that period, as Anselm himself reports (col. 263).

## Judgment of the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*

This book is read in all manuscript and printed volumes of St. Anselm’s works. In a manuscript at Cambridge, no. 235 of St. Benedict’s College, it is attributed to Augustine—undoubtedly through an error involving the initial letter A, which made Augustine stand for Anselm.

Although Eadmer does not explicitly state in the books *On His Life* that Anselm published this work—he says only in book II, col. 102, that the Greeks were refuted by Anselm in a Catholic disputation—it nevertheless becomes clear from the same author in book II of the *History of Recent Events*. There he says that Anselm himself, after the Council of Bari, which was convened in 1098, treated the matter more carefully and subtly, wrote an outstanding work, and sent it to his friends in many places at their request.

This is also evident from Anselm’s book or letter *On Unleavened Bread*, in chapter 1 of which he says that he sent Walerannus the little work he had published on the procession of the Holy Spirit. The same disputation is mentioned in letters 53 and 160 of book III and in letter 11 of book IV.

In the Gothic and Cologne editions this book is entitled *Letter*, and so forth. I conjecture that this was because Anselm composed it at Hildebert’s request and sent it to him, as is clear from the letters cited.

It may therefore be inferred that this work was published before the completion of the year 1101, in which the schism was extinguished, from the aforesaid letter in which Anselm writes that he had sent this little work to Walerannus, who was still adhering to the schism. The previously cited words of Eadmer also establish with certainty that it was composed only after the Council of Bari, which was held not in 1097, as the compilers of councils incorrectly calculate, but in 1098. For in 1097 Anselm departed from the court on Thursday, which was the Ides of October, and on the following day came to the port of Dover, intending to travel from England to Rome. He remained at Lyon until the Tuesday before Palm Sunday—therefore in the year 1098—on which day he departed from Lyon; after several days he reached Rome, and, because of the excessive heat, withdrew to the estate of Schiavia. From there he traveled with Urban II to Bari and attended the council. Eadmer recounts these events at length in Book II of the *History of Recent Events*. From them it is clear that the Council of Bari was convened in 1098, and that the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* was not published until after that year had elapsed.

I therefore judge, first, that Anselm was prompted to undertake this work by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, in the year 1100, after the month of August, when King William laid down both his kingdom and his life—that is, immediately after Hildebert was released from the prison in which he had been confined, and after Anselm had returned to England. That Anselm was then in England is clearly indicated by the aforesaid letter of Hildebert to Anselm, which is Letter 160 of Book III, in these words:

> “Happy should I be if I had deserved to be instructed even while present. But this place begrudges me that, and has granted me no other service of greeting unless I first consult half the world; for it is necessary to test the mildness of the sea and of the air, etc.”

In this letter he also indicates that he had not yet crossed over to England. Hence I infer that it was written before the year 1101, at the beginning of which—namely, shortly before spring—Hildebert crossed into England, before Elias, after capturing the city, had besieged the fortress of Le Mans, as D. de Bondonnet observes concerning Hildebert in his book *On the Lives of the Bishops of Le Mans*.

Second, I judge that this work was composed by Anselm between the beginning of 1101 and 1103, when Anselm again left England, and that he sent it to Hildebert and Walerannus at that very time.

## Censure of the Book *On the Will of God*

This little book is found in none of the manuscripts that have come to my notice. Nevertheless, since it is read in all printed editions under the name of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and since the words and judgments of Saint Anselm are discernible in it, we have not relegated it to the appendix. I am indeed aware that Anselm of Laon disputed *On the Will of God* in that century, and that his opinion on this matter was sharply attacked by Rupert of Deutz, not only in words but also in writing, as I discussed at length in Rupert’s *Apology* (in the prologue and in Part I, pp. 10, 11, 12, 13, 16, 17, 43, and 81). But why should not Anselm of Canterbury also have written on the same question, together with that of the harmony of foreknowledge, etc., toward the end of his life, when minds were then inflamed over this question concerning the will of God—only a few years before Rupert confronted Anselm of Laon? For Rupert wrote against him around the year 1116, as I observed in his *Apology*, whereas Anselm had died in 1109.

## Censure of the Book *On the Fall of the Devil*

Saint Anselm himself mentions this dialogue in chapter 17 of Book I of *Why God Became Man*, near the end of chapter 5 of *On the Virginal Conception*, and in chapter 7 of *On the Harmony of Foreknowledge, Predestination, and Grace with Free Choice*. The subject of the book is explained in the prologue to the dialogue *On Truth*.

Eadmer records that Saint Anselm wrote this work, as well as three others, while he was still prior at Bec—that is, from the year 1063, when he was appointed prior, until 1077, when he was elected abbot.

One point should be noted here: the treatise *On Evil*, which he himself wrote to Mauritius, is nothing other than an excerpt from chapter 11 of this dialogue, with the conversational form removed, as anyone will readily observe who compares the letter to Mauritius, Letter 8 of Book II, with the aforementioned chapter 11 [or 10]. For this reason we have not published that writing separately, since it is found complete, in one continuous context, both in that chapter and in this letter.

## Censure of the Books *Why God Became Man*

Saint Anselm began this work in England at the request of Boso and completed it in the region of Capua, before he was compelled to attend the Council of Bari, as he himself testifies in the preface and Eadmer reports in Book II of *The Life of Anselm*. It necessarily follows that this work appeared before the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which, as we have shown, was not written until after the Council of Bari.

Accordingly, in 1094, after completing the book *On the Incarnation of the Word*, Saint Anselm undertook these books, while, during the king’s absence, he devoted himself entirely to sacred studies, according to Eadmer, Book II of *The Life of Anselm* (col. 84). He completed them at the estate of Schiavia, to which he had withdrawn in 1098 and where he was forced by the excessive heat to remain until the appointed day of the council was approaching—namely, the Kalends of October of that year, 1098, and not of 1097, as we have demonstrated from Eadmer in the censure of the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*.

Eadmer himself transcribed these books for the Church of Bec, of which he was a son, as Saint Anselm testifies in Letter 25 of Book II. Saint Anselm also asked that they be transcribed by the monks of Canterbury and sent to Paschal II, if we are to believe his Letter 55 of Book IV.

It should also be noted that at the end of chapter 17 of Book II Anselm says that he intended to write about original sin. It follows that the book *On the Virginal Conception and Original Sin* is later than this one. The same is indicated by its prologue and by chapter 22 of this book, where it mentions the books *Why God Became Man*.

## Censure of the Book *On the Virginal Conception and Original Sin*

After the Council of Bari and the Roman synod, Saint Anselm, while residing at Lyon, wrote this work after completing the books *Why God Became Man* and before the meditation *On Human Redemption*, as Eadmer establishes in Book II of *The Life of Anselm* (col. 107). It is therefore clear that this book was composed in 1099, the year in which the Roman council was held under Urban II, specifically on the feast of the Apparition of Saint Michael. That feast was the expiration of the truce which the king of England had obtained at the feast of the Nativity of the Lord after the Council of Bari, according to Eadmer, Book II of the *History of Recent Events*.

Saint Anselm attended this Roman synod, and did not return to Lyon until after it had been completed, as is clear from Eadmer in the same place. Nor did he leave Lyon until after the death of the king, which occurred in August 1100—one year after the death of Urban II, who had departed this life in October [corrected to July] of the preceding year, as Eadmer observes at the end of Book II of the *History of Recent Events*.

This book is sometimes entitled simply *On the Virginal Conception*. Thus it appears at Cambridge in manuscript 161 of the Public Library, in manuscript 217 of Caius College, in manuscript 203 of Pembroke Hall, and elsewhere. Sometimes it is entitled simply *On Original Sin*, as at Cambridge in manuscript 235 of Saint Benedict’s College and in other manuscripts, as may be seen in the various readings. This may perhaps explain Trithemius’s error in distinguishing a book *On the Virginal Conception* from a book *On Original Sin*.

In the preface and in chapter 22 of this little work Saint Anselm mentions the books *Why God Became Man*, which are therefore earlier than it. This work, however, preceded the book *On the Harmony of Foreknowledge*, in whose chapter 7 mention is made of this little work.

Finally, in the letter to Theodoric, which is Letter 42 of Book IV, he writes about this work and orders that it be transcribed together with the books *Why God Became Man*, so that all of them might be sent to Paschal II. See Letter 55 of Book IV.

## Censure of a Certain Explanation of the Preceding Book

Although this explanation does not occur in the manuscripts of Saint Anselm’s works, it is nevertheless found in all editions of those works. Its occasion and subject can be learned from the work itself. Concerning its author and date, however, we know nothing other than that he was a contemporary of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, whom he calls “the instrument of the Holy Spirit of his age.” It follows that this explanation is later than Anselm, who died in 1109. Bernard, however, became a monk in 1113.

## Censure of the Dialogue *On Truth*

Saint Anselm wrote this dialogue while still prior, as Eadmer testifies in Book I of *The Life of Anselm* (col. 62), at the same time, namely, as the dialogues *On the Fall of the Devil*, *On Freedom*, and *On the Grammarian*. See Saint Anselm’s prologue to this dialogue, which he himself also mentions in chapter 5 of the book *On the Virginal Conception*. The same censure therefore applies to the dialogues *On Free Choice* and *On the Grammarian*, with the addition that in chapter 4, question 3, of *On the Harmony of Grace*, etc., mention is made of the dialogue *On Free Choice*.

## Censure of the Treatise *On the Will*

In Book *On the Harmony of Grace with Free Choice*, chapter 11, Saint Anselm promised, despite his very poor health, that he would at some time discuss the manifold division of the will that is customary. Since he never touched upon this subject anywhere, I reasonably infer that shortly before his death he composed this little book, which I published from manuscript Victorinus C. d. 12. I do so all the more willingly because it bears not only Anselm’s name but also his judgments.

## Censure of the Book *On the Harmony of Foreknowledge, Predestination, and Grace with Free Choice*

After peace had been restored to the English Church, Saint Anselm wrote this work near the end of his life—that is, in the year 1109—according to Eadmer, Book II of *The Life of Anselm* (col. 114).

The arrangement of this work varies, as has been noted in the various readings. To these variations may be added the fact that in manuscript 142 of Saint Peter’s House in England this book is divided into two treatises: the first is on foreknowledge and predestination; the second on grace and free choice. More properly, however, it is divided into three parts in manuscript 203 of Pembroke Hall: first, on foreknowledge and free choice; second, on predestination and free choice; third, on grace and free choice. In the manuscript of the Villers Library in Brabant it is called *The Book of Three Questions*. It is certainly a worthy book with which to close the life of so great a man.

## Censure of the Book or Letter *On Unleavened and Leavened Bread*

All printed and manuscript copies declare this book, or letter, to be Anselm’s; Dodechin himself does so under the year 1094. The book itself also declares in chapter 1 that it was written by the author who had published the treatise *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, of which we spoke above.

In manuscript 22 of the Lincoln Library, in manuscripts 217 of the Caius Library, in manuscript 145 of the Public Library at Cambridge, and in a Cistercian manuscript, it is entitled *On the Sacrifice of Unleavened and Leavened Bread*. In the manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai it is entitled *On the Sacrificial Bread against the Greeks*. Among the letters it was printed in the Cologne edition of 1612; in all other editions it was published among the books under the title that we have prefixed to it. See the various readings.

Since the aforementioned book *On the Procession*, etc., mentioned in chapter 1 of this letter, was published between 1101 and 1103, as we have demonstrated above, and since this letter was addressed to Walerannus of Noviomagus while he was still adhering to the schism—which began to be extinguished with the death of Guibert, which occurred, according to Dodechin, in 1100—it is absolutely certain that it was not written by Anselm before 1101, but shortly after the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, around 1102.

It would be unreasonable to extend its date to 1106, near the end of which Anselm returned to England and in which the emperor Henry IV died at Liège, since by that time the schism had completely ended and Henry V was already emperor. This letter preceded the other, *On the Diversity of the Sacraments*, at the end of which the author mentions it.

## Censure of the Book or Two Letters *On the Diversity of the Sacraments*

The inscriptions in all printed and manuscript copies present the first of these letters as Walerannus’s and the second as Anselm of Canterbury’s. Eadmer does not mention this work, nor the preceding little work, because he considered it necessary to list it among the letters. We have counted it among the books, in accordance with nearly all editions and most manuscripts.

In manuscript 22 of the Lincoln Library, manuscript 217 of the Caius Library, manuscript 203 of Pembroke Hall, the Cistercian manuscript, and the Nuremberg edition of 1491, this book is entitled *On the Sacraments of the Church*. Saint Bonaventure cites it under this same title in volume VII, Part IV, chapter 1 of the Third Response of the *Apology of the Poor*. See the various other titles in the various readings.

We conjecture the date of composition of these two letters as follows. Anselm had already sent Walerannus the letter on unleavened bread, as he himself indicates at the end of this little work. Then, from the final chapter of Walerannus’s letter and from chapter 1 of Saint Anselm’s letter, it is clear that Walerannus had by then been reconciled with Paschal II and was so close to him that he was already his co-secretary among the cardinals, as Paul Langius reports in the *Chronicle of Zeitz*.

I therefore judge that this letter of Saint Anselm was written in 1102, when Anselm devoted all his attention to the good of the Church, before he again traveled from England to Rome, where he arrived around the end of 1103. Thus, in the two years 1101 and 1102, Saint Anselm wrote the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, then the book *On Unleavened Bread*, and finally the letter *On the Differences among the Sacraments*.

## Censure of *The Offence of Priests*

This book exists at Cambridge in manuscript 235 of Saint Benedict’s College, in the Corbie manuscript E 10, and in the manuscript of Saint Évroult, from which we published it. It is nothing other than an excerpt from Saint Anselm’s letter to William, abbot, which is Letter 56 of Book I, as is evident to anyone who reads both. Dodechin says under the year 1094 that this William was abbot of Dersay; but he is called abbot of Hirsau in the old *Records against the Schismatics*, edited by Sebastian Tengnagel in 1612 and communicated to me by the most learned D. Baluze, where this letter is found. From the foregoing it is clear how falsely this little book is attributed to Honorius of Autun in volume XII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

## Censure of the Book *On the Marriage of Blood Relatives*

As far as I know, this book was first printed in the Cologne edition of 1612, and there among the letters. Since it is doctrinal, however, we have joined it to the other little works.

The inscription bearing Anselm’s name, the title *Method for Investigating the Reasons for the Things We Observe*, and the statement in chapter 6 that the whole of nature was corrupted through Adam, because the whole of it was then in him and was outside him, assign it to Anselm of Canterbury. All these points belong to Anselm.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that in chapters 3 and 7 of this book Anselm defines marriage between relatives as permissible in the sixth degree, whereas in the older councils of England, including those over which he himself presided, unions were prohibited through the seventh degree. The apparent discrepancy is easily reconciled if one observes that the canons prohibited marriage within the seventh degree until the relationship on either side reached the seventh degree, as the Council of London under Lanfranc in 1075 expresses it. Thus, if the sixth degree is reached on one side only and the seventh on the other, marriage may be contracted in the sixth degree.

Father Raynaud, in order to resolve this difficulty, judged in his *Syntax* that Anselm had counted the degrees of kinship at this point not from brother and sister but from nephew and niece, according to the definition of the Council of Szabolcs. But what reason would Anselm have had to enumerate these degrees here according to a different order from that used in the book *On Unleavened Bread* and in the canons that he himself enacted at the Council of London in 1102?

There is therefore no contradiction; everything suggests that this letter was written by Anselm. But to whom, and at what time, I have no basis for conjecture. Its inscription is mutilated: the name of the person to whom it is written is not preserved, nor is Anselm called archbishop.

Saint Anselm wrote Letter 142 of Book III to Murierdach, or Murchertach, king of Ireland, urging him to prohibit marriages between relatives. From Eadmer, Book II of the *History of Recent Events*, we learn that this king sent letters to Saint Anselm in 1095 and 1096 concerning the consecration of the bishop of Dublin and the bishop of Waterford. Hence it may reasonably be conjectured that this letter was written by Anselm to some Irishman around that time, namely around 1096.

## Censure of the Dialogue *On the Grammarian*

(See the censure of the dialogue *On the Fall of the Devil* and of the dialogue *On Truth*.)

## Censure of the Homilies

Since it is the duty of a pastor to feed the flock with the word of God, no one can doubt that Anselm, who was always ready and prepared to speak with eloquence and zeal, frequently delivered sermons to the people. Eadmer testifies that he preached in various places.

Of all Saint Anselm’s sermons or homilies, however, very few survive. In the older editions—namely, two Gothic editions, one Nuremberg edition of 1491, two Parisian editions of 1544 and 1549, and one Venetian edition of 1549—there is only one homily, the one on the passage: “Jesus entered,” etc. In the Cologne edition of 1573, expositions or homilies on several Gospel passages and on the words of Ecclesiasticus XXIV, “In all things, rest,” etc., were first printed under the name of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

A second Cologne edition, in 1612, and the Lyon edition, in 1630, published the same works under the same name. We therefore published them with that degree of confidence, although no manuscript known to me supports them and Eadmer says nothing about them; we assert nothing on that account, but transmit what we received. We changed only their order, arranging them according to the sequence of the passages of Scripture that they explain.

It is enough to note that these homilies are written in the same style and spirit as the expositions on Matthew which the Cologne edition assembled in the same volume under Anselm’s name. Anyone can readily discern this, in my opinion, by comparing the passages treated in both works.

At Oxford, in manuscript 242 of the Merton Library, there are homilies of Blessed Anselm; but I have not been able to learn which ones or how many.

In manuscript S 15 of Saint Évroult there is one homily with the title: “Here begins Anselm’s sermon on ‘When Jesus saw the crowds,’” etc. We inserted this, which was sent to us, as the second in order among the others.

We also added one on the Apostle’s words, “For it was fitting,” etc., from Corbie manuscript S 596, under this title: “According to Master Anselm on the verse: ‘For it was fitting,’” etc.

The homily on “Jesus entered,” etc., which we placed as the ninth, is repeated in all manuscripts and printed editions, including the oldest. In the manuscripts it bears Anselm’s name and has this title in manuscript 1106 of the Royal Library: “For the Assumption of Blessed Mary: Anselm on ‘He entered,’” etc. In Corbie manuscript P 307: “Anselm’s sermon for the Assumption, on ‘He entered,’” etc. In Corbie manuscript 596: “From the sayings of the lord archbishop Anselm.” In the breviary of the Church of Carcassonne: “For the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary: ‘At that time, he entered,’” etc., “Homily of the venerable archbishop Anselm.” Consult the various readings.

Saint Anselm wrote this homily at the request of William, abbot of Fécamp, and Arnulf, abbot of Troarn, as we learn from its prologue, which we published from a Corbie manuscript.

That he wrote it before becoming archbishop, and therefore before 1093, he himself sufficiently indicates in the prologue, where he says that he committed it to writing out of obedience, having delivered it more than once in the assembly of the brothers. It was therefore written between 1088, when Arnulf was elected abbot of Troarn according to the Chronicle of Gofernius cited by the author of *Pious Neustria* in chapter 2, *On the Abbey of Troarn*, and 1093, when Anselm was placed in charge of the Church of Canterbury.

Finally, in the library manuscript of the distinguished V. D. Bigot there is a homily entitled: “Here begins Blessed Anselm’s homily on John, concerning the lament of Magdalene.” This is the same work commonly but falsely attributed to Origen. Since I am not entirely certain that it is Anselm’s, and since it has been published elsewhere in several places, we have omitted it.

## Censure of the Exhortations

Father Theophilus, as far as I know, was the first to publish these exhortations or maxims. If he had explained where he obtained them and by what right he attributed them to Saint Anselm, we would know; therefore we published them among Saint Anselm’s works with the degree of confidence due to him.

One point is certain to me: they were written by a Benedictine monk. Several are drawn from the Rule of Saint Benedict, as when it says:

> “Why, by your evil deeds, do you grieve the most loving Father, who has deigned to count you among his children?”

Likewise:

> “Lest the Lord, provoked by your evil deeds, hand you over as a most wicked servant to everlasting punishment,” etc.

Likewise:

> “About to serve the eternal King, renounce your own wills,” etc.

Likewise:

> “While you have the opportunity, do what will profit you forever.”

All these statements are expressed in the prologue of the Rule of Saint Benedict. And when it says:

> “Be content with every kind of lowliness or extremity.”

Likewise:

> “Declare yourself inferior to everyone,”

which is found in chapter 5 of the Rule. And when it says:

> “Fear the day of judgment; guard the deeds of your life at every hour; make yourself a stranger to the deeds of the world,” etc.,

all these points are set forth in chapter 6 of the holy Rule.

## Censure of the *Admonition for One Who Is Dying*

Father Theophilus first made this public from a manuscript of the Vatican Library. The version transmitted to us from there, however, differs from it in some respects, as is evident from the various readings placed at the end of the work.

This formula of admonition is found in the manuscript of the library of Saint Martin of Tournai under the following title: “Treatise of Blessed Anselm: how a brother approaching death ought to be questioned, and how he ought to respond.” See the various readings.

I have no basis for conjecturing at what time Saint Anselm prescribed this formula.

## Censure of the Poem *On Contempt for the World* and Two Other Poems

This poem was first printed at Cologne in 1573, but in an incomplete and mutilated form. It was published there in full from the Paris manuscript of Saint Victor in 1612.

It exists in several manuscripts, with which we compared it, but in none of them does it bear Saint Anselm’s name. Indeed, in the manuscript of the Aldenburg Library the poem *On Contempt for the World* is attributed to Bernard of Cluny. In Gembloux manuscript C. 70 there are two poems *On Contempt for the World*: one begins, “Our little scroll to you,” etc.; the other is the one added to Anselm’s works and entitled “Claudianus to the Monks.” In Bec manuscript K 10 it is attributed to Roger of Caen, a monk of Bec.

I therefore do not dare to determine what claim Anselm has to this work. It is true that this holy teacher composed some verses, both hexameters and pentameters; but what follows from that? I will say only that this poem was composed by a monk who professed the holy Rule. For it contains many statements in accordance with the spirit of the Rule of Saint Benedict, as when it speaks explicitly to those who have promised conversion of life and exhorts the monk to believe that God is present everywhere and always, etc.

We appended the other two poems solely on the authority of D. Picard, who was the first to publish them.

## Censure of the Treatise *On Peace and Concord*

It is attributed to Anselm in a manuscript from Leuven, from which we published the transcript sent to us. Behold: it is foreign to Anselm’s style and thought.

## Censure of the Book of Meditations and Prayers

Eadmer testifies that Saint Anselm wrote prayers or meditations in Book II of *The Life of Anselm* (col. 56). Durandus, abbot of Casa-Dei, testifies to the same in his letter to Anselm, which is Letter 61 of Book I. Anselm himself also testifies to it in Letter 20 of Book I and Letter 51 of Book II. Finally, almost innumerable manuscripts testify to it.

He did not write them all at one time, but at different times, as will become evident from the censures of the individual works. These will also establish which works, and how many, truly proceeded from Saint Anselm.

### Censure of the Prologue

Anyone who recognizes in it both the words and the thought of the letter in which Saint Anselm writes to Gondulf that he divided his arguments into paragraphs so that their length would not produce weariness, and so that the reader might enter them—that is, stop or begin wherever he wished—will judge with me that this prologue was written by Saint Anselm. The same points occur in the prologue.

### Censure of Meditation 1

Father Theophilus first published it among Saint Anselm’s *Meditations*. He does not himself state from whom he obtained it.

The Reverend Father D. Franciscus Pommeraye assured us that it is found among Saint Anselm’s *Meditations* in the manuscript of D. Bigot’s library, which he had in his hands.

It certainly contains Saint Anselm’s judgments. For what it says in section 1—that the soul which does not awaken at the voice of God is dead rather than asleep—is the same thought expressed in Meditation 2. What it says there, that the soul was made in the image of God so that it might remember, understand, and love the supreme good, is precisely what he taught in the *Monologion*, the *Proslogion*, and elsewhere throughout his works. In section 3 it says that God alone truly is, and is true being, without whom nothing can be well. Saint Anselm explained this same point in the *Monologion* and in many other places.

Although this meditation is found in only a few manuscripts, at least under Anselm’s name, I nevertheless cannot deny it to Saint Anselm.

### Censure of Meditation 2

In all printed editions it appears under the title *The Book on Human Misery*. It is also found in all the manuscripts, but under different titles. In the manuscript of D. Bigot it is entitled *On the Terror of the Last Judgment*. In manuscript 2024 of the Royal Library, in the Cistercian manuscript, and in others, it is entitled *Meditation to Stir Up Fear*. Consult the various readings.

Durandus writes that he received it from Anselm’s monks, in Letter 61 of Book I. From that letter and from Anselm’s reply it is clear that it was published by Anselm before he became abbot—that is, before 1078. In it Anselm is not addressed as abbot, nor is he described as such. Durandus had received this meditation while he was abbot of the monastery of Casa-Dei, whose government he held from 1068 until 1078, when he was elected bishop of Clermont. It is therefore evident that it was written between 1068 and 1078, when Anselm became abbot of the monastery of Bec.

Saint Bonaventure cites it in chapter 3 of the *Soliloquy*, and Saint Antoninus transcribes it in full, Part II, title 16, chapter 12, section 7.

I note two points here. First, among Saint Bernard’s works there is a book bearing the same title, *On Human Misery*, but it is entirely different from this one. Second, it is found among the prayers collected by Abbot John in a manuscript codex from Metz. This is no slight argument that those prayers were copied by him rather than composed by him, as we shall demonstrate more fully below.

### Censure of Meditation 3

This is found in all printed and manuscript copies of Saint Anselm’s *Meditations*. See the diversity of its titles in the various readings.

I judge it to be one of those little works of a contrite heart which the aforementioned Durandus rejoices that he received in the previously cited letter. I therefore readily grant that it was composed at the same time as the preceding meditation was published.

In his *Syntax* of this meditation, Father Theophilus asks whether Saint Anselm is here reproaching and describing his own crimes under his own name; he concludes by denying this, lest the holy teacher be judged excessively prodigal of his reputation. To me, however, this seems an overly delicate scruple. Why investigate Anselm’s conscience, when Eadmer himself writes that he withdrew from the pursuit of piety in order to indulge himself? Let it be enough that Anselm washed away the sins of his youth with the tears of true repentance.

Several sentences of this meditation are found in chapter 39 of the book of *Meditations* falsely attributed to Saint Augustine.

### Censure of Meditations 4, 5, and 6

All the manuscripts with which these were compared, as well as manuscript 2024 of the Royal Library and the manuscript of D. Bigot, contain them among Saint Anselm’s *Meditations*. See the various readings.

### Censure of Meditation 7

Father Raynaud published it as composed from various sections that occur in other prayers whose author is certainly Saint Anselm. We, having set those sections aside, presented only what is proper to this work and does not occur in the others.

The first two paragraphs of this meditation are found in the manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai, a transcript of which was sent to us. I found the other two in no manuscript and published them solely on Father Theophilus’s authority, all the more willingly because I recognized in them Anselm’s thought and language.

I cannot conceal that the first two paragraphs are read in full in the book *On Contrition of Heart*, which is found in the appendix to volume IX of Saint Augustine’s works. But this takes nothing away from Saint Anselm’s claim, since that book is nothing other than an excerpt from various meditations and prayers which are beyond all doubt Anselm’s. We shall demonstrate this below in the judgment on the book *On Contrition of Heart*.

### Censure of Meditation 8

Father Theophilus first published it from a manuscript of the Vatican Library, and nothing occurs in it unworthy of Saint Anselm.

### Censure of Meditation 9

This meditation, which begins “Jesus of Nazareth,” etc., is read among Saint Anselm’s works in all printed editions under the title *Mirror of Evangelical Speech*; elsewhere it is called *The Goad of Love*. In the manuscript of D. Bigot it is entitled *On the Humanity*. In the manuscript of the Paris Oratory it bears the title: *The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the World, According to Blessed Anselm, Archbishop*.

In volume VII of Saint Bonaventure’s works there is a book entitled *The Goad of Love*, but it is entirely different from this one. I admit that this meditation occurs among Saint Bernard’s works under the title *Sermon of Blessed Bernard on the Passion of the Lord*. But those who observe that it is not written in Bernard’s style at all deny it to Saint Bernard; nor will I assert it more firmly to Anselm, since I do not recognize Anselm’s words in it. Nevertheless, it conflicts in no respect with his doctrine or piety, and it bears his name in all the printed editions, including the oldest, as well as in some manuscripts.

### Censure of Meditation 10

Father Theophilus published it from a Vatican manuscript, and I have no basis for judging that it is not Saint Anselm’s.

### Censure of Meditation 11

This is read among Saint Anselm’s meditations in all printed and manuscript copies. In manuscript 22 of the Lincoln Library it bears the title *On the Recreation of Man*. See the various titles in the various readings.

Eadmer, Book II of *The Life of Anselm*, testifies that Anselm wrote it at Lyon in 1099, after the book *On the Virginal Conception*, etc.

### Censure of Meditations 12 and 13

If I am not mistaken, Father Raynaud was the first to publish them among Saint Anselm’s meditations. I learned that they are counted among Saint Anselm’s meditations in only one manuscript, that of D. Bigot. In the twelfth I perceive Anselm’s phrasing; in the thirteenth I see a style entirely different. Nevertheless, both are congenial to devout minds.

### Censure of Meditation 14

Father Theophilus was the first to publish this under Saint Anselm’s name from manuscript “e” of the library—of the Viennese College, I believe. It also occurs among Saint Anselm’s *Meditations* in the manuscript of D. Bigot; I have not read it in the others.

It should be observed, however, that it contains the first nine chapters of the little book commonly called Saint Augustine’s *Manual*. We shall therefore give below a critical judgment of this book, as well as of the *Meditations* and the book *On Contrition of Heart*.

### Censure of Meditations 15, 16, and 17

In the Lyon edition of 1630 they appear as one meditation divided into three parts; we divided them into three meditations. Father Theophilus first brought this work to light from a manuscript and writes that it was sent by Anselm to his sister. I have indeed been reliably informed that this tripartite meditation addressed to his sister is found in the aforementioned manuscript of D. Bigot; I confess, however, that I have read it in no manuscript.

The following facts about its author are certain:

1. He was the brother of the virgin to whom the meditations are addressed; for in the second he declares that the same father begot them, the same womb embraced them, and the same entrails brought them forth.

2. He had fallen into the vices of youth, as he admits to her in the same place.

3. At last he had been converted from the world by the mercy of God.

4. His sister was living in a commitment to virginity, as is clearly indicated in these works.

It is known, however, that Saint Anselm had only one sister, named Richera, who married Burgondio and bore him a son named Anselm. Several letters written by Anselm to Burgondio, to Richera, and to his nephew Anselm testify to this. In one of them, Letter 67 of Book III, he writes to his sister that no one except her husband exists whose welfare she desires to know and hear about as much as that of herself and her son, because he is her only brother and the other her only son. These words clearly indicate that Saint Anselm had no other sister; for if he had had one, Anselm would not have been the only person, after her husband, whom Richera loved together with her nephew. This is the one point that prevents me from believing that Anselm wrote these meditations.

Some have attributed them to Saint Augustine; indeed, in the little book *On the Eremitical Life to a Sister*, chapter 47, near the end, these three meditations are read in their entirety. But Augustine is not the author of that little book either. Its author was some younger follower of Saint Benedict and Saint Gregory, for he mentions the former in chapters 14 and 19 and the latter in chapter 46. Add that I have found this work transcribed in none of the older manuscripts of Saint Augustine.

The author of this little book admits in its final chapter that he added to these meditations *On Divine Benefits* a form of life that he prescribed there in forty-six chapters. It is therefore clear that the same person was the author both of this form of life and of these meditations.

### Censure of Meditation 18
From the manuscript of the Viennese College, Father Theophilus, as he says in his preface to the *Mantissa*, was the first to bring this meditation, among all the others which he calls “little lights,” or “conversations” of Saint Anselm, into the light of day. Its beginning is found in the first part of chapter 18 of the book of *Meditations* circulated among the works of Saint Augustine.

Of its author this one thing is known: that he lived in a community of brothers over whom he presided; for he indicates this there at several points. There is nothing in it, however, that does not have the character of Anselm [Col. 0032B], and therefore I would readily believe that it was written by Anselm while he governed the monastery of Bec.

**Censure of Meditation 19**

Father Raynaldus was the first to publish it from the Vatican manuscript. We have given it from the manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai, corrected. It is entirely worthy of Anselm.

**Censure of Meditation 20**

This is found among Saint Anselm’s prayers in manuscript 267 of the Thuana Library, from which we printed it. It expresses Saint Anselm’s teaching and piety in every respect.

**Censure of Meditation 21**

I regard this as nothing other than flowers of piety collected from the *Proslogion*, whether by Anselm himself or by someone else; [Col. 0032C] and it is therefore rightly attributed to Anselm in several manuscripts and in Father Theophilus’s edition.

## Censure of the Prayers

**Censure of Prayer 1**

It was first published by Father Raynaldus from a manuscript of the Viennese College, and I have found it neither in any printed edition nor in any manuscript. Nevertheless, it does not depart from Anselm’s style, and it distinguishes its author by his purpose and religious manner of life.

**Censure of Prayer 2**

It is found even in the older printed editions, as though it were part of the prayer beginning, “My God, give to my heart,” and so forth. We have not separated it from that prayer except in order to place before those passages which are composed for obtaining virtues the passages which arouse compunction. [Col. 0032D] Chapters 5, 6, 7, and 8 of the book of *Meditations*, falsely attributed to Augustine, consist of this prayer, which nevertheless is attributed to Saint Anselm in the manuscript and in all the printed editions. See below the judgment on this book of *Meditations*.

**Censure of Prayers 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7**

These are read among Saint Anselm’s prayers in the manuscripts whose variant readings we have recorded. Add to them the manuscript of Dom Bigot and the manuscript of the Viennese College, from which Father Raynaldus first published them. The fifth is chapter 34 of the aforementioned book of *Meditations*.

**Censure of Prayer 8**

Several lamentations of Saint Anselm—that is, meditations—[Col. 0033A] are read in the manuscript of the Library of Saint Martin of Tournai. Among them is this prayer, which we received in transmission and have published.

Prayer 9 is the same as Prayer 2; see its censure.

**Censure of Prayer 10**

This prayer forms the first four chapters of the aforementioned book of *Meditations*. Nevertheless, all the older editions of Saint Anselm’s *Meditations* also contain it, as do manuscript 267 of the Thuana Library and the manuscript of the Viennese College.

**Censure of Prayer 11**

This is read among Saint Anselm’s prayers in several manuscripts, in which it bears various titles, as may be seen in the variant readings. In the manuscript of Dom Bigot this prayer is joined to two others. Father Raynaldus was the first to make it public from the Vatican manuscript.

**Censure of Prayers 12 and 13**

[Col. 0033B] Father Theophilus was the first, from the Viennese manuscript, to include these among Saint Anselm’s conversations.

**Censure of Prayer 14**

This is found in all the printed editions, as well as in the manuscript of Dom Bigot, the Thuana manuscript, and the Viennese manuscript. It is nevertheless chapter 9 of the often-mentioned book of *Meditations*, on which we shall give our judgment below.

**Censure of Prayer 15**

This prayer is found among Saint Anselm’s prayers in manuscript Corbeiensis 160, the manuscript of Vallis Lucana, the manuscript of Saint-Germain, and the manuscript of the Viennese College, from which Father Theophilus first published it.

**Censure of Prayers 16, 17, 18, and 19**

These complete chapters 36 and 37 of the aforementioned book of *Meditations*. Nevertheless, and not without reason, Father Raynaldus counted them among Saint Anselm’s conversations from the manuscript of the Viennese College.

[Col. 0033C]

**Censure of Prayer 20**

The aforementioned book of *Meditations* closes with this prayer. Nevertheless, it is read among Saint Anselm’s prayers not only in the manuscript indicated in our variant readings, but also in the manuscript of Saint-Germain, the Louvain manuscript, and the Viennese manuscript, from which Father Raynaldus first added it to Saint Anselm’s conversations.

**Censure of Prayers 21 and 22**

Father Raynaud received and published these from the Vatican manuscript. They are indeed found in the book *On Contrition of Heart* and in chapter 10 of the book of *Meditations*. But below we shall demonstrate how falsely these books bear the name of Augustine.

**Censure of Prayers 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 28**

[Col. 0033D]

Besides the manuscripts noted in the variant readings, the Louvain manuscript, the manuscript of the Royal Library, the Floriac manuscript, and also the Vatican and Cologne manuscripts, from which Father Theophilus drew them, attest that these are Anselm’s.

**Censure of Prayer 29**

Since full confidence must be placed in manuscript witnesses wherever no other means of judgment is available, and since nothing elsewhere contradicts the attribution, we have judged that this prayer should be assigned to no one other than Saint Anselm. We have read it among the other prayers of this holy teacher in several manuscripts of no inferior reputation; anyone who wishes may consult those marked in the variant readings. To these should be added manuscript 2024 of the Royal Library and another manuscript of Dom Bigot. Anyone familiar with Anselm’s writings knows well that this prayer is written in his style [Col. 0034A]. But what follows from the fact that it is found among the pious collections of John, abbot of Fécamp, in a manuscript of Metz? Nothing other than that this abbot—who was still flourishing at the time when many people requested from Saint Anselm the pious prayers he had composed—received this prayer from him and copied what he had received. We shall demonstrate this below.

**Censure of Prayers 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, and 36**

Father Raynaudus first published all these from the Viennese manuscript. The thirty-third is also found in the manuscript of Dom Bigot under the title *Apologetic Prayer of Saint Anselm*. The thirty-fourth is found in the Thuana manuscript and in the Bec manuscript, as we indicated in the variant readings.

**Censure of Prayers 37, 38, 39, and 40**

We published these from manuscript Corbeiensis 160 and attributed them to Anselm. The fortieth is also found in manuscript Victorinus KK. 16.

[Col. 0034B]

**Censure of Prayers 41, 42, 43, and 44**

The first of these is read among Saint Anselm’s prayers in almost all the manuscripts. See the variant readings. I would not assert the others to Anselm with equal confidence, although Father Raynaldus published the forty-second from the Viennese manuscript and the others from the Vatican manuscript.

**Censure of Prayers 45, 46, 47, and 48**

Father Raynaldus was the first to print these four prayers to the Blessed Virgin from the manuscript of the Viennese College among the Anselmian works.

**Censure of Prayers 49, 50, and 51**

These are found not only in the manuscript of the Viennese College, the Vatican manuscript, and the manuscript of Saint-Germain, but also in all those which I have examined, as I have marked in the variant readings. I therefore believe them to be the prayers which Anselm, while not yet an abbot, says he composed at greater length in his letter to Gondulphus, letter 20 of Book I.

One point should be noted here: in the earlier editions, Prayers 40 and 50 are abbreviated and combined into one under the title *Invocation of the Virgin Mother Mary and of Her Son*. It begins, “Holy One, and among…”

[Col. 0034C]

**Censure of Prayers 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, and 59**

Father Raynaldus first published Prayer 52 from the Viennese manuscript and the others from the Vatican manuscript among the Anselmian works.

[Col. 0034D]

**Censure of Prayer 60**

This hymn is found among Saint Anselm’s prayers in manuscript Corbeiensis 160 and in manuscript Victorinus KK. 16; from these we committed it to the press, inserted among Saint Anselm’s prayers.

**Censure of Prayer 62 and of the Others to the Saints**

William of Jumièges writes of Anselm in Book VI, chapter 9, that he published a book of prayers to the saints. There is no reason to doubt that these are Anselm’s unless one denies all credibility to manuscript witnesses. In some manuscripts Prayer 64, which is addressed to Saint Andrew, Prayer 68, which is addressed to Saint Lawrence, and Prayer 71, which is addressed to Saint Dunstan, are absent. But since the first is read in the Viennese manuscript, the manuscript of Theophilus, and the manuscript of Saint-Germain; the second in the manuscripts of Theophilus and Vienna [Col. 0035A]; and the third in the Viennese manuscript, these witnesses should be sufficient to establish confidence in this matter.

It remains to make the following observations.

1. In the manuscript of Saint Arnulf of Metz, many of the above-mentioned *Meditations* and *Prayers* of Saint Anselm—specimens of which Dom Mabillon presented in volume I of the *Analecta*—are found among various devotional works which Abbot John dedicated to Augusta. They were not composed by him, but collected from the *Meditations* and *Prayers* already published by Saint Anselm. This is shown, first, by the fact that of all the manuscript codices of Saint Anselm’s prayers which I have seen, and which are identified both in the preface and in the variant readings, there is not one which does not attribute at least most of these prayers to Saint Anselm. By what scale of equity, I ask, will one [Col. 0035B] raise a single manuscript against the testimony of so many others, when no other consideration supports it?

2. The letters of Saint Anselm which we identified in the first censure of the *Meditations*, together with the testimony of Eadmer himself (*Life of Saint Anselm*, Book I, col. 56), establish that Anselm published prayers while he was still prior—that is, before the year 1078—and that they were copied by many people. I therefore do not conjecture lightly that John of Fécamp, who was closer to Anselm of Bec, received them from him.

3.
