The prayers which Anselm’s own letters attribute to him are repeatedly copied among them: namely, the three prayers to Saint Mary which he claims as his own in his letter to Gondulphus, letter 20 of Book II, and the meditation beginning “I am terrified…” (see the censure [Col. 0035C] of Meditation 2), together with others on contrition of heart, for which Durand, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, congratulates him in letter 61 of the same book.

From these facts it follows: first, that this manuscript of Metz was not copied until after Saint Anselm had published his *Meditations* or *Prayers*; second, that this abbot John copied several prayers composed by Anselm and sent the copies to Augusta; and third, that John should therefore be regarded not as the author of these prayers, but merely as their pious collector.

Nothing, moreover, conflicts with the well-founded attribution of these prayers to Saint Anselm. The fact that the aforementioned Metz manuscript was written in an excellent hand toward the end of the eleventh century, and that John of Fécamp died in 1078—although the *Pious Neustria* [Col. 0035D], citing Orderic Vitalis, reports that he governed the monastery until 1082, in Book IV under the year 1072 and Book II under the year 1107—not only presents no obstacle but strongly supports the attribution. For, as has already been mentioned, it is certain that Anselm wrote several prayers while he was prior at Bec, an office which he held from 1063 until 1078, when he was made abbot.

Their author calls himself a “little man.” But since this statement was made not with reference to bodily stature but from a humble estimation of himself, it does not help us identify this John, who was called “Little John” because of his small physical stature. Rather, it openly reveals Anselm, who frequently used the words *homuncio* and *homunculus*, as is clear to anyone who reads the third meditation and [Col. 0036A] Prayer 69. These are unquestionably Anselm’s, and in them he himself calls himself a “little man” and a “little human being.”

In Conversation 12, which in our edition is Meditation 181, the author indicates that he held the office of shepherd, under the burden of which he groaned. This fits Anselm as prior extremely well; Eadmer describes his sighs and tears beneath the weight of that office (*Life of Saint Anselm*, Book I):

> When he was weeping most bitterly over the loss of the tranquillity of his former state, he began earnestly to ask Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, that he might deserve to be relieved from the burden of the office of prior, which he confessed to be unbearable. But Maurilius ordered him to retain the office he held.

[Col. 0036B]

Finally, what does the author’s request for grace to order the places entrusted to him prove against John of Fécamp, who governed two monasteries? It proves nothing—as though every priest were thought to govern several churches simply because, at the end of brief litanies, he recites a prayer containing the words “the places entrusted to us.”

We have therefore rightly attributed these prayers to Anselm of Canterbury alone. They were received and collected, with great devotion, not only by John of Fécamp, but also by Durand, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, from 1068 to 1078, and by many others.

A second observation: numerous excerpts from prayers which are unquestionably Anselm’s—namely, the prayers to Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint Nicholas, and Saint Benedict—[Col. 0036C] were used to compose, for the most part, the book *On Contrition of Heart* and the book of *Meditations*, which are found in volume IX of the works of Saint Augustine. We shall therefore pronounce below what judgment should be formed concerning them.

Third, Prayer 69 is incorrectly entitled as a prayer to Saint Martin, since Anselm himself writes in his letter to Baldric, letter 51 of Book II, that he composed it for Saint Nicholas. In that same letter he indicates that it was composed shortly before he crossed over to England, that is, around the time when he had begun the book *On the Incarnation of the Word* against Roscelin. This prayer is found under the name of Saint Nicholas in the manuscript of the monastery of Lira.

## Censure of the Psalter of the Blessed Virgin

Dom Picard was the first to publish this, undoubtedly [Col. 0036D] from some manuscript bearing the name of Saint Anselm. Father Raynaldus admits that he possessed no manuscript of the work. I myself came upon two: one Victorine and the other Floriac, in which the beginning of this Psalter up to Compline is found. But in both, the remainder is absent, and neither contains the author’s name. I also encountered in manuscript 345 of our library a *Psalter of the Blessed Virgin*, and another in a manuscript of the Royal Library. But these two are entirely different both from the work published here and from the work composed by Saint Bonaventure.

## Judgment on the Book *On Contrition of Heart*

The final part of the first chapter, together with the second chapter, [Col. 0037A] is taken word for word from the final part of Meditation 2, which Saint Anselm wrote in 1099 concerning human redemption.

The latter part of the third chapter, beginning “What kind of person you made me,” and the first part of chapter 4, up to the words “My soul, before all things,” are excerpted from Saint Anselm’s prayer to Saint John the Baptist. The other part of chapter 4, beginning “But these are…” is transcribed from Prayer 4 to God, which begins “Most High…” Finally, the last part, beginning with the words “How much more tolerable…” and the beginning of the following chapter up to “Do not, Lord…,” have been transferred from Saint Anselm’s second and undisputed meditation, which begins “I am terrified…”

From the words “Do not, Lord…” [Col. 0037B] up to “Spare my sinful soul…” the text is drawn from the final part of Saint Anselm’s third meditation, which is a lament over virginity wrongly lost.

From the words of chapter 5, “Alas! always miserable…” up to “even perverse…” the material has been borrowed, though in reverse order, from Saint Anselm’s third prayer to God. From “even perverse…” up to “O sins…” excerpts have been taken, with the order changed, from the prayer to Saint Benedict, which is known to be Saint Anselm’s.

From the words “O sins…” up to “Hear, therefore…,” which begins chapter 10, the material is taken from the prayer to Saint Nicholas, which Anselm himself declares in Letter 51 [Col. 0037C] of Book II that he composed. From “Hear, therefore…” up to “But whence, my God…” it is likewise extracted from the aforementioned prayer to Saint Nicholas.

From “But whence, O God…” up to “Remember…” the material comes from Saint Anselm’s third meditation, which concerns wrongly lost virginity.

From “Remember…” up to “My God, in you I place…” it is drawn from the end of the prayer to Saint Nicholas and from the meditation on wrongly lost virginity.

The words of the final chapter, “To sin is to dishonor God…” are taken from Meditation 11, which Saint Anselm composed at Lyons, and from several other chapters of his [Col. 0037D].

The passage in the same chapter beginning “Alas, I have sinned…” and ending “God the Lord, whose…” is copied from Saint Anselm’s second meditation. The words “Woe to the one who does evil…” are nevertheless transcribed from the prayer to Saint Paul; from that prayer these words are also excerpted: “God, whose goodness…” up to “I know indeed and confess…”

From all this it is evident that the book *On Contrition of Heart*, whose author was uncertain even to the censors of Saint Augustine, was composed by some later writer who most diligently collected the sayings of Saint Augustine and Saint Anselm that could most effectively move the heart to contrition, and skillfully arranged this book from them.

[Col. 0038A]

## Judgment on the Book of *Meditations* Circulated among the Works of Saint Augustine

Two books of *Meditations* are found in volume IX of the works of Saint Augustine: one among his works and another published in the Appendix. Concerning the second, which has nothing in common with Anselm’s *Meditations*, we make no judgment here. But in order to conclude what should be thought of the first, two preliminary points must be made.

1. Almost the whole of this book is found in Saint Anselm’s *Meditations* and *Prayers*. The first four chapters of this book constitute Prayer 10, which begins “Lord God, give to my heart…” and continues up to “How great, Lord…” The next four chapters are reproduced word for word in Prayer 2, which begins “I invoke you.”

Chapter 9 of this little book is filled by Saint Anselm’s Prayer 14 [Col. 0038B], beginning “Now, O divine love…”

Chapter 10 is Prayer 21 itself, beginning “I know, Lord…”

The beginning of chapter 18 begins Meditation 18, with several verses omitted that precede it.

Chapters 22 and 23 contain many passages found in sections 5, 6, and 7 of Meditation 14, which is also called the *Enchiridion*.

Chapters 29 and 30 are contained in section 1 of the aforementioned Meditation 14.

Chapter 34 is the complete prayer which we numbered as Prayer 5.

Chapter 35 constitutes Prayer 17.

Chapter 36 supplies Prayer 16.

Chapter 37 completes Prayers 18 and 19.

Chapter 39 contains some sayings that occur in Prayer 62 [Col. 0038C], some that occur in Meditation 3, some that are read in Prayer 2, and some that are found in chapter 1 of the *Proslogion*.

Finally, chapters 41 and the last chapter constitute Prayer 20 in its entirety.

From these facts it is clearer than daylight that either these meditations and prayers were copied from the aforementioned book, or that this book was composed from these prayers and meditations—especially the prayers—not by Anselm but by a later writer.

To determine which is true, I observe the following.

1. The *Proslogion*, and at least some of the prayers which contain the same material as this book, are unquestionably works of Saint Anselm. It is therefore more probable [Col. 0038D] that this book was transcribed from Saint Anselm’s prayers than that these prayers were copied by Anselm from the little book whose author is not certainly known to have existed before Anselm, and which is read only in more recent manuscripts. Nor was this the disposition of Saint Anselm.

2. This book of *Meditations* is nothing other than a patchwork, sometimes sewn together rather ineptly. In Saint Anselm’s prayers, however, the sayings fit more closely with sayings and the parts with the parts. It is therefore more likely that the book was composed from these prayers than that the prayers were composed from the book.

[Col. 0039A]

## Judgment on the Book Called the *Manual*

That this book is not Augustine’s is established: first, because it is not read in the older manuscripts; second, from its own prologue, in which the author states that he collected this *Manual* from the more elegant sayings of the holy Fathers; and third, because the final six chapters of the book are transcribed word for word from Saint Anselm’s *Proslogion*.

[Col. 0040A] Whether this book is Anselm’s, however, I cannot determine. I would nevertheless judge more fairly that the work was produced neither by Augustine nor by Anselm, but by someone later than both, who stitched this book together from various sayings and chapters, especially those of Saint Augustine and Saint Anselm.

## Censure of Works Published in the Appendix

### Censure of the *Elucidarium*

At Oxford, in manuscript 223 of the Merton Library, this book is entitled: “The Book Called the *Elucidarius* of Blessed Anselm.” At Cambridge, in manuscript 123 of the Benedictine College, it is called “Anselm’s *Elucidarium*.” It is found in several other manuscripts, [Col. 0039B] but without the author’s name. I have also been reliably informed by a friend, who had the manuscript before him, that this work exists in French in a manuscript belonging to an English library.

Espencaeus was the first to commit this book, marked with Anselm’s name, to the press at Paris in 1560; it was subsequently printed among the works of Saint Anselm at Cologne in 1573. Since, however, it contains many vain and foolish things contrary to Saint Anselm’s teaching, it was judged entirely unworthy of being numbered among his works. What is said in Book I, chapter 15, concerning the mourning of Adam and the slain Abel, and what is related in the same book, chapter 19, concerning the miracles said to have occurred at the Lord’s birth, is worthy neither of a theologian nor of a sound mind. And when free choice is defined in Book III, chapter 3, as “the freedom to choose good or evil,” [Col. 0039C] the work departs from Anselm’s teaching. The statement made in Book II, chapter 15, concerning the impurity of semen likewise contradicts Anselm’s position.

Furthermore, in the prologue to his dialogue *On Truth*, Saint Anselm himself writes that he composed and enumerated four dialogues, but he does not mention this one. No one should reply that the dialogue had not yet been published by him at that time. For the preface to the *Elucidarium* makes it clear that it was composed by someone who was still teaching in the schools and had not yet become a prelate, whereas Anselm had already assumed the government of the monastery of Bec when he wrote the prologue to his dialogues.

Trithemius attributed the work to Honorius of Autun in Book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Father Theophilus, in the *Eromata*, assigned it to William of Coventry, a Carmelite who lived around 1360. Father Labbe, however, refutes this opinion on the basis of a manuscript of the College of Clermont, [Col. 0039D] which predates that Carmelite’s lifetime. I shall attribute the work to neither of them, but to some student of Saint Anselm who composed this “summary of Christian theology,” as he calls it, chiefly from Anselm’s own sayings.

### Censure of the Dialogue *On the Passion of the Lord*

This dialogue is found in manuscript 519 of the Thuana Library under the title: “The Lament of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin to Anselm concerning the Passion of Christ.” It is also found in all the printed editions. Nevertheless, I am convinced that it is not Saint Anselm’s: first, from the prologue, where the words “Blessed Anselm…” are found; second, because it is not among the four dialogues which Anselm himself lists in the preface to the dialogue *On Truth* as having been composed by him; third, because Eadmer says nothing about it; and fourth, and especially, because the dialogue is filled with fables and childish nonsense.

### Censure of the Book *On the Measurement of the Cross*

This book is found in all the printed editions of Saint Anselm’s works, even the older ones. But since it is found in no manuscript, and since the author cites Bernard [Col. 0040B] in chapter 5, it is evident that he is later than Anselm, who died in 1109, before Bernard had even become a monk. The fact that the work speaks of merit *ex condigno*—merit according to strict desert—in chapter 1 likewise indicates that it was not produced before the thirteenth century.

### Censure of the Book *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*

Father Raynaldus was the first to publish fragments of this treatise under the heading *On the Passive Virginal Conception*, and he argues throughout that the treatise was composed by Saint Anselm.

I myself know that in manuscript 271 of the Merton Library in England this work is read before the treatise *On the Excellence of Blessed Mary* under the title “Anselm on the Conception of Blessed Mary.” In manuscript 22 of the Lincoln Library it is found among other works of Saint Anselm under the title *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*. At Cambridge, in manuscript 338 of the College of Saint Benedict, a treatise *On the Conception of Saint Mary* likewise appears after Eadmer’s works. In the Cluniac manuscript we also read: “Treatise of Blessed Anselm on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary.” This treatise is likewise found among Saint Anselm’s works in the Corbie manuscript [Col. 0040C], under the title *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary*. From these two manuscripts we published the complete treatise.

We nevertheless did not publish it among Saint Anselm’s works, since these few manuscripts—which also contain treatises by authors other than Saint Anselm—cannot overturn the testimony of the countless other manuscripts of Saint Anselm’s works preserved in the Royal, Victorine, and Thuana libraries and in many other libraries in France, England, and Belgium. In none of all these is even a fragment of these [Col. 0040D] treatises to be found. Nor do I know what treatise those three English codices call *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*. This title could have been prefixed by copyists to the book *On the Virginal Conception*.

Moreover, the whole of Saint Anselm’s doctrine protests against the false attribution of this book to him, as anyone who has read Book II of *Why God Became Man*, especially chapters 16 and 17, will understand. In his *Syntax* of this little book, Father Raynaldus maintains that Anselm was speaking there, like other Fathers, of the first conception, which consists in the reception of the father’s seed and through which the debt of contracting original sin is incurred.

But Anselm is wholly opposed to this in the passages cited, especially where he proves that there is no impurity in the seed [Col. 0041A] requiring purification, and where he demonstrates to his disciple Boso that it was necessary for God to become man so that the Blessed Virgin might be purified, and that she was purified by the Holy Spirit through Christ.

Others object that Saint Anselm held the same view in his expositions of Saint Paul’s Epistles as this book sets forth. For on the Apostle’s words, “He condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8), he says: “Mary, dead through Adam, unless she had been divinely exempted, and so forth.” And on the words, “All have died” (2 Corinthians 5), he explains: “All, therefore, died in sins, absolutely no one being excepted, apart from the Mother of God, whether from original sins or from those added by the will.”

Why is this relevant? Anselm did not write these expositions; they were written by Hervaeus of Bourg-Dieu, as Bellarmine and Labbe themselves observe [Col. 0041B] in their book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. This is also established for us by the manuscript in our possession, from which it is clear that the clauses “unless she had been divinely exempted” and “apart from the Mother of God” were inserted by someone else, as Estius had already suspected. They are not read in the manuscript.

There is therefore no way to reconcile Saint Anselm’s contradictory doctrine if this book was published by him. I would consequently judge, not unfairly, that the book has been falsely attributed to Anselm rather than that Anselm is inconsistent with himself.

By the same line of argument, Angelus Rocca, an Augustinian, when arranging the works of Saint Bonaventure for printing at Rome, concluded in the margin [Col. 0041C] of the second sermon on Blessed Mary that this sermon is not Saint Bonaventure’s, since it explains the same doctrine as this book, although Bonaventure elsewhere repeatedly and consistently defends the opinion affirmed in Book III of the *Sentences*.

Baronius himself observes in his notes on the *Martyrology* that whether the treatise *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin* is Anselm’s is rightly disputed, since it contains much that conflicts with that author, as John de Turrecremata notes in his treatise *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*, Part XII, chapter 3. This is Baronius’s own judgment.

The treatise itself, now restored to its integrity and purity, declares that it was not published until after Anselm’s time. From the very beginning of the sermon it is clear [Col. 0041D]:

1. that in many places the solemn feast of the Conception of Blessed Mary was already being celebrated;

2. that in ancient times it was celebrated more frequently, while pure simplicity still prevailed;

3. that the discernment and examination of certain modern people, who surpassed others in secular and ecclesiastical authority and in abundance of wealth, removed this solemnity as though it were irrational and reduced it to nothing; and

4. that the charity of the simple faithful was then mourning the abolition of so great a feast.

But these circumstances cannot belong to Anselm’s time, any more than can the story that Anselm instituted this feast while he was staying at Lyons. Eadmer, who describes with the greatest care everything—even the smallest matters—that Anselm did at Lyons, says nothing of these events either in his books on Anselm’s life or in his *History of Recent Events*. Nor did anyone at that time write of the institution or abolition of this [Col. 0042A] feast, although so many writers have transmitted the events of that age to us.

Finally, how can one say that a feast instituted in ancient times was abolished during Anselm’s lifetime because of the prevailing authority of certain people who held ecclesiastical rank over the charity of the simple, when Anselm lived scarcely ten years after his first return from the city of Lyons, where the feast is said to have been instituted by him?

This, therefore, belongs not to Anselm’s age but to Bernard’s. For at that time, around the year 1140, the Church of Lyons wished to celebrate the conception of the Blessed Virgin as a feast. Since Saint Bernard and many others regarded this unfavorably, serious controversies arose. Their arguments were [Col. 0042B]:

1. that there was no reason to commemorate this conception specially; and

2. that if the Blessed Virgin had died before the birth of Christ, she would not have escaped the lot of original sin, as the author of this book himself reports.

Among others, Potho of Prüm appears to be indicated and refuted here. In Book III of *On the State of the House of God*, written in 1151, he says toward the end that it seemed especially absurd that the feast of the Conception of Saint Mary had been newly introduced, although he did not wish to detract from the devotion of the faithful by asking the reason for this feast. There Potho reproduces the thought and words of Saint Bernard in Letter 174 to the canons of Lyons.

It should also be noted that in that letter Saint Bernard says that, before writing it, he had already discovered this “error”—his own word—among certain [Col. 0042C] people, but had spared the devotion of the simple by concealing it. He had tolerated it less patiently among learned men and in a distinguished church.

From this it is evident: first, that in the time of Saint Bernard, who flourished after Anselm, only certain simpler people—those mentioned in the aforementioned treatise—venerated the conception of Blessed Mary; second, that it was not yet customarily commemorated publicly and solemnly by the churches; and third, that this feast was therefore celebrated by the Church of Lyons neither on Anselm’s initiative nor during his lifetime, since Saint Bernard rebuked the canons of that church for the celebration as soon as he discovered it: “When the superstition was discovered…” He would not have been unaware of it if it had been instituted in that church during Anselm’s time, since he himself says there [Col. 0042D] that he was specially a son of that church.

Since, therefore, the statements found in this treatise concerning the institution and abolition of that feast do not at all fit the times of Saint Anselm, the treatise was composed not by Anselm but by a later writer.

## Censure of the Letter or Sermon *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*

Father Raynaldus published this sermon from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Raguebertus in the Jura, under the title: “Letter of Saint Anselm on the Conception of Blessed Mary.”

> Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and shepherd of the English, sends greetings and perpetual blessing in Christ to his fellow bishops and to all who venerate the mysteries of Blessed Mary.

Many considerations persuade us that this letter is fictitious [Col. 0043A].

1. The inscription is not Anselm’s. Nowhere in his letters does he call himself “shepherd of the English,” a title which might have aroused no small envy against him.

2. Saint Anselm would not have addressed fellow bishops in these words—“Most beloved brothers,” “your love”—without any indication of dignity or paternal reverence, which he always observed elsewhere.

3. His letters do not close with these words: “With the Lord Jesus Christ, His Son, granting it, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through infinite ages of ages. Amen.”

4. None of the writers of English history reports that William the Conqueror sent Elsinus to Denmark to investigate shrewdly whether a fleet was being prepared, as was rumored, to be directed against England. On the contrary, they all relate that William, immediately after he had been consecrated king of England, crossed over to Normandy, and that somewhat later the Danes invaded England with their most powerful fleet [Col. 0043B].

The opening narrative of this letter or sermon is plainly inconsistent with these facts. If Elsinus had reported to William that the fleet was ready, either he himself would not have left England, or at least the Danes would not have invaded it while William was unprepared.

Saint Elsinus, called Aiegelsin in English, was not elected abbot of Ramsey until the year 1080, as is recorded in the *Register of Ramsey*, folio 218. It is therefore a fable that Elsinus, abbot of the monastery of Ramsey, was summoned and sent to Denmark by William I immediately after William had subjected England to his rule—that is, in the year 1066 [Col. 0043C].

It is said in another account that this Elsinus once resided in the church of Saint Augustine. Indeed, William Thorne, in his *Chronicles*, lists Egelsinus among the abbots of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury, under the year 1059; and, among other things, he writes of him that, with Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, as their leaders, the people of Kent went to meet William in 1066; and that, after an agreement and treaty had been made between them, this abbot sailed to Denmark—but as an exile, to escape William’s anger, not as his legate or spy, as the fable pretends. Finally, he states that Egelsinus was not only never advanced to the church of Ramsey, but also never appeared again from that time onward, so that the king appointed another in his place, named Scotland, at whose insistence the king ordered all the goods restored to the monastery of Saint Augustine which this abbot Egelsinus—whom the king himself calls a fugitive in his rescript—had either granted away or allowed to be seized [Col. 0043D].

Therefore, this is not the Elsinus who was sent by the king to Denmark, and who, after reaching an agreement with the Danes, received the aforesaid revelation while returning to England. For he was never the father of the monastery of Ramsey, nor did he cross over to the Danes except as a fugitive; and consequently he never returned from anywhere.

Nor could the abbot of Ramsey have been chosen by the king for that office, since this Elsinus was not elected abbot until the year 1080, and never migrated to Denmark [Col. 0044A]—least of all to investigate the plans of the Danes, who shortly afterward invaded England.

Who, then, is this Elsinus, or Egelsinus, to whom such great mysteries were revealed as he returned from Denmark? I should say that he was neither the Ramsey nor the Canterbury Elsinus, but a figure fabricated from both: one who would cross over to Denmark, as the Canterbury abbot did, and who would govern the monastery of Ramsey, lest he still be believed to be an exile or fugitive in Denmark. Thus the poorly woven narrative collapses of its own accord.

6. This Elsinus, being so near shipwreck, investigates so scrupulously not only the day but also the office of the feast, that the narrative may easily be believed to have been artfully composed.

7. This letter has been transmitted in such varying forms that it is closer to a falsehood wavering uncertainly [Col. 0044B] than to a truth that stands firm. In the version published by Father Yenez in the appendix to volume VII of the *Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*, it is declared that the saintly mitred figure who comes to Elsinus’s aid in his shipwreck is Saint Nicholas, and only one apparition is narrated. In the version published here, two other apparitions have been added in the same style. Finally, the version which I appended from the Jumièges manuscript, under the title *Miracle of the Conception of Blessed Mary*, is composed partly in verse and partly in prose, and reports only a single apparition. In conclusion, Durand himself, bishop of Mende (1296), in book VII of *On the Divine Offices*, concludes that this revelation, said to have been made to an abbot caught in a shipwreck, is neither authentic nor deserving of approval.

8. What is narrated about a certain deacon, the brother of the king of Hungary, has no greater appearance of truth. They wish this man—[IVION I. II. *Ligni vita*]—to have been Frederick, the forty-third patriarch of the Church of Aquileia, whom they falsely represent as a son of Charles the Bald and a monk of Fulda, and then as the person who, after being appointed archbishop by him, instituted this feast. Ughellus, in volume V of *Sacred Italy*, published at Rome, rejects and refutes this fable on the grounds that this archbishop is not listed among the sons of Charles in the Carolingian genealogy; that no mention of such a relationship appears in the epitaph engraved on his tomb; and that Christoph Brower makes no mention of him in his book *Antiquities of Fulda*, where he treats expressly of the distinction, learning, and piety of the illustrious monks of Fulda. Finally, no patriarch of Aquileia is known to have been the brother of the king of Hungary. Nor would Bernard, Potho, and others have complained about a newly introduced feast around the year 1140, if it had been celebrated in the patriarchal see of Italy from the year 884, when this archbishop of Aquileia was elected, or shortly afterward, together with its octave.

9. The third narrative of this letter is excessively favorable to final impenitence—that sin which will not be forgiven even in the future age—and is too plainly opposed to Scripture’s declaration that where the tree falls, there it will remain, and to the Church’s confession that there is no redemption in hell, for it to deserve belief [Col. 0044D].

10. The argument that the conception of Blessed Mary should therefore be exalted, [Col. 0045A] just as her birth is, because unless she had been conceived she would not have been born, is reported and refuted by Saint Bernard (*Letter* 174). This proves that the fable was fabricated in that period.

11. The author attacks those who refused to celebrate this feast as insane and senseless. Anyone who has even casually examined Anselm’s writings knows how foreign this is to Anselm’s modesty and gentleness.

Concerning the miracle of the conception of Saint Mary, which comes from chapter 40 of the Gembloux manuscript, judge it in the same way as the preceding letter.

In all these matters, I have pursued only this one aim: to demonstrate that these treatises are not by Saint Anselm. I have said nothing about the feast and mystery of the Conception [Col. 0045B], concerning which I shall always hold whatever accords with the judgment of the Church.

## Censure of the Passion of Saints Guignerus and Others

D. Joannes Picardus was the first to publish this history—if it ought to be called a history—from a manuscript of the Victorine Library, and he attributed it to Saint Anselm. Nevertheless, we judged it scarcely worthy of Anselm, since it contains many things which sensible people will regard as very unlike the truth, and which may provoke laughter more readily than move anyone to piety.

## Censure of the Judgment concerning Stability

There is nothing in it unworthy of Saint Anselm, nor does it disagree with what Saint Anselm wrote to Lanzoni in the letter that is book I, letter 29.

[Col. 0045C]

## Censure of the Disputation of a Jew with a Christian

The letter placed before this work as a prologue plainly indicates both the author and the subject of this disputation. It had hitherto remained unpublished, although it is found in several manuscripts: namely, in the manuscript of the Elno Library, that of Longpont, that of the cathedral church of Tournai, and that of Saint Lambert; as well as in the manuscripts of the Library of Saint-Remi at Reims, the Victorine Library, and the Library of Saint-Germain. From these copies we have brought it into the public domain.

## Censure of the Ring

We successfully recovered this dialogue, which for five hundred years and more had lain hidden in the chests of libraries, from the Laetian manuscript. We learn from Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz, that he composed this *Ring* and divided it into three books, like three jewels, in his own prologue to the books *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. There he states that, at the request of Cunon, formerly abbot of Siegburg and then bishop of Regensburg, he wrote this *Ring* after completing thirteen little books *On the Glory of the Son of Man* and before undertaking the books *On the Glorification*, and so forth—that is, around the year 1127. I have discussed these matters at greater length in my *Apology for Rupert*.

## Censure of the Little Book Entitled *Certain Useful Sayings*, etc.

Father Raynaudus was the first to bring this work to light from manuscripts of the Vatican Library. It certainly bears the stamp of Anselm. We have appended to it some passages from the Corbie manuscript, which likewise are not foreign to Anselm.

[Col. 0046A]

What should be judged concerning the homily on the words, “For it was fitting,” and so forth, I have stated in the censure of the other homilies.

## Censure of Two Miracles

In the Saint-Germain manuscript 608, these two miracles are said to have been published by Saint Anselm. Therefore, so that nothing might be lacking in this volume among the works attributed to him, we have added them, however fabulous and unworthy of belief they may be. They are of the same kind as the aforesaid treatise *On the Conception* and the miracle of the abbess who gave birth with angels acting as midwives.

## Censure of the Book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*

In the Cambron manuscript this book is found under the following title: “Here begins the book of Lord Anselm *On the Sacrament of the Altar*.” It is also read under the same title in the Arras manuscript [Col. 0046B]. But since in this work certain things are refuted which we read in the books *On the Divine Offices*, written by Rupert of Deutz in the year 1111, whereas Anselm was removed from human life in 1109, it is clear that this work did not proceed from Anselm. I have explained this more fully in Rupert’s *Apology*. We have therefore left this book to its author, William of Saint-Thierry, whose name it bears in the Longpont manuscript and in others, and have judged that it should not be printed here, since it has already been published among the works of William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, in the Cistercian Library.

## Censure of the Book *On the Members and Acts Attributed to God*

This book is found in volume IV of Saint Augustine’s works under the title *On the Essence of Divinity*. In volume IX of Saint Jerome’s works it is letter 15, *On Those Things Attributed to God in the Holy Scriptures*; it also appears among the minor works of Saint Bonaventure. Therefore, although it is included in earlier editions of Saint Anselm’s works, since no manuscript assigns Anselm’s name to it, we have omitted it [Col. 0046C].

## Censure of the Books *On the Image of the World*

This work exists in manuscript 14 of the Library of Oriel College under the following title: “Epilogue of the Map of the World by the same author, Peter of Ailly, bishop of Cambrai.” In manuscript 12 of Corpus Christi College it is *Two Books on the Image of the World*, among the works of Hugh. In manuscript 7 of Trinity College it is “The Book of Henry of Huntingdon, called *The Image of God*.” In manuscript 367 of Saint Benedict’s College it is “The Image of the World, composed by H., a canon.” In the same library, manuscript 32 has *The Image of the World with a Prologue by the Most Distinguished Doctor Anselm on a Book Whose Author Is Gregory of Huntingdon*. In manuscript 280 of the Royal Library it begins: “Here begins the prologue of Blessed Anselm, bishop, on the book called *The Image of the World*.” In manuscript 512 of our Saint-Germain Library there is a book entitled *The Mirror or Image of the World*, published by Brother Vincent of the Order of Friars Preachers; but this is different from the work that was published among Saint Anselm’s works. In manuscript 513 of the same library another book is found under the title *The Mirror or Image of the World*, without the author’s name; but this too is not identical with the others.

Yet these two books are found in all printed editions of Saint Anselm’s works, even the older ones.

Nevertheless, we have excluded them from this volume and have not even given them a place in the Appendix, since it is not established that they are Anselm’s, and since elsewhere—that is, among the works of Honorius of Autun—we have read them expressly published in volume XII of the *Library of the Fathers* [Col. 0047A].

## Censure of the Book *On the Blessedness of the Heavenly Homeland*

In the manuscripts of the libraries of Clairvaux, Saint-Ebrulf, Longpont, and Saint Martin of Tournai, Saint Anselm’s name is prefixed to this book. In the Corbie manuscript E. 10 and in the Bec manuscript, however, it is attributed to Eadmer; and there is found with it his letter to William the monk, which, together with the prologue, explains the circumstances of the book’s transcription and clearly identifies Eadmer as its author. Many passages from it are also cited in book *On Similitudes*, chapters 47 through 71. The name of Saint Anselm is not improperly prefixed to it in several manuscripts, since it is a sermon which Saint Anselm delivered at Cluny [Col. 0047B] and which his inseparable companion Eadmer wrote down in book form.

## Censure of the Book *On Similitudes*

In the Lira manuscript and in the manuscript of Pembroke Hall, this book is entitled *On Human Morals*. It appears among Saint Anselm’s works in all printed editions and in many manuscripts. Consequently, Saint Thomas, Saint Bonaventure, Saint Antoninus, and others have assigned it to Saint Anselm. Only Father Theophilus listed the work among the spurious writings—and not without reason. For it is proved that this book was not composed by Anselm, first from chapters 186–192, which were the final chapters in earlier editions; from the manuscript of Saint-Germain and the Bec manuscript, however, we have appended two chapters that were not read in the earlier printed editions. In those seven chapters the author speaks of Saint Anselm [Col. 0047C]; hence it necessarily follows that he is someone other than Saint Anselm. Nor should anyone say that these chapters were added later—as indeed they are absent from the Nuremberg edition—for they are found in all the manuscripts, and one of them is cited by Saint Bonaventure under Anselm’s name.

The error arose from the fact that this book was composed from the similes which Saint Anselm regularly employed in order to shape moral conduct readily. Hence it could properly be called Anselm’s *Book of Similitudes*, or entitled *The Similitudes of Saint Anselm*. For Eadmer presents very many of those used by Saint Anselm in the book *On His Life*: namely, the simile of the bear-tamer, column 58; of wax, 59; of the plant, 67; of the fishpond, 76; of the owl, 83; of the mill, 85; of the hare, 91; of the little bird, 92; and of the soldier paid in solidi, column 94. We read these same similes collected together in this book of *Similitudes*. This, together with the entire structure of the book, is certain evidence to me that it was composed by Eadmer himself from the materials he had collected—not only from Saint Anselm’s similes but also from his sayings, especially those concerning the will, humility, blessedness, and misery. Hence one part of it is sometimes found entitled *The Book on the Threefold Will*, another *On the Mountain of Humility*, and a third *On the Fourteen Beatitudes and an Equal Number of Miseries*.

## Censure of the Book *On the Excellence of the Glorious Virgin*

This book is not found in the Nuremberg edition; in the other editions, however, including the Gothic ones, it is read among Saint Anselm’s works. We have restored it from the Bec manuscript E 10 to Eadmer, in whose style it is written [Col. 0048B].

## Censure of the Book *On the Four Virtues of Blessed Mary*

Father Raynaudus was the first to publish this book and assign it to Saint Anselm. Since, however, I have found it neither in any manuscript nor in earlier editions of Saint Anselm’s works, although it does contain some of Saint Anselm’s sayings—especially where it discusses God’s power—and since it seemed to me so closely related in both wording and meaning to the preceding book that I do not lightly conjecture it to be the work of Eadmer, who adhered firmly and consistently to Saint Anselm’s opinions, I nevertheless have not dared to prefix Eadmer’s name to this work on this single ground.

In the manuscripts of the Alne Library there is a treatise entitled *Anselm on the Double Robe*. In manuscript G. 6 of the Bodleian Library, among Saint Anselm’s works, there is a book *On the Double Robe after the Resurrection*. I was unable to obtain a copy of this work [Col. 0048C]; but I do not think it was composed by Anselm of Canterbury, since neither Eadmer nor anyone else mentions it.

One book *On the Antichrist* is attributed to Anselm in manuscripts 122 and 134 of Saint Benedict’s College Library at Cambridge, and in manuscript 203 of Pembroke Hall. I conjecture that this book is excerpted from chapter 30 and following of the *Elucidarium*, which is attributed to Anselm, though falsely.

The book *On Good Occupation* is likewise attributed to Anselm by manuscript 134 of the aforesaid Saint Benedict’s College and manuscript 16 of the Library of Magdalen College, Oxford.

I have not been able to discover what this book actually concerns. Finally, I judge it, like the other works bearing Anselm’s name, to be a spurious offspring foisted upon so great a Father; it would not be appropriate to spend more time cataloguing them.

[Col. 0049]

# LIFE OF SAINT ANSELM, BY EADMER, MONK OF CANTERBURY, DISCIPLE AND INSEPARABLE COMPANION OF SAINT ANSELM

## Prologue

[Col. 0049A]

Since we have observed that many changes in affairs, unprecedented in the times of our predecessors, have occurred and taken shape in England during our own days, we have committed some brief excerpts from them to the written record, lest those changes entirely escape the knowledge of posterity. But since this work is chiefly concerned with accurately setting out what took place between the kings of the English and Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and with describing, in an unpolished but nevertheless straightforward style, those matters which could then have become known to all who wished to learn their history in its purity, and since it seemed to contain little that concerned Anselm’s private life, the quality of his character, or the performance of miracles, some of my friends persuaded me by their prayers [Col. 0049B] to undertake, just as I had recorded known events for posterity, to try by setting down unknown matters to render some service both to those who would come and to those who are now living. Because I was especially careful not to offend them, I made every effort to comply with their wishes as far as I could.

Accordingly, I have arranged this work, entitled *On the Life and Conduct of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury*, with God’s help in such a way that, although the other work mentioned above consists for the most part of an account of this same man’s conduct, this work nevertheless presents the form of a complete narrative within its own subject matter, so that neither work seems to require much assistance from the other for a mutual understanding of its contents. Yet for those who wish to know his deeds fully, I declare that neither work can suffice without the other [Col. 0050B].

# BOOK ONE: THE DEEDS OF SAINT ANSELM BEFORE HIS EPISCOPATE

## Chapter One

### The Birth of Saint Anselm, His Studies, His Departure for Gaul, and His Deliberation about the State of Life He Should Embrace

1. Since I am about to commit to the written record the institutions of life and conduct of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, I shall first call upon the supreme mercy and majesty of God, and briefly say something about his birth and the character of his parents, so that the reader may perceive from what root there later sprang what shone forth in the studies of their offspring.

His father was called Gundulf, and his mother Ermemberga. Both were nobly born according to the dignity of the world, and nobly lived in the city of Augusta [Note: [Col. 0049C] [Migne gives the source of these notes as *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, April, volume II, day 21.] This is not Augusta of the Taurini, as Thomas Unionatus appears to have understood, but Augusta Praetoria, formerly made the capital of the Salassi by its founder Augustus—commonly called Aosta—and now the capital of a duchy in Piedmont. Solinus and Capella call it a boundary of Italy, just as this place is called a boundary of Burgundy and Lombardy. It is an episcopal city in the province of the Graian Alps, under the metropolitan see of Tarentaise; the latter is one of the six metropolitan sees of Burgundy according to Gervase of Tilbury in his description of Gaul, published by André du Chesne in volume I of the *Writers of the History of the Franks*, p. 22. For this reason Anselm is considered Italian by Orderic Vitalis, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, under the year 1072; he was born there around the year 1033.] Augusta. This city, bordering Burgundy and Lombardy, gave Ermemberga birth; Gundulf, born in Lombardy, it made one of its citizens despite his foreign origin.

They were joined by the law of marriage. Both were not undistinguished in wealth, but in character they differed to some extent. Gundulf, devoted to secular life, did not take very great care of his possessions, but frequently distributed what he had without regard to circumstances, so that some judged him not merely generous and beneficent, but also wasteful and ruinous. Ermemberga, devoted to good pursuits, managing her household well and dispensing and preserving her goods with discretion, fulfilled the duties of a good housewife. Her conduct was upright and irreproachable, supported by reason according to sound judgment. Such was her life; in it she remained while she lived, and in it she deserved to meet the end of life. Gundulf, however, around the time of his death, rejected the world, became a monk, and died a monk.

2. Anselm, their son, while still a little boy, gladly gave his attention to his mother’s conversations as far as his age permitted. When he heard that there was one God above in heaven, ruling and containing all things, he suspected [Note: [Col. 0050C] Augusta is surrounded on every side by mountains.]—being a child raised among mountains—that heaven rested upon the mountains, that God’s palace was there, and that it could be reached through the mountains.

As he often revolved this thought in his mind, it happened that one night in a vision he saw that he ought to climb to the summit of a mountain and hasten to the palace of the great King, God. Before he began to climb the mountain, however, he saw women in the plain through which he was traveling, at the foot of the mountain. They were the king’s maidservants, harvesting the crops, but they were doing so very carelessly and lazily. The boy, grieving over and reproving their laziness, resolved to accuse them before their lord the king.

Then, having crossed the mountain, he entered the royal palace. He found the Lord with only his steward. For, as it seemed to him, since it was autumn, the Lord had sent his household to gather the harvest. As the boy entered, the Lord summoned him. He approached and sat at his feet. He was asked, with pleasant friendliness, who he was, where he came from, and what he wanted. He answered the questions according to his understanding of the truth.

Then, at the Lord’s command, the steward brought him exceedingly pure bread, and he was refreshed with it in the Lord’s presence. In the morning, when he recalled before the eyes of his mind what he had seen, the simple and innocent boy truly believed that he had been refreshed in heaven with the Lord’s bread, and he openly affirmed before others that this was so.

3. The boy therefore grew and was loved by everyone. For he possessed upright character, which made him greatly loved. He was entrusted to teachers, learned, and made very great progress in a short time. He had not yet reached his fifteenth year, yet he was already considering in his mind how he might order his life better according to God, and he conceived the conviction that nothing in human society was superior to the life of monks. Wishing to attain it, he went to an abbot whom he knew and asked him to make him a monk.

But the abbot, recognizing his desire, refused to do what he requested without his father’s knowledge, lest he offend his father’s feelings. The boy, however, persisting in his resolve, prayed to God that he might deserve to fall ill, so that at least in this way he might be received into the monastic order he desired.

A remarkable thing! To show how much he could trust, even in other matters, in what he had heard of God’s goodness, God heard his prayers and immediately sent him a severe bodily weakness. Having therefore fallen seriously ill, he sent to the abbot, declared that he feared death, and asked to become a monk. Because of the fear just mentioned, what he requested was not done—at least so far as human judgment was concerned [al., “so far as it concerned”]. But God, whom future things do not deceive, did not wish his servant to become attached to the life of that place, because he had hidden other people in the bosom of his mercy, whom, as later became clear, he intended through Anselm to shape for his will in the future.

After this the young man recovered his health. What he could not do then, he resolved in his mind to accomplish later by God’s grace.

4. Then, as bodily health, youthful age, and worldly prosperity smiled upon him, the fervor of his spirit for his religious purpose gradually grew cold, so that he began to desire rather to enter the paths of the world than to abandon them and become a monk [Col. 0052A]. He also began gradually to set aside the study of literature, in which he had been accustomed to exercise himself diligently, and to devote himself to youthful amusements.

Nevertheless, the devout affection and careful piety that he had toward his mother restrained him somewhat from these things. When she died, the ship of his heart, as though it had lost its anchor, almost wholly drifted into the waves of the world. But almighty God, foreseeing what he intended to do with him, and lest Anselm should lose his soul after attaining transitory peace, stirred up against him a hostile and inward war. That is, he inflamed his father’s mind with such bitter hatred against him that his father pursued equally—or certainly more severely—those things which he did well and those which he did wrongly.

Anselm could not soften his father by any humility; the humbler he showed himself toward him, the harsher he felt his father to be toward him. Seeing that this was intolerable and fearing that something worse might result from it, he chose to renounce his father’s possessions and his homeland rather than cause any disgrace either to his father or to himself through living together. Having therefore prepared what was necessary for the journey, he left his homeland accompanied by one cleric to serve him.

When he was subsequently exhausted while crossing Mount Cenis [Note: [Col. 0051D] Mount Cenis is very well known, as is its difficult ascent, by which one crosses from Italy into Gaul, as happened here—or conversely from Gaul into Italy.], and his body was failing because he could not endure the labor, he tried to restore his strength by chewing snow. For there was nothing else available for him to eat. His attendant noticed this, grieved, and began carefully to investigate whether perhaps there might be something edible in the sack carried by their donkey. Soon, contrary to expectation, he found in it an exceedingly pure loaf of bread [Col. 0052C]. Refreshed by it, Anselm recovered his strength and was restored safely to life [al., “restored”].

5. After spending nearly three years partly in Burgundy and partly in France, he went to Normandy [al. omits], and sought out Avranches, the city of that province, where he stayed for some time. After this he came to Bec, wishing to see, speak with, and live alongside a certain master named Lanfranc [Note: [Col. 0052D] Blessed Lanfranc was by origin from Pavia in Italy and later became archbishop of Canterbury.], a very good man, truly noble in religious excellence and wisdom.

His outstanding reputation had spread everywhere and drew to him the most distinguished clerics from every part of the world. Anselm therefore approached the man and, recognizing that he possessed an exceptional kind of wisdom, submitted himself to his instruction. Before long he became more familiar with him than the other students.

He occupied himself day and night with literary study, not only reading with Lanfranc what he wished to learn, but also diligently teaching others whatever he was asked to teach. Because of these studies, when his body was being wearied by vigils, cold, and hunger, it occurred to him that if he should ever become a monk, as he had formerly resolved, he would not have to endure hardships more severe than those he was then suffering; nor would he then lose the merit of his present labor, though he did not see whether it would remain his [al., “did not understand”] [Col. 0053A].

Having conceived this thought, he began to direct his whole intention toward pleasing God. He despised the world and its delights and truly desired to become a monk.

6. Why say more? He considered where he might better accomplish what he desired to do, and reasoned with himself as follows:

“Look,” he said, “I shall become a monk. But where? If at Cluny or Bec [Note: [Col. 0053D] These are very famous monasteries. We have often discussed Cluny, especially on 13 January in the life of Blessed Berno, its first abbot. Bec is in the diocese of Rouen, across the Seine, on the Bec stream near the River Risle; it was endowed by William, duke of Normandy, in 1034. In both monasteries, in the year 1662, we experienced singular charity when we went there because of the monuments concerning the lives and veneration of the saints.], I shall have wasted all the time I spent learning literature. For the strictness of the order at Cluny and the superior wisdom of Lanfranc, who is a monk there, will prove either that I am useful to no one or that I am worth nothing. Therefore I shall perfect what I intend in such a place as will allow me to display what I know and to benefit many.”

He used to relate these words himself, as though in jest [al., “willingly”], and would meditate on them [Col. 0053B]. He added:

“I had not yet been subdued; contempt of the world had not yet become strong in me. Therefore, when I spoke as I thought, relying on the affection of others, I did not realize how harmful it was. Later, coming to my senses, I said: ‘What? To wish to become a monk—is that to wish to be placed above others, to be honored above others, to be magnified before others? No. Therefore I shall become a monk at Bec, having laid aside my arrogance, where, as is right, I shall be placed after everyone for God’s sake, regarded as lower than everyone, and thought little of before everyone. And where could this be possible? Surely at Bec. There I shall be of no account, since there is one there who, shining with the light of preeminent knowledge [al., “wisdom”], is sufficient for all, honored and beloved by all.

“‘There, then, shall be my rest; there, God alone shall be my intention; there, the contemplation of his love alone shall be mine; there, the blessed and constant remembrance of him shall be my happy consolation and satisfaction.’”

These were his thoughts, these were his desires, and these were the things he hoped would come to him.

7. During that period his mind was also drawn toward other paths of life to be pursued, but the force of his desire inclined most strongly toward this one. Knowing that it is written, “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (*Ecclesiasticus* 32:24), he did not wish rashly to entrust himself to any one of the ways of life he was considering, lest in some respect he appear disobedient to the precepts of Scripture.

He had many friends, but when he sought one adviser to whom he could entrust himself completely in this matter, he chose the aforesaid Lanfranc from among a thousand. He went to him and explained that his will was divided among three possibilities, but that, following Lanfranc’s counsel, he wished to hold to whichever of the three he judged best, abandoning the other two.

He explained the three possibilities to him as follows:

“Either I wish to become a monk, or I desire to be a hermit, or, living from my own inheritance, I wish, if you advise it, to provide from it as far as I can for any needy people for God’s sake. For my father has now died, and the whole inheritance falls to me.

“Know, then, Lord Lanfranc, that my will fluctuates among these three possibilities; but I beg you to establish me in whichever of them is best.”

Lanfranc delayed giving his judgment and advised him instead to refer the matter to the hearing of the venerable Maurilius [Note: [Col. 0053D] Maurilius governed the Church of Rouen from 1055 to 1067.] of Rouen, bishop [al., “archbishop”]. Anselm accepted the advice, and, accompanied by Lanfranc, sought the bishop.

Such was the force of devotion then possessing Anselm’s heart, and such was his belief that Lanfranc possessed true counsel, that, as they traveled toward Rouen through the great forest above Bec, he confessed that if Lanfranc had said to him, “Remain in this forest, and take care not to leave it as long as you live,” he would undoubtedly have obeyed the command.

When they reached the bishop, they explained the reason for their arrival and asked what he thought. Without delay, he praised the monastic order above the others and preferred Anselm’s purpose to all the alternatives.

## Chapter Two

### Monastic Life; Administration of the Priorship; Assistance Given to a Young Man in Life and in Death

8. Hearing and approving this, Anselm abandoned the other possibilities, left the world, and became a monk at Bec in the twenty-seventh year of his age [Note: [Col. 0053D] In the year of Christ 1060.].

At that time the monastery itself was governed by Lord Herluin, the abbot, an elderly man distinguished by great uprightness [Col. 0054C]. He was the first abbot of that place and had built the monastery from its foundations out of his own inheritance. The often-mentioned Lanfranc held the office of prior.

Anselm, now a new monk, diligently imitated those who lived more religiously than others. Indeed, he served religion in every respect so faithfully that anyone who wished to live religiously within the entire community found enough in his life to imitate. Thus, over the course of three years, progressing daily and continually toward what was better, he came to be regarded as a great and honorable man.

9. When the venerable Lanfranc had assumed the governance of the monastery at Caen [Note: Caen is the principal city of Lower Normandy, on the River Orne, with a celebrated academy and various monasteries.], [Note: The monastery was dedicated to Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and founded by William the Conqueror, king of England and duke of Normandy; it was later destroyed by the most wicked Calvinists. Lucas d’Achery published its foundation charters in his notes to the Life of Blessed Lanfranc, issued before his works.] [Note: Blessed Lanfranc was appointed its first abbot in 1062, as we reported above from the Chronicle of Bec.], Anselm himself served as prior. Thus, having obtained greater freedom for serving God, he began to devote himself entirely, and all his time, to God’s service, and to remove the world and all its affairs entirely from his attention. It came about that, being continually occupied with God alone and with heavenly disciplines, he ascended so high to the summit of divine contemplation that, with God revealing them, he perceived the most obscure questions concerning God’s divinity and our faith—questions unresolved before his time [al., unfamiliar]—and, having perceived them, unraveled them. By explanations laid open, he proved that what he said was sound and catholic.

For he placed such faith in the divine Scriptures that, with unshakable firmness of heart, he believed that there was nothing in them that could in any way depart from the path of solid truth. Therefore, with the utmost zeal he directed his mind toward this end: that, in accordance with his faith, he might be found worthy by the reasoning of his mind to perceive what he sensed lay hidden beneath much darkness in those Scriptures.

It happened one night that, occupied with such thoughts, he lay awake in bed before the nocturnal office and tried by meditation to investigate how the prophets had once known past and future things together as though they were present, and had proclaimed them without hesitation either by word or in writing. And behold, while he was wholly absorbed in this and ardently desired to understand it, he fixed his eyes and saw through the walls between the oratory and the dormitory the monks whose duty it was to go around the altar and the other places of the church in preparation for Matins, lighting the lamps. Finally, he saw one of them take a cord in his hands and strike the bell to awaken the brothers. At its sound, when the community rose from their beds, Anselm marveled at what had occurred. He therefore concluded that it was a very small matter for God to show prophets future events in the spirit, since God had granted him to see bodily, with his physical eyes, what was happening through so many obstacles.

[Col. 0055C]

10. From that time, suffused inwardly with the light of a more penetrating wisdom, he so pierced the character of people of every sex and age, as reason disclosed it, that when you heard him openly discussing such matters, you would notice that he was revealing to each person the secrets of his own heart. He also uncovered the origins and, so to speak, the very seeds and roots, as well as the development, of all virtues and vices; and he taught with the utmost clarity how the former could be attained and the latter avoided or overcome.

You would see such power of every good counsel shining forth in him that you could not doubt that the spirit of counsel presided in his breast. How ready and constant he was in holy exhortations it is unnecessary to say, since nearly all who heard him agree that, though he himself was indefatigable in them, he often exhausted his listeners. What is said of Saint Martin—that Christ was never absent from his mouth—we may confidently affirm, without falsehood, can be said of Anselm, whether concerning justice or anything else pertaining to true life. In this connection, it is worth noting that, not without a certain presage, he had once already been refreshed in a vision by the bright bread of the Lord’s table.

11. As for his bodily exercises—I mean his fasts, prayers, and vigils—I think it better to remain silent than to speak. For what could I say about his fasting, when from the beginning of his priorate he so weakened his body by hunger that not only was every enticement of the appetite afterward completely extinguished in him, but, as he used to say, he never afterward suffered hunger or the pleasure of eating, no matter what abstinence he practiced? [Note: From the year of Christ 1063 to the year 1078, for fifteen years.] Nevertheless, he ate as other people do, but very sparingly, knowing that his body could not subsist [al., endure] without food.

As for the prayers that he himself published, written according to the desire and requests of his friends [Note: These were perhaps the *Heavenly Colloquies*, or *Flames of Pious Affections toward God, Christ the Lord, the Mother of God, and many saints*, published by Rainaudus, beginning on page 197.], it is enough, even without my speaking, to see with what solicitude, fear, hope, and love he appealed to God and his saints, and also taught others how to appeal to them. Let anyone simply attend to them devoutly, and I hope that he will joyfully perceive in them and through them the affection of Anselm’s heart and his own spiritual progress.

What shall I say of his vigils? Frequently the whole day was insufficient for giving counsel; a large part of the night was added to it. Moreover, he corrected at night books that before that time had been exceedingly corrupt throughout the world; he persisted in holy meditations; and, from contemplating supreme blessedness and desiring eternal life, he poured forth immense showers of tears. He wept most bitterly over the miseries of this life, over his own sins, if he had any, and over those of others. He scarcely slept at all before the nocturnal vigils, and often obtained no sleep whatsoever. His life was adorned by such pursuits.

12. May God grant that something, even a little, may be said of how he conducted himself toward his subjects, for the emulation of prelates. When he had first become prior, certain brothers of the monastery became jealous of him, seeing—and, in seeing, envying—that he had been placed above them, although they judged that, according to the order of their conversion, he ought to have been placed below them. Thus disturbed, and disturbing others, they stirred up scandals, produced dissensions, fostered factions, and nourished hatred. But Anselm was peaceable with those who hated peace (Psalm 119:7), returning their slanders with acts of brotherly charity and preferring to conquer evil with good rather than to be conquered by their evil with evil (Romans 12:21).

By God’s mercy, this came to pass: when they observed that he conducted himself in all his actions with complete purity and simplicity, and that nothing remained in him which could rightly be condemned, their evil will was changed into a good one, and they began to imitate his words and deeds for the better. But, to make clear how this happened, I shall present one of them as an example, so that, once it is recognized by what artifice Anselm changed him from his wickedness, it may be understood how the others too were corrected through him.

13. A certain man named Osbern, still a youth, was a monk of that monastery. He was shrewd by nature and skilled with his artful hands in various tasks, and he displayed in himself promising material for good hope. But the habits that were very perverse in him greatly disfigured these qualities; in addition, he practiced an utterly dog-like hatred against Anselm.

Anselm himself did not consider this hatred important. Yet, greatly desiring that Osbern’s conduct should correspond to his intelligent nature, he began, with a certain holy cunning, to draw the boy in by pious caresses, kindly tolerating his childish actions and granting him many things, so long as they could be tolerated without harm to discipline—things in which his age might take pleasure and his unbridled spirit might be bent toward gentleness.

The boy rejoiced in such treatment, and gradually his spirit was brought down from its fierceness [al., truth]. He began to love Anselm, accept his admonitions, and regulate his conduct. When Anselm noticed this, he embraced him familiarly above the others [al., omit], nurtured and cherished him, and urged and instructed him in every way to advance continually toward better things. Then, little by little, he withdrew the childish privileges he had granted him and strove to lead him toward honorable maturity of conduct.

His pious solicitude was not frustrated: Anselm’s sacred admonitions advanced and grew strong in the young man. Therefore, when he perceived that he could rely on the firmness of the youth’s good purpose, he immediately cut away all childish behavior in him. If he discovered that the young man had admitted anything deserving correction, he punished it severely in him not only with words but also with blows [al., more severely].

What did the young man do? He endured everything calmly; he was strengthened in his resolve to practice the whole of religious life; he burned with zeal in learning every holy action; he patiently bore the insults, reproaches, and slanders of others, preserving toward all the affection of sincere love. The father rejoiced in these things beyond what can be expressed and loved his son with the holy fire of charity more than can be believed.

14. But when Anselm hoped—as he later reported in tears—that Osbern would advance to the great benefit of the Church, behold, the young man was suddenly taken away by a serious bodily illness and confined to bed. You would then have seen the good father, the friend of the fortunate young man, sitting beside the bedridden youth day and night, supplying him with food and drink, taking upon himself the duties of all the attendants, and behaving in every respect as a true friend. He himself carefully restored both the young man’s body and his soul.

When Osbern drew near to death, Anselm instructed him in a familiar conversation that, after his death, if possible, he should reveal to him what had become of him. Osbern promised, and died. The dead man’s body was washed according to custom, clothed, placed in a coffin, and carried into the church. The brothers sat around it, chanting psalms for his soul. Anselm, however, withdrew to a more secluded part of the church so that he might pour out his prayers for him more freely.

When, amid his tears, his body was weakened by the heavy sorrow of his heart [al., torpor], and he lowered his eyes for a little sleep, he saw in the spirit of his mind certain persons of venerable appearance, clothed in brilliant white garments, enter the house in which Osbern had ended his life and sit around to pronounce judgment. Yet, since he did not know the sentence of the judgment and anxiously desired to learn it, behold, Osbern appeared, resembling a man who, having been brought near death either by illness or by excessive loss of blood, is returning to consciousness [al., omit].

The father said to him, “What is it, my son? How are you?”

He answered him: “The ancient serpent rose up against me three times, and three times fell back upon himself, and the Lord God’s bear-keeper delivered me.”

At these words Anselm raised his eyes from sleep, and Osbern disappeared. Thus the dead man displayed obedience to the living, just as, while alive, he had been accustomed [al., used] to display it to the living Anselm.

15. If anyone wishes to hear how Anselm himself interpreted these words of the obedient dead man, let him lend his ears briefly.

“The ancient serpent,” he said, “rose up against him three times because the devil accused him of the sins he had committed after baptism and before his parents offered him to the service of God in the monastery [al., omit]; he accused him also of the sins he had committed after his parents’ offering and before his profession; and likewise he accused him of the sins he had committed after his profession and before his death.

“But he fell three times upon himself because he found that the sins he had committed while still in the world had been erased by the faith of his parents when they offered him to God. And the sins he had committed later, while living in the monastery but before his profession, he found erased at the very moment of his profession. The sins also that he had committed after his profession and before his death, he found at the moment of his death to have been erased and forgiven through true confession and repentance; and, confounded, he lamented that the malicious [al., malignant] stratagems by which he had enticed him to sin had, by God’s just judgment, been turned back upon himself to increase his own condemnation.

“And the Lord God’s bear-keeper delivered him. God’s bear-keepers are the good angels. For just as bear-keepers restrain bears, so the angels restrain and crush the evil demons in their ferocity, so that they may not harm us as much as they wish [al., may harm us only].”

16. After this, so that Anselm would not deny to the dead the gift of holy affection that he had bestowed upon Osbern while alive, he celebrated Mass for his soul every day for an entire year. If he was ever prevented from celebrating that sacrament himself, he arranged for those who were obliged to celebrate the familiar Masses to say his Mass for his brother’s soul; and, when the opportunity arose, he himself celebrated their Masses before the Mass for his deceased brother.

Thus, on every day of the entire year, either Anselm himself celebrated Mass for Osbern or, by borrowing another Mass celebrated by someone else [al., by being changed], he supplied it. In addition, by letters sent everywhere, he asked that prayers be offered in Masses for the soul of his Osbern, and he obtained this.

When the brothers saw these things and reproached the sluggishness of their own hearts, they proclaimed themselves wretched and unhappy, and Osbern blessed and fortunate, since he had deserved to find such love and such assistance. From that time, therefore, each and every one of them submitted himself in body and soul to Anselm, desiring to succeed Osbern by hereditary right in Anselm’s friendship. Anselm, for his part, giving thanks to God for their conversion, became all things to all people, so that he might save all (1 Corinthians 9:22).

[Col. 0059A]

17. Nevertheless, he devoted particular care to adolescents and young men, and when they asked him the reason, he gave it by means of an example. He compared youth to wax, which is suitably tempered for forming a seal. “For,” he said, “if wax is too hard or too soft, when it is pressed with a seal it does not fully receive the seal’s shape. But if, possessing in proper measure both hardness and softness, it is impressed with a seal, then the form of the seal is made entirely clear and complete.

“So it is with the ages of human beings. You may see a man who has lived in the vanity of this world from childhood to extreme old age, wise only in earthly things and completely hardened in them. Speak to him of spiritual matters; teach him to investigate the secrets of heavenly contemplation; and you will see that he cannot even perceive what you want. No wonder: he is hardened wax. He has spent no part of his life in these matters and has learned to pursue what is alien to them.

“On the other hand, consider a boy tender in age and understanding, unable to distinguish good from evil and unable even to understand you when you discuss such things. Clearly, he is soft wax, almost liquid, and in no way able to receive the image of a seal.

“Between these two stands the adolescent and the young man, suitably tempered between tenderness and hardness. If you instruct him, you will be able to form him into whatever shape you wish. Recognizing this, I watch over young men with greater solicitude, striving to uproot in them every shoot of vice, so that afterward, properly instructed in the practice of holy virtues, they may transform within themselves the image of a spiritual man.”

18. But while various affairs belonging to various people wearied Anselm amid these activities and sometimes disturbed his mind from its tranquillity, he came to Rouen to seek counsel about them from the aforementioned archbishop of Rouen, Maurillus, of venerable memory.

When he explained to the bishop the reason for his arrival and, in the course of his words, wept most bitterly over the tranquillity of his former condition, he began earnestly to beg that he might deserve to be relieved of the burden of prelateship, which he confessed to be unbearable.

But that man of great holiness said: “Do not seek, my dearest son, what you are seeking; and do not wish to withdraw from bearing the burden of others while caring only for yourself. For I tell you truly that I have heard of many, and have seen many, who, because they refused, for the sake of their own peace, to watch over the benefit of their neighbors through pastoral care, have always advanced from bad to worse as they walked in idleness.

“Therefore, lest the same thing happen to you—which God forbid—I command you by holy obedience to retain the prelateship you now possess and not to abandon it in any way unless your abbot commands you to do so [al., now]. If at any time you are called to a greater office, do not refuse to accept it under any circumstances. For I know that you will not remain long in the office you now hold; rather, before long you will be advanced to a higher degree of prelateship.”

When Anselm heard this, he said, “Woe to me, wretched man that I am! I am failing beneath what I carry; and if a heavier burden is imposed, I do not dare reject it.”

The bishop repeated his command and ordered him, as before, not to transgress it.

## CHAPTER III

### Kindness toward Everyone. Certain Books and Letters Written

19. Thereafter Anselm returned to the monastery and presented himself to everyone in such a way that all loved him as a most dear father. He bore the character and infirmities of all with equanimity and offered each person whatever he knew to be necessary and beneficial.

O how many people who had already despaired because of their infirmity were restored to their former health through his pious solicitude! You, Herewald, decrepit old man, experienced this in yourself when, weighed down not only by age but also by a serious illness, you had nothing of your body under your control except your tongue. Fed by his hands, and with wine pressed from grapes into his other hand, you drank from that very hand, were refreshed, and were restored to your former health [al., and]. For, as you reported, you could take no other drink, nor drink from any other source, that was agreeable to you.

Anselm himself was accustomed to visit the house of the sick, carefully investigate the illnesses of the individual brothers, and without delay or annoyance supply each one with whatever his illness required. Thus he was a father to the healthy and a mother to the sick—indeed, a father and mother alike to the healthy and the sick.
