Hence whatever secret any of them kept within himself, each strove to reveal to Anselm as to the sweetest of mothers. Yet his diligent care was especially exercised toward the young.

[Col. 0060C]

20. One of these young men had resolved within himself that, on no occasion whatsoever, would he place his hand upon his own private parts. The devil, jealous of this resolve, caused him to feel such pain and anguish in those same parts that the young man could not endure himself in any way. His flesh seemed to feel so heavy that it was as though an exceedingly massive weight of lead were hanging from that part of his body and dragging him downward.

Since he could not conceal the extent of his distress in his bearing, Anselm asked him what was wrong, and he could not hide the matter. Anselm advised him to test the extent of his illness by placing his hand there, but the young man refused out of shame, fearing that he would violate his resolve.

Then Anselm took with him a certain elderly and religious brother and led the suffering young man to a more secluded place, intending to discover the nature of his illness and offer whatever help was possible. What more need be said? The flesh was found to be perfectly healthy, and they were greatly astonished. Immediately all that diabolical affliction fell away, and it no longer troubled the young man in this way; Anselm’s simple presence had made him immune to so great a calamity.

21. Moreover, one of the older brothers of the monastery, who was deeply hostile to Anselm because of an old hatred and could in no way look upon him with a simple eye, was afflicted by illness and brought to the point of death.

While the brothers were resting in their beds at midday according to custom, he began, in the house of the sick where he lay, to utter pitiable cries. As though eager to escape the dreadful appearances of certain beings, he grew pale, trembled anxiously, and kept hiding and turning his face from side to side.

The frightened brothers who were present asked what was wrong. He replied: “You see two monstrous wolves holding me squeezed between their paws and now strangling my throat with their teeth sunk into it, yet you ask what is happening to me?”

When he heard this, one of the monks, named Riculphus, hurried to Anselm, who at that time was occupied in the cloister correcting books. He led Anselm outside the cloister and explained what was happening to the sick brother.

Riculphus was then ordered to return to the sick man, while Anselm withdrew alone to a more secluded place. Shortly afterward he entered the room in which the brother was suffering, raised his hand, and made the sign of the holy cross, saying: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

At this action the sick man immediately became calm. His face brightened, and he began from the depths of his heart to give thanks to God. He said that, when Anselm entered through the door and extended his hand to make the sign of the holy cross, he had seen a flame of fire issue from Anselm’s mouth in the form of a lance. It was hurled at the wolf, frightened them, and drove them far away in swift flight.

Anselm then approached the brother and spoke with him privately about the salvation of his soul. He inclined his heart to repentance and confession of everything in which he could remember having offended God. Then, by paternal authority, he absolved him from all these things [Col. 0061C] and told him that he would depart from the present life at the hour when the brothers rose for None.

And so it happened. For when the monks rose from their beds, the sick man was placed on the ground, and, while they gathered around him, he died.

22. The aforementioned Riculphus served as secretary in the monastery itself. One night, while he was walking through the cloister and watching for the time and hour at which he should awaken the brothers for the vigils, he happened to pass before the door of the chapterhouse. Looking inside, he saw Anselm standing in prayer, surrounded by a great globe of shining flame.

He marveled and did not know what new thing the sight signified. He supposed that at that hour Anselm was occupied with sleep rather than prayer. He therefore hurried up to the dormitory and went to Anselm’s bed, but found him nowhere there. Returning, he found the man in the chapterhouse, but did not find the globe of fire that he had left behind.

23. At another time, one of the princes of Normandy sent word to Anselm, who wished to cross to England, asking him to come both for other business and so that, through the prince’s prayer, Anselm’s journey might be protected from the dangers of the sea [al., might wish him to come; al., omit].

Anselm set out. The day of their intended conversation was already declining into evening, but the prince was taking no thought about providing lodging for him. When Anselm learned this, he said nothing to anyone about the matter; he obtained permission and departed.

As he went, uncertain where he should turn aside—for Bec was far away—one of the monks of Bec met him, intending to go there, since he knew that Anselm was being detained for conversation with the prince. Anselm asked him where he was going and then what provision he had made for his lodging.

He replied: “Indeed, Father, we have some sort of lodging not far away, but we have nothing to set before you and the brothers except bread and cheese.”

Smiling, Anselm said: “Good man, do not be afraid. Rather, go quickly, cast a net into the nearby river, and you will immediately find a fish sufficient for all of us.”

Having received this command, the monk hastened ahead. He summoned a fisherman, explained what Anselm had ordered, and commanded, urged, and entreated him to cast his net into the river more quickly.

The fisherman was astonished. He hesitated to obey the petitioner, declaring that what the monk said would happen was more fit to be laughed at than attempted. At last, compelled by the brother, he cast the net against all expectation and immediately caught a trout of extraordinary size together with another small fish.

A third fisherman, astonished at what had happened, asserted that he had investigated the retreats of that water for twenty years and had never been able to find a trout of that kind in it.

When the fish had been prepared and set before the man, it abundantly sufficed for him and his companions, exactly as Anselm had said, with plenty left over.

24. On another occasion, a man named Walter, surnamed Tirellus, detained Anselm while he was passing through his land, unwilling to let him depart without having eaten with him. But when Walter complained of the scarcity of fish and said jokingly that he had nothing to set before so great a man and his monks except certain worthless things, Anselm said to him: “A sturgeon is being brought to you—yet your mind complains about a lack of delicacies?”

Walter laughed, entirely unable to believe what he heard. Immediately after Anselm’s words, two of the man’s servants brought one enormous sturgeon. They said that their shepherds had found it on the bank of the River Authie [Note: The Authie is a stream in Picardy, near the town of Dourlens; it is mentioned in the Acts of Saint Fursa on 16 January.] and had sent it to them.

If anyone doubts that the spirit of prophecy was present in the man in these matters, the truth of what happened makes clear what must be held.

[Col. 0062D]

25. During this period he wrote three treatises [Note: These first four books are written in the form of a dialogue between master and disciple and are contained in the first part among the didactic minor works.], namely, *On Truth*, *On the Freedom of Choice*, and *On the Fall of the Devil*. In them it is sufficiently clear where he fixed his mind, although in considering such matters he in no way withdrew from the concerns that the care of others required of him.

He also wrote a fourth work entitled *The Grammarian*. In it, introducing a disciple who disputes with him, he proposes and resolves many dialectical questions and explains and teaches how qualities and qualified things are to be distinguished and understood.

He also composed a little book that he called the *Monologion* [Note: This *Monologion*, divided into seventy-seven chapters, is extant among the didactic minor works.]. In it he speaks alone and with himself. Setting aside all authority from divine Scripture, he seeks by reason alone to discover what God is; and he proves and establishes by invincible reasoning that what true faith holds concerning God is so, and can be so in no other way.

26. After this, it occurred to him to investigate whether what is believed and proclaimed concerning God could be proved by one single and brief argument: namely, that God is eternal, immutable, omnipotent, wholly present everywhere, incomprehensible, just, pious, merciful, truthful, truth, goodness, justice, and several other things, and how all these things are one in him (John 17:21).

As Anselm himself reported, this matter caused him great difficulty. For this thought partly took away his food, drink, and sleep; partly—and this burdened him even more—it disturbed the attention with which he ought to have devoted himself to Matins and the other service of God.

When he noticed this, and still could not fully grasp what he was seeking, he supposed that such a thought was a temptation of the devil and strove to drive it far from his mind. Yet the more he labored at this, the more and more the thought itself afflicted him.

And behold, one night during the nocturnal vigils, the grace of God shone into his heart. The matter became clear to his understanding and filled all his inmost being with immense joy and exultation.

Considering that this discovery might please others if it became known, and free from envy, he immediately wrote it on wax tablets and entrusted them to one of the monastery’s brothers, instructing him to guard them carefully.

After several days he asked the custodian for the tablets. They were sought in the place where they had been stored but were not found. The brothers were questioned, in case someone had taken them, but to no avail. To this day no one has been found who acknowledged knowing anything about them.

Anselm composed another statement on the same subject on other tablets and entrusted them to the same custodian, ordering him to guard them with greater caution. The custodian placed the tablets in a more secluded part of his bed. The next day, suspecting nothing amiss, he found the tablets scattered on the floor before the bed, with the wax that had been on them dispersed here and there in fragments.

The tablets were lifted, the wax gathered, and both were returned to Anselm [Col. 0063D]. He joined the wax together and, though with difficulty, recovered the writing. Fearing that it might be completely lost through some negligence, he ordered it to be transferred, in the name of the Lord, onto parchment.

From this he composed a small volume, but one great in the weight of its arguments and in the subtlety of its contemplation, which he called the *Proslogion* [the text has *Prostagion*]. [Note: This *Proslogion* is substituted for the work called the *Monologion* and is divided into twenty-six chapters.]

In that work he addresses either himself or God. When the work came into the hands of a certain person, and that person was considerably offended by one of its arguments, he judged [al., became angry] that the argument was not sound. Eager to refute it, he composed a certain writing against it [al., against him] and appended it to the end of Anselm’s work. [Note: It is substituted under the title *Book on Behalf of the Fool, against the Reasoning of Blessed Anselm in the Proslogion*, by an unknown author; and there is added: *The Apologetic Book of Blessed Anselm against the Fool*, comprising ten chapters.]

When Anselm examined this writing, which had been sent to him by one of his friends, he rejoiced. He thanked his critic and published his own response to the objection. He sent it back to the friend who had transmitted the writing, appended and subscribed to a little book addressed to Anselm himself.

He desired that this response should be requested by that critic and by others who might wish to possess the little book, so that at the end of the work [see the variant readings] the criticism of his argument and his response to the criticism might be appended.

[Col. 0064B]

27. During this period he also wrote very many letters [Note: These are contained in Book I of the letters that Anselm wrote before becoming abbot; there are seventy-seven of them, together with a few letters from others addressed to him.]. Through them he instructed certain people to attend to matters that concerned them according to the diversity of their circumstances [al., their causes], and he answered, in proportion to the matter, those who asked him for advice concerning their affairs.

We shall refrain from mentioning the various matters that diverse circumstances compelled him to address in writing. But I have taken care to insert into this work the advice he sent in one letter to a certain Lanzon, recently made a monk at Cluny, so that from this one letter it may be understood what may be judged concerning the others [Note: This is Letter 29, which contains more material at the beginning that is omitted here.].

Among other things, he wrote as follows:

“You have entered, dearest one, and professed the military service of Christ. In that service, not only must the violence of an openly resisting enemy be driven back, but the cunning of one who appears to give counsel must also be avoided.

“For often, when the malevolent enemy cannot openly destroy Christ’s recruit by wounding him with evil will, he maliciously and craftily tries to extinguish him with the cup of poisonous reasoning when he thirsts for it. When he cannot overwhelm a monk through hatred of the life he has professed, he strives to overthrow him through disgust with the way of life in which he is living.

“And although he seems to grant that the monk’s purpose ought to be maintained, nevertheless, because he began it under such conditions, among such people, or in that place, the enemy never ceases, by many cunning devices, to accuse him of being exceedingly foolish and imprudent. He does this so that, by persuading him to be ungrateful for the benefit which God granted in his undertaking, the monk may, by a just judgment, neither advance to better things, nor retain what he has received, nor persist uselessly [al., profitably] in it.

“For while he continually labors in troubled thoughts about changing his beginning—or, if it cannot be changed, at least about condemning it—he never strives toward the goal of perfection. Since he dislikes the foundation he has laid, he is in no way willing to build the structure of a good life upon it.

“Hence it happens that, just as a little tree, if it is often transplanted [al., transported], or if, newly planted, it is disturbed in the same place by frequent uprooting [al., turning], cannot take root and quickly becomes dry, never reaching any fruitfulness, so the unhappy monk, if he is repeatedly moved from place to place by his own desire, or, while remaining in one place, is frequently shaken by hatred of it, never becoming firmly rooted in the roots of love, grows weak in every useful exercise and is enriched by no abundance of good works.

“And when, if he happens to reflect upon it, he perceives that he is advancing not toward good but toward evil, he unjustly attributes the whole cause of his misery not to himself but to the conduct of others. From this he inflames himself still more unhappily with hatred of those among whom he lives.

“Therefore, whoever undertakes the monastic way of life should find it beneficial, in whatever monastery he has made his profession—unless it is such a place that he is forced against his will to do evil there—to strive with the full intention of his mind to take root there in the roots of love. He should refuse to judge the conduct of others or the customs of the place, provided that they are not contrary to the divine commandments, even if they appear useless.

“Let him rejoice that at last he has found a place where he may resolve to remain for his whole life, not unwillingly but voluntarily, having driven away every concern about migration, so that in tranquillity he may devote himself diligently to seeking only the exercises of a pious life.”

28. But if he seems to himself to desire certain greater and more useful things with spiritual fervor than the regulations of his present monastery permit, let him judge either that he is deceived—whether by preferring equal things to equal or lesser things to greater [another reading: lesser things]—or by presuming himself capable of what he is not capable of; or else let him believe that he has not deserved what he desires. If he is deceived, let him give thanks to divine mercy, by which he is protected from his error, lest, by changing his place or way of life without benefit, or even [Col. 0065C] with loss, he incur in vain the charge of fickleness and frivolity, or, exhausted by attempting things greater than his strength, fail into a condition worse than the former, or even worse than that. But if, though he has not yet deserved them, he truly desires things better than those that are available, let him patiently endure the divine judgment, which unjustly denies nothing to anyone [another reading: to him] [MS: *haec* omitted]; let him not offend God by murmuring or speaking against Him, but bear everything with equanimity and strive, by enduring, to lead everything toward better things, lest by provoking the just Judge through impatience he deserve both not to receive what he does not have and to lose what he has received, or, because [another reading: that] he does not love it, to hold it uselessly. Whether, then, he perceives [Col. 0065D] mercy or judgment toward himself in those things that he does not have but desires, let him rejoice in what he has received and render worthy thanks to the generosity of heaven. And because he has been able to reach some kind of harbor from the stormy whirlwinds of the world, let him beware of bringing into the harbor’s tranquility the storm of fickleness and impatience, so that his mind, kept safe by steadfastness and gentleness, may be free for the anxious care of divine fear and the delight of love. For fear guards through watchfulness, whereas love brings to completion through delight.

I know that these matters require greater breadth in writing or conversation if it is to be understood more fully by what devices the ancient serpent ensnares the inexperienced monk in this kind of temptation, and by what arguments the prudent monk dissolves and destroys its [another reading: these] cunning persuasions. But since I have already exceeded the brevity that the [Col. 0066A] letter requires, and since everything I have said here—or ought to have said—pertains to preserving peace of mind, let a brief exhortation on this matter [another reading omits “this”] bring our letter to an end. Nor should you think, dearest friend, that I say these things because I suspect you of suffering from any disturbance of mind. But since Lord Ursio [another reading: Ursus] compels me to write some admonition to you, I do not know what I should advise more than that you beware of this thing which I know commonly steals upon certain novices under the appearance of a right intention.

Therefore, my friend and most beloved brother, your beloved lover [i.e. he who loves you] advises, admonishes, and entreats you with all the depths of his heart to devote all your strength to peace of mind, without which no one can discern the ambushes of the crafty enemy or perceive the exceedingly narrow paths of the virtues. Yet the monk who lives in a [Col. 0066B] monastery can in no way reach this peace without steadfastness and gentleness—which gentleness is the inseparable companion of patience—and unless he strives religiously to observe the institutions of his monastery, which are not forbidden by the divine commandments, even if he does not see their rationale.

Farewell, and may the omnipotent Lord perfect your steps in His paths, so that your footsteps may not be moved, that you may appear in righteousness before the sight of the Lord [the text is uncertain here], and be satisfied when His glory appears.

## CHAPTER IV

Visions granted by God; advice concerning the governance of boys; love of the common life and discernment

[Col. 0066C]

29. Meanwhile, when his conduct no longer disagreed in any respect with his words and writings, and he had composed the whole intention of his mind toward contempt of the world and fixed all his zeal upon those things alone that belonged to God, it happened that, seized by illness, he was grievously afflicted. But while he himself always remained the same in God [another reading omits “always”], when his sickness had somewhat subsided, he was carried outside himself in an ecstasy of mind and saw a single swift and headlong river into which flowed the washings of all streams [another reading: rivers] and the waters that washed every earthly thing. The water itself appeared exceedingly turbid and filthy, horrible with every kind of foul pollution. It seized whatever it could touch and swept along men and women alike, rich and poor together.

When Anselm saw this, and, pitying their shameful whirling, asked how they could live, or from what source they could refresh their thirst, those who were being carried along in this fashion, he received the answer that they delighted to live upon and take pleasure in the water by which they were being dragged away. Then, in an indignant voice, he said [another reading: “he said”]: “How? Could anyone be so drenched with such filth, or even carry himself for shame among human beings?”

The one who accompanied him replied: “Do not wonder. What you see is the torrent of the world, in which the people of the world are swept away and engulfed.” And he added: “Do you wish to see what true monastic life is?”

He answered: “I do.”

So he led him, as it were, into the enclosure of a certain large and spacious cloister and said to him: “Look around.” He looked, and behold, the walls of that cloister were covered with the purest silver [Col. 0067A] [another reading omits “and brightest”]. The grass in the middle of the level ground was also silver, green, soft, and more delightful [another reading: “not”] than human imagination could conceive. Like other grass, it gently bent beneath those who rested upon it, and when they rose, it too rose again. Thus the whole place was pleasant and filled with exceptional delight, and Anselm chose it for his dwelling.

Then his guide said to him: “Come! Do you wish to see what true patience is?”

When Anselm ardently desired this and replied that he wanted it exceedingly, he suddenly returned to himself and, grieving and lamenting, lost both the vision and the one who had shown it to him. Understanding the two visions that he had seen and turning them over within himself, he strove all the more to flee the horror of the one as he endeavored to delight in the pleasantness of the other.

From then on he devoted himself entirely to being a true [another reading: truly] monk, and, in order to grasp the monastic life through firm reasoning and propose it to others [another reading: place it before others], he was not deprived of his desire. Something of this, I believe, may be perceived from his words, which we have resolved to insert at intervals into this little work, as the sequence of the events we have undertaken to narrate shall require. For it does not seem to me that one can fully attain knowledge of the ordering of his life if, after describing his actions, one remains silent in speech about what kind of person he was.

30. At a certain time, when a certain abbot who was regarded as exceedingly religious was speaking with him about matters belonging to monastic religion, and, among other things, had begun speaking about boys brought up in the cloister [another reading: had discussed them], he added: “What, I ask, will become of these boys? They are perverse and incorrigible. Day and night we do not cease beating them, and they continually become worse in their own regard.”

Anselm, astonished at this [another reading: him], said: “You do not cease beating them?” And when they are grown, what are they like?”

“Dull and bestial,” he replied.

Then Anselm said: “With what good omen do you spend your nourishment on them, when you have raised beasts from human beings?”

“And what can we do about it?” he said. “By every means we constrain them to improve, and we accomplish nothing.”

“Constrain them?” said Anselm. “Tell me, please [another reading: Tell me, please, my lord abbot], lord abbot: if you planted a tree in your garden and immediately enclosed it on every side so tightly that it could not extend its branches in any direction, when after some years you released it, what kind of tree would emerge?”

“Certainly,” he replied, “one with useless, crooked, and tangled branches.”

“And whose fault would this be except yours, since you had enclosed it without measure? This is exactly what you do with your boys. Through their oblation they have been planted in the garden of the Church so that they may grow and bear fruit for God. But you constrain them on every side [another reading: by every means] with such terror, threats, and beatings that they are entirely denied any freedom of their own. Thus, crushed without discernment, they heap up within themselves thoughts that are twisted and tangled like thorns [another reading: within]; they foster and nourish them, and support [another reading: supply] them so strongly in their growth that, with an obstinate mind, they evade everything that might aid in correcting them.

“As a result, since they feel no love, no compassion, no goodwill, and no sweetness toward themselves in you, they later place no trust in any good [another reading omits “any”] within you, but believe that everything you do proceeds from hatred and envy against them. And it happens, in a pitiable way, that just as they grow in body, so hatred and suspicion of every evil grow in them; they are always inclined and bent toward vices. Since they have been nurtured in no true charity toward anyone, they are able to look upon no one except with lowered brows or a sidelong glance.”

31. “But for God’s sake, I wish you would tell me why you are so hostile to them. Are they not human beings? Are they not of the same nature as you? Would you want what you inflict upon them to be done to you? If only you were what they are!

“But let it be so. Do you intend to shape them toward good conduct solely through blows and scourges [another reading: threaten them]? Have you ever seen a craftsman form a beautiful image from a sheet of gold or silver by blows alone? I do not think so. What does he do, then? In order to shape the sheet into a suitable form [another reading: fit it], he sometimes gently presses and strikes it with his tool, and sometimes, by measured relief, he gently raises and forms it.

“So too, if you wish your boys to be adorned with good conduct, it is necessary that, together with the depressions inflicted by blows, you provide them with the relief and support of fatherly compassion and gentleness.”

At this the abbot said: “What relief? What support? We labor to constrain them into grave and mature forms.”

Anselm replied: “Quite right. Bread and every solid, wholesome, and good food is indeed useful to one who is able to use it. But remove the milk and feed a nursing infant on solid food, and you will see that the child is thereby strangled rather than refreshed. Why is this? I do not wish to say, since it is obvious.

“Nevertheless, hold firmly to this: just as a fragile or strong body has food suited to its condition, so a fragile or strong soul has nourishment suited to its measure. A strong soul delights in and feeds upon solid food—namely, patience in tribulations, not coveting what belongs to others, offering the other cheek to one who strikes one cheek, praying for enemies, loving those who hate, and many things of this kind.

“But a fragile soul, still tender [another reading: tenderly] in the service of God, needs milk—namely, the gentleness of others, kindness, mercy, cheerful encouragement, charitable support, and many things of this sort. If you adapt yourselves in this way to your strong and weak alike, then, by God’s grace, you will gain all of them for God, insofar as it depends upon you [another reading: by your care, for God].”

When the abbot heard this, he groaned and said: “Truly we have strayed from the truth, and the light of discernment has not shone upon us.” Falling to the ground at Anselm’s feet, he confessed that he had sinned and was guilty; he asked forgiveness for the past and promised amendment in the future.

We have related these things so that through them we may recognize how full of devout discernment and discerning compassion he was toward everyone.

32. He devoted himself to such pursuits, served God in them, and through them pleased all good people greatly. Hence his good reputation was spread not only throughout all Normandy, but also throughout all France, all Flanders, and all the lands adjoining them [another reading: the whole adjoining land]; [Col. 0069A] indeed, it crossed the sea and filled England as well. Many nobles, learned clerics, and vigorous soldiers were stirred throughout the various regions and flocked to him; they surrendered themselves and their possessions to the service of God in that monastery. That community grew both within and without: within, in holy religion; without, in possessions of many kinds.

33. But when Abbot Herluin, whom we mentioned above, had grown very old and was no longer able to attend to the affairs of the monastery or assist them, everything that had to be done was carried out under the direction of Anselm, as prior. Since many matters required it, he often had to go outside the monastery. When horses and other necessities for travel were sometimes lacking, the abbot ordered everything he needed to be prepared and supplied to him alone as his personal property.

But at the very mention of personal ownership Anselm recoiled. When he returned from a journey, he ordered whatever had been specially prepared for him to be made available collectively to those who were traveling on the road. Nor, because he might perhaps suffer want afterward, did he ever hold back from supplying the poverty of the others from his own abundance.

This should not be surprising. Since he had already triumphed over the world [another reading: the world had shone upon him], he showed himself in this way to his brothers, for, as he himself was accustomed to relate, even while he was still living a secular life he burned with such love toward others that whenever he saw anyone of his own rank less well provided for than himself, he willingly supplied that person’s want from his own abundance, as far as he was able.

Even then reason taught him that all the riches of the world had been created by the one Father of all for the common benefit of human beings, and that according to natural law nothing belonged more to one person than to another. I say nothing of the fact that some people often offered him considerable weights of gold and silver so that he might accept, keep, and spend them for his own use and that of his people. He would never accept them on any terms unless they were presented to the abbot for the common benefit of the brothers. But when the person offering his possessions replied that he had no intention at that time of giving anything to the abbot or the monks, but only to Anselm himself, Anselm answered that he had no need of such things and did not wish to receive anything from anyone on any other terms.

34. I shall say briefly that, amid such pursuits, one day, as he turned aside to his bed in the dormitory, he unexpectedly found a golden ring upon it [Col. 0069D], and was exceedingly astonished. Considering whether perhaps someone who administered the monastery’s affairs had left the ring there by some chance, he picked it up and showed it to each person. They were astonished and emphatically denied knowing anything about it. It was shown to others and still others, but no one could identify where or by whom it had been brought there.

The ring was then expended for the work of the Church, and the matter ended there. Later, when Anselm himself was raised to the episcopate, there were some who asserted that this very event had already been marked out by that ring as a kind of omen. We, however, set down what happened in a simple style only.

35. He was also invited by various abbeys so that there, both publicly in the chapterhouse to the brothers and privately to those who wished to speak with him, he might offer words of life. For it had become customary for everyone to regard whatever they heard from his mouth as though it were plainly a divine answer. Thus people hurried to him from various places in order to seek counsel.

This matter wounded the devil with grave envy [another reading: was wounding him]. Those whom he could not turn away from that purpose by secret fraud, he attempted to divert through open rebuke. For example, there was a certain soldier named Cadulus. Once, while he was intent upon God through vigils and prayers, he heard the devil, using the voice of his shield-bearer outside the church in which he was, shouting and complaining in a troubled murmur that his horses and all his possessions had already been seized and carried off by robbers after his lodging had been broken into, and that nothing could be recovered unless he hurried there at once.

When Cadulus was not moved in the least by this—judging it a greater loss to yield to the prayer than to lose his possessions—the grieving devil, perceiving that he had been despised, changed himself into the form of a bear and slipped through the roof of the church, falling headlong before him, so that at least by the horror and crash of his fall he might drive the man from what he had begun [another reading: disturb him].

But the soldier remained unmoved and safely mocked the monster. After this, wishing to establish the course of his life upon a holier purpose, he went to Anselm, desiring to learn his advice on the matter. As he hurried along the road toward him, behold, the evil enemy, producing a human voice from the opposite direction, burst out with these words: “Cadulus, Cadulus, where are you going?”

When Cadulus stopped at this voice [Col. 0070C], wishing to know who was saying such things, the demon repeated: “Where are you going, Cadulus? What compels you to go so eagerly to that hypocrite of a prior? His reputation is entirely different from the conduct of his life. Therefore I advise you—indeed, I urge you—to return quickly, lest, deceived by him, you be dragged into the folly by which you are now being led and ensnared. His hypocrisy has already deceived many and, having lulled them with empty hope, has made them bereft of their own resources and defenseless.”

Hearing this and recognizing that the speaker was a demon, Cadulus armed himself with the sign of the cross and, despising the enemy, continued where he had intended to go. What more need be said? After hearing Anselm, he renounced himself and the world, gave himself to the religious life, and became a monk at the Greater Monastery.

Anselm had this practice: he never advised anyone who wished to renounce the world to do so for the sake of any advantage in his monastery rather than in another. He acted in this way, evidently, from this consideration: lest someone later, when troubled by some difficulty—as commonly happens—should disparage the place he had not entered by his own deliberation and attribute the murmuring of his scandal and impatience to Anselm’s persuasion, and thus make himself burdensome to others and others burdensome to him in many ways.

## CHAPTER V

The kindness of the elected abbot toward guests and members of his household. His journey to England. His conversation with Blessed Lanfranc concerning the veneration of Saint Elphegus.

36. After the death of Abbot Herluin, mentioned so often above [Col. 0071A] [Note: Blessed Herluin died in the year 1078, on 26 August], Anselm was elected abbot by the unanimous consent of all the brothers of Bec [another reading: by the complete consent of all]. He tried with every effort to avoid this, putting forward many different reasons why it should not happen. But when they were unwilling even patiently to listen to his arguments, his spirit became anxious within him, and he did not know what to do.

Some days passed in this way. But when Anselm saw that he could not change the monks’ unanimous determination by words, he tried whether he might somehow bend it through prayers. The brothers having therefore assembled under their prior and insisting that he consent to become abbot, setting aside his customary objections, he fell on his face before them all, weeping and uttering pitiable sobs. He prayed and entreated them by the name of almighty God, by whatever compassion [another reading: mercy] they possessed within them, to consider God’s mercy [another reading: compassion toward him], desist from what they had begun, and allow him to remain free from so great a burden.

But they all, for their part, prostrated themselves on the ground and prayed that he instead have mercy upon that place and upon them, lest, by setting aside the common good, he be shown to love himself alone, in a singular manner, above the rest.

Many things were done on both sides in this fashion; but we shall now pass over their manner of speaking [another reading: “the importunity of speaking”]. In the end the diligent importunity and importunate diligence of the brothers prevailed—those who wished to bear the yoke of the Lord under his rule. The command also prevailed, and prevailed most of all: as we related above, Archbishop Maurilius had enjoined him under obedience that, if a greater office than his priorate were ever imposed upon him, he should in no way refuse to accept it.

For, as Anselm himself testified, he would never have consented to become abbot unless the command of which we speak had compelled him to do so. Thus, by such force, he was made abbot and was consecrated at Bec with due honor [Note: Anselm was consecrated on the feast of Saint Peter at the Chair in the year 1079 by Gislebert, bishop of Évreux].

What sort of person he thereafter showed himself to be in all the practices of holy virtue may be gathered from this: he never diminished anything from the holiness of his former conduct on account of the abbacy, but always strove to ascend from virtue to virtue, so that he might deserve to see the God of gods in Zion.

37. Having entrusted the affairs of the monastery to the care and concern of the brothers, whose life and vigor he knew well, he himself continually devoted himself to contemplation of God, to the instruction, admonition, and correction of the monks. Whenever some important matter in the affairs of the Church had to be undertaken and was not thought proper to be settled in his absence, he arranged the matter, according to the time and the circumstances, through justice.

For he considered it utterly detestable to obtain any gain from what another could lose through some trick contrary to the restraints of law. Thus he allowed no one in lawsuits to be deceived by any fraud on the part of his men, observing that he should not do to anyone what he would not wish done to himself.

This was the reason that, while sitting among litigants, when his opponents were seeking through their counsels by what ingenuity or cunning they might support their own case and fraudulently lay snares for his, he paid no attention to such matters. Instead, to those who wished to listen to him he discoursed either from the Gospel, or from some other divine Scripture, or certainly on instruction in good conduct.

Often, too, when there were no such listeners, he would sleep bodily, resting sweetly in the purity of his heart. It sometimes happened that frauds devised by subtle contrivance, as soon as they were brought to his hearing, were exposed and dissected—not as by one who was then sleeping, but as by someone keenly awake and attentive.

For the charity that “does not envy, does not act perversely, and does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:4) flourished in him, and through it he immediately perceived, as truth revealed them, the things that ought to be seen.

38. How watchful and solicitous he was in receiving guests and relieving them in every service of hospitality [another reading: humility] is proved by the fact that we know he devoted both himself and his possessions to this with pious zeal: himself with complete cheerfulness, and his possessions with complete generosity.

If at any time the food available for the bodily refreshment of the guests fell altogether short of what he desired, his goodwill and cheerful expression graciously supplied among the guests what was lacking. Moreover, sometimes the brothers’ food was removed from the refectory at his command and brought and set before the guests [Col. 0072C], for at that moment there was nothing else readily available that could suitably be placed before them.

The monks’ provisions, however, were distributed by God’s providence in such a way that none of what necessity demanded was lacking for them, although very often matters reached the point at which it was feared that they would have nothing at all for the following day. Thus they sometimes hovered between something and almost nothing: they had no excess, but what was almost nothing did not burden them through want.

39. This happened to them entirely in accordance with the words of their father, who used to foretell such things when the ministers of the Church complained to him of fear concerning the need that threatened. For he was frequently approached by the cellarers, chamberlains, and secretaries, and asked what counsel he would give against the shortage that was ruining each person’s obedience [Col. 0072D].

When he answered them, “Hope in the Lord, and I hope that He Himself will provide you with whatever you need,” what he said in hope wonderfully came to pass in reality. For after these words one would see, immediately that same day or certainly the next morning—or, what could not fail, before the shortage afflicted anyone at all—ships from England loaded with every abundance drawing near the harbor for their use; or one of the wealthy of the land, seeking fellowship with the Church, arriving with a large sum of money; or someone wishing to leave the world offering himself and his possessions to the monastery; or finally something being brought from elsewhere, from which all necessities could be supplied for many days.

40. The community itself also had several possessions in England, which had to be visited from time to time by the abbot’s presence for the common benefit of the brothers. Therefore, in the very year of his appointment, Anselm departed for England.

Although the reason I have mentioned was sufficiently weighty, there was another no less important: namely, that he might see the venerable Lanfranc, whom we mentioned above, and speak with him familiarly about the matters he carried in his heart. That venerable man had by then been made [Note: In the year 1070] archbishop of Canterbury from abbot of Caen, highly honored by all and distinguished by sublime excellence [Col. 0073B].

41. When Anselm, having crossed the sea, came to Canterbury, he was received honorably by the community of Christ’s Church situated in that city, out of reverence for him and for his holiness known to all [Note: This is the cathedral church, dedicated by Saint Augustine, its first bishop, in honor of Jesus Christ the Savior; a community of monks was attached to it. Its antiquity and possessions are discussed in volume I of the Monasticon Anglicanum, pp. 18 and following].

Not wishing to appear ungrateful for this honor, he later began his thanks to that monastic community and, as his speech proceeded, spoke about charity. He showed reasonably that the person who has charity toward another possesses something greater than the person toward whom that charity is directed:

“He who has charity,” he said, “among other things has this for which God knows to give him thanks; but the one toward whom charity is merely directed does not. For what thanks does God owe me if you or anyone else loves me? But if it is greater to possess that for which God knows how to give thanks to a human being than that for which He gives no thanks—since He knows to give thanks for charity bestowed, but not so much for charity received—it follows that the one who has charity toward another possesses something greater than the one upon whom it is bestowed.

“Furthermore, the person to whom another’s love serves receives only the gift of some benefit in passing: for example, one honor, one favor, one meal, or some service of that kind. But the other retains for himself the charity that offered the benefit.

“Let us consider this at present in the case of you and me, most holy brothers. Behold, you have bestowed upon me one service of charity. You have bestowed, I say, one service of charity upon me, and that service has now passed away from me; but the charity itself, which is pleasing to God, has remained with you. Do you not judge a lasting good better than a passing good?

“Moreover, if through that very service some charity toward you has grown in me, this too will be added to the abundance of your reward, since you have done that from which so great a good has come to me. Even if your charity alone has remained with you, the service you offered has entirely passed away from me.

“Therefore, if we attend to these matters with right consideration, we shall certainly perceive that we ought to rejoice more if we love others than if we are loved by others. Because not everyone does this, many prefer to be loved by others rather than to love others.”

He spoke many other things of this kind. After accepting the brotherhood of the monks, he became one of them. He stayed among them for several days and every day, either in the chapterhouse or in the cloister, discoursed before them with remarkable eloquence—remarkable and unusual in those times—about the life and conduct of monks.

At other hours he also spoke privately with those who possessed deeper understanding, proposing profound questions to them from divine and secular books and explaining the questions they had proposed. At that time I too was granted the opportunity to come to know his holiness and, as far as my youthful smallness allowed—for I was then a young man—to enjoy no little of his blessed intimacy.

42. What was done or said in those days between the venerable Archbishop Lanfranc and this Abbot Anselm is easy to understand for those who know the life and conduct of both. Those who do not know them may understand it from this: insofar as the opinion of ourselves and many others can tell, at that time there was no one who surpassed Lanfranc in authority or in his manifold [another reading: triple] knowledge of matters, or Anselm in holiness and wisdom concerning God.

Moreover, Lanfranc was still, as it were, a newcomer to England, and certain customs he had found in England had not yet settled firmly in his mind. Therefore, relying greatly on his reason in some cases, he changed certain practices [another reading omits “certain”] by the sole deliberation of his authority.

While he was occupied with changing them and had Anselm with him as a like-minded friend and brother, he spoke with him more familiarly one day and said:

“These English people among whom we live have established for themselves certain saints whom they venerate. When I sometimes turn over in my mind who these people were, according to their own account, I cannot turn my mind away from doubt concerning the merit of their holiness.

43. “And behold, one of them is resting in the holy see over which, with God’s authority, we now preside: a man named Elfegus [another reading: “not”] [Note: Saint Elphegus is commemorated on 19 April, on which day some matters concerning his veneration are proposed]. He was indeed a good man and, in his own time, presided there in the rank of archbishop. They count him not only among the saints but also among the martyrs, although they do not deny that he was killed not for confessing the name of Christ, but because he refused to ransom himself with money.

“For when, to use the words of the English, his pagan rivals and enemies of God had captured him, and nevertheless, out of reverence for him, had granted him the opportunity to ransom himself, they demanded an immense sum of money from him for this purpose. Since he could not obtain it by any means except by stripping his own people of their money and perhaps subjecting some of them to hated poverty, he chose to lose his life rather than preserve it in such a manner.

“I wish to hear what your fraternity thinks about this.”

As a new citizen of England, Lanfranc presented this matter to Anselm in a brief summary. Yet when we examine historically the cause of the blessed Elfegus’s death, we see that it was not only this, but that another cause preceded it. For he was captured and cruelly put to death not merely because he refused to ransom himself with money, but also because, when his pagan persecutors were burning Canterbury and the Church of Christ situated there and killing innocent citizens with a savage death [another reading omits: “and when ...”], he attempted, in Christian freedom, to resist them and convert them from their unbelief.

44. But Anselm, as a prudent man answering a prudent man according to the question put to him, replied simply:

“It is clear that one who does not admit even a slight sin against God does not hesitate to die; still less would he hesitate to die before provoking God through some grave sin. And indeed it seems a graver sin to deny Christ than, for the sake of his life’s ransom, to burden for a short time any earthly lord by taking away his people’s money. But Elfegus refused to do this lesser thing. Therefore he would much less have denied Christ if a mad hand, by threatening him with death, had forced him to do so.

“From this it is understood that his breast possessed an extraordinary justice, since he preferred to give his life rather than, by despising charity, scandalize his neighbors. For this reason that woe was far from him which the Lord threatens against the one through whom scandal comes (Matt. 18:7). Nor, as I think, is he counted among the martyrs without reason, since he is truly proclaimed to have willingly endured death for such great justice.

“For blessed John the Baptist, whom the whole Church of God both venerates and believes to be an outstanding martyr, was killed not because he refused to deny Christ, but because he refused to remain silent about the truth. And what difference is there between dying for justice and dying for truth?

“Further, since, as the sacred word testifies and your fatherhood knows very well, Christ is truth (John 14:6) and is justice, one who dies for justice and truth dies for Christ; and one who dies for Christ is regarded as a martyr by the testimony of the Church.

“Blessed Elfegus likewise suffered for justice, just as blessed John suffered for truth. Why, then, should anyone doubt more about the true and holy martyrdom of one than of the other, when the same cause holds both in the endurance of death?

“These things reason itself teaches me to be sound, venerable Father, insofar as I am able to perceive them. Nevertheless, it belongs to your prudence both to restrain me from this judgment by correcting me if you think otherwise and to show the Church of God, by your teaching, what ought chiefly to be believed in so great a matter.”

To this Lanfranc replied:

“I confess that I greatly approve and venerate the subtle insight and insightful subtlety of your intellect. Instructed by your firm reasoning, I trust, with God’s help, that from now on I shall honor and venerate the blessed Elfegus from my heart as a truly great and glorious martyr of Christ.”

He later devoted himself to this with piety, and indeed ordered a history of Elfegus’s life and passion to be composed with diligent care. This history was nobly produced by Osbern, of joyful memory, a monk of the Church of Canterbury, both in plain prose for reading and in musical composition for singing. Lanfranc, through his prudence and out of love for that martyr, raised it to greater distinction, authorized the distinguished work, instituted that authorized work to be read and sung in the Church of God, and thereby greatly glorified the martyr’s name.

## CHAPTER VI

The sweetness and effectiveness of admonitions; miracles
45. After this Anselm went through England to attend to the matters for which he had come, [Col. 0076B] diligently serving in every respect, according to God, the interests of his monks. As he traveled, visiting various monasteries of monks, canons, and nuns, as well as the courts of different nobles wherever circumstances led him, he was received with the greatest joy, and after his reception every service of charity was most gratefully offered him. For his part, he displayed his customary pleasantness and accessibility to everyone, and, insofar as he could without sin, adapted himself to the manners of each person. For, in accordance with the Apostle, he became as one without the law to those who were without the law (1 Cor. 9:21), although he was not without the law of God but was within the law of Christ; he adapted himself in order to win those who were not only without the law—as was thought, the law of blessed Benedict—but also those devoted to secular life, who in many respects lived without the law of Christ. Thus, in a wonderful way, the hearts of all were turned toward love of him, and they were filled with a hungry eagerness to hear him.

46. He also adapted his speech to each order of people so appropriately that his hearers acknowledged that nothing could be said more harmoniously with their way of life. To the monks he distributed one kind of instruction, to the clerics another, and to the laity another, according to each person’s purpose. He urged monks not to despise even the smallest matters belonging to their order, warning them that through contempt for small things they would fall into the ruin and disregard of all good things. He presented this teaching by the example of a fishpond, saying that its enclosure could be compared to the strict discipline of the monastic order. “For,” he said, “just as the fish in a fishpond die when its enclosure cracks little by little and frequently, and is not repaired, so the whole religious life of the monastic order perishes utterly if its discipline gradually grows lukewarm through contempt for minor faults, as Scripture testifies when it says: ‘He who despises small things will gradually fall’ (Ecclus. 19:1).”

He also instructed clerics how they ought to guard themselves in the portion allotted to God, and warned them above all to beware lest, if they fell from God’s portion, they should through neglect of their manner of life and order fall into the devil’s portion. He taught married people with what faith, love, and intimacy they ought to be joined to one another, both in relation to God and in relation to the world: the husband, to love his wife as himself and to know no other woman besides her, and to care for her as for his own body, without any sinister suspicion; the wife, to obey her husband with complete submission and love, diligently urging him toward good conduct, and, if his spirit should swell against anyone contrary to justice, calming him with graciousness.

47. The teachings which, as we have said, he gave by admonition, instruction, and explanation, he did not deliver in the manner customary among other teachers. Instead, he presented each point in a very different way, using ordinary and familiar examples, supporting it with the testimony of sound reasoning, removing every ambiguity, and fixing it in the minds of his hearers. Everyone who could converse with him therefore rejoiced, because whatever was asked of him, divine counsel was readily at hand. For this reason every sex and every age admired him and, in admiring him, embraced him; and the more powerful and distinguished someone was, the more devoted and eager that person was to serve him. There was no count or countess in England, nor any person of influence, who did not judge that he had forfeited his merits before God if it happened that he had failed to show Anselm, abbot of Bec, the favor of any service then within his power [alt., “had failed to possess” such favor].

King William himself [Note: [Col. 0077D] William the Conqueror occupied England in 1066 and reigned until 1087], who had taken England by arms and was ruling at that time, although because of his greatness he seemed to almost everyone harsh and terrifying, was nevertheless so inclined and approachable toward Anselm that, when Anselm was present, he became—amid the astonishment of the others—entirely different from what he was accustomed to be.

48. Thus, because of his outstanding reputation, Anselm was known throughout every part of England [Col. 0077C] and, because of his revered holiness, was in fact beloved by all. He entered upon the journey back to Normandy, enriched by many gifts which, as is recognized, continue to serve the honor and usefulness of his church to this day. From then on England became familiar to him, and he frequently visited it as the variety of circumstances required.

But so that almighty God might show that he was the author of the favor Anselm had found among human beings, and that Anselm had found greater favor with God than with human beings, God deigned to visit certain men through visions and to reveal to them how they might recover through Anselm from the illnesses by which they were being grievously afflicted. Of those whom I have mentioned, I shall present two, by way of example, who were not without reputation among their own people and who, as they were reported by truthful monks of the monastery of which Anselm had long been abbot, were healed through him in that same monastery, in the presence of those monks.

49. There was a certain noble and vigorous man who was considered very powerful in the borderland between Ponthieu and Flanders. [Note: [Col. 0077D] Concerning the region of Ponthieu, on the right bank, discussion will be found in the Life of St. Riquier, 16 April. Artois adjoins it; it was then regarded as part of Flanders, was separated from it in 1192, and thus “Flanders” is used here in a broad sense.] When leprosy struck his body, he was afflicted with the greater sorrow because he saw himself, on account of the ugliness of so great an illness, despised and abandoned by his own people in a manner unworthy of his noble birth. He therefore turned to God and, with frequent prayers and generous almsgiving, begged help from him. One night, a certain figure appeared to him in a vision and warned him that, if he wished to be restored to his former health, he should go to Bec and arrange with Abbot Anselm that he be given, as a drink, the water with which Anselm washed his hands during his Mass.

Trusting the vision, the man promptly set out to do what he had been instructed to do, and secretly informed Anselm why he had come. Anselm was astonished at his words and tried in many ways to persuade the man to abandon such a request. But the man persisted in his entreaties, begged Anselm still more earnestly to have compassion on him, and pleaded that he not be deprived of the remedy through which, on the strength of the divine promise, he believed he would quickly recover.

What more is there to say? Compassion overcame the heart of humility, and, intending to pray to God for the man, Anselm celebrated Mass more privately in the morning. The sick man was admitted and received from Anselm’s hand the water he had requested. As soon as he drank it, it restored the diseased man to complete health and opened the mouths of many in praise of God.

Anselm therefore sent the man who had come to him away secretly, warning him in the name of the Lord never to attribute what had happened to Anselm himself, but to know with complete certainty that it had been accomplished solely through divine mercy. He further instructed him to answer those who asked about it that this was so, while saying nothing at all about Anselm’s role.

50. At that same time, a certain brother from the community was struck by a severe bodily illness and brought to the point of death. In a dream, someone appeared to him and promised that he would recover life and health if he were sprinkled with water blessed by Anselm. The sick man therefore asked Anselm, who was visiting him, for water, in accordance with the vision [alt., “without mentioning the vision”]; and, having obtained what he desired, he was immediately restored to health.

51. These few things have been said for the present to display the man’s grace. Yet I do not find the favor he had earned among human beings particularly surprising to those who knew his way of life, because wherever he was, a certain desirable sweetness arose from his company, drawing everyone into his friendship and intimacy. For it had always been his practice toward all people to do above all what he understood could be most advantageous to others.

Thus, when he was asked what benefit those acquired who, while preserving justice, tried to agree with the wishes of others wherever they could, and what harm befell those who strove to fulfill their own wishes rather than those of others, he replied in this way:

“Whoever strives in all things, insofar as goodness permits, to agree with the wishes of others earns this from God, the just judge: just as that person in this life agrees with the wishes of others, so in the next life God and all that belongs to him will agree with that person’s will. But whoever, disregarding the wishes of others, insists on fulfilling his own will will suffer this loss by the judgment of the same judge: because in the present life he was agreeable to no one’s will, no one in the future will wish or be obliged to agree with his will. ‘With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you’ (Luke 6:38).”

Strengthened by reflection on this principle, Anselm therefore wished to be burdensome to no one and a weight to no one, even if for this reason he had to moderate somewhat the austerity of monastic discipline. Indeed, as the order of discretion taught him, he sometimes tempered his own severity by accommodating himself to others. We cannot know what those who will perhaps read or hear these things after us will think about this. But we who were privileged to know the manner of his life judge that what deserves greater praise in him is that he sometimes descended from the rigor of his purpose when reason required it, rather than that he should have persisted constantly and indiscriminately in severity. To act according to reason is virtue; to act contrary to it is vice.

52. In the midst of these events, a certain young cleric named Boso came to Bec, seeking a conversation with the abbot. He was sharp-minded and had entangled his mind in certain perplexing questions, but could find no one who could unravel them to his satisfaction. Speaking with Anselm and laying open to him the knots of his heart, he received from him, without fear of deception [alt., “disputation”], everything he desired. He was astonished at the man and became bound to him by an excessive love. Thereafter, once he had gained the intimacy of Anselm’s conversation, he was drawn, within a short time, to contempt for the world and became a monk at Bec.

The devil, grievously envious of both his conversion and his new way of life, plunged him into so great a storm of temptation that, as one tumult of thoughts followed another, he could scarcely remain master of his own mind. Several days passed, and the same temptation continually grew more monstrous. Troubled and confused in mind, he went to Anselm and laid before him the agitation of his spirit. When Anselm had understood each part of the matter, he replied to him only this, with pious affection: “May God take care of you!” He then immediately dismissed the brother.

At once such tranquility of mind followed that, as he himself later reported to me, he suddenly became a different person from the one he had been, beyond what can be believed in words. Thus the whole temptation completely vanished, and he never again experienced anything of the kind.

53. Many other things of this sort also took place through Anselm, but, because we are striving for brevity, we deliberately pass them over. We have also decided to pass over in silence the countless people who were cured of various illnesses, especially fevers, either by water in which he had washed his hands or by scraps of food secretly taken away from before him, God distributing his gifts according to the merit of each person’s faith.

For if we wished to describe everything we have learned from the most truthful men, we might be judged—as I think—to be devoting ourselves more to talkativeness than to the straightforward narration of events. Therefore, so that we do not make this account excessively long by lingering over such matters, let us omit these things and proceed to others. But lest an uncultivated style, prolonged by its own continuation, burden readers or hearers with boredom, let us here bring the work begun to its first conclusion, so that, refreshed by what is more pleasing, those who wish to know what follows may find us ready for a new beginning.

# BOOK TWO. DEEDS DURING THE ARCHIEPISCOPATE OF CANTERBURY

## CHAPTER ONE

The archbishopric assumed. Monastic repose postponed. A disagreement with the king.

1. After the death of the aforementioned king of the English, William, his son William obtained the kingdom. After the venerable Father Lanfranc had been removed from this life, this William afflicted the churches and monasteries of all England with exceedingly severe oppression.

In the fourth year of this oppression, Anselm entered England, having been invited—or rather adjured by an urgent appeal—by Hugh, earl of Chester, and by many other leaders of the English kingdom, who had chosen him as physician and advocate of their souls. Moreover, he had been compelled to come for the common good by the prayer and command of his own church.

On the day before the Nativity of blessed Mary, Mother of God and perpetual virgin, he came to Canterbury. There, since many monks and laypeople were loudly proclaiming, as though by foreknowledge of what was to come, that he would be archbishop, he departed from the place early in the morning and would in no way consent to the requests that he celebrate the feast there.

When he came to the king’s court, all the nobles eagerly went out to meet him and received him with great honor. The king himself sprang from his throne and joyfully came to meet the man at the door of the house; rushing to kiss him, he led him by the right hand to his own seat. They sat down and exchanged some cheerful words. Then Anselm privately wished to transact business with the king and instructed the others to withdraw.

Setting aside the matters of his monastery, for which he was thought chiefly to have come there, Anselm began to rebuke the king concerning the things that rumor reported about him, and he suppressed nothing that he knew had to be said to him. For nearly everyone throughout the kingdom was saying such things about him daily, sometimes secretly and sometimes openly, as were wholly unbecoming to royal dignity. When the conversation ended, they separated from one another, and on that occasion Anselm did nothing concerning the affairs of his church.

2. He then went to Chester to the earl and was compelled by necessity to remain in that region for several days. Meanwhile King William was seized by a severe illness and brought almost to the point of death. Among other advice, the nobles urged him to think about the mother of the entire kingdom, namely the church of Canterbury, and to relieve it from its former widowhood and calamity by appointing a bishop.

He accepted their counsel and declared Anselm to be the worthiest person for this task. Everyone acclaimed the decision, and both clergy and people praised the king’s decree [alt., “edict”]; no contradiction from anyone was heard there.

Anselm heard this and resisted, opposed, and objected almost to the point of collapse. Nevertheless, the assembly of the Church of God prevailed. He was therefore seized and carried—more forcibly borne than led—to a nearby church amid hymns and praises. This took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, on the day before the Nones of March, the first Sunday of Lent.

3. At the following feast of Easter Anselm came to Winchester and lodged in a suburb of the city. One night, through carelessness, fire broke out in the roofs of the suburb. As it grew, it consumed the various buildings all around. The fire was already approaching Anselm’s lodging and was about to consume it, with only two houses between.

While some people were carrying away the things that were in the house, the mistress of the house forbade them, declaring that she and her household had no reason to fear any damage, since they had been deemed worthy to have so great a guest—namely, Anselm the archbishop—with them.

Moved by the woman’s words, Baldwin, a vigorous man and a monk, took pity on her and advised Anselm to help his hostess. But Anselm said, “In what way can I help?”

“Go out,” Baldwin replied, “and oppose the fire with the sign of the cross. Perhaps God will hold it back.”

“On my account?” Anselm answered. “What you are saying is nothing.”

Nevertheless, driven by fear of the fire, he left the house. When he saw the flaming masses, the venerable Bishop Gundulf and Baldwin themselves compelled him to make the sign of the cross against the fire, raising his right hand upward.

Wonderful to relate: no sooner had he extended his hand than one could see the fire turned back upon itself and the flames fail, so that they left even the house they had begun to devour only half burned.

4. For many reasons that had intervened, Anselm had not yet consented to the election that had been made concerning him, that he should become bishop. But because the king detained him, he remained in England, while the aforementioned Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, stayed with him at the king’s command and supplied him with what was necessary.

When those reasons had been removed, at last, after a long period of time, constrained at once by obedience and necessity, Anselm consented. On the day before the Nones of December he was consecrated at Canterbury, with due honor, by all the bishops of England.

At this consecration the following evangelical sentence was found written over him: “He called many, and sent his servant at supper time to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready. And they all began together to make excuses” (Matt. 22:3).

Afterward, when he had presented himself at the royal court on the Nativity of the Lord Jesus, and had been honorably received by the king, spending the first three days of the feast happily with him [alt., “being led about with him”], the king’s disposition was changed against him through the instigation of the devil and evil men. Anselm had refused to give the king a thousand pounds in money from the goods stripped from his subjects, as a reward for carrying out [alt., “completing”] the king’s munificence. Thus, with the ruler disturbed, Anselm withdrew from the court.

5. When he came to his own village, called Berg, he dedicated there a church belonging to a parish. His predecessor Lanfranc had built it but, overtaken by death, had been unable to dedicate it.

Among those coming to the dedication from London was a certain cleric who, presenting himself among the man’s clerics as though to assist, secretly stole the bishop’s chrism-vessel, plunged into the crowd, and took flight.

When he had entered upon the road leading to London with the stolen object, he turned back, not thinking that he should hasten toward the place to which he was fleeing [alt., “thinking that he should turn his steps [lacuna]”]. But when, on returning, he encountered a gathered multitude of people, he realized that he had changed the road he intended to take and retraced the way by which he had come.

He had gone on for some distance when once again it seemed to him that he should proceed in the direction in which he had been fleeing. This happened repeatedly, and, not knowing where he was going, he was carried about in error, now this way and now that.

The people who observed him in this condition wondered what was wrong with him. But when the bishop’s attendants discovered that the chrism-vessel had been lost, they ran about in confusion and uproar, searching here and there for what had been lost, not knowing from whom or where they should certainly seek it.

News of the loss spread among the people, and many suspected the wandering cleric. He was seized, and the stolen vessel was found beneath his cloak. What had happened was reported to the bishop. But he, with a composed expression and tranquil mind, immediately ordered that the fault be forgiven and that the cleric be released to return home.

Then, once freed from the burden of the theft, the man immediately entered upon the road which he had been entirely unable to keep to before, and proceeded without hesitation.

6. After this, a few days having passed, Anselm was ordered to go to court to accompany the king with his blessing as the king crossed the sea. While the crossing was delayed by contrary winds, Anselm thought he had found a suitable opportunity and began to appeal to the king for the relief of the churches, which were being destroyed day by day; for the restoration of Christian law, which was being violated in many ways; and for the correction of the various customs that were being corrupted excessively each day among every order of people.

The king received all this with great indignation, declared that he would do nothing in any of these matters on Anselm’s account, ordered him to leave, and angrily commanded that he not wait there any longer for the king to cross the sea.

7. Considering afterward how much rest he had lost and how much labor he had found, Anselm was troubled in spirit and worn down by intense grief. Before the eyes of his mind he brought the life he used to lead when he was prior and abbot: how pleasantly he rested and rejoiced in the love of God and neighbor; how devoutly he spoke the words of life and was heard by all; how devotedly the things he said were carried out in practice, as he hoped, for the increase of their reward.

Now, by contrast, although through the episcopate he ought to have progressed toward what was better, he saw himself laboring day and night amid secular affairs, unable to devote himself to God or neighbor according to God as he had done formerly. Nor did he see anyone willing to hear from his mouth a word of life that could be fulfilled in action, to the detriment—as he reckoned—of his reward.

To these things were added, increasing his distress, the cruel oppressions of his people, which sounded daily in his ears, and the threats of evildoers, resounding all around with promises of worse things in the future. For it was known that the king’s mind had been stirred into fury against him; and for this reason every wicked person thought himself blessed if he could contrive by any means to do something that would anger Anselm.

He was therefore wearied by many and various storms of injuries, and was comforted by no sweetness of earthly honor or advantage.

8. Yet, with the innocence of his conscience [alt., “the purity of his conscience”] preserved in every respect and toward everyone, he breathed a little from these troubles and was greatly consoled whenever he could enter the monks’ cloister and speak before them about what their manner of life required.

On one occasion, while presiding over their chapter and speaking more freely than usual about such matters, he finished his discourse and, playfully alluding to it in cheerful good humor, made the matter known through a humorous comparison, saying:

“Just as an owl, while it is in a cave with its young, rejoices and is well off in its own way, but when it is among crows, jackdaws, or other birds, is attacked and torn apart and is altogether ill at ease, so it is with me. When I am with you, I am well, and my life has a delightful and singular consolation. But when, removed from you, I live among secular people, attacks from various affairs tear me apart here and there, and the secular business I do not love torments me. I am therefore ill at ease when I am in that condition, and I tremble and fear greatly lest such a state bring about terrible loss for my soul.”

Although, as I have said, he introduced this remark playfully, he began to follow it with bitter weeping and said: “But, I beg you, have pity on me, have pity on me—at least you, my friends—for the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job 19:21).

Because he found such great relief in this way of living, he sighed heavily when it was unavailable to him. I call God as my witness that I often heard him solemnly declare, under oath to the truth, that he would rather live in the community of monks as a boy among boys, trembling under the master’s rod, than, placed over all Britain through pastoral care, preside in the episcopal chair amid assemblies of people.

9. Someone may perhaps say: “If it was so good and pleasant for him to live with monks, why did he not continually live at Canterbury with his own?”

My answer is this: if that alone had been possible for him, he would have considered himself greatly consoled. But this was taken away from him partly by the remoteness of his estates, partly by the custom and practice of his predecessors [alt., omission: “partly by the custom and practice of his predecessors”], and partly by the number of people without whom episcopal dignity did not allow him to be. These things compelled him to travel through his estates and remain there.

Moreover, if he had lived continually at Canterbury, his people would have been heavily burdened by transporting provisions. In addition, when those oppressed by their officials—as often happened—appealed to him for many reasons, they would never have found him present; oppressed more and more, they would have gone utterly to ruin.

Nevertheless, he was never anywhere or at any time without his monks and clerics, apart from those who, coming to him from various places, were rarely absent. For he received everyone who came to him with sweet readiness and gave each person an effective answer according to the nature of the person’s business.
