You could see some people, entangled in scriptural sayings and questions, immediately disentangled by the reasoning he supplied; others, wavering in the discernment of conduct [alt., “of lesser matters”], instructed no less diligently; and still others, struggling with poverty in necessities, relieved from want when he gave them what they needed.

Nor did this generosity relieve only the poverty of monks or clerics. It also overflowed, according to the pious Father’s ability—and sometimes beyond his ability—toward any laypeople who needed help and asked him for it.

10. Whenever an opportunity presented itself, he was accustomed to withdraw to a more secluded part of his chamber and devote himself alone to heavenly studies. Moved by zeal for the Christian faith, he therefore composed the excellent and, for the circumstances of that time, exceedingly necessary work *On the Incarnation of the Word*. He wrote this work in the style of a letter and dedicated and sent it to the venerable Urban, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church.

Urban received it graciously and, recognizing that it was supported by invincible reasoning concerning the truth, held it in such high authority that later, disputing against the Greeks at the Council of Bari, which will be mentioned in its proper place, he drew strength for his argument from it and demonstrated how condemnable their error was in denying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.

11. But setting these matters aside and returning to the narrative begun, let us say that when Anselm sat down to refresh his body, he sometimes took a subject for conversation from the sacred reading being read aloud before him and edified those dining with him; sometimes, on his own initiative, he expounded sacred words and instructed the minds of those present in place of the sacred reading; and sometimes, when questioned about something useful or necessary, he refreshed both the questioner and the others listening with marvelous sweetness.

To make this known, I shall add one example that comes readily to hand—not to indicate by it the full effectiveness of his teaching, but simply to show for a little while the matters among which his speech was accustomed to move during earthly meals [alt., “letters”].

12. On one occasion a certain man who had become a monk from secular life came to him, seeking advice about his way of life. Since he had previously spoken with Anselm more intimately, he found an opportunity during the meal and said that, while he was still living in secular life, he had realized that the path he had taken toward life was not a straight one.

“Therefore,” he said, “I left the world and came to the order of monks, hoping that there I could devote myself entirely to eternal life and to God. But now, at the command of my abbot, I attend to secular affairs; and while I desire to defend and protect the church’s possessions against secular people, I make settlements, I litigate, and perhaps I am not greatly concerned if others lose through my gain. Thus I am almost forced to despair, since I seem to be administering with so many sins the things I abandoned.”

Anselm answered this with the following example:

“The whole life of human beings can be compared to a mill established above a precipitous river. Let there be in this mill, within a person’s reach, a millstone grinding. Some who grind neglect their flour so completely that it flows and runs away into the river; others retain part of it but allow part to go over the precipice; others collect all of it and store it under their protection.

Of those who have kept none of the flour for themselves, the one who has done so will have nothing to eat in the evening. The one who retained little will find little in proportion to what was retained. The one who collected all of it will be able to feed himself abundantly.

13. “Thus, as I have said, let human life be compared to a mill, and human actions to its grinding. For just as a millstone, while it grinds something, is moved around in a circle and, having completed its circuit, is brought back again in a similar course, so human actions return upon themselves at their appointed times.

“For example: people plow, sow, reap, grind, make bread, and eat. The millstone has completed its circuit. Does it then rest? Not at all. The same process is repeated. The land is plowed, sown, and reaped; grain is ground, bread is made, and it is eaten. These things happen every year and return upon themselves like the motion of a millstone.

“Thus you see a person performing all his works for earthly advantage, desiring nothing in them except something transitory. This person grinds because he works; but all his flour, which is the fruit of his work, is seized and swept away by the river—that is, by the flow of secular desire—and hurled down the precipice.

“When, at the end of his life, he leaves the mill, returns to his house, and wishes to eat the fruit of his works, he will find nothing, because the rushing river has swallowed everything. He will therefore fast forever—woe to the wretched man.

“There is another person who does not lose his flour entirely, because now he gives some alms for God, now he goes to church in God’s service, now he visits a sick person, now he buries the dead, and now he devotes himself to other good works of this kind. Yet, when he serves the pleasures of the flesh, rages with hatred over an injury inflicted upon him, feeds upon human praise, is lulled to sleep by gluttony and drunkenness, and is weakened by similar things, he does not watch carefully enough to prevent the greater part of his flour from being lost. What will become of him in the future except that he will receive according to what he has done?

14. “Now consider a third kind, within the order of monks. There is a monk placed under the authority of his abbot, professing obedience in everything enjoined upon him according to God, and, so far as depends on him, never wishing to leave the monastery cloister for any secular business.

“Suppose he is ordered to go outside the cloister to guard one of the church’s estates. He excuses himself and begs that it not be done. The abbot persists in his decision and orders him, under obedience, to carry out what has been commanded. Not daring to refuse [alt., “to excuse himself”], he obeys.

“Look: he has come to the mill; he must necessarily grind. Complaints, settlements, and lawsuits rise up on every side. Let the wise monk therefore guard his flour and carefully receive it into his vessel, lest it flow away into the river.

“‘How,’ you ask, ‘is he to do this?’

“Let him do nothing out of empty boasting, and let him do nothing for the sake of any gain that God forbids. Let him devote himself to the obedience enjoined upon him in such a way that he both vigorously and justly defends and protects the church’s possessions against everyone, and does not try to bring anything belonging to another unjustly under the church’s control.

“If he conducts himself and lives in this way, even though on account of such matters he sometimes misses Masses, sometimes speaks while the brothers in the cloister are silent, and does or omits certain similar things which they neither do nor omit, the virtue of obedience that he practices consumes all these things. Preserving his vessel intact, he collects and stores all the flour flowing from his mill—flour that will feed him eternally—pure and whole.

“For he proceeds not according to the flesh but according to obedience; and therefore, as the Apostle says, ‘there will be no condemnation for him’ (Rom. 8:1).”

15. “And what,” he asked, “should be thought about the man who voluntarily offers himself for the administration of estates, and, in order to bring about what he desires, secretly calls in assistants [alt., “hearers”], promises gifts, and pledges favor?”

He replied: “This has nothing to do with the monk’s purpose.”

He said: “Why? Is it not the case that, although such a man desires what I have described, he nevertheless attempts nothing without the permission of his superior?”

He answered: “Permission deceives many. Obedience and disobedience are opposites; permission lies between them. The person whom obedience does not constrain wishes to leave the monastery cloister for worldly business and to evade the strictness of the rule with permission, although he does not wish to presume to do so without permission. For this reason he may defend his action by appealing to the permission on which he relies; nevertheless, he is guilty because of his unlawful desire.

“After he had died to the world and entered the cloister, he ought not to have returned to worldly business in any way, not even in his will. Yet because he wished to fulfill this very desire in action only after permission had been granted, the obedience he embraced in this matter will excuse the action itself. But the desire he held against obedience will be dangerous for him unless he repents. Many people, paying insufficient attention to this, are often deceived by the permission they seek in order to fulfill their own will.”

16. As I said, I have not presented these matters to display the quality of his teaching, but have shown by a slight example the subjects with which he was accustomed to occupy himself during meals. For if I were to introduce him expounding on humility, patience, gentleness, and the obedience that I have now touched on briefly, as well as on countless other profound sayings—as we heard him do almost every day—another work would have to be composed, and the work we have in hand would have to be interrupted.

“When, then,” someone may ask, “did he eat?”

He certainly ate while speaking, but sparingly—so sparingly that one might wonder how he remained alive. Nevertheless, he admitted, and we learned that it was true, that when he was occupied in some lengthy discussion, he unknowingly ate more than usual, while we who sat nearer to him sometimes secretly supplied him with bread.

But when, in the absence of guests, he ate privately with his own people, and no spiritual question arose from anyone, he would soon stop after merely tasting rather than consuming the food, and, attending to the reading, would wait for the others to finish eating.

If he noticed someone either eating more quickly because of waiting for him or perhaps leaving food behind, he rebuked both, and affectionately urged them to attend to their own needs without hesitation. But whenever he noticed some people eating gladly, he looked upon them with the pleasant friendliness of an approachable face, rejoiced with them, and, raising his right hand slightly, blessed them, saying: “May it go well with you!”

## CHAPTER II

The exercise of various virtues.

[Col. 0087B]

17. Having explained by what manner Anselm was accustomed to be refreshed during his meals, let me briefly set forth what he also applied himself to at other hours. I shall repeat what I remember having said about him above: namely, that Christ was never absent from his lips, whether in the form of justice or of anything whatsoever pertaining to true life. He maintained that every period was wasted which did not serve good studies or necessary usefulness.

I consider it impious to suppose that he lived otherwise than he taught. For since it is certain that, from the time when he assumed the religious habit until he received the dignity of the pontificate, he diligently pursued [variant: “shone with”] every adornment of virtue, and that by word and example he was able to implant those virtues in the minds of anyone whatsoever, we likewise affirm it as certain that, after he had been made primate of all Britain, he shone in every respect in this regard. Hence, because of his indiscriminate guardianship of those virtues—as it often seemed to some, and at times to me also—he was frequently reproved, and it was judged against him that he ought to be a cloistered monk rather than primate of so great a people. This was said, censured, and condemned as a consequence of his outstanding humility, his immeasurable patience, and his excessive abstinence.

Above all, however, he was accused of indiscretion in preserving gentleness, since, as many supposed, numerous people whom ecclesiastical discipline ought to have corrected, perceiving his leniency, remained in their wrongdoing as though with permission. Yet when his explanation of these matters had been heard—for he despised no one and did not disdain to give an account to anyone who questioned him—it immediately became clear that, in such matters, he neither ought nor was able to act otherwise than he did, since he wished to hold himself without error to the rule of true discernment.

18. He could not, however, bear secular affairs with equanimity; rather, as far as he could, he withdrew his presence from them in every possible way. Whenever some matter arose in which his presence was necessarily required, he devoted himself solely to truth and, insofar as it concerned him, allowed no fraud or injury of any kind to be inflicted upon anyone. If empty shouting, disputes, or quarrels arose, as they commonly do, he sought either to calm them or to withdraw from them as quickly as possible. For if he did not do so, he was immediately overcome inwardly by weariness and, in addition, suffered severe bodily illness.

Having learned this habit of his, we often led him away from the midst of the crowd when circumstances themselves compelled it; then, by proposing to him some question from Holy Scripture, we immediately restored body and mind—as though treated by a health-giving antidote—to their accustomed condition [variant: “state”]. When asked why he was so weak and faint-hearted in secular matters, he replied:

“Since I expelled from my mind long ago every love and desire for secular affairs, how could I be strong and diligent in their cases? Indeed, I speak the truth and do not lie: when they themselves intrude upon me importunately and of necessity, my mind is shaken by horror of them just as an infant is when some terrifying image is thrust before his face. Nor do I take any more pleasure in arranging them than a child delights in his mother’s breasts when, smeared with bitter bitterness, he is weaned from them.”

Driven by these necessities, he entrusted the entire care and administration of his household to the monk Lord Baldwin, whom we mentioned above, so that everything should depend upon his direction and that arrangements made against [variant: “outside”] his order should be invalid. Thus, having obtained security, he devoted himself to spiritual disciplines and contemplation.

19. Nevertheless, various tribulations and anxieties interrupted this tranquility and compelled him to reflect upon matters outside himself: partly because of the lands of the Church, which certain wicked men invaded while the king did not prevent them; partly because of the exactions of money, which were devastating the whole kingdom, and especially his own people, beyond measure; partly because of the oppressions of monasteries, which he could not calm and which were reported to him daily; and partly because of many other matters of this kind that he often had to endure.

Moreover, those who before his episcopate had submitted themselves to him, loved him, and by loving him showed him favor, and who, by showing him favor, eagerly contributed whatever was chosen from their own possessions [variant: omits “by showing him favor”], now asked him for Church lands, now begged for horses, now for money, and now for this or that toward which each person’s desire [variant: “will”] drew him. You would therefore notice that those who obtained what they requested rejoiced in his presence with feigned peace and promised repayment and service, while others, having fallen into opposition, disparaged his honor, attacked his men as far as they could, and threatened them without measure.

20. But he, knowing that in his patience he possessed his soul, was peaceful with those who hated peace (Psalm 109:7), always returning words of gentleness and peace to his attackers and wishing to overcome their evil with good. Nevertheless, he by no means tolerated with equanimity, or allowed to fall through negligence, those things that could later become harmful to his Church.

But what shall I say? Such great greed dominated the minds of certain people in that period that neither softened by his patience did they yield to his admonitions, nor shaken by his threats did they cast off the blindness of their hearts. Yet there might perhaps be little reason for wonder concerning outsiders. His own people, his household servants, lied to him and became faithless. Observing that his heart was gentle, mild, and simple, they often deceived him in many matters by fraudulent cunning and carefully constructed speeches. By diminishing what ought to have belonged to his jurisdiction, and thereby unlawfully increasing their own possessions, they lost the fidelity by which they had been bound to him.

For this reason, when he was familiarly reproved by Baldwin and by his other faithful servants for excessive simplicity and insufficient prudence, he replied with innocent amazement:

“What is this? Are they not Christians? And if they are Christians, would they knowingly wish to lie against their faith for the sake of some advantage [variant: ‘not to lie’]? It is nothing. They compose their words to me with such care, and swear, invoking their faith, that what they say is true, that it might seem imputable to unbelief not to wish to believe that their words rest upon the very firmness of truth.”

He said this, supposing that they did not wish for him what he knew he himself wished to do to no one. When it was answered that their conduct was not in keeping with his custom, he said:

“I admit it: I would rather be deceived by believing good things about them, even if they are evil without my knowing it, than deceive myself by believing evil things about those whom I have not yet truly proved not to be good.”

21. I should remember, however, that these things were said at the beginning of his pontificate. Later the truth of the matter became known to the man, and he discovered that what his own people had truly been saying to him was altogether true. Although thereafter he did not grant their words his customary faith in every respect, nevertheless the fact that at the beginning he had been so trusting toward them did considerable harm to his affairs in the future.

For they, knowing for certain that he did not have the heart to repay evil with evil for the wrongs inflicted upon him, and freed from fear, became worse in themselves and advanced from bad to worse. Reflecting on this matter, the Father grieved more for their ruin, which he foresaw would follow, than for his own temporary deception.

Nevertheless, on account of this deception and the corruption of faith not kept, Anselm often used to say that one day they would either be disinherited, in their own persons or through their children, of the Church’s possessions by which they were then being raised to high position, and would be subjected to the ancient poverty in which they had been born and brought up; or, certainly, that before death or in death—which would be worse—they would be punished by some grave and shameful vengeance. We already see this saying of his fulfilled in certain cases, and from it we infer what others too may have to fear.

He was unable to correct them because, entangled like dense thorns, they asserted through clever arguments and verbal claims that they were not the sort of people who needed such correction.

22. But he, avoiding service to contention, let them go, fearing for himself lest he exceed the measure of discernment if he became too intent upon investigating their actions. For he feared nothing in the world as much as sinning.

I do not lie, with my conscience as witness, because we often heard him openly affirm under the testimony of truth that, if he could bodily see on one side the horror of sin and on the other the pain of hell, and had necessarily to plunge into one of them, he would choose hell rather than sin. He was also accustomed to say something else that was perhaps no less astonishing to some: that he would rather, being pure from sin and innocent, possess hell than, polluted by the filth of sin, possess the kingdoms of heaven.

When this statement seemed strange to some, he moderated it by giving the reason, saying:

“Since it is established that only the wicked are tormented in hell and only the good are comforted in the heavenly kingdom, it is clear that the good, if they entered hell, could not be held there by the punishment owed to the wicked; nor could the wicked, if they should happen to ascend [variant: ‘approach’] into heaven, enjoy the blessedness of the good.”

For this reason he always strove with great zeal to avoid the contagion of sins and, with every care, to drive away from his purpose whatever could provide them with any opportunity for arising. Nor was he momentary in these matters. His daily formation of character revolved around them; his continual manner of life stood firm in them; the tireless execution of his resolve flourished in them. In these things he served God; for these things he was acceptable to all good people; through these things he labored to attain eternal life.

## CHAPTER III

### Having with difficulty obtained permission to go to Rome from the angry king, he takes leave of his people

23. Anselm approached the king after he had returned from across the sea and humbly asked him to grant permission for him to go to Rome, to Pope Urban, concerning the pallium of his archiepiscopate. But at the name of Urban the king became agitated and said that he did not acknowledge him as pope, and that it was not his custom to permit anyone in his kingdom to name someone pope without his election.

A serious disagreement consequently arose, but its discussion was postponed to another time. It was therefore ordered that all the bishops, abbots, and princes of England should come together to discuss this dispute at the castle called Rochingeham. This was done, and in the third week of Lent [variant: omits “the third week of Lent”] they assembled according to the decree.

The case was brought forward, and Anselm was shaken by various complaints from every side. Many, especially the bishops who wished to favor the royal will, disregarding the judgment of equity, tried to establish that Anselm could in no way, without violating the faith he owed the king, recognize Urban as the pontiff of the Apostolic See within the king’s kingdom.

When several arguments that reason had supplied had been brought against them, and Anselm had completely silenced them with the words of the Lord, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew XII, 17), together with several other arguments that no reason could refute, they, having nothing to say in reply, shouted all together that he was blaspheming against the king, since he had dared to ascribe anything whatsoever to God in the king’s kingdom without the king’s permission.

24. Therefore, at a single word expressing the king’s indignation, certain bishops, in one sudden movement, renounced every subjection and professed obedience to their archbishop and primate, and with an equally deplorable agreement abjured their unity of brotherly fellowship with him. Others, however, denied that they would obey him even in those matters only that he might command on behalf of Pope Urban.

Thus all the bishops who were present, except the bishop of Rochester, renounced their due subjection and obedience to him in one way or another. The king himself also deprived him of every confidence and security in all his affairs, and swore that he would no longer regard him as archbishop or father unless he immediately denied that he would thereafter obey the vicar of blessed Peter.

Three days were spent in that affair, filled with shouting and insults against Anselm, and finally they concluded it with the outcome I have described.

25. Anselm, steadfast in his purpose, then requested through intermediaries a safe-conduct from the king, so that he might depart the kingdom safely. Recognizing that this would be harmful to many, the princes begged that a truce be granted on both sides until Pentecost, for the restoration of peace, and they obtained it. Thus they prevented him from leaving the kingdom.

The king therefore promised that until the appointed time of the truce he would grant complete peace and tranquility to Anselm’s possessions, and that then, for the sake of his religion, he would yield considerably to his wishes in the matter that had arisen. But he fell entirely into the opposite course. Lord Baldwin was driven out of the kingdom, Anselm’s men were captured and stripped of their possessions, and his lands were devastated without measure, causing him great distress.

26. Nevertheless, after these events, he accepted Urban as pope through Walter, bishop of Albano, who brought Anselm’s pallium from Rome to Canterbury. Then, acting on the advice of his princes, the king received the man into his friendship.

After some time, however, the same king returned victorious from the Gauls, and his anger was renewed. He was disturbed against Anselm on account of the soldiers whom, as the wicked falsely claimed, Anselm had sent on campaign badly instructed.

Then Anselm considered within himself that such matters could arise for no reason at any time, and that he could always be prevented by them from carrying out his pontifical office. He therefore resolved that he ought to go to Rome and seek counsel on these matters from the See of blessed Peter.

When he had come to the royal court at Windsor on the solemnity of Pentecost, he sent word through his household servants to the king that it was absolutely necessary for him to go to Rome, and that, if it pleased the king, he wished to do so with his permission.

But the king replied:

“By no means. We do not know him to be ignorant of any counsel concerning what must be done, or liable to any grave sin, so that he should need either to consult the pope or to implore absolution from him.”

Thus the matter remained at that time.

27. When Anselm had departed from the court and was traveling toward his village called Heysem, the boys whom he was raising pursued with dogs a hare that had encountered them on the road. As it fled, the hare reached the feet of the horse on which the Father himself was seated and crouched beneath them.

Knowing that the wretched animal had sought refuge beneath him, he held the reins and fixed the horse in place, unwilling to deny the creature the protection it desired. The dogs surrounded it and, licking it here and there with their tongues in an unkind service [variant: omits “with their tongues”], could neither drive it out from beneath the horse nor harm it in any way.

We were astonished when we saw this. But when Anselm saw some of the riders laughing and, as though over a captured animal, giving free rein to their amusement, he burst into tears and said:

“Are you laughing? Surely there is no laughter or joy for this unfortunate creature. Its enemies are around it, and, anxious for its life, it has fled to us, seeking protection. This is precisely the case with the human soul. When it departs from the body, its enemies immediately appear: the evil spirits who, while it lived in the body, pursued it in many ways through the winding paths of vice, and who are then cruelly prepared to seize it and hurl it into eternal death.

“But the soul, in the greatest anxiety, looks around here and there, and longs with indescribable desire for the hand of defense and help to be extended to it, so that it may be protected. The demons, on the contrary, laugh and rejoice greatly when they find it unsupported by any aid.”

After saying this, he loosened the reins and resumed the journey, forbidding the dogs in a loud voice to pursue the animal any further. Then, unharmed by every injury, the hare leapt joyfully and cheerfully away at full speed and returned to the fields and woods. We, having laid aside our joking, yet becoming not a little cheerful over the pious liberation of the frightened animal, continued the journey we had begun and made our way onward.

28. On another occasion he saw a boy playing in the road with a little bird. The bird had one foot tied by a thread, and whenever it was allowed to go somewhat more freely, it tried to fly away, wishing to secure its escape. But the boy, holding the thread in his hand, pulled it back and threw it down at his feet; this was a great delight to him.

This happened repeatedly. When the Father saw it, he pitied the bird deeply and wished that, when the thread broke, it might be restored to freedom. And behold, the thread broke, the bird flew away, the boy wept, and the Father rejoiced.

Calling us, he said:

“Did you notice the boy’s game?”

When we admitted that we had noticed it, he said:

“The devil plays in a similar way with many people whom he has entangled in his snares and drags at his pleasure into various vices. Some people—for example, those inflamed by the fires of avarice, lust, or similar passions—become addicted to them through evil [variant: ‘great’] habit. At times it happens that they consider their actions, grieve over them, and promise themselves that from then on they will refrain from such things. Like the bird, they suppose that they are flying free.

“But because they are entangled [variant: ‘enticed’] by depraved habit and held by the enemy, they are thrown back, while flying, into the same vices. This happens repeatedly. They are not freed altogether unless, through a great effort and by turning to the grace of God, the cord [variant: ‘thread’] of depraved habit is broken.”

29. From there Anselm again came to the court and asked the king for the permission to go to Rome that he had already requested, but he did not obtain it.

After this, in the month of October, he was invited by the king to Winchester. What he had already asked twice, he requested a third time, more earnestly, through intermediaries. The king became agitated and complained anxiously that Anselm was troubling him excessively.

To this Anselm replied:

“Let him believe that I am doing this because I have determined to go to Rome for the sake of the holy Christian religion, whose governance in this land I have undertaken; for the sake of the salvation of my soul; and also for the sake of his honor and advantage. If he grants me permission to go with good will, I shall accept it gratefully. But if he does not, I certainly ought not to set aside what God commands, since it is written: ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts V, 28).”

Hearing this, the king, disturbed in spirit, ordered him either to abandon what he had begun and swear that he would never appeal to blessed Peter or to his See for any matter, or to leave his kingdom without delay, abandoning every hope of returning.

He added:

“But if, frightened by these things, he chooses to abandon what he has begun and remain rather than go, then I wish him to make whatever amends my court judges appropriate, since he has asked me for the third time to grant him something in which he was not certain that he would persevere.”

Anselm replied:

“He is the Lord; he says what he wishes. Yet, knowing for what purpose I have been appointed and what I have undertaken to carry out in England, I declare that it would not be honorable for me, for the sake of any passing advantage, to omit what I hope will in future times be useful to His Church through the work of God’s mercy.”

Many more things were done in this matter, which we have written elsewhere and therefore touch upon briefly here. When the king and his courtiers had been stirred to anger against the man, Anselm himself approached him with a peaceful countenance, sat down at his right hand as usual, and said:

“I, my lord, am going as I have resolved. But first I shall give you my blessing, if you do not reject it.”

When the king replied that he did not reject it, Anselm blessed the king, who sat quietly, raising his right hand. Then he left the court and came to Canterbury.

30. The following day, he addressed the monks gathered in that very church and serving the Lord Jesus Christ, in these words:

“Dearest brothers and sons, as you have heard and know, I am soon to depart from this kingdom [variant: ‘to leave’]. For the cause that has long existed between our lord the king and me concerning the correction of Christian religion has finally been brought to this point: either I must do what is contrary to God and to my honor, or I must leave this kingdom without delay.

“I willingly go, hoping, through the mercy of God, that my journey will in future be of some value to the liberty of the Church. Yet I am moved by no small affection for you whom I am now leaving behind, since I see that, in my absence, you will suffer tribulations and anxieties, oppressions and insults, more bitterly than usual.

“For although it is certain that these things were not entirely removed even while I was present, nevertheless, whenever they arose, I was for you something like a shelter against them. So that they might not strike you without measure, I placed myself between them and you as a shield [variant: ‘I made myself a shield’] for your protection.

“I believe, indeed, that you enjoyed greater peace and security after I came among you than you had enjoyed from the departure of our venerable Father Lanfranc until my arrival. Hence I seem to see that those who used to trouble you will rage against you all the more when I depart, since they see that, because of my presence, they have been cast down from the domination by which they oppressed you.

“But you are not inexperienced or dull in the school of the Lord, so that you need instruction concerning how you should conduct yourselves if such things arise. Nevertheless, I offer a brief exhortation: since you have gathered within the enclosure of this monastery to serve as soldiers of God, always keep before your eyes how you are to serve as soldiers.

“For not everyone serves in the same way. This is also plainly seen in the earthly courts of princes. A prince has soldiers of different orders in his court. He has those who, for the lands they hold from him, devote themselves to his service; he has those who, for their pay, labor for him in military arms; and he also has those who, in order to recover the inheritance that they lament having lost through the fault of their parents, strive with unconquered strength of mind to obey his will.

“Those, then, who serve for the lands they possess are already rooted and founded, and they do not fear being uprooted so long as they preserve themselves in the will of their lord. But those who have given themselves to military service for pay sometimes, wearied by their labors, fall away sluggishly from the service they undertook, when perhaps, as they themselves suppose, the greatness of the exertion and labor does not equal the magnitude of the expense and reward.

“Those, however, who have undertaken the condition of service in order to recover an inheritance, although now they are oppressed by one kind of labor and now by another, and now suffer one insult and now another, endure everything with equanimity if they hold a firm love for recovering their inheritance because of a sure hope.”

31. “It is clear that such things occur among human beings. From this, with reality itself showing us what takes place in the court of the Prince of all, it is useful to observe the matter.

“God, to whom belong all things that exist, has in these three orders a court distinguished for His service. He has angels who, established in eternal blessedness, minister to Him. He also has human beings who serve Him for the sake of earthly advantages, like soldiers serving for pay. He likewise has certain people who, clinging to His will day and night, strive to reach by hereditary right the kingdom of heaven that they lost through the fault of their father Adam.

“But our longing should be directed more toward the fellowship of the blessed spirits than toward discussing here their military service, by which they perpetually stand before God.

“Let us turn our words to the soldiers serving for pay. Consider how many people living a secular life love God merely in outward appearance for the things they possess, and devote themselves to His service through certain good works that they perform. Some temptation comes upon them by God’s judgment, and they lose their possessions. What shall I say? Their mind immediately changes: they fly away from the love of God, abandon the good works they had been doing, murmur, and accuse God of injustice.

“What is to be said of such people? They are soldiers serving for pay, and in them is fulfilled what the Psalm says: ‘He will give thanks to you when you have done him good’ (Psalm XLVIII, 19).

“This has been said about secular people. But would that we monks were such that we were not like them! For those who refuse to stand by the rule of their profession unless they possess everything they desire in abundance, and who are unwilling to suffer either poverty of anything for God’s sake or the discipline of the Rule—by what arguments, I ask, will they help themselves not to be regarded as like them?

“In all their works they demand their reward before they offer the service for which the reward is owed. And will such people be heirs of the heavenly kingdom? I say confidently: certainly not, unless they repent of having been such.”

32. “But the person who directs the intention of his service toward recovering the kingdom of life strives in all things to cling to God and to fix all his trust upon Him with an unbending disposition of mind. No adversity draws him away from God’s service; no pleasure of passing life restrains him from God’s love.

“He walks through hard and rough places along the path of His commandments, and kindles his heart with the unfailing ardor of charity through hope of future reward. Thus, relying in all things upon true patience, he joyfully sings with the Psalmist: ‘Great is the glory of the Lord’ (Psalm XX, 6).

“While placed in this pilgrimage, he tastes that glory; by tasting it he ruminates upon it; by ruminating he desires it; by desiring he greets it from afar. Thus, strengthened by the hope of reaching it, he consoles himself amid worldly dangers and sings cheerfully: ‘Great is the glory of the Lord.’

“And know that this man will in no way be deprived of the glory of the Lord, since everything that lives in him serves the Lord’s will and is directed toward obtaining it.

“But, my brothers, I see that I must now cease speaking to you about these matters. I beg you: if we now separate from one another in sorrow, strive so that in the future we may be joyfully joined to one another before God. Become people who truly wish to be made heirs of God.”

33. At these words, tears bursting from his eyes prevented him from speaking further. Who could recount the groaning of the brothers that followed? Weeping filled everything, so that no one’s voice remained for words.

At last the Father, breaking through his sobs, said:

“My dearest ones, you know what I wish you to be and toward what I wish you to strive. But this hour forbids me to say more. I commend you to almighty God and to the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, so that God Himself may recognize you among His sheep and blessed Peter may receive you into his protection as sheep entrusted to him by God.

“With your permission and blessing I go, and I pray that the God of peace and love may remain with you.”

After this he rose, gave the kiss of peace to everyone, and went into the oratory, where the people were awaiting his holy address. In keeping with the urgency of the matter before him, he offered them a word of consolation and exhortation.

When he had performed this excellently, in the presence of a multitude of monks, clerics, and people, he received before the altar a traveling bag and staff in the manner of pilgrims. After commending everyone to Christ, he departed amid great weeping and lamentation.

## CHAPTER IV

### His departure for Gaul, then to Rome and into Samnium

34. That same day we went to the port of Dover, and there found a certain cleric named William, sent by the king to Anselm. We were detained there for fifteen days because the wind prevented our crossing. During this delay William went in and out with the Father and ate daily at his table, but he did not wish to disclose to anyone why he had been sent.

On the fifteenth day, when the sailors urged us to board the ships and our eagerness to cross was making us weary, behold, you would have seen a pitiable spectacle: William detained the father of his country and primate of all Britain on the shore like a fugitive and a criminal, and, on behalf of his lord, ordered that he should not cross the sea until he had revealed to him one by one everything he was carrying with him.

His bags and pouches were therefore brought before him and opened. All his belongings were overturned and thoroughly searched in the hope of finding money, while a great crowd of common people stood around, watching this wicked deed with astonishment because of its novelty and, as they watched, cursing it.

When everything had been overturned, but none of the objects for which it had been overturned was found among them, the searcher’s anxious effort was mocked, and Anselm was permitted to depart with his companions.

35. Thus he boarded the ship, and the sails were spread to the winds. We advanced a considerable distance over the sea when suddenly the sailors, first murmuring among themselves and then expressing their complaint in an audible voice, declared that, despite every effort and the thrust of numerous oars, we could not reach Wissant with the wind that was carrying us. Rather, unless we wished to be engulfed together in the waves of the sea, we must return without delay.

Anselm groaned at this and said:

“If it pleases the judgment of almighty God that I should return to my former miseries rather than, freed from them, proceed toward what He knows I have resolved in my heart, let Him see to it; let Him dispose of it. I am prepared to obey His will, for I belong not to myself but to Him.”

He spoke, and his eyes filled with tears; our hearts, which heard and saw these things, were shaken into groaning. Immediately a wind rose from the opposite side and struck the sail, forcing the sailors, who had already turned the sail and were making for land, to return to their former course.

We were therefore greatly heartened, and, carried swiftly over the waves of the sea, reached Wissant shortly afterward in accordance with our wish.

36. When we were leaving the ship, those to whom the ship belonged detained Lord Baldwin—the man whom we said above was Anselm’s steward and administrator of his affairs—and showed him something remarkable that had happened.

In the bottom of the ship that had carried the man across the waves, a hole had been made by the breaking of one plank. It was nearly two feet in size and presented a broad opening to the water [variant: “a pool”], yet, for as long as Anselm had been in the ship, it admitted no entry at all.

If this event caused astonishment to those who looked upon it, I do not think that surprising. Baldwin then ordered everyone with the utmost care to conceal the matter, and for some time it became known to only a few.

I, however, having later heard certain things about it and, after a long interval, applying my mind to writing the work that we now have in hand, did not wish to record anything about which even slight doubt might remain for me. I therefore questioned that same man about the matter and earnestly sought the truth.

He, affirming the truth on which a servant of God and true monk ought to rely, confessed that the event had occurred in every respect as I have related it and that nothing in it had been fabricated.

37. Once outside England, Anselm rejoiced greatly in this and gave manifold thanks to God, because he saw that he had escaped, as it were, the immense furnace of Babylon and had in some fashion reached the summit of peaceful quiet.

When King William heard that Anselm had crossed the sea, he immediately ordered everything that had belonged to Anselm’s jurisdiction to be transferred into his own control and all the arrangements that could be proved to have been established by Anselm since he had become archbishop to be declared void.

What tribulations the Church of Christ suffered within and without, I declare difficult to comprehend by thought, let alone to express in words.

38. Anselm therefore departed from Wissant in the morning and, after several days, came to Saint-Bertin. He was received there with great eagerness by the people, clerics, and monks, and was detained for five days.

Meanwhile, at the request of the canons [variant: “friends and canons”], he consecrated an altar at Saint-Omer. After this had been done, certain honored men from among the inhabitants came to him and, kneeling, begged him to mark their sons with the anointing of sacred chrism through the laying on of his hands.

He immediately replied:

“I shall gladly receive these for whom you ask on this occasion, and I shall not reject others in need of this sacrament if they are present.”

Amazed at the man’s kindness in granting this request, they rejoiced greatly and gave thanks. After their boys had been confirmed, they immediately filled the entire city with what they had received from his mouth.

You would therefore have seen men and women, great and small, rushing from their houses and hurrying competitively to our lodging for the sake of the aforesaid sacrament. For several years had already passed among them during which none of the bishops there had been willing to undertake such a duty.

39. Finally, on the sixth day, when he had already confirmed an innumerable multitude and the long journey awaiting us on that day compelled us to hasten our departure from the place, a certain girl entered the house from which we were coming out to mount our horses. With a sorrowful and pious appeal, she begged to be confirmed.

When some of our companions heard this, they were greatly displeased. Since they were already weary of such matters, they silenced her words by contradicting her.

What more is there to say? Although the man wished to grant the girl’s request, they detained him by pointing out the length of the day’s journey, the dangers that commonly confront travelers by night in a foreign land, and the fact that many people were lying in wait outside for this very reason, prepared to break in if he yielded to her alone. They prevailed upon him not to listen to her voice.

But after we had proceeded some distance, the Father remembered what he had agreed to and what he had done. Immediately accusing himself of great impiety, he conceived such grief in his heart that, for as long as he remained in this present life, regret for that deed, as he often admitted, never departed from his mind.

40. As we hastened our journey from day to day, the man’s reputation advanced far more rapidly and filled the people with manifold reports. Thus crowds of common people, gatherings of clerics, and troops of monks came out to meet him wherever he went: some resounding with joy [Col. 0098B] and exultation, others rejoicing together in God’s honor for his arrival with banners and sonorous hymns. When he had come to Lyons and had been gloriously received by the city’s archbishop, after a few days he sent a letter asking the lord pope for advice concerning his affair, and informed him that, partly because of his bodily weakness and partly because of many other causes, he could in no way proceed beyond Lyons. He therefore settled at Lyons, awaiting there the return of his messengers. After some time the messengers returned from Rome and reported that, with every excuse removed, the pope had ordered him to hasten to him. Unaware of delay, he obeyed the pontiff’s commands and, not fearing death for God, entrusted himself to the dangers of the road.

[Col. 0098C]

41. From there we came to Susa [Note: [Col. 0097D] Secusia, commonly called Susa, is not far from Mount Cenis, in the territory of Piedmont. There is there an abbey of Saint Justus, founded in the year 1029; Francis Augustine ab Ecclesia presents the instrument of its foundation, together with a chronology of its abbots, in *Chronological History of the Piedmont Region*, p. 237 and following.] and presented ourselves to the abbot of that place. We were three monks: namely, the lord and Father Anselm, Lord Baldwin, and I, Brother Eadmer, who write this account. We traveled as though we were equals, displaying before others no indication of who was superior to whom. When the abbot asked who we were and where we came from, we answered briefly. Having heard that some of us were monks of Bec, he inquired:

“Brothers, I beg you, is that man still alive—that friend of God and of all good people, Anselm, namely the abbot of that monastery, a man approved and esteemed in every form of religious life?”

Baldwin replied: “He has been carried away to the archbishopric in another kingdom.”

“I have heard that,” he said. “But now, I ask you, how is he? Is he well?—For my part,” he continued, “from the time when he assumed the episcopate I have not seen him at Bec; yet he is said to be well where he is.”

Then the abbot said: “And I pray that he may be well.”

Hearing these things said about him, Anselm immediately covered his head with the hood of his cowl, lowered his face, and sat silently. We did not wish to be recognized, lest the reputation of so great a man’s arrival should run ahead of us and, through our carelessness, expose us to some danger. Thereafter, having celebrated the solemnities of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection in the monastery [Note: [Col. 0098D] This was then the celebrated monastery of Saint Michael, consecrated in the year 966, to which various abbeys were subject. It is now a collegiate church of secular canons, as is recorded in the chronology cited above, p. 209 and following.] of Saint Michael the Archangel, which is situated on a mountain called Clusa, we resumed our journey and hastened toward Rome.

Strange to relate: we traveled through foreign places few in number and unknown, recognizing no one and making known to no one who or where we were; yet the mere sight of Anselm aroused the people’s wonder and marked him as a man of exceptional life. Thus, even after we had lodged among people whose ambushes we feared, men and women sometimes entered our lodging [variant: *intravere*, “entered”] and earnestly begged [variant: *precari*, “to beg”] to see the man and to be found worthy to receive his blessing.

42. Accompanied all the way to Rome by such favor from the common people, he arrived at the Lateran, where the supreme pontiff was then residing. The pontiff was informed of the Father’s arrival and, rejoicing, ordered him to lodge in a part of his own palace and to devote that day to rest.

In the morning the Roman nobility flocked to the pope, and conversation arose about the arrival of the new guest. The man was brought respectfully into their midst, and a chair was produced in which he could sit decorously before the pope. Having entered, he humbly lowered himself according to custom at the feet of the supreme pontiff, but was immediately raised by him to receive his kiss. Anselm sat, and the apostolic lord declared, with the Roman curia, that he rejoiced at his arrival; the curia echoed the declaration.

After silence had been made, the pope spoke at length in praise of the man, affirming that he was a man of virtue and of complete religious devotion.

“Indeed,” he said, “that is what he is. Although we hold him as a teacher, since he has been nurtured in every discipline of the liberal arts, and deem him worthy to be honored as our equal, or as an apostle of another world and a patriarch; nevertheless, such outstanding constancy in humility presides over his mind that he could not be deterred either by dangers at sea or by the vast distances of a foreign land from presenting himself at the blessed Peter’s shrine for the service of our littleness. He has come to consult us concerning his affairs, even though we need his counsel more than he needs ours. Consider, therefore, with what love and honor he ought to be received and embraced.”

When Anselm heard these and many more words spoken in his praise, he was, as he himself often admitted, not a little embarrassed, because he did not at all recognize himself as being, in his own estimation, the sort of man whom so great a man proclaimed him to be. Nevertheless, he remained silent throughout the speech, judging that it was more fitting to be silent in such circumstances than to speak.

Afterward, when the pope asked him the reason for his arrival, he recounted it to him in the manner demanded by truth and discretion. The pope marveled at what he heard and promised full assistance. He therefore ordered Anselm to await the effect of this assistance from him.

43. But because the summer heat was burning everything in those regions, and the city’s habitation was extremely unhealthy, especially for foreigners, a certain John—formerly a monk of Bec and then abbot of the monastery of Saint Saviour at Telesia—received him, with the pope’s approval, as his own father in his own [household: the text breaks off], and led him to his estate called Sclavia, situated on the summit of a mountain, where the air was perpetually healthy and mild and where those living there found it a suitable place.

Our dwelling, therefore, was located at the mountain’s summit, free from the tumult of crowds and resembling a solitude. Perceiving this, Anselm, cheered by the hope of future quiet, said: “This is my rest; here I shall dwell” (Psalm 131:14).

He therefore ordered his life according to the pattern of religious observance that he had possessed before becoming abbot, and which he lamented having lost most completely after entering the episcopate. Day and night he devoted his mind to holy works, divine contemplation, and the explanation of mystical matters. Moved by love for the Christian faith, he produced the distinguished volume that he entitled *Why God Became Man*. As he himself testifies in its prologue, he began this work in England but completed it here, in the province of Capua.

Amid all these activities he made himself available to everyone, assisting all as far as he could. He admitted to conversation all who wished to hear him, without considering anyone’s rank, and answered each person with kindly and accessible generosity according to the nature of the question presented. Consequently, his reputation quickly spread all around, and he turned everyone’s hearts toward love and veneration of him. Whoever was able to see him and receive his blessing judged himself blessed according to his own judgment.

44. A monk who, by order of the abbot, was caretaker of that estate and who, like a good host, ministered to us in various ways [Col. 0100C], observed the Father’s life and actions. He conceived within himself a hope of great good and believed that God’s grace was active in him; he also believed that God would willingly accomplish many things on account of his merits.

The people of the estate, however, suffered many daily hardships because of a scarcity of water. On the sloping side of the mountain there was one well of enormous depth, but it was emptied so thoroughly each day that from the ninth hour of the day until morning no water that could be drawn was found in it. Wishing this hardship to be relieved, the brother reported the matter to Anselm in the manner of one making a complaint, and added that he wished to construct a well at the very place where we lived, if God in his mercy should deign to remove the problem.

Anselm praised the brother’s pious intention and encouraged him to attempt it. The brother rejoiced at this and asked Anselm to inspect the place himself and, after offering a prayer, to open the earth first with his blessing. Anselm consented to the request, unwilling to offend the will of his host.

What shall I say? A rock of astonishing height could be seen, and it seemed almost madness to wish to seek a spring of water in such a place. Nevertheless, Anselm went with us to the site. After first offering a humble prayer—that God might grant there an abundance of perpetual and wholesome water—he struck the ground three times, opened it, and ordered the rest of the work to be undertaken.

Only a very few days had passed since the work began when suddenly a living spring burst from the hardness of the rock and struck everyone with immense astonishment. Nor is this surprising: since the master of the work thought that he would not find water even after many days, it is no wonder that finding it so quickly caused amazement.

The well was therefore completed. It was of moderate depth, but overflowed with a perpetual spring of the clearest and most wholesome water. The event was immediately reported and became a source of considerable wonder; everyone who heard of it attributed it to the man’s merits. Thus, to this day, the inhabitants of that land call the well “the well of the Archbishop of Canterbury.”

Those who have often come to us from there report that many people afflicted by various illnesses and fevers are restored immediately to their former health after drinking this same water [Note: [Col. 0101D] We have a letter witnessing this matter from the distinguished man Lord Silvester Ayossa, a Capuan priest. In the year 1640, he went out of devotion to that well and found it fifty units deep and six palms wide. He drew water from it, filled a small vessel, and carried it to Capua; he then gave it to a woman suffering from fever to drink, and she immediately recovered. At the request of the same man, he also shared some with a notary, Leonardo Pizzo, who was despairing of life, and experienced a similar result. That young man was still alive in the year 1660, when, in a written letter, he proclaimed the miracle performed upon him. That water, distributed in small portions, lasted for exactly three years without spoiling. Later, at the urging of the same Silvester, in the year 1650 a physician offered water from the well in faith to a certain bedridden patient and suddenly made him well, to his own great astonishment. Ayossa explains that the castle of the Sclavians lies in the district of the city of Calatia or Cajazzo, about nine miles east of Capua.] 

## CHAPTER V

### Excursion into Campania. Return to Gaul. Various miracles.

45. During these days Duke Roger of Apulia had laid siege to the city of Capua. Moved by the man’s reputation, he sent to ask him to come to him. We mounted, went there, and spent several days at the siege, withdrawn in tents from the crowds and tumult of the resounding army.

Near the place where we were was a small church, completely deserted. Beside its entrance was a cistern, ruined above, whose collapse had opened a deep chasm. We used the church as a chamber according to our needs, devoting ourselves there to quiet and to work; and each day we had the duke himself and his men readily available to us for whatever we wished.

One night, while we were sleeping there, Anselm happened to rise silently because of a bodily necessity. Following his custom, he proceeded toward the entrance with slow steps so as not to disturb us. After he had gone out and, forgetting the pit, had turned aside in the darkness, he fell into its depth, crying out loudly as he fell: “Holy Mary!”

Awakened by the sound, we and our companions who were resting in the tents leapt from our beds. We ran up, saw the man in the depths, and were nearly deprived of life by fear and anguish of heart. Perceiving this, he immediately raised his head and, with a gracious face and cheerful look, signaled to us that he had suffered no injury.

Some of our men then descended by another side of the precipice, where there was a way down, and brought him out completely safe and unharmed.

[Col. 0101D]

46. After this, when Urban, pontiff of the apostolic see, was approaching that place, Anselm and the leaders of the entire army went out to meet him. He was escorted with the immense pomp of worldly glory and led to a tent which, as was customary for him, had been set up more splendidly than the others.

Thus, until the city surrendered, the siege placed the lord pope and Anselm in neighboring quarters, so that the households of the two seemed more like one than two. No one easily went to the pope without also turning aside to Anselm.

The pope was honored by everyone as their common father and shepherd. Anselm was loved by all as a gentle and mild man, one to whom, in their judgment, no one owed anything. In the pope there prevailed a lofty power joined to the authority of his dignity; in Anselm there shone a wonderful humility, pure and simple, which charmed everyone.

Many whom fear prevented from approaching the pope hurried to Anselm, led by a love that knows no fear. The pope’s majesty admitted only the wealthy; Anselm’s humanity welcomed everyone without distinction of persons. And whom did it welcome? Pagans too, to say nothing of Christians.

For Duke Roger, count of Sicily, had brought many thousands of such people with him on the expedition [alternative reading: omission, with the scope indicated only by the printed abbreviation *s. a.*]. Some of them, stirred among their own people by the reputation of Anselm’s goodness, frequently visited our lodging and returned gratefully after receiving bodily food from him, proclaiming among their fellows the man’s admirable kindness, which they had themselves experienced.

Consequently, he was thereafter held in such great veneration even among them that, when we passed through their camps [or: enclosures], which had been set up together, a huge crowd of them raised their hands to heaven and invoked prosperity upon him. According to their custom they kissed their own hands, and also bent their knees before him, venerating him while giving thanks for his kindly generosity.

As we learned, many of them would gladly have submitted themselves to his instruction and placed their necks under the yoke of the Christian faith through him, if they had not feared that their count would rage against them for doing so. For in truth he did not want any of them to become Christians with impunity. By what policy, so to speak, he did this is of no concern to me; let God and he see to it.

47. After the siege had been lifted, Anselm tried with many prayers to persuade the pope to release him from the burden of the episcopate and allow him to devote himself freely to quiet. But when his labor achieved nothing, at least as far as its outcome was concerned, he returned to Sclavia, relying on the pope’s blessing, and there awaited the time of the council that the same pope was to celebrate at Bari on the Kalends of October.

When Anselm presented himself at that council and, persuaded by the pope, refuted in a rational and Catholic disputation the Greeks who were held to be in error concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, since they asserted that the Spirit proceeded from the Father and not from the Son, he was held in high regard by everyone and judged worthy of the greatest veneration.

48. When the council had ended, we set out for Rome with the apostolic lord. After several days had passed, that William arrived in Rome whose departure from England we mentioned earlier. Among other things, he secured from the apostolic lord a truce for the king of England concerning Anselm’s case until the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel.

When Anselm learned this, he immediately wished to return to Lyons; but the pope prevented him on account of the council that he had determined to hold at Rome during the third week of Easter. We therefore remained in Rome for nearly half a year, continually living near the pope and, as it were, sharing one household.

For this reason the pope himself sometimes came to Anselm, spending time happily with him and holding court in his presence. He also granted him the lodging in which we lived, on the condition that, if he ever returned to Rome, he could claim it against everyone.

At gatherings of the nobility, in processions, at stations, always and everywhere, Anselm was second to the pope: honored above all, accepted by all, and himself submissive to everyone with simple humility.

Moreover, Englishmen who came to Rome in those days wished to honor his feet with their offerings, as they honored the feet of the Roman pontiff. Anselm would not consent to this at all; he fled to a more secluded part of the house and allowed no one to approach him for such a purpose.

When this was reported to the pope, he marveled at the man’s humility and contempt for the world. He ordered Anselm to keep such offerings for himself (variant: *in eo*, “in him,” for *in se*, “in himself”) and forbade him to prevent anyone who wished to do good, but to admit patiently all who came for that reason.

Moved (*actus*; variant *ictus*, “struck”) by a certain modest shame, Anselm would certainly have disregarded the order if he had not feared being stained by the blemish of disobedience.

49. What shall I say of certain citizens of Rome—an immense crowd of them—who, because of their loyalty to the emperor, were hostile to the pope? Sometimes they gathered together, wishing to seize Anselm and his companions as they went from the Lateran to Saint Peter’s, out of hatred for the pope. But as soon as they saw his face, they were terrified, cast their weapons upon the ground, fell prostrate, and begged to be marked by his blessing.

These and similar honors and popular favors accompanied him everywhere, because his conduct in all things served God. This also explains why at Rome he was not ordinarily called simply “a man” or “an archbishop,” but rather, by his proper name, “the holy man.”

Therefore, all of us who served him were objects of love and honor to everyone.

When, however (*vero*; variant *ergo*, “therefore”), we came to the aforementioned council, and the matters that seemed necessary to be cut away had been cut away and those that seemed necessary to establish had been established, the pope, together with the entire council, pronounced a sentence of excommunication both against laymen who granted investitures of churches and against those who received them from their hands.

The same sentence also condemned those who consecrated anyone to an office after he had obtained such an honor.

50. When the assembly had been dissolved and we had received permission, we departed from Rome. The road of return was exposed to many dangers, but, with the Lord protecting us, we escaped all of them and reached Lyons unharmed.

There we were received with the greatest honor and joy and were detained by the city’s venerable pontiff, Hugh [alternative reading: omits “venerable Hugh”]. We established our residence there, having entirely abandoned hope of returning to England while King William was alive.

Anselm was therefore lodged there not as a guest or foreigner, but truly as a native and lord of the place. Accordingly, while he was present, the city’s own bishop nowhere wished to preside in his proper position. With Anselm presiding everywhere, that bishop, endowed with remarkable humility and propriety, performed the role and office of an inferior, almost like a suffragan.

Moreover, he placed the exercise of episcopal office throughout his entire parish at Anselm’s will and discretion. When this became known in the neighboring places, crowds immediately began to gather, asking that the anointing of the sacred chrism be conferred upon them through the laying on of his hands.

He admitted everyone to the grace of that sacrament, so that very often the entire day was spent in this activity, and we who served him were afflicted with severe weariness, while he always maintained a joyful and cheerful expression.

From this there grew in everyone an extraordinary and incredible affection for him, and his goodness was spread far and wide.

51. Thus, in those days, whoever could obtain even a remnant from his table believed himself enriched with a health-giving medicine against every danger and illness. Nor did this faith deceive them. For we truly know that some people afflicted with fevers and oppressed by other illnesses were restored to complete health immediately after taking remnants of his food.

For example, the feast of blessed Maurice is celebrated solemnly at Vienne [Note: [Col. 0103D] Saint Maurice of Agaunum is honored there twice with a solemn office: on 22 September, the day of his death, and again on 26 October. The latter is called the feast of the revelation of Saint Maurice and his companions, when their sacred bodies were brought there. This passage seems to refer to that feast; a cathedral church is dedicated to him there.].

Anselm was therefore invited by Guido, archbishop of that city [Note: [Col. 0104D] Guido, archbishop of Vienne, appointed in 1083, became pope in 1119 under the name Calixtus II.], and came there for the feast itself. After celebrating the solemn office of Mass and preaching, he sat down for bodily refreshment. Two soldiers then came before him, displaying in voice and face the illness that oppressed them, and asking him to give them some crumbs of his bread.

“Not at all,” he said. “I see that you do not need an entire loaf, much less crumbs. But if you wish to eat, there is ample room: sit down, and with God’s blessing eat what is set before you.”

They replied that this was not why they had come.

“Nor shall I do anything else for you,” he said.

For he understood what they intended.

One of those sitting at his right, realizing that they were concerned for their own health and that the man wished to do nothing that could be attributed to a miracle, apparently weary of their insistence, seized fragments from the table and gave them to the soldiers, warning them to withdraw and not weary the man.

As soon as they had tasted a little of them, they departed with the man’s blessing.

After the meal they took me aside and earnestly begged that, aided by my assistance, they might be found worthy to receive the Lord’s body and blood from the Father’s hand at Mass. When I gladly listened to them and informed them when and where this would occur, they replied in gracious tones:

“We shall indeed come, as you say, after setting aside every excuse, if we are not freed by this medicine, which we have now received from his table, from the quartan fevers and deadly fevers and intestinal pains by which we are shaken with unbearable torment. And this shall be the sign [variant: *signi*, “of the sign”] between you and us: if we recover, we shall not come; we shall come if we do not recover.”

I agreed to their statement [variant: *quibus dictis*, “when these things had been said”], and we separated from one another. They did not come, because, as I learned from those who knew both men, they were completely restored by God’s grace through what they had received from the table.

Indeed, if this had not happened, it would be credible that, just as they wished to be restored from their severe illness, so they would not have been unwilling to seek the later medicine.

[Col. 0105C]

52. They were certainly convinced that they could not be deceived in this matter and fail to recover, knowing that a man of no obscure reputation had recovered from an identical illness simply by attending that Mass in the hope of regaining his health.

One of the leading men of that land had long been afflicted by the same painful illness as they. Having learned that Anselm was going to celebrate Mass according to custom in the church of Saint Stephen [Note: [Col. 0105D] The town of Saint Stephen of Furennis, within nine leagues of Vienne, may be intended; if this church is to be sought outside the city of Vienne, Lyons, or some similar city, however, the identification remains uncertain.], he hurried there, thinking that it would be useful for recovering his health if he could obtain the Mass and blessing of so great a man.

I confess that we saw the man enter the church leaning on the hands of his attendants, more like a dead man than a living one. He sat down and left when the Mass had ended.

We, however, neither knowing nor caring who he was, where he came from, or why he had come, saw the same man return to the Father after a few days had passed. He knelt before him and gave thanks for the health he had obtained.

Anselm was astonished at this. The man explained the sequence of events, affirming that from the hour when he presented himself at Anselm’s Mass, every affliction of pain had been driven away and he had been restored to health.

Anselm asserted that this had nothing to do with him, but was to be attributed to the man’s faith and to the merits of the blessed martyr to whom he had turned. He instructed him in what was suitable for the salvation of his soul and, as we later learned from the testimony of many, made him his intimate associate and restored him to a more disciplined life.

53. At about this time, as we were traveling to Cluny, a man of the sacred order met us. With tearful prayers he begged the man to look upon him with the eye of mercy and to regard with the right hand of his blessing his sister, who had recently become insane.

He added: “Behold, she is being held by many people along the road on which you are going to travel. They hope that, if you, lord, place your hand upon her, she may immediately, with God’s grace assisting, be restored to her mind.”

At this Anselm passed by with silent speech and, as it were, a deaf ear. The priest, however, pressed him all the more insistently and multiplied his entreaties. Anselm rejected him, asserting in every way that such an extraordinary act was in no manner to be attempted by him.

As we continued, we saw the woman being held at close quarters amid a crowd gathered together. In her face, mouth, eyes, and the gestures of her whole body she displayed furious movements and inhuman signs.

The people surrounded the approaching man. Holding back his reins, they repeated their prayers, asking him to lay his hand upon the wretched woman; they begged and implored him.

He resisted, saying that what they requested was not at all wise. Like the common people, they brought forward every argument that occurred to them, striving to overcome him at least by their persistence.

Then, realizing that he could not escape in any other way, he accommodated them in this one respect: he did what he never used to refuse anyone. Raising his right hand, he marked her with the sign of the holy cross.

Having done this, he rode away faster than the reins could be released. He placed the hood of his cowl over his head and, leaving his companions behind, went on alone, tenderly lamenting the unfortunate woman’s misery with tears overflowing from a compassionate heart [alternative reading: omission indicated by the printed abbreviation *p. l.*].

We, afflicted by this grief, proceeded to Cluny, while the woman was taken home by the hands of the crowd. Her foot had not yet worn down the threshold of her house when she was granted complete health and set every tongue praising the man.

When we received a reliable report at Cluny that this had happened, we rejoiced and gave God thanks and glory for his mercy.

54. After completing the matters for which we had come to Cluny, we began our return journey to Lyons by way of the city of Mâcon. There, at the request of the bishop [Note: [Col. 0106D] This was Bernard, who became bishop of Mâcon in the year 1097.] and the canons, Anselm publicly celebrated Mass at Saint Vincent.

During the sermon that he delivered to the people, he urged everyone to pray together to the Lord concerning the drought by which the land had been parched beyond measure. They said that they had already done this many times but had achieved nothing. For that reason they earnestly begged and implored him to make their prayers effective before God by adding his own prayer.

What shall I say? We had not yet eaten our midday meal when, suddenly, to everyone’s astonishment, the clear sky turned cloudy. On that very day, before we departed from the city, gentle and abundant rain fell upon the earth.

The people, seeing this event, therefore blessed the Lord and proclaimed Anselm, after God, its author, with great praise.

Returning to our dwelling at Lyons, we then led a quiet life free from all the tumult of worldly affairs. Anselm, for his part, lived the life of a true servant of God in holy meditations, in the edification of people of every sex, age, and rank who came to him, and in the practice of the remaining virtues.

During this period he also wrote one book, *On the Virgin’s Conception and Original Sin*, and another little work, pleasing and agreeable to many, which he entitled *Meditation on Human Redemption*.

## CHAPTER VI

### The death of King William and a new difficulty with his successor Henry concerning investitures. The Roman embassy. Return forbidden.

55. Meanwhile Urban, pontiff of the apostolic see, departed from this life and did not reach the truce that he had granted the king concerning Anselm’s case.

At that time many people also predicted the king’s death. It was reported that divine vengeance was soon to overwhelm him for his persecution of Anselm, both because of signs—new and unusual phenomena displayed throughout England—and because of visions revealed to several religious persons.

Anselm, however, placed no confidence in any of these things and prayed daily to God for the king’s conversion and salvation.

In the third year of our exile—which was the second year from the time we came from Rome to Lyons—Anselm went to Marcigny [Note: [Col. 0107D] Marcigny was a monastery of nuns in the diocese of Autun, constructed by Saint Hugh, as we explain at length in his Life under 29 April.], to speak with Lord Hugh, the abbot of Cluny, and with the nuns.

While we were seated before the abbot and, as usually happens, various remarks were being exchanged about what had thus far taken place between Anselm and the king, that venerable abbot declared, under the testimony of truth, that on the immediately preceding night the same king had been accused before God’s throne, judged, and condemned, and that a sentence of damnation had been pronounced against him.

We were considerably astonished by these words. Yet, taking into account the eminence of his holiness and authority, we could not withhold belief from what he said.

56. The following day we departed from there and came to Lyons. On the feast of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0108D] This is the feast of the Chains of Saint Peter.], which is celebrated on the Kalends of August, after the Matins had been said, we who were constantly with Anselm wished to devote ourselves to rest.

Then a certain young man, not mean in dress or appearance, stood beside our cleric Adam, who was lying near the door of the chamber. Adam was not yet asleep, though he kept his eyes closed as if for sleep. The young man called him by name:

“Adam,” he said, “are you sleeping?”
