When Adam replied, “No,” the young man said: “Do you want to hear some news?”

“Gladly,” Adam answered.

“Know for certain,” the young man said, “that the entire dispute between Archbishop Anselm and King William has been settled and brought to an end.”

Adam immediately raised his head, becoming more alert. But when he opened his eyes and looked around, he saw no one.

On the following night, during Matins, one of us was standing with his eyes closed and singing psalms. Suddenly someone presented him with a very small slip of paper to read. He looked at it and found written there: “King William has died.”

At once he opened his eyes, but saw no one except his companions.

57. Three days later Anselm went, after many invitations, to the abbey called Casa Dei. He was honorably received and lodged there.

One day, after the meal, while the brothers of the place were resting on their beds, the sky suddenly thundered with a great crash. Frequent flashes of lightning darted across the mountain. The storm increased, and multiplied bolts of lightning descended violently upon the house where the monastery’s hay was stored.

At once a dreadful fire was kindled and sent an extremely terrible and foul-smelling smoke through the air. Everyone who was lodging with Anselm leapt up, shaken by fear.

I therefore remained alone with him. When he wished to lie down on the bed, he asked me whether the fire that had broken out had been extinguished.

When I answered that it had increased rather than been extinguished, he rose and said with a calm and modest expression: “It is better that we take care of ourselves, because your own property is at stake when the wall next to you is burning.”

Having said this, he hurried to the fire. When he saw it, he immediately confronted it with the sign of the holy cross, made with his raised right hand.

You would have seen the flame instantly lowering itself, as though it were becoming quiet in order to receive his blessing. The fire therefore immediately withdrew into itself and completely weakened; it advanced no farther to consume anything.

And something that you may perhaps find no less astonishing: although it devoured certain buildings that stood nearby, it caused no damage to the monks’ hay, since the hay was what filled almost the entire house upon which the lightning itself had first fallen.

58. From there two of his monks came to Anselm, announcing the death [or: departure] of the aforementioned king. For on the second day of August—the second day after the first vision, which I have just reported as having occurred at Lyons, and the first day after the second vision—the same king went hunting in the forest in the morning. There, an arrow struck him in the heart and killed him without any intervening delay.

Struck by profound astonishment at this, Anselm immediately burst into the bitterest weeping. We were greatly astonished when we saw it. But with sobs interrupting his words, he declared that, if he could have brought it about, he would much rather have chosen to be dead in body himself than to have the king dead as he was.

After this, when we had returned to Lyons, messengers came to Anselm one after another, bringing letters and urgent requests on behalf of the mother Church of the English, on behalf of the new king Henry, who had succeeded his brother, and also on behalf of the kingdom’s nobles. They earnestly begged him to return with all speed, declaring that the entire land was stunned in anticipation of his arrival and that all the kingdom’s affairs had been postponed pending his decision.

After receiving these messages, Anselm hastened toward England [alternative reading: omits this final clause].

59. But when he came to the king at Serberia and explained to him in plain speech what he had learned at the Roman council concerning the investitures of the churches, the king was troubled and deeply grieved. Nor did he wish, in any matter, to await his decision, as the messengers had said. What was done between them over this affair during two and a half years [variant: omits *s*], how many and how great were the threats and tribulations Anselm endured, how the messengers were sent once and again to Rome to seek a change in those decrees, and what they achieved—whoever wishes to know these things should read that work which we mentioned in the prologue to this little book; there he will find each matter fully [variant: plainly], as I think, set forth.

After all this, the king asked Anselm to go to Rome himself and, together with the messenger whom he intended to send there, to assist the case that had arisen, for the sake of the king’s honor. Since all the bishops [variant: *ipsi*, “the bishops themselves”], abbots, and princes of England agreed to this and loudly declared that, in so great a matter, he ought by no means to delay going, Anselm replied that he would indeed go, but solemnly promised in person [variant: replied] that he would never, either at the king’s request or on his advice, induce the pope to do anything that might oppose either the liberty of the churches or his own honor. Thus, when he had come to Rome, he was honorably received by Pope Paschal, who had succeeded Urban, and by all the nobility of the city.

Then, on the appointed day, that William whom we mentioned above, sent by the king, brought the king’s case forward and, among other things, asserted in threatening words that the king himself would not tolerate losing the investitures of the churches even at the cost of losing his kingdom. To this the pope replied:

“If, as you say, your king will not suffer the donations of the churches to be taken from him even at the cost of losing his kingdom, know this—for I speak here before God—that Pope Paschal will never permit him to retain them with impunity, even for the ransom of his own head.”

60. At that time the king’s business thus came to an end. Anselm, after conducting various discussions with the pope concerning the regulation of ecclesiastical affairs, resumed his journey and reached the city of Florence, where he rested for one night. When the bishop had lain down on the bed in which he had indulged in sleep, the master of the house, after Anselm’s departure, lay down there as was customary. As he fell asleep, a man of unfamiliar appearance stood beside him and warned him to leave the bed without delay. “For,” he said, “it is not fitting that your presence should deprive this place of what it deserved to obtain through the presence of so great a man.”

When he rose in the morning and turned the vision over in his mind, he attributed it to a phantom; and the following night he confidently placed himself in the same bed. He fell asleep, and behold, the one who had come stood beside him a second time, now with a somewhat threatening expression, repeating what he had said before. But he awoke and, as before, dismissed the vision, and on the third night gave himself over to sleep in his usual place. As he slept, the same figure who had appeared the second time appeared a third time, displaying anger in face and voice.

“Why,” he said, “do you do what I have already told you once and again not to do? Now, warned for the third time, rise and henceforth keep yourself away from the bishop’s bed. For I tell you that, if you are found in it again, you will discover that there is nothing phantom-like in what you hear.”

Then, greatly terrified, the man leapt from the bed and hastened to the bishop of the city [Note: This was Rainerius, who held the see of Florence for forty-two years, from 1071 to 1113], wishing to consult him about the matter. In the presence of many people he explained the entire sequence of events. The bishop, who had long since learned of the man’s holiness through widespread report and had recently experienced something of it in conversation with him, sternly rebuked the man’s boldness. He declared that the man had acted foolishly and like an ignorant person in daring to lie in the bed where so great a man had rested.

Accordingly, he ordered that the same bed thereafter be reverently preserved and commanded that no one presume to lie in it again. This, as we have learned, has been observed to the present day.

61. When Anselm, having completed his journey, had drawn near to Lyons, the aforementioned William, wishing to leave his company, forbade him, on behalf of his lord the king, to return to England unless he would firmly promise to observe for the king all the customs of his father and brother, setting aside submission and obedience to the apostolic see. When Anselm heard this, he was astonished, knowing that he had not been in England on any other condition [variant: not on another condition].

When he reached Lyons, he settled there, as in former times, in peace and quiet, inhabiting the private house of the aforementioned venerable Hugh, archbishop of that city, and never for even an hour withdrawing in word or deed from the things of God.

62. It happened one day that, after celebrating the solemn office of the Mass, the Father was alone in the oratory, as was his custom, offering himself to God through tears. A certain man, guiding his feet with a staff, came wishing to break into the oratory. Our brother and companion Alexander, a monk of the Church of Canterbury, happened to be waiting outside for the Father to come out. Seeing the man attempting to enter the church, he stopped him and asked what he wanted.

The man replied in a loud voice that he had lost the light of his eyes and wished the servant of God to lay his hand upon him, knowing that Anselm’s holy merits would assist him. The Father heard the shouting but could not make out the words. He motioned to the aforementioned brother to come to him and explain the cause of the shouting.

Then Alexander said: “Lord Father, a poor man has come, complaining that his eyes are afflicted, and asking that through you the sign of the holy cross be placed upon him.”

The Father, with a compassionate expression, said: “Let him come.”

Then, tracing the sign of the cross with his thumb three times over the man’s eyes, as the man had requested, he prayed:

“May the power of Christ’s cross enlighten these eyes, drive all illness from them, and restore them to complete health.”

After sprinkling them with consecrated water, he ordered the man to depart. Alexander immediately led him out and advised him that, if the deed of the man of God had not entirely benefited him on this first occasion, he should return in the morning; he promised that he would obtain for him a repetition of the same action.

The man replied: “Indeed, good sir, I will not return for this reason: by the grace of God and of his faithful servant, all blindness has been driven away, and I see most clearly.”

I have written this just as I received it from Alexander’s own mouth; he testified that he had been present.

63. When King Henry learned that the pope was standing by his decision, he immediately brought the archbishopric under his own control and stripped Anselm of all his possessions. Many things were done between them after this, and for a year and a half the king’s anger was not quieted.

64. In the midst of these events Walo, bishop of Paris, came to us—a deeply religious man, instructed from early youth in the regulations governing ecclesiastical customs. Known at Rome and having served in the office of an apostolic legate, he enjoyed the friendship of Father Anselm.

This man, coming to us from Rome, was carrying with him certain relics of saints, which, as we learned with certainty, had been given to him at Rome. While speaking with Anselm in my presence, he told him what relics he had brought with him from Rome. When Anselm gave thanks to God for them, the bishop brought from a reliquary a bone which he asserted was from the head of God’s holy martyr Prisca. Immediately explaining how he had obtained it, he said:

“I was at Rome. The oratory of the aforementioned martyr, in which the blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, had consecrated an altar, had been consumed and ruined by age. In my presence the martyr’s body was raised in order to be placed in a new church. Since the cardinal of that place held the holy relics under his authority, and since he himself was my friend, he gave me this bone, taken from the sacred body, as a token of our mutual affection.”

The bishop had finished speaking. But I, enticed by a desire to possess some of these relics, began to beg him to give me a portion of the bone. He replied:

“Take it, and whatever you can break off from it at the first attempt shall be yours.”

I took it, and behold, beyond what I had hoped, at the beginning of my attempt a single fragment remained in my right hand. Since I could not conceal my grief at its smallness and was eager to be permitted to break off another piece [variants: *frangere*, “to break,” / *frangerem*, “that I might break”; *gestirem*, “I was eager,” / *gestire*, “to be eager”], Father Anselm interrupted my desire and said:

“No, no; let what you have be sufficient for you. For I tell you truthfully that, for all the gold found in Constantinople and everywhere beyond or this side of it, the lady herself to whom it belongs would not fail to claim it for herself on the day of the resurrection of all. Therefore, if you show her the reverence due to her, she will receive it just as though you were showing reverence to her entire body.”

Hearing this, I agreed, and from that time to this I have preserved it as decently as I could. Many days later, Peter, a Cluniac monk, a man of great authority in his time [Note: If this refers to a later period, and to the authority in which Peter flourished under Paschal until the year 1118, one might suspect that he was the same famous Peter known for his deeds, writings, and holiness who became abbot of Cluny in 1122. But the conjecture is impeded not so much by the year of his death, which was 1157—for why should he not have reached or exceeded his eightieth year?—as by the fact that nothing has been found concerning Peter’s affairs before his prelacy that supports this identification, and by the fact that Eadmer, writing after the election of this Peter as abbot—a matter which certainly soon became known at Canterbury—did not expressly add that the Peter of whom he is speaking had recently been made abbot], who had been chamberlain to Pope Urban and Pope Paschal, came to us and asked me what I thought of it. When I told him how I had obtained it, he acknowledged that what the bishop had said about it was entirely true, and asserted that he himself had been present when the cardinal had received that same bone after it had been removed from the martyr’s body.

## Chapter VII

Reconciliation with the King. Return to England. Illness, Death, and Miracles.

65. After this, both to exercise the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline and to bring relief to the churches established in England, Anselm left Burgundy and went to France. When King Henry of England learned of this, Anselm, having been summoned, came to him in Normandy. There the king, seized at once by fear and love of God, restored Anselm to his possessions and received him back into friendship.

While Anselm was thereafter staying in Normandy, Baldwin and William returned. They had been sent, at the command of the king and the bishop, to Rome to conclude the matter of the investitures of the churches, which had continued between them until then. William went to the king in England and shortly afterward returned to Anselm at Bec. On the king’s behalf he asked him, now that their former disputes had been quieted, to visit England without delay.

Anselm readily agreed. But when he set out and reached Jumièges, illness detained him there so that he could not complete the journey. When it had subsided, he returned to Bec to await the crossing of the king of England. While extraordinary joy possessed everyone at his return, behold, Anselm’s illness was renewed, and it confined him to bed, overturning the joy and casting everyone down in deep sorrow.

He could neither eat nor do anything from which we might hope for his recovery, and an overwhelming fear of his death held us [variant: *tamen*, “nevertheless”]. Meanwhile, we carefully urged him to take some food [variant: *in cibum*, “for food”], but he confessed, as best he could, in labored breath that he had no desire for anything. Yet when we multiplied our pleas, at last, lest by refusing entirely he burden us still more, he said:

“Perhaps I would eat some partridge, if I had one.”

What more need be said? His servants scattered through the fields and woods, and one day was spent in fruitless labor searching for a partridge. It happened that one of the monastery’s servants, on that very day, happened to take a path through a nearby wood, paying no attention to the task with which the others were occupied. Behold, on the road along which he was walking, a little animal called a *martira* [Note: *Martira*, commonly *martre*, elsewhere *fovine*, is called *martes* in Latin; it is a small animal hostile to sheep and chickens, able easily to creep through any narrow passage] was carrying a partridge in its mouth.

When the little animal saw the man, it abandoned its prey to him and sought safety in flight. He took the partridge and brought it to us. Our sick man, refreshed by it, immediately began to improve from his illness; and finally, growing better day by day, he recovered his former health.

66. After the bishops and abbots who had assembled for his funeral rites had returned to their own places, Radulphus also returned [Note: Shortly afterward—namely, in 1108—he was made bishop of Rochester, and in 1114 archbishop of Canterbury. He had succeeded the first abbot of the abbey of Sées, Robert, in 1089; the abbey had been restored in 1060 by Roger of Montgomery, viscount, and his wife Mabel]. He was abbot of the monastery of Sées and had been one of those men.

One of his men began, on the journey, to disparage Anselm and to assert in a slanderous voice that no one ought rightly to pity his illness, especially since, as he said, Anselm could easily assist his own health with food and drink if he wished, without boastfulness, to do so. When the abbot heard this, he warned the man to be silent and not to say anything further that was evil about so great a man.

The man contemptuously disregarded the warning. Agitated by a kind of madness, he persisted in what he had begun, and spurred his horse so that he might get farther away from the abbot and more freely utter what the bitterness of his mind suggested. But while he desired to be carried along at full speed, and, with the reins slackened, began to go faster, the four-footed animal on which he sat fell and threw him from its back with great disgrace. Then, rolling him down a steep mountain in a long fall, it taught him to restrain his tongue from slandering the man of God.

67. Later, on the Assumption of the blessed Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary, King Henry came to Bec and, with the sanction of the apostolic see governing the matter, erased everything that had been settled between himself and Anselm concerning that oft-mentioned affair. In every matter toward which he had been striving, he made Anselm master of his wishes.

Since Anselm’s journey to return to England was delayed for a while for certain reasons, he was asked by the abbot of Bec to dedicate a chapel situated within the court of that monastery. During the dedication, a certain cleric who had recently been seized by an illness of frenzy was brought by his people before the bishop, and immediately, through his blessing, was healed of his mental derangement.

[Col. 0113D]

68. After this, when he came to England with a favorable journey, he was received with great joy and honor by the holy Church. Some days later, a certain English nobleman, both wealthy and distinguished, afflicted by a severe bodily illness, sent a messenger to Anselm asking that bread blessed by him be sent to him, and he received it. After tasting a little of it, he immediately began to recover according to his faith; restored to complete health, he gave heartfelt thanks to God and to the man of God.

69. Meanwhile, the king, staying in Normandy, was greatly rejoicing—as those who came to us from there reported—because he had obtained peace with Anselm. He therefore also congratulated himself in firm hope that he would bring all Normandy under his dominion. And so it happened. For, after joining battle in a serious conflict, he captured his brother Robert, count of Normandy, and the other princes who had gone to war against him. After killing countless men, he gained possession of the entire land as victor, and promptly informed Anselm of this by letter, joyfully and graciously.

Everyone who heard of these events at that time attributed them to the merits of the reconciliation that the king had made with Anselm.

70. That same year, after celebrating the solemnity of Easter, Anselm went from the king’s court at London to the abbey of Saint Edmund, intending to confirm by his authority the abbot elected there [Note: The *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 295, says that after the death of Abbot Robert, who died in 1107, the abbey of Saint Edmund was vacant for seven years, and that finally in 1115 Abbold was confirmed; he had been prior of Saint Nicaise of Meulan. But who can say whether he had been elected while Saint Anselm was alive or was substituted later after the earlier election had been annulled?], and to perform there certain other pontifical offices belonging to his right.

When he had solemnly completed all these duties, he was seized by a very severe fever and afflicted for many days, almost until he breathed his last. Because of this he was detained there until the octave of Pentecost, and the council which the king had proposed to hold concerning the bereaved churches was postponed until the Kalends of August because of his absence.

At that time, when all the leading men of England had assembled in the king’s palace at London, Anselm obtained the victory concerning the liberty of the Church, for which he had labored so long. For the king, abandoning the practice of his predecessors, neither personally chose the persons appointed to govern the churches nor invested them in the churches over which they were placed by the giving of the pastoral staff.

71. During these events Anselm wrote a small book, *On the Agreement of Foreknowledge and Predestination and the Grace of God with Free Will*. In this work he suffered an unusual delay in writing, because from the time he had fallen ill at Saint Edmund’s until the end of his present life, his body was weaker than usual. Therefore, as he moved from place to place, he was afterward carried in a litter rather than riding a horse.

Moreover, he was afflicted by frequent and severe illnesses, so that we scarcely dared hope to promise him life. Yet he never forgot his former way of life, but was always occupied either with good meditations, holy exhortations [variant: exercises], or other pious works.

72. In the third year after he had been recalled from his second exile by King Henry, all foods by which human nature is strengthened and nourished became repulsive to him. Nevertheless, he ate by forcing his nature, knowing that he could not live without food. Passing his life in this way for about half a year, he gradually grew weaker in body, while in strength of spirit he remained always the same as he had been.

Thus strong in spirit but exceedingly frail in the flesh, he could not walk to the oratory. Yet because he desired to attend the consecration of the Lord’s body, which he venerated with a special devotion, he had himself carried there each day in a chair. We who served him tried to prevent this because he was greatly fatigued by it, but we could barely prevail upon him until the fifth day before his death.

From then on, lying constantly in bed, he urged in a breathless voice all who were privileged to approach him to live for God, each according to his proper order. The Lord’s Day of Palms had dawned, and we were sitting around him as usual. One of us then said to him:

“Lord Father, as we understand it, you are leaving the world and going to the paschal court of your Lord.”

He replied:

“Indeed, if that is his will, I will willingly obey his will [variant: I will not resist it]. But if he preferred me to remain among you a little longer, at least until I could complete the question about the origin of the soul which I turn over in my mind, I would receive that favor gratefully, since I do not know whether anyone will complete it after my death. For if I could eat, I hope I would recover. I feel no pain in any part of my body, except that, because my stomach is distressed by the food it cannot take [variant: I cannot take], I am entirely failing.”

[Col. 0115C]

73. Later, as Tuesday evening approached, when he was no longer able to utter any words that could be understood, Radulphus, bishop of Rochester [Note: He had previously been taken from the abbacy of Sées, as has been stated], asked him to grant his absolution and blessing to us who were present and to his other sons, and also to the king and queen with their children, and to the people of the land who under God had kept themselves in his obedience.

Anselm raised his right hand as though he were suffering no harm, made the sign of the holy cross, and sat with his head bowed.

Meanwhile, the community of the brothers was singing the morning praises in the greater church. One of those keeping watch around the Father took up the Gospel book and read the Passion before him. It was the Passion that was to be read at Mass that same day.

When he came to the Lord’s words, “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint to you, just as my Father appointed to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22:29), Anselm began to breathe more slowly than usual.

We therefore perceived that he was about to die, and he was placed from the bed upon sackcloth and ashes. With the entire company of his sons gathered around him, he gave up his last breath into the hands of the Creator and slept in peace.

He died at daybreak on the Wednesday preceding the Lord’s Supper, which was the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1109. This was the sixteenth year of his episcopate [variant: thirteenth] and the seventy-sixth year of his life.

74. After his body had been washed according to custom, Baldwin, the aforementioned steward and administrator of Anselm’s affairs, asked that the Father’s face be anointed with the balsam which, after most of its contents had been lost, remained in a very small vessel in his possession. He hoped and earnestly desired that in this way the face might be preserved a little longer, so that it would not decay.

We agreed, embracing the man’s diligence. The bishop therefore took the vessel of liquid into his hand and, intending to anoint the dead man’s face, dipped his finger to the bottom of the vessel. When he immediately withdrew it and found scarcely the tip of his finger moistened, he judged that the balsam would in no way suffice to anoint the face.

He therefore asked that the balsam kept in the greater church for the preparation of chrism be brought, wishing that, together with the head, Anselm’s right hand—through which he had spoken and written many good and divine things—might be honored by such anointing.

I was with the bishop during this and assisted him in the ministry. I dipped my finger into the vessel of balsam after him and withdrew it equally moist, or certainly less moist, than his finger. The bishop was then asked to turn the vessel into my palm, in case some drop might fall from it. He agreed, and immediately, to everyone’s astonishment, the liquid sprang out, filled my hand with its abundance, and overflowed.

The same thing happened a second and a third time, and again thereafter. What more shall I say? The almost-empty vessel supplied such an abundance of balsam that, without touching the church’s vessel, we anointed not only his head and hands but also his arms, breast, feet, and entire body, not once but repeatedly, on every side.

After this he was clothed in sacred garments according to the custom of the supreme pontiff and carried with due reverence into the oratory.

75. On the following day, when he was being committed to burial, the sarcophagus that had been prepared for him several days earlier was found to be suitable in length and width but, in large part, insufficient in depth. Considering this, we were disheartened, since we could in no way endure that he should be pressed by the upper stone and thereby suffer any impairment of his bodily integrity.

While many people were wavering over the matter, and some repeatedly proposed one solution and others another, a certain man from the dense crowd of brothers took the staff of the bishop of Rochester, who was present performing the funeral office, and began to draw it crosswise over the sarcophagus above the Father’s body. He discovered that it already projected above the body of the one lying there on every side, greatly astonishing us.

Thus the venerable body of Father Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury [variant: Dorobernia] and primate of all Britain, was enclosed in the tomb. By his example he warns all who pass by to consider what the condition of human mortality entails.

Certainly, many things are reported to have been seen by many people at his death and after his death, testifying to the glory which we do not doubt he received from God in accordance with his merits. Yet we have not wished to undertake the labor of writing them down. We prefer, rather, by our silence, to make all who saw such things in sleep equal to one another than, by writing some and omitting others, to make one person appear to prefer certain accounts to others as though they were more important.

To write everything down would, in the end, be an undertaking of infinite magnitude. The manifest deeds which God deigned to perform through him, and which we, being unworthy of such things, have set forth as best we could, seem sufficient, I think, to make known the reward and manner of life [variant: reward of life] that he received.

Therefore, to God the Father almighty, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, be praise and thanksgiving, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0117A]

## Supplement to Eadmer’s Books on the Life of Saint Anselm

*(Warthon, Anglia Sacra, vol. II, p. 181.)*

[Col. 0117B]

[Note: In the printed editions these two final chapters of the *Life of Saint Anselm* are lacking, although they are found in all the manuscript copies that I have seen and are cited by Eadmer in the prologue to his book on the miracles of Saint Anselm. There Eadmer says that he dealt with the miracles of Count Arnulf and the monk Robert at the end of the books *On the Life of Saint Anselm*. Warthon.]

Certain events that are said to have occurred not in a dream, but within a short time after his death, when people were in grave danger, through the remembrance of his devout name, compel me—because of the force of the love with which some of my fellow monks still burn for him—to record them briefly.

### Chapter LXVI

A certain man named Arnulf, son of Count Roger of Montgomery, and himself a count, was returning from Normandy to England. He had successfully completed the middle portion of his sea voyage when, behold, contrary to the expectations of everyone aboard the ship, a fog of extraordinary density suddenly arose, grew thicker, and increased. Moreover, all the wind by which they had been carried fell, disappeared, and died away.

The ship, in the middle of the sea, had no wind to carry it onward. Nor could the multitude of men aboard discern what course to hold through the density of the fog. The ship drifted here and there among the heaps of waves, unable to make any headway, and the crowd of men aboard, stricken by great weariness, was losing heart.

For two days the sea thus held them in an unwelcome service and stirred their minds and mouths toward conflicting prayers, so that they might be released from its restraint. At last the aforementioned count, remembering Father Anselm, whose memory deserves remembrance, broke off everyone’s prayers and urged them in a brief address to attend to him for a little while:

“Let us set aside all other matters,” he said, “and in the present danger turn our heart and tongue toward our father and bishop, the holy Anselm, whom we often saw, to whom we clung, whose sacred teaching instructed us, and whose blessed blessing we often enjoyed. Let us implore the well-known compassion of his heart, so that by his holy merits he may obtain from our Creator and Lord of all, Jesus Christ, both the forgiveness of our sins and a speedy release from this most serious hardship, which we justly suffer because of them.”

All agreed to his exhortation.

Great is the mercy of God; great is his power. They had not yet completed the Lord’s Prayer, which they had begun immediately at the count’s words, when suddenly the fog vanished, the entire serenity of the sky returned, and they happily saw that the shore toward which they had first been hastening was not far away.

They therefore gave thanks to God and to his faithful servant. Their spirits restored, they spread their sail and were carried most successfully into the desired harbor. From there they went to the court of Henry, king of the English, and explained to the king himself, in the presence of the bishops and the leading men of the kingdom, everything that had happened to them, in the order set out above.

The report pleased many people greatly. They did not doubt that his life in the world had been such that, once taken from the world, he deserved to obtain this and much greater things from God.

[Col. 0118C]

There was also a monk named Robert, constantly in the service of Radulphus, bishop of Rochester, who was mentioned above. At about that time, as he was crossing London Bridge, he was suddenly struck by misfortune when the horse carrying his pack fell.

The horse, being led by a servant with insufficient care across a place where the bridge was broken here and there, fell into the river where the force of the current and the depth of the water were greatest. Although the aforementioned brother, to whom all these things belonged, was somewhat distressed by the loss of the animal and of the goods kept in the pack, he was nevertheless almost oblivious to all of them and was very anxious about one of the books of blessed-memory Father Anselm, which was among the other contents.

He therefore proceeded across the bridge as best he could, praying for the book’s preservation and recovery through the merits of the man who had made it. Meanwhile the horse, in the depth of the swollen current, was swimming with strong effort toward the bank.

What more shall I say? Each had completed his journey—the one across the bridge, the other through the river—and they came upon each other on opposite sides. The pack was immediately taken down and opened, so that the water with which it was feared to be filled might be shaken out. Everything inside was found dry, except for one linen garment, as though the pack had never been immersed in water.

He returned to the bishop and, in my presence, reported what had happened, opening the mouths of those who heard him in praise of God.

Here I shall bring this little work to an end, after first briefly reminding all who consent to read or hear it not to wound their minds through disbelief in the things described. For in writing these matters I have used authorities whose testimony leaves me in no doubt that every suspicion of falsehood is far removed.

Indeed, I gathered much of what the sequence of the first book contains from the words of Father Anselm himself. For he was a man of exceptional cheerfulness and would sometimes, among his other remarks, recount in simple speech, as though in play, what he had done as a boy, as a young man, before taking the monastic habit, after entering that habit, as prior, and as abbot. He assumed that his listeners would receive these things with the same intention with which they were told and only superficially.

As for the events counted among the miracles in the little book itself, I received some from Baldwin, some from Boson, and some from Riculf, monks of Bec. I, Eadmer, a monk of the Church of the Savior at Canterbury, remember having mentioned them there. According to their own accounts, these men either were present at the events, experienced them in their own persons, or heard them from those who testified that they had been present when the events occurred.

Almost everything recorded in the second book I either saw with my own eyes, perceived by hearing, or was able in some other way to learn personally, since I, Eadmer, continually enjoyed his presence from the time he assumed the episcopate.

I declare that it is a wicked thing knowingly to write anything false in sacred histories. For whenever such things are either read or heard, the soul of the writer is destroyed, because through the things he has falsely written he lies to everyone with an abominable mouth.

[Note: In the margin of another manuscript there is this note: “Eadmer, who composed this Book II, here brings it to an end. He who saw it bore witness. And at the command of Bishop Ralph he completed it.”]

## Chapter LXVII

Furthermore, when I had first set my hand to the work and had transferred to parchment a considerable part of what I had dictated on wax tablets, Father Anselm himself came to me one day privately, asking what I was dictating and what I was writing. Since I preferred to conceal the matter in silence rather than disclose it, he ordered me either to abandon what I had begun and devote myself to other things, or to show him what I was writing.

But I, who had already been strengthened in some of what I had written by reliance upon his assistance and correction, willingly obeyed, hoping that, with the benevolence inherent in him, he would correct whatever needed correction and arrange each point differently expressed in its proper place. Neither my hope nor my expectation deceived me. For in the little work itself he corrected some things, overturned others, changed certain passages, and approved others.

When I was therefore rejoicing somewhat in my heart, and perhaps boasting within myself, Eadmer, more than was proper that what I had published was supported by such great and such authoritative approval, a few days after the work had been corrected the bishop summoned me to him and ordered me to destroy completely the quires in which I had composed the work. He judged himself wholly unworthy that posterity should derive from written memorials praise of him at any price.

I found this very painful. Yet, not daring to disobey his command outright, and not wishing the work that I had assembled with so much labor to perish altogether, after noting his words, I destroyed those very quires, having first inscribed them on other quires. Nevertheless, this action of mine perhaps was not free from the sin of disobedience. For I knew that his command was to be carried out otherwise, and that he had understood it otherwise.

Therefore, on behalf of all into whose hands these writings may perhaps fall, I earnestly beg that, if they find in them anything that does not entirely displease them so far as the foolishness of the narrative is concerned, they will deign to intercede for me, for this and for my other sins, lest the weight of them press me down so heavily that I cannot reach him whose Life and deeds I have set forth in whatever style I could.

For I cannot forget how he answered me when once I asked him that, just as he had made me his companion in labor here below, so he might make me a sharer in his reward above. He said that he would indeed do this willingly and gladly, provided only that I took care not to make myself too heavy in this matter.

If, however, the justice of the righteous Judge, removing all mercy, weighs the burden of my sins, my soul will surely rush downward, not upward, into the depths of the abyss. Therefore, just as I, Eadmer, began, I continue to press forward with whatever prayers I can, asking that they obtain from God for me, together with themselves, relief and forgiveness of sins such as they desire to have rendered to them, lest the merciful Father be unable to lift me up, burdened as I am with excessive sins, to the place where he promised.

May his clemency keep this far from me—he who, above all, lives, rules, and reigns as God. Amen.

[Col. 0119D]

# The Miracles of Saint Anselm

*(Drawn by Mabillon from the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. Edited by D. Martène, Amplissima Collectio, vol. VI, col. 983.)*

Since many miracles are reported of Father Anselm,

which Christ specially worked through him,

and since the matter is now scarcely known except to a few,

so that it may be clear how great was the merit of this blessed man,

I have distinguished certain events that I judged worthy of being written,

adding them to the subject matter of the work mentioned above.

[Note: In the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden these verses appear at the end of the Life of Saint Anselm composed by Eadmer. From this one may infer that the author of these verses was likewise the aforementioned Eadmer.]

There was a man in the district of Pontif, adjoining Augo,

known for his wealth, but with his flesh weakened by an ulcer,

surrounded by servants, but contaminated by leprosy.

He himself persevered daily in good works,

mingling tears with multiplied prayers.

He besought Christ, thus imploring the Lord:

that he might deign to bend his gaze upon the afflicted man,

and, cleansing his skin, himself grant him salvation.

But he who looks upon a contrite heart and sees it fashioned for himself

did not fail the anxiety of the sick man.

Rather, he came to his aid wondrously and with evident care.

Accordingly, one night in a dream he was warned

that, if he now wished to become and appear well,

he should rise confidently and go to Bec,

and privately entreat the father of the monastery,

striving by every means to prevail upon him

to deign to give him water to drink,

with which he washed his hands while celebrating the rites of Mass.

Believing these instructions and made more certain by them,

he hastily climbed there and immediately went on his way.

He briefly disclosed to kindly Anselm

what had been shown to him from above in the vision.

Anselm was astonished at his words and at first repelled him with harsh speech,

warning him not to trouble himself with such requests.

He declared that what the man sought was not his task,

but that of the blessed men who had gone before him.

He was a sinner, far removed from them and inferior to them,

and, because of his own faults, unworthy to be heard in matters so great.

Yet the pitiable man persisted all the more in his prayers,

repeating more loudly that the venerable man should bring him aid

and should not allow him to be deprived of the remedy

from which he believed that healing would quickly come to him.

At last the man of God, urged on by these cries

and, according to his custom, moved with compassion for the afflicted man,

entered the church and went up in prayer to the altar.

In the morning, intending to pray for the healing of this man’s body,

clad in sacred vestments like a soldier in armor,

he celebrated Mass, though not without tears.

The sick man also stood near, prostrate in complete prayer,

praying from the depths of his spirit and the marrow of his heart

that what had been promised him from heaven might now be fulfilled.

[Col. 0121D]

When the sacred mysteries had been completed

—I shall relate a wonder, and yet expound a wonder—

he received water from the abbot’s hands, thirsty as he was.

After he had devoutly tasted it and drunk more deeply of it,

the desired health was immediately poured into his limbs.

His flesh was cleansed; his foul skin was restored.

Breaking forth in praise of the Almighty,

he exalted Anselm no less with loud praises.

The holy man restrained him and warned him

not to attribute to himself so great a deed,

but to render the offices of praise to God alone,

from whom the care of all salvation proceeds.

Instructed by these words and greatly overjoyed,

cleansed and unharmed, with his skin renewed, he returned home.

At the time when the saint was exercising pastoral care

and was rightly renowned as primate over the English,

many disturbances had arisen throughout the kingdom,

especially through the violence of King William, the younger,

whose madness was accompanied by the savagery of his mind.

He harassed and plundered the churches of the kingdom,

showing no reverence for God or restraint toward men in his greed.

Since Anselm could not completely settle these matters by himself,

he left his beloved homeland and set out for Rome

to seek the counsel of the lord pope concerning them.

The pope received him with extraordinary honor,

and all the nobility of the city venerated him.

For, hastening pompously to meet him,

he hurried toward so great a prelate, racing to honor his reputation,

both because Anselm had come there from distant regions of the world

to seek the assistance of holy Peter,

and because he was known for his wondrous religious observance

and for deeds that had proved his great practical wisdom.

But when the reason for Anselm’s arrival had become clear,

having been reported to the supreme pontiff by Anselm himself,

the pope then displayed even greater honor toward him,

as was fitting for so distinguished a person.

Keeping him with him, he made Anselm his second,

in all matters both private and public,

often speaking at great length in his praise,

sometimes privately and sometimes before a larger assembly,

so that Anselm was often truly embarrassed by it.

The site of the city, however, is known to be unhealthy and not salubrious

during the summer season, especially for visitors.

Therefore, with the consent and counsel of the lord pope,

Anselm went to a village called Sclavia,

where he often rested and refreshed his body.

The village stands high upon a mountain;

the air there is healthier, and its slope is considered salubrious.

It is not far from the walls of the city of Rome.

Anselm himself frequently returned there at the father’s command,

especially whenever he openly discussed important matters.

But the people of that mountain had long been exhausted

by an extreme scarcity of water.

The guardian of the village, carefully considering this,

as well as the holy man’s life

and the fact that Christ had already granted many benefits

through Anselm’s prayers to people afflicted by the corruption of disease,

addressed the saint and surrounded him with prayers,

asking him to mark out a place for a well there,

where he might judge that water would more conveniently be found.

He said that he wished it, if it could perhaps be accomplished,

and that it would be a great help if Anselm’s prayers brought it about,

so that there would be no need to descend to the bottom of the valley

to bring water up to the height of the mountain.

Anselm heard him and at last consented to his prayers.

He praised what the man declared he had resolved to do.

Taking companions with him, including two monks,

he went out to carry out what he had so often been asked to do.

But the mountain was lofty, steep, and exceedingly rugged,

and above it the mountain itself was covered with cliffs.

It therefore seemed the height of madness

for anyone even to contemplate digging a well there.

Nevertheless, the bishop, mindful of the Scripture,

which says that one who possesses faith as great as a mustard seed

commands a mountain to be moved, and it will move quickly,

trusting in hope, as he was well accustomed to do,

examined the place and carefully surveyed it.

Then, after offering the prayer that was always ready upon his lips,

and kneeling down and making the sign of the cross,

he struck the ground three times near a stone and rock,

and ordered them to begin the work and prepare a well.

They did not doubt, but placed their hope in him

who once produced firm waters from a rock

for a thirsty people traveling through the desert.

After only a few days had passed

from the time when they began to dig into the summit of the mountain,

a spring suddenly burst forth from the rock,

and its water struck those standing there with great and sudden astonishment.

Then, in the joy of their hearts and with the honor of praise,

they magnified Christ and acclaimed the saint of God

with repeated voices,

both because of the novelty of the event

and because of the wondrous novelty of the divine gift.

This too is regarded there as a miracle.

For although the mountain is lofty and only moderately hollowed out,

a perennial spring of wholesome water appears and fills the place.

When taken as a drink, it cures those suffering from fever

and is also found suitable for various illnesses.

This unquestionably redounds to the praise of the Lord,

who mercifully gives such gifts to his people.

The prelate himself is not without a share in the praise,

for God appears to have performed this work out of love for him.

Thus throughout the whole region the well of Sclavia

is called “the well of Prelate Anselm,”

with praise that never perishes.

[Col. 0123B]

# The Shorter Life of Saint Anselm

*From a manuscript of the library of Victorina.*

Anselm was born in Aosta, a city of Burgundy situated at the foot of the Alps, and was descended from distinguished parents, his father Gundulf and his mother Hermenberga. From childhood he was educated liberally and in a manner befitting a gentleman. Moved by the fame of Lanfranc and by a desire for learning, he came to the monastery of Bec.

There, in the twenty-seventh year of his age, he first became a monk. Later, when Lanfranc had been placed in charge of the abbey of Caen, Anselm succeeded him in the priory of Bec. He remained in that office for fifteen years. Then, after Erluin, abbot of Bec, had died, Anselm was created abbot, an office that he likewise held for fifteen years.

At last, when Hugh, count of Chester, was gravely ill and Anselm’s fame had become widely known, he was summoned to England. He was to attend to certain affairs of the count and to fill the community of the monastery of Chester with monks, excluding priests.

When William Rufus learned of this, he appointed Anselm archbishop of Canterbury. For the king had received all the revenues of the archbishopric for four years, had held many churches for sale, had turned thirty cemeteries into pastures for wild beasts, because of the ruin of the churches, and had reserved for himself the revenues of vacant churches.

When he realized, upon granting the archbishopric, that this profitable arrangement would either have to be abandoned altogether or greatly reduced, he immediately regretted his ready and generous beneficence toward Anselm. Therefore, in order to turn Anselm’s mind away from accepting the archbishopric offered to him, he first pretended that, although love for Anselm and his merits had led him to confer the archbishopric of Canterbury upon him, he now saw that the difficulty and magnitude of the province of Canterbury were greater than could be endured and sustained by a man devoted to monastic duties, vigils, and sacred studies.

When this persuasion accomplished nothing, and he discovered with certainty that the nobles and people of England, opposed to him or less loyal to him, favored Anselm and demanded that he accept the office of archbishop already offered to him, he did not dare openly to object. Nevertheless, he stipulated that the possessions of the churches which he had appropriated during the four-year vacancy should be confirmed by Anselm’s authority and judgment as well.

Anselm replied that he did not wish to harm the Church, to which he had contributed nothing in his office. Accordingly, after obtaining the permission of the bishop of Rouen, in whose diocese Bec was situated, he left the abbey of Bec. He was confirmed as archbishop of Canterbury by Walchelin, then bishop of Winchester, and, as was customary, swore fidelity to King Rufus.

Once installed and established in that see, he began to admonish the king more freely and severely concerning his insatiable greed and plunder of ecclesiastical property. Nothing, he said, could be more certain than that the king had made so many cemeteries into common pastures for beasts through the ruin of the churches.

But when Anselm could form no hope from his prayers and exhortations that the king’s mind would change, he sought permission to go to Rome to obtain the pallium from Pope Urban. Whether disturbed and inflamed by this request or by the mention of Urban, the king vehemently asserted and insisted that Anselm had acted against the bond of the fidelity he had promised. His father, he said, had decreed that no one whom the king had not named should be acknowledged as pope in the kingdom of England in the pope’s name; anyone who acted otherwise was to be judged guilty of lèse-majesté and an enemy of the king, because he had violated the custom of the kingdom.

Eadmer describes the truth of this matter in these words:

> “When the king had returned from overseas, Anselm approached him and humbly asked that he grant him permission to go to Rome to Pope Urban for the pallium of his archbishopric. But the king, disturbed at the name of Urban, said that he did not recognize him as pope, and that it was not his custom to allow anyone in his kingdom to name a pope without his authorization.”

A serious disagreement therefore arose, but its examination was deferred to another time. The king accordingly ordered all the bishops, abbots, and nobles of England to come together for the discussion of this dispute at the castle called Rockingham.

This was done, and in the third week of Lent they assembled as ordered. The matter was brought forward, and Anselm was assailed by various accusations from every side. Many—especially the bishops, who wished to favor the king’s will—disregarding the judgment of equity, sought to prove that Anselm could not, while preserving the fidelity he owed the king, recognize Urban as pope and as the prelate of the apostolic see within the king’s realm.

When several arguments dictated by reason had been brought against them, and Anselm had completely silenced them with the words of the Lord, “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21), together with other arguments that no reason could refute, they, having nothing to say in reply, shouted all together that he was blaspheming against the king, since he had dared to ascribe anything to God in the king’s realm without the king’s permission.

Accordingly, at a single outburst of royal indignation, certain bishops suddenly renounced all subjection and professed obedience to their archbishop and primate, and, with an equally pitiable unanimity, abjured their unity of fraternal fellowship with him. Others among them declared that they would not obey him in anything he commanded on behalf of Pope Urban.

Thus all the bishops, with the sole exception of the bishop of Rochester, in one way or another renounced the subjection and obedience they owed him. The king himself also deprived him of all confidence and security in everything of his, and swore that he would no longer regard him as archbishop or father unless Anselm denied that he would henceforth obey the vicar of Saint Peter.

Three days were spent in this affair amid clamors against Anselm and loaded with insults. At last they reached this conclusion.

But Anselm, steadfast in his purpose, asked the king to allow him to leave the kingdom safely. When this was denied him, both sides made pledges until Pentecost, and full peace and tranquility were promised.

Nevertheless, Anselm was afflicted beyond measure: his men were captured and despoiled, and his lands were devastated. After these events he accepted Urban as pope through Walter, bishop of Albano, who brought the pallium from Rome to Anselm at Canterbury.

While this controversy was being handled, the king dealt privately with Pope Urban about removing Anselm entirely from England. But since, on account of the man’s exceptional learning and integrity of character, he could not accomplish this, Anselm, having received the pallium, exercised his archiepiscopal care and authority with the king’s acquiescence.

At the request of King Muirchertach and of the people of Ireland, he consecrated at Lambeth Samuel as archbishop of Dublin and Malchus as the first bishop of Waterford, together with other bishops, after receiving their profession of subjection.

But after returning from the Welsh expedition, the king began to reproach Anselm concerning the soldiers he had sent to conduct so great a war, claiming that they were poorly suited to the task. He also brought new accusations against the matters on which Anselm had spoken more freely and openly, both publicly and privately to the king, concerning the recovery and preservation of ecclesiastical liberty and the devastation and ruin of churches caused by the king’s invasion.

After these actions of Anselm had been reviewed, he was immediately given the choice between two courses: either to remain in the kingdom of England, with the fidelity and service to the king that he had promised by oath and that earlier archbishops had customarily rendered, and not to appeal to the pope or to the apostolic see concerning anything against the king; or to depart from the kingdom of England, which would not have been difficult for a foreigner and newcomer.

Accordingly, Anselm obtained an eleven-day respite, within which he would settle his affairs and cross the sea. “I am going,” he said to the king and nobles, “but I impart my blessing to you, if you do not despise it.”

When the king said that he would not reject it, Anselm blessed him with his right hand raised and departed from Canterbury. He remained there for fourteen days. On the following day, when he was about to board a ship at Dover, a certain William, a cleric and messenger of the king, detained him as though he were guilty of some grave crime.

While a great crowd of common people stood by, all his baggage was searched, he was stripped of all his possessions, and, once he had crossed the sea, he was put ashore naked on a foreign coast.

After his departure, the king outlawed everything that belonged to Anselm, transferred it to his own ownership, and declared all that Anselm had established null and void. Anselm, however, went to Lyon and from there was summoned to Rome by the pope, who received him with the greatest kindness and hospitality.

Meanwhile William—the man who had searched Anselm as he departed from the shore—came to Rome as the king’s envoy, in order to obtain a postponement of Anselm’s case until the following feast of Saint Michael the Archangel.

When this was granted, Anselm, displeased by it, resolved to return to Lyon, but the pope detained him for the council that was then being convened. Among the other decrees of this council, a sentence of excommunication was issued against laymen who gave investitures of churches and against clerics who received them from laymen.

While the postponement concerning Anselm’s case was still in effect, the pope died, and shortly afterward King Rufus died. During his lifetime the king had allowed neither ecclesiastical synods to be held for the correction of abuses nor many churches to be held by clerics. Instead, he received their revenues, always jokingly mocking the entire clergy with this verse:

> “Christ’s bread is rich bread.”

After Rufus died, his brother Henry succeeded him. He was consecrated by Maurice, bishop of London, and repaired the church’s condition, which his brother had made miserable and divided. He recalled Anselm from exile and entrusted ecclesiastical administration to him.

How greatly Henry favored Anselm may be understood from the charter he sent to the people of London concerning the immunity of Anselm’s servants and attendants, and asking them to treat Anselm and his men kindly and humanely. He requested that Anselm and his people be as free as Lanfranc and his men had been, as may be understood from the grant of William the Conqueror.

To show how open and simple that age was, and how little given to prolixity and over-elaboration in words, it will not be out of place to insert the charter itself word for word, written in both Latin and English. The whole text, in both languages, does not even reach the width of a palm.

The great royal seal, which is now customarily attached at the end of charters, is affixed to this ancient charter on a small, gradually extended and cut portion of parchment attached to the left side of the charter. In ancient times kings did not append seals to their charters. This practice was introduced by Edward I, king of England, who appended impressed wax to his charters as testimony to their truth.

## Charter of King Henry

> “Henry, king of the English, to Hugh de Boclande and W. Baynard, and to all my officers of London, greeting. I command and will that all the men of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, whom he has in London, and all his people going and returning in that town, be as free from all customs as Lanfranc, archbishop, ever had his men there at their best and freest in the time of my father. And see that you do them no injury. Witness Hugh, count of Chester, at Westminster.”

Anselm, diligently exercising his ecclesiastical administration, summoned a synod of the entire clergy at London. In it he deposed many from ecclesiastical dignities on account of simoniacal agreements and other offenses: Guido, abbot of Wymondham, and Ælwin of Ramsey, as simonists; Geoffrey of Peterborough; Haimo of Châlons; and Robert of Saint Edmund’s, on account of various defects and excesses.

This synod was also commonly known as the London Synod, but its constitutions were immediately despised and disregarded. For when Girard, archbishop of York, had ordered that its canons be observed, the entire clergy of his province refused.

Therefore he wrote to Anselm:

> “I thirst for the integrity of my clerics; but, except in very few, I find either the deafness of an asp or the changeability of some fabulous Proteus. With various stings of the tongue they inflict now threats, now insults. Those canons who have been irregularly advanced to holy orders without a profession flatly refuse to make their profession to me. So too do those who, established in the priesthood or diaconate, have until now publicly kept wives or concubines and have shown no reverence at the altar. When I invite them to receive any of the orders, they resist stubbornly, refusing to profess chastity when they are ordained.”

A great conflict and disagreement also arose between the king and Anselm concerning the investiture of churches, preventing the canons of this synod from acquiring the force and authority of law.

For during the entire three years of Anselm’s absence, while episcopal sees and churches were vacant, the king had appointed ecclesiastics to them at his own discretion. Through investiture, by the gift of the pastoral staff and ring, he had handed over possession of them.

At that time Christian rulers claimed for themselves this right of investing and inducting into possession. Accordingly, from among those who had been installed in bishoprics and churches by royal authority, the king asked Anselm to consecrate those who had not yet been consecrated; and those who had been consecrated by other bishops in Anselm’s absence, he asked him to admit into his fellowship and customary association and into the company of the bishops.

In both matters Anselm resisted the king: first, because other laymen, following the king’s example and by private authority, might appoint priests to benefices without the lawful approval of bishops; and second, because Urban, the Roman pontiff, had decreed at the preceding council that no one should receive the investiture of any church from the hand of a king or layman, or seize authority by a layman’s power.

But the king, the nobles of the kingdom, the bishops, and courtiers of every kind, indignant that Anselm had done this contrary to the custom of the kingdom, declared that they would never accept so unjust a decree of the pope. They would rather drive Anselm from the kingdom and withdraw entirely from the Roman Church than confirm this decision of the pope, wholly alien as it was to royal right and the custom of the kingdom.

When the king observed that the nobles and bishops were conspiring and agreeing with him in this sentiment, he persuaded and commanded Girard, archbishop of York, to undertake and complete the office of consecration himself.

Girard accepted this burden and appointed a day for the celebration of the consecration at London, in the church of Saint Paul. When many had gathered there, William, then bishop-elect of Winchester, returned to the king the pastoral staff and ring that he had received from him. He said that he could no longer retain what he had received unjustly.

The king was struck by the novelty of this deed, which had occurred so suddenly and unexpectedly, contrary to everyone’s expectation. He outlawed William’s goods and expelled him from the kingdom.

After many people, as is usual in every dispute, had leaned now one way and now the other, the disagreement grew so great that it threatened to become dangerous for the king, the son of the recent conqueror of the kingdom, and had to be settled. It was therefore agreed that Anselm and William Warelwast, the king’s envoy, who had always opposed Anselm’s party, should go to Rome to seek the pope’s judgment.

When they presented the case at Rome before the pope’s tribunal, Anselm argued the pope’s cause before the pope, who was present and judge; William argued the cause of his absent king, who was not judge.

When William, passionately devoted to the king’s position, said that his king would not surrender the right to give churches and transfer possession of them even at the cost of losing the kingdom of England, Pope Paschal replied—as I shall quote the words of Eadmer, the author:

> “If, as you say, your king will not allow himself to lose the right of giving churches even at the cost of losing his kingdom, know this: behold, I say before God, that Paschal the pope will not permit him to retain them with impunity even for the redemption of his own head.”

By this response of the pope, the case was decided against the king in Anselm’s favor.

Others write that Anselm heard Pope Paschal thundering the sentence of excommunication against laymen who gave investitures and clerics who received them from laymen, and that, terrified by it, he did not dare consent to his prince, who claimed a right handed down from his ancestors.

For in that excommunication the pope used words such as these:

> “It is abominable that hands which have risen to so great an eminence that, by their ministry, they create the Lord who creates all things—a privilege granted to no angel—and offer that same Lord for the redemption and salvation of the whole world before the eyes of God the supreme Father, should be subjected to this disgrace: that they become handmaids of hands polluted day and night by obscene contaminations, stained by plunder and the unjust shedding of blood.”

It is certain that the emperor Henry came to Rome to settle the dispute that had begun between the king and the clergy, regarding it as a scandal to the Christian world.

This right of investiture began to be taken away from kings by Gregory VII, called Hildebrand. Thereafter his successors, Victor and Urban, and especially Paschal, forbade it under threat of excommunication.

But from the time of Charlemagne, king and emperor of the Franks, and under the emperors who followed him—who ruled for more than three hundred years, during which period sixty-three Roman pontiffs succeeded one another in order—the practice of investing clerics in ecclesiastical benefices and inducting them into possession through the delivery of the staff and ring was frequently exercised and maintained.

Against the authority and custom of these emperors and princes, the pontiffs, by synodal judgment, declared that no one could or should receive the investiture and possession of a bishopric or any church from the hand of a prince or layman through a staff or ring, and that those who did so should be excommunicated by sentence duly issued.

For this principal reason, therefore, Emperor Henry hastened to Rome and bravely struck down the Lombards who resisted him on the way. Then, having entered Rome and received the diadem, he seized the pope together with the bishops and cardinals and held them under strict guard.

On Easter Day a reconciliation took place. On that day, after the Gospel had been read during the solemn Mass, at the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the sight of very many princes, Pope Paschal handed the emperor a privilege allowing him alone in his kingdom to transfer the investitures of churches to clerics through the delivery of the staff and ring, provided that after the investiture they canonically received consecration from the bishop in whose diocese the churches were situated.

Thus the right of investing, removed from the other princes solely by a synodal decree of the pope, was retained in that kingdom alone. Yet the thunderbolts of anathemas and excommunications hurled by the pope had struck such terror into kings that they had, as the saying goes, wrested the club from a timid and trembling Hercules. But Henry silenced those thunderclaps.

This peace, arranged during the solemn Mass through the privilege of investiture, was confirmed by the sacrament of the papal altar in the following manner. As the pope celebrated, he offered the sacrament to the emperor with these words:

> “Lord emperor, this body of the Lord, born of the Virgin Mary and suffering on the cross for us, as the holy and apostolic Church holds, we give you as confirmation of the true peace between you and me.”

After the emperor had received the sacrament, the pope obtained peace from the emperor at the cost of surrendering investitures.

Let us now return to Anselm, who, departing from Rome, reached Lyon. As Anselm was setting out for that place, the king’s envoy William, acting on the king’s command, forbade him to return to England unless he firmly promised that he too would observe all the customs retained and practiced by the king’s father and brother, setting aside subjection and obedience to the Roman see.

Anselm, however, refused to abandon his position. Accordingly, he remained at Lyon with Archbishop Hugh for almost the entire period of three years.

The king ordered all the revenues of the archbishopric to be placed in the treasury. At last Anselm was reconciled with the king through Adela, countess of Blois and the king’s sister, and was restored to the rights of the archbishopric.

Adela had long suffered from a very grave and dangerous illness. Anselm came to console her in the midst of such bodily weakness. His arrival brought the sick countess such great and sudden joy that, when the disease had been driven away, she recovered her health.

She therefore approached her brother, who was occupied in bringing Normandy under his rule, on Anselm’s behalf, and brought Anselm into a conference with the king.

After Anselm had been received back into the king’s favor, the earlier controversy over the investiture of churches, which had previously separated them, was again referred to Paschal for judgment.

To avoid inflaming against Anselm the king’s temper, which he had already found irritable, while nevertheless not yielding anything concerning the right of investiture, Paschal followed a middle course in deciding the case. The bishops whom the king had previously invested, and whom Paschal had excommunicated, were released from that sentence and confirmed in their sees; but Paschal took precautions and decreed that nothing of this kind should be done in the future by the king or by any layman.

The king accepted the pope’s decree and fully restored Anselm all the goods and revenues that he had received and retained during Anselm’s exile.

Anselm therefore returned to England and was received into the kingdom with the greatest honor by the queen and the nobles, amid the enthusiastic acclamation of the entire people. The king himself had been detained by a revolt in Normandy; after it had been settled, he again subjected Normandy to his rule.

When he returned, he summoned a public council of the kingdom at London. It was decreed there that neither the king nor any layman might invest any bishop or priest through the staff and ring; it was sufficient for bishops to render homage to the king for their temporal possessions.

After these matters had been carried out according to Anselm’s judgment, he began to enforce the decrees of the earlier London Synod that he himself had celebrated and to dissolve the marriages of priests.

At about this time, after the death of Girard, archbishop of York, Thomas was elected archbishop. [Col. 0131A] When he was to be consecrated by Anselm, he refused—at the urging and instigation of the clergy of his province—to profess the subjection owed to the see of Canterbury and previously rendered by the archbishops of York. Because of this defiance, Anselm was unwilling to consecrate him and forbade by letter that he be consecrated by any other bishop. Thus Thomas remained merely elected, without consecration, throughout Anselm’s lifetime.

After Anselm’s death, the king, the nobles of the kingdom, and the bishops summoned a council at London to deliberate on the consecration of the archbishop of York. The bishops, forbidden by Anselm, were unwilling to consecrate him. When Thomas, formerly of Meletus, who at that time enjoyed the king’s closest and greatest favor, perceived this, he asked, with a harsher expression and tone, whether anyone would dare obey such letters without the king’s authority and judgment. [Col. 0131B] Terrified and astonished by this, the bishops asked Samson, bishop of Worcester, to consecrate Thomas as archbishop of York. He declared that he would do so only if Thomas promised to profess, according to custom, his subjection to the see of Canterbury. The king also agreed to this and ordered that Thomas be consecrated in St Paul’s church on the fifth day before the Kalends of July next, in the presence of the bishops, and that he make the profession rendered by his predecessors.

When the bishops assembled at that time to complete the sacred ceremonies, a profession sealed with a seal was presented to Thomas, such as his predecessors had long been accustomed to read. After reading it openly with the utmost gravity and reverence, [Col. 0131C] as was fitting, he handed it to the bishop of London, dean of the Church of Canterbury, in the presence also of the prior of that same Church. The form of the profession was as follows:

> “I, Thomas, who am to be consecrated metropolitan of the Church of York, profess subjection and canonical obedience to the holy Church of Canterbury, to the canonically elected and consecrated primate of that Church, and to his successors canonically enthroned, saving the fidelity I owe to King Henry and saving my obedience to the Roman Church.”

At Canterbury, on the fourth day before the Ides of August, Anselm consecrated William, bishop of Winchester; Roger, bishop of Salisbury; Rainald, bishop of Hereford; and Urban, bishop of Glamorgan, in the presence of Girard, archbishop of York, and the other bishops of the province of Canterbury.

He devoted much labor and expense to adorning and restoring Christ Church at Canterbury, and to establishing the monastery of monks at Chester, previously built by Count Hugh; [Col. 0132B] he made his own chaplain, Richard, its abbot. He was frequent and constant in writing letters, of which 367 have been preserved to our own time.

He wrote various treatises:

1. *On Truth*.
2. *On the Freedom of Choice*.
3. *On the Fall of the Devil*.
4. *On the Grammarian and the Disciple*.
5. One called the *Monologion*.

He proposed and resolved many dialectical questions. He also wrote a little book of Sentences; the *Proslogion*; a book of letters to various persons; the book *On the Incarnation of the Word*; the book *Why God Became Man*; and, in addition, *On the Virgin Birth*, *On Contemplative Prayers*, and *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*.

Two years after his second return to England from exile, he was seized by a very serious fever at the abbey of Saint Edmund. He hastened to Canterbury, where he lay sick in bed for a long time, and died there on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1109, in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the sixteenth year of his pontificate. He was buried and lies entombed at the head of Lanfranc.

[Col. 0131C]

# Chronological Synopsis of the Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury

| Christian year | Supreme pontiffs | Events |
|---|---|---|
| 1033 | Benedict VIII | Anselm was born at Aosta, at the foot of the Alps, to his father Gondulf and his mother Ermengard. |
| 1060 | Nicholas II | Having lost his parents, Anselm, in the twenty-seventh year of his age, came to Bec. There, under Herluin, founder and first abbot of that monastery, and under Lanfranc, its prior, he received the monastic habit. |
| 1063 | Alexander II | When Lanfranc had been appointed abbot of the monastery at Caen, Anselm became prior of the monastery of Bec. He wrote the *Monologion*, the *Proslogion*, *Against Gaunilo’s Reply on Behalf of the Fool*, *On Truth*, *On the Fall of the Devil*, *On the Freedom of Choice*, *On the Grammarian*, and the meditation beginning “I fear,” and others. |
| 1078 | Gregory VII | After Herluin had been taken from human affairs on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, Anselm was elected abbot. |
| 1079 | — | He was blessed in the church of Bec by Gislebert, bishop of Évreux. He departed for England. At Canterbury, in the assembly of the brethren, he delivered a sermon on fraternal charity. |
| 1088 | Urban II | King William I of England summoned Anselm to him as the illness from which the king shortly afterward died grew worse. Anselm went to the king, but, having himself fallen ill, could not be present at the king’s death. |

[Col. 0133]  

| Christian year | Supreme pontiffs | Events |
|---|---|---|
| 1090 | — | At the request of William, abbot of Fécamp, and Arnulf, abbot of Troarn, Anselm wrote about this time a homily on the passage “Jesus entered …,” which he had often delivered in the assembly of the brethren. |
| 1092 | — | He began the book or letter *On the Incarnation of the Word*. Summoned to England by Count Hugh of Chester, he set out and arrived at Canterbury on the day before the Nativity of Blessed Mary. |
| 1093 | — | Anselm was elected archbishop of Canterbury at Gloucester on the day before the Nones of March, the First Sunday of Lent.
