At Winchester he extinguished a fire by making the sign of the Cross. On the seventh day before the Kalends of October he entered Canterbury and ascended the pontifical see. There he was consecrated on the day before the Nones of December. |
| 1094 | — | King William demanded money from Anselm; Anselm refused to give it and withdrew from the royal court. He dedicated a church in a village called Berga. He assembled at Hastings with other bishops and nobles to bless the king, who was about to cross over to Normandy. While delayed there, he consecrated Robert of Lincoln. At the beginning of Lent, on Ash Wednesday, during the celebration of Mass, he preached against those who cultivated long hair. Many repented after having their hair cut; Anselm suspended the rest from receiving ashes and from the blessing of his absolution. He completed the book *On the Incarnation of the Word* and dedicated it to Urban II. He began to write the books *Why God Became Man*. |
| 1095 | — | On the fourth day before the Ides of June, Walter, bishop of Albano and legate of the apostolic see, brought Anselm the pallium. |
| 1096 | — | On the octave of Easter and on the octave of Pentecost, Anselm consecrated several bishops. He wrote the book *On the Marriages of Blood Relatives*. |
| 1097 | — | After asking for permission to go to Rome for the third time and being refused for the third time, Anselm left the king on the Ides of October. The following day he departed from Canterbury and reached the port of Dover; fifteen days later he boarded a ship and left England for Lyon. |
| 1098 | — | Anselm left Lyon on the Tuesday before Palm Sunday and reached Rome. Ten days later he withdrew to a village called Schlavium in the province of Campania. He completed the books *Why God Became Man*. He was present with Urban II at the siege of Capua. On the Kalends of October he attended the Council of Bari. There he disputed against the Greeks and, on bended knees, begged the fathers of the council not to excommunicate the king. |
| 1099 | — | Anselm attended the Roman council at which those who gave or received investitures were excommunicated, and so forth. He left Rome for Lyon; while staying there, he learned that Urban II had died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. There he wrote the book *On the Virgin Birth*, and so forth, and a meditation on human redemption. |
| 1100 | Paschal II | While staying at Cluny, he delivered a sermon *On the Blessedness of the Heavenly Homeland*; there he was informed of the death of William II, which had occurred in August of that year. He was recalled to England by Henry II and landed at Dover on the Kalends of October. He refused to do homage to the king. A postponement was granted in the matter until the following Easter. |
| 1101 | — | On the feast of Pentecost, England was disturbed by the return from Palestine of Robert, brother of Henry II. Anselm stood by King Henry. He wrote the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* and a letter *On Unleavened Bread* to Walerannus. |
| 1102 | — | Anselm summoned a council at London. He refused to consecrate bishops invested by the king. He wrote a letter *On the Diversity of the Sacraments* to Walerannus. |
| 1103 | — | After Easter, with the king’s consent, Anselm left England on the fifth day before the Kalends of May and came to Chartres. He celebrated Pentecost at Bec; after the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, he proceeded to Rome. Toward the end of November he left Rome and shortly before Christmas arrived at Lyon. |
| 1104 | — | He remained at Lyon until March of the following year. |
| 1105 | — | A Roman council was held under Paschal II. On the seventh day before the Kalends of April, it excommunicated the Count of Meulan. Anselm withdrew to the Cell of Charity of the Cluniac order; from there he went to Blois, to the countess, sister of Henry II. With her he came to a castle called L’Aigle, where, on the second day before the Kalends of August, he met with Henry II. He then stayed sometimes at Reims, sometimes at Bec. |
| 1106 | — | In the presence of Henry II, on the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, Anselm celebrated the solemn Mass at Bec. After settling matters with the king, he returned to England. |
| 1107 | — | From Easter until Pentecost, Anselm was detained by illness at the king’s court. On the Kalends of August, an English council was held; at it peace and liberty were restored to the Church. On the third day before the Ides of August, he consecrated several bishops. |
| 1108 | — | At the beginning of Lent, Anselm came to a place near London for a conference with the king. At Pentecost, the king discussed with him the incontinence of the clergy. After the royal court was dissolved, Anselm ordained several men at the village of Murtelac during the fast of the fourth month. After the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, he came to Canterbury. At Pagham he consecrated the bishop of London, and at Canterbury the bishop of Rochester. |
| 1109 | — | Anselm wrote the treatise *On the Will*, three questions *On the Agreement of Foreknowledge*, and so forth, and began to write *On the Origin of the Soul*. Engaged in these studies, Anselm, in the sixteenth year of his pontificate and the seventy-sixth year of his age, died a precious death at Canterbury. He lived three years in the world, three as a monk without office, fifteen as prior, fifteen as abbot, and sixteen as archbishop; when these years were completed, he died a blessed death. |

[Col. 0135]

# A Poem in Praise of Saint Anselm

[Col. 0135A]

Do not expect, gracious Father, a greeting equal  
to that which my Muse carries on uneven feet.  
That my Muse, writing to you, has no balanced feet  
is the result of the poverty of my talent.

The offspring of nobles ought to be praised in Homer’s metre.  
Forgive me: I feared to undertake so great a burden.  
I confess that I am weighed down by the greatness of the subject,  
and my Muse cannot bear the burden of this matter.

Even if my heart should cry out without ceasing,  
and my mouth should resound with a hundred voices;  
even if Apollo should sprinkle me from the Caballine spring,  
I alone would still not be enough to praise you.

You are a noble man, born of great parents,  
yet you surpass your lineage in nobility of character.  
Already your fame has filled both houses of the sun, [Col. 0135B]  
and the world rejoices to possess such a Father.

The northern axis knows you, and the southern,  
and no part of the world is without your merits.  
If the English land were not supported by your merits,  
it would collapse, shaken by the weight of its own vice.

By your merits, I confess, it both stands and will stand;  
and by your prayers it is enabled not to fall.  
Who does not know that you live according to the measure of righteousness?  
Who does not know that you possess the faith of the saints?

You chastise sinners with a gentle scourge;  
you yourself warn people lest they wish to sin.  
You rebuke those who profit from the sins of others.  
Before you as judge, truncated faith is deprived of its reward.

Before you as judge, the wealthy sinner lives as a pauper,  
and the wicked master is a sufficiently wretched servant. [Col. 0135C]  
Alone in this age, Father, you are worthy of praise in this age;  
alone, venerable man, you possess the measure of life.

Alone on earth you mourn the sins of the wicked;  
you alone are medicine for guilty men who fear.  
Because of these merits, and deservedly, Father most excellent,  
your name has been spread throughout the whole world.

Things that were once great perish by chance,  
and fate governs no one within a fixed limit.  
The man who was recently rich falls at fortune’s blow;  
and though I am what I am now, I do not think I shall be so for long.

Those whom the world’s glory leads astray do not attend to this,  
nor those whom an unsatisfied love of riches has deceived.  
But you, who look upon what has passed and what follows,  
know that what exists now will soon meet destruction. [Col. 0135D]

You believe that things which scarcely last for the space of one hour  
should be compared with everlasting goods.  
Whatever mortal thing is created obeys nature;  
what once existed now ceases to exist.

You too will be subject to death, but by a different course;  
nor will you yourself be placed among the rejected.  
When you exchange earth, you will possess heaven, [Col. 0136A]  
and yet you will remain a survivor upon the earth,

because the court of heaven will first receive you joyfully,  
and you will be established in the seat promised to you.  
I believe that no one will succeed to the reins of men  
who can govern them with your goodness.

When almighty God made the first human being foolish—*ἄβουλος*, “without counsel,” “incited by evil counsel” [Note: [Col. 0135D]—he willed you to be born in our time.  
Why, however, did he will this, unless he knew beforehand  
that you could prepare bridles for bloodstained wolves?

Look: the bloodstained wolf stands near and attacks  
the folds which remain secure while you keep watch.  
If by chance the savage wolf stains a sheep with his mouth,  
the sheep escapes the wolf’s jaws when you hasten to its aid.

If the storm of the world has driven someone to you,  
you repair the ship’s equipment so that it may not perish. [Col. 0136B]  
With divine weapons you strike the attacking enemy;  
with divine weapons the sheep rests safely.

Although you did not wish it, one of your sheep nevertheless perished;  
yet it does not perish entirely, if you are willing to keep watch.  
The one of whom I speak is the bleating priest Hugh.  
His own folly carried him away onto the rocks.

But since your compassion, Father, is a wall around the wretched,  
I beg that he may experience your help.  
That he is still alive, that his eyes have not been gouged out—  
who could deny that this is the result of your care?

For unless the savage fury of the wolves had feared you,  
the man whom prison does not hold would have been held by the cross.  
It is a grave matter, I confess, that the wretched man committed;  
but his grave fault does not exceed the possibility of pardon.

Who ever sinned more grievously than the first man? [Col. 0136C]  
Yet his guilt perished through pardon.  
I shall begin higher: who could be equal to Judas in crime?  
I think no pardon could accompany him.

Yet if, drenched in sacred bloodshed, he had repented,  
he who is compassionate toward all would not have been savage toward him.  
You say that one should place a hand beneath the drowning man,  
lest the wave that comes from the sea submerge him.

This man is sinking, struck by a great storm;  
and unless you hurry now, life is leaving him.  
Only his head emerges from all those waters;  
if it too is submerged, alas for me—his life is gone.

Therefore I beg you to come to the aid of his broken little boat,  
which can have no shore unless you grant one.  
Either your care, hastening to him, will heal him,  
or certainly he will never again be sound. [Col. 0136D]

He was supported by many powerful friends  
while the goddess who rules the world smiled upon him.  
But after she suddenly changed her smile into anger,  
they were not ashamed to turn their backs on him.

Some attack him without reason  
and refuse to acknowledge him because he acted foolishly. [Col. 0137A]  
Yet, I think, when he was able to avoid the ruin,  
they ought to have said to him: “Take this road.”

Now that his ship is broken, what good is it to tell him:  
“You ought to have sailed more cautiously across this sea”?

Since, then, you are the common protector of the guilty,  
holy Father, I beg you to protect this guilty man. [Col. 0138A]  
Holy worshiper of God, fountain of faith, lover of the flock,  
hope, honor, help, life, and salvation of men,

I shall say what you are:  
the asylum of the whole homeland.  
Unfallen ladder of heaven, farewell.

[Col. 0137A]

# Funeral Poem on His Death

Our poem desires to be suited to the praises  
of the prelate Anselm, whose recent death we mourn.  
Yet something about so great an undertaking deters me,  
lest a beloved subject fail to love my talent.

Nevertheless, trusting in Christ’s gift, [Col. 0137B]  
I shall attempt to say what I can about the man’s goodness.  
He was an exceedingly precious, useful, and noble thing,  
a distinguished, wise, and upright man.

Known and unknown, wise and foolish alike,  
the whole world loved him equally.  
His love was sweet and carried no weariness;  
whatever anyone loved him for seemed too little.

And, to make his possession of virtue seem even more remarkable,  
he was held dear even by his own enemies.  
There were indeed men [Note: [Col. 0137D] The king and his accomplices.]  
whom his cause troubled; nevertheless they praised him as good.

Whatever they disliked about him  
was plainly their error, not his.  
His whole life—for what could so great a man possess that was evil?—[Col. 0137C]  
was a sweet fragrance of goodness.

It is difficult to believe how greatly that man shone,  
and no tongue can adequately recount it for you.  
God himself knows that I hope to speak the truth  
and do not wish, in praising the man, to deceive anyone.

For I call Jesus to witness, and empty opinion does not mislead me:  
he had led his days with sufficient innocence.  
Whom did he injure by his speech except one whom he thought had sinned?  
And even this—how soberly and devoutly he did it!

Who received a harsh insult from his mouth?  
Who could say that he mocked anyone?  
Whom did he treat badly or unjustly provoke to anger?  
Whom did he harm while living through his own deceit?

It would not have been much to lead a life without crime  
if it had not also been full of the beauty of virtue. [Col. 0137D]  
If it pleases you, listen to how precious that holiest of men was  
by the merit of his virtues.

Yet it is uncertain—because great abundance confounds us—  
what I should say first and what afterward.  
You might see someone enter a pleasant field in springtime  
to gather flowers.

He thinks, “Shall I pluck this one?” But that one is much more beautiful.  
“Shall I pick that one?” But others surpass it.  
For a long time, not knowing what to do, he desires them all;  
he marvels and does not know which one to choose.

So I, turning over within myself for a long time  
the many things that ought to be said,  
think of the many things I should like to recount.  
Finally, if I report with what splendor of wisdom

that man shone, who will believe me?  
Unless I am mistaken, he surpassed all the eminent and chosen men  
whom we see in our present age.

If you do not believe me, at least his little works [Col. 0138B]  
will not be able, once seen, to deny me credibility.  
Whoever wishes to read the little books he wrote  
will perceive there how wise he was.

And rightly was he wise, since he always loved Christ  
and never offered obedience to wickedness.  
For that wisdom is proved pleasing to God  
which forbids vice and teaches justice.

But concerning the justice in which he flourished more fully,  
I think the time has come to say something.  
Oh, how just he was, since he feared no adversity  
and loved prosperity no more than was sufficient.

Among all the things we see in the world,  
there was nothing that could force him through frivolity into vice.  
Among the riches he possessed sufficiently,  
he was full of virtues but poor in material things. [Col. 0138C]

He lived for himself in such a way  
that you would have thought he possessed nothing.  
He clung to the world in body, not in spirit.  
Weighing everything prudently and courageously,  
he did not wish to displease God.

Remaining between the two, he handled everything with moderation.  
He hated whatever was excessive in excess.  
There are, however, some who may perhaps criticize me  
because I have raised him so high with such praises.

For they will say: “He ought not to have been raised so high,  
since he was excessively simple and indulgent;  
since, as we read, like a deceived dove,  
which is quickly tricked, he was without understanding;

since, as a prelate, he did not strive sufficiently to forbid wrongdoing,  
nor rebuke the wretched conduct of the people;  
since he did not utter a worthy bark from his discerning mouth, [Col. 0138D]  
but showed himself to be a mute dog;

since he did not guard the sheepfold entrusted to him,  
but rather gave wrongdoing room by concealing it.”

O utterly insane, headlong audacity of mind!  
O blind fury, puffed up in place of piety!  
Who are you that you can condemn another man’s servant?  
Every human being is subject not to you but to the Lord.

What good does it do if you see others with a sharp eye,  
when you yourself do not see your own mist?  
Look back at your own heart, you who thus attack sins;  
everything done there will appear black. [Col. 0139A]

You will scarcely be able to discern your own life  
if you alone condemn whatever others do.  
It is no obstacle to the talkative to pursue idleness.  
The inactive man knows how to mourn the fault of one who fights.

Spare, wretched man, to tear the just with a dog’s bite;  
do not attribute to the innocent the harm done by the wicked.  
Unfamiliar with truth, she despises treaties, laws, and faith;  
she hates a superior and does not love an equal.

When, then, would such people be pleased to have a teacher  
who would correct the untamed habits of human beings,  
who would teach that it is not good to despise the law,  
who would preach and uphold the commandments of God?

Moreover, when did he fail to urge people to fear God?  
Or when was God absent from his mouth?  
If he had sent away empty-handed someone he knew wished to be taught, [Col. 0139B]  
then you could justly have been displeased with him.

If, when anyone asked him for a word about any matter,  
he had not immediately given a full answer,  
it would be exceedingly unworthy if I wished  
either to criticize you without cause or to magnify him falsely.

But what harm will it do if I describe a deed,  
one that truly proves his pontifical merit?  
It is clear to many that royal commands wanted  
something to be done which divine law teaches to be less than good.

But the prelate bravely resisted this  
and repeatedly forbade it to be done.  
Thus, at last, by the command of the law,  
it was established that he should be guilty of exile.

What would the prudence of a holy mind do after this?  
Would he despise God at the king’s command? [Col. 0139C]  
Therefore he preferred to withdraw from his position  
rather than subject his neck to a sinful man against the will of God.

Why delay? He was driven from his homeland  
and, suffering exile, was compelled to travel distant roads.  
This happened once, and again, compelled by love of virtue;  
he deserved to wage a happy battle.

There is also, I confess, something wonderful to relate  
that enlarges the title of our prelate.  
For who would not approve that, although he was more worthy  
than all, he nevertheless preferred to be inferior?

No one is more inferior than one subject to an inferior,  
who judges himself not equal even to the least.  
Thus, as a cultivator and guardian of his own salvation,  
he had as many masters as he had servants, [Col. 0139D]

considering it more beneficial for himself,  
after abandoning his own will,  
to run submissively according to another’s judgment.

Praise belongs to the Lord alone, from whose gift  
such great grace of virtue came to this man.  
Blessed is the man whom it is pious to praise  
and salutary to remember.

For such remembrance will be an act of piety.  
But I confess my fault, because both my understanding and my hand,  
at least in what I know how to write, fail me.  
Much is hidden from me; for who could think he knew  
everything that man had done throughout his life?

Indeed, by a certain reckoning, he was dearer  
than any human being could fully perceive.  
Nor does he seem deserving of being deprived of praise  
who was worthy of receiving so much praise.

Why, moreover, do you marvel if he could not immediately drive  
the great crime from an unjust people? [Col. 0140A]  
Cease marveling. It is God who judges the world.  
It is not a human being but God himself who draws our hearts.

To rebuke evil or give words of salvation  
to one who has gone astray is something anyone among humankind can do;  
but neither planting nor watering what has been planted accomplishes anything  
unless God himself gives the increase.

Whomever God hardens, no human care will make gentle;  
without God’s command, no human being has any power.  
The shoots of the human mind will always be dry  
unless God moistens them with his own dew.

This, then, was such a man, so faithful a lover of what is honorable;  
this was the leader of faith and the glory of the Church;  
this was the ram driving away the enemy with twin horns;  
this was the vine, the branch, the fragrance of piety; [Col. 0140B]

this was the stone glowing in the image of the eternal King.  
He left behind a great burden: the remains of his body.

Alas, how mournfully, with what abundant grief,  
the mind recalls the funeral rites of so great a prelate!  
Oh, how precious he was, how useful to so many!  
Therefore his death weighs heavily upon many.

Happy Italy, before all the regions of the world,  
which deserved to bring forth such a man.  
Unhappy again, because it loses such a foster-son;  
utterly unhappy, deprived of its own pledge.

You too, once-thriving monastery of Bec,  
flourished while your Anselm was both leader and monk.  
Your appearance almost lost its former beauty  
when your Anselm ceased to be Father.

Canterbury, once venerable throughout the whole world, [Col. 0140C]  
you displayed your glory in the time of the prelate Anselm.  
The world was less than you; your fame spread through all peoples,  
welcome to the good and hateful to the wicked.

Monks, clergy, and people who needed instruction  
came to you while your good Anselm lived.  
There was no one on earth who wished to say:  
“Anselm is less than I, or like me.”

Now your brow is drawn down, covered with rough wrinkles;  
now your bowed neck suffers a wretched collapse,  
though once it was like a lofty tower.  
Now you lie uncultivated, deprived of so great a shepherd,  
as great as no other holy man remains in the world.

When he died, the religious faith of the mother Church  
suffered many losses at the same time. [Col. 0140D]  
For there appears to have been no sex, no age,  
to which his goodness could not have given aid.

Happy the man followed by so many sweet prayers of the people,  
commended by so many and redeemed by so many tears.  
This death brought common grief to many;  
the death of one became a public punishment.

What are we—what are we, wretched men who bear the name of monks?  
This grief will always be our own.  
He was the ornament of our order, its leader and pathway,  
its chariot and charioteer, its harbor and its breeze.

In him our greatest hope of life has escaped us,  
and no one like him remains,  
no one who could bless us with equal honor  
and raise our head as he did. [Col. 0141A]

O Father Anselm, O pontifical glory,  
O honor, O light, O devout prelate, farewell.  
You have now deserved to overcome the world’s varied disturbances;  
now you remain secure in a peaceful dwelling.

You hasten into the embraces and kisses of the heavenly King.  
From now on there will be no end to your honor: [Col. 0142A]  
you always have Christ, whom you always wished to have;  
Christ will always be your single portion.

Songs of joy are never absent from you,  
and without end you sing: “Great glory to God.”

Amen.

[Col. 0141A]

# Threefold Epitaph of Saint Anselm

*(From the manuscript of the Victorines and the manuscript of Bec.)*

[Col. 0141B]

## I

Noble and wise, good and radiant in speech,  
abbot of Bec, afterward prelate of Canterbury;  
renowned for intellect, deeply learned in Scripture,  
well instructed in natural philosophy, logic, and moral matters;

an arranger of things, a frequent observer of truth;  
writing down what he contemplated in polished composition;  
sound in counsel, and a giver to the needy;  
concerned for himself, yet becoming all things to all people;

wishing to save himself, but unwilling to put others second;  
a despiser of the world, a perfect lover of Christ;  
watering his face with tears through the heart’s great sweetness;  
sorrowful with the sorrowful, joyful with the joyful;

rigid toward the unjust, gentle as a lamb toward the meek;  
quickly granting the fulfillment of a request;  
generously giving to one who desired what was right,  
scarcely demanding others’ goods for himself;

composed in his actions, grave and witty in speech;  
accomplishing many miracles through his prayers; [Col. 0141C]  
a despiser of praise, endowed with so many qualities worthy of esteem.

Released from the flesh on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May,  
Anselm is believed to have been joined to the heavenly beings.

## II

*(From the manuscript of the Victorines and the manuscript of Bec.)*

If you wish to know what you are and what you will be, reader,  
you can learn it from me, if you know my fate.  
Believe that this same fate is prepared for you,  
since the substance of a human being is earth, ashes, and matter. [Col. 0142B]

Religion, moral uprightness, and the splendor of ancestors,  
learning, delights, bodily form, and the face—  
if these could make one live, my limbs would not lie here,  
confined in this house. Thus it will be for every human being.

## III

*(From manuscript 30 of the Thuani.)*

Whoever strives to embrace a disciplined life,  
look upon this man distinguished by his merits.  
He offers a living mirror for your conduct.  
Stand beside this man; hasten to follow him.

Here, halt your step, you who run toward impious acts,  
restraining your horse with the bridle of justice after this man’s example.  
Sanctifying grace made him, holy in mind, bright and pure in body,  
its own inner sanctuary.

The glory and honor of the world, things driven suddenly by chance,  
became displeasing to the man who sought heavenly things.  
He judges that whatever falls in time must be rejected,  
teaching that the highest things are to be sought in mind, hand, and tongue. [Col. 0142C]

With the radiance of virtues he adorned the regions of the cosmos.  
Shining with sacred light, he drives away our clouds.

Let the envious enemy grieve that this man reigns above the ether,  
since, defeated, he returns to the depths;  
let the heavenly beings yield to him, while the court of heaven applauds.  
Let the Church, exulting, proclaim his titles.

Let the earth rejoice, supported by so illustrious a patron,  
and let the starry axis rejoice in possessing so great a companion.  
This standard-bearer of God, granted the honor of a trophy,  
this standard-bearer of God teaches the weapons of faith.

[Col. 0141C]

# The First Part of the Works of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury: Dogmatic Works

[Col. 0141C]

# On the Essence of Divinity: The *Monologion*

[Note: [Col. 0141C] The *Monologion* has been collated with the manuscripts of Jumièges, Corbie, Séez 16, Saint Michael in the Mount, the Thuani manuscripts 30 and 90, the Victorine manuscripts RR 13 and EE 13, and the Cistercian manuscript. A manuscript begins: “Prologue to the book *Monologion* of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.” The Cistercian manuscript begins: “Preface to Anselm’s *Monologion*.”]

## 1–3. Preface

Here Anselm discusses the essence of divinity by way of meditation, not on the authority of Scripture but by the force of arguments. He said nothing inconsistent with the writings of the holy Fathers, especially blessed Augustine. When, in chapter 76, he said that the Trinity could be called three substances—that is, three persons—he was speaking in agreement with the Greeks.

Certain brothers often and earnestly begged me [Col. 0143A] to write down, under a certain example of meditation, certain matters which I had set before them in ordinary conversation concerning the divine essence to be meditated upon, together with certain other matters connected with that meditation [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Certain matters concerning them which concerning” in MSS Gem., Corb., Sag., Vict., and Cister. (a corrupt or incomplete reading); “connected with this meditation” in MSS Cister., Vict. 3, Gem., Corb., Sag., and S. Mich.; “connected with a meditation of this kind” in the same witnesses; “under some example of it” in one manuscript; “under some example for them” in another]. They prescribed for me the following form for writing this meditation—more in accordance with their will than with the practicability of the matter [Note: [Col. 0143C] “The capacity of the matter” in the MSS.; “the practicability of the matter”] or my own ability [Note: [Col. 0143C] “They prescribed the form” in the MSS.; “they prescribed for me the form”]: namely, that absolutely nothing in it should be established by the authority of Scripture; rather, whatever the conclusion of each investigation affirmed should be compelled briefly by the necessity of reason, and displayed openly by the clarity of truth, in plain style, with common arguments [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Augmentations” for “arguments” in MSS Vict., Sag., and S. Mich. and the Cologne edition of 1572] and simple disputation [Note: [Col. 0143C] “The clarity of truth” is altered to the accusative “the clarity of truth” in the MSS.]. They also wished me not to disdain meeting even simple and almost foolish objections [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Almost foolish” in MS Cister.; “not foolish” in the variant reading].

For a long time I refused to attempt this, and, considering the matter carefully with myself, tried to excuse myself on many grounds: for the easier they found the use of what they requested and desired for themselves, the more difficult they imposed its execution upon me. At last, however, I was overcome both by the modest persistence of their requests and by the commendable seriousness of their study. Reluctantly, because of the difficulty of the matter and the weakness of my intellect, I began what they were asking; but willingly, because of their affection, I completed it as far as I could, according to their own [Note: [Col. 0143C] “I was able, among them” in the MSS.; “I completed it as far as I could, according to their own”] definition.

Since I was led to this with the expectation that whatever I did would be known only to those who had demanded it [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Whatever I did alone” in the MSS.; “whatever I did for them alone” in MS S. Mich.; “whatever I did for them alone”], and that shortly afterward it would be buried in contempt as a worthless thing by those who had grown tired of it [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Would be contemptuously buried” in the MSS.; “would be buried in contempt” in MS Thuan.], I know that in this I was able not so much to satisfy those who asked as to bring to an end the prayers with which they pressed me [Col. 0143C] [Note: [Col. 0143C] “I know that in this I was not so much able to satisfy those asking as to bring to an end the prayers” in MS Corb.; “You know that in this I was not so much able to satisfy those asking as…”]. Yet somehow, contrary to expectation, it turned out that not only the brothers mentioned above, but also many others, endeavored to commit the work itself to lasting memory by copying it out for themselves [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Into permanence” in the MSS. Corb. and Vict. 13; “into length”].

When I repeatedly reconsidered it [Note: [Col. 0143C] “When I often examined it” in the MSS.; “when I repeatedly reconsidered it”], I could find nothing in it that I had said which was not consistent with the writings of the Catholic Fathers, and especially those of blessed Augustine. Therefore, if anyone should think that in this little work I have put forward something either excessively novel or contrary to the truth, I ask that he not immediately denounce me as an advocate of novelties [Note: [Col. 0143C] “As an advocate of novelties” in the MSS.; “as a presumptuous advocate of novelties”] or an assertor of falsehood; instead, let him first examine carefully the books of the aforesaid teacher Augustine [Note: [Col. 0143C] “The books of blessed Augustine” in the MSS.; “the books of the aforesaid Doctor Augustine”] on the Trinity [Col. 0144A] [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Let him examine” in the MSS. Gem., Corb., Vict. 13; “let him look into”], and then judge my little work in accordance with them.

For when I said that the supreme Trinity could be called three substances, I followed the Greeks, who confess three substances in one essence [Note: [Col. 0143C] “That there are three substances in one essence” in the MSS.; MS Cister. omits “there are” and omits “substances”], with the same faith with which we confess three persons in one substance [Note: [Col. 0143C] “In one person” in MS Vict. 3; “in one essence”]. For in God they signify by “substance” what we signify by “person.”

Whatever else I said there [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Whatever I said” in the MSS.; “whatever I said there”] was expressed in the person of someone arguing and investigating these matters in thought by himself, as though he were considering things he had not previously noticed—just as I knew those wished who were asking me and whose request I intended to fulfill. I earnestly beg and implore anyone who wishes to copy this little work to place this preface at the beginning of the booklet, before the chapters themselves. For I think it will be of great assistance in understanding what he reads there, if he first learns with what intention and in what manner the arguments were conducted [Col. 0144B]. I also think that, if anyone sees this very preface first, he will not rashly pass judgment if he finds something expressed contrary to his own opinion [Note: [Col. 0143C] “If he finds something expressed both against…” in the MSS.; “both” omitted].

[Note: [Col. 0143C] MS Sag.: “An example of meditating on the reason of faith.” MS Vict. 3: “Here begins the Monologion, the book of Anselm.” MS Vict. 13: “Here begins Anselm’s Monologion, archbishop.” MS S. Mich.: “Here begins the book of Anselm’s Monologion.” MS Cister.: “Here begins Anselm’s Monologion.”]

## CHAPTER ONE

### That there is something which is the best, the greatest, and the supreme of all things that exist

[Note: “That there is a certain thing” in the manuscripts, in place of “something.”]

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

Reason alone can persuade us to a considerable extent that there exists one supreme nature, sufficient to itself, from whose omnipotent goodness all other things derive the fact that they are, as well as many other things that we believe concerning God. The most straightforward method of investigating the supreme nature is the following.

We desire only what we believe to be good, and by reason we discern that there are many good things. It is utterly certain that whatever is said to be something, in such a way that things are said of one another to be more, less, or equally so, is said through something that is understood not as one thing and another, but as the same thing in the different things that participate in that one thing. Therefore, all things must be good through something that is one and the same in different good things. Thus there is one thing through which all things are good, and in which different good things agree.

Who, then, would doubt that that very thing through which all things are good is itself a great good, and is good through itself? Therefore all other good things are good through something else, while that alone is good through itself. But what is good through another is less than that which is good through itself. Therefore what is good through itself is supremely good, and the supreme of all things that exist; for what is supremely good is supremely great. There is therefore one thing that is supremely great and supremely good—that is, the supreme of all things that exist.

If anyone is unaware—whether because he has not heard or because he does not believe—that there is one supreme nature among all things that exist, sufficient by itself in its own eternal blessedness, and that by its omnipotent goodness it gives and makes all other things be what they are or be good in some way [Note: [Col. 0143C] “And sufficient” in MS Corb.; “sufficient”], together with many other things that we necessarily believe concerning God or his creation, he may think that, if he possesses even an average intellect [Note: [Col. 0145C] “If he has an intellect” in MS Corb.; MS Corb. omits “is”], he can persuade himself of these things, at least by reason alone [Note: [Col. 0145C] MS Corb. omits “he himself”].

Although he can do this in many ways, I shall present one method that I judge to be the most straightforward. Since everyone desires to enjoy only those things that he believes to be good, it is easy for him at some point to turn the eye of his mind toward investigating the source of the goodness of those very things he desires only because he judges them to be good. Then, with reason leading and with himself following it, he may advance rationally toward those matters that he irrationally fails to understand [Note: [Col. 0145C] MS Sag.: “He may advance. Since he can do this in many ways, I think this method is the most straightforward and easiest for him, so that he may say silently to himself: Since there are so many innumerable…”].

If, however, I say anything for which greater authority does not provide evidence [Note: [Col. 0145C] The MSS.: “does not show”; “does not show”], I wish it to be accepted in this way: even if what appears to me to be concluded as necessary from these arguments is presented as such, it should nevertheless not for that reason be said to be altogether necessary, but only to appear for the time being to be so.

It is easy, then, for someone to say silently to himself: Since there are so many good things, whose great diversity we experience both through bodily senses and distinguish by the reasoning of the mind, ought we to believe that there is one thing through which all things that are good are one [Note: [Col. 0145C] “They are one” in MSS Gem., Corb., and Vict.; “they may be one” in the received text], or are some things good through one thing and others through another?

It is perfectly certain and clear to everyone willing to pay attention that whatever is said to be something, so that things are said of one another to be more, less, or equally so [Note: [Col. 0145C] MS Corb.: “Whatever is said to be something, so that things are said of one another to be more … are said through another thing, which is understood not as one thing and another, but…”; another form reads, “whatever is said to be something, so that things are said of one another to be more … is said through something that is understood not as one thing, but…”], is said through something that is understood as the same thing in different things, whether it is considered equally or unequally in them [Col. 0145C] [Note: [Col. 0145C] MS Gem., Sag., Vict. 3, S. Mich., and Cister.: “Whatever is said to be something, so that things are said of one another to be more … is said through something …”; MSS Thuan. and Vict. 13: “Whatever is said in relation to something, so that things are said of one another to be more … is said through something…”].

For whatever things are said to be just in relation to one another, whether equally or more or less, cannot be understood as just except through justice, which is not one thing and another in different things. Therefore, since it is certain that all good things, when compared with one another, are good either equally or unequally [Note: [Col. 0145C] “Or are unequally good” in MS Vict. 3; the latter phrase is omitted], all must be good through something that is understood as the same in different good things [Note: [Col. 0145C] “In different good things” in MS Corb.; “good things” omitted], even though at times they appear to be called good through different things.

A horse appears to be called good through one thing because it is strong, and good through another because it is swift. Although it appears to be called good through strength and good through swiftness, strength and swiftness nevertheless do not appear to be the same thing. But if a horse is good because it is strong and swift [Note: [Col. 0145C] “Or swift, it is good” in the MSS.], why is a strong and swift robber evil? Rather, just as a strong and swift robber is evil because he is harmful [Note: [Col. 0145C] “Is evil because” in the MSS. Gem., Corb., Vict., Sag., and Cister.; “is therefore evil because”], so a strong and swift horse is good because it is useful.

Indeed, nothing is usually thought good except either on account of some usefulness, as health is called good, along with the things that benefit health, or on account of some form of moral excellence, as beauty is considered good, along with the things that enhance beauty. But since the reasoning already established cannot be overturned in any way [Note: [Col. 0145C] “Perfect reasoning” in the Venetian edition; “established reasoning”], it is necessary that everything useful or honorable, if it is truly good, should also be good through that very thing through which all things must be good, whatever that may be [Note: [Col. 0145C] “To be good through itself” in MSS Vict. and Sag.; “to be good through that very thing”].

Who, then, would doubt that that very thing through which all things are good is a great good? [Col. 0146B] It is therefore good through itself, since every good is good through it. It follows, then, that all other good things are good through something other than what they themselves are [Note: [Col. 0145C] “Other than what they themselves are: and…” in MS Corb.; “other than what they themselves are”; MSS Thuan. and others read “and” differently], while it alone is good through itself. But no good that is good through another is equal to or greater than that good which is good through itself. Therefore that alone is supremely good which alone is good through itself [Note: [Col. 0145C] “Therefore it is supremely good” in the MSS.; “therefore that alone is supremely good”].

For that is supreme which so surpasses others that it has neither an equal nor anything superior to it [Note: [Col. 0145C] “Which surpasses others through itself, so that…” in the MSS.]. But what is supremely good is also supremely great. There is therefore one thing that is supremely great and supremely good—that is, the supreme of all things that exist.

## CHAPTER TWO

### On the same subject

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

Just as there is one thing that is supremely good, because all good things are good through one thing that is good through itself, so there exists one thing that is supremely great, because whatever things are great are great through one thing that is great through itself. By “great” I do not mean spatially extended, as a body is, but wisdom, which is better and more worthy.

Just as it was discovered that there is something supremely good, since all good things are good through one thing that is good through itself [Note: [Col. 0145C] “One thing” in the Venetian edition: “some one thing”], so it is necessarily inferred that there is something supremely great, since whatever things are great are great through one thing that is great through itself. I mean not something great in spatial extent, as some body is, [Col. 0147A] but something such that the greater it is, the better or more worthy it is [Note: [Col. 0147C] MS Gem., Corb., Thu., and S. Mich.: “But something such that the greater it is, the better or more worthy it is”; MSS Vict. and Sag.: “But something that is better or more worthy in proportion to its greatness”; MS Cister.: “But the greater it is, the better or more worthy it is”], as wisdom is. And since nothing can be supremely great unless it is supremely good, there must be something greatest and best—that is, the supreme of all things that exist.

## CHAPTER THREE

### That there is a certain nature through which whatever exists exists, which exists through itself and is the supreme of all things that exist

[Note: MS S. Mich.: “Which exists through itself and is supreme”; MSS Thuan.: “And which exists through itself and is supreme”; MS Sag.: “Which exists through itself and is the supreme”; other manuscripts: “Which exists through itself and is supreme.”]

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

Everything that exists exists either through something or through nothing. It does not exist through nothing; therefore it exists through something. But that through which all things exist is either one thing or many. If many, these many things exist individually through themselves; and thus there is one principle or power through which these many things have their being through themselves. Therefore there is one thing through which whatever exists exists, and that alone exists through itself.

Nothing exists through one another—not the things that are related, nor the relations themselves. But what exists through another is less than that which exists through itself. Therefore there is one thing that alone exists most greatly and supremely of all, and that exists as supremely good and supremely great, since through it whatever is good, great, or anything at all exists.

Finally, not only are all good things good through the same thing, and all great things great through the same thing; whatever exists also appears to exist through one thing. For everything that exists exists either through something [Note: [Col. 0147C] “Or through something” in the MSS.; “or exists through something”] or through nothing; but nothing exists through nothing. For it cannot even be conceived that something should exist without existing through something [Note: [Col. 0147C] MS Corb.: “For it does not exist, nor can it be conceived that, if it is something…”; MSS Gem. and Thu.: “For it does not wish to be conceived that, if it is something…”; MSS Vict.: “For it cannot even be conceived that something should exist…”].

Whatever exists, therefore, exists only through something. Since this is so, either there is one thing through which all existing things exist, or there are several. But if there are several, either they themselves are related to one thing through which they exist, or the same several things exist individually through themselves, or they themselves exist through one another [Note: [Col. 0147C] MS Corb.: “They exist individually through themselves, or they exist through one another”].

If these several things exist through one thing, then all things do not exist through several things, but rather through that one thing through which these several things exist [Note: [Col. 0147C] MS Corb. omits “one”; “through which several things exist”]. If, however, these several things exist individually through themselves, then there is certainly one power or nature of existing through oneself, by which they have it that they exist through themselves [Note: [Col. 0147C] “By which they have it that they exist through themselves” in the MSS.; MS Corb. reads “by which they themselves become through themselves” and omits the intervening words]. There is no doubt that they are one through that same thing through which they have it that they exist through themselves. Therefore all things exist more truly through that one thing than through several things that cannot exist without that one.

But that several things should exist through one another is permitted by no rational account. It is an irrational thought that something should exist through that to which it gives existence. For even relative things do not exist through one another in this way [Note: [Col. 0147C] MS Corb.: “Exist through one another”]. Although master and servant are related to one another, the men who are related in this way do not exist through one another at all; nor do the relations through which they are related exist through one another at all, since those relations exist through their subjects [Note: [Col. 0147C] “They are the same through their subjects” in the MSS.].

Since truth therefore entirely excludes the possibility that there are several things through which all things exist [Note: [Col. 0147C] “Through which all things exist”], it is necessary that there be one thing through which all existing things exist. Since all things that exist exist through this one thing, undoubtedly this one thing itself exists through itself. Therefore all other things exist through another, while it alone exists through itself.

But whatever exists through another is less than that through which all other things exist and which alone exists through itself. Therefore that which exists through itself exists most greatly of all. There is therefore one thing that alone exists most greatly and supremely of all. But that which exists most greatly of all, and through which whatever is good or great exists—and indeed whatever is anything at all—is necessarily supremely good, supremely great, and the supreme of all things that exist.

Therefore there is something that may be called essence, substance, or nature, which is the best and greatest and the supreme of all things that exist.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### On the same subject

[Note: [Col. 0147C] MS Corb.: “On the same subject. That, just as it exists through itself and other things through it, so it exists from itself and other things from it.” MSS Thu. and Cister.: “That it was not brought into being with the aid of any cause, nor is it through nothing or from nothing, and how it can be understood to exist through itself and from itself.”]

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

Not all natures are equal in dignity; some are better than others. Therefore there is one nature that so surpasses the rest that it has none superior to it; otherwise the multitude of natures would have no limit, which is absurd. The superior nature is either alone or there are several equal natures. If there are several, they are equal only through something identical that constitutes their essence. For if they were equal through something else, they would be less than that thing and consequently would not be supreme or superior to the rest.

Therefore there is one nature or essence that is the supreme of all things that exist; that is good and great through itself; that exists through itself as what it is; and through which whatever is good, great, or anything at all exists.

Moreover [Note: [Col. 0147C] MS Cister. omits “moreover”], if anyone directs his attention to the natures of things, whether he wishes to or not, he perceives that they are not all contained within an equality of dignity [Note: [Col. 0147C] “Equality” in MS Cister.; “likeness of rank”]. For who would doubt that, in its own nature, a horse is better than wood, and a human being superior to a horse? Anyone who doubts this surely ought not to be called a human being.

Since it cannot be denied that some natures are better than others [Note: [Col. 0147C] “Cannot be denied” in the MSS.; “cannot be denied”], reason nevertheless persuades us that one of them so surpasses the others [Col. 0149A] that it has none superior to it. For if this distinction of ranks [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Of these ranks” in the MSS.] is infinite, so that there is no rank there [Note: [Col. 0149C] MS Cister. omits “there is”] beyond which another higher rank cannot be found, reason is led [Note: [Col. 0149C] “From this reason” in the MSS.] to the conclusion that the multitude of natures has no limit. But everyone considers this absurd, except one who is himself excessively absurd.

Therefore, necessarily, there is some nature that is superior to one or more others in such a way that there is none to which it is inferior. This nature, being such, is either alone, or there are several such natures and they are equal. But if there are several and they are equal, they cannot be equal through different things, but through one and the same thing. That one thing through which they are equally great is either identical with what they themselves are—that is, their very essence—or it is something other than what they are [Col. 0149B].

If it is nothing other than their essence, then, just as their essences are not several but one, so their natures are not several but one. For here I understand “nature” to mean the same as “essence.” If, however, that through which these several natures are so great is something other than what they are, then they are certainly less than that through which they are great. For whatever is great through another is less than that through which it is great. Therefore they are not so great that nothing else is greater than they are.

If it is impossible for several natures to be such either through what they are or through something else [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Neither through what they are nor through another” in MS Corb.], that nothing is superior to them [Note: [Col. 0149C] “That nothing is superior” in the MSS.], then in no way can there be several natures of this kind [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Several such natures”]. It remains, therefore, that there is one and only one nature that is superior to the others in such a way that it is inferior to none. But what is such is the greatest and best of all things that exist [Note: [Col. 0149C] The MSS. continue: “... that exist. Therefore there is a certain nature that is the supreme of all things that exist. But this…”]. Therefore there is a certain nature that is the supreme of all things that exist. But this [Note: [Col. 0149C] The MSS. repeat: “... that exist. Therefore there is a certain nature that is the supreme of all things that exist. But this…”] cannot be unless it exists through itself as what it is, and all things that exist exist through it as what they are. For since reason shortly before demonstrated that what exists through itself, and through which all other things exist, is the supreme of all existing things [Col. 0150A], either, conversely, what is supreme exists through itself and all other things through it, or there will be several supreme things. But it is evident that there are not several supreme things [Note: [Col. 0149C] “That there are not several” in the MSS.; “that there are not several supreme things”].

Therefore there is a certain nature, substance, or essence that is good and great through itself [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Good or great” in the MSS. Thu.; “good and great”], that exists through itself as what it is [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Exists through itself as what it is” in MS Thu.; “exists through itself as this is what it is”], and through which whatever is truly good, great, or anything at all exists [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Great or anything” in MS Vict.]. It is the supreme good, the supreme great, the supreme being or subsistent [Note: [Col. 0149C] “The supreme great and supreme good, the supreme being or existent” in the MSS.]—that is, the supreme of all things that exist.

## CHAPTER FIVE

[Note: [Col. 0149C] In some copies this is part of Chapter Four. In MSS Gem., Corb., Thuan., and Cister., Chapter Five begins here under this title. MSS Gem., Thuan., and Cister. give the title: “That just as it exists through itself and other things through it, so it exists from itself and other things from it.” MS Corb.: “How all other things exist through it and from it.” MS Cister. reads “Since thus” for “Since therefore.”]

### That just as it exists through itself and other things through it, so it exists from itself and other things from it

Since this has been established, it is worth investigating whether this nature itself, and all things that are anything at all, exist only from it [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Do not exist except from it” in the MSS.], just as they exist only through it [Col. 0150B] [Note: [Col. 0149C] In MS Corb.: “But it may be said that whatever is from something is also through that same thing—that is, whatever is through something is also from that very thing, as…”; another reading: “But it may be said that what is from something is also through that very thing, and what is through something is also from that very thing, as…”].

But it is clear that it can be said that whatever is from something is also through that very thing, and whatever is through something is also from that very thing. Thus what is from matter and through an artisan can also be said to be through matter and from the artisan; for through both, and from both—that is, from each—it has its being, although it is through matter and from matter in one way, and through the artisan and from the artisan in another [Note: [Col. 0149C] MS Corb. expands: “What is from matter and through an artisan can also be said to be through matter and from the artisan, since it has its being through both and from both, although it is through matter in one way…”].

It follows, then, that just as all things that exist are what they are through the supreme nature, and therefore that nature exists through itself while other things exist through another, so everything that exists is from the same supreme nature; and therefore that nature exists from itself, while other things exist from it [Note: [Col. 0149C] “Consequently, therefore” in the MSS.; “whatever exists is from” in the MSS., for “whatever exists is from”; “therefore it is from itself” in the MSS., for “therefore it exists from itself.”]

## CHAPTER SIX [in other copies, Chapter Five]

[Note: [Col. 0149C] It is Chapter Five in MSS Corb., Gem., Thuan., and Cister.]

### That it was not brought into being with the aid of any cause; yet it is not through nothing or from nothing; and how it can be understood to exist through itself and from itself

[Note: [Col. 0149C] MS Corb.: “How it should be understood that it made all things from nothing.”]

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

How should the supreme nature be said to exist through itself? For whatever exists through something appears to exist either through an efficient cause, through matter, or through an instrument. But what exists in any of these ways exists through another and is consequently less than that through which it has its being. The supreme nature, however, exists neither through another nor as less than or posterior to itself or to anything else.

Therefore the supreme nature cannot be made either by itself or by another; nor was it itself the matter from which it came to be, whether for itself or for anything else; nor did anything assist it in coming to be. But it cannot even be conceived that what is something exists through nothing.

If, then, the supreme nature is from nothing, it is either from nothing through itself or from nothing through another. Not through itself, for otherwise it would be prior to itself; nor through another, for otherwise it would not be supreme, but inferior to that through which it exists.

Furthermore, if the supreme nature is from nothing through something, that which was the cause of so great a good is itself a great good. But no good can be conceived before that good without which nothing is good—that is, before the supreme nature. Therefore no thing can be conceived to precede the supreme nature, through which the supreme nature exists from nothing.

Again, if this nature is something from nothing, it is either through nothing, or it is not from itself and through itself, or it is nothing. Therefore it is in no way through nothing or from nothing; rather, it exists through itself and from itself, in the manner in which light is understood to shine and to be luminous through itself and from itself [Col. 0151B].

Source preparation: Exact canonical local source; no recovery placeholders.

Since, then, “to be through something” and “to be from something” do not always have the same meaning [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “or to be through” in place of “or to be from”], we must inquire more carefully how all things that exist are through the highest nature or from it. Since that which exists through itself and that which exists through another do not have the same mode of existence, let us first examine separately the highest nature itself, which exists through itself [Note: [Col. 0151D] Gem., Corb., and Cist. read “let us examine concerning”; one manuscript reads “let it be examined concerning”], and afterward those things that exist through another.

Since it is established that it itself is, through itself, whatever it is, while everything else is what it is through it, how does it itself exist through itself? For what is said to exist through something [Note: [Col. 0151D] St. Michael reads “but what is said”] appears to exist either through an efficient cause, or through matter, or through some other assistance, such as through an instrument [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “or an instrument”; Cist. reads “as an instrument”]. But whatever exists in one of these three ways [Note: [Col. 0151D] The manuscripts read “through any one of these three ways”] exists through another; it is also subsequent to, and in some way less than, that through which it has existence. The highest nature, however, is in no way through another; nor is it subsequent to, or less than, itself or anything else.

Therefore the highest nature could not have been made either by itself or by another; nor was it itself matter for itself, nor was anything else its matter [Note: [Col. 0151D] Manuscript Corb. reads “anything else was its matter”], from which it might have been made; nor did it in any way assist itself, nor did anything assist it, so that it might be what it previously was not.

What, then? For whatever has not come into existence through a maker, from some matter, or through some assistance seems either to be nothing, or, if it is something, to exist through nothing and from nothing. Although I think that this cannot in any way apply to the highest substance, in view of what I have already observed by the light of reason [Note: [Col. 0151D] The manuscripts read “Although this, in view of what I have already observed …”], I shall nevertheless set out a proof of the matter.

Since this meditation of mine has suddenly led me to something great and delightful [Note: [Col. 0151D] Vict. reads “has suddenly led me to a certain thing”], I do not wish to pass over, by neglect, any objection—even a simple and almost foolish one—that occurs to me as I argue [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “negligently” instead of “by neglect”]. In this way, I may leave nothing doubtful in what has preceded and proceed more confidently to what follows; and, if I should wish to persuade someone of what I am contemplating, then, with every obstacle, however slight, removed, even a slow understanding may easily approach what has been heard [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “receive what has been heard” instead of “approach what has been heard”].

That the nature without which no nature exists is nothing is as false as it would be absurd to say that whatever exists is nothing. Yet it does not exist through nothing, because it cannot in any way be understood that something which exists should exist through nothing.

But if it exists in some way from nothing, it is from nothing either through itself, through another, or through nothing. Yet it is established that nothing can in any way exist through nothing [Col. 0152B] [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “something else exists through nothing” instead of “something exists through nothing”]. If, then, it exists in some way from nothing, it is from nothing either through itself or through another [Note: [Col. 0151D] Manuscript Corb. reads “through another it exists; it is from nothing”].

Nothing can be from nothing through itself, because if anything is from nothing through something, that through which it exists must necessarily exist first [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “through some thing it is necessary” instead of “through something it is necessary”]. Since, therefore, this essence is not prior to itself, it is in no way from nothing through itself [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “it is in no way from nothing” instead of “it is in no way from nothing through itself”].

But if it is said to have arisen from nothing through some other nature, then it is not the highest of all things, but something inferior [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts, including Gem. and Corb., read “but something inferior”]; nor is it through itself what it is, but through another [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “but through another”].

Again, if it is from nothing through something [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “if it is from nothing through another”], that through which it exists was a great good, since it was the cause of a good. But no good can be understood to exist before that good without which nothing is good. It is sufficiently clear that this good, without which no good exists [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “without which nothing is good”], is the highest nature under discussion.

Therefore no thing, even in thought [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts, including Vi. and Thu., read “no thing, even conceived”], preceded it, through which it could exist from nothing.

Finally, if this nature itself is something either through nothing or from nothing, then without doubt either it is not through itself and from itself whatever it is, or it is said to be nothing. It would be superfluous to explain how false both alternatives are.

Although, then, the highest substance is not through an efficient cause or from some matter, and although it was not assisted by any causes so as to be brought into existence [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts, including Thu. and Vict., read “so as to be produced into existence”], nevertheless it is in no way through nothing or from nothing, because whatever it is, it is through itself and from itself.

How, then, should its being through itself and from itself finally be understood? It is to be understood in such a way that it neither made itself, nor was itself its own matter, nor in any way assisted itself so that what was not might exist [Note: [Col. 0151D] Some manuscripts read “assists” instead of “assisted”], unless perhaps it is to be understood in the manner in which it is said that light shines, or is luminous, through itself and from itself.

For just as light, shining, and that which shines are related to one another, so essence, being, and being—that is, an existing or subsisting thing—are related to one another [Note: [Col. 0153D] Vict. reads “are related to one another” in place of “are related to one another among themselves”]. Therefore highest essence, supreme being, and supreme being—that is, a thing supremely existing or supremely subsisting—correspond to one another no less than light, shining, and that which shines.

## CHAPTER VII [elsewhere VI]

How all other things are through and from it [Note: [Col. 0153D] Manuscript Corb. has as the title of chapter 8 in the printed editions: “That things which were made from nothing were not nothing before they were made, with respect to the maker’s reason.”]

### Summary of the Chapter

The question whether all things are through that highest nature as their efficient cause, or from it as from matter, is investigated as follows. The four elements can be understood without the forms that we observe in formed things. Whence does this unformed or confused nature of theirs exist?

1. If it is from some matter, it is either from the highest nature, from itself, or from some third essence—which does not exist.

It is not from itself: first, because it exists not through itself but through another; and second, because, since nothing is subsequent to itself, nothing is materially from itself. It is not from the matter of the highest nature; otherwise something less than it would be made from it, and consequently it would be changed and corrupted—which it is impious to say.

2. That through which the highest good is changed or corrupted is not good. But whatever exists exists through the highest essence. Therefore, if anything exists from the matter of the highest good, the highest good is changed and corrupted through the highest essence. Thus the highest good is in no way good, which is inconsistent.

Therefore no lesser nature is materially from the highest nature. Consequently the essence of the elements is from no matter. Therefore the highest essence alone, through itself, produced from nothing so great a mass of things.

It remains now to examine the totality of things that exist through another, and how they exist through the highest substance: whether because it made the universe, or because it was the matter of the universe. There is no need to ask whether all things exist through it merely because, while another was making them or another matter existed, it assisted them in some way so that all things might exist [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “whether all things exist from God” instead of “whether they exist through it for this reason”]. For it is contrary to what has already been made clear that whatever exists should exist through it in a secondary and non-primary way.

I therefore think that the first question to be asked is whether the totality of things that exist through another is from some matter. I do not doubt [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “I do not doubt this” instead of “I do not doubt the whole of this”] that the whole mass of the world, with its parts, is formed, as we see it, from earth, water, air, and fire—namely, the four elements [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “which are the four elements”]. These can in some way be understood [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “can be understood”] without the forms that we observe in formed things, so that their unformed, or even confused, nature appears to be the matter of all bodies distinguished by their forms. I do not doubt this; rather, I ask from where this very matter [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “from where this matter itself”] of the worldly mass that I have described exists.

For if this matter has some matter of its own, that other matter [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “another matter”] is more truly the matter of the bodily universe. If, then, the universe of things, whether visible or invisible, is from some matter, it certainly cannot exist—and cannot even be said to exist—from any matter other than the highest nature, itself, or some third essence, which plainly does not exist [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “some other third essence” instead of “some third essence”].

For nothing at all can be conceived to exist besides the highest of all, which exists through itself, and the totality of those things that do not exist through themselves but through that same highest nature. Therefore what in no way exists is the matter of nothing.

The totality of things, which does not exist through itself, cannot exist from its own nature. For if this were so, it would in some way exist both through itself and through something other than that through which all things exist, and it would not be solely that through which all things exist. All of this is false [Note: [Col. 0153D] Manuscript Corb. reads: “since they exist through that through which all things exist, and not solely through that through which all things exist; all of these things are false.” Other manuscripts read: “than through that through which all things exist; and it would not be solely that through which all things exist; all of these things are false.”].

Again, everything that is from matter is from another [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “is from something else”] and is subsequent to it. Since, therefore, nothing is other than itself or subsequent to itself, it follows that nothing is materially from itself.

But if something less than the highest nature can exist from the matter of the highest nature, the highest good can be changed and corrupted—which it is impious to say. Since everything that is other than it is less than it, it is therefore impossible for anything else to exist from it in this way [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “to exist greater than it” instead of “to exist from it”].

Furthermore, there is no doubt that what changes or corrupts the highest good is in no way good. If, then, some lesser nature is from the matter of the highest good, since nothing exists from anywhere whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “from anything whatsoever”] except through the highest essence, the highest good is changed and corrupted through the highest essence [Note: [Col. 0153D] The manuscripts read *summum per ipsum bonum* (“the highest [is changed] through the good itself”) for *summum bonum per ipsam* (“the highest good through it,” where *ipsam* refers to the highest essence)]. Therefore the highest essence, which is the highest good itself, is in no way good—which is inconsistent.

Thus no lesser nature is materially from the highest nature. Since it is established that the essence of those things that exist through another is not from the highest essence as from matter, nor from itself, nor from another [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “nor from anything else”], it is clear that it is from no matter.

Since whatever exists exists through the highest essence, and since nothing else can exist through it except either because it makes it or because it is its matter, it necessarily follows that nothing exists besides it except through its making. And since nothing else exists or existed except it and the things made by it, it could make nothing through another, an instrument, or any assistance, but only through itself.

Everything that it made, without doubt, it made either from something, as from matter, or from nothing [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some manuscripts read “and everything” instead of “everything”]. Since it is most certainly clear that the essence of everything existing besides the highest essence was made by that same highest essence, and that it is from no matter [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “because there is no matter” instead of “because it is from no matter”], nothing is clearer than that the highest essence alone, through itself, produced from nothing so great a mass of things, so numerous a multitude, so beautifully formed, so orderly in its variations, and so fittingly diverse.

## CHAPTER VIII [elsewhere VII]

How it should be understood that it made everything from nothing [Note: [Col. 0155C] Manuscript Corb. has as the title of chapter 9 in the printed editions: “What that reasoning is,” etc. Manuscripts Gem., Corb., and Thuan. number chapter 7 as chapter 8.]

### Summary of the Chapter

Nothing itself cannot be the cause of anything that exists; and everyone says, “Nothing comes from nothing.” Hence it seems that whatever comes to be, comes to be from something. If this is true, everything previously established about the highest essence—that it made all things from nothing—collapses.

A substance can be said to have been made from nothing in three ways:

1. It may be understood as not having been made at all; thus, of a silent person, one says, “He speaks from nothing,” that is, “He does not speak.”

2. It may be signified as having been made from nothing as though from something; this meaning is always false.

3. It may be said to have been made from nothing in the sense that it is understood to have been made not from something.

In this third sense all things besides the highest essence are said to have been made from nothing: that is, things that previously were nothing are now something, just as someone is said to become rich from being poor, or healthy from illness. In this sense, the person who was poor or ill is now rich or healthy.

A certain difficulty concerning “nothing” nevertheless arises [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “a certain person concerning nothing”]. For whatever something comes from is the cause of what comes from it [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “is its cause”], and every cause must provide some assistance toward the essence of its effect [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “some assistance toward the essence of the effect”].

Everyone holds this so firmly through experience that it cannot be wrested from anyone by argument, and can scarcely be stolen from anyone by deception [Note: [Col. 0155C] Manuscript St. Michael reads “so that it is not wrested from anyone” and the manuscripts read “and scarcely stolen from anyone”]. If, therefore, something was made from nothing, nothing itself was the cause of what was made from it. But how did that which had no existence assist something to come into existence?

If no assistance toward something comes from nothing, who, or by what means, can be persuaded that something is made from nothing?

Moreover, “nothing” either signifies something or does not signify something. But if nothing is something, whatever has been made from nothing has been made from something. If, however, nothing is not something, then, since it cannot be understood that something should come from what entirely does not exist, nothing comes from nothing, as everyone says: “Nothing comes from nothing.” Hence it seems to follow that whatever comes to be comes from something; for it comes either from something or from nothing.

Whether, then, nothing is something or nothing is not something, it seems to follow that whatever has been made has been made from something.

If this is accepted as true, it conflicts with everything established above. For if what was nothing will be something, then what was most of all something will be nothing [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “what was most of all something will be nothing”; others read “what was most of all was something; nothing will be something.”].

For, reasoning from the fact that I had discovered a certain substance existing most of all, I had reached the conclusion that all other things were made by it in such a way that there was nothing from which they were made [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “the other things were made by it, so that there was nothing”]. Therefore, if that from which they were made, which I thought was nothing, is something, then whatever I had discovered concerning the highest essence is nothing.

What, then, should be understood concerning nothing? For I have already resolved in this meditation to disregard any objection that I can see, even one that is almost foolish [Note: [Col. 0155C] One manuscript reads “an objection that could be raised against me, which I had already judged almost foolish”].

[Elsewhere, Chapter 8.] [Note: [Col. 0155C] In manuscripts Gem., Corb., and Thu., the preceding chapter continues for thirty sections.]

I think, then, that there are three ways—sufficient to resolve the present difficulty—in which it can be explained if a substance is said to have been made from nothing.

The first is the way in which we intend it to be understood that what is said to be from nothing was not made at all [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “what is said to have been made from nothing”]. This is like the answer given when someone asks of a silent person where he is speaking from: “From nothing,” that is, “He is not speaking.”
