In this sense, when someone asks from what the highest essence itself, or that which neither was nor is at all, was made, it is rightly answered, “From nothing,” that is, “It was not made in any way.” This meaning, however, cannot be understood of any of the things that were made.

The second meaning is one that can indeed be stated but cannot be true: namely, that something was made from nothing in such a way that it was made from nothing itself, that is, from what entirely does not exist [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “from that nothing” instead of “from nothing itself”]. This would mean that nothing itself was some existing thing from which something could be made [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “was something else existing” instead of “was some existing thing”]. Since this is always false, whenever existence is attributed to it, an impossible absurdity follows.

The third interpretation of the statement that something was made from nothing is that we understand it to have been made, but not to have anything from which it was made [Note: [Col. 0155C] One manuscript, Corb., reads “from nothing is that it was made, but …”].

By a similar usage, someone who is saddened without cause is said to be saddened “from nothing” [Note: [Col. 0155C] Manuscript Thu. reads “to be saddened from nothing”].

If, then, what was concluded above is understood in this sense—namely, that all things besides the highest essence were made by it from nothing, that is, not from something—then, just as the conclusion itself follows appropriately from what preceded [Note: [Col. 0155C] Some manuscripts read “will follow appropriately”], nothing inconsistent follows from that conclusion.

Indeed, without inconsistency or contradiction, the things made by the creative substance can be said to have been made from nothing [Note: [Col. 0157C] Some manuscripts read “can be from nothing”], in the same way that someone is said to have become rich from being poor, or to have recovered health from illness: that is, someone who was previously poor is now rich, possessing what he did not previously have; and someone who previously had an illness now has health, which he did not previously have.

In this sense, then, it is not inconsistent to understand the statement that the creative essence made the universe from nothing, or that the universe was made by it from nothing: that is, things that previously were nothing are now something.

Indeed, by the very expression “it made these things,” or “these things were made,” it is understood that when it made them, it made something, and that when these things were made, they were made only as something [Note: [Col. 0157C] The manuscripts read “they were made only as some things”].

Thus, when we see someone raised from a very humble condition to great wealth or honors by another, we say: “Behold, he made this man from nothing,” or “That man was made by this man from nothing.” This means that he who was previously regarded as almost nothing is now, through the other’s action, considered truly something [Note: [Col. 0157C] Some manuscripts read “was regarded” instead of “was considered”].

## CHAPTER IX

That things which were made from nothing were not nothing before they were made, with respect to the maker’s reason.

[Note: [Col. 0157C] Elsewhere this is part of chapter 8.]  
[Note: [Col. 0157C] Manuscripts Gem., Corb., Thu., Vict., and Sag. begin chapter 9 with these words, “But I seem to see”; manuscript Corb. has no title here, while other manuscripts precede it with the title “That things which were made …,” which is the title of chapter 8 in the printed editions.]

### Summary of the Chapter

Nothing is rationally made by anything unless the form of the thing to be made precedes in the maker. Therefore, before the universe was made, there was in the reason of the highest nature what things would be, what sort of things they would be, and how they would be.

Therefore, before they existed, they were not nothing; nor, when they exist, are they from nothing with respect to the maker’s reason.

But I seem to see something that compels me to distinguish carefully in what respect the things that were made can be said to have been nothing before they were made [Note: [Col. 0157C] Some manuscripts read “something that compels me to distinguish nothing carefully”].

For it is in no way possible for anything to be made rationally by anyone unless, in the reason of the maker, there first exists something like an example of the thing to be made, or—as it is more aptly called—a form, likeness, or rule.

It is therefore clear that, before the universe was made, there existed in the reason of the highest nature what it would be, what sort of thing it would be, and how it would be [Note: [Col. 0157C] Some manuscripts read “there existed” in the plural]. Thus, although it is clear that the things that were made were nothing before they were made, insofar as they were not what they now are and there was nothing from which they could be made, nevertheless they were not nothing with respect to the reason of the maker, through which and according to which they were to be made.

## CHAPTER X [elsewhere IX]

That this reason is a certain speaking of things, just as a craftsman first says within himself what he is going to make [Note: [Col. 0157C] Some manuscripts read “what has been made” instead of “what he is going to make.” Manuscript Corb. has the title “That nevertheless …,” as in the printed editions for chapter 10; other manuscripts have “That this reason is …,” as in the printed editions for chapter 9.]

### Summary of the Chapter

The form of things in the divine mind is a kind of speaking of them in the divine reason. Thus a craftsman says within himself the work he is going to make.

We can speak one thing in three ways:

1. Sensibly, by using sensible signs.

2. Insensibly, by thinking these signs insensibly within ourselves.

3. Neither sensibly nor insensibly, by speaking mentally not signs but the things themselves.

Each of these three kinds of speaking has its corresponding words. The words of the third kind of speaking are natural and therefore the same among all people. Wherever these words exist, no other word is necessary for knowing the thing; where they cannot exist, every other word is useless for displaying the thing.

Natural words are truer because they are more like the things. Therefore a natural word is the most proper and principal word of a thing. This, then, was the speaking by which the highest essence spoke all things before they existed, so that through it they might come to be.

The form of things that preceded the things to be created in its reason—what else is it than a kind of speaking of things in its own reason? It is like a craftsman who, intending to make some work of his art, first says it within himself through a conception of the mind.

By mental or rational speaking I mean here not the thinking of words signifying things, but the things themselves—whether future or already existing—being viewed in the mind by the mind’s power of thought [Note: [Col. 0157C] Some manuscripts omit “conception and,” reading simply “rational speaking”; manuscript Vict. reads “are conceived” instead of “are viewed”].

For frequent experience makes it clear that we can speak one thing in three ways. Either we speak of the thing through sensible signs—that is, by using signs that can be perceived by bodily senses—in a sensible manner; or we think within ourselves, insensibly, the same signs that are outwardly sensible; or, without using these signs either sensibly or insensibly, we speak the things themselves inwardly in our mind, either through an image of bodies or through the understanding of reason, according to the differences among the things themselves.

For example, I speak of a human being in one way when I signify him by the name “human being”; in another way when I think the same name silently; and in another way when the mind itself beholds that human being either through a bodily image or through reason.

It beholds him through a bodily image when it imagines his perceptible shape; through reason when it thinks his universal essence, namely, “a rational mortal animal.”

Each of these three varieties of speaking consists of words belonging to its own kind. But the words of the third kind of speaking, which I placed last, are natural when they concern things that are not unknown, and they are the same among all peoples.

Since all other words were invented for the sake of these, wherever these exist no other word is necessary for knowing the thing; and where these cannot exist, no other word is useful for showing it.

They may also reasonably be called truer in proportion as they are more like the things whose words they are and signify them more distinctly [Note: [Col. 0159D] One manuscript reads “signify them more distinctly” as “mark them more distinctly”].

For, except for those things that we use in place of their own names to signify them—such as certain sounds, for example the vowel “A”—no other word seems so like the thing of which it is the word, or expresses it so fully, as that likeness which is expressed in the mind’s direct apprehension when it thinks the thing itself [Note: [Col. 0159D] Some manuscripts read “which the thinker expresses” instead of “which is expressed when it thinks”].

Therefore it is rightly called the most proper and principal word of the thing.

Since no speaking of anything approaches the thing so closely as that which consists of words of this kind, and since nothing else can be so like either a future thing or one already existing in someone’s reason, it may reasonably seem that such a speaking of things existed in the highest substance before they existed, so that through it they might come to be, and that it exists when they have been made, so that through it they may be known [Note: [Col. 0159D] Some manuscripts omit “the very” before “highest substance”].

## CHAPTER XI [elsewhere X]

That there is nevertheless much dissimilarity in this likeness to a craftsman [Note: [Col. 0159D] Printed editions have “That this [speaking] of the highest …”; other manuscripts have the same title as the printed editions.]

### Summary of the Chapter

The highest artisan differs from a craftsman:

1. In that the highest artisan does not assemble the form from elsewhere.

2. In that the highest artisan requires no matter from which to complete the work conceived beforehand.

3. In that the works of the creative substance are nothing except what they are through it; whereas things made by a craftsman would not exist at all unless they were something that they are not through him.

Although it is established that the highest substance first, as it were, spoke the whole creation within itself before establishing it according to, and through, that same intimate speaking of its own—just as a craftsman first conceives in his mind what he afterward completes in his work according to the conception of his mind—I nevertheless perceive much dissimilarity in this likeness.

For the highest substance took nothing at all from elsewhere from which it might construct within itself the form of the things it was going to make, or by which it might bring those things themselves to be what they are [Note: [Col. 0159D] Some manuscripts read “what they were going to be” instead of “what they are”].

A craftsman, however, cannot even mentally conceive anything bodily through imagination unless he has already learned it in some way, either as a whole or in parts, from certain things. Nor can he complete the work conceived in his mind if matter or anything else is lacking without which the work previously conceived cannot be made [Note: [Col. 0159D] Manuscript Thu. reads “matter, or an instrument, or something else”].

Although a human being can invent by thought or painting an animal of a kind that exists nowhere, he can do so only by combining in it parts that he has drawn into memory from other things previously known [Note: [Col. 0159D] Manuscript Thu. reads “other parts that he has drawn from other known things”].

Thus the intimate speakings of works to be made differ in the creative substance and in a craftsman. The former, neither derived nor aided from elsewhere, could, as the first and sole cause, suffice for its artisan in completing his work [Note: [Col. 0159D] One manuscript reads “it alone could suffice for its own work”; Vict. reads “the highest artisan” for “its artisan”]. The latter, however, is neither first, nor sole, nor sufficient for beginning its work.

Therefore all things created through the creative substance are not what they are except through it [Note: [Col. 0159D] Some manuscripts read “what is not through it”]. But things made through the craftsman would not exist at all unless they were something that they are not through him [Note: [Col. 0159D] Some manuscripts read “unless it were something” and “which is not through him”].

## CHAPTER XII [elsewhere XI]

That this speaking of the highest essence is the highest essence [Note: [Col. 0159D] Manuscript Corb. has as the title of chapter 12: “That just as all things are through the highest …”]

### Summary of the Chapter

The highest substance made all things through itself. It made all things through a natural and intimate speaking. Therefore this natural speaking is the highest substance itself.

Since reason equally teaches that whatever the highest substance made, it made through no other but through itself, and that whatever it made, it made through its intimate speaking—whether by saying each thing through its own word, or rather by saying all things together in one word—what could appear more necessary than that this speaking of the highest essence should be nothing other than the highest essence?

I do not think, then, that consideration of this speaking should be passed over negligently. But before it can be discussed, I think that certain properties of that same highest substance must first be carefully and diligently investigated [Note: [Col. 0159D] Some manuscripts, including Vict. and Sag., read “through certain properties” instead of “certain properties”].

## CHAPTER XIII [elsewhere XII]

That just as all things were made through the highest essence, so they persist through it [Note: [Col. 0159D] Manuscript Corb. has as the title of chapter 13 in the printed editions: “That it is …”]

### Summary of the Chapter

Just as all things that exist exist through one thing, which alone exists through itself, so all things persist through one thing, which alone persists through itself.

Therefore, just as nothing was made except through the creative essence, so nothing persists except through that same preserving presence.

## Complete textual apparatus and editorial matter

This register restores the supplied edition's readings that are not already attached to the translated prose above. Quoted Latin is retained wherever English alone would conceal a change of inflection, connective, or word order; each entry gives its scope, sense, and witnesses exactly as printed.

### [Col. 0151D–0153D]: Chapters VI–VII

- In the opening contrast, MSS read *aut per esse ex* (“or to be through, to be from”) for *aut esse ex* (“or to be from”); after “let us examine,” Gem., Corb., and Cist. read *videamus de* (“let us consider concerning”), while the passive is *videatur de* (“let it be considered concerning”). St Michael has *quod enim dicitur* (“for what is said”); the contrasting printed reading is *quod autem dicitur* (“but what is said”).
- At the three modes of causation, MSS have *vel instrumentum* (“or an instrument”), and Cist. *velut instrumentum* (“as an instrument”); for “by any one of these three ways,” MSS read *ex aliquo his tribus*, an altered ordering/case beside *aliquo ex his tribus*. Corb. reads *aliud illa materia* (“something else [was] its matter for it”) for *aliquid aliud illi materia*.
- At “through what aids,” Vict. reads *aut ex quibus* (“or from which [aids]”) for *aut quibus* (“or by which [aids]”). At “or, if it is something,” MSS read *aut si aliud est* (“or, if it is another thing”) for *aut si aliquid est* (“or, if it is something”). For “Although,” MSS read *quod licet ex his* (“although this from these [things]”) for *quae licet ex iis* (“which, although, from those [things]”). Vict. has *quoddam me* (“a certain thing led me”) for *quiddam me* (“something led me”); MSS have *negligenter* (“negligently”) for *negligendo* (“by neglect”), and *audita ... accipere* (“receive what has been heard”) for *ad audita ... accedere* (“approach what has been heard”).
- In “it would be absurd to say,” MSS read *erit aut si dicatur* (“it will be, or if it is said”) for *erit si dicatur* (“it would be if it is said”). At the next conditional they read *aut si quomodo* (“or if in some way”) for *at si quo modo* (“but if in some way”); at “something exists through nothing,” *aliud est per* (“something else is through”) for *aliquid est per* (“something is through”). Corb. reads *per aliud est, est ex nihilo* (“it is through another; it is from nothing”) for the joined phrase.
- At the necessity claim, MSS read *per aliquod necesse* (“through some thing it is necessary”) for *per aliquid necesse*; at the conclusion they omit *est* in *nullo modo ex nihilo* (“in no way from nothing”). At “something inferior,” Gem. and Corb. read *sed aliquo inferior*: *aliquo* is ablative (“inferior by/in some respect”), whereas the text's *aliqua inferior* is feminine nominative (“some inferior [nature]”). They also read *hoc est, sed* (“this is, but”) for *hoc quod est, sed* (“what it is, but”).
- At “if it is through something,” MSS read *si per aliud est* (“if it is through another”) for *si per aliquid est* (“if it is through something”); at “without which no good exists,” *sine quo nihil est* (“without which nothing exists”) for *sine quo nullum est* (“without which no [good] exists”). Vi. and Thu. have *nulla vel intellecta* (“no thing, even one understood”) for *res nulla vel intellectu* (“no thing even in thought”). Thu. and Vict. read *ad esse produceretur* (“might be produced into being”) for *perduceretur* (“brought into being”); MSS have present *adjuvat* (“assists”) for past *adjuvit* (“assisted”).
- At the light comparison, the manuscript heading is *Quod dicitur* (“What is said”); Vict. has *sunt ad invicem* (“are related to one another”) for *sunt ad se invicem* (“are related among themselves”).
- Chapter VII’s alternate title in Corb. is: “That things made from nothing were not nothing before they were made, with respect to the maker’s reason.” At “whether all things are through it,” MSS read *utrum a Deo sint* (“whether they are from God”) for *utrum ideo sint* (“whether for this reason they are”). At “it assisted,” MSS read *essent adjuvat* (“it assists that they may be”) for *essent, adjuverit* (“it assisted so that they might be”).
- In the account of the elements, MSS read *dubito hanc* (“I doubt this”) for *non autem dubito omnem hanc* (“I do not doubt this whole”); *quae sunt quatuor* (“which are four”) for *quae, scilicet, quatuor* (“which, namely, [are] four”); *intelligi posse* (“can be understood”) for *intelligi possunt* (“are able to be understood”); *unde hic ipsa* (“whence this [one] itself”) for *unde haec ipsa* (“whence this matter itself”); and *alia verius* (“another more truly”) for *illa verius* (“that [matter] more truly”).
- At the exhaustive alternatives, Gem., Corb., Vict., and St Michael read *potest ex alia* (“can [be] from another”) for *non ... potest ... ex alia* (“cannot ... be from another”); Thu. reads *ex alia tertia essentia* (“from another third essence”) for *ex aliqua tertia essentia* (“from some third essence”). Corb.’s full altered sentence is *quoniam per id per quod sunt cuncta: et non solum id per quod cuncta sunt, quae sunt omnia falsa*; the other MSS have *quam per id per quod sunt cuncta sunt; quae omnia falsa sunt*. Both preserve a word-order/construction variant in the inference that the universe would exist through itself and not solely through that through which all things exist.
- For “is from another,” MSS read *ex aliquo est* (“is from something”) for *ex alio est* (“is from another”); for “but if,” *ac si ex* (“and if from”) for *at si ex* (“but if from”); and for *nihil sit undecunque* (“nothing is from anywhere whatever”), *sit unumcunque* (“let it be any one whatever”). MSS read *esse majus ipsa* (“to be greater than it”) for *esse ex ipsa* (“to be from it”).
- The crucial argument reads in the supplied source: *mutatur et corrumpitur summum bonum per ipsam* — “the highest good is changed and corrupted through it,” with *ipsam* referring to *summam essentiam* (“the highest essence”) in “nothing exists except through the highest essence.” The manuscript reading is exactly *summum per ipsum bonum* (“the highest [is changed] through the good itself”), for printed *summum bonum per ipsam* (“the highest good through it”). It does **not** say that a lesser nature is the pronoun’s antecedent.
- At “nor from another,” MSS read *nec alio* (“nor another”) for *nec ex alio* (“nor from another [source]”); at “but everything it made,” *ac omne* (“and every [thing]”) for *at omne* (“but every [thing]”); and at “from no matter,” MSS read *quia nulla materia* (“because [there is] no matter”) for *quia ex nulla materia* (“because [it is] from no matter”).

### [Col. 0155C–0157C]: Chapter VIII

- In the opening difficulty, MSS read *quidam de nihilo* (“a certain [man] concerning nothing”) for *quaedam dubitatio de nihilo* (“a certain difficulty concerning nothing”); *causa ejus* (“its cause”) for *causa est ejus* (“is its cause”); *quod ex se fit* (“which is made from itself”) for *quod ex eo fit* (“which is made from it”); and *aliquid ad essentiam effectus* (“something toward the essence of the effect,” differing in case) for *aliquod ad essentiam effecti*.
- At universal assent St Michael reads *ut et nulli rapiatur* (“so that it is not wrested even from anyone”) for *ut etiam nulli rapiatur* (“so that even from no one is it wrested”); MSS read *ut vix ulli*, Thu. *et vix illi*, for *et vix ulli* (“and scarcely from anyone”). Vict. reads *sed ergo* (“but therefore”) for *si ergo* (“if therefore”).
- At “how did it assist something,” MSS read *adjuvit aliud* (“assisted another thing”) for *adjuvit aliquid* (“assisted something”). At the following transition they read *propterea* (“therefore/on that account”) for *praeterea* (“moreover”); in “from that which wholly is not,” *potest ut eo* (“it can [be] that from that”) for *potest ut ex eo* (“it can [be] that from that”). At the next conclusion MSS have *si igitur nihil* (“if therefore nothing”) for *sive igitur nihil* (“whether therefore nothing”).
- For the premise “everything established above,” Corb. reads *disputata sunt* (“has been argued/disputed”) and the MSS *dicta sunt* (“has been said”) for *disposita sunt* (“has been set out”). Thu. reads *maxime erat, aliquid nihil erit* (“what most was, something will be nothing”) for *maxime aliquid erat, nihil erit* (“what was most of all something will be nothing”). MSS also read *alia ab ea facta essent: sic ut nihil* (“the other things were made by it: so that nothing ...”) for *alia sic facta essent ab ea, ut nihil*.
- The objection’s alternate form is *posse objici sibi pene jam fatuum statui* (“which could be objected to him, almost foolish, I had already decided”) for *posse objici vel pene fatuum jam statui*. Gem., Corb., and Thu. continue the preceding chapter for thirty sections.
- At the first meaning, MSS read *quod factum dicitur ex nihilo* (“what is said to have been made from nothing”) for *quod dicitur ex nihilo esse* (“what is said to be from nothing”). Thu. reads *dici potest quidem vera, esse tamen non potest* (“it can indeed be said true, yet cannot be true”) for the printed word order; MSS read *dicatur sic esse factum* (“it is said to have been so made”) for *dicatur aliquid sic esse factum* (“something is said to have been so made”). Vict. and Sag. have *ut ex ipso nihil* (“as from that nothing”) for *ut ex ipso nihilo* (“as from nothing itself”).
- At “as though nothing were an existing thing,” MSS read *sit aliud existens* (“were another existing thing”) for *sit aliquid existens* (“were some existing thing”); *quotiens est* (“whenever it is”) for *quotiens esse* (“whenever being is”); and *de nihilo est, cum* (“from nothing is, when”) or Corb.’s *de nihilo est quod* (“from nothing is that which”) for *de nihilo, cum* (“from nothing, when”). Thu. has *per similem enim significationem* (“for by a similar usage”) and *contristari de* (“to be saddened from”) for *per similem significationem* and *contristatus de* (“saddened from”).
- Thu. reads *secundum enim* (“according to/for”) for *secundum igitur* (“therefore according to”); MSS have *convenienter sequetur* (“will follow fittingly”) for *convenienter consequetur* (“follows fittingly”). At creation MSS read *facta a creatrice* (“made by the creative”) for *facta sunt a creatrice* (“were made by the creative”); *possunt ex nihilo* (“can [be] from nothing”) for *possint esse ex nihilo facta* (“may be made from nothing”); and Vict. and Sag. *per illa facta sunt* (“were made through that [neuter]”) for *per illam facta sint* (“may have been made through her/it”).
- At the two clauses about making, MSS read *sive quod ista* (“or that these things”) for *sive quia ista* (“or because these things”), *aliqua fecit* (“made some things”) for *aliquid fecit* (“made something”), and *nisi aliqua facta sunt* (“were made only as some things”) for *nisi aliquid facta sunt* (“were made only as something”). Vict. 13 has *sic autem* (“but thus”) for *sic enim* (“for thus”); Vict. and Sag. *honoribusque* (“and honours”) for *honoribusve* (“or honours”); and their *deputabatur* (“was reckoned/assigned”) for *reputabatur* (“was regarded”).

### [Col. 0157C–0160C]: Chapters IX–XIII

- At the distinction before the maker’s reason, MSS read *quoddam quod negligenter* (“a certain thing which carelessly …”; the witness omits the negation in *non negligenter*, “not carelessly”) for *quiddam quod non negligenter* (“something which [one should] not carelessly [fail to distinguish]”), and *dici possunt* (“can be said”) for *dici possint* (“may be said”). At “nothing can be made rationally,” MSS read *aliud rationabiliter* (“another thing rationally”) for *aliquid rationabiliter* (“anything rationally”); at “or, more aptly,” *sive aptius* (“or more aptly”) for *sive ut aptius dicitur* (“or, as it is more aptly called”). Vict., Sag., Gem., and Corb. have plural *erant in ratione* (“there were in the reason”) for singular *erat in ratione*.
- In the account of inward speech, MSS read *mentem autem* (“the mind, however”) for *mentis autem* (“of the mind, however”), and omit *conceptionem* in *rationis conceptionem et locutionem* (“the conception and speech of reason”). Vict. 3 reads *concipiuntur* (“are conceived”) for *conspiciuntur* (“are beheld”).
- The three modes are distinguished as: *sensibiliter utendo* (“using sensibly”), MSS *sensibiliter cogitando* (“thinking sensibly”) for printed *insensibiliter cogitando* (“thinking insensibly/inwardly”), and *nec sensibiliter his* (“not sensibly with these [signs]”) for *nec sensibiliter nec insensibiliter his* (“neither sensibly nor insensibly with these signs”). In the illustration MSS have *cum ejus* (“when his”) for *ut cum ejus* (“as when his”).
- At the third and final speech, MSS read singular *non ignoratur* (“is not unknown”) for plural *non ignoratis sunt* (“are [speech-words] about things not unknown”); one manuscript has *expressius signant* (“signify more expressly”) for *expressius significant* (“signify more expressly”). In “no other word appears similar to the thing,” a manuscript reads *sic dicitur rei* (“is thus said of the thing”) for *sic videtur rei* (“thus appears [similar] to the thing”). Vict. and Sag. read *cogitantis exprimit* (“expresses [it] of one thinking”) for *cogitantis exprimitur* (“is expressed by one thinking”).
- At “a thing, future or already existing,” MSS read *rei futurae* (“of a future thing”) for *rei vel futurae* (“of a thing either future”), and omit *ipsam* (“itself”) in *apud ipsam summam substantiam* (“in the highest substance itself”).
- In the craftsman comparison Corb. reads *quae futura erant* (“which were going to be”) for *quae factura erat* (“which it was going to make”); Vict. and Sag. read *hoc quod sunt* (“that which they are”) for *id quod sunt* (“what they are”). Thu. has *materia, aut instrumentum, aut aliquid* (“matter, or an instrument, or something”) for *materia, aut aliquid*; MSS *aliud, sine quo* (“another thing, without which”) for *aliquid, sine quo* (“something, without which”); Thu. *partes alias, quas* (“other parts, which”) for *partes, quas*; and MSS *rebus aliis cognitis* (“things known elsewhere/other things known”) for *rebus alias cognitis* (“things known at other times”).
- At the two inner speeches, the manuscript wording *sola eam sufficere potuit suo* (“it alone could suffice him for his”) differs from *sola causa sufficere potuit suo* (“as sole cause it could suffice for its”); Vict. 15 reads *summo artifici* (“the supreme craftsman”) for *suo artifici* (“its craftsman”). MSS have *quod non sit per illam* (“which is not through it”) for *quod non sunt per illam* (“which they are not through it”). At the contrasting artisan’s speech, MSS read *per ipsam fiunt* (“are made through that very one”) for *per istam fiunt* (“are made through this one”), *nisi esset aliquid* (“unless there were something”) for *nisi essent aliquid* (“unless there were some things”), and again *quod non sit per ipsam* for the plural printed construction.
- Finally, at “whatever the highest substance made,” MSS read *substantia fecit, per aliud* (“the substance made, through another”) for *substantia fecit, non fecit per aliud* (“the substance made, did not make through another”); at “through its innermost speech,” *per intimam* (“through an innermost [speech]”) for *per suam intimam* (“through its own innermost [speech]”). Vict. and Sag. read *per proprietates* (“through properties”) for *proprietates* (“properties”). Chapter XIII is chapter XII in the manuscripts; Corb.’s alternate heading is “That it is [the case], etc., as in the heading of chapter 13 in the printed editions.”

Therefore it is established that whatever is not identical with the supreme nature was made by the supreme nature. [Col. 0161A] It can be doubtful only to a rational mind that all things which have been made are sustained and continue to exist for as long as they exist by that same power by which they were made to have from nothing the existence they possess. For by an entirely similar argument—by which it was gathered that everything which exists exists through one thing, which alone exists through itself, while other things exist through another—it can likewise be proved that whatever things are sustained are sustained through one thing [Note: [Col. 0161D] The Victor and Sag. manuscripts read *aliquid vigent*; the reading is *aliquid vigeant* (“that something may flourish / be sustained in vigour”).]; and that this one thing alone is sustained through itself, while other things are sustained through another. Since this cannot be otherwise, except that things which have been made are sustained through another, while that by which they were made is sustained through itself, it is necessary that, just as nothing was made except through the creative presence of that essence, so nothing is sustained except through the preserving presence of that same essence [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read “power” instead of “presence.”].

## CHAPTER XIV [elsewhere XIII] [Note: [Col. 0161D] Chapter 13 in the manuscripts is chapter 14.]

That it is in all things and through all things, and that all things are from it, through it, and in it [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read: “in all things, and all things”; the Thuanus manuscript reads: “in all things, and through all things, and all things”; “that it is in all things,” etc., as in the printed editions.].

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

It follows that where it is not, nothing exists. Therefore it is everywhere, through all things, and in all things. Since what is created cannot in any way escape the immensity of the creator and sustainer, while the creator and sustainer can surpass everything that has been created, it is clear that the supreme essence itself carries, surpasses, encloses, and penetrates all other things; and that it is in all things and through all things; and that all things are from it, through it, and in it.

If this is so [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read “that it is so.”]—indeed, because it is necessarily so—it follows that where it is not, nothing exists. Therefore it is everywhere, through all things, and in all things. But since it is absurd that, just as nothing created can in any way escape the immensity of the creator and sustainer, so the creator and sustainer should be unable in any way to surpass the totality of created things [Col. 0161C] [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read the plural *valeant aliquo* (“should be able in some way”) for the singular *valeat aliquo*.] [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts of Thuanus, Corbeiensis, Gemblacensis, and Saint-Michael read “and since.”], it is clear [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read *liquet quomodo* (“it is clear how”) for *liquet quoniam* (“it is clear that”).] that it is itself which carries, surpasses, encloses, and penetrates all things [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read “and encloses”; Victor omits “and.”]. If, then, these points are joined to what was discovered above, it is the same reality which is in all things, through all things, and from which, through which, and in which all things exist.

## CHAPTER XV [elsewhere XIV] [Note: [Col. 0161D] Chapter 14 in the manuscripts is chapter 15.] [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript of Corbeiensis reads “What is identical with it,” etc., as in the title of chapter 15.]

What can or cannot be said substantially of it [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts of Victor, Sigebert, Saint-Michael, and Thuanus read “what can be said.”].

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

No relative property among created things is substantial to the thing of which it is predicated relatively. Therefore what is said relatively of the supreme nature—for example, that it is greater than all things—does not signify its essence. [Col. 0161D] For it is whatever it is through itself and not through another or in relation to another. Apart from relative properties, whatever exists is either better in itself than its negation, or its negation is in some respect better than it. “Itself” and “not itself” are understood as, for example, “true” and “not true,” “body” and “not body,” and things of this kind. “Itself,” as in “wise,” is simply better than “not itself,” that is, than “not wise.” “Not itself,” as in “not gold,” is in some respect better than “itself,” that is, than “gold.” “Supreme” is not altogether and simply better than “not supreme,” because it is relative. “Not supreme” is not in any respect better than “supreme.” Neither term designates the essence of the supreme nature. The supreme nature is whatever is altogether better than its negation: for it alone is that than which nothing is better, and it is better than all things. Therefore it is not a body or anything corporeal, since something is better than a body—namely, a rational mind. Therefore it is living, wise, powerful, true, just, blessed, eternal, and whatever is absolutely better than its negation.

Now I am not without reason deeply moved to inquire, as carefully as I can, what among all the things that can be said of something can substantially apply to this nature, so astonishing. Although I would be surprised if words or names that we adapt to things made from nothing could be found [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read *reperire, quod* (“to find that”) for *reperiri, quod* (“that there may be found”).] that are worthy to be said of the substance that created the universe, nevertheless we must attempt to see where reason will lead this inquiry [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts of Thuanus and Saint-Michael read “may lead.”].

Regarding relative properties, then, no one doubts that none of them is substantial to that of which it is predicated relatively. Therefore, if anything is said relatively of the supreme nature, it does not signify its substance [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read “its substantial signification.”]. Thus, when it is said that it is supreme over all things or greater than all things made by it—or anything else that can similarly be said relatively—it is clear that this does not designate its natural essence [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts, except Thuanus, read “which is supreme over all things”; Thuanus omits “is.”] [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts, except Thuanus, read “anything else that is similarly”; the manuscript of Saint-Michael reads “something else similarly.”]. For if none of those things ever existed in relation to which it is called supreme and greater, it would neither be understood as supreme nor as greater; yet it would not on that account be less good, nor would its essential greatness suffer any diminution. This is clearly recognized from the fact that whatever good or greatness it possesses, it possesses not through another but through itself.

If, therefore, the supreme nature can be understood as non-supreme while nevertheless being neither greater nor less than when it is understood as supreme over all things, it is clear that “supreme” does not simply signify that essence [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript of Thuanus, at folio 30, omits this sentence.] which is altogether greater and better than whatever is not what it is [Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscripts read “which is not what it is”; another reading is “which it is.”]. What reason teaches about “supreme” is found in the same way in other relative terms.

Let us therefore set aside those things which are said relatively, since none of them simply demonstrates the essence of anything [Col. 0162D], and let our attention turn to the examination of other matters. If someone considers each thing carefully, whatever exists apart from relative properties is either such that it is altogether better than its negation, or such that its negation is in some respect better than it. By “itself” and “not itself” I understand here nothing other than “true” and “not true,” “body” and “not body,” and similar terms.

Something is altogether better than its negation—for example, “wise” is better than “not wise” [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read *quam non sapiens* (“than not-wise”) for *quam non ipsum sapiens* (“than not-itself-wise”).]. For although a just person who is not wise may seem better than an unjust person who is wise, “not wise” is not thereby simply better than “wise”: everything that is not wise, simply insofar as it is not wise, is less than what is wise, because everything that is not wise would be better if it were wise. Similarly, “true” is altogether better than its negation, that is, than “not true”; “just” is better than “not just”; and “living” is better than “not living.”

But in some respect the negation is better than the thing itself—for example, “not gold” is better than “gold.” For it is better for a human being to be not gold than to be gold, although perhaps it would be better for something else to be gold than not gold—for example, for lead. Since both a human being and lead are, of course, not gold, a human being is better than gold to the extent that it would be a lower nature if it were gold; and lead is correspondingly more worthless to the extent that it would be more precious if it were gold [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts of Victor omit “to be.”].

It is evident from the fact that the supreme nature can be understood as non-supreme in such a way that “supreme” is neither altogether better than “not supreme,” nor “not supreme” better in any respect than “supreme,” that there are many relative terms which are not contained within this division. I refrain from investigating whether any are contained within it, since for the present purpose it is enough to know this about them: none of them designates the simple substance of the supreme nature [Col. 0163C] [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read “and for the purpose.”].

Since, then, whatever else exists, when each thing is examined, is either better than its negation or its negation is in some respect better than it [Note: [Col. 0163D] Thuanus reads “or if it is better”; the manuscripts of Victor, Gemblacensis, Corbeiensis, and Sigebert read “or is better.”], just as it is impious to suppose that the substance of the supreme nature is something whose negation is in any respect better, so it is necessary that it be whatever is altogether better than its negation [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read “human nature” instead of “the supreme nature.”]. For it alone is that than which absolutely nothing is better, and it is better than all things that are not what it is.

Therefore it is not a body, nor any of those things discerned by the bodily senses. For something that is not what these things are is better than all of them. A rational mind, which is not perceived by any bodily sense—neither what it is, nor what kind, nor how great it is—would be so much less if it were one of the things subject to bodily senses [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read *si esset aliud* (“if it were something else”) for *si esset aliquid* (“if it were something”).], and is therefore greater than any of them [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts of Corbeiensis and Victor read “it would be better than,” rather than “it is greater than.”]. For it must be understood that the supreme essence is none of those things above which stands something that is not what they are; and, exactly as reason teaches, it must be said to be whatever is above all those things below which stands everything that is not what they are.

Therefore it must be living, wise, powerful and omnipotent, true, just, blessed, eternal, and whatever is similarly absolutely better than its negation [Note: [Col. 0163D] One manuscript reads “whatever is simply better,” rather than “whatever is similarly better.”]. What more, then, is there to ask about what that supreme nature is, if it is clear what it is among all things and what it is not among all things [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read “and what it is not”; the Gothic edition reads “or what it is not among all things.”]?

## CHAPTER XVI [elsewhere XV] [Note: [Col. 0163D] Chapter 15 in the manuscripts is chapter 16.] [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript of Corbeiensis reads “That it is so,” etc., as in the title of chapter 16 in the printed editions.]

That for it to be just is the same as for it to be justice [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read *illi justa quod* (“that it is just for it”), omitting *esse* (“to be”) from *illi esse justam quod*.]; and the same applies to those things that can similarly be said of it; and that none of these shows what kind or how great it is, but what it is.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

The supreme nature is whatever it is not through another but through itself; and it is just, indeed through justice. Therefore the supreme nature is its own justice; and when it is called just through justice, it is understood to be just through itself. Then, if one asks what the supreme nature is, what answer is truer than “justice”? Therefore one does not properly say of the supreme nature that it has justice, but that it exists as justice; and when it is said to exist as justice, one does not say what kind it is, but what it is. Therefore, when it is called just, one does not say what kind it is, but what it is; and it is the same as if one said, “It is justice.” Understand the same concerning the other things that are said similarly of God. Moreover, whatever good the supreme nature is, it is that good supremely. Therefore it is supreme essence, supreme life, supreme reason, supreme justice, and so forth; this is nothing other than supremely existing, supremely living, supremely rational, supremely just, and so forth.

10 But perhaps when it is called just, or great, or something similar [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read “or another similar thing.”], it does not show what it is, but rather what kind or how great it is. For each of these terms appears to be predicated through quality or quantity [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript of Saint-Michael reads “each of these things.”]. Everything that is just is just through justice, and likewise with other such things [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read “other such things.”]. Therefore the supreme nature is not just except through justice. It thus appears to be called just through participation in a quality—namely, justice—so that the supremely good substance would be just; but if this is so, it is just through another, not through itself.

Yet this is contrary to perfect truth, because whatever is good, or great, or subsistent, and is so altogether, is so through itself, not through another. If, therefore, it is not just except through justice, it cannot be just except through itself [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscripts read “nor can the supreme be [so]” rather than “nor can it be just.”]. What is more evident, what more necessary, than that the same nature is justice itself? And when it is said to be just through justice [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript of Corbeiensis reads: “When it is said to be just through itself, nothing other than ‘through justice’ is understood.” The manuscripts of Victor, Sigebert, and Gemblacensis read: “When it is said to be just through justice, it is the same as ‘through itself’; and when it is said to be just through itself, nothing other than ‘through justice’ is understood.” The manuscripts of Thuanus and Saint-Michael read: “When it is said to be just through itself, nothing other than ‘through justice’ is understood.”], this is the same as being just through itself; and when it is said to be just through itself, nothing other than being just through justice is understood [Col. 0165A].

Therefore, if one asks what the supreme nature under discussion is, what answer is truer than “justice”? We must therefore consider how it should be understood when that nature, which is justice itself [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “which is justice,” rather than “which is justice itself.”], is called just. Since a human being cannot be justice, but can have justice, a human being who is called just is not understood to exist as justice, but to possess justice.

Since, therefore, one does not properly say of the supreme nature that it has justice [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts of Victor, Sigebert, and Thuanus omit “is just.”], but that it exists as justice, when it is called just it is properly understood to exist as justice, not to possess justice [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thuanus reads “when it is called justice,” rather than “when it is called just.”]. Therefore, if when it is said to exist as justice one does not say what kind it is but what it is, it follows that when it is called just one does not say what kind it is [Col. 0165B], but what it is.

Furthermore, since of that supreme essence it is the same to say that it is just and that it exists as justice; and since, when it is said to exist as justice [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thuanus reads “when it is said to exist,” omitting “is.”], this means nothing other than that it is justice, there is no difference in it whether one says “it is justice” or “it is just” [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts of Victor and Sigebert read “it is just; or it is justice.”]. Therefore, when one asks what it is, it is no less appropriate to answer “just” than “justice.” What is clearly established in the example of justice, reason compels the intellect to understand concerning all the things that are similarly said of the supreme nature. Whatever of these things is said of it does not show what kind or how great it is, but rather what it is.

It is obvious, moreover, that whatever good the supreme nature is, it is that good supremely. Therefore it is supreme essence, supreme life, supreme reason, supreme salvation, supreme justice, supreme wisdom, supreme truth, supreme goodness, supreme greatness, supreme beauty, supreme immortality, supreme incorruptibility, supreme immutability, supreme blessedness, supreme eternity, supreme power, and supreme unity. This is nothing other than supremely existing, supremely living, and similarly with the rest [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “the rest simply,” rather than “the rest similarly.”].

## CHAPTER XVII [elsewhere XVI] [Note: [Col. 0165D] Chapter 16 in the manuscripts is chapter 17.] [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript of Corbeiensis reads “That it is without …,” etc., as in the title of chapter 18 in the printed editions.]

That it is so simple that all the things which can be said of its essence are one and the same in it; and that nothing can be said of it substantially except insofar as it is what it is.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

Everything composite requires the things of which it is composed, owes to them what it is, and through them is whatever it is; but what those things are, they are not through it. Therefore it is not supreme. It is impious to say these things of the supreme nature. [Col. 0165D] Therefore it is not composite. Since it is itself so many goods—life, reason, goodness, justice, and so forth, which are said of God [Col. 0166A]—it is necessary that all these goods be not many but one. Therefore any one of them is identical with all of them, whether taken together or individually. And since, in a single consideration, the supreme nature is whatever it is, because essentially it is the whole of what it is, nothing is said of it insofar as it is what kind or how great, but insofar as it is what it is.

What, then? If that supreme nature is so many goods, will it be composed of so many goods [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “so many goods,” rather than the alternate construction “so many goods.”]; or rather are there not many goods, but one good signified by so many names? Everything composite, in order to subsist, requires the things of which it is composed; and it owes to them what it is, because whatever it is, it is through them; but what those things are, they are not through it [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thuanus omits “indeed.”]. For that reason it is not supreme at all.

If, therefore, that nature is composed of many goods, all the features that belong to every composite must necessarily fall upon it [Col. 0166B]. But the whole necessity of truth that was made evident above destroys and overwhelms this impious falsehood by a clear argument [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts of Victor, Sigebert, and Saint-Michael read “an appropriate argument,” rather than “a clear argument.”]. Since, then, that nature is in no way composite and yet is in every respect so many goods, it is necessary that all those goods be not many but one [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “it is necessary that [they be] one,” omitting “is.”]. Therefore any one of them is identical with all of them, whether together [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “all are together.”] or individually; thus when “justice” or “essence” is said, it signifies the same as the others, whether all together or individually [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “one signifies,” rather than “it signifies the same.”].

Therefore, just as whatever is said essentially of the supreme substance is one, so in a single way and in a single consideration it is whatever it is essentially. When someone is called both a human being and a body and rational, these three predicates are not said in one way or under one consideration. In one respect he is a body, and in another he is rational [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read *aliud rationale* (“rational in another respect”) rather than *aliud rationalis* (“in another he is rational”).], and neither of these individually is the whole of what a human being is [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “the whole of this” rather than “the whole of what a human being is.”]. But the supreme essence is not in any way something such that it is not that same thing in another mode or under another consideration, because whatever it essentially is in any mode is the whole of what it is.

Therefore nothing that is truly said of its essence is understood insofar as it is what kind or how great, but insofar as it is what it is. For whatever is or is of some kind or magnitude is also something else insofar as it is what it is [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “is also something else” rather than the alternate reading “and is something else”]; hence it is not simple but composite [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscripts read “not simple, but” rather than “not simple but composite.”].

## CHAPTER XVIII [elsewhere XVII] [Note: [Col. 0165D] Chapter 17 in the manuscripts is chapter 18.] [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript of Corbeiensis reads “How there was nothing,” etc., as in the title of chapter 18 in the printed editions.]

That it is without beginning and without end.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

If the supreme substance has a beginning, it has it either from itself, from another, or from nothing. It does not have it from another or from nothing, since it has been proved that it is not from another or from nothing. Nor does it have a beginning from itself or through itself: for it is from itself and through itself in such a way that there is not one essence which is through itself and from itself, and another through which and from which it exists; otherwise it would no longer be through itself but through another. Therefore the supreme nature did not begin through itself or from itself.

Nor will it have an end. For if it is going to have an end: (1) it is not supreme life, that is, immortal and incorruptible; (2) it will perish either willingly or unwillingly: not willingly, because it is not a simple good by whose will the supreme good perishes; but if unwillingly, it is not supremely powerful; (3) it would not be eternal; (4) truth cannot be conceived as having a beginning or an end. For it was never untrue that something was going to be, and it will never be untrue that something has been.

From what point, then, has this supremely simple nature, the creator and vigor of all things, existed, and until what point will it exist? Or rather, does it exist neither from some point nor until some point, but without beginning and without end [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “without end? If it is,” rather than “without end is it?”]?

For if it has a beginning, it has it either from or through itself, or from or through another, or from or through nothing [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “or in place of nothing. But,” rather than “or through nothing. But.”]. But it is established through the truth already examined that it is in no way from another, from nothing, through another, or through nothing. Therefore it has in no way received a beginning through another or from another, through nothing or from nothing.

Nor can it have a beginning from itself or through itself, although it exists from itself and through itself. For it is from itself and through itself [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “it is from itself through itself,” omitting the conjunction.] in such a way that there is in no way one essence which exists through itself and from itself, and another through which and from which it exists. Whatever begins to exist from something or through something is not altogether identical with that from which or through which it begins to exist. Therefore the supreme nature did not begin through itself or from itself [Col. 0167C].

Since, then, it has a beginning neither through itself nor from itself, neither through another nor from another, neither through nothing nor from nothing, it has a beginning in no way.

Nor will it have an end. For if it is going to have an end, it is not supremely immortal and supremely incorruptible; but it is established that it is supremely immortal and incorruptible. Therefore it will not have an end.

Furthermore, if it is going to have an end, it will perish either willingly or unwillingly. But it certainly is not a simple good whose will causes the supreme good to perish; and it is itself the true and simple good. Therefore it will not perish of its own accord, since it is certain that it is the supreme good.

But if it is going to perish unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript of Saint-Michael reads “if, then, it is unwilling.”], it is not supremely powerful or omnipotent; yet the necessity of reason has affirmed that it is supremely powerful and omnipotent. Therefore it will not perish unwillingly. [Col. 0167D] Thus, if the supreme nature will have an end neither willingly nor unwillingly [elsewhere omitted], it will in no way have an end [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “if the supreme nature will have an end unwillingly, it will in no way have an end”; the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “unwillingly; in no way.”].

Furthermore, if that supreme nature has an end [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts of Victor, Sigebert, and Saint-Michael read “has, or will have, an end,” rather than “has an end.”], or a beginning, it is not true eternity. But it has been shown above that it is true eternity [Col. 0168A] [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “which has been found above,” rather than “that it is … found above.”].

Let anyone who can consider when it began, or when this was not true—namely, that something was going to be—or when it will cease, and this will not be true—namely, that something will have been. But if neither of these can be conceived, and neither can be true without truth, it is impossible even to conceive that truth has a beginning or an end.

Finally, if truth had a beginning or will have an end, before it began it was then true that truth did not exist [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “it was true because then,” rather than “it was then true because.”]; and after it has ended, it will be true that it does not exist [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “then it will be true that,” rather than “it will be true because.”]. But the true cannot exist without truth. Therefore truth existed before truth existed, and truth will exist after truth has ended, which is utterly absurd.

Whether, then, truth is said to have, or is understood not to have, a beginning or an end, truth cannot be enclosed by any beginning or end. The same therefore follows concerning the supreme nature, since it is supreme truth.

## CHAPTER XIX [Note: [Col. 0167D] Chapter 18 in the manuscripts is chapter 19.]

How there was nothing before it, or will be nothing after it.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

There are two meanings of the statement, “There was nothing before the supreme essence.” One meaning is: before the supreme essence existed, there was a time when there was nothing. The other is: before the supreme essence, there was not anything. In the first sense the statement is false; in the second it is true. There is likewise a double meaning when it is said: “After the supreme essence there will be nothing.”

But behold, “nothing” rises up again; and whatever reason has so far argued, with truth and necessity jointly bearing witness [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts of Victor, Gemblacensis, Sigebert, Saint-Michael, and Corbeiensis read “reason in truth,” rather than “reason bearing witness through truth.”], it now asserts to be nothing. For if what was set out above has been secured by the protection of necessary truth, there was nothing before the supreme essence, nor will there be anything after it [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “something before … something after,” rather than “anything before … anything after.”]. Therefore there was nothing before it, and there will be nothing after it. For it is necessary that either something or nothing preceded it or will follow it [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “for something or nothing must have preceded or will follow.”].

But someone who says that there was nothing before it and that there will be nothing after it appears to be declaring this: there was a time before it when there was nothing, and there will be a time after it when there will be nothing. Therefore, when there was nothing, it did not exist; and when there will be nothing, it will not exist. How, then, did it not begin from nothing, or how will it not come to nothing, if it did not yet exist when there was already nothing [Note: [Col. 0167D] The Venice edition, except for the manuscripts of Thuanus, reads: “there was nothing, and the same will no longer exist when there will still be nothing. What, then?” The Gothic edition reads: “there was nothing; and the same will no longer exist, although there will still be nothing. What, then?”], and if it will no longer exist when there will still be nothing?

What, then, has such a great mass of arguments accomplished, if “nothing” so easily demolishes the constructions of those arguments [Col. 0168D]? For if it is established that supreme being succeeds preceding nothing and yields to subsequent nothing [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscripts read “it was saying,” rather than “it yields.”] [Col. 0169A], whatever was established above as true is necessarily deprived of its foundation by empty nothing [Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscripts read “is deprived by the necessity,” rather than “is necessarily deprived.”].

Or rather, must we resist nothing, lest so many structures of necessary reason be stormed by nothing, and the supreme good, sought and found by the lamp of truth, be lost for nothing? It should therefore rather be asserted, if possible, that nothing did not exist before the supreme essence and will not exist after it, than that, when a place is given to nothing before or after it, that being which through itself brought what was nothing into existence should through nothing be reduced to nothing [Note: [Col. 0169D] One manuscript reads “nothing into being”; the manuscripts and Gothic edition read “nothing to nothingness”; the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “nothing exist, to exist.”].

A single statement, “There was nothing before the supreme essence,” carries two meanings. One meaning is that before the supreme essence existed, there was a time when there was nothing. The other meaning is that before the supreme essence there was not anything [Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscripts read “there was not another thing,” rather than “there was not anything.”].

It is as if I said, “Nothing taught me to fly.” I could explain this either as meaning that nothing itself—which signifies “not anything” [Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscripts read “which signifies not,” rather than “which signifies not anything.”]—taught me to fly, which would be false; or as meaning that no thing taught me to fly [Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscripts of Victor, Sigebert, and Saint-Michael read *non me docuit volare* (“it did not teach me to fly”) for *non me docuit aliquid volare* (“no thing taught me to fly”).], which is true.

The first meaning, then, is the one that entails the absurdity discussed above, and it is rejected as false by every argument. The second is the one that agrees perfectly with what was said above [Note: [Col. 0169D] Thuanus reads “agrees with what was perceived,” rather than “agrees perfectly.”] and is compelled to be true by the whole connection of those arguments.

Therefore, when it is said that there was nothing before it, it must be understood according to the latter meaning. It must not be explained as meaning that there was ever a time when it did not exist and nothing existed; rather, it must be understood to mean that before it there was not anything.

The same reasoning applies to the two meanings if it is said that nothing will be after it. If, then, this interpretation of “nothing” is carefully distinguished, it is most truthfully concluded that neither something nor nothing preceded or will follow the supreme essence, and that nothing existed before it or will follow after it [Note: [Col. 0169D] Thuanus reads “will follow after it,” rather than “will follow it”]. Yet the solidity of everything already established is not shaken by the emptiness of nothing.

## CHAPTER XX [elsewhere XIX] [Note: [Col. 0169D] Chapter 19 in the manuscripts is chapter 20.]

That it is in every place and time.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

The creative essence exists everywhere and always: (1) because it never began or will cease to exist; (2) because the supreme nature either exists everywhere and always, or only somewhere and at some time, or nowhere and never. But it is contradictory: (1) that what exists most truly and supremely should exist nowhere and never; (2) that any good or anything should exist without the creative essence, without which nothing exists anywhere or at any time [Col. 0170A].

Finally, it is not located determinately somewhere and at some time; for where it is not, there is no essence. Nor is it determinately present through itself in one place and time and present in the others through its power, since its power is its essence. Therefore it exists everywhere and always.

Although it has already been concluded that this creative nature is everywhere, in all things, and through all things, and from the fact that it neither began nor will cease to exist [Note: “nor does it cease to exist” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition] it follows that it always was, is, and will be [Note: “always was, is” in the manuscripts of Vict., Gem., Corb., and Sag., and in the Gothic edition: “always was, is, and will be”]. I nevertheless [Note: “however, someone” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition] sense something murmuring in contradiction [Note: manuscript S. Mich.: “of the murmur of contradiction”], which compels me to investigate more carefully where and when it exists. Thus the supreme essence either exists everywhere and always, or only somewhere and at some time, or nowhere and never—that is, either [Col. 0170B] in every place and time [Note: “in every place or time” in the manuscripts], or determinately [Note: “or determining” in the manuscripts] in some place or time, or in none. But what could be more contrary to reason than that what exists most truly and supremely should exist nowhere and never [Note: “that it should exist nowhere and never” in the manuscripts]? It is therefore false that it exists nowhere or never [Note: “therefore it exists nowhere and never” in the manuscripts of Gem., Vict., and Sag., and in the Gothic edition].

Moreover, since no good, indeed nothing at all, exists without it [Note: the manuscripts of Vict., Gem., and Sag. read: “How [can there be] no good?”], if it exists nowhere or never, then nowhere or never does any good exist, and nowhere or never does anything at all exist. There is no need to say how false this is [Note: “Although it is false” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition]. It is therefore also false that it exists nowhere or never [Note: “that it exists nowhere and never” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition].

It must therefore either exist determinately somewhere and at some time, or everywhere and always. But if [Note: the manuscripts of Thu. read “or if it exists determinately”] it exists determinately in some place or time, then only there and then—where and when it exists—can anything [Col. 0170C] exist. Wherever and whenever it does not exist, there is then absolutely no essence, because nothing exists without it. It would therefore follow [Note: the manuscripts of Vict. and Sag., and the Gothic edition, read “it follows”] that there is some place and some time where and when absolutely nothing exists. Since this is false—for that place and time themselves are something—it cannot be that the supreme nature exists determinately somewhere or at some time [Note: “somewhere and at some time determinately” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition].

But if it is said [Note: the manuscripts of Vict., Thu., Gem., and Sag. read “because it exists determinately”] that it exists determinately somewhere and at some time through itself, while through its power it exists wherever or whenever anything exists, this is not true. For it is clear that its power is nothing other than its very being; therefore its power cannot in any way exist without it. Since, then, it does not exist determinately somewhere or at some time, it must exist everywhere and always, [Col. 0170D] that is, in every place and time.

[Col. 0171A]

## CHAPTER XXI [alternatively XX]

That it is in no place or time.

**Summary of the chapter.**—It is entirely alien to the supreme nature to have a composition of parts or a division. Therefore it is not wholly in all places and times in such a way that it is present by parts in each. Whether it is wholly and simultaneously in each place and time is investigated as follows: if it is wholly and simultaneously in each place, then in each place there is a distinct whole. For what is wholly in some place has nothing of itself outside that place; but of that from which nothing exists outside that place, nothing can simultaneously be in another place. Therefore one whole cannot simultaneously be wholly in different places. Hence there are distinct wholes in the several places. Therefore, if the supreme nature is wholly and simultaneously in each place, then as many supreme natures exist as there can be separate places. It is therefore not wholly and simultaneously in all places.

Nor is it wholly and simultaneously in all times, since the times themselves are not simultaneous; nor is it wholly and distinctly in each time. Otherwise its eternity, which is its very essence, would have parts—present, past, and future. Therefore it is in no way in every place or time. Yet since nothing exists without it anywhere or at any time, it must be everywhere and always.

### 12

But if this is so, then either it is wholly in every place or time, or only some part of it is, so that another part is outside every place and time. If it is partly present and partly not present everywhere and always, it has parts; but that is false. It is therefore not partly everywhere and always.

How, then, is it wholly everywhere and always? [Note: An alternate text omits this sentence; the Gothic edition also omits it.] It must either be understood as wholly and simultaneously in all places or times, and by parts in the several places or times [Note: “so that it is wholly and simultaneously” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Gem.], or as wholly present even in each [Note: “or so that it is wholly present even” in the manuscripts]. But if it is present by parts in each, it does not escape composition and division into parts; and this has been found to be entirely alien to the supreme nature. Therefore it is not wholly in all places and times in such a way that it is present by parts in each.

The other possibility remains to be examined: namely, how the supreme nature is wholly in all places and times and in each place and time [Note: “in places or times” in the manuscripts of Vict. and Sag.]. This plainly cannot be unless it is so either simultaneously or at different times. But since the account of place and the account of time, which our inquiry had previously been able to pursue together on the same path [Note: the manuscripts of Gem., Vict., Sag., Thu., and Cister. read “pursuit” or “prosecution”], here appear to diverge from one another [Note: “here they diverge from one another” in the Gothic edition; “departing” in the manuscripts] and to flee the discussion by different, almost winding routes, they must be investigated separately in their own examinations. First, therefore, let it be considered [Col. 0171D] whether the supreme nature can be wholly in each place [Note: the manuscripts read “whether in the supreme nature”], either simultaneously or at different times. Then the same question will be investigated with respect to times.

If, then, it is wholly and simultaneously in each place [Col. 0172A], there are distinct wholes in the several places. For just as one place is distinguished from another so that there are distinct places, so what is wholly in one place is distinguished from what is wholly, at the same time, in another place, so that there are distinct wholes. For what is wholly in some place has nothing of itself that is not in that place. But of that of which there is nothing that is not in some place, nothing exists of it at the same time outside that same place. Therefore what is wholly in some place has nothing of itself that at the same time is outside that place. But of that of which nothing is outside any given place, nothing of it is at the same time in another place. Therefore what is wholly in any place has nothing of itself simultaneously in another place [Note: “nothing is simultaneously in another” in the manuscripts].

If, then, something is wholly in some place, how can it also be wholly in another place at the same time [Note: “how can it also be wholly at the same time” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., S. Mich., and Cister.] if nothing of it can be in another place? Since, therefore, one whole cannot simultaneously be wholly in different places, it follows that there are distinct wholes in the several places, if something wholly is simultaneously in each place.

Consequently, if the supreme nature is wholly at one time in all the several places, then as many supreme natures exist as there can be separate places. It is unreasonable to believe this. Therefore it is not wholly at one time in the several places.

But if it is wholly in each place at different times [Note: “but if it is wholly in different times” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition], when it is in one place, no good and no essence exists meanwhile in the other places, because nothing at all exists without it. The places themselves, which are not nothing but something, prove this absurd. The supreme nature is therefore not wholly in each place at different times.

If it is wholly in each place neither at the same time nor at different times [Note: “nor in different times” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Cister.], it is clear that it is in no way wholly in all the several places.

It must now be investigated [Note: the manuscripts of Vict., Thu., and Cister. read “Now it must be investigated”] whether the same supreme nature is wholly in each time, either simultaneously or distinctly through the several times [Note: “Here chapter 21 begins in another place.”] [Note: “Chapter 21 is chapter 22 in the manuscripts”].

But how can something be wholly and simultaneously in each time, if the times themselves are not simultaneous? If, however, it is wholly and distinctly in each time, in the way that a whole man is wholly yesterday, today, and tomorrow, it is properly said to have been, to be, and to be going to be. Therefore its age, which is nothing other than its eternity, is not wholly simultaneous, but is extended in parts through the parts of time.

Yet its eternity is nothing other than itself [Note: the manuscripts read “than the supreme essence itself”]. The supreme essence will therefore be divided into parts according to the distinctions of time [Col. 0172D]. For if its age is extended through the courses of time, it has, together with time, present, past, and future. But what else is its age, or duration of existence, than its eternity? Therefore, since its eternity is nothing other than its essence, as the reasoning set out above proves beyond doubt, if its eternity has past, present, and future, then consequently its essence also has past, present, and future.

But what is past is not present or future; what is present is not past or future [Note: “will not be past or future” in the manuscripts; “is not future or past” in the manuscript of S. Mich.; “is not past or future” in the manuscripts]; and what is future is not past or present [Note: “is not past or present” in the manuscripts of Thu.; “is neither past nor present” in the manuscripts]. How, then, can what was established above with rational and evident necessity [Note: the manuscripts of Gem., Vict., Sag., and Cister. read: “namely, that the supreme nature is in no way …”] stand—namely, that this supreme nature is in no way composite, but supremely simple and supremely immutable—if one thing and another exist at different times [Note: the manuscripts and Gothic edition read “but if another and another”], and it has parts distributed through time? Or rather, if those propositions are true [Col. 0173B]—indeed, because they are plainly true [Note: “plainly” in the manuscripts of Vi. and Sag.; “plain”]—how can this be possible?

Therefore, in no way does the creative essence, its age, or its eternity admit a past or a future. For how could it not have the present, if it truly exists? But “it was” signifies the past, and “it will be” the future. Therefore it never was and never will be; hence it is not distinct [Note: “is not distinct” in the manuscripts], just as it is not wholly simultaneous in the several times.

If, then, as has been examined [Note: the manuscripts and Gothic edition read “Thus, then, it has been examined”], it is neither wholly in all places or times in such a way that it is wholly once in all of them and by parts in each, nor in such a way that it is wholly in each, it is clear that it is not wholly in every place or time in any way. And since it has likewise been seen [Note: “has been foreseen” in the manuscripts of Thu. and the Gothic edition] that it is not everywhere and always in such a way that one part is everywhere and another part is outside every place or time, it is impossible for it to be everywhere and always.

For it cannot be understood to be everywhere and always unless it is either wholly or partly so. If, then, it is in no way everywhere and always, it must either be determinately in some place or time, or in none. But that it cannot be determinately in some place has already been examined. It is therefore in no place or time—that is, nowhere and never [Note: “nowhere or never” in the manuscripts of Thu.]. For it cannot exist except either in every place or in some place.

Yet it is established incontrovertibly not only that it exists through itself, without beginning and without end, but also that nothing exists anywhere or at any time without it. Therefore it must be everywhere and always [Note: “it is necessary that it be” in the manuscripts of Vi., Gem., and Sag.].

## CHAPTER XXII [alternatively XXIII]

How it is in every place and time and in no place or time [Note: Chapter 22 is chapter 23 in some manuscripts, under the title: “How it can be understood better as being everywhere than as being in every place”; Gem. has: “How it is in every and in no place and time.” In the manuscripts of Vict., Thu., Gem., Cister., and Sag., chapter 21 continues here; S. Mich. and Thu. have the heading “place and time.”]

[Col. 0173D]

**Summary of the chapter.**—These propositions, so contrary in their wording and so necessary according to their proof, are mutually compatible.
