The assertion that one whole cannot simultaneously be wholly in different places or times is true only of things that are in place and time in such a way that they do not exceed the spatial extent of the place or the duration of the time. For a place belongs only to that whose quantity the place circumscribes and contains; and a time belongs only to that whose duration it terminates by measuring it.

But the supreme nature is enclosed by no boundaries; rather, its power, which is its very essence, comprehends all things beneath itself. Therefore no spatial or temporal confinement contains it. Since it receives neither the magnitude nor the smallness of any local or temporal extension, nor any part of such extension, it is circumscribed by no place or time.

Nevertheless, necessity requires that the supreme essence, wholly, be absent from no place or time; and no law of place or time prevents it from being wholly present simultaneously in every place and time. Therefore it is wholly and simultaneously present in all places and times and in each of them. For it is said to be in a place or time not because it is contained, but because it is present. Yet it would be more aptly said to be with a place or time than in a place or time [Col. 0174B], because “to be in a place or time” properly signifies being contained.

Thus the supreme nature is in every place and time because it is absent from none; and it is in no place or time because it is enclosed by none and subject to no laws of place or time.

How, then, are these propositions—so necessary according to their wording and so necessary according to their proof—compatible? Perhaps the supreme nature is in a place or time in a manner that does not prevent it from being wholly and simultaneously in each place or time [Note: “in places or times” in the manuscripts of Vict., Gem., Sag., and Cist.], while nevertheless there are not several wholes, but one single whole, and while its age, which is nothing other than true eternity, is not divided into past, present, and future.

For it seems that the law of place and time compels only those things that are in place or time in such a way that they do not exceed the extent of the place or the duration of the time. Therefore, just as it is asserted with complete truth of things of this kind that one and the same whole cannot simultaneously be wholly in different places or times [Note: “in places or times” in the manuscripts of Vict., Gem., Sag., and Cist.], so in the case of things that are not of this kind, the same conclusion is not established by any necessity.

For it seems rightly said that a place belongs only to that whose quantity the place circumscribes by enclosing it, and encloses by circumscribing it; and that a time belongs only to that whose duration time, by measuring it, terminates in some way, and by terminating measures. Therefore, where no boundary is imposed by either place or time upon a thing’s magnitude or duration, it is truly proposed that no place or time belongs to it.

Since place does not perform for it what place performs, nor time what time performs, it is not irrationally said that no place is its place and no time is its time. But whatever is seen to have no place or time is plainly proved not to be subject in any way to the law of place or time.

Therefore no law of place or time compels any nature [Note: the manuscripts read “that nature”] in any way if no place or time [Note: the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Gem. read “place and time”] encloses it by containment [Col. 0175A]. What rational consideration [Note: the manuscripts and Gothic edition read “what rational consideration indeed”; the manuscripts except Thu. read “would not exclude”] would not conclude in every respect that the creative and supreme substance of all things—necessarily alien and free from the nature and law of all the things it made from nothing—cannot be enclosed by any confinement of place or time [Note: the manuscripts of Vi., Sag., and S. Mich. read “any confinement of place”; the manuscripts read “which is nothing,” for “which is nothing other than”], since its power, which is nothing other than its essence, encompasses beneath itself all things made by it?

How could it not be an instance of shameless folly to say that the quantity of supreme truth is circumscribed by place or its duration measured by time, when it admits absolutely neither magnitude nor smallness of local or temporal extension [Note: “division” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition]?

Since, then, the condition of place or time is that only whatever is enclosed by their boundaries is subject to them, and that it cannot escape the logic of parts—whether according to the quantity its place contains or according to the duration its time undergoes—and since in no way can a whole be simultaneously contained by different places or times, whatever is not at all constrained by the containment of place or time is not compelled by any law of places or times into a plurality of parts, nor is it prevented from being wholly present simultaneously in several places or times.

Since, I say, this is the condition of place or time, the supreme substance, which is enclosed by no containment of place or time, is bound by none of their laws. Therefore, since both unavoidable necessity requires the supreme essence, wholly, to be absent from no place or time [Col. 0175C], and no reasoning concerning place or time prevents it from being wholly present simultaneously in every place and time, it must be wholly and simultaneously present in all places and times and in each of them.

For the fact that it is present to this place or time does not prevent it from being present simultaneously and in the same way to that place or time; nor, because it was, is, or will be, has some part of its eternity vanished from the present together with the past [Note: “and the past” in the manuscripts of Vi., Sag., Gem., and Cister.], which no longer exists, or passed away with the present, which scarcely exists, or arrived with the future, which does not yet exist [Note: “some part of it” in one manuscript and the Gothic edition].

For what in no way encloses its being within a place or time is neither compelled nor prevented by the law of places or times from being or not being somewhere or at some time. Now, if the supreme essence itself is said to be in a place or time, although the same expression is used of it and of local or temporal natures because of customary speech, the meaning is nevertheless different because the things themselves are dissimilar [Note: One manuscript of Sag. omits “because of the dissimilarity of things”; the manuscript of Vict. 13. has “because of the similarity of things.”]

In the case of those other things, the same expression signifies two facts: namely, that they are present in the places and times in which they are said to exist, and that they are contained by them. In the case of the supreme essence, only one fact is signified: that it is present, not also that it is contained. Hence, if usage permitted it, it would seem more appropriate to say that it is with a place or time than that it is in a place or time.

For when something is said to be in another, its being contained is signified more truly than when it is said to be with another. Strictly speaking, therefore, it is in no place or time, because it is contained by nothing else [Col. 0176B]; yet in a certain manner it can be said to be in every place or time, since whatever else exists is sustained by its presence lest it fall into nothingness.

It is in every place and time because it is absent from none; and it is in no place or time because it has no place or time, nor does it receive within itself distinctions of places or times. It is neither here nor there [Note: the manuscripts read “nec habet nec illic,” in place of “nec hic vel illic”], nor somewhere, nor then, nor now, nor at some time. Nor does it exist according to the fleeting present time that we use, nor was it according to the past, nor will it be according to the future, because these are proper to things that are circumscribed and mutable, whereas it is not.

Yet these expressions can in some manner be said of it, because it is present to all circumscribed and mutable things as though it were itself circumscribed by those same places and changed through times.

It is therefore clear, insofar as is sufficient to dissolve the contradiction that was murmuring, how the supreme essence of all things is everywhere and always, and nowhere and never—that is, in every place and in no place, or in every time and in no time—according to the concordant truth of the different meanings [Note: One manuscript of Cister. omits “of the different meanings.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII [alternatively XXIV] [Note: In some manuscripts, chapter 23 is chapter 24, under the title: “How it can be understood better as being everywhere than as being in every place.”]

How it can be understood better as being everywhere than as being in every place.

**Summary of the chapter.**—Local words—“where,” “there,” and so forth—are often applied without error to things that are neither places nor contained by local circumscription, as when it is said that understanding is there in the soul where rationality is. Thus it is more aptly said that the supreme nature is everywhere, that is, in all things that exist, than that it is in all places. It is not in all things as though it were contained by them, but as that which, by penetrating all things, contains them [Col. 0176D].

[Col. 0177A]

Since it is established that the same supreme nature is no more in all places than in all things that exist—not as something contained, but as that which, by penetrating all things, contains them—why should it not be said to be everywhere in this sense, so that it is understood to be in all things that exist rather than merely in all places, since both the truth of the matter supports this meaning and the proper use of the local word in no way forbids it?

For we are accustomed to apply local words frequently and without error to things that are neither places nor contained by local circumscription, as when I say that understanding is there in the soul where rationality is. Although “there” and “where” are local adverbs [Note: the manuscripts read “ibi et ubi adverbia localia sint”; Thu. reads “ubi et ibi sint localia verba” (“where and there are local words”)], nevertheless neither does the soul contain anything by local circumscription, nor is understanding or rationality contained.

Therefore, according to the truth of the matter, the supreme nature is more aptly said to be everywhere [Note: “is more aptly said everywhere” in the manuscripts] in the sense that it is understood to be in all things that exist than if it is understood to be merely in all places [Note: “than if it is understood in all places, and” in the manuscripts]. And since, as the reasons set out above teach, it cannot be otherwise, it must be in all things that exist in such a way that it is one and the same, perfectly whole, simultaneously in each.

## CHAPTER XXIV [alternatively XXV] [Note: In some manuscripts, chapter 24 is chapter 25. In Gem. and Cister. the title is: “How it can be understood better as being always than as being in every time.”]

How it can be understood better to “be always” than to “be in every time.”

**Summary of the chapter.**—The supreme nature has neither beginning nor end, nor present, past, or future, which are temporal distinctions, because its eternity, which is nothing other than itself, is immutable and without parts. Since the word “always” more properly signifies eternity, while time signifies variation, it is more fitting to say that the supreme nature always exists than that it exists in every time. And since eternity is interminable life existing wholly and perfectly at once, it belongs exclusively to this supreme nature, which lacks a beginning, an end, and every limit.

It is likewise established that this same supreme substance exists without beginning and without end; nor does it have a past or future, nor anything temporal—that is, the fleeting present that we use—because its age or eternity, which is nothing other than itself, is immutable and without parts.

Does “always,” then, which seems to designate the whole of time, not much more truly, when it is said of it, signify eternity, which is never unlike itself, than the variation of times, which is always unlike itself in some respect [Col. 0177D]? Therefore, if it is said to exist always, since for it to exist and to live are the same, nothing is better understood than that it exists or lives eternally—that is, that it possesses interminable life wholly and perfectly at once [Col. 0178A].

For its eternity seems to be interminable life existing wholly and perfectly at once [Note: “but its eternity seems” in the manuscripts of Gem. and Sag.]. Since it is already sufficiently clear from what was said above that this same substance is nothing other than its life and its eternity, and since it is in no way terminable [Note: “determinable” in the manuscript of Thu.], nor exists except wholly, simultaneously, and perfectly, what else is true eternity—which belongs to it alone—than interminable life existing wholly, simultaneously, and perfectly?

Indeed, even from this alone it is clearly understood that true eternity belongs only to that substance which alone is found not to have been made but to be the maker, since true eternity is understood to lack the boundary of a beginning and an end. That this can belong to none of created things is demonstrated by the very fact that they were made from nothing.

## CHAPTER XXV [Note: Elsewhere this is part of chapter 24.]

That it is not mutable through any accidents.

**Summary of the chapter.**—Some accidents produce change; others, such as relations, introduce no change. But the supreme nature, because it is simple, is not subject to accidents that produce change. Therefore it is not susceptible to any accident; for those things are improperly called accidents that do not alter the thing. The supreme essence is therefore in no respect mutable, since it is always substantially the same and is never accidentally different in any way.

But this essence [Note: In the manuscripts of Gem., Thu., and Cister., “But this essence,” and so forth, begins chapter 25 here under the title “That it is not mutable through any accidents.”], which has been shown to be wholly the same substantially in itself, is it not at some time different from itself, even accidentally [Note: “Is it not at some time …?” in the manuscripts except Thu.]? But how is it supremely immutable if through accidents it can be not merely existent but even conceivable as variable?

Conversely, how is it not a participant in accidents, when even the fact that it is greater than all other natures and that it is dissimilar to them [Note: “and that it itself is” in the manuscript of S. Mich.; “and that it is at the same time” in the Gothic edition] seems to accrue to it [Note: “is dissimilar” in the manuscripts and Gothic edition]? But what conflict is there [Note: the manuscripts read “what conflict is there,” for “what conflicts are there”] between the susceptibility of certain things called accidents and natural immutability, if no variability of substance follows from their assumption [Note: the manuscripts read “no variability follows to the substance”; the Gothic edition: “no variability of substance follows”]?

For among all things called accidents, some are understood to be present and absent only with some alteration in the thing that participates in them, such as all colors. Others are known to produce absolutely no change, whether by accruing to or withdrawing from the thing of which they are predicated, such as certain relations.

It is clear, for example, that I am neither greater, nor smaller, nor equal, nor similar to a man who will be born after the present year. Yet, once he has been born, I will be able to have and to lose all these relations to him without any change in myself, according as he grows [Note: “according as he grows” in the manuscripts of Thu.; “according as he is growing”] or is changed by different qualities.

It is therefore evident that, among the things called accidents, some in a certain measure draw change toward themselves, while others in no way detract from immutability [Note: “draw … detract from immutability” in the manuscript of Sag.]. Just as the supreme nature never grants a place in its simplicity to accidents that produce change, so it does not refuse, with respect to those that in no way conflict with supreme immutability [Note: “immutably conflict” in the manuscripts], to be called something at some time; yet nothing belonging to its essence accrues to it from which it could be understood as variable [Note: “the being of its essence” in the manuscript of Vict. 3.].

From this too it can be concluded that it is susceptible to no accident. For just as those accidents that produce some change by accruing to or withdrawing from a thing are judged, by their very effect, truly to accede to the thing they change [Note: “by their effect” in the manuscripts], so those that lack a similar effect are found to be improperly called accidents.

Therefore, just as it is always wholly and substantially the same in itself [Note: “to be the same in itself” in the manuscripts], so it is never in any way different from itself, not even accidentally. Whatever the reasoning concerning the propriety of the name “accidents” may be, this is undoubtedly true: nothing can be said of a supremely immutable nature from which it could be understood to be mutable.

## CHAPTER XXVI [alternatively XXV] [Note: Chapter 25 is chapter 26 in the manuscripts. In the manuscript of Thu. the title is: “How it should be said to be substance; that it is outside every substance; that it is individually whatever exists in the common category of substances; and yet that it is a substance and an individual spirit.”]

How it should be said to be substance; that it is outside every substance; and that it is individually whatever exists.

**Summary of the chapter.**—Since the supreme nature is susceptible to neither change nor accident, it is called substance only if “substance” is used in the sense of “essence” [Col. 0179C]. Yet it is both outside and above every substance, because it alone exists through itself. Thus it shares with created things only a common name.

*[The supplied source ends here, within the summary of Chapter XXVI.]*
But if what has been discerned concerning the simplicity of this nature [Note: [Col. 0179D] “It has been discerned” is the reading of the Vict. manuscripts; the text reads “it is clear.”] is established, how is it a substance? For since every substance is susceptible either of the admixture of differences or of the alteration of accidents, while the complete purity of this immutable nature is inaccessible to every admixture or alteration, how, then, can it be maintained that it is any substance at all, unless “substance” is said in the sense of “essence,” and thus it is outside, just as it is above, every substance? For by as much as that being which exists through itself is whatever it is and makes everything else exist from nothing, differs from that being which, through another, becomes from nothing whatever it is [Note: [Col. 0179D] “From that being which, through another, becomes from nothing whatever it is”: MS Gem. has, “from that being which, through another being, differs from that being which, through another, becomes from nothing whatever it is”], by so much in every respect the highest substance is distant from those things that are not identical with it. And since it alone, among all natures, has from itself, without the aid of another nature, to be whatever it is [Col. 0180A], how is it not, in a unique manner and apart from association with its creature, whatever it itself is? Hence, if it ever shares with other things some name in common, the signification must undoubtedly be understood as very different.

## CHAPTER XXVII [formerly XXVI] [Note: [Col. 0179D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 26 is Chapter 27.]

### That it is not included in the common treatment of substances, and yet is a substance and an individuated spirit

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Every substance is either universal—that is, common to several—or individual, though it has an essence in common with others. The highest nature, however, neither divides itself among several substances nor joins itself in communion with another essence. Therefore it is not included in the common treatment of substances. Yet because it exists in the highest degree, it can most properly be called a substance; and because it is more excellent, it is not a body but a spirit—indeed, an individuated spirit, since it consists neither of parts nor of differences or accidents, is not subject to change, and consequently is in no way divisible.

It is therefore established that this substance is not included in any common treatment of substances, since every nature is excluded from communion in its essence with it. For every substance is treated either as universal, which is essentially common to many substances—as “being human” is common to individual human beings—or as individual, which has a universal essence in common with others, just as individual human beings have in common with one another that they are human. How, then, can anyone understand the highest nature as included in the treatment of other substances, when it neither divides itself among several substances nor joins itself to any other through essential communion? Yet since it not only exists with the greatest certainty but also exists in the highest degree among all things [Note: [Col. 0179D] The manuscripts read “the highest of all”; the text has “exists in the highest degree among all”], and since the essence of anything whatsoever is customarily called a substance, then, if anything can properly be called a substance, it is certainly not forbidden to call it one [Note: [Col. 0179D] The manuscripts read, “Therefore, if anything can properly be called…”; the text reads, “If anything can properly be called…”]. And since no essence is known to be more excellent than spirit or body [Note: [Col. 0179D] The manuscripts read “spirit and body”; the text reads “spirit or body”], and among these spirit is more excellent than body, it must accordingly be affirmed to be spirit, not body [Note: [Col. 0179D] MS Vict., Sag., Thu., and Cister. read “to be spirit and not body”; MS text omits “and”]. Since, moreover, there are no parts of this spirit, nor can there be several spirits of this kind, it must be altogether an individuated spirit. For since, as has been established above, it is composed neither of parts [Col. 0180D] nor can it be understood to be changeable through any differences or accidents, it is impossible for it to be divisible by any kind of partition.

[Col. 0181A]

## CHAPTER XXVIII [formerly XXVII] [Note: [Col. 0181D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 27 is Chapter 28.] [Note: [Col. 0181D] MS Thu. 90 reads “the creature … is not” for “created things … are not.”] That this same spirit simply is, and that created things, compared with it, are not

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Because of its immutable eternity, the highest spirit cannot in any way be said either to have been or to be going to be, but simply is. Other things, however, because they are mutable, have at some time been something they are not, or will be something they are not; and what they are scarcely exists. Moreover, they come from non-being into being not through themselves but through another, and so return to non-being unless they are sustained through another. Therefore the highest spirit alone truly, perfectly, and absolutely is in the simple sense; other things either are not or scarcely are. Yet they are not altogether nothing, for they have been made something from nothing by him who alone exists absolutely.

15. It therefore seems to follow from what has preceded that this spirit, which exists in such a wonderfully singular and singularly wonderful manner [Col. 0181B], is in one respect alone; while all other things that appear to exist in comparison with it are not. For if one attends carefully, he will see that it alone simply, perfectly, and absolutely is; whereas almost all other things are not [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts of Vict., Sag., Thu., S. Mich., and Cister. read “truly are not”; the text reads “almost are not”] and scarcely are. For this same spirit, because of its immutable eternity, cannot in any way, according to any movement, be said either to have been or to be going to be; but simply is. Nor does it mutably exist as something that at some time was not or will not be; nor is it something that at some time was or will be not. Rather, whatever it is, it is once and simultaneously and without end. Since, I say, its being is of this kind, it is rightly said simply, absolutely, and perfectly to be [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and S. Mich. read “since, inasmuch as…”; the text reads “since, I say…”].

But since all other things, mutably and in some respect, either once were or will be [Col. 0181C] what they are not, or are what at some time they were not or will not be; and since the fact that they were is now no longer, while the fact that they will be is not yet; and since that which they are in the fleeting, exceedingly brief, and scarcely existing present scarcely is [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts read “that which they are”; the text reads “since that which…”], they are rightly denied to exist simply, perfectly, and absolutely, and are asserted almost not to be, scarcely to be.

Furthermore, since everything that is other than he has come from non-being into being not through itself but through another, and since, insofar as it depends upon itself, it returns from being to non-being unless it is sustained through another, how can simple, perfect, or absolute being properly belong to such things, rather than their scarcely, or almost not, being? And since the being of that ineffable Spirit alone [Col. 0181D] cannot in any way be understood either to have begun from non-being [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts read “or to have been begun from non-being”; the text reads “or to have begun from non-being”] or to be capable of suffering, from what it is, a falling away into non-being [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts read “or to suffer any [such thing]”; the text reads “or to be capable of suffering some [such thing]”]; and since whatever he is does not exist through another [Col. 0182A] but through himself—that is, through the fact that he is himself—is it not on account of this being rightly understood to be simple, perfect, and absolute alone [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Cister. read “alone is understood to be simply perfect”; the text reads “on account of this alone is understood to be simple, perfect…”]?

Whatever is thus simply and in every respect alone perfect, simple, and absolute may, with very good reason, be called “alone existent.” Conversely [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts read “a contrario” (“on the contrary”); the text reads “e contra”], whatever by the preceding reasoning is recognized neither simply, nor perfectly, nor absolutely to be, but scarcely to be or almost not to be, is rightly said in some manner not to be. According to this reasoning, therefore, that Spirit alone is the creator, and created things are not; yet they are not altogether nothing, because they have been made something from nothing by him who alone exists absolutely.

## CHAPTER XXIX [formerly XXVIII] [Note: [Col. 0181D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 28 is Chapter 29.] [Col. 0182B] That his utterance is identical with himself and is consubstantial with him, since they are not two but one Spirit

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The highest Spirit made nothing except through himself; and whatever he made, he made through his utterance. Therefore his utterance, or Word, is nothing other than the highest Spirit himself. Moreover, this utterance through which everything created was made is not a creature but exists before every creature. Therefore it is the creating Spirit. Again, this utterance is the intelligence of the highest Spirit; but the highest nature, being simple, is its own intelligence. Therefore the highest nature is its own utterance; and this utterance is consubstantial with it, because it is an individuated Spirit.

Now, having examined what has occurred to me, as I follow reason as my guide, concerning the properties of this highest nature [Col. 0182C] [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts, except Thu., read “what has occurred as I follow”; Thu. reads “what has occurred to me as I follow”], I think it appropriate to consider, if I can, its utterance, through which all things were made. For since the force of reason firmly maintains everything that could be observed above concerning it, this in particular compels me to investigate it more carefully: namely, that it is proved to be identical with the highest Spirit himself. For if he made nothing except through himself, and whatever was made by him was made through it, how is it other than what is identical with himself [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts read “than what is identical”; the text reads “than what is identical with himself”]?

Furthermore, the things already established assert, in a manner that cannot be explained otherwise, that nothing whatsoever has ever been or can subsist except the creating Spirit and his creature. But it is impossible for this utterance of the same Spirit to be included among created things, since whatever created thing subsists [Col. 0182D] [Note: [Col. 0181D] The manuscripts read “whatever created thing subsists”; Thu. reads “whatever created thing exists”] was made through it, whereas it could not have been made through itself. For nothing can be made through itself, since whatever comes to be is posterior to that through which it comes to be; and nothing is posterior to itself. It therefore remains that this utterance of the highest Spirit, since it cannot be a creature, is nothing other than the highest Spirit.

Finally, this very utterance can be understood as nothing other than the intelligence of the same Spirit, by which he understands all things. For what else is it for him to utter a thing in this manner of uttering than to understand it? For he does not, like a human being, fail to say at all times what he understands [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “a human being always says”; the text reads “like a human being, he does not always say”]. If, therefore, the supremely simple nature is nothing other than what its intelligence is, just as it is identical with what its wisdom is [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “is what its being is”; the text reads “is identical with what its wisdom is”], it must likewise be nothing other than what its utterance is. But since it is now evident that there is only one highest Spirit, wholly individuated, this utterance of his must be consubstantial with him [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “so that his utterance may be consubstantial with him”; the text reads “so that this utterance of his may thus be consubstantial with him”], so that they are not two but [Col. 0183B] one Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXX [formerly XXIX] [Note: [Col. 0183D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 29 is Chapter 30.] That the same utterance does not consist of several words but is one Word

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Since this utterance is consubstantial with the highest nature, which is simple and one, it is likewise simple and one; consequently, it does not consist of several words but is one Word.

Why, then, should I hesitate over what I previously left uncertain—namely, whether this utterance consists in several words or in one word? For if it is consubstantial with the highest nature in such a way that they are not two but one Spirit, then, just as that nature is supremely simple, so is this utterance. It therefore does not consist of several words but is one Word [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “but one”; the text reads “but is one Word”], through which all things were made.

[Col. 0183C]

## CHAPTER XXXI [formerly XXX] [Note: [Col. 0183D] In the printed editions, Chapter 31 appears under this title: “That the Word itself…” as in the title of Chapter 30.] That the Word itself is not the likeness of things made, but the truth of essence; and that created things are some imitation of truth. And which natures are more real and more excellent than others

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The Word by which all things are spoken and through which all things were made is consubstantial with supreme immutability, because it is consubstantial with the highest nature, which is its own immutability. Therefore that Word is not a true likeness of mutable things, although they were made according to its pattern. Since its essence exists in the highest degree and alone truly exists, it is the truth of existence; other things are nothing but its imitation. Hence a creature exists to a greater degree and is more excellent to the extent that it is more like that Word which exists supremely and is supremely great. Hence living natures are superior to nonliving ones, sentient to nonsentient, rational to nonrational. It is likewise clear that some things exist more than others: for that nature exists more which is more like the highest essence. And that which participates in more things is more like it, or is like the highest essence in more respects; moreover, that participates in more things from which more can be removed, at least in thought. Since every essence exists and is more excellent precisely to the extent that it is more like that essence which exists and excels supremely [Col. 0184A], it is clear that the Word is not the likeness of a creature but true essence, whereas in created things there is not absolute essence but an imitation of true essence. Thus created things themselves are more or less true to the extent that they approach it more or less.

But behold, it seems to me that a question is arising—neither easy nor one that should in any way be left in ambiguity [Note: [Col. 0183D] The passage beginning “But behold, it seems…” begins in MSS Gem. and Cister.]. For all such words by which we speak of things in the mind—that is, think of them—are likenesses and images of the things whose words they are; and every likeness or image [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “likeness and image”; the text reads “likeness or image”] is more or less true according as it imitates more or less the thing of which it is the likeness. What, then [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “What, then”; the text reads “But what…”], are we to maintain concerning the Word by which all things are spoken and through which all things were made? Will it be, or will it not be [Note: [Col. 0183D] MS Sag. reads “will it be or will it not be”; the text reads “will it be, or will it not be”], a likeness of those things that were made through it?

For if it is the true likeness of mutable things, it is not consubstantial with supreme immutability—which is false. But if it is not altogether true [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Cister. read “is not altogether”; the text reads “if it is not altogether true”], but is some kind of likeness of mutable things, the Word of supreme truth is not altogether true—which is absurd. But if it has no likeness whatsoever to mutable things, how were they made according to its pattern?

Perhaps none of this ambiguity will remain if, just as in a living human being the truth of humanity is said to exist, while a painted human being is said to be the likeness or image of that truth, so the truth of existence is understood to be in the Word, whose essence exists in such a supreme manner that, in a certain sense, it alone exists, while in those things that, in comparison with it, in some sense do not exist, yet have been made through it and according to it, some imitation of that highest essence is discerned [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Cister. read “alteration”; the text reads “imitation”].

For the Word of supreme truth—which is itself supreme truth—will thereby suffer neither increase nor diminution, according as it is more or less like creatures. Rather, everything created must exist more and be more excellent to the extent that it is more like that which exists supremely and is supremely great. Hence, perhaps—indeed, not perhaps, but certainly—every intellect judges that natures living in any manner are superior to nonliving ones, sentient to nonsentient, rational to irrational [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “every intellect”; Thu. reads “this intellect”].

For since the highest nature, in its own singular manner [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscripts read “in a certain singular manner”; Vict. and Sag. read “in a certain manner singularly”], not only exists but also lives, senses, and is rational [Col. 0184D], it is clear that among all things that exist, whatever lives in any manner is more like it than what does not live at all; whatever in any manner, or by bodily sense, knows something is more like it [Col. 0185A] than what senses nothing whatsoever; and whatever is rational is more like it than what is incapable of reason [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts read “more than what is incapable of reason”; the text reads “more than what is incapable of the reason”].

Since, by a similar reasoning, some natures exist more or less than others [Note: [Col. 0185D] Thu. reads “less than some other natures”; the text reads “less than others”], this is plain. For just as that nature is more excellent which is closer in its natural essence to the most excellent, so that nature exists more whose essence is more like the highest essence.

I think this can also easily be recognized in the following way. Suppose that, from any substance which lives, senses, and is rational, what is rational is removed in thought, then what is sentient, then what is vital, and finally the bare existence itself that remains. Who does not understand that the substance which is thus gradually destroyed is led step by step to less and less existence, and finally to non-being [Col. 0185B]? The things whose separate removal reduce any essence to less and less existence, when taken in order, lead it to greater and greater existence [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts read “will lead”; the text reads “lead”].

It is therefore evident that a living substance exists more than a nonliving one, a sentient substance more than a nonsentient one, and a rational substance more than a nonrational one. There is no doubt, then, that every essence exists and is more excellent precisely because it is more like that essence which exists and excels supremely.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that in the Word through which all things were made there is not their likeness but a true and simple essence; whereas in things made there is not simple and absolute essence but scarcely any imitation of that true essence. Hence the Word itself does not become more or less true according to the likeness of created things [Col. 0185C]; rather, every created nature stands at a higher level of essence and dignity to the extent that it appears more nearly to approach it [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts read “but, if all [created nature]…”; the text reads “but every created nature…”].

## CHAPTER XXXII [formerly XXX] [Note: [Col. 0185D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 30 is Chapter 31; in MSS Gem. and Cister. it is Chapter 32, under this title: “That the highest Spirit…” as in the title of Chapter 31 in the printed editions.] That the highest Spirit speaks himself through a coeternal Word

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—1. The highest Spirit is supreme wisdom itself. Supreme wisdom understands itself eternally and supremely, and for it to speak is identical with understanding. Therefore the highest Spirit speaks himself eternally and consequently has a coeternal Word. 2. Since a rational mind understands both itself and supreme wisdom, the highest Spirit, who is eternal, understands himself eternally and primarily. But if he understands himself eternally, he speaks himself eternally; if he speaks himself eternally, his Word is eternally with him. Thus, even if no other essence existed, his Word would necessarily be coeternal with him [Col. 0185D].

But since this is so [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts read “since these things are so”; Thu. reads “since this is so”], how can that which is simple truth be the Word of things of which it is not the likeness, when every word by which some thing is thus spoken in the mind is a likeness of that same thing? And if it is not the Word of the things that were made through it, how will it be established that it is a Word? For every word is the word of something.

Finally, if no creature ever existed [Note: [Col. 0185D] Thu. reads “if no nature ever existed”; MS S. Mich. reads “if nothing created ever existed”], there would be no word belonging to it. What, then? Are we to conclude that if there were no creature at all, that Word—which is the supreme essence needing nothing—would in no way exist? Or perhaps that supreme essence itself, which is the Word, would indeed be an eternal essence but would not be a Word if nothing were ever made through it? For there can be no word of what has not been, is not, and will not be [Note: [Col. 0185D] Thu. 90 reads “of what has not been, is not, and will not be”; the text has “of what has not been, is not, and will not be”].

According to this reasoning, then, if no essence existed besides the highest Spirit [Col. 0186B], there would be no word in him at all. If there were no word in him, he would say nothing to himself [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts, except S. Mich., read “he would say nothing to himself”; S. Mich. has “he would say nothing to himself if he said nothing to himself”]. And if he said nothing to himself, then, since for him to say something is identical with understanding something [Note: [Col. 0185D] Thu. reads “since for it”; the text reads “since for him”], he would understand nothing. If he understood nothing, then supreme wisdom—which is nothing other than that same Spirit—would understand nothing, which is utterly absurd.

What, then? If he understood nothing, how would he be supreme wisdom? Or if nothing existed in any way besides that essence, what would it understand? But surely it would understand itself? Yet how can it even be conceived that supreme wisdom at some time does not understand itself, when a rational mind can remember not only itself but also that supreme wisdom, and can understand both it [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts read “both it and itself”; the text reads “both it, and itself”] and itself [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts read “and understand itself”; Thu. reads “understand through itself”]?

For if the human mind could have no memory or understanding either of it or of itself [Col. 0186C] [Note: [Col. 0185D] The manuscripts read “or understanding”; Thu. reads “nor understanding”], it would never distinguish itself from irrational creatures, nor distinguish it from every creature, by silently debating with itself alone, as my mind now does. Therefore, just as that highest Spirit is eternal, so he is eternally mindful of himself and understands himself, after the likeness of a rational mind; indeed, not after the likeness of anything, but he is primary, while the rational mind is after his likeness.

But if he understands himself eternally, he speaks himself eternally. If he speaks himself eternally, his Word is eternally with him. Therefore, whether he is conceived as existing with no other essence or with other essences existing, his Word must be coeternal with him.

## CHAPTER XXXIII [formerly XXXI] [Col. 0186D] [Note: [Col. 0185D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 31 is Chapter 32; in MSS Gem. and Cister. it is Chapter 33 under this title: “That with one Word…” as in the title of Chapter 32. MS Thu. 30 has the title “With a coeternal Word”; another reading is “coeternal Word.”] That he speaks himself and what he makes with one consubstantial Word

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The Word by which the highest Spirit speaks himself is identical with the highest Spirit, as was demonstrated above. The Word by which he speaks the things that were made is likewise the highest Spirit himself, as was also proved above. Therefore there is one consubstantial Word, by which the highest Spirit speaks himself and by which he speaks the things he makes.

Moreover, the Word by which supreme wisdom speaks itself may most appropriately be called its Word, because it perfectly preserves its likeness. For a word is an image of a thing formed from thought, and the truer the mind’s thought of a thing, the truer the word is. Again, when a rational mind understands itself by thinking, it produces an image or word of itself, which can be separated from it only by reason. Therefore supreme wisdom too, when it understands itself by speaking, brings forth a likeness of itself consubstantial with itself—that is, its Word.

This Word may also be called its image, figure, and character. But the Word by which it speaks the creature cannot be called the word, image, or figure of the creature [Col. 0187B], because it is the creature’s primary essence. Therefore the highest Spirit does not speak the creature with the creature’s word but with his own. Therefore whatever he speaks, he speaks with his own Word. Therefore with one and the same Word he speaks himself and all that he has made.

But behold: as I was asking about the Word by which the Creator speaks everything he makes, there presented itself to me the Word by which he who makes all things speaks himself. Does he therefore speak himself with one word and the things he makes with another [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “the things he made”; the text reads “the things he makes”]? Or rather, does he speak whatever he makes with the very Word by which he speaks himself [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “whatever he made”; the text reads “whatever he makes”]?

For this Word also, by which he speaks himself, must be identical with what he is [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “which is itself”; the text reads “which is he himself”], just as is established concerning that Word by which he speaks the things that were made by him. For even if nothing else had ever existed except that highest Spirit, reason would nevertheless compel us to affirm that the Word by which he speaks himself exists necessarily [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “nevertheless compels”; the text reads “would nevertheless compel”]. What, then, could be truer [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “what is truer”; the text reads “what could be truer”] than that this Word of his is nothing other than what he is?

Therefore, if he speaks both himself and the things he makes [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “the things he made”; the text reads “the things he makes”] with a Word consubstantial with himself, it is clear that the substance of the Word by which he speaks himself and of the Word by which he speaks the creature is one. How, then, if there is one substance, are there two Words [Note: [Col. 0187D] MS Thu. reads “if it is one highest substance”; the text reads “if there is one substance”]?

Perhaps the identity of the substance does not compel us to admit the unity of the Word [Note: [Col. 0187D] MS Vict. 3 reads “to abandon unity”; the text reads “to admit unity”]. For the same person who speaks these words has the same substance as they do, and yet is not a word. But certainly the word by which supreme wisdom speaks itself may, according to the preceding reasoning, most appropriately be called its Word, because it perfectly preserves its likeness.

For it cannot be denied on any account that when a rational mind understands itself by thinking, an image of it arises in its thought—indeed, that its very thought of itself is its image [Col. 0187D] [Col. 0188A] [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “is an image of itself”; the text reads “is its own image”], formed in its likeness [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “in its own likeness”; the text reads “in its [the mind’s] likeness”], as though from an impression made by it. For whatever thing the mind seeks truthfully to think, whether through bodily imagination or through reason, it strives, as far as it can, to express its likeness in the thought itself [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “in its own cognition”; Thu. reads “in its own thought”]. The more truly it does this, the more truly it thinks the thing itself.

This is especially clear when it thinks of something other than itself, and most clearly when it thinks of a body. For when I think of an absent person known to me, the focus of my thought is formed into an image of him such as I drew into my memory through the sight of my eyes. This image in my thought is the word of that same person, whom I speak by thinking [Note: [Col. 0187D] Thu. 90 reads “of whom I speak by thinking”; the text reads “whom I speak by thinking”].

A rational mind, then, when it understands itself by thinking [Col. 0188B], has with itself an image of itself born from itself—that is, a thought of itself formed in its own likeness, as though by an impression made by itself—although it can separate itself from its image only by reason. This image is its word. [Note: [Col. 0187D] In another arrangement, Chapter 32 begins here.] [Note: [Col. 0187D] In all the manuscripts, Chapter 32 continues as part of the preceding chapter.]

In this way, then, who would deny that supreme wisdom, when it understands itself by speaking [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts read “understands by speaking”; the text reads “understands itself by speaking”], brings forth a likeness of itself consubstantial with itself—that is, its Word? Although, because of the singular eminence of the matter, nothing can properly be said of this Word with complete adequacy, it may nevertheless appropriately be called not only its likeness but also its image, figure, and character [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts of Thu. 90 omit “both image and figure”].

The Word, however, by which it speaks the creature is in no similar way the word of the creature, because it is not its likeness but its primary essence. It follows, therefore, that it does not speak the creature with the word of the creature. With whose word, then, does it speak it, if it does not speak it with its word? For whatever it says, it says with a word; and a word of something is the word—that is, the likeness—of that thing.

But if it speaks nothing other than itself or the creature, it can speak only with either its own Word or the creature’s word. Therefore, if it does not speak with the creature’s word, whatever it says, it says with its own Word. With one and the same Word, therefore, it speaks itself and whatever it has made.

## CHAPTER XXXIV [formerly XXXIII] [Note: [Col. 0187D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 33 is Chapter 34 under this title: “How with his Word he may…” as in the title of Chapter 33.] [Col. 0188D] How he can be seen to speak the creature with his Word [Note: [Col. 0187D] The title in the manuscripts reads “that he speaks with his Word”; the text reads “how with his Word”] [Note: [Col. 0187D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “to see”; the text reads “to be seen”]

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—He himself is the highest reason in which are all things that have been made. Therefore, when he speaks himself, he speaks all things that have been made. In themselves, creatures are mutable essence; in him, they are the first essence itself and the first truth of existence.

[Col. 0188D]

But how can such different things—namely, creating and created essence—be spoken with one Word, especially since the Word itself is coeternal with the one who speaks, whereas the creature is not coeternal with him? Perhaps because he is supreme wisdom and supreme reason, in which are all things that have been made. In the same way, a work made according to some art is always in the art itself—not only when it is being made, but also before it is made and after it has been destroyed—not as something other than the art itself, but as what the art itself is.

Therefore, when the highest Spirit speaks himself, he speaks all things that have been made. For both before they were made, and when they have already been made, and when they are corrupted or altered in any way, they are always in him—not what they are in themselves, but what he himself is [Note: [Col. 0189D] MS Thuan. 30 reads “what the same being is”; Thu. 90 reads “what is identical”; another reading is “what he is”]. In themselves they are mutable essence [Note: [Col. 0189D] Thu. reads “mutable essence”; the text reads “essence that is mutable”], created according to an immutable reason [Note: [Col. 0189D] Vict., Sag., and Gem. read “mutable reason”; the text reads “immutable reason”]; but in him they are the first essence itself and the first truth of existence. To the extent that they are in any way more like it [Note: [Col. 0189D] The manuscripts read “to the extent that they may be more like it”; the text reads “to the extent that they are more like it”], they exist more truly and more excellently.

In this way, then, it can reasonably be maintained that, when that highest Spirit speaks himself, he also speaks whatever has been made, with one and the same Word.

## CHAPTER XXXV [formerly XXXIV] [Note: [Col. 0189D] In the manuscripts, Chapter 34 is Chapter 35 under this title: “That whatever…” as in the title of Chapter 34 in the printed editions.] That whatever has been made is life and truth in his Word and knowledge

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—All things that are in the highest Spirit are in his Word identically and in the same manner, because the Word is consubstantial with him. Therefore all things are life and truth in the Word. And since for him knowing is identical with speaking, just as all things are life and truth in the Word, so they are in his knowledge.

But since it is established that his Word [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Because [the] Word,” in the manuscripts except Thuan.; “because his Word,” in Thuan.] is consubstantial with him [Col. 0189C] and perfectly like him, it necessarily follows that everything which is in him is in his Word, identically and in the same manner. Whatever, therefore, has been made—whether it lives or does not live, or however it may be in itself [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Or whatever,” in the manuscripts; “or however”]—in him is life itself and truth. But since, for the supreme Spirit, knowing is the same as understanding or speaking, it must know everything that it knows in the same manner in which it speaks or understands it [Note: [Col. 0189D] “That in the same manner,” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., Thuan., Gem., and Cister.; “in the same manner”]. Therefore, just as everything is life and truth in his Word, so it is in his knowledge.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 34.]

How incomprehensibly he says, or knows, things made by him.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Things exist in our knowledge not according to their essence, but according to their likeness; therefore they exist more truly in themselves than in our knowledge. Yet it is established that they exist much more truly in the Word than in themselves, inasmuch as the creative essence exists more truly than the created essence. Human knowledge cannot comprehend this.

From this [Note: [Col. 0189D] In the manuscripts Chapter 36 begins here under this title, “How incomprehensibly,” etc., as in the title of Chapter 35 in the printed editions] it can be understood most clearly how that same Spirit says, or knows, things which cannot be comprehended by human [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Or human,” in the manuscripts; “by human”] knowledge [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Cannot be comprehended,” in the manuscripts; Thuan. 90 omits “cannot be”]. For no one doubts that created substances [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Created substances,” in the manuscripts; Thuan. 30: “uncreated substances”] exist in themselves in a very different way from that in which they exist in our knowledge. In themselves, they exist through their own essence; but in our knowledge they are not their essences [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Their essence,” in the manuscripts; “their essences”], but their likenesses. It follows, then, that they exist more truly in themselves [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Be in themselves,” in the manuscripts; “exist in themselves”] than in our knowledge, inasmuch as they exist somewhere more truly through their essence than through their likeness.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Elsewhere Chapter 35 begins here.] [Note: [Col. 0189D] In the manuscripts this continues the preceding chapter.]

Since it is also established that every created substance [Col. 0190B] exists more truly in the Word—that is, in the Creator’s understanding [Note: [Col. 0189D] “And understanding,” in the manuscripts; “that is, in the Creator’s understanding”]—than in itself, inasmuch as the creative essence exists more truly than the created essence, how can the human mind comprehend what that speaking and that knowledge are like, which are so far superior and more true than created substances, when our knowledge is surpassed by them [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Is surpassed so greatly,” in the manuscripts; “is surpassed so far”] as far as their likeness is removed from their essence?

## CHAPTER XXXVII [alternatively XXXVI]

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Chapter 36 is found in the manuscripts; Chapter 37 here.]

Whatever he is in relation to creation, such also is his Word; yet the two are not together plural [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Similarly, plural,” in the manuscripts except Thuan.; “together, plural”].

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The supreme Spirit made all things through the Word. Therefore the Word itself also made all those same things: for what the supreme Spirit does through the Word, he does through himself; and the Word and the supreme Spirit have one essence, which alone is creative and the beginning [Col. 0190C] of all that exists. Whatever, therefore, the supreme Spirit is in relation to creation, such also is his Word; and consequently, just as the former is Creator, so is the latter. Yet they are not two, but one Creator and one beginning.

Since the foregoing arguments plainly teach that the supreme Spirit made all things through his Word, did not the Word itself also make those same things? Because it is consubstantial with him whose Word it is, it must be the supreme essence. But there is only one supreme essence, which alone is creative and the sole beginning of all that has been made. For it alone made everything from nothing, not through another but through itself. Therefore, whatever the supreme Spirit does, the Word also does, and likewise [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Does likewise,” in the manuscripts; “does, and likewise”].

[18] Whatever, then, the supreme Spirit is in relation to creation, this his Word also is [Col. 0190D] [Note: [Col. 0189D] “This the Word also is,” in the manuscripts; Thuan.: “but this the Word is”], and likewise. Yet the two are not together plural [Col. 0191A], because there are not several creative supreme essences. Therefore, just as he is the Creator and beginning of things, so is his Word; yet they are not two, but one Creator and one beginning.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [alternatively XXXVII]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Chapter 37 is found in the manuscripts; Chapter 38 here.]

That it cannot be said what the two are, although they necessarily exist as two.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Whatever the supreme Spirit and the Word are in essence and in relation to creation—namely, truth and Creator—belongs to each individually and to both together, so that they are not two, nor two truths, nor two Creators, but one. Yet he whose Word it is cannot be his own Word, nor can the Word be he whose Word it is. Therefore plurality is admitted only in this respect: that he is not from the Word, whereas the Word is from him. It is established, then, that they are two; but it cannot be expressed what the two are. For they are not two spirits, nor two Creators, nor two Words, nor two images.

One must therefore attend carefully to something which appears to occur in the supreme Spirit and his Word, though it is highly unusual in other things. For it is certain that whatever they are in essence and whatever they are in relation to creation belongs both to each individually [Note: [Col. 0191D] “Is, to each individually,” in the manuscripts; “be, to each individually”] and to both together [Note: [Col. 0191D] “And to both together,” in the manuscripts; Thuan.: “from both”], so that each individually is perfect [Note: [Col. 0191D] “Is perfect individually,” in the manuscripts; Thuan.: “is perfect individually and”] and both together are perfect, yet plurality is not admitted in the two.

For although individually he is perfectly the supreme truth and Creator, and his Word is the supreme truth and Creator, nevertheless together they are not two truths or two Creators. Yet, although this is so, it is nevertheless wonderfully and entirely clear that neither he whose Word it is can be his own Word, nor can the Word be he whose Word it is [Col. 0191C] [Note: [Col. 0191D] “Can be whose it is,” in the manuscripts; “can be he whose it is”], so that, in whatever signifies either what they are substantially or what they are in relation to creation, they always retain indivisible unity.

But in this respect—that he is not from the Word, whereas the Word is [Note: [Col. 0191D] “But thus it is,” in the manuscripts; “whereas the Word is”] from him—they admit an ineffable plurality: ineffable indeed. For although necessity compels them to be two, it can in no way be expressed what the two are [Note: [Col. 0191D] “What the two are,” in the manuscripts; Thuan. 90: “that they are two”]. For even if they might perhaps be called two equal things, or something else similarly related to one another, if one asks what the things are of which these relations are predicated, they cannot be spoken of in the plural, as one speaks of two equal lines or two similar human beings.

For they are not two equal spirits, nor two equal Creators, nor two things signifying either their essence or their relation to creation [Col. 0191D]; nor are they two things designating the proper relation of one to the other [Col. 0192A], since they are not two Words or two images. For a Word, precisely insofar as it is a Word, or an image, is relative to another, since it is the Word or image of something; and these relations belong so properly to one of the two that they cannot at all be transferred to the other.

For he whose Word or image it is is neither an image nor a Word. [Note: [Col. 0191D] Chapter 38. In the manuscripts the preceding chapter continues. “That the same Word,” in the manuscripts of S. Mich.; “that the same word.”] [Note: [Col. 0191D] Elsewhere Chapter 38 begins here.] It is therefore established [Note: [Col. 0191D] “It is established, therefore, that,” in the manuscripts; “but it is established that”] that it cannot be expressed what the two are—the supreme Spirit and his Word—although certain properties belonging to each compel them to be two. For it is proper to one to be from the other, and it is proper to the other to be from the former [Note: [Col. 0191D] “To be from him,” in the manuscripts; Thuan. omits “to be”].

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 38.]

That the same Word is from the supreme Spirit by being born.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The Word of the supreme Spirit is from him as the very same thing from the very same thing. Thus it possesses his perfect likeness, as offspring possesses the likeness of its parent. Therefore it cannot more suitably be conceived as being from him than by being born. Indeed, it is more appropriately said to be born from him than are many things said to be born from something from which they derive their existence but with which they have no likeness—for example, hair, which is said to be born from the head.

This point itself [Note: [Col. 0191D] “This point itself,” etc.: Chapter 39 begins here in the manuscripts] could evidently be expressed in no more familiar way than by saying that it is proper to one to be born from the other, and proper to the other that the first be born from it. For it is already certain [Note: [Col. 0191D] “It is now established that,” in the manuscripts; “it is already certain that”] that the Word of the supreme Spirit is not from him in the manner of things made by him, but as Creator is from Creator [Note: [Col. 0191D] “As from the Creator,” in the manuscripts except Thuan.; “as Creator from Creator”], the supreme from the supreme.

And, to express the likeness with complete brevity, it is the very same thing from the very same thing, and in such a way [Col. 0192C] that it exists only from him. Since it is therefore evident that the Word of the supreme Spirit is from him alone in such a way that it possesses his perfect likeness, as offspring possesses the likeness of its parent, and since it is from him not in order to be made by him [Note: [Col. 0191D] “From that very one in order to be,” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., Thuan. 30, and Cister.; “from him in order to be”], it certainly cannot more suitably be conceived as being from him than by being born.

Indeed, innumerable things are unquestionably said to be born from those from which they derive their existence, although they possess no likeness of the things from which they are said to be born, as offspring possesses the likeness of its parent. We say that hair is born from the head and fruit from a tree, although the former is not like the head and the latter not like the tree. If, then, many such things are not absurdly said to be born, the Word of the supreme Spirit can be said all the more appropriately to exist from him [Note: [Col. 0191D] “To exist from him,” manuscript of Vict. 13; “to subsist from him”], by being born, inasmuch as, like offspring from its parent, it derives his likeness more perfectly by existing from him [Note: [Col. 0191D] “It derives his likeness,” manuscript of Vict. 13; “may derive his likeness”].

[Col. 0193A]

## CHAPTER XL [alternatively XXXIX]

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Chapter 39 is found in the manuscripts; Chapter 40 here.]

That he is most truly the parent, and that is most truly the offspring.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—He is called parent, and this offspring, all the more truly inasmuch as he alone is sufficient for this generation and this offspring expresses his likeness without any admixture of unlikeness. Therefore, it is proper to him to be the truest parent, and to the other to be the truest offspring.

If, then, it is most appropriately said to be born, and it is so like him from whom it is born [Note: [Col. 0193D] “That which is born,” in the manuscripts; “him from whom it is born”], why should it be judged merely like him, as offspring is like its parent? Why should it not rather be asserted that he is all the more truly the parent, and this the offspring [Note: [Col. 0193D] “And this offspring,” in the manuscripts; “and this the offspring”], inasmuch as he alone is sufficient for the perfection of this birth [Note: [Col. 0193D] “For his birth,” in the manuscripts of Vict. and Sag.; “for this birth”], and what is born expresses his likeness?

Among other things in which it is certain that there is a relation of parent and offspring, no one generates in such a way that, entirely needing nothing else, it alone by itself is sufficient to generate offspring; nor is anything generated in such a way that, with no admixture of unlikeness, it exhibits the complete likeness of its parent. If, then, the Word of the supreme Spirit exists entirely from his essence alone, and is singularly so like him that no offspring is so entirely from its parent’s essence or so like its parent, the relation of parent and offspring evidently seems to be applied to nothing so appropriately as to the supreme Spirit and his Word.

Therefore, it is proper to him to be the truest parent [Note: [Col. 0193D] “The truest proper [one],” in the manuscripts; “proper to him to be the truest”], and to the other to be the truest offspring [Note: [Col. 0193D] “The most genuine offspring,” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and S. Mich.; “the truest offspring”].

## CHAPTER XLI [alternatively XL]

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Chapter 40 is found in the manuscripts; Chapter 41 here.]

That he most truly begets, and that is most truly begotten. [Note: [Col. 0193D] “That he is most truly begotten,” in the manuscripts; “that is most truly begotten,” in Cister.; “that he is begotten.”]

[Col. 0193C]

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Therefore, it is proper to the supreme Spirit most truly to generate, and to his Word most truly to be generated.

But this [Note: [Col. 0193D] “But this,” in the manuscripts of Vict. 13 and Sag.; “and this”] cannot be established unless, correspondingly, he most truly generates and this is most truly generated. Therefore, just as the former is evident, so the latter must be entirely certain. Hence it is proper to the supreme Spirit most truly to generate, and to his Word most truly to be generated.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 40.]

That it is most truly proper to one to be begetter and Father, and to the other to be begotten and Son.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Therefore, the one is Father and the other Son; the one should not instead be called mother and the other daughter—not because there is any difference of sex between them, nor because the male sex is generally stronger, but rather because the name “Father” is more appropriate than “mother” to the one to whom no other cause is joined in generating, and the name “Son” is more appropriate than “daughter” to the one who is more like the Father, since a son is always more like his father than a daughter is, being of a different sex.

[Col. 0194A]

I should now like [Note: [Col. 0193D] “I should now like,” etc.: Chapter 42 begins here in the manuscripts under this title, “That it is most truly proper,” etc., as in the title of Chapter 41 in the printed editions], and perhaps I could, conclude that he is most truly Father and that this is most truly Son. But I do not think [19] it should be neglected to ask whether the names “Father” and “Son,” or “mother” [Note: [Col. 0193D] “And whether mother,” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Cister.; “whether mother”] and “daughter,” are more suitable for them, since there is no distinction of sex in them. For if he is appropriately Father and his offspring Son for the reason that both are Spirit, why, by the same reasoning, should it not be appropriate for one to be mother and the other daughter, since both are truth and wisdom?

Or is it because, among natures that have a difference of sex, it belongs to the better sex to be father or son, and to the inferior sex to be mother or daughter? And this is indeed [Note: [Col. 0193D] “And this indeed,” in the manuscripts; “this indeed”] naturally the case in many species; in some, however, the reverse is true, as in certain kinds of birds, where the female sex is always greater and stronger [Col. 0194B], while the male is smaller and weaker.

Or, certainly, is it for this reason that it is more appropriate to call the supreme Spirit Father than mother: because the first and principal cause of offspring is always in the father? For if the maternal cause is always preceded in some way by the paternal cause, it is exceedingly inappropriate to apply the name “mother” to that parent to whom no other cause is either joined or prior in generating offspring [Note: [Col. 0193D] “Be adapted,” in the manuscripts of Vict. and Sag.; “be fitted”].

It is therefore most true that the supreme Spirit is the Father of his offspring. And if a son is always more like his father than a daughter is, while nothing is more like another than his offspring is like the supreme Father, it is most true that this offspring is not a daughter but a Son.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Elsewhere Chapter 41 begins here.] [Note: [Col. 0193D] In the manuscripts this continues the preceding chapter.]

Therefore, just as it is proper to the one most truly to generate and to the other to be generated, so it is proper to the one to be the truest begetter and to the other to be the truest begotten [Note: [Col. 0193D] “To be the truest begotten,” in the manuscripts of Vict. and Sag.; they omit “to be”]. And just as the one is the truest parent and the other the truest offspring, so the one is the truest Father and the other the truest Son.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Note: [Col. 0194D] Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 41.]

A reconsideration of the communion of both and of the properties of each.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—It is impossible for the one who generates to be the same as the one who is generated, yet it is necessary that the one who generates and the one who is generated be the same. Thus the begetter is one and the begotten another, yet the begetter is not something other than what the begotten is. It is therefore evident that they are two, but what the two are remains hidden: for they are not two Spirits, nor two Fathers, nor two Sons. They are opposed only by relations, so that one never assumes what is proper to the other; yet they agree in nature, so that one always possesses the essence of the other. Hence the Father is never called Son, nor the Son ever called Father; but the essence of the Son is in the Father, and the essence of the Father is in the Son.

[Col. 0195A]

Having discovered so many and such great properties of each [Note: [Col. 0195D] “Having discovered so many and such great,” etc.: Chapter 43 begins here in the manuscripts under this title, “A reconsideration,” etc., as in the title of Chapter 42 in the printed editions], through which a remarkable plurality—both ineffable and unavoidable—is shown to exist within supreme unity, I find it exceedingly pleasing to reconsider again and again so impenetrable a mystery. For behold: although it is impossible for the one who generates to be the same as the one who is generated, and for the parent to be the same as the offspring, so that the begetter must be one and the begotten another, and the Father one and the Son another, nevertheless it is necessary that the one who generates be the same as the one who is generated, and likewise the parent and the offspring, so that it is impossible for the begetter to be something other [Note: [Col. 0195D] “For one begetter … another,” in the manuscripts; “for something other … something other”] than what the begotten is, or for the Father to be something other than what the Son is.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Elsewhere Chapter 42 begins here.] [Note: [Col. 0195D] In the manuscripts this continues the preceding chapter.]

And although one is distinct from the other, so that it is entirely evident that they are two [Note: [Col. 0195D] “What the two are,” in the manuscripts of Thuan.; “that they are two”], nevertheless what the one and the other are is one and the same [Col. 0195B] [Note: [Col. 0195D] “One and the very same,” in the manuscripts of Gem. and Cister.; “one and the same”], so that what the two are remains completely hidden.

For the Father is one and the Son another, so that, when I have named both, I see that I have named two; yet what both the Father and the Son are is the same, so that I do not understand what two things I have named. Although each individually—the Father and the Son—is perfectly the supreme Spirit, nevertheless the Father as Spirit and the Son as Spirit are one and the same Spirit [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript of S. Mich. omits “supreme”], so that the Father and the Son are not two Spirits but one Spirit.

Thus, just as the individual properties of each do not admit plurality, because they do not belong to two, so what is common to both retains indivisible unity, although it wholly belongs to each individually. For just as there are not two fathers or two sons, but one Father and one Son, because the individual properties belong individually to each [Col. 0195C], so there are not two but one Spirit, although both the Father individually and the Son individually possess the perfect being of Spirit.

They are opposed by their relations in such a way that one never assumes what is proper to the other; they agree in nature in such a way that one [Note: [Col. 0195D] “Just as they agree in nature, and one,” in the manuscripts; “they agree in nature in such a way that one”; Cister. omits “are”] always possesses the essence of the other.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Elsewhere Chapter 43 begins here.] [Note: [Col. 0195D] In the manuscripts this continues the preceding chapter.]

For they are distinct in that one is Father and the other Son [Note: [Col. 0195D] “And otherwise the Son,” in the manuscripts of Vict. and Sag.; they omit “and”], so that the Father is never called Son, nor the Son Father; yet they are the same in substance, so that the essence of the Son is always in the Father, and the essence of the Father in the Son. For their essence is not different but the same—not many essences but one essence belonging to both.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0196D] Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 43.]

How one is the essence of the other.

[Col. 0195D]

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—One may rightly be called the essence of the other, in order to emphasize the unity and simplicity of their common nature [Col. 0196A]. Yet the Father is not called the essence of the Son, and the Son the essence of the Father, as though one existed not through itself but through the other. For the supreme essence always exists through itself, just as supreme wisdom always knows through itself. Thus the Father exists through himself, and likewise the Son exists through himself, because the Father is the supreme essence and likewise the Son is the supreme essence. The Son is indeed an essence born from the Father’s essence, and wisdom from wisdom; but he is no less perfect for this, since he nevertheless exists through himself and knows through himself. Nor is it contradictory that the Son subsists through himself and has his being from the Father. For he has from the Father the fact that he exists and knows through himself; otherwise the being of the Father and the Son would not be the same. Finally, for both, to have essence is nothing other than to be essence. Therefore, just as one has the essence of the other, so one is the essence of the other—that is, what one is, the other also is.

[Col. 0196B]

Hence, even if one is called the essence of the other [Note: [Col. 0195D] “Hence, even if …” In the manuscripts Chapter 44 begins here, with the title “How one is the essence …,” as in the title of Chapter 43 in the printed editions], one does not depart from the truth; rather, the supreme unity and simplicity of their common nature is emphasized.
