For it cannot be understood in the same way as human wisdom, through which a human being is wise, although he cannot be wise through himself [Note: [Col. 0195D] “Cannot be through himself,” in the manuscripts; “cannot through himself be”]. Thus, if the Father is called the essence of the Son and the Son the essence of the Father, it cannot be understood as though the Son exists through the Father and the Father through the Son [Note: [Col. 0195D] “So that he exists in the same way,” in the manuscripts; “as though he exists in the same way”], as though one could exist only through the other, just as a human being cannot be wise except through wisdom.

For just as supreme wisdom [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript of Thuan. 30 omits “supreme”] always knows through itself, so the supreme essence always exists through itself. The Father is perfectly the supreme essence [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript of Vict. 3 omits “perfectly”], and the Son is perfectly the supreme essence; therefore the perfect Father exists through himself, and likewise the perfect [Col. 0196C] [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscripts of Vict., Sag., and Thuan. omit “likewise”] Son exists through himself, just as each knows through himself.

The essence or wisdom of the Son is not less perfect because it is an essence born from the Father’s essence and wisdom from wisdom; rather, it would be a less perfect essence or wisdom if it did not exist through itself or did not know through itself. For it is in no way contradictory that the Son both subsists through himself [Note: [Col. 0195D] “It is contradictory that the Son exists through himself,” in the manuscripts of Vict., Sag., Thuan., and Cister.; “it is contradictory that the Son both exists”] and has his being from the Father.

For just as the Father possesses essence, wisdom, and life in himself, so that he exists not through another’s essence but through his own essence, knows through his own wisdom, and lives through his own life, so by begetting he gives the Son to possess essence, wisdom, and life in himself, so that the Son subsists, knows, and lives not through an alien essence, wisdom, or life but through his own [Col. 0196D]. Otherwise the being of the Father and the Son would not be the same, nor would the Son be equal [Col. 0197A] to the Father—a claim whose falsity was seen with complete clarity above [Note: [Col. 0197D] “And how false this is,” in the manuscripts; “the falsity of which”].

Therefore it is not contradictory that the Son both subsists through himself and is from the Father, because he necessarily has from the Father this very capacity—that is, the ability to subsist through himself [Note: [Col. 0197D] “To have from the Father,” in the manuscripts of Thuan.; “to have from the Father”].

For if a wise person were to teach me his wisdom, of which I had previously been without, it could rightly be said that this was accomplished by that person’s wisdom. Yet although my wisdom would derive its being and its knowing from his wisdom, once it existed it would exist only through its own essence [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Yet when it no longer existed except through its wisdom,” in the manuscripts except S. Mich.; “yet once it existed, it would exist only through its own essence”; Thuan.: “yet once it existed, it would exist through its wisdom”; Cister.: “yet once it existed, it would exist only in its own essence”], and it would know only through itself [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Nor would it know except through itself,” manuscript of Cister.; “nor would it know except in itself”].

How much more, then, does the coeternal Son of the eternal Father, who has his being from the Father in such a way that there are not two essences, subsist, know, and live through himself.

The statement that the Father is the essence of the Son, or the Son the essence of the Father, therefore cannot be understood as though one could not subsist through himself but only through the other [Col. 0197B]. Rather, it signifies the communion they possess of a supremely simple and supremely one essence. In this sense it can appropriately be said and understood that one is the very same thing as the other, so that one possesses the essence of the other [Note: [Col. 0197D] “To designate,” in the manuscripts; “to signify”].

For this reason, since to have essence is nothing other than to be essence [20], just as one possesses the essence of the other, so one is the essence of the other—that is, what one is, the other also is.

## CHAPTER XLV [alternatively XLIV]

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Chapter 44 is found in the manuscripts; Chapter 45 here.]

That the Son can more appropriately be called the essence of the Father than the Father the essence of the Son; and that the Son is likewise the Father’s power, wisdom, and similar attributes.

[Col. 0197C]

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—It is nevertheless more appropriate to call the Son the essence of the Father than to call the Father the essence of the Son. Since the Son has his essence from the Father, he can be said to possess the Father’s essence and consequently to be the Father’s essence. Thus the Son is called the Father’s power, wisdom, truth, justice, and so forth, because he has these from the Father.

Although this is true according to the reasoning established above, it is nevertheless much more appropriate to call the Son the essence of the Father than the Father the essence of the Son. Since the Father has his essence from no one but himself, it is not sufficiently appropriate to say that he possesses the essence of anyone other than his own. But since the Son has his essence from the Father, and has the same essence as the Father [Note: [Col. 0197D] “And has the same,” in the manuscripts; “and has the same essence that the Father has”], he can most appropriately be said to possess the Father’s essence.

Therefore, since neither possesses essence in any other way than by existing as essence [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Since neither,” in the manuscripts of Thuan. 30; “since neither of the two”], just as the Son is more appropriately understood to possess the Father’s essence than the Father the Son’s, so the Son can more suitably be called the Father’s essence than the Father the Son’s.

For this one expression, with sufficiently incisive brevity, emphasizes that the Son not only possesses the same essence as the Father, but possesses it from the Father: so that “the Son is the essence of the Father” means that “the Son is an undifferentiated essence from the Father’s essence,” indeed, “an essence from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Rather, from the Father’s essence,” in the manuscripts; “rather, an essence from the Father”].

Similarly, then, the Son is the Father’s power and wisdom, or truth and justice, and whatever belongs to the essence of the supreme Spirit.

## CHAPTER XLVI [alternatively XLV]

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Chapter 45 is found in the manuscripts; Chapter 46 here.]

How some of the things expressed in this way can also be understood in another manner.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The Son can also be called the understanding and wisdom, knowledge and cognition of the Father, because he understands, knows, and recognizes the Father’s essence itself [Col. 0198B]. He can also be called the Father’s truth in the sense that he is not an imperfect imitation but the complete truth and the very essence of the Father’s substance, and is nothing other than what the Father is.

Certain of the things which can be expressed and understood in this way appear nevertheless to admit another, no less appropriate interpretation under the very same wording. For it is clear that the Son is the true Word—that is, the perfect understanding, or the perfect cognition, knowledge, and wisdom of the whole paternal substance, which itself understands, recognizes, knows, and is wise concerning the Father’s essence.

If, therefore, in this sense the Son is called the Father’s understanding, wisdom, knowledge, cognition, or awareness, because he understands, knows, and recognizes the Father, one does not depart from the truth. The Son can also most appropriately be called the Father’s truth—not only in the sense that the Son’s truth is the same as the Father’s truth, as has already been established, but also in the sense that he is understood to be not some imperfect imitation but the complete truth of the Father’s substance, because he is nothing other than what the Father is.

## CHAPTER XLVII

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 45.]

That the Son is the understanding of understanding and the Truth of truth.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—This is clear because the Son is the understanding, knowledge, wisdom, and truth of the Father’s substance, which itself is understanding, knowledge, wisdom, and truth.

[Col. 0198D]

But if the Father’s substance itself is understanding [Col. 0199A], knowledge, wisdom, and truth, it follows consequently that, just as the Son is the understanding, knowledge, wisdom, and truth of the Father’s substance, so he is the understanding of understanding, the knowledge of knowledge, the wisdom of wisdom, and the truth of truth.

## CHAPTER XLVIII [alternatively XLVI]

[Note: [Col. 0199C] Chapter 46 is found in the manuscripts as Chapter 48, under this title: “That and how the Son is the understanding or wisdom of memory, and the memory of the Father and of memory.”]

That and how the Son is the understanding or wisdom of memory, and the memory of the Father and of memory.

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The Word of a thing is the very thought formed from memory according to the thing’s likeness. Therefore the Word is born from memory. Therefore, just as the Son is called the Word, so the Father, from whom he is begotten, can be called memory. Therefore, just as the Son is the understanding and wisdom of the Father, so he is the understanding and wisdom of the Father’s memory. And because whatever the Son understands and knows, he also remembers, the Son is the memory of the Father and the memory of memory—that is, a memory mindful of the Father [Col. 0199B], who is memory born from no one; whereas the Son is memory born from memory, that is, from the Father.

What, then, should be understood concerning memory? Is the Son to be considered the intelligence of memory, or the memory of the Father, or the memory of memory? Indeed, since it cannot be denied that supreme Wisdom remembers itself, nothing is more fitting than that the Father should be understood in memory, just as the Son is understood in the Word; for the Word appears to be born from memory, which is perceived more clearly in our own mind. Since the human mind does not always think of itself, although it always remembers itself, it is evident that, when it thinks of itself, its word is born from memory.

[Note: The manuscripts read “which is its word” (quod verbum ejus), rather than “because its word” (quia verbum ejus).] Hence it appears that, if it always thought of itself, its word would always be born from memory. For to think of a thing whose memory we possess is to speak of it in the mind; but the word of a thing is the thought itself, formed from memory according to its likeness. From this, therefore, it can clearly be discerned concerning supreme Wisdom—which always speaks itself in the same way as it always remembers itself—that its coeternal Word is born from its eternal memory.

[Note: The manuscripts read “memory coeternal,” rather than “its memory coeternal.”]

Therefore, just as the Word is fittingly understood as offspring, so memory most appropriately assumes the name of parent. If, then, the offspring—which was born wholly from the one supreme Spirit—is the offspring of its memory, nothing is more consequent than that it is itself its memory.

[Note: The manuscripts read “nothing more fitting.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “his memory is” (memoria ejus est), rather than “his own memory is” (memoria sua est).]

For it is not the case that, because it remembers itself, it is in its memory as one thing is in another, as those things are which are so in the memory of the human mind that they are not themselves our memory; rather, it remembers itself in such a way that it itself is its memory.

[Note: The manuscripts read “for it is not in it.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “so it is in the memory of itself.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “itself in our memory.”]

It follows, therefore, that just as the Son is the intelligence or wisdom of the Father, so he is also the intelligence or wisdom of the Father’s memory. But whatever the Son knows or understands, he likewise remembers it.

[Note: In some copies, Chapter 47 begins here.]

[Note: In the manuscripts, the preceding chapter continues here.]

The Son, therefore, is the memory of the Father and the memory of memory—that is, the memory which remembers the Father, who is memory, just as he is the wisdom of the Father and the wisdom of wisdom—that is, wisdom which knows the Father as Wisdom. The Son, indeed, is memory born from memory, just as wisdom is born from wisdom; but the Father is memory or wisdom born from no one.

## CHAPTER XLIX [elsewhere XLVII]

[Note: Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 47.]

### That the supreme Spirit loves himself

**Summary of the chapter.—** Just as the supreme Spirit remembers himself and understands himself, so he loves himself. For the rational mind itself is shown to be capable of loving both itself and him by the fact that it can understand both itself and him.

But while I delightfully contemplate these properties and the communion of the Father and the Son, I find nothing more delightful to contemplate in them than the affection of mutual love.

[Note: In the manuscripts, “I found,” rather than “I find.”]

For how could it be denied, however absurdly, that the supreme Spirit loves himself, just as he remembers himself and understands himself, when even the rational mind is shown to be capable of loving both itself and him because it can remember both itself and him and can understand both itself and him? For the memory and understanding of anything whatever are idle and utterly useless unless the thing itself is loved or rejected, as reason requires. The supreme Spirit therefore loves himself, just as he remembers himself and understands himself.

[Note: In the manuscripts, this section begins Chapter 49 under the title “That the supreme Spirit loves himself,” as in the title of Chapter 48 in the printed editions.]

[Note: The manuscripts read “when the mind.”]

[Col. 0200C]

## CHAPTER L [elsewhere XLVIII]

[Note: Chapter 48 in the manuscripts is Chapter 50 under the title “That the same love proceeds equally from the Father and the Son,” as in the title of Chapter 48 in the printed editions.]

### That the same love proceeds equally from the Father and the Son

**Summary of the chapter.—** It is evident that the love of the supreme Spirit proceeds from the fact that he remembers himself and understands himself, for nothing is loved without its memory and understanding. Therefore that love proceeds from the Father, who is memory, and from the Son, who is intelligence.

It is certainly clear to anyone who reasons that he does not remember himself or understand himself because he loves himself, but that he loves himself because he remembers himself and understands himself; nor can he love himself if he does not remember himself or understand himself.

[Note: The manuscripts read “because he does not understand himself.”]

For nothing is loved without its memory or understanding, while many things are retained in memory and understood without being loved. It is therefore evident that the love of the supreme Spirit proceeds from the fact that he remembers himself and understands himself. And if the Father is understood in the memory of the supreme Spirit and the Son in its intelligence, it is manifest that the love of the supreme Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and from the Son.

[Note: The manuscripts read “and from the Son,” rather than “and the Son.”]

## CHAPTER LI [elsewhere XLIX]

[Note: Chapter 49 in the manuscripts is Chapter 51 under the title “That each loves himself and the other with equal love,” as in the title of Chapter 49 in the printed editions. Manuscript Thu. 90 omits “and the other.”]

### That each loves himself and the other with equal love

**Summary of the chapter.—** The supreme Spirit loves himself. Therefore the Father loves himself, and the Son loves himself, and each loves the other; for the Father and the Son are the supreme and undivided Spirit, and together they are one spirit. Each also understands himself and the other, because each remembers himself and the other. And since in both that which loves is identical with that which is loved, each loves himself and the other with equal love.

But if the supreme Spirit loves himself, without doubt the Father loves himself, the Son loves himself, and each loves the other; for the Father individually is the supreme Spirit, and the Son individually is the supreme Spirit, while together they are one spirit. And because each equally remembers himself and the other and understands himself and the other, and because in the Father that which loves or is loved is altogether identical with what it is in the Son, it is necessary that each love himself and the other with equal love.

[Note: The manuscripts read “the Father is the supreme,” rather than “the Father individually is the supreme.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “in the Father,” rather than “from the Father.”]

## CHAPTER LII [elsewhere L]

[Note: Chapter 50 in the manuscripts is Chapter 52 under the title “That this love is as great as the supreme Spirit,” as in the title of Chapter 50 in the printed editions. Manuscript Thu. 30 reads, “That this love is as great as the supreme Spirit himself.”]

### That this love is as great as the supreme Spirit himself

**Summary of the chapter.—** This is established because this love is as great as the extent to which he understands himself; and he understands himself to the extent that he is.

How great, then, is this love of the supreme Spirit, which is common to the Father and the Son! But if he loves himself to the extent that he remembers himself and understands himself, and remembers and understands himself to the extent of his essence—which cannot be otherwise—then surely his love is as great as he is.

[Note: The manuscripts read “the love of the supreme,” rather than “this love of the supreme.”]

## CHAPTER LIII [elsewhere LI]

[Note: Chapter 51 in the manuscripts is Chapter 53.]

### That this same love is identical with the supreme Spirit, and yet is one spirit with the Father and the Son

**Summary of the chapter.—** Nothing can be equal to the supreme Spirit except the supreme Spirit. Since, therefore, this love is as great as the supreme Spirit, it is clear that this love is the supreme Spirit. Moreover, even if nothing had ever existed except the supreme Spirit, the Father and the Son would nonetheless love themselves and each other. Therefore this love is nothing other than what the Father and the Son are, namely, the supreme essence.

[Col. 0201D] Finally, there cannot be several supreme essences. Therefore the love of both is one supreme essence with the Father and the Son. Consequently, this love is supreme wisdom, supreme truth, the supreme good, and whatever can be said concerning the substance of the supreme Spirit.

But what can be equal to the supreme Spirit except the supreme Spirit? This love, therefore, is the supreme Spirit.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the love of the supreme Spirit? This, then,” rather than “the supreme Spirit? This, then.”]

Finally, if no creature had ever existed—that is, if nothing had ever existed other than the supreme Spirit—the Father and the Son would nonetheless love themselves and each other, the Father and the Son. It follows, therefore, that this love is nothing other than what the Father and the Son are, namely, the supreme essence. But since there cannot be several supreme essences, what is more necessary than that the Father, the Son, and the love of both be one supreme essence? This love, therefore, is supreme wisdom, supreme truth, the supreme good, and whatever can be said concerning the substance of the supreme Spirit.

## CHAPTER LIV [elsewhere LII]

[Note: Chapter 52 in the manuscripts is Chapter 54.]

### That it proceeds wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son, and yet is only one love

[Col. 0202B]

**Summary of the chapter.—** This love does not proceed from that in which the Father and the Son are plural, but from that in which they are one. For it does not proceed from the relations, which are plural, since the relation of the Father is one and the relation of the Son another; rather, from their very essence, which admits no plurality, the Father and the Son emit so great a good. Yet it proceeds wholly from the Father, wholly from the Son, and wholly from both as one and the same thing, because from the Father, who individually is the supreme Spirit, nothing but the supreme Spirit proceeds; from the Son, who likewise individually is the supreme Spirit, nothing but the supreme Spirit proceeds; and from the Father and the Son, who are not two but one Spirit, nothing but one supreme Spirit can proceed.

It must be carefully considered whether there are two loves, one proceeding from the Father and another from the Son; or one love which does not proceed wholly from one, but partly from the Father and partly from the Son; or neither several loves nor one proceeding partly from each, but one love proceeding wholly from each individually and wholly from both together. The certainty of this question is known beyond doubt from the following consideration: it does not proceed from that in which the Father and the Son are plural, but from that in which they are one. For it does not proceed from their relations, which are plural—for the relation of the Father is one and that of the Son another—but from their very essence, which admits no plurality, the Father and the Son together emit so great a good.

Thus, just as the Father individually is the supreme Spirit, the Son individually is the supreme Spirit, and together the Father and the Son are not two but one spirit, so from the Father individually flows the whole love of the supreme Spirit, and from the Son individually the whole love; while together from the Father and the Son there proceed not two wholes, but one and the same whole.

[Note: One manuscript reads “the Son, not two but one,” rather than “the Son, not—I say—two but one.”]

[Col. 0202D]

## CHAPTER LV [elsewhere LIII]

[Note: Chapter 53 in the manuscripts is Chapter 55 under the title “That this is not their Son.”]

### That this love is not their Son

**Summary of the chapter.—** Yet this love is neither the Son of the Father nor the Son of the Word, from whom it proceeds, because, although it is altogether identical with what the Father and the Son are, it does not, by proceeding from them, display their likeness. Moreover, if it is their offspring, then either one of them will be its father and the other its mother—which is contrary to the case, since it proceeds from the Father no differently than from the Son—or both will be its father or its mother. But no nature admits two things which individually have toward one and the same thing a complete and wholly identical relation of father and mother.

What, then? Since this love exists equally from the Father and the Son and is so similar to both that it is in no way unlike them, but is altogether identical with what they are, should it be considered their Son or offspring? But just as the Word, as soon as he is considered, most clearly proves himself to be the offspring of him from whom he is, by presenting the manifest image of his parent, so love openly denies that it is offspring. For although it is understood to proceed from the Father and the Son, it does not at once display to the contemplative an equally evident likeness of that from which it is, even though reason, when it considers the matter, teaches that it is altogether identical with what the Father and the Son are.

[Note: The manuscripts read “it is considered” (mox consideratur), omitting “as soon as” (mox ut).]

[Note: Manuscript Thu. 90 reads promptam praeferendo, “by presenting a ready image”; the text has promptam referendo, “by referring [to] a ready image.”]

Finally, if it is their offspring, then either one of them will be its father and the other its mother, or both are its father or its mother. All these alternatives appear contrary to the truth. Since it proceeds from the Father in no way differently than from the Son, truth does not permit the Father and the Son to be related to it by different names. Therefore one is not its father and the other its mother. Nor does any nature permit any example to show two things which individually have, equally toward one thing, a complete and in no respect differing relation of father or mother. Therefore the Father and the Son together are not the father or mother of the love proceeding from them. It consequently does not at all appear consistent with the truth that this same love should be their son or offspring.

## CHAPTER LVI [elsewhere LIV]

[Note: Chapter 54 in the manuscripts is Chapter 56.]

### That the Father alone is begetter and unbegotten; the Son alone begotten; and love alone neither begotten nor unbegotten

**Summary of the chapter.—** Therefore this love cannot properly be called begotten, as the Word is; but neither should it be called wholly unbegotten, because it is not wholly unrelated to another. Thus it belongs to the Father alone to be begetter and unbegotten; to the Word alone to be begotten; and to love alone to be neither properly begotten nor wholly unbegotten, but proceeding, because it is neither offspring nor wholly unrelated to another.

Yet it seems that this same love cannot, according to ordinary usage of speech, be called wholly unbegotten, nor can it be called begotten as properly as the Word.

[Note: The manuscripts read “the manner of speech,” rather than “the usage of speech.”]

For we often say that something is generated from the thing from which it exists, as when we say that brightness or heat is generated from fire, or that some effect is generated from its cause. According to this reasoning, therefore, love proceeding from the supreme Spirit cannot be asserted to be wholly unbegotten; but it cannot be called begotten as properly as the Word, because it is clear that the Word is a true offspring and a true son, whereas love is in no way a son or offspring.

[Note: The manuscripts read “some effect,” rather than “an effect.”]

It is therefore possible—indeed, it is necessary—to call him alone whose Word it is both begetter and unbegotten, because he alone is Father and parent and in no way exists from another. The Word alone is begotten, because he alone is son and offspring. Love alone, however, belonging to both, is neither begotten nor unbegotten, because it is neither son nor offspring, nor is it wholly unrelated to another.

[Note: The manuscripts read “neither son nor unbegotten,” rather than “neither son nor offspring.”]

## CHAPTER LVII [elsewhere LV]

[Note: The printed text has “Chapter 35”; in the manuscripts this is Chapter 57 under the title “That this same love is uncreated, etc.,” as in the title of Chapter 55 in the printed editions.]

### That this same love is uncreated and creator in the same way as the Father and the Son; and yet that it, together with them, is not three but one uncreated being and one creator; and that it may likewise be called the Spirit of the Father and the Son

**Summary of the chapter.—** Since this love is one and the same supreme essence with the Father and the Son, and since that essence alone was made by no one and made all things through itself, it is necessary that this love, like the Father and the Son, be uncreated and creator. Thus these three are not several but one uncreated being and one creator. No one makes, creates, or begets the Father. The Father alone begets the Son, but does not make him. The Father and the Son neither make nor beget, but breathe forth their love, because it proceeds from them—not by departing from that supreme essence, but by existing from it. For this reason it may rightly be called the Spirit of the supreme essence. It may also be called the communion of the Father and the Son, both because it has a name common to the Father and the Son and because it is altogether identical with what the Father and the Son are.

Since, then, this same love is individually the supreme essence, just as the Father and the Son are, while together the Father, the Son, and the love of both are not several but one supreme essence—which alone was made by no one and made all things through no other than itself—it is necessary that, just as the Father individually and the Son individually are uncreated and creator, so love individually is uncreated and creator, while all three together are not several but one uncreated being and one creator.

[Note: One manuscript reads “love not several,” rather than “love not several” with the present grammatical form.]

[Note: The manuscripts read “together, and not,” rather than “together, not.”]

No one, therefore, makes, creates, or begets the Father. The Father alone begets the Son, but does not make him.

[Note: Manuscript Thu. reads “the Father alone does not make but begets.”]

The Father and the Son together neither make nor beget; but, if it may be said in this way, they breathe forth their love. Although the supremely immutable essence does not breathe in our manner, it nevertheless seems that it cannot be said to emit its own love—which proceeds ineffably from it, not by departing from it but by existing from it—in any more appropriate way than by breathing.

[Note: The manuscripts read “not with our love,” rather than “not in our manner.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “yet the love itself,” rather than “yet its own love.”]

If this may be said, then just as the Word is the Son of the supreme essence, so its love may quite appropriately be called its Spirit. Thus, although it is essentially spirit itself, just as the Father and the Son are, the Father and the Son should not be thought to be the spirit of anyone, since the Father is from no other and the Son is not born from the Father as from one breathing. This love, however, may be considered the Spirit of both, because it proceeds wondrously from both, by their own ineffable mode of breathing.

Because it is the communion of the Father and the Son, it also seems not without reason able, as though as its own, to assume some name common to the Father and the Son, if the need for a proper name requires it. If this is done—that is, if this love is designated, as though by a proper name, by the name Spirit, which equally signifies the substance of the Father and the Son—it will also serve the useful purpose of indicating through this name that it is identical with what the Father and the Son are, although it has its existence from them.

[Note: Manuscript Thu. 30 reads “if this same thing,” rather than “if this is done.”]

[Col. 0205D]

## CHAPTER LVIII [elsewhere LVI]

[Note: Chapter 56 in the manuscripts is Chapter 58.]

### That just as the Son is the essence or wisdom of the Father in the sense that he has the same essence or wisdom as the Father, so the same Spirit is the essence and wisdom of the Father and the Son, and likewise in other respects

Moreover, just as the Son is the substance, wisdom, and power of the Father in the sense that he has the same essence, wisdom, and power as the Father, so the Spirit of both may be understood as the essence, wisdom, or power of the Father and the Son, because he has altogether the same essence, wisdom, and power as they have.

[Note: The manuscripts read “because he may have,” rather than “because he has.”]

## CHAPTER LIX [elsewhere LVII]

[Note: Chapter 57 in the manuscripts is Chapter 59.]

### That the Father, the Son, and their Spirit are equally in one another

**Summary of the chapter.—** These three are one and the same supreme essence, which cannot exist without itself, outside itself, or greater or less than itself. Therefore these three are in one another, so that none surpasses another. Moreover, the memory of the supreme essence is wholly in its intelligence and love, its intelligence in its memory and love, and its love in its memory and intelligence. Therefore the whole Father, who is memory, is in the Son, who is intelligence, and in the Spirit, who is love; the whole Son is in the Father and the Spirit; and the whole Spirit is in the Father and the Son. One of them cannot exist without the others.

It is pleasant to contemplate how the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both are in one another with such equality that none surpasses another. In addition to the fact that each of them is so perfectly the supreme essence that all three together are nevertheless only one supreme essence—which cannot exist without itself or outside itself, nor be greater or less than itself—the same conclusion can also be proved concerning each individually.

For the whole Father is in the Son and in the common Spirit; the Son is in the Father and in that same Spirit; and the same Spirit is in the Father and the Son. The memory of the supreme essence is wholly in its intelligence and in its love, its intelligence in its memory and in its love, and its love in its memory and in its intelligence.

[Note: The manuscripts read “and in love and intelligence,” rather than “and in its love and intelligence.”]

The supreme Spirit understands and loves his entire memory; remembers his entire intelligence and loves it all; remembers the whole of his love and understands it all. The Father is understood in memory, the Son in intelligence, and the Spirit of both in love. Thus the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both embrace one another and are in one another with such equality that none of them can be shown to surpass another or to exist without it.

[Note: The manuscripts read “the whole supreme,” rather than “his entire.”]

## CHAPTER LX [elsewhere LVIII]

[Note: Chapter 58 in the manuscripts is Chapter 60.]

### That none of them needs another in order to remember, understand, or love, because each individually is memory, intelligence, love, and whatever must belong to the supreme essence

**Summary of the chapter.—** Yet none of them needs another either in order to remember, to understand, or to love. Since each is the supreme essence, each individually is memory, intelligence, and love through himself; and thus each individually remembers, understands, and loves through himself, just as he exists through himself.

I believe that what occurred to me while considering these matters should by no means be carelessly entrusted to memory. For the Father must indeed be understood as memory, the Son as intelligence, and the Spirit as love; but not in such a way that the Father needs the Son or the common Spirit, or the Son the Father or that same Spirit, or that same Spirit the Father or the Son—as though the Father could remember through himself alone, but could understand only through the Son and love only through his own Spirit and that of the Son; and as though the Son could understand only through himself, but remember through the Father and love through his Spirit; and as though that same Spirit could do nothing through himself except love, while the Father remembered for him and the Son understood for him.

For since each individually among these three is the supreme essence and perfect supreme wisdom, so that each through himself remembers, understands, and loves, it is necessary that none of these three need another in order to remember, understand, or love.

[Note: The manuscripts read “none of the three of them,” rather than “none of these three.”]

Each individually is essentially memory, intelligence, love, and whatever must belong to the supreme essence.

[Note: The manuscripts read “whatever must belong to the supreme essence,” rather than “whatever must belong to the supreme.”]

## CHAPTER LXI [elsewhere LIX]

[Note: Chapter 59 in the manuscripts is Chapter 61.]

### That nevertheless they are not three but one, whether Father, Son, or Spirit of both

**Summary of the chapter.—** Although the Father is intelligence and love, he is not the Son or the Spirit of anyone, because he is neither begotten intelligence nor love proceeding from another. Although the Son is memory and love, he is not the Father or the Spirit of anyone, because he is neither begetting memory nor love proceeding from another, as the Spirit does. Likewise, although the Spirit is memory and intelligence, he is not the Father or the Son, because he is neither begetting memory nor begotten intelligence. Thus there is one Father, one Son, and one Spirit in the supreme essence, not three Fathers, three Sons, or three Spirits.

I see a certain question arising here. For if the Father is intelligence and love just as he is memory, and if the Son is memory and love just as he is intelligence, and if the Spirit of both is no less memory and intelligence than love, how is the Father not the Son and the Spirit of someone? Why is the Son not the Father and the Spirit of someone, and why is the same Spirit not the Father and the Son of someone? For memory was understood to be the Father, intelligence the Son, and love the Spirit of both.

[Note: The manuscripts read “the Father and the Son and the Spirit of someone,” rather than “the Father, the Son, or the Spirit of someone.”]

But this question is not difficult to solve if what has already been discovered by reason is considered. The Father is not the Son or the Spirit of someone, even though he is intelligence and love, because he is not begotten intelligence or love proceeding from another; rather, whatever he is, he is only begetting, and he is the one from whom another proceeds.

The Son likewise is not the Father or the Spirit of someone, although through himself he remembers and loves, because he is not begetting memory or love proceeding from another, in likeness to his Spirit; rather, whatever he is, he is only begotten, and he is the one from whom the Spirit proceeds.

The Spirit, too, is not thereby forced to be Father or Son because he is satisfied with his memory and intelligence, since he is neither begetting memory nor begotten intelligence, but only proceeds, whatever he is.

[Note: The manuscripts read “his intelligence; since he is not,” rather than “his memory and intelligence, since he is not.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “whatever he is, proceeds,” rather than “whatever he is, may proceed.”]

What, then, prevents us from concluding that in the supreme essence there is only one Father, one Son, and one Spirit, and not three Fathers, Sons, or Spirits?

[Col. 0207C]

## CHAPTER LXII [elsewhere LX]

[Note: Chapter 60 in the manuscripts is Chapter 62.]

### How several sons appear to be born from these three

**Summary of the chapter.—** Since each of the three understands himself and the others and consequently speaks them, it appears that each individually produces his own Word or Son, and that consequently there are several Sons.

But lest what I am considering conflict with this assertion, there should be no doubt that the Father, the Son, and their Spirit each speaks himself and the other two, just as each understands himself and the others. If this is so, how are there not in the supreme essence as many words as there are speakers and as many as there are those who are spoken? For if several people speak one thing in thought, there appear to be as many words of it as there are thinkers, because its word is in the thought of each. Likewise, if one person thinks several things, there are as many words in the mind of the thinker as there are things thought.

But in human thought, when a person thinks of something that exists outside his mind, the word of the thing thought does not arise from the thing itself, because the thing is absent from the gaze of thought; rather, it arises from some likeness or image of the thing that is in the thinker’s memory, or perhaps from the thing itself when, at the moment he thinks of it, it is drawn into the mind through bodily sense.

In the supreme essence, however, the Father, the Son, and their Spirit are always present to one another. For, as has already been seen, each is no less in the others than in himself, so that when they speak one another, it appears that the very one who is spoken generates his own word in the same way as when he is spoken by himself.

How, then, does the Son generate nothing, nor the Spirit of the Son and the Father, if each of them generates his own word when he is spoken by himself or by another?

[Note: The manuscripts read “when he is spoken by himself or by another,” rather than “when he is spoken by himself or by another” in the present abbreviated wording.]

But as many words as can be shown to arise from the supreme substance, so many sons it must, according to the foregoing consideration, beget and so many spirits emit.

## CHAPTER LXIII

[Note: Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 60.]

### How there is only one of one; that is, one Word, and from the Father alone

**Summary of the chapter.—** Nevertheless, since there are neither several speakers nor several things spoken, but one essence which understands and is understood, it is clear that there are neither several fathers nor several words nor several sons. Rather, there is one speaker, namely the Father, and one Word, namely one Son. Although the Father, the Word, and the Spirit equally speak themselves and the other two, there is only one Word there, which cannot in any way be called the Word of all three, but only the Word of one of them, namely the Father.

For it is neither the image nor the Son of itself or of the Spirit proceeding from it. It is neither born from itself nor from what proceeds from itself, nor does it imitate itself or what proceeds from itself by existing. It remains, therefore, that this one Word belongs solely to him from whom it has its existence by being born and according to whose complete likeness it exists.

By this reasoning, therefore [Note: [Col. 0207D] In the manuscripts, “By this reasoning, etc.” begins Chapter 63 here, under the heading “How there is only one of one,” as in the heading of Chapter 61 in the printed editions], they seem to contain not only many fathers, sons, and proceeding beings, but also other relations; or certainly the Father, the Son, and their Spirit—of whom it is already most certain that they truly exist—are not three speakers, although each individually is a speaker; nor are there several things that are spoken, since each speaks of himself and of the other two.

For just as knowing and understanding belong to supreme wisdom, so it is naturally characteristic of eternal and unchangeable knowledge and understanding always to behold as present what it knows and understands. But for such a supreme spirit to speak is nothing other than, as it were, to behold by thinking, just as the speech of our mind is nothing other than the inspection of one who is thinking [Note: [Col. 0207D] The manuscripts read “to speak of this spirit”; Thu. reads “to speak of such a spirit”]. The arguments already considered have made it entirely certain that whatever exists essentially in the supreme nature belongs perfectly, individually, to the Father, the Son, and their Spirit; and yet, when that same thing is predicated of the three together, it does not admit plurality. [Col. 0208D]

Since, then, it is established that, just as knowledge and understanding belong to its essence, so its knowing and understanding are nothing other than speaking [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts read “is not something to speak”; the printed reading is “is not other than to speak”], that is, always beholding as present what it knows and understands, it must follow that, just as the Father individually, the Son individually, and the Spirit of the Father and Son individually are knowing and understanding, yet these three together are not several knowers or understanders but one knower and one understander, so each individually is a speaker, yet the three together are not three speakers [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts read “yet all three together are not three speakers”; others read “yet these three together are not three speakers”], but one speaker.

From this it can also be clearly understood that, when these three are spoken of, whether by themselves or by one another, they are not several things that are spoken. For what is spoken there except their essence? If that essence, then, is one alone [Note: [Col. 0209D] Codex Thuaneus reads “if that alone is one”], what is spoken is one alone. Therefore, if there is one alone in them that speaks, and one that is spoken—since there is one wisdom that speaks in them and one substance that is spoken—it follows that there are not several words there, but one.

Although, therefore, each speaks of himself and all speak of one another, it is nevertheless impossible that there should be in the supreme essence any word other than that one which, as is already established, is born from that of which it is the Word in such a way that it can also be called its true image and truly be its Son [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts read “so that it may also be its true image”; the printed reading is “so that it can also be called its true image”]. In this I see something astonishing and inexplicable. For although it is manifest that each one—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son—simultaneously speaks of himself and of the other two, and that there is only one Word there [Col. 0209C], nevertheless that Word cannot in any way be called the Word of all three, but only of one of them.

For it is established that it is the image and Son of the one whose Word it is; and it is evident that neither an image nor a son can properly be called the image or son of itself, or of the Spirit proceeding from itself [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts read “nor of what proceeds from itself”; the manuscript of Saint Michael reads “or of itself”]. For it is born neither from itself nor from what proceeds from itself; nor does it, by existing, imitate itself or what proceeds from itself. It does not imitate itself, since it does not draw from itself the likeness of existence; for imitation and likeness do not exist in one alone but in several. Nor does it imitate that other or exist according to its likeness, because this one does not have existence from that other, but that other from this one [Note: [Col. 0209D] In the manuscripts, the preceding chapter continues here. A. reads in the heading “Let there be one of one”; another manuscript reads “let there be only one of one”; Thu. 30 reads “let there be only one Son of one.”]. [Note: [Col. 0209D] In some editions, Chapter 61 begins here.]

It remains, therefore, that this one Word belongs only to the one from whom, by being born, it has its existence, and according to whose complete likeness it exists. [Col. 0210A] Thus there is one Father, not several fathers; one Son, not several sons; one proceeding Spirit, not several proceeding spirits, in the supreme essence. Although these three are such that the Father is never the Son or the proceeding Spirit; the Son is never the Father or the proceeding Spirit; and the Spirit of the Father and the Son is never the Father or the Son; and although each individually is so perfect that it lacks nothing [Note: [Col. 0209D] One manuscript reads “if he is perfect”; the printed reading is “is so perfect”], nevertheless what they are is one in such a way that, just as it cannot be said plurally of each individual, so neither can it be said plurally of the three together. And although each simultaneously speaks of himself and all speak of one another, there are nevertheless not several words there, but one; and that one belongs not to each individually or to all together, but to one alone.

## CHAPTER LXIV [alternatively LXII]

[Note: [Col. 0209D] Chapter 62 is Chapter 64 in the manuscripts.] [Col. 0210B]

### That, although this is inexplicable, it must nevertheless be believed

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The human mind should recognize that this is most certainly so, even if it cannot penetrate how it is so. It is incomprehensible how supreme wisdom knows the things it has made. Therefore, much less can it be explained how it knows or speaks of itself.

It seems to me that the secret of this matter, so sublime, surpasses every power of the human intellect; and for that reason I think that the attempt to explain how this is so should be restrained. For I think it ought to be sufficient for one investigating an incomprehensible matter to reach, by reasoning, the point of knowing with complete certainty that it exists, even if he cannot understand intellectually how it is so. Nor should the certainty of those things be diminished for that reason when they are asserted by necessary proofs and no other reasoning contradicts them, even if the incomprehensibility of their natural sublimity does not allow them to be explained. [Col. 0210C]

For what is so incomprehensible, so ineffable, as that which is above all things? [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts read “incomprehensible as”; the printed reading is “so incomprehensible, so ineffable, as”]. Therefore, if the things so far argued concerning the supreme essence have been established by necessary arguments, even though they cannot be penetrated by the intellect in such a way that they can also be explained in words, the solidity of their certainty nevertheless does not waver in the least.

For if the preceding consideration rationally understood that it is incomprehensible how the same supreme wisdom knows the things it has made—things which we necessarily know so much about—who could explain how it knows or speaks of itself, concerning which it is possible for a human being to know either nothing or scarcely anything? [Col. 0210D] Therefore, if the Father does not generate and the Son is not generated by the fact that he speaks of himself [Note: [Col. 0209D] Thu. 30 reads “by the fact that he speaks of that one,” rather than “of himself”], who will recount his generation? (Isaiah 53:8.)

[Col. 0211A]

## CHAPTER LXV [alternatively LXIII]

[Note: [Col. 0211D] In the manuscripts, the material beginning “But again, if it is so…” begins Chapter 65 here, under the heading “How one may argue truly about an ineffable matter,” as in the heading of Chapter 63 in the printed editions.]

### How one may argue truly about an ineffable matter

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Although this matter is ineffable in its proper nature, nothing prevents what has so far been argued about the supreme nature through riddles, images, and likenesses from being true. Whatever names are spoken of that nature indicate not so much its proper nature as a likeness. For they signify what we conceive in created things; yet what is intimated or estimated concerning it through words is not false. What is known concerning it is true, although not everything that it truly is is known.

But again, if the nature of its ineffability is as described—or rather, because it is so—how can anything stand that has been argued concerning it according to the relation of Father, Son, and proceeding Spirit? For if that has been unfolded rationally and truly [Note: [Col. 0211D] One manuscript reads “has been explained rationally”; others read “has been explained by reason”; the printed reading is “has been unfolded rationally”], how is it ineffable? Or if it is ineffable [Note: [Col. 0211D] Several manuscripts read “if that is ineffable”; others omit “that”], how is it as it has been argued?

Or is it that something concerning it could be explained to some extent, and therefore nothing prevents what has been argued from being true? But because it could not be comprehended completely, it is therefore ineffable.

Yet what answer can be given to what was already established above in this same discussion: that the supreme essence is so far above and beyond every other nature that, whenever something is said of it in words common to other natures, the meaning is in no way common? What meaning did I understand in all these words that I have considered except the common and customary one? If, then, the customary meaning of the words is foreign to it [Note: [Col. 0211D] The manuscripts read “is foreign with respect to those things”], whatever I have reasoned does not pertain to it. [Col. 0211C]

How, then, is it true that something concerning the supreme essence has been discovered, if what has been discovered is entirely different from it? What, then? Is something in one respect discovered concerning an incomprehensible matter, while in another respect nothing about it has been perceived?

For often we say many things without expressing properly what they are as they are; rather, through something else we signify what we either do not wish or are unable to express properly, as when we speak in riddles. And often we see something not properly as the thing itself is, but through some likeness or image, as when we examine someone’s face in a mirror [Note: [Col. 0211D] The manuscripts read “the face of someone”; the printed reading is “someone’s face.”]

Thus we both speak and do not speak of one and the same thing; we both see and do not see it. We speak and see through something else; we do not speak and do not see it according to its proper nature [Note: [Col. 0211D] In the manuscripts, the preceding chapter continues here.] [Note: [Col. 0212D] In some editions, Chapter 63 begins here.]

For this reason, then, nothing prevents what has so far been argued about the supreme nature from being true while it nevertheless remains ineffable, provided that it is not thought to have been expressed through the proper nature of its essence, but signified in some way through something else. [Col. 0212A]

For whatever names seem capable of being spoken of that nature do not, in my view, show it through its proper nature so much as suggest it through some likeness. Indeed, when I consider the meanings of those same words, I conceive in my mind more familiarly what I see in created things than what I understand to transcend every human intellect. For, by their signification, those words establish in my mind something much lesser—or rather, something entirely different—from what my mind itself strives to approach by means of this slight signification.

For neither does the name “wisdom” suffice to show me that through which all things were made from nothing and are preserved from nothing; nor can the name “essence” express that which, by its singular sublimity, is far above all things and, by its natural properness, is far beyond all things. [Col. 0212B] Thus that nature is ineffable, because it cannot in any way be intimated through words as it is; yet it is not false if something concerning it can, under the guidance of reason, be estimated through something else, as though in a riddle.

## CHAPTER LXVI [alternatively LXIV]

[Note: [Col. 0211D] Chapter 64 is Chapter 66 in the manuscripts.] [Col. 0212B]

### That the rational mind approaches most closely to knowledge of the supreme essence

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Nothing concerning that nature can therefore be apprehended according to its proper nature, but only through something else. Thus the more closely the creative essence is investigated through a creature resembling it, the more deeply it is known. Just as only the rational mind can rise to investigate it, so it alone is able to advance most effectively toward discovering it, because it is close to it. Hence, the more diligently the mind applies itself to learning about itself, the more effectively it ascends to knowledge of that supreme essence; and the more it neglects to look upon itself, the further it descends from the contemplation and vision of the creative essence.

Since it is evident that nothing concerning this nature can be apprehended through its proper nature, but only through something else, it is certain that one approaches knowledge of it more closely through that which more closely approaches it by likeness [Note: [Col. 0211D] One manuscript reads “its thought” rather than “its knowledge”]. For whatever among created things is established to be more like it must necessarily be superior in nature [Note: [Col. 0211D] Thu. 30 reads “through that which more closely approaches it” rather than “through that which more closely approaches it by likeness”].

Therefore, by a greater likeness, that thing both helps the mind investigating to draw nearer to supreme truth and, through the more excellent created essence, teaches the mind more about what it ought to judge concerning the Creator. Without doubt, then, the creative essence is known more deeply the more it is investigated through a creature more closely resembling it.

For reason, already considered above, does not allow us to doubt that every essence, insofar as it exists, is insofar like the supreme essence. It is therefore evident that, just as the rational mind alone among all creatures can rise to investigate it, so likewise it alone is able to advance most effectively toward discovering it. For it is already known that the rational mind approaches it most closely through the likeness of its natural essence. [Col. 0212C]

What, then, is clearer than this: the more diligently the rational mind applies itself to learning about itself, the more effectively it ascends to knowledge of that essence; and the more it neglects to look upon itself, the further it descends from its contemplation? [Col. 0212D]

## CHAPTER LXVII [alternatively LXV]

[Note: [Col. 0213D] Chapter 65 is Chapter 67 in the manuscripts.] [Col. 0213B]

### That the mind itself is its mirror and its image

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—Since only the mind can be mindful, understanding, and loving both itself and this supreme essence, it alone is the true image of that essence, which consists in an ineffable Trinity through memory, understanding, and love of itself. The mind is especially like the supreme essence in that it can remember, understand, and love what is best and greatest—that is, the supreme essence.

It can therefore most appropriately be called, as it were, a mirror for itself, in which it may contemplate, so to speak, an image of that which it cannot see face to face. For if the mind alone, among all things that have been made, can be mindful, understanding, and loving of itself, I do not see why it should be denied that there is in it a true image of that essence which consists in an ineffable Trinity through memory, understanding, and love of itself.

Or certainly it proves itself more truly to be that essence’s image for this reason: it can remember it, understand it, and love it. For in whatever respect it is greater and more like it, in that respect it is recognized as being more truly its image. [Col. 0213C]

It is altogether impossible to conceive that anything so remarkable and so like supreme wisdom has been naturally granted to a rational creature as this: that it can remember, understand, and love what is the best and greatest of all things. Therefore nothing else has been implanted in any creature that so represents the image of the Creator.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0213D] In some editions, this is part of Chapter 65.]

### That the rational creature was made in order to love it

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The rational mind ought therefore to strive above all else to express, by a voluntary act, this image naturally impressed upon it. Since its foremost capacity is to remember, understand, and love the supreme good, it ought above all to will this; for whatever is better within its power ought more greatly to be within its will.

Moreover, to be rational is nothing other than to be able to distinguish the just from the unjust, the true from the non-true, the good from the non-good, and the better good from the lesser good. Yet this ability is useless unless it loves or rejects what it distinguishes, according to the judgment of true discrimination—loving more or less what it judges to be more or less good.

Therefore the rational creature was made for this purpose: to love the supreme essence, which is the supreme good, above all goods; indeed, to love nothing except it, because it is good through itself, and nothing is good except through it.

It consequently seems to follow that the rational creature ought to strive above all else to express, through voluntary action, this image impressed upon it by its natural power. For, apart from the fact that it owes to its Creator the very fact that it is, it is also recognized that it has no more distinguished ability than to remember, understand, and love the supreme good; and so it is clearly established that it ought to will nothing more especially [Note: [Col. 0213D] In the manuscripts, “Consequently, therefore, etc.” begins Chapter 68 here, under the heading “That the rational creature was made…,” as in the heading of Chapter 66 in the printed editions.]. [Col. 0214B]

For who could deny that whatever is better within one’s power ought more greatly to be within one’s will? Finally, for a rational nature, to be rational is nothing other than to be able to distinguish the just from the unjust, the true from the non-true, the good from the non-good, and the better good from the lesser good [Note: [Col. 0213D] One manuscript reads “the greater good from the lesser good”; the printed reading is “the better good from the lesser good.”]

But this ability is altogether useless and superfluous to it unless it loves or rejects what it distinguishes according to the judgment of true discrimination [Note: [Col. 0213D] In the manuscripts, the preceding chapter continues here.] [Note: [Col. 0214D] In some editions, Chapter 66 begins here.]

From this it is sufficiently clear that every rational being exists for this purpose: just as by the judgment of reason it judges something to be more or less good or non-good, so it should love or reject it more or less [Note: [Col. 0213D] The manuscripts read “something greater or lesser”; Victor, Sag., Thu., and Cister. read “something more or less.”].

Nothing, therefore, is clearer than that the rational creature was made to love the supreme essence above all goods, just as it is itself the supreme good; indeed, to love nothing except it or for its sake, because it is good through itself, and nothing else is good except through it. But it cannot love it unless it remembers it and strives to understand it.

It is therefore clear that the rational creature ought to devote all its ability and will to remembering, understanding, and loving the supreme good, to which it recognizes that it owes its very existence [Note: [Col. 0213D] The manuscripts read “its will and ability” rather than “its ability and will.”].

## CHAPTER LXIX [alternatively LXVII]

[Note: [Col. 0213D] Chapter 67 is Chapter 69 in the manuscripts.] [Col. 0214D]

### That the soul, always loving it, will at some time live truly blessed

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The human soul is a rational creature. It was therefore made to love the supreme essence, and to love it without end. For it is impious to suppose that supreme wisdom made it for the purpose that it should at some time, either voluntarily or by force, lose this love.

It remains, therefore, that it was made to love the supreme essence without end. But it cannot do this unless it lives forever. Thus it was made to live forever if it always wills to do that for which it was made.

Moreover, it is not fitting for a good God that what he made to exist for the purpose of being loved by him should cease to exist as long as it has truly loved him; nor that he should take away, or permit to be taken away from one who loves, what he freely gave to one who did not love, so that it might always love and then, by necessity, not love—since there should be no doubt that he himself loves every nature that truly loves him.

Therefore it is clear that human nature will never have its life taken from it if it always strives to love the supreme life. But it is absurd for any nature that always loves the one who is supremely good and omnipotent to live always in misery. Therefore the human soul, because it is rational, was made for this purpose: if it preserves what it was made for, it will at some time live securely and blessedly, free from death and every affliction. [Col. 0215A]

There is no doubt that the human soul is a rational creature. It must therefore have been made for the purpose of loving the supreme essence. It must consequently have been made either to love without end or to lose this love at some time, voluntarily or by force.

But it is impious to suppose that supreme wisdom made it for the purpose that it should at some time either despise such a great good or, while willing to retain it, lose it through some force. It remains, therefore, that it was made to love the supreme essence without end.

But it cannot do this unless it lives forever [Note: [Col. 0215D] The manuscripts read “and it cannot do this”; the printed reading is “but it cannot do this.”]. Thus it was made to live forever if it always wills to do what it was made for.

Furthermore, it is exceedingly unfitting for the supremely good, supremely wise, and omnipotent Creator that what he made to exist for the purpose of being loved by him should cease to exist as long as it has truly loved him; and that what he freely gave to one who did not love, so that it might always love, should be taken away from one who loves, or allowed to be taken away, so that it might not love by necessity—especially since there should be absolutely no doubt that he himself loves every nature that truly loves him. [Col. 0215C]

Therefore it is manifest that the life of the human soul will never be taken away if it always strives to love the supreme life. How, then, will it live? For what great thing is a long life unless it is truly secure from the assault of afflictions? Whoever, while living, is subject to afflictions either through fear or suffering, or is deceived by false security—what is he doing except living miserably? But whoever lives free from these things lives blessedly [Note: [Col. 0215D] The manuscripts read “lives freely”; Victor, Sag., Gem., and Cister. read “lives free from these things.”].

It is therefore utterly absurd that any nature should live always in misery while always loving him who is supremely good and omnipotent. It is consequently clear that the human soul is such that, if it preserves what it was made for, it will at some time live truly secure and blessed, free from death itself and every other affliction.

[Col. 0216A]

## CHAPTER LXX [alternatively LXVIII]

[Note: [Col. 0215D] Chapter 68 is Chapter 70 in the manuscripts.]

### That it gives itself in return to the soul that loves it, so that she may be eternally blessed

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—It is contrary to justice that the one who is most just should fail to distinguish between one who loves and one who despises what ought to be supremely loved; that he should not love one who loves him; or that being loved by him should be of no benefit. It is therefore contrary to reason that he should give nothing in return to one who loves him.

But for this love, by which the rational creature surpasses other creatures, there can be no reward except that which surpasses all natures. For the good that requires itself to be loved in this way also compels itself to be desired no less. Therefore supreme goodness can give nothing to one who loves and desires it except itself.

For if it wishes to be loved in order to give something else in return, it does not wish to be loved for its own sake but for the sake of something else; and thus it wishes not itself but something else to be loved. It is therefore established that whoever has desired it as he ought will enjoy supreme blessedness, and that she will never lose it, because she will be unable not to love it, nor will it be able to abandon one who loves it. Therefore she will be eternally blessed.

Finally, it cannot in any way seem true that the most just and most powerful being gives nothing in return to one who perseveres in loving him, when he gives existence to one who does not love him [Note: [Col. 0215D] The manuscripts read “that he should give existence”; the printed reading is “when he gives existence”], so that he might be able to become a lover.

For if he gives nothing in return to one who loves him, then the supremely just one does not distinguish between one who loves and one who despises what ought to be supremely loved [Note: [Col. 0215D] The manuscripts read “what ought supremely to love”; the printed reading is “what ought to be supremely loved.”]. Nor does he love one who loves him, or is being loved by him of no benefit. All these alternatives are inconsistent with him. He therefore gives a reward to everyone who perseveres in loving him.

What, then, does he give in return? If he gave rational being to what was nothing, so that it might love, what will he give to one who loves, if that one does not cease loving? If what serves love is so great, how great must be what is repaid to love? And if the support of love is such, what must be the profit of love? [Col. 0216C]

For if the rational creature, which is useless to itself without this love, surpasses all creatures, then nothing can be the reward of this love except that which surpasses all natures. Indeed, the very same good that requires itself to be loved in this way also compels itself to be desired by the lover no less [Note: [Col. 0215D] The manuscripts read “is compelled”; the printed reading is “compels.”]

For who would love justice, truth, blessedness, or incorruptibility without desiring to enjoy them? What, then, can supreme goodness give in return to one who loves and desires it except itself? For whatever else it gives is not a repayment, because it neither compensates for the love, nor consoles the lover, nor satisfies the one who desires.

Or if it wishes to be loved and desired in order to give something else in return, it does not wish to be loved and desired for its own sake but for the sake of something else; and thus it does not wish itself to be loved but something else—a thought that it would be impious to entertain [Note: [Col. 0215D] The manuscripts read “it is impious to entertain”; the printed reading is “it would be impious to entertain.”] [Col. 0216D]

Nothing, therefore, is more certain than that every rational soul, if it strives, as it ought, by loving to desire supreme blessedness, will at some time receive it for enjoyment, so that what it now sees as though through a mirror and in a riddle it will then see face to face [Col. 0217A] [Note: [Col. 0217C] In some editions, Chapter 69 begins here.] [Note: [Col. 0217C] In the manuscripts, the preceding chapter continues here.]

But it would be the height of folly to doubt whether she will enjoy it without end. For, once enjoying it, the soul will be unable to be tormented by fear, deceived by deceptive security, or experience its want again; she will be unable not to love it; nor will it abandon one who loves it; nor will there be anything more powerful that could separate them against their will.

Therefore whatever soul has once begun to enjoy supreme blessedness will be eternally blessed.

## CHAPTER LXXI

[Note: [Col. 0217C] In some editions, this is part of Chapter 69.] [Col. 0217B]

### That the one who despises it is eternally miserable

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—By contrast, whoever despises the love of the supreme good will be eternally miserable, for he will either cease to exist or exist in eternal misery. It is not sufficient as a punishment that he should not exist; for after his guilt he would be what he was before his guilt, and thus justice would not distinguish between one who can have no good and wills no evil, and one who can have the greatest good and wills the greatest evil. Therefore, if he despises loving the supreme essence, he will exist in eternal misery.

From this it follows consequently that the one who despises the love of the supreme good will incur eternal misery [Note: [Col. 0217C] The manuscripts of Victor, Sag., Thu. 30, and Cister. read “will incur”; Victor 13 reads “may incur.”].

For if it is said that he is punished justly for such contempt by losing existence or life, because he does not use himself for that for which he was made, reason in no way permits him to receive as punishment, after so great a guilt, the existence that he had before every guilt. For before he existed, he could neither have guilt nor feel punishment.

If, then, the soul that despises what it was made for dies in such a way that it feels nothing, or so that it is altogether nothing [Note: [Col. 0217C] The manuscripts of Victor, Sag., and Thu. read “or so that it is altogether nothing”], its condition will be the same both in the greatest guilt and without any guilt; and supremely wise justice will not distinguish between one who can have no good and wills no evil, and one who can have the greatest good and wills the greatest evil.

How unfitting this is is sufficiently clear [Note: [Col. 0217C] In the manuscripts, the preceding chapter continues here.] [Note: [Col. 0218C] In some editions, Chapter 70 begins here.]. Nothing, therefore, can appear more consistent, nor ought anything to be believed with greater certainty, than that the human soul was made in such a way that, if it despises loving the supreme essence, it will suffer eternal misery [Note: [Col. 0217C] The manuscript of Cister. reads “if it despises loving supreme justice, it will suffer eternally”; another reading is “if it despises justice, it will suffer eternally.”]: just as the one who loves will rejoice in an eternal reward, so the one who despises will suffer under eternal punishment; and just as the former will experience unchangeable sufficiency, so the latter will experience inconsolable [Note: [Col. 0217C] Thu. 90 reads “incomprehensible”] want.

[Col. 0218A]

## CHAPTER LXXII

[Note: [Col. 0218C] In some editions, this is part of Chapter 70.]

### That every human soul is immortal, and that it is either always miserable or at some time truly blessed

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—The soul would be neither eternally blessed nor eternally miserable if it were mortal. It is therefore immortal. All souls, moreover, are of the same nature; therefore all are immortal, since at least some are immortal. Further, everything that lives will either never or at some time be truly secure from every affliction. Therefore every human soul will either always be miserable or at some time be truly blessed.

But neither must the soul that loves be eternally blessed, nor the soul that despises be miserable, if it is mortal. Whether, therefore, it loves or despises that for which it was created to love, it must be immortal.

But if there are some rational souls that should be judged neither lovers nor despisers—such as the souls of infants seem to be—what should be thought about them? Are they mortal or immortal [Note: [Col. 0217C] The manuscripts read “or are they immortal”?] [Col. 0218B]

Without a doubt, all human souls are of the same nature. Since it is therefore established that some are immortal, every human soul must be immortal.

Yet since everything that lives will either never or at some time be truly secure from every affliction, it is nevertheless necessary that every human soul be either always miserable or at some time truly blessed [Note: [Col. 0217C] In the manuscripts, this sentence begins Chapter 73 under the heading “That it is either always miserable or at some time truly blessed,” as in the heading of Chapter 70 in the printed editions.].

## CHAPTER LXXIII [alternatively LXXI]

[Note: [Col. 0217C] In the manuscripts, this is Chapter 74, under the heading “That no soul is unjustly deprived of the supreme good, and that one must strive toward it,” as in the heading of Chapter 71 in the printed editions. The manuscripts Thu. 60 and Cister. read “That no soul is unjustly deprived of the supreme good, and that one must wholly direct oneself toward it”; one manuscript has “supreme sound” for “supreme good.”]

### That no soul is unjustly deprived of the supreme good, and that one must strive toward it with one’s whole being

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—What souls are such that they love in a way that they will at some time be blessed, or despise in a way that they will at some time be miserable, cannot be comprehended by a human being. It is enough that the supremely just one deprives no one unjustly of the supreme good. Every human being must therefore strive toward it by loving and desiring it with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind.

But which souls should unquestionably be judged to love that for which they were made, so that they will at some time enjoy it; which should be judged to despise it so that they deserve always to lack it; and how, or on what merits, those that seem able to be called neither lovers nor despisers are distributed to eternal blessedness or misery—whether any mortal can comprehend this by argument, I consider either exceedingly difficult or impossible.

Nevertheless, it must be held with complete certainty that no soul is unjustly deprived by the supremely just and supremely good Creator of creatures of the good for which it was made [Note: [Col. 0219D] The manuscripts read “deprived of the good from which it was made”; the printed reading is “deprived of the good for which it was made.”]. And every human being must strive toward that same good by loving and desiring it with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind.

## CHAPTER LXXIV [alternatively LXXII]

[Note: [Col. 0219D] Chapter 73 is Chapter 75 in the manuscripts.] [Col. 0219D]

### That the supreme essence is to be hoped for

**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**—No one can strive toward it if he despairs of being able to reach it. Therefore, besides love, hope is necessary.
