- [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts read “the Father individually, the Son individually”; Victor and Sag. add *et*: “the Father individually, and the Son individually.” The manuscripts read *unus sciens, et unus*, “one knower, and one [understander]”; Victor and Sag. omit *et*, “and.”
- [Col. 0209D] Thu. 30 reads “if that essence alone is one”; The manuscripts have *ergo unum solum est*, “therefore there is one alone”; Cister. has *ergo si unum est*, “therefore, if there is one,” against *ergo si unum solum est*, “therefore, if there is one alone.” The manuscripts read “it is established that it is”; the printed reading adds *ipsum* (“it itself”). The manuscripts read corrupt *et pater, quod nec*, literally “and the Father, which not”; the printed reading is “and it is evident that.”
- [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts read “Spirit of the Father or of the Son”; Victor and Sag. read “Spirit of the Father and of the Son.”
- [Col. 0211D] Victor, Sag., Thu., and Gem. omit *substantia* (“essence/substance”) from *de illa substantia*, “concerning that substance.” The apparatus gives manuscript *aut quodantenus*, “or to some extent,” against *an quodam tenus*, “or whether to some extent,” preserving the conjunction and spacing distinction. The manuscripts transpose to *verum inventum est esse*, “it has been discovered to be true”; the contrasting form in the apparatus is *verum est inventam esse*, “it is true that [something] has been discovered,” with anomalous feminine *inventam* where the narrative prints neuter *inventum*. The manuscripts read *aut volumus aut*, “either we wish, or,” where the narrative has *aut nolumus, aut*, “either we do not wish, or,” before the following “cannot.” They also read *non prope* (“not near”), instead of *non proprie* (“not properly”).
- [Col. 0211D] The manuscripts read *pateat quod* (“it is evident that”), rather than “it is evident because.” Thu. 30 reads *quo illi magis* (“through that which is more like it”), rather than *quod illi magis* (“that which is more like it”).
- [Col. 0213D] Thu. 30 reads *apertissime igitur* (“therefore, most plainly”), rather than *aptissime igitur* (“therefore, most fittingly”); the manuscripts read *at certe* (“but certainly”), rather than *aut certe* (“or certainly”). The manuscripts read *huic quoque, quia*, “to this also, because”; Gem. and St Michael have *hinc quoque, quia*, “from this also, because”; Cister. has *hic quoque quia*, “here also, because.” The manuscripts read *satis patienter* (“sufficiently patiently”), rather than *satis patenter* (“sufficiently clearly”). Victor, Sag., Thu., St Michael, and Cister. read “nothing is more fitting,” rather than “nothing is clearer.”
- [Col. 0215D] The manuscripts read *tribuat* (“may give”), rather than *retribuat* (“may give back”). The manuscripts read *rationabilem* (“rational”), rather than *rationalem* (“rational”). Victor, Sag., Thu., and St Michael read *nec se vult* (“nor does it wish itself”), rather than *non se vult* (“it does not wish itself”). Victor, Sag., St Michael, and Thu. read *nunc videat* (“may now see,” subjunctive), rather than *nunc videt* (“now sees,” indicative).
- [Col. 0217C] In the manuscripts, the preceding words begin Chapter 71 under the heading “That the one despising it is eternally miserable”; Thu. 30 reads the same heading. Victor 3, Sag., Thu. 30, and Cister. read *incurrit* (“incurs”), and Victor 13 *incurrat* (“may incur”), rather than *incurret* (“will incur”). Cister. reads “receives non-existence, which,” rather than “receives the existence which.” The manuscripts read *culpa sine*, “guilt without,” rather than *culpa et sine*, “guilt and without”; they read *nec discernit* (“does not distinguish”) and *sapiens justitiam* (the phrase “wise justice,” but with anomalous accusative *justitiam*), rather than “will not distinguish” and *sapiens justitia*, “wise justice,” with nominative *justitia*. Gem., St Michael, and Cister. read *ita ista sentiet* (“thus this one will experience”), rather than *sentiat* (“may experience”).

The manuscripts read *quod tam a* (“which so by”), rather than *quod tamen a* (“which nevertheless by”); they read *ex bono ad* (“from the good toward”), rather than *eo bono, ad* (“of that good, for”); Thu. 30 reads *certissimum est* (“it is most certain”), rather than *certissime est* (“it is most certainly [to be held]”).

But the human soul will in no way be able to exercise itself in this intention if it despairs of being able to reach what it aims at. Therefore, as the effort to strive toward it is useful to the soul, so necessary is the hope of attaining it.

[Note: The manuscripts read *adnittendum* (“that one must strive”) for *adnitendi* (“of striving”).]

[Col. 0219B]

## 27. CHAPTER LXXV

[Note: In some manuscripts this is part of Chapter 72.]

### That one ought to believe in it—that is, by believing, to strive toward it.

**Summary of the chapter.**—One cannot love or hope for what one does not believe. Faith, therefore, is also necessary—not merely faith by which one believes the supreme essence and those things without which it cannot be loved, but faith by which, through believing, one strives toward it. For to believe in it is to strive toward it by believing. Therefore, whoever does not move toward it through what he believes does not believe in it. Whoever, however, strives toward it by believing will reach it in such a way that he will remain within it. Hence it is more appropriately said that one must believe and strive *into* it than that one must believe or strive *toward* it.

[Note: At this point the manuscripts begin Chapter 76, under the title “That one ought to believe,” etc., as in the printed title of Chapter 73. Victor., Sagiens, and Cistercian manuscripts read *et sperare* (“and hope”) for *aut sperare* (“or hope”).]

But one cannot love or hope for what one does not believe. It is therefore beneficial for the human soul to believe the supreme essence, and those things without which it cannot be loved, so that by believing it may strive toward it. I think this same point can be expressed suitably and more briefly if, instead of saying “to strive by believing into the supreme essence,” one says “to believe in the supreme essence.”

[Note: The manuscripts read *ut illa credendo* (“so that, by believing, it”) for *ut illam credendo* (“so that, by believing, [the soul] may strive toward it”), and *signari posse* (“can be indicated”) for *significari posse* (“can be signified”).] For if someone says that he believes in it, he seems sufficiently to show both that, through the faith he professes, he is striving toward the supreme essence, and that he believes those things which pertain to this striving. For he does not seem to believe in it either if he believes something that does not pertain to striving toward it, or if, through what he believes, he does not strive toward it.

[Note: Thu. 30 reads *non videntur credere* (“they do not seem to believe”) for *non videtur credere* (“he does not seem to believe”).]

[Note: In the manuscripts this continues the preceding chapter.]  
[Note: Elsewhere this is where Chapter 73 begins.]

And perhaps one may indifferently say “to believe in it” and “to believe toward it,” just as “to strive by believing into it” and “to strive toward it” may be taken as equivalent—except that whoever reaches it by striving toward it will not remain outside it, but will remain within it. This is expressed more explicitly and familiarly when one says that one must strive *into* it rather than *toward* it. For this reason, I think it can more appropriately be said that one must believe *in* it rather than *toward* it.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

[al. LXXIV]  
[Note: In the manuscripts this is Chapter 74; Chapter 77 in the present arrangement.]

### That one ought equally to believe in the Father, the Son, and their Spirit individually and together in all three.

**Summary of the chapter.**—One ought to believe in them in this way because the three together, and each one individually, are one supreme essence. It is in this essence alone that every human being ought to believe, just as it alone is the one end at which a human being ought, through love, to aim in every thought and action. But just as no one can strive toward it unless he believes it, so believing it is of no benefit to anyone unless he strives toward it.

One must therefore believe equally in the Father, the Son, and their Spirit, both in each individually and together in all three, because the Father individually, the Son individually, and their Spirit individually are the supreme essence; and the Father, the Son, together with their Spirit, are one and the same supreme essence, in which alone every human being ought to believe. For it is the sole end at which, through love, he ought to aim in every thought and action. Hence it is clear that, just as no one can strive toward it unless he believes it, so believing it benefits no one unless he strives toward it.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

[al. LXXV]  
[Note: In the manuscripts this is Chapter 75; Chapter 78 in the present arrangement.]

### What living faith and dead faith are.

**Summary of the chapter.**—Faith without love is therefore useless, and something like a dead thing. Faith accompanied by love, however, is not idle; for whoever loves supreme justice is unable to despise anything just or admit anything unjust. Thus active faith lives, because it possesses the life of love, without which it would not act; and idle faith does not live, because it lacks the life of love, with which it would not remain idle. Faith is called dead because it does not possess the life it ought always to possess. Moreover, living faith is said to be that which believes in what ought to be believed; dead faith, that which merely believes what ought to be believed.

Therefore, no matter how firmly so great a matter may be believed, faith will be useless, and something like a dead thing, unless it is effective and alive through love. For that faith which is accompanied by fitting love is in no way idle when an opportunity for action presents itself, but rather demonstrates itself through a certain abundance of works—something it could not do without love. This alone can prove the point: whoever loves supreme justice is unable to despise anything just or admit anything unjust.

[Note: The manuscripts read *offerat* (“may offer”) for Thu.’s *conferat* (“may contribute”), and *facere non possit* (“could not do”) for *facere non posset* (“could not have done”).]  
[Note: The manuscripts read *magis esse quadam* (“rather, to be engaged in a certain frequency of works”); Thu. and Gem. read *magna se quadam* (“itself by a certain great [frequency]”) for *magis se quadam*.]

Therefore, since something that acts shows that life is present in it, without which it could not act, it is not unreasonable to say that active faith lives, because it possesses the life of love, without which it would not act, and that idle faith does not live, because it lacks the life of love, with which it would not remain idle.

[Note: “Active faith is said” in the manuscripts: “active faith is said to live.”]  
[Note: “Idle faith” in the manuscripts: “and idle faith.”]  
[Note: “Would not live” in the manuscripts; Thu. has “would not live”; Vict., Sag., and Cister. have “not justly.”]

Accordingly, if someone is called blind not only when he has lost his sight, but also when, although he ought to have sight, he does not have it, why may faith without love not likewise be called dead—not because it has lost its life, that is, love, but because it does not possess the life it ought always to possess?

[Note: Thu. reads *quicunque quod debet habere* (“whoever does not have what he ought to have”) for *qui cum debet habere* (“who, although he ought to have [it]”).] Just as that faith which acts through love is recognized to be living, so that which remains idle through contempt is shown to be dead. It may therefore be said quite appropriately that living faith believes in what ought to be believed, whereas dead faith merely believes what ought to be believed.

[Note: The manuscripts read *in quo credi* (“in which one ought to believe”) for *in quod credi* (“in what one ought to believe”).]

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

[al. LXXVI]  
[Note: In the manuscripts this is Chapter 76; Chapter 79 in the present arrangement.]  
[Col. 0221B]

### That the supreme essence may in a certain sense be called three.

**Summary of the chapter.**—It is beneficial for every human being to believe in a certain ineffable threefold unity and one Trinity: one, on account of the essence; threefold, on account of three—I do not know what. For it cannot be said what the three persons are in such a way that they thereby become several. Nor are there as many substances as persons, as there are among human beings, where there are as many individual substances as persons. Thus, in the supreme essence, just as there are not several substances, so neither are there several persons. The only reason for calling there “three persons” or “three substances” in one supreme essence or nature is the lack of a name by which plurality in a single essence might be signified.

Individuals are, above all, subjects of accidents; hence they more properly receive the name “substance.” Therefore the supreme essence, which is subject to no accidents, cannot properly be called a substance, unless “substance” is taken to mean “essence.” In this way, that supreme and one Trinity can irreproachably be called one essence and three persons, or three substances.

It is therefore evident that it is beneficial for every human being to believe in a certain ineffable threefold unity and one Trinity: one, indeed, and unity, because of the one essence; threefold, and Trinity, because of three—I do not know what. For although I can say “Trinity” because of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both, who are three, I cannot express in a single name what the three are for—such as if I were to say “three persons”—just as I can say “unity” because of one substance.

[Note: The manuscripts omit “yet I cannot.”]  
[Note: The manuscripts omit “if.”]

They are not to be considered three persons because all groups of several persons subsist separately from one another in such a way that there must be as many substances as persons. This is recognized in the case of several human beings, where there are as many individual substances as persons. Therefore, in the supreme essence, just as there are not several substances, so neither are there several persons.

If, then, someone wishes to explain to another what the three are, he will say that they are the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both—unless, compelled by the lack of a properly suitable name, he chooses one of those names which cannot be used in the plural of the supreme essence to signify what cannot be named appropriately.

[Note: “Some of those names” in Thu. 30; “several of those names” in Ms. S. Mich.; “one of those names” in the present text.]

Thus he may say that the admirable Trinity is one essence, or nature, and three persons, or substances. These two names are more suitably chosen to signify plurality in the supreme essence, because “person” is said only of an individual rational nature, while “substance” is principally said of individuals, which subsist most especially in plurality.

[Note: At both occurrences, the manuscripts read *ad designandum/ad designandam* (“to designate”) for *ad significandum/ad significandam* (“to signify”).]  
[Note: The manuscripts read *dici non possint* (“cannot be said”) for *dici non possunt* (“cannot be said”), and *pluralitate constunt* (“stand in plurality”) for *pluralitate subsistunt* (“subsist in plurality”).]

For individuals are above all “substantial”—that is, they are subject to accidents—and therefore more properly receive the name “substance.” Hence it has already been made clear above that the supreme essence, which is subject to no accidents, cannot properly be called a substance, unless “substance” is taken to mean “essence.” For this reason of necessity, then, that supreme and one Trinity, or threefold unity, may irreproachably be called one essence and three persons, or three substances.

## 28. CHAPTER LXXIX

[Note: Elsewhere this is part of Chapter 76.]

### That it is God, who alone rules over everything and governs everything.

**Summary of the chapter.**—The name “God” properly belongs to this supreme essence alone, which rules over everything and governs everything. For by the name “God” is understood only a substance that is above every nature, to be venerated by human beings because of its dignity and entreated because of any urgent necessity. Just as everything was made by the supremely good and supremely wise Spirit, so he himself rules over everything and governs everything. Therefore all things are governed neither by another nor by chance. He alone, then, is the one whom every other nature ought to venerate through love; from him alone prosperity is to be hoped for; to him alone one must flee from adversity; to him alone one must pray for every need. He alone, therefore, truly is and is called God, ineffably three and one.

[Col. 0223A]

It therefore seems—or rather, it is asserted without hesitation—that what is called God is not nothing, and that the name “God” properly belongs to this supreme essence alone.

[Note: “For indeed nothing” in the manuscripts, rather than “for indeed what is called God is not nothing.”]  
[Note: In the manuscripts the following begins Chapter 80 under the title “That it rules,” as in the title of Chapter 77 in the present editions.]  
[Note: Elsewhere this is where Chapter 77 begins.]

For whoever says that God exists, whether he means one or several, understands only some substance which he considers to be above every nature that is not God, and which is to be venerated by human beings because of its eminent dignity and entreated by them because of any urgent necessity.

[Note: The manuscripts read “against any necessity” rather than “because of any necessity.”]  
[Note: In the manuscripts this continues the preceding chapter.]

What, then, is as worthy of veneration because of its dignity, and of supplication for every need, as the supremely good and supremely powerful Spirit who rules over everything and governs everything? For just as it is certain that all things were made and endure through his supremely good and supremely wise omnipotence, so it is exceedingly inappropriate to suppose that he does not rule over the things he made;

[Note: Victor., Sagiens, and Cistercian manuscripts read *nimis inconveniens est*, omitting *et* in *nimis et inconveniens est*.] or that what was made by him is governed by another who is less powerful, less good, or less wise; or that it is governed by no reason at all, but only by the disordered turning of chance.

For he alone is the one through whom all things are well for anyone, and without whom nothing is well, and from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. Since he alone is not only the good Creator but also the most powerful Lord and the wisest ruler of all, it is perfectly clear that he alone is the one whom every other nature, with all its power, ought to venerate through loving him and love through venerating him; from him alone prosperity is to be hoped for; to him alone one must flee from adversity; to him alone one must pray for every need.

[Note: The manuscripts read “in adversity” rather than “from adversity.”]

Truly, then, he is not only God but the only God, ineffably three and one.

[Note: S. Mich., Vict. 3, and Cister.: “The Monologion of Anselm ends.”]

[Col. 0223A]

# SAINT ANSELM’S PROSLOGION, OR ALLOQUY, CONCERNING THE EXISTENCE OF GOD

29

[Note: The book of the Proslogion was collated with the manuscripts of Gemmeticum, Bec, three Victorine manuscripts—RR 3, EE 13, CC 9—the Corbie manuscript 307, four manuscripts from Thouars—90, 391, 451, and 633—one Cistercian manuscript, and one from the monastery of Saint Michael at the Peril of the Sea. Ms. Cist.: “Here begins the Prologue to Anselm of Canterbury’s Proslogion.” Ms. Gem.: “Here begins the Preface to the book Proslogion of Anselm, archbishop.” Ms. Vict. 3: “Here begins the Preface to Anselm’s book Proslogion.” Ms. Thua. 391: “Here begins the Preface to the book Proslogion of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.” Ms. Thu. 633: “Here begins Anselm’s Proslogion, that is, his Alloquy.” Ms. S. Mich.: “Here begins the Preface to the book Proslogion of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.”]

## PROLOGUE

In this little work he intends, by a single argument, to prove that God exists, and whatever we believe about God. The work is difficult. The author writes in the person of one contemplating God and seeking to understand what he believes. He had given this little work the title “Faith Seeking Understanding.” He later named it Proslogion, that is, “Alloquy.”

After I had published a certain work, the *Monologion*, as an example of meditation on the reasonableness of faith, at the insistence of certain brothers, reasoning silently with himself in the person of someone investigating what he did not know,

[Note: The manuscripts read “investigating” rather than “someone investigating.”]

I began to ask myself whether perhaps a single argument could be found which would need no other argument than itself in order to establish itself, and which would suffice by itself to prove that God truly exists, that he is the supreme good needing nothing else, while all things need him in order to exist and to exist well, and whatever we believe concerning the divine substance.

[Note: Thu. and Cistercian manuscripts read *ut sint bene* (“that they may exist well”) for *ut sint et bene sint* (“that they may exist and exist well”).]

Whenever I repeatedly and carefully directed my thought to this, sometimes it seemed that what I was seeking could already be grasped, while at other times it entirely eluded the mind’s vision.

[Note: The manuscripts read “I directed my thoughts” rather than “I directed my thought.”]

At last, despairing, I wanted to stop, as though I were searching for something that could not be found. But when I wished completely to exclude that thought from me, lest by occupying my mind uselessly it should hinder me from other things in which I might make progress,

[Note: The manuscripts read “in which they might make progress” rather than “in which I might make progress.”]

it began more and more insistently to force itself upon me, although I did not want it and resisted it.

[Note: Thu. reads “although I wanted it more and more” rather than “although I did not want it more and more.”]

One day, then, when I was exhausted from strongly resisting its importunity, in the very conflict of my thoughts it presented itself in such a way that I embraced eagerly the thought which I had anxiously driven away, believing that I had found what I had despaired of finding.

I therefore judged that, if it were written down, it might please someone who read it, and I wrote the following little work about this very matter and certain others, in the person of one striving to raise his mind to contemplate God and seeking to understand what he believes.

[Note: Ms. S. Mich. reads “and certain other things” rather than “and certain others.”]  
[Note: The manuscripts read *exigere mentem* (“to direct or raise his mind”) for *erigere mentem* (“to raise his mind”).]

Since I judged neither this work nor the one I mentioned above worthy of the name of a book, or of having the author’s name placed before it,

[Note: The manuscripts read “of having the name of love placed before it” rather than “the author’s name.”]

yet I did not think they should be left without some title by which they might in some way invite anyone into whose hands they came to read them, I gave each its own title:

[Note: The manuscripts read *tamen sine* (“yet without”) for *tamen eadem sine* (“yet those same [works] without”).]

[Note: The manuscripts read “I gave each a title” rather than “I gave each its own title.”]

the first was to be called “An Example of Meditation on the Reason of Faith,” and the following one “Faith Seeking Understanding.”

[Note: Ms. S. Mich. reads “and the frequent one” rather than “and the following one.”]

But when both works had already been copied by many under these titles,

[Note: The manuscripts read “under these titles” with a slightly different word order.]

many people compelled me—and especially the most reverend archbishop of Lyon, named Hugh, who was serving as papal legate in Gaul and who ordered me by apostolic authority to place my name before them—to do so.

[Note: The manuscripts punctuate this as: “apostolic authority. He ordered me by apostolic authority.”]

To make this more suitable, I named the first *Monologion*, that is, “Soliloquy,” and the latter *Proslogion*, that is, “Alloquy.”

[Note: The manuscripts conclude the Prologue here. They then begin: “Proslogion, the book of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.”]

## CHAPTER I

### The awakening of the mind to the contemplation of God

He casts away cares and excludes everything except God in order to seek God. Human beings were made to see God. A sinful human being lost the blessedness for which he was made and found the misery for which he was not made. He did not preserve the good, although he could easily have done so. Without God we are in misery. Our labors and efforts are fruitless without God. A human being cannot seek God unless God himself teaches him, nor find him unless God himself reveals himself. God created the human being in his own image so that he might remember God, think of God, and love God. The faithful person does not seek to understand in order to believe; rather, he believes in order to understand, because unless he believes, he will not understand.

Come now, little man, leave your occupations for a while; hide yourself for a short time from your tumultuous thoughts. Cast aside your burdensome cares and postpone your laborious distractions.

[Note: The manuscripts read “burdensome things and” rather than “burdensome cares and.”]  
[Note: Some manuscripts read “disputes”; Vict. 9 reads “intentions,” rather than “distractions.”]

Give a little time to God and rest for a little while in him. Enter into the chamber of your mind; exclude everything except God and whatever helps you to seek him; and, with the door closed, seek him. Say now, my whole heart, say now to God: “I seek your face; your face, Lord, I seek” (Psalm 26:8).

Come now, then, Lord my God, teach my heart where and how to seek you, where and how to find you. Lord, if you are not here, where shall I seek you in your absence? But if you are everywhere, why do I not see you present?

[Note: Some manuscripts read “if, then, you are everywhere” rather than “but if you are everywhere.”]  
[Note: The manuscripts read “I see you present” and some omit “you.”]

Yet surely you dwell in inaccessible light. And where is that inaccessible light, or how shall I approach inaccessible light? Or who will lead me and bring me into it, so that I may see you in it? Then, by what signs and with what appearance shall I seek you? I have never seen you, Lord my God; I do not know your face.

What will he do, most high Lord? What will this exile of yours, far away, do?

[Note: The manuscripts read “What will this exile of yours do?” rather than “What will this far-away exile of yours do?”]

What will your servant do, anxious with love for you and cast far away from your face? He longs to see you, yet your face is exceedingly far from him. He desires to approach you, yet your dwelling is inaccessible. He longs to find you, yet he does not know your place. He seeks you, yet he does not know your face.

Lord, you are my God and my Lord; and I have never seen you.

[Note: Some manuscripts rearrange this as: “your place. He seeks you and does not know your face. Lord, you are my God and my Lord; and I have never…”]

You made me and remade me, and you bestowed all my good things upon me, yet I do not know you. Finally, I was made to see you, yet I have not done that for which I was made.

O miserable fate of humanity, when it lost what it was made for! O harsh and dreadful fall! Alas, what did it lose, and what did it find? What departed, and what remained? It lost the blessedness for which it was made and found the misery for which it was not made. He departed without whom nothing is happy, and there remained what in itself is nothing but miserable.

[Note: The manuscripts read “without whom it is unhappy” rather than “without whom nothing is happy.”]

Then the human being ate the bread of angels, which he now hungers for; now he eats the bread of sorrows, which he did not know then. Alas, the public mourning of humanity, the universal lamentation of the sons of Adam! He then belched from satiety; we sigh from hunger. He abounded; we beg. He held blessedly and abandoned miserably; we lack unhappily and desire miserably—and alas, we remain empty!

Why did he not preserve for us, when he could easily have done so, what we would lack so grievously?

[Note: The manuscripts read “what we lack” rather than “what we would lack.”]

Why did he bar the light from us in this way and cover us with darkness? Why did he take life away from us and inflict death upon us? Wretched beings, from where have we been expelled, and where have we been driven? From where have we been hurled down? Where have we been buried? From our homeland into exile, from the vision of God into our blindness, from the delight of immortality into the bitterness and horror of death. A miserable change from so great a good to so great an evil! A grievous loss, a grievous sorrow—everything grievous.

But alas for me, miserable as one among the other miserable sons of Eve, who have been separated from God! What did I begin? What did I accomplish? Toward what was I striving? Where have I arrived? What was I aspiring to? In what do I sigh? I sought good things, and behold, confusion. I was striving toward God, and I stumbled over myself. I sought rest in my solitude, and found tribulation and sorrow in my innermost being. I wanted to laugh from the joy of my mind, and I am compelled to roar from the groaning of my heart. Joy was hoped for, and behold, from here my sighs grow thick.

And you, Lord, how long? How long, Lord, will you forget us? How long will you turn your face from us? When will you look upon us and hear us? When will you illuminate our eyes and show us your face? When will you restore yourself to us? Look upon us, Lord; hear us, illuminate us, show yourself to us. Restore yourself to us, so that it may be well with us; without you it is so ill with us.

Have mercy on our labors and efforts toward you, for without you we have no power.

[Note: The manuscripts read “Have mercy on our labors” rather than “Have compassion on our labors.”]

You invite us; help us.

[Note: The manuscripts read “Invite us” rather than “You invite us.”]

I beseech you, Lord: let me not despair through sighing, but let me breathe again through hoping. I beseech you, Lord: my heart has become bitter through its desolation; sweeten it through your consolation. I beseech you, Lord: hungry, I began to seek you; do not let me cease while still fasting from you. Famished, I approached you; do not let me depart unfed. Poor, I came to the rich; miserable, to the merciful; do not let me return empty and despised. And if I sigh before I eat, give me, even after my sighs, something to eat.

Lord, bent down, I can look only downward; raise me up so that I may be able to direct my attention upward. My iniquities have risen above my head and envelop me; like a heavy burden, they weigh me down. Unwind me, unload me, lest their pit press its mouth over me. Let me look up toward your light, whether from far away or from the depths.

[Note: The manuscripts read “receive your light” rather than “look up toward your light.”]

Teach me to seek you and reveal yourself to the one who seeks you, because I cannot seek you unless you teach me, nor find you unless you reveal yourself. Let me seek you by desiring you; let me desire you by seeking you; let me find you by loving you; let me love you by finding you.

I confess, Lord, and I give thanks, because you created in me this image of yourself, so that I may remember you, think of you, and love you. But it has been so obliterated by the abrasion of vices and so darkened by the smoke of sins that it cannot do what it was made to do unless you renew and reform it.

I do not attempt, Lord, to penetrate your loftiness, for I do not at all compare my understanding with it; but I desire to understand in some way your truth, which my heart believes and loves. For I do not seek to understand in order to believe; rather, I believe in order to understand. For I also believe this: unless I believe, I shall not understand.

[Note: Vict. 3 omits the second occurrence of “for.”]

## CHAPTER II

### That God truly exists, even though the fool has said in his heart, “There is no God”

Therefore, Lord, who gives understanding to faith, grant me to understand, insofar as you know it to be beneficial, that you exist, as we believe, and that you are what we believe you to be.

Indeed, we believe that you are something than which nothing greater can be conceived. Is there, then, no such nature, because the fool has said in his heart, “There is no God”? (Psalm 13:1.) But surely that same fool, when he hears this very thing that I say—“something than which nothing greater can be conceived”—understands what he hears, and what he understands is in his understanding, even if he does not understand that it exists.

[Note: In Thu. 451 the words “that same fool” are missing from the passage.]

For it is one thing for a thing to be in the understanding and another to understand that the thing exists. When a painter first conceives what he is going to make, he has it in his understanding, but he does not yet understand it to exist, because he has not yet made it. Once he has painted it, however, he both has it in his understanding and understands that what he has made exists.

The fool, then, is convinced that something than which nothing greater can be conceived exists even in his understanding, because when he hears it, he understands it, and whatever is understood is in the understanding.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the fool is convinced,” while others read “the fool is also convinced,” or “therefore the fool is also convinced.”]

And surely that than which nothing greater can be conceived cannot exist in the understanding alone. For if it exists in the understanding alone, it can be conceived to exist also in reality, which is greater. Therefore, if that than which nothing greater can be conceived exists in the understanding alone, then that very thing than which nothing greater can be conceived is something than which something greater can be conceived—which is impossible.

[Note: One manuscript reads: “that than which nothing greater can be conceived is not that than which nothing greater can be conceived, because…” Another reads: “that than which nothing greater can be conceived is greater than itself, because…”]

Therefore, beyond doubt, something than which nothing greater can be conceived exists both in the understanding and in reality.

[Col. 0228B]

## CHAPTER III

### That God cannot be conceived not to exist

God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived. That which can be conceived not to exist is not God.

This is so truly that it cannot even be conceived not to exist. For one can conceive something that cannot be conceived not to exist; and that is greater than something whose nonexistence can be conceived.

Therefore, if that than which nothing greater can be conceived can be conceived not to exist, then that very thing than which nothing greater can be conceived is not that than which nothing greater can be conceived—which cannot be the case.

[Note: Thu. 451 reads: “that than which nothing greater cannot be conceived is greater than itself, which …”; the Cistercian manuscript reads: “that than which nothing greater cannot be conceived is not that than which something greater cannot be conceived.”]

Thus there truly exists something than which nothing greater can be conceived, and it cannot be conceived not to exist; and this is you, Lord our God. You truly exist, Lord my God, in such a way that you cannot be conceived not to exist—and rightly so.

For if some mind could conceive something better than you, the creature would rise above the Creator and judge the Creator, which is utterly absurd. Moreover, whatever exists besides you alone can be conceived not to exist. You alone, therefore, have existence most truly of all, and for that reason most fully of all, because whatever else exists does not exist in this same true way and therefore possesses less existence.

[Note: One manuscript reads “exists truly, and therefore” rather than “does not exist in this same true way and therefore.”]

Why, then, did the fool say in his heart, “There is no God”? (Psalm 13:1.)—when it is so evident to a rational mind that you exist most of all? Why, except because he is foolish and a fool?

## CHAPTER IV

### How the fool said in his heart what cannot be conceived

[Note: The Thuan, Victorine, and Cistercian manuscripts transpose the words, reading “The fool said in his heart,” and omit *insipiens* (“the fool”) at its printed position.]

Things are conceived in two ways: first, when the voice signifying them is conceived; second, when the thing itself is understood.

[Col. 0228D]

According to the word, God can be conceived not to exist; according to the thing itself, he cannot.

But how did the fool say in his heart what he could not conceive? Or how could he not conceive what he said in his heart, since saying something in the heart and conceiving it are the same?

If, indeed—rather, because indeed—he conceived it because he said it in his heart, and did not say it in his heart because he could not conceive it, then something is said or conceived in the heart in more than one way.

[Note: Thu. 451 reads *et vere cogitavit* (“and truly conceived it”) for *imo quia vere et cogitavit* (“indeed, because he truly conceived it”); it also reads *aliquid in corde dicere et cogitare* (“to say and conceive something in the heart”) for *aliquid in corde vel cogitatur* (“something is said or conceived in the heart”).]

For a thing is conceived in one way when the voice signifying it is conceived, and in another when that very thing which the thing is is understood. In the former way, God can be conceived not to exist; in the latter, absolutely not.

For no one who understands what fire and water are can conceive that fire is water in reality, although he can do so according to the words. Thus no one who understands what God is can conceive that God does not exist, although he may say these words in his heart either without any meaning or with some extraneous meaning.

[Note: Thu. 391 reads “who understands what fire and water are can conceive that fire is not water in reality, although he can do so according to the words.” Thu. 451 reads “who understands what fire and water are can conceive that fire is water in reality, although he can do so according to the words. Thus no one who understands what God is…”]

For God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived. Whoever understands this properly certainly understands that it exists in such a way that it cannot be nonexistent even in thought. Whoever, therefore, understands that God exists in this way cannot conceive that he does not exist.

Thanks be to you, good Lord, thanks be to you, because what I first believed through your gift, I now understand through your illumination in such a way that, even if I did not wish to believe that you exist, I could not fail to understand it.

## CHAPTER V

### That God is whatever is better to be than not to be, and that he alone exists through himself and makes everything else from nothing

[Note: Victor., Bec, Gem., and S. Mich. manuscripts add *alia* (“other”) in “makes all other things”; Thu., Victor., and Cistercian manuscripts read *qui* (“who”) for *quid* (“what”); and the manuscripts read *quis es nisi quod* (“who are you, except that which”) for *quid es, nisi id quod* (“what are you, except that which”).]

What, then, are you, Lord God, than whom nothing greater can be conceived? But what are you except that which, existing alone through itself and supreme of all things, made everything else from nothing?

For whatever is not this is less than can be conceived; but this cannot be conceived of you.

[Note: Thu. 451 reads *minus est quam cogitari* (“is less than to be conceived”) for *minus est quam quod cogitari* (“is less than that which can be conceived”).] What good, then, is lacking from the supreme good, through which every good exists? You are therefore just, truthful, blessed, and whatever is better to be than not to be. For it is better to be just than not just, and blessed than not blessed.

## CHAPTER VI

### How God is perceptive although he is not a body

[Note: The manuscripts read *Quomodo sit* (“How he is”) for *Quomodo Deus sit* (“How God is”).]

God is perceptive, omnipotent, merciful, and impassible, because it is better to be these things than not to be them. It is not improperly said that one who knows in some way perceives in some way.

But since it is better for you to be sensible, omnipotent, merciful, and impassible [Note: [Col. 0229D] “To be sensible” is found in the manuscripts instead of “for you to be sensible”], than not to be so, how are you sensible if you are not a body; or omnipotent if you cannot do all things [Note: [Col. 0229D] “If you cannot do all things” is found in Thuan. 451 instead of “if you cannot do everything”]; or merciful and impassible at the same time? For if only bodily things are sensible [Note: [Col. 0229D] “Bodies alone” is found in the manuscripts instead of “only bodily things”], since the senses are concerned with bodies and exist in the body, how are you sensible, since you are not a body but the supreme Spirit, which is better than a body?

But if to sense is nothing other than to know, or exists only for knowing—for whoever senses knows according to the particular character of the senses, as colors through sight and flavors through taste—then it is not inappropriate to say that whatever knows in some way senses in some way. Therefore, Lord, although you are not a body, you are nevertheless truly supremely sensible in the manner in which you supremely know all things—not in the manner in which an animal knows through bodily sense.

## CHAPTER VII

### How he is omnipotent, although he cannot do many things

To be capable of being corrupted or of lying is not power but impotence. God can do nothing through impotence, and nothing can do anything against him.

But how are you omnipotent if you cannot do everything? Or if you cannot be corrupted, or lie, or make what is true become false—so that what has been done should not have been done, and similarly other things [Note: [Col. 0229D] Thuan. 451 reads “to make what is true false, and other things” instead of “to make what is true become false, so that what has been done should not have been done, and similarly other things”—how can you do everything? Or to be able to do such things [Note: [Col. 0229D] “Or to be able to do such things” is found in Vict. 3; “to such things” in Vict. 13] is not power but impotence.

For whoever can do these things can do what is not expedient for him and what he ought not to do; and the more he can do so, the more adversity and perversity can act against him, while he himself is less able to oppose them. Whoever therefore can act in this way can do so not by power but by impotence. For he is not said to be able because he himself has the power, but because his impotence makes something else capable of acting against him—or, by a certain manner of speaking, just as many things are said improperly: for example, when we use “to be” for “not to be,” and “to do” for what is “not to do,” or for “to do nothing.”

For we often say to someone who denies that a thing exists, “It is as you say it is,” although more properly it seems one should say, “It is not as you say it is not.” Likewise, we say, “This man sits as that man does,” or, “This man rests as that man does,” although sitting is a kind of not-doing, and resting is doing nothing.

Thus, when someone is said to have the power to do or suffer what is not expedient for him or what he ought not to do, impotence is understood through the word “power”: for the more of this power he has, the more powerful adversity and perversity are against him, and the more impotent he is against them. Therefore, Lord God, you are all the more truly omnipotent because you can do nothing through impotence [Note: [Col. 0229D] “You can do nothing through impotence” is found in the manuscripts instead of “you can do nothing by impotence”], and nothing can do anything against you [Note: [Col. 0229D] The manuscripts of S. Mich. and Vict. read “nothing can do anything against you” instead of “you can do nothing against”].

## CHAPTER VIII

### How he is merciful and impassible

God is merciful according to us, who experience the effect of his mercy. God is not merciful according to himself, since he does not experience the feeling of compassion.

But how are you both merciful and impassible? For if you are impassible, you do not suffer with others; if you do not suffer with others, you do not have a pitiable heart through compassion for the wretched—and that is what it means to be merciful. But if you are not merciful, whence comes such great consolation to the wretched [Note: [Col. 0231D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “whence are you for the wretched” instead of “whence is there for the wretched”]?

How, then, are you, and are not merciful, Lord, unless because you are merciful according to us and are not so according to yourself? You are so according to our experience, and are not so according to your own. For when you look upon us in our misery, we experience the effect of your mercy [Note: [Col. 0231D] Manuscripts of Vict. 3 and 13 read “you experience the feeling of compassion”]; you do not experience the feeling. Thus you are merciful because you save the wretched and spare your sinners; and you are not merciful because you are affected by no compassion for misery [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. 451 reads “you are affected by no compassion for misery”; the manuscripts of S. Mich. and Cister. read “you are affected by no misery arising from compassion”].

## CHAPTER IX

### How he is wholly and supremely just, yet spares the wicked, and how he justly has mercy on the wicked

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. 90 reads “wholly and supremely just.”]

The one who is good to both the good and the wicked is better than the one who is good only to the good. Since God is supremely just, it is hidden how he is merciful. God is supremely merciful because he is supremely just. He saves the just, with justice accompanying them; he liberates sinners, with justice ruling. God spares the wicked by justice, because it is just that God—than whom no one is better or more powerful—should also be good to the wicked and should make the good out of the wicked. If God ought not to have mercy, he has mercy unjustly; but to say this is impious. Therefore God has mercy justly.

But how do you spare the wicked if you are wholly just and supremely just [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. 451 reads “if you are wholly and supremely just”]? For how does one who is wholly and supremely just [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. and Vict. read “wholly and supremely just”] do something unjust [Note: [Col. 0231D] The manuscripts read “do some unjust thing”]? Or what justice is it to give eternal life to one who deserves eternal death?

Whence, therefore, good God, good to the good and the wicked, does it come that you save the wicked, if this is not just and you do nothing unjust [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. and Vict. read “something unjust”]? Is it because your goodness is incomprehensible, and this is hidden in the inaccessible light in which you dwell?

Truly, in the highest and most secret place of your goodness lies hidden the fountain from which the river of your mercy flows. For although you are wholly and supremely just, you are also kind to the wicked precisely because you are wholly and supremely good. You would be less good if you were kind to no wicked person [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan., Vict., and S. Mich. read “if you were kind to be wicked”]. For the one who is good to both the good and the wicked is better than the one who is good only to the good; and the one who is good to the wicked both by punishing and by sparing is better than the one who is good only by punishing.

Therefore you are merciful because you are wholly and supremely good. And although it may perhaps seem clear why you repay good to the good and evil to the wicked, this is certainly utterly marvelous: why you, wholly and supremely just [Note: [Col. 0231D] The manuscripts of Thuan. 451 and S. Mich. read “since you are wholly just”], and lacking nothing, bestow good upon the wicked and upon those guilty before you.

O the depth of your goodness, God! It is seen whence you are merciful, but it is not fully discerned. One sees from where the river flows, but does not perceive the fountain from which it arises [Note: [Col. 0231D] The manuscripts of Bec., Gem., and S. Mich. read “is perceived” instead of “is fully discerned”] [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. and the Gothic edition read “from which it is born” instead of “from which it arises”]. For it is from the fullness of your goodness that you are gracious to your sinners; but in the height of your goodness [Note: [Col. 0231D] The manuscripts of Thuan. read “in the height of your goodness”] lies hidden the reason why you are this way.

For although you repay good to the good and evil to the wicked out of goodness, the reason of justice nevertheless seems to demand this. But when you bestow good upon the wicked, it is known that the supremely good willed to do this, and it is marvelous how the supremely just could will it.

O mercy, from what rich sweetness, and with what sweet richness, you pour forth upon us! [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan., Vict., Bec., Gem., and Cister. read “O mercy of God, from which.”] [Col. 0232B] O immeasurable goodness of God, with what affection ought you to be loved by sinners! For you save the just, with justice accompanying them; but you liberate these others, with justice ruling [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. reads “with justice condemning” instead of “with justice ruling”]. You aid the former by their merits; the latter despite their merits. You save the former by their recognizing the good things you have given; the latter by forgiving the evils you hate [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. and Vict. read “their own evils” instead of “the evils”].

O immeasurable goodness, which thus surpasses all understanding, may that mercy which proceeds from such richness of yours come upon me! May that mercy which flows forth [Note: [Col. 0231D] S. Mich. reads “which flows down from” instead of “which flows forth”] from you flow into me. Spare me through clemency, so that you may not punish me [Note: [Col. 0231D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “and do not punish me” instead of “so that you may not punish me”] through justice.

For although it is difficult to understand how your mercy is not absent from your justice, it is nevertheless necessary to believe that what overflows from goodness—which is not without justice in any way, but rather truly agrees with justice—does not oppose justice at all. Indeed, if you are merciful only because you are supremely good, and you are not supremely good unless you are supremely just, then you are truly merciful precisely because you are supremely just.

Help me, just [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. and Vict. omit “and supremely”] and merciful God, whose light I seek; help me to understand what I say. Truly, then, you are merciful for this reason: because you are just. Does your mercy, then, arise from your justice? Do you therefore spare the wicked by justice? If this is so, Lord, if this is so, teach me how it is.

Is it because it is just that you should be so good that no one can be understood to be better, and should act so powerfully that no one can be thought more powerful? For what is more just than this? Certainly [Note: [Col. 0231D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “this therefore”] this would not happen if you were good only by rewarding and not by sparing; and if you made good only out of those who are not good, and not also out of the wicked [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. reads “and if you did not make good only out of those who are not good”].

In this way, then, it is just that you spare the wicked and make the good out of the wicked. Finally, what is not done justly ought not to be done; and what ought not to be done is done unjustly. If, therefore, you do not have mercy on the wicked justly, you ought not to have mercy. And if you ought not to have mercy, you have mercy unjustly. But since it is impious to say this, it is right to believe that you have mercy on the wicked justly.

## CHAPTER X

### How he justly punishes and justly spares the wicked

In sparing the wicked, God is just according to himself, because he does what accords with his goodness; but he is not just according to us, because he does not exact the punishment that is owed.

But it is also just that you punish the wicked: for what is more just than that the good should receive good and the wicked evil? How, then, is it both just that you punish the wicked and just that you spare the wicked? Do you justly punish the wicked in one way and justly spare them in another?

When you punish the wicked, it is just because it accords with their merits; but when you spare the wicked, it is just not because of their merits, but because it is fitting to your goodness. For in sparing the wicked you are just according to yourself [Note: [Col. 0233D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “wicked, just”], and not according to us, just as you are merciful according to us, and not according to yourself. When you save us, whom you would justly destroy, you are merciful—not because you experience the feeling, but because we experience the effect. So also you are just, not because you repay what is owed to us, but because you do what is fitting for you, who are supremely good. Thus, without contradiction, you justly punish and justly spare.

## CHAPTER XI

### How all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, and yet the Lord is just in all his ways

It cannot in any way be grasped why, through supreme goodness, you save some of the wicked rather than others, and why, through supreme justice, you condemn some rather than others.

But is it not also just according to you, Lord, that you punish the wicked? It is just that you should be so just that one more just than you cannot be conceived [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. 451 reads “that one more just than you cannot be conceived”]; and you would by no means be this if you repaid good only to the good and not evil to the wicked [Note: [Col. 0231D] Thuan. 451 reads “and evil to the wicked”]. For the one who repays merits to both the good and the wicked is more just than the one who does so only to the good.

It is therefore just according to you, just and kind God, both when you punish and when you spare. Truly, then, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10); and yet the Lord is just in all his ways (Ps. 144:17). And certainly without contradiction, because for those whom you wish to punish, it is not just that they be saved; and for those whom you wish to spare, it is not just that they be condemned. For only what you will is just, and what you do not will is not just.

Thus your mercy arises from your justice, because it is just that you should be so good that you are good even by sparing. And perhaps this is why the supremely just can will good for the wicked. But although it can somehow be grasped [Note: [Col. 0233D] The manuscripts read “both can be grasped”] why you can wish to save the wicked, this certainly cannot be comprehended by any reasoning: why, from wicked people who are alike, you save some more than others through supreme goodness, and condemn others more than these through supreme justice.

Thus you are truly sensible, omnipotent, merciful, and impassible, just as you are living, wise, good, blessed, eternal, and whatever it is better to be than not to be.

## CHAPTER XII

### That God is the very life by which he lives, and likewise with similar attributes

But certainly, whatever you are, you are through nothing other than yourself. You are therefore the very life by which you live, and the wisdom by which you are wise, and the very goodness by which you are good to the good and the wicked—and likewise with similar attributes.

## CHAPTER XIII

### How he alone is uncircumscribed and eternal, although other spirits are also uncircumscribed and eternal

No place or time confines God. He himself is everywhere and always. Alone, just as he does not cease to be, so he does not begin to be.

Everything that is enclosed to some extent by place or time is less than what no law of place or time constrains [Note: [Col. 0233D] Thuan. 451 reads “what the law of place or time does not constrain”]. Since, therefore, nothing is greater than you, no place or time confines you, but you are everywhere and always. Because this can be said of you alone, you alone are uncircumscribed and eternal.

How, then, are other spirits also said to be uncircumscribed and eternal? You alone are eternal, since alone among all things you neither cease nor begin to be. But how are you alone uncircumscribed? Is a created spirit, compared with you, circumscribed, but compared with a body, uncircumscribed [Note: [Col. 0233D] Thuan. and Vict. read “compared with you, is it circumscribed”]?

That is wholly circumscribed which, while it is entirely somewhere, cannot at the same time be elsewhere; this is seen only in bodily things. Uncircumscribed, however, is that which is wholly everywhere at once; this is understood of you alone. Circumscribed and uncircumscribed at the same time is that which, while it is wholly somewhere, can at the same time be wholly elsewhere, though not everywhere; this is recognized in created spirits.

For if the soul were not wholly present in each of the members of its body, it would not wholly sense in each of them. You, therefore, Lord, are uniquely uncircumscribed and eternal; and yet other spirits also are uncircumscribed and eternal [Note: [Col. 0233D] The Cistercian manuscript omits the second “also”].

## CHAPTER XIV

### How and why God is seen and is not seen by those who seek him

Have you found, my soul, what you were seeking? You were seeking God. You found him to be something supreme among all things, than which nothing better can be conceived; and you found him to be life itself, light, wisdom, goodness, eternal blessedness, and blessed eternity; and you found him to be everywhere and always.

For if you have not found your God, how is he what you found, and how did you understand him with such certain truth and true certainty? But if you have found him, what is it that you do not perceive what you found? Why does your soul not perceive you, Lord God, if it has found you? Or has it not found the one whom it found to be light [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts read “or has it not found him to be light”] and truth?

For how did it understand this unless by seeing the light and truth? Or could it understand anything about you at all except through your light and your truth? If, therefore, it saw the light and truth, it saw you; if it did not see you, it did not see the light or truth.

Or is what it saw both truth and light, and yet it has not yet seen you because it saw you to some extent [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts of Vict. and Thuan. 451 read “to a little extent”], but did not see you as you are [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts read “and did not see you”]? Lord my God, my maker and reformer, tell my desiring soul what else you are than what it saw, so that it may clearly see what it desires.

It strains itself so that it may see more, and sees nothing beyond what it saw except darkness. Rather, it does not see darkness [Note: [Col. 0235D] Some manuscripts read “rather, it did not see darkness”], which does not exist in you; but it sees that it cannot see more because of its own darkness.

Why is this, Lord, why? Is its eye darkened by its weakness, or dazzled by your radiance? Certainly it is both darkened in itself and dazzled by you. It is both obscured by its smallness and overwhelmed by your immensity. Its narrowness is truly contracted and overcome by your greatness.

For how great is that light from which every truth shines that illuminates the rational mind [Note: [Col. 0235D] Thuan. and Vict. read “that shines in the mind”]? How vast is that truth in which everything that is true exists [Note: [Col. 0235D] Thuan. and Vict. omit “also”], and outside which there is nothing but nothingness and falsehood? How immense is the one who, with a single gaze, sees whatever things have been made, and from whom, through whom, and how they were made from nothing? What purity, what simplicity, what certainty and splendor are found there? Certainly more than a creature can understand.

## CHAPTER XV

### That he is greater than can be conceived

Therefore, Lord, you are not only that than which nothing greater can be conceived; you are something greater than can be conceived. For since it can be conceived that something of this kind exists, if you are not this very thing, something greater than you can be conceived—which cannot happen.

## CHAPTER XVI

### That this is the inaccessible light in which he dwells

Truly, Lord, this is the inaccessible light in which you dwell; truly, there is nothing else that can penetrate this light [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts read “penetrate it” instead of “penetrate this light], so as to see you there.

Truly, I do not see it for this reason: it is too much for me. Yet whatever I see, I see through it, just as a weak eye sees whatever it sees through the light of the sun, although it cannot look upon that light in the sun itself.

My intellect cannot reach it; it shines too brightly. It cannot grasp it, nor can the eye of my soul gaze upon it for long. It is dazzled by the radiance, overcome by the greatness, overwhelmed by the immensity, and confounded by capacity.

O supreme and inaccessible light! O complete and blessed truth, how far you are from me, who am so near to you! How remote you are from my sight, although you are so present to your own sight of me! You are wholly present everywhere [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts read “wholly everywhere”], and I do not see you. In you I move and in you I am, yet I cannot approach you. You are within me and around me, and I do not perceive you.

## CHAPTER XVII

### That in God there are harmony, fragrance, flavor, lightness, and beauty, in his own ineffable manner

You still lie hidden from my soul in your light and blessedness, Lord; and therefore it still moves about in its own darkness and misery. It looks around, but does not see your beauty. It listens, but does not hear your harmony. It smells, but does not perceive your fragrance. It tastes, but does not know your flavor. It touches, but does not feel your lightness [Note: [Col. 0235D] Vict. 3 reads “gentleness” instead of “lightness”].

For you possess these things, Lord God, in yourself, in your own ineffable manner—you who gave them to the things created by you in their own sensible manner. But the senses of my soul have grown stiff, become numb, and been obstructed by the old sickness of sin.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### That God is life, wisdom, eternity, and every true good

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Thuan. 90 has the heading: “That God is all things, and how.”]

Whatever is joined together from parts is not wholly one; it can be dissolved either in actuality or in thought. Wisdom, eternity, and so forth are not parts in God, but one thing, the very whole that God is, or the unity itself, which is not divisible even in thought.

And again, behold confusion; behold, sorrow and grief once more confront the one seeking joy and gladness. My soul had already hoped for satisfaction, and behold, it is again overwhelmed by want. I had already longed to eat, and behold, I am hungrier still [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts of Thuan., Vict., and Cist. read “to hunger”; manuscript 451 reads “I hunger for you”]. I tried to rise toward the light of God, and fell back into my darkness. Indeed, I have not merely fallen into it; I feel myself wrapped in it.

Before my mother conceived me, I fell. Certainly I was conceived in them, and was born wrapped in them [Note: [Col. 0235D] Manuscript 451 omits “formerly”]. Certainly we all fell in the one in whom we all sinned. In him we all lost what he easily possessed, and through his own and our fault lost it; when we wish to seek it, we do not know it; when we seek it, we do not find it; when we find it, it is not what we seek.

Help me, for the sake of your goodness, Lord. I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts of Vict. and Cister. read “then I shall seek”]. Do not turn your face away from me (Ps. 26:8). Reveal me from myself [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscripts read “raise me from myself” instead of “reveal me from myself”] to yourself. Cleanse, heal, sharpen, and illumine the eye of my mind, so that it may contemplate you. May my soul gather its strength and again direct itself toward you with its whole understanding [Col. 0237A] [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan. omits “again”].

What are you, Lord, what are you? What will my heart understand you to be? Certainly you are life, wisdom, truth, goodness, blessedness, eternity, and every true good. These are many things; my narrow intellect cannot see so many all at once [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan. 451, Vict., and Mich., Bec., and Gem. read “so many as one”]. It cannot delight in them all at once.

How, then, are you all these things, Lord? Are they parts of you, or rather is each of these wholly what you are [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan. reads “of you, or rather”]? For whatever is joined together from parts is not wholly one, but in some manner is many and different from itself, and can be dissolved either in actuality or in thought—things alien to you, than whom nothing better can be conceived.

There are therefore no parts in you, Lord, nor are you many; but you are so entirely one and identical with yourself that in no respect are you unlike yourself [Col. 0237B]. Rather, you are unity itself, divisible by no understanding.

Therefore life, wisdom, and the rest are not parts of you, but all are one; and each of them is wholly what you are [Note: [Col. 0237D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “is wholly what you are”] and what all the others are.

How, then, do neither you nor your eternity—which you are—have parts? [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan., Vict., S. Mich., Gem., and Bec. read “Therefore neither”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “How therefore neither.”] Nowhere and never is any part of you or of your eternity. Rather, you are wholly everywhere, and your eternity is wholly always.

## CHAPTER XIX

### That he is not in place or time, but all things are in him

But if through your eternity you were, are, and will be; and to have been is not to be going to be; and to be is not to have been or to be going to be—how is your eternity wholly always?

Does nothing pass away from your eternity so as no longer to be, nor is anything future as though it did not yet exist? You were not therefore yesterday, nor will you be tomorrow; rather, you are yesterday, today, and tomorrow. Indeed, you are neither yesterday, nor today, nor tomorrow [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan. and Vict. read “indeed, not yesterday”], but simply are, outside all time.

For “yesterday,” “today,” and “tomorrow” mean nothing other than being in time. You, however, although nothing exists without you, are not in place or time; rather, all things are in you. Nothing contains you, but you contain all things.

## CHAPTER XX

### That he is before and beyond all things, even eternal things

God’s eternity is wholly present to him; other things, in their eternity, do not yet possess what will be future, and no longer possess what is past.

You therefore fill and embrace all things; you are before and beyond all things. You are before all things because, before they were made, you are.

But how are you beyond all things? For how are you beyond things that will have no end? Is it because they cannot exist in any way without you, while you are in no way less—even if they should return to nothingness? For in this way [Note: [Col. 0237D] Gem., Bec., and Cister. read “if in this way”] you are, in a certain manner, beyond them.

Or is it also because they can be conceived as having an end, whereas you cannot in any way? For in this way they do, in a certain manner, have an end [Note: [Col. 0237D] The Cistercian manuscript omits “in a certain manner”], whereas you do not in any way.

And certainly you also surpass all eternal things in this respect: your eternity and theirs are wholly present to you, while they do not yet possess from their eternity what is to come, just as they no longer possess what is past. In this way you are always beyond them, since you are always present there, or since that to which they have not yet arrived is always present to you.

## CHAPTER XXI

### Whether this is the age of the age, or the ages of ages

God’s eternity contains the very ages of times, and may be called the age of the age, or the ages of ages.

Is this, then, the age of the age, or the ages of ages? For just as the age of time contains all temporal things, so your eternity contains even the ages of time themselves. It is called “the age” because of its indivisible unity, and “the ages” because of its boundless immensity [Note: [Col. 0237D] The manuscripts read “which age” instead of “it is called the age”].

And although you are so great, Lord, that all things are full of you and are in you, you are nevertheless without any spatial extension, so that neither a middle, nor a half, nor any part exists in you.

## CHAPTER XXII

### That he alone is what he is and who he is

All things need God in order to exist and in order to exist well.

You alone, therefore, Lord, are what you are, and you are who you are. For whatever is one thing in its entirety and another in its parts, and in which something is changeable, is not wholly what it is.

And whatever began from not being, and can be conceived as not being; and unless it subsists through something else, returns to not being; and whatever has a past that no longer is and a future that does not yet exist—that is not properly and absolutely.

You, however, are what you are, because whatever you are at any time or in any manner, you are wholly and always this. And you are who you properly and simply are, because you do not have a past or a future being, but only present being, nor can you be conceived at any time not to exist [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan. 451 reads “nor can it be conceived”].

But you are also life [Note: [Col. 0237D] The manuscripts read “but life”], light, wisdom [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan. 451 reads “and you are light, and you are wisdom, and”], blessedness, eternity, and many such good things; yet you are nothing other than one and supreme good, wholly sufficient to yourself and lacking nothing [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thuan. and Vict. omit “and”], which all things need in order to exist and in order to exist well.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### That this good is equally the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that this is the one necessary thing, which is every good, the whole good, and the only good

[Note: [Col. 0239D] Thuan. 90 reads “who is” instead of “which is.”]

Since the Word is truthful and truth itself, there is nothing in the Father who speaks that does not come to be in the Word by which he speaks himself. Nor is the love proceeding from the Father and the Son unequal to the Father or the Son, because the Father and the Son love each other as greatly as the Father and the Son are good. From supreme simplicity nothing can be born or proceed except what is the same as that from which it is born or proceeds.

You, God the Father, are this good [Note: [Col. 0239D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “this good being, you”]. This is your Word, that is, your Son. For nothing other than what you are, nor anything greater or less than you, can be in the Word by which you speak yourself [Note: [Col. 0239D] Bec. and Gem. read “in your Word by which”], since your Word is true in the same way that you are truthful [Note: [Col. 0239D] Manuscript 451 and Cister. read “as you are truthful”].

And therefore it is truth itself just as you are—not something other than you [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thuan. 451 reads “not something else than”]—and you are so simple that nothing other than what you are can be born from you.

This same thing is the one love common to you and your Son [Note: [Col. 0239D] The manuscripts read “your Son, that is, the Holy Spirit”], namely, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both. For this love is not unequal to you or to your Son, because you love yourself and him, and he loves you and himself, as greatly as you and he are; and nothing that is unlike you and him can be different from you [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thuan. reads *non est tibi* (“is not [unequal] to you”) instead of *non sit tibi*].

Nor can anything proceed from supreme simplicity other than what is the same as that from which it proceeds [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thuan. reads “what is the same as that from which it proceeds”].

Whatever each one individually is, this the whole Trinity is together—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—because each one individually is nothing other than supreme simple unity and supremely one simplicity, which can neither be multiplied nor be one thing and another.

Moreover, there is one necessary thing. This, then, is that one necessary thing in which every good exists [Note: [Col. 0239D] The manuscripts read “in which every good exists”]; indeed, which is every good, one whole [Note: [Col. 0239D] S. Mich., Bec., and Gem. read “and one whole”; manuscript 451 reads “which is both the whole and the one”], and the only good.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### An estimation of what kind and how great this good is

[Note: [Col. 0239D] The Bec. manuscript has “What and how great the good things are for those who enjoy it.”]

If created life is good, how good is creative life?

Now, my soul, rouse yourself and raise your whole understanding, and consider as much as you can what kind and how great that good is. If individual good things are delightful, consider attentively how delightful that good must be which contains the pleasantness of all good things—not such pleasantness as we have experienced in created things, but differing from it as much as the Creator differs from the creature.

If created life is good, how good is creative life! If created salvation is pleasant, how pleasant is the salvation that made all salvation [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thuan. reads “that makes all salvation”]! If wisdom in the knowledge of created things is lovable, how lovable is the wisdom that created all things from nothing! Finally, if there are many and great delights in delightful things, what kind and how great is the delight in the one who made the delightful things themselves!

## CHAPTER XXV [Note: [Col. 0239D] In the Bec. manuscript this is joined to the preceding chapter.]

### What and how great the good things are for those who enjoy this good

Joy in the blessed will be multiplied through the blessedness and joy of others.

Source preparation: supplied local canonical restoration, exact generator-equivalent alignment.

O you who enjoy this good! And what will there be for him, and what will not be there for him? Certainly, whatever he wishes will be; and what he does not wish will not be. For there will be there the goods of body and soul, such as neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart conceived (Isaiah 64:4; 1 Corinthians 2:9).

Why, then, do you wander through so many things, little man, seeking the goods of your soul and your body? Love the one good in which all goods are found, and it is sufficient. Desire the simple good which is every good, and that is enough. For what do you love, my flesh? What do you desire, my soul? There it is—there is whatever you love, whatever you desire.

If beauty delights you, the righteous will shine like the sun (Matthew 13:43). If speed, strength, or bodily freedom delights you—freedom against which nothing can prevail—you will be like the angels of God, because “the animal body is sown, and a spiritual body will rise” (1 Corinthians 15:44), in power, certainly, though not in nature.

If you desire long and healthy life, there is healthy eternity and eternal health, because “the righteous will live forever” (Wisdom 5:16), and “the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Psalm 36:39). If satiety, “they will be satisfied when the glory of God appears” (Psalm 16:15). [Note: Col. 0239D: the Cistercian manuscript reads *gloria Dei* (“the glory of God”); the note then gives the unassigned contrast *gloria Domini* (“the glory of the Lord”).] If drunkenness, “they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35:9). If melody, there the choirs of angels sing together to God without end.

If any pleasure that is not unclean but pure delights you, “you will give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure,” O God (ibid.). [Note: Col. 0239D: the Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Thuanus, and Cistercian manuscripts read *tuae potabis* (“you will give [them] drink from your [pleasure]”); the note then gives the unassigned contrast *suae potabit* (“he will give [them] drink from his [pleasure]”).]

If wisdom, God’s Wisdom itself will show itself to them. If friendship, they will love God more than themselves, and one another as themselves; and God will love them more than they love themselves, because they love him, themselves, and one another through him, while he loves himself and them through himself.

If harmony, all will have one will, because they will have no will except the will of God. If power, they will be omnipotent with respect to their own will, as God is with respect to his. For just as God will be able, through himself, to do whatever he wishes, so they will be able, through him, to do whatever they wish. For just as they will wish nothing other than what he wishes, so he will wish whatever they wish; and what he wishes cannot fail to be.

If honor and riches, God will set his good and faithful servants over many things (Luke 13:42); indeed, they will be called children of God and gods. And where his Son will be, there they also will be, “heirs indeed of God, but joint heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). [Note: Col. 0239D: the manuscripts read *vocabuntur et ubi* (“they will be called, and where”); the note then gives unassigned *vocabuntur et erunt et ubi* (“they will be called and will be, and where”).] [Note: “there they also will be, heirs”: the Thuanus and Victorinus manuscripts read “there they also will be, and heirs.”]
