If true security, they will certainly be so assured that this good—or rather, this one good—will never and in no way be lacking to them: just as they will be assured that they will not lose it of their own will, that God, who loves them, will not take it away from those who love it against their will, and that nothing more powerful than God will separate God and them against their will.

But what kind and how great is the joy where such a great good exists? Human heart, needy heart, heart acquainted with sorrows—indeed, overwhelmed by sorrows—how greatly 35 would you rejoice if you abounded in all these things! Ask your inmost being whether it can contain its joy at such great blessedness.

Yet certainly, if someone else whom you loved altogether as yourself possessed the same blessedness, your joy would be doubled, because you would rejoice for him no less than for yourself. If two or three, or many more, possessed the same thing, you would rejoice for each one as much as for yourself, if you loved each one as yourself.

Therefore, in that perfect charity of innumerable blessed angels and human beings, where no one will love another less than himself, each person will rejoice for every other person no differently than for himself. If, then, the human heart can scarcely contain its joy over its own great good, how will it be capable of so many and such great joys?

And certainly, since each person rejoices in another’s good as much as he loves that person, just as in that perfect happiness each will love God incomparably more than himself and all others together, so he will rejoice immeasurably more in God’s happiness than in his own and that of all others together.

But if they love God with all their heart, all their mind, and all their soul, while their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul do not suffice for the dignity of that love, surely they will rejoice with all their heart, all their mind, and all their soul, so that their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul will not suffice for the fullness of their joy.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Whether this is the full joy that the Lord promises. [Note: The Thuanus manuscript reads: “Whether this joy, which God promises.”]

The blessed will rejoice as much as they love; they will love as much as they know.

My God and my Lord, my hope and the joy of my heart, tell my soul whether this is the joy of which you speak to us through your Son: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full” (John 16:24).

For I have found a certain full joy, and more than full. Indeed, with that joy filling the heart, the mind, the soul, and the whole person, joy will still abound beyond measure. Therefore, all that joy will not enter into those who rejoice; rather, all those who rejoice will enter into the joy.

Tell me, Lord, tell your servant inwardly in his heart whether this is the joy into which your servants will enter—those who will enter into the joy of their Lord. But certainly that joy in which your chosen ones will rejoice is what neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart (Isaiah 64:4; 1 Corinthians 2:9).

I have not yet said, nor have I conceived, Lord, how greatly those blessed ones of yours will rejoice. Certainly, they will rejoice as much as they love; they will love as much as they know. How greatly will they know you then, Lord, and how greatly will they love you! Certainly, neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, how greatly they will know and love you in that life.

I pray, O God, that I may know you and love you, so that I may rejoice in you. And if I cannot do so fully in this life, may I at least advance day by day until that fullness comes. May knowledge of you advance in me here [Note: “knowledge of you”: the Thuanus manuscript reads “your knowledge.”] and there become complete; may your love increase, and there be complete, so that here my joy may be great in hope, and there complete in reality.

Lord, through your Son you command—or rather, counsel—us to ask, and you promise that we will receive, so that our joy may be full. I ask, Lord, for what you counsel through our wondrous Counselor; may I receive what you promise through your truth, so that my joy may be full.

True God, I ask; may I receive, so that my joy may be full. Meanwhile, let my mind meditate upon it; let my tongue speak of it. Let my heart love it; let my mouth converse about it. Let my soul hunger for it, my flesh thirst for it, and my whole being desire it, until I enter into the joy of the Lord, who are the triune and one God, blessed forever. [Note: Col. 0241C: the manuscripts, including Thu., read *saecula. Amen* (“forever. Amen”); the note then gives the unassigned contrast *saecula saeculorum. Amen* (“forever and ever. Amen”).]

Amen. [Note: The manuscripts add: “Here ends the book of the Proslogion of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.”]

# A BOOK ON BEHALF OF THE FOOL

[Note: This work has been collated with two Victorine manuscripts, EE. 13 and RR. 3; one Gemmeticensis manuscript, C. 54; one Corbeiensis manuscript, 307; one manuscript from the Thuanus Library, 90; one Cistercian manuscript; and one from the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount. The Gemmeticensis, Victorine 3, and Saint Michael manuscripts prefix this title: “What someone replies to these arguments on behalf of the fool.” The Thuanus manuscript reads: “Here begins the disputation of the fool, saying in his heart: ‘There is no God.’” The Corbeiensis manuscript reads: “A response concerning how someone replies.” The Victorine 13 manuscript reads: “Here begins the disputation on behalf of the fool.” The Cistercian manuscript reads: “What someone replies to these arguments on behalf of the fool.” In the Gemmeticensis and Saint Michael manuscripts, the author of this book is identified as the monk Gaunilo of Major Monastery, commonly called Mair-Moutier.]

## AGAINST THE REASONING OF SAINT ANSELM IN THE PROSLOGION

By Gaunilo, monk of Major Monastery

### 1

To one who doubts or denies that there exists some nature such that nothing greater can be conceived, it is nevertheless said first to be proved that this nature exists: because the very person who denies or doubts concerning it already has it in his understanding, since, when he hears it spoken of, he understands what is said.

Next, it is said to be proved that what he understands must exist not only in the understanding but also in reality. This is proved as follows: to exist in the understanding and in reality is greater than to exist in the understanding alone. And if it exists in the understanding alone, whatever also exists in reality will be greater than it. Thus, what is greater than everything will be less than something; and it will not be greater than everything, which is contradictory.

Therefore, what is greater than everything, which has already been proved to exist in the understanding, must exist not in the understanding alone but also in reality [Note: The manuscripts read: “which has already been proved to exist in the understanding, and not in the understanding alone but in reality.”], since otherwise it could not be greater than everything.

### 2

Perhaps it can be answered that this is now said to exist in my understanding for no other reason than that I understand what is said. But could I not similarly be said to have in my understanding anything false, and indeed anything that does not exist in itself at all, whenever, if someone said such things, I understood whatever he said? [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript reads “simply could be said.”]

Unless, perhaps, this thing is established as being such that it cannot be held in thought in the same way as any false or doubtful thing; and therefore I am not said to think about or have in thought what I have heard, but to understand it and have it in my understanding—because, evidently, I cannot think of it otherwise than by understanding it, that is, by grasping through knowledge that it really exists. 

But if this is so, then first, having a thing in the understanding at one time and understanding that the thing exists at a later time will not be two different things occurring at different times, as happens with a picture, which is first in the mind of the painter and afterward in the work.

Furthermore, it will scarcely ever be credible that, once this has been said and heard, it cannot be thought not to exist in the same way in which God too can be thought not to exist. For if it cannot, why has this entire disputation been undertaken against someone who denies or doubts that such a nature exists?

Finally, that this thing is such that, as soon as it is thought of, the certainty of its existence must be perceived by an unshakable understanding must first be proved to me by some argument. But the present argument cannot prove it: namely, that it is already in my understanding when I understand it after hearing it. For in the same way anything else uncertain, or even false, could be in my understanding when spoken by someone whose words I understood. I think this would be even more the case if, deceived by it—as often happens—I believed what I do not yet believe.

### 3

Hence the example of the painter, who already has in his understanding the picture he is going to make, cannot sufficiently 36 fit this argument. For before it is made, that picture is held in the painter’s art; and something of that kind in the art of any craftsman is nothing other than a part of his understanding.

For—as Saint Augustine says—when a craftsman is about to make a chest in his work, he first has it in his art: the chest that is made in the work is not life, but the chest that exists in the art is life, because the craftsman’s soul lives, and in it all these things exist before they are brought forth.

For what else are these things, as life in the living soul of the craftsman, except the knowledge or understanding of that soul?

But whatever is perceived as true outside those things which are known to belong to the nature of the mind itself—whether heard or conceived by the understanding—is without doubt one thing as the truth itself, and another thing as the understanding by which it is grasped.

Therefore, even if it is true that there exists something than which nothing greater can be conceived, nevertheless what has been heard and understood is not of the same kind as the picture not yet made in the painter’s understanding.

### 4

To this is added what was stated above: namely, that what is greater than everything that can be conceived—said to be nothing other than God himself—I cannot have in my understanding, on the basis of anything known to me either in reality or by its kind or form, any more than I can have God himself in my understanding. Indeed, for this very reason I can think that God does not exist. [Note: Col. 0243C: Victorine 13 reads *non esse cogitare possum* (“I can think that he does not exist”); the note then gives *non esse cogitare non possum* (“I cannot think that he does not exist”) as the unassigned contrast.]

For I neither know the thing itself that is God, nor can I infer it from anything similar, since you assert that it is such that nothing similar can exist. For if I heard something said about a certain person entirely unknown to me, whom I did not even know to exist, I could nevertheless think about him according to the actual thing that is a human being, through the particular or general knowledge by which I know what a human being or human beings are.

And yet it could happen that, since the person speaking was lying, the one whom I was thinking about was not a human being, although I would still be thinking about him according to the true thing—not what that individual was, but what any human being is.

Therefore, even if I had that false thing in thought or in my understanding, I cannot, upon hearing the words “God” or “something greater than everything,” have it in the same way. When I can think of something according to a true reality known to me, I cannot think of this thing at all except according to the word—according to which alone, or scarcely or never, can anything true be thought.

For when it is thought in this way, it is not so much the word itself—which is certainly a true thing, namely, the sound of letters or syllables—as the meaning of the word that has been heard which is thought. Yet it is not thought in the same way by one who knows what that word ordinarily signifies. Such a person thinks it either according to the thing itself or as true in thought alone. But one who does not know it merely tries to form for himself a meaning according to the movement of his mind produced by hearing the word, and according to the meaning he has perceived in the word he has heard. It is no wonder if he is ever able to form it according to the truth of the thing.

Thus, it is not yet established that this thing exists in my understanding in any other way when I hear and understand someone saying that there exists something greater than everything that can be conceived. This is what I have to say concerning the claim that that supreme nature is already said to exist in my understanding.

### 5

But that it must exist not only in the understanding but also in reality is proved to me as follows: unless it exists, whatever exists in reality will be greater than it. Consequently, it will not be greater than everything, although it has already been proved to exist in the understanding.

I answer further: if one is to say that something is in the understanding when it cannot even be thought except in accordance with the truth of some thing, then I do not deny that this is so in my case as well. But because its existence in reality cannot in any way be established from this fact, I still do not concede that it exists until it has been proved to me by an indubitable argument. For whoever says that it exists because otherwise that which is greater than everything would not be greater than everything does not sufficiently consider to whom he is speaking. [Note: Col. 0245C: Vict., Thu., Gem., and Cister. read *non erit omnibus minus* (“will not be less than everything”) for *non erit omnibus majus* (“will not be greater than everything”).] For I do not yet say—and indeed I deny or doubt—that this thing is truly greater than anything. Nor do I concede to it any other existence than this: if it is to be said to exist, it exists only as something that the mind tries to fashion from a word it has merely heard, while the thing itself is completely unknown.

How, then, is it proved to me from the fact that it is established as greater than everything that this greater thing subsists in the truth of reality, when I still deny or doubt that it is established at all? I do not even say that it exists in my understanding or thought in the way that many doubtful and uncertain things exist.

First, it is necessary to establish with certainty that this greater thing really exists somewhere; and only then will it be clear, from its being greater than everything, that it also subsists in itself.

### 6

By way of example, some say that somewhere in the ocean there is an island which, because of the difficulty—or rather the impossibility—of finding what does not exist, some call “Lost.” They relate that it surpasses all other lands inhabited by human beings by an immeasurable abundance of every kind of wealth and delight, much more than is reported of the Fortunate Isles, and that, having no owner or inhabitant, it surpasses all other lands everywhere in the abundance of possessions.

Let someone tell me that this is so, and I will easily understand what he says; there is nothing difficult about it. But if he then adds, as though by consequence, and says: “You can no longer doubt that this island, more excellent than all lands, truly exists somewhere in reality, since you do not doubt that it exists in your understanding; and because it is more excellent to exist not only in the understanding but also in reality, it must necessarily exist. For if it did not, whatever other land exists in reality would be more excellent than it; and thus the island which you have already understood to be more excellent would not be more excellent,”

if, I say, he wished by this reasoning to establish for me that this island truly exists and that there can no longer be any doubt about it, I would either think that he was joking, or I do not know whom I ought to consider the greater fool: myself, if I granted his claim, or him, if he thought that he had established the existence of that island with any certainty.

He would not have done so unless he had first shown that its excellence exists in my understanding merely as something truly and indubitably existing, and not at all as something false or uncertain. [Note: Col. 0247C: the manuscripts read *intellectu in eo* (“in his understanding”); Corb. reads *intellectu meo* (“in my understanding”); the note then gives the unassigned contrast *intellectu mero* (“in [the] bare understanding”).]

### 7

Let him who has begun to respond to these objections give this answer for the present. When it is subsequently asserted to him that the greater thing is such that it cannot fail to exist even in thought alone, and when this is again proved from nothing other than the fact that otherwise it will not be greater than everything, he can offer the same response and say:

“When did I say that anything of this kind—that is, something greater than everything—exists in the truth of reality, so that from this it ought to be proved to me that it exists in reality to such an extent that it cannot be thought not to exist?

Therefore, it must first be proved by some most certain argument that there exists some nature superior—that is, greater and better—than all things that exist, so that from this we may then prove everything that necessarily belongs to what is greater and better than all things.

When it is said that this supreme thing cannot be thought not to exist, it might perhaps be better to say that it cannot be understood not to exist, or even to be able not to exist. For, according to the proper meaning of the word, false things cannot be understood; yet they can certainly be thought in the way in which the fool thought that God does not exist.

I know with complete certainty that I exist, and I also know that I can fail to exist. But as for that supreme thing which is God, I understand without doubt both that it exists and that it cannot fail to exist. [Note: The Thuanus manuscript reads: “that thing which is, namely, God”; the Victorine and Corbeiensis manuscripts read “that thing which is God.”]

I do not know whether, while I know with complete certainty that I exist, I can think that I do not exist. But if I can, why could I not also think in the same way anything else whose existence I know with equal certainty? If I cannot, then this will no longer be something proper to God.”

### 8

The rest of that little book is argued so truthfully, so brilliantly, and so magnificently; it is finally so filled with usefulness and fragrant with the intimate scent of pious and holy feeling, that it should in no way be despised because of those arguments at its beginning which, though correctly understood, are argued less firmly. Rather, those arguments should be supported more robustly, and the whole work should be received with great veneration and praise.

---

# THE APOLOGETIC BOOK OF SAINT ANSELM AGAINST GAUNILO, WHO RESPONDED ON BEHALF OF THE FOOL

[Note: The Victorine 13 manuscript reads: “Here begins the book of Anselm, archbishop and abbot, against the respondent on behalf of the fool.” The Gemmeticensis, Victorine, and Cistercian manuscripts read: “What the editor of that little book—the Proslogion—replies to these arguments.” The Thuanus manuscript reads: “Here begin Anselm’s replies to the respondent on behalf of the fool, who says in his heart, ‘There is no God’; or, A response against the fool.” The Saint Michael manuscript reads: “Anselm’s response to the same man, namely Gaunilo.”]

37 Since the fool against whom I spoke in my little work did not criticize me in these statements, but rather someone who is not a fool—and a Catholic—who responded on behalf of the fool, it is sufficient for me to respond as a Catholic to a Catholic.

## CHAPTER ONE

The opponent’s reasoning is refuted in general, and it is shown that that than which nothing greater can be conceived exists in reality.

---

## Complete textual apparatus from the supplied source

The following register preserves every printed note in this chunk. Latin forms are retained where English cannot show an orthographic, inflectional, or word-order distinction; each has an English gloss or explanation and its witnesses.

### Closing Proslogion material

- **“O you who enjoy this good” (0239D):** Gem., Bec., and Thu. read *Qui hoc bono* (“Who [enjoys] this good”) for *O qui hoc bono* (“O you who enjoy this good”). Thu. reads *Quid illi … et quid illi* (“What [will be] for him … and what [will be] for him”) for *Et quid illi … et quid illi* (“And what … and what”).
- **“the glory of God” (0239D):** Cister. has *gloria Dei* (“the glory of God”); the note gives *gloria Domini* (“the glory of the Lord”) as the unassigned contrast. **“you will give them drink from your pleasure” (0239D):** Gem., Bec., Thu., and Cister. have *tuae potabis* (“you will give [them] drink from your [pleasure]”); the note gives *suae potabit* (“he will give [them] drink from his [pleasure]”) as the unassigned contrast.
- **“they will be called, and where” (0239D):** the manuscripts read *vocabuntur et ubi* (“they will be called, and where”); the note gives *vocabuntur et erunt et ubi* (“they will be called and will be, and where”) as the unassigned contrast. Thu. and Vict. read *illi, et haeredes* (“they, and heirs”) for *illi, haeredes* (“they, heirs”).
- **“such and so great a good” (0241C):** Vict. and S. Mich. have *tale aut* (“such or”) for *tale ac* (“such and”). The printed marker **35**, after *quantum* (“how greatly”), is retained as a source boundary marker.
- **Chapter 26 heading (0241C):** the Bec. manuscript numbers the printed chapter 26 as chapter 25 (*CAP. 26. est 25. in Bec. ms.*). Thu. 90 reads *An hoc gaudium, quod promittat Deus* (“Is this the joy which God promises?”) for *An hoc fit gaudium plenum quod promittit Dominus* (“Is this the full joy which the Lord promises?”). the manuscripts have *amabunt in* (“they will love in”) for *et amabunt in* (“and they will love in”); The manuscripts have *ut proficiam* (“that I may advance”) for *vel proficiam* (“or at least may I advance”); Thu. has *notitia tua* (“your knowledge”) for *notitia tui* (“knowledge of you”); and they have *interim mens* (“meanwhile [let] the mind”) for *interim inde mens* (“meanwhile [let] my mind [meditate] on it”). The manuscripts, including Thu., read *saecula. Amen* (“forever. Amen”); the note gives *saecula saeculorum. Amen* (“forever and ever. Amen”) as the unassigned contrast. The manuscripts add: *Explicit Proslogion liber Anselmi Cantuariensis archiepiscopi* (“Here ends the book of the Proslogion of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury”).
- **Gaunilo title notice (0241D):** the work was collated with Vict. EE.13 and RR.3, Gem. C.54, Corb. 307, Thu. 90, a Cistercian MS, and S. Mich. Gem., Vict. 3, and S. Mich. prefix *Quid ad haec respondeat quidam pro insipiente* (“What someone replies to these things on behalf of the fool”); Thu. has *Incipit disputatio insipientis dicentis in corde suo: Non est Deus* (“Here begins the disputation of the fool saying in his heart, There is no God”); Corb. has *Responsio qualiter respondeat quidam* (“A response, how someone replies”); Vict. 13 has *Incipit disputatio pro insipiente* (“Here begins the disputation on behalf of the fool”); Cister. has the same *Quid ad haec…* title. Gem. and S. Mich. name the author Gaunilo, monk of Majoris Monasterii, commonly Mair-Moutier.

### Gaunilo, §1 (0241D–0243C)

- Corb. reads singular *dubitanti … neganti* (“to one doubting … denying”); the note contrasts plural *dubitant … negant* (“they doubt … deny”). Gem., Corb., and Thu. have *tamen esse* (“nevertheless to exist”); the note contrasts *cum esse* (“that it exists”).
- Vict. 13 and Cister. omit *in intellectu et* (“in the understanding and”) from *esse in intellectu et in re* (“to exist in the understanding and in reality”). Vict. and Cister. read *ac si majus* (“and if [it is] greater”) for *ac sic majus* (“and thus greater”).
- The manuscripts read *quod esse jam probatum est in intellectu, non in solo intellectu, sed et in re* (“that it has already been proved to exist in the understanding, not in the understanding alone but also in reality”) for *quod est jam probatum, esse in intellectu, et non in solo intellectu, sed in re* (“which has already been proved to exist in the understanding, and not in the understanding alone but in reality”); this preserves the disputed order, the *et* (“also”), and the omission of the second *in intellectu*.

### §2 (0243A–0244A)

- The manuscripts read *Responderi potest* (“It can be answered”) for *Respondere forsitan potest* (“Perhaps one can answer”). Vict. 3 has *in seipsis existentia* (“existing in themselves”) for *in se existentia* (“existing in itself”); Corb., Vict., and Thu. omit *esse* (“to exist”) after *existentia* (“existing”). The manuscripts have *similiter dici posset* (“could similarly be said”); Corb. has *simpliciter dici possent* (“could simply be said”) for printed *similiter dici possem* (“I could similarly be said”). Corb. reads *cum ea dicente* (“with him saying”) for *cum dicente* (“with someone saying”).
- The manuscripts have plural *haberi possint* (“can be held”) for singular *haberi possit* (“can be held”). They read *intelligitur habere esse, quia, scilicet, licet non possum* (an altered construction: “it is understood to have being because, namely, although I cannot…”); Corb. has *in intellectu habere, quia, scilicet, non possum* (“to have in the understanding, because, namely, I cannot”), and the note gives unassigned *intellectu habere quia solum non possim* (“to have by understanding, because I may not merely be unable”). These are preserved because they alter the relation of “being in the understanding” to inability to think otherwise.
- The manuscripts read *Sed hoc non est. Primo quidem non hoc erat* (“But this is not so. First, this was not…”) for *Sed si hoc est: primo quidem non hic erit* (“But if this is so, first there will not here be…”). Vict. and Cister. have *et aliud, idque* (“and another, and that”) for *et aliud, idemque* (“and another, and the same”); Corb. has *aut aliud idemque* (“or another and the same”). Vict., Thu., and Cister. read plural *in animo pictorum* (“in the minds of painters”); Corb. omits *quae prius est* (“which is first”).
- Vict., Corb., Thu., and Cister. read *fuerit illud non eo* (“that thing will have been not in the way”) for *fuerit istud non eo* (“this will have been not in the way”); Corb. has *potest non esse Deus* (“God can not be”) for *potest cogitari non esse Deus* (“God can be thought not to be”). Corb. has *certo percipi* (“be certainly perceived”) for *pro certo percipi* (“be perceived as certain”).
- The note at 0243C reads *intelligerentur dicta: adhuc* (“were understood as said: still”) for printed *intelligerem, dicta adhuc* (“I understand [them], still said”); Corb. has *et insuper* (“and moreover”) for *insuper* (“moreover”), *illa deceptus* (“deceived by it”) for *ipsa deceptus* (“deceived by those things”), and *ut saepe fit* (“as often happens”) for *ut secum* (“as with himself”), *credentur* (“they will believe”) for *crederem* (“I would believe”), and the manuscripts have *credentur quod istud nondum* (“they will believe that this not yet…”). Vict. 13 has *quia istud nondum* (“because this not yet…”). These forms must not be collapsed into “various readings.”

### §3 (0243C–0244B)

- Corb. omits *unde* (“whence/therefore”) in *unde nec* (“therefore not even”). The printed boundary marker **36**, after *satis* (“sufficiently”), is retained. The manuscripts have past *antequam fieret* (“before it was made”) for present *antequam fiat* (“before it is made”); Corb. reads *pictoris arte* (“the painter’s art”) for *pictoris mente* (“the painter’s mind”).
- Thu., Vict., and Corb. read *quia, sicut* (“because, just as”) for *quia et (sicut* (“because also, as”); the manuscripts have *vivente anima, vita* (“in the living soul, [they are] life”) for *in vivente artificis anima vita* (“in the living soul of the craftsman, [they are] life”). Corb. omits *vero* (“indeed”) after *at*; it reads *extra illa* (“outside those things”) for *non extra illa* (“not outside those things”).
- Gem., Vict., and Thu. read *percipitur verum, aliud est sine dubio verum illud, aliud intellectus* (“truth is perceived; without doubt that truth is one thing, the understanding another”); Corb. has *percipitur verum; aliud sine dubio est, verum illud, aliud intellectus* (“truth is perceived; without doubt one thing is that truth, another the understanding”); the note then gives unassigned *percipitur, verum aliud sine dubio est. Unde illud aliud intellectus* (“it is perceived, but without doubt it is another thing; hence the understanding is another”). These preserve the source’s alternatives for “the truth itself” and “the understanding.”

### §4 (0244C–0245C)

- Vict., Corb., and S. Mich. read *majus, nihil aliud* (“greater, nothing else”) for *majus, quod nihil aliud* (“greater, which nothing else”). The manuscripts read *tam ergo* (“therefore so”) for *tam ego* (“so I”); Corb. has *cogitare auditum vel intellectum* (“think [it] heard or understood”), while Vict. and Gem. have *cogitare auditu, vel intellectu* (“think [it] by hearing or understanding”), for printed *cogitare auditum vel in intellectu habere* (“think [it] heard or have [it] in the understanding”). Vict. 13 reads *non esse cogitare possum* (“I can think [him] not to be”); the note contrasts *non esse cogitare non possum* (“I cannot think [him] not to be”).
- Vict. 13 has *rem ipsam novi, aut ex alia possum conjicere simili* (“I know the thing itself, or can infer it from another similar [thing]”) for *rem ipsam, quae Deus est, novi; aut ipsam possum conjicere ex alia simili* (“I know the thing itself, which is God; or I can infer it from another similar thing”); the note then gives *rem ipsam, quae Deus est, novi; aut ipsam possum convincere ex alia simili* (“I know the thing itself, which is God; or I can prove it from another similar thing”) as the unassigned contrast. Corb. has *et tu talem* (“and you [say it] such”) for *et cum talem* (“and since [you say it] such”).
- the Vict. manuscripts read *et tamen* (“and nevertheless”) for *sed tamen* (“but nevertheless”); the manuscripts omit *esse* (“to be”) in *quem esse cogitarem* (“whom I thought to exist”); Corb. has *cum tamen ego* (“although nevertheless I”) for *cum tamen esse* (“although nevertheless to be”). The manuscripts have *non qui esset … sed qui est* (“not what he was … but what [a man] is”) for *non quae esset … sed quae est* (“not what [thing] he was … but what [a man] is”).
- Vict. 13 has *possum illud* (“I can have it”) for *possem illud* (“I could have it”); it has *aut aliud omnibus* (“or something else [greater] than everything”) for *aut aliquid omnibus* (“or something [greater] than everything”). Corb. has *quando illud* (“when that thing”) for *quando aut illud* (“when or that thing”); Corb., S. Mich., Vict., and Thu. omit *secundum* (“according to”) in *secundum rem veram* (“according to a true reality”). Vict. 3, Corb., Cister., and the 1612 edition have *cogitare posse illud* (“to be able to think it”) for *cogitare possum* (“I can think”); Vict. 13 reads *possem istud* (“I could think this”) for *possum cogitare istud* (“I can think this”).
- Gem., Vict., Thu., S. Mich., and Cister. read *nequeam, potest ullum cogitari verum, siquidem* (“I cannot; anything true can be thought, for…”) where the printed text reads *nequeam, nisi tantum secundum vocem, secundum quam solam aut vix aut nunquam potest ullum cogitari verum. Siquidem* (“I cannot, except according to the word alone, according to which scarcely or never can anything true be thought. For…”); Corb. preserves that longer reading, while the note gives unassigned *nisi tamen secundum vocem … aut vix aut nunquam potest illum cogitare. Verum siquidem* (“except nevertheless according to the word … scarcely or never can he think it. But indeed…”). Gem., Vict., Cister., and Thu. have *cogitatione vera, verum ut ab* (“in true thought, but as by”), while Corb. has *cogitatione veram, verum ut ab* (“a true thought, but as by”); the note then gives *cogitatione vera fit ab* (“in true thought it is made by”) as the unassigned contrast. Corb. has *secundum animi motum* (“according to the movement of the mind”) for *animi motu* (“by the movement of the mind”). Corb. has *auditu vocis effectum* (“produced by hearing the word”), Vict. 13 has *auditu vel vocis effectum* (“produced by hearing or by the word”), and the note gives the unassigned *auditu vocisque affectum* (“the impression from hearing and from the word”). The manuscripts preserve *effingere: sibi: quod* (“to form: for himself: which”) and Corb. *effingere sibi: quod* (“to form for himself: which”); the note then gives unassigned *effingere sibi: quid* (“to form for himself: what”). Vict. 13 reads *veritate potuerit* (“may [form it] by the truth”) for *veritatem potuerit* (“may [form] the truth”).
- The manuscripts read *ab intellectu meo* (“away from my understanding”) for *in intellectu meo* (“in my understanding”); at the next clause they read *hoc de eo* (“this concerning him”) for *haec de eo* (“these things concerning him”). Corb. has *jam esse dicitur in intellectu meo* (“is now said to be in my understanding”) for *jam dicitur intellectu meo* (“is now said [to be] [in] my understanding”).

### §5 (0245C–0246B)

- Corb. has *quam autem et in re* (“but [that it is] also in reality”) for *quod autem non solum in intellectu, sed et in re* (“but that it is not only in the understanding but also in reality”). The manuscripts’ long alternative is *quia ubi fuerit quidquid est majus, in re illa erat: ac si per hoc* (“because where it will have existed, whatever is greater was in that reality; and as if through this”); it changes the conditional relation in printed *quia nisi fuerit, quidquid est in re, majus illa erit: ac per hoc* (“unless it exists, whatever is in reality will be greater than it”).
- Vict. and Thu. read *ad hoc respondeo, si esse dicendum est in intellectu, quod secundum veritatem cujusque rei* (“to this I answer: if one must say [it is] in the understanding, according to the truth of each thing”); Cister. has *adhuc respondeo. Si esse dicendum est… cujusquam rei* (“I answer further: if one must say that it exists … according to the truth of any thing”); Corb. has *ad hoc ego respondeo…* (“to this I answer…”); the note then gives the unassigned alternative *respondeo. Sic enim dicendum est in intellectu quidem secundum veritatem cujusquam rei* (“I answer: for thus it must be said to be in the understanding according to the truth of some thing”). The source also prints an identical *et hoc in meo* (“and this in mine”) on both sides of a general-manuscript note. These readings govern the crucial “in intellectu” argument.
- The manuscripts read *non potest nullatenus* (“cannot in no way”) for *non potest ullatenus* (“cannot in any way”); Cister. omits *adhuc* (“still”); Thu. has *quod qui esse* (“that [one] who says [it] exists”) for *quod si esse* (“that if [it] exists”); Vict. 13 reads *dicit hoc* (“says this”) for *esse dicit, sed hoc* (“says it exists, but this”). Vict., Thu., Gem., and Cister. have *non erit omnibus minus* (“will not be less than everything”) for *non erit omnibus majus* (“will not be greater than everything”).
- Thu. reads *ulla re* (“by any real thing”) for *nulla re* (“by no real thing”); Corb. has *si dicendum est* (“if it must be said”) for *non dicendum est* (“it must not be said”). The manuscripts read *quando igitur* (“when therefore”) for *quomodo igitur* (“how therefore”); in the next note Vict. 13 and Cister. read *quia constet* (“because it is established”), with *quomodo igitur* (“how therefore”) as the unassigned contrast. Corb. reads *eo usque negem adhuc dubitemve* (“to that extent I deny, still, or doubt”) for *adhuc dubitem, negemve* (“I still doubt and deny”). The manuscripts omit *in* in *in intellectu*; Vict. 13 omits *mihi* (“to me”) in *certum mihi necesse est* (“it is necessary for it to become certain to me”) and omits *ipsum* (“itself”) in *alicubi majus ipsum* (“the greater thing itself [exists] somewhere”). The manuscripts have *et tamen deinde ex* (“and nevertheless afterwards from”) for *et tum demum ex* (“and only then from”).

### §6 (0245C–0247B)

- The manuscripts omit *ex* in *vel potius ex impossibilitate* (“or rather from the impossibility”); Vict. and Corb. read *hoc ita esse* (“this is so”) for *haec ita esse* (“these things are so”). The source prints *quisptam* (“someone,” orthographic form).
- The manuscripts have *ac si tunc velit* (“and if he then wishes”) for *at si tunc velut* (“but if then, as it were”); Vict. 13 has *consequenter* (“consequently”) for *contingenter* (“contingently”); the manuscripts read *ac si dicat* (“and if he says”); the note gives *ac dicat* (“and says”) as the unassigned contrast to printed *adjungat ac dicat* (“adds and says”). Corb. has *vere esse alicubi* (“truly exist somewhere”) for *nec esse alicubi* (“nor exist anywhere”). Vict. reads *quam in intellectu* (“than in [the] understanding”); Corb. reads *quam et in intellectu* (“than also in [the] understanding”); the note gives *quam et intellectu* (“than also understanding”) as the unassigned contrast.
- A Corb. note repeats *non in intellectu solo* (“not in the understanding alone”) identically on both sides. Corb. and the other readings retain that phrase; Thu. has *ideo sic* (“therefore thus”) for *ideoque sic* (“and therefore thus”); the manuscripts read masculine *quicunque alia* (“whatever other [one]”) for neuter *quaecunque alia* (“whatever other [thing]”); they have *praestantior et intellecta praestantior* (“more excellent, and understood more excellent”) for printed *praestantior intellecta, praestantior* (“understood as more excellent, [it] will not be more excellent”). The manuscripts read *per hoc ille* (“by this he”) for *per haec ille* (“by these things he”), Thu. *ambigendum* (“[there is] to be doubted”) for *et ambigendam* (“and [it] to be doubted”), Corb. *jocari ipsum* (“that he was joking”) for *altercari illum* (“that he was disputing”), and Corb. *credam … debeam* (“I may think … ought I”) for *credant … debeant* (“they may think … ought”); the source repeats this same note at both verb positions. Corb. also reads *an illum* (“or him”) for *aut illum* (“or him”), a conjunction-level variant.
- At the conclusion, the manuscripts have *intellectu in eo* (“in his understanding”) for *intellectu meo* (“in my understanding”); Corb. has *intellectu meo* (“in my understanding”); the note gives *intellectu mero* (“in [the] bare understanding”) as the unassigned contrast.

### §7 (0247C–0248B)

- Corb., Gem., Vict., and Cister. have *hoc interim* (“this meanwhile”) for *haec interim* (“these things meanwhile”); Vict. 13 has *responderit* (“will have replied”); the note gives *responderet* (“might reply”) as the unassigned contrast. In a separate note, the manuscripts generally have *possit respondere* (“can reply”) for *possit referre responsum* (“can return the answer”). Gem., Vict., and S. Mich. read *rei veritatem* (“the truth of the thing”) for *rei veritate* (“in the truth of the thing”).
- Thu. has *in tantum etiam* (“to such an extent even”); the note gives *in tantis etiam* (“even in such great [matters]”) as the unassigned contrast. The manuscripts read *ex hac alia* (“from this [nature], other [things]”) for *ex hoc, alia* (“from this, other [things]”), the manuscripts read *nec posset cogitari* (“nor could it be thought”) for *nec possit cogitari* (“nor can it be thought”); and Vict., Thu., and Cister. read *probare* (“prove”) for *comprobare* (“confirm”). Gem., Vict., S. Mich., and Cister. have *necesse est, ac quod majus ac melius est illud omnibus* (“it is necessary, and that which is greater and better than all things”) for the printed order.
- Thu. reads *illud, quod est scilicet, et Deus* (“that thing which is, namely, and God”); Vict. and Corb. read *illud quod Deus* (“that thing which [is] God”); the note gives *illud quod est, scilicet, est Deus* (“that which is, namely, is God”) as the unassigned contrast to the printed *summum vero illud quod est Deus* (“that supreme thing which is God”). Cister., Gem., Corb., and Vict. have *cur et nunquid aliud* (“why also anything else”) for *cur non et quidquid aliud* (“why not also whatever else”).

### §8 and transition (0247C–0249A)

- Thu., Gem., Vict., and Cister. read *praestantia* (“distinguished”); Corb. reads *disserta* (“discussed”); and the note gives *diserta* (“eloquently argued”) as an unassigned contrast to the printed *praeclare … disserta* (“brilliantly … discussed”). The manuscripts have *restricta* (“restricted”) for *referta* (“filled”). The manuscripts have *quae videntur* (“which seem”) and the Venetian edition *quae virtus* (“which power”) for *quae in initiis* (“which at the beginnings”); they read *argumentata, sibi ista sint contemnenda* (“having been argued, these things themselves should be despised”) for *argumentata sunt, ista sint contemnenda* (“have been argued, these things should be despised”). Cister. reads *ac omnia* (“and all [things]”) for *ac sic omnia* (“and thus all [things]”).
- **Apologetic title notice (0249):** Vict. 13 has *Incipit Liber Anselmi archiepiscopi et abbatis contra respondentem pro insipiente* (“Here begins the book of Anselm, archbishop and abbot, against the respondent on behalf of the fool”); Gem., Vict., and Cister. have *Quid ad haec respondeat editor ipsius libelli (Proslogion.)* (“What the editor of that little book, the Proslogion, replies”); Thu. has *Incipiunt responsiones. Anselmi contra respondentem pro insipiente dicente in corde suo; Non est Deus: sive Responsio contra fatuum* (“Here begin Anselm’s replies against the respondent on behalf of the fool who says in his heart, ‘There is no God’; or, A reply against the fool”); S. Mich. has *Responsio Anselmi ad eumdem, id est, Gaunilonem* (“Anselm’s reply to the same man, namely Gaunilo”).
- The printed boundary marker **37** precedes *Quoniam non me* (“Since [he] did not [criticize] me”). Vict. 13 omits *non* (“not”); Thu. has *in meo opusculo* (“in my little work”) for *in eo opusculo* (“in that little work”); Corb. reads *quinam non insipiens* (“what non-fool?”) for *quidam non insipiens* (“a certain non-fool”), and *quidam insipiens* (“a certain fool”) is also attested. The chapter heading is: “The opponent’s reasoning is refuted in general, and it is shown that that than which a greater cannot be thought exists in reality.”

Provenance: original Luna translation; saved Terra review did not certify coverage; native Terra canonical-source adjudication and repair. No external source or deterministic translator was used.

You do indeed say [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Thu reads “you say a certain thing” (`dicis quidam`) instead of “you do indeed say” (`dicis quidem`)—whoever you are who say that these things can be said by a fool—that there is something in the intellect than which a greater cannot be conceived only in the way in which, according to the true nature of each thing, it cannot even be conceived; and because what I call “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” does not follow any more from its being in the intellect than its existing in reality follows for the Lost Island’s certainly existing, from the fact that, when it is described in words, the hearer does not doubt that it is in his intellect. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts Gem. and S. Mic. read “this can be said” (`hoc posse dicere`) instead of “can say this” (`haec dicere posse`).]

[Col. 0249B] I, however, say: If “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” is neither understood nor conceived, then either God is not that than which a greater cannot be conceived, or he is not understood or conceived and is not in the intellect or in thought. How false this is, I employ your faith and conscience as an exceedingly firm argument for how false this is. Therefore “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” is truly understood and conceived, and is in the intellect and in thought.

Consequently, either the propositions by which you try to prove your case are not true, or what you think follows from them does not follow. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “which you try to prove against” (`conaris contra`) instead of “by which you try to prove” (`quibus contra conaris`).] But as for your supposition that, from the fact that something than which a greater cannot be conceived is understood, it does not follow that it is in the intellect, nor, if it is in the intellect, that it therefore exists in reality: I certainly say [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “therefore I say” (`certe, ergo dico`) instead of “I certainly say” (`certe ego dico`)]: if it can even be conceived as existing, it must exist. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Thu reads “it is necessary that it exist, that than which…” (`necesse illud est esse quo`) instead of “it must exist” (`necesse est illud esse`).]

For “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” cannot be conceived as existing except without a beginning. [Col. 0249C] Whatever, however, can be conceived as existing and does not exist [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “can be conceived as existing and as not existing” (`cogitari esse et non esse`) instead of “can be conceived as existing and does not exist” (`cogitari esse, et non est`)]: can be conceived as existing through a beginning. Therefore “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” cannot be conceived as existing and not exist. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts Gem., Thu., and Vict. read “can be conceived as existing and not exist” (`potest esse et non esse`) instead of “can be conceived as existing and does not exist” (`potest esse et non est`).] If, then, it can be conceived as existing, it exists necessarily. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “that thing necessarily exists” (`illud ex necessitate`) or omit “that thing” (`illud`).]

Furthermore, if it can even be conceived, it must exist. For no one who denies or doubts that there is something than which a greater cannot be conceived denies or doubts that, if it existed, it could not fail to exist either actually or in the intellect. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts Thu. and Vict. 13 read “could not fail to exist in the intellect” (`intellectu posse non`) instead of “could not fail to exist either actually or in the intellect” (`nec actu nec intellectu posset non esse`).] Otherwise it would not be that than which a greater cannot be conceived. [Col. 0250A] But whatever can be conceived and does not exist could, if it existed, not exist either in reality or in the intellect. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Vict. 13 reads “even if it existed, it could not exist” (`etiam si esset, posset`) instead of “if it existed, it could not exist” (`si esset, posset`).] Therefore, if it can even be conceived, it cannot not exist—namely, that than which a greater cannot be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “Therefore, if nothing can be conceived…” (`quare si nihil cogitari`) instead of “Therefore, if it can even be conceived” (`quare si vel cogitari`).]

But let us suppose that, if it can be conceived, it does not exist. Yet whatever can be conceived and does not exist would, if it existed, not be that than which a greater cannot be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “or whatever…” (`aut quidquid`) instead of “yet whatever…” (`at quidquid`).] If, therefore, it existed as that than which a greater cannot be conceived, it would not be that than which a greater cannot be conceived—which is altogether absurd. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read: “If, therefore, there were that than which a greater cannot be conceived, there would not be that than which a greater cannot be conceived; which is altogether absurd” (`Si ergo esset quo majus cogitari non possit, non esset quo majus cogitari non possit; quod nimis`).] It is therefore false that there is nothing than which a greater cannot be conceived, if it can even be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “if something greater cannot be conceived” (`majus aliquid cogitari non possit, si`) instead of “if there is nothing than which a greater cannot be conceived” (`majus cogitari non possit, si`).] And much more so if it can be understood or be in the intellect. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “much more so if…” (`multo magis si`) instead of “much more so, therefore, if…” (`multo itaque magis, si`).] [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “understood and be in the intellect” (`intelligi et in intellectu`) instead of “understood or be in the intellect” (`intelligi aut in intellectu`).]

I shall say something more: without doubt, whatever is not wholly present somewhere or at some time, even if it exists somewhere or at some time, [Col. 0250B] can nevertheless be conceived never to exist and nowhere to exist, just as it is not present somewhere or at some time. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “even if it exists” (`etiam si est`) or “and if it exists” (`et si est`) instead of “even if it exists somewhere or at some time” (`etiamsi est alicubi aut aliquando`).] For what was not yesterday and exists today can be understood as not having existed yesterday, and can consequently be understood as never existing. Likewise, what is not here and exists elsewhere can be conceived as existing nowhere, just as it is not here. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “what is not there … is not there” (`quod hoc non est … non est hoc`) instead of “what is not here … is not here” (`quod hic non est … non est hic`).]

Similarly, when the individual parts of something are not where or when its other parts are, all its parts, and therefore the whole itself, can be conceived as existing never or nowhere. For even if time is said always to exist and the world to be everywhere [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts Vict. 13, Thu., Corb., and Cister. read “and the world” (`et mundus`) instead of “or the world” (`aut mundus`)]: nevertheless the whole of time is not always present, nor is the whole world everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “this whole is always present” (`iste semper est`) instead of “this whole is not always present” (`iste totus est`).] Just as the individual parts of time do not exist when the other parts exist, so they can be conceived as never existing. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “I can also conceive them as never existing” (`possum etiam nunquam cogitari`) instead of “they can be conceived as never existing” (`possunt nunquam esse cogitari`).] And the individual parts of the world, just as they are not where the other parts are, [Col. 0250C] can accordingly be conceived as existing nowhere. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “and the individual parts there of the world” (`et singulae ibi mundi`) instead of “and the individual parts of the world” (`et singulae mundi`).] Moreover, what is joined together from parts can be dissolved in thought and can not exist. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Vict. 13 reads “but also what…” (`sed etiam quod`) instead of “moreover, what…” (`sed et quod`).] [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “is joined” (`junctum est`) instead of “is joined together” (`conjunctum est`).]

Therefore whatever is not wholly present somewhere or at some time, even if it exists, can be conceived as not existing. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “and so whatever…” (`ac quo majus`) instead of “but whatever…” (`at quo majus`).] But “that than which a greater cannot be conceived,” if it exists, cannot be conceived as not existing. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “as it cannot exist” (`sicut non potest`) instead of “if it exists, it cannot…” (`si est, non potest`).] Otherwise, if it exists, it is not that than which a greater cannot be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscripts read “it is not that than which a greater…” (`non quo majus`) instead of “it is not that than which a greater…” (`non est quo majus`).] This is impossible. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Vict. 13 reads “it cannot be: this…” (`non potest: quod`) instead of “which is impossible” (`quod non convenit`).] It is therefore in no way wholly absent somewhere or at some time; rather, it is wholly present always and everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0249C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “therefore that which is wholly absent somewhere … you think” (`nullatenus ergo quod alicubi … putas`) instead of “therefore it is in no way wholly absent somewhere … do you think” (`nullatenus ergo alicubi … putas`).]

Do you think that what these propositions are understood of can in any way be conceived or understood, or be in thought or in the intellect? [Col. 0251A] [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Cister. reads “in thought or in the intellect” (`in cogitatione vel in intellectu`) instead of “in thought or the intellect” (`in cogitatione vel intellectu`).] For if it cannot, these propositions cannot be understood of it. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Vict. 13 read “these propositions cannot be understood of God” (`non de Deo possunt haec intelligi`) instead of “these propositions cannot be understood of it” (`non possunt haec intelligi de eo`); the manuscript Cister. reads “these propositions cannot be understood of him” (`non de eo possunt haec intelligi`).] If you say that what is not completely understood is neither understood nor in the intellect, then say that someone who cannot gaze upon the purest light of the sun does not see the light of day, which is nothing other than the sun’s light. Certainly “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” is understood at least to this extent and is in the intellect [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Vict. read “and is not in the intellect” (`et non est in intellectu`) instead of “and is in the intellect” (`et est in intellectu`)], so that these things may be understood of it. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Corb. and Vict. 13 read “so that these things may be understood of God” (`de Deo intelligantur`) instead of “of it” (`de eo intelligantur`).]

## CHAPTER II

The foregoing reasoning is pressed more strongly; and it is shown that “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” can be conceived, and therefore also exists.

I said, then, in the argument that you criticize, that when the fool hears “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” pronounced, he understands what he hears. Indeed, if someone does not understand it when it is spoken in a familiar language, he has either no intellect or an exceedingly dull one. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts read “indeed, if he does not understand” (`utique si non`) instead of “indeed, if someone does not understand” (`utique qui non`).] [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Vict. 13 reads “exceedingly obstructed” (`nimis obrutum`) instead of “exceedingly dull” (`nimis obtusum`).]

Then I said that, if it is understood, it is in the intellect. Is that which has been shown necessarily to exist in reality in no intellect? [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Thu. omits “to exist” (`esse`); the manuscript of Corb. omits “has been shown” (`monstratum`).] But you will say that, even if it is in the intellect, it does not therefore follow that it exists because it is understood. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts read “it does not follow” (`tamen consequitur`) instead of “it does not therefore follow” (`tamen consequenter`).] See that its being in the intellect follows from its being understood. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “from the fact that it is understood” (`ex eo quod`) instead of “from the fact that it is understood” (`ex eo quia`).] For just as what is thought is thought by thought, and what is thought by thought is in thought in the same way in which it is thought [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Vict. 13 reads “and is likewise in thought” (`sic et est in cogitatione`) instead of “is in thought” (`sic est in cogitatione`)], so what is understood is understood by the intellect; and what is understood by the intellect is in the intellect in the same way in which it is understood. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “it is understood by the intellect, and is understood in the intellect in the way in which it is understood” (`intelligitur intellectu, ita, sicut intelligitur, intellectum est`).] What could be clearer?

Afterward I said that, if it exists even in the intellect alone, it can be conceived as existing also in reality, which is greater. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “in reality, because it is greater” (`in re, quia majus`) instead of “in reality, which is greater” (`in re, quod majus`).] If, therefore, it exists in the intellect alone, then that same thing—namely, “that than which a greater cannot be conceived”—is something than which a greater can be conceived. I ask: what could follow more logically? [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Cister. reads “for is it, if it exists…” (`an enim est, si est`) instead of “for if it exists…” (`an enim si est`).]

For if it exists even in the intellect alone, can it not be conceived as existing also in reality? [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts read “as existing in reality, or…” (`esse in re, aut`) instead of “as existing also in reality” (`esse et in re, aut`).] Or if it can, does not the person who conceives this conceive something greater than it, if it exists in the intellect alone? [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts read “he conceives something else” (`cogitat, aliud cogitat`) instead of “he conceives something” (`cogitat, aliquid cogitat`).] What could follow more logically, then, than that, if “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” exists in the intellect alone, it is itself something than which a greater can be conceived? [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Thu. reads “that is, it is something than which…” (`id est, esse quo`) instead of “it is itself something than which…” (`idem esse quo`).]

But certainly something than which a greater can be conceived is in no intellect that contains nothing greater than it. Does it not therefore follow [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Thu., Corb., and Vict. read “therefore it does not follow” (`ergo non sequitur`) instead of “does it not therefore follow” (`ergo non consequitur`)] that, if “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” exists in any intellect, it does not exist in the intellect alone? [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts read “it is not in the intellect alone” (`non est in solo`) instead of “it does not exist in the intellect alone” (`non esse in solo`).] For if it exists in the intellect alone, it is something than which a greater can be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Gem., Corb., and Vict. read “if, then, it exists, it exists in the intellect alone, and is something than which…” (`si enim est, in solo intellectu est, quo`); Thu. reads “if it exists in the intellect alone, it is something than which greater…” (`si enim in solo intellectu, est quo majus`).] This is impossible.

[Col. 0252B]

## CHAPTER III

In response to the adversary’s objection: it would follow that a fictitious island exists in reality because it is conceived.

“But such a case,” you say, “is like someone saying that an island in the ocean, surpassing all lands in fertility, which is called Lost because of the difficulty—or rather the impossibility—of finding what does not exist, cannot for that reason be doubted to exist truly in reality, since anyone can easily understand it when it is described in words.” [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Gem. reads “such a greater thing is like…” (`sed tale est majus ac si`); the manuscripts Thu., Vict., S. Mich., and Cister. read “such a case, you say, is like…” (`sed tale est, inquis, ac si`); Corb. reads “such a case, he says, is like…” (`sed tale est, inquit, ac si`).]

I speak confidently [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “I shall speak confidently” (`fidens loquar`) instead of “I speak confidently” (`fidens loquor`)]: if someone finds for me anything existing either in reality or in mere thought, apart from “that than which a greater cannot be conceived,” to which he can apply the structure of my argument [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “to which it may be suitable” (`cui competere`) instead of “to which he can apply” (`cui aptare`)], I will find it and give him the Lost Island, so that it will no longer be lost. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Gem., S. Mich., and Vict. read “if someone does not find…” (`si quis non venerit nisi`) instead of “if someone finds…” (`si quis invenerit`); the manuscripts Corb., Vict., and Cister. read “if someone finds for me something or other…” (`si quis invenerit mihi aliquid aut`).]

It is already evident, however, that what cannot be be conceived as greater cannot be conceived as not existing, since it exists by so certain a reasoning of truth. Otherwise it would not exist at all. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Thu., Vict., Corb., and S. Mich. read “what exists, than which a greater cannot be conceived” (`existens, quod majus`) instead of “what cannot be conceived as greater” (`quo non valet cogitari majus`).]

Finally, if someone says that he conceives it as not existing, I say that, when he conceives this, he either conceives something than which a greater cannot be conceived, or he does not. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “I say that when he conceives this…” (`dico quia cum hoc`) instead of “I say that, when he conceives this…” (`dico quod tum cum hoc`).] If he does not conceive it, he does not conceive as not existing what he does not conceive. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts omit “if” (`quod si`) before “he does not conceive” (`non cogitat`).]

But if he does conceive it, then he certainly conceives something that cannot be conceived as not existing. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts read “he certainly conceives something” (`utique cogitat aliquod`) instead of “he certainly conceives something” (`utique cogitat aliquid`).] For if it could be conceived as not existing, it could be conceived as having a beginning and an end; but this cannot be the case. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscript of Vict. 13 reads “which cannot be conceived as existing” (`cogitari non possit esse`) instead of “which cannot be conceived as not existing” (`cogitari possit non esse`).] Therefore the person who conceives it conceives something that cannot be conceived as not existing. Whoever conceives this does not conceive that very thing as not existing. [Note: [Col. 0251C] The manuscripts Gem., Vict., Thu., and Cister. read “does not conceive that very thing as existing” (`idipsum esse`) instead of “does not conceive that very thing as not existing” (`idipsum non esse`).] Otherwise he conceives what cannot be conceived. Therefore “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” cannot be conceived as not existing.

## CHAPTER IV

The difference between being conceivable and being intelligible as nonexistent.

As for your statement that, when it is said that this supreme thing cannot be conceived as not existing [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscripts Vict. read “cannot be conceived not to exist” (`non esse queat cogitari`) instead of “cannot be conceived as not existing” (`non esse nequeat cogitari`)], it might perhaps be better said that it cannot be understood as nonexistent, or even as capable of not existing: rather, it should have been said that it cannot be conceived as nonexistent. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Vict. 13 reads “perhaps I should have said” (`fortasse dicerem`) instead of “it might perhaps be better said” (`fortasse diceretur`).] [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “that it cannot be conceived as not existing” (`non posse cogitari`) instead of “that it cannot be conceived” (`non possit cogitari`).]

For if I had said that the thing itself cannot be understood as nonexistent, perhaps you yourself—who say that, according to the proper meaning of this expression, false things cannot be understood—would object that it is false that nothing that exists can be understood as nonexistent, since what exists is not nonexistent. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “you would object to me that…” (`objiceres mihi quod`) instead of “you would object that…” (`objiceres nihil quod`).] Therefore it would not be peculiar to God that he cannot be understood as nonexistent. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscripts Thu., Gem., and Vict. 3 read “it would not be peculiar” (`non esse proprium`) instead of “it would not be peculiar” (`non esset proprium`).]

If this were so, then some of the things that most certainly exist could be understood as nonexistent, and other certain things could likewise be understood as nonexistent. [Col. 0253B] But this objection cannot properly be made concerning conception, if it is carefully considered. For although no things that exist can be understood as nonexistent [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “no things that do not exist” (`nulla quae non sunt`) instead of “no things that exist” (`nulla quae sunt`], all things can nevertheless be conceived as nonexistent except that which supremely exists. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Cister. reads “all things only” (`omnia tantum`) instead of “all things nevertheless” (`omnia tamen`).]

Those things, and those alone, can be conceived as nonexistent that have a beginning, an end, or a conjunction of parts; and, as I have already said, whatever is not wholly present somewhere or at some time. But that alone cannot be conceived as nonexistent in which there is neither a beginning, nor an end, nor a conjunction of parts, and which no thought finds except as wholly present always and everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscripts Thu. and Vict. 13 read “which that thought finds” (`illa invenit`) instead of “which no thought finds” (`ulla invenit`).]

Know, therefore, that you can conceive yourself as nonexistent so long as you know with complete certainty that you exist—something that I am surprised you said you did not know. [Col. 0253C] For we think many things nonexistent that we know to exist, and many things existent that we know not to exist [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “that we do not know to exist” (`nescimus esse`) instead of “that we know not to exist” (`non esse scimus`)]: not by judging them to be so, but by imagining them to be as we think them. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “by signifying” (`significando`) instead of “by imagining” (`fingendo`).]

Indeed, we can conceive something as nonexistent so long as we know it to exist, because we can do both at once: conceive that and know this. Yet we cannot conceive it as nonexistent while we know it to exist, because we cannot conceive it to exist and not exist at the same time. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscripts Gem., Thu., Vict. 13, S. Mich., and Cister. give an expanded form: “Indeed, we can conceive something as nonexistent while we know it to exist, because we can do both at once, conceive that and know this; and we cannot conceive it as nonexistent while we know it to exist, because we cannot conceive it to exist and not exist at the same time.” The manuscript Vict. 3 gives the same wording in a slightly shorter form. The manuscript Corb. reads only: “Indeed, we can conceive something as nonexistent while we know it to exist. We cannot conceive it to exist and not exist at the same time.”]

If, then, one distinguishes the two propositions in this utterance in this way, one will understand that nothing can be conceived as nonexistent so long as it is known to exist; and that anything other than “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” can, even while it is known to exist, be conceived as nonexistent. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “it is known to exist, but according to the sense of composition it can be understood as not existing” (`scitur, sed secundum sensum compositionis posse intelligi non esse`); Vict. 13 reads “it is known to exist, and it cannot be conceived as not existing” (`scitur, esse non posse non esse cogitari`).]

Thus it is proper to God that he cannot be conceived as nonexistent; nevertheless, many things cannot be conceived as nonexistent while they exist. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “many things cannot be understood” (`multa non possunt intelligi`) instead of “many things cannot be conceived” (`multa non possunt cogitari`).] How God is said to be conceived as nonexistent, I think has been sufficiently explained in the work itself. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscripts Thu., Corb., Vict., and Cister. read “in that work” (`in isto`) instead of “in the work itself” (`in ipso`).]

## CHAPTER V

A specific examination of various statements by the adversary, beginning with his unfaithful report of the reasoning he undertook to refute.

It is easy to detect what sort of things the others are that you bring against me on behalf of the fool—or of someone only slightly wise—and for that reason I had thought it unnecessary to point them out. But since I hear that, to some readers, they appear to have some force against me, I shall mention them briefly.

First, you repeatedly say that I claim that what is greater than everything is in the intellect, and that, if it is in the intellect, it is also in reality; otherwise what is greater than everything would not be greater than everything. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscripts Gem. and Vict. 3 read “what is greater than everything is in the intellect” (`majus omnibus est et in intellectu`); the manuscripts Thu., Corb., Vict. 13, and S. Mich. read “what is greater than everything is in the intellect” (`majus omnibus est in intellectu`).] Nowhere in all my statements is such a proof found.

For “greater than everything” does not have the same force as “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” for proving that what is spoken of exists in reality. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “greater, indeed, than everything” (`majus quidem cogitari nequit`) instead of “that than which a greater cannot be conceived.”] [Col. 0254C] If someone says that “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” is not something in reality, or can not exist, or cannot even be conceived as not existing, he can easily be refuted. For what does not exist can not exist; and what can not exist can be conceived as not existing. [Note: [Col. 0253C] The manuscript of Corb. omits the following: “For if it does not exist, then, if it existed, it would not be that than which a greater cannot be conceived.”]

But whatever can be conceived as not existing, if it exists, is not that than which a greater cannot be conceived. If it does not exist, then, if it existed, it would not be that than which a greater cannot be conceived. Yet one cannot say that “that than which a greater cannot be conceived,” if it exists, is not that than which a greater cannot be conceived, or that, if it existed, it would not be something than which a greater could not be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts read “because that which is greater cannot be conceived” (`quia qui majus`) instead of “because that than which a greater cannot be conceived” (`quia quo majus`).] [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts read “cannot be conceived” (`non possit cogitari`) instead of “cannot be conceived” (`non possit cogitari`); the manuscript of Corb. reads “if it exists, if it is not that than which a greater cannot be conceived” (`si est, si non qui majus cogitari non potest`).]

It is therefore evident that it neither does not exist, nor can not exist, nor can be conceived as not existing. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Thu. reads “that it neither does not exist”; Cister. reads “that it neither exists”; the better reading is “that it neither does not exist.”] Otherwise, if it exists, it is not what is said; and if it existed, it would not be what is said.

[Col. 0255B] This, however, does not appear equally easy to prove concerning what is called “greater than everything.” For it is not equally evident that what can be conceived as nonexistent is not greater than everything that exists, as it is that it is not that than which a greater cannot be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Vict. reads “nor, if it exists” (`nec si est`) instead of “nor is it equally…” (`nec sic est`); the manuscript of Corb. reads “nor is it so” (`nec est`).] Nor is it equally indubitable that, if there is something greater than everything, it is nothing other than that than which a greater cannot be conceived; or that, if it existed, there would similarly be nothing else greater than it. This is certain concerning what is called “that than which a greater cannot be conceived.” [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Corb. omits the words “or that, if it existed, there would similarly be nothing else greater than it.”]

For what if someone says that there is something greater than everything that exists, but that this same thing can nevertheless be conceived as nonexistent, and that something greater than it can be conceived—even if that greater thing does not exist, it can nevertheless be conceived? [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts Gem., Vict., Thu., and Cister. read “is greater, even if…” (`majus esse, etiamsi`) instead of “something greater than it can be conceived, even if…” (`majus eo, etiamsi`).] Can it then be inferred as plainly as it would be in the former case: “Therefore it is not greater than everything that exists,” as it would there be most plainly said: “Therefore it is not that than which a greater cannot be conceived”? [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts read “as it would be said there” (`sicut ubi`) instead of “as it would be in the former case” (`sicut ibi`).] [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “it will be said” (`dicetur`) instead of “it would be said” (`diceretur`).]

That requires an argument other than the phrase “greater than everything.” In the other case, however, no argument is needed beyond what the phrase itself signifies: “that than which a greater cannot be conceived.” [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “which signifies” (`qui sonat`) instead of “what the phrase itself signifies” (`quod sonat`).]

[Col. 0256A] Therefore, if it cannot be proved in the same way of what is called “greater than everything” what the phrase “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” proves by itself, you have unjustly criticized me for saying what I did not say, since the two expressions differ so greatly.

But even if another argument can be supplied [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “if another argument is proposed” (`si vero proponi aliud`); the manuscripts read “you have supplied an argument” (`argumentum posuisti`) instead of “another argument can be supplied” (`argumentum potest`)], you still should not have criticized me for saying something that can be proved. Whether it can be proved is readily discerned by anyone who understands that there is something than which a greater cannot be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts read “can be discerned” (`perpendi`) instead of “is readily discerned” (`perpendit`).] For it cannot be understood that there is something than which a greater cannot be conceived unless that thing alone is greater than everything.

Therefore, just as “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” is understood and is in the intellect [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “is understood to exist in the intellect” (`et intelligitur esse in`) instead of “is understood and is in the intellect” (`intelligitur, et est in`)] and for that reason is asserted to exist in reality, so what is called “greater than everything” is understood and is in the intellect, and for that reason its existence in reality is necessarily concluded. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript reads “so that what is called greater…” (`sic quo majus`) instead of “so what is called greater…” (`sic quod majus`).]

You see, then, how rightly you compared me with that fool who wanted to assert that the Lost Island exists merely because it was understood when described.

## CHAPTER VI

The adversary’s statement in section 2 is examined: that any false things could likewise be understood and therefore exist.

As for your objection that any false or doubtful things can likewise be understood and be in the intellect, just as in the case of what I was saying, I am surprised what you meant here, when you wished to establish a doubtful point against me. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts read “what you meant by this” (`quod hoc sensisti`) instead of “what you meant here” (`quid hic sensisti`).] For it was enough at first that I show it to be understood in some manner and to be in the intellect, so that it might subsequently be considered whether it existed in the intellect alone, as false things do, or also in reality, as true things do. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “I should show it to be in the intellect” (`intellectu ostenderem`); Vict. 13 reads “I should show it to be understood” (`intellectum ostenderem`).]

For if false and doubtful things are understood in this way and are in the intellect because, when they are spoken, the hearer understands what the speaker signifies, nothing prevents what I said from being understood and being in the intellect.

But how the following statements agree with one another is your concern: you say that, when someone says something false, you would understand whatever he said; yet, when what exists is not in the same way in which false things are held in thought, you do not say that you think what is heard or have it in thought, because, as you claim, you cannot think it in any other way except by understanding it—that is, by comprehending through knowledge that it exists in reality.
