[Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts Gem., Thu., and Vict. read “how what you say agrees: when someone says something false…” (`quomodo autem sibi conveniat quod dicis, quod falsa dicente`); Corb. reads “how your statements agree, since when someone says something false…” (`quomodo autem sibi conveniant quod dicis quia falsa dicente`); Cister. reads “how they agree, since when someone says something false…” (`quomodo sibi conveniant qui dicis quia falsa dicente`).] [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts Gem., Thu., and Vict. read “what does not exist, in the way in which false things are held in thought, you do not say…” (`quod non est, eo modo quo etiam falsa habentur in cogitatione, non dicens`); Corb. reads “what is not, in the way in which false things are held in thought, you do not say…”; Cister. reads “what exists, not in the way in which false things are held in thought, you do not say…”; the printed reading is uncertain.] [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts read “namely, I cannot” (`scilicet non possum`) instead of “namely, you cannot” (`scilicet non possis`).]

How, I ask, do these statements agree: that false things are understood, and that to understand is to comprehend through knowledge that something exists? [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscripts read “that something else exists” (`existere aliud`) instead of “that something exists” (`existere aliquid`).] You must see to that.

But if false things are understood in some manner, and this is not the whole definition of understanding but only a certain kind of understanding, I should not have been criticized for saying that “that than which a greater cannot be conceived” is understood and is in the intellect even before it was certain that it existed in reality. [Note: [Col. 0255C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “that it is also in the intellect” (`in intellectu etiam esse`) instead of “that it is in the intellect” (`in intellectu esse, etiam`).]

[Col. 0257A]

## CHAPTER VII

Against another statement of the adversary in the same place: namely, that the supreme magnitude could equally be conceived as nonexistent, just as God is conceived by the fool.

Next [Note: [Col. 0257C] The manuscripts Corb. and Vict. 13 read “finally” (`denique`) instead of “next” (`deinde`)], you say that it can scarcely ever be believed that, once this has been stated and heard, it can be conceived as nonexistent in a way different from that in which God can be conceived as nonexistent. [Note: [Col. 0257C] The manuscript of Corb. omits “can be” (`posse esse`).] [Note: [Col. 0257C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “in the way in which it also cannot be conceived as nonexistent” (`quo etiam non potest`) instead of “in the way in which it can also be conceived as nonexistent” (`quo etiam potest`).]

[Col. 0257B] Let those who have acquired even a little knowledge of disputation and argumentation answer for me. Is it reasonable for someone to deny what he understands merely because it is said to exist that which he denies for the reason that he does not understand it? [Note: [Col. 0257C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “because that is said to exist which he denies” (`quia id esse dicitur, quia id negat`) instead of “because it is said to exist that which he denies” (`quia esse dicitur, id quod ideo negat`).] Or, if something that is understood to some extent is at times denied, and the same thing is for that person equivalent to something not understood at all, is it not easier to prove what is doubtful concerning something that is in the intellect to some degree than concerning something that is in no intellect at all?

Therefore it cannot be believed that anyone denies “that than which a greater cannot be conceived,” which he understands to some extent when he hears it, for the reason that he denies God, whose meaning he does not conceive in any way.

Or if something else is also denied because it is not wholly understood, is it not nevertheless easier to prove what is understood in some manner than what is understood in no manner? [Note: [Col. 0257C] The manuscripts read “nevertheless not at all” (`minime tamen`) instead of “is it not nevertheless” (`nonne tamen`).] It was therefore not unreasonable, in proving that God exists against the fool, to introduce “that than which a greater cannot be conceived,” since the former is understood in no way, while the latter is understood in some way.

## CHAPTER VIII

The comparison of the picture proposed in section 3 is examined; and the basis is shown from which one may infer the supreme magnitude about which the adversary had inquired in section 4.

### Restored apparatus entries

The following source-keyed entries restore readings omitted from the inherited queue draft. In each entry, the form before the witness label is the witness reading; the final form is the contrasting printed reading.

- At “than which a greater can be conceived,” the manuscripts read `suo majus quod cogitari`, “his greater which can be conceived,” for `quo majus cogitari`, “than which a greater [can be conceived].”
- The manuscripts read `et quod non magis consequitur`, “and that it does not follow any more,” for `et quia non magis consequitur`, “and because it does not follow any more.”
- Corb. reads `quam praedictam`, “than the aforesaid [island],” for `quam perditam`, “than the lost [island].”
- The manuscripts read `certissime existere ex eo quia cum`, “to exist with certainty from the fact that, when,” for `certissime ex eo cum`, “with certainty from the fact that, when.”
- Corb. reads `possit, aut intelligitur`, “can [be conceived], or is understood,” for `possit, aut non intelligitur`, “can [be conceived], or is not understood.”
- Vict. reads `cogitari posset`, “could be conceived,” for `cogitari non posset`, “could not be conceived.”
- Corb. reads `quod hoc non est ... non est hoc`, “what is not there ... is not there,” for `quod hic non est ... non est hic`, “what is not here ... is not here.”
- Vict. 13, Thu., Corb., and Cister. read `esse et mundus`, “to exist and the world,” for `esse, aut mundus`, “to exist, or the world.”
- Vict. 13 reads `non potest: quod`, “cannot [be conceived]: which,” for `non possit: quod`, “could not [be conceived]: which.”
- Corb. reads `nullatenus ergo quod alicubi ... putas`, “therefore in no way that which is somewhere ... do you think,” for `nullatenus ergo alicubi ... putas`, “therefore in no way somewhere ... do you think.”
- The manuscripts read `quod si dicitur`, “but if it is said,” for `quod si dicis`, “but if you say.”
- Corb. and Vict. 13 read `de Deo intelligantur`, “these things are understood of God,” for `de eo intelligatur`, “this is understood of it.”
- Thu. omits `esse`, “to be,” in `necessario in rei veritate esse monstratum est`, “has necessarily been shown to exist in reality”; Corb. instead reads `necessario tamen consequitur in rei veritate esse monstratum`, “yet it necessarily follows that it has been shown in reality.”
- Corb. reads `sed dicis quia si est`, “but you say that if it is,” for `sed dicis quia etsi est`, “but you say that although it is.”
- Corb. reads `intelligitur intellectu, ita, sicut intelligitur, intellectum est`, “it is understood by the intellect, and thus, as it is understood, it has been understood”; Vict. 13 reads `intellectu intelligitur, ita est in intellectu sicut intelligitur`, “it is understood by the intellect, and thus it is in the intellect as it is understood.”
- The manuscripts read `aut cogitat aliquod`, “or thinks some thing,” for `aut cogitat aliquid`, “or thinks something.”
- The manuscripts omit `quod`, “that,” in `quod si non cogitat`, “but if he does not think.”
- Corb. reads `cogitari non possit esse`, “cannot be conceived to be,” and Vict. 13 `cogitari possit non esse`, “can be conceived not to be,” for `cogitari non esse possit`, “can be conceived not to be.”
- The manuscripts read `hoc vero quod cogitat`, “but this which he thinks,” for `hoc vero qui cogitat`, “but he who thinks this.”
- The manuscripts read `nihil, quod est, posse intelligi non esse; falsum est enim`, “nothing which exists can be understood not to exist; for it is false,” for the malformed printed division `nihil quod est, posse intelligi, non est falsum, est enim`.
- Thu., Gem., and Vict. 3 read `non esse proprium`, “not to be peculiar,” and Corb. `non est proprium`, “is not peculiar,” for `non esset proprium`, “would not be peculiar.”
- The manuscripts omit `esset`, “were,” in `quod si esset aliquid`, “if something were.”
- Corb., Thu., and Vict. 3 read `non esse posset intelligi`, “could be understood not to be”; Vict. 13 `non esse posse intelligi`, “to be able to be understood not to be,” for `posse intelligi non esse`, “to be able to be understood not to be.”
- Thu. reads `haec utique non possunt`, “these certainly cannot,” for `hoc utique non potest`, “this certainly cannot.”
- Corb. reads `solummodo potest`, “can only,” and Vict. 13 `solum potest`, “alone can,” for `solum non potest`, “alone cannot.”
- Vict. 13’s corrupt `cogitarerem non esse quam` is retained as an unresolved reading; it stands against `cogitare te non esse quandiu`, “to think that you do not exist while.”
- The manuscripts read `ita esse cogitamus`, “we think [them] to be so,” for `ita esse ut cogitamus`, “to be so as we think.”
- Corb. omits `sic`, “thus,” in `sic distinguat`, “distinguishes thus”; the manuscripts read `intelligit nihil`, “he understands that nothing,” for `intelliget nihil`, “he will understand that nothing.”
- Corb. reads `scitur, sed secundum sensum compositionis posse intelligi non esse`, “it is known, but according to the composite sense it can be understood not to be”; Vict. 13 `scitur, esse non posse non esse cogitari`, “it is known not to be able to be thought not to be,” for `scitur, posse cogitari non esse`, “it is known [to be], [yet] able to be thought not to be.”
- The manuscripts read `multa possunt cogitari`, “many things can be thought,” and Corb. `multa non possunt intelligi`, “many things cannot be understood,” for `multa non possunt cogitari`, “many things cannot be thought.”
- The manuscripts read `argumentum posuisti`, “you have put forward an argument,” for `argumentum potest`, “an argument can [be supplied]”; this is a reading, not a sentence addressed to the reader.
- Corb. reads `si vero proponi aliud`, “but if another [argument] is proposed,” for `si vere vel post aliud`, “but if truly or after another.”
- Corb. reads `in intellectu ostenderem`, “I should show [it] in the intellect,” and Vict. 13 `intellectum ostenderem`, “I should show [it] understood,” for `intellectu ostenderem`, “I should show [it] to the intellect.”
- The manuscripts read `quod hoc sensisti`, “what you thought by this,” for `quid hic sensisti`, “what you thought here.”
- Corb. reads `quia cum dicuntur`, “because when they are said,” for `quod cum dicitur`, “that when it is said.”
- Corb. omits `posse esse`, “to be able to be,” in the assertion that it can be believed.
- Corb. reads `quia id esse dicitur, quia id negat`, “because that is said to be which he denies,” for `quia esse dicitur, id quod ideo negat`, “because that is said to be which he therefore denies.”
- Gem., Thuan., Vict. 3, S. Mich., and Cister. read `aut si et illud`, “or if that too,” while Corb. has `aut si illud`, “or if that,” and Vict. 3 `aut si id`, “or if it,” for `ac si et illud`, “and as if that too.”


### Restored column-boundary register

+[Col. 0249B] begins the reply “I, however, say”; [Col. 0250B] begins the argument that what is absent at some place or time can be conceived never and nowhere to be; [Col. 0250C] continues with the parts of the world; [Col. 0251B] begins Chapter II; [Col. 0252A] continues the inference from existence only in the intellect; [Col. 0252B] begins Chapter III; [Col. 0252C] begins the alternative “if he does not think”; [Col. 0253A] concludes that it cannot be conceived not to be; [Col. 0254A] begins the paired distinction of thinking and knowing; [Col. 0254B] begins Chapter V; [Col. 0254C] begins the contrast between “greater than all” and “than which a greater cannot be conceived”; [Col. 0255A] continues the modal proof; [Col. 0255B] begins the limitation concerning “greater than all”; [Col. 0256A] concludes that comparison; [Col. 0256B] begins Chapter VI; and [Col. 0256C] continues its distinction concerning false and doubtful things.

What you so earnestly prove—that it is not such a thing as “that than which nothing greater can be conceived”—is no more relevant than the fact that a picture not yet made, but conceived in the painter’s mind, is made without cause. For I did not introduce a preconceived picture in order to assert that the thing under discussion was such; I introduced it only so that I might show that something can exist in the understanding which is understood not to exist. [Note: Col. 0257C: The manuscripts read *ut aliquid esset* (“that something might be”), for *ut aliquid esse in intellectu* (“that something be in the understanding”); the Corbie manuscript reads *esse non intelligeretur* (“that being might not be understood”), for *non esse intelligeretur* (“that non-being might be understood”).]

Likewise, when you say that you cannot conceive or have in your understanding “that than which nothing greater can be conceived” according to a thing known to you either by its genus or by its species, because you know neither the thing itself nor can know it from another similar thing, it is clear that the matter is otherwise. [Note: Col. 0257C: The manuscripts read “or have understanding” (*vel intellectum habere*) for “or have it in the understanding”; “you know the thing” for “you know the thing itself”; and, for “can know,” Corbie and Victorine 13 read *potes conjicere* (“can infer”), while Victorine 3 reads *convincere* (“establish”).]

Since every lesser good is similar to a greater good insofar as it is good, it is evident to every rational mind [Note: Col. 0257C: The manuscripts read *rationabili menti* (“to a reasoning mind”) for *rationali menti*.] that, by ascending from lesser goods to greater ones [Note: Col. 0257C: Corbie reads *ascendendo* (“ascending”) for *conscendendo*.], we can infer from those things from which something greater can be conceived [Note: Col. 0257C: The witnesses vary between *ex his quibus*, *ex his*, and *ex quibus*; they also read *aliud quid majus cogitari potest* (“some other greater thing can be conceived”) for *aliquid cogitari potest majus*.] that than which nothing greater can be conceived. [Note: Col. 0257C: Corbie and Victorine 13 read *possumus convincere* (“we can establish”) for *possumus conjicere* (“we can infer”); Victorine 13 also reads *quod*, omitting *illud*, where the text has *illud quo*.]

For who, for example, cannot conceive—even if he does not believe that what he conceives exists in reality—that if something is good which has a beginning and an end, it is much better to be good in such a way that, although it begins, it does not cease? And just as this is better than that, so that is better than this which has neither an end nor a beginning, even if it always passes from the past through the present into the future. [Note: Col. 0257C: The witnesses read *bonum est aliquod* (“some good”) for *bonum est aliquid*; they vary between *istud esse melius illo* and *isto esse melius illud*, a word-order variation; and Victorine 3 omits *per* in *per praesens* (“through the present”).] Whether or not something of this kind exists in reality [Note: Col. 0257C: The manuscripts read “whether or not some such thing exists in reality”], nevertheless that which in no way needs or is compelled to change or move is much better than it. [Note: Col. 0257C: One manuscript reads “is much greater than it.”]

Can this not be conceived? Or can something greater than it be conceived? Or, from things of this kind, can one not infer that than which nothing greater can be conceived? [Note: Col. 0257C: The manuscripts variously read *ex his tribus* (“from these three [things]”); *ex iis quibus cogitari valet* (“from those things by which it can be conceived”); and formulations that repeat, “Can something greater than this be conceived?” Gemmeticum reads *conjicere in quo* (“infer that in which”), Corbie *cogitare id quo* (“conceive that than which”), and some witnesses *convincere id quo* (“establish that than which”).]

There is, therefore, a basis from which that than which nothing greater can be conceived may be inferred. Thus the fool who does not accept sacred authority can easily be refuted if he denies that “that than which nothing greater can be conceived” can be inferred from other things. [Note: Col. 0257C: The manuscripts read “from these things” instead of “from other things”; another reads “can be conceived.”]

But if some Catholic denies this, let him remember that “the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made since the creation of the world; and likewise his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20).

[Col. 0258C]

## CHAPTER IX

That the greatest conceivable thing can be conceived and understood, and the argument made against the fool is strengthened.

But even if it were true that that than which nothing greater can be conceived could not be conceived or understood, it would nevertheless not be false that that than which nothing greater can be conceived can be conceived and understood. [Note: Col. 0257C: Saint-Michael’s manuscript reads *sed et si* for *sed etsi*. Corbie reads “to conceive that thing, or to understand the thing subject to that than which …” (*cogitari illud vel intelligi rem subjectam illi quo*); Victorine 13 omits *cogitari* in the following assertion that it can be conceived and understood; Corbie omits *ista* (“this”).]

For just as nothing prevents something from being called “ineffable,” although what is called ineffable cannot be said; and just as “the inconceivable” can be conceived, although that to which the name “inconceivable” applies cannot be conceived; so, when it is said, “that than which nothing greater can be conceived,” there can be no doubt that what is heard can be conceived and understood, even if the thing than which nothing greater can be conceived cannot itself be conceived or understood. [Note: Col. 0257C: Some manuscripts read *si enim nihil* (“for if nothing”) for *sicut enim nihil* (“for just as nothing”). The printed apparatus repeats the reading concerning *non cogitabile* (“the inconceivable”); Corbie reads *quod non auditur* (“what is not heard”) for *quod auditur* (“what is heard”), and the witnesses vary between *quo majus* and *qua majus* in the relative phrase.]

For even if someone is so foolish as to say that there is not something than which something greater cannot be conceived [Note: Col. 0259B: The manuscripts read *aliquod* rather than *aliquid*, an indefinite-form variation.], he will not be so shameless [Note: Col. 0259B: Some manuscripts read “so imprudent”; another reads “so foolish”] as to say that he cannot understand or conceive what he is saying. [Note: Col. 0259B: Some manuscripts read “that he cannot understand what he is saying.”] And if such a person is found, not only must his speech be rejected, but he himself must also be spat upon. 40

Whoever, therefore, denies that there is something than which nothing greater can be conceived, certainly understands and conceives the denial that he makes. [Note: Col. 0259B: The manuscripts read “the denial” or “because of the denial” instead of “the denial that he makes.”] But he cannot understand or conceive that denial without its parts; and one of its parts is “that than which nothing greater can be conceived.” Whoever, therefore, denies this understands and conceives that than which nothing greater can be conceived.

It is also clear that, in the same way, one can conceive and understand that which cannot not exist. [Note: Col. 0259B: One manuscript reads “that which can fail to exist.”] But the person who conceives this conceives something greater than the person who conceives what can fail to exist. [Note: Col. 0259B: One manuscript omits this comparison.]

When, therefore, one conceives that than which nothing greater can be conceived, if one conceives that it can fail to exist, one does not conceive that than which nothing greater can be conceived. [Note: Col. 0259B: The manuscripts variously read: “When that than which nothing greater can be conceived is conceived, if what can be conceived as greater is conceived…”; “When that than which nothing greater can be conceived is conceived, but what can fail to exist is conceived…”; and “When that than which nothing greater can be conceived is conceived, if what can fail to exist is conceived, that than which nothing greater can be conceived is not conceived.”] Yet the same thing cannot simultaneously be conceived and not conceived.

Therefore, whoever conceives that than which nothing greater can be conceived does not conceive something that can fail to exist, but something that cannot fail to exist.

It is therefore necessary that what he conceives exist, because whatever can fail to exist is not that which he conceives.

[Col. 0260A]

## CHAPTER X

The firmness of the foregoing argument, and the conclusion of the little book.

I think I have shown that, in the little book mentioned above, I proved by an argument that is not weak but sufficiently necessary that something exists in reality than which nothing greater can be conceived, and that the strength of this argument cannot be weakened by any objection. [Note: Col. 0259B: One manuscript reads “that something greater than which nothing can be conceived”; another reads “that the argument cannot be weakened by weakness” instead of “by any objection.”]

For the meaning itself contains such force that what is said is, by necessity, proved by that very fact by which it is understood or conceived to exist in reality; and it is proved to be precisely whatever must be believed concerning the divine substance. For we believe concerning the divine substance whatever can absolutely be conceived to be better than not to be. [Note: Col. 0259B: One manuscript reads “whatever can absolutely be conceived”; the Corbie manuscript reads “by you.”]

For example, it is better to be eternal than not eternal; good than not good; indeed, goodness itself than not goodness itself. But nothing of this kind can fail to exist which is that than which something greater cannot be conceived. [Note: Col. 0259B: One manuscript reads “nothing of this kind can not exist,” that is, “nothing of this kind can fail to exist.”]

Therefore, that than which nothing greater can be conceived must exist, whatever ought to be believed concerning the divine essence.

I give thanks to your kindness [Note: Col. 0259B: Victorine 13 reads “your goodness.”] both for your criticism and for your praise of my little work. [Note: Col. 0259B: Victorine 3 and Cîteaux read *hujus prolationis* (“of this statement”) for *hujus probationis* (“of this proof”); Corbie reads *quo majus aliquid cogitari* (“than which something greater can be conceived”); and the source’s *infirmari infirmitate* is the Victorine-3 reading for *infirmari firmitate*.] For when you have extolled with such praise those things which seemed to you worthy of acceptance, it is sufficiently evident that you criticized those things which seemed weak to you out of benevolence, not malevolence. [Note: Col. 0259B: The manuscripts read “you detected” rather than “you criticized.”]

[Note: The manuscripts Gemmeticum and C. 54, together with Saint-Michael’s manuscript, conclude: “Here ends Anselm’s response to Gaunilo, monk of Marmoutier.”]

[Col. 0259B]

# SAINT ANSELM’S BOOK ON THE FAITH OF THE TRINITY AND ON THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD, AGAINST THE BLASPHEMIES OF RUZELINUS OR ROSCELINUS

[Note: Col. 0259C: The book on the faith was collated with the manuscripts of Gemmeticum, Corbie 307, Cîteaux, Saint-Michael-on-the-Mount, and the two Victorine manuscripts EE 13 and RR 3, as well as the two Thuan manuscripts 30 and 546. The Corbie manuscript begins: “Here begins Anselm’s Letter on the Incarnation of the Word, or on the Christian faith, to Pope Urban.” Thuan manuscript 90 begins: “Here begins Anselm’s Letter on the Incarnation of the Word to Pope Urban, against the blasphemies of Ruzelinus of Compiègne.”]

[Col. 0259C]

## 41. PREFACE

Although after the apostles many holy Fathers and teachers of ours have said so many and such great things about the rationale of our faith, in order to refute the foolishness and break the hardness of unbelievers, and to feed those who, with their hearts already cleansed by faith, take delight in the rationale of that same faith—which, after its certainty has been established, we ought to hunger for—so that we may expect no one, either in our own times or in the future, to equal them in contemplation of the truth, nevertheless I do not think anyone should be reproached if, firmly established in faith, he wishes to exercise himself in investigating its rationale. [Note: Col. 0259C: Corbie reads *ratione dicunt* (“they speak concerning the rationale”) for *ratione dicant*, and *confundendam* (“to confound”) for *confutandam* (“to refute”). It also reads *possent dici, si* (“might be said, if …”) for *possent, si* (“might [have said], if …”).]

For they too, because “our days are short” (Job XIV, 58), could not say everything they might have said had they lived longer; and the rationale of truth is so vast and so profound that it cannot be exhausted by mortals; and the Lord does not cease to bestow the gifts of his grace upon his Church, with which he promises to be until the consummation of the age.

To say nothing of the other passages by which sacred Scripture invites us to investigate its rationale, when it says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VII, 9), it openly urges us to extend our intention toward understanding, while teaching how we ought to advance toward it. [Note: Col. 0261D: The Corbie manuscript reads “it openly urges” rather than “it openly urges us.”]

Finally, since I understand that the intellect which we attain in this life stands midway between faith and vision, I believe that the more anyone advances toward it, the nearer he approaches vision, for which we all long.

Strengthened, therefore, by this consideration, although I am a man of very little learning, I sometimes try to rise toward contemplating the rationale of the things we believe, insofar as heavenly grace deigns to grant me the ability. [Note: Col. 0261D: The Corbie manuscript reads “I shall try to rise” instead of “I sometimes try to rise.”] And whenever I discover something that I did not previously see, I gladly disclose it to others, so that I may learn from another’s judgment what I ought to hold securely.

Therefore, my father and lord, Pope Urban—beloved with reverence by all Christians and to be revered with love, whom God’s providence has established as supreme pontiff in his Church—since I can present it to no one more appropriately, I submit the little work that follows to the sight of your holiness, so that by your authority the things in it that ought to be accepted may be approved, and those that ought to be corrected may be amended.

To the lord and father of the whole Church that is journeying on earth, the supreme pontiff URBAN: brother ANSELM, a sinner in life, a monk in habit, called bishop of the metropolitan see of Canterbury, whether by God’s command or permission, offers due submission, with humble service and devoted prayers.

Since divine providence has chosen your holiness as the one to whom it would entrust the preservation of the Christian life and faith and the governance of its Church, it is most appropriately referred to no one else if anything contrary to the Catholic faith arises in the Church, so that it may be corrected by his authority. Nor is anything more safely presented to anyone else if a response is made against error, so that it may be examined by his prudence.

Therefore, just as I can entrust this letter to no one more worthily, so I send it to no one more willingly than to your wisdom, so that, if anything in it requires correction, it may be disciplined by your judgment, and whatever adheres to the rule of truth may be strengthened by your authority. [Note: Col. 0261D: Thuan manuscript 546 reads “and whatever holds to the rule of truth may be strengthened by your authority.” Thuan manuscript 30 omits this clause; another reads “and whatever the rule of truth holds.”]

## CHAPTER I

The occasion for writing, and the state of the question.

While I was still abbot at the monastery of Bec, a certain cleric in France ventured to make the following assertion:

“If in God,” he said, “the three persons are only one thing, and are not three things, each separately in itself, as are three angels or three souls, though they are entirely the same in power and will, then the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate together with the Son.”

When this was reported to me, I began a letter against this error, but, after publishing part of it, I abandoned its completion, believing that it was not necessary. For the man against whom it had been written had abjured his error at a council gathered by the venerable archbishop of Reims, Raynald, and no one seemed unaware of his error.

Nevertheless, certain brothers, without my knowledge, transcribed the part I had written and gave it to others to lament. I say this so that, if that portion should come into anyone’s hands, although there is nothing false in it, it may nevertheless be left as incomplete and unpolished; and so that what I began there may here be sought more carefully begun and completed.

After I had been seized and detained in England for the episcopate, by some disposition of God of which I know nothing, I heard the author of the aforementioned novelty persisting in his opinion and saying that he had abjured what he said for no other reason than that he feared being killed by the people. [Note: Col. 0261D: The manuscripts read “he heard” instead of “I heard.”]

For this reason certain brothers compelled me by their prayers to resolve the question in which he was so entangled that he believed he could in no way extricate himself from it, unless he either became entangled in the incarnation of God the Father and the Holy Spirit or in a plurality of gods. [Note: Col. 0261D: The manuscripts read *expediri ab ea crederet* (“believed that he was being extricated from it”) for *expediri ab ea posse crederet* (“believed that he could be extricated from it”); the printed Gothic edition reads *de eorum* (“of them”) for *deorum* (“of gods”); and several witnesses read *multiplicatione se* for *multitudine se*.]

I beg that no one think I presumed to do this as though I considered the firmness of the Christian faith to need the assistance of my defense. For if I, a contemptible little man, with so many holy and wise men existing everywhere to confirm the bulwark of the Christian faith, were to attempt to write as though it needed my defense, I could rightly be judged presumptuous and might seem worthy of ridicule.

If people saw me trying to support Mount Olympus with stakes, ropes, and other things by which unstable objects are usually laboriously tied and stabilized, lest it waver or be overturned by anyone’s push, it would be astonishing if they restrained themselves from laughter and ridicule. [Note: Col. 0261D: The manuscripts read “they would restrain themselves” instead of “they restrain themselves.”] How much more would this be so when the stone cut from the mountain without hands struck and crushed the statue that Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream, and, having become a great mountain, filled the whole earth? [Note: Col. 0261D: The manuscripts variously read “the stone that was cut from the mountain”; “and it struck”; “in his dream”; “it became a mountain”; and “and it filled.”] If I should strive to support it with my arguments and stabilize it as though it were wavering, all the holy and wise men who rejoice that they are themselves established upon its eternal firmness might rightly be indignant with me, and attribute this not to serious diligence but to the lightness of boastful vanity. [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts read “to boastful lightness” instead of “to the lightness of boastful vanity.”]

If, therefore, I discuss anything about the firmness of our faith in this letter, it is not to confirm that faith, but to satisfy the prayers of the brothers who demanded this of me. [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts read *petitionibus* (“petitions”) for *precibus* (“prayers”); several witnesses read *in epistola* for *in hac epistola*; and the source records *jactabundae levitati* (“boastful lightness”) for *jactantiae levitati* (“the lightness of boastfulness”).]

But if the man who put forward the aforementioned opinion has returned to the truth through God’s correction, let him not suppose that I am speaking against him in this letter, for he is no longer what he was. If he was once darkness, but now is light in the Lord, the darkness that no longer exists should not be reproved, but the light that shines should be approved.

Nevertheless, whether he has already returned to the light or not, since I perceive that many are troubled by the same question, and that faith in them surpasses the reasoning which seems to oppose their faith, it does not seem useless to me to dissolve this apparent opposition.

[Col. 0263B]

## CHAPTER II

That the questions of sacred faith which we discuss or investigate should be undertaken humbly not by just any dialecticians, but by those experienced in the sacred Scriptures.

Before I discuss the question, however, I shall say something to restrain the presumption of those who, with unspeakable recklessness, dare to dispute against something confessed by the Christian faith because they cannot grasp it intellectually. In foolish pride they judge that what they cannot understand cannot exist at all, rather than acknowledging with humble wisdom that many things can exist which they themselves cannot comprehend. [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts and printed Gothic edition read *multa quae* (“many things which”) for *multa posse quae* (“many things can [exist] which”); the manuscripts also read *quoniam quod catholica* for *quomodo quod catholica*.]

No Christian ought to dispute how something that the Catholic Church believes in her heart and confesses with her mouth can fail to be. Rather, always holding the same faith without doubt, loving it, and living according to it, he should humbly seek, insofar as he can, the rationale of how it is. [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts read “how it cannot be”; the printed Gothic edition omits “how.”]

If he can understand, let him give thanks to God; if he cannot, let him not thrust out horns to toss it about, but bow his head in veneration. For human wisdom, trusting in itself, can more quickly stumble and tear out its own horns than it can, by straining against it, uproot this rock. [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts read “by leaning upon it, uproot it”; another reads “by striving, overturn it.”]

Some people, when they begin, as it were, to grow the horns of their confident knowledge, do not know that “if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know how he ought to know.” [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts variously read “the horns of confidence”; “the horns of professed knowledge”; and “the horns of confessing knowledge.”] Before they have acquired spiritual wings through the solidity of faith, they presumptuously attempt to rise into the highest questions concerning faith.

Thus it happens that, while they try prematurely to ascend by understanding to those matters which first require the ladder of faith, as it is written, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VII, 5), through the failure of their understanding they are compelled to descend into manifold errors.

For it is clear that those who, because they cannot understand what they believe, dispute against the truth of that same faith confirmed by the holy Fathers do not possess the firmness of faith. They are like bats and owls who, seeing the sky only at night, argue about the rays of the midday sun against eagles who gaze upon the sun itself with an unflinching sight.

The heart must therefore first be cleansed by faith, as is said of God: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 9). The eyes must first be illuminated through keeping the Lord’s commandments, because “the commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm XVIII, 9). And through humble obedience to the testimonies of God we must first become little ones, so that we may learn the wisdom which “the faithful testimony of the Lord gives, granting wisdom to the little ones” (Psalm XVIII, 8).

Hence the Lord says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones” (Matthew XI, 25). [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts read “Father, Lord” rather than “Lord, Father.”]

First, I say, we must put aside the things of the flesh and live according to the spirit before we investigate the profound matters of faith by judgment. [Note: Col. 0263D: One manuscript reads “propose” instead of “put aside.”] For the one who lives according to the flesh is carnal, or animal, and of him it is said: “The animal person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians II, 14).

But the one who puts to death the deeds of the flesh through the spirit becomes spiritual; of him it is written that “the spiritual person judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one” (ibid., 15).

It is true that the more abundantly we are nourished in sacred Scripture by those things which feed us through obedience, the more sublimely we are advanced toward those things which satisfy us through understanding. [Note: Col. 0263D: Thuan omits *quia* in “For it is true that”; other witnesses read *sine vitae* (“without life”) for *sine fide* (“without faith”) in the ensuing statement.] For he tries in vain to say, “I have understood more than all who teach me” (Psalm CVIII, 99), if he does not dare to say, “For your testimonies are my meditation” (ibid.).

And he falsely declares, “I have understood more than the elders,” if what follows is not familiar to him: “Because I sought your commandments.” [Note: Col. 0263D: The manuscripts read “the commandment” instead of “your commandments.”] Certainly, this very thing that I am saying is true: whoever does not believe will not understand. For whoever has not believed will not experience; and whoever has not experienced will not understand. [Note: Col. 0263D: One manuscript reads “will not know” instead of “will not understand.”]

As experience surpasses merely hearing about a thing, so the knowledge of one who has experienced it surpasses the knowledge of one who has merely heard. The mind is not only prevented from ascending to higher understanding without faith and obedience to God’s commandments, but sometimes even the understanding that has been given is withdrawn, and faith itself is overturned when a good conscience is neglected.

For the Apostle says of certain people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Romans I, 21). And when he commanded Timothy to wage the good warfare, he said: “Having faith and a good conscience; by rejecting these, some have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith” (1 Timothy I, 19). [Note: Col. 0263D: The printed Gothic edition reads “But he says” instead of “For the Apostle says.”]

Let no one, therefore, recklessly plunge into the dense thickets of divine questions unless he has first acquired, in the solidity of faith, the gravity of character and wisdom, lest, running about with incautious levity through the many byways of sophisms, he become caught in some tenacious falsehood. [Note: Col. 0265D: The witnesses read *mergat in* for *immergat in*; some read *difficillimarum* (“most difficult”) for *divinarum* (“divine”); and others read *in tanta levitate* (“with such levity”) for *incauta levitate*.] [Note: Col. 0265D: The manuscripts read “the most difficult questions” instead of “divine questions”; other manuscripts and the printed Gothic edition read “with such incautious levity.”]

And while everyone must be admonished to approach the questions of sacred Scripture with the greatest caution, those dialecticians of our time—or rather, heretics in dialectic—who think that universal substances are nothing but a breath of voice, who cannot understand color as anything other than a body, and who understand the wisdom of a human being as nothing other than the soul, must be expelled entirely from discussion of spiritual questions. [Note: Col. 0265D: The manuscripts and printed Gothic edition variously read “dialectical heretics”; “who indeed do not think…”; and “who cannot understand color as anything except a body.”]

For in their souls reason—which ought to be both ruler and judge of everything that exists in a human being—is so wrapped up in bodily images that it cannot free itself from them, nor distinguish from them those things which it ought to contemplate by itself and in purity. [Note: Col. 0265D: Some witnesses omit *et* in “both ruler and judge”; Thuan 546 reads *in imaginibus* (“in images”) for *in imaginationibus* (“in imaginings”); and the witnesses vary between *quae ipsa sola et pura* and *quae sola et pura ipsa* (“those things which it itself alone and purely ought to contemplate”).] [Note: Col. 0265D: One Thuan manuscript reads “bodily likenesses” instead of “bodily images”; the manuscripts variously read “those things which it alone and purely ought to contemplate.”]

Whoever does not yet understand how several human beings are one human being in species, how will he comprehend, in that most secret and exalted nature, how several persons, each one of whom is perfect God, are one God?

And whose mind is too obscure to distinguish between his horse and its color—how will he distinguish between one God and his several relations? [Note: Col. 0265D: The manuscripts read “obscured” or “darkened” instead of “too obscure,” and “to judge” instead of “to distinguish.”]

Finally, whoever cannot understand that something is a human being except as an individual will in no way understand a human being except as a human person. Every individual human being is a person. How, then, will such a person understand that a human being was assumed by the Word, but not a person—that is, that another nature, not another person, was assumed?

I have said this so that no one may presume to investigate the highest questions concerning faith before he is fit to do so; or, if he does presume, so that no difficulty or impossibility of understanding may be able to shake him loose from the truth to which he has adhered through faith. [Note: Col. 0265D: One manuscript reads “discuss him” instead of “shake him loose.”]

Now we must come to the matter for which we began.

## CHAPTER III

That there are not three gods; and although there are three personal things, there is nevertheless one essential thing.

He says (as I hear) that the one who is said to maintain that the three persons are like three angels or three souls argues as follows. [Col. 0266A] The pagans defend their law; the Jews defend their law; therefore we Christians too ought to defend our faith. Let us hear how this Christian defends his faith.

“If,” he says, “the three persons are only one thing, and are not three things, each separately in itself, as three angels or three souls are—yet in such a way that they are altogether identical in will and power—then the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate together with the Son.”

See what this man says; see how this Christian defends his faith. Surely he either wishes to confess three gods, or does not understand what he is saying. But if he confesses three gods, he is not a Christian; and if he asserts what he does not understand, he must not be believed.

This man should not be answered by the authority of sacred Scripture, because either he does not believe it, or he interprets it in a perverse sense. For what could sacred Scripture say more clearly than that God is one and alone? [Note: [Col. 0265D] “Than that God is one”: the manuscripts of Thuanus read “than because God is one.”] His error, therefore, must be demonstrated by the reasoning with which he attempts to defend himself.

To do this more easily and briefly, I shall speak only of the Father and the Son, since these two persons are plainly designated as distinct from one another by their proper names. For the name “Holy Spirit” is not alien from the Father and the Son, because each is both Spirit and holy. Whatever, then, we discover in the Father and the Son concerning unity of substance or plurality of persons, we shall undoubtedly recognize in the three. [Note: [Col. 0265D] “We shall undoubtedly recognize”: the manuscripts read “we undoubtedly recognize.”]

Let him therefore say: If the two persons, the Father and the Son, are not two things, let us first ask what he wishes to mean by “two things.” For we believe that each person is what is common to both and what is proper to that person.

The person of the Father is God, which is common to him with the Son; and he is Father, which is proper to him. [Note: [Col. 0265D] “Which is proper to him”: the manuscripts of Victorinus, Corbie, Cisterciensis, the edition, and the Gothic edition read “which is proper to him.”] Likewise, the person of the Son is God, which is common to him with the Father; and he is Son, which is said of this person alone. Thus, in these two persons there is one common element, namely God, and two proper elements, namely Father and Son. [Note: [Col. 0265D] “One common element, namely”: the manuscripts of Thuanus read “one element which is common, namely.”]

Whatever is common to them—such as omnipotent and eternal—is understood in this one common element. What is proper to each—such as “begetter” or “begetting” with respect to the Father, and “Word” or “begotten” with respect to the Son—is signified by these two names, Father and Son. [Note: [Col. 0265D] “As is Father, begetter”: the edition and Gothic edition read “as is for the Father, begetter.”]

When, therefore, he says that these two persons are two things, I ask what he says are the two things: is it what is common to them, or what is proper to each? [Note: [Col. 0265D] “What he says are two things”: the manuscripts of Cisterciensis, Saint Michael, Gembloux, Victorinus, and the Gothic edition read “what he says there are two things.”]

But if he says that the two things are the two proper elements, namely the Father and the Son, while the common element is not several things but one and only one thing, he says this superfluously. For no Christian confesses that the Father and the Son, according to these two proper elements, are one thing; rather, he confesses them to be two.

We customarily use the word “thing” of whatever we in some manner say to be something. Whoever says “Father” or “Son” of God says something of him. Everyone knows that in God the Father is not the Son and the Son is not the Father, although in one human being the father may be the son and the son may be the father, if the same person is both father and son. This occurs because in God these terms are spoken in relation to one another, whereas in one human being they are not spoken in relation to one another: he is called father in relation to one son and son in relation to another father.

In this sense, therefore, there is nothing to prevent us from saying that the two persons, the Father and the Son, are two things—provided that we understand what sort of things they are. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “What sort of things they are”: the manuscripts read “what sort of things are the things.”]

For the Father and the Son are not two things in such a way that their substance is understood in these two things, but rather their relations. Yet by what he adds he plainly shows that he does not understand “two persons are two things” in this way.

For when he says, “If the three persons are only one thing and not three things,” he adds, “each separately in itself.” [Note: [Col. 0267D] “There are two things there”: the manuscripts of Cisterciensis, Saint Michael, Gembloux, Victorinus, and the Gothic edition read “that there are two things there.”] He seems to posit a separation of such a kind as would prevent father and son from being simultaneously in the same human being. Through this separation alone he thinks he can free the Father from sharing in the incarnation with the Son. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “He can free himself”: the manuscripts of Gembloux, Victorinus, Thuanus, and Saint Michael read “free himself.”] For by that separation whereby being Father is one thing and being Son another—since paternity and sonship are distinct from one another—if he believes that there is one and only one God who is both Father and Son, he does not see that the Father and the Son can be separated without nevertheless being simultaneously in the same human being. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “And being Son is another”: the manuscripts of Victorinus and Cisterciensis read “and being Son is another”; the manuscript of Corbie reads “another being Son.”] [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Since paternity and sonship are distinct”: the manuscripts read “for paternity and sonship are distinct.”]

Either, then, he means a separation of the persons of the Father and the Son other than that by which, according to their proper relations, the Father and the Son are distinct from one another—for by this separation he does not understand the incarnation to be alien from the Father; indeed, if the Father and the Son are together, he supposes that it follows that the Father shares in the incarnation with the Son—or, if he means that separation, he labors in vain, as I have already said, because the Christian faith understands the Father and the Son to be two things in this sense.

But when he says, “As there are three angels or three souls,” he plainly shows that he is not speaking of that plurality or separation which exists in those persons according to what is proper to them. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Which exists in those”: the manuscripts read “which is in them.”]

Certainly, two angels are never said of one and the same thing numerically, nor are two souls; nor is one thing numerically said of two angels or of two souls, as we say “Father” and “Son” of one God numerically, and “one God” numerically of the Father and the Son.

For we believe and say that God is Father and that God is Son; and conversely, that the Father is God and the Son is God. Yet we neither believe nor say that there are several gods, but that there is one God numerically, just as there is one nature, although the Father and the Son are not one person but two.

We speak of an angel and a soul according to substance, not according to relation. For although the name “angel” is taken from an office, because an angel is called a messenger, nevertheless, just as “soul” is taken as a kind of substance, so too is “angel.” [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Is taken from an office”: the manuscripts of Gembloux, Corbie, Victorinus, and Cisterciensis read “is said from an office.”]

He shows that he understands this when he says together, “As there are three angels or three souls.” Thus he signifies a plurality and separation such as several angels or souls possess, that is, such as several substances possess. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “He signifies a plurality”: the manuscripts read “he indicates a plurality.”] [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Such”: the manuscripts of Corbie, Gembloux, Victorinus, and Cisterciensis read “and such.”]

He seems to show this even more plainly when he adds, “Yet in such a way that they are altogether identical in will and power.” For he understands will and power in those several things as they exist in several angels or souls. This cannot be understood if those several things are thought to exist according to the properties of the persons, rather than according to what is predicated of them in common. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “According to what is predicated of them in common”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “or according to what is predicated of them in common.”]

For, according to their proper properties—that is, according to paternity and sonship—the Father and the Son have no will or power; they have these according to the substance of divinity, which is common to them. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “And sonship”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “or sonship.”]

Therefore, if he says that the three persons are three things according to their proper properties, it is obvious how superfluously he says this, and how inappropriately, when he adds, “As there are three angels or three souls.” [Note: [Col. 0267D] “When he adds: ‘As’”: the manuscripts read “when he adds; ‘as.’”]

But if he says that the same persons are two things according to what is common to them, namely according to the fact that each individually and all together are one perfect God, I ask first whether he is a Christian. He will answer, I think, that he is. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “That he is”: the manuscripts read “that he is this.”]

Then he believes that there is one God, and that this God is three persons, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that only the person of the Son was incarnate, while the other two cooperated with him.

Whoever believes this declares that the one who wishes to assert anything contrary to these points is not a Christian. If, then, he himself believes this, he denies that the one who argues against these points is a Christian. Let us see, therefore, whether he himself attempts to subvert this faith. [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Against these”: the manuscripts read “against this.”]

When, then—to speak of two persons as I began, though the same applies to the three—he says that if the two persons are one thing and not two, as there are two angels or two souls, it follows that the Father too is incarnate if the Son is incarnate, I think he reasons with himself in this way: [Note: [Col. 0267D] “He reasons with himself”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis omits “with himself.”]

“If God is one and the same thing numerically, and that same thing is both Father and Son, then, since the Son is incarnate, how can the Father not also be incarnate?” [Note: [Col. 0267D] “And is Son”: the manuscripts read “and is Son”; the manuscript of Corbie reads “and Son.”]

For of one and the same thing it is not possible for an affirmation and its negation to be true simultaneously; but it is entirely possible to affirm something of one thing and deny that same thing of another. Peter the apostle, for example, is not both an apostle and not an apostle. But if the same person is affirmed to be an apostle under one name and denied to be an apostle under another—“Peter is an apostle, and Simon is not an apostle”—the two statements are not both true; one of them is false.

But “Peter is an apostle, and Stephen is not an apostle” can be true, since Peter is one person and Stephen another. Therefore, if the Father is the same thing numerically as the Son, and not another thing, it is not true that something should be affirmed of the Son and denied of the Father, or affirmed of the Father and denied of the Son. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Affirmed of the Father”: the manuscripts of Thuanus, Victorinus, Gembloux, and Corbie read “affirmed of the Father.”]

Whatever the Father is, therefore, the Son also is; and whatever is said of the Son ought not to be denied of the Father. Now the Son is incarnate; therefore the Father too is incarnate.

But if this reasoning is true and valid, it is the heresy of Sabellius. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “If this reasoning is true and valid”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “if this reasoning is true”; the manuscript of Corbie reads “if this reasoning is valid.”] For if whatever is said of one person is also said of the other because one thing is two persons, then just as “Son,” “Word,” and “begotten” are said of the Son, so they will be said of the Father. And just as the Father is Father, begetter, and unbegotten, so these terms must be said of the Son.

But if this is so, the Father is not other than the Son, nor is the Son other than the Father. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Nor is the Son other than the Father”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “nor is the Son another than the Father.”]

Therefore there are not two persons but one person. For they are called two persons precisely because the Father and the Son are believed to be distinct from one another—provided that God is Father and Son.

For the Father is always the father of someone, and the Son is always the son of someone; the Father is never the father of himself, nor is the Son the son of himself. Rather, the father is one person and the one whose father he is another; likewise, the son is one person and the one whose son he is another.

Therefore, if in God there is not one who is Father and another whose Father he is, nor one who is Son and another whose Son he is, then it is falsely said that God is Father or Son. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “There is one who is Father and another whose Father he is”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “there is one who is Father, another whose Father he is.”] For if in God there is no one other than the Father of whom he is Father, he cannot be Father; and likewise, if there is no one in him other than the Son of whom he is Son, he cannot be Son. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Nor the Son”: the manuscripts read “nor likewise the Son.”]

Consequently, there will be no basis for calling those two persons persons in God—although they are called so because God is Father, God is Son, and the Father is always one and the Son another. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “And the Son another”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “and another son.”] [Note: [Col. 0269D] “And another son”: the manuscript of Cisterciensis reads “and another son. You see.”]

You see, then, how according to the reasoning of the one who thinks that the Father must be incarnate together with the Son our faith is destroyed, if the several persons in God are one thing and not several things.

For if his inference is true, not only will this follow concerning the Father and the Son, but in all three persons such confusion will result that whatever is said properly of each individual person must be said commonly of all.

Accordingly, there will be no basis for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son to be distinct from one another, as I have shown in the case of the Father and the Son. Therefore there will be no relation there either, since relation exists there only according to the fact that they are distinct from one another. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “According to the fact”: the manuscripts of Victorinus, Thuanus, and Saint Michael read “according to this, according to which.”]

Nor, then, will there be several persons.

For if three persons are posited as one thing, either what he says will not follow, or all the consequences I have mentioned will follow together; for the force of the inference is the same in every case. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “What he says will not follow”: the manuscripts read “what follows does not follow.”] Why, then, does he proceed to the incarnation as though that alone created the difficulty, rather than saying instead: “If the three persons are one thing, they are not three persons”? For this difficulty can be raised no less before the incarnation than after it.

But if he wishes to maintain outright that the three persons, insofar as each is God, are not one thing but three things, each existing separately, as three angels do, it is perfectly clear that he establishes three gods.

Perhaps, however, he himself does not say, “As there are three souls or three angels,” but the one who submitted his question to me supplied this comparison from his own resources; perhaps he merely asserts that the three persons are three things, without adding any comparison. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Only three persons”: the manuscripts read “only three persons.”]

Why, then, does he deceive himself or deceive others under the name “thing,” when the same meaning is expressed under the name “God”? Either he will deny that God is the thing in which—or rather whom—we confess the three persons to exist, or, if he does not deny this, it follows that, just as he asserts that the three persons are not one thing but three things, so he must also affirm that the same persons are not one God but three gods. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “But three gods”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “that they are three gods, which.”]

Let Christians judge how impious this is.

But he will say that what I say does not force him to admit that three things are three gods, because those three things together are one God.

And we reply: Then each individual thing among those three—that is, each individual person—is not God, but God is composed from the three things. Therefore the Father is not God, the Son is not God, and the Holy Spirit is not God, since God is to be predicated neither of each one individually nor of two, but only of the three named together. This too is impious.

For if this is so, the nature is not simple but composed of parts. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “The nature is not simple”: the manuscripts read “God is not a simple nature.”]

But if he has a simple understanding and is not clouded by a multiplicity of imaginings, he understands that simple things are superior to composite things insofar as simplicity and composition are concerned. For every composite thing must be capable of being divided either in reality or in thought; whereas this cannot be understood of simple things. No intellect can dissolve into parts what cannot be conceived as having parts.

If, then, God is composed of three things, either no nature is simple, or there is some other nature superior in some respect to God’s nature. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Must be capable of being divided either in reality or in thought”: the manuscripts read “must be capable of being divided either in thought or in reality.”] It is obvious how false both alternatives are.

And if this man belongs to those modern dialecticians who believe that nothing exists except what they can grasp through their imaginings, and who do not think that anything exists in which there are no parts, he will either not deny that he understands the following: if there were something that could be dissolved neither in reality nor in thought, it would be greater than what can be dissolved even in thought. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “He does not think”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “they do not think.”]

Thus, if every composite can at least be dissolved in thought, when he says that God is composite, he says that he can understand something greater than God. His intellect therefore passes beyond God—something no intellect can do.

But let us see what he adds, as though to ward off the absurdity that seems to arise if those three persons are three things. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “What he adds”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “what he adds.”]

“Yet,” he says, “in such a way that one will and power belong to the three things.”

Here we must ask whether those three things are divine according to the fact that they are understood separately from one another; or according to their common will and power; or neither according solely to what they possess separately nor according to what they have in common, but according to both together.

For if they possess divinity according to what they are separately, there will be three gods; and they could be understood without will and power. Proper properties are always understood distinctly from common properties, and common properties from distinct ones.

But the divine nature cannot be understood at all without will and power. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Without will and power”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “without will.”] If, then, according to one common will and power, each individually, each pair, and all three together are God, what do those three discordant things contribute? They cannot agree into the unity of divinity except through something else, nor do they contribute anything toward perfection or toward any assistance by which God might be God. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “So that they may be God”: the manuscripts read “so that they may be.”]

For if one will and power is sufficient for God’s perfection, what are those three things which God needs, or for what does he need them? We believe that God needs nothing. Those three things, therefore, are conceived in God to no purpose.

But if neither those three things alone nor will and power alone, but all these together, constitute God, I say again that he is composite, and that things which are not God in themselves, or gods, make God. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “If not the three things alone”: the manuscripts read “but if not the three things alone.”] [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Those three things alone”: the manuscripts read “the three things alone.”] [Note: [Col. 0271D] “I say again”: the manuscripts read “I say again.”]

Or if he says that those three things have the name “God” through power and will, just as a man is called king through royal power, then “God” is not the name of a substance; rather, those—I know not what—three things are called three gods accidentally, just as three men possessing the same royal power are called three kings. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Three things, three gods”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “three things, three gods.”] For three men cannot be one king. It is unnecessary to say how impious this is.

A large book would have to be filled if I wished to write out the absurdities and impieties that follow if it is true that, when one person of God is incarnate, the other two must also be incarnate because the three persons are one thing according to what we say of the three in common; or if they are three separate things, as the man against whom I have argued thinks, since only the Son is incarnate. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “What we say of the three”: the manuscripts read “what is said of the three.”] [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Since only”: the manuscripts read “how only.”]

It is therefore clear that one should not be eager to debate profound matters, especially matters in which one cannot err without danger.

## CHAPTER IV

It is impossible for the three persons to be incarnate when the Son is incarnate; yet incarnation is more fitting for the Son than for the Father or the Holy Spirit.

But perhaps this man will say to me: “Just as you think that the things you mention follow together by necessity, so the consequence that I assert appears necessary to me. Therefore show that what I say does not follow, and I will agree with you that no absurdity follows if only the Son is incarnate, or if the three persons are one thing.

“If you fail to demonstrate this, you do not resolve the question but entangle it further, since you yourself prove with me that innumerable absurdities arise. If these absurdities are to be denied, then we must both conclude alike either that the three persons are not one thing if only the Son is incarnate, or that, if they are one thing, all three are equally incarnate.” [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Innumerable absurdities arise”: the manuscripts of Gembloux, Victorinus, Corbie, and Thuanus read “innumerable absurdities arise from this.”]

It must therefore be shown where this man is mistaken, and how the incarnation of the Son alone does not entail that the three persons are three separate things, or, if the three persons are one thing, that all of them are incarnate.

That God is one and only one, individual and simple in nature, and three in persons, has been argued by the holy Fathers—and especially by blessed Augustine, after the apostles and evangelists—with unconquerable arguments.

And if anyone should be willing to read my two short works, the *Monologion* and the *Proslogion*, which were composed especially so that what we hold by faith concerning the divine nature and its persons, apart from the Incarnation, might be proved by necessary reasoning without the authority of Scripture; if, I say, anyone wishes to read them, I think that there too he will find arguments concerning this matter which he will neither be able to reject nor wish to disregard. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Especially for this”: the manuscripts read “especially for these things.”]

If in those works I have set down something which I have either not read elsewhere or do not remember having read—not as though I were teaching something unknown to our teachers, or correcting what they stated inadequately, but perhaps as saying what they left unsaid, though it does not conflict with their statements but coheres with them—I do not think that I ought on this account to be reproached. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Which I have either not read”: the manuscripts read “or which I have not read.”] [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Or correcting”: Thuanus reads “or not correcting.”]

I wrote these things either to respond in defense of our faith against those who, unwilling to believe what they do not understand, mock believers; or to assist the devout study of those who humbly seek to understand what they firmly believe. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Unwilling to believe”: the manuscripts read “willing to believe.”] I therefore do not think that I should be censured for this.

Nevertheless, so that I do not impose upon the readers of this letter the labor of seeking out other writings in order to know not only by faith but also by evident reasoning that the three persons are not three gods but one alone, and yet that, when God is incarnate according to one person, it does not follow by necessity that the same God is incarnate according to the other persons, I believe that I should add here something sufficient to repel the opinion of this defender of our faith, as he himself thinks.

He plainly says either that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate together with the Son, or that the three persons are three separate things. He evidently considers this separation to be such that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit is in the Son. For if the two other persons are in the Son, and the Son is in the human being, then those two persons are in the human being as well. Hence he thinks it follows that, since the three persons are simultaneously in the same human being if they are one thing, the person of the Son cannot be incarnate in that human being without the other two persons.

Yet he does not deny that there are three persons, nor that the Son is incarnate.

Therefore, since it has been shown above that, if the three persons are three separate things, either it follows that there are three gods or that there are the other absurdities already discussed, I shall now show briefly, with the assistance of the one and only God, first that even if there were three gods, this would not help him defend the Father and the Holy Spirit against incarnation—which he thinks cannot be done without a plurality of gods. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “This would help him”: the manuscript of Saint Michael reads “these would help him.”]

Next I shall show that there are not several gods but one alone. Finally, I shall make clear that, although there is one God and three persons, the incarnation of one person does not make it necessary for the others also to be incarnate; rather, this is impossible. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “But this is impossible”: the manuscripts of Gembloux, Saint Michael, and Thuanus read “it would be impossible.”]

It belongs to the divine nature always and everywhere to exist in such a way that nothing ever or anywhere exists without its presence. Otherwise it would not be powerful everywhere and always; and what is not powerful everywhere and always is in no way God.

If he says that it is not the divine substance itself but its power that is always and everywhere, he will nevertheless not deny that power is either accidental or substantial to it. Power is not accidental to God, because, since every subject can exist or be understood without an accident, God cannot exist or be understood without power.

If power is substantial to God, then either it is a part of his essence or it is identical with his entire essence. But it is not a part, because, as was said above, whatever has parts is divisible either in reality or in thought; and this is wholly foreign to God. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Or is a part of it”: the manuscripts read “or is its part.”]

Therefore God’s being and his power are identical. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “His power”: the manuscripts of Gembloux, Victorinus, Corbie, and Thuanus read “his powers.”]

Just as God’s power is always and everywhere, so whatever is God is always and everywhere.

Therefore, when the aforementioned defender of our faith asserts, in accordance with his own position, that there are three gods, he cannot show how they are separate according to the separation by which he thinks he can free the Father and the Holy Spirit from incarnation.

The plurality of gods therefore cannot help him defend the Father and the Holy Spirit against incarnation, because in that multiplication of gods he cannot find the distinction without which he thinks this defense cannot be made. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “The distinction”: Thuanus, Gembloux, and Cisterciensis read “the disjunction.”]

That there is one and only one God, and not several, is easily proved as follows: either God is not the supreme good, or there are several supreme goods, or there are not several gods but one alone.

No one denies that God is the supreme good, since whatever is less than something else is in no way God, and whatever is not the supreme good is less than something, because it is less than the supreme good.

The supreme good certainly does not admit plurality in itself, so that there might be several supreme goods. For if there were several supreme goods, they would be equal. But the supreme good is that which surpasses other goods in such a way that it has neither an equal nor anything superior to it. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “But the supreme good”: the manuscripts read “therefore the supreme good is.”]

The supreme good, therefore, is one and alone. There are not several gods, then, but one and only one God, just as the supreme good is one and alone; and just as supreme substance, or essence, or nature is proved by the same reasoning to be incapable of being spoken of in the plural. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “So supreme substance”: the manuscripts read “so supreme substance.”] [Note: [Col. 0273D] “In the plural”: the manuscripts read “the supreme good cannot be spoken of in the plural.”]

Although this one and only God is three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—it does not follow, when the Son is incarnate, that the other persons too must be incarnate, as that disputant thinks; rather, it is impossible. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Although this one God is three”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “although they are three.”]

He does not deny that there are several persons, precisely because they are distinct from one another. For if they were not distinct from one another, they would not be several.

To explain this more briefly and speak more easily about what I want, I shall speak only of the Father and the Son, as I did above, because through them it will be clear what should be understood concerning the Holy Spirit.

According to substance, then, the Father and the Son are not several, nor are they distinct from one another, because they are not two substances, nor is the Father one substance and the Son another; rather, the Father and the Son are one and the same substance. [Note: [Col. 0275D] “The Father one substance, the Son another”: the manuscripts read “the substance of the Father, another of the Son.”] According to person, however, they are several and distinct from one another, because the Father and the Son are not one and the same person, but two persons, distinct from one another. [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Distinct from one another”: the manuscripts read “distinct from one another.”]

He therefore says: “If the Son is incarnate, and the Son is not another thing but one and the same thing numerically as the Father is, then the Father too must be incarnate.” [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Which the Father is”: the manuscripts read “which the Father is.”] For it is impossible for one and the same thing numerically both to be incarnate and not to be incarnate in the same human being.

And I reply: If the Son is incarnate, and the Son is not one and the same person numerically as the Father, but another, it does not follow for that reason that the Father too is incarnate. [Note: [Col. 0275D] “For that reason it is necessary that the Father be incarnate”: the manuscripts read “for that reason it is necessary that the Father too be incarnate.”] For it is possible for one person to be incarnate in one human being and another person simultaneously not to be incarnate in that same human being.

And he says: “If God the Son is incarnate, and God who is Son is not another but one and the same God numerically as the Father, then, although the Father and the Son are distinct persons, it nevertheless seems more necessary that the Father too be incarnate with the Son, because of the identity of the Godhead, than that he be able, because of the diversity of the persons, not to be incarnate together with him.” [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Because of the identity”: Victorinus and Corbie read “because of the unity.”] [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Not to be incarnate together with him”: the manuscripts read “that he not be incarnate together with him.”]

See how the one who says this limps on both feet in the incarnation of the Son of God. For whoever rightly accepts his incarnation believes that he did not assume a human being into unity of nature, but into unity of person.

This man, however, dreams that the human being was assumed by the Son of God more into unity of nature than into unity of person. For if he did not think this, he would not say that it is more necessary for the Father to be incarnate with the Son because the Father and the Son are one God than that it is possible for him not to be incarnate simultaneously because they are several persons. [Note: [Col. 0275D] “For the Father to be incarnate with the Son”: the manuscripts of Gembloux, Corbie, Victorinus, and Thuanus read “for the Father to be with the Son incarnate.”]

Thus whoever thinks of the incarnation of the Son of God—who is one in nature with the Father and distinct in person from the Father—as being according to unity of nature, so that the Son cannot be incarnate without the Father, and fails to understand it as being according to unity of person, so that the Father cannot be incarnate with the Son, limps on both feet—that is, in both respects—in the incarnation of the Son of God. [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Because he is one”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “because he is one.”]

God did not assume a human being in such a way that the nature of God and of the human being is one and the same, but in such a way that the person of God and of the human being is one and the same; and this can occur only in one person of God.
