For it cannot be understood that diverse persons are one and the same person with one and the same human being. If one human being is one person with each of several persons, it necessarily follows that several persons, who are distinct from one another, are one and the same person—which is impossible.

Consequently, when God is incarnate according to one person, it is impossible that he should also be incarnate according to another person.

## CHAPTER V [formerly IV]

Why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, was incarnate.

Why, then, did God assume man into the unity of the person of the Son rather than into the unity of one of the other persons? Although this was not our purpose in this letter, nevertheless, since mention of the matter has arisen, I think that some explanation ought to be given.

[Col. 0275D] **Note:** The manuscripts read *propositum non fuit* (“this was not the purpose”); the base text has *propositum non fuerit* (“this may not have been the purpose”). Indeed, if the Holy Spirit had become incarnate, just as the Son became incarnate, the Holy Spirit would be the son of a human being. There would therefore be two sons in the Trinity of God: namely, the Son of God and the son of man. Hence a certain confusion of doubt would arise whenever we spoke of God the Son; for each would be God and Son, although one would be the Son of God and the other the son of man. There would also be a kind of inequality among the different persons insofar as they were sons—although they ought to be altogether equal—since one son would excel through the dignity of the greater parent, while the other would be subject to the lowliness of the lesser parent. For just as the nature of God is greater than that of man, so it is more worthy to be the Son of God than to be the son of man.

[Col. 0275D] **Note:** Manuscripts S. Mich. and the Gothic edition read *qui omnino* (“who altogether”), rather than *quae omnino* (“which altogether”). Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. read *quam Filium hominis* (“than the Son of Man”), rather than *quam esse Filium hominis* (“than to be the Son of Man”).

[Col. 0275D] **Note:** *Magis assumpsit* (“he assumed more readily”) is found in the manuscripts Gem., Vict., and Corb.; the base text has *magis assumpserit* (“he should have assumed more readily”).

Therefore, if the Holy Spirit had been born of the Virgin, while the Son of God possessed only the more excellent birth, which is from God, and the Holy Spirit only the lesser birth, which would be from a human being, one person would be greater and the other lesser according to the dignity of birth.

[Col. 0275D] **Note:** *Secundum dignitatem nativitatis* (“according to the dignity of birth”) is found in manuscript Cister.; another reading is *secundum nativitatem dignitatis* (“according to the birth of dignity”).

This is not fitting. But if the Father had assumed man into the unity of his own person, the plurality of sons would produce the same improprieties in God, and yet another one. For if he were the son of the Virgin, two persons in the Trinity would assume the name “grandson”: the Father would be a grandson of the Virgin’s parents, and her Son would also be a grandson, although he himself would have received nothing from the Virgin.

[Col. 0275D] **Note:** *Pater nepos* (“the Father would be a grandson”) is the reading here; manuscripts Vict. and Corb. and the Gothic edition have *Pater et nepos* (“the Father and a grandson”).

Since, therefore, even the slightest impropriety in God is impossible, no person of God other than the Son ought to have become incarnate.

[Col. 0275D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *quodlibet parvum* (“any small [impropriety]”); the base text reads *quamlibet parvum* (“however small [an impropriety]”).

Once he became incarnate, no impropriety follows. For although the Son is said to be less than the Father and the Holy Spirit according to his humanity, those two persons do not therefore surpass the Son, because the Son also possesses that same majesty by which they are greater than the Son’s humanity, and by which he himself, together with them, presides over his humanity.

[Col. 0275D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *debuit alia persona* (“another person ought to have”); the base text reads *debuit alia Dei persona* (“another person of God ought to have”).

There is another reason why incarnation is more fitting for the Son than for another person. The one who was to become incarnate was to pray for the human race; and the human mind much more readily accepts that the Son should make petition to the Father than that one person should supplicate another, although this supplication is made not by divinity but by humanity toward divinity. The Son of God does this because, through the unity of person, he is the Son of God as man.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *satis convenientius* (“more fittingly enough”); the base text reads *convenientius satis* (“quite suitably”).

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. has *alii supplicare* (“that another should supplicate another”); the base text reads *alium aliis supplicare* (“that one should supplicate another”).

Moreover, the one who was to assume man was to come to fight against the devil and to intercede, as I said, for human beings.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** Manuscript Vict. 3 has *si hominem* (“if he were to assume man”); the base text reads *qui hominem* (“the one who was to assume man”).

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. has *pro homine* (“for man”); the base text reads *pro hominibus* (“for human beings”).

Both the devil and man sought through usurpation to make themselves like God, since they used their own will. And because they sought this through usurpation, they could do so only through falsehood, since they could will it only unjustly.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *nisi per falsitatem* (“only through falsehood”); another reading is *nisi falsitatem* (“only falsehood”).

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *injuste potuerunt* (“they could do so unjustly”); another reading is *injuste voluerunt* (“they willed it unjustly”).

For the will proper to an angel or a human being is that which is contrary to the will of God. When someone wills what God forbids him to will, he has no author of his will except himself; and therefore it is his own will. For although a human being sometimes submits his will to the will of another human being, it is nevertheless his own if it is contrary to God, since he submits it only in order to attain something that he wills; and therefore he himself is the author of the reason for which he submits it to another.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts Gem., Corb., S. Mich., and Vict. 3 have *ut ad aliquid quod* (“in order to attain something which”); the base text reads *ut aliquid quod* (“in order to attain something which”).

Accordingly, the will is proper to someone when it is subject to no other will. God alone has a will proper to himself—that is, one subject to no other will. Whoever, therefore, uses a will proper to himself strives through usurpation to become like God and is convicted, insofar as it lies within him, of depriving God of his proper dignity and unique excellence. For if there were some other will that was subject to no one, God’s will would not be supreme over all, nor would it alone be the will over which no other will presides.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts Vict. and Corb. and Cister. have *erit ipsa sola* (“it alone will be”); Thu. omits *ipsa* (“it”).

Therefore, among the three persons of God, none could more fittingly have emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), in order to overthrow the devil and intercede for man, than the Son—against whom both the devil and man, in presuming a false likeness of God by usurpation, had sinned. He is the radiance of eternal light and the true image of the Father, and he did not consider it usurpation to be equal with God (ibid., 6); rather, through true equality and likeness, he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts Corb. and Vict. 3 have *praesumpserat* (“had presumed”); the base text reads *praesumpserant* (“had presumed,” plural).

For no one more justly attacks the guilty, punishes him, spares him more mercifully, or intercedes for him than the one against whom the wrong is shown to have been committed in a special way. Nor is anything more fitting set against falsehood to defeat it, or applied to heal it, than truth.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. has *excellunt filio* (“they surpass the Son”); another reading is *excellent filio* (“they excel the Son”).

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *opponitur ad salvandum* (“is set against [falsehood] for salvation”); the Gothic edition has *apponitur ad sanandum* (“is applied for healing”), as in the base text.

For those who presumed upon a false likeness of God seem to have sinned especially against the one who is believed to be the true likeness of God the Father.

## CHAPTER VI [alternatively IV]

### How there are not two persons in Christ, as there are two natures

As has been said, he assumed man into the unity of person, so that there are two natures—namely, divine and human—but one person. We most firmly believe that this unity of person does not arise from two persons in Christ. Nevertheless, since one may say something from which it could appear to those who look upon the matter carelessly that Christ exists from two persons and in two persons, it does not seem useless to me to say something about it.

For some say: How can we say that there are not two persons in Christ, as there are two natures? God was already a person before the assumption of man, and after he assumed man he did not cease to be a person. The assumed man is also a person, since every individual human being is known to be a person. Therefore, the person of God, which existed before the incarnation, is one person, and the assumed man is another, just as Christ is God and man. Thus there appear to be two persons in him.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *quia alia* (“because [the person] is another”); the base text has *quare alia* (“therefore [the person] is another”).

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *quomodo dicis* (“how do you say”); the base text reads *quomodo dicimus* (“how do we say”).

This reasoning seems to prove that there are two persons in Christ because God is a person and the assumed man is a person. But this is not so. Just as in God there is one nature and several persons, and several persons are one nature, so in Christ there is one person and several natures, and several natures are one person.

For just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and yet there are not three gods but one God, so in Christ God is a person and man is a person, and yet there are not two persons but one person.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts Vict., Corb., Cister., and the Gothic edition have *duae sunt personae, sed* (“there are two persons, but”); the base text has *duae sunt, sed* (“there are two, but”).

For Christ is not one person as God and another as man, although God is one thing and man another; rather, the very one who is God is also man.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *Deus, qui et homo* (“God, who is also man”); the base text reads *Deus, et qui homo* (“God, and he who is man”).

The Word made flesh assumed another nature, not another person. For when the word “man” is uttered, it signifies only the nature common to all human beings. But when we say demonstratively “this man” or “that man,” or use the proper name “Jesus,” we designate a person who, together with the nature, has a collection of properties by which the common human nature is individualized and distinguished from other individuals.

[Col. 0277D] **Note:** The base text has *quibus homo communis sit singulus* (“by which the common human being is an individual”). Manuscripts Corb. and Vict. read *communis fit singulis* (“becomes common to individuals”); another reading is *communis fit singulus* (“becomes common to each individual”).

For when he is designated in this way, just any human being is not understood, but the one who was announced by the angel, who is God and man, the Son of God and the Son of the Virgin. Whatever is said about him is truly said either according to God or according to man.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *angelo annunciatus* (“announced by the angel”); another reading is *angelo nunciatus*, with the same meaning.

The Son of God cannot be designated or named personally without the son of man, nor the son of man without the Son of God, because the very one who is the Son of God is the son of man; and the collection of the properties of the Word and of the assumed man is one and the same.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *quicquid de illo dicitur* (“whatever is said about him”); manuscript Cister. omits *dicitur* (“is said”).

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** Manuscripts Corb. and Vict. read *cum vero Verbum* (“but when the Word”), rather than *cum ergo Verbum* (“therefore, when the Word”).

It is impossible, however, for different persons to have the same collection of properties or to be predicated of one another. For the collection of properties belonging to Peter and Paul is not the same; Peter is not called Paul, nor Paul Peter.

Therefore, when the Word became flesh, he assumed a nature that alone is signified by the name “man,” and that is always different from the divine nature. He did not assume another person, because he has the same collection of properties as the assumed man.

For “man” and “the man assumed by the Word,” that is, Jesus, are not the same thing. In the name “man,” as has been said, only the nature is understood; whereas in “the assumed man,” or in the name “Jesus,” what is understood together with the nature—that is, with the man—is the collection of properties that is the same in the assumed man and in the Word.

Therefore, we do not say that the Word and man simply considered are the same person, lest we say that that man has the same person as the Word no more than any other man does. Rather, we say that the Word and that assumed man, namely Jesus, are the same person.

Likewise, we do not believe that the same man is simply the same person as God, but that he is the same person as that person who is the Word.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** Manuscripts Corb., Vict., and Cister. have *quae Verbum est, et* (“which is the Word, and”); another reading is *quae Verbum et* (“which is the Word and”).

Otherwise, we might appear to confess that the man himself is the same person as the Father or the Holy Spirit. But since the Word is God and that assumed man is man, it is true to say that God and man are the same person. In the name “God,” however, the Word must be understood, and in the name “man,” the Son of the Virgin must be understood.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *subintelligendus est* (“must be understood”); the base text reads *subaudiendus est* (“must be understood”).

## CHAPTER VII [alternatively VI]

### That the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three separate things, demonstrated by the natural example of Adam and Abel

Of the position of the man to whom I am replying in this letter, I have been able to see nothing except what I set out above.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *supra dixi* (“I said above”); the base text reads *supra posui* (“I set out above”).

But I think that the truth of the matter is so evident from what I have said that no intelligent person can fail to see that nothing said against it possesses the force of truth.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *nulli lateat intelligenti* (“may be hidden from no intelligent person”); Thu. has *nullum lateat intelligenti* (“may hide no one intelligent”).

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *quod ab illo dicitur* (“what is said by him”); the base text reads *quod contra illam dicitur* (“what is said against it”).

But if, having been recalled from a multitude of gods, he rejects plurality among the persons in God, he does this because he does not know what he is talking about. For he does not conceive of God or his persons, but something like this: persons such as the several human persons are. And because he sees that one human being cannot be several persons, he denies the same of God.

For the three persons are not called three because they are three separate things, as three human beings are, but because they bear a certain likeness to three separate persons.

Let us consider this in the Father and the Son, and let the same be understood of the Holy Spirit. Let us suppose, then, a man who is only a father and not a son, and his son, who is only a son and not a father—that is, Adam and Abel.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts Thu. and the Gothic edition have *qui tantum filius sit* (“who is only a son”); another reading omits *sit* (“be”).

We therefore say of Adam the father and of Abel the son that the father is not the son and the son is not the father, because Adam and Abel are two human beings and separate persons. Adam is not anyone’s son, nor is Abel anyone’s father.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *et de Abel Filio* (“and concerning Abel the Son”); the base text reads *et Abel Filio* (“and Abel the Son”).

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** Manuscripts Corb. and Vict. have *pater sit Abel* (“Abel be a father”); another reading is *pater est Abel* (“Abel is a father”).

Thus we confess in God that the Father is not the Son and the Son is not the Father, although there are not two gods, because the Father does not have a father, nor the Son a son. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son, because he is not anyone’s father or anyone’s son.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. have *nec de* (“nor of”); another reading is *et nec de* (“and not of”).

Therefore, since the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three, distinct from one another, and cannot be predicated of one another—as we have shown with the father and son among separate human persons—they are called three persons, not because they are three separate things.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *at si negat* (“but if he denies”); other readings are *ac si negat* (“and if he denies”) and *aut si negat* (“or if he denies”).

But if he denies that three can be said of one and one of three, while the three are not said of one another—as we affirm concerning these three persons and one God—because he does not see this in other things and therefore cannot understand it in God, let him for a little while endure something that his intellect cannot penetrate as existing in God.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *ut tria* (“so that three”); another reading is *cum tria* (“when three”).

Let him not compare a nature that is above all things, free from every law of place, time, and composition of parts, with things confined by place or time or composed of parts. Rather, let him believe that something exists in that nature which cannot exist in these things, and let him submit to Christian authority; let him not argue against it.

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The base text has *sufferat aliquid* (“let him endure something”); one manuscript has *sufferat paulisper per aliquid*, apparently “let him endure for a little while through something.”

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. has *liberam ab omni lege* (“free from every law”); the base text reads *libera ab omni lege* (“free from every law”).

[Col. 0279D] **Note:** The base text has *auctoritati Christianae* (“to Christian authority”); the manuscripts have *auctoritate Christi* (“by the authority of Christ”).

48 ## CHAPTER VIII [alternatively VII]

### He explains the origin of the persons in the divine nature by the likeness of a spring, a stream, and a pool

Let us nevertheless see whether, among created things—which are subject to the law of place, time, and composition of parts—what he denies in God can be found to some extent.

Let us suppose a spring from which a stream is born and flows, and which afterward gathers into a pool; and let its name be Nile. We accordingly speak distinctly of the spring, the stream, and the pool, so that we do not call the spring the stream or the pool; nor the stream the spring or the pool; nor the pool the spring or the stream.

Yet the spring is called Nile, the stream Nile, and the pool Nile. The spring and stream together are Nile; the spring and pool are Nile; the stream and pool are Nile; and all three together—the spring, the stream, and the pool—are Nile. Nevertheless, there is not one Nile and another Nile, but one and the same Nile, whether each one individually, two together, or all three are called Nile.

There are therefore three—the spring, the stream, and the pool—and one Nile, one river, one nature, one water. Yet it cannot be said what the three are. For there are neither three Niles, nor three rivers, nor three natures, nor three waters; nor are there three springs, three streams, or three pools.

Thus one is predicated of the three, and three of one; yet the three are not predicated of one another.

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *hic de tribus* (“this is predicated of the three”); another reading is *hoc de tribus* (“this is predicated of the three”).

If he objects that each individual thing—the spring, the stream, or the pool—or the two together is not the perfect Nile but a part of the Nile, let him consider the whole Nile, from the moment it begins until it ceases to be, throughout what may be called its entire lifetime. For the whole Nile itself is not simultaneously present either in place or in time, but exists in parts, nor will it be complete until it ceases to be.

In this respect the Nile has a certain likeness to speech: as long as speech is proceeding, as it were, from the spring of the lips, it is not complete; and when it is complete, it no longer exists.

For if someone considers the matter in this way and understands it carefully, he will recognize that the whole Nile is the spring, the whole Nile is the stream, and the whole Nile is the pool; yet the spring is not the stream or the pool, nor the stream the spring or the pool, nor the pool the spring or the stream.

The spring itself is not the stream or the pool, although the stream and the pool are the very same thing as the spring—namely, the same Nile, the same river, the same water, and the same nature.

Three things, then, are here predicated of one complete whole, and one complete whole is predicated of the three; yet the three themselves are not predicated of one another. Although the matter is very different and much more perfect in that most simple nature, which is entirely free from every law of place, time, and composition of parts, nevertheless, if this can be seen to some extent in a thing composed of parts and subject to place and time, it is not incredible that it exists perfectly in that supremely free nature.

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The base text reads *tria igitur hic* (“three things, therefore, are here”); the manuscripts and Gothic edition have *tria igitur haec* (“these three things, therefore”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscripts Vict., Corb., and the Gothic edition have *de uno toto perfecto* (“of one complete whole”); another reading is *de uno perfecto* (“of one complete thing”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. has *quamvis hoc aliter* (“although this is otherwise”); another reading is *quamvis haec aliter* (“although these things are otherwise”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. has *omni lege loci vel temporis liberrima* (“entirely free from every law of place or time”); the fuller reading is “free from every law of place, time, or composition of parts.”

Here, too, we must observe that the spring does not come from the stream or from the pool; the stream, however, comes from the spring alone, not from the pool; while the pool comes from the spring and from the stream. Thus the entire stream comes from the entire spring, and the entire pool both from the entire spring and from the entire stream, just as we say of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscripts S. Mich., Cister., and the Gothic edition have *de solo fonte est, non* (“comes from the spring alone, not”); another reading is *de solo fonte, non* (“from the spring alone, not”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. have *et ita totus* (“and thus the entire”); another reading is *et ita ut totus* (“and thus so that the entire”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscripts Vict., Corb., and Cister. have *sicut dicimus in* (“just as we say in”); another reading is *sic dicimus in* (“so we say in”).

And because the stream comes from the spring in one way, while the pool comes from the spring and the stream in another way, so that the pool is not called the stream, in another corresponding way the Word is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Word in another way, so that the Holy Spirit is not the Word or the Son, but the one proceeding.

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. omits *modo* (“way”) in *et alio modo* (“and in another way”). Manuscripts Cister., Vict., Corb., and Gem. read *sic suo quodam modo alio* (“thus in some other way of its own”), rather than *sic suo quodam alio modo* (“thus in some other way of its own”).

I still wish to say something which, although it has great dissimilarity, nevertheless bears some likeness to the incarnation of the Word. Perhaps someone reading this will despise it, but I shall say it nonetheless, because if someone else had said it, I would certainly not despise it.

If the stream flows through a conduit from the spring all the way to the pool, is not the stream alone—as I may put it, although it is not a different Nile from the spring and the pool—“conduited”? So only the Son became incarnate, although he is not a different God from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscripts Corb., Vict., and S. Mich. have *sic solus Filius* (“thus the Son alone”); another reading is *sicut solus Filius* (“just as the Son alone”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** Manuscript S. Mich. has *quam Pater et Spiritus sanctus* (“than the Father and the Holy Spirit”); manuscripts Cister. and Vict. 3 have *quam Pater et Filius et Spiritus* (“than the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit”).

[Col. 0282B]

## CHAPTER IX [alternatively VIII]

### That eternity is one and simple; he compares it with a point

Since these earthly things are very far removed from the supreme nature, let us, with its assistance, raise our mind toward it and contemplate in it, briefly and to some extent, what we are saying.

God is nothing other than simple eternity itself.

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *simpliciter aeternitas* (“simply eternity”); the base text reads *simplex aeternitas* (“simple eternity”).

Several eternities cannot be understood. For if there are several, they are either outside one another or within one another. But nothing is outside eternity; therefore eternity is not outside eternity. Again, if they are outside one another, they are in different places or times, which is alien to eternity. Thus there are not several eternities outside one another.

But if several are said to exist within one another, it must be understood that however often eternity is repeated within eternity, it is only one and the same eternity.

For a nature that, when repeated within itself, always agrees with itself in perfect unity is more worthy than one that admits plurality within itself. For where there is plurality, there is diversity; but where there is diversity, there is not perfect harmony. Perfect harmony is that which converges into one identity and the same unity.

If, then, perfect harmony is better than imperfect harmony, and it is impossible for anything imperfect to exist in the supreme good, which is eternity itself, the nature of eternity cannot admit plurality.

Therefore, however often eternity is repeated within eternity, it is always one and the same eternity.

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The manuscripts read *una et eadem aeternitas est* (“it is one and the same eternity”); manuscript Cister. reads *una eademque et sola aeternitas est* (“it is one, the same, and sole eternity”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The base text has *dignior est natura* (“the nature is more worthy”); other readings are *dignior est autem natura* (“the nature, however, is more worthy”) and *dignior enim natura est* (“for the nature is more worthy”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The base text has *ubi diversitas est, non est perfecta concordia* (“where there is diversity, there is not perfect harmony”); another reading is *ubi diversitas, ibi non est perfecta concordia* (“where there is diversity, there is not perfect harmony”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The manuscripts have *perfecta namque est* (“for that is perfect”); another reading is *perfecta namque concordia est* (“for perfect harmony is”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The base text has *quae in unam identitatem et eandem* (“which converges into one identity and the same [unity]”); another reading is *quae in identitatem et eandem* (“which converges into identity and the same [unity]”).

[Col. 0281D] **Note:** The base text and the Gothic edition have *si ergo* (“if, then”); the manuscripts have *sic ergo* (“thus, then”).

The same is said similarly of many other things: omnipotence within omnipotence is nothing but one omnipotence.

And, to give one example among things that do not possess the divine nature, in which the same principle is found: a point within a point is nothing but a point. For a point—such as the central point of the world, or a point of time, that is, the present moment in relation to eternity—bears a considerable likeness useful for contemplating that same eternity. This must be discussed more fully elsewhere.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The manuscripts vary considerably here. One reading is: “Let me offer this: a point in a point is nothing but a point. For a point, as the center of the world, and a point of time, that is, the present moment, has some likeness to eternity.” Another has: “Let me offer this: a point in a point is nothing but one point, like the center of the world. For a point, and a point of time—that is, the present moment—has some likeness to eternity.” Other manuscripts read: “Let me offer this: a point in a point is nothing but one point. For a point, like the central point of the world, and the middle point of time, that is, the present moment, has some likeness to eternity.”

For the present, let this suffice: a point is simple—that is, without parts—and indivisible, like eternity. Therefore, a point together with a point, without any interval, is nothing but one point, just as eternity together with eternity is nothing but one eternity.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The base text has *hic tantum hoc sufficiat* (“for the present let this suffice”); manuscript Thu. has *hoc tantum hic sufficiat* (“let this alone suffice here”).

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** Manuscript Thu. has *simplex, id est, sine partibus, et indivisibile est, velut* (“simple, that is, without parts, and indivisible like”); other manuscripts slightly alter the word order but retain the same distinction.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The manuscripts have *sic aeternitas* (“so eternity”); the base text reads *sicut aeternitas* (“just as eternity”).

Therefore, since God is eternity, there are not several gods, because God is not outside God, nor does God within God add number to God.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The base text has *nec Deus est extra* (“nor is God outside”); the manuscripts have *nec Deus extra* (“nor God outside”).

God is therefore always one and the same and alone.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The base text has *idem et solus est* (“is the same and alone”); manuscripts Vict. and Corb. have *idem est solus* (“is the same alone”).

When, then, God is born from God—for what is born is not outside that from which it is born—the offspring is in the parent and the parent in the offspring: one God, namely the Father and the Son. And when God proceeds from God the Father and the Son, he does not go outside God; God remains in God, namely the Holy Spirit in the God from whom he proceeds.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** Manuscript Cister. omits *cum* (“when”) in *vel cum Deus procedit* (“or when God proceeds”). Thus there is one God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

And because this birth and this procession are without beginning—for otherwise eternity would have been born and eternity would have proceeded, which is false—we must neither think nor can we think that God began to be Father, Son, or Holy Spirit.

Just as the divine substance preserves eternal and singular unity, so the nature of these relative terms—namely, Father and Son, the one proceeding and the one from whom he proceeds—maintains an inseparable plurality.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The manuscripts read *tenet cum unitate pluralitatem* (“maintains plurality together with unity”), omitting *cum unitate* (“together with unity”) in the alternative reading.

For just as it is necessary that God always be one and the same, and not one and another, so the Father is never the same as his Son, nor is the one proceeding the same as the one from whom he proceeds, according to these relations. The Father is always one and the Son another; the one proceeding is another and the one from whom he proceeds another; and they can never be predicated of one another.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The manuscripts have: “The Father is one, and the Son is another; the one proceeding is another than the one from whom he proceeds.” The base text reads: “The Father is always one and the Son another; and the one proceeding is another and the one from whom he proceeds another.”

Therefore, since when God is born from God, or when God proceeds from God, neither can the substance lose its singularity nor the relation its plurality, there is here one and three, and three and one; yet the three are not predicated of one another. Nor should it be considered incredible that in a nature which is above all things and unlike all other things there should be something whose example cannot be perfectly found in other things.

The Latins call these three “persons”; the Greeks call them “substances.” Just as we say in God that there is one substance and three persons, so they say that there is one essence and three substances.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** Manuscript S. Mich. has *unam essentiam, tres substantias* (“one essence, three substances”); another reading is *unam personam, tres substantias* (“one person, three substances”).

By “substance” they signify there the same thing that we signify by “person,” and they do not differ from us at all in faith.

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The base text has *idipsum ibi per substantiam* (“the same thing there by ‘substance’”); the manuscripts have *idipsum per substantiam* (“the same thing by ‘substance’”).

How the Son is born from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and yet is not the Son—since how this is so cannot be seen in this life—blessed Augustine carefully contemplated, as in a mirror and in an enigma, in his book on this very Trinity (Book IX, chapter 12; Book II, chapter 3; Book XII, chapter 5; Book XV, chapter 26). I too discussed it, according to my ability, in my *Monologion* (chapter 55, alternatively 53).

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The manuscripts have *in aenigmate* (“in an enigma”); another reading is *et in aenigmate* (“and in an enigma”).

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The manuscripts have *meo, pro* (“in my [work], for”); another reading is *meo, cuius supra memini, pro* (“in my [work], which I mentioned above, for”).

Anyone who wishes to know why, although there is no sex in the supreme essence, the parent is called Father rather than Mother, and the offspring Son rather than Daughter; or why the Father alone is unbegotten, the Son alone begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, will find the answer clearly in the same little book (chapter 56, alternatively 55).

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The manuscripts have *cur in summa* (“why in the supreme [essence]”); the base text reads *cur cum in summa* (“why, although in the supreme [essence]”).

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. omit *cur* (“why”) in the question “why the parent is called Father rather than Mother.”

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** The base text has *aperte inveniet* (“will find clearly”); the manuscripts have simply *inveniet* (“will find”).

[Col. 0283C] **Note:** Manuscript Gemm.: “The Book of Saint Anselm on the Incarnation is complete.” The Venetian edition of 1547: “The Letter of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Incarnation of the Word is complete.” Manuscript Thu. 30: “The Letter of Anselm to Pope Urban, on the Incarnation of the Word, against the blasphemies of Roscelin of Compiègne, is complete.”

[Col. 0285]

# THE BOOK OF SAINT ANSELM ON THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AGAINST THE GREEKS

[Col. 0285A]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** This book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* was collated with the manuscripts from Bec, Gembloux, and three Victorine manuscripts previously designated CC 9, EE 13, and RR 3; with two manuscripts from the Thuane collection, namely 30 and 90; with one Corbie manuscript, 307; with one Cistercian manuscript; with one manuscript from the library of Saint Michael on the Mount, in which the work is incomplete; and with the Gothic edition. Manuscript Vict. 3: “A little book published by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Procession of the Holy Spirit.” Manuscript Cister.: “Here begins the book of the same author on the Procession of the Holy Spirit.” Manuscript Corb. 307: “The Book of Anselm on the Procession of the Holy Spirit.” In the Corbie manuscript it appears in the form of a prologue.

The Greeks deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, as we Latins confess. Nor do they accept our Latin teachers, whom we follow in this matter. Since they venerate the Gospels together with us and, in other matters concerning the triune and one God, believe in every respect what we do, and since we are certain about the same reality, I hope—through the help of that same Holy Spirit—that, if they prefer to submit to solid truth rather than contend for an empty victory, they can be rationally led, by means of what they confess without ambiguity, to accept what they do not accept.

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** Manuscripts Bec., Gem., Vict., Corb., and the Gothic edition have *auxilium ejusdem Spiritus* (“the help of that same Spirit”); another reading is *auxilium Spiritus* (“the help of the Spirit”).

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** The base text has *inani victoria* (“empty victory”); the manuscripts have *inani gloria* (“empty glory”).

Although there are many who could accomplish this better than I, nevertheless, since many impose this task upon me, I dare not resist their request, both because of my duty to the love of truth and because of their affection and religious purpose.

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** The base text has *multi sint* (“there may be many”); the manuscripts have *multi sunt* (“there are many”).

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** The base text has *a pluribus hoc injungitur* (“this is imposed upon me by many”); another manuscript has *a pluribus injungitur* (“is imposed upon me by many”).

I invoke that same Holy Spirit, asking him to deign to guide me toward this end. Therefore, with this hope, and in the humility of my knowledge, leaving higher matters to those more learned, I shall undertake what they request.

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** The base text has *meae scientiae* (“of my knowledge”); manuscript Vict. 13 has *meae conscientiae* (“of my conscience”).

I shall use the faith of the Greeks and the things that they believe and confess confidently as the most certain arguments for proving what they do not believe.

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. have *quae credunt* (“the things which they believe”); another reading is *qui credunt* (“those who believe”).

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** The base text has *et confitentur* (“and confess”); the manuscripts have *et confidenter* (“and confidently”).

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** The Gothic edition and the base text have *pro certissimis argumentis ad probandum quod* (“as the most certain arguments for proving what”); the manuscripts have *pro certissimis argumentis ad reprobandum quod* (“as the most certain arguments for refuting what”).

## CHAPTER ONE

### The faith concerning the Trinity that is common to Latins and Greeks

[Col. 0285C] **Note:** Manuscript Corb. contains the heading “Chapter 1.”

They indeed believe that there is one and only one perfect God, that he has no part, but is wholly whatever he is. They also confess that this one is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that whether only the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit is named; whether two together—the Father and the Son, the Father and the Holy Spirit, or the Son and the Holy Spirit; or whether all three together—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are named, the same whole and perfect God is designated [Note: [Col. 0285C] “The whole perfect” in the manuscripts: “whole and perfect”]. Yet the name “Father” or “Son” does not signify the same thing as the name “God.” For “to be God” is not the same as “to be Father” or “to be Son.”

The name “Holy Spirit,” however, is used as a relative name, because the Holy Spirit is understood to be the spirit of someone. For although the Father is spirit and holy, and the Son is spirit and holy, the Father is not the spirit of someone, nor is the Son the spirit of someone [Note: [Col. 0285C] “Yet the Father is not someone’s father” in the manuscripts: “the Father is not the spirit of someone”]. The Holy Spirit, however, is the spirit of someone: he is the Spirit of God, and the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. Although the Greeks deny that he proceeds from the Son, they do not nevertheless deny that he is the Spirit of the Son.

They also believe and confess that God is from God by being born, and that God is from God by proceeding [Note: [Col. 0285C] “That God is from God by proceeding” in the manuscripts: “that God is God from God by proceeding”], because the Son is God from God the Father by being born, and the Holy Spirit is God from God the Father by proceeding [Note: [Col. 0285C] “The Holy Spirit is from the Father” in the manuscripts: “the Holy Spirit is God from the Father”]. Nor do they think that the God who is born is other than the one from whom he is born, or that the one who proceeds is other than the one from whom he proceeds. Nevertheless, according to the names signifying that there is one from whom someone is born, one who is born from someone, and one who proceeds from someone, plurality is admitted; and according to this plurality the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are more than one and are distinct from one another.

For when God is called “Father,” he is signified as the one from whom someone is born; when he is called “Son,” he is understood to be the one who is born from someone; and when the Holy Spirit is named [Note: [Col. 0285C] “The Holy Spirit is named” in manuscript Cistercianus: “is called”], because we understand not simply spirit but the Spirit of God, he is shown to be the one who proceeds from someone. But when it is said that the Son is from the Father and that the Holy Spirit is from the Father [Note: [Col. 0285C] “And the Holy Spirit from the Father” in the manuscripts: “and the Holy Spirit is from the Father”], it is understood that what the Son is or what the Holy Spirit is, they have from the Father [Note: [Col. 0287D] “He has from the Father” in the manuscripts and the Goth edition: “they have from the Father”].

Yet the Son is understood to be from the Father in one way, and the Holy Spirit in another. The Son is from his Father, that is, from God who is his Father; but the Holy Spirit is not from God as his Father, but only from God who is the Father. Therefore, insofar as the Son is from God, he is called God’s Son, and the one from whom he is, his Father. The Holy Spirit, however, is not God’s son insofar as he is from God [Note: [Col. 0287D] “He is called his son” in the manuscripts: “he is his son”], nor is the one from whom he is his father.

It is also certain that God is not the Father, Son, or Spirit of anyone except God [Note: [Col. 0287D] “Or the Spirit of anyone except God” in the manuscripts of Corbie and Victor 3: “or the Holy Spirit of anyone except God”], and that nothing is God except the same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And just as there is one God, so there is only one Father, one Son, and one Holy Spirit.

Thus it follows that in that Trinity the Father is father only of that same Son; the Son is son only of that same Father; and the Holy Spirit is the spirit of no one except that same Father and Son. This, then, is the sole reason for plurality in God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit cannot be said of one another, but are distinct from one another [Note: [Col. 0287D] “Distinct, as from one another” in the manuscripts: “distinct from one another”], because God is from God in the two ways stated above.

All of this can be called relation. For since the Son exists from God by being born, and the Holy Spirit by proceeding, they are related to one another by the very difference between birth and procession, as distinct and different from one another. And when substance has being from substance, two incompatible relations arise there if names are assigned to the substances according to those relations. For when a man is generated from a man, the man from whom the man exists is called “father,” and the man who exists from the man is called “son.” It is therefore impossible for the father to be the son whose father he is, or for the son to be the father whose son he is. Yet nothing prevents the father from being a son and the son from being a father when one man is both father and son, because he is father in relation to one person and son in relation to another [Note: [Col. 0287D] “He is father in relation to one and son in relation to another” in the manuscripts: “he is father in relation to one, and son in relation to another”; in Corbie: “he is Father in relation to one, and Son in relation to another”].

Thus Isaac, for example, is the father of Jacob and the son of Abraham: he is both father and son without contradiction, because he is called father in relation to someone other than his own father, and son in relation to someone other than his own son. But it is impossible, in the same Isaac, for the father to be that son whose father he is, or for the son to be that father whose son he is [Note: [Col. 0287D] “Or for that Son to be that Father” in the manuscripts; in Corbie: “or for the Son to be that Father”; another reading: “or for that Son to be that Father”]; [Note: [Col. 0287D] “Whose son he is” in manuscript Corbie: “whose son he may be”].

So, in God, since God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and the Father is father only of that same Son, the Son is son only of that same Father, and the Holy Spirit is the spirit of no one except that same Father and Son [Note: [Col. 0287D] “Of the Father, nor the spirit of anyone except” in the manuscripts: “of the Father, and the spirit of no one except”], the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; the Son is not the Father; and the Holy Spirit is not the Father [Note: [Col. 0287D] “The Son is not the Father or the Holy Spirit, nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son” in the manuscripts; “the Son is not the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit the Father” in another reading]. For the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father [Note: [Col. 0287D] “The Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Father” in the manuscripts and the Goth edition: “the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father”]. The one from whom someone exists cannot be the one who exists from him; nor can the one who exists from someone be the one from whom he exists, as has already been said. Therefore the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit, and the Son or the Holy Spirit is not the Father.

Moreover, to mention another reason for the moment, since it has not yet been established that the Holy Spirit is from the Son and proceeds from him, the Son is not the Holy Spirit, nor is the Holy Spirit the Son. The Son has being from the Father by being born; the Holy Spirit, however, has being not by being born but by proceeding. The Son therefore cannot be his own spirit, nor can the Holy Spirit be the one whose spirit he is.

## CHAPTER II [Note: [Col. 0287D] In manuscript Corbie: “Chapter 3.”]

### How indivisible unity and incompatible plurality coincide in God

With these points established, let us inquire how indivisible unity and incompatible plurality are related to one another in God. Since we believe and confess all that has been said with equal certainty—both we, who say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, and the Greeks, who do not agree with us on this matter—we ought by common consent to accept without any ambiguity whatever necessarily follows from these premises.

It follows, according to the character of God’s unity, which has no parts, that whatever is said of the one God, who is wholly whatever he is, is said of the whole God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—because each one alone is whole and perfect God. The opposition of the relations described above, however, which arises because God is from God in the two ways mentioned, prevents the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit from being said of one another and prevents what belongs properly to each from being attributed to the others.

Thus the consequences of this unity and of this relation are harmonized in such a way that the plurality following from relation does not extend to those matters in which the simplicity of the unity stated above is expressed [Note: [Col. 0287D] “The simplicity of the aforementioned unity sounds forth” in the manuscripts of Corbie and Victor 13: “the unity of the aforementioned simplicity sounds forth”], nor does unity suppress plurality where the same relation is signified. In this way unity never loses its consequence where no opposition of relation intervenes, and relation does not lose what belongs to it except where inseparable unity resists it.

If we consider the matter through examples, it will become clearer [Note: [Col. 0287D] “It will be clearer” in the manuscripts of Victor, Saint Michael, Corbie, and Cistercianus: “it will appear more clearly”] how the simplicity of unity excludes from itself the plurality contained in the signification of relative names. We confess that the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; that the Son is not the Father or the Holy Spirit; and that the Holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son. It follows, therefore, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are distinct from one another and more than one.

But the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. What, then, would be more consistent, if the aforementioned plurality of the persons preserves its proper character, than for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be several gods, distinct from one another? Yet the inviolable simplicity of the Godhead, which we believe to be one and only one God, absolutely refuses this. Thus the unity of God’s essence rejects the consequence of the relative terms.

It should also be considered how the plurality of relations opposes the consequence of unity, if we first set forth certain matters in which no opposition intervenes. We say that one God is Father, is Son, and is Holy Spirit, and that the one and same God is meant whether each individually, two together, or all three together are named [Note: [Col. 0289D] “The three are named together” in manuscript Victor 3: “the three are said to be together.”]

If, then, God is eternal, the unity of the Godhead necessarily entails that the Father is eternal, the Son is eternal, and the Holy Spirit is eternal. And since whether individually or several together they are one God, there is only one eternal being. The same consequence follows if God is called Creator, or just, or anything else in which none of the relations mentioned above is understood.

## CHAPTER III

### How relation restricts the consequence of God’s unity

Let us now see how relation restricts this consequence of God’s unity [Note: [Col. 0289D] “Let us now see, etc.” In manuscript Corbie, Chapter 3 begins here]. We say that God is Father. Since, therefore, one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the unity of God requires that the Son be Father and that the Holy Spirit be Father. But relation intervenes and prevents the Son or the Holy Spirit from being Father. For neither nature permits nor understanding comprehends that one who exists from someone should be the one from whom he exists, or that the one from whom he exists should be the one who exists from himself.

The Son and the Holy Spirit exist from the Father. Therefore the Son or the Holy Spirit cannot be Father, although God is Father and the one same God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The same point is recognized [Note: [Col. 0289D] “The same point is also recognized” in the manuscripts of Victor, Gembloux, Bec, Corbie, and Cistercianus: “the same point is recognized”] if God is said to be Son. The consequence of God’s unity requires that the Father [Note: [Col. 0289D] “That the Father also is” in the manuscripts of Victor and Corbie: “that the Father and also”] and the Holy Spirit be Son. But the Father, from whom the Son exists, cannot be the one who exists from himself. Likewise, the Holy Spirit, who exists from the Father by proceeding, is not the one who exists from the Father by being born.

Again, when it is said, “God is the Holy Spirit,” the unity stated above requires the Father and the Son also to be the Holy Spirit. But the Father, from whom the Holy Spirit exists, cannot be the one who exists from himself; nor is the Son, who exists from the Father by being born, the one who exists from that same Father by proceeding—that is, the Holy Spirit. When it becomes clear that the Holy Spirit is from the Son, it will also be clear that for this reason the Holy Spirit cannot be the Son, nor the Son the Holy Spirit.

Let us consider further [Note: [Col. 0289D] “Let us consider further, etc.” In manuscript Victor 13, Chapter 4 begins here] how the oppositions mentioned above resist the consequence of the unity stated above. “God is from God.” Once it is accepted that the one same God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it follows according to this identity that God the Father is God from God and God from whom God exists; likewise the Son is God from God and God from whom God exists; and in the same way the Holy Spirit.

To ask whether each one is God from whom God exists [Note: [Col. 0289D] “Whether each person is God” in the manuscripts of Victor, Corbie, Saint Michael, Cistercianus, and the Goth edition: “whether each one is God”] is nothing other than to consider whether each one individually is God from God. For God cannot be God from God unless he is the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, and unless he is from the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit.

Let us therefore examine whether each one is God from God, and it will become clear whether each one individually is God from whom God exists. The Father cannot be from God because of the opposition stated above. Since God is none other than the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—whether one of them, two together, or all three together—the Father cannot be God from God unless he is from the Father, that is, from himself; or from the Son; or from the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0289D] “That is, from the Son or from the Holy Spirit” in the manuscripts and the Goth edition: “that is, from himself, or from the Son, or from the Holy Spirit”]; or from two; or from three.

He cannot be from himself, because one who exists from someone cannot be identical with the one from whom he exists. He is not from the Son, because the Son is from him; and therefore he cannot be from the Son. He is not from the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is from him; nor can he be the one who exists from himself [Note: [Col. 0289D] “Nor can he be the one” in the manuscripts and the Goth edition: “nor can he be the one who exists from himself”]. Nor can the Father be from two or three together, for the same reason of opposition.

The Son, however, necessarily is God from God the Father, because the Father is not from him. He cannot be from the Son—that is, from himself—for the one existing from someone cannot be identical with the one from whom he exists. Whether he is from the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit from him, will be shown later.

But first we shall speak about the Holy Spirit: whether, according to the consequence stated above, he is from the Father and from himself. He must indeed be from the Father, because no opposition intervenes; the Father is not from him. But he cannot be from himself, because the one existing from someone cannot be identical with the one from whom he exists.

In all these matters nothing opposes the consequence of the one identity [Note: [Col. 0289D] “The identity of the one” in the manuscripts of Victor, Corbie, and the Goth edition: “the identity of the one”] except one of the oppositions stated above. Whatever is recognized in these matters must necessarily occur immutably in everything said of God.

## CHAPTER IV [Note: [Col. 0291D] In manuscript Victor 13: “Chapter 5.”]

### Since the Son is not from the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son

We must now inquire, by means of the irrefragable arguments stated above, whether the Son is from the Holy Spirit or the Holy Spirit from the Son. I say that just as, according to the reasoning already given, either the Father is from the Son or the Son from the Father, and likewise either the Father is from the Holy Spirit or the Holy Spirit from the Father [Note: [Col. 0291D] “From the Father, and likewise either the Father is from the Holy Spirit” in the manuscripts: “from the Father, or likewise the Father is from the Holy Spirit”], so either the Son is from the Holy Spirit or the Holy Spirit is from the Son.

Whoever denies this must also deny that there is one and only one God, or that the Son is God, or that the Holy Spirit is God, or that God is from God, because what I say follows from these premises.

Furthermore, neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is from the Father except from the Father’s essence, which is one and the same for him, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When it is said that the Son is from God the Father, then, since the Father and the Holy Spirit are the same God, it follows according to the unity of the Godhead that the Son is also from the Holy Spirit. In the same way, when we confess that the Holy Spirit is from God the Father, since the Father and the Son are the same God, it follows according to that same unity of the Godhead that he is also from the Son.

From this it is clearly understood that either the Son is from the Holy Spirit or the Holy Spirit is from the Son, since both cannot be true or both false. It is therefore necessary that the Holy Spirit be from the Son if it can be shown that the Son is not from him.

If someone says that it does not follow that the Son is from the Father and from the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0291D] “To be from the Father and the Spirit” in the manuscripts of Cistercianus, Corbie, and Saint Michael: “to be from the Father and from the Holy Spirit”], merely because the Father and the Holy Spirit are one God [Note: [Col. 0291D] “Because they are one” in the manuscripts: “because they are one God”], even if nothing else opposes the Holy Spirit’s being from the Father and the Son, because the Father and the Son are one God, although the Son is not from the Holy Spirit, then let him consider this. When God is from God, he is either wholly from the whole, partly from the part, wholly from the part, or partly from the whole. But God has no part. It is therefore impossible for God to be from God as wholly from a part, or as a part from the whole, or as a part from a part [Note: [Col. 0291D] “Partly from a part, or partly from the whole; but God” in the manuscripts: “partly from a part, or wholly from a part, or partly from the whole; but God”]. Consequently, if God is from God, he must be wholly from the whole [Note: [Col. 0291D] “So that, if God is from God, he is wholly from a part” in the manuscripts; “so that, if God is from God, he is wholly from the whole” in the Goth edition].

When, therefore, the Son is said to be from God who is the Father and the Holy Spirit, either the Father will be one whole and the Holy Spirit another whole, so that he is from the whole Father and not from the whole Holy Spirit; or, if the one whole God is Father and Holy Spirit, then, since he is from the whole God who is one whole Father and Holy Spirit, he is necessarily from both the Father and the Holy Spirit, unless something else stands in opposition [Note: [Col. 0291D] “The whole, because it is one whole, both Father and Holy Spirit; he is likewise” in the manuscripts: “the whole, who is one whole, Father and Holy Spirit. He is likewise”; in Corbie: “the whole, who is one whole, Father and Son and Holy Spirit; and likewise”].

In the same way, when the Holy Spirit is said to be from the whole God who is Father and Son, either the Father will be one whole and the Son another whole, so that the Holy Spirit is from the whole Father and not from the whole Son; or, since the Holy Spirit is from the Father, he cannot fail to be from the Son if the Son is not from the Holy Spirit. For no other reason can it be denied that the Holy Spirit is from the Son.

Someone may say: “If, because the Father and the Holy Spirit are one God, when the Son is from the Father he follows as being from the Holy Spirit; and if, because the Father and the Son are the same God, when the Holy Spirit is from the Father he is also from the Son, then, when the Father begets the Son, he must also beget the Holy Spirit, because the Son and the Holy Spirit are one and the same God. And when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, because of the same unity of the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Son also proceeds from the Father just as the Holy Spirit does. But if the unity of God [Note: [Col. 0291D] “The unity of the Godhead” in the manuscripts: “the unity of God”] in the Son and the Holy Spirit does not have such force as a consequence that both are similarly begotten and proceeding, it appears that from the fact that the Father and the Holy Spirit are one God [Note: [Col. 0291D] “The Father is one God” in the manuscripts of Victor and Corbie: “the Father and the Holy Spirit are one God”] it does not follow that the Son is from the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is from the Son, because, as you say, the Father and the Son are the same God.”

To this I reply:

The Son and the Holy Spirit certainly have being from the Father, but in different ways: one by being born, the other by proceeding. Thus, by this difference they are distinct from one another, as has been said [Note: [Col. 0291D] “So that they are distinct from one another by this, as has been said” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Victor, Thuaneus, and Cistercianus: “so that by this they are distinct from one another, as has been said”; in Corbie: “so that by this they are distinct from one another, because, as has been said”].

Therefore, when one is born, the one who is distinct from him by not being born in the same way cannot be born together with him, but proceeds; and when one proceeds, the one who is distinct from him by not proceeding in the same way cannot proceed together with him, but is born. Thus unity does not have that force as a consequence, because plurality intervenes, arising from birth and procession. Even if the Son and the Holy Spirit were not plural in any other respect, they would be distinct by this alone.

When I say that from the fact that the Father is one God with the Son or with the Holy Spirit it follows that the Son is from the Holy Spirit or that the Holy Spirit is from the Son [Note: [Col. 0293D] “It follows that the Son is” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, and the Goth edition: “that it follows that the Son is”], no plurality is generated there to oppose the consequence of unity, because I do not say that both are so, but only one.

It is therefore concluded with complete and invincible necessity that, if the things I have said above are true—things which we believe together with the Greeks—either the Son is from the Holy Spirit or the Holy Spirit is from the Son.

That the Son is not from the Holy Spirit, however, is clear from the catholic faith. God is from God only either by being born, as the Son, or by proceeding, as the Holy Spirit. The Son is not born from the Holy Spirit. For if he were born from him, he would be the son of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit would be his father; but neither is the father nor the son of the other [Note: [Col. 0293D] “Neither Father nor Son” in the manuscripts and the Goth edition: “neither is Father nor Son”]. Therefore the Son is not born from the Holy Spirit, and it is no less clear that he does not proceed from him. For he would be the spirit of that same Holy Spirit. This is plainly denied when the Holy Spirit is called and believed to be the Spirit of the Son. For no one can be the spirit of his own spirit.

Therefore the Son does not proceed from the Holy Spirit. The Son is in no way from the Holy Spirit. It follows, then, by an invincible argument that the Holy Spirit is from the Son, just as he is from the Father.

## CHAPTER V [Note: [Col. 0293D] In manuscript Victor 13: “Chapter 6.”]

### It is proved that the Holy Spirit has from the Father what he is, against a certain bishop favoring the Greeks

Perhaps the Greeks will deny that the Holy Spirit is God from God, as the Son is God from God, because by this we prove that he is and proceeds from the Son; and because his procession from the Son was not placed in that Creed in which they reproach us for having added it.

But whoever thinks this denies either that the Father is God from whom the Holy Spirit is, or that the Holy Spirit is God who is from the Father, or that the very thing which is the Holy Spirit is from the Father. No Christian accepts that the Father is not God or that the Holy Spirit is not God [Note: [Col. 0293D] “No one accepts that the Holy Spirit is not God” in manuscript Cistercianus: “no one accepts that the Holy Spirit is not God”]. Let us therefore see whether the very thing that the Holy Spirit essentially is, is from the Father [Note: [Col. 0293D] “Whether the Spirit is essentially” in the manuscripts and the Goth edition: “whether, essentially, it is the Holy Spirit”]. I perceived that a certain bishop, perhaps favoring the Greeks, did not wish to hold this view in the city of Bari.

For if what the Holy Spirit is is not from the Father, then, since the Father and the Holy Spirit are one and the same God, there is no way to discover in what respect the Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father. For he is not distinct merely because the Father has a Son while the Holy Spirit does not have a Son. This can prove that they are distinct from one another, but it is not the cause that they are different persons.

Suppose there are two men, one of whom has a son and the other does not. Although this may show that they are distinct, they are not thereby distinct from one another, since however they may stand with respect to having or not having a son, they nevertheless remain distinct in whatever way they are distinct. So with the Father and the Holy Spirit: they are not distinct because one has a Son and the other does not [Note: [Col. 0293D] “One has a son and the other does not” in manuscript Corbie: “one has, and the other does not have, a son”]; rather, because they are distinct, nothing prevents them from being unlike one another with respect to having and not having a Son [Note: [Col. 0293D] “Therefore they are distinct” in manuscript Victor 3: “therefore they are not distinct”].

A similar answer can be given if the Holy Spirit is called distinct because he does not proceed from another as he himself proceeds from the Father. For, to speak according to those who deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son: just as it is not the reason why the Son is distinct from the Father that he does not have the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself as the Father does—for it would follow that if the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Son, the Son would not be distinct from the Father—so the Holy Spirit is not distinct from the Father because he does not have a Son or the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself as the Father does [Note: [Col. 0293D] “Or the Holy Spirit proceeding from him” in manuscript Cistercianus: “or the Spirit proceeding from him”].

And just as the Son is not distinct from the Father merely because the Son has a Father while the Father has no father—for even if the Father had a father, he would still be distinct from the Son [Note: [Col. 0293D] “He would still be distinct from the Father” in the manuscripts: “he would still be distinct from the Son”]—so the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from someone while the Father proceeds from no one, is not for that reason distinct from the Father. For if the Father proceeded from someone, he would nevertheless be distinct from the one from whom he proceeded.

It is therefore clear that the Holy Spirit is not distinct from the Father because he does not have a Son or the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself as the Father does, nor because he proceeds from someone while the Father proceeds from no one.

Nor can it be understood from this that he is distinct from the Father because he is the Father’s Spirit, if he does not have being from him. For someone can be understood to be distinct from another before he is that other’s, although he cannot be someone’s unless he is distinct from him. Thus when a man is called someone’s master, or another man’s man, he is first understood to be distinct from the one whose master or man he is [Note: [Col. 0293D] “For he is first understood to be distinct from him” in the manuscripts: “for” is omitted in some witnesses].

Likewise, if the Holy Spirit is not from the Father, nothing prevents him from being understood to be distinct from the Father before he is the Father’s. Therefore the fact that he is the Father’s Spirit does not make him distinct from the Father, if through this he does not have being as distinct from him [Note: [Col. 0293D] “By the fact that he is his Spirit” in manuscripts of Victor, Bec, and Gembloux: “by the fact that he is his Spirit”; in Corbie: “by this, because he is his Spirit”], just as the Son is distinct from the Father by being his Son, which means nothing other than that he exists from him by being born [Note: [Col. 0295D] “Which means nothing other than that he exists from him by being born” in the manuscripts of Victor, Bec, and Gembloux: “which means nothing other than that he exists from him by being born”; in Victor 3: “which is not otherwise than that he exists from him by being born”; in Corbie: “which is not another, except that he exists from him by being born”].

Let it therefore be seen whether the Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father for any other reason than that he has from him the being that he is, although in a way different from the Son.

Let us nevertheless investigate this more carefully [Note: [Col. 0295D] “Let us investigate this more carefully, etc.” In manuscript Corbie, Chapter 6 begins here; in manuscript Thuaneus 90, Chapter 7 begins here]. Either, after the Holy Spirit came to be what he is, it happened to him to be distinct from the Father, or he has in his existence the reason why he is called distinct.

It can happen that someone is what he is before he is distinct, and it can happen that someone becomes distinct in existing. But it is impossible for anyone to be distinct before he is what he is. The first man, for example, before there was another man from him, was himself a man but was not distinct. When the first person came to exist from him, then the one from whom that person existed, after the other had come to be, became distinct [Note: [Col. 0295D] The manuscripts give expanded and variant forms: “When someone first came forth from him, then the one from whom he came forth, after this one existed, was made distinct; and the one who came forth from him simultaneously had being and became distinct”; manuscript Corbie: “when someone first came forth from him, and the one from whom he came forth, after this one existed, was made distinct; and the one who came forth from him simultaneously had both being and being distinct”; another manuscript reads: “when the first one came forth, etc., as in the other manuscripts”]. The one who came forth from him simultaneously had both being and distinctness.

Therefore either the Holy Spirit, as I said, became distinct from the Father after he came to be, or he has in his existence the reason why he is called distinct. But if it happened to him to become distinct from the Father after he came to be, and if there is no other person except insofar as he is distinct from another, then the three persons were not always three, because this person did not always exist, just as the Holy Spirit was not always distinct from the Father.

Since these propositions are false [Note: [Col. 0295D] “How, therefore” in the manuscripts: “since, therefore”], it is clear that he has in his existence the reason why he is distinct. But he cannot exist except either from something, as the Son does, or from nothing, as the Father does.

If he exists from nothing, as the Father exists, then either each exists independently, so that neither has anything from the other, and there are two gods—the Father and the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0295D] “But there are two gods” in the manuscripts: “there are two gods”]—or, since they are one God [Note: [Col. 0295D] “Since there is one God” in the manuscripts: “since they are one God”], if both are from nothing, nothing at all can be found in the Christian faith by which they are distinct from one another. The Father and the Holy Spirit would be one and the same, and one person. True faith recoils from this.

It is therefore not true that the Holy Spirit is from nothing. If he is from something, he can be from none other than God, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But he cannot be from himself, because no person can exist from himself [Note: [Col. 0295D] “To exist from himself, except the Father alone. Therefore” in the manuscripts: “to exist from himself. Therefore”]. Therefore, if someone denies that he is from the Son, he cannot deny that he is from the Father.

If someone says that, although he does not have being from the Father, he can nevertheless be understood to be distinct through procession, I think that this too must be answered, so that nothing may be brought against our assertion in this question to which our reply does not respond. Nor should anyone wonder that I dwell so long on this matter [Note: [Col. 0295D] “To dwell on this matter” in the manuscripts of Victor: “to linger on this matter”; in Corbie: “to linger in this matter”], since the man whom I perceived not to share the view that the Holy Spirit has from the Father the being that he is was a person of no small authority among his own people, and at that time I had no opportunity to answer him.

## CHAPTER VI [Note: In manuscript Corbie the preceding chapter continues. In manuscript Victor 13 it is Chapter 7.]

### Unless the Holy Spirit has being from the Father, he cannot be understood to be distinct from him through mission or procession
Whoever, then, wishes to say that the Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father solely by procession, although he does not derive his being from Him, understands either that “to proceed from the Father alone” means the same as “to be sent or given by the Father,” so that He proceeds from the Father only when the Father sends or gives Him [Note: [Col. 0295D] The manuscripts of Victor 19 and 3, Gem., and Bec. read *tunc tantum procedit* (“then only He proceeds”); the text reads *tunc tantum procedat* (“then only He may proceed”).]; or that “to proceed” means “to be from the Father.” But if [Note: [Col. 0295D] The manuscripts read *si idem est* (“if it is the same”), while the text reads *sed si idem est* (“but if it is the same”).] “to proceed” means the same as “to be given or sent,” [Col. 0296B] the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Son as from the Father, since He is likewise sent and given by Him.

Again, if the Holy Spirit’s proceeding means nothing other than His being sent or given, then He is distinct from the Father and proceeds from the Father only when He is given or sent—which, I think, no one understands. For the Holy Spirit is always distinct from the Father, even before creation; but He is given or sent only to creation. Yet it must not be said that being given or sent happens to Him. Since He Himself is everywhere and immutable, something happens to the recipient, because something takes place in relation to that recipient which previously did not exist and can be absent; but nothing happens in relation to the Holy Spirit that previously did not exist [Note: [Col. 0295D] “Something happens which did not exist”: the manuscripts of Victor, 3, and Corb. read “something happens which previously did not exist”]. When a blind person, in the presence of light, does not perceive the light, the light has neither more nor less [Note: [Col. 0295D] Victor 3 reads *non magis nec*; Corb. *nec magis nec*; another reading is *nec majus nec* (“neither greater nor”).]; and when, after blindness has been removed, the blind person perceives the light, a change occurs in him, not in the light.

It is therefore clear [Note: [Col. 0295D] “It is therefore clear, etc.”: in the manuscript of Corb. Chapter 7 begins here] that the Holy Spirit is not distinct from the Father by a procession understood in such a way that proceeding means nothing other than being given or sent. It is therefore evident [Note: [Col. 0295D] The manuscripts read “It is also evident” (*est quoque patens*), while the text reads “It is therefore evident” (*est ergo patens*).] that through procession He has His being from the Father; and by this He is distinct from the Father, just as the Son is distinct from the Father by no other means than that He exists from Him.

He is therefore God from God, and proceeds from God, because He Himself is God, and the Father is God, from whom He is and from whom He proceeds.
