But if we say that two processions of the Holy Spirit may be named—one when He exists from the Father, the other when He is given or sent—I do not think this should be denied, provided that each is understood in its proper sense [Note: [Col. 0295D] “In its proper sense”: the manuscripts of Victor, Corb., and Cister. read “is received in its proper sense”].

[Col. 0297A] With regard to that procession by which He is given or sent, we may appropriately understand the Lord to have spoken as follows: “The Spirit breathes where He wills, and you hear His voice, but you do not know where He comes from or where He goes” (John 3:8). For this may be understood as having been said thus: “You do not know from where He proceeds or to what hidden place He withdraws.” When He is given, He comes and proceeds, as it were, from a hidden place; but when He is withdrawn, He goes and departs, as it were, to a hidden place. Of this procession it may be said that proceeding is the same as being sent.

## CHAPTER VII [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Chapter 7”: in the manuscript of Corb. this continues the preceding chapter; in the manuscript of Victor 13 it is Chapter 8.]

### The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father entails His procession from the Son

Whether, then, He proceeds only by existing from the Father; or proceeds only when He is given or sent, proceeding in order to sanctify creation [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Or sent to sanctify”: the manuscripts of Victor, Corb., Bec., Gem., and Cister. read “or sent and proceeds to sanctify”]; or proceeds in both ways [Col. 0297B]—it follows that He proceeds from the Son.

For if He is from the Father, He is God from God; hence, as has been said, it is proved that He is also from the Son and proceeds from Him. For He proceeds from the one from whom He is, and exists from the one from whom He proceeds. But if He proceeds only when He is sent or given, He proceeds from the Son, by whom He is given and sent. And if He proceeds in both ways, it is likewise understood that in both ways He proceeds from the Son [Note: [Col. 0297D] “It is understood that He proceeds”: the manuscripts read “it may be understood that He proceeds”].

Behold, we see that the Holy Spirit is God from God [Note: [Col. 0297D] “That the Holy Spirit is God from God”: the manuscripts read “that the Holy Spirit is from God”], and proceeds from God—something that is not stated in the aforementioned creed. If, then, they deny that He is and proceeds from the Son because this is not stated there, let them likewise deny that He is from God and proceeds from God [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Likewise that He is from God”: the manuscript of Corb. reads “likewise that He is from God”]—which is likewise not said there [Note: [Col. 0297D] “And proceeds, because it is not said there”: the manuscripts read “and proceeds, which is not said there”]. Or, if they cannot deny this, let them not fear confessing with us that the Holy Spirit is and proceeds from the Son [Col. 0297C], since they do not find this stated in the same creed [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Since they do not find this”: the manuscripts of Corb. read “since it is not found”].

But they will say [Note: [Col. 0297D] “But if they say”: the manuscripts read “But if they say”]: It is sufficiently signified there that He is and proceeds from God, when it is said that He proceeds from the Father, since the Father is God [Note: [Col. 0297D] “He proceeds from God because He proceeds from the Father”: the manuscripts read “He proceeds from God when it is said that He proceeds from the Father; insofar as the Father is God”]. And we likewise say that it is plainly shown that He proceeds from the Son when it is said that He proceeds from God, since the Son is God [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Since the Son is God”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “since the Son is God”].

For I ask whether the Holy Spirit is to be understood as being from the Father because He is from God, or whether He is from God because He is from the Father. Although one can prove the one from the other reciprocally—for if He is from the Father, He is from God; and if He is from God, He is from the Father, since none of the relations stated above contradicts this—nevertheless, they are not reciprocally the cause of one another in the same way [Col. 0297D] [Note: [Col. 0297D] “The one the cause of the other”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “the one the cause of the other”].

For if the fact that the Holy Spirit is from the Father is the cause of His being from God, then, when it is said that He is from the Father, it must not be understood that He is from that which the Father is—namely, from the divine essence—but from that by which the Father is God, that is, from that by which He is related to the Son [Note: [Col. 0297D] “But from that by which”: the manuscript of Victor 9 reads “but from that from which”]. The divine essence in the Holy Spirit would therefore be from the relation, not from the Father’s deity; and this is most foolish to say.

Even if someone wished to understand it in this way, it would no less follow that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father. For there is no relation of the Father without the relation of the Son, just as there is no relation of the Son without the relation of the Father. If, then, one is nothing without the other [Note: [Col. 0297D] “If, then”: the manuscripts read “If, then, one of the two”], something cannot be from the relation of the Father without being from the relation of the Son. Therefore it follows [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Therefore it follows”: the manuscripts of St. Michael, Thu., 30, and Gem. 45 read “Therefore it will follow”] that the Holy Spirit is from both, if He is from one.

Thus, if He is from the Father according to relation, He will likewise be from the Son in the same sense [Note: [Col. 0297D] “He will likewise be from”: the manuscripts read “He will be at the same time from”]. But since no one is so foolish as to hold this view, we must believe and confess that the Holy Spirit is from the Father because He is from God. Yet the Father is no more God than the Son is; rather, the Father and the Son are one single true God. Therefore, if the Holy Spirit is from the Father because He is from God who is the Father, it cannot be denied that He is also from the Son, since He is from God who is the Son.

## CHAPTER VIII [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Chapter 8”: in the manuscript of Victor 13 it is Chapter 9.]

### The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son because He proceeds from the one true God, who is Father and Son

Let us also consider what the Lord says in the Gospel. For He says: “This is eternal life: that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent” (John 17:3).

Either, then, “the only true God” is to be understood in such a way that, when we name the Father alone, He is not signified as the only true God, nor when we name the Son alone; rather, He is understood as the only true God only when we name the Father and the Son together [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Or the Father alone”: the manuscripts of Victor 3 and 9 read “or the Father alone”; Victor 13 omits “or alone”]; or the only true God is understood when we name the Father alone [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Or the Father alone”: the manuscripts of Victor 3 and 9 read “or the Father alone”; Victor 13 omits “or alone”], or the Son alone.

But if, when the Father alone or the Son alone is named, the only true God is not understood without excluding the name of the other, then neither the Father nor the Son is perfect God; rather, God is composed of Father and Son [Note: [Col. 0297D] “But God is composed”: the manuscript of Corb. reads “if God is omnipotent, He is composed”]. Yet we believe the Father to be perfect [Col. 0298D], the only true God, and likewise the Son to be perfect [Col. 0299A], the only true God.

Therefore, when we name the Father alone or the Son alone, apart from the relation by which they are related to one another, we understand nothing other than the only true God—the same God whom we recognize in the utterance of both names.

Thus, when the Lord said: “This is eternal life: that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent” (John 17:3), if He had added, saying, “And from this only true God the Holy Spirit proceeds,” who would dare to separate the Son from that procession, since the only true God is no more or less Father than Son?

Therefore, if the same only true God is understood when the Father alone or the Son alone is named and when both are named together, what could be clearer than that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the only true God, who is Father and Son, when He is said to proceed from the Father? Just as He would be understood to proceed from the Son if the Son Himself had said that He proceeded from the only true God, when He said that He and the Father are the only true God, so, when He says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father [Note: [Col. 0299D] “So, when He says that He proceeds from the Father”: the manuscript of Corb. reads “so, when He said that the same one proceeds”], He undoubtedly signifies that He proceeds from Himself [Note: [Col. 0299D] “He signifies that He proceeds from Himself”: the manuscripts of Victor read “without doubt He proceeds from Himself”; the manuscript of Corb. reads “without doubt He signifies that He proceeds from Himself”].

## CHAPTER IX [Note: [Col. 0299D] “Chapter 9”: in the manuscript of Victor 13 it is Chapter 10.]

### The Spirit’s mission in the Son’s name and from the Son confirms His procession from the Son

The Lord also says: “But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). And again: “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26) [Note: [Col. 0299D] “And when”: the manuscripts of Victor read “And, when”; the manuscript of Corb. reads “And again: when”; another reading is “And again: when”].

What, then, is to be understood when He says, “whom the Father will send in my name”? Is it because the Holy Spirit will have His name, so that, when the Father sends the Holy Spirit, this is the same as sending the Son? But what He says—“whom I will send to you from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0299D] The manuscripts of Victor and Corb. omit “to you”]—does not admit this interpretation, because the very same Holy Spirit whom the Father sends is also sent by the Son; and the Son does not send the Son [Note: [Col. 0299D] “The Son sends, nor”: the manuscripts read “the Son sends, and neither”].

Finally, nowhere do we read—and we categorically deny—that the Holy Spirit is the Son. What, then, does “whom the Father will send in my name” mean, except “whom the Father will send, the Son also will send”? Just as when He says, “whom I will send from the Father,” it means nothing other than “I will send, and the Father will send.”

For “the Son” is the name of the one who said, “The Father will send in my name.” [Note: [Col. 0299D] The manuscripts place the numeral 54 here.] “The Father will send in my name” therefore means nothing other than “the Father will send in the name of the Son.”

What, then, does “the Father will send in the name of the Son” mean except “the Father will send as though the Son were sending, so that in the Father’s mission the Son’s mission may be understood”? But what does He mean by saying, “whom I will send to you from the Father”? Clearly, the one from whom the Son sends Him is the one by whom He is sent. Now the Son sends Him from the Father; therefore He is sent by the Father. But the one who sends is the one by whom He is sent. Thus the Father is understood to send when the Son says, “I will send from the Father.”

What, then, is “I will send from the Father” except “I will send as though the Father were sending, so that my mission and the Father’s may be one and the same”? Therefore, since the Son shows with such care that the Father’s mission and His own are one—that neither does the Father send unless the Son sends, nor does the Son send unless the Father sends [Note: [Col. 0299D] The manuscripts of Victor, Corb., and Cister. omit “send”]—what does He wish to signify [Note: [Col. 0299D] The manuscripts read “what does He wish to be signified”], or what does He wish to be understood [Note: [Col. 0299D] The manuscripts of Victor and Corb. omit “what does He wish”], except that the Holy Spirit does not stand in one relation to the Father and another to the Son, and is no more the possession of one than of the other? [Col. 0300B]

For this reason it is exceedingly difficult—indeed impossible—to show how He does not proceed from both. For how can the Son, together with the Father, have the power to give or send the Holy Spirit, and for that Spirit to belong to both, if He is not simultaneously from both? Why does the Son give the Holy Spirit rather than the Holy Spirit give the Son? Or why is the Holy Spirit the Son’s rather than the Son the Holy Spirit’s, unless the Son is not from the Father together with the Holy Spirit in the same way that the Holy Spirit is from the Father together with the Son? [Note: [Col. 0299D] “From the Father and from”: the manuscripts of Victor, Corb., and Cister. read “from the Father and from”].

If, then, the Holy Spirit is not from the Son, let Him not be given by the Son, nor be called the Son’s [Note: [Col. 0299D] “Not from the Son, not given, nor called”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “is not from the Son, let Him not be given by the Son, nor be called”], just as the Son is not given by the Holy Spirit, nor called the Holy Spirit’s, since He is not from the Holy Spirit.

But if they say that the Holy Spirit also sends the Son, just as He Himself says through the prophet: “And now the Lord God has sent me, and His Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16), this is to be understood according to the human being whom He bore, who appeared in the world in order to redeem it by the one will and disposition of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, I ask those who deny that the Holy Spirit is and proceeds from the Son how they understand Him to be the Spirit of the Son in such a way that the Son sends Him as His own Spirit. Do they think that the Father gave the Holy Spirit to the Son as though the Son did not have Him from Himself? Either He has Him from Himself or from another. But He cannot have Him from another except from the Father. Therefore He received Him from the Father, from whom He has His being; and the Father gave the Son the Holy Spirit as though the Son did not have Him from Himself.

Let them show, since the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are equal and each is sufficient for Himself [Note: [Col. 0299D] “Sufficient for Himself”: the manuscripts of Victor, Corb., and the Gothic edition read “is sufficient for Himself”], what reason or what need the Son had for the Father to give Him His Spirit, rather than for the Holy Spirit to be given the Son.

We do not deny that the Son has the Holy Spirit from the Father in this manner: since He has His being from the one from whom He has the being by which He has the Spirit existing from Himself, as the Father does [Note: [Col. 0301C] “The Holy Spirit existing from Himself”: the manuscripts read “the Holy Spirit existing from Himself”; Corb. reads “existing from Himself”], for the being of the Father and the Son is the same.

For it is not the same thing for the Son to receive from the Father the essence from which the Holy Spirit proceeds and for Him to receive the Holy Spirit from the Father. When it is said that He has from the Father the essence from which the Holy Spirit proceeds, no need of the Son is indicated. But when it is said that the Son receives from the Father the Holy Spirit, whom He does not have from Himself as the Father does, the Son appears to have something less than the Father has, and the Holy Spirit appears to be given to Him as a supplement [Note: [Col. 0301C] “To give Him as a supplement”: the manuscripts of Victor 3 and 13 and Corb. read “to be given to Him as a supplement”].

[Col. 0301B] Yet it is not apparent why the Son should need the Holy Spirit more than the Holy Spirit needs the Son [Note: [Col. 0301C] “Than the Spirit needs the Son”: the manuscripts of Victor and Corb. read “than the Holy Spirit needs the Son”].

If it is answered that the Holy Spirit was given to the Son so that, when He too gave the same Holy Spirit together with the Father, an equal share of grace might be attributed to Him [Note: [Col. 0301C] The manuscripts read: “so that, when He Himself also had the same Holy Spirit with the Father, He might be an equal”; “so that, when He Himself also gave the same Holy Spirit together with the Father, He might be equal”; the manuscript of St. Michael and the Gothic edition read “so that, when He Himself also gave the same Holy Spirit together with the Father, He might be equal”; Corb. reads “and when He Himself also gave the same Holy Spirit together with the Father, and might be equal”]—this is an earthly opinion, far removed from an understanding of divinity: as though God were to assist God in need, as a human being assists a human being.

For if the Father gives the Holy Spirit to the Son, God gives God to God [Note: [Col. 0301C] “God gives God to God”: the manuscript of St. Michael reads “God gives God from God”]. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and there is one and the same God. Yet we do not understand God to receive God from God unless this is said when God is from God, as the Son and the Holy Spirit are.

The Holy Spirit is therefore called the Spirit of the Son for no other reason than that He is from Him [Col. 0301C].

## CHAPTER X [Note: [Col. 0301C] “Chapter 10”: in the manuscripts of Victor 13 it is Chapter 11.]

### The same procession is proved from Christ’s breathing upon the apostles

After the Resurrection, we read that the Lord breathed upon His disciples [Note: [Col. 0301C] The manuscripts read “the Lord [breathed upon] His disciples”; the manuscript of Victor 9 reads “the Lord [breathed upon] His disciples”] and said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

What is the meaning of this breathing? For we know that the breath which then proceeded from His mouth was not the Holy Spirit. We therefore do not believe that He breathed without some mystery.

What, then, can more correctly or appropriately be understood here [Note: [Col. 0301C] The manuscripts read “or more clearly”] than that He did this in order that we might understand that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him? It is as though He had said:

“As you see this breath, through which I signify to you—just as sensible things can signify invisible things—that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the innermost part of my body and from my person, so know that the Holy Spirit whom I signify to you through this breath proceeds from the hidden depths of my divinity and from my person.”

For we believe and confess one person of the Word and the human being, and in that one person two natures, namely the divine and the human.

But perhaps they will say: That breath was certainly not of human substance, and yet He emitted it as though it were His own [Note: [Col. 0301C] “As though it were His own”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “as though it were His own”; the manuscript of Corb. reads “as though it were the Spirit”]. Therefore, through this kind of giving of the Holy Spirit, we are taught that when the Son gives the Holy Spirit, He gives and sends His Spirit, but not from the essence of His divinity.

Let those who hold this opinion say, then, that just as the breath is not human nature when it is emitted by a human being, so the Holy Spirit is not divine substance when He is given or sent by God the Son—which no Christian confesses.

Let them also say, when we hear: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of His mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6), that if they do not deny that the Holy Spirit is to be understood there by “the spirit of the Lord’s mouth,” then He is not of the essence of the Lord whose mouth-spirit He is said to be, because the spirit that normally proceeds from a human mouth is not of the substance of the one from whose mouth it proceeds.

But if no one dares say that the Spirit of God is not of the essence of God, and by means of words concerning sensible things—that is, by “the spirit of His mouth”—they understand the Holy Spirit to proceed from the hidden depths of the essence whose mouth-spirit He is called, let them also confess that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the essence of the one whose lips’ spirit He is called.

For we read in the prophet concerning Christ that “by the breath of His lips He will slay the wicked” (Isaiah 11:4). Either, then, let them show a distinction between “the spirit of the mouth” and “the spirit of the lips” [Note: [Col. 0301C] “Between the spirit of the lips”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “between the spirit of the mouth and the spirit of the lips”]—which cannot be done—or let them equally admit that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the one whose mouth-spirit and from the one whose lips-spirit is signified.

But if they say that “the spirit of the lips” there is by no means to be understood as the Holy Spirit, but rather the words of His preaching, which He formed in His mouth from this aerial human breath [Note: [Col. 0301C] The manuscripts of Victor and the Gothic edition read “from the airy human breath in His mouth He will form”; Corb. reads “from the aerial breath He formed in human fashion”], because by His words He slays the wicked [Note: [Col. 0301C] Corb., St. Michael, Victor 13, 3, and Cister. read “He will slay the wicked”; Thu. 90 and Victor 9 read “He slew the wicked”], turning a person away from wickedness by teaching [Note: [Col. 0301C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “turning him away by teaching”]—then it is certainly not sensible words, nor this sensible breath, but the Holy Spirit of whom God says through the prophet:

“I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will place my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The Holy Spirit therefore slays the wicked [Note: [Col. 0303C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “the Holy Spirit will slay”] when He turns his heart from wickedness to righteousness [Note: [Col. 0303C] The manuscripts read “his heart is turned”; the manuscript of Victor 9 reads “He will turn his heart”].

And if we understand that wicked person to be the Antichrist, whom the Lord Jesus will slay by the spirit of His mouth, I do not think anyone attributes to the power of the spirit of the human voice as much as to the divine Spirit. If, then, the Holy Spirit is understood in these statements, when “the spirit of the Lord’s mouth”—whose word established the heavens, that is, the Father’s—is spoken of together with the spirit of the mouth of the Lord Jesus and the spirit of His lips, it is not apparent why He should be understood to proceed more from the Father’s mouth than from the Son’s mouth.

And if by the Father’s mouth we understand the Father’s essence—for His mouth is nothing other than His essence, so that just as the Lord’s word is His essence, so the spirit of His mouth is from nothing other than His essence—what could be clearer than that, just as the spirit of the Father’s mouth is from the Father’s essence and proceeds from it, so the spirit of the Son’s mouth and lips is from the Son’s essence and proceeds from it?

For I think no one will understand in a merely literal way the statement: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of His mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6), as referring to transitory words and to a spirit taken from the air and emitted through the mouth of the speaker.

But however anyone may try to explain this, it is enough that in the Lord’s breathing upon the disciples, which I mentioned, the action was performed to signify that the Spirit whom He gave proceeded from the hidden depths of that same person, from whose hidden depths the Spirit whom He breathed proceeded [Note: [Col. 0303C] The manuscripts of Victor read “from whose hidden depths that Spirit proceeded”].

Finally, when divine Scripture signifies something hidden through likenesses of sensible things, the things that signify and the things signified cannot be similar in every respect [Note: [Col. 0303C] The manuscript of St. Michael reads “the things that signify and the things signified”]. For otherwise it would not be likeness but identity—unless someone should wish to say that the Lord’s breathing upon the disciples was performed by God’s wisdom in such a simple way, without any spiritual signification. But I do not think anyone is so senseless as to hold this view.

[Col. 0304A]

## CHAPTER XI [Note: [Col. 0303C] “Chapter 11”: in the manuscript of Victor 13 it is Chapter 12.]

### The same procession is argued from Christ’s words: “He will receive from what is mine”

The Son also says concerning the Holy Spirit: “For He will not speak from Himself, but whatever He hears He will speak” (John 16:13).

What does “He will not speak from Himself” mean except that He will have from another what He will speak? And what does “He will have from another what He will speak” mean except “He will have from another the knowledge of what He will speak”? Hence, after saying, “He will not speak from Himself,” He added, “but whatever He hears He will speak.”

What does it mean for the Holy Spirit to hear except, as it were, to learn? And what does it mean to learn except to receive knowledge? If, then, His knowledge is nothing other than His essence, He has His essence from the one from whom He hears what He speaks and teaches, since speaking and teaching are the same for Him.

But He neither hears nor has His essence from another except either from the Father or from the Son [Note: [Col. 0303C] The manuscripts read “except from the Father and the Son”]. If, however, He has His being from the Father, according to the reasoning stated above, He also has it from the Son [Note: [Col. 0303C] Corb. reads “He also has it from the Son”; the manuscripts of Victor read “He also has it from the Son as well”].

Hence the same Son says: “He will glorify me, because He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:14). For what else does this mean than “He will hear from me”—that is, “He will know from me what He will announce to you”?

When He said, “Whatever He hears He will speak,” He did not specify from whom He would hear. But when He says, “He will receive from what is mine,” lest anyone attribute solely to the Father what He hears from another, He plainly shows that He is the one from whom, just as from the Father, He receives knowledge or essence.

For just as, when it is said, “He will not speak from Himself, but whatever He hears He will speak and announce to you,” it is signified that He is and proceeds from the one from whom He hears [Col. 0304C], so, when the Son says, “He will receive from what is mine,” He openly shows that He has and proceeds from what is His—namely, from His essence [Note: [Col. 0303C] The manuscripts read “He will receive, and announce to you, openly”; Gem. reads “from His essence, an essence”; Thu. 90 reads “from His essence, an essence”; another reading is “from His essence, an essence”].

For whatever is not the divine essence is beneath the Holy Spirit; and He Himself does not receive anything from that which is beneath Him. Therefore, when the Son says, “He will receive from what is mine,” He signifies by “what is mine” nothing other than His essence.

## CHAPTER XII [Note: [Col. 0303C] “Chapter 12”: in the manuscript of Victor 13 it is Chapter 13.]

### Other words of Christ press the same point: “No one knows the Son except the Father,” and so forth

Perhaps they will try to understand in another way than I have explained what the Son said: “He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:14) [Note: [Col. 0303C] The manuscript of Corb. reads “Perhaps what He said”; another reading is “Perhaps He also said”]. But what will they say when He declares: “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him”? (Matthew 11:27.)

We hear that no one knows the Father or the Son except the Father or the Son, and the one to whom the Son reveals Him [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts of Victor 3 and 9 read “knows the Father, or the Father or the Son, and the one”; another reading is “knows the Father or the Son, except the Father or the Son, and the one”]. He does not say “no one,” as though he meant no human being, but as though he meant absolutely no one. For if this were what He meant, He would not add “except the Father,” since the Father is not a human being.

And when He says, “Nor does anyone know the Father,” in this monosyllabic word—namely, “anyone”—a human person is no more understood than any other person. Therefore, absolutely no one possesses this knowledge except the Father and the Son, and the one to whom the Son Himself reveals it.

Either, then, the Holy Spirit does not know the Father and the Son—which it is impious to think—or the Son reveals to Him the knowledge of Himself and of the Father, and this knowledge is nothing other than the essence of that same Holy Spirit.

But if they say that, although the Son, insofar as His utterance is concerned, admits no one to this knowledge except Himself, the Father, and the one to whom He reveals it [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts of Victor 3 and 9 and Corb. read “admits [him] to the knowledge”], nevertheless the Holy Spirit is not to be confessed as either separated from that knowledge or receiving it from the Son [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts read “or receiving that one from the Son”], because the Father and the Son know each other only by virtue of being one with the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when He says that the Father and the Son know each other, the Holy Spirit is to be understood as included; and when the Son reveals, He reveals not to the Holy Spirit but to creation.

If, I say, they make this argument, we immediately and firmly draw the following conclusion [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts read “If this is said … we will infer”]: If, where the truth plainly denies—according to the words uttered by His mouth—that the Holy Spirit knows the Father and the Son except when the Son reveals them [Col. 0305C], they also say that we ought to attend not so much to the words as to the unity of essence, which is one and inseparable in the three, since no authority either in writing or in meaning denies this unity and no statement is produced that is contrary to or in any way conflicts with it—then let the Greeks choose one of two alternatives, if they wish openly to resist the truth:

Either they must say that the Holy Spirit does not know the Father and the Son except when the Son reveals them [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts of Victor, Corb., and Cister. read “or the Son except”]; or, because the Father and the Son are one in that by which they know each other [Note: [Col. 0305D] Gem., Bec., Victor, and Thu. read “in that by which they know themselves”], they must necessarily conclude that, when they are said to know each other, the Holy Spirit is understood in that same knowledge [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts read “since they themselves are said to know”].

There is no middle position if they do not wish entirely to disavow either this knowledge from the Holy Spirit or the truth from the words of Truth [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts read “from the words”].

[Col. 0306A] For Truth says: “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him” (Matthew 11:27).

If, then, they choose to say that the Holy Spirit knows the Father and the Son through the Son’s revelation, He has from the Son the knowledge that is nothing other than His being. He therefore is and proceeds from the Son, since He proceeds from the one from whom He is.

But if they say that, when the Father and the Son are said to know each other, the Holy Spirit necessarily shares in the same knowledge because the essence by which they know each other is the same in the Holy Spirit, then, when they read that He proceeds from the Father, of whom the Son says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), let them confess with us that, because of the essential identity of the Father and the Son, He undoubtedly proceeds also from the Son [Col. 0306B] [Note: [Col. 0305D] “Also from the Son, undoubtedly”: the manuscripts read “from the Son, without doubt”].

## CHAPTER XIII [Note: [Col. 0305D] “Chapter 13”: in the manuscript of Victor 13 it is Chapter 14.]

The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Son, is not later than or lesser than he.

But if someone objects [Note: [Col. 0305D] The Saint-Mihiel manuscript reads “But if someone objects”; “But if they object”] that, when we say [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts read “when it is said”; “when we say”] that the Son is born from the Father and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, we establish certain degrees and intervals—as though the Holy Spirit could not exist unless the Son were first born from the Father, so that the Holy Spirit would be later than the Son—and therefore that it would be more correct to say that they are equally from the Father, the Son by being born and the Holy Spirit by proceeding, so that neither the Son is from the Holy Spirit nor the Holy Spirit from the Son, just as radiance and heat are equally from one sun, and neither radiance is from heat nor heat from radiance: if, I say, someone raises this objection against our assertion, we reply:

We neither posit degrees of dignity in God, who is one, nor establish intervals in eternity—which is outside all time—between the Son’s existing from the Father or the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Father and the Son. For, similarly, all who hold the Christian faith confess that the Son is neither lesser nor later than the Father, although he exists only from him. Thus we too, who say that the Holy Spirit is from, or proceeds from, the Son, confess that he is neither lesser nor later than the Son [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts read “later with the Son”; “later than the Son”].

Indeed, although radiance and heat proceed from the sun and cannot exist unless that from which they are exists, we nevertheless understand nothing earlier or later among the three—that is, the sun, radiance, and heat [Col. 0306D] [Note: [Col. 0305D] The manuscripts of Victor, Corbie, and Cîteaux read “in the sun and radiance”; “in the sun, namely, and radiance”]. Therefore, since this is so even in temporal things, much less can the aforesaid three persons be understood as susceptible of an interval in their existence within eternity, which is not enclosed by time [Col. 0307A] [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts read “may be understood”; “can be understood”].

## CHAPTER XIV [Note: [Col. 0307D] Chapter 14; in the Corbie manuscript the preceding chapter continues as Chapter 14.]

### The difference between the procession of the Son and of the Holy Spirit from the Father, and the procession of radiance and heat from the sun

But when it is said that the Son and the Holy Spirit can be from the Father alone in such a way that neither the Son is from the Holy Spirit nor the Holy Spirit from the Son, just as radiance and heat proceed together from one sun so that one is not from the other, this is not rightly brought against us.

For when we say that the Son is from the Father [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts of Victor and Corbie read “that the Son is from the Father”; “that the Son is from the Father and exists”], and that the Holy Spirit is from the Father, we confess that the Son is God, and that the Holy Spirit is God from God the Father [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *Spiritum sanctum esse de* (“the Holy Spirit to be from”), rather than *Spiritum sanctum Deum esse de* (“the Holy Spirit to be God from”)], and that these three persons are one God, and that this same one is from that same one.

In the case of the sun, however, we do not say that the sun is from the sun when radiance or heat is from the sun; nor that the sun and what is from the sun are the same [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts of Thuringia, Gembloux, Bec, Saint-Mihiel, and Corbie, and the Gothic edition read “and what is from the sun”; the manuscripts of Victor 9 and 13 read “what is from the sun”]; nor that those three are one sun.

For if the sun and radiance were one sun, or if the sun and heat were likewise one sun [Note: [Col. 0307D] The Saint-Mihiel manuscript reads “would together be one sun”; “would be one sun together”], it would necessarily follow either that radiance was from heat, since it would be from the whole sun, which would be the same as heat; or that heat was from radiance, since it would have its existence from the sun [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts read “which would have its existence from the sun”; “since it would have its existence from the sun”], whose essence would not differ from that of radiance.

Let us nevertheless suppose that the Son and the Holy Spirit are equally from the Father alone, just as heat and radiance are from one sun. But if this is so, from where do those who say this derive the fact that they confess the Holy Spirit to be the Son’s, while denying that the Son is the Holy Spirit’s? For just as no reason permits heat to be radiance’s, or radiance heat’s, so truth does not allow the Holy Spirit to be the Son’s more than the Son is the Holy Spirit’s.

Therefore, if they do not dare deny that the Holy Spirit is the Son’s, let them deny that the Son and the Holy Spirit are equally from the Father alone in the same way that radiance and heat are from one sun. Thus, if they bring against us what I said about the sun’s radiance and heat, it supports neither them nor us.

## CHAPTER XV [Note: [Col. 0307D] Chapter 15; in the Corbie manuscript it is Chapter 14. Formerly it continued the preceding chapter.]

### That the Greeks do not correctly say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, through whom all things exist; rather, he proceeds from the Godhead, which is one belonging to the Father and the Son

When we are told not to separate the Son entirely from communion with the Father in this procession of the Holy Spirit, they assert that he proceeds from the Father through the Son [Col. 0307D]. But how this can be understood is not apparent, especially since nowhere do they read anything by which they could prove it openly [Col. 0308A].

For if they think they can support this view by what we read about God—“For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36)—so that “from whom” all things are may be the Father, “through whom” the Son, and “in whom” the Holy Spirit, and so that the Holy Spirit may be understood among all the things that are through the Son [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts read “the Holy Spirit is understood”; “the Holy Spirit is received”—and the Corbie manuscript reads “what is said, namely, to be from,” rather than “what is said to be from”], then we accept without hesitation that all things are from the Father, through the Son, and in the Holy Spirit; but to assert that the Holy Spirit is among all the things of which the Apostle speaks is excessively problematic.

For it is impossible to include any one of those three persons among all those things while excluding the other two [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts read “to enclose all those things”; the manuscripts of Corbie and Cîteaux read “to include all those things”]. But if the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are among all the things that are from the Father, through the Son, and in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts read “if the Father and the Son are”; “if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are”], let the rational mind consider how great a confusion follows [Col. 0308B].

Therefore, when the Apostle says, “From him and through him and in him are all things,” we must undoubtedly understand him to mean all created things, which are from him, through him, and in him in the same way that one thing is from another, through another, and in another. Whatever has been made is not the same as God, but is other than him.

The Holy Spirit, however, is not other, but is the very same as the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts of Victor, Corbie, and Cîteaux read “the very same as the Father and the Son”; “the very same as the Father”]. Nothing else can be understood by which they could show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, as they say [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts read “by which it could be shown”; “by which they could show”].

Since the Father and the Son do not differ in the unity of the Godhead, and since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father only from the Godhead, if the Son’s Godhead is the same, it cannot be understood how he proceeds from the Father’s Godhead through the Son’s Godhead and not from that same Son’s Godhead—unless someone should say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father’s Godhead but from his fatherhood, and not through the Son’s Godhead but through his sonship. This opinion chokes itself by its manifest foolishness [Col. 0308C].

But if someone says [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts of Victor, Corbie, Saint-Mihiel, and Cîteaux read “but if someone says”; “but if someone says”] that, when I say that he proceeds from the Godhead of the Father and the Son, I cannot separate the Godhead of the Holy Spirit from this Godhead of the Father and the Son, because the Godhead of the three is one and the same, and that consequently, if he proceeds from the Godhead of the Father and the Son, he proceeds from his own Godhead also, and therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself:

I have already, as I remember, answered this sufficiently above: no person can exist from himself. For just as the Son, although he is from the Father’s essence, and although the Son’s essence is not other than the Father’s but the same, is nevertheless not from himself but from the Father alone [Note: [Col. 0307D] The manuscripts of Victor 9 and 13 read “from him, but”; “from himself, but”], so the Holy Spirit, although he is from the essence of the Father and the Son—which is the same essence as his own—is nevertheless not from himself, but solely from the Father and the Son [Col. 0308D–0309A].

## CHAPTER XVI [also XV] [Note: [Col. 0309D] “They will say: Why not likewise, etc.” In the Corbie manuscript Chapter 15 begins here; formerly it continued the preceding chapter.]

### That the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father through the Son in the same way that all things were made from the Father through the Word

They will say: Why can we not similarly say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, just as we say that all things were made from the Father through the Word, who is the Son? For when the Father acts through his Word, he does not act through anything other than what he himself is—that is, through the essential power that is the same as the Word’s—and yet he is said to act through the Word [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts read “and yet he is not said to act except through the Word”; “and yet he is said to act through the Word”]. Why, then, do we not similarly say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Word, when he proceeds from the Father only from and through that which is the same in him and in the Son, although not as a creature but as the very same from the very same [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “does not proceed from the Father except from that which is the same”; “does not proceed from the Father except from and through that which is the same”]?

Let us see what follows if we say this, and let there be peace between us. Certainly, the things that were made by the Father through the Word were made by the Word himself. For the Word himself says, “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John 5:19) [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts read “Whatever the Father does”; “whatever indeed the Father does”].

Let us therefore say that, when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, he also proceeds from the Son in the same way, just as the things made by the Father through the Word were likewise made by the Word himself. Unless perhaps they understand the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father through the Son in the manner in which, when a spring flows into a stream and the stream is gathered into a lake, the lake is said to be from the spring through the stream.

But there the stream is not in the spring, but outside the spring, whereas the Son is in the Father and not outside the Father. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not from the Father through the Son in the way that the lake is from the spring through the stream [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts of Victor 9 and Corbie read “Therefore the Holy Spirit is not so from the Father through the Son”; “therefore he is not so”].

If, nevertheless, this is the case, it cannot be denied that he is from the Son, although he is from the Father through the Son—just as one must admit that the lake is from the stream, although it is from the spring through the stream. For whoever denies that the lake is from the stream [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts of Victor, Corbie, and Saint-Mihiel read “that the lake is from the stream”; “that the lake is from the stream”] because the stream is first from the spring should say that he is not from his father but from Adam, because through his father he is from Adam.

Let him also say that the Virgin’s Son is not from Mary, nor from David, nor from Abraham, because they existed first from Adam. And let him say that what was said to Abraham is false: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18); and what was said to David: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11); and what was said to Mary: “Blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42) [Col. 0309D].

Let him say that Christ is not the seed or fruit of these persons, but of Adam, because they descended from him [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts of Saint-Mihiel and Cîteaux read “they descended”; “they descend from him”].

But neither, in this sense, is the Virgin’s Son from Adam; rather, he is from the clay from which Adam was made [Col. 0310A].

They will then object [Note: [Col. 0309D] “But they will object, etc.” In the Corbie manuscript this is where Chapter 16 begins; formerly it continued the preceding chapter]:

“We rightly say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, but from the Father through the Son, although he is from the Father and from the Son, just as you say that the lake is from the spring and from the stream. For the question between us concerns the word ‘proceed’: you assert that it is from the Son, whereas we deny this [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts read “from the Son, we deny”; “from the Son, and we deny”].

“For behold, you see that the stream proceeds from the spring, as from an original principle, whereas the lake does not proceed but is gathered from the stream, although it has its existence from it. Thus, even if the Holy Spirit has his existence from the Son, he is not properly said to proceed from the Son, but from the Father as from the principle.

“This might rightly be said if, when born from the Father, the Son proceeded outside the Father, and if, with some intervening interval, the Holy Spirit were first understood to be from the Father rather than from the Son; just as the stream flowing from the spring proceeds outside the spring, and, after a certain interval, is gathered into the lake, so that the lake is from the spring before it is from the stream. Therefore it is from the spring through the stream, not from the stream through the spring.

“But since, when born from the Father, the Son does not go out beyond the Father, but remains in him, undivided from the Father in place, time, or essence [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts of Saint-Mihiel and Corbie read “is different from the Father”; “is divided from the Father”], and since that from which the Holy Spirit proceeds is one and the same for the Father and the Son, it can neither be understood nor said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and not from the Son.

“Therefore it does not appear on what grounds it is said that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son but from the Father through the Son, since, even if it cannot be said to be through the Son, it cannot be said not to be from the Son.”

If, nevertheless, someone wishes to say that the Son proceeds from the Father more properly than the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, although the Holy Spirit is from him—just as the stream seems to him to proceed more properly from the spring than the lake from the stream—let him not concede that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son [Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscripts read “let him not concede the Holy Spirit”; the Corbie manuscript reads “let him not concede the Holy Spirit”; another reading is “nor let him concede the Holy Spirit”], from whom he has his existence, as the lake does from the stream.

We do not deny that what is born proceeds in some manner from that from which it is born; and we assert that the Holy Spirit proceeds in his own manner, not as from two springs but truly from one spring, in such a way, however, that the Son’s procession does not lose the name of birth, nor does the procession of the Holy Spirit receive it.

There is therefore no reason why the Son should be said to proceed from the Father more than the Holy Spirit from the Son [Col. 0310B–C].

## CHAPTER XVII [also XVII] [Note: [Col. 0309D] Chapter 16; in the Corbie manuscript it is Chapter 17. Formerly, in the same manuscript, it was Chapter 14.]

### That, just as the lake is from the stream and the spring, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son

Let us consider more carefully how the lake is from the spring and equally from the stream, so that through this example—by which something eternal can be understood through something temporal and spatial—we may recognize that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son.

Many things are found in this consideration, as in the letter on the incarnation of the Word that I wrote to Pope Urban, of venerable memory [Col. 0311A] [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “to Urban from”; “to Pope Urban from”].

It is established that one and the same water is called the spring, the stream, and the lake—not three waters, although there are three things: a spring, a stream, and a lake [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “For it is established that one”; “it is established that one”].

Let us therefore distinguish between the spring, the stream, and the lake, and see how each of these, although they are three, is understood in one water [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “how each is understood”; “what each of these is”].

In the spring, water rising from the abyss bubbles up; in the stream, descending from the spring, it flows; in the lake, it is gathered and remains [Col. 0310D] [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “it is gathered into the lake”; the Corbie manuscript reads “it is gathered in the lake”; another reading is “it is gathered through the lake”].

Thus, by the spring is understood water bubbling up from the abyss; by the stream, the fact that it flows from the spring; and by the lake, the fact that it is gathered together there [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “it flows into the lake”; another reading is “it flows through the lake”].

We see, however, that the stream is not from that by which the water is called a spring, but from that which it is—that is, from water. Nor is the lake from that by which the water is called a spring or a stream, but from the water itself, which is one and the same in the spring and in the stream [Col. 0311B].

The lake therefore exists not from that in which the spring and the stream differ, but from that in which they are one. If, then, the spring is not more truly that from which the lake is than the stream is, the lake cannot be understood to be more from the spring than from the stream.

Thus, when God is called Father, Son, or Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “If, therefore, when”; the Saint-Mihiel manuscript adds that the remainder of this book is lacking], one essence and one God are understood in the three; and the name “God” signifies his essence. But in the Father the begetter is understood, in the Son the begotten, and in the Holy Spirit one who proceeds in a singular and ineffable manner.

Therefore, just as the lake is not from that by which the spring and the stream are distinct from one another, but from the water in which they are one [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “water in which they are one”; “water into one”], so the Holy Spirit is not from that by which the Father and the Son are distinct from one another [Col. 0311C], but from the divine essence in which they are one.

If, then, the Father is not more truly that from which the Holy Spirit is than the Son is, it cannot be understood why he is more from the Father than from the Son.

## CHAPTER XVIII [also XVII] [Note: [Col. 0311D] Chapter 17; in the Corbie manuscript it is Chapter 18. Formerly it was Chapter 15.]

### The Father and the Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit

But if they say that he cannot be from two causes or from two principles, we reply:

Just as we do not believe that the Holy Spirit is from that by which the Father and the Son are two, but from that in which they are one, so we do not say that he has two principles but one principle [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “we say two of him”; “we say that he has two”].

For when we call God the principle of creation, we understand the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as one principle, not three principles, just as one Creator, not three creators [Col. 0311D], although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three. For it is by that in which they are one, not by that in which they are three [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “in which there are three, exists”; “by that in which they are three, exists”], that the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit is principle or creator.

Therefore, although the Father is principle, the Son is principle, and the Holy Spirit is principle, they are nevertheless not three principles but one. Likewise, when the Holy Spirit is said to be from the Father and the Son, he is not from two principles but from one, which is the Father and the Son, just as he is from one God, who is the Father and the Son—if, that is, God ought to be said to have a principle or cause [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “and the Son, if nevertheless”; another reading is “and the Son, just as he is from one God who is the Father and the Son, if nevertheless”].

For “principle” seems to belong only to something that begins to exist [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “begins to exist”; “began to exist”], and “cause” only to an effect. The Holy Spirit, however, never began to exist and is not the effect of anything [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts of Victor and Cîteaux read *affectus* (“affection”), rather than *effectus* (“effect”); they omit *alicujus* (“of anything”).]

For what begins to exist advances from non-being to being, and the term “effect” seems properly applicable to something that comes to be. Nevertheless, since it is true that the Son is from the Father and the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, if this is understood in some ineffable manner of its own, since it cannot be expressed otherwise, it may appropriately be said that the Father is, in a certain manner, the principle of the Son, and the Father and the Son the principle of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “but in a certain manner”; “if in a certain manner”].

Yet we do not confess two principles: one, the Father in relation to the Son [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts of Victor 9 and 13 read “principles, one, the Father in relation to the Son”; another reading is “a principle, but one, the Father and the Son”]; the other, the Father and the Son in relation to the Holy Spirit.

Nor do we believe in one God the Father from whom the Son is, and another God, the Father and the Son, from whom the Holy Spirit is, although each is from the same God, or from the same principle, in his own manner—one by being born, the other by proceeding—if this procession is understood in some singular and ineffable manner [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts of Victor and Corbie read “in a certain and ineffable manner”; “in an ineffable and singular manner”].

For “procession” is spoken of in many ways, and this one is understood in a unique way, just as the Son’s birth is recognized as singular.

The same thing is understood if we say that the Father is the cause of the Son, and the Father and the Son the cause of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “we say that he is the cause”; “we say that the Father is the cause”]. For we cannot say that there are two causes, one of the Son and another of the Holy Spirit, but one—just as there are not two gods but one God, from whom the Son and the Holy Spirit are [Col. 0312A–C].

## CHAPTER XIX [also XVIII] [Note: [Col. 0311D] Chapter 18; in the Corbie manuscript it is Chapter 19. Formerly it was Chapter 16.]

### The argument drawn from Christ’s expressing the Holy Spirit’s procession from the Father alone is overturned

But if it is asked why, when the Lord said, “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), he did not add “and from the Son,” or “from me,” if he wished it to be understood in that way, this is not unusual in his sayings: when he attributes something to the Father as though to him alone, or to himself, or to the Holy Spirit, he may intend what he says of one to be understood of the others [Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscripts read “what he says of one”; “what he says in one”].

For when he says, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17), must not the Son himself and the Holy Spirit be understood to have revealed it together with the Father?

Since the Father does not reveal by that in which he is Father [Note: [Col. 0313D] The Corbie manuscript omits everything from “For the Father does not reveal by that in which he is Father” through “Although what was said above”], but by that in which he is God—and the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same God [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “by that in which he is God, and the Father and the Son are the same God”; “by that in which he is God, and the Son is the same God”—the source reading is materially uncertain]—it follows that what the Father reveals, the Son and the Holy Spirit reveal.

Likewise, when he says, “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27), as though the Son alone knows and reveals the Father and himself, and the Father alone knows the Son [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “the Father and himself, and the Father alone”; another reading is “the Father and the Father alone”], it must be understood that revealing and knowing are common to the three persons. For they know and reveal not by that in which they are distinct from one another, but by that in which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one [Col. 0313B] [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts of Gembloux and Bec read “in which the Father and the Spirit are one”; “in which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one”].

When he also says [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “when he says”; “when he also says”] that the Father knows the Son, and the Son knows the Father, and reveals himself and the Father, he plainly intends it to be understood that the Father knows the Holy Spirit, and the Son knows and reveals the Holy Spirit; for what the Father and the Son are is also what the Holy Spirit is [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts of Victor and Cîteaux read “is also the Spirit”; “is also the Holy Spirit”].

Similarly, when he says, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9), the Holy Spirit must not be separated from this. For whoever sees that in which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “from which they are one”; “that in which they are one”] cannot see one of these three without the other two.

He also says of the Holy Spirit to the apostles, “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13), as though the Holy Spirit alone teaches all truth, although he does not teach all truth without the Father or without the Son [Col. 0313C]. For he teaches all truth not by being the Spirit of someone—namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit—but by being one with the Father and the Son, that is, by being God.

You see, therefore, how in the passages I have cited [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “which I have set forth”; the manuscripts of Victor 9 and 13 also read “which I have set forth”; another reading is “which he set forth”], what he attributes to one as though to him alone [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “what I attribute to one as though to him alone”; “what he attributes to one as though to him alone”] cannot be separated from the other two persons [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “cannot be separated from the other persons”; “cannot be separated from the other two persons”].

We read many things of this kind in sacred Scripture: what is said individually of one person is to be understood indiscriminately of the three. Whatever is pronounced of one person must equally be understood of the others, unless it is recognized that this concerns that by which, as I have said, they are distinct from one another [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “when this concerns”; “unless this concerns”].

Therefore, when we believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, because God is from God—that is, because the essence of the Holy Spirit is understood to be from the essence of the Father, which is one in the three [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “is one in three”; “is one in the three”]—we must necessarily confess that he is likewise from the Son, if the Son is not from him; for the Holy Spirit is from that which the Son is and from that which the Father is [Col. 0314A].

## CHAPTER XX [also XIX] [Note: [Col. 0313D] Chapter 19; in the Corbie manuscript it is Chapter 20.]

### The confirmation of the same argument is refuted

But someone will say: We understand the Son and the Holy Spirit to reveal what is said to be revealed by the Father alone; and the Father and the Holy Spirit to reveal and know what the Son alone is said to do; and the Father and the Son to teach what the Holy Spirit alone is promised to teach, because what is read of one alone in one place is openly signified of the others elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0313D] The Gembloux manuscript reads “is openly signified”; the manuscript of Victor 13 reads “is openly figured”; another reading is “is openly shown”].

But when it says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, we do not read anywhere that he proceeds from the Son. By this we are warned not to assert, according to our own judgment, what has nowhere been said [Note: [Col. 0313D] The Gembloux manuscripts read “by this we are warned”; another reading is “by this we warn”].

To this we reply that, rather, through these statements—which are expressed in this way—we are taught to understand similarly what is left unsaid in similar statements, especially since we see with complete clarity that, from what is said, what is not said follows by rational necessity, with no reason contradicting it [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “we see most clearly”; “we have seen most clearly”].

For when the Lord says to the Father, “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3), are we therefore to separate the Holy Spirit from this saving and life-giving knowledge because nowhere do we read, “This is eternal life: that they know the Father, the only true God, and the Holy Spirit”? Or: “This is eternal life: that they know the Son, the only true God, and the Holy Spirit”?

Or, when we read, “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26), are we to say that the Holy Spirit does not have life from the Father, from whom he is, so as to have life in himself, as the Father and the Son have it, because the Son nowhere says this of the Holy Spirit as he says it of himself?

Likewise, when he says, “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father,” and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:10), are we to deny that the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son, and that the Father and the Son are in the Holy Spirit? Or are we to deny that whoever sees the Son sees the Holy Spirit, just as he sees the Father, if these things are not read with the same wording with which they are spoken of the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscripts read “are read, which”; “are read, with which”]?

On the contrary, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same God, when it is said that knowing the Father and the Son, the only true God, is eternal life, the Holy Spirit must be understood inseparably in that knowledge [Col. 0314D].

And when we read, “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he granted the Son to have life in himself,” we must not regard that same life as foreign to the Holy Spirit, or suppose that he does not have it in himself [Note: [Col. 0315D] The manuscripts of Thuringia, Gembloux, and Bec read “not from himself”; “not in himself”].

And when we hear, “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father,” and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father,” we must understand through these statements that the Holy Spirit is not outside the Father and the Son, nor the Father and the Son outside the Holy Spirit; and that through the vision of the Son the Holy Spirit is seen just as the Father is [Note: [Col. 0315D] The manuscripts read “as also the Father”; “as the Father”].

For just as there is not one God the Father, another God the Son, and another God the Holy Spirit, so God does not have anything other than God within himself; God is not outside God; and God is not unlike God [Note: [Col. 0315D] The manuscripts read “Thus God does not have anything other than God in himself; God is not outside God; God is not unlike God. Finally”; the manuscript of Thuringia 30 reads “thus he does not have anything other than God in himself, nor is God outside God, nor is God unlike God. Finally”; another reading is “thus God does not have anything other than God in himself, etc., as in the other manuscripts”].

Finally, where do we read [Note: [Col. 0315D] The manuscripts read “Where do we not read”] in a prophet, evangelist, or Apostle, in these words, that God is one, three persons; or that one God is the Trinity; or that God is from God? [Col. 0315B] Yet neither in that Creed, in which the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is not expressed, do we find the word “person” or “Trinity” [Note: [Col. 0315D] The manuscripts read “we find the name ‘Trinity.’ But how, from these things”; another reading is “we find the name ‘person’ or ‘Trinity.’ Nevertheless, from these things”].

Nevertheless, since these conclusions follow most openly from what we read, we steadfastly believe them in our hearts and confess them with our mouths. Therefore, we must receive with certainty not only what is read in sacred Scripture, but also what follows from it by rational necessity, when no other reason contradicts it [Col. 0315B].

## CHAPTER XXI [also XX] [Note: [Col. 0315D] Chapter 20; in the Corbie manuscript it is Chapter 21.]

### The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is expressed when the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son
Although what has already been said above may suffice, I shall nevertheless add something further, by which the Holy Spirit may be known to be from the Son. The Greeks confess with us that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father, and the Spirit of the Son. I ask, therefore, whether they understand him to be the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father, and the Spirit of the Son in the same way, or differently. [Note: At Col. 0315D: *intelligitur esse*, “is understood to be,” mss.; *intelligunt esse*, “they understand [him] to be,” ms. Corb.; *intelligatur eum esse*, “that he be understood to be,” [another reading].]

It is certain, however, that he is not called the Spirit of God in the sense of a possession, as when one says someone’s horse or house. For the possessor is greater than what is possessed. But God is not greater than the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is God, and God is not greater than God. Nor is he called the Spirit of God as a member of God, like a man’s hand or foot: for God has no member or any part. How, then, is the Spirit to be understood as being of God, unless because that which he is is from God? [Note: At Col. 0315D: *nisi hoc quod est*, “unless [because] that which [he] is,” mss.; *nisi quia hoc quod est*, “unless because that which [he] is,” [another reading].]

Now the name Father signifies nothing other than God who is Father, or his relation to the Son, through which he has the name Father. The same must be said of the Son. For what is understood in the name Son, except God who is Son, or the relation by which he is referred to the Father, through which he is called Son? [Note: At Col. 0315D: *quae refertur ad Patrem*, “which is referred to the Father,” mss.; *qua refertur ad Patrem*, “by which he is referred to the Father,” [another reading].] But no understanding permits the Holy Spirit to be the Spirit of the Father or of the Son insofar as the Father is one and the Son another; rather, he is so insofar as both are one and the same God.

Therefore the meaning is the same when he is called the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father, and the Spirit of the Son. [Note: At Col. 0315D: *cum dicitur Spiritus sanctus Spiritus Dei*, “when the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of God,” mss.; *cum dicitur Spiritus Dei*, “when the Spirit of God is called,” [another reading].] But he is called the Spirit of God and the Spirit of the Father because he is and proceeds from God and from the Father. Thus he is and proceeds also from the Son, because in the same sense he is called the Spirit of the Son. [Note: At Col. 0315D: *et procedit de Filio*, “and proceeds from the Son,” mss. Vict., Corb., and Cister.; *et procedit etiam de Filio*, “and also proceeds from the Son,” [printed reading].]

For, when the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of God or the Spirit of the Lord, if we do not understand there the Spirit of the Son in the same sense as the Spirit of the Father, we shall either separate the Son from the name God or Lord, or the Spirit of God, or the Spirit of the Lord, will be understood in two ways. [Note: At Col. 0315D: *cum dicitur Spiritus sanctus Spiritus Dei*, “when the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of God,” mss.; *cum dicitur Spiritus Dei*, “when the Spirit of God is called,” [another reading].]

[Col. 0316B] But whence do they have this understanding, or where is it read in sacred Scripture that the same is not to be understood of the Father and of the Son when we read “Spirit of God” or “Spirit of the Lord”? [Note: At Col. 0315D: *Spiritum Dei et Spiritum Domini, aut*, “the Spirit of God and the Spirit of the Lord, or,” mss.; *Spiritum Dei aut Spiritum Domini*, “the Spirit of God or the Spirit of the Lord,” [printed reading].] Or what is found from which this follows? [Note: At Col. 0315D: *unde hoc non sequatur*, “from which this does not follow,” mss.; *unde hoc sequatur*, “from which this follows,” [printed reading].]

For if they say, “When the Spirit of the Father is mentioned, it is understood in two ways: he is the Spirit of the Father because he is from the Father and because he is given by the Father; but he is the Spirit of the Son only because he is given by the Son,” this is what I ask: whence do they have this? [Note: At Col. 0315D: *Filius vero Patris non*, “but the Son is not [the Father’s],” mss. and Edit. Goth.; *Filii vero Spiritus non*, “but the Spirit of the Son is not,” [printed reading].] And if they say that it has been stated on no authoritative page, nor does it follow from what is written there, why do they rebuke us when we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son because they do not read these words, while we understand that this necessarily follows from what they read and believe? [Note: At Col. 0315D: *ex eo quod scriptum*, “from that which is written,” mss.; *ex eo quod ibi scriptum*, “from that which is written there,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0315D: *sequi intelligimus*, “we understand [it] to follow,” mss.; *consequi intelligamus*, “we understand [it] to follow as a consequence,” [printed reading].]

Let them also judge for themselves what ought rather to be accepted, although sacred Scripture is silent about both: whether what we say, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son—which we show follows from what we truly believe—or what they say, that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father in one way and the Spirit of the Son in another—a proposition which they can show neither by authority nor by reason nor from what is certain. [Note: At Col. 0315D: *aliter esse Patris*, “to be [the] Father’s in another way,” mss.; *aliter esse Spiritum Patris*, “to be the Spirit of the Father in another way,” [printed reading].]

Certainly, they ought either to abandon this opinion of theirs—if indeed they say, as I hear, that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son in a different way from that in which he is the Spirit of the Father—since they nowhere read this or have anything from which to prove it; or at least they ought not to rebuke us who say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, although we do not read it in these words, because we show that it follows from what we believe together. [Note: At Col. 0315D: *audio quod Spiritus*, “I hear that the Spirit,” mss.; *audio quia Spiritus*, “I hear because the Spirit,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0315D: *debent quod dicimus*, “they ought [that] we say,” mss.; *debent qui dicimus*, “they ought [not to rebuke us] who say,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0315D: *verbis non legamus*, “we do not read [it] in words,” mss.; *verbis hoc non legamus*, “we do not read this in these words,” [printed reading].]

But if they abandon this assertion of theirs, let them believe with us that the Holy Spirit is equally the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, and understand that he proceeds from the Son as from the Father. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *et intelligent eum*, “and they will understand him,” mss. and Edit. Goth.; *et intelligant eum*, “and let them understand him,” ms. Corb.; *intelligant eum*, “let them understand him,” [another reading].] And if they cease to rebuke us, let them acknowledge with us that on account of this they know that we ought not to be rebuked.

## CHAPTER XXII [otherwise XXI]

[Note: At Col. 0317D: “Chapter 21” in ms. Corb.; “Chapter 22” [in the printed text].]

### Why the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son was not expressed in the Creed, and why it was added by the Latins without consulting the Greeks

As to their rebuking us for having added to that Creed—which both they and we accept and hold—that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, and asking why this was done and why it was not first shown to their Church, so that it might be considered jointly and, by common consent, that which ought to be added might be added: to this, I say, we have a sufficient answer.

For if it is asked why it was done, we say that it was necessary on account of certain persons of limited understanding, who did not perceive that the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is contained in, and follows from, those things which the universal Church believes, lest perhaps they should hesitate to believe it. How necessary this was, we learn from those who deny it because it is not stated in that Creed. Therefore, since necessity compelled it, no reason forbade it, and the true faith admitted it, Latin Christianity confidently asserted what it recognized ought to be believed and confessed.

For we know that not everything which we ought to believe and confess is stated there; nor did those who composed that Creed intend that the Christian faith should consist in believing and confessing only those things which they set down there. To say nothing of other matters, it is not stated there that the Lord descended into hell, though both we and the Greeks equally believe this. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *ut alia taceam*, “to say nothing of other matters,” mss.; *ut enim alia taceam*, “for, to say nothing of other matters,” [printed reading].]

But if they say that a Creed established by such great authority ought in no way to be corrupted, we do not judge there to be corruption where we add nothing contrary to what is stated there. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *auctoritate firmatum*, “confirmed by authority,” mss.; *auctoritate taxatum*, “established/authorized by authority,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0317D: *ubi nihil addidimus*, “where we added nothing,” mss. Vict. and Corb.; *ubi nihil addimus*, “where we add nothing,” [printed reading].]

And although we could defend this addition as not being a corruption, if anyone nevertheless wishes to maintain this contentious claim, we answer that we did not corrupt that Creed but issued another, new one. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *defendere possemus*, “we could defend,” mss. Vict. and Corb.; *defendere possimus*, “we can defend,” [another reading].] For we preserve intact and venerate with them that Creed which was translated according to the character of Greek diction; but this one, which we use more frequently in the hearing of the people, we have issued in Latin fashion with the aforesaid addition. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *illud secundum*, “that according to,” mss.; *illud enim secundum*, “for that according to,” ms. Corb.; *illud quod secundum*, “that which according to,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0317D: *illud autem quo*, “but that by which,” mss.; *istud autem quo*, “but this by which,” [printed reading].]

As to the question why this was not done with the consent of the Greek Church, [Col. 0318A] we answer that it was exceedingly difficult for the Latins to assemble the Greek bishops for consultation on this matter; nor was it necessary to bring into question what they do not doubt.
