[Note: At Col. 0317D: *in hoc quaestionem*, “into question in this,” mss.; *hoc in quaestionem*, “this into question,” [printed reading].] For what Church, even one spread throughout the extent of a single kingdom, is not permitted to establish something in accordance with the right faith, to be usefully read or sung in an assembly of the people? [Note: At Col. 0317D: *regni dilatatur*, “is spread through the extent of a kingdom,” mss. Vict. and Corb.; *regni dilatetur*, “may be spread through the extent of a kingdom,” [another reading].] How much more, then, was it permitted to the Latins steadfastly to proclaim this, in which all peoples and all kingdoms that use Latin letters agree together.

## CHAPTER XXIII [otherwise XXII]

[Note: At Col. 0317D: “Chapter 22” in ms. Corb.; “Chapter 23” [in the printed text].]

### Summary of the doctrine and proofs of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son

Let us briefly collect what has been established above by many arguments. [Col. 0318B] It is evident by an unassailable argument that the Holy Spirit is from the Son as he is from the Father, though not as from two different things, but as from one. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *esse de duobus diversis, sed de uno*, “to be from two different [things], but from one,” mss.; *esse quasi de duobus diversis, sed quasi de uno*, “to be as from two different [things], but as from one,” [printed reading].]

For the Holy Spirit is from that in which the Father and Son are one—that is, from God—not from that in which they are distinct from one another, but because God, from whom the Holy Spirit is, is Father and Son. Therefore he is truly said to be from the Father and the Son, who are two. And because the Father is neither prior nor posterior to the Son, neither greater nor less, nor is either more or less God than the other, the Holy Spirit is not first from the Father rather than from the Son, nor from the Son rather than from the Father; nor is he greater or less as existing from the Father than as existing from the Son; nor is he more or less from the one than from the other.

For if he were first or later, greater or less, or more or less from one than from the other, it would necessarily follow either that the Holy Spirit was not from that in which Father and Son are one, or that that unity itself was not perfectly and simply one, but that there was in it some diversity from which there would be the variation of which I have spoken in the Holy Spirit’s existing from that one and same unity. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *nam de altero si prior aut posterior, vel*, “for if from the other [he were] earlier or later, or,” mss.; *nam si prius aut post, vel*, “for if [he were] first or later, or,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0317D: *de uno eodem Spiritu Sancto*, “of the one and same Holy Spirit,” mss.; *de eodem uno Spiritum sanctum*, “of the Holy Spirit from that same one,” [printed reading].]

But it cannot be said that the Holy Spirit is not from that in which Father and Son are one; otherwise he would not be from God. Nor should it be believed that there is, in that very unity insofar as it is, any diversity. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *quod in ipso uno*, “that in that very one,” ms. Vict. 13; *quod ex ipso uno*, “that from that very one,” [another reading].]

Therefore the Holy Spirit is neither first nor later, neither greater nor less, neither more nor less from the Father than from the Son, nor from the Son than from the Father. For the one and same Holy Spirit, who is once wholly from the whole God, cannot be more or less from the one supremely simple God. [Note: At Col. 0317D: *qui simul est totus, de Deo toto, magis*, “who is wholly at once, from the whole God, more,” mss.; *qui semel totus est de Deo toto, magis*, “who is once wholly from the whole God, more,” ms. Thu. 90; *qui semel totus est de Deo, magis*, “who is once wholly from God, more,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0317D: *magis aut minus*, “more or less,” mss.; *magis et minus*, “more and less,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0317D: *et summo simplici*, “and the supremely simple,” mss.; *summe simplici*, “supremely simple,” [printed reading].]

[Col. 0319A]

## CHAPTER XXIV [otherwise XXIII]

### That the Holy Spirit is not principally from the Father

If it is said that the Holy Spirit is principally from the Father, as though he were more from the Father than from the Son, this must not be said so as to imply that any of the varieties mentioned above is present. Rather, because the Son has from the Father that which he is, it is not unfittingly maintained that the Son has from the Father the very fact that the Holy Spirit is from the Son, from whom the Son has being. [Note: At Col. 0319D: “If it is said, because, etc.” Here Chapter 24 begins in ms. Corb.]

Yet because the Son has being from the Father in such a way that he is altogether the same thing as the Father, one and the same God, just as the one simple God cannot be greater or less than himself, nor prior or posterior, nor have anything diverse within himself, so the Son is neither prior nor posterior, neither greater nor less than the Father, [Col. 0319B] nor has anything diverse in himself from him. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *de Patre ut omnino*, “from the Father, so that altogether,” mss.; *de Patre Filius ut omnino*, “the Son from the Father, so that altogether,” [printed reading].]

Rather, just as he has perfect being from him, so he has from the same source, in every respect, being equal and like to him—indeed, the very same being. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *aequale illi et simile*, “equal and like to him,” mss.; *ille aequalem et similem*, “him equal and like,” [another reading].]

Therefore, just as the Father is not more God than the Son, although the Son has being from the Father, so the Holy Spirit is not more from the Father than from the Son, although the Son has from the Father that the Holy Spirit is from him. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *habebat esse de*, “had being from,” mss. Vict. and Corb.; *habeat esse a*, “has being from,” [another reading].]

For in that in which he is one and the same with the Father—that is, in that which is God—he is not one and the Father another; nor does he have anything differently, because the Father is not one God and the Son another God; nor are they differently what they are. Rather, in that he is Father and this one Son, the former is one and the latter another. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *nec est alius*, “nor is he another,” mss.; *non est alius ille*, “that one is not another,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *neque dissimiliter sunt id quod sunt*, “nor are they differently what they are,” mss. Gem., Bec., Vict., Thu. 90, Cister.; *neque dissimiliter habet aliquid*, “nor does he have anything differently,” [printed reading]: “because the Father is not one God and the Son another God; nor are they differently what they are.”] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *iste Filius, alius est ille, et alius est iste*, “this one [is] Son; the former is one and the latter another,” ms. Corb.; *iste Filius est, alius ille, et alius iste*, “this one is Son; the former one and the latter another,” mss. Vict. 9 and 13, Cister.; *iste est Filius, est alius ille, et alius iste*, “this one is Son; the former is one and the latter another,” [printed reading].]

And just as the Son is not another God than the Father, so, insofar as he is God, he has nothing from another than from himself. [Col. 0319C] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *aliquid ab alio*, “anything from another,” mss.; *aliquid ab illo*, “anything from him,” ms. Corb.; *aliquid aliud ab alio*, “anything else from another,” [another reading].] For when we say “God from God, Son from Father,” we do not understand another God from another God, but the very same God from that very same God, although we say one from another, namely, Son from Father. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *Deum de Deo, Filium de Patre*, “God from God, Son from Father,” ms. Vict. 9; *Deum Filium de Deo Patre*, “God the Son from God the Father,” [another reading].]

For, as was said above, just as God, according to the name which signifies unity, admits no diversity, so, according to names signifying God from God, he necessarily admits plurality. If, therefore, it is said that the Holy Spirit is principally from the Father, nothing else is signified than that the Son himself, from whom the Holy Spirit is, has from the Father the very fact that the Holy Spirit is from him, because he has from the Father that which he is. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *Sanctus a Patre habet hoc*, “the Holy Spirit has this from the Father,” mss.; *Sanctus habet hoc*, “the Holy Spirit has this,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *sit de illo: quoniam*, “is from him: because,” mss.; *sit de illo a patre: quoniam*, “is from him, from the Father: because,” [another reading].]

This is not as in created things, where, when we assert that something is principally [something], we mean to signify that it is more that which it is said to be principally than that to which it is referred. Thus, when the steward of a certain lord feeds the household of the house at his master’s command, the lord is rightly said to feed it principally and more than the steward. [Col. 0320A] For not all things which are the lord’s are equally the steward’s, as those things which are the Father’s are also the Son’s without inequality. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *nam omnia quae sunt*, “for all things which are,” mss.; *nam non omnia quae sunt*, “for not all things which are,” [printed reading].]

## CHAPTER XXV

[Note: At Col. 0319D: “Chapter 23” in ms. Corb.; “Chapter 25” [in the printed text].]

### This procession introduces no priority within God except that of origin

Perhaps someone will ask and wonder, saying: How can it be understood that something has being from something else, and yet that from which it is is not in some way more principal and more worthy, while what is from it is somehow less and, as it were, secondary? [Note: At Col. 0319D: *habeat aliquid esse de*, “has something to be from,” ms. Vict. 9; *habeat esse de*, “has being from,” [printed reading].] Especially since that which is from something appears to need, in order to be, that from which it is; while that from which it is does not at all need that which is from itself? [Note: At Col. 0319D: *ut sit ex eo de quo*, “that it may be from that from which,” mss.; *ut sit eo de quo*, “that it may be [by] that from which,” [printed reading].]

The answer is that, just as the essence of God is very different and alien from created essence, so, when we say that God exists from God by being begotten or by proceeding, this generation or procession must be understood very differently from when we say that in other things something is born or proceeds.

For there nothing is earlier or later by nature, time, or any respect; nothing is greater or less; and nothing needs anything else for any reason. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *nihil est aut natura*, “nothing is either by nature,” mss.; *nihil aut natura*, “nothing, or by nature,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *aut in aliquo prius*, “or in any respect earlier,” mss. Gem., Vict., Thu. 30 and 90, and Cister.; *aut vi aliqua prius*, “or earlier by some force,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *aut aliqua ratione*, “or for any reason,” mss. Vict.; *aut ulla ratione*, “or for any reason whatsoever,” [printed reading]; *ut nulla ratione*, “so that for no reason,” ms. Corb.]

Rather, all that is is not so much equal or like to itself and coeternal with itself as identical with itself, and through itself wholly sufficient to itself. [Col. 0320C] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *non tam aequale*, “not so much equal,” mss.; *non tamen aequale*, “not, however, equal,” mss. Vict. 13 and Cister.; *tam aequale*, “so equal,” [another reading].] Nor is anything there born or proceeds as though advancing from non-being to being.

Therefore, just as our understanding cannot pass beyond eternity so as, as it were, to judge concerning its beginning, so it cannot, and ought not, to think or judge concerning this generation or procession by the likeness of a creature. But since that which is begotten and that which proceeds is nothing other than that from which it is begotten or proceeds—and that is the sole and one God—just as the same God is not greater or less than himself, so in the three, that is, in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, there is nothing greater or less, nor is one other than another in that which is greater or less, although it is true that God is from God by being begotten and proceeding. [Note: At Col. 0319D: *aliud nisi id*, “other than that,” mss. Vict., Corb., and Cister.; *aliud quam id*, “other than that,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0319D: *verum sit quod Deus est*, “although it is true that God is,” mss.; *verum sit quia Deus est*, “although it is true because God is,” [printed reading].]

[Col. 0321A]

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Note: At Col. 0321D: “Chapter 24” in ms. Corb.; “Chapter 26” [in the printed text].]

### The truth of the Holy Spirit’s procession from the Son is especially confirmed because the things from which it necessarily follows are certain by faith

Behold, we have seen with how much truth and how much necessity it follows that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *ecce videmus quanta*, “behold, we see how great,” mss.; *ecce vidimus de quanta*, “behold, we have seen from how great,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0321D: *et quanta*, “and how great,” ms. Corb.; *et etiam quanta*, “and also how great,” [another reading].]

If this is not true, then either something from which we said this follows is false—which is contrary to the Christian faith which we hold with the Greeks—or we have not concluded consequentially, which cannot be shown. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *quod contra Christianam*, “which [is] against the Christian,” mss.; *quod est contra Christianam*, “which is against the Christian,” [printed reading].] Therefore, if it is not true, the Christian faith is destroyed. It is also plain to one who understands that, if it is held to be false, no truth is born from this.

Let us consider also what follows if it is asserted to be true. Certainly, if it is true that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, it follows that he is the Spirit of the Son as of the Father, and is sent and given by the Son as by the Father; this divine authority teaches, and absolutely no falsehood follows.

But since denial of the Holy Spirit’s procession from the Son introduces so great a falsehood that it destroys, contrary to the Christian faith, those things from which we showed that it follows, and produces no truth; while its assertion proves so great a truth, as we have shown, and in no way brings any falsehood with it, let the rational mind consider by what reasoning it can exclude this from the Christian faith. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *nec ullam ullatenus*, “and no [falsehood] whatever,” mss.; *nec aliquam ullatenus*, “and not any [falsehood] whatever,” [printed reading].]

Finally, if it is an error to believe this procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, divine authority itself leads us into error, since it teaches us both those things from which this procession follows and those things which follow from it; [Col. 0321C] and nowhere either denies it or declares that anything opposes it in any way. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *pronuntiat auctoritas. Si*, “authority declares. If,” mss.; *pronuntiet. Si*, “may declare. If,” [another reading].]

If, therefore, it is objected that divine authority nowhere states it, and that for this reason it ought not to be said, let it likewise be said that, because it nowhere denies it and says nothing which opposes it, it ought not to be denied. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *esse dicenda*, “ought to be said,” mss. Vict. and Corb.; *esse dicendam*, “ought to be said,” [printed reading].] We say also that it sufficiently affirms it when it asserts those things from which it is proved, and in no way signifies anything from which it should be denied. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *aliquid significet sic*, “may signify something thus,” ms. Corb.; *sed alia*, “but other things,” mss.; *aliquid significat*, “signifies something,” [printed reading].]

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Note: At Col. 0321D: “Chapter 23” in ms. Corb.; “Chapter 27” [in the printed text].]

### If the Holy Spirit did not proceed from the Son, there would be no reason why the Son should not proceed from the Holy Spirit

It is clear, therefore, as I stated above, that, in addition to the fact that the Son exists by being begotten and the Holy Spirit by proceeding, there is also this reason—namely, that the Holy Spirit is from the Son—why they cannot be said to be from one another, and why, for this reason alone, the Son cannot be from the Holy Spirit. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *praemisi*, “I stated beforehand,” mss. and Cister.; *promisi*, “I promised,” [another reading].]

For, as has been said, either the Son is from the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit is from the Son. If the Holy Spirit were not from the Son, it would follow that the Son is from the Holy Spirit.

It is therefore apparent from the reasons given above that the Father is God from whom God is, and is not God from God; that the Son is God from God and God from whom God is; and that the Holy Spirit is God from God and is not God from whom God is. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *Spiritus Sanctus Deus de*, “the Holy Spirit [is] God from,” mss.; *Spiritus Sanctus est Deus de*, “the Holy Spirit is God from,” [printed reading].]

And although two are from the Father, namely Son and Holy Spirit, there are nevertheless not two gods from the Father, but one God who is Son and Holy Spirit. And though there are two—the one from whom the Son is and the one who is from the Son, namely Father and Holy Spirit—there are nevertheless not two gods, but one God who is Father and Holy Spirit. And although the Holy Spirit is from two, namely Father and Son, he is nevertheless not from two gods, but from one God, who is Father and Son. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *quanquam Spiritus*, “although the Spirit,” mss.; *et quanquam Spiritus*, “and although the Spirit,” [printed reading].]

But if Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are considered in pairs, it is clear from what has been said that one must either be from the other, because that one is not from himself, or not be from the other, because that other is from himself. [Col. 0322B] [Note: At Col. 0321D: *si conferamus*, “if we compare,” mss.; *si conferimus*, “if we are comparing,” [another reading].]

For if we compare Father and Son, we see that the Son is from the Father because the Father is not from him; and that the Father is not from the Son because the Son is from the Father. Likewise, if we consider Father and Holy Spirit, we find that the Holy Spirit is from the Father because the Father is not from him; and that the Father is not from the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit is from him. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *si consideremus conferendo Patrem*, “if, comparing, we consider the Father,” mss.; *si consideramus Patrem*, “if we consider the Father,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0321D: *inveniemus*, “we shall find,” mss.; *invenimus*, “we find,” [printed reading].]

So too, if we consider how Son and Holy Spirit stand toward one another, we understand that the Holy Spirit is from the Son because the Son is not from him; and that the Son is not from the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit is from the Son. [Note: At Col. 0321D: *quomodo sunt*, “how they are,” mss. Vict. and Corb.; *quomodo sint*, “how they may be,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0321D: *intelligimus*, “we understand,” mss. Vict. and Corb.; *intelligemus*, “we shall understand,” [another reading].]

It appears, therefore, as I said above, that although the aforesaid relations are in one, they cannot introduce their plurality into unity, nor can unity introduce its singularity into the relations. [Col. 0322C]

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Note: At Col. 0321D: “Chapter 26” in ms. Corb.; “Chapter 28” [in the printed text].]

### What is common and what is proper to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit

Moreover, there are six differences of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, arising from these names: having a Father and not having a Father; having a Son and not having a Son; having the Holy Spirit proceeding from oneself and not having the Holy Spirit proceeding from oneself.

Of these differences, each has one proper to himself, by which he differs from the other two; and two which are both common and proper, so that by that which he shares with one he differs from the other. [Col. 0322D] [Note: At Col. 0321D: *ut qua communicat*, “so that by that which he shares,” mss.; *ut quam communica*, “so that that which [he] shares,” [another reading].]

For the Father alone has a Son, by which he differs from the other two; he has the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself, which is common to him and the Son, and by which he differs from the Holy Spirit; but he does not have a Father, as neither does the Holy Spirit, and in this he differs from the Son. [Col. 0323A] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *sicut nec Spiritus sanctus, et in hoc*, “as neither does the Holy Spirit, and in this,” mss. Gem., Bec., Vict., Thu. 30, Corb., and Cister.; *sicut Spiritus sanctus, sed in hoc*, “as the Holy Spirit, but in this,” ms. Thu. 90; *ut Spiritus sanctus, et in hoc*, “as the Holy Spirit, and in this,” [another reading].]

The Son alone has a Father, in which he differs from Father and Holy Spirit; and he shares with the Father, as has been said, the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, by which he is distinguished from that same Holy Spirit; but he lacks a Son, as does the Holy Spirit, and in this he differs from the Father.

The Holy Spirit alone is one from whom another does not proceed. He shares with the Father, as I said, not having a Father, in which he is unlike the Son; and he shares with the Son, as has now been shown, not having a Son, in which he does not agree with the Father. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *et illi commune cum Patre*, “and it is common to him with the Father,” mss.; *est illi commune cum Patre*, “it is common to him with the Father,” [printed reading].]

Thus the Father alone is from no one and is the one from whom the other two are. Conversely, the Holy Spirit alone is from two and is one from whom no one is. [Col. 0323B] The Son alone is from one and is one from whom one is.

It is common to all three to have a relation to two: for the Father is related to the Son and the Holy Spirit, as to those who are from himself; the Son to the Father and the Holy Spirit, because he is from the Father and the Holy Spirit is from him; and the Holy Spirit to Father and Son, because he is from both.

Each, therefore, possesses his own properties, whose collection is not the same in another, after the likeness of the distinct persons of different human beings. For human persons are distinct from one another because the collection of the properties of each is not the same in another. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *quia unaquaeque*, “because each [collection],” mss.; *quia uniuscujusque*, “because [the collection] of each,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *in alio eadem*, “the same in another,” mss.; *in alia eadem*, “the same in another [feminine],” ms. Thuan. 30; *in alio*, “in another,” [another reading].]

There is, however, a difference. For among human persons, if there is one person, there is one human being; and if there is one human being, there is one person. Likewise, if there are several persons, there are also several human beings; and if these are several, the former do not escape plurality. [Col. 0323C] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *et istae plures*, “and if these [persons are] several,” mss. Gem. and Bec.; *et si isti plurales sunt*, “and if these [men] are plural,” mss. Vict., Thu. 30, Corb., and Edit. Goth.; *et si isti plures*, “and if these [men] are several,” [printed reading].]

In God, however, although there are three persons, there is nevertheless one God; and although there is one God, the persons do not at all lose their plurality. In that in which God is relatively called God in relation to God, he admits, as do several human beings, plurality and diversity of persons; but in that which he is through himself—that is, in God—he preserves inseparable singularity, after the likeness of one human being. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *admittit pluralitatem et diversitatem*, “admits plurality and diversity,” mss.; *admittit diversitatem*, “admits diversity,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *quod per se, id est, in*, “that which is through itself, that is, in,” mss.; *quod per se est, id est in*, “that which is through itself is, that is, in,” [printed reading].]

For plurality of human persons exists only among several human beings, nor does one human being receive plurality of persons; but God is one [and] three persons, and the three persons are one God. [Col. 0323D] In this way, therefore, he preserves completely neither the property of one person nor that of distinct persons. [Col. 0324A]

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: At Col. 0323D: “Chapter 27” in ms. Corb.; “Chapter 29” [in the printed text].]

### In God the plurality of persons is by what is proper; by what is common, the unity of essence

Why this is so, although I have said something about it in the aforesaid letter on the Incarnation of the Word, I shall nevertheless repeat it briefly here. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *aliquantulum diximus*, “we have said something,” mss.; *aliquantulum dixerim*, “I have said something,” [printed reading].]

It often happens that several things come together into one under the same name and with the same quantity which each had before they became one. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *eadem qualitate, quam*, “with the same quality which,” mss.; *eadem quantitate et quam*, “with the same quantity and which,” ms. Corb.; *eadem quantitate, quam*, “with the same quantity which,” [printed reading].] For if we add point to point without an interval, or set an equal line upon an equal line, or an equal surface upon an equal surface, there results only one point, one line, one surface. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *inaequali lineae*, “upon an unequal line,” mss.; *in aequali linea*, “upon an equal line,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *inaequali superficiei*, “upon an unequal surface,” mss. and Edit. Goth.; *in aequali superficie*, “upon an equal surface,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *nisi unus punctus*, “except one point,” mss. Gem., Bec., Thu., Corb., and Cister.; *nisi unum punctum*, “except one point,” [another reading].] Whoever wishes to inquire will find similar instances in many things. [Col. 0324B] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *inveniet simile*, “will find a similar [thing],” mss.; *inveniet similia*, “will find similar [things],” [printed reading].]

In this way, although there are not several eternities, if eternity is said to be in eternity, there is only one eternity; and light in light is only one light. In the same way, whatever is said of God’s essence, if it is replicated in itself, neither increases quantity nor admits plurality.

Now because God is eternity, just as absolutely nothing exists outside eternity, so absolutely nothing exists outside God. And as eternity in eternity is only one eternity, so God in God is one sole God. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *sicut aeternitas non est nisi una aeternitas in aeternitate, sic Deus*, “as eternity is only one eternity in eternity, so God,” mss.; *sicut aeternitas in aeternitate non est nisi una aeternitas; sic Deus*, “as eternity in eternity is only one eternity, so God,” ms. Corb.; *sicut aeternitas in aeternitate non est nisi summa aeternitas, sic Deus*, “as eternity in eternity is only supreme eternity, so God,” [another reading].]

But we have from the true faith that God is from God by being begotten, and God from God by proceeding. Yet because nothing is outside God, when God is begotten from God or proceeds from God, the one begotten or proceeding does not go outside God but remains in God. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *non erit nascens vel procedens*, “the one being born or proceeding will not be,” mss.; *non exit nascens vel procedens*, “the one being born or proceeding does not go out,” ms. Thuan. 90; *non exit nascens, vel procedit*, “the one being born does not go out, or proceeds,” [another reading].]

Therefore, because God in God is only one God, when God is begotten from God there is one sole God, begetting and begotten; and when God [Col. 0324C] proceeds from God, there is only one God, proceeding and that from whom he proceeds. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *cum procedit Deus*, “when God proceeds,” mss.; *et cum procedit*, “and when [he] proceeds,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *Deus est et procedens*, “God is and [he is] proceeding,” mss.; *Deus est procedens*, “God is proceeding,” [printed reading].] [Note: At Col. 0323D: *et de Deo quae procedit*, “and that which proceeds from God,” mss.; *et de quo procedit*, “and that from whom he proceeds,” [printed reading].]

Hence it follows inevitably that, since God has no parts but is wholly whatever he is, the one same God, and not another God, is wholly Father, wholly Son, wholly Holy Spirit. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *eumdemque et non alium, et alium Deum totum esse Patrem*, “the same and not another, and another God to be wholly Father,” mss. Vict. 3 and 9; *eundemque et non alium Deum totum esse Patrem*, “the same and not another God to be wholly Father,” [another reading].]

Therefore Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because, when God is from God and God in God, there is only one God, preserve in the Godhead, after the likeness of one human being, singularity. [Note: At Col. 0323D: *cum est Deus, in Deo non est*, “when God is, in God there is not,” mss.; *cum est Deus de Deo, et Deus in Deo, non est*, “when God is from God and God in God, there is not,” [printed reading].] But because, when God is from God either by being begotten or by proceeding, the same one cannot be both the one who is from another and the one from whom he is, they maintain plurality, according to the names signifying these relations, as distinct human persons do. [Col. 0325A]

It must nevertheless be noted that God is not without person, nor person without God; and that we sometimes attribute to individual persons their individual properties, and sometimes to one as though proper to him what is common to the others. For when we say: “The Father alone among the three persons is from no one; the Son alone is from one and is one from whom one is; the Holy Spirit alone is one from whom no one is,” by naming the individual persons we attribute to each what is proper to it. [Note: At Col. 0325D: *quia nullo est*, “because he is from no one,” ms. Vict. 3 and ms. Vict. 13; *quia a nullo est*, “because he is from no one,” ms. Corb.; *quia nulla est*, “because there is no one,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0325D: *solus Filius qui est de uno, et de quo unus, solus*, “the Son alone who is from one, and from whom one [is], alone,” ms.; *solus Filius est, qui de uno est, et de quo unus est, solus*, “the Son alone is from one and from whom one is, alone,” ms. Thu. 30; *solus Filius, qui de uno et de quo unus est. Solus*, “the Son alone, who is from one and from whom one is. Alone,” ms. Thu. 90; *solus Filius est, qui de uno et de quo unus est. Solus*, “the Son alone is from one and from whom one is. Alone,” [another reading].] [Note: At Col. 0325D: *Spiritus sanctus de quo*, “the Holy Spirit from whom,” mss.; *Spiritus sanctus est de quo*, “the Holy Spirit is one from whom,” [printed reading].]

But when we read, “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11:27), and “No one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11), although Scripture seems to deny of the other persons what it says of one, nevertheless that which it attributes to each as though proper to him is common to all. [Col. 0325B; Col. 0326A] For neither the Father nor the Son is ignorant of himself and of the things of God, nor is the Holy Spirit ignorant of the Father or the Son. Why and when that which is said of one as though of him alone is to be understood of the others has been sufficiently stated above.

### Conclusion of the work

Compelled by others, and trusting not in myself but in the same Holy Spirit, I have presumed to write for the Latins against the Greeks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit; and on that occasion to add something concerning the unity of the Godhead and the Trinity of persons, although there are innumerable persons among those who use Latin letters who could do this better than I.

Whatever, therefore, I have said that ought to be accepted should not be attributed to me but to the Spirit of truth. But if I have put forward anything which ought in some respect to be corrected, [Col. 0326B] let it be imputed to me, not to the understanding of Latin Christianity [the Latin Church]. [Note: At Col. 0325D: “Here ends the book of St Anselm, *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*,” mss.]

[Col. 0325B]

# THE DIALOGUE OF SAINT ANSELM ON THE FALL OF THE DEVIL
Provenance: original Luna translation and Luna repair; saved Terra review did not certify coverage; native Terra canonical-source adjudication completed the repair. No external source or deterministic translator was used.

## 62 CHAPTER ONE

**[Note: [Col. 0325D] The book *On the Fall of the Devil* was collated with three Victorine manuscripts, CC 9, EE 13, and RR 3; with the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Cîteaux, and Saint Michael in the Mount; and with the Gothic edition. The Cîteaux manuscript begins: “Here begins the treatise on the fall of the devil, published by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.” Victorine manuscript 9: “The book of Master Anselm, *On the Fall of the Devil*.” Victorine manuscript 3: “Here begins the treatise of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the fall of the devil.”]**

That this saying may also be applied to the angels: “What do you have that you did not receive?”; that there is nothing from God except goodness and being; that every good is essence, and every essence is good. **[Col. 0325D]**

**[Note: [Col. 0325D] See below, the prologue to the *Dialogue on Truth*.]**

**DISCIPLE.** Is that saying of the Apostle, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7), spoken only to human beings, or also to angels?

**MASTER.** No creature has anything from itself. For what does not possess itself from itself, how can it possess anything from itself? Moreover, if there is nothing except the one who made and the things made by the one **[Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts read: “The things made are by the one.”**, it is clear that nothing can be possessed except by the one who made it or by what he made.

**DISCIPLE.** It is truly clear. **[Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts read: “It is truly clear indeed.”]**

**MASTER.** Neither the maker himself nor what has been made can be possessed except by the maker himself.

**DISCIPLE.** This too is no less clear.

**MASTER.** He alone, therefore, has from himself whatever he has; and all other things have something only from him. And just as they have nothing from themselves, so they have something only from him. **[Col. 0325D–0326C]**

**DISCIPLE.** I do not at all see what you mean when you say that other things have from God nothing except something. For who else causes the many things that we see passing from being into non-being not to be what they were, even if they do not pass wholly into nothing? Or who causes whatever is not to be, except the one who causes everything that is to be? Again, if nothing is anything except because God makes it so **[Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “because God made it so.”**, it must be that what is not is not for this reason: because he does not make it so. Therefore, just as things that are have from him the fact that they are something, so things that are not, or things that pass from being into non-being, seem to have from that same one the fact that they are nothing. **[Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “to have nothing.”]**

**MASTER.** It is not only the one who makes something be, or makes something not be **[Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts read: “or makes nothing be”; the Cîteaux manuscript reads: “or makes something not be”; the Gothic edition reads: “and makes something not be.”**, who is said to make it be when he makes what is not exist, or makes what is exist not to exist **[Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts read: “or makes what is not exist.”**]; the one who can make something not exist and does not do so is also said to make it exist, and the one who can make something exist and does not do so is said to make it not exist. **[Col. 0326D–0327A]**

For example, not only is the person who strips someone said to make him naked or not clothed; so too is the person who, although able to prevent the one stripping him, does not prevent him. But the former is properly said to do this **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts read: “The former is properly said to do this.”**, while the latter is said to do it improperly **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts read: “The latter improperly.”]**. When the latter is said to have made someone naked or not clothed, nothing else is meant except that, although he could have done so, he did not make the person not be naked or remain clothed. **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The Cîteaux manuscript reads: “or remain clothed.”]**

In this way God is said to do many things which he does not do: for example, to lead into temptation, because, although he can, he does not defend someone from temptation; and to make what is not not exist, because, although he can, he does not make it exist. But if you consider things that exist when they pass into non-being, he himself makes them not exist.

For not only is there no other essence except through his making it **[Note: [Col. 0327D] Saint Michael’s manuscript omits “other.”**; what has been made cannot remain in any way unless that same one preserves it **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts read: “unless that same one makes it remain.”**]. When he ceases to preserve what he made, what was does not return to non-being because he makes it not exist, but because he ceases to make it exist. **[Col. 0327B]**

Even when, as though angered, he removes existence from something by destroying it, its non-being is not from him. Rather, when he removes what he had granted as his own—what had been made by him and preserved by him so that it might exist—it returns to the non-being that it possessed, not from him but from itself, before it was made.

If you reclaim from someone a tunic that you had voluntarily lent him for a time while he was naked **[Note: [Col. 0327D] One manuscript reads: “which you had lent him just for a time.”**, he does not receive nakedness from you. Rather, when you remove what was yours, he returns to what he was before being clothed by you.

Indeed, just as there is nothing from the highest good except goodness, and every good is from the highest good, so there is nothing from the highest essence except essence, and every essence is from the highest essence. Since, therefore, the highest good is the highest essence, it follows that every good is essence and every essence is good. **[Col. 0327C]**

Nothing, therefore, and non-being, just as they are not essence, are not good. **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts read: “Just as it is essence, it is not good.”]** Nothing and non-being, then, are not from him, from whom there is nothing except goodness and essence.

**DISCIPLE.** Now I clearly see that, just as goodness and being are only from God, so nothing except goodness and being is from God.

**MASTER.** Be careful not to suppose that, when we read in the divine books—or when, following them, we say—that God makes evil or makes non-being, I deny the reason for which this is said **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts read: “non-being, which I deny.”]**, or criticize the way it is said. Rather, we should not cling so much to the impropriety of the words, which conceals the truth, as we should long for the propriety of the truth concealed beneath the manifold forms of expression. **[Note: [Col. 0327D] Victorine, Gembloux, and Bec read: “form of expression.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** You need say this only to someone who does not understand or who is contentious. **[Col. 0328A]**

**MASTER.** Return to what you began **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “Return to what you began.”**, and see whether it can be said not only of a human being but also of an angel that he does not have what he did not receive.

## CHAPTER II

### Why the devil appears not to have received perseverance because God did not give it

**DISCIPLE.** It is sufficiently clear that this applies no less to an angel than to a human being. It is therefore established that the angel who stood in the truth persevered because he had perseverance; that he had perseverance because he received it; and that he received it because God gave it. It follows, then, that the one who did not stand in the truth did not persevere because he did not have perseverance; that he did not have perseverance because he did not receive it; and that he did not receive it because God did not give it.

If you can, I want you to show me his guilt, since he did not persevere because the one without whose giving he could possess nothing did not give it. **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts read: “since he did not persevere.”]** For I am certain—even if I do not understand it—that he was condemned only justly by the supremely just one, and that he could not have been justly condemned without guilt. **[Col. 0328B]**

**MASTER.** Why do you think it follows that, if the good angel received perseverance because God gave it, the evil angel did not receive it because God did not give it?

**DISCIPLE.** Because if giving is the cause of receiving in the good angel, I think that not giving is the cause of not receiving in the evil angel. And if non-giving is posited, I see that not receiving necessarily follows. **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscripts read: “I see that it is necessary from this.”]** We all know that, when we do not receive what we want, it is not because we do not receive it that it is not given; rather, we do not receive it because it is not given. **[Note: [Col. 0327D] The Venetian edition reads: “when we do not receive”; the manuscripts read: “when we did not receive.”]**

Finally, all those whom I have read or heard raising this question formulate it, as far as I remember, in this way: if the good angel received because God gave, the evil angel did not receive because God did not give. I do not yet remember seeing a solution to this inference. **[Col. 0328C]**

## CHAPTER III

### That God did not give because the devil did not receive

**MASTER.** Your inference is invalid. Not giving can fail to be the cause of not receiving, even if giving were always the cause of receiving.

**DISCIPLE.** Then, if not giving is posited, it does not necessarily follow that there is no receiving. Therefore, receiving can occur even if there is no giving.

**MASTER.** That is not so.

**DISCIPLE.** I want you to show me by an example what you mean. **[Col. 0328D]**

**MASTER.** If I extend something to you and you receive it, I do not give it because you receive it; rather, you receive it because I give it, and giving is the cause of receiving.

**DISCIPLE.** So it is.

**MASTER.** What if I extend that very thing to someone else and he does not receive it? **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “and he did not receive it”; the printed text adds: “here, therefore, not.”]** Does he therefore not receive it because I do not give it?

**DISCIPLE.** It seems rather that you do not give it because he does not receive it.

**MASTER.** In this case, then, not giving is not the cause of not receiving. Yet if I posit that I did not give it, that is the cause of the consequence that he did not receive it.

For it is one thing for a matter to be the cause of another matter; it is another for the positing of a matter to be the cause of something else following. **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “for something to follow.”]** Since a fire is not the cause of fire, but fire is the cause of a conflagration, nevertheless the positing of a conflagration is always the cause of fire’s following. For if there is a conflagration, fire must exist. **[Col. 0329A]**

**DISCIPLE.** I must acknowledge that this is so.

**MASTER.** You see, then, I think, that although you received because I gave, it does not nevertheless follow that the person who did not receive did not receive because I did not give; and yet it does follow that, if I did not give, he did not receive.

**DISCIPLE.** I see it, and I am pleased that I see it. **[Col. 0329B]**

**MASTER.** Do you still doubt that, just as the angel who stood received perseverance because God gave it, so God did not give it to the one who did not stand because he did not receive it? **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “so God did not immediately give it to the one who did not stand.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** You have not yet demonstrated this to me. You have demonstrated only this sufficiently: namely, that it does not follow from the fact that the good angel received because God gave that the evil angel did not receive because God did not give. **[Note: [Col. 0329D] Some manuscripts read: “received because he gave,” omitting “God.”]** If you wish to assert that God did not give it to him because he did not receive it, I ask why he did not receive it. Was it because he could not, or because he did not want to?

For if he lacked either the power or the will to receive it, God did not give it. For if God had given it, he certainly would have possessed it. Therefore, if he could not have the power or the will to receive perseverance except through God beforehand, what did he do wrong if he did not receive what God did not give him the power or will to receive? **[Col. 0329C]**

**MASTER.** God gave him the power and the will to receive perseverance.

**DISCIPLE.** Then he received what God gave, and had what he received.

**MASTER.** Indeed, he had it and received it.

**DISCIPLE.** Therefore he received and had perseverance.

**MASTER.** He did not receive it, and therefore did not have it.

**DISCIPLE.** Did you not say that God gave him, and that he received, the power and will to receive perseverance?

**MASTER.** I did; but I did not say that God gave him the act of receiving perseverance. I said only that he gave him the will and power to receive perseverance.

**DISCIPLE.** Therefore, if he willed and was able, he received perseverance.

**MASTER.** That does not necessarily follow. **[Col. 0329D]**

**DISCIPLE.** I do not see why not, unless you show me. **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “I do not see why—unless.”]**

**MASTER.** Have you ever begun something with the will and ability to complete it, which nevertheless you did not complete because your will changed before the matter was finished?

**DISCIPLE.** Often.

**MASTER.** Then you willed and were able to persevere in something in which you did not persevere.

**DISCIPLE.** Certainly I willed to do so; but I did not persevere in the will, and therefore did not persevere in the action.

**MASTER.** Why did you not persevere in the will?

**DISCIPLE.** Because I did not want to.

**MASTER.** As long as you wanted to persevere in the action, did you not want to persevere in that very will?

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny it.

**MASTER.** Why, then, do you say that you did not want to persevere in it? **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “Why do you say, ‘I did not want’?”]**

**DISCIPLE.** I would answer again: because I wanted to persevere, but I did not persevere in this will—unless I were to see the matter proceeding to infinity, with you always asking the same question and me giving the same answer. **[Col. 0330A]**

**MASTER.** You should not, then, say, “I did not want to persevere in the will because I did not want to persevere in the will of this will.” **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts vary: some read, “I did not want to persevere in the will of this will”; Saint Michael’s reads, “I did not want to persevere, because I did not want to persevere in the will of this will.”]** Rather, when you are asked, “Why did you not persevere in the action in which you willed and were able to persevere?” you can answer **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “you can or ought to answer,” with “or ought” omitted here.**: “Because I did not persevere in the will.”

If it is then asked, “Why did you not persevere in the will?” another cause must be given—namely, the cause from which the failure of that will occurred—rather than saying that you did not persevere in willing the will. For in answering thus you show nothing other than the very thing being asked: that you did not persevere in the will to persevere in the action. **[Col. 0330B]**

**DISCIPLE.** I see that I did not see what I should say.

**MASTER.** Say, then, in one word what it is to persevere, insofar as the matter requires, in doing something.

**DISCIPLE.** To complete it. For to persevere in writing something, we say *perscribere*, “to write through to completion”; in leading, *perducere*, “to lead through to completion.”

**MASTER.** Let us therefore say similarly—even if the expression is not customary—that to persevere in willing is *pervelle*, “to will through to completion.” **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “that to persevere is to will through,” rather than the rare form *pervelle*.]**

**DISCIPLE.** Let it be so.

**MASTER.** Since, then, you did not complete what you willed and were able to complete, why did you not complete it?

**DISCIPLE.** Because I did not will it through to completion. **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “because I did not will to persevere.”]**

**MASTER.** Say, then, that the devil, who received the will and ability to receive perseverance—and the will and ability to persevere—did not receive perseverance and did not persevere because he did not will it through to completion. **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “because he did not will to persevere.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** I ask again why he did not will it through to completion. **[Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscripts read: “Why did he not will to persevere?”]** For when you say that he did not will through to completion what he willed, it is as though you said: “What he willed beforehand, he later did not will.” When, then, he did not will what he had previously willed, why did he not will it, unless he lacked the will? I do not mean the will that he previously had when he willed, but the will that he lacked when he did not will.

Why, moreover, did he lack this will, unless because he did not receive it? And why did he not receive it, unless because God did not give it? **[Note: [Col. 0331C] The manuscripts continue: “God did not give it? But God did not give it for this reason: because he did not receive it. M. Again.”]**

**MASTER.** I say again that he did not fail to receive it because God did not give it; rather, God did not give it because he did not receive it.

**DISCIPLE.** Show this.

**MASTER.** He voluntarily abandoned the will that he had. **[Note: [Col. 0331C] The manuscripts read: “that he had had.”]** And just as he received the possession of it for as long as he had it, so he could always have received and retained what he abandoned. **[Note: [Col. 0331C] The manuscripts read: “he could receive it and always retain it.”]** But because he abandoned it, he did not receive it.

Therefore, because he abandoned it, he did not receive the retaining of what he had abandoned. **[Note: [Col. 0331C] The manuscripts read: “to retain it because he abandoned it.”]** He did not fail to receive it because God did not give it; rather, God did not give it because he did not receive it. **[Note: [Col. 0331C] Saint Michael’s manuscript reads: “he did not receive it,” rather than “he did not fail to receive it”; the manuscripts continue: “Who did not?”]**

**DISCIPLE.** Who does not see that he did not fail to will to retain it because he abandoned it, but abandoned it because he did not will to retain it? For, in one who is retaining something, not willing to retain always comes before willing to abandon. Someone wants to abandon what he is holding precisely because he does not want to hold it.

I ask, therefore, why he did not will to retain what he was holding, unless God did not give him the will to do so. **[Col. 0331B]**

**MASTER.** Not always does not willing to retain come before willing to abandon.

**DISCIPLE.** Show me when it does not.

**MASTER.** When you do not want to retain something for its own sake but want to abandon it, as with a burning coal placed in your bare hand: then perhaps not willing to retain comes first, and you want to abandon it because you do not want to retain it. Before you hold it, you do not want to hold it; but you cannot want to abandon it until you are holding it.

When, however, you are holding something that you do not want to retain except for the sake of something else, and that you do not want to abandon except for the sake of something else; and when you prefer something else—which you cannot have unless you abandon what you are holding—then willing to abandon comes before not willing to retain.

For when a miser wants to retain a coin but prefers bread, which he cannot have unless he gives up the coin, he first wants to give up—that is, abandon—the coin, before he does not want to retain it. He does not want to give up the coin because he does not want to retain it; rather, he does not want to retain it because he must give it up in order to have the bread. **[Note: [Col. 0331C] The manuscripts read: “but because he must give it up”; the Gothic edition reads: “but he does not want to retain it because he must give it up”; another reading is: “because he does not want anything.”]**

Even before he has it, he wants to retain and possess it; and when he has it, he certainly does not fail to want to retain it as long as he does not need to abandon it.

**DISCIPLE.** It is true.

**MASTER.** Therefore, not always does not willing to retain come before willing to abandon; sometimes willing to abandon comes first. **[Col. 0332A]**

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny it.

**MASTER.** I say, then, that he did not fail to will what he ought to have willed, and what he ought to have willed, because the will failed and God failed to give it; rather, by willing what he ought not to have willed, he drove out the good will when the evil will came upon it. **[Note: [Col. 0331C] The manuscripts read: “the will fails.”]**

Therefore he did not lack, and did not fail to receive, a good persevering will because God did not give it. Rather, God did not give it because, by willing what he ought not to have willed, he abandoned that will, and by abandoning it he did not retain it.

**[Note: [Col. 0331C] In the margin of the Cîteaux manuscript, in the same hand, are written the following words: “God created among the other angels one—not an order, but an individual spirit—who is commonly called Lucifer in Holy Scripture; and in his creation he made him worthier than all the others. Speaking of him, the Lord says to blessed Job: ‘He is the beginning of the ways of God,’ that is, the chief among the works of God. And Gregory, on the same passage: ‘God, who created all things, made this one more eminent than all; and although he had an equal over him—which is not certain—he nevertheless had none above himself.’ And Ezekiel says of him: ‘Every precious stone was your covering,’ that is, all the angelic spirits were subject to you, offering you veneration and adorning you about, as though with a precious garment. Therefore this Lucifer, because he saw himself exalted to so great a dignity and wished inordinately to become like his Creator, sinned without possibility of remission; and, falling below the blessedness which he would have had if he had persevered, he lost [his] joys, together with all who agreed with him in this will.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** I understand what you are saying.

## CHAPTER IV

### How he sinned and willed to be like God

**MASTER.** Do you still doubt that the devil did not want to abandon what he had because he did not want to retain it, but that he did not want to retain it because he wanted to abandon it?

**DISCIPLE.** I do not doubt that this is possible, but you have not yet made me certain that this is what happened. First, then, show what he wanted to have that he did not have, so that he might want to abandon what he was holding, as you demonstrated in the case of the miser. Then, if nothing can be objected to its being so, I shall acknowledge that I have no doubt.

**MASTER.** You do not doubt that he sinned, since he could not have been unjustly condemned by a just God; but you ask how he sinned.

**DISCIPLE.** So it is.

**MASTER.** If he had preserved justice perseveringly, he would never have sinned and would not have been miserable.

**DISCIPLE.** We believe this.

**MASTER.** No one preserves justice except by willing what he ought to will, nor abandons it except by willing what he ought not to will.

**DISCIPLE.** No one doubts this.

**MASTER.** By willing something, then, which at that time he ought not to have willed, he abandoned justice, and thus sinned.

**DISCIPLE.** That follows. But I ask what else he wanted besides what he had.

**MASTER.** Whatever he had, he ought to have willed. **[Note: [Col. 0331C] One manuscript reads: “It is true that he ought to have willed what he had.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** He truly ought to have willed what he had received from God; and he did not sin by willing this.

**MASTER.** Therefore he wanted something that he did not have and ought not then to have willed, just as Eve wanted to be like the gods before God willed this.

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny that this follows.

**MASTER.** He could want nothing except justice or advantage. For blessedness consists of advantages, and every rational nature wants blessedness.

**DISCIPLE.** We can recognize this in ourselves, since we want nothing except what we think just or advantageous. **[Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscripts read: “just and advantageous.”]**

**MASTER.** He could not have sinned by willing justice.

**DISCIPLE.** True.

**MASTER.** Therefore he sinned by willing an advantage that he neither had nor ought then to have willed, although it could have existed for him as an increase of blessedness.

**DISCIPLE.** It is evident that he could not have sinned in any other way.

**MASTER.** You see, I think, that by disorderly willing something more than he had received, he extended his will beyond justice. **[Note: [Col. 0333D] Victorine manuscript 3 reads: “he displayed,” rather than “he extended.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** Now I clearly see that he sinned both by willing what he ought not to have willed and by not willing what he ought to have willed. And it is evident that he did not want more than he ought to have wanted because he did not want to retain justice; rather, he did not retain justice because he wanted something else, and by willing it he abandoned justice, just as you demonstrated in the case of the miser with the coin and the bread. **[Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscripts read: “because he wanted something.”]**

**MASTER.** But when he wanted what God did not want him to will, he wanted, in a disorderly way, to be like God.

**DISCIPLE.** If God cannot be conceived except as so uniquely constituted that nothing like him can be conceived, how could the devil have wanted what he could not conceive? He was not so dull-minded that he did not know that nothing else could be conceived as like God.

**MASTER.** Even if he did not want to be altogether equal to God, but wanted something less than God **[Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscripts read: “he wanted to be altogether equal to God in some respect, something less than God.”]**, nevertheless, by wanting this against God’s will, he wanted, in this very act, to be disorderly like God. For it belongs to God alone to will something by one’s own will in such a way as not to follow a higher will.

**DISCIPLE.** So it is.

**MASTER.** He not only wanted to be equal to God by presuming to have a will of his own; he also wanted to be greater, by willing what God did not want him to will, since he placed his own will above God’s will.

**DISCIPLE.** It is sufficiently clear.

**MASTER.** I think, then, that it is now manifest to you, from the arguments stated above, that the devil voluntarily abandoned willing what he ought to have willed and justly lost what he had, because he voluntarily and wrongly willed what he did not have and ought not to have willed. **[Note: [Col. 0333D] Victorine manuscripts 9 and 13 read: “and willed what he ought not to have willed.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing could be clearer.

**MASTER.** Although the good angel received perseverance because God gave it, the evil angel did not therefore fail to receive it because God did not give it. Rather, God did not give it because he did not receive it; and he did not receive it because he did not want to receive it.

**DISCIPLE.** You satisfy me so fully concerning the matters I ask about **[Note: [Col. 0333D] Saint Michael’s manuscript reads: “You have satisfied me concerning”; the manuscripts of Gembloux and Bec read: “You satisfy me concerning.”]**, that neither in what you propose nor in the very sequence of your conclusions do I see truth wavering in any way, as far as my judgment goes. **[Col. 0334A]**

## CHAPTER V

### That the good angels could have sinned before the fall of the evil angels

**MASTER.** Do you think that the good angels could likewise have sinned before the evil angels fell?

**DISCIPLE.** I think so, but I would like to grasp this by reasoning.

**MASTER.** You hold it as certain that, if they could not sin, they preserved justice not by power but by necessity. Why, then, would they have deserved greater grace from God because they stood when others fell than because they preserved rationality **[Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscripts read: “reasonableness.”]**, which they could not lose? Indeed, if you consider the matter carefully, they would not rightly be called just.

**DISCIPLE.** Reason demonstrates this.

**MASTER.** Therefore, if those who fell had not sinned when they could have sinned, they would have been so much better than these as they would truly have been just and would have deserved grace from God. It follows either that the elect human beings will be greater and better than the good angels, or that the fallen angels will not be perfectly restored, since the human beings who are assumed in their place will not be such as those angels would have become. **[Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscripts of Bec, Gembloux, Cîteaux, and Saint Michael read: “who are assumed for them”; Victorine manuscripts 3 and 9 read: “who will be assumed for them.”]**

**DISCIPLE.** I consider both of these conclusions wholly unacceptable. **[Col. 0334B]**

**MASTER.** The good angels, then, could have sinned before the fall of the evil angels **[Note: [Col. 0333D] Victorine manuscript 3 omits “of the evil angels.”]**, and could have sinned in no other way than was shown concerning those who did sin.

**DISCIPLE.** I see no other possibility.

## CHAPTER VI

### How the good were confirmed in their state and the evil in their fall

**MASTER.** Those angels, then, who preferred the justice they had to that additional good which they did not have, lost that good, as far as their will was concerned, as though for the sake of justice. In return, justice granted them also a share of that good, and they remained in true security in what they had. **[Col. 0334C]**

Therefore they advanced so far **[Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscripts read: “They advanced from God.”]** that they attained whatever they could have willed. **[Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscripts read: “so that they have attained.”]** They no longer see anything more that they could will. **[Note: [Col. 0333D] Victorine, Bec, Gembloux, and Saint Michael read: “anything more that they can will.”]** For this reason they cannot sin.

But those angels who preferred the additional good that God did not yet wish to give them to standing in the justice in which they had been created, were judged by that same justice. They did not obtain at all the thing for which they had despised justice, and they lost the good that they held.

Thus the angels were divided: those who clung to justice can will no good thing that they do not enjoy, while those who abandoned it can will no good thing of which they are not deprived. **[Col. 0334D–0335A]**

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing is more beautiful or more just than this division. But if you could say what sort of advantage that was, I would like to hear it—what advantage the good angels justly advanced by willing, and the evil angels fell by unjustly desiring.

**MASTER.** I do not see what it was. But whatever it was, it is enough to know that it was something toward which they could grow, which they did not receive when they were created, so that they might advance to something else through their merit. **[Col. 0335A]**

## CHAPTER VII

### Whether the will, and its turning toward what it ought not to will, is itself the evil that makes the wicked; and why a rational creature cannot turn by itself from evil to good, as it can from good to evil

## Complete textual apparatus and editorial matter

This register restores every textual note in the supplied chunk. Each item is keyed to the clause it affects. The first Latin form is the witness reading specified by the source; the second is the contrasting printed form. The English gloss states the difference, so Latin is never left untranslated.

### [Col. 0325D]

- At “the things made by the one,” the manuscripts read *facta sunt ab* (“the things made are by”) for *facta sunt ab uno* (“the things made are by one”). Victorine manuscripts read *quia a se nullatenus* (“because in no way from itself”) for *quia nullatenus* (“because in no way”); Cîteaux reads *habere aliquid* (“to possess something”) for *haberi aliquid* (“for something to be possessed”).
- At “It is truly clear,” the manuscripts read *vere clarum est* (“it is truly clear”) for *vere clarum* (“truly clear”).
- At “Who else causes,” Victorine, Cîteaux, and Saint Michael read *quis fecit alius* (“who else caused”) for *quis facit alius* (“who else causes”). At “because God makes,” the manuscripts and Gothic edition read *quia Deus fecit* (“because God made”) for *quia Deus facit* (“because God makes”); at “have the fact that they are nothing,” they read *habere nihil* (“to have nothing”) for *habere esse nihil* (“to have being nothing”).
- At “makes something not be,” Victorine reads *aut non esse aliquid* (“or not to be something”), Cîteaux *aut aliquid non esse* (“or something not to be”), and the Gothic edition *aut esse non aliquid* (“or to be not something”), for *aut aliquid non esse* in the printed sequence. The manuscripts read *aut ut non sit* (“or that it not be”) for *aut non sit* (“or not be”), and *aliquid ut non sit* (“something so that it not be”) for *ut non sit aliquid* (“so that something not be”).

### [Col. 0327D]

- At the beginning of the nakedness example, Victorine and Saint Michael read the whole preceding continuation *facere esse non esse. Quippe* (“to make be, not be. For indeed”) for the printed restart *... dicitur facere non esse. Quippe* (“... is said to make not be. For indeed”). This is a boundary/wording variant, not an added doctrine.
- At “the former is properly said,” the manuscripts read *ille dicitur proprie facere* (“the former is said properly to do”) for *ille proprie dicitur hoc facere* (“the former is properly said to do this”); at “the latter improperly,” they read *iste improprie* (“the latter improperly”) for *iste vero improprie* (“but the latter improperly”). At “is said to have made,” manuscripts and Gothic edition read *quia facit esse* (“because he makes be”) for *quia fecit esse* (“because he made be”); Cîteaux reads *aut ut maneret* (“or that he might remain”) for *aut ut maneret* in the printed construction, preserving the differing connective scope.
- Saint Michael omits *alia* (“other”) in *aliqua alia essentia* (“any other essence”). The manuscripts read *quae facta est* (“which was made,” feminine) for *quod factum est* (“what was made,” neuter); and *nisi eodem ipso faciente ut maneat* (“unless that same one makes it remain”) for *nisi eodem ipso servante* (“unless that same one preserves it”).
- In the tunic example, the manuscripts read *quam praestiteras illi modo ad tempus* (“which you had lent him only for a time”) for *quam illi nudo sponte ad tempus praestiteras* (“which you had voluntarily lent him while naked for a time”).
- At “just as it is not essence, it is not good,” the manuscripts read *sicut est essentia, non est bonum* (“just as it is essence, it is not good”) for *sicut non est essentia, ita non est bonum* (“just as it is not essence, so it is not good”); the source preserves this problematic variant without resolving it.
- At “I deny the reason,” the manuscripts read *non esse, quod negem* (“non-being, which I deny”) for *non esse, quia negem* (“non-being, because I deny”). Victorine, Gembloux, and Bec read *genere locutionis* (“under a kind of expression,” singular) for *genere locutionum* (“under kinds of expressions,” plural). At “Return,” manuscripts and Gothic edition read *redi ad quod* (“return to what”) for *redi ad id quod* (“return to that which”).

### [Col. 0327D–0329D]: Chapters II–III

- At “God gave; consequently,” Gembloux, Bec, Victorine, and Cîteaux read *dedit, consequens est* (“gave; consequently it follows”) for *dedit. Consequens est* (“gave. It follows”). At “because he did not persevere,” manuscripts read *cum ideo non perseveravit* (“since for that reason he did not persevere,” indicative) for *cum ideo non perseveraverit* (“since ... he may not have persevered”). At “by the supremely just one,” manuscripts read *a summo justo* (“by the highest just one”) for *a summe justo* (“by the supremely just one”).
- At “I see a necessary consequence,” manuscripts read *inde necessariam* (“from this, necessary”) for *video necessariam* (“I see [it] necessary”); at “we all know,” *ut omnes scimus* (“as we all know”) for *et omnes scimus* (“and we all know”). Venetian, Cologne, and Gothic editions read *quia non accipimus* (“because we do not receive”) while manuscripts read *quia non accepimus* (“because we did not receive”), for the printed *qui non accipimus* (“we who do not receive”). Cîteaux omits *angelus* (“angel”) in *malus angelus ideo* (“the evil angel therefore”).
- At “that very thing,” manuscripts read *quid si ipsum* (“what if [I extend] the thing itself”) for *quid si id ipsum* (“what if [I extend] that very thing”); at “and he does not receive,” they read *et non accepit* (“and he did not receive”), with the printed text adding *hic igitur non* (“here, therefore, not”). At “not giving,” manuscripts read *hoc igitur non* (“therefore this not-giving”) for *hic igitur non* (“here, therefore, not-giving”); at “I did not give,” *non me dedisse* (“that I did not give”) for *me non dedisse* (“that I had not given”). At “for something to follow,” *sequatur aliquid* (“something may follow”) for *sequatur aliud* (“another thing may follow”).
- At “to the one who did not stand,” Cîteaux and Saint Michael read *ita non statim* (“thus not immediately”) for *ita non stanti* (“thus to the one not standing”). Cîteaux reads *monstrasti* (“you showed”) for *demonstrasti* (“you demonstrated”). Victorine and Saint Michael read *accepit, quia dedit* (“he received because he gave”), omitting *Deus* (“God”), for *accepit, quia Deus dedit*.
- At “I do not see why, unless,” Victorine, Gembloux, and Bec read *non video cur nisi* (“I do not see why unless”) for *non video cur non, nisi* (“I do not see why not, unless”). At “you say you did not want,” manuscripts read *dicis, non voluisse* (“you say, [that you] did not want”) for *dicis te non voluisse* (“you say that you did not want”); Cîteaux reads *semper idem ipsum* (“always the very same thing”) for *semper idipsum* (“always the same thing”).
- At the infinite-regress sentence, manuscripts read *ideo non volui perseverare in voluntate, quia non volui perseverare in voluntate hujus voluntatis* (“therefore I did not will to persevere in the will because I did not will to persevere in the will of this will”) for the shorter printed form; Saint Michael reads *ideo non volui perseverare; quia ...* (“therefore I did not will to persevere; because ...”). At “you can answer,” manuscripts read *potes vel debes* (“you can or ought to”) for *potes* (“you can”), omitting *vel debes* in the printed line; at “because I did not persevere,” they read the first person *quia non perseveravi* for printed *quia non perseverasti* (“because you did not persevere”).
- At the coined *pervelle*, manuscripts read *sit perseverare velle* (“to persevere is to will”) for *sit pervelle* (“to will through to completion”). Saint Michael reads *cur ergo non* (“why then did you not”) for *cum ergo non* (“since then you did not”). Manuscripts read *quia non perseverare volui* (“because I did not will to persevere”) for *quia non pervolui* (“because I did not will through”).
- At the devil’s case manuscripts read *quia non perseverare voluit* (“because he did not will to persevere”) for *quia non pervoluit* (“because he did not will through”); at the question, *quare non perseverare voluit?* (“why did he not will to persevere?”) for *quare non pervoluit?* (“why did he not will through?”). Their longer reading begins *cum enim dicis, quia non perseverare voluit quod voluit* (“for when you say that he did not will to persevere in what he willed”), while the printed text has *quia quod voluit, non pervoluit* (“that what he willed, he did not will through”); Saint Michael retains the same contrast with *non perseverare voluit*.
- Manuscripts read *quoniam ergo* (“since therefore”) for *quando ergo* (“when therefore”), and *habuit cum voluerit* (“he had when he had willed,” perfect subjunctive) for *habuit cum voluit* (“he had when he willed”). Gembloux, Bec, and Saint Michael continue “God did not give? But God did not give for this reason: because he did not receive it. M. Again”; the printed text has only “God did not give? M. Again.”

### [Col. 0331C]: retaining and abandoning

- At “the will that he had,” manuscripts read *quam habuit* (“which he had”) for *quam habebat* (“which he was having”). At “received the ability to have,” they read *sicut accepit habuit* (“just as he received, he had”) for *sicut accepit habere* (“just as he received to have”). At “could always retain,” manuscripts read *potuit accipere semper tenere* (“he could receive [it] always to retain”) for *potuit accipere semper* (“he could always receive”); at “retain what he abandoned,” *tenere quia deseruit* (“to retain because he abandoned”) for *tenere quod deseruit* (“to retain what he abandoned”).
- At “did not receive the retaining,” manuscripts read *tenere quia deseruit* (“to retain because he abandoned”) for *tenere quod deseruit* (“to retain what he abandoned”). Saint Michael reads *non ideo accepit* (“not for that reason he received”) for *non ideo non accepit* (“not for that reason he did not receive”); manuscripts read *sed Deus non* (“but God did not”) for *sed ideo Deus non* (“but for that reason God did not”). At the next clause manuscripts continue *non accepit. Quis non* (“he did not receive. Who does not”), while printed has *non accepit. D. Quis non* (“he did not receive. Disciple: Who does not”).
- Venetian reads *ideo non voluit* (“for that reason he did not will”) for *non ideo non voluit* (“not for that reason he did not will”). At “retain. I ask,” manuscripts have corrupt *terere. Quaero* (“to rub. I ask”) for *tenere. D. Quaero* (“to retain. Disciple: I ask”); the corruption is retained as unresolved.
- At the hot-coal example, manuscripts read *quando aliquando rem* (“when at some time [you hold] a thing”) for *quando aliquam rem* (“when [you hold] some thing”). At “what you do not want to retain except for something else,” manuscripts read *quod propter aliquid non vis* (“which you do not want because of something”) for *quod nonnisi propter aliud non vis* (“which you do not want except because of something else”); Cîteaux reads *quod nonnisi propter aliud non vis* (“which you do not want except because of something else”); the Gothic edition reads *quod nisi propter aliud non vis* (“which you do not want unless because of something else”). The final unassigned contrast is *quod non propter aliquid vis*: “which you will, though not for the sake of something [else]”; its *non* qualifies *propter aliquid*, not *vis*..
- At “nor want to abandon except for something else,” manuscripts read *nec tamen propter aliquid* (“nor nevertheless because of something”) for *nec nisi propter aliud* (“nor except because of something else”). At “you prefer something else,” manuscripts read *et magis vis aliquid* (“and you prefer something”) for *et magis vis aliud* (“and you prefer something else”). These are separate entries and do not inherit a witness label from the previous note.
- In the miser sentence, manuscripts read *tenere: sed ideo non vult tenere, quia ut* (“to retain; but therefore he does not want to retain, because in order that”) for *tenere: sed quia ut* (“to retain; but because in order that”). At “willing to abandon,” the printed *vellere deserere* is a corruption for *velle deserere* (“to will to abandon”); it is preserved as a printed corruption rather than normalized.
- At “the will failed,” manuscripts read *voluntas deficit* (“the will fails,” present) for *voluntas defecit* (“the will failed,” perfect). The Cîteaux marginal note is: “God created among the other angels one individual spirit, not an order, commonly called Lucifer in Holy Scripture ... and, falling below the blessedness he would have had had he persevered, together with all who consented to him in this will, he lost [his] joys.” The source’s *gaudia amisit* is plural: “he lost joys,” not “he lost joy.” It also quotes Job, Gregory, and Ezekiel as translated in the main note.

### [Col. 0331C–0335D]: Chapters IV–VI

- At “Whatever he had,” manuscripts read *verum quod habebat* (“true, what he had”) for *quidquid habebat* (“whatever he had”). At “just or advantageous,” manuscripts read *justum et commodum* (“just and advantageous”) for *justum aut commodum* (“just or advantageous”). At “what he had received,” manuscripts read *accepit inordinate* (“received disorderly”) for *acceperat inordinate* (“had received disorderly”); Victorine 3 reads *ostendit* (“he displayed”) for *extendit* (“he extended”).
- Manuscripts read *et nolendo quod* (“and by not willing what”) for *et non volendo quod* (“and by not willing what”): the substantive English sense is the same, while the Latin differs by the placement of *non*.
