Victorine reads *quia ideo non voluit* (“because for that reason he did not will”) for *quia non ideo voluit* (“because he did not for that reason will”); manuscripts read *quia aliquid voluit* (“because he wanted something”) for *quia aliud voluit* (“because he wanted something else”).
- On being like God, manuscripts read *voluit omnino par esse Deo secundum aliquid minus Deo* (“he wanted to be wholly equal to God in some respect less than God”) for *noluit omnino par esse Deo, sed aliquid minus Deo* (“he did not wish to be altogether equal to God, but [to be] something less than God”). At “in this very act,” they read *hoc voluit inordinate* (“he willed this disorderly”) for *hoc ipso voluit inordinate* (“by this very act he willed disorderly”).
- Cîteaux, Victorine, and Saint Michael read *jam tibi* (“now to you”) for *jam igitur tibi* (“now therefore to you”). Victorine 9 and 13 read *et velle quod non debebat* (“and to will what he ought not”) for *et velle non debebat* (“and ought not to will”). Victorine 13 reads *malus tamen non ideo non accepit, quia Deus* (“yet the evil [angel] did not for that reason fail to receive, because God”) for *non ideo tamen malus non accepit, quia Deus*.
- At “you satisfy me,” Saint Michael reads *satisfecisti ad* (“you satisfied [me] concerning,” perfect), while Gembloux, Bec, and Victorine read *satisfacis ad* (“you satisfy [me] concerning”), for the printed phrase.
- In Chapter V, manuscripts read *rationabilitatem* (“reasonableness”) for *rationalitatem* (“rationality”); Victorine 3 reads *quam justi* (“than [those who are] just”) for *quam isti* (“than these”). Bec, Gembloux, Cîteaux, and Saint Michael read *illis assumuntur* (“are taken for them”), Victorine 3 and 9 *illis assumentur* (“will be taken for them”), for *qui pro illis assumentur* (“who will be taken in their place”). Manuscripts read *poterant igitur* (“therefore could,” imperfect) for *potuerunt igitur* (“therefore could,” perfect); Victorine 3 omits *malorum* (“of the evil [angels]”).
- Chapter VI begins at this sentence in the manuscripts. Victorine 9 reads *illud quod plus non* (“that which [is] more not”) for *illud plus quod non* (“that additional [good] which not”). Manuscripts read *a Deo sunt profecti* (“they have advanced from God”) for *adeo sunt provecti* (“they have advanced so far”); *ut sunt adepti* (“so that they have attained”) for *ut sint adepti* (“so that they may have attained”); and Victorine, Bec, Gembloux, Saint Michael *quod plus velle* (“what more [they can] will”) for *quid plus velle* (“what more to will”). The manuscripts read *possunt, et* (“they can, and”) for *possint, et* (“they may be able, and”).
- At the final question, manuscripts read *volendo sic perfecerunt* (“by willing thus brought [it] to completion”) and *nolendo sic profecerunt* (“by not willing thus advanced”) for *volendo sic profecerunt* (“by willing thus advanced”). These are the two distinct source readings; neither is a general paraphrase.

DISCIPLE. And for now let it suffice that we have investigated this matter thus far [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Victorinus manuscript reads *investigasse* (“to have investigated”); *investigare* (“to investigate”) in the text.] [Note: [Col. 0335D] In the Cistercian manuscript this chapter begins with the words: “But I do not know what it is,” etc.] But I do not know what it is that, when I hope I am already reaching the end of the question [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Cistercian manuscript reads *jam pertingere*, omitting *jam* (“already”); the Victorinus and Cistercian manuscripts read *me sperem* (“I may hope”), rather than *me spero* (“I hope”)], I then see other questions springing up and rising as though from the roots of questions that have been cut down [Col. 0335B]. For behold, although I see most clearly that the perverse angel could by no means have fallen into an immoderate lack of the good except because of an immoderate desire, I am greatly troubled as to where he obtained that disordered will itself.

For if it was good, then because of a good will he fell from so great a good into so great an evil. Again, if it was good, God gave it to him, since of himself he had nothing except nothing. If, therefore, he willed what God gave him to will, what did he sin? Or if he had this will from himself, then he had some good which he did not receive [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Victorinus and Cistercian manuscripts read *habuit a se aliquod* (“he had some good from himself”); they omit *a se* in this position]. But if it is evil, and is something, the same difficulty arises again: it can only be from God, from whom everything that is something comes [Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *a quo omne quod est, aliquid est* (“from whom everything that is is something”), rather than *a quo est omne quod aliquid est* (“from whom everything that is something comes”)]. Likewise, one may ask what he sinned by having a will that God gave him, or how God could give an evil will.

But if this evil will [Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *si vero mala* (“but if [it is] evil”), rather than *si vero haec mala* (“but if this [will is] evil”)] came from the devil himself, and is something, then he had something from himself; and not every essence is good, nor will evil be nothing, as we are accustomed to say—since an evil will is an essence. Or if an evil will is nothing, then he was condemned so severely on account of nothing, and therefore without cause.

What I say about the will can likewise be said about desire, or longing [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Cistercian and Victorinus manuscripts read *hoc idem dici* (“the same thing can be said”), rather than *hoc ipsum dici* (“this very thing can be said”)], since desire and longing are also will. And just as there is a good and an evil will, so there is a good and an evil desire [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Victorinus manuscripts read *ita est et bona* (“so there is also a good”), rather than *ita est bona* (“so there is a good”)], and a good and an evil longing. If it is said that the will is some essence, and is therefore something good, but that, when turned toward what it ought to will, it becomes a good will, while, when turned toward what it ought not to will, it is called an evil will, then I see that whatever I have said about the will can also be said about the turning of the will itself.

For I am greatly troubled as to where the devil obtained that perverse turning of his will, and the other questions I have just raised concerning the will [Col. 0336A] [Note: [Col. 0335D] *De voluntate modo dixi* (“what I have just said concerning the will”) in the Victorinus manuscript; *de voluntatis conversione modo dixi* (“what I have just said concerning the turning of the will”)].

There is still another matter [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Victorinus, Gembloux, and Bec manuscripts read *est adhuc aliquid* (“there is still something else”), rather than *est adhuc aliud* (“there is still another matter”)] that I find very surprising when I consider this turning of the will: namely, why God made that nature—which He had exalted to such excellence—in such a way that it could turn its will away from what it ought to will toward what it ought not to will, but could not turn it from what it ought not to will toward what it ought to will [Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *possit convertere* (“can turn”), rather than *posset convertere* (“could turn”)].

[Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *cum magis videatur* (“since it seems more”), rather than *cum multo magis videatur* (“since it seems much more”).] It would seem much more appropriate that such a creature should have received from such a maker the power to do the good for which it was made [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Venetian edition, Cologne edition, and Gothic version read *ad quod facta sunt* (“for which they were made”), rather than *ad quod facta est* (“for which it was made”)], rather than the power to do the evil which it was made to avoid. The same question can also be raised concerning our nature, since we believe that no human being can have a good will unless God gives it, whereas anyone can always have an evil will merely by God’s permitting it.

## CHAPTER VIII

### The proposed question is resolved: the will and its turning are not themselves evil

[Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *conversio sit, non ipsum* (“the turning is not itself”), rather than *conversio non sit ipsum* (“the turning is not itself”).]

MASTER. I do not think it can be denied that either the will or the turning of the will is something. Even if they are not substances, it nevertheless cannot be proved that they are not essences, since there are many essences besides that which is properly called a substance.

In short, a good will is no more something than an evil will [Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *bona non magis* (“the good is no more something”), rather than *bona voluntas non magis* (“a good will is no more something”)]. Nor is the latter more evil than the former is good. For the will that wishes to give mercifully is no more something than the will that wishes to seize violently; nor is the former more good than the latter is evil [Col. 0336C].

Therefore, if an evil will is the very evil by which someone is called evil, then a good will will also be the very good by which someone becomes good. But an evil will will be nothing if it is the very evil that we believe to be nothing. A good will, therefore, will also be nothing, since it is no more something than an evil will. Consequently, we shall not be able to deny that the very good which makes good people is nothing, since it is a good will, which will be nothing. Yet no one doubts that it is false that a good will, or goodness itself, is nothing.

Accordingly, an evil will is not the very evil that makes evil people, just as a good will is not the very good that makes good people.

What I have said about the will can likewise be considered in the case of the turning of the will [Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *potest considerari* (“can be considered”), omitting *etiam* (“also”)]. For the turning that turns the will from plunder to giving is no more something than the turning that turns that same will from generosity to avarice [Col. 0336D] [Note: [Col. 0335D] The manuscripts read *quam illa quae* (“than that which”), rather than *quam est illa quae* (“than is that which”)]; and the same applies to the other points that I made shortly before concerning the will [Col. 0337A].

DISCIPLE. The very same thing seems to me to be true, as you assert [Note: [Col. 0337C] *Idipsum videtur* (“the very same thing seems so”) in the Cistercian and Saint-Michael manuscripts; *hoc ipsum videtur* (“this very thing seems so”) in the text; *ut asseris* (“as you assert it”) in the manuscripts, rather than *quod asseris* (“what you assert”)].

MASTER. Therefore neither an evil will nor a perverse turning of the will is the very evil by which an angel or a human being becomes evil, and which we say is nothing. Nor is a good will, or a good turning of the will, the good by which good people become good [Note: [Col. 0337C] The Cistercian, Victorinus 3, and Saint-Michael manuscripts read *nec bona voluntatis* (“nor of a good will”); Victorinus 13 reads *aut bona voluntatis* (“or of a good will”); Victorinus 9 reads *aut bonae voluntatis* (“or of a good will”), or *aut malae voluntatis* (“or of an evil will”)].

## CHAPTER IX

### Injustice is the very evil, and is nothing

DISCIPLE. What, then, shall we say is the very evil that makes evil people, and what is the very good that makes good people?

MASTER. We must believe that justice is the very good by which good people—that is, the just, angels, and human beings—are good [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *credere dicimus ipsum bonum quo fiunt boni* (“we say that justice is the very good by which they become good”), rather than *credere debemus esse ipsum bonum quo sunt boni* (“we must believe that it is the very good by which they are good”)], and by which the will itself is called good or just. Injustice, however, is the very evil which we say is nothing other than the privation of good, and which makes people evil and makes the will evil. Therefore we maintain that this same injustice is nothing other than the privation of justice.

For as long as the will, first given to a rational nature and, in the very act of being given, turned—or rather, not turned but made straight—by the giver himself toward that which it ought to will, remained in that uprightness which we call truth or justice, in which it was made, it was just [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *facta fuit, justa* (“it was made and was just”); the Victorinus, Saint-Michael, and Cistercian manuscripts read *facta est, justa fuit* (“it was made; it was just”)].

But when it turned away from what it ought to will and turned toward what it ought not to will [Note: [Col. 0337C] The Cistercian manuscript omits *se* (“itself”)], did it not remain in its original—as I might call it—uprightness, in which it was made? When it abandoned that uprightness, it lost something great; and in its place it received nothing except its privation, which has no essence and which we call injustice.

[Col. 0337C]

## 66 CHAPTER X

### How evil appears to be something

DISCIPLE. I grant what you say, that evil is a privation of good. Nevertheless, I see that good is likewise a privation of evil. And just as I perceive that, in the privation of evil, something else comes to be which we call good, so I observe that, in the privation of good, something else comes to be which we call evil [Note: [Col. 0337C] The Victorinus and Cistercian manuscripts read *dicimus* (“which we say”), rather than *nominamus* (“which we call”)].

Therefore, although evil is proved by certain arguments to be nothing—for evil is only vice or corruption, which cannot exist except in some essence, and the more they exist in that essence, the more they reduce it to nothing; and if that same essence should come wholly to nothing, vice and corruption too are found to be nothing—although, I say, evil is proved to be nothing in this or some other way, my mind [Note: [Col. 0337C] One manuscript reads *minus mens* (“the mind less”), rather than *animus meus* (“my mind”)] cannot be satisfied except by faith alone, unless what also proves to me that evil is nothing but something is taken away from me [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *mihi etiam probat* (“also proves to me”), rather than *mihi e contra probat* (“proves to me on the contrary”)].

For when the name “evil” is heard, our hearts are needlessly horrified by what they understand to be signified by this name, if nothing is signified by it [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *significetur hoc* (“if this is signified”), rather than *significatur hoc* (“if this is signified”)].

Again, if this utterance—namely, “evil” [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *hoc scilicet* (“this, namely”), rather than *haec, scilicet* (“this utterance, namely”)]—is a name, it is certainly significative [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *utique significatum* (“certainly signified”), rather than *utique significativum* (“certainly significative”)]. But if it is significative [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *si autem significatum* (“but if it is signified”), rather than *si autem significativum* (“but if it is significative”)], it signifies; and it signifies nothing except something. How, then, is evil nothing, if what its name signifies is something?

Finally, while justice remains, such tranquility and such repose seem to exist that in many cases justice appears to be nothing other than resting from evil, as with chastity and patience. But when justice departs, such a varied, laborious, and multifaceted passion takes possession of the mind [Col. 0338A] that, like a cruel master, it compels the miserable little human being to be anxious with concern for so many shameful and laborious deeds [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *operum sollicitum* (“anxious for the deeds”), rather than *operum cura sollicitum* (“anxious with concern for the deeds”)], and to labor so grievously at those very deeds [Note: [Col. 0337C] The Victorinus, Gembloux, Corbie, and Bec manuscripts read *occupat animum* (“takes possession of the mind”), rather than *occupet animum* (“may take possession of the mind”)]. It is astonishing if it can be shown that all these things accomplish nothing.

## CHAPTER XI [otherwise X]

### That evil and nothing cannot be proved by their names to be something, but only quasi-something

MASTER. I suppose you are not so insane [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts begin with: “I suppose you are not insane, etc.”] as to say that nothing is something, although you cannot deny that “nothing” is a name. Therefore, if nothing cannot prove itself to be something by means of the name “nothing” [Note: [Col. 0337C] The Cistercian manuscript reads *nihil potest probari* (“nothing can be proved”); the other manuscripts read *nihil potes probare* (“you can prove nothing”)], how do you think you can prove evil to be something by means of the name “evil”?

DISCIPLE. That example accomplishes nothing; it resolves one dispute by another. For I do not know what this very “nothing” is. Therefore, since the question at hand concerns evil [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *quaestio est de malo in manibus* (“the question concerning evil is at hand”); Victorinus reads *de malo quaestio est in manibus* (“the question concerning evil is in hand”)], which you say is nothing, if you wish to teach me what I should understand evil to be [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *docere quid si malum* (“teach what evil is”)], first teach me what I should understand nothing to be [Note: [Col. 0337C] Victorinus 13 reads *quid intelligam esse nihil* (“what I should understand nothing to be”)]. Then you will answer the other points by which, because of the name “evil,” I said I was moved to think that it is something.

MASTER. Since “to be nothing” and “not to be something” differ in no way, how can it be said what that is which is not something [Note: [Col. 0337C] The manuscripts read *quid sit, et quod non est aliquid* (“what it is, and that it is not something”); Victorinus 3 reads *quid si quod est aliquid* (“what if it is something”)]?

DISCIPLE. If what is signified by this name is not something, then it signifies nothing. But if it signifies nothing, it is not a name. Yet it certainly is a name. Thus, although no one says that nothing is something, but we are always compelled to admit that nothing is nothing [Note: [Col. 0339C] The Victorinus, Bec, Gembloux, and Corbie manuscripts read *nihil esse, cogamur fateri nihil* (“we are compelled to admit nothing to be nothing”), rather than *nihil esse nihil cogamur fateri*], no one can deny that the name “nothing” is significative [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *significatum esse* (“is signified”), rather than *significativum esse* (“is significative”)].

But if this name itself does not signify nothing but something, then what is signified appears unable to be nothing and instead to be something. If, therefore, what is signified is not nothing but something, how will it be true that nothing is signified by this name, which is “nothing” [Note: [Col. 0339C] Victorinus 6 reads *ut significetur* (“that it be signified”), rather than *ut nihil significetur* (“that nothing be signified”)]? For if it is truly called nothing, it truly is nothing, and therefore it is not something.

Accordingly, if what is signified by this name is not nothing but something—as the reasoning seems to show—then it is falsely and incongruously called by this name [Note: [Col. 0339C] Victorinus 9 reads *falso et incongrue* (“falsely and incongruously”)]. Conversely, if, according to everyone’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *judicium omne* (“every judgment”), rather than *judicium omnium* (“everyone’s judgment”)], what is called “nothing” is truly nothing, then it is in no way something. Is anything more consequent than that this very name “nothing” should signify—or rather, not signify—something [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *id non significet* (“not signify it”), rather than *id est non significet* (“that is, not signify”)][Col. 0339B]?

What, then, is the explanation for the fact that this name, namely “nothing,” does not signify nothing but something, and does not signify something but nothing [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *videlicet non significat* (“namely, does not signify”), omitting *nihil* (“nothing”) before it]?

MASTER. Perhaps signifying nothing and something are not contradictory.

DISCIPLE. If they are not contradictory, then either this utterance signifies nothing and something under different considerations, or some thing must be found that is both something and nothing [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *aut aliquid: aut* (“or something; or”) rather than *aut invenienda res est aliqua* (“or some thing must be found”)].

MASTER. What if both can be found: both a different consideration of signification in this name and the same thing’s being something and nothing?

DISCIPLE. I should like to understand both.

MASTER. It is clear that, as far as signification is concerned, this utterance—“nothing”—differs in no way from what I say, “not something” [Note: [Col. 0339C] Some manuscripts read *dicit non aliquid* (“it says ‘not something’”); the Gothic edition reads *dico non aliquid* (“what I say, ‘not something’”)]. Nothing is clearer than that this utterance, “not something,” removes from the intellect every thing and everything that is something, and by its signification establishes that no thing, or anything that is something, is to be retained in the intellect at all [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *in intellectu retinendum* (“to be retained in the intellect”), rather than *intellectu retinendum*].

But the removal of some thing cannot be signified at all except together with the signification of that very thing whose removal is signified. No one understands what “not human” signifies without understanding what a human being is. Therefore it is necessary that this utterance, “not something,” by destroying what is something, should signify something [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *necesse ut haec* (“necessary that this”), omitting *est*].

Yet, by taking away everything that is something, it signifies no essence which it establishes as something to be retained in the hearer’s understanding. Hence the utterance “not something” signifies no thing, or anything that is something. Thus, by these different considerations, the utterance “not something” signifies a thing and something to some extent, and in no way signifies a thing or something: it signifies by removing, and does not signify by establishing.

For this reason the name “nothing,” which destroys everything that is something, in destroying does not signify nothing but something; while, in establishing, it does not signify something but nothing. Therefore it is not necessary that nothing be something because its name signifies something in some manner [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *nomen significet aliquid* (“because its name signifies something”), omitting *ejus* (“of it”)]. Rather, it is necessary that nothing be nothing, because its name signifies something in this way.

In this manner, then, it is not contradictory that evil is nothing and that the name “evil” is significative: it signifies something by destroying it, in such a way that it establishes nothing [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts here begin Chapter 11; in the title they read *Quomodo malum* (“How evil”) rather than *Quod malum* (“That evil”)][Col. 0340A].

DISCIPLE. I cannot deny that the name “nothing,” according to the account you have given, signifies something in some way. But it is sufficiently clear that the something signified in this way is not called “nothing”; nor, when we hear this name, do we take it for that thing which it signifies in this way [Note: [Col. 0339C] The Cistercian manuscript omits *illud* (“that”) and *re* (“thing”)].

That, then, is what I ask about: what this name stands for, and what we understand when we hear it [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *et quid intelligimus* (“and what we understand”); the Victorinus manuscripts read *et quod intelligimus*; the Cistercian manuscript reads *cum ipsum nomen audimus* (“when we hear the name itself”)]. That, I say, is what I ask: what is it? For this name properly signifies that thing [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *hoc nomine proprie* (“by this name properly”), rather than *hoc nomen proprie* (“this name properly”)]; and it is a name because it is significative of that thing [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *ejus significatum est* (“its signified thing is”), rather than *ejus significativum est* (“it is significative of it”)], not because, by the method described above, it signifies something through negation.

For it is the name of that for whose signification it is counted among names, and that thing is called “nothing.” I ask how that thing can be something if it is properly called “nothing,” or how it can be nothing if the name signifying it signifies something [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *significatum significat nihil* (“the signified thing signifies nothing”); the Saint-Michael manuscript reads *significativum ejus significat nihil* (“its significative term signifies nothing”)], or how the same thing can be both something and nothing.

I ask the same concerning the name “evil,” and concerning what it signifies and what is called evil [Col. 0340C].

MASTER. You ask rightly. For although, according to the reasoning set out above, “evil” and “nothing” signify something, what is signified is not evil or nothing [Note: [Col. 0339C] The Cistercian manuscript reads *significatur, non est malum aut nihil* (“what is signified is not evil or nothing”)]. Rather, there is another reason [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *sed et alia ratio* (“but there is also another reason”), rather than *sed est alia ratio* (“but there is another reason”)] by which they signify something, and what is signified is something—but not truly something [Note: [Col. 0339C] The Cistercian manuscript reads *sed non vere est aliquid* (“but is not truly something”)], only quasi-something.

Many things are said to exist [Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscripts read *multa quidem dicuntur* (“many indeed are said”), rather than *multa quippe dicuntur* (“for many are said”)] according to the form of speech that are not so according to reality. For example, “to fear,” according to the form of the word, is called active, although in reality it is passive [67]. Likewise, blindness is called something according to the form of speech, although in reality it is not something.

For just as we say of someone that he has sight, and that sight is in him, so we say that he has blindness, and that blindness is in him. Yet blindness [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *cum hoc non sit* (“although this is not”), rather than *cum haec non sit* (“although this is not”)] is not something, but rather not-something; and to have it is not to have something, but rather to lack what is something.

For blindness is nothing other than non-sight, or the absence of sight where sight ought to be [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *non visus, vel* (“non-sight, or”), rather than *non vero visus vel*]. But non-sight or the absence of sight is no more something where sight ought to be than it is where sight ought not to be. Therefore blindness is no more something in the eye, because sight ought to be there, than non-sight or the absence of sight is something in a stone, where sight ought not to be.

Many other things are likewise called something according to the form of speech, although they are not something, because we speak of them as we speak of existing things. In this way, therefore, “evil” and “nothing” signify something; and what is signified is something, not according to reality, but according to the form of speech [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *et quod significatur, est* (“and what is signified is”), rather than *et quod significat, est* (“and what signifies is”)][Col. 0341B].

For “nothing” signifies nothing other than “not something,” or the absence of things that are something. And evil is nothing other than “not good,” or the absence of good where good ought and is appropriate to be. But whatever is nothing other than the absence of what is something is itself not something.

Evil, therefore, is truly nothing; and nothing is not something. Yet, in a certain way, they are something, because we speak of them as though they were something when we say, “He did nothing,” or “He did evil,” or “What he did is nothing” or “evil”—just as we say, “He did something” or “He did good,” or “What he did is something” or “good.”

This is why, when we deny altogether that something exists which someone asserts, we say: “What you are saying is nothing.” For “this” and “what” properly are said only of that which is something [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *nam hoc, et quod proprie non dicuntur: nisi de eo* (“for ‘this’ and ‘what’ properly are not said except of that”)]. Yet when they are used in the way I have just described, they are not said of something that is something, but of what is spoken of as quasi-something [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read: *quod est aliquid, et cum ita dicuntur, sicut modo dixi, non dicuntur de eo quod sit aliquid; sed quod quasi aliquid dicitur* (“what is something; and when they are spoken in the way I have just described, they are not said of something because it is something, but what is said is quasi-something”)].

DISCIPLE. You have satisfied me concerning the reasoning about the name “evil,” by which I thought I could prove that evil is something.

## CHAPTER XII

### That an angel could not have his first will from himself; and that many things are said to be possible by another’s power, and impossible by another’s inability

It remains for you to teach me what answer I can give to the other considerations that try to persuade me that evil is something.

MASTER. In order that we may unravel the truth of the matter [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Victorinus manuscript reads *enucleare* (“to uncover thoroughly”), rather than *enodare* (“to unravel”)], we must begin somewhat farther back [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *longe* (“far back”), rather than *longius* (“somewhat farther back”)]. But you must not be content merely to understand each thing I say separately; you must gather everything together in your memory, as though under a single glance [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Cistercian manuscript reads *uno contuitu* (“under a single gaze”), rather than *uno intuitu* (“under a single glance”)].

DISCIPLE. I shall certainly be attentive as far as I can. Nevertheless, if I should prove slower in some respect than you wish, do not be displeased to wait for me, according as you see that my slowness requires.

MASTER. Let us suppose, then, that God is now making an angel whom He wishes to make blessed, and that he is not made all at once but in stages, and has by now been made far enough that he is already capable of having a will, although he does not yet will anything [Col. 0342A].

DISCIPLE. Suppose whatever you wish, and explain what I am asking.

MASTER. Do you think, then, that this angel can will something by himself?

DISCIPLE. I do not clearly understand what you mean by “by himself.” For, as you have already said above concerning every creature, nothing has anything that it did not receive; therefore nothing can do anything by itself.

MASTER. I mean “by himself” through what he already has. Someone who has feet and everything sufficient for the power of walking can walk by himself; but someone who has feet without healthy feet cannot walk by himself. In this sense, then, I ask whether that angel who is already capable of willing, but does not yet will anything, can by himself will something [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *quae sufficiant* (“which may suffice”), rather than *quae sufficiunt* (“which suffice”)].

DISCIPLE. I think he can, if at some time he wills [Col. 0342B].

MASTER. You are not answering my question.

DISCIPLE. How so?

MASTER. I am asking about one who wills nothing, and about a power that precedes the act; but you answer about one who wills [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *de voluntate* (“about the will”), rather than *de volente* (“about one who wills”)], and about a power that comes into being with the act. For everything that exists, by the very fact that it exists [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *et ipso quod est* (“by the very fact that it is”), rather than *eo ipso quia est* (“by the very fact that it exists”)], can exist; but not everything that exists could have existed before it existed [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Cistercian manuscript reads *priusquam esset* (“before it existed”), rather than *antequam esset*].

When I ask whether one who wills nothing can will, I am asking about a power preceding the will, by which he could move himself to willing. But when you answer that if he wills he can, you are speaking of a power that comes into being with the will itself. For if he wills, it is necessary that he be able to will.

DISCIPLE. I know that there are two powers: one that does not yet exist in actuality, and another that already exists in actuality. But I also cannot fail to know this: whatever can be in such a way that it already is, if at some time it was not, could have been earlier. For if it could not have been, it would never exist.

I therefore think I have answered well: one who can will because he already wills must necessarily have been able to do so before he willed.

MASTER. Do you think that what is nothing has absolutely nothing, and therefore has no power at all, and that without power nothing can do anything?

DISCIPLE. I cannot deny this.

MASTER. I suppose that the world, before it was made, was nothing.

DISCIPLE. You are speaking the truth.

MASTER. Therefore it could do absolutely nothing before it existed.

DISCIPLE. That follows.

MASTER. Therefore it could not have existed before it existed.

DISCIPLE. And I say: if it could not have existed, it was impossible that it should ever exist.

MASTER. Before it existed, it was both possible and impossible. It was impossible in the power of that in whose power it was not that it should exist; but it was possible in God’s power, in whose power it was that it should be made. Therefore the world exists because God was able to make it before it existed [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscripts read *mundum facere poterat prius* (“was previously able to make the world”), rather than *prius mundum potuit facere* (“was able first to make the world”)], not because the world itself was previously able to exist [Col. 0342D].

DISCIPLE. I cannot contradict the reasoning, but ordinary usage does not agree with it.

MASTER. That is not surprising [Col. 0343A]. Many things are spoken improperly in common speech. But when it is necessary to seek the marrow of truth, one must separate out the disturbing impropriety, insofar as the matter requires and it is possible to do so [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *sed tamen oportet* (“but nevertheless it is necessary”), rather than *sed cum oportet* (“but when it is necessary”)].

From this impropriety of speech it happens that we very often say that a thing can do something, not because that thing can do it, but because another thing can; and that a thing which can do something cannot, because another thing cannot. For example, if I say, “The book can be written by me,” the book can do nothing; rather, I can write the book. And when we say, “This man cannot be overcome by that man,” we mean nothing other than that the other man cannot overcome him.

This is why we say that God cannot do anything contrary or perverse to Himself: because He is powerful in blessedness and justice—or rather, because blessedness and justice are not different from Him but one good, He is omnipotent in the simple good, so that no thing can do what harms the highest good [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *quae noceat* (“which may harm”), rather than *quod noceat* (“what harms”)]. For this reason He cannot be corrupted or lie [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *ideo non potest* (“therefore He cannot”), rather than *ideo namque non potest* (“for this reason He cannot”)].

Thus, whatever does not exist cannot exist by its own power before it exists. But if another thing can make it exist, then in this way it can exist by another’s power. Although power and inability can be divided in many ways, let this much suffice for now: many things are said to be possible not by their own power but by another’s power, and many things are said to be impossible not by their own power but by another’s inability [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *non posse sua sed* (“impossible by their own power but by another’s inability”); the Victorinus and Saint-Michael manuscripts read *non posse non sua sed* (“not possible by their own power but by another’s inability”)].

When I ask about the angel whom we have posited as newly being made, and who has already been made far enough to be capable of having a will [Note: [Col. 0343D] The Victorinus and Saint-Michael manuscripts read *ut et aptus jam*; the Cistercian manuscript reads *ut aptus*, rather than *ut jam aptus* (“so that he is already capable”)], but still wills nothing, I am speaking of his own power. I ask whether he himself can will something by himself, and I ask you to answer me about that power [Col. 0343C].

DISCIPLE. If he is already so capable of willing that nothing else is lacking to him except willing [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *si jam sit aptus* (“if he is already capable”), rather than *si jam sic aptus* (“if he is already so capable”)], I do not see why he could not will by himself. For anyone capable of seeing who is placed in the light with his eyes closed sees nothing, yet he can see by himself [Note: [Col. 0343D] The Victorinus manuscripts omit *tamen* (“yet”)]. Why, then, should one who does not will likewise not be able by himself to will, just as one who does not see can by himself see [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *non volens simpliciter* (“one simply not willing”), rather than *non volens similiter* (“one not willing likewise”)]?

MASTER. Because the one who does not see has sight and a will by which he can move his sight; but now we are speaking of one who has no will at all [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *nos vero de* (“but we speak of”), rather than *nunc vero de* (“but now we speak of”)]. Therefore answer me this: if something moves itself from not-willing to willing, does it itself will to move in that way [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *ut sic ipsa* (“that it itself thus will”), rather than *utrum sic ipsa* (“whether it itself thus wills”)]?

DISCIPLE. If I say that it is moved while not willing, it will follow that it is moved not by itself but by another—unless, perhaps, someone suddenly closes his eyes against an approaching blow, or someone is compelled by some difficulty to will what he previously did not will. For I do not know whether in such a case he first wills to move himself to this will [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *enim tunc* (“for then”), rather than *enim an tunc* (“for whether then”)].

MASTER. No one is compelled by fear or by the perception of some difficulty, nor is anyone drawn by love of some advantage to will something, unless he already has a natural will to avoid difficulty or possess advantage; for by that will he moves himself to other wills.

DISCIPLE. I cannot deny it.

MASTER. Say, then, that whatever moves itself to willing first wills to move itself in that way.

DISCIPLE. So it is.

MASTER. Therefore what wills nothing can in no way move itself to willing.

DISCIPLE. I cannot contradict that.

MASTER. It remains, then, that the angel who has already been made capable of having a will, but nevertheless wills nothing, cannot have his first will from himself.

DISCIPLE. I must admit that one who wills nothing can in no way will anything by himself.

MASTER. But he cannot be blessed if he does not will blessedness. I am speaking now of blessedness not joined with justice, but of that blessedness which everyone wills, including the unjust [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *dico enim nunc* (“for I say now”), rather than *dico autem nunc* (“but I say now”)]. For everyone wishes himself to fare well.

Apart from the fact that every nature is called good, common usage speaks of two goods and two evils opposed to them [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *dividitur in duo bona et duo his* (“it is divided into two goods and two evils opposed to them”), rather than *duo bona et duo his contraria mala usu dicuntur* (“two goods and two evils opposed to them are spoken of in common usage”)]. One good is what is called justice, whose contrary evil is injustice. The other good is what seems to me able to be called advantage, and the evil opposed to it is disadvantage.

Not everyone wills justice, nor does everyone avoid injustice. But not only every rational nature, but everything capable of sensation, wills advantage and avoids disadvantage [Note: [Col. 0343D] The Cistercian manuscript reads *sed etiam omne* (“but also everything”), rather than *sed et omne*]. For no one wills anything except what he in some way thinks advantageous to himself.

In this sense, then, everyone wishes to fare well, and no one wishes to fare badly. It is of this blessedness that I now speak: no one can be blessed who does not will blessedness [Note: [Col. 0343D] The Cistercian manuscript reads *non dico quia* (“I do not say that”), rather than *nunc dico quia* (“I now say that”)]. For no blessed person can be blessed either by possessing what he does not will or by not possessing what he wills [Col. 0344C].

DISCIPLE. This cannot be denied.

MASTER. Nor ought one to be blessed who does not will justice [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read *beatus esse potest* (“can be blessed”), rather than *beatus esse debet* (“ought to be blessed”)].

DISCIPLE. That too must no less be granted.

## CHAPTER XIII

### That, having received only the will for blessedness, he could neither will anything else nor not will it; and that whatever he willed would not be a just or unjust will

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Victorinus 9 reads *quidquid non vellet* (“whatever he did not will”), rather than *quidquid vellet* (“whatever he willed”).]

TEACHER. Let us say, then, that God gives that angel at first only the will for blessedness, and let us see whether, merely because he has received some will, he can now move himself to will something other than what he has received the will to desire.

STUDENT. Continue what you have begun; I am ready to understand.

TEACHER. It is clear that he does not yet will anything other than blessedness, because he has not received the will to desire anything else.

STUDENT. That is true.  
[Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscripts read: “It is clear that he has not yet received the will to desire anything else.”]

TEACHER. I ask you, then, whether he can move himself to will something else.

STUDENT. I cannot see how one who does not will anything else can move himself to will something other than blessedness. For if he wills to move himself to will something else, then surely he wills something else.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The Cistercian manuscript omits *utique* (“surely”).]

TEACHER. Just as, then, when no will had yet been given, he could not by himself will anything, so, once he has received only the will for blessedness, he cannot have any other will from himself.

STUDENT. That is so.

TEACHER. If he thinks that something contributes to attaining blessedness, can he not move himself to will that thing?

STUDENT. I hesitate how to answer. For if he cannot, I do not see how one who cannot will what he thinks enables him to attain blessedness can will blessedness; but if he can, I do not understand how he cannot will something else.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read “what he may will,” rather than “how he can will.”]

TEACHER. When someone wills something not for the sake of the thing he appears to will, but for the sake of something else, what should he properly be judged to will: the thing he is said to will, or that for the sake of which he wills?

STUDENT. Surely that for the sake of which he wills, he appears to will.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read “that which he wills appears,” rather than “he appears to will.”]

TEACHER. Therefore, one who wills something for the sake of blessedness wills nothing other than blessedness. Consequently, he can will both what he thinks contributes to blessedness and blessedness alone.

STUDENT. That is sufficiently clear.

TEACHER. I ask further whether, having received this will for blessedness alone, he can not will blessedness.

STUDENT. He cannot both will and not will the same thing simultaneously.

TEACHER. That is true. But that is not what I am asking. I ask whether he can abandon this will and move himself from willing to not willing blessedness.

STUDENT. If he does this unwillingly, he does not do it himself; but if he does it willingly, he wills something other than blessedness. Yet he does not will anything else. Therefore, I think it is evident that he cannot by himself not will what he alone received the will to desire.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “But if he does it willingly, he wills something else.” Victorinus 9 reads: “But if he does it willingly, he wills something else.”]

TEACHER. You understand well. But answer me this also: if he can not will blessedness, how much greater will he understand blessedness to be, who wills nothing but blessedness and cannot not will blessedness?  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] Some manuscripts read: “If he cannot not will”; Geminianus, Corbeiensis, and Beccensis read: “If he can will”; Victorinus, the Cistercian manuscript, and Saint Michael’s read: “If he can not will.”]

STUDENT. If he did not will blessedness all the more insofar as he considered it better and greater, then either he would not will blessedness at all, or he would will something else for the sake of which he would not want blessedness to be better. But we say that he wills blessedness and nothing else.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “Either, if he willed blessedness at all, he would will something else,” rather than “he would not will blessedness at all, or he would will something else.”]

TEACHER. Therefore, he wants to be blessed to the degree that he recognizes that this is possible to a higher degree.

STUDENT. Without doubt, he does.

TEACHER. Therefore, he wants to be like God.

STUDENT. Nothing is clearer.

TEACHER. What do you think? If he wanted in this way to be like God, would his will be unjust?

STUDENT. I do not want to call it just, because he would will what was unfitting; nor unjust, because he would will it necessarily.

TEACHER. Yet we have supposed that the one who wills blessedness alone wills only advantageous things.

STUDENT. That is so.

TEACHER. If, then, the one who would will nothing except advantageous things could not have greater and truer advantages, would he will the lesser ones that were available to him?

STUDENT. Rather, if he could not have greater ones, he could not fail to will even the lowest.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “Nor would he will any of the lowest things, if there were greater ones,” rather than “he could not fail to will any of the lowest things, if there were greater ones.”]

TEACHER. If he willed the lowest and most unclean advantages, in which irrational animals take pleasure, would not that same will be unjust and blameworthy?

STUDENT. How could the will be unjust or blameworthy, since he would will what he had received the inability not to will?  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “He had received the inability to will,” rather than “he had received the inability not to will.”]

TEACHER. Nevertheless, the will itself—whether it wills the highest advantages or the lowest—is evidently the work and gift of God, just as life or sentience is; and it contains neither justice nor injustice.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] One manuscript reads “nor is there injustice in it,” rather than “it contains neither justice nor injustice.” The Cistercian manuscript reads “in him” rather than “in it.”]

STUDENT. There is no doubt of that.

TEACHER. Therefore, insofar as it is an essence, it is something good; but insofar as justice or injustice is concerned, it is neither good nor bad.

STUDENT. Nothing could be clearer.

TEACHER. But he ought not to be blessed if he does not have a just will. Indeed, he cannot be perfectly or laudably blessed if he wills what neither can nor ought to be.

STUDENT. This is very evident.

## CHAPTER XIV

That the same is true if only the will for rectitude is received; and that he therefore received both wills simultaneously, so that he might be both just and blessed.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “And so that he might be just,” rather than “so that he might both be just.”]

TEACHER. Let us consider, then, the will for justice. If the same angel were given the will to desire only what it was fitting for him to will, could he will something else? Or, if he could, could he by himself not will what he had received the will to desire?

STUDENT. Whatever we saw occur in the will for blessedness must necessarily occur in this will as well.

TEACHER. Therefore, he would have neither a just nor an unjust will. For just as there the will would not be unjust if he willed what was unfitting, since he could not fail to will it, so here, if he willed what was fitting, his will would not thereby be just, since he had received this in such a way that he could not will otherwise.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “If he willed what was unfitting, it would not therefore be just,” rather than “if he willed what was fitting, it would not therefore be just.”]

STUDENT. That is so.

TEACHER. Since, then, by willing blessedness alone, or by willing only what is fitting, when he wills in this way necessarily, he can be called neither just nor unjust—and since he can neither be nor ought to be blessed unless he wills, and unless he wills justly—it is necessary that God make both wills meet in him in such a way that he wills both to be blessed and to be just. By adding justice, God must so regulate the will for blessedness and cut off the will’s excess, without removing the power to exceed, that although through willing to be blessed he can exceed the proper measure, through willing justly he does not will to exceed it. Thus, possessing a just will for blessedness, he can and ought to be blessed: by not willing what he ought not to will, although he is able to do so, he may merit that he never be able to will what he ought not to will; and by always retaining justice through a moderate will, he may in no way stand in need [of correction]; but if he abandons justice through an immoderate will, he may stand in need in every way.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “So that he may will to be,” rather than “so that he may will to be and justly will, so that…”]  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] The manuscripts read: “Through the fact that he will,” rather than “through the fact that he wills.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscripts read: “Through the fact that he will justly, he will not will,” rather than “through the fact that he wills justly, he does not will.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscripts of Victorinus, Geminianus, Beccensis, and Corbeiensis read: “He will need entirely.”]

STUDENT. Nothing more fitting can be conceived.

TEACHER. Remember that, when earlier we were considering the will for blessedness alone, without this limit that we have added so that it might restrain itself beneath God, we said that whatever it willed contained neither justice nor injustice.

STUDENT. I remember well.

## CHAPTER XV [elsewhere XIV]

[Col. 0347B] That justice is something.

TEACHER. Do you think that there is something which, when added to the same will, regulates it so that it does not will more than it ought and is advantageous for it to will?  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] “M. Do you think there is something…” Here, in the manuscripts, chapter 15 begins.]

STUDENT. No intelligent person would think that this is nothing.

TEACHER. I believe you recognize sufficiently that this is nothing other than justice.

STUDENT. Nothing else can be conceived.

TEACHER. It is therefore certain that justice is something.

STUDENT. Indeed, something very good.

TEACHER. Before it received this justice, ought that will to will and not will according to justice?

STUDENT. It ought not to have what it did not have for that reason: it had not received it.  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscripts read: “It therefore ought not to have it,” rather than “it did not have it for that reason.”]

TEACHER. But after it received it, you do not doubt that it ought to retain it unless it loses it through some violence?

STUDENT. I think it is always bound to this obligation, whether it retains what it received or voluntarily abandons it.

TEACHER. You judge correctly. But what if this same will, without any need or force compelling it, abandons the justice so usefully and wisely added to it, exercising its own power voluntarily—that is, by willing more than it ought? When justice has been removed, will anything else remain with the will itself besides what we considered before the addition of justice?

STUDENT. Since nothing else was added except justice, it is certain that, once justice is separated, nothing else remains except what was there before, except that, having received justice, it made the will indebted; and, as it were, that same justice, once abandoned, left behind certain beautiful traces of itself. For by the very fact that it remains indebted to justice, it is shown to have been adorned by the beauty of justice. It is also quite just that what once received justice ought always to preserve it, unless it loses it by force. And certainly that nature is proved much more worthy which is shown to have possessed at some time, and always to possess, so honorable a good than one which is recognized as neither having nor ever having been obliged to have this good.  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] The Cistercian, Geminianus, Beccensis, and Corbeiensis manuscripts omit “to preserve it.”]

TEACHER. You consider this well. But add to your judgment that, in proportion as the nature that possessed and ought to possess this is shown to be more praiseworthy, so the person who does not possess what he ought to possess is proved more blameworthy.

STUDENT. I strongly agree.

TEACHER. Explain well to me what there demonstrates a praiseworthy nature and what makes a person blameworthy.

STUDENT. Having possessed it, or being obliged to possess it, demonstrates natural dignity; not possessing it produces personal dishonor. Being obliged to possess it was brought about by the one who gave it; not possessing it was brought about by the one who abandoned it. For the one who received it is therefore obliged to possess it; and he does not possess it because he abandoned it.  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] Some manuscripts read: “Having it adorns,” rather than “being obliged to possess it adorns.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscripts read: “Not having it was brought about by him,” rather than “not possessing it was brought about by the one who abandoned it.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] Victorinus and the Cistercian manuscript read: “because he left it behind,” rather than “because he abandoned it.”]

TEACHER. Therefore, you do not criticize in the will itself, which did not stand in justice, that it is obliged to possess justice; rather, you criticize it for not possessing justice.

STUDENT. I criticize nothing else there than the absence of justice, or the fact that it does not possess justice. For, as I have already said, being obliged to possess it adorns; not possessing it disfigures. And the more the former is fitting, the more the latter is unfitting. Indeed, the will is disfigured by not possessing justice through its own fault for no other reason than that it is adorned by being obliged to possess it through the goodness of the giver.  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscripts read: “Having it adorns,” rather than “being obliged to possess it adorns.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] Geminianus, Beccensis, Corbeiensis, and Victorinus read: “the giver’s obligation to have it,” rather than “the giver’s goodness in obliging it to have it.”]

TEACHER. Do you not now judge the will itself, which does not possess the justice it ought to possess, to be unjust, and injustice to be in it?

STUDENT. Who would not judge so?

TEACHER. If it were not unjust, there would be no injustice in it; I think you would criticize nothing in it.

STUDENT. Nothing at all.

TEACHER. Therefore, you criticize nothing else in it than injustice, and the fact that it is unjust.

STUDENT. I cannot criticize anything else in it.

TEACHER. If, then, you criticize nothing else there than the absence of injustice—and, as you said shortly before, its not possessing justice—and if it is again true that you criticize nothing else in it than that injustice is in it, or that it is unjust, it is evident that injustice in it, or being unjust, is nothing other than the absence of justice, or not possessing justice. [The printed text says “absence of injustice”; the argument requires the absence of justice.]

STUDENT. These cannot in any way be different things.

TEACHER. Therefore, just as the absence of justice and not possessing justice has no essence, so injustice and being unjust have no being; and for this reason they are not something, but nothing.

STUDENT. Nothing follows more necessarily.

TEACHER. Remember also that it has already been established that, when justice departs, apart from the obligation to justice, nothing else remains in it except what it had before it received justice.  
[Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscripts read: “remained there,” rather than “remained in it.”]

STUDENT. That is certainly established.

TEACHER. But it was not unjust, nor did it have injustice, before it possessed justice.

STUDENT. No.

TEACHER. Therefore, either, when justice departs, there is no injustice in it and it is not unjust—or injustice and being unjust are nothing.

STUDENT. Nothing could appear more necessary.

TEACHER. Yet you have conceded that, after justice has been abandoned, it has injustice and is unjust.

STUDENT. Indeed, I cannot fail to see it.

TEACHER. Therefore injustice, or being unjust, is nothing.

STUDENT. You have made me, as a believer, know what I believed without knowing.

## CHAPTER XVI

That injustice is nothing other than the absence of the justice that is owed.  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] The manuscripts read: “That injustice is not,” rather than “That injustice is nothing other than…”]

TEACHER. I think you now understand that, since injustice is nothing other than the absence of justice, and being unjust nothing other than not possessing justice, why this same absence of justice is called injustice, and not possessing justice is called being unjust, not before justice is given but after it has been abandoned, and why both are blameworthy: it is unbecoming for justice to be absent only where it ought to be present. Just as a man who does not yet ought to have a beard is not disfigured by not having one, but when he ought already to have it, it is unbecoming for him not to have it, so not possessing justice does not deform a nature that ought not to possess justice; but it dishonors one that ought to possess it. And just as being obliged to possess it shows a more manly nature, so not possessing it disfigures the manly form.  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] Victorinus, Geminianus, Beccensis, and Corbeiensis read “being obliged to possess,” rather than “ought to possess.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] Victorinus 9 reads: “the manly nature shows,” rather than “shows a manly nature.”]

STUDENT. I see sufficiently that injustice is nothing other than the absence of justice where justice ought to be.

## CHAPTER XVII [elsewhere XVI]

Why the angel who deserted cannot return to justice.

TEACHER. When we supposed that only the will for blessedness was given to the aforementioned angel, we saw that he could will nothing else.  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] In the manuscripts and the Gothic edition: “When we are able…” The heading of chapter 17 begins here.]

STUDENT. We saw clearly what you are saying.

TEACHER. Now, with justice abandoned and that sole will for blessedness—which had existed before—remaining, can the same deserter return by himself to the will for justice, to which he could not come before it was given?

STUDENT. Much less now. Then he could not possess it by the condition of his nature; now, by the desert of his fault, he ought not to possess it.

TEACHER. Therefore, he can in no way possess justice from himself, since he does not have justice—neither before he receives it nor after he has abandoned it.

STUDENT. He ought not to possess anything from himself.

## CHAPTER XVIII [elsewhere XVII]

How the evil angel made himself unjust and the good angel made himself just; and that the evil angel ought in this way to give thanks to God for the good things he received and abandoned, just as the good angel does, who preserved what he received.

TEACHER. Could he not in some way, even while he possessed justice, give it to himself?

STUDENT. How could he have done so?

TEACHER. We are said to do something in several ways. We are said to do something when we cause a thing to exist; and when we can cause it not to exist but do not do so. In this way, then, he could give justice to himself, because he could take it away from himself and could refrain from taking it away—just as the one who stood in the truth in which he was created did not, when he could, cause himself not to have it. In this way he himself gave it to himself, and he received the whole of this from God. For both received from God the possession of justice, the ability to retain it, and the ability to abandon it. God gave them this last ability so that they could in some way give justice to themselves. For if they could in no way take it away from themselves, they could in no way give it to themselves. Therefore, the one who gave it to himself in this way receives from God the very fact that he gave it to himself.  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “Both had received,” rather than “both received.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] In the manuscripts, this continues the preceding chapter.]

STUDENT. I see that they could give justice to themselves by not taking it away; but one gave it to himself, while the other took it away from himself.

TEACHER. You see, then, that they owe God equal thanks as regards his goodness, and that the devil does not for that reason owe God less in return for what belongs to God, because he took away from himself what God gave and refused to receive what God offered.  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “that they have thanks,” rather than “that they owe thanks.”]

STUDENT. I see it.

TEACHER. Therefore, the evil angel must always give thanks to God for the blessedness that he took away from himself, just as the good angel must give thanks for the blessedness that he himself gave himself.

STUDENT. It is most true.

TEACHER. I think you understand that God can in no way make someone unjust except by not making just one whom he can make just. For before justice is received, no one is just or unjust; and after justice is received, no one becomes unjust except by voluntarily abandoning justice. Therefore, just as the good angel made himself just by not taking justice away from himself when he could, so God makes the evil angel unjust by not restoring justice to him when he can.  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “God makes the unjust one unjust when he does not make just the one whom he can make just,” and omit the intervening wording.]

STUDENT. This is easily understood.

## CHAPTER XIX

That the will, insofar as it exists, is good, and that no thing is evil.  
[Note: [Col. 0349D] The manuscripts read: “That it is good insofar as it exists, and that no thing is evil.”]

TEACHER. Let us return to our consideration of the will and recall what we are considering: namely, that the will for blessedness, whatever it wills, is not evil but some good before it receives justice. Hence it follows that, when it abandons the justice it received—if it is the same essence that it was before—it is something good insofar as it exists; but insofar as the justice that was in it is absent, it is called evil and unjust. For if wanting to be like God were evil, the Son of God would not want to be like the Father; or, if wanting any of the lowest pleasures were evil, the will of irrational animals would be called evil. But neither is the will of the Son of God evil, because it is just; nor is an irrational will called evil, because it is not unjust. Hence it follows that no will is evil, but is good insofar as it exists, because it is God’s work; and that it is evil only insofar as it is unjust. Since no thing is called evil except an evil will, or on account of an evil will—as with an evil man or an evil action—nothing is clearer than that no thing is evil, and that evil is nothing other than the absence of abandoned justice in the will, or in some thing on account of an evil will.  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscripts read: “to be unjust is evil,” rather than “to be evil insofar as it is unjust.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscripts read: “to be evil,” rather than “to be an evil thing.”]

## CHAPTER XX

How God makes evil wills and actions, and how they are received from him.  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscripts read: “evil wills,” rather than “evil and wills.”]

STUDENT. Your argument is so closely linked by true, necessary, and evident reasons that I see no way in which what you say can be dissolved—except that I see something following from it which I believe ought not to be said, yet I do not see how it is not so if what you say is true. For if wanting to be like God is not nothing or evil, but some good, it could have been received only from him from whom everything that exists comes. If, then, the angel did not have what he did not receive, what he had he received from the one from whom he had it. But what did he receive from him that he did not give? Therefore, because he had the will to be like God, he had it because God gave it.

TEACHER. What is surprising if, just as God is said to lead someone into temptation when he does not deliver him from it, we likewise admit that he gives an evil will by not preventing it when he can—especially since the power to will anything whatsoever comes only from him?  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscripts read: “to will anything,” rather than “to will anything whatsoever.”]

STUDENT. In this way it does not seem inappropriate.

TEACHER. If giving is not possible without receiving, then, just as it is customarily said that one gives both when one willingly grants something and when one permits it without approving it, so it is not improperly said that one receives both when one accepts what has been granted and when one presumes upon what is unlawful.

STUDENT. What you say seems neither inappropriate nor unusual.

TEACHER. What, then, are we saying against the truth if we say that, when the devil willed what he ought not to have willed, he both received this from God, because God permitted it, and did not receive it, because he did not consent?

STUDENT. Nothing here seems contrary to the truth.  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscripts read: “Nothing in this is contrary,” rather than “Nothing here seems contrary.”]

TEACHER. When, then, the devil turned his will toward what he ought not to will, both the willing itself and the turning were something; yet he had something only from God and from God’s will, since he could neither will anything nor move his will unless the one who made all substantial and accidental natures, universal and individual, permitted it. Insofar as the will, and the turning or movement of the will, is something, it is good and belongs to God; but insofar as it lacks justice, without which it ought not to exist, it is not simply evil but something evil. And what is evil belongs not to God but to the one willing or moving the will. For simple evil is injustice, since it is nothing other than evil—which is nothing. But the nature in which injustice exists is something evil, because it is something and is other than injustice, which is evil and nothing. Therefore, what is something is made by God and belongs to God; but what is nothing—that is, evil—is made by the unjust one and belongs to him.  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “who makes all,” rather than “who made all.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscripts read: “and individual,” rather than “and individual” in the feminine form.]  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] Victorinus, Beccensis, Geminianus, Corbeiensis, and the Gothic edition read “the will,” without the final “is.”]

STUDENT. We must admit that God makes the natures of all things. But who would grant that he makes the individual actions of perverse wills, as though he made the very perverse movement by which the evil will moves itself?

TEACHER. What is surprising if we say that God makes the individual actions performed by an evil will, when we admit that he makes the individual substances that come to be through an unjust will and a dishonorable action?

STUDENT. I have nothing to say in opposition. For I cannot deny that every action is truly something; nor do I want to admit that what truly has some essence is not made by God. Nor does this argument of yours in any way accuse God or excuse the devil; rather, it wholly excuses God and accuses the devil. But I would like to know whether that same deserter angel foresaw these things about himself.

[Additional textual notes: Col. 0345D: The manuscripts read “he could not will anything by himself,” for “he could not by himself will anything”; and “because he does not will anything else,” for “one who does not will anything else.” They read “that, therefore,” for “surely that.” They also read “he cannot but will blessedness,” for “he cannot not will blessedness.” “Would his will be just?” is the manuscript reading for “would his will be unjust?” The manuscripts begin the next question, “We have supposed: if, then, that man…”.

Col. 0345D: The manuscripts read “nor would he will any lowest things, if he could [have] greater things,” for “he could not fail to will even the lowest, if he could not have greater ones.” They read “nor is there [justice or injustice] in it,” for “and it contains neither justice nor injustice”; the Cistercian manuscript has masculine “in him.”

Col. 0345D: The manuscripts read “or if he could not,” for “or, if he could”; “if he willed what was unfitting, nor would the will thereby be just,” for the corresponding clause concerning willing what is fitting; and “Since, therefore, neither merely…,” for “Since, then, by…”. They read “that he may will to be [blessed]. Wherefore…,” for “that he wills both to be blessed and to be just. By…”.

Col. 0347D: Victorinus reads “regulate it,” for “regulates it”; Victorinus 3, “and that it not will more,” for “so that it does not will more.” The manuscripts read “But after it has not received it,” for “But after it received it,” and Victorinus and the Cistercian manuscript read “You rightly maintain,” for “You judge correctly.” They read “Justice? Since…,” for “justice? When…”. The manuscripts read “Justice: it ought always to preserve it”; the Cistercian, Geminianus, Beccensis, and Corbeiensis manuscripts omit “to preserve.” “They are proved” is the common manuscript reading for “is proved”; “than because this very thing,” for “than one which”; “had it, which it ought [to have],” for “possessed and ought to possess it”; and “what shows you,” for “what there demonstrates.” The manuscripts read “Having it was brought about by the one who gave it,” for “Being obliged to possess it was brought about by the one who gave it,” and “You criticize,” for “you do not criticize.”

Col. 0349D: The manuscripts read at the opening of Chapter XVI, “I think that you also now understand why, since…,” and read “he gives the angel,” for “was given to the angel”; “that will alone,” for “that sole will”; “before he receives it,” for “before he receives it”; and “after he abandons it,” omitting “it.” At Chapter XVIII the manuscripts begin, “Could he not in some way…?” and the Cistercian manuscript reads “while he himself possessed it,” omitting *ipse* in other witnesses. The manuscripts read “they owe him thanks,” for “they owe God equal thanks,” and the Saint Michael manuscript has the same wording *quantum ad* (“as regards”).

Col. 0351D: The manuscripts read “some other thing,” for “something”; “ought not to be said,” for “ought not to be said”; and “how it is not,” for “how it is not so.” They read “God is said to lead [one] into temptation,” and “does not deliver [one] out of it,” for “from it.” The manuscripts read “what he may will,” for “anything whatsoever.”

## CHAPTER XXI

That the evil angel could not foresee that he would fall.

MAGISTER: When you ask whether that angel who did not stand in the truth foresaw that he would fall [Note: [Col. 0351D] The Cistercian manuscript omits *to be* (*esse*) in “that he would fall.”], it must be distinguished what kind of knowledge you mean. For if the question concerns that knowledge which exists only when something is understood with certain reasoning, I answer categorically that what can fail to be cannot be known in that way [Note: [Col. 0351D] “Cannot be known” in the edition and Gothic manuscript; “cannot know” in the manuscripts]. For what can fail to be cannot in any way be established by certain reasoning [Col. 0352D]. Therefore it is clear that he could in no way have foreseen his fall, which was not necessary to occur in the future [Note: [Col. 0351D] “Which was not necessary to occur in the future” in the manuscripts: “which was not necessary to be future”]. Let us suppose, then, that that fall was not going to occur; do you think it could have been foreseen if it was not going to occur? [Col. 0353A]

STUDENT: It seems that what can fail to be future cannot be foreseen, and that what is foreseen cannot fail to be future. But I now remember that famous question concerning divine foreknowledge and free choice. Although it is asserted with such authority and held with such usefulness that there must be no doubt, for any human reason, that divine foreknowledge and free choice agree with one another, nevertheless, insofar as the consideration of reason appears to be concerned [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “appears to concern”; Victor, Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, Corbey, and the Gothic edition read “appears, is concerned”], they seem irreconcilably to disagree. Hence in this question we see some inclining so entirely to one side that, as the wave of unbelief submerges them, they perish, abandoning the other altogether [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “abandoning all”; “abandoning the other altogether” in the supplied text]; while many others, as though contrary winds were shaking them from opposite directions while they tried to support both positions against one another, are endangered. Yet since it is established that divine foreknowledge embraces all things that occur by free choice, and that none of these occurs by necessity [Col. 0353B] [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “since, then, it is established”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “since it is established”], nevertheless what is foreknown seems able not to be future [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “something else of these things”].

MAGISTER: For the moment I answer briefly. God’s foreknowledge is not properly called foreknowledge: for one to whom all things are always present has not foreknowledge of future things, but knowledge of present things. Since, then, the reasoning concerning foreknowledge of a future thing differs from that concerning knowledge of a present thing, it is not necessary that divine foreknowledge have the same consequence as the foreknowledge about which we are asking.

STUDENT: I agree.

MAGISTER: Let us return to the question that was in hand.

STUDENT: I am pleased with what you say. But on this condition: whenever I ask you about the question I mentioned [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “which we mentioned”], do not refuse to answer me what God will deign to show you concerning it. Its solution is exceedingly necessary, if it has already been made by someone or is to be made. For I confess that, apart from divine authority, which I believe without hesitation, I have not yet read anywhere a reason sufficient for me to understand the solution of this question.

MAGISTER: When we come to it—if indeed we do come to it—it will be as God grants. But now, since by the reasoning already given it is clear that the apostate angel could not have foreseen his ruin by that foreknowledge which is followed by the necessity of the thing, receive another argument, which excludes not only foreknowledge but also any anticipation of, or whatever suspicion concerning, his fall.

STUDENT: I am waiting for it [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “I accept this”].

MAGISTER: If, while still standing in a good will, he foresaw that he would fall, either he wanted it to happen or he did not want it.

STUDENT: One of these two must be true.

MAGISTER: But if, together with his foreknowledge, he had at some point the will to fall, he had already fallen by that very evil will.

STUDENT: What you say is clear.

MAGISTER: Therefore he did not know before he fell that he would fall by wanting to fall [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “before he would fall”].

STUDENT: Nothing can be brought against your conclusion [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “something else can be brought against it”].

MAGISTER: But if he foresaw that he would fall and did not want to fall, he was as miserable in grieving as he wanted to remain standing.

STUDENT: That cannot be denied.

MAGISTER: But he was all the more just the more he wanted to remain standing; and the more just he was, the happier he ought to have been.

STUDENT: It cannot be denied [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read: “The more he wanted to remain standing, and the more just he was, the happier he ought to have been. The Student: It cannot be denied. The Master: He was all the more just, the more he wanted to remain standing; and the more just he was, the happier he ought to have been. The Student: It cannot be denied”; another manuscript omits “the more he wanted to remain standing”].

MAGISTER: Therefore, if by not wanting to fall he foresaw that he would fall, he was all the more miserable the happier he ought to have been—which is incongruous.
