STUDENT: I cannot deny that this follows. But we often know that something of this kind occurs, not only without incongruity, but laudably and through heavenly grace. For, to mention briefly a few of the afflictions of the just, the more just someone is, the more he is affected by compassionate grief at another’s fall. Often, too, we see someone who possesses greater steadfastness in justice suffer a more savage assault of persecution from the unjust [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “suffer a greater assault”; the supplied text reads “a more savage assault”].

MAGISTER: The reasoning is not the same in human beings and in that angel. Human nature, because of the sin of our first parent, has already become susceptible to innumerable afflictions [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “the nature of man”]; and through this susceptibility grace works for us in many ways toward incorruptibility. But that angel, before any sin had preceded, had not deserved the experience of any evil [Note: [Col. 0353C] The manuscripts read “had not found”; the supplied text reads “had not deserved”].

STUDENT: You have satisfied my objection. For it is clear that this same argument, just as it separates from the evil angel foreknowledge of his fall, likewise excludes every supposition concerning it.

MAGISTER: There is also something else that seems to me to show sufficiently that he could in no way have previously supposed his future transgression. He would either have supposed it forced upon him or voluntary; but there was no basis for him to suspect that he would ever be forced, and as long as he wanted to persevere in the truth, he could in no way suppose that he would abandon it by will alone. For it has already been shown above that, as long as he had a right will, he wanted to persevere in that very will. Therefore, since he wanted steadfastly to retain what he held, I in no way see how he could have suspected that, without any other cause intervening, he would abandon it by will alone. I do not deny that he knew he could change the will he held; but I say that he could not suppose that, when every other cause had ceased, he would voluntarily change the will he wanted to hold steadfastly. [Col. 0355A]

STUDENT: Whoever carefully understands what you say clearly sees that the evil angel could in no way know or suppose that he would do what he did wickedly.

## CHAPTER XXII

### That he knew he ought not to will what he sinned by willing, and that he ought to be punished if he sinned

But I also want you to show equally whether he knew that he ought not to will what he willed by transgressing.

MAGISTER: You should have no doubt about this if you consider what was said above. For if he had not known that he ought not to will what he unjustly willed, he would not have known that he ought to retain the will he abandoned. Therefore he would neither have been just in retaining it nor unjust in abandoning a justice of which he was ignorant. Indeed, he could not have failed to will more than he possessed if he did not know that he ought to be content with what he had received. Finally, since he was rational in such a way that nothing prevented him from using reason, he was not ignorant of what he ought or ought not to will. [Col. 0355B]

STUDENT: I do not see how your reasoning can be weakened, but nevertheless it seems to me that a certain question arises from it. For if he knew that he ought not to abandon what he had received, surely he likewise knew that he ought to be punished if he abandoned it. How, then, could he voluntarily will that by which he would be miserable, when he had received an inseparable will to be blessed? [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscripts read “by which he would be blessed,” rather than “so as to be blessed”].

## CHAPTER XXIII

### That he ought not to have known that he would be punished if he sinned

MAGISTER: Just as it is certain that he could not have been ignorant that he ought to be punished if he sinned, so he ought not to have known that he would be punished if he sinned.

STUDENT: How could he have been ignorant of this, if he was rational in such a way that his rationality was not impeded from knowing the truth, as ours is often impeded by the burden of corruptible flesh? [Col. 0355C] [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscripts read “while corruptible flesh reigns”; the supplied text reads “while corruptible flesh burdens us”].

MAGISTER: Because he was rational, he could understand that, if he sinned, he would justly be punished. But because “the judgments of God are a great deep” (Psalm 35:7), and “his ways are unsearchable” (Romans 11:33), he could not comprehend whether God would do what he could justly do. But if someone says that he could in no way have believed that God would condemn his creature on account of its fault, when he had created it with such great goodness—especially since no example of justice avenging injustice had preceded, and since he was certain that the number of those who had been made to enjoy God had been fixed with such wisdom that, just as it had nothing superfluous, so, if it were diminished, it would be incomplete; nor would so splendid a work of God remain incomplete in any respect; and since there was no way he could know, if the human being had already been made, that God would substitute human nature for angelic nature, or angelic nature for human nature, if it fell, but rather that he would restore each nature to that for which it had been made, for its own sake and not for another’s [Col. 0356A] [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscripts read “restored”; the supplied text reads “would restore”]; or, if the human being had not yet been made, he could much less suppose that it was to be made for the substitution of another nature—if, I say, someone says this, what incongruity is there in it?

STUDENT: It seems to me to contain more congruity than incongruity.

MAGISTER: Let us return [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscripts read: “Is there incongruity? But let us return, and so forth”; the supplied text has “Is there incongruity? The Student: It seems to me to contain more congruity than incongruity. The Master: Let us return”] to what I had said: namely, that he ought not to have possessed this knowledge. For if he had known, he could not, while possessing blessedness and willingly, have voluntarily willed that by which he would be miserable. Therefore he would not have been just, since he would not have willed what he ought not to will, because he could not have willed it. But consider for this reason also whether he ought to have known what you ask. For if he had known, would he have sinned or not?

STUDENT: One of these two would have occurred.

MAGISTER: If, with such punishment foreseen, he had sinned when there was no need and nothing compelling him, he would have deserved punishment all the more.

STUDENT: That is so.

MAGISTER: Therefore this foreknowledge would not have been advantageous to him.

STUDENT: It would not have been advantageous for one who was going to sin to foresee the punishment.

MAGISTER: And if he had not sinned, would he have refrained from sin by good will alone, or from fear of punishment?

STUDENT: Nothing else can be said.

MAGISTER: But the fact that he did not avoid sin solely through love of justice, he demonstrated by the deed itself.

STUDENT: There is no doubt of that.

MAGISTER: But if he had avoided it through fear, he would not have been just.

## CHAPTER XXIV [also XXIII]

### That the good angel, too, ought not to have known this

STUDENT: It is clear that he ought in no way to have known that the punishment announced to him would follow his sin [Note: [Col. 0355D] In the manuscripts, this is where Chapter 24 begins]. But since we believe that the angel who stood and the angel who did not stand in the truth were endowed with equal knowledge at their first creation [Col. 0356C], I do not see why this knowledge was denied to the former, whose good will was so steadfast that it would have sufficed to prevent sin.

MAGISTER: Nevertheless, he could not and ought not to have disregarded a punishment that he had foreseen.

STUDENT: So it seems.

MAGISTER: Therefore, just as love of justice alone would have sufficed, hatred of punishment alone would also have sufficed to prevent sin.

STUDENT: Nothing could be clearer.

MAGISTER: Thus he would have had two reasons not to sin: one honorable and useful, the other neither honorable [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscripts read “dishonorable”; Gemmeticensis and Beccensis read “not honorable”] nor useful—that is, love of justice and hatred of punishment. For it is not honorable not to sin solely from hatred of punishment [Note: [Col. 0355D] Some manuscripts read “it is not sufficiently honorable,” and omit “sufficiently”]; and hatred of punishment is useless for preventing sin where love of justice alone is sufficient.

STUDENT: I have nothing I can object to.

MAGISTER: What, then? Does not his perseverance seem much more splendid when the only reason for persevering in him appears to be that which is useful and honorable because voluntary, than if that other reason also appeared alongside it, which is useless and dishonorable because understood as necessary? [Note: [Col. 0355D] In the manuscripts, the Student’s reply continues Chapter 23].

STUDENT: What you say is so evident that, whereas a little earlier I wanted him to have known this, I now rejoice that he did not know it; for now we cannot deny that he possesses the same knowledge that the example of the sinning angel cannot allow him to be ignorant of. [Col. 0357A]

MAGISTER: Now, then, both the good angel and the evil angel are certain that such a fault is followed by such a punishment. But just as their knowledge is different, so the cause of their knowledge is not the same, and its end is dissimilar. What the one knows through his own experience, the other learned solely through the example of the first. The former learned it in that way because he did not persevere; the latter in another way because he persevered [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “the former in that way”]. Therefore, just as the knowledge of the former, because he blameworthily did not persevere, is for disgrace [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “for punishment”], so the knowledge of the latter, because he persevered [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “so the knowledge of this one, because”], is for glory [Note: [Col. 0357D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “his knowledge is”; the supplied text reads “his knowledge is for glory”]. If, then, he is said to be unable to sin now merely because he has this knowledge [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “if, then, the former is said”; Victor and the Cistercian manuscript read “if, then, the latter is said”], it is sufficiently clear that, just as the knowledge acquired from praiseworthy perseverance is glorious, so the inability to sin that arises from glorious knowledge is for glory. Therefore, just as the evil angel must be blamed because he cannot return to justice, so the good angel must be praised because he cannot depart from it. For just as the former can no longer return because he departed through an evil will alone, so the latter can no longer depart because he remained through a good will alone. It is therefore clear that, just as for the former the inability to recover what he abandoned is the punishment of sin, so for the latter the inability to abandon what he retained is the reward of justice.

## CHAPTER XXV

### That although he is said to be unable to sin now merely because he has this knowledge from the devil’s fall, it is nevertheless for his glory

Your contemplation of this knowledge and inability would be very beautiful if, as you maintain, the good angel had acquired this same knowledge and inability because he persevered. For he does not seem to have acquired them because he himself persevered [Note: [Col. 0357D] The Cistercian manuscript omits “he himself”], but because the deserter did not persevere.

MAGISTER: If it is as you say, the good angel can rejoice at the apostate angel’s fall, since it was advantageous for him that the other should fall: he acquired this knowledge by which he can no longer sin or be miserable—not because he himself merited well, but because another merited evil. All of this is filled with excessive absurdity.

STUDENT: The more absurd it seems—as you show—that the fall of the sinning angel benefited the angel who stood, the more necessary it is that you show that the latter did not acquire the knowledge in question because the former sinned [Note: [Col. 0357D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “As you show that the fall of the sinning angel benefited the one who stood, so it is all the more necessary”; the supplied text reads “all the more necessary”].

MAGISTER: You should not say that the good angel advanced to this knowledge because the evil one sinned, but that the good angel advanced to this knowledge through the example of the one who fell because he sinned [Note: [Col. 0357D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “through the example of the one who fell because he did not sin”]. For if neither had sinned, God would have given both the same knowledge as a merit of perseverance, but in another way, without the example of anyone’s fall. No one will say that God could not have given this knowledge to his angels in another way [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “no one says”; Victor and the Cistercian manuscript read “no one will say”]. Since, then, the one sinned, God taught the other through his example what he was going to teach him—not through inability, as though he could not do it in another way, but through greater power, by which he could bring good out of evil, so that evil, though disordered, would not remain in the kingdom of omnipotent wisdom.

STUDENT: I am very pleased with what you say.

MAGISTER: It is therefore clear that, even if the good angel could no longer sin merely because he knows that the evil angel’s sin was followed by punishment, this inability would not be to the diminution of his praise [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “to the diminution of praise”; another reading is “to the strengthening of praise”], but to the reward of preserved justice. But you know that it was made clear above that he cannot sin for this reason: through the merit of perseverance he has advanced so far [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “was perfected by God”] that he no longer sees anything more that he could will. [Col. 0358B]

STUDENT: Nothing that we discovered above through the investigation of reason has slipped from my memory.

73

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Why we shudder when the name of evil is heard, and what makes the deed called injustice, when evil itself is nothing

But although you have satisfied all my questions, I still await an explanation of what it is that makes us shudder when the name of evil is heard, and what makes a deed seem to be performed by injustice, which is evil, as in the case of a robber or a lustful person, when evil is nothing.

MAGISTER: I answer you briefly. The evil that is injustice is always nothing; but the evil that is affliction is sometimes undoubtedly nothing, as blindness, and sometimes something, as sadness and pain. And we always hate this affliction, which is something. Therefore, when we hear the name “evil,” we do not fear the evil that is nothing, but the evil that is something and follows upon the absence of good. For injustice and blindness, which are evil and nothing, are followed by many afflictions, which are evil and something; and these are what we shudder at when we hear the name of evil.

When we say that injustice causes robbery, or that blindness causes a person to fall into a pit, this must in no way be understood to mean that injustice or blindness makes anything. Rather, it means that, if there were justice in the will and sight in the eye, neither robbery nor the fall into the pit would occur [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “but if justice were in the will”; the supplied text reads “but that, if justice were in the will”]. It is like saying, “The absence of a rudder drives a ship onto the rocks,” or “The absence of a bridle makes a horse run about”: this means nothing other than that, if a rudder were present in the ship and a bridle in the horse [Note: [Col. 0357D] The manuscripts read “the rudder is absent from the ship”; one group reads “if these were present”; another omits “these”], neither would the winds drive the ship nor would the horse run about [Col. 0359A]. For just as a ship is steered by a rudder and a horse by a bridle, so the will of a human being is governed by justice, and the feet by sight.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### From where evil comes into the angel who was good

STUDENT: You have satisfied me concerning the evil that is injustice so completely that every question which used to exist in my heart concerning it has now been resolved [Note: [Col. 0359C] The manuscripts read “all the questions in my heart concerning it have been wiped away”; the Cistercian and Saint Michael manuscripts read “every question in my heart concerning it has been resolved”]. For a question seems to arise concerning this evil because, if it were some essence, it would be from God, from whom everything that is something must exist, whereas it is impossible for sin or injustice to exist from him [Note: [Col. 0359C] The Cistercian manuscript reads “it is impossible for it to exist from him”]. As for the evil that is affliction, if it is sometimes something [Note: [Col. 0359C] The Saint Michael manuscript reads “if it is sometimes nothing, I see something”], I see nothing contrary to right faith. But, so that you will not be wearied by briefly answering my foolish question—for it is not always easy for a wise person to answer wisely a foolish person who asks foolishly [Note: [Col. 0359C] The Cistercian manuscript omits “a foolish person”]—I ask, so that I may know how to answer those who ask this same question: from where did the evil called injustice, or sin, first come into the angel who was made just?

MAGISTER: Tell me: from where does nothing come into something?

STUDENT: Nothing neither comes nor departs.

MAGISTER: Why, then, do you ask from where injustice came, when it is nothing?

STUDENT: Because when justice departs from where it was, we say that injustice approaches.

MAGISTER: Then state what is more properly and clearly said, and ask about the departure of justice. For a suitable question often makes the answer easier, while an unsuitable one makes it more difficult.

STUDENT: Why, then, did justice depart from the just angel?

MAGISTER: If you wish to speak precisely, it did not depart from him; rather, he abandoned it by willing what he ought not to will.

STUDENT: Why did he abandon it?

MAGISTER: When I say that he abandoned it by willing what he ought not to will, I plainly show both why and how he abandoned it. For he abandoned it because he willed what he ought not to will; and in this way, by willing what he ought not to will, he abandoned it [Note: [Col. 0359C] The manuscripts read “and how he abandoned it”].

STUDENT: Why did he will what he ought not to will?

MAGISTER: No cause preceded this will except that he was able to will.

STUDENT: Did he will it because he was able to?

MAGISTER: No; for the good angel was likewise able to will it [Note: [Col. 0359C] The manuscripts read “the good angel is able”; Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, and Saint Michael read “the good angel was able”], yet he did not will it. For no one wills what he is able to will merely because he is able to.

STUDENT: Why, then, did he will it?

MAGISTER: Only because he willed it. For this will had no other cause by which it was in any way driven or attracted; rather, it was itself, if one may say so, its own efficient cause and effect [Note: [Col. 0359C] The manuscripts read “and it can be the effect”; the supplied text has “and effect”].

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### That the power to will what he ought not to have willed was always good, and that the willing itself was good insofar as it existed

STUDENT: If the power itself to will, and the willing itself, were something, they were good and from God [Note: [Col. 0359C] The manuscripts read “it was some good; it was from God”; the supplied text reads “it was something, it was good, and it was from God”].

MAGISTER: Both were something. The power was nothing other than something good, and a voluntary gift of God; the willing, according to its essence, was good. But because it was done unjustly, it was evil, and yet it was from God, from whom everything that is something exists. Indeed, a person has from God not only what God voluntarily gives, but also what he unjustly seizes, with God permitting it. And just as God is said to do what he permits to be done, so he is said to give what he permits to be seized. Since, therefore, with God permitting it, the evil angel used by seizure a power voluntarily given by God, he had from God the very act of using it [Note: [Col. 0359C] The manuscripts read “he had the use”; the supplied text reads “he had the very use”], which is nothing other than the willing itself. For willing is nothing other than using the power of willing, just as speaking is the same as using the power of speech.

[Col. 0360C]

# TWO BOOKS OF SAINT ANSELM: WHY GOD BECAME MAN

## PREFACE

74 [Note: [Col. 0359C] The books *Why God Became Man* were collated with three Victorine manuscripts, P. 19, R.R. 3, and E.E. 13; with one belonging to Lord Joly; with one from the Cistercian library; with one from the library of Saint Michael in Peril-of-the-Sea; with three others from the monasteries of Gemmeticum and Bec; and with the Gothic edition. The Gothic manuscript C. 19 and the Cistercian manuscript begin: “Here begins *Why God Became Man*, the book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.” The Saint Michael manuscript begins: “Anselm’s *Why God Became Man*.”] [Note: [Col. 0359C] The Joly manuscript begins: “Here begins the preface to *Why God Became Man*, the book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.” The Gemmeticensis manuscript C. 9 begins: “Here begins the preface to the book *Why God Became Man*.”]

I was compelled to complete the work submitted here because certain people, before it was finished and carefully revised, were copying its first parts for themselves without my knowledge, more hastily than was suitable for me, and therefore I was forced to finish it, as best I could, more briefly than I wished [Col. 0361A]. For I would have inserted and added many things that I omitted, if I had been allowed to publish it in quiet and with adequate time. In the great anguish of heart which God knows both how and why I suffered, I began it in England [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “God knows: I began it in England”], at the request of others, and completed it as a stranger in the province of Capua.

I named it *Why God Became Man* according to the subject on which it was written, and divided it into two books. The first contains the objections of unbelievers who reject the Christian faith because they think it contrary to reason, together with the responses of the faithful; and finally, with Christ removed—as though nothing had ever been said about him—it proves by necessary arguments that no human being can be saved without him [Col. 0362A].

In the second book, likewise as though nothing were known about Christ, it is shown by equally evident reason and truth that human nature was instituted for this purpose: that at some time the whole human being—that is, body and soul—might enjoy blessed immortality [Note: [Col. 0361D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “and soul”]. It is shown that this must happen to human beings, because for this they were made; but that it can happen only through the God-man, and that everything we believe concerning Christ must necessarily occur.

I ask all who wish to copy this book to place this little preface, together with the chapter headings of the entire work, before its beginning, so that whoever receives it into his hands may see, as though on its forehead, whether there is anything in the whole body that he should not despise.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE

### The question on which the whole work depends

I have often and most earnestly been asked by many people, both orally and in writing, to commit to writing for memory’s sake the reasons concerning a certain question of our faith which I customarily give in answer to those who ask [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts, Victorine P. 1, and Joly read “which I may commend”]. For they say that they are pleased by these reasons and judge that they provide satisfaction. What they request is not that they should approach faith through reason, but that they may delight in the understanding and contemplation of what they believe [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts read “that they may delight in understanding and may delight in contemplation”; Victor, Joly, Saint Michael, and the Gothic edition read “that they may delight in understanding and contemplation”], and that, insofar as they can [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts, Victor, Joly, and Saint Michael read “insofar as they may be able”], they may always be prepared to give an answer to anyone who asks them for a reason concerning the hope that is in us.

This is the question which unbelievers customarily put to us, deriding Christian simplicity as though it were foolish, and which many of the faithful turn over in their hearts: by what reasoning or necessity God became man, and by his death, as we believe and confess, restored life to the world [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition omit “we believe”]. They ask how this could be, when he could have done it through another person, whether angelic or human [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “whether through another person, either angelic or human”], or by will alone. Many ask this question—not only the educated but also the uneducated—and desire its explanation.

Since, then, many have requested that this matter be treated [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “how many have requested that this matter be treated”], and although it appears very difficult in the inquiry, it is nevertheless intelligible to all in the exposition, and lovable because of the usefulness and beauty of its reasoning [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts of Victor and Joly read “and the beauty of the truth”], I shall endeavor to show those who ask what God will deign to reveal to me concerning it, although the holy Fathers have said enough about it that ought to suffice. [Col. 0361D]

And because matters investigated through question and answer are more evident to many people, especially those of slower understanding, and therefore please them more [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “therefore one pleases more”; another reading is “therefore one of those matters pleases more”], I shall take as my interlocutor one of those who demand this, a man who presses me more insistently than the others on this subject [Note: [Col. 0361D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “who presses me”]. Thus Boso will ask and Anselm will answer in the following manner.

## CHAPTER TWO

### How the matters that are to be discussed should be understood

[Supplementary apparatus omitted from the draft: [Col. 0351D] The manuscripts read “by which only,” rather than “which exists only”; manuscripts read “for any human reason,” rather than “for any reason whatever”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “and hence we see,” rather than “hence we see”; manuscripts read “with the wave of their unbelief submerging them,” rather than “with the wave of unbelief submerging them.” [Col. 0353C] Manuscripts read “for the moment I shall answer,” and Saint Michael and Cistercian manuscripts, “for the moment I shall answer this”; manuscripts read “if it happened, or did not want it,” rather than “either he wanted it to happen or he did not want it”; manuscripts read “but if,” rather than “but if”; manuscripts read “often indeed,” rather than “often too”; the Cistercian manuscript omits *for* in “for it is clear”; manuscripts read “indeed, either,” rather than “indeed, either.”

[Col. 0354A–C] Manuscripts read “finally, since,” rather than “finally, because”; manuscripts read “the judgments of God [are] many,” rather than “the judgments of God are a great deep”; manuscripts read “there was the number in which those who were to enjoy God would be,” rather than “he was certain that the number in which they had been made”; the Cistercian manuscript reads *inditam sibi* (“placed in him”), rather than *indictam sibi* (“announced to him”); manuscripts read “since the angel who stood, and the one who did not stand,” rather than “since also the angel who stood, and the one who did not stand.”

[Col. 0356B, D–0358A] The chapter heading has the manuscript variant “That the good angel ought not to have known this also”; manuscripts read “from where evil may come,” rather than “from where evil comes”; manuscripts read “what evil does,” “what it may do,” and “which seems,” in the heading; manuscripts read “what it is that,” rather than “what it is which”; Victor’s manuscript reads “I shall answer you briefly”; manuscripts read “justice, which is,” rather than “injustice, which is”; manuscripts read “when justice departs,” rather than “when justice departs from where it was”; Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, and Saint Michael manuscripts read “and why concerning,” rather than “and ask concerning”; manuscripts read “but it itself,” rather than “but it was itself”; manuscripts read “if it can be [called] an effect,” rather than “and effect.”

[Col. 0359C–0361D] Manuscripts read “because it was not done justly,” rather than “because it was done unjustly”; manuscripts read “the work which follows because of certain people,” rather than “the work submitted because of certain people”; God knows “from what source and why,” not “how and why,” the author suffered this anguish; Cistercian, Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Joly, Saint Michael, and Gothic witnesses read “earnestly,” rather than “most earnestly”; manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “they judge that they are satisfied; what they desire,” rather than “they judge that they provide satisfaction; what they request”; Cistercian, Saint Michael, and Gothic witnesses read “although in investigating,” rather than “although in asking”; manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “if he should deign to reveal it to me,” rather than “what he will deign to reveal to me.”]

BOS. Just as the right order requires us to believe the profound truths of the Christian faith before we presume to examine them by reason, so it seems to me negligence if, after we have been established in faith, we do not strive to understand what we believe. Therefore, since, by God’s prevenient grace, I think I hold the faith of our redemption so firmly that, even if I could comprehend by no reasoning what I believe, nevertheless nothing could tear me away from its firmness, I ask you to explain to me what, as you know, many others along with me are asking: namely, by what necessity and reason God, although he is omnipotent, assumed the humility and weakness of human nature for its restoration.

ANS. What you ask of me is beyond me, and for that reason I fear to discuss matters too lofty, lest perhaps, when someone thinks—or even sees—that I do not satisfy him, he should suppose that the truth of the matter is lacking to me rather than that my understanding is insufficient to grasp it.

BOS. You should fear this no more than you should remember that, when people converse about some question, it often happens that God reveals what previously lay hidden. You should also hope in God’s grace: if you willingly share what you have freely received, you will deserve to receive higher things, which you have not yet reached.

ANS. There is another reason as well why I see that we can now discuss this matter either only with difficulty or not at all in full. For an understanding of power, necessity, and will, together with certain other matters, is required; and these are so interconnected that none of them can be fully considered without the others. Consequently, their treatment calls for a work of its own—not, as I think, a very easy one, nor altogether useless. For ignorance of these matters makes certain things difficult which become easy through knowledge of them.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] “Which become easy through knowledge of them” is absent from the Joly manuscript.]

BOS. You can speak briefly about these matters in their proper places, so that we may have what is sufficient for the present work, while postponing to another time what requires fuller discussion.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The manuscripts read “so that we may have what”; Victor and Joly read “so that we may have what.”]

ANS. This too greatly holds me back from granting your request, because the subject is not only precious, but, just as it is “beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3), so it also concerns a reasoning beautiful beyond human understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] “Beautiful in form” is found in the manuscripts Victor 3 and 13, Bec, Gembloux, and Cistercian.]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] “Beautiful in reasoning” is found in the manuscripts Victor and Cistercian; the word “beautiful” is omitted in some.]

Thus I fear that what happens to me may resemble what I myself commonly feel when I see our Lord painted by poor artists in a distorted figure: I might likewise be indignant with myself if I presume to set down so beautiful a subject in an inelegant and contemptible style.

BOS. This too should not hold you back. Just as you permit someone who can speak better to do so, you do not thereby forbid anyone to write more beautifully if your style does not please him. But, to remove all your excuses, you will not do what I ask for the learned; you will do it for me and for those who, together with me, ask the same thing.

ANS. Since I see your persistence and that of those who, with you, ask this out of charity and religious devotion, I shall attempt, according to my ability—with God’s help and with your prayers, which you who make this request have often promised me when I asked for them for this very purpose—to show you what you seek, or rather to seek it together with you. But I ask that everything I say be received on these terms: if I say something that a greater authority does not confirm, even though I may appear to prove it by reasoning, let it be accepted with no other certainty than that, for the present, it seems so to me, until God reveals something better to me in some way.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] “For the present, unless it seems so to me” is the reading of some manuscripts; others read “unless for the present it seems so to me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The manuscripts Victor and Joly read “until God reveals something better to me in some way.”]

If I can satisfy your question to some extent, it ought to be certain that someone wiser than I will be able to do so more fully. Indeed, it must be understood that, whatever a human being may be able to say or know about such a matter,

[Note: [Col. 0363D] Some manuscripts read “whatever a human being may be able to say,” omitting “or know.”]

deeper reasons concerning so great a subject still remain hidden.

BOS. Allow me, then, to use the words of unbelievers. For when we strive to investigate the reasons for our faith, it is right that we put forward the objections of those who are in no way willing to approach that faith without reasons. Although they seek a reason because they do not believe, whereas we seek one because we believe, what we seek is nevertheless one and the same. And if you give an answer that sacred authority seems to oppose,

[Note: [Col. 0363D] Some manuscripts read “that sacred authority seems to contradict.”]

let me bring that authority forward, so that you may explain how it does not oppose your answer.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Victor, Joly, and Saint-Michel read “let me bring it forward.”]

ANS. Say what seems right to you.

## CHAPTER III

### The objections of unbelievers and the answers of believers

[Col. 0364B]

BOS. Unbelievers mock our simplicity and bring this objection against us: we do God an injury and an insult when we assert that he descended into a woman’s womb,

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The Joly manuscript reads “a virgin’s womb.”]

was born of a woman, was nourished and grew by human milk and food, and—not to mention many other things that do not seem fitting for God—underwent weariness, hunger, thirst, blows, and, among thieves, the cross and death.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] Some manuscripts read “and endured death” instead of “and underwent death.”]

ANS. We do not do God any injury or insult. Rather, with our whole heart giving thanks, we praise and proclaim the ineffable greatness of his mercy,

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The Joly manuscript omits “of his mercy.”]

because the more wondrously, and contrary to expectation, he restored us from such great and deserved evils, in which we were trapped, to such great and undeserved goods, which we had lost,

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The Joly manuscript reads “through which we had fallen” instead of “which we had lost.”]

the greater love and compassion he showed toward us.

For if they carefully considered how fittingly human restoration was accomplished in this manner, they would not mock our simplicity; rather, they would praise God’s wise kindness toward us.

For just as death had entered the human race through a human being’s disobedience, so life had to be restored through a human being’s obedience. And just as sin, which was the cause of our condemnation, began with a woman, so the author of our righteousness and salvation had to be born of a woman.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Victor, Joly, and Cistercian read “the author of true righteousness and salvation.”]

And just as the devil had overcome the human being through the tasting of the tree that he persuaded him to taste, so he had to be overcome by a human being through the suffering of the tree that he inflicted.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The manuscripts read “through the tasting of the tree that he persuaded him to taste,” but omit “so.”]

There are also many other things which, when carefully considered, reveal an ineffable beauty in our redemption, accomplished in this manner.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] The manuscripts Victor P. 19 and RR. 3 read “ineffable”; manuscripts EE. 13 read “inexpressible”; others read “venerable.”]

[Col. 0364D]

[Col. 0365A]

## CHAPTER IV

### That these answers appear to unbelievers to be without necessity and like mere pictures

BOS. All these things are beautiful and should be received as something like pictures. But if there is nothing solid on which they rest, they do not seem sufficient to unbelievers as an explanation of why we ought to believe that God wished to undergo the things we describe.

For someone who wishes to make a picture chooses something solid on which to paint, so that what he paints may remain. No one paints on water or in the air, because no trace of the painting remains there.

Therefore, when we offer these correspondences, which you describe, to unbelievers as pictures of the event, since they think that what we believe is not an event but a fabrication, they suppose that we are painting, as it were, upon a cloud.

The solid rational foundation of the truth must therefore first be displayed—that is, the necessity which proves that God ought or could have humbled himself to undergo the things we proclaim.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Some manuscripts read “the rational solidity of the truth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Some manuscripts read “which prove.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] The Joly manuscript omits “or could have.”]

Then, so that the body of the truth itself may shine forth more clearly, these correspondences must be explained as the pictures of that body.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] The Joly manuscript reads “the pictures themselves … may shine forth,” with a different grammatical construction.]

ANS. Does it not seem sufficiently necessary that God ought to have done the things we describe, because the human race—so precious a work—had been utterly ruined? It was not fitting that what God had purposed concerning humanity should be completely annihilated. Nor could his purpose be brought to fulfillment unless the human race were liberated by its own Creator?

## CHAPTER V

### That the redemption of humanity could not be accomplished by any person other than God

[Col. 0365C]

BOS. If this very liberation were said to have been accomplished in any way by someone other than a divine person—whether by an angel or by a human being—the human mind would accept it much more readily.

For God could have made some human being without sin, not from the sinful mass and not from any human being,

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Manuscript Victor reads “from another human being.”]

but just as he made Adam,

[Note: [Col. 0365D] The Joly manuscript reads “just as God made Adam.”]

through whom this very work could apparently have been accomplished.

ANS. Do you not understand that, if any other person were to redeem humanity from eternal death, that human being would rightly be judged to be that person’s servant?

If that were so, he would in no way have been restored to the dignity he would have possessed had he not sinned. For he, who was destined to be nothing but God’s servant and in every respect equal to the good angels, would be the servant of one who was not God and whose angels were not servants.

[Col. 0365D] [Note: The manuscripts Victor and Joly read “nothing but God’s servant.”]

[Col. 0366A]

## CHAPTER VI

### How unbelievers criticize our assertion that God redeemed us by his death, thereby showed his love toward us, and came to defeat the devil on our behalf

BOS. This is what they find especially astonishing: that we call this liberation a redemption. “From what captivity,” they ask us, “or from what prison, or from whose power, were you being held, from which God could not liberate you unless he redeemed you through so many labors and finally by his own blood?”

When we say to them, “He redeemed us from sins, from his own anger, from hell, and from the power of the devil. Because we could not defeat the devil, he himself came to conquer him on our behalf; and he redeemed the kingdom of heaven for us. Because he did all these things in this manner,

[Note: [Col. 0365D] The manuscripts Victor, Joly, and Saint-Michael read “he did everything in this manner.”]

he showed how greatly he loved us,” they respond:

“If you say that God could not do all these things by a mere command—although you say that he created everything by commanding it—you contradict yourselves, because you make him powerless.

“Or if you admit that he could have done so, but did not wish to do so except in this manner,

[Note: [Col. 0365D] The Saint-Michael manuscript reads “except in this manner” with a slightly different form.]

how can you show him to be wise, when you assert that, without any reason, he wished to undergo such unbecoming things?

“All these things that you put forward depend upon his will. The anger of God is nothing other than the will to punish. If, therefore, he does not wish to punish human sins, a human being is free from sins, from the anger of God, from hell, and from the power of the devil. All these things are endured because of sins, and human beings receive the things from which they are deprived because of those same sins.

“For in whose power are hell, the devil, or the kingdom of heaven, except in the power of him who made everything? Whatever you fear or desire is subject to the will of the one whom nothing can resist.

“Therefore, if he did not wish to save the human race except in the manner you describe,

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Some manuscripts read “except in the manner that you describe.”]

although he could have done so by his will alone—to put it mildly,

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Some manuscripts read “although he could have done so by his will, to put it less strongly”; others read “although he could have done so by his will alone, to put it mildly.”]

consider how you contradict his wisdom.

“For if a human being were to do with great labor, and without reason, what he could easily do, no one would judge him wise.

“Indeed, your claim that God showed how greatly he loved you by acting in this way cannot be defended by any reasoning unless it is shown that he could not have saved humanity in any other way. For if he could not have done otherwise, then perhaps it would have been necessary for him to show his love in this manner. But now, since he can save humanity in another way, what reason is there for him to do and suffer the things you describe in order to show his love?

“Did he not show the good angels how greatly he loved them, even though he did not suffer such things for them?

“As for your claim that he came to defeat the devil on your behalf, in what sense do you dare to say this?

[Col. 0367A]

“Does not the omnipotence of God reign everywhere?

[Note: [Col. 0367D] The Joly manuscript reads “Does not God reign by his omnipotence?”]

How, then, did God need to descend from heaven in order to overcome the devil?”

These objections, it seems, unbelievers can bring against us.

## CHAPTER VII

### That the devil had no right against humanity; why he appears to have had such a right; and why God liberated humanity in this manner

[Note: [Col. 0367D] The manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, and Victor read “appears to have had such a right, and why God liberated humanity in this manner.” The Joly manuscript reads “appears to have had such a right, and why God liberated humanity in this manner.”]

There is also the argument we commonly make: namely, that God ought first to have acted against the devil by justice, in order to liberate humanity, and only afterward by force. When the devil killed one in whom there was no cause of death and who was God, he would justly lose the power he had over sinners. Otherwise, he would have inflicted unjust violence upon him,

[Note: [Col. 0367D] The Joly manuscript reads “he would have inflicted injustice upon him.”]

since he rightly possessed the human being, whom he had not himself violently drawn to him,

[Col. 0367B]

but who had voluntarily gone over to him. I do not see what force this argument has.

For if either the devil or the human being belonged to himself or to someone other than God, or remained under a power other than God’s, perhaps this could rightly be said. But since neither the devil nor the human being belongs to anyone except God,

[Note: [Col. 0367D] The Joly manuscript reads “neither belongs except in the power of God.”]

and neither exists outside God’s power, what case did God have to bring against his own servant, concerning his own property and within his own authority, except to punish his servant, who had persuaded his fellow servant to abandon their common Lord and cross over to him—and who, as a traitor receiving a fugitive, and as a thief receiving another thief together with his Lord’s stolen property, had taken him in?

For both were thieves: one stole himself from his Lord when persuaded by the other.

What could be more just than for God to act in this way?

Or if God, the judge of all, were to snatch the human being, who had been so possessed, from the power of one who possessed him so unjustly—either in order to punish him by some means other than the devil, or in order to spare him—what injustice would that be?

Although the human being was justly tormented by the devil, the devil nevertheless tormented him unjustly.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] The manuscripts Victor, Joly, and Cistercian read “but he nevertheless tormented him.”]

The human being had deserved to be punished, and by no one more fittingly than by the one to whom he had consented when he sinned.

But the devil had no merit entitling him to punish. Indeed, he acted all the more unjustly because he was not drawn to this by love of justice, but was driven by the impulse of wickedness.

He did not do this at God’s command; rather, God permitted it through his incomprehensible wisdom, by which he orders even evil things well.

And I think that those who suppose the devil to possess some right in possessing the human being are led to this conclusion because they see that the human being is justly subjected to the devil’s torment, and that God justly permits this. For that reason they think that the devil justly inflicts it.

The same thing can be just and unjust when considered from different perspectives. Consequently, those who do not look carefully may judge the whole thing to be either just or unjust.

For it may happen that someone unjustly strikes an innocent person, and thus deserves himself to be justly struck. Yet if the one who has been struck ought not to avenge himself and strikes the person who struck him, he acts unjustly.

This striking, therefore, is unjust from the perspective of the one who strikes back, because he ought not to avenge himself; but it is just from the perspective of the one who was struck, because the person who struck unjustly deserved to be struck justly.

Thus the same action is just and unjust when viewed from different perspectives, because one person may judge it to be only just, while another judges it to be unjust.

In this way, then, the devil is said to torment the human being justly, because God justly permits it and the human being justly suffers it.

[Col. 0368B]

The human being is also said to suffer justly—not because he suffers justly through any righteousness of his own, but because he is punished by God’s just judgment.

But if someone adduces that “record of the decree” which the Apostle says was against us and was erased by Christ’s death (Colossians 2:14), and supposes that it signifies that the devil, as though under the record of some agreement, justly demanded from the human being, before Christ’s Passion, the sin that he had committed—as interest on the original sin that the devil had persuaded him to commit—and the punishment of sin, so that by this he might appear to establish his right over the human being, I do not think that it should be understood in this way.

For that record is not the devil’s, since a *chirographum* means a written decree; and that decree did not belong to the devil but to God.

By God’s just judgment it had been decreed, and confirmed as though by a written record, that the human being, who had sinned voluntarily, could not by himself avoid either sin or the punishment of sin.

“For he is a spirit that goes and does not return” (Psalm 77:39); and “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). Nor should the one who sins be released without punishment, unless mercy spares the sinner, liberates him, and brings him back.

Therefore, through this record we must believe that no right of the devil can be found in the devil’s tormenting of humanity.

Finally, just as there is no injustice at all in the good angel, so there is absolutely no justice in the evil one.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] The manuscripts read “so there is absolutely no justice in the evil one.”]

There was therefore nothing in the devil that should have prevented God from using his power against him in order to liberate humanity.

[Col. 0368D]

[Col. 0369A]

## CHAPTER VIII

### How, although the humiliations we ascribe to Christ do not pertain to his divinity, they nevertheless seem unfitting to unbelievers when said of him according to his humanity, and why it appears to them that this same human being did not die voluntarily

[Note: [Col. 0369D] The manuscripts Victor and Joly omit “nevertheless.”]

ANS. God’s will ought to be sufficient for us as a reason when he does something, even if we do not see why he wills it. For God’s will is never irrational.

BOS. That is true if it is established that God wills the matter under discussion. For many people are by no means willing to accept that God wills something if it appears to contradict reason.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Some manuscripts read “if reason appears to contradict it.”]

ANS. What do you think contradicts reason when we affirm that God willed the things we believe concerning his incarnation?

BOS. To put it briefly: that the Most High should incline himself to such lowliness, and that the Almighty should do something with such great labor.

ANS. Those who say this do not understand what we believe. We unquestionably affirm that the divine nature is impassible, that it cannot in any way be humbled from its exalted state, and that there is no labor in its doing what it wills.

But we say that the Lord Jesus Christ is true God and true human being: one person in two natures, and two natures in one person.

Therefore, when we say that God underwent something lowly or weak, we do not understand this according to the majesty of his impassible nature, but according to the weakness of the human substance that he bore. In this way no reason of our faith is seen to oppose us.

For we signify no humiliation of the divine substance; rather, we show that there is one person of God and of the human being.

Thus, in the incarnation of God no humiliation of his nature is understood to have occurred; rather, human nature is believed to have been exalted.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Victor and Cistercian read “Thus, in the incarnation,” omitting “of God.”]

BOS. Let it be so: let nothing be attributed to the divine nature that is said of Christ according to the weakness of his humanity. But how can it be proved just or reasonable that God treated, or permitted to be treated in this way, that human being whom the Father called his beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased (Matthew 12:18), and whom the Son made himself?

What justice is there in delivering the most righteous of all human beings to death for a sinner? What human judge would not himself be judged worthy of condemnation if he condemned an innocent person in order to free a guilty one?

This seems to lead to the same absurdity that was mentioned above. For if God could not save sinners in any other way than by condemning the just, where is his omnipotence?

[Note: [Col. 0369D] The manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Victor, and Joly read “where is his omnipotence?”]

But if he could have done so and did not wish to, how shall we defend his wisdom and justice?

ANS. God the Father did not treat that human being in the way you seem to understand, nor did he deliver an innocent man to death for the guilty.

For he did not force him to death against his will, nor did he permit him to be killed. Rather, he himself voluntarily endured death in order to save humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Several manuscripts read “he voluntarily endured death.”]

BOS. Even if he was not unwilling, since he consented to the Father’s will,

[Note: [Col. 0369D] The manuscript reading is “he consents to the Father.”]

it nevertheless seems that the Father compelled him in some way by commanding him.

For it is said that “Christ humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross.” For this reason “God also exalted him” (Philippians 2:8). It is also said that “he learned obedience through the things that he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), and that “the Father did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

[Note: [Col. 0369D] The Joly manuscript omits “for us all.”]

The Son himself also says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

And as he was going to his Passion he says: “As the Father gave me a commandment, so I do” (John 14:31).

Likewise: “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John 18:11.)

And elsewhere:

[Note: [Col. 0369D] The Joly manuscript omits “and elsewhere”; the Saint-Michael manuscript reads “and again.”]

“Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).

And again: “Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (ibid., 42).

[Note: [Col. 0369D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “in all these things.”]

In all these statements Christ appears to have endured death more because obedience compelled him than because his own spontaneous will directed him toward it.

## CHAPTER IX

### That he died voluntarily; what is meant by “he became obedient unto death”; why God exalted him; what is meant by “I have not come to do my will”; by “the Father did not spare his own Son”; and by “not as I will, but as you will”

[Note: [Col. 0369D] The manuscripts Gembloux, Victor, and Joly read “spared God, and.”]

Additional textual apparatus for passages translated above:

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “higher things, which”: the manuscripts read *altiora, ad quae* (“higher things, to which”) for *altiora, quae* (“higher things, which”).]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “power, necessity, and will”: the Victor, Joly, and Cistercian manuscripts read “of power and necessity and will.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “so that we may have what”: Victor and Joly read “and so that we may have what.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “This too greatly holds me back”: the manuscripts read “greatly holds me back.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “our Lord”: the Cistercian manuscript omits “our.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “Allow me, then”: in the Cistercian and Bec manuscript C. 3, the chapter begins at these words.]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “we put forward the objections”: Gembloux, Bec, Victor, and Cistercian read “I put forward the objections.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “let me”: Gembloux, Bec, Victor, Joly, and Saint-Michel read “it is permitted to me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “let me bring that authority forward”: Gembloux, Bec, Joly, two Victor manuscripts, and Cistercian read “let me show it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “things that do not seem fitting for God”: the manuscripts read “for our God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363D] At “because the more wondrously”: the manuscripts read “so that the more wondrously.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] At “so precious a work”: the manuscripts read “so, namely, precious a work.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] At “the human mind”: the manuscripts read “this human mind.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] At “From what captivity”: Joly reads “But in what captivity?”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] At “but did not wish to do so except in this manner”: Joly reads “but did not wish to, unless”; Victor reads “but did not wish to, unless.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] At “how can you show him to be wise”: some manuscripts read “how will you be able to show him wise”; Victor 13 reads “how can you show him wise.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] In the Chapter VII heading, Gembloux, Bec, and Victor read “is said to have had, or appears to have had; and why in this manner humanity”; Joly reads “appears to have had, and why God liberated humanity.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] At “if either the devil or the human being”: the manuscripts read “if the devil himself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] At “in possessing the human being”: Victor and Saint-Michel read “in possessing humanity.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] At “those who do not look carefully”: the manuscripts read “and therefore by those who do not look carefully.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] At “the one who strikes back”: Victor and Joly read “the one who strikes.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] At “because one person may judge it”: Joly reads “which may happen.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] At “the devil is said to torment the human being justly”: some manuscripts read “the devil is not said to torment the human being justly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] At “written record”: the Venice edition of 1547 reads *chyrographum confirmatum* (“a confirmed written record”) for *chyrographo confirmatum* (“confirmed by a written record”).]

[Note: [Col. 0369D] At “delivering the most righteous … to death for a sinner”: Joly reads “for the most righteous to die for a sinner.”]

[Note: [Col. 0369D] At “But if he could have done so and did not wish to”: Victor 13, Joly, and Cistercian read “But if he did not wish to, how”; the alternate reading is “But if he did not wish, how.”]

[Note: [Col. 0369D] At “he himself voluntarily endured death”: Victor, Gembloux, Bec, and Cistercian read *sponte suam*; the text reads *sponte sua*, both meaning “of his own accord.”]

ANS. As it seems to me, you do not properly distinguish between what he did because obedience required it and what, because he preserved obedience, he endured as something inflicted upon him, although obedience did not require it.

BOS. I need you to explain this more clearly.

ANS. Why did the Jews pursue him even unto death?

BOS. For no other reason than that, by living and speaking, he unwaveringly upheld truth and justice.

ANS. I think that God requires this from every rational creature, and that the creature owes it to God through obedience.

BOS. We must admit this.

ANS. Therefore, that man owed this obedience to God the Father, and his humanity owed it to his divinity; and the Father required this obedience from him.

BOS. No one doubts this. [Col. 0369D] 

[Col. 0370D]

ANS. There you have what he did because obedience required it.

BOS. It is true; and now I see what he endured as something inflicted upon him because he persevered in obedience. For death was inflicted upon him [Col. 0371A] [Col. 0371D] , because he persisted in obedience and endured it. But I do not understand how this obedience did not require it. 

ANS. If man had never sinned, would he have had to suffer death, or would God have had to require this of him?

BOS. As we believe, neither would man have died nor would this have been required of him; but I want to hear the reason for this from you.

ANS. You do not deny that the rational creature was made just and for the purpose of being blessed through enjoyment of God.

BOS. No.

ANS. Surely you will not consider it fitting for God to compel the creature whom he made just for blessedness to be miserable without guilt; for a man to die unwillingly is misery.

BOS. It is clear: if man had not sinned, God should not have required death from him.

ANS. Therefore God did not compel Christ to die, in whom there was no sin. Rather, he willingly endured death—not through obedience in abandoning life, but because of obedience in preserving justice, in which he persevered so steadfastly that he incurred death because of it. It may also be said that the Father commanded him to die, since he commanded what caused him to incur death. [Col. 0371B] Thus: “As the Father gave him commandment, so he did” (John 14:31); and he drank “the cup which the Father gave him” (John 18:11); and he became obedient to the Father unto death. In this way he “learned obedience from the things which he suffered,” that is, he demonstrated how far obedience ought to be preserved.

The verb used here, “learned,” [Col. 0371D]  can be understood in two ways. It may mean that he learned in the sense that he caused others to learn.  Or it may mean that, although he did not lack knowledge of this through understanding, he learned it through experience.

When the Apostle, after saying, “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross,” added, “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:8), this resembles what David said: “He shall drink of the torrent in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Psalm 109:7). [Col. 0371C] [Col. 0371D] 

This was not said as though he could in no way have attained that exaltation except through this obedience unto death, nor as though that exaltation had been bestowed solely as a recompense for this obedience. Before he suffered, he himself said that everything had been delivered to him by the Father (Luke 10:22), and that everything belonging to the Father was his (John 16:15). [Col. 0371D] 

But because he had determined, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to display to the world the greatness of all his power only through death—since it had been ordained that this should be accomplished only through that death—when it is accomplished through it, it is not improperly said to happen because of that death. [Col. 0372A] [Col. 0371D] 

For if we intend to do something but propose first to do something else through which it will be accomplished, then, once what we wanted to precede it has been done, if the intended act follows, it is rightly said to happen because what had delayed it has been done; for it had been ordained that it should be accomplished only through that prior act. [Col. 0371D] 

For example, if I can cross a river by horse or by boat, but propose to cross it only by boat, and therefore delay crossing because the boat is absent, then, once the boat is available, if I cross, it is rightly said of me: “The boat was ready; therefore he crossed.” [Col. 0372B] [Col. 0371D] 

We speak in this way not only when we intend to do something through what we want to precede it, but also when we decide to do something afterward—not through that prior act, but merely after it. If someone delays taking food because he has not yet attended the celebration of Mass that day, then, once he has completed what he wanted to do first, it is not improperly said to him: “Now take food, because you have now done what caused you to delay taking it.”

The expression is therefore much less unusual when Christ is said to have been exalted because he endured death, through which and after which he had determined to bring about that exaltation. [Col. 0371D] 

This may also be understood in the manner in which the same Lord is read to have advanced in wisdom and grace with God—not because he was actually such, but because he conducted himself as though he were. For after his death he was exalted as though this had happened because of that death. [Col. 0372C] [Col. 0371D] 

When he says, “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38), this is like the statement, “My doctrine is not mine” (John 7:16). [Col. 0371D]  For what someone does not have from himself but from God, he ought to call not so much his own as God’s. No human being has from himself the truth that he teaches or the just will that he possesses, but from God. Christ therefore did not come to do his own will but the Father’s, because the just will he possessed came not from his humanity but from his divinity.

The statement, “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), [Col. 0372D] [Col. 0373A] [Col. 0373D]  means nothing other than that he did not release him.  For many such expressions are found in Holy Scripture. 

When he says, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39), and, “If this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (ibid., 42), he signifies through his own will his natural desire for salvation, by which his human flesh recoiled from the pain of death.

He speaks of the Father’s will not because the Father preferred the Son’s death to his life, but because the Father did not wish the human race to be restored unless man did something as great as that death. Since reason did not demand something that another man could not do, the Son says that the Father willed his death because the Father preferred that he suffer rather than that the human race not be saved. [Col. 0373B] [Col. 0373D]  It is as though he said: “Since you do not wish the reconciliation of the world to occur in any other way, I say that you will my death in this way. Therefore let your will be done—that is, let my death occur, so that the world may be reconciled to you.” [Col. 0373D] 

We often say that someone wills something because he does not will something else which, if he did will it, would prevent what is said to be his will. For example, we say that someone wants to extinguish a lamp when he does not want to close the window through which the wind enters and extinguishes the lamp.

Thus the Father willed the Son’s death because he did not will the world to be saved in any other way than through man’s doing something so great, as I have already said. [Col. 0373C] [Col. 0373D]  For the Son, who desired the salvation of mankind, this was equivalent to the Father’s commanding him to die, since no one else was able to do it.  Hence, “as the Father gave him commandment, so he did”; and he drank the cup which the Father gave him, obedient unto death.

## CHAPTER X

### Further discussion of the same matters; how they may rightly be understood in another way

It may also rightly be understood that, through that devout will by which the Son wished to die for the salvation of the world, the Father gave him—not by compelling him—a commandment and the cup of suffering; that he did not spare him but delivered him up for us; that he willed his death; and that, because the Son himself was obedient unto death, he “learned obedience from the things which he suffered.”

For just as, according to his humanity, he did not have from himself the will to live justly but from the Father, so also he could not have from any source other than the Father of lights that will by which he wished to die in order to accomplish so great a good. [Col. 0374A] From him comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James 1:17). And just as the Father is said to draw by giving the will, so it is not improper to assert that he impels. [Col. 0373D] 

For just as the Son says of the Father, “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6:44), so he could have said, “unless he impels him.” Similarly, he could have said: “No one runs to death for my name’s sake unless the Father impels or draws him.” Since each person is drawn or impelled by his will toward what he unwaveringly wills, God is not improperly said to draw or impel when he gives such a will. [Col. 0373D]  In this drawing or impulse, no necessity of violence is understood, but rather the spontaneous and cherished steadfastness of the good will received.

If, then, it cannot be denied that the Father, by giving that will, drew or impelled the Son to death, who does not see that, by the same reasoning, he gave him a commandment to endure death willingly and the cup which he would drink without reluctance? [Col. 0374B] [Col. 0373D] 

And if it is rightly said that the Son did not spare himself but delivered himself up for us by spontaneous will, who can deny that it is rightly said that the Father, from whom he received such a will, did not spare him but delivered him up for us and willed his death?

In this way also, by unwaveringly and willingly preserving the will received from the Father, the Son became obedient to him unto death and learned obedience from the things which he suffered—that is, how great a thing must be done through obedience. For obedience is then true and simple when rational nature preserves the will received from God not by necessity but willingly. [Col. 0374C]

We can also rightly understand in other ways that the Father willed the Son’s death, although these may suffice. For just as we say that someone wills what he causes another to will, so we also say that someone wills what he does not cause another to will but approves because the other wills it. [Col. 0373D]  For example, when we see someone willing to endure hardship courageously in order to complete what he rightly desires, although we admit that we want him to endure that punishment, we do not thereby want or love his punishment, but his will.

We likewise customarily say that someone who can prevent a thing but does not prevent it wills what he does not prevent. Since, therefore, the Son’s will pleased the Father, and he did not prevent him from willing or accomplishing what he willed, the Father is rightly affirmed to have willed that the Son should endure death so devoutly and so beneficially, although he did not love his punishment.

Yet he said that the cup could not pass unless he drank it—not because he could not avoid death if he wished, but because, as has been said, it was impossible for the world to be saved in any other way, and he unwaveringly preferred to suffer death rather than that the world not be saved. [Col. 0375A]

He therefore spoke those words to teach the human race that it could not otherwise be saved than through his death, not to show that he had no power to avoid death. [Col. 0375D] 

Whatever is said about him must be explained in a manner similar to these statements, so that he is understood to have died not by any necessity but by free will.  For he was omnipotent, and it is written of him: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isaiah 53:7). [Col. 0375B]

He himself also says: “I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay down my life and to take it again” (John 10:17). [Col. 0375D]  Therefore, since he himself does this by his own power and will, it cannot rightly be said that he was compelled to do it. 

BOS. The fact that God permits him to be treated in this way, even though he is willing, does not seem fitting for such a Father with regard to such a Son.

ANS. On the contrary, it is especially fitting for such a Father to consent to such a Son if he wills something praiseworthy for the honor of God and beneficial for the salvation of mankind—something that could not otherwise be accomplished.

BOS. We are still concerned with how that death can be shown to be reasonable and necessary. Otherwise, it seems that neither the Son himself ought to will it nor the Father compel or permit it. For the question is why God could not save man in another way; or, if he could, why he willed this way. It also seems unfitting that God should have saved man in this manner, and it is not apparent what value that death has for saving man. It is indeed astonishing if God so delights in or needs the blood of the innocent that he wishes or is able to spare the guilty only after the innocent has been killed. [Col. 0375C] [Col. 0375D] 

ANS. Since in this question you assume the role of those who wish to believe nothing unless reason has first demonstrated it, I want us to agree that we will accept no incongruity, even the smallest, in God, and that we will reject no reason, however small, provided that a greater reason does not contradict it. For just as any incongruity in God entails impossibility, so any reason, however small, is accompanied by necessity if it is not overcome by a greater reason. [Col. 0375D] 

BOS. I accept nothing in this matter more willingly than that we should jointly observe this agreement between us.

ANS. Our question concerns only the incarnation of God and what we believe about the man assumed by him. [Col. 0376A]

BOS. So be it.

ANS. Let us therefore suppose that God’s incarnation and everything we say about that assumed man had never occurred. Let us agree that man was made for blessedness, which cannot be attained in this life; that no one can reach it unless his sins are forgiven; that no human being passes through this life without sin; and other matters whose belief is necessary for eternal salvation.

BOS. Let it be so, because none of these things seems incongruous or impossible for God.

ANS. The forgiveness of sins is therefore necessary for sinful man to attain blessedness.

BOS. We all hold this.

## CHAPTER XI

### What it is to sin, and what it is to make satisfaction for sin

[Col. 0376B]

ANS. We must therefore inquire by what reasoning God forgives sins to human beings. To make this clearer, let us first see what it is to sin and what it is to make satisfaction for sin.

BOS. It is your task to demonstrate this, and mine to pay attention.

ANS. If an angel or a human being always rendered to God what he owes, he would never sin.

BOS. I cannot contradict that.

ANS. Is sinning, then, anything other than failing to render to God what is owed?

BOS. What is it that we owe God? [Col. 0375D] 

ANS. Every will of a rational creature ought to be subject to the will of God.

BOS. Nothing is truer.

ANS. This, then, is the debt that an angel and a human being owe God: when it is paid, no one sins; and everyone who does not pay it sins. This is the justice, or rectitude, of the will that makes people just, or upright in heart—that is, in will. [Col. 0376C] This is the sole and entire honor that we owe God and that God demands from us. For only such a will makes actions pleasing to God when it can act; and when it cannot act, the will alone is pleasing in itself, because no work is pleasing without it.

Whoever does not render this owed honor to God takes from God what belongs to him and dishonors God; and this is sinning. As long as he does not repay what he has taken, he remains guilty. Nor is it sufficient merely to restore what was taken; he must repay more than he took because of the insult inflicted. [Col. 0375D] 

For just as someone who injures another’s health is not cleared merely by restoring that health unless he makes some recompense for the injury and pain inflicted, so someone who violates another’s honor does not sufficiently restore that honor unless, in proportion to the harm caused by the dishonor, he restores something that pleases the person whom he dishonored. [Col. 0376D] [Col. 0375D] 

This too must be observed: when someone repays what he unjustly took, he must give what could not have been demanded from him if he had not seized what belonged to another. [Col. 0377A]

Thus everyone who sins must repay to God the honor he has taken; and this is the satisfaction that every sinner must make to God.

BOS. In all this, since we have resolved to follow reason, although you frighten me somewhat, I have nothing I can say against it.

## CHAPTER XII

### Whether it is fitting for God to forgive sins by mercy alone, without any payment of the debt

ANS. Let us return and see whether it is fitting for God to forgive sins by mercy alone, without any restoration of the honor taken from him.

BOS. I do not see why it would not be fitting.

ANS. To forgive sin in this way is nothing other than not punishing it. And since rightly ordering sin without satisfaction is nothing other than punishing it, if it is not punished, it is left disordered. [Col. 0377B]

BOS. What you say is reasonable.

ANS. It is not fitting for God to leave anything disordered in his kingdom.

BOS. If I want to say something else, I fear that I shall sin. [Col. 0377D] 

ANS. Therefore it is not fitting for God to leave sin unpunished in this way.

BOS. That follows.

ANS. Another consequence follows if sin is left unpunished: with God, the sinner and the one who does not sin will be treated alike. This is not fitting for God.

BOS. I cannot deny it.

ANS. Consider this also: everyone knows that human justice is subject to law, so that according to its measure the measure of recompense is repaid by God.

BOS. We believe this.

ANS. But if sin is neither paid for nor punished, it is subject to no law. [Col. 0377C]

BOS. I cannot understand it otherwise.

ANS. Injustice is therefore freer if it is forgiven by mercy alone than justice is, which seems highly improper. [Col. 0377D]  This impropriety extends even to making injustice like God, because just as God is subject to no law, so injustice would be subject to none.
