BOS. I cannot resist your reasoning. But since God commands us to forgive completely those who sin against us, it seems contradictory for him to command us to do what it is not fitting for him himself to do.

ANS. There is no contradiction here, because God commands us not to presume to do what belongs to God alone. For vengeance belongs to no one except the one who is Lord of all. When earthly authorities rightly exercise it, God himself does so through them, since he has appointed them for this very purpose. [Col. 0377D] 

BOS. You have removed the contradiction that I thought existed. But there is another matter to which I want your answer. Since God is so free that he is subject to no law or anyone’s judgment, and is so good that nothing more benevolent can be imagined, and since nothing is right or fitting except what he wills, it seems strange if we say that he absolutely does not will, or is not permitted, to forgive an injury done to himself—even though we customarily ask him to forgive the injuries we do to others. [Col. 0378A] [Col. 0377D] 

ANS. What you say about his freedom, will, and goodness is true. But we must understand these qualities reasonably, so that we do not see them as contrary to his dignity. Freedom exists only with respect to what is advantageous or fitting; nor should that be called goodness which does something unfitting for God. [Col. 0377D] 

As for the statement that what he wills is just and what he does not will is not just, it must not be understood to mean that if God willed any incongruity, it would be just simply because he willed it. For it does not follow that, if God wills to lie, lying is just; rather, it would follow that he is not God. A will can in no way will to lie unless truth has been corrupted in it—indeed, unless it has been corrupted by abandoning truth.

Therefore, when it is said, “If God wills to lie,” this means no more than: “If God is a nature that wills to lie.” [Col. 0378B] [Col. 0377D]  It does not follow that lying is just, except in the same way that we speak of two impossibilities when we say: “If this is so, that is so,” even though neither this nor that is so. For example: “If water is dry, fire is wet.” Neither statement is true.

It is therefore true to say, “If God wills this, it is just,” only with respect to things whose willing by God is not incongruous. If God wills it to rain, it is just that it rain; and if he wills that a person be killed, it is just that the person be killed. [Col. 0378C]

Consequently, if it is not fitting for God to do anything unjustly or disorderly, it does not belong to his freedom, goodness, or will to leave unpunished the sinner who does not repay to God what he took.

BOS. You have taken away everything that I thought I could bring against you.

ANS. Consider further why it is not fitting for God to do this. [Col. 0377D] 

BOS. I gladly listen to whatever you say.

## CHAPTER XIII

### That nothing in the order of things is less tolerable than for a creature to take away from the Creator the honor owed to him and not repay what it takes

ANS. Nothing in the order of things is less tolerable than for a creature to take away from the Creator the honor owed to him and not repay what it takes. [Col. 0378D]

BOS. Nothing could be clearer in judgment. [Col. 0377D] 

ANS. Nothing is tolerated more unjustly than that which is least tolerable.

BOS. This too is not obscure.

ANS. Therefore, I think you will not say that God ought to tolerate that which is tolerated more unjustly than anything: namely, that a creature should not repay to God what it takes. [Col. 0379A] [Col. 0379D] 

BOS. On the contrary, I see that this must be utterly denied. [Col. 0379D] 

ANS. Again, if nothing is greater or better than God, nothing is more just than that which preserves his honor in the ordering of things: supreme justice, which is nothing other than God himself. [Col. 0379D] 

BOS. This too is completely clear.

ANS. Therefore God preserves nothing more justly than the honor of his dignity.

BOS. I must concede this. [Col. 0379D] 

ANS. Do you think that he preserves it wholly if he permits it to be taken from him in such a way that it is neither repaid nor does he punish the one who takes it?

BOS. I do not dare say so.

ANS. It is therefore necessary either that the honor taken away be repaid or that punishment follow. Otherwise God would either not be just toward himself or would be powerless with respect to both—and it is impious even to think this. [Col. 0379B] [Col. 0379D] 

BOS. I understand that nothing more reasonable can be said. [Col. 0379D] 

## CHAPTER XIV

### What kind of honor the punishment of the sinner is

BOS. But I want to hear from you whether the punishment of the sinner is an honor to God, and what kind of honor it is. For if the punishment of the sinner is not his honor, then, when the sinner does not repay what he took but is punished, God loses his honor without recovering it. [Col. 0379C] [Col. 0379D]  This seems contrary to what has been said.

ANS. It is impossible for God to lose his honor. Either the sinner willingly repays what he owes, or God takes it from him against his will. For either a human being offers God the submission he owes, whether by not sinning or by repaying what he has taken through sin, of his own free will; or God subjects him against his will by tormenting him, and thus shows that he is his Lord—a fact which the man himself refuses willingly to acknowledge. [Col. 0379D] 

Here we must consider that just as a human being takes what belongs to God by sinning, so God takes away what belongs to the human being by punishing. For not only is something said to belong to someone when he already possesses it, but also when it lies within his power to possess it. Since, therefore, man was made so that he could possess blessedness if he did not sin, when he is deprived of blessedness and every good because of sin, he repays from his own property, though unwillingly, what he took.

Although God does not transfer what he takes to the use of his own advantage, as a person converts money taken from another to his own benefit, he nevertheless uses what he takes for his honor by the very act of taking it. [Col. 0380A] For by taking these things from the sinner, he proves that the sinner and everything belonging to him are subject to God.

## CHAPTER XV

### Whether God permits his honor to be violated even for a short time

## Textual apparatus

The following notes follow the supplied apparatus in source order. Manuscript sigla and abbreviated edition names are retained. Paired readings are translated even where the supplied note repeats the narrative reading or gives an inconsistent form; those inconsistencies have not been silently resolved.

### Col. 0369D

2. *Verum est et jam videre*, “It is true, and now to see …,” Vict. 13 and Joly; *Verum etiam video*, “I also see [that it is] true …,” the contrasting reading. The former has the infinitive *videre*, unlike the narrative's *video*, “I see.” Both quotations are abbreviated in the source.

### Col. 0371D

3. Joly omits *Nam illata est illi mors: quia perstitit in obedientia, et hanc sustinuit*, “For death was inflicted on him because he persisted in obedience, and he endured it.”
4. *Hanc obedientiam exigat*, “requires this obedience,” Gem., Vict., Joly, Cister., and the Gothic edition; *haec obedientia non exigat*, “this obedience does not require [it],” the contrasting reading. The case and the negation both differ.
5. *Praecepit pater, unde incurreret*, “the Father commanded [that] from which he would incur [death],” manuscripts; *praecepit, unde incurrit*, “commanded [that] from which he incurred [death],” the contrasting reading.
6. *Dedit ei, bibit*, “gave to him; he drank,” Vict., Joly, Cister., and S. Mich.; *dedit, bibit*, “gave; he drank,” without *ei*, “to him.”
7. *Propositum est*, “has been set forth,” manuscripts; *positum est*, “has been placed [here],” the contrasting reading.
8. The variants explaining “he learned” are: *dictum est pro eo quod est alios dicere fecit*, “was said for ‘he made others speak,’” Gem., Bec., Joly, and Vict. 19; *dictum est pro, alios fecit discere*, “was said for ‘he made others learn,’” Vict. 3 and 19; *dictum est, per alios fecit discere*, “was said, ‘through others he made [them] learn,’” Vict. 13; *dictum est pro eo quod per alios fecit discere*, “was said for ‘through others he made [them] learn,’” S. Mich.; and *dictum est; quod alios fecit discere*, “was said, ‘that he made others learn.’” The source assigns Vict. 19 to two readings and prints *dicere*, “speak,” in the first; neither feature is silently corrected.

62. *Quod cum aliquis*, “that when someone,” manuscripts; *quia cum aliquis*, “because when someone,” the contrasting reading.

### Col. 0377D

63. *Et hoc est*, “and this is,” manuscripts; *et haec est*, “and this is,” with a feminine rather than neuter demonstrative referring to satisfaction.
64. *Si aliquid aliud volo*, “if I wish something else,” manuscripts; *si aliud volo*, “if I wish otherwise,” the contrasting reading without *aliquid*, “something.”

66. *Ad haec etiam*, “in addition to these things,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *ad hoc etiam*, “in addition to this,” the contrasting reading.

68. *Nulli legi*, “to no law,” manuscripts; *nullius legi*, “to no one's law,” the contrasting reading.
69. *Ut haec praecipiat*, “that he should command these things,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *ut hoc praecipiat*, “that he should command this,” the contrasting reading.
70. *Facit Deus, a quo*, “God does [it], by whom,” Cister.; *facit a quo*, “does [it], by whom,” the contrasting reading without the expressed *Deus*, “God.”
71. *Anselm. Removisti*, “ANSELM. You have removed …,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *Boso Removisti*, “BOSO. You have removed …,” the contrasting speaker attribution.
72. *Deus sit liber*, “God is free,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *Deus sic sit liber*, “God is thus free,” the contrasting reading.
73. *Nullius legis subjacet juditio*, “he is subject to the judgment of no law,” Vict., Joly, Cister., Mich., and the Gothic edition; *nulli legi, nullius subjaceat judicio*, “he should be subject to no law, to no one's judgment,” the contrasting construction. The printed spelling *juditio* is retained in the first form.
74. *Aut decet*, “or is fitting,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *aut quod decet*, “or what is fitting,” the contrasting reading.
75. *Operetur*, “should bring about,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *operatur*, “brings about,” the contrasting mood.
76. *Talis naturae*, “of such a nature,” Vict., Joly, and the Gothic edition; *talis natura*, “such by nature,” the contrasting case form.
77. *Deceat haec facere*, “it is fitting to do these things,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *deceat hoc facere*, “it is fitting to do this,” the contrasting reading.
78. *Et quod non*, “and that not,” Gem., Bec., Vict., and the Gothic edition; *et non*, “and not,” without the additional *quod*.
79. *Nihil clarius judicio*, approximately “I judge nothing clearer,” manuscripts, with the anomalous printed *judicio*; *hoc nihil clarius*, “nothing [is] clearer than this,” the contrasting reading.

### Col. 0379D

80. In *debere tolerare*, “ought to tolerate,” Joly omits *debere*, “ought.”
81. *Ut quod creatura*, “that what the creature …,” Vict., Joly, Cister., and S. Mich.; *ut creatura*, “that the creature …,” the contrasting reading without *quod*, “what.”
82. *Esse judico*, “I judge [it] to be,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *esse video*, “I see [it] to be,” the contrasting reading.
83. In *aut melius est*, “or is better,” Cist. and the Gothic edition omit *est*, “is.”
84. In *quam quae*, “than what [preserves his honor],” Gem., Bec., Joly, Vict. 3 and 13, and the Gothic edition omit *quae*, “what/which.”
85. *Illius servet*, “should preserve his [honor],” Vict., Gem., Bec., and Joly; *illius servat*, “preserves his [honor],” the contrasting reading; the Gothic edition has *illius servare*, “to preserve his [honor].”
86. *B. Quod utique necessario concedi oportet*, “BOSO. That certainly must necessarily be conceded,” manuscripts; *B. concedere me oportet*, “BOSO. I must concede [it],” the contrasting reading.
87. *Est etiam cogitare*, “even to think [it] is [impious],” Vict., Gem., Bec., Joly, Cister., and the Gothic edition; *est vel cogitare*, also “even to think [it] is [impious],” with *vel* rather than *etiam*.
88. *Dici potest, ut puto*, “can be said, as I think,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *dici posse intelligo*, “I understand that [it] can be said,” the contrasting reading. Both complete the assertion that nothing more reasonable can be said.
89. *Non recuperetur*, “[his honor] is not recovered,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *non recuperet*, “he does not recover [his honor],” the contrasting active form.
90. *Invito accipit*, “takes from the unwilling person,” Vict. 19; *invito recipit*, “receives back from the unwilling person,” the contrasting reading.
91. *Deus invitum*, “God [subjects] the unwilling person,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *Deus cum invitum*, literally “God when [he subjects] the unwilling person,” the contrasting wording as supplied. The narrative prints *eum invitum*, “him unwilling,” rather than this apparatus's *cum invitum*.
92. In *Dominum ejus esse ostendit*, “shows that he is his Lord,” Joly omits *esse*, “to be”; Vict. 19 omits *ejus esse*, “to be his.”
93. *Non solum id suum*, “not only that which is his own,” Vict. 19; *non solum suum*, “not only his own,” Vict. 3 and 13; *non solum idipsum*, “not only that very thing,” the contrasting reading.
94. *Homo factus est*, “man was made,” Vict. and the Gothic edition; *homo ita factus est ut*, “man was so made that,” the contrasting reading.
95. *Cum ergo propter*, “since therefore because of,” Gem., Bec., Vict., Joly, and the Gothic edition; *cum propter*, “since because of,” the contrasting reading without *ergo*, “therefore.”

BOS. I approve what you say. But there is another matter to which I demand your answer: for if God, as you prove, ought to preserve his honor, why does he allow it to be violated even for a little while? For whatever is permitted to be harmed in any way is not preserved wholly and perfectly [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Or perfectly”; the manuscripts read “nor perfectly”].

ANS. Nothing can be added to or subtracted from God’s honor insofar as it pertains to him. For he himself is that honor, incorruptible and in no way changeable. [Col. 0380B] Nevertheless, whenever each creature [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Nevertheless, when each creature” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition] preserves its own order, as though prescribed for it, whether naturally or rationally, it is said to obey and honor God [Note: [Col. 0379D] “And is said to honor God” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition]. This applies especially to rational nature, which has been given understanding of what it ought to do [Note: [Col. 0379D] “This is especially true of rational creation … what it ought to do” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition].

When it wills what it ought, it honors God—not because it confers anything upon him, but because it voluntarily subjects itself to his will and disposition and, insofar as it is able, preserves its own order within the universe and the beauty of that same universe [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Is, preserves” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition]. But when it does not will what it ought, it dishonors God, insofar as this pertains to it [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Pertains to it” in the manuscript of Victor 19; “pertains to him” in the manuscripts of Victor 3 and 13], because it does not voluntarily submit to his disposition and, insofar as it is able, disturbs the order and beauty of the universe, although it in no way harms or disfigures God’s power or dignity.

For if the things contained within the circuit of heaven [Col. 0380C] wished not to be beneath heaven or to move away from heaven, they could in no way be anywhere except beneath heaven, nor could they flee from heaven except by drawing nearer to heaven. For wherever, and toward whatever, and by whatever route they went [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Wherever and toward whatever and by whatever route they went” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition], they would still be beneath heaven [Note: [Col. 0379D] “They would be beneath heaven” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Victor, and Joly; one reading has the singular “it would be beneath heaven”], and the farther they withdrew from any part of heaven, the nearer they would draw to the opposite part [Note: [Col. 0379D] “They would draw nearer” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Victor 3, and 19].

Thus, although a human being or an evil angel does not wish to be subject to the divine will and ordinance, he nevertheless cannot escape it [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Escape it” in the manuscript of Joly; “escape it” in another reading]. For if he wishes to flee from beneath the commanding will, he runs beneath the punishing will [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Runs beneath the will” in the manuscript of Victor 19; “runs into the will” in another reading]. And if you ask [Note: [Col. 0379D] “If you ask” in the Victor manuscripts; “if he asks” in another reading] under what will he passes, it is only under the permitting will [Col. 0380D] [Note: [Col. 0379D] “Under the will of the one permitting” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition]. And this very thing, which he perversely wills or does, the highest wisdom converts into the order and beauty of the universe [Col. 0381A] [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Wisdom converts” in the manuscripts of Saint Michael; “wisdom overturns” in that witness].

For the voluntary satisfaction arising from perversity, or the infliction of punishment upon one who does not make satisfaction—apart from the fact that God makes good things from evil in many ways [Note: [Col. 0381C] “That God makes good things from evil in many ways” in the manuscripts of Victor, Gembloux, Bec, and Joly; “because God makes good things from evil in many ways” in another reading]—occupies its own place in that same universe [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Occupies its place” in the manuscript of Victor 19; “would occupy its place” in that witness], and belongs to the beauty of its order.

If divine wisdom did not add these things when perversity attempts to disturb the right order, a kind of deformity arising from the violation of order would come to exist in the very universe which God ought to order, and God would appear to fail in his disposition. 81 Since these two consequences are as inappropriate as they are impossible, it is necessary that satisfaction or punishment follow every sin.

BOS. You have satisfied my objection.

ANS. It is therefore clear that no one can honor or dishonor God insofar as this depends upon God himself; but insofar as it depends upon the person, someone appears to do so when he subjects his will to God’s will or withdraws it from that will.

BOS. I do not know what I can say against this [Note: [Col. 0381C] “What I can answer” in the manuscript of Saint Michael].

ANS. I will add something further.

BOS. Speak until I grow weary of listening.

## CHAPTER XVI

### The reason why the number of angels who fell must be restored from among human beings

ANS. It is established that God purposed to restore from human nature, which he made without sin, the number of angels who had fallen.

BOS. We believe this, but I should like to have some reason for it [Note: [Col. 0381C] “To hear a reason” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition].

ANS. You are misleading me. We had proposed to discuss nothing except the Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0381C] “The Incarnation alone” in the manuscript of Joly] of God, and you are inserting other questions for me [Col. 0381C].

BOS. Do not be angry, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). No one proves more cheerfully that he gives what he promises than one who gives more than he promises. So tell me willingly what I ask [Note: [Col. 0381C] “A cheerful giver” in the manuscripts of Victor 19, Joly, and the Gothic edition].

ANS. It must not be doubted that rational nature [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Rational creation” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition], which is blessed—or is to be blessed [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Is blessed” in Joly and Victor 19]—by the contemplation of God, was foreknown by God in a certain rational and perfect number [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Foreknown by God” in the manuscript of Cister; “was foreknown by God” in another reading], so that it would be fitting for it to be neither greater nor smaller.

For either God does not know in what number it would be better for it to be established—which is false—or, if he knows, he will establish it in the number that he understands to be more suitable for this purpose. Therefore either those angels who fell had been made to exist within that number [Note: [Col. 0381C] “To remain within that number” in the manuscripts; another reading has “to remain outside that number”], or they fell of necessity because they could not remain outside that number. But it is absurd to think this.

BOS. What you say is plainly true.

ANS. Since, then [Note: [Col. 0381C] “How, then” in the Victor manuscripts and the Gothic edition], they ought to belong to that number, either their number must necessarily be restored [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Must be restored … or [the rational nature] will remain incomplete” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition], or rational nature, which was foreknown in a perfect number, will remain in an incomplete number. That cannot be.

BOS. They must undoubtedly be restored.

ANS. Therefore they must be restored from human nature [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Therefore them, from” in the manuscript of Victor 19; another reading omits “them”], since there is no other nature from which they can be restored [Note: [Col. 0381C] “From which they can be restored” in the manuscript of Cister; “from which they can naturally be restored” in another reading].

## CHAPTER XVII

### Why other angels cannot be restored in their place [Note: [Col. 0381C] “In their place” in the manuscript of Joly; “in their very place”]

BOS. Why can they themselves not be restored, or why can other angels not be restored in their place [Note: [Col. 0381C] The manuscripts begin: “Why can they themselves, or other angels, not …”; the manuscripts of Bec, Gembloux, Victor, and the Gothic edition read, “Why can they themselves, or other angels, not be restored in their place”? The heading reads: “Why other angels cannot be restored in their place”?]

ANS. When you see the difficulty of our restoration, you will understand the impossibility of their reconciliation.

Other angels cannot be restored in their place for this reason—leaving aside how this might seem contrary to the perfection of the first creation [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Because this” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Victor, Joly, and the Gothic edition]—because they ought not to be, unless they could be such as those angels would have been had they not sinned. Those angels, having seen no punishment for sin, would have persevered; but after their fall this would be impossible for others who were restored in their place [Note: [Col. 0381C] “And when those angels,” in the manuscripts; the source distinguishes those who would have persevered from those restored after the fall].

For the one who stands in the truth and has never known the punishment of sin is not equally praiseworthy with the one who continually sees that punishment as eternal [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Who had never known” in the manuscript of Victor 19]. It must by no means be thought that the good angels were confirmed by the fall of the evil ones, but rather by their own merit.

For just as [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Just as” in the manuscripts], if the good had sinned together with the evil, they would have been condemned together, so the unjust [Note: [Col. 0381C] “The just” in the manuscript of Joly], if they had stood together with the just, would likewise have been confirmed. Indeed, if some of them were to be confirmed only through the fall of others, then either no one would ever be confirmed, or someone would necessarily have to fall and be punished in order to confirm the others [Note: [Col. 0381C] “To confirm them” in the manuscript of Joly]. Both alternatives are absurd.

Thus those who stood were confirmed in the same way in which all would likewise have been confirmed [Note: [Col. 0381C] The manuscript of Joly omits “confirmed”] if they had stood. I explained this manner [Note: [Col. 0381C] “How” (*quemadmodum*) in the manuscripts of Gembloux and Bec; “the manner” (*quem modum*) in the text], as best I could, when I discussed why God did not give the devil perseverance.

BOS. You have proved that the evil angels must be restored from human nature. It is clear from this argument that the elect human beings will not be fewer in number than the reprobate angels. But show, if you can, whether they will be more numerous [Note: [Col. 0381C] “The elect will be” in the manuscript of Joly; “are the elect” in another reading].

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Whether there will be more holy human beings than evil angels

ANS. If, before some angels fell, the angels were already in that perfect number of which we spoke [Col. 0383A; Note: [Col. 0383D] “Were in” (*erant in*) in the text; “would be in” (*essent in*) in Joly], then human beings were made only for the restoration of the lost angels, and it is clear that there will not be more human beings than those angels.

But if that number did not exist among all those angels, then both what was lost and what had previously been lacking must be completed from among human beings. The elect human beings will be more numerous than the reprobate angels. Thus we shall say [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Thus we say” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition] that human beings were made not only to restore the diminished number, but also to complete what was not yet complete.

BOS. Which should we hold: that the angels were first made in a perfect number, or that they were not? [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Or that the angels were [made in that number]” in the manuscripts]

ANS. I will say what seems to me correct.

BOS. I cannot demand more from you [Note: [Col. 0383D] “I demand no more from you” in manuscript B].

ANS. If human beings were made after the fall of the evil angels, as some understand the account in Genesis, I do not see how I can determine by this argument which of the two alternatives is correct [Col. 0383B].

It may be, as I think, that the angels were first in a perfect number [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Were first in a perfect number” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Joly, and Victor 13; “were first in a number” in the manuscript of Victor 19], and that human beings were afterward made to restore their diminished number. It may also be that they were not in a perfect number [Note: [Col. 0383D] “They were not” (*non fuerunt*) in the manuscripts; “they were not” (*non fuerint*) in the text], because God postponed—as he still postpones—completing that number until he would make human nature at its proper time.

Accordingly, he would either merely complete the number that was not yet full, or, if it were diminished, restore it as well.

But if the whole creation was made simultaneously, and those days in which Moses appears to say that this world was not made simultaneously are to be understood otherwise than as we understand the days in which we live, I cannot understand how the angels were made in that perfect number [Note: [Col. 0383D] “In that complete number” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Victor, and Joly].

For if this were so, it seems to me that necessarily either some human beings or angels would have to fall, or there would be more in that heavenly city than the harmony of that perfect number required.

Therefore, if all things were made simultaneously, the angels and the first two human beings appear to have existed in an incomplete number [Note: [Col. 0383D] “In a perfect number” in the manuscripts of Bec, Gembloux, Victor 13 and 19, and the Gothic edition], so that, if no angel fell, only what was lacking would be completed through human beings [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Would be completed only” in the manuscript of Joly; “would be completed solely” in another reading], while, if someone were lost, what fell would also be restored.

And human nature, which was weaker, would, as it were, excuse God and confound the devil if the devil attributed his fall to his own weakness while human nature, though weaker, stood firm. And if that same human nature also fell, it would defend God all the more against the devil and against itself: for although it was made much weaker and subject to death, in the elect it would rise from such great weakness much higher than the point from which the devil had fallen, in proportion as the good angels—whose equality is owed to it—advanced after the ruin of the evil angels because they persevered [Col. 0383D–0384A].

For these reasons it seems to me rather that the perfect number by which that heavenly city would be completed did not exist among the angels [Note: [Col. 0383D] The manuscripts read, “that heavenly city would be completed, for if a human being”; Joly, “that heavenly city will be completed, since if a human being”]. For if human beings were not made simultaneously with the angels, this is possible [Note: [Col. 0383D] “It is possible” in the manuscripts of Bec, Victor, Joly, and Cister; “it is impossible” in the manuscript of Gembloux]; and if they were made simultaneously—which many think, since we read, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Sirach 18:1)—it seems necessary.

Moreover, if the perfection of the worldly creation is to be understood not so much in the number of individuals as in the number of natures, then human nature must either have been made to complete that same perfection or be superfluous to it. We would not dare say this even of the nature of the smallest worm.

Therefore human nature was made there for its own sake, and not only to restore individuals of another nature. 82 Hence it is clear that even if no angel had perished [Note: [Col. 0383D] “For even if” (*quia si etiam*) in the manuscripts of Bec, Gembloux, Victor, and Joly; “even if” (*quia etiam si*) in the text], human beings would nevertheless have had their place in the heavenly city.

It follows, then, that before some angels fell, the perfect number did not exist among the angels. Otherwise it would necessarily have been the case that either human beings or some angels would fall, since no one could remain there outside the perfect number [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Outside that perfect number no one could remain” in the manuscript of Victor 19].

BOS. You have accomplished something.

ANS. There is also another reason, as it seems to me, which strongly supports the opinion that the angels were not made in a perfect number.

BOS. State it.

ANS. If the angels were made in that perfect number, and human beings were not made at all except for the restoration of the lost angels, it is clear that, unless those angels [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Unless those angels” in the manuscripts of Victor 3 and 13; “unless the angels” in another reading] had fallen from that blessedness [Note: [Col. 0383D] “From that city” in the manuscript of Victor 19], human beings would not ascend to it.

BOS. That is certain.

ANS. But if someone should say [Note: [Col. 0383D] “If, therefore, someone should say” in Joly; “if someone should say” in the text] that the elect human beings will rejoice over the loss of the angels as much as they will rejoice over their own assumption, since undoubtedly the latter would not have occurred unless the former had occurred, how could they be defended against this perverse rejoicing?

Or how shall we say that the fallen angels are restored from among human beings [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Restored in human beings” in the manuscript of Cister; “restored from human beings” in the text] if, had those angels not fallen, they would have remained without this fault—that is, without rejoicing over the fall of others—while these human beings cannot be without it [Note: [Col. 0383D] “The fall of others” in the manuscript of Joly; “the fall of those others” in another reading]? Rather, how ought they to be blessed while possessing this fault? [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Could not be without it” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Victor 3 and 19, and Saint Michael; “could not have been without it” in another reading.]

Furthermore, with what boldness shall we say that God neither wills nor is able [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Was unable” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition] to accomplish this restoration without that fault?

BOS. Is it not similar in the case of the Gentiles who were called to the faith because the Jews rejected it? [Col. 0384D–0385A]

ANS. No. For even if all the Jews had believed, the Gentiles would nevertheless have been called, because “in every nation, whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:35) [Note: [Col. 0385D] Victor 19 reads, “who cooperates (*cooperatur*) and has attained righteousness” (*justitiam adeptus est*)].

But because the Jews despised the apostles, this then became the occasion for the apostles to turn to the Gentiles.

BOS. I see no way at all in which I can answer this [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Answer this” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Victor, and Cister].

ANS. From what, then, does that singular joy over another’s fall seem to you to arise? [Note: [Col. 0385D] “That individual joy” in the manuscript of Cister]

BOS. From what else, except that each person will be certain that he would by no means be where he will be unless another had fallen from there [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Unless another had not fallen from there” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition]?

ANS. If, then, no one had this certainty, there would be no reason for anyone to rejoice over another’s loss.

BOS. That seems so [Note: [Col. 0385D] “That seems so to me” in the manuscript of Joly].

ANS. Do you think that any of them will have this certainty if there will be many more of them than those who fell? [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Than those who fell” in the manuscripts of Bec, Gembloux, Victor, and Joly.]

BOS. I cannot at all suppose that he will or ought to have it. For how could anyone know whether he was made to complete what had been diminished, or to complete what had not yet been perfect, in the number from which the city was to be constituted? But all will be certain that they were made for the completion of that city.

ANS. Therefore, if there will be more of them than there are reprobate angels, no one can or ought to know that he was assumed there only because of another’s fall.

BOS. That is true.

ANS. Therefore no one will have reason to rejoice over another’s destruction.

BOS. That follows.

ANS. Since, then, we see that if there will be more elect human beings than reprobate angels, the impropriety that necessarily follows if there are not more will not follow [Note: [Col. 0385D] “The impropriety does not follow” in the manuscripts of Bec, Gembloux, Victor 3 and 13; “will not follow” in the manuscript of Victor 19; “that impropriety will not follow” in the manuscript of Joly], and since it is impossible that anything improper should occur in that city, it seems necessary that the angels were not made in that perfect number and that there will be more blessed human beings than there are miserable angels.

BOS. I do not see how this can be denied [Note: [Col. 0385D] “That can be denied” in the manuscript of Cister; “it can be denied” in another reading].

ANS. I think another reason for the same opinion can also be given.

BOS. You ought to present that one as well.

ANS. We believe that this bodily mass of the world is to be renewed for the better. Nor will this happen until the number of elect human beings has been completed and that blessed city has been perfected; nor is this to be postponed after its perfection [Note: [Col. 0385D] “This is not to be postponed” in the manuscripts of Bec, Gembloux, Victor, and Joly; “this” is omitted in another reading].

From this it can be inferred that from the beginning God purposed to perfect both simultaneously, so that neither the lesser nature, which does not perceive God, would be completed before the greater nature, which ought to enjoy God, nor, when the greater nature had been changed for the better in its perfection, would it fail in its own way to rejoice with it.

Indeed, every creature would rejoice eternally in its own manner over such a glorious and wondrous consummation, rejoicing with the Creator and with one another, so that what the will spontaneously does in rational nature, insensible creation would also, by God’s disposition, naturally display [Note: [Col. 0385D] “And this it already does” in the manuscripts of Victor, Gembloux, and Bec; “this also” in another reading].

We ordinarily rejoice in the exaltation of those who belong to us, as when on the birthdays of the saints we are gladdened by festive celebration, rejoicing in their glory [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Exulting” in the manuscripts of Victor 3 and 19; “rejoicing”].

This opinion also seems to be supported by the fact that, even if Adam had not sinned, God would nevertheless have postponed perfecting that city until, when the number he was awaiting had been completed from among human beings, the human beings themselves were transformed in their bodies into, so to speak, immortal immortality [Col. 0386A] [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Were transformed into immortal immortality” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Victor 3 and 13, Saint Michael, and the Gothic edition; the supplied wording is “were transformed into immortal immortality”].

For in paradise they had a certain immortality—that is, the power not to die—but this power was not immortal, because it could die [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Because they could die” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Saint Michael, and Victor 13; “because it could die” in the manuscripts of Victor 3 and 19; “because they could not die” in another reading], so that they themselves could not die [Note: [Col. 0385D] “That is, they themselves could not die” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Saint Michael, Cister, and Victor 13; “that is, they themselves could not fail to die” in another reading].

But if this is so [Note: [Col. 0385D] “But if this is so” in the manuscript of Victor 19], namely, that God purposed from the beginning to perfect simultaneously rational nature, the blessed city, and this worldly, insensible nature [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Sensible nature” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition], it seems that either that city was not complete in the number of angels before the fall of the evil ones, but God was waiting to complete it from human beings when he would change the bodily nature of the world for the better [Note: [Col. 0385D] “When he would renew the bodily nature for the better” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Victor, Joly, and Saint Michael; “and renew it for the better” in another reading];

or, if it was perfect in number, it was not perfect in confirmation, and its confirmation was to be postponed—even if no one in it had sinned—until the renewal of the world that we await [Col. 0386B];

or, if that confirmation was not to be postponed any longer, the renewal of the world had to be hastened so that it would occur together with that confirmation.

But that God should have instituted the immediate renewal of a newly made world and the destruction, at the very beginning before it became apparent why they had been made, of those things that would not exist after that renewal [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Should have instituted renewal and …” in the manuscript of Victor 19; “had instituted” in the manuscript of Saint Michael] is wholly without reason.

It follows, therefore, that the angels were not made in such a perfect number that their confirmation would not be long postponed, on the grounds that the renewal of the new world would then immediately have to occur [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Would have to occur” in the manuscripts of Joly and Victor 13; “must occur” in another reading; “may occur” in the manuscript of Victor 13]. That is not fitting.

But that God should have wished to postpone that same confirmation until the future renewal of the world seems inappropriate, especially since he completed it so quickly in some, and since it can be understood that he would have completed it in the first human beings when they sinned, had they not sinned, just as he did in the angels who persevered.

For although they had not yet advanced to that equality with the angels which human beings were going to attain when the perfect number was taken from among them, nevertheless, in the justice in which they stood, it seems that if, when tempted, they had conquered so as not to sin [Note: [Col. 0387C] “In the justice in which they stood, it seems that if, when tempted, they had conquered so as not to sin” in the manuscripts; one witness reads “in which they stood, it seems that if they had lived without being tempted, they would not sin”], they would have been confirmed, together with all their offspring, so that thereafter they could not sin [Note: [Col. 0387C] “So that thereafter they could sin” in one manuscript], just as, because they were defeated and sinned, they were weakened so that, insofar as depended on them, they could not be without sin [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Could not be” in the manuscript of Saint Michael; “could not have been”].

For who would dare say that injustice [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Justice” (*justitiam*) in the manuscript and Gothic edition; “injustice” (*injustitiam*) in the text] was more powerful for binding in slavery [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Into slavery” in the manuscripts] a human being who consented to it at the first persuasion [Note: [Col. 0387C] “At the first temptation” in the manuscripts] than justice would have been for confirming in liberty one who adhered to it during that same first temptation?

For just as, because the whole of human nature was in the first parents [Note: [Col. 0387C] “The whole which was in the parents” in the manuscripts], it was wholly defeated in them so as to sin—except for that one human being whom God, just as he knew how to make without the seed of a man from a Virgin, also knew how to separate from Adam’s sin [Note: [Col. 0387C] “He knew how to make him, and thus willed to separate him from Adam’s sin” in one reading; “he knew how to make him and thus knew how to separate him from Adam’s sin” in another]—so the whole of human nature would have conquered in them if they had not sinned [Note: [Col. 0387C] “If he had not sinned” in the manuscripts].

It remains, therefore, to say that the heavenly city was not completed in that first number of angels, but was to be completed from human beings. If these things are sound, there will be more elect human beings than there are reprobate angels.

BOS. What you say seems highly reasonable. But what shall we say about the passage that is read concerning God: “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deuteronomy 32:8)? Some, because in place of “the children of Israel” the reading “the angels of God” is found, interpret it in such a way that the number of elect human beings to be assumed is understood to correspond to the number of good angels.

ANS. This does not conflict with the opinion stated above [Note: [Col. 0387C] “This conflicts with it” in the manuscript of Victor 19], if it is not certain that as many angels fell as remained.

For if the elect angels are more numerous than the reprobate, and it is necessary that the reprobate be restored by elect human beings, it can happen [Note: [Col. 0387C] “It can also happen” in Joly] that they become equal in number to the blessed; and thus there will be more just human beings than unjust angels. 83

But remember how I began to answer your question: namely, that if I say something which a greater authority does not confirm [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Namely, if I say something which a greater authority does not confirm” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition], then, even if I seem to prove it by reason, it must not be accepted with any other certainty than that, for the time being, it appears so to me, until God reveals something better to me in some way.

For I am certain that if I say anything which without doubt contradicts Sacred Scripture, it is false, and I do not wish to hold to it if I come to know this.

But in matters about which different opinions may safely be held, such as the matter we are now discussing—since we do not know whether more human beings are to be chosen than there are fallen angels [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Than the fallen angels” in the manuscripts of Victor, Gembloux, and Bec; “than the fallen angelic beings” in the manuscript of Joly], or not, and we judge one alternative more likely than the other—I do not think there is any danger to the soul.

If, I say, in matters of this kind [Note: [Col. 0387C] “In these matters” in the manuscripts] we interpret divine statements so that they appear to support different opinions, and nowhere is it found where they definitively determine what must be held without doubt [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Where they determine” in the manuscripts of Victor 19; “where it is determined” in the manuscript of Cister], I do not think that we should be censured.

As for what you said—“He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God,” as it is read in one translation, and “according to the number of the children of Israel” in another—since both translations either signify the same thing or signify different things without contradiction, it is to be understood in the following ways.

By “the angels of God” and by “the children of Israel” may be signified only the good angels; or only the elect human beings; or together the angels and the elect human beings—that is, the entire heavenly city.

Or “the angels of God” may signify the holy angels alone, and “the children of Israel” the just human beings alone.

Or the angels alone may be signified by “the children of Israel,” and the just human beings by “the angels of God.”

If only the good angels are designated by both expressions, the meaning is the same as if the expression were only “the angels of God.” But if the whole heavenly city is intended, the meaning is that peoples—that is, multitudes of elect human beings—will continue to be assumed, or peoples will continue to exist in this world, until the predestined number of that city, which is not yet complete from among human beings, has been completed [Col. 0388C] [Note: [Col. 0387C] One manuscript reads: “If only the good angels are designated by both, the meaning is the same. But if the whole heavenly city is intended by ‘the angels of God,’ this is the meaning: for as long as …”].

But I do not now see how only angels, or angels and holy human beings together, can be understood by “the children of Israel.” It is not foreign to usage, however, for holy human beings [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Holy angels” in Victor 19; “holy human beings” in the text] to be called “the children of Israel,” just as they are called “the children of Abraham.”

They can also rightly be called angels of God [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Could be called” in the manuscripts], because they imitate an angelic life, and because the likeness and equality of angels is promised to them in heaven, and because all who live justly are angels of God.

Hence confessors and martyrs themselves are also called such [Note: [Col. 0387C] “The confessors and martyrs themselves” in the manuscripts]. For one who confesses and bears witness to the truth is God’s messenger—that is, his angel [Col. 0389A] [Note: [Col. 0389C] “He is an angel” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition; “he is his angel” in the manuscripts of Victor; “he is an angel of God” in another reading].

And if an evil human being is called “the devil,” as the Lord calls Judas on account of the likeness of his wickedness, why should a good human being not also be called an angel [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Why is a good person not [called one]” in the manuscript of Victor], on account of the imitation of righteousness? [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Why should a good human being not be called an angel” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition.]

Therefore, as I think [Note: [Col. 0389C] “As I judge” in the manuscripts], we can say that God established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of elect human beings. For peoples will continue to exist, and the procreation of human beings will continue in this world, until the number of those elect human beings has been completed [Note: [Col. 0389C] “The number of elect human beings has been completed” in the manuscripts; Joly and Victor omit “human beings”]. Once it has been completed, the generation of human beings that occurs in this life will cease [Note: [Col. 0389C] “The existence of human beings will cease” in the manuscript of Victor 19; it omits “to be”].

But if by “the angels of God” we understand only the holy angels, and by “the children of Israel” only the just human beings, then “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God” can be understood in two ways:

either that as many people—that is, as many human beings—will be assumed as there are holy angels of God [Note: [Col. 0389C] “As many as there are angels of God” in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Joly, Saint Michael, and Victor 19];

or that peoples will continue to exist until the number of God’s angels is completed from among human beings.

I see only one way in which “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel” can be explained: namely, that [Note: [Col. 0389C] “The children of God; likewise, that” in one reading], as stated above, peoples will continue to exist in this world until the number of holy human beings has been assumed.

From both translations it is inferred that as many human beings will be assumed [Note: [Col. 0389C] “As many will be assumed” in the manuscript of Victor] as there are angels who remained.

It does not follow from this, however, although the fallen angels are to be restored from among human beings [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Are to be restored” in the manuscripts of Victor, Gembloux, Bec, and Joly], that as many angels fell as persevered.

But if this is said [Note: [Col. 0389C] “If it were said” in the manuscripts], it will have to be discovered how the arguments stated above are not valid [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Are not valid” in the manuscripts of Victor; “are valid” in another reading], since they seem to show that before some angels fell there was not among the angels that perfect number of which I spoke above, and that more elect human beings will be future than there are evil angels.

BOS. I do not regret compelling you to speak about these matters concerning the angels; for it was not done in vain [Note: [Col. 0389C] “It was done in vain” in the Victor manuscripts; “this was done in vain” in another reading]. Now return to the matter from which we digressed.

## CHAPTER XIX [alternatively, XVIII]

### That a human being cannot be saved without satisfaction for sin
ANS. It is established that God purposed to restore, from among human beings, the angels who had fallen. [Note: [Col. 0389C] In the manuscripts, chapter 19 begins with these words: “It is established that God,” etc.]

BOS. It is certain.

ANS. Therefore the human beings who are to be assumed into that heavenly city in place of the angels must be such as those were who were to be there in whose place they will be there; that is, such as the good angels now are. Otherwise those who fell will not be restored; and it will follow that God either will not be able to complete the good work he began, or will repent of having begun so great a good work. Both are absurd. [Note: [Col. 0389C] One Cistercian manuscript omits *illi* (“those”) in “such as those who were to be there.”] [Note: [Col. 0389C] The manuscripts read “and it follows that” (*et sequitur quia*) for “and it will follow that” (*et sequetur quia*).]

BOS. Truly, human beings must be equal to the good angels. [Note: [Col. 0389C] The Victor manuscripts read: “Whence it is necessary that” (*unde oportet quod*), for “Truly, it is necessary that” (*vere oportet ut*).]

ANS. Have the good angels ever sinned?

BOS. No.

ANS. Can you conceive that a human being who has sinned at some time and has never made satisfaction to God for his sin, but is merely dismissed unpunished, is equal to an angel who has never sinned? [Note: [Col. 0389C] Joly reads *pro peccato suo satisfecit* (“made satisfaction for his sin”); the text has *pro peccato satisfecit* (“made satisfaction for sin”).]

BOS. I can conceive and speak these words, but I cannot so conceive their sense, just as I cannot understand falsehood to be truth.

ANS. Therefore it is not fitting for God to assume a sinful human being without satisfaction into the restoration of the lost angels, since truth does not permit that person to be raised to equality with the good. [Note: [Col. 0389C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *hominem peccatorem* (“a sinful human being”) for *hominem peccantem* (“a human being sinning”).] [Note: [Col. 0389C] Victor, Joly, and Saint-Michel read *assumere perditorum* (“to assume of the lost”) for *sumere perditorum* (“to take of the lost”).] [Note: [Col. 0389C] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Victor 3 and 13, Cisterciensis, Saint-Michel, and Joly read *aequalitatem angelorum* (“equality with the angels”); Beccensis 2, Victor 19, and the Gothic edition read *aequalitatem beatorum* (“equality with the blessed”); the text reads *aequalitatem bonorum* (“equality with the good”).]

BOS. Reason shows this.

ANS. Consider also the human being alone, apart from the fact that he ought to be made equal to the angels, whether God ought to raise him to any blessedness, or to such blessedness as he had before he sinned. [Note: [Col. 0389C] Joly reads *consideratio etiam* (“consideration also”) for *considera etiam* (“consider also”).] [Note: [Col. 0389C] The manuscripts read *sine eo quod* (“apart from the fact that”) for *sine hoc quia* (“apart from this, that”).] [Note: [Col. 0389C] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Victor, Joly, and the Gothic edition read *ad beatitudinem illam* (“to that blessedness”) for *ad beatitudinem ullam* (“to any blessedness”).]

BOS. Say what you think, and I shall consider it as I can. [Note: [Col. 0389C] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Joly, Victor 3 and 13, Cisterciensis, and the Gothic edition read *dic quae cogitas* (“say the things you think”); Victor 19 reads *dic tu prout cogitas* (“speak as you think”).]

ANS. Let us suppose a certain rich man holding in his hand a precious pearl, which no pollution has ever touched, and which no one else can remove from his hand unless he himself permits it; and that he intends to place it in his treasury, where are the dearest and most precious things he possesses. [Note: [Col. 0389C] Victor reads *nullo unquam pollutio* (“by no pollution ever”) for *nunquam pollutio ulla* (“no pollution ever”).]

BOS. I conceive it as though it were before us.

ANS. What if he permitted that same pearl to be knocked out of his hand into mud by some envious person, though he could prevent it, and afterwards, taking it from the mud, placed it, polluted and unwashed, in some clean and dear place of his, intending thereafter to preserve it thus? Would you think him wise? [Note: [Col. 0389C] The manuscripts read *tamen prohibere posset* (“although he could nevertheless prevent it”) for *cum prohibere posset* (“though he could prevent it”).]

BOS. How could I? For would it not be far better for him to keep and preserve his pearl clean rather than polluted? [Note: [Col. 0391D] One manuscript reads *esset hoc satis* (“would this be sufficiently”); another omits *hoc* (“this”).]

ANSEL. Would God not act similarly? He held in paradise, as though in his hand, the human being who was to be joined to the angels without sin; and he permitted the devil, inflamed by envy, to cast him—though consenting—into the mire of sin. For, had he wished to prevent the devil, the devil could not have tempted the human being. Would he not, I say, act similarly if he restored, at least to paradise from which he had been expelled, a human being stained with the filth of sin, without any elevation—that is, without all satisfaction—one who was to remain such forever? [Note: [Col. 0391D] Victor 3 reads *sociatum sine* (“joined without”) for *sociandum sine* (“to be joined without”).]

BOS. If God did this, I do not dare deny the resemblance, and therefore I do not grant that he could do it. [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts read *et idcirco ... non abnuo* (“and therefore I do not deny”), for *et idcirco ... non annuo* (“and therefore I do not grant”).] For it would seem either that he had been unable to accomplish what he had purposed, or that he had repented of his good purpose. Neither can befall God.

ANS. Hold, then, as utterly certain that without satisfaction—that is, without voluntary payment of the debt—God cannot dismiss sin unpunished, nor can the sinner attain blessedness, even such blessedness as he had before he sinned. For in this way the human being would not be restored, nor would he be such as he had been before sin. [Note: [Col. 0391D] In the manuscripts this is the final part of chapter 19.] [Note: [Col. 0391D] Victor 19 omits *sine* (“without”) in “that is, without voluntary payment of the debt.”]

BOS. I cannot wholly contradict your arguments. But what is it that we say to God: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6); and why does every people pray the God whom it believes in to forgive its sins? If we pay what we owe, why do we pray that he forgive it? Is God unjust, to demand again what has been paid? But if we do not pay, why do we vainly pray him to do what, since it is unfitting, he cannot do? [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts read *quoniam credit* (“because it believes”) for *quem credit* (“whom it believes”).]

ANS. Whoever does not pay says “Forgive” in vain; but whoever pays makes supplication, because supplication itself belongs to payment. For God owes nothing to anyone, but every creature owes to him; and therefore it is not appropriate for a human being to deal with God as equal with equal. But you need not answer about this now. For when you know why Christ died, perhaps you will see for yourself what you are asking. [Note: [Col. 0391D] Cisterciensis omits *nunc* (“now”).] [Note: [Col. 0391D] Victor 19 reads *qui autem solvitur* (“but he who is paid”) for *qui autem solvit* (“but he who pays”).]

BOS. For the present, what you answer concerning this question is enough for me. But you have shown so plainly that no human being can attain blessedness with sin, or be released from sin unless he pays what he seized by sinning, that even if I wished I could not doubt it. [Note: [Col. 0391D] Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, Victor, Joly, and the Gothic edition read *sufficit mihi nunc* (“it is enough for me now”); the text reads *sufficit ergo mihi nunc* (“therefore it is enough for me now”).]

[Col. 0392A]

## CHAPTER XX

That satisfaction must be in proportion to the measure of sin, and that a human being cannot make it by himself.

ANS. You will not doubt this either, I think: satisfaction must be in proportion to the measure of sin.

BOS. Otherwise sin would remain disordered in some respect; and that cannot be, if God leaves nothing disordered in his kingdom. For it has been established that any incongruity, however slight, is impossible in God. [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts read *quodlibet parvum* (“any small [incongruity]”) for *quamlibet parvum* (“however small”).]

ANS. Tell me, then, what will you pay God for your sin? [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts read *solves pro* (“will you pay for”) for *solves Deo pro* (“will you pay God for”).]

BOS. Repentance, contrition and humility of heart, abstinences, manifold bodily labours, mercy in giving and forgiving, and obedience.

ANS. What do you give God in all these things?

BOS. Do I not honour God when, from fear and love of him, I cast away temporal joy in contrition of heart; trample underfoot, in abstinences and labours, the pleasures and repose of this life; am generous with what is mine in giving and forgiving; and subject myself to him in obedience? [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *in abstinentiis* (“in abstinences”) for *abstinentiis* (“abstinences”).] [Note: [Col. 0391D] Victor 13 reads *delectationem* (“pleasure”) for *delectationes* (“pleasures”).] [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *sunt largiendo* (“are [given] in giving”) for *sunt largior* (“I am generous with [them]”).]

ANS. When you return something which you owe God, even if you had not sinned, you must not count it as payment of the debt that you owe for sin. Yet all those things which you mention, you owe God. [Note: [Col. 0391D] Victor 19 reads *non debet* (“he must not”) for *non debes* (“you must not”).] [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *computare hoc pro* (“count this as”) for *computare pro* (“count as”).]

For love in this mortal life ought to be so great; and, as regards prayer, desire to attain that for which you were made; and grief because you are not yet there; and fear lest you should not attain it; that you ought to feel no joy except in those things which give you help or hope of attaining it. [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts read *pertinet omne desiderium* (“every desire pertains [to this]”); the Gothic edition reads *pertinet omnino desiderium* (“desire wholly pertains [to this]”); the text reads *pertinet oratio, desiderium* (“prayer pertains [to this], desire”).]

For you do not deserve to possess what you do not love and desire according to what it is; and you do not grieve for that which you do not yet possess, and about which, since you are still in such danger whether you will possess it or not, you ought to grieve. [Note: [Col. 0391D] Victor, Joly, and the Gothic edition read *quod es, amas* (“what you are, you love”) for *quod est, amas* (“what it is, you love”).] [Note: [Col. 0391D] Victor 13 reads *non dolore* (“not grieving”) for *non doles* (“you do not grieve”).]

To this also belongs fleeing rest and worldly pleasures, which call the mind back from that true rest and delight, except insofar as you recognize them to suffice for your purpose of attaining it.

As for giving, you must understand that you give out of debt, just as you understand that what you give you do not have from yourself, but from him whose servant both you and the person to whom you give are. Nature also teaches you to do for your fellow, that is, human being for human being, what you wish him to do for you; and that one unwilling to give what he has ought not receive what he does not have.

As for forgiving, I say briefly that vengeance would in no way belong to you, as we said above, because you are not your own; nor is he who injured you either yours or his own. Both of you, made servants of one Lord, are from him out of nothing; and if you take vengeance upon your fellow servant, you arrogantly usurp over him the judgment which properly belongs to the Lord and judge of all. [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *dimissione breviter* (“briefly, concerning forgiving”) for *dimissione vero breviter* (“but briefly, concerning forgiving”).] [Note: [Col. 0391D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *pertineat* (“would belong”) for *pertinet* (“belongs”).] [Note: [Col. 0393D] Victor, Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Joly, and the Gothic edition read *etsi de* (“even if [you take vengeance] upon”) for *et si de* (“and if [you take vengeance] upon”).]

And in obedience, what do you give God that you do not owe him, since you owe to his command everything that you are, have, and can do?

BOS. I no longer dare say that in all these things I give God anything that I do not owe.

ANS. What, then, will you pay God for your sin?

BOS. If I owe him myself and all that I can do, even when I do not sin, in order that I may not sin, I have nothing to render him for sin. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Victor omits *illi* (“to him”) in *peccato illi reddam* (“render to him for sin”).]

ANS. What, then, will become of you? How can you be saved?

BOS. If I consider your arguments, I do not see how. But if I turn to my faith, I hope that I can be saved in the Christian faith which works through love (Galatians 5:7), and because we read: if the unjust person turns from his injustice and does justice, all his injustices are handed over to oblivion (Ezekiel 18). [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *injustitias suas* (“his own injustices”) for *injustitias ejus* (“his injustices”).]

ANS. This is said only of those who either awaited Christ before he came or believe in him after he came. But we set Christ and the Christian faith aside, as though they had never existed, when we proposed to inquire by reason alone whether his coming was necessary for human salvation. [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *nisi de illis* (“only of those”) for *nisi illis* (“only to those”).] [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *expectabant Christum* (“were awaiting Christ”) for *exspectaverunt Christum* (“awaited Christ”).] [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *nunquam fuisset* (“as though he had never existed”) for *nunquam fuissent* (“as though they had never existed”).]

BOS. We did so.

ANS. Let us therefore proceed by reason alone.

BOS. Although you lead me into certain straits, I nevertheless greatly desire you to proceed as you began. [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts read *deducas* (“lead”) for *ducas* (“bring”).]

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0393C] How great the weight of sin is.

ANS. Let us suppose that you do not owe for sin all those things which you just proposed as being able to pay for sin, and let us see whether they can suffice as satisfaction for one sin as small as a single glance contrary to God’s will. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Victor reads *ponamus ergo omnia* (“let us suppose, therefore, all”) for *ponamus omnia* (“let us suppose all”).] [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *modo proposuisti* (“just proposed”) for *modo posuisti* (“just set forth”).] [Note: [Col. 0393D] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Victor 3 and 19, Cisterciensis, Saint-Michel, Joly, and the Gothic edition read *utrum possit* (“whether it can”) for *utrum possint* (“whether they can”).] [Note: [Col. 0393D] Joly reads *non sufficere* (“not suffice”) for *sufficere* (“suffice”).]

BOS. Had I not heard you propose this as a question, I should have thought that I could erase this sin by one act of contrition.

ANS. You have not yet considered how great the weight of sin is.

BOS. Show me now. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Victor reads *ostende* (“show”) for *nunc ostende* (“show me now”).]

ANS. If you saw yourself in God’s presence, and someone said to you, “Look there,” while God, on the other hand, said, “I do not in any way wish you to look,” search your own heart for what there is among all things for which you ought to make that glance contrary to God’s will.

BOS. I find nothing for which I ought to do this, unless perhaps I were placed in such necessity that I must commit either this or a greater sin. [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *pro quo hic* (“for which here”) for *propter quod hoc* (“for the sake of which this”).]

ANS. Remove that necessity, and consider this sin alone: whether you could commit it in order to redeem yourself. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Victor, Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, Joly, and the Gothic edition read *et de solo* (“and concerning the alone”) for *de solo* (“concerning the alone”).]

BOS. I clearly see that I cannot.

ANS. Not to detain you longer: what if it were necessary either that the whole world, and everything which is not God, perish and be reduced to nothing, or that you do so small a thing against God’s will?

BOS. When I consider the act itself, I see it as something exceedingly slight. But when I consider what it is to act against God’s will, I understand it to be something most grave and incomparable with any loss. Yet we sometimes act contrary to someone’s will without blame, in order that his goods may be preserved; and afterwards he is pleased that we acted against his will.

ANS. This occurs with a human being who sometimes does not understand what is useful to him, or cannot restore what he has lost. But God needs nothing and, if all things perished, could restore them just as he made them. [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts read *aut non posset* (“or could not”) for *aut non potest* (“or cannot”).] [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts read *fecit restaurare* (“made [them] restore”) for *fecit restituere* (“made [them] restore them”).]

BOS. I must admit that I ought to do nothing contrary to God’s will for the preservation of the whole creation.

ANS. What if there were many worlds full of creatures, as this one is? [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts read *pleni creaturae* (“full, [of] creature”) for *pleni creaturis* (“full of creatures”).]

BOS. If they were multiplied to an infinite number and shown to me in the same way, I should give the same answer. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Victor 19, Cisterciensis, and Joly read *obtenderentur* (“were presented”) for *ostenderentur* (“were shown”).]

ANS. You could answer nothing more correctly. But consider also, if it happened that you made that glance contrary to God’s will, what could you pay for this sin?

BOS. I have nothing greater than what I said above.

ANS. Thus we sin grievously whenever we knowingly do anything, however small, contrary to God’s will; for we are always in his presence, and he has always commanded us not to sin. [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts read *quantumlibet parvum* (“however small”) for *quamlibet parvum* (“however small”).]

BOS. As I hear it, we live in very great danger.

ANS. It is evident that God requires satisfaction according to the magnitude of sin.

BOS. I cannot deny it.

ANS. Therefore you do not make satisfaction unless you restore something greater than that for the sake of which you ought not to have committed sin. [Note: [Col. 0393D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *ergo satisfacies* (“therefore you will make satisfaction”) for *ergo satisfacis* (“therefore you make satisfaction”).]

BOS. I see that reason requires this, and that it is altogether impossible.

ANS. Nor can God admit to blessedness anyone in any degree bound by the debt of sin, because he ought not to do so.

BOS. This conclusion is exceedingly harsh.

ANS. Hear still another reason why it is no less difficult for a human being to be reconciled to God. [Note: [Col. 0393D] In the manuscripts chapter 22 begins here.]

BOS. Unless faith consoled me, this alone would compel me to despair.

ANS. Listen nevertheless.

BOS. Speak.

[Col. 0395A]

## CHAPTER XXII

What an insult the human being inflicted on God when he allowed himself to be conquered by the devil, for which he cannot make satisfaction. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly reads *quod contumeliam* (“that [he inflicted] an insult”) for *quam contumeliam* (“what an insult”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly reads *non potest Deo* (“cannot [make satisfaction] to God”) for *non potest* (“cannot”).]

ANS. The human being, created in paradise without sin, was placed, as it were, on God’s side between God and the devil, so that by not consenting to the devil urging sin he might conquer the devil, for the vindication and honour of God and for the devil’s disgrace: the weaker being on earth would not sin, though persuaded by the same devil who, being stronger, sinned in heaven without anyone persuading him. And though the human being could easily have accomplished this, compelled by no force, by persuasion alone he willingly allowed himself to be conquered according to the devil’s will and against God’s will and honour. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts read *et ad confusionem* (“and for the disgrace”) for *ad confusionem* (“for the disgrace”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly omits: “who, being stronger, sinned in heaven without anyone persuading him.”] [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts read *hoc facile* (“this easily”) for *hoc homo facile* (“the human being [could do] this easily”).]

BOS. What are you aiming at?

ANS. Judge for yourself whether it is not contrary to God’s honour that the human being should be reconciled to him while this injury inflicted upon God remains as an accusation, unless first he honours God by conquering the devil, as he dishonoured him by being conquered by the devil. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Gemmeticensis and Beccensis read *homo reconciliaretur* (“the human being might be reconciled”) for *homo reconcilietur* (“the human being is reconciled”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, Victor, and Joly read *inhonoraverit illum* (“has dishonoured him”) for *inhonoravit illum* (“dishonoured him”).]

Moreover, the victory must be such that, just as a strong being, immortal by power, easily consented to the devil in order to sin, and thereby justly incurred the punishment of mortality, so a weak and mortal being—such as he made himself—must conquer the devil through the difficulty of death, so as in no way to sin. This he cannot do so long as, from the wound of the first sin, he is conceived and born in sin.

BOS. Again I say that reason proves what you say, and that it is impossible. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Victor, and Joly read *quia ratio* (“because reason”) for *quia et ratio* (“because both reason”).]

ANS. Receive yet one further point, without which the human being is not justly reconciled; and it is no less impossible. [Note: [Col. 0395D] In the manuscripts chapter 23 begins here.] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Cisterciensis omits *est* (“is”) in *impossibile est* (“is impossible”).]

BOS. You have already set before us so many things which we must do that, whatever you add, cannot frighten me more.

ANS. Listen nevertheless.

BOS. I am listening.

## CHAPTER XXIII

What the human being took from God when he sinned, which he cannot restore. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts, Gothic edition, and Venetian edition read *quod abstulit* (“what he took”) for *quid abstulit* (“what did he take”).]

ANS. What did the human being take from God when he allowed himself to be conquered by the devil?

BOS. You say it, as you began; for I do not know what he could add to the evils which you have shown.

ANS. Did he not take from God everything which God had purposed to make from human nature?

BOS. It cannot be denied.

ANS. Attend to strict justice, and judge by it whether the human being makes satisfaction to God in proportion to his sin unless, by conquering the devil, he restores to God that very thing which, by allowing himself to be conquered by the devil, he took from God. Thus, just as through his defeat the devil seized what was God’s and God lost it, so through his victory the devil must lose it and God recover it. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *attendere in* (“attend to”) for *intende in* (“direct [your attention] to”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts read *utrum et aequalitatem* (“whether and [in] equality”) for *utrum ad aequalitatem* (“whether in proportion”).]

BOS. Nothing stricter or more just can be conceived.

ANS. Do you think that supreme justice can violate this justice?

BOS. I do not dare think so.

ANS. Therefore the human being neither ought nor can receive from God what God purposed to give him, unless he restores to God all that he took from him; so that, as God lost through him, God may also recover through him. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Victor reads *aut totum* (“or wholly”) for *aut potest* (“or can”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Victor reads *illum recuperet* (“may recover him”) for *illum Deus recuperet* (“God may recover him”).]

This cannot happen otherwise than that, as through the defeated one all human nature was corrupted and, as it were, leavened with sin—together with which God admits no one to complete that heavenly city—so through the victor as many human beings must be justified from sin as were to complete the number for the completion of which the human being was made. But this the sinful human being cannot do in any way, because a sinner cannot justify a sinner. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly reads *vivificentur* (“may be made alive”) for *justificentur* (“may be justified”).]

BOS. Nothing is more just and nothing more impossible. Yet from all this God’s mercy and human hope seem to perish, as concerns the blessedness for which the human being was made.

ANS. Wait a little longer.

BOS. What more have you? [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly and Victor omit *adhuc* (“still”).]

## CHAPTER XXIV

That, so long as the human being does not render God what he owes, he cannot be blessed; nor is he excused by inability. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts read *quia quandiu* (“because so long as”) for *quod quandiu* (“that so long as”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Beccensis and Gemmeticensis omit *homo* (“the human being”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly and Victor read *reddet Deo* (“will render God”) for *reddit Deo* (“renders God”).]

ANS. If the person who does not return to another human being what he owes is called unjust, much more unjust is one who does not return to God what he owes.

BOS. If he can and does not return it, he is indeed unjust. But if he cannot, how is he unjust?

ANS. Perhaps, if there is no cause of inability in him, he may in some degree be excused. But if guilt lies in the inability itself, then, just as it does not lighten sin, so it does not excuse one who does not repay the debt. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly reads *in ipso impotentia est culpa* (“in him inability is guilt”); Victor 3 and 19, Cisterciensis, and the Gothic edition read *in ipsa potentia est culpa* (“in power itself there is guilt”); Saint-Michel reads *in ipsa impotentia culpa est* (“in inability itself there is guilt”); Victor 13 reads *ipsa impotentia est culpa* (“inability itself is guilt”); the text reads *si nulla in illo est impotentiae causa* (“if there is no cause of inability in him”).]

For if someone assigned a task to his servant, and commanded him not to throw himself into a pit which he showed him and from which he could by no means emerge; and if that servant, despising his master’s command and warning, voluntarily threw himself into the pit shown beforehand, so that he could in no way perform the assigned task: do you think that such inability could in any degree serve him as an excuse for not doing the task assigned?
