[Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly reads *servo et* (“to a servant, and”) for *servo suo* (“to his servant”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, and Victor read *illi monstrat* (“shows him”) for *illi demonstrat* (“points it out to him”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Joly reads *opus perficere* (“complete the task”) for *opus efficere* (“perform the task”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] Victor omits *illi* (“to him”) after *putasne* (“do you think”).] [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *cum opus* (“when [he does] the task”) for *cur opus* (“why [he does] the task”).]

BOS. By no means; rather, it increases his guilt, because he himself brought that inability upon himself. For he sinned twice: he did not do what he had been commanded to do, and he did what he had been commanded not to do.

ANS. So too the human being, who voluntarily bound himself by that debt which he cannot pay, and by his own fault cast himself into this inability, so that he cannot pay either what he owed before sin—that is, not to sin—or what he owes because he sinned, is inexcusable. [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *illi debito* (“by that debt”) for *illo debito* (“by this debt”).] [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *nec quod debet* (“nor [pay] what he owes”) for *nec hoc quod debet* (“nor this which he owes”).] [Note: [Col. 0397C] Joly reads *inexcusabile est* (“it is inexcusable”) for *inexcusabilis est* (“he is inexcusable”).]

For inability itself is guilt, because he ought not to have it; indeed, he ought not to have it. For, just as it is guilt not to have what one ought to have, so it is guilt to have what one ought not have. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Joly omits from “Thus, therefore” through “For this reason.”]

Therefore, just as it is guilt for a human being not to possess that power which he received in order to be able to avoid sin, so it is guilt for him to possess the inability by which he can neither maintain justice and avoid sin, nor render what he owes for sin. For he voluntarily did that through which he lost that power and came into this inability. Not possessing the power which one ought to possess is the same as possessing the inability which one ought not to possess. [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts read *per quam nec* (“through which he can neither”) for *qua nec* (“by which he can neither”).]

Therefore inability to render God what one owes, which causes one not to render it, does not excuse the human being if he does not render it; for the effect of sin does not excuse the sin which produces it. [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts read *effectus peccati* (“the effect of sin”) for *effectum peccati* (“the effect of sin”).] [Note: [Col. 0397C] Saint-Michel reads *quod fecit* (“which it committed”) for *quod facit* (“which it commits”).]

BOS. It is exceedingly grave, and it must be so.

ANS. Therefore the human being who does not render God what he owes is unjust.

BOS. It is very true; for he is unjust because he does not render it, and unjust because he cannot render it.

ANS. No unjust person, however, will be admitted to blessedness; for just as blessedness is sufficiency in which there is no want, so it befits no one except one in whom justice is so pure that there is no injustice in that person. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Victor and the Gothic edition read *admittitur ad* (“is admitted to”) for *admittetur ad* (“will be admitted to”).]

BOS. I do not dare believe otherwise.

ANS. Whoever does not pay God what he owes cannot be blessed. [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *non potest esse* (“cannot be”) for *non poterit esse* (“will not be able to be”).]

BOS. Nor can I deny this consequence. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Joly reads *nec hoc consequi possum* (“nor can I attain this”); Victor 19 reads *nec hoc consequenter* (“nor this consequently”); Victor 3 and 13 read *nec consequi negare possum* (“nor can I deny attaining”); Saint-Michel and the Gothic edition read *et hoc consequi non possum* (“and I cannot attain this”).]

ANS. But if you wish to say that merciful God forgives the suppliant what he owes because he cannot repay it, it cannot be said that he forgives except either what the human being ought voluntarily to repay but cannot—that is, what could be compensated for by a sin which ought not be committed, even for the preservation of every thing that is not God—or what he was going to take away from one unwillingly by punishment, as I said above, namely blessedness.

But if he forgives what the human being ought voluntarily to repay because he cannot repay it, what else is this than God forgiving what he cannot have? It is mockery to ascribe such mercy to God.

But if he forgives what he was going to take away from one unwillingly, on account of inability to repay what that person ought voluntarily to repay, God remits punishment and makes the human being blessed on account of sin, because he has what he ought not have. For he ought not have that inability itself, and therefore, so long as he has it without satisfaction, it is sin in him. But mercy of this kind is very contrary to God’s justice, which permits nothing but punishment to be rendered for sin. Therefore, just as it is impossible for God to be contrary to himself, so it is impossible for him to be merciful in this way. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, and Victor 19 read *Dei est nimis* (“is exceedingly of God”) for *Dei nimis est* (“of God is exceedingly”).]

BOS. Another mercy of God must be sought than this.

ANS. Let it be true, then: God forgives one who does not pay what he owes, because he cannot. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Joly reads *verum est* (“it is true”) for *verum esto* (“let it be true”).] [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *dimittat Deus ei, qui non solvit debitum* (“may God forgive one who does not pay the debt”) for *dimittit Deus ei, qui non solvit quod debet* (“God forgives one who does not pay what he owes”).] [Note: [Col. 0397C] Victor, Joly, Cisterciensis, Saint-Michel, and the Gothic edition read *idcirco quod non potest* (“because he cannot”); Gemmeticensis and Beccensis omit *idcirco* (“because”).]

BOS. I should like that to be so.

ANS. But so long as he does not render it, he either will wish to render it or will not wish to render it. If he wishes what he cannot do, he will be needy; but if he does not wish to do it, he will be unjust. [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *quod si volet* (“but if he wishes”) for *sed si volet* (“but if he wishes”).]

BOS. Nothing is clearer. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Joly reads *mihi clarius* (“clearer to me”) for *nihil clarius* (“nothing clearer”).]

ANS. Whether he is needy or unjust, he will not be blessed.

BOS. This too is clear. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Victor reads *apertum est* (“it is clear”) for *hoc apertum* (“this [is] clear”).]

ANS. Therefore, so long as he does not render it, he cannot be blessed. [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *quandiu non* (“so long as not”) for *quandiu ergo non* (“therefore, so long as not”).]

BOS. If God follows the rule of justice, there is no escape for the wretched little human being, and God’s mercy seems to perish.

ANS. You asked for reason; receive reason. I do not deny that God is merciful, who saves human beings and animals, according as he has multiplied his mercy. But we are speaking of that final mercy by which he makes the human being blessed after this life. I think I have sufficiently shown, by the arguments set out above, that this blessedness ought to be given to no one except one whose sins have been wholly forgiven, and that this forgiveness cannot occur unless the debt due for sin has been paid according to the magnitude of the sin. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Joly, Cisterciensis, Victor 19, and the Gothic edition read *dare debere* (“ought to give”) for *dari debere* (“ought to be given”).] [Note: [Col. 0397C] Victor 19 reads *penitus demissa* (“wholly remitted”) and omits *penitus* (“wholly”) in the text’s *penitus dimissa* (“wholly forgiven”).]

If you think that any argument can be raised against these reasons, you ought to say so. [Note: [Col. 0397C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *dicere deberes* (“you ought to say”) for *dicere debes* (“you must say”).]

BOS. I certainly see that none of your arguments can be weakened in any respect.

ANS. Nor do I think so, if they are well considered. Nevertheless, if even one of all the arguments I have put forward is established by unconquerable truth, it ought to suffice. For whether truth is shown invincibly by one argument or by several, it is equally protected from every doubt.

BOS. So it is. How, then, will the human being be saved, if he neither pays what he owes nor ought to be saved if he does not pay? [Note: [Col. 0397C] In the manuscripts chapter 25 begins here: “B. So it is,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts read *nec salvari valet* (“nor can be saved”), omitting *valet* (“can”) in some witnesses.] [Note: [Col. 0399C] Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, Victor 3, Joly, and Saint-Michel read *si non solvit quod debet* (“if he does not pay what he owes”); Victor 19 reads *si non solvit, debet* (“if he does not pay, [what] he owes”); the text has *si non solvitur, debet* (“if it is not paid, [what] is owed”).]

Or with what face shall we assert that God, rich in mercy beyond human understanding, cannot exercise this mercy? [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *fronte asserimus* (“with what face do we assert?”) for *fronte asseremus* (“with what face shall we assert?”).] [Note: [Col. 0399C] Gemmeticensis, Beccensis, Victor, and Joly read *super humanum* (“beyond human [understanding]”) for *supra humanum* (“above human [understanding]”).]

ANS. You must now demand this from those whose part you are taking—those who believe that Christ is not necessary for that salvation of the human being—that they say how a human being can be saved without Christ. If they cannot do so in any way, let them cease mocking us, come and join themselves to us who do not doubt that a human being can be saved through Christ, or despair that this can happen in any way. But if they recoil from that, let them believe with us in Christ, that they may be saved. [Note: [Col. 0399C] Joly reads *ab illis non* (“not from those”) for *nunc ab illis* (“now from those”).] [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *ad salutem* (“for salvation”) for *ad illam salutem* (“for that salvation”).] [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *ut jungant se* (“that they may join themselves”); Joly reads *et adjungant se* (“and let them join themselves”) for *et jungant se* (“and let them join themselves”).]

BOS. As I began, I shall ask you to show me by what reasoning a human being is saved through Christ. [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts read *a te quaero* (“I ask you”) for *a te quaeram* (“I shall ask you”).] [Note: [Col. 0399C] Victor reads *sicut incepisti* (“as you began”) for *sicut incoepi* (“as I began”).]

## CHAPTER XXV

That the human being is saved through Christ by necessity.

### Apparatus completion record (source-keyed)

The following five printed entries were consolidated or absent from the repaired candidate's inline notes; this register preserves their actual scope and source direction.

- [Col. 0389C], pearl-parable clause: *nisi ipso* — “unless by him himself,” ms. Joly; contrasting reading *non ipso* — “not by him himself.”
- [Col. 0389C], pearl-parable location clause: *ubi sunt* — “where they are,” ms. Joly; contrasting reading *ubi sint* — “where they may be.”
- [Col. 0391D], repayment qualification: *omnimodo* — “in every way/altogether,” mss. and Edit. Goth.; contrasting reading *omnino* — “wholly.”
- [Col. 0397C], mercy objection: *dicere quia misericors* — “to say, because [he is] merciful,” mss.; contrasting reading *dicere; misericors* — “to say; [he is] merciful.”
- [Col. 0397C], inability objection: *negare possum* — “I can deny,” ms. Vict. 19; *nec consequi negare possum* — “nor can I deny attaining,” mss. Vict. 3 and 13; *et hoc consequi non possum* — “and I cannot attain this,” ms. S. Mich. and Edit. Goth.; contrasting reading *nec hoc consequi negare possum* — “nor can I deny attaining this.”

ANS. Is it not sufficiently proved through Christ that a human being can be saved, since even unbelievers do not deny that a human being can in some way become blessed, and since it has been sufficiently shown that, if we suppose Christ not to exist, human salvation can in no way be found? For either through Christ, or in some other way, or in no way can a human being be saved [Note: [Col. 0399C] The Cistercian and Saint-Michael manuscripts read *aut alio aliquo modo aut nullo* (“either in some other way or in no way”), instead of *aut alio aliquo aut nullo modo* (“either in some other way or in no manner”)]. Therefore, if it is false that this can occur in no way or in some other way, it is necessary that it occur through Christ [Note: [Col. 0399C] The Saint-Michael manuscript omits *est* in *necesse est fieri* (“it is necessary that it occur”).] [Note: [Col. 0399C] Victorinus, Cistercian, and Saint-Michael manuscripts, and the Gothic edition, read *poterit salvus* (“will be able to be saved”), rather than *poterit homo salvus* (“a human being will be able to be saved”).]

BOS. If someone, seeing the reasoning that it cannot occur in any other way, but not understanding how it can occur through Christ, should wish to assert that it can occur neither through Christ nor in any way, what shall we answer him? [Note: [Col. 0399C] Victorinus reads *esse valet* (“can occur”) rather than *esse valeat* (“may be able to occur”).]

ANS. What should be answered to one who asserts that what must exist is impossible for the sole reason that he does not know how it exists? [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts read *quod respondendum* (“what is to be answered”) rather than *quid respondendum* (“what should be answered”); Joly, Victorinus, thirteen Saint-Michael manuscripts, and the Gothic edition have the former reading.]

BOS. That he is foolish.

ANS. Therefore, what he says must be disregarded.

BOS. That is true; but the manner in which what he considers impossible exists must itself be shown to him [Note: [Col. 0399C] The Joly manuscript reads *respondendum est* (“must be answered”) rather than *ostendendum est* (“must be shown”).]

ANS. Do you not understand from what we said above that it is necessary for some human beings to attain blessedness? For if it is unfitting for God to bring a human being with any stain to the state for which he made that person without any stain [Note: [Col. 0399C] The Joly manuscript reads *sine macula fecit* (“he made him without stain”)], lest he appear either to repent of a good beginning or to be unable to fulfill his purpose, then, much more on account of the same unfittingness, it is impossible that no human being be advanced to the state for which he was made. Therefore either satisfaction for sin of the kind we showed above to be necessary must be found outside the Christian faith—which no reasoning can demonstrate—or it must unquestionably be believed to exist within that faith [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition omit *in* in *in necessaria ratione* (“by necessary reasoning”).] For whatever is truthfully inferred by necessary reasoning to exist must not be reduced to doubt [Note: [Col. 0399C] Victorinus, Joly, Gembloux, Bec, and Saint-Michael read *duci dubietatem* (“be led into doubt”), rather than *deduci dubietatem* (“be reduced to doubt”); the Cistercian manuscript has *dubitationem* (“doubt”).], even if the manner in which it exists is not perceived [Note: [Col. 0399C] The Cistercian manuscript reads *ratio quomodo* (“the reasoning how”); another reading is *ratione quomodo* (“by the reasoning how”), in place of *ratio, quomodo sit* (“the reasoning, how it is”).]

BOS. What you say is true.

ANS. What more, then, are you asking?

BOS. I did not come to remove from me the doubt of faith [Note: [Col. 0399C] Gembloux, Bec, Victorinus, and Joly read *mihi dubitationem* (“to remove doubt from me”), rather than *mihi fidei dubitationem* (“to remove the doubt of my faith”)], but to show me the reasoning for my certainty. Therefore, just as you led me rationally to see that a sinful human being owes God, on account of sin, what he is unable to repay [Note: [Col. 0399C] Victorinus reads *quod reddere* (“what he is unable to repay”), rather than *quod et reddere* (“what he is also unable to repay”)], and that unless he repays it he cannot be saved, so I want you to lead me to the point where I may understand by rational necessity that all those things which the Catholic faith commands us to believe about Christ are necessary if we wish to be saved; what they accomplish for human salvation [Note: [Col. 0399C] Joly reads *quomodo valeant* (“how they avail”) rather than *quid valeant* (“what they avail”)]; and how God saves a human being by his mercy, although he does not forgive that person’s sin unless he has repaid what he owes on account of it. And, so that your arguments may be more certain, begin from a distance, so that you may establish them upon a firm foundation.

ANS. May God now help me [Col. 0400C], since you spare me not at all and do not consider the weakness of my knowledge, to which you assign so great a task. Nevertheless, since I have begun, I shall try, trusting not in myself but in God, and I shall do what I can with his help. But lest excessive length generate weariness in anyone wishing to read this, let us distinguish what is to be said from what has been said by beginning a new division [Note: [Col. 0399C] The manuscripts read *generetur, a dictis* (“lest it be generated, from what has been said”), rather than the printed *generem, a dictis*.]

## BOOK TWO

[Note: [Col. 0399C] The Gembloux manuscript reads: “Book Two of Anselm, Bishop of Canterbury: That a human being cannot be made blessed except through the God-man.”]

## CHAPTER ONE

### That the human being was made righteous by God so that, by enjoying God, he might be blessed

[Note: [Col. 0399C] The Gothic edition reads *ut Deo favendo beatus esset*: “so that, by favouring God, he might be blessed.”]

It must not be doubted that a rational nature was made by God righteous so that, by enjoying him, it might be blessed [Note: [Col. 0399C] Saint-Michael reads *rationalem creaturam* (“a rational creature”), rather than *rationalem naturam* (“a rational nature”); Joly reads *unde beatus* (“whence blessed”) rather than *ut beatus* (“so that blessed”).] For this is why it is rational: that it may distinguish between the just and the unjust [Note: [Col. 0399C] Victorinus and Joly read *injustum, et inter* (“the unjust, and between”)], between good and evil [Note: [Col. 0399C] Victorinus, Joly, and Saint-Michael read *malum, et inter* (“evil, and between”)], and between the greater good and the lesser good [Note: [Col. 0399C] Gembloux, Bec, Victorinus, and Joly read *magis bonum* (“the better good”) rather than *majus bonum* (“the greater good”)]. Otherwise it would have been made rational in vain. But God did not make it rational in vain. Therefore it is certain that it was made rational for this purpose [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *factam rationalem esse constat* (“it is clear that it was made rational for this purpose”), rather than *factam esse rationalem* (“it was made rational for this purpose”).]

By similar reasoning it is proved that it received the power of distinguishing in order to hate and avoid evil, and to love and choose the good, and to love and choose the greater good more [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *amaretque et diligeret bonum, atque majus bonum magis diligeret* (“would love and cherish the good, and would love the greater good more”); the Cistercian manuscript reads *majus magis bonum magis amaret* (“would love the greater, better good more”).] For otherwise God would have given it that power of distinguishing in vain [Note: [Col. 0401D] The Cistercian manuscript reads *potestatem istam* (“this power”), rather than *potestatem illam* (“that power”)], since it would distinguish in vain if it did not love and avoid things according to its discernment. But it is unfitting that God should have given so great a power in vain.

It is therefore certain that rational nature was made for this purpose: to love and choose the highest good above all things [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *omnia amaret et diligeret* (“would love and cherish all things”), rather than *omnia amaret et eligeret* (“would love and choose all things”)], not for the sake of anything else but for its own sake. For if it loves it for the sake of something else, it loves not the highest good but that other thing. Yet it cannot do this unless it acts justly [Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus, Joly, and Saint-Michael read *ad hoc nisi* (“for this purpose, unless”), rather than *at hoc nisi* (“yet this, unless”).] Thus, so that it would not be rational in vain, it was made both rational and righteous for this purpose [Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus reads *simul rationalis* (“similarly rational”); Saint-Michael reads *simul rationalis* (“rational”); another witness reads *simul ad hoc et rationalis* (“both for this purpose and rational”).]

If it was made righteous for choosing and loving the highest good, it was either made such that it would at some time attain what it loved and chose, or it was not [Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus reads *at talis ad hoc* (“but such for this purpose”), rather than *aut talis ad hoc* (“or such for this purpose”).] But if it was not made righteous for this purpose—that it might attain what it so loves and chooses [Note: [Col. 0401D] The Victorinus manuscript reads *si ad hoc justa non est facta* (“if it was not made righteous for this purpose”), rather than *si non ad hoc justa est facta* (“if it was not made righteous for this purpose”) ]—then it was made such in vain, that it should love and choose that good in this way; nor would there be any reason why it ought ever to attain it. As long, therefore, as by loving and choosing the highest good it does what it was made to do, it will be miserable, because it will be needy against its will, not possessing what it desires. That is exceedingly absurd.

Therefore rational nature was made righteous so that, by enjoying the highest good—that is, God—it might be blessed [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *bono, id est Deo, fruendo* (“by enjoying the good, that is, God”), rather than *bono fruendo* (“by enjoying the good”).] Thus the human being, who is a rational nature [Col. 0401C], was made righteous for this purpose: that, by enjoying God, he might be blessed.

## CHAPTER II

### That the human being would not die if he had not sinned

ANS. That he was made such that he would not die by necessity is easily proved from this [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *hoc facile* (“this is easily proved”), rather than *hinc facile* (“from this it is easily proved”).] For, as we have already said, it is contrary to the wisdom and justice of God to compel a human being whom he made righteous for eternal blessedness to suffer death without guilt [Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus reads *cogeret mortem* (“compel death”); other manuscripts read *cogeret hominem mortem justum fecerat* (“compel a human being to suffer death whom he had made righteous”), while the printed text has *justum fecit* (“whom he made righteous”).] It follows, therefore, that if he had never sinned, he would never die.

## CHAPTER III

### That the human being will rise again with the body in which he lives in this life

[Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus reads *resurgat* (“may rise again”) rather than *resurget* (“will rise again”).]

ANS. From this the future resurrection of the dead is clearly proved [Col. 0401D]. For if the human being is to be perfectly restored [Col. 0402A], he ought to be restored such as he would have been if he had not sinned.

BOS. It cannot be otherwise.

ANS. Therefore, just as, if the human being had not sinned, he would have been transformed into incorruptibility with the same body that he bore, so, when he is restored, he must be restored with his own body, in which he lives in this life.

BOS. What shall we answer if someone says that this must be understood of those in whom the human race will be restored, but that it is not necessary in the case of the reprobate? [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition assign *quid* (“what?”) to Anselm rather than to Boso.]

ANS. Nothing more just or fitting can be understood than that, just as, if the human being had persevered in righteousness, he would have been eternally blessed in his entirety—that is, in soul and body—so, if he perseveres in unrighteousness, he should likewise be eternally miserable in his entirety [Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus reads *miser erit* (“he will be miserable”) rather than *miser sit* (“he should be miserable”).]

BOS. You have satisfied me briefly concerning these matters.

[Col. 0402B]

## CHAPTER IV

### That God will complete in human nature what he began

ANS. From these considerations it is easy to recognize that God will either complete in human nature what he began [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *ad hoc de humana natura* (“for this purpose in human nature”), rather than *aut hoc de humana natura* (“either in human nature”).], or else he made so exalted a nature for so great a good in vain. But if it is acknowledged that God made nothing more precious than rational nature, in order that it might rejoice in him, it is wholly alien to him to allow any rational nature to perish utterly [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts read *ab eo ut illam* (“for him to allow it”), rather than *ab eo ut ullam* (“for him to allow any”).]

BOS. A rational heart cannot think otherwise.

ANS. It is necessary, then, that he complete in human nature what he began. But, as we said, this cannot happen except through complete satisfaction for sin, which no sinner can make.

BOS. I now understand that it is necessary for God to complete what he began, lest he appear to depart from his own beginning in a manner unbecoming to him.

## CHAPTER V

### That although this must happen, God will not do it under compulsion of necessity; what necessity removes or diminishes grace, and what necessity increases it

[Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus reads *et quod sit necessitas* (“and what necessity is”) for “and what necessity”; it also reads *et sit necessitas quae augeat* (“and what necessity increases it”).]

BOS. But if this is so, it seems as though God is compelled by the necessity of avoiding impropriety to procure human salvation. How, then, can it be denied that he does this more for his own sake than for ours? But if that is so [Note: [Col. 0401D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *aut si ita est* (“or if that is so”), rather than *at si ita est* (“but if that is so”)], what gratitude do we owe him for doing what he does [Note: [Col. 0401D] Victorinus and the Gothic edition read *quod fecit* (“what he did”), rather than *quod facit* (“what he does”)] for his own sake? And how shall we ascribe our salvation to his grace if he saves us by necessity?

ANS. There is a necessity that takes away or diminishes gratitude from one who does good [Note: [Col. 0401D] Joly, Victorinus, three and thirteen Saint-Michael manuscripts, the Cistercian manuscript, and the Gothic edition read *benefaciendi* (“of doing good”), rather than *benefacienti* (“to one doing good”)], and there is a necessity through which greater gratitude is owed for a benefit [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *major ex beneficio* (“greater from a benefit”).] [Col. 0402D]. When someone does good under a necessity to which he is subject unwillingly, little or no gratitude is owed him. But when he voluntarily subjects himself to the necessity of doing good, and does not endure it unwillingly, then he certainly deserves greater gratitude for the benefit. For this should not be called necessity but grace: he undertook or maintains it freely, with no one compelling him.

For if what you freely promise today that you will give tomorrow you give tomorrow with the same willingness, although tomorrow you must fulfill your promise if you can, or else lie [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *si non poteris aut non vis mentiri* (“if you cannot, or if you are unwilling, lie”), rather than *si potes aut mentiri* (“if you can, or lie”)], nevertheless the person to whom you give it owes you no less gratitude for the benefit bestowed than if you had not promised it. For you were not compelled to make yourself his debtor before the time of giving [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts omit *nec coactus* (“nor were you compelled”).]

The same is true when someone freely vows the purpose of a holy way of life [Col. 0403B] [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *sponte vovet* (“freely vows”).] Although after the vow he must keep it under necessity, lest he incur the condemnation of an apostate, and although he can be compelled to keep it if he is unwilling [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *possit, si nolit* (“can be compelled if he is unwilling”), rather than *posset si nolit* (“could be compelled if he is unwilling”)], nevertheless, if he keeps what he vowed without unwillingness, he is no less, but more, pleasing to God than if he had not vowed. For he has denied himself, for God’s sake, not merely the common life but also its freedom; and he should not be said to live holily by necessity, but by the same freedom with which he vowed.

Therefore, much more, if God does for a human being the good that he began, although it is unfitting for him to abandon the good beginning [Note: [Col. 0403D] The Joly manuscript reads *bono proposito* (“the good intention”), rather than *bono incepto* (“the good beginning”)], we must ascribe the whole of it to grace. For he began this for our sake, not for his own, since he lacks nothing. He was not unaware of what the human being would do when he made him; nevertheless, by creating him in his goodness, he freely bound himself, as it were, to complete the good he had begun [Col. 0403C].

In conclusion, God does nothing by necessity, because he is in no way compelled or prevented from doing anything. And when we say that God does something as though by the necessity of avoiding dishonor—which he certainly does not fear—we should rather understand that this is what he does [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *est quia hoc facit* (“it is because he does this”), rather than *est quod facit* (“it is what he does”)], by the necessity of preserving honor. This necessity is nothing other than the unchangeableness of his honor, which he has from himself and not from another; and for that reason it is improperly called necessity.

Nevertheless, let us say [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *dicimus tamen* (“nevertheless, we say”) rather than *dicamus tamen* (“nevertheless, let us say”).] that it is necessary for God’s goodness, on account of its unchangeableness, to complete in humanity what it began, although all the good that he does is entirely grace [Note: [Col. 0403D] Gembloux, Bec, Victorinus, Joly, and the Gothic edition read *gratia bonum quod facit* (“the good that he does is grace”), rather than *gratia quod fecit bonum* (“the good that he did is grace”).]

BOS. I grant it.

## CHAPTER VI

### That the satisfaction through which the human being is saved can be made only by the God-man

[Col. 0403D]

ANS. This, however, cannot happen unless there is someone who pays God for human sin something greater than everything that exists apart from God [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *quod Deus non est* (“that which is not God”), rather than *quod praeter Deum est* (“that which exists apart from God”).]

BOS. That is established.

ANS. It is also necessary that the one who can give God something of his own that surpasses everything subject to God be greater than everything that is not God [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *superat omne* (“surpasses everything”), rather than *superet omne* (“may surpass everything”).]

BOS. I cannot deny it.

ANS. But there is nothing above everything that is not God except God [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *nihil autem est quod super omne sit quod Deus non est* (“there is nothing that is above everything that is not God”).]

BOS. That is true.

ANS. Therefore no one except God can make this satisfaction.

BOS. It follows.

ANS. But neither ought anyone except a human being to make it; otherwise it is not a human being who makes satisfaction.

BOS. Nothing seems more just.

ANS. If, then, as is established, it is necessary that the heavenly city be completed from human beings, and if this cannot happen unless the satisfaction mentioned above is made—a satisfaction that can be made by none but God and ought to be made by none but a human being—it is necessary that the God-man make it.

BOS. Blessed be God! We have already found something great concerning what we seek. Continue, then, as you began. For I hope that God will help us.

ANS. We must now investigate how it is possible for God to become human [Note: [Col. 0403D] In the manuscripts this marks the beginning of Chapter 7; another reading has *quomodo possit esse Deus homo* (“how God can be God-man”).]

## CHAPTER VII

### That the same person must be perfect God and perfect human being

For the divine and human natures cannot be changed into one another [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition omit *enim* (“for”); they also read *possunt invicem* (“can mutually”) or *possunt ab invicem* (“can from one another”) for *possunt in invicem* (“can into one another”).], so that the divine becomes human or the human divine; nor can they be so mixed that some third thing arises from the two, which is neither wholly divine nor human. Finally, if it were possible for one to be converted into the other, the result would be either God alone and not human, or human alone and not God. Or, if they were mixed in such a way that a third thing arose from the two corrupted natures—just as from two individual animals of different species, male and female, a third is born that preserves neither the complete nature of the father nor that of the mother, but a third nature mixed from both [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *tertiam mixtam* (“a third mixed nature”)])—it would be neither human nor God.

Therefore the God-man whom we seek cannot arise from the divine and human natures either by conversion of one into the other or by the destructive mixing of both into a third, because these things cannot happen; or, if they could happen, they would contribute nothing to what we seek [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts read *valerent. Si* (“would contribute nothing. If”), rather than *valeret. Si* (“would contribute nothing. If”).]

But if these two complete natures are said to be joined in any manner so that one is human and another is God [Note: [Col. 0403D] The manuscripts read *ut cum alius sit homo, alius Deus* (“so that one is human and the other God”); Victorinus reads *ut tamen aliud sit homo, aliud sit Deus* (“so that one thing is human and another thing God”)], and the one who is God is not the same as the one who is human [Note: [Col. 0403D] Joly reads *et idem sit Deus* (“and the same is God”)], it is impossible for both to accomplish what must be accomplished. For God will not do it because he ought not; and the human being will not do it because he cannot. Therefore, for the God-man to do this, the very same person who is to make this satisfaction must be perfect God and perfect human being [Note: [Col. 0405D] The manuscripts variously read “because he ought not; and the human being will not do it, because he cannot. Therefore”; or “what he ought not do, and the human being will not do, because he cannot. Therefore”]. For he cannot make it unless he is true God [Note: [Col. 0405C] The manuscripts read *nisi sit verus Deus* (“unless he is true God”)], nor ought he make it unless he is true human being [Note: [Col. 0405C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *nisi sit verus homo* (“unless he is true human being”).]

Since, therefore, while the integrity of both natures is preserved, it is necessary that a God-man be found, it is no less necessary that these two complete natures come together in one person, just as body and rational soul come together in one human being. Otherwise it cannot happen that the very same person is perfect God and perfect human being.

BOS. Everything you say pleases me.

## CHAPTER VIII

### That God must assume a human being from Adam’s race and from a virgin woman

[Note: [Col. 0405C] Victorinus 13 and 19 read *Deum oportebat* (“God had to”); the manuscripts and Gothic edition read *sumere* (“take”) rather than *assumere* (“assume”).]

ANS. It remains now to ask from where and how God will assume human nature. For either he will assume it from Adam [Note: [Col. 0405C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *eam Adam* (“it Adam”), omitting *de* (“from”)], or he will make a new human being, just as he made Adam from no other human being. But if he makes a new human being not from Adam’s race, that person will not belong to the human race born from Adam. Therefore he ought not to make satisfaction for it, since he will not be from it [Note: [Col. 0405C] The Cistercian manuscript reads *de illo* (“from him”), rather than *de eo* (“from it”).]

For just as it is right that a human being make satisfaction for human guilt, so it is necessary that the one making satisfaction be either the same person as the sinner or belong to the same race. Otherwise neither Adam nor his race would make satisfaction for itself [Note: [Col. 0405C] The Victorinus manuscripts read *satisfaciet pro se* (“would make satisfaction for itself”), rather than *satisfaceret pro se* (“would make satisfaction for itself”).] Therefore, just as Adam’s and Eve’s sin was propagated to all human beings, so no one except Adam and Eve themselves, or one born from them, ought to make satisfaction for human sin [Col. 0405C]. Since they themselves cannot do so, it is necessary that the one who will do this be from them.

Furthermore, just as Adam and his entire race [Note: [Col. 0405C] The Cistercian manuscript reads *genus humanum* (“the human race”), rather than *genus ejus* (“his race”)] would have stood by themselves, without the support of any other creature, if he had not sinned, so, if that same race is raised after its fall, it ought to rise and be restored by itself [Note: [Col. 0405C] The manuscripts read *genus resurgit* (“the race rises”), rather than *genus resurget* (“the race will rise”).] For by whoever it is restored to its original state, by that one it will stand—by the one through whom it will recover its original state.

Moreover, when God first made human nature in Adam alone, and did not wish to make the woman except from him, so that human beings might multiply from both sexes, he clearly showed that he wished to make from Adam alone what he was going to make from human nature [Note: [Col. 0405C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition omit *unde ipse* (“therefore he himself”).]

Therefore, if Adam’s race is raised up by a human being who is not from that same race [Col. 0406A], it will not be raised to the dignity it would have had if Adam had not sinned [Note: [Col. 0405C] Gembloux, Bec, Victorinus, Saint-Michael, and the Gothic edition read *habiturus erat* (“it would have had”), rather than *habiturum erat* (“it would have had”)], and thus it will not be restored completely, and God’s purpose will appear to fail. Since both of these consequences are unfitting, it is necessary that the human being through whom Adam’s race is restored be assumed from Adam [Note: [Col. 0405C] The manuscripts read *restaurandum est genus Adae* (“Adam’s race must be restored”); the Gothic edition has *restauretur genus Adae* (“Adam’s race may be restored”).]

BOS. If we follow the reasoning, as we proposed, this must inevitably be so.

ANS. Let us now investigate whether God ought to assume human nature from a father and mother [Note: [Col. 0405C] The Victorinus manuscripts read *de patre et matre* (“from a father and mother”), rather than *de patre et de matre* (“from a father and from a mother”)], as other human beings are [Note: [Col. 0405C] Victorinus, Bec, Gembloux, and Joly read *sicut alii homines* (“as other human beings”), rather than *sicut alii sunt homines* (“as other human beings are”)]; or from a man without a woman; or from a woman without a man. For whichever of these three ways it may be, he will be from Adam and Eve, from whom every human being of either sex is descended. Nor is any one of these three ways easier for God than the others [Note: [Col. 0405C] Joly reads *quam alius* (“than another”), rather than *quam alii* (“than the others”)], so that he ought to assume him in that way rather than another.

BOS. You are proceeding well.

ANS. It requires no great labor to show that this human being will be begotten more purely and honorably from a man alone or from a woman alone than from the union of both, as are all other children of human beings [Note: [Col. 0405C] Joly reads *quam quod de* (“than that he should be from”), rather than *quam ut de* (“than from”).]

BOS. That is sufficient.

ANS. Therefore he must be assumed either from a man alone or from a woman alone.

BOS. It cannot be from anywhere else.

ANS. God can make a human being in four ways: from a man and a woman, as ordinary experience shows; from neither man nor woman, as he created Adam; from a man without a woman, as he made Eve; or from a woman without a man, which he has not yet done. Therefore, in order to show that this manner too lies within his power, and that it has been reserved for this very work, nothing is more fitting than that he assume from a woman without a man the human being whom we seek.

Whether this should more worthily be done from a virgin or from a non-virgin need not be debated; but it must be asserted without any doubt [Note: [Col. 0405C] Victorinus, Joly, Bec, Gembloux, and the Gothic edition read *dubitatione* (“without doubt”), rather than *disputatione* (“without debate”) ] that the God-man must be born from a virgin [Note: [Col. 0405C] Joly, Victorinus, three and thirteen Saint-Michael manuscripts, and the Gothic edition read *Deum et hominem* (“God and man”); Victorinus 19 reads *hominem Deum* (“the human God”).]

BOS. You speak according to the desire of my heart.

ANS. Is what we have said solid, or is it something empty, like a cloud—the kind of thing you said unbelievers object to us?

BOS. Nothing is more solid.

ANS. Paint, then, not upon fabricated emptiness [Note: [Col. 0405C] The Saint-Michael manuscript reads *siccam vanitatem* (“dry emptiness”)], but upon solid truth, and say that, just as human sin and the cause of our condemnation took its beginning from a woman [Note: [Col. 0405C] Victorinus, Joly, and the Cistercian read *principium sumpsit* (“took its origin”), rather than *initium sumpsit* (“took its beginning”)], so the remedy for sin and the cause of our salvation [Note: [Col. 0405C] Victorinus, Joly, the Cistercian, Saint-Michael, and the Gothic edition read *nostrae salutis* (“of our health/salvation”), rather than *nostrae salvationis* (“of our salvation”)] should be born from a woman. And so that women may not despair of belonging to the lot of the blessed because so great an evil came from a woman, it is fitting that, to restore their hope, so great a good should come from a woman [Col. 0407A].

Paint this also [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *pinge et hic* (“picture also here”) rather than *pinge et hoc* (“picture this also”).]: if a virgin was the cause through which all evil came to the human race, it is much more fitting that a virgin be the cause through which all good will come. Paint this too: if the woman whom God made from a man without a woman was made from a virgin, it is very fitting that the man who will be made from a woman should likewise be made from a virgin without a man [Note: [Col. 0407D] The Joly manuscript reads *foemina facta est, de virgine convenit* (“the woman was made; from a virgin it is fitting”), rather than the printed reading.]

But for the pictures that can be painted on this subject—that the God-man ought to be born from a virgin woman—let these now suffice [Note: [Col. 0407D] The Cistercian manuscript reads *sed et de picturis* (“and let the pictures also suffice”).]

BOS. These pictures are exceedingly beautiful and rational.

89 ## CHAPTER IX

### That the Word alone and the human being must come together in one person

ANS. We must now ask in which person God, who is three persons, assumes the human being. For several persons cannot assume one and the same human being into the unity of one person [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *in unitate personae* (“in the unity of the person”), rather than *in unitatem personae* (“into the unity of the person”).] Therefore this must necessarily occur in one person only.

But concerning this unity of the person of God and the human being [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition have *hominis: et in* (“of God and the human being; and in”), continuing with “and in which person of God”], and concerning in which person of God this ought more fittingly to occur, I have spoken in the fifth—or, according to another numbering, fourth—letter on the Incarnation of the Word, addressed to Lord Pope Urban, as far as I think sufficient for the present investigation [Note: [Col. 0407D] Victorinus 19 reads *quae locutus sum* (“which I have discussed”), rather than *locutus sum* (“I have spoken”).]

BOS. Touch briefly here, nevertheless, on why the person of the Son ought to become incarnate [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts read *debet incarnari* (“must become incarnate”), rather than *debeat incarnari* (“ought to become incarnate”).], rather than that of the Father or the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0407D] Gembloux, Bec, Victorinus, and Saint-Michael read *aut Spiritus sancti* (“or the Holy Spirit”), rather than *et Spiritus sancti* (“and the Holy Spirit”).]

ANS. If any other person were to become incarnate [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *incarnaretur* (“were incarnated”), rather than *incarnetur* (“were to become incarnate”)], there would be two sons in the Trinity: namely, the Son of God, who was already Son before the incarnation, and the one who through the incarnation would be the Son of the Virgin. And among the persons, who must always be equal, there would be inequality according to the dignity of their births. For the one born from God would have a more excellent birth than the one born from the Virgin.

Again, if the Father were incarnate, there would be two grandsons in the Trinity. For the Father would be the grandson of the Virgin’s parents through the human being he assumed; and the Word, although he has nothing from the human being, would nevertheless be the Virgin’s grandson because he would be the son of her son [Note: [Col. 0407D] Joly reads “the Virgin’s grandson through the human being assumed, because he would be her son’s son.”] All these consequences are unfitting, whereas they do not occur in the incarnation of the Word.

There is also another reason why it is more fitting for the Son to become incarnate than the other persons: it is more fitting for the Son to entreat the Father than for one other person to entreat another [Note: [Col. 0407D] Victorinus 19 reads *personam. Iterum* (“another person. Again”), rather than *personam alii* (“one person to another”).]

Furthermore, the human being for whom he was to pray and the devil whom he was to conquer had both presumed upon a false likeness to God through their own will [Col. 0407D]. Thus they sinned, as it were, more particularly against the person of the Son, who is believed to be the true likeness of the Father [Note: [Col. 0407D] Joly reads *dicitur* (“is called”), rather than *creditur* (“is believed”).] Therefore, to the one against whom the injury was more particularly committed, the punishment or pardon of the fault is more fittingly attributed.

Since, therefore, unavoidable reasoning has led us to the conclusion that the divine and human natures must come together in one person, and since this cannot occur in several persons of God, while it is evident that it is more fittingly accomplished in the person of the Word than in the others, it is necessary that the Word, God and human being, come together in one person.

BOS. This is the road by which you lead me, fortified on every side by reasoning, so that I do not see how I could deviate from it either to the right or to the left.

ANS. It is not I who lead you; rather, he of whom we speak, without whom we can do nothing, leads us wherever we hold to the way of truth.

[Col. 0408B]

## CHAPTER X

### That the same human being does not die by obligation; how he can or cannot sin; and why he or an angel should be praised for his righteousness when they cannot sin

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Victorinus and the Gothic edition read *homo idem* (“the same human being”) rather than *idem homo*; Victorinus 19 and the Gothic edition read *non possint* (“they cannot”) rather than *non possit* (“he cannot”).]

**ANS.** Whether that man is to die by obligation, as all other men die by obligation [Note: [Col. 0407D] As others do: other manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “as all others”], we ought not investigate [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Now investigate”: manuscript Joly reads “now investigate”]. But if Adam would not have died had he not sinned, much more ought this man not to suffer death, in whom sin cannot exist, because he will be God [Note: [Col. 0407D] “He will be God”: manuscript Victor 19 omits “will be”].

**BOS.** I want you to dwell on this for a little while. For whether it is said that he can sin or that he cannot sin, in either case a considerable question arises for me. For if he is said to be unable to sin, this seems difficult to believe [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition punctuate and read: “It is said. It seems difficult to believe. For as…”]. To speak briefly—not as though we were speaking about one who never existed [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *nunquam fuisset* (“had never existed”) for *nunquam fuerit* (“has never existed”)], as we have done up to now, but as though we were speaking about one whose existence and deeds we know—who could deny that he was able to do many things that we call sins? Indeed, to pass over everything else, how shall we say that he could not lie, which is always a sin? For when he says to the Jews concerning the Father, “If I say that I do not know him, I shall be like you, a liar” (John 8:55) [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Ei similis* (“like him”): the manuscripts and the Gothic edition omit *ei* (“him”)], and among these words says, “I do not know him,” who could say [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts Joly, Victor 3 and 19 read *eum dicet* (“would say it”) for *eum dicat* (“could say it”)] that he was unable to utter those same three words—or the same statement in other words—namely, “I do not know him” [Note: [Col. 0407D] Joly reads *nescio eum* (“I do not know him”) for *non scio eum*, with the same English sense]?... If he did this, as he himself says, he would be a liar, which is to be a sinner. Therefore, since he was able to do this, he was able to sin.

**ANS.** He was able to say this, and yet he was unable to sin.

**BOS.** Demonstrate this [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Demonstrate this”: manuscript Victor 19 omits “this”].

**ANS.** Every power follows the will. When I say that I can speak or walk, the qualification “if I wish” is understood. For if the will is not implied, there is no power but necessity. When I say that, unwillingly, I can be dragged or conquered [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Dragged and conquered”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “dragged or conquered”], this is not my power [Note: [Col. 0409D] “This is not, nor is it my”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “this is not my”], but necessity, and another’s power. Indeed, “I can be dragged or conquered” means nothing other than “another can drag or conquer me.”

We may therefore say of Christ that he could lie, if the qualification “if he wished” is understood. And since he could not lie unwillingly, neither could he wish to lie; thus it can equally be said that he was unable to lie [Note: [Col. 0409D] “And he could not”: manuscripts Victor 3 and 19, Saint-Michel, Gembloux, Bec, and the Gothic edition read “he could not”]. Thus he both could and could not lie.

**BOS.** Let us now return to investigating the matter as though he did not yet exist, as we began. I say, then, that if he cannot sin [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Cannot sin”: manuscripts Victor, Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Saint-Michel, and the Gothic edition read “could not sin”], because, as you say, he cannot wish to sin, he will preserve righteousness by necessity. Why, then, will he not be righteous through freedom of choice? What grace, therefore, will be owed him for his righteousness? For we are accustomed to say that God made the angel and man such that they could sin so that, although they could abandon righteousness, if they preserved it through freedom of choice they would merit grace and praise—things that would not be owed them if they were righteous by necessity.

**ANS.** Are not the angels, who now cannot sin, to be praised?

**BOS.** Certainly; because they earned what they now cannot do through the fact that they could do it and did not wish to do it.

**ANS.** What do you say of God, who cannot sin? He did not earn this through the power of sinning by which he did not sin. Is he nevertheless not to be praised for his righteousness?

**BOS.** I want you to answer on my behalf. For if I say that he is not to be praised, I know that I am lying. But if I say that he is to be praised, I fear weakening the argument I gave concerning the angels [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Weakening the argument”: manuscript Victor 19 reads “the argument being weakened”].

**ANS.** The angels are not to be praised for their righteousness because they were able to sin, but because, through the fact that they were able to sin, they in a certain manner possess from themselves the fact that they cannot sin. In this respect they are in some degree like God, who possesses from himself whatever he possesses.

For someone is said to give something when he does not take it away, although he can [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Who does not take away”: the manuscripts Victor, Joly, Gembloux, Bec, and the Gothic edition read “when he does not take it away”]; and someone is said to make something exist when, although he can make that same thing not exist, he does not. Thus, since an angel was able to take righteousness away from himself and did not take it away, and was able to make himself unrighteous and did not do so, it is rightly asserted that he gave righteousness to himself and made himself righteous.

In this way, therefore, he possesses righteousness from himself—for a creature cannot possess it from itself in any other way—and for this reason he is to be praised for his righteousness, and he is righteous not by necessity [Note: [Col. 0409D] “And not by necessity”: the manuscripts Victor, Joly, Gembloux, Bec, and the Gothic edition read “not by necessity”], but by freedom, because necessity is improperly spoken of where there is neither any compulsion nor any prohibition.

Since God, therefore, perfectly possesses from himself whatever he possesses, he is supremely to be praised for the good things that he possesses and preserves—not by any necessity, but, as I said above, by his own proper and eternal immutability.

Thus that man, who will himself be God, since every good that he possesses he will possess from himself, will possess it not by necessity but by freedom [Note: [Col. 0409D] “But by will and freedom”: the manuscripts omit “by will and”]. He will be righteous from himself and therefore will be worthy of praise. For although human nature will have from the divine nature what it will possess, nevertheless he himself will possess it from himself, since the two natures will be one person.

**BOS.** You have satisfied me on this point, and I clearly see that he will be unable to sin and yet will be worthy of praise for his righteousness. But now I think we must ask: since God could make such a man [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Could make such”: the manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Victor, and Joly read “can make such”], why did he not make the angels and the first two men such that they likewise could not sin and would be worthy of praise for their righteousness?

**ANS.** Do you understand what you are saying [Note: [Col. 0409D] “What you are saying?”: manuscript Joly reads “What do you mean?”]?

**BOS.** I seem to understand, and therefore I ask why he did not make them such.

**ANS.** Because it neither could nor ought to have happened that each of them should himself be God [Note: [Col. 0409D] Joly reads *fieri. Unusquisque* (“to happen. Each one”), rather than *fieri ut unusquisque* (“to happen that each one”)], as we say concerning this man [Note: [Col. 0409D] Joly reads *Deus. Nunc de* (“God. Now concerning”); Victor 19, *Deus sic de* (“God, thus concerning”), for *Deus, sicut de* (“God, as concerning”)]. And if you ask why he did not do this for as many as there are persons of God, or at least for one [Note: [Col. 0409D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition add *vel* (“or”) before *tot quot* (“as many as”)], I answer: because reason in no way required that this be done then; rather, it wholly prohibited it, since God does nothing without reason.

**BOS.** I am ashamed that I asked this. Say what you were going to say [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Say what”: the manuscripts read “Say that”].

**ANS.** Let us say, then, that he ought not to die, because he will not be a sinner.

**BOS.** I must concede this.

## CHAPTER XI

### That he dies by his own power, and that mortality does not belong to the pure nature of man

[Note: [Col. 0409D] The Victor manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “that mortality” rather than “and that mortality.”]

[Col. 0410C]

**ANS.** It remains to investigate whether he can die according to his human nature, for according to his divine nature he will always be incorruptible.

**BOS.** Why should we doubt this [Note: [Col. 0409D] Victor 19 reads *de hoc hic* (“about this here”) for *de hoc cur* (“why about this”)], since he himself will be the old man, and every man is naturally mortal?

**ANS.** I do not think that mortality belongs to the pure nature of man, but to his corrupt nature. For if man had never sinned and his immortality had been immutably established [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Had been established”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “were firm”], he would nevertheless still be true man. And when mortal men rise in incorruption, they will no less be true men. For if mortality belonged to the truth of human nature, a man who was immortal could in no way exist. Therefore corruptibility or incorruptibility does not belong to the integrity of human nature, since neither makes or destroys man; rather, the one contributes to his misery and the other to his blessedness.

But since there is no man who does not die, philosophers place “mortal” in the definition of man, because they did not believe that the whole man could ever have been or could be immortal. Therefore it is not sufficient to demonstrate that this man ought to be mortal merely from the fact that he will be true man.

**BOS.** Then seek another reason, because I do not know it if you do not know the one by which he can be proved able to die [Note: [Col. 0411D] “If you do not know”: the manuscripts Victor, Joly, Gembloux, Bec, and the Gothic edition read “if you know”].

**ANS.** There is no doubt that, just as he will be God [Note: [Col. 0411D] “Just as he will be God”: manuscript Joly reads “just as God will be God”], so he will be omnipotent.

**BOS.** It is true [Note: [Col. 0411D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition attribute this reply as “B. Where does that come from?” rather than “It is true”].

**ANS.** If, then, he wishes, he will be able to lay down his soul and take it up again.

**BOS.** If he cannot do this, he does not seem to be omnipotent.

**ANS.** He will therefore be able never to die, if he wishes; and he will be able to die and rise again. Whether he lays down his soul with no one else acting, or another causes him to lay it down with his permission, there is no difference as far as power is concerned.

**BOS.** There is no doubt of this.

**ANS.** If, then, he wishes to permit it, he will be able to be killed; and if he does not wish it [Note: [Col. 0411D] “But if he does not wish it”: manuscripts of Cistercian origin, Saint-Michel, Joly, and the Gothic edition read “and if he does not wish it”], he will not be able to be killed.

**BOS.** Reason leads us to this conclusion without deviation.

**ANS.** Reason has also taught us that he ought to possess something greater than anything that is beneath God, something that he may give spontaneously and not by obligation [Note: [Col. 0411D] “By obligation, to God”: manuscript Saint-Michel reads “by obligation”].

**BOS.** So it is.

**ANS.** But this cannot be found either beneath him or outside him [Note: [Col. 0411D] “Nor beneath him, nor”: manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Cistercian, and the Gothic edition read “beneath him, nor”] [Note: [Col. 0411D] “Can be found”: the Cistercian manuscript reads “cannot be found”].

**BOS.** It is true.

**ANS.** It must therefore be found in him.

**BOS.** That follows.

**ANS.** Either, then, he will give himself, or he will give something of himself.

**BOS.** I cannot understand it otherwise.

**ANS.** We must now ask what sort of giving this ought to be. For he cannot give himself to God, or something of himself as though God did not possess it and it needed to become his, since every creature belongs to God.

**BOS.** So it is.

**ANS.** This giving must therefore be understood as follows: he will in some way offer himself for the honor of God, or something of himself in a way in which he will not be under obligation.

**BOS.** That follows from what has been said.

**ANS.** Let us see whether perhaps this might be giving or laying down his life, or surrendering himself to death for the honor of God. For God will not demand this from him by obligation, since, because there will be no sin in him, he will not be obliged to die [Note: [Col. 0411D] “He will not be obliged to die”: manuscript Joly reads “he is not obliged to die”], as we have said.

**BOS.** I cannot understand it otherwise.

**ANS.** Let us consider further whether this is fitting according to reason.

**BOS.** You speak, and I shall gladly listen.

**ANS.** If man sinned through pleasure, is it not fitting that he make satisfaction through hardship? And if he was so easily overcome by the devil that, by sinning, he dishonored God—so easily that he could not have been overcome more easily—is it not just that, in making satisfaction to God for sin [Note: [Col. 0411D] “To God for sin”: the manuscripts Victor and Joly omit “to God”], man should conquer the devil with such difficulty for the honor of God that he could not do so with greater difficulty? Is it not fitting that he who, by sinning, so took himself away from God that he could not take himself away further should, in making satisfaction, give himself to God in such a way that he could not give himself more fully?

**BOS.** Nothing could be more reasonable [Note: [Col. 0411D] “More reasonable”: manuscripts Joly, Victor, and the Gothic edition read “reasonable”].

**ANS.** Nothing more difficult or arduous can man spontaneously and not by obligation suffer for the honor of God than death; and man cannot give himself more fully to God than when he surrenders himself to death [Note: [Col. 0411D] “When he surrendered himself to death”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “when he surrenders himself to death”] for his honor.

**BOS.** All this is true.

**ANS.** He who wishes to make satisfaction for human sin must therefore be such that he can die if he wishes.

**BOS.** I plainly see that the man we seek must be such that he does not die by necessity, since he will be omnipotent [Note: [Col. 0411D] “Since he will be omnipotent”: the manuscripts read “because he will be omnipotent”]; nor by obligation, since he will never be a sinner; and that he can die by free will, since this will be necessary.

**ANS.** There are also many other reasons why it is highly fitting that he should possess the likeness and manner of life of men without sin. These reasons are more easily and clearly evident in his life and works themselves than they could be demonstrated by reason alone before the event.

For who could explain how necessary and how wisely it was done [Note: [Col. 0411D] Joly, Victor, and Saint-Michel read *factum sit* (“it was done”) for *factum est* (“it has been done”)] that he who was going to redeem men and, by teaching, lead them back from the way of death and destruction to the way of life and eternal blessedness should live among men? And, while living among them [Note: [Col. 0411D] Joly omits *in ipsa* (“in that very”)], when he taught them by word how they ought to live, should present himself as an example? But how could he give himself as an example to the weak and mortal, so that they would not depart from righteousness because of injuries, insults, sufferings, or death, if they did not know that he himself experienced all these things?

## CHAPTER XII

### That although he shares in our afflictions, he is nevertheless not miserable

**BOS.** All these things plainly show that he ought to be mortal and to share in our afflictions. But all these things belong to our misery. Will he, then, be miserable?

**ANS.** Not at all. For just as the advantage that someone possesses against his will does not belong to blessedness, so it is not misery wisely to undergo some affliction willingly and without necessity.

**BOS.** This must be conceded.

[Col. 0413A]

## CHAPTER XIII

### That, together with our other weaknesses, he does not possess ignorance

**BOS.** But in this likeness that he ought to have with men, tell me whether he will also possess ignorance, like our other weaknesses [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Ignorance also”: manuscript Joly reads “ignorance,” omitting “also”].

**ANS.** Why do you doubt whether God is all-knowing?

**BOS.** Because although he will be immortal by his divine nature, he will nevertheless be mortal by his human nature. Why, then, could he not similarly be truly ignorant in that nature, just as he will be truly mortal? [Note: [Col. 0413D] The manuscripts read *cur ergo* (“why then”) for *nam cur* (“for why”).]

**ANS.** The assumption of that man into the unity of the person of God [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Of the person”: the manuscripts read “of the person of God,” and manuscript Saint-Michel reads “of the divine person”] will be accomplished only wisely by supreme Wisdom. Therefore God will not assume in the man anything that is in no way useful but highly harmful to the work that this same man is going to perform.

Ignorance would be useful to him for nothing, but harmful in many ways. For how will he perform the many great works that he is going to perform without supreme wisdom [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Supreme wisdom”: the manuscripts read “immense wisdom”]? Or how will men believe him if they know him to be ignorant [Note: [Col. 0413D] “If they know him to be ignorant”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “if they know him ignorant,” while manuscript Victor 13 reads “if they know that he is ignorant”]? And if they do not know this [Note: [Col. 0413D] “But will not know”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “will not know”], what use will that ignorance be to him?

Moreover, if nothing is loved except what is known, then, just as there will be no good that he does not love, so there will be no good that he does not know [Note: [Col. 0413D] “There will be no good”: manuscript Joly reads “nothing good”]. But no one perfectly knows the good unless he knows how to distinguish it from evil. No one knows how to make this distinction [Note: [Col. 0413D] The manuscripts read *facere, nisi qui* (“make it, unless one who”) for *facere, qui* (“make it, one who”)] who is ignorant of evil [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Who is ignorant of evil”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “unless he is not ignorant of evil”].

Therefore, just as the one of whom we speak will know every good perfectly, so he will be ignorant of no evil. He will thus possess all knowledge, although he may not publicly display it in his dealings with men.

**BOS.** In mature age this seems to be as you say. But in infancy, just as there will not be an appropriate time for wisdom to appear in him, so there will be no need for it, and therefore it will not be fitting for him to possess it.

**ANS.** Did I not say that this incarnation will be accomplished wisely? God will wisely assume mortality, which he will wisely use because it is highly useful [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Wisely, because highly usefully”: manuscript Victor reads “wisely, and it is highly useful”]. But he cannot wisely assume ignorance, because it is never useful and always harmful—unless perhaps [Note: [Col. 0413D] The manuscripts read *forte per eam* (“perhaps through it”) for *forte cum per eam* (“perhaps when through it”)], through it, an evil will, which will never exist in him, is restrained from its effect [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Restrained from its effect”: manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Saint-Michel, and the Gothic edition read “restrained from its inclination”].

For even if ignorance sometimes does no harm in some other respect, it harms in this respect alone [Note: [Col. 0413D] Saint-Michel reads *hoc solum tamen* (“this alone, however”) for *hoc solo tamen* (“by this alone, however”)]: it removes the good of knowledge. To give a brief answer to what you ask: from the moment that he is man, he will always be full of God, as he will be full of himself [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Will always be in him”: the manuscripts read “will always be in him”], and therefore he will never be without his power, strength, and wisdom.

**BOS.** Although I had no doubt that this had always been true in Christ [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Had always been”: the manuscripts read “had always been” in a different word order], I nevertheless asked so that I might also hear the reasoning for it. We are often certain that something is true, yet we do not know how to prove it by reason.

## CHAPTER XIV

### How his death surpasses the number and magnitude of all sins

Now I ask you to teach me how his death surpasses the number and magnitude [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Number and magnitude”: manuscript Saint-Michel reads “number and multitude”] of all sins, when you show that one sin—which we think exceedingly small—is so immeasurable that, even if an infinite number of worlds were displayed [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Were displayed”: manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Cistercian, and the Gothic edition read “were shown”], filled with creatures as this world is, and unable to be preserved from being reduced to nothing unless someone were to cast a single glance against the will of God, nevertheless that glance ought not to be cast.

**ANS.** If that man were present, and you knew who he was, and you were told, “Unless you kill that man [Note: [Col. 0413D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *nisi occidas* (“unless you kill”) for *nisi occideris*], this entire world and everything that is not God will perish,” would you do it in order to preserve every other creature?

**BOS.** I would not, even if an infinite number of worlds were placed before me [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Were placed before me”: manuscripts Joly, Victor 13, Cistercian, and the Gothic edition read “were to be displayed”].

**ANS.** What if you were told again, “Either kill him [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Or you kill him”: manuscript Joly reads “you will kill him,” or “you will kill him”], or all the sins of the world will come upon you”?

**BOS.** I would answer that I would rather take upon myself all the other sins—not only those of this world, past and future, but also whatever sins can be conceived beyond these—than that one sin alone [Note: [Col. 0413D] “All the other”: manuscript Joly and the Gothic edition read “all the others.”] I think I ought to give the same answer not only concerning his killing but also concerning any slight injury that might touch him.

**ANS.** You are right to think so. But tell me why your heart judges in such a way that it dreads one sin committed by injuring this man more than all other sins that can be conceived, since every sin that is committed is against him?

**BOS.** Because the sin committed against his person incomparably surpasses all those that can be conceived outside his person.

**ANS.** What will you say to this? [Note: [Col. 0413D] The manuscripts read *quid dicis* (“what do you say?”) for *quid dices* (“what will you say?”)] Often someone willingly suffers certain troubles in his own person so as not to suffer greater troubles in his possessions [Note: [Col. 0413D] Joly reads *nec majora* (“nor greater ones”) for *ne majores* (“lest greater ones”)].

**BOS.** God does not need this suffering [Note: [Col. 0413D] “This suffering”: manuscript Joly reads “this knowledge”], since everything is subject to his power, as you answered earlier to one of my questions [Note: [Col. 0413D] “To one of my questions”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “to one of my questions above”].

**ANS.** You answer well. We see, then, that no immensity or multitude of sins outside the person of God can be compared with the violation of this man’s bodily life.

**BOS.** It is perfectly clear [Note: [Col. 0413D] “It is most evident”: the manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “it is most wise”].

**ANS.** How great a good does that life seem to you to be, when its killing is so great an evil?

**BOS.** If his existence is as great a good [Note: [Col. 0415C] “If all good”: the Gothic edition reads “if all good is as…,” and the printed wording is uncertain] as its destruction is an evil, then its goodness is incomparably greater than the evil of those sins that his killing surpasses beyond all estimation [Note: [Col. 0415C] The Gothic edition reads the fragmentary variant *Si omne bonum tam* (“If every good [is] so…”); the transmitted continuation is materially uncertain. “Without estimation”: the manuscripts read *existimatione* for *aestimatione*, with no material difference in sense].

**ANS.** You speak truly. Consider also that sins are hateful to the extent that they are evil, and that this life is lovable to the extent that it is good [Note: [Col. 0415C] “This life is so lovable”: manuscript Victor reads “this life is lovable”]. Hence it follows that this life is more lovable than sins are hateful [Note: [Col. 0415C] “From this it follows”: manuscripts Victor, Joly, Saint-Michel, and Cistercian read “from this it follows”; “this life”: manuscripts Victor and Joly read “this life”].

**BOS.** I cannot fail to understand this [Note: [Col. 0415C] Manuscripts Joly and Victor 19 read “I cannot fail to understand this”; manuscript Victor 13 reads “I cannot deny this”].

**ANS.** Do you think that so great and lovable a good can suffice to pay what is owed for the sins of the whole world?

**BOS.** Indeed, it has infinitely greater power [Note: [Col. 0415C] “It can do more than infinitely”: the manuscripts read “it can do more than infinity”].

**ANS.** You see, then, how this life conquers all sins if it is given for them.

**BOS.** Clearly.

**ANS.** If, then, giving life means accepting death, just as the giving of this life surpasses all human sins, so also does the acceptance of death.

## CHAPTER XV

### How the same death also blots out the sins of those who killed him

**BOS.** It is established that this is so concerning all sins that do not touch the person of God. But now I see that another question must be asked. For if killing him is as great an evil as his life is a good, how can his death overcome and blot out the sins of those who killed him? Or if it blots out the sin of some of them [Note: [Col. 0415C] Victor 19 reads *peccati delet* (“blots out of the sin”) for *peccatum delet* (“blots out the sin”)], how can it not also blot out some sin of other men? [Note: [Col. 0415C] Joly reads *aliquot* (“some [persons]”) for *aliquod* (“some [sin]”).] For we believe that many of them were saved, while countless others are not saved [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Others are saved”: the Cistercian manuscript reads “others are saved,” omitting the negation].

**ANS.** The Apostle resolves this question when he says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). So great is the difference [Note: [Col. 0415C] Victor reads *differt scienter* (“differs knowingly”) for *differunt scienter* (“differ knowingly”)] between a sin committed knowingly and one committed through ignorance that an evil which, if it were known, they could never commit because of its enormity is venial because it was done unknowingly.

No human being could ever wish, even knowingly, to kill God [Note: [Col. 0415C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *velle possit* (“can wish”) for *velle posset* (“could wish”)]. Therefore those who killed him in ignorance did not rush into that infinite sin to which no other sins can be compared. For we did not consider [Note: [Col. 0415C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *nam si consideravimus* (“for if we considered”) for *nam non consideravimus* (“for we did not consider”)] the greatness of his life in order to see how good that life was, since the deed was committed in ignorance; rather, we acted as though what no one ever did or could do had been knowingly done [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Would be done knowingly”: manuscripts Joly and Victor read “would be knowingly done”].

**BOS.** You have shown reasonably that Christ’s killers could attain forgiveness for their sin [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Could attain forgiveness”: manuscript Saint-Michel reads “you have shown that they could attain forgiveness,” omitting “could” before “attain”].

**ANS.** What more do you ask now? Behold, you now see [Note: [Col. 0415C] The manuscripts read *ecce jam vides* (“behold, now you see”), and some read *ecce vides* (“behold, you see”), for the printed *ecce jam dives*] how rational necessity demonstrates [Note: [Col. 0415C] Joly, Victor, Saint-Michel, Cistercian, and the Gothic edition read *ostendit* (“demonstrates”) for *ostendat* (“may demonstrate”)] that the heavenly city must be completed from among human beings, and that this cannot happen except through the remission of sins.
