No human being can receive this remission except through a man who is himself God and who, by his death, reconciles sinful men to God [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Reconciles to God”: manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Victor, Joly, and the Gothic edition read “unites to God”].

We have therefore clearly found that Christ, whom we confess to be God and man, died for us [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Whom we confess, and who died”: manuscripts Gembloux and Bec read “whom we confess, and who died”]. Once this is known without any doubt [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Without any doubt”: manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, Cistercian, Victor 3, Saint-Michel, and the Gothic edition read “without any doubt”; manuscript Victor 19 reads “without any doubting”; manuscript Victor 13 reads “without any ambiguity”], we must not doubt that everything he says is certain, since God cannot lie, nor that the things he did were done wisely, even though their reason is not understood by us.

**BOS.** What you say is true. I do not doubt in the least either that what he said is true or that what he did was done reasonably. But I ask you to explain to me how what seems to unbelievers either ought not or cannot happen must or can happen within the Christian faith—not so that you may strengthen me in the faith, but so that, strengthened already, you may make me rejoice through understanding the truth itself.

## 92. CHAPTER XVI

### How God took a sinless man from the sinful mass, and concerning the salvation of Adam and Eve
Provenance: original Luna translation and Luna repair; saved Terra review did not certify coverage; native Terra canonical-source adjudication completed the repair. No external source or deterministic translator was used.

Therefore, just as you have explained the reasoning of what was said above, so I ask you to set forth the reasoning of what I am [Col. 0416C] still going to ask. First, namely, how God took from a sinful mass—that is, from the human race, which was wholly infected by sin—a man without sin, as though unleavened bread from leavened dough [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Sinful and human”: all manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “sinful, that is, from human”; Victor 3 reads “from leavened dough”; another witness reads “from leaven.”]. For although the conception of this same man was pure and without the sin of carnal pleasure, the Virgin herself, from whom he was taken, was conceived in iniquities, and her mother conceived her in sins [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Her mother”: the Victor manuscripts read “her mother”], and she was born with original sin, since she too sinned in Adam, in whom all sinned.

**ANSELM:** Once it is established that that man is God [Note: [Col. 0415C] “That he is God”: Joly, Victor, Cistercian, and Saint Michael read “that he is God and”], and the reconciler of sinners [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Reconciler of sinners”: Joly, Victor, Cistercian, and Saint Michael read “that he is the reconciler of sinners”], there is no doubt that he is entirely without sin [Col. 0417A] [Note: [Col. 0417D] “He is without sin”: Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Victor 3 and 13, and the Gothic Edition read “he is entirely without sin”; Victor 19 reads “he is without any sin”]. But this cannot be so unless he was taken from the sinful mass without sin. If we cannot understand the manner in which the wisdom of God did this [Note: [Col. 0417D] “In what manner”: Victor 3 reads “in what manner, however”; another manuscript reads “because, indeed, by intention”], we ought not to be astonished; rather, with reverence we should accept that something in the secrets of so great a matter remains unknown to us.

For God restored human nature more wondrously [Note: [Col. 0417D] “More wondrously”: Victor and the Gothic Edition read “wondrously”] than he created it. Both are equally easy for God; but, before he existed, man did not sin, so that he ought not to have been made. After he had been made, however, by sinning he deserved to lose what he was made and destined to be—although he did not altogether lose what he had been made to be, so that there would remain one who could be punished [Note: [Col. 0417D] “Who could be punished”: the manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “who could be punished”] or upon whom God could have mercy. Neither of these could happen if he had been reduced to nothing.

God therefore restored him more wondrously than he created him [Col. 0417B], insofar as he did the one for a sinner, contrary to merit, whereas he did the other neither for a sinner nor contrary to merit. How great, moreover, is it that God and man should come together as one, while the integrity of both natures is preserved, so that the same one is both man and God? Who, then, would presume even to think that human understanding could penetrate how wisely and wondrously so inscrutable a work was made [Note: [Col. 0417D] “That human understanding”: Joly reads “that human understanding”; Victor 13 reads “or whether any human [understanding]”; another manuscript reads “or any human being”?].

**BOSO:** I agree that no human being can fully disclose so great a secret in this life. Nor do I ask you to do what no human being can do, but only as much as you can. You will persuade me more effectively that deeper reasons lie hidden in this matter if you show that you perceive some reason than if, by saying nothing, you prove that you understand no reason in it.

**ANSELM:** I see that I cannot escape your persistence [Col. 0417C]. But if I can in some measure show what you ask, let us give thanks to God. If I cannot, let what has been proved above suffice. Since it is established that God ought to become man, there is no doubt that he possesses the wisdom and power for this to occur without sin.

**BOSO:** I readily accept that.

**ANSELM:** It was necessary, certainly [Note: [Col. 0417D] “It was necessary, certainly”: Joly reads “it was necessary, therefore”], that the redemption Christ accomplished should benefit not only those who existed at that time but also others. Let there be, then, some king whose entire people of a certain city sinned against him, except for one man, who nevertheless belonged to their race, in such a way that none of them could do anything by which he might escape condemnation to death. But let the one who alone is innocent enjoy such favor with the king that he can reconcile them, and such love for the guilty that he wishes to reconcile all who believe his counsel through some service highly pleasing to the king, which he is going to perform [Col. 0417D] on a day appointed according to the king’s will.

And since not all those who are to be reconciled can assemble on that day, let the king, because of the greatness of that service, [Col. 0418A] grant that whoever, either before or after that day, confesses that he wishes through the work performed on that day to obtain pardon and to enter into the covenant established there, should be absolved from all past guilt. If it should happen that, after receiving this pardon, he sins again, then, provided he wishes thereafter to make worthy satisfaction and amend his conduct, let him receive pardon again through the efficacy of the same covenant. Yet no one may enter his palace until the deed has been accomplished by which their guilt is released [Note: [Col. 0417D] “Until the deed has been accomplished by which guilt is released”: the manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “until the deed by which guilt is released”; Victor and the Gothic Edition have “is released” in the present tense].

In accordance with this likeness, since not all the human beings who were to be saved could be present when Christ accomplished that redemption, such power was present in his death that its effect extends even to those absent either in place or in time [Col. 0418B]. That it ought to benefit not only those present [Note: [Col. 0417D] “Not only those present”: Joly, Victor 3 and 19 read “not only those who are present”] can easily be recognized from this: not as many people could be present at his death [Note: [Col. 0417D] “Could be present at his death”: the manuscripts of Victor and Joly read “could be present in his death”] as are necessary for the building of the heavenly city—even if all those who were alive anywhere at the time of that death were admitted to that redemption.

For there are more demons than there would have been human beings living on that day from whom their number is to be restored. Nor should we believe that, from the time man was made, there was ever a period when this world, together with the creatures made for human use [Note: [Col. 0417D] “The creatures made for their use”: the manuscripts of Joly and Victor, and the Gothic Edition, read “the creatures made for their use”; the Gothic Edition omits “their”], was so empty that no one of the human race belonging to that purpose for which man was made existed in it. For it seems incongruous that God should have permitted the human race, and the things he made for the use of those from whom the heavenly city is to be completed, to exist even for a single moment as though in vain. They would seem in some measure to exist in vain so long as they did not appear to continue for the purpose for which they had been made above all [Note: [Col. 0417D] “For which they had been made”: the manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “for which they had been made,” agreeing grammatically with “things,” rather than “they had been made”].

**BOSO:** You show, by a fitting argument against which nothing seems to conflict, that from the time man was made there was never any period without someone belonging to that reconciliation—for otherwise every human being would have been made in vain. We can conclude that this was not only fitting but also necessary [Note: [Col. 0417D] “Fitting but also necessary”: the manuscripts read “fitting, but also necessary,” with the same sense]. For if it is more fitting and reasonable than that there should ever have been no one through whom God’s purpose in making man would be fulfilled, and if nothing opposes this reasoning, then it is necessary that there always was someone belonging to the aforesaid reconciliation [Col. 0418D]. Hence there is no doubt that Adam and Eve belonged to that redemption, although divine authority does not openly declare this.

**ANSELM:** It also seems incredible that, when God made them and unchangeably purposed to make from them all the human beings whom he was going to take into the heavenly city [Col. 0419A], he excluded those two from this purpose.

**BOSO:** Rather, it should be believed that he made them especially for this purpose: that they might be among those for whose sake they were made.

**ANSELM:** You consider the matter well. Nevertheless, before Christ’s death no soul could enter the heavenly paradise, just as I said above concerning the king’s palace.

**BOSO:** That is what we hold.

**ANSELM:** But that Virgin from whom the man of whom we are speaking was taken belonged to those who were cleansed from sins through him before his birth [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Before his birth”: the manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “before his necessity”; the contextual reading is evidently “before his birth”]. It was in that very purity of hers that he was taken from her.

**BOSO:** I would greatly approve what you say [Note: [Col. 0419D] “I would approve”: Joly reads “I approve”], except that, since he ought to have his purity from himself, he seems to have it from his mother and therefore to be pure not through himself but through her [Note: [Col. 0419D] “To be pure through himself”: Joly and the Gothic Edition read “not to be pure through himself”].

**ANSELM:** It is not so. Rather, since the mother’s purity, through which he is pure, came only from him, he too was pure through himself and from himself.

## CHAPTER XVII [alternatively XVI]

### How he who could exist only because he was going to die did not die by necessity

**BOSO:** That is satisfactory concerning this matter. But I still seem to have another question to ask [Note: [Col. 0419D] In the manuscript of Victor 19, the seventeenth chapter begins here]. For above we said that he was not going to die by necessity, and now we see that his mother was made pure through his future death; if that future death had not been, he could not have been taken from her. How, then, did he not die by necessity, when he could exist only because he was going to die? For if he was not going to die, the Virgin from whom he was taken would not have been made pure [Col. 0419C], since this could in no way have happened except by believing in his true death; nor could he have been taken from her in any other way. Therefore, if he did not die by necessity, then, after he had been taken from the Virgin, he could have not been taken from the Virgin after he had been taken from her—which is impossible.

**ANSELM:** If you had carefully considered what was said above, you would have understood, I think, that the question had already been solved in those statements [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Solved in those statements”: Victor 19 reads “solved together with those statements”].

**BOSO:** I do not see how.

**ANSELM:** When we asked whether he could have lied, did we not show that there are two powers involved in lying: one, namely, the power of willing to lie, and the other, the power of lying? And since, although he possessed the power of lying, he had from himself the fact that he could not will to lie, was he not for this reason worthy of praise for his righteousness, by which he preserved the truth?

**BOSO:** That is so.

**ANSELM:** Similarly, in preserving life there is a power of willing to preserve it and a power of preserving it. When, then, it is asked whether the same God-man could preserve his life so that he would never die, there is no doubt that he always possessed the power of preserving it [Note: [Col. 0419D] “He always possessed”: Victor 19 reads “he always possessed” in the past tense], although he could not will to preserve it so that he would never die. And since he had this from himself—namely, that he could not will it—he laid down his soul not by necessity but by free power.

**BOSO:** Those powers in him—namely, of lying and of preserving life—were not altogether similar. In the former case it follows that, if he wished, he could lie. Here, however, it seems that, if he did not wish to die [Note: [Col. 0419D] Victor 19 reads “if he did not wish not to die”], he could no more do this than he could not be what he was. For he was man for the purpose of dying; and because of the faith in this future death, as you said above, he could be taken from the Virgin.

**ANSELM:** Just as you suppose that he could not not die, or that he died by necessity [Note: [Col. 0419D] Victor 19 reads “was going to die” rather than “died”], because he could not not be what he was, so you may assert that he could not will not to die, or that he willed to die by necessity, since what he was could not not be. For he was made man no more for the purpose of dying than for the purpose of willing to die. Therefore, just as you ought not to say that he could not will not to die [Note: [Col. 0419D] Victor 19 reads “he could not will not to die,” rather than “he could not not will to die”], or that he willed to die by necessity, so it should not be said that he could not not die, or that he died by necessity.

**BOSO:** Rather, since both dying and willing to die are subject to the same reasoning [Note: [Col. 0419D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “namely, both willing to die and dying,” reversing the order], both seem to have been necessary in him [Note: [Col. 0419D] Victor 19, the Cistercian manuscript, and the Gothic Edition read “in that necessity”].

**ANSELM:** Who freely willed to make himself man so that, by the same unchangeable will, he would die, and so that through the certainty of this event the Virgin from whom that man would be taken might become pure?

**BOSO:** God the Son of God [Col. 0420C].

**ANSELM:** Was it not shown above that God’s will is compelled by no necessity, but preserves itself by its own spontaneous unchangeability when it is said to do something by necessity [Note: [Col. 0419D] Joly and Victor read “because God’s will”; Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Victor, the Cistercian manuscript, and the Gothic Edition read “but he himself preserves himself”]?

**BOSO:** It was truly shown. But, on the other hand, we see that what God wills unchangeably cannot fail to be; it is necessary that it be. Therefore, if God willed that that man should die, he could not not die.

**ANSELM:** From the fact that the Son of God assumed man with the will to die, you prove that the same man could not not die?

**BOSO:** That is how I understand it.

**ANSELM:** Did it not likewise appear from what has been said that the Son of God and the assumed man are one person, so that the same is both God and man, Son of God and son of the Virgin [Note: [Col. 0419D] Joly and the Cistercian manuscript read “man and son”; another reading is “man, son”]?

**BOSO:** It is so.

**ANSELM:** Therefore, the same man, by his own will, could not not die [Col. 0420D], and he died.

**BOSO:** I cannot deny it.

**ANSELM:** Since, then, God’s will does nothing by necessity [Col. 0421A], but by its own power, and his will was the will of God, he died not by necessity but by his own power.

**BOSO:** I cannot oppose your arguments. For I am in no way able to weaken either the propositions you put forward or the conclusions you draw. Yet this always occurs to me, as I said [Note: [Col. 0421D] The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “as you said”]: if he wished not to die, he could no more do this than he could not be what he was. For he truly was going to die [Note: [Col. 0421D] Joly reads “if he wished not to die, it would not be more possible for him to do this than not to be what he was: for truly”; Victor, the Cistercian manuscript, and the Gothic Edition read “if he wished not to die, he could no more do this than not be what he was: truly”]. For if he truly had not been going to die, faith in his future death would not have been true—the faith through which both that Virgin from whom he was born and many others were cleansed from sin. For if it had not been true, it could have benefited no one. Therefore, if he could have not died [Note: [Col. 0421D] The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “if he could have not died”], he could make false what was true.

**ANSELM:** Why was it true, before he died, that he was going to die [Col. 0421B]?

**BOSO:** Because he himself freely willed this by an unchangeable will [Note: [Col. 0421D] The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “how this,” rather than “because this”].

**ANSELM:** If, then, as you say, he could not not die for this reason: that he truly was going to die—and if he truly was going to die for this reason: that he himself freely and unchangeably willed it—it follows that he could not not die for no other reason than that by an unchangeable will he willed to die.

**BOSO:** That is so. But whatever the cause may have been, it nevertheless remains true that he could not not die and that it was necessary for him to die.

**ANSELM:** You cling too much to nothing and, as the saying goes, seek a knot in a rush.

**BOSO:** Have you forgotten what I objected to your evasions at the beginning of our discussion? Namely, that you should not do what I asked for the learned, but for me and for those who make the same request with me? Bear with me, then, so that, in view of the slowness and dullness of our understanding [Col. 0421C], you may satisfy me and them even in childish questions, as you have begun to do.

## CHAPTER XVIII [alternatively XVII] [Note: Victor 19 has “Chapter 18.”]

### What necessity or impossibility is not in God; and what is compelling necessity and non-compelling necessity

**ANSELM:** We have already said that God is improperly said either to be unable to do something or to do something by necessity. For every necessity and impossibility is subject to his will, whereas his will is subject to no necessity or impossibility. Nothing is necessary or impossible except because he wills it so; but for him to will or not will something because of necessity or impossibility is contrary to the truth.

Therefore, since he does everything that he wills, and only what he wills, just as no necessity or impossibility precedes his willing or not willing, so neither does any precede his doing or not doing—although he wills and does many things unchangeably [Col. 0422A]. And just as, when God does something, once it has been done it can no longer not have been done, but it is always true that it has been done, yet it is not rightly said that it is impossible for God to make what is past not be past [Note: [Col. 0421D] Saint Michael reads “to make what is past not be past”; another reading ends the phrase after “what is past”], so likewise, if he declares that he will do something unchangeably, although what he declares cannot, before it happens, fail to be future, there is nevertheless no necessity in him for doing it or impossibility of not doing it, because only his will is operative in him.

Whenever God is said to be unable to do something, no power in him is being denied; rather, an unconquerable power and strength are being indicated [Note: [Col. 0421D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “power is signified,” rather than “an unconquerable power and strength are indicated”]. Nothing else is meant except that no thing can cause him to do what he is said to be unable to do.

This manner of speaking is very common: something is said to be able, not because there is power in it, but because power exists in something else; and it is said to be unable, not because there is impotence in it, but because impotence exists in something else. Thus we say, “This man can be defeated,” meaning, “Someone can defeat him”; and, “That man cannot be defeated,” meaning, “No one can defeat him.” For the ability to be defeated is not a power but an impotence; and the inability to be defeated is not an impotence but a power.

Nor do we say that God does something by necessity because there is any necessity in him, but because there is necessity in something else, just as I spoke of impotence when he is said to be unable [Note: [Col. 0421D] The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “as I said concerning impotence”]. Every necessity is either compulsion or prohibition; and these two necessities are mutually opposed, just as the necessary and the impossible are opposed [Col. 0422C]. Whatever is compelled to be is prohibited from not being, and whatever is compelled not to be is prohibited from being—just as what must be cannot not be, and what must not be cannot be, and conversely.

When we say that something must be or must not be in God, we do not mean that there is in him a necessity that compels or prohibits. Rather, we signify that in all other things there is a necessity prohibiting them from doing what is said of God and compelling them not to do it. Thus, when we say that God must always speak the truth and must never lie [Note: [Col. 0421D] The Cistercian manuscript and the Gothic Edition read “it is necessary that he never lie”], we mean only that his constancy in preserving the truth is so great that no thing can cause him not to speak the truth or to lie [Col. 0422D] [Note: [Col. 0421D] The manuscripts continue the preceding chapter. Victor 19 and the Gothic Edition read “and not,” possibly beginning the alternative division of the chapter].

Therefore, when we say that that man, who according to the unity of person—as was said above—is himself the Son of God, God, could not not die or will not to die after he was born from the Virgin, we do not signify in him any inability to preserve or to will to preserve his life immortal. We signify rather the unchangeability of his will, by which he freely made himself man for the purpose of dying while persevering in that same will; and we signify that no thing could change that will.

For it would be more impotence than power if he could will to lie, deceive, or change a will that he had previously willed to be unchangeable. And if, as I said above, when someone freely proposes to do some good thing and later completes what he proposed with the same will, although he can be compelled, if he is unwilling, to fulfill his promise, he should nevertheless not be said to do what he does by necessity, but by the free will with which he made the proposal.

Something should not be said to be done or not done by necessity or impotence where neither necessity nor impotence operates, but the will does. If this is so in a human being, then necessity or impotence should much less be named in God, who does nothing except what he wills [Note: [Col. 0423D] Joly, Victor, Saint Michael, the Cistercian manuscript, and the Gothic Edition read “what he wills, he did”], and whose will no force can compel or prohibit.

For this purpose the diversity of natures and unity of person existed in Christ: so that what needed to be done for the restoration of human beings, if human nature could not do it, divine nature might accomplish; and if it was wholly unsuitable to divine nature, human nature might perform it; and so that there would not be one person and another, but the very same one, existing perfectly as both, might through the human nature discharge what the human nature owed, and through the divine nature be able to do what was expedient [Col. 0423C].

Finally, the Virgin, who was made pure through faith so that he could be taken from her, did not believe that he would die [Note: [Col. 0423D] Joly, Victor, and the Cistercian manuscript read “that he would die”; another reading is “that she believed”] except because he willed it—just as she had learned through the prophet who said of him: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isaiah 53:7). Therefore, since her faith was true, it was necessary that it happen as she believed.

If it troubles you again that I say “it was necessary” [Note: [Col. 0423D] The manuscripts of Victor and Joly read “that I say,” rather than “because I say”], remember that the truth of the Virgin’s faith was not the cause of his freely dying; rather, because this was going to happen, her faith was true. Accordingly, if it is said that it was necessary for him to die by his will alone, because the faith or prophecy that had preceded this event was true [Note: [Col. 0423D] Joly, Victor 3, Gembloux, and Bec read “that had preceded”; the Cistercian manuscript and the Gothic Edition read “that had proceeded”], this means nothing other than that it was necessary for the event to happen in this way because it was going to happen in this way.

Such necessity does not compel a thing to exist; rather, it makes the necessity belong to the thing’s existence [Col. 0424A]. There is a preceding necessity, which is the cause of a thing’s existence, and there is a subsequent necessity, which the thing itself causes. The preceding and efficient necessity is present when it is said, “The heavens revolve,” because they must revolve. The subsequent necessity, which effects nothing but comes into being, is present when I say, “You speak by necessity,” because you are speaking [Note: [Col. 0423D] Gembloux, Bec, Victor, and the Gothic Edition read “but comes into being”; another reading is “but thus is, when”].

When I say this, I mean that nothing can cause you not to be speaking while you are speaking—not that someone else is compelling you to speak [Note: [Col. 0423D] Victor reads “something causes you,” rather than “someone else”]. For the violence of natural condition compels the heavens to revolve, but no necessity makes you speak [Note: [Col. 0423D] Joly reads “compels you to speak,” rather than “makes you speak”].

Wherever there is preceding necessity, there is also subsequent necessity; but wherever there is subsequent necessity, preceding necessity does not immediately follow. We can say, “The heavens must revolve,” because they revolve; but it is not similarly true that you speak because you must speak.

This subsequent necessity runs through all times in the following way: whatever was, must have been; whatever is, must be; whatever will be, must have been going to be [Note: [Col. 0423D] Gembloux and Bec read: “Whatever is must be; and whatever will be, it must have been future.” Joly, Victor, the Cistercian manuscript, Saint Michael, and the Gothic Edition read: “Whatever is must be; and whatever will be, it must have been future; whatever will be, it must have been future.” The text is repetitive in the witnesses].

This is the necessity that, when Aristotle treats of singular and future propositions, seems to destroy the possibility of either alternative and to establish that everything exists by necessity [Note: [Col. 0423D] The manuscripts read “when he treats,” rather than “where he treats”].

By this subsequent and non-efficient necessity, because the faith or prophecy concerning Christ was true—that he was going to die by his will, not by necessity [Note: [Col. 0423D] Joly, Victor, the Cistercian manuscript, and the Gothic Edition read “not by necessity”]—it was necessary that it be so. By this necessity he was made man; by it he did and suffered whatever he did and suffered; by it he willed whatever he willed.

For they were by necessity because they were future; they were future because they were; and they were because they were [Col. 0424C]. And if you wish to know the true necessity of everything he did and suffered, know that everything happened by necessity because he willed it. But no necessity preceded his will.

Therefore, if things existed only because he willed them, then, had he not willed them, they would not have existed. Thus no one took his soul from him; rather, he himself laid it down and took it up again, because he had the power to lay down his soul and to take it up again, as he himself said [Note: [Col. 0423D] The Cistercian manuscript and Saint Michael read “as he himself says,” rather than “as he himself said”] (John 10:18).

**BOSO:** You have satisfied me that he cannot be proved to have undergone death by any necessity, and I do not regret having been persistent with you so that you would do this.

**ANSELM:** We have shown, I think, a certain reason by which God took a man without sin from a sinful mass. Nevertheless, I by no means think it should be denied that there is another reason besides the one we have stated [Note: [Col. 0423D] Joly reads “I do not at all think that there is another”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “except the reasoning we have stated”]—except for this: God can do what human reasoning cannot comprehend [Col. 0425A] [Note: [Col. 0425D] Joly reads “because God”; another reading is “that God”; Joly also reads “what human reasoning”].

But since this explanation too seems to me capable of sufficing, and since, if I wished now to seek another, it would be necessary to investigate what original sin is and how it is spread from our first parents through the entire human race, apart from the man of whom we are speaking, thereby entering into other questions that require their own treatment, let us be content with the explanation that we have given [Note: [Col. 0425D] The manuscripts read “with the explanation that we have given”] and continue the work we began [Note: [Col. 0425D] Gembloux, Bec, Joly, and Victor read “let us pursue”].

**BOSO:** As you wish—but on the condition that, at some time, with God’s help, you discharge as a debt that other explanation which you now avoid investigating [Note: [Col. 0425D] Saint Michael reads “which you forbid investigating,” rather than “which you avoid investigating”].

**ANSELM:** Since I know that I have this intention, I do not refuse what you ask. But because I am uncertain about the future, I do not dare to promise; rather, I entrust it to God’s disposition [Note: [Col. 0425D] Gembloux reads “disposition” rather than “dispensation.”] But tell me now what you think remains to be answered concerning the question you proposed at the beginning [Note: [Col. 0425D] Joly reads “which I proposed”], on account of which many other questions arose.

**BOSO:** The main question was why God became man in order to save man through his death, when it appears that he could have done this in another way. In answering this question with many necessary arguments, you showed that the restoration of human nature ought not to be left undone and could not be accomplished unless man paid what he owed to God for sin. That debt was so great that it ought to be paid by none but man, yet could be paid by none but God, so that the same one would be both man and God [Note: [Col. 0425D] Joly reads “the man who is God” rather than “the same one who is both man and God.”]

Hence it was necessary for God to assume man into the unity of person, so that the one who, in his nature, ought to pay the debt but could not, would exist in a person who could [Note: [Col. 0425D] Gembloux reads “so that he would exist in the person who could”].

Then, because that man who was God was to be taken from the Virgin and from the person of the Son of God, you showed how he could be taken without sin from a sinful mass. You also proved most clearly that the life of this man was so exalted and so precious that it could suffice to pay what is owed for the sins of the whole world, and infinitely more [Note: [Col. 0425D] Joly reads “and more than infinitely,” rather than “and infinitely more”]. It remains, therefore, to show how that life is paid to God for the sins of human beings.

95

## CHAPTER XIX [alternatively XVIII] [Note: The manuscripts have “Chapter 18.”]

### How Christ’s life is paid to God for the sins of human beings; and how Christ both ought and ought not to have suffered

[Col. 0425D]

## Complete textual apparatus and editorial matter

This source-keyed register supplies every reading in the canonical chunk. In each item, the form before its siglum is that witness’s reading; the last form is the contrasting printed reading. Latin is retained only with an English gloss where wording, inflection, or order cannot otherwise be represented.

### [Col. 0415C–0418D]

- At “from a sinful mass, that is, from the human race,” all manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *peccatrice et humano* (“sinful and human”) for *peccatrice, id est, de humano* (“sinful, that is, from the human”). Victorine 3 reads *de fermentato* (“from leavened [dough]”) for *de fermento* (“from leaven”). Victorine manuscripts read *mater sua* (“his own mother”) for *mater ejus* (“her mother”).
- Joly, Victorine, Cîteaux, and Saint Michael read *illum esse Deum et* (“that that man is God and”) for *illum Deum et* (“that that God and”); the same witnesses read *peccatorum esse reconciliatorem* (“to be reconciler of sinners”) for *peccatorum reconciliatorem* (“reconciler of sinners”).
- Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Victorine 3 and 13, and the Gothic edition read *eum sine peccato* (“him without sin”); Victorine 19 reads *eum omnino sine peccato* (“him entirely without sin”) and *eum sine omni peccato* (“him without any sin”), against the printed wording. Victorine 3 reads *quia vero intentione* (“because truly by purpose”) for *qua vero ratione* (“by what reason”); Victorine and the Gothic edition read *mirabilis Deus* (“wonderful God”) for *mirabilius Deus* (“God more wonderfully”).
- At “one who might be punished,” manuscripts and Gothic edition read *quod puniretur* (“that which might be punished,” neuter) for *qui puniretur* (“one who might be punished,” masculine). Joly reads *quod humanus* (“that [a] human”), Victorine 13 *quis quod humanus* (“who [is] that human”), for *vel quis humanus* (“or what human [being]”). Joly reads *oportuit itaque* (“therefore it was fitting”) for *oportuit utique* (“indeed it was fitting”).
- At “all who will believe,” Joly reads *qui credent* (“who will believe”) and Victorine 3 *qui credunt* (“who believe”) for *qui crederent* (“who would believe”). Joly reads *sed digne* (“but worthily”) for *si digne* (“if worthily”); manuscripts and Gothic edition read *sit, unde culpae* (“let it be, from which sins”) for *sit hoc unde culpae* (“let this be, from which sins”), while Victorine and Gothic read *relaxantur* (“are remitted”) for *relaxentur* (“may be remitted”).
- Victorine 19 reads *non potuerunt* (“could not,” perfect) for *non poterant* (“could not,” imperfect). Joly and Victorine 3 and 19 read *non solum praesentibus* (“not only those present”) for *non solis praesentibus* (“not those present only”); Victorine and Joly read *ejus esse morti potuerunt* (“could be present at his death”) for *esse ejus morti poterant* (“could be at his death”). Joly, Victorine, Cîteaux, and the Gothic edition read *creaturis suis quae* (“his creatures which”) for *creaturis quae* (“creatures which”), omitting *suis* in the printed text.
- At “things made chiefly for this,” manuscripts and Gothic edition read *factae essent* (“had been made,” feminine) for *facta essent* (“had been made,” neuter). Manuscripts read *convenire sed etiam necesse esse* (“to be fitting and also necessary”) for *conveniens sed etiam necessarium esse* (“to be fitting and also necessary,” neuter construction).

### [Col. 0419D–0421D]: the death discussion

- Manuscripts and Gothic edition read *necessitatem ejus* (“his necessity”) for *nativitatem ejus* (“his birth”). Joly reads *placet mihi* (“it pleases me”) for *placeret mihi* (“it would please me”); Joly and Gothic read *per se mundus non esse* (“not clean through himself”) for *non per se mundus esse* (“clean not through himself”). Victorine 19 begins Chapter 17 at *verum adhuc mihi* (“but still to me”).
- Manuscripts read *quomodo non* (“how not”) for *quomodo ergo non* (“how therefore not”); Victorine 19 reads *cum illis, ut puto* (“with those [things], I think”) for *in illis, ut puto* (“in those [things], I think”). Joly reads *habet, hoc* (“has, this”) for *haberet, hoc* (“had, this”). Manuscripts read *cum autem* (“but when”) for *cum ergo* (“therefore when”).
- Victorine 19 reads *idem Deus homo* (“the same God-man”) for *idem homo* (“the same man”), and *semper habuit* (“always had”) for *semper habuerit* (“always had,” perfect subjunctive). It reads *non mori vellet, non* (“if he wished not to die, not”) for *mori non vellet, non* (“if he did not wish to die, not”); *mortuum esse* (“to have died”) for *moriturum esse* (“to be going to die”); and *non potuit velle non mori* (“he could not will not to die”) for *non potuit non velle mori* (“he could not not will to die”).
- Cîteaux reads *scilicet et mori et velle mori* (“namely both dying and willing to die”) for *scilicet et velle mori, et mori* (“namely both willing to die and dying”). Victorine 19, Cîteaux, and Gothic read *in illa necessitate* (“in that necessity,” feminine) for *in illo necessitate* (“in that necessity,” masculine). Joly and Victorine read *quod Dei voluntas* (“that God’s will”) for *quia Dei voluntas* (“because God’s will”); Gembloux, Bec, Joly, Victorine, Cîteaux, and Gothic read *sed ipse* (“but he himself”) for *sed ipsa se* (“but it itself”).
- Manuscripts label the next “truly” *A. vere* (“Anselm: truly”) for *B. vere* (“Boso: truly”). Joly reads *moreretur, probas eundem hominem non potuisse non mori* (“he would die, you prove the same man could not not die”) for *moreretur, non potuit non mori* (“he would die, [he] could not not die”). Joly and Cîteaux read *homo, et filius* (“man, and son”) for *homo filius* (“man son”).
- Manuscripts and Gothic read *quomodo ergo* (“how therefore”) for *quoniam ergo* (“since therefore”). Victorine 19 reads *hic mihi semper* (“this always occurs to me”) for *hoc mihi semper* (“this always [thing] to me”); manuscripts and Gothic read *quod dixisti* (“what you said”) for *quod dixi* (“what I said”).
- At “if he wished not to die,” Joly reads the expanded *non mori, non magis hoc posset, quam posset non esse quod erat vere* (“not to die, he could no more do this than he could not be what he was, truly”); Victorine, Cîteaux, and Gothic read *non mori, non esset magis hoc posse, quam non esse quod erat: vere* (“not to die, it would not be more possible than not to be what he was: truly”), for the printed order. Manuscripts and Gothic read *si potuisset non mori* (“if he could have not died”) for *si potuit non mori* (“if he could not die”); they read *quomodo hoc* (“how this”) for *quoniam hoc* (“because this”). Joly reads *quod objecerim* (“that I objected”) for *quid objecerim* (“what I objected”).

### [Col. 0421D–0424C]: necessity

- Victorine 19 has “Chapter 18” at the chapter heading. Saint Michael’s reading is *faciat quod praeteritum est non esse praeteritum* (“make what is past not be past”) for the truncated printed *faciat quod praeteritum est* (“make what is past”). Victorine, Joly, Cîteaux, and Gothic read *quae veritatem* (“which [wills] truth,” feminine) for *qui veritatem* (“who [wills] truth,” masculine). Cîteaux reads *signatur potentia* (“power is signified”) for *significatur potentia* (“power is indicated”).
- Manuscripts and Gothic read *dixi, impotentia* (“I said, impotence”) for *dixi de impotentia* (“I spoke of impotence”). Cîteaux and Gothic read *necesse eum nunquam* (“it is necessary for him never”) for *necesse est nunquam* (“it is necessary never”). The manuscripts continue the preceding chapter; Victorine 19 and Gothic read *vel non* (“or not”) for *et non* (“and not”).
- At freely proposing and completing a good work, Joly, Victorine, Saint Michael, Cîteaux, and Gothic read *perfecit quod* (“completed what”) for *perficit quod* (“completes what”). At “does what he wills,” Joly, Victorine, Saint Michael, Cîteaux, and Gothic read *quod vult, fecit* (“what he wills, he did”) for *quod vult, facit* (“what he wills, he does”).
- In the Virgin’s faith, manuscripts read *crediderit illum* (“she will have believed him”) for *credit illum* (“she believes him”); Joly and Victorine read *moriturum* (“going to die”) for *esse moriturum* (“to be going to die”). Victorine and Joly read *quod dico* (“that I say”) for *quia dico* (“because I say”). Joly, Victorine 3, Gembloux, and Bec read *praecesserat* (“had preceded”); Cîteaux and Gothic *processerant* (“had proceeded”), for *praecesserant* (“had preceded”).
- Gembloux, Bec, Victorine, and Gothic read *sed sic est, cum* (“but it is thus, when”) for *sed fit, est cum* (“but it happens, it is when”). Victorine reads *aliquid te* (“something [causes] you”) for *alius te* (“someone else [causes] you”); Joly reads *facit loqui* (“makes [you] speak”) for *cogit loqui* (“compels [you] to speak”).
- The subsequent-necessity formula has three exact witness arrangements: Gembloux and Bec read *quicquid est, necesse est esse. Quicquid futurum est, necesse est futurum fuisse* (“whatever is must be; whatever will be must have been future”); Joly, Victorine, Cîteaux, Saint Michael, and Gothic read *quicquid est necesse est esse: et necesse est futurum fuisse quicquid futurum est* (“whatever is must be; and whatever will be must have been future”); the printed text repeats *quicquid futurum est, necesse est futurum fuisse* (“whatever will be must have been future”). The repetition is preserved.
- Manuscripts read *ut tractat* (“when he treats”) for *ubi tractat* (“where he treats”). Victorine 19 reads *omnia esse ex* (“all things to be from”) for *omnia ex* (“all [things] from”). Joly reads *vel prophetia* (“or prophecy”) for *et prophetia* (“and prophecy”); Joly, Victorine, Cîteaux, and Gothic read *non necessitate moriturus* (“going to die not by necessity”) for *non ex necessitate moriturus* (“going to die not from necessity”). Manuscripts and Gothic read *voluntatem ergo* (“therefore [his] will”) for *voluntatem vero* (“but [his] will”), and *sic utique* (“thus indeed”) for *sic itaque* (“thus therefore”). Cîteaux and Saint Michael read *sicut ipse dicit* (“as he himself says”) for *sicut ipse dixit* (“as he himself said”).

### [Col. 0423D–0425D]: close of the chapter

- Joly reads *nequaquam negandum aestimo, aliam* (“I judge that another is by no means to be denied”) for *nequaquam aestimo aliam* (“I by no means judge another”). Cîteaux reads *quam diximus, excepto* (“which we stated, except”) for *quam diximus, rationem, excepto* (“the reason which we stated, except”).
- Joly reads *quia Deus* (“because God”) for *quod Deus* (“that God”). Its following *hominis ratio* (“human reasoning”) stands for the printed corrupt *quod Deus*; the source preserves the corruption rather than supplying an invented expansion. Joly reads *quoniam et ista* (“since this too”) for *quoniam ista* (“since this”); manuscripts read *ea qua diximus* (“that which we stated”) for *ea, quam diximus* (“that [explanation] which we stated”); Gembloux, Bec, Joly, and Victorine read *persequamur* (“let us pursue”) for *prosequamur* (“let us continue”).
- Saint Michael reads *inquirere vitas* (“to investigate lives”), a printed corruption, for *inquirere vetas* (“you forbid [us] to investigate”); it remains unresolved. Gembloux reads *dispositioni* (“to disposition”) for *dispensationi* (“to dispensation”). Victorine 19, Gembloux, Bec, and Cîteaux begin Chapter 18 at *sed dic nunc* (“but tell me now”). Joly reads *proposuisti* (“you proposed”) for *proposui* (“I proposed”).
- Joly reads *videretur. Ad quod* (“it would seem. To which”) for *videatur. Ad quam* (“it may seem. To which [feminine]”). It reads *homo qui Deus* (“the man who is God”) for *homo qui et Deus* (“the man who is also God”). Gembloux reads *in persona esset qui posset* (“he who could would exist in the person”) for *in persona esset quae posset* (“that which could would exist in the person”). Joly reads *et plus in infinitum* (“and more into infinity”) for *et plus infinitum* (“and more infinitely”). The manuscripts title the next section “Chapter 18.”

ANS. If he allowed himself to be killed for the sake of justice, did he not give his life for the honor of God? [Col. 0426A]

BOS. If I can understand what I do not doubt—although I do not see how he did this reasonably, when he could have preserved both justice without deviation and his life eternally—I shall admit that he voluntarily gave such a thing to God for the honor of him beside whom nothing that is not God can be compared, and which can be recompensed for all the debts of all human beings. [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Fecerit, cum et* (“he did this, when also”), manuscript Joly: *fecerit, et cum et* (“he did this, and when also”). *Tale quid* (“such a thing”), manuscript Joly: *talem quid* (“such a [thing]”). *Cui quidquid quod Deus non est* (“to whom whatever is not God…”), manuscripts: *cui quicquid Deus non est* (“to whom whatever is not God…”). *Pro omnibus omnium hominum debitis* (“for the debts of all human beings”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *pro omnibus omnium debitis* (“for all debts”).]

ANS. Do you not understand that, when he patiently endured the injuries, insults, and death on the cross with thieves—as we said above—which were inflicted on him for the sake of the justice he obediently observed, he gave human beings an example, so that they would not depart from the justice they owe God on account of any hardships they may experience? He certainly would not have given this example if, according to his power, he had avoided a death inflicted for such a cause. [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Tali causa* (“for such a cause”), manuscript Joly: *tali culpa* (“for such a fault”).]

BOS. It seems that he himself gave this example without any necessity, since many before his coming, and John the Baptist after his coming but before his death, are known to have given it sufficiently by bravely enduring death for the truth. [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Exemplum necessitate* (“the example by necessity”), manuscripts S. Michaelis, Vict. 3 and 13, and the Gothic edition: *exemplum ipse necessitate* (“he himself [gave] the example by necessity”).]

ANS. No human being ever, by dying, gave God something that he was not at some time going to lose by necessity, or paid what he did not owe. But he voluntarily offered to the Father what he was never going to lose by necessity, and he paid on behalf of sinners what he did not owe on his own behalf. [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Patri obtulit* (“offered to the Father”), manuscripts Vict. 3 and 13: *pati obtulit* (“offered to suffer”). *Quod pro se non debebat* (“what he did not owe on his own behalf”), manuscript Joly: *quod ipse non [debebat]* (“what he himself did not owe”).] Therefore he gave an example all the more powerfully, so that everyone would not hesitate, when reason requires it, to render to God on his own behalf what he will certainly lose at some time—he who, since he had no need of it for himself and was not compelled to give it for others, to whom he owed nothing but punishment, gave so precious a life—indeed, gave himself, so great a person, with such great willingness (*tanta voluntate*; the printed OCR reading is uncertain). [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Ille multo magis* (“he all the more”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *ille magis* (“he more”). *Qui cum* (“he who, since”), manuscripts Gem., Bec., Joly, Vict., and the Gothic edition: *quia cum* (“because, since”).]

BOS. You are coming very close to what I desire; but allow me to ask something which, although you may perhaps think it foolish to ask, I nevertheless do not readily know how to answer if I am asked. You say that, when he died, he gave what he did not owe. Yet no one will deny that he acted better when he gave this example in such a manner, and that this pleased God more than if he had not done so. Or will anyone say that he ought not to have done what he understood to be better and more pleasing to God? [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Quiddam quaeram* (“I shall ask something”), manuscripts Vict., Joly, and the Gothic edition: *quoddam quaeram* (“I shall ask a certain thing”). *Tamen in promptu* (“nevertheless readily”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *tamen promptum* (“nevertheless readily”). *Hoc exemplum* (“this example”), manuscripts Vict., Gem., and Bec.: *illud ad exemplum* (“that as an example”). *Aut dicet* (“or will anyone say”), manuscript Vict. 19: *aut dices* (“or will you say”). *Melius esse* (“to be better”), manuscript Joly: *melius esset* (“would be better”). *Deo intellexit* (“he understood to be pleasing to God”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *Deo cognovit* (“he recognized to be pleasing to God”).]

How, then, shall we assert that he did not owe God what he did—that is, what he understood to be better and more pleasing to God—especially since a creature ought to give God everything that it is, everything that it knows, and everything that it can? [Col. 0426D–0427A] [Note: [Col. 0425D] *Melius esse et magis* (“to be better and more”), manuscripts: *melius esse magis* (“to be better, more”). *Deo intellexit* (“he understood to be pleasing to God”), manuscripts: *Deo cognovit* (“he recognized to be pleasing to God”). *Quod scit et quod potest* (“what it knows and what it can”), manuscript Cisterciensis: *quod scit, et potest* (“what it knows and can”).]

ANS. Although a creature has nothing from itself, nevertheless, when God grants it permission to do or not to do something lawfully, he gives it both alternatives as its own, so that, although one may be better, neither is required in a determinate way. Whether it does what is better or the other, it is said to be obliged to do what it does; and if it does what is better, it receives a reward because it freely gives what is its own.

Since virginity is better than marriage, yet neither is required of a human being in a determinate way, both the person who chooses marriage and the person who prefers to preserve virginity are said to be obliged to do what they do. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Cum virginitas* (“since virginity”), manuscript S. Michaelis: *cum licet virginitas* (“although virginity is [better]”). *Mavult, quod* (“prefers, what”), manuscripts Gem., Bec., Vict., and the Gothic edition: *mavult, et quod* (“prefers, and what”).]

No one says that virginity or marriage ought not to be chosen. Rather, we say that, before a person determines either of these, he ought to do what he prefers; and if he preserves virginity, he expects a reward for the voluntary gift that he offers to God.

Therefore, when you say that a creature owes God what it knows and can do better, if you understand this as an obligation and do not supply the qualification “if God commands,” it is not always true. As I have said, a person does not owe virginity as a matter of obligation; but if he prefers marriage, he ought to make use of marriage.

If the word *ought* troubles you, and you cannot understand it without some kind of obligation, know that, just as “being able” and “not being able” occur, and necessity is sometimes spoken of—not because these things exist in the realities of which they are predicated, but because they exist in something else—so it is with *owing*. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Contingit posse et non posse, et necessitatem aliquando dici* (“it happens that being able and not being able are spoken of, and that necessity is sometimes spoken of”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *contingit posse et necesse aliquando dici* (“it happens that being able and necessary are sometimes spoken of”).]

For when we say that the poor ought to receive alms from the rich, this means nothing other than that the rich ought to give alms to the poor. This obligation is not to be exacted from the poor, but from the rich. God, too, is said to be obliged to rule over all things, not because he is in any way a debtor in this matter, but because everything ought to be subject to him; and he is said to be obliged to do what he wills, because what he wills ought to be. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Et debere facere* (“and [he is said] to be obliged to do”), manuscripts Vict., S. Michaelis, and the Gothic edition: *et debent facere* (“and they ought to do”). *Quoniam quod vult* (“because what he wills”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *quomodo quod vult* (“how what he wills”).]

Thus, when a creature wishes to do what it is its own to do or not to do, it is said to be obliged to do it, because what it wills ought to be.

Accordingly, when the Lord Jesus chose to endure death, as we said, since it was his own to suffer or not to suffer, he was obliged to do what he did, because what he willed to happen ought to happen; and he was not obliged to do it, because he did not do it from obligation. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Quod voluit fieri* (“what he willed to happen”), manuscripts: *quod vult fieri* (“what he wills to happen”).]

Indeed, since he himself is both God and human being, according to his human nature, from the time he became human, he received from the divine nature—which is other than the human nature—his entire being and everything he possessed, so that he owed nothing except what he willed to give. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Humanam quidem naturam; ex quo fuit homo* (“according to the human nature, from the time he became human”), manuscripts: *humanam ex qua fuit homo* (“the human nature from which he was human”); the Gothic edition: *humanam quidem naturam; ex qua fuit homo* (“according to the human nature, from which he was human”). *Suum quicquid habebat* (“everything that he possessed”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *suum quod habebat* (“what he possessed”).]

According to his person, however, he possessed from himself everything that he possessed, and was so perfectly sufficient to himself that he neither owed anyone anything in return nor needed to give anything in order to receive a return. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Habebat quicquid habebat* (“he possessed everything that he possessed”), manuscript Vict. 19: *habebat quod habebat* (“he possessed what he possessed”).]

BOS. I now see clearly that, for no reason, did he give himself to death from obligation for the honor of God, as my reasoning seemed to show; and yet he ought to do what he did. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Aperte nunc video* (“I now see clearly”), manuscripts Gem., Bec., Joly, Vict., and the Gothic edition: *aperte ut video* (“I see clearly”).]

ANS. That honor certainly belongs to the whole Trinity. Therefore, since he himself is God, the Son of God, he offered himself to himself for his own honor, just as he offered himself to the Father and to the Holy Spirit—that is, he offered his humanity to his divinity, which is one and the same divinity of the three persons. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Id est humanitatem* (“that is, his humanity”), manuscript Vict. 19: *et humanitatem* (“and his humanity”). *Eadem trium* (“the same [divinity] of the three”), manuscripts: *eademque trium* (“the same and identical [divinity] of the three”).]

Nevertheless, in order to speak more openly, while remaining within the truth of the matter itself, let us say, as common usage has it, that the Son voluntarily offered himself to the Father. In this way it is stated most plainly that the whole God, in one person, to whom he offered himself according to his humanity, is understood; and, through the names “Father” and “Son,” an immense piety is felt in the hearts of the hearers when the Son is said in this manner to plead for us before the Father. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Quia et in una persona* (“because also in one person”), manuscripts: *quia in persona* (“because in the person”).]

BOS. I accept this most willingly.

## CHAPTER XX [elsewhere part of Chapter XIX]

### How human salvation follows from his death

ANS. Let us now consider, as far as we can, by how great a rational necessity human salvation follows from it. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Intueamur nunc* (“let us now consider”), manuscripts: *intueamur nunc etc.* (“let us now consider, etc.”). *Quanta inde* (“how great [a necessity] follows from it”), manuscripts Joly, Vict., Cister., S. Michaelis, and the Gothic edition: *quanta mihi* (“how great [it seems] to me”).]

BOS. My heart is directed toward this. For although I seem to understand this, I want you to set out the very sequence of the reasoning. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Ad hoc tendit* (“my heart is directed toward this”), manuscript Joly: *attendit* (“it attends”); manuscript Vict. 13: *ad hoc intendit* (“it is directed toward this”). *Volo fieri* (“I want [it] to be done”), manuscripts Gem., Bec., Joly, Vict. 3 and 13, and the Gothic edition: *volo audire* (“I want to hear [it]”).]

ANS. There is no need to explain how great a thing it is that the Son freely gave.

BOS. It is sufficiently clear.

ANS. You will not judge that the one who freely gives so great a gift to God ought to be without recompense. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Tantum donum* (“so great a gift”), manuscript S. Michaelis: *tantum bonum* (“so great a good”).]

BOS. On the contrary, I see that it is necessary for the Father to recompense the Son; otherwise he appears either unjust, if he were unwilling, or powerless, if he were unable—things that are alien to God. [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Judicabis. Immo* (“you will judge. On the contrary”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *judicabis. B. Immo* (“you will judge. Boso: On the contrary”).]

ANS. Whoever recompenses someone either gives him what he does not have or remits what may be exacted from him. But before the Son did so great a thing, everything that belonged to the Father belonged to him, and he had never owed anything that could be remitted to him. What, then, will be recompensed to one who lacks nothing, and for whom there is nothing that can be given or remitted? [Note: [Col. 0427D] *Tantam rem Filius* (“the Son did so great a thing”), manuscript Joly: *rem facilius Filius* (“the Son did the matter more easily”). *Aut cui non* (“or for whom there is not”), manuscripts Joly, Vict., and Cister.: *et cui non* (“and for whom there is not”).]

BOS. On one side I see the necessity of recompensing, and on the other its impossibility: for it is necessary that God give back what he owes, yet there is no one to whom he can give it back. [Col. 0428D–0429A] [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Non est cui reddat* (“there is no one to whom he can give it back”), manuscript S. Michaelis: *non est quod reddat* (“there is nothing that he can give back”).]

ANS. If such a great and so deserved reward is given neither to him nor to anyone else, the Son will seem to have done such a great thing in vain.

BOS. It is impious to think this.

ANS. It is therefore necessary that it be given to someone else, since it cannot be given to him.

BOS. It follows inevitably.

ANS. If the Son wishes to give to someone else what is owed to him, will the Father be able to prohibit him by right, or deny it to the person to whom he gives it? [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Alii dare* (“to give to someone else”), manuscripts Joly, Vict., Cister., and the Gothic edition: *alteri dare* (“to give to another”). *Poteritne Pater* (“will the Father be able?”), manuscript Vict. 19: *poterit, nec Pater* (“will he be able, and not the Father…”). *Jure illum* (“by right prohibit him”), manuscript Joly omits *jure* (“by right”). *Aut alii cui* (“or deny it to someone else”), manuscripts Vict. and Joly: *aut illi cui* (“or deny it to the one to whom…”).]

BOS. On the contrary, I understand it to be both just and necessary that what the Son wishes to give be given to him by the Father: for the Son is permitted to give what is his, and the Father can give back what he owes only to someone else.

ANS. To whom could he more appropriately attribute the fruit and recompense of his death than to those for whose salvation—as the reasoning of truth has taught us—he made himself human, and to whom, as we said, by dying he gave an example of dying for the sake of justice? For his imitators will imitate him in vain if they do not share in his merit.

Or whom would he more justly make heirs of the debt that he does not need, and of the abundance of his fullness, than his parents and brothers, whom he sees wasting away in want under the burden of so many and such great debts, sunk in the depths of misery, so that what they owe for their sins may be remitted to them and what they lack because of their sins may be given to them? [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Frustra quippe* (“for in vain”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *frustra quidem* (“indeed in vain”). *Exundantiae* (“of the abundance”), manuscripts Gem., Bec., Vict.: *ex abundantia* (“from abundance”); manuscript Joly: *et exabundantiae* (“and of abundance”); manuscript Bec.: *et exundatione* (“and of overflowing”). *Plenitudinis* (“of fullness”), manuscripts Vict.: *plenitudine* (“from fullness”).]

BOS. The world can hear nothing more reasonable, nothing sweeter, nothing more desirable. I derive such confidence from this that I can no longer say with what joy my heart exults. For it seems to me that God rejects no person who approaches him under this name.

ANS. That is so, if he approaches as he ought. Sacred Scripture teaches us everywhere how one must approach participation in so great a grace and how one must live under it. It is founded upon the solid truth which, with God’s help, we have in some measure perceived, as upon a firm foundation. [Col. 0429C] [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Firmum fundamentum fundata* (“founded upon a firm foundation”), manuscript Joly: *firmum firmamentum fundata* (“founded upon a firm support”); manuscript S. Michaelis: *firmum illud firmamentum fundata* (“founded upon that firm support”); another reading: *firmamentum firmum fundatum firmata* (“established and made firm upon a firm foundation”).]

BOS. Truly, whatever is built upon this foundation is founded upon solid rock.

ANS. I think that I have now satisfied your question to some extent, although a fuller treatment could do this better, and although the reasons for this matter are greater and more numerous than my mortal intellect can comprehend. [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Sint rationes* (“may the reasons be”), manuscript S. Michaelis: *sunt rationes* (“the reasons are”).] It is also clear that God had no need whatsoever to do what we have said. Rather, immutable truth required it. For although, on account of the unity of the person, God is said to have done what that human being did, God did not need to descend from heaven in order to conquer the devil, nor did he need to act against him through justice in order to free humanity. Instead, God required from a human being that he conquer the devil, and that the one who had offended God through sin make satisfaction through justice.

For the devil was owed nothing by God except punishment, nor by humanity anything except repayment—that is, that the one conquered by him should conquer him in return. [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Nisi vicem* (“except repayment”), manuscript Joly: *nisi vincere* (“except to conquer”).] But whatever was required from him, he owed to God, not to the devil.

## CHAPTER XXI

### How great and how just the mercy of God is

When we considered the justice of God and the sin of humanity, God’s mercy, which seemed to you to have perished, proved to be so great and so perfectly harmonious with justice that nothing greater or more just can be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Tam magnam tamque* (“so great and so perfectly”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *tam magnam tanquam* (“as great as”).]

For what can be understood as more merciful than when God the Father says to a sinner condemned to eternal torments, who has nothing with which to redeem himself: “Take my Only-Begotten Son and give him for yourself”; and the Son himself says: “Take me and redeem yourself”? For this is, as it were, what they say when they call and draw us to the Christian faith. [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Quam cum peccatori* (“than when to a sinner”), manuscripts Vict., Joly, Gem., Bec., S. Michaelis, and the Gothic edition: *quam peccatori* (“than to a sinner”). *Damnato* (“condemned”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *deputato* (“assigned”). *Ipse Filius* (“the Son himself”), manuscripts Joly, Vict., S. Michaelis, Cister., and the Gothic edition: *et ipse Filius* (“and the Son himself”). *Quasi enim hoc* (“for it is as though they say this”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *quasi haec* (“as though they say these things”).]

What is also more just than that he to whom a price greater than every debt is given should, if it is given with the proper affection, remit every debt?

## CHAPTER XXII

### That it is impossible for the devil to be reconciled

You will understand the impossibility of the devil’s reconciliation, about which you asked, if you carefully consider the case of humanity. Just as humanity could not be reconciled except through the God-human being who could die, through whose justice what God had lost through human sin would be restored to God, so condemned angels cannot be saved except through an Angel who is God, who can die, and who by his justice can restore to God what the sins of others took away. [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Angelum Deum* (“an Angel who is God”), manuscripts Gem., Bec., Vict., and the Gothic edition: *Angelum Domini* (“an Angel of the Lord”). *Restitueretur* (“would be restored”), manuscripts Vict. 19: *restauraretur* (“would be repaired”).]

And just as humanity ought not to have been restored through another human being who was not of the same kind, although he was of the same nature, so no angel ought to be saved through another angel, although all angels are of one nature, because they are not of the same kind as one another, as human beings are. For all angels do not derive from one angel in the way that all human beings derive from one human being.

This, too, rules out their restoration: just as they fell without anyone else harming them so as to make them fall, so they ought to rise again without anyone else helping them—which is impossible. [Note: [Col. 0429D] *Nullo alio nocente* (“with no one else harming them”), manuscripts: *alio suadente* (“with another persuading them”). [Col. 0431C] *Resurgere debent* (“they ought to rise again”), manuscripts Cister. and Vict. 19: *surgere debent* (“they ought to rise”).]

For otherwise they cannot be restored to the dignity they would have possessed, since, without external help, through the power they had received they would have stood firm in the truth if they had not sinned. [Note: [Col. 0431C] *Sine alieno* (“without another’s [help]”), manuscript Vict. 19: *sine alio* (“without another’s [help]”).]

Therefore, if anyone thinks that the redemption of our Savior ought at some time to extend even to them, he is reasonably convicted of being reasonably deceived. I do not say this as though the price of his death did not, by its greatness, surpass all the sins of human beings and angels; rather, immutable reason opposes the restoration of the fallen angels.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### That the truth of the Old and New Testaments has been demonstrated in what has been said

[Col. 0431B]

BOS. Everything you say seems to me reasonable and incapable of contradiction. Through the solution of the one question we proposed, I understand everything contained in the New and Old Testaments to have been demonstrated. For since you prove the necessity of God’s becoming human in such a way that, even if the few points you drew from our books are removed—such as what you touched upon concerning the three persons of God and Adam—you satisfy not only the Jews but also the pagans by reason alone; and since this same God-human being established the New Testament and approved the Old, just as it is necessary to confess him to be truthful, so no one can deny that what is contained in those books is true. [Note: [Col. 0431C] *Deum fieri* (“God’s becoming”), manuscript Vict. 19: *Deum sic fieri* (“God’s becoming in this way”). *Sed etiam paganis* (“but also the pagans”), manuscript Cisterciensis: *sed et paganis* (“and also the pagans”).]

ANS. If we have said anything that ought to be corrected, I do not refuse correction, provided that it is made reasonably. But if the testimony of truth strengthens what we reasonably believe we have discovered, we ought to attribute it to God, not to ourselves, who is blessed forever. Amen. [Col. 0432A–B]

[Note: [Col. 0431C] Manuscript Gem., chapter 19: “The Book of Anselm, *Cur Deus Homo*, ends.” Manuscript Cisterciensis: “The *Cur Deus Homo*, the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, ends.”]

[Col. 0431B]

# SAINT ANSELM’S BOOK ON THE VIRGINAL CONCEPTION AND ORIGINAL SIN

## PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 0431C] This book was collated with the Beccensis, Gemmeticensis, and four Victorine manuscripts formerly designated CC 9, EE 13, RR 3, and P 19; with one manuscript from the library of Saint Michael on the Mount; with two Thuan manuscripts, numbered 391 and 546; with one Cistercian manuscript; and with the Gothic edition.

After the title and the list of chapters, manuscript Thu. 361 reads: “Here begins the Book of the Lord Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgininal Conception and Original Sin.”

Manuscript Thu. 546 reads: “Here begin the chapters of Anselm’s book on the Virgininal Conception.” After prefacing these titles and numbers, it continues: “Here begins Anselm the Archbishop’s Book on the Virgininal Conception.”

Manuscript Vict. 3 reads: “Here begins the Preface to the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgininal Conception and Original Sin.” After the preface: “Here begins the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgininal Conception and Original Sin.”

Manuscript Vict. 19 reads: “The chapters of the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgininal Conception.” After this: “Here begins the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgininal Conception.”

Manuscript Vict. 9 reads: “The Book of Master Anselm on the Virgininal Conception.”

The Cistercian manuscript reads: “Here begins the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgininal Conception and Original Sin.”]

Since I wish, if I can, to comply with all your devout wishes, dearest brother and son Boso, I consider myself especially obliged when I understand that you are stirring such a wish in me. I am certain that, when you read in the book *Cur Deus Homo*—which you above all others urged me to publish, and in which I took you as my interlocutor—that another account than the one I presented there may be proposed for how God took a human being from the sinful mass of the human race without sin, your eager mind is strongly impelled to seek what that account might be.

Therefore, I fear that I might appear unjust to you if I concealed from your affection whatever I think about it. I shall therefore speak briefly about what I believe, without condemning anyone’s faithful opinion concerning the same matter, and without stubbornly defending my own if it can reasonably be shown to conflict with the truth. [Note: [Col. 0431C] *Poterit ostendi* (“can be shown”), manuscripts: *probari poterit* (“can be proved”). *Pervicaciter* (“stubbornly”), manuscript Thu. 546: *pertinaciter* (“obstinately”); omitted in manuscripts Vict. 19.]

Nevertheless, I consider the account of the same matter that I set out in that work entirely sound and sufficient, if it is properly considered. For there is nothing to prevent there being several explanations of the same matter, each of which by itself may be sufficient. [Note: [Col. 0431C] *Sufficientem* (“sufficient”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *sufficienter* (“sufficiently”).]

## CHAPTER I

### What original and personal justice—or injustice—is

[Note: [Col. 0433D] Manuscripts and the Gothic edition read: “and personal nature”; manuscript Vict. 19 reads: “and what personal justice or injustice is.”]

In order to see, then, how God took a human being from the sinful mass of the human race without sin, we must first investigate original sin, because this question arises from that alone. For if it becomes clear how Christ could not have been subject to it, and how the assumption or conception of that human being was free from every sin, the matter will be evident. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Nascitur haec* (“this question arises”), manuscript Cisterciensis omits *haec* (“this”). *Non potuit* (“could not”), manuscript Vict.: *non poterit* (“will not be able”). *Palam erit* (“it will be evident”), manuscripts Vict., Cister., Thu., S. Michaelis, and the Gothic edition: *palam erit qualiter assumptio* (“it will be evident how the assumption…”).]

There is no doubt that *original* is named from *origin*. If, then, original sin exists only in a human being, it seems to be called “original” either from the origin of human nature—which is original because it is from the beginning of that nature, since it is transmitted from the very origin of human nature—or from the origin, that is, from the beginning of each person, because it is transmitted in the origin of that person. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Dici aut ab originale* (“to be called from the original”), manuscripts: *dici ab origine* (“to be called from the origin”). *In ipsa ejus trahitur* (“is transmitted in its origin”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *in ipsa trahatur* (“is transmitted in it”).]

But that it descends from the beginning of human nature does not seem possible, since its origin was just when the first parents were made just, without any sin. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Quoniam origo* (“since its origin”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *quando origo* (“when its origin”). *Sine omni peccato* (“without any sin”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *sine peccato* (“without sin”).]

It therefore seems to be called original from the very origin of each individual human person. Nevertheless, if someone says that sin is called original because it descends upon individuals from those from whom they derive the origin of their nature, I shall not contradict him, provided that he does not deny that original sin is transmitted together with the origin of each individual person. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Si tamen* (“provided that”), manuscript Vict. 19: *sed tantum* (“but only”).]

For although in each human being there are simultaneously nature, by which he is human like all others, and person, by which he is distinguished from others—as when one says “that one” or “this one”—whether by a proper name, such as Adam and Abel, each person’s sin exists both in nature and in person. Adam’s sin existed in the human being, which pertains to nature, and in the one called Adam, which pertains to person. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Simul sint et natura* (“there are simultaneously nature”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *simul fuit natura* (“nature was simultaneous”). *Sicut omnes* (“like all others”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *sicut sunt omnes* (“as all are”). *Iste, sive proprio nomine* (“this one, or by a proper name”), manuscript Thu. and manuscripts Gem. and Bec.: *iste, suo proprio nomine* (“this one, by his own proper name”); the Gothic edition: *iste, sive proprio nomine* (“this one, or by a proper name”). *Nomine, ut Adam et Abel* (“by name, such as Adam and Abel”), manuscripts Thu., Gem., Bec., and Cister.: *nomine, ut Adam aut Abel* (“by name, such as Adam or Abel”).]

There is, however, a sin that each person draws along with nature at the very beginning of his existence, and there is a sin that he does not draw along with nature itself, but commits after he has become a person distinct from other persons. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Cum natura in ipsa sui origine* (“with nature at the origin of itself”), manuscripts Thu., Gem., Bec., Vict., and the Gothic edition: *natura in ipsa* (“nature in itself”). *Non trahit cum ipsa* (“does not draw along with it”), manuscripts: *non trahit ab ipsa* (“does not draw from it”).]

The former, which is transmitted at the very beginning, is called original; it can also be called natural—not because it belongs to the essence of nature, but because, on account of nature’s corruption, it is assumed along with it. The sin that each person commits after becoming a person can be called personal, because it is committed through the defect of the person.

By a similar reasoning, justice can be called original and personal. Adam and Eve were originally—that is, at the very beginning of their existence, as soon as they became human beings—just without interruption. Personal justice, however, can be called that which an unjust person receives, although he did not possess it from the beginning. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Quam ab origine* (“which he did not have from the beginning”), manuscripts: *quam in origine* (“which he did not have in the origin”).]

## CHAPTER II [elsewhere I]

### How human nature was corrupted

Therefore, if Adam and Eve had preserved original justice, those who were born from them would have been just originally, as they themselves were. [Note: [Col. 0433D] In manuscript Thu. 391 and the Cistercian manuscript, Chapter II begins here.] But because they sinned personally, [Note: [Col. 0433D] In manuscript Thu. 391 and the Cistercian manuscript, Chapter II continues here.] although originally strong and incorrupt they possessed the power always to preserve justice without difficulty, everything they were became weakened and corrupted.

The body became what it was after sin: subject to the corruption and carnal appetites characteristic of brute animals. The soul, through the corruption of the body and those same appetites, and through the lack of the good things it had lost, became infected with carnal affections. And because the whole of human nature was in them, and nothing of it existed outside them, the whole was weakened and corrupted.
