[Note: [Col. 0433D] *Eisdem appetitibus* (“those same appetites”), manuscripts Vict. and Cister.: *ejusdem appetitibus* (“the same appetites”). *Infecta est* (“became infected”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *infecta* (“infected”). *Extra illos de illa nihil* (“nothing of it existed outside them”), manuscripts and the Gothic edition: *extra ipsos de illa nihil* (“nothing of it existed outside them”).]

There therefore remained in it the obligation of the complete justice it had received, without any injustice, and the obligation of making satisfaction because it had abandoned that justice, together with the corruption it incurred on account of sin. [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Sine omni injustitia* (“without any injustice”), manuscripts Vict., Gem., Bec., and S. Michaelis: *sine omni justitia* (“without any justice”).]

Thus, just as, if it had not sinned, it would have propagated the condition in which God had made it, so after sin it propagates the condition into which it brought itself by sinning.

Since, therefore, human nature is unable by itself either to make satisfaction for sin or to recover the justice it abandoned, and since the body, which is corruptible, weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15), especially when it is weaker—as in infancy and in the mother’s womb, when it cannot even understand justice—it seems necessary [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Infirmius est* (“it is weaker”), manuscripts Vict., Gem., and Bec.: *infirmum est* (“it is weak”); manuscripts Thu. and Vict. 19: *infirmius est* (“it is weaker”); another reading: *infirmus est* (“he is weak”).] that infants be born with the obligation of making satisfaction for the first sin, from which they could always have abstained, and with the obligation of possessing the original justice that they were always able to preserve. [Note: [Col. 0433D–0435A] *Eam in infantibus* (“that [obligation] in infants”), the Gothic edition: *eam ut in infantibus* (“that [obligation] as in infants”). *Quod semper cavere potuit* (“from which he could always have abstained”), manuscript Vict. 19: *quo semper carere* (“which he could always lack”); manuscript Thu. 390: *cavere non potuit* (“he could not abstain from”). *Servare valuit* (“was able to preserve”), manuscript Vict. 19: *servare voluit* (“wished to preserve”); *servare noluit* (“did not wish to preserve”).]

Nor does inability excuse it in infants, since even in them it does not pay what it owes: it makes this obligation for itself by abandoning the justice in the first parents, in whom the whole of human nature existed. [Note: [Col. 0435D] *Ipsa sibi* (“it for itself”), the Gothic edition: *ex ipsa* (“from itself”). *Primis parentibus* (“the first parents”), manuscripts: *primis hominibus* (“the first human beings”).] It is always a debtor in respect of possessing the power that it received in order always to preserve justice. This may be understood as original sin in infants.

Let us add also the sins of near ancestors, which are repaid to the third and fourth generation. Although it may be asked whether all these things are to be understood as belonging to original sin or not, nevertheless, lest I appear to lessen it by raising this question, I shall posit that original sin is such that it cannot be shown to be more serious by anyone.

[Note: [Col. 0435D] *Quaeri possit* (“it may be asked”), manuscript Vict. 19: *dubitari possit* (“it may be doubted”).]

## CHAPTER III

### That there is no sin except in a rational will
Source preparation: exact local restored source; no recovered placeholders.

But whether this whole matter is original sin, or something less [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Or something else, less” in the manuscripts; “or something less”], I think it can in no way be asserted to exist in an infant before the infant possesses a rational soul, just as justice did not exist in Adam before he became a rational human being. For if Adam and Eve had begotten children without prior sin [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts read *generassent sine* ("had begotten without"); Cister. reads *generassent filios sine* ("had begotten children without")], justice would nevertheless not have been in the seed, nor could it have been there before the seed was formed into a living human being. If, therefore, human seed is not capable of receiving justice before it becomes a human being, it cannot receive original sin before it is human [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Before it becomes a human being” in the manuscripts; “before it is human”].

Indeed, there should be no doubt that original sin is injustice. For if every sin is injustice, and original sin is sin, then it is certainly also injustice. But if someone says, “Not every sin is injustice,” let him say that something can at the same time be a sin in someone and yet no injustice exist there [Note: [Col. 0435D] “And be a sin” in the manuscripts; “and yet be some sin”]. This seems incredible.

If, however, original sin is said not to be called sin absolutely, but with the addition of the term “original”—just as a painted man is not truly a man [Note: [Col. 0435D] The Gothic edition has “is not truly a man”; “is not a true man”] but is truly a painted man [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts Thuan. and Vict. 19, and Cister., have “but is truly a painted man”—], then it necessarily follows that an infant who has no sin except original sin is free from sin. Nor was the Son of the Virgin alone among human beings conceived in his mother’s womb and born of his mother without sin. Either, then, an infant who dies without baptism, having no sin besides original sin, is not condemned; or it is condemned without sin. But we accept none of these conclusions [Col. 0435D].

Therefore every sin [Note: [Col. 0435D] Vict. 19 reads *quare et omne* ("therefore also every")] is injustice [Col. 0436A], and original sin is sin absolutely; hence it follows that it is injustice [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts have “it follows that it is injustice”; Thuan. and Cister. have “it follows that it is also injustice”].

Moreover, if God condemns only on account of injustice [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “condemns a human being only”;], and he condemns someone on account of original sin, then original sin is nothing other than injustice. But if this is so, and injustice is nothing other than the absence of the justice that is owed [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts have: “If this is so, original sin is nothing other than injustice, that is, the absence of the justice that is owed”;], for injustice seems to exist only in a nature that, while it ought to have justice, does not have it, then original sin is included under the same definition as injustice.

But if justice is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake, and this rectitude can exist only in a rational nature, then no nature is debtor to justice except a rational nature, just as no nature is capable of receiving justice except a rational nature [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have: “Therefore, in this way, no nature is debtor to justice except a rational nature, just as no nature is capable of receiving justice except a rational nature”]. Since injustice, then, can exist only where justice ought to exist, original sin—which is injustice—exists only in a rational nature.

Now rational nature is found only in God, in an angel, and in the human soul, by which the human being is called rational and without which he is not human. Since, therefore, original sin exists neither in God nor in an angel, it exists only in the rational soul of a human being.

It must also be understood that justice can exist only in the will, if justice is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake; therefore, neither can injustice exist except in the will. For the absence of justice is not called injustice except where justice ought to exist [Note: [Col. 0435D] “For the absence of justice is not called …,” etc.]. Nothing, therefore, apart from justice or injustice itself, is called just or unjust except the will, or something on account of a just or unjust will. Through the will we call a human being or an angel just or unjust, and a soul or an action just or unjust.

## CHAPTER IV. That nothing is just or unjust in itself except justice or injustice itself, and that nothing is punished except the will [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Or injustice” is omitted by the manuscripts Vict., Gem., and Bec.].

For nothing—whether substance, action, or anything else considered in itself—is just except justice, or unjust or sinful except injustice; nor is the will itself, in which justice or injustice exists, just or unjust in itself.

For one thing is that power of the soul by which the soul wills something [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “wills something”;], a power that may be called the instrument of willing, just as sight is the instrument of seeing; this is what we call the will. Another thing is justice: by possessing it, the will is called just, and by lacking it, unjust. The affections and uses of this same instrument are also called volitions [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *dicuntur enim* ("are indeed called") for *dicuntur etiam* ("are also called"); Col. 0437D reads *affectionis et usus* ("of affection and use") for *affectiones et usus* ("affections and uses")], but it would take too long to insert that discussion here.

Nor are the appetites that the Apostle calls “the flesh,” which desires against the spirit (Romans 8), or “the law of sin,” which is in the members and resists the law of the mind (Galatians 5), just or unjust when considered in themselves [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts have “when they are considered in themselves”;]. They do not make the person who experiences them just or unjust; rather, they make him unjust only through the will, when he consents to them when he ought not.

The Apostle says that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh (Romans 8)—that is, who do not consent by the will of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “that is, who do not consent to the flesh by their will”; Vict. 19 has “that is, who do not consent to carnal desire”]. For if the experience of these impulses, without consent, made a person unjust, condemnation would follow [Note: [Col. 0437D] Thuan. 391 has “would make him unjust; it would not follow”;]. Thus it is not experiencing them but consenting to them that is sin.

For if they were unjust in themselves [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts have “if they were just in themselves unjust”; the Gothic edition has “if they were unjust in themselves”; some manuscripts have “if they were just in themselves”], then whenever one consented to them, they would make him unjust. But when brute animals consent to them, they are not called unjust. Again, if they were sins, they would be removed in baptism, when every sin is wiped away; but it is plainly evident that this does not happen. Therefore there is no injustice in their essence, but in the rational will that follows them disorderly.

When the will resists them, delighting in the law of God according to the inward person, the will is just. He calls the justice commanded by the law the law of God because it is from God, and the law of the mind because it is understood through the mind. Likewise, the old law is called the law of God because it comes from God, and the law of Moses because it was administered through Moses.

What I said—that no action is called unjust in itself, but on account of an unjust will—is clear in the case of actions that can sometimes be performed without injustice, such as killing a human being, as Phinehas did (Numbers 25), or sexual union between the two sexes, as in marriage, or even among brute animals [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts Vict., Bec., Gem., Thuan. 391, and Cister. have “and likewise among brute animals”;].

In the case of things that can never exist except unjustly, such as perjury and certain other things that ought not even to be named, this is not so easily understood. But if some action by which something is done [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “by which something else is done”;] exists only while something is being done [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “while something else is being done”;] and passes away once it has been completed, so that it no longer exists; or if it is a work that comes into being and remains—for example, when something that ought not to be written is written, the act of writing passes away while the written forms remain—then, if the action were a sin, once the action had passed away and no longer existed, the sin would likewise pass away and no longer exist. Or, if the work that comes into being remained, the sin would never be erased.

Yet we see that sins are often not erased when the action has passed away, and that they are erased while the work remains. Therefore neither the action, which passes away, nor the work, which remains, is ever itself a sin [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “Therefore the action …”;].

Finally, if the members and senses through which voluntary actions are unjustly performed were accused, they could reply:

“God subjected us, and the power that is in us, to the will, so that at its command we cannot refrain from moving ourselves and doing what it wills. Indeed, the will moves us as its instruments and performs the works that we seem to perform. We cannot resist it by ourselves, nor can the works that it performs fail to occur. We cannot and ought not disobey the mastery that God has given us; when we obey it, we obey God, who gave us this law. What fault, then, lies with the members, senses, or works that God subjected in this way to the will, if they preserve what God ordained for them?”

Whatever they do, therefore, must be attributed wholly to the will.

Since this is so, someone may perhaps wonder why, on account of the will’s guilt, the members and senses are punished [Note: [Col. 0437D] Thuan. has “are punished or”]. But this is not so: only the will is punished. For nothing is punishment to anything except what is against its will, and nothing experiences punishment except what has a will. The members and senses, however, will nothing in themselves.

Therefore, just as the will operates in the members and senses, so it is itself tormented or delighted in them. If someone does not accept this, let him understand that in the senses and members it is only the soul—in which the will exists—that experiences and acts, and that therefore it is in them that the soul is tormented or delighted.

It remains customary, however, to call the actions performed by an unjust will sins, because the sin is in the will through which they are performed. Certain names are also given to actions to signify that they are performed unjustly, such as fornication and lying. But one thing is meant when the action or utterance itself is considered [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts Gem., Vict., and S. Mich. have “something else is understood”;], and another when it is considered whether it is performed justly or unjustly.

## CHAPTER V. That evil, which is sin or injustice, is nothing

Finally, every essence is from God, and nothing from God is unjust [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts have “nothing unjust”;]. Therefore no essence is unjust in itself.

Injustice, however, is altogether nothing, like blindness. For blindness is nothing other than the absence of sight where sight ought to be. It is no more something in an eye where sight ought to be than in a piece of wood where sight ought not to be [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts have “something else in the eye”;].

Injustice is not some substance by which the soul is infected and corrupted like a body by poison [Col. 0438D], and which causes it to do something [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts have “causes it to do something else”;], as seems to happen when a malicious person performs evil deeds.

For just as, when an untamed beast breaks its chains and rages about, and when a ship, if the pilot lets go of the rudder, wanders among the winds and mountains of the sea and is driven into every danger, we say that the absence of the chain or rudder causes this—not because their absence is something or does anything, but because, if they were present, they would prevent the beast from raging or the ship from perishing—so, when an evil person rages and is driven into every danger of his soul, which consists in evil deeds, we cry out that injustice produces these things [Note: [Col. 0439D] Thuan. 546 has “injustice produces this”; Thuan. 391 has “injustice produces these works”;].

Yet injustice is not any essence, nor does it do anything. Rather, the will—to which all the voluntary movements of the whole human being are subject—when justice is absent, is driven by various appetites and, light-minded, unrestrained, and without a guide, hurls itself and everything subject to it into manifold evils [Col. 0439B]. Justice, if it were present, would prevent all this from occurring [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts Vict., Gem., Bec., Thuan., and Cister. have “and this whole thing”;].

From this it is easily understood that injustice has no essence, although custom calls the affections and acts of an unjust will—which, considered in themselves, are something—injustice [Note: [Col. 0439D] In Thuan. 391, “From this, then, it is easily understood…”;].

By the same reasoning we understand that evil is nothing. For just as injustice is nothing other than the absence of the justice that is owed, so evil is nothing other than the absence of the good that is owed. No essence, even though it is called evil, is nothing; nor does being evil mean being something for any essence [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “nor does being evil mean being evil”;].

For, in the case of no essence, being evil means anything other than lacking the good that it ought to have. But lacking the good that ought to be present is not being something [Col. 0439C]. Therefore, being evil is not being something for any essence [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts Vict., Gem., Bec., and Thuan. 391 have “Therefore, being evil…”].

I have spoken briefly and without hesitation about evil, which is always nothing, namely, insofar as it is injustice [Note: [Col. 0439D] Cister., Thuan., Vict., and the Gothic edition have “without hesitation, just as concerning injustice”;].

For a privation or disadvantage (*incommoditas*) is evil—whence disadvantages are called evils—which is sometimes nothing, as deafness and blindness; sometimes it seems to be something, as pain and sadness [Note: [Col. 0439D] Thuan. has “which sometimes are nothing”; Vict. has “sometimes seem to be something”;].

That justice is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake; that injustice is nothing other than the absence of the justice that is owed, and has no essence [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts Vict., Gem., and Bec. have “and has no essence”;]; that every essence is from God, and that nothing is from God except what is good—I think I have sufficiently demonstrated in the treatise I wrote *On the Fall of the Devil* (Book 1, chapters 15–16). But I discussed justice more fully in the work I published *On Truth* (chapter 13).

[Col. 0440A]

## CHAPTER VI. That when God punishes for sin, he does not punish for nothing

When some people hear that sin is nothing, they usually say: “If sin is nothing, why does God punish a human being for sin, since no one ought to be punished for nothing?” Although the question is humble, something must nevertheless be said briefly to them, because they are ignorant of what they ask.

Although the absence of justice is equally nothing both where justice ought to be and where it ought not to be, God nevertheless rightly punishes sinners not for nothing but on account of something. For, as I said in the aforementioned book, he both exacts from the unwilling the honor owed to him, which they refused willingly to render [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts Vict., Bec., Gem., Thuan., S. Mich., and Cister. have “on account of something, because, as I said in the aforementioned book, the honor owed”;], and, so that nothing disordered may exist in his kingdom, assigns them a separate place from the just, according to a fitting order [Col. 0440B].

He does not punish creatures in whom justice ought not to exist for the absence of justice—that is, for nothing—for there is nothing that he demands from them, nor does the appropriate order of the universe require this [Note: [Col. 0439D] Vict. 13 has “demand”].

Thus, when God punishes for sin, which is the absence of the justice that is owed and is itself nothing, he does not punish altogether for nothing. It is true that unless there is something on account of which he ought to punish, he does not punish for nothing [Note: [Col. 0439D] The Cistercian manuscript deletes “he does not punish for nothing”].

That sin and injustice are nothing; that they exist only in a rational will; and that no essence properly speaking is called unjust except the will: from what has been said, I think this is clear.

## CHAPTER VII. How human seed is called unclean, and how a human being is conceived in iniquities, although sin is not in the seed

It therefore seems to follow either that an infant has a rational soul immediately from conception [Note: [Col. 0439D] Vict. 19 has “had a rational soul”;], without which it cannot have a rational will, or that original sin is not in it as soon as it is conceived.

But that it has a rational soul immediately from conception is accepted by no human understanding. For it would follow that whenever human seed is received and perishes from the very moment of its reception, before it reaches human form [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts have “is born before it reaches”;], the human soul in it is condemned, since it is not reconciled through Christ. This is altogether too absurd.

This part of the division must therefore be entirely rejected. But if the infant does not have sin immediately from conception, what does Job mean when he says to God [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “What does Job say?”]:

“Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” (Job 14:4.) [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts Vict. and the Gothic edition have “Is it not you who alone…”.]

And how is what David says true?

“In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50:7).

I shall therefore ask, if I can, how human beings are said to be conceived from unclean seed, in iniquities and in sins, even though sin is not in infants immediately from conception [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “to be conceived in iniquities and sins”;].

Sacred Scripture often asserts that something exists which at present does not exist [Note: [Col. 0441D] Vict. 19 has “when it does not exist”;], simply because it is nevertheless destined to exist. Thus God says to Adam concerning the forbidden tree: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Genesis 2:7). He does not mean that Adam died bodily on that day, but that on that day he received the necessity of dying at some time.

Paul likewise says, because of the necessity of dying at some time: “But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification” (Romans 8:10) [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts Vict. 9 and 13 have “Christ is in us”;]. The bodies of those to whom he spoke were not dead, but were destined to die because of sin, since “through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin, death” (Romans 5:12).

In Adam we all sinned when he sinned—not because we ourselves, who did not yet exist, sinned at that time, but because we were destined to exist from him. And at that time the necessity arose that, once we existed, we would sin, since “through the disobedience of one, many were constituted sinners” (ibid. 5:19).

In the same way, a human being may be understood to be conceived from unclean seed, in iniquities and in sins—not because the uncleanness of sin, or sin or iniquity, is in the seed [Col. 0441C], but because from that seed and from conception itself, from which the human being begins to exist, he receives the necessity [Note: [Col. 0441D] Vict. 19 has “receives the power”;] that, once he has a rational soul, he will possess the uncleanness of sin, which is nothing other than sin and iniquity.

For even if the infant is generated from a vicious desire [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts have “even if the infant is generated from seed of vicious desire”;], guilt is no more in the seed than it is in spittle or blood if someone spits with an evil will or emits some of his blood. It is not the spittle [Note: [Col. 0441D] Vict. 19 has “not spittle”;] or the blood that is accused, but the evil will.

It is therefore clear how sin is not in infants immediately from conception and yet the things I have cited from sacred Scripture are true [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts have “are true”;]. Sin is not in them because they do not have a will, without which sin does not exist [Note: [Col. 0441D] Thuan. and Cister. omit “sin”;], and yet it is said to be in them because in the seed they draw the necessity of sinning [Col. 0442A] when they will already be human beings [Note: [Col. 0441D] Vict. 19 has “when they were no longer human beings”;].

If these things are true, as I think they are, then the conclusion concerning parent and child holds: because the child has no will, there is no sin in it.

## CHAPTER VIII. That in the seed taken from the Virgin there is neither sin nor the necessity of future sin

It is therefore evident that in what the Son of God assumed from the Virgin into his own person there could be no stain of sin. But it has been said that seed is drawn from parents with the necessity of future sin, once it has been animated by a rational soul. This is so for no other reason than that human nature, as I said, is born in infants with the obligation of making satisfaction for the sin of Adam and, as I have maintained, of their immediate parents—a satisfaction it cannot make; and so long as it does not make it, it sins.

It is also so because human nature, by itself, cannot possess the justice it abandoned [Note: [Col. 0441D] Cister. has “which it abandons”;], and because the soul, burdened by the corruptible body [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “which is burdened”;], cannot even understand that justice which cannot be preserved or possessed without being understood.

Therefore, if it can be shown that the seed taken from the Virgin was free from these necessities, it will be clear that it drew with it no necessity of sin. It can easily be shown that the necessity by which human nature, by itself, cannot recover justice, and the necessity by which the corruptible body burdens the soul so that it can neither preserve that same justice, once received, at mature age without the help of grace, nor even understand it in infants [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts have “nor even in infants”;], are foreign to that seed, through the personal unity of the nature that assumes and the nature that is assumed—provided first that the necessity by which it seems bound to make satisfaction for the sins of its first and immediate parents is removed.

But there will be no doubt that no debt follows from the immediate parents if it can be understood to be free from the debt of the first parents [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscripts Thuan., Vict., and Cister. have “free from the debt of the first parents”;]. With God’s help, I shall therefore first investigate how this can be known, so that, once it has been demonstrated, there will be no need to labor at length over the remaining points.

## CHAPTER IX. Why the sin by which the human race is condemned is imputed more to Adam than to Eve, although he sinned afterward and through her

First, it seems to me that we must ask why the sin by which the human race was condemned is more frequently and specifically imputed to Adam than to Eve [Col. 0442D], although she sinned first and Adam afterward and through her [Note: [Col. 0443C] Cister., Thuan., Vict., and the Gothic edition have “although she sinned first”; Vict. 19 has “although she was first”].

For the Apostle says: “But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14).

Many other passages are also read that seem to accuse Adam more than Eve. I think this happens either because the union of the two is entirely understood under the name of the principal part, just as the whole is often signified through a part; or because Adam, together with his rib—which had been built into a woman—could still be called Adam, as it is written: “Because God made them male and female, and blessed them” (Genesis 1:17). “And he called their name Adam on the day when they were created.”

Or it is because, if it had been not Adam but Eve alone who sinned, the whole human race would not have had to perish, but Eve alone. For God could have made another woman from Adam, in whom he had created the seed of all human beings [Note: [Col. 0443C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “in whom he had created all human beings”;], through whom God’s purpose concerning Adam could be fulfilled.

For these same reasons I shall use the name Adam to signify both of them, except when it is necessary to distinguish them [Note: [Col. 0443C] Thuan. 546 has “signifying”;].

## CHAPTER X. Why those who were not aware of Adam’s sin are burdened by it

Each person is Adam’s son and a human being by creation, Adam by propagation, and a person by individuality [Note: [Col. 0443C] Vict. 13 has “by individual identity”;], by which he is distinguished from others.

For a human being does not have existence from Adam, but through Adam. Just as Adam did not make himself human, so he did not make the nature of propagation in himself. Rather, God, who created him human, placed this nature in him [Note: [Col. 0443C] Cister., Vict., S. Mich., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition have “placed this creation in him”;] so that human beings might be propagated from him.

There is no doubt about the source from which each person is bound by the debt under discussion. It is not because he is a human being, nor because he is a person. For if each person were liable for this debt because he is a human being or a person, Adam would necessarily have been bound by this debt before he sinned, because he was a human being and a person. That is utterly absurd.

It therefore remains that he is a debtor solely because he is Adam—not simply because he is Adam, but because he is sinful Adam. It would follow, indeed, that if Adam had never sinned, those propagated from him would nevertheless have been born with this debt. That is impious.

It is not inappropriate to repeat here what was said above: namely, why each person is burdened by Adam’s sin or debt simply because he is propagated from him, even though he was not aware of that sin.

When God made Adam, he placed in him the nature of propagation. He subjected it to Adam’s power, so that Adam might use it according to his will, so long as he himself wished to remain subject to God. He would not use it with a bestial [Note: [Col. 0443C] Vict. 19 has “not so that he would use it as something bestial”;] and irrational [Note: [Col. 0443C] Thuan. and Cister. have “or irrational”;] pleasure, but with a human and rational will.

For just as it belongs to beasts to will nothing rationally, so it would belong to human beings to will nothing without reason [Note: [Col. 0443C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “so it belongs to human beings”;]. They ought always to do this, because Adam received this power and was always able to preserve it.

God also gave him this grace [Note: [Col. 0443C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “God gave him this grace”;]: just as, when he created Adam, without any nature of propagation or will of a creature operating, he made him at once both rational and just, so, if Adam did not sin, those whom he would generate through the operation of nature and will would likewise be just as soon as they had a rational soul.

For by the same reasoning by which it is shown that a rational nature was created just—which he demonstrated in the aforementioned treatise (*On the Fall of the Devil*, Book 2, chapter 1)—it is also proved that those propagated from human nature without prior sin would necessarily have justice together with rationality.

Indeed, the one who created the first human being without generation from parents also creates those who come from him through the created nature of propagation [Note: [Col. 0443C] Thuan. 546 has “through the creature”;]. Every human being, therefore, if sin had not preceded, would have been, like Adam, both just and rational.

But because Adam did not wish to remain subject to God’s will, the nature of propagation, although it remained, was not subject to his will as it would have been if he had not sinned. He lost the grace that he could have preserved for those propagated from him [Note: [Col. 0443C] The manuscripts have “that he could have propagated from himself”;]. And all who are propagated through the operation of the nature he had received are born bound by his debt.

Therefore, because human nature—which was wholly in Adam, so that nothing of it existed outside him—sinned without any necessity and dishonored God, and consequently could not make satisfaction by itself [Note: [Col. 0443C] Thuan. 546 has “and therefore by itself”; Vict., Thuan. 391, and the Gothic edition have “because by itself”; Vict. 19 has “and therefore in his place by himself”;], Human nature lost the grace that, once received, it could always have preserved for those propagated from it [Note: [Col. 0443C] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read *propagandi de se* ("to be propagated from itself") for *propagandis de se* ("for those propagated from it")]. And human nature carries sin, accompanied by the punishment of sin, with it, however extensively it is propagated through the given nature of propagation.

[Col. 0445A]

## CHAPTER XI. That propagation from the Virgin is not subject to the law and merits of natural propagation, and that there are three courses of things [Note: [Col. 0445D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have “and that there are three courses of things”].

### Additional textual apparatus

The following notes preserve readings omitted from the first draft. Each entry is keyed to its exact source locus; quoted Latin is retained where English cannot represent an inflection, word order, or spelling distinction.

- **[Col. 0435D], “original sin … something less”:** manuscripts read *sive aliud minus* (“or something else, less”) for *sive aliquid minus* (“or something less”).
- **[Col. 0435D], “before it is human”:** manuscripts read *homo fiat* (“before the human being comes to be”) for *homo sit* (“before it is human”).
- **[Col. 0435D], “something can be sin”:** manuscripts read *et esse peccatum* (“and be sin”) for *et esse aliquod peccatum* (“and be some sin”).
- **[Col. 0435D], “not truly a man”:** the Gothic edition reads *non vere homo est* (“is not truly a man”) for *non verus est homo* (“is not a true man”); manuscripts Thuan., Vict. 19, and Cister. read *homo pictus* (“a painted man”) for *sed vere est homo pictus* (“but is truly a painted man”).
- **[Col. 0435D], “hence every sin”:** Vict. 19 reads *quare et omne* (“therefore also every”) for *quare omne* (“therefore every”).
- **[Col. 0435D], “hence it follows”:** Vict. reads *sequitur, quod est injustitia* (“it follows that it is injustice”); Thuan. and Cister. read *sequitur, quod est et injustitia* (“it follows that it is also injustice”), for *sequitur, quia est et injustitia*.
- **[Col. 0435D], “God condemns only”:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *damnat hominem nisi* (“condemns a human being only”) for *damnat nisi* (“condemns only”).
- **[Col. 0435D], definition of injustice:** manuscripts read *originale peccatum non est aliud quam injustitia, id est absentia debitae justitiae* (“original sin is nothing other than injustice, that is, absence of owed justice”) for the printed *et injustitia non est…* (“and injustice is nothing other than…”).
- **[Col. 0435D], rational nature:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *ergo ita non est ulla natura debitrix justitiae… sicut nulla natura susceptibilis…* (“therefore no nature is debtor to justice… just as no nature is capable…”) for the printed wording.
- **[Col. 0435D], will:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *vult aliud* (“wills another thing”) for *vult aliquid* (“wills something”); they also read *dicuntur enim* (“are indeed called”) for *dicuntur etiam* (“are also called”).
- **[Col. 0437D], appetites:** manuscripts read *per se considerandi* (“to be considered in themselves”) for *per se considerati* (“considered in themselves”); manuscripts and the Gothic edition omit *hominem* (“the human being”) in *non enim hominem justum*.
- **[Col. 0437D], Apostle and walking:** manuscripts read *dicit enim idem Apostolus* (“for the same Apostle says”) for *dicit enim Apostolus*; Vict. 19 reads *ambulant, sed secundum spiritum, id est* (“walk, but according to the Spirit, that is”) for *ambulant, id est*.
- **[Col. 0437D], consent and condemnation:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *id est, non carni voluntate* (“that is, not consenting to the flesh by will”); Vict. 19 reads *id est qui non carnali voluntati* (“that is, those who do not consent to carnal desire”). Thuan. 391 reads *faceret, non sequeretur* (“would make [him unjust], condemnation would not follow”) for *facerent, sequeretur* (“would make [him unjust], condemnation would follow”).
- **[Col. 0437D], unjust in themselves:** manuscripts read the corrupt alternative *si enim injusti justi per se essent*; the Gothic edition reads *si enim per se injusti essent* (“if they were unjust in themselves”); another manuscript reading is *si enim justi per se essent* (“if they were just in themselves”).
- **[Col. 0437D], examples:** Vict. reads *ut hominem* (“as [to] killing a human being”) for *ut est hominem*; Vict., Bec., Gem., Thuan. 391, and Cister. read *et sicut in brutis* (“and likewise among brute animals”) for *sive in brutis* (“or among brute animals”).
- **[Col. 0437D], action and work:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *qua fit aliud* (“by which something else is done”) and *dum fit aliud* (“while something else is being done”); they read *fiunt figurae* (“figures are made”) for *fiunt scripturae* (“writings are made”). Manuscripts read *saepe non* (“often not”) for *saepe et non* (“often and not”), and *quare actio* (“therefore action”) for *quare nec actio* (“therefore neither action”).
- **[Col. 0437D], members and senses:** manuscripts read *non possimus movere nos* (“we cannot move ourselves”) for *non possimus non movere nos* (“we cannot fail to move ourselves”). Vict. reads *dominae quam* (“the mistress whom”); the Gothic edition *Domine quam* (“the Lord whom”); another reading *dominationi quam* (“the dominion which”), for the printed *dominae, quam*.
- **[Col. 0437D], punishment and agency:** Thuan. reads *puniantur vel* (“are punished, or…”) for *puniuntur et* (“are punished and…”). Manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *si igitur* (“if therefore”) for *sicut igitur* (“just as therefore”). Cister., Vict., Thuan., S. Mich., and the Gothic edition read *quas fecit* (“which [the unjust will] performed”) for *quas facit* (“which it performs”).
- **[Col. 0437D], action/utterance:** Gem., Vict., and S. Mich. read *aliud intelligi* (“something else to be meant”) for *aliud intelligitur* (“one thing is meant”); manuscripts read *cum quasi actio* (“when, as it were, an action”) for *cum ipsa actio* (“when the action itself”).
- **[Col. 0437D], injustice as no thing:** Thuan. reads *nihil injustum* (“nothing unjust”) for *nihil est injustum* (“nothing is unjust”); manuscripts read *quae res non magis* (“which thing no more”) for *quae non magis* (“which no more”), and *aliud in oculo* (“something else in the eye”) for *aliquid in oculo* (“something in the eye”).
- **[Col. 0437D], infection:** manuscripts read *res quia inficiatur* (“a thing because/by which it is infected”) for *res qua inficiatur* (“a thing by which it is infected”).
- **[Col. 0439D], ship and injustice:** manuscripts read *dimittit eam* (“lets it go”) for *dimittat eam* (“should let it go”). Thuan. 546 reads *hoc operatur injustitia* (“injustice produces this”); Thuan. 391 *haec operatur injustitia* (“injustice produces these [things]”); the other reading is *haec opera facit injustitia* (“injustice performs these deeds”).
- **[Col. 0439D], Chapter V continuation:** Vict., Gem., Bec., Thuan., and Cister. read *et quod totum* (“and all of which”) for *quod totum* (“all of which”); in Thuan. 391 *et his ergo facile etc.* (“and from these, therefore, easily, etc.”) begins here.
- **[Col. 0439D], evil:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *nec malum esse* (“nor to be evil”) for *nec malam esse* (“nor to be evil [feminine]”); the Gothic edition reads *illi esse* for *ulli esse* (“to be for it / for any [essence]”). Manuscripts read *malam essentiam esse* (“for an essence to be evil”) for *malam esse* (“to be evil”), and Vict., Gem., Bec., Thuan. 391 read *quare malum esse* (“therefore, to be evil”) for *quare malam esse*.
- **[Col. 0439D], disadvantage:** manuscripts read *indubitanter sicut de injustitia* (“without hesitation, as concerning injustice”) for *indubitanter quod est injustitia* (“without hesitation, insofar as it is injustice”); they read *enim non est malum* (“for it is not evil”) for *enim est malum* (“for it is evil”). Thuan. has *aliquando nihil sunt* (“are sometimes nothing”), and Vict. *videntur esse* (“seem to be”), for the singular printed forms.
- **[Col. 0439D], Chapter VI:** Vict., Gem., and Bec. read *et nullam habet* (“and has no essence”) for *et nullam habeat* (“and may have no essence”). Thuan. 391 reads *ab injustis* (“from the unjust”) for *ab invitis* (“from the unwilling”). Vict. 13 reads *expostulat* (“demands”) for *postulat* (“requires”). Cister. deletes *non* in *non punit pro nihilo* (“does not punish for nothing”).
- **[Col. 0439D], Chapter VII heading and readings:** Vict., Gem., Bec., and S. Mich. read *quod semen* (“that seed”) for *quomodo semen* (“how seed”); Vict. 19 reads *animam habebat rationalem* (“had a rational soul”) for *animam habet rationalem* (“has a rational soul”), and manuscripts *parit antequam* (“gives birth before”) for *perit antequam* (“perishes before”).
- **[Col. 0439D–0441D], Job and conception:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *quid dicit Job* (“what does Job say?”) for *quid est quod dicit Job*; Vict. and the Gothic edition *nisi tu qui* (“unless you who”) for *nonne tu qui* (“is it not you who”). Manuscripts and the Gothic edition omit the first *in* in *iniquitatibus et peccatis concipi* (“to be conceived in iniquities and sins”). Vict. 19 reads *quando non est* (“when it does not exist”) for *quod modo non est* (“which now does not exist”).
- **[Col. 0441D], Paul and Adam:** Vict. 9 and 13 read *Christus in nobis est* (“Christ is in us”) for *in vobis* (“in you”); Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read *sic in Adam omnes* (“thus in Adam all”) for *sicut in Adam omnes* (“as in Adam all”); manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *facta est illi* (“it was made to him”) for *facta est illa* (“that arose”).
- **[Col. 0441D], seed and infant:** Vict. 19 reads *accipit potestatem* (“receives the power”) for *accipit necessitatem* (“receives the necessity”). Manuscripts read *et si ex vitiosa concupiscentia semine generetur* (“even if generated from seed of vicious desire”) for *etsi vitiosa concupiscentia generetur*; Vict. 19 reads *non sputum* (“not spittle”) for *non enim sputum* (“for not spittle”). Manuscripts read *vera sunt quae* (“the things are true which”) for *vera sint quae* (“may the things be true which”), and Thuan. and Cister. omit *peccatum* (“sin”) in *non inest peccatum*.
- **[Col. 0441D–0442A], future humanity:** Vict. 19 reads *homines jam non erant* (“they were no longer human beings”) for *homines jam erunt* (“they will already be human beings”).
- **[Col. 0441D], Chapter VIII:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *quod in eo* (“that in it”) for *quoniam in eo* (“because in it”); Vict. 19 *hoc itaque* (“therefore this”) for *hoc utique* (“certainly this”); manuscripts *cum debeo* (“when/since I owe”) for *cum debito* (“with a debt”). Cister. reads *quam deserunt* (“which they abandon”) for *quam peccando deseruit* (“which it abandoned by sinning”); manuscripts and the Gothic edition *quae gravatur* (“which is weighed down”) for *quae aggravatur* (“which weighs down”).
- **[Col. 0441D], satisfactions:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *quod sola quidem* (“that alone indeed”) for *quod illa quidem* (“that it indeed”); manuscripts *nec infantibus saltem* (“nor even infants”) for *nec in infantibus saltem* (“nor even in infants”). At *Sed quod illud nullum*, Thuan. 546 reads *sed quia illud nullum* (“but because that is no…”), Thuan. 391 *sed quod nullum* (“but that no…”), manuscripts *sed quod illum* (“but that him…”), against the printed *sed quod illud nullum*. Manuscripts Thuan., Vict., and Cister. read *a debito primorum parentum intelligi* (“to be understood free from the debt of the first parents”) for *a debito primorum liberum intelligi*.
- **[Col. 0441D–0443C], Chapters IX–X:** manuscripts read *imputatur* (“is imputed”) for *imputetur* (“may be imputed”); Cister., Thuan., Vict., and the Gothic edition *cum ipsa prius* (“although she herself first”), while Vict. 19 has *quanquam illa prior* (“although she [was] first”), for *cum illa prior*. Manuscripts Thuan. read *et ille* (“and he”) for *et Adam*; Thuan. and Cister. *totum hominum genus* (“the whole race of human beings”) for *totum humanum genus*; manuscripts and the Gothic edition *omnium creaverat* (“had created [the seed] of all”) for *omnium hominum creaverat*.
- **[Col. 0443C], Chapter X opening:** Thuan. 546 reads *significando* (“by signifying”) for *significabo* (“I shall signify”). Vict. 3 reads *filius Adae homo per* (“Adam's son, human by”); Vict. 19, S. Mich., Gem., and Bec. *filius Dei et per* (“son of God and by”), for *filius Adae et homo per*. Vict. 13 reads *per individualitatem* (“by individuality”) for *per individuitatem* (“by individual identity”).
- **[Col. 0443C], Adam and existence:** manuscripts read *habet homo esse ab Adam* (“a human being has being from Adam”) for *habet esse hominem ab Adam* (“has being a human from Adam”). Cister., Vict., S. Mich., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read *hanc creaturam* (“this creature/creation”) for *hanc naturam* (“this nature”). Manuscripts read *ad hoc debitum* (“to this debt”) for *hoc debito* (“by this debt”). In Thuan. 391 Chapter 10 begins at *Non incongruum est etc.*; Vict., Gem., Bec., and Cister. read *hoc repetere* (“to repeat this”) for *hic repetere* (“to repeat here”).
- **[Col. 0443C], propagation:** manuscripts read *cum enim fecit Deus Adam* (“for when God made Adam”) for *cum fecit Deus Adam* (“when God made Adam”). Vict. 19 reads *non ut illa uteretur bestiali* (“not that he would use it bestially”); other manuscripts *non illa uteretur ut bestiali*; the printed reading is *nam non illa uteretur bestiali*. Thuan. and Cister. read *vel irrationali* (“or irrational”) for *et irrationali* (“and irrational”). Manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *ita hominum est* (“so it is of human beings”) for *ita hominum esset* (“so it would be of human beings”).
- **[Col. 0443C], grace and final sentence:** manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *illi Deus gratiam* (“God [gave] him grace”) for *illi Deus hanc gratiam* (“God [gave] him this grace”), and *creat etiam omnes qui* (“also creates all who”) for *creat etiam eos qui* (“also creates those who”). Thuan. 546 reads *per creaturam* (“through the creature”) for *per creatam* (“through the created [nature]”). Manuscripts read *de se propagandi* (“to be propagated from himself”) for *de se propagandis* (“for those propagated from himself”).
- **[Col. 0443C–0445D], conclusion:** Thuan. 546 reads *unde et per se* (“whence also by itself”); Vict., Thuan. 391, and the Gothic edition *unde quia per se* (“whence because by itself”); Vict. 19 *unde pro eo per se* (“whence in its place by itself”), for printed *unde per se*. Manuscripts and the Gothic edition read *propagandi de se* (“of propagating/begetting from himself”) for *propagandis de se* (“for those propagated from himself”). At the Chapter XI heading they read *et quod tres sint cursus rerum* (“and that there are three courses of things”) for *et quod tres sint* (“and that there are three”).

Provenance: Luna translation/repair; Terra review did not certify; native Terra source repair.

Now it must be carefully considered whether this supposed inheritance of sin and of the punishment of sin justly passes through the Virgin to the man propagated from Adam. [Note: “Now, therefore, the manuscripts and Gothic Edition read ‘now diligently.’”] [Note: The manuscripts of Bec, Gem, Victor 3 and 9, and Saint Michael, and the Gothic Edition read “and the punishment of sin.”] [Note: The Gothic Edition reads “to man through the Virgin,” rather than “through man to the Virgin.”] [Note: “Propagated” is feminine in the manuscripts of Bec, Gem, Victor 3, 9, 19, and Saint Michael.] [Note: Thu. 546 reads “may pass through.”]

It is certain that Adam received the nature of propagation only through a man and a woman together. For human nature does not possess—and it is recognized as impossible—that a man alone or a woman alone should generate a human being, with nature and its own will alone operating. [Note: The manuscripts read “may be able to generate” rather than “should generate.”] [Note: The manuscripts read “by will alone” rather than “by nature and its own will.”]

For just as the clay of the earth had not received the nature or will by which, through its operation, the first man might be made from it—although it was the material from which God could make him—so woman was not made from the man’s rib, nor man from woman alone, through the operation of nature or human will. [Note: Victor 19 reads “did not receive” rather than “had not received.”] But God, by his own will and power, made one man from clay, another from woman alone, and woman from man alone. For although nothing happens except by God’s will, whether he acts or permits it, nevertheless some things are effected solely by his power and will, some by created nature, and some by the will of a creature. [Note: The manuscripts read “the will of nature,” but the manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “the will of a creature.”]

But just as created nature can do nothing by itself except what it has received from God’s will, [Note: The manuscripts of Victor, Gem, Bec, Cister, and the Gothic Edition read “what it has received from God.”] so the will of a creature cannot operate anything by itself except what nature assists or permits. [Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “the will of a creature cannot,” rather than “the will of nature cannot.”]

God’s will alone made the natures of things in the beginning, assigning to some of them wills suited to each one, so that natures and wills, according to the order handed down to them, might perform their own work in the course of things. And even now he does many things when he operates through those same natures and wills what they could in no way accomplish according to their own use and purpose. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor, Thu, Saint Michael, and the Gothic Edition read “they could in no way accomplish”; some manuscripts read “it could in no way accomplish.”]

For the work is solely God’s will when the sea provides a dry path through itself for the people; when the dead rise; when water is suddenly changed into wine; when human hearts are taught by the Holy Spirit things that they know neither by themselves nor through any other creature; when harmful wills, under the sole direction of grace, are turned from their impulse toward what is beneficial; and when many other things occur [Note: Thu. 391 reads “many things occur”; Thu. 546 reads “many things do” and omits “occur.”] that neither a creature nor its will would accomplish according to its customary course. [Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “would accomplish”; the present text has “operates.”]

Nature draws light things upward and heavy things downward. It causes the earth—sometimes after the will has first cultivated and sown it, and sometimes with no work of the will preceding—to produce countless herbs and trees and make them bear fruit, along with many other things that we recognize more easily through experience than through instruction. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor, Gem, and Bec read “more easily through experience”; some manuscripts read “more easily by sight.”]

Those things of this kind are attributed to the will, [Note: The Gothic Edition reads “are of this kind”; some manuscripts read “are human.”] such as traveling, building, writing, speaking, and similar activities, which the will alone performs. [Note: The manuscripts of Gem, Bec, and Saint Michael read “also to do”; the present text reads “to travel.”]

Since, then, everything that happens, if carefully considered, happens either by the will of God alone, or by nature according to the power God has implanted in it, or by the will of a creature—and since those things that neither created nature nor the will of a creature performs, but God alone performs, are always miraculous—it is evident that there are three courses of things: namely, the miraculous, the natural, and the voluntary.

The miraculous course is in no way subject to the others or to their law; rather, it freely rules them. [Note: Victor 19 reads “or to their law,” rather than “or to their laws.”] Nor does it wrong them when it appears to oppose them, because they possess nothing except what they have received from it, and it gave them nothing except under its authority. [Note: The manuscripts read “anything else” rather than “anything.”]

Since, therefore, the propagation of a man from a virgin alone is neither natural nor voluntary, but miraculous—like the event in which woman was produced from man alone, and like the creation of man from clay—it is clear that it is in no way subject to the laws and merits of that propagation which both will and nature, though distinctly, bring about. [Note: Thu. 391 reads “to the law and merits” (legi et meritis), rather than “to the laws and merits” (legibus et meritis).] For there the will does one thing and nature another; nevertheless a true man is produced: Adam from what was not man, Jesus from woman alone, and Eve from man alone, just as every man or woman is a true human being when born from man and woman.

Every human being is either Adam or from Adam. [Note: Thu. reads “is from Adam.”] But Eve is from Adam alone, and all the others are from Adam and Eve. Since Mary, from whom Jesus alone derives, is from Adam and Eve, he cannot fail to be from them also. For it was fitting that the one who was to redeem the human race should be and be born from the father and mother of all.

## CHAPTER XII

### That Adam’s evils do not pass to that man by any justice or right

How, moreover, the Son of the Virgin is not subject to Adam’s sin or debt is likewise not difficult to understand. Adam was made just, free from sin, from the aforesaid debt, and from the punishment of sin, and blessed; he was able always to preserve the justice he had received and, through that justice, the freedom and blessedness I have mentioned. [Note: The manuscripts read “was made, and just,” rather than “was made just.”]

Since, therefore, Adam could always preserve these good things for himself without any difficulty, but did not preserve them, he himself took them away from himself and subjected himself to their opposites. Thus he became a slave of sin, or injustice; of the debt that he cannot repay [Note: The manuscripts of Victor read “that he could not repay.”]; and of misery, from which comes the inability to recover the good things he had lost. [Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “to restore.”]

Just as, therefore, he could not take away from himself the good things he possessed and draw upon himself the evils he did not possess except by failing to preserve the good things for himself when he could have done so, [Note: Thu. 391 reads: “to take away the good things he possessed and draw upon himself the evils he did not possess except when he could have preserved them,” and so forth.] so he could not take those same good things away from anyone else or inflict evils upon anyone except by failing to preserve the good things for one for whom he was able to preserve them. [Note: The manuscripts of Thu, Gem, Bec, Victor 3 and 13, and the Gothic Edition read “for one for whom he could preserve them.”]

But he could preserve those good things for no one except those whose power of generation he had received subject to his will. Therefore he could transmit the aforesaid evils to no person propagated from him whose generation involved neither a nature of propagation given to him nor any operation of his will, nor anything that his will could operate. [Note: The manuscripts of Thu. and Victor 19 continue the preceding chapter here.]

Therefore Adam’s aforesaid evils pass to the man conceived from the Virgin by no reason or right.

## CHAPTER XIII

### That, even if he were not God but merely man, he would nevertheless have to be such as the first man was made

[Note: In the manuscripts of Cister, Thu, Victor 9, and the Gothic Edition, this is where Chapter XIII begins.]

Again, if with the pure gaze of reason we contemplate God’s wise justice, it is understood to be exceedingly absurd that through that seed—which neither created nature nor the will of a creature produces or sows, and over which no power was granted to anyone [Note: The manuscript of Cister reads “no power of generation was granted to anyone.”]—but through God’s will alone, by his own power, a man should be procreated from the Virgin, newly separated from sin, and that any necessity of another’s sin, debt, or punishment should pass to that same man; even if he were not assumed into the person of God but became merely a man.

For by the very reasoning by which God ought not to have made Adam except just and unburdened by any debt or affliction, the rational mind clearly recognizes that the one whom God likewise procreates by his own will and power ought not to be subjected to any evil. [Note: The manuscripts read “procreated” (procreavit) rather than “procreates” (procreat).] For it is exceedingly unfitting to the goodness of the omnipotent and wise God to make a rational nature solely by his own will from matter in which there is no sin, and yet make that nature unjust or miserable. Whoever does not understand this does not recognize what is unfitting for God. [Note: The manuscripts read “does not recognize what is fitting for God”; Victor 19 reads “what is not fitting for God.”]

Therefore, even if God were to make a mere man in the manner stated, he would necessarily be endowed with no less justice and blessedness than Adam had when he was first made.

## CHAPTER XIV

### That what is written—“man is from unclean seed” and “conceived in iniquities”—does not oppose the proposed reasoning, even if it was properly said of certain cases

If someone’s mind does not grasp what I have said about human seed—namely, that there is no sin in it before the rational soul, but that it is called unclean because of sin and iniquity on account of the uncleanness that will occur when the man already exists—and if he thinks that it is unclean at conception because, as I myself raised against my own argument, it is written, “Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed?” (Job 14), and, “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50), I am not concerned with this difficulty. [Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “I do not labor over this.”] I do not need to make him understand what he cannot grasp; I ask him only to attend to what I shall say briefly.

Those who said these things either intended them to be understood of every human seed, or only of that seed which is sown with the sensation of sexual pleasure—which would belong only to brute animals if man had not sinned. [Note: The manuscripts read “with consent” (consensu) rather than “with sensation” (sensu).] But if they meant this of every seed, then they asserted that the seed taken from the Virgin was unclean—a belief that it is impious to hold. Therefore they did not write this about it.

But if, according to this meaning, they uttered it concerning some human seed, they intended it to be understood only of that which is conceived with the aforesaid pleasure. This in no way opposes our reasoning, which asserts that the seed taken from the Virgin is clean, although it is taken from a sinful mass. [Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “although it is from the mass.”]

## CHAPTER XV

### How the sinful mass is not wholly sinful

For just as blindness is not in every part of a man, although a man is called blind, but only in the eye where sight ought to be—for it is not in the hand or the foot—and just as deafness is only in the ear when a man is called deaf, [Note: Thu. and the Gothic Edition read “deafness is only in the ear.”] so, although the mass of the human race is called sinful, sin is not in any part of it except, as I have said, in the will. [Note: The Gothic Edition reads “in pleasure” rather than “in the will.”] The seed is recognized as having this in no conception of a human being. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor read “which is present in no conception.”]

Therefore, if what has been said above is considered, no true or plausible reason contradicting it, we can now freely conclude that no reason, no truth, and no understanding permits anything from the sin of the sinful mass—although he was taken from it—to have been able or obliged to pass to the man conceived from the Virgin, even if he were not God.

## CHAPTER XVI

### Why John and others who were conceived in a similar miraculous manner were not, by themselves, free from sin

[Col. 0449B]

If John the Baptist and others who were propagated from barren women, in whom, because of old age, the generative power of nature had already died, are brought forward against me, and if they are thought, by a similar reasoning, to have had to be born without sin and the punishment of sin because they were conceived miraculously, then the reasoning that shows the virginal conception to be free from every necessity of sin must be understood to be entirely different from theirs.

For it is one thing to make something unheard-of, unexpected, and unknown to nature; it is another to heal nature weakened by age or by some defect and restore it to its proper work. For if Adam had not sinned, just as he himself would not have been weakened by old age or by any cause, so the nature of propagation created in him and, as has already been said, subjected to his power for use would not have been hindered in its course by any accident. [Note: The manuscripts read “weakened and failing” rather than “weakened.”]

Therefore, in John and those like him, something new was not given to Adam’s nature, as it was in the Son of the Virgin; rather, what had been weakened by its causes is understood to have been restored. Since, then, they were generated through the natural propagation given to Adam, they neither can nor ought to be compared with the one under discussion in the miracle of conception, so that they could be shown to have been released from the bond of original sin. [Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic Edition read “so that they can be shown.”]

## CHAPTER XVII

### Why God became incarnate, although he could have made from Adam as many sinless men, not gods, as would suffice

[Col. 0449D]

Perhaps someone will say: If a mere man, who was not God, could be made from Adam without any contamination of sin, as you say, why was it necessary for God to become incarnate? For either through one such man, who would be without all sin, God could redeem sinners, [Note: The manuscripts read “God could redeem sinners,” rather than “he could redeem sinners.”] or he could make, by a similar miracle, as many men as were necessary to complete the heavenly city.

To this I answer briefly. God became man because a man, not God, would not suffice to redeem others, as was shown in the aforesaid work. [Note: The manuscripts of Cister, Victor, and the Gothic Edition read “the aforementioned work.”] For this reason also he did not make as many such men as were necessary, lest, if no one were saved through natural propagation, he should appear to have created that nature in Adam to no purpose and, as though he had not made it, to have corrected it—a thing that is unfitting for supreme wisdom to do with any nature. [Note: Thu. 546 omits “that.”]

Not long above I proposed to investigate how the seed taken from the Virgin—of which it had been shown that there was no sin, and which was free from the aforesaid necessities in which I had posited that all other human beings were conceived—could be understood to be free: both from the necessity by which human nature cannot by itself recover the justice it abandoned, and from the necessity by which the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, especially in infants. [Note: The manuscripts read “from the necessity by which the body” rather than “from that necessity.”] I was confident that this man could be freed from these necessities because he would be God, provided that the necessity of Adam’s sin and debt, and of the debts of his nearest parents, were first rationally removed from him. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor, Gem, Bec, and the Gothic Edition read “from Adam and the nearest parents.”]

I therefore began, in Book I, to ask how this could be understood with respect to the necessity of Adam’s sin and debt, so that afterward what I was seeking concerning other matters might more easily be found. And through the abundant grace and purity of the one whose conception is under discussion (Book I, chapter 16), it came about that he should be recognized as free not only from every sin, debt, and the aforesaid necessities, but also, by intelligible reasoning, that the man so conceived ought to be endowed with no less justice or blessedness than that in which Adam was made, even if he were not God but merely a man. [Note: The Gothic Edition reads “no greater” rather than “no less.”] [Note: Thu. 391 reads “if he were merely man, it would be proved.”]

For it seemed equally unreasonable both that sin or the punishment of sin should descend from any parents to him through such propagation, and that God should willingly make a rational nature unjust or miserable without any injustice of its own deserving it. [Note: Thu. 546 reads “equally reasonable,” rather than “equally unreasonable.”] [Note: Victor 19 reads “it will seem.”] [Note: The manuscripts read “the punishment of sin from them,” rather than “from any parents.”]

[Col. 0451A]

## CHAPTER XVIII

### That God was conceived from a just Virgin, not by necessity—as though he could not be born from a sinful woman—but because it was fitting

Although, therefore, the Son of God was truly conceived from the most pure Virgin, this did not happen by such necessity that a just offspring could not reasonably be generated through such propagation from a sinful parent; rather, it happened because it was fitting that the conception of that man should take place from a most pure mother.

It was fitting that the Virgin should shine with that purity than which no greater can be conceived beneath God, since God the Father was preparing to give her his only Son, whom he loved as begotten equal to himself from his own heart, as his very self, so that naturally he might be one and the same Son common to God the Father and the Virgin; and whom the Son himself chose to make his mother substantially; and from whom the Holy Spirit willed, and was about to bring it about, that he should be conceived and born, he from whom the Spirit himself proceeds. [Note: The manuscripts read “he from whom he proceeds.”] [Note: The manuscripts of Victor and Thu. omit “his” in “his only Son.”] [Note: Victor 19 reads “whom he loved as though from his heart” rather than “whom he loved as begotten from his heart.”] [Note: Victor 19 omits “as his very self.”]

How this same Virgin was cleansed through faith before the conception itself, I explained in Book II, chapters 16 and 17, where I gave another account of the very matter under discussion here.

[Note: In Victor 19, the following begins Chapter XIX.]

## CHAPTER XIX

### How this reasoning and the other given elsewhere agree and differ

These two explanations seem to me each sufficient by itself for the question; but together they abundantly satisfy the mind seeking both the force of reason and the fittingness of the action. Although they aim at the same result, they differ in this respect: the explanation I have set forth here shows that God ought to produce, by such propagation, a just offspring—indeed, only a just offspring—from the substance even of a sinful Virgin, since nowhere in human nature is there sin apart from the will, and since nothing opposes this conclusion. [Note: The manuscripts read “the one itself which I have set forth here”; Thu. reads “this question which I have set forth.”]

The other explanation proves that even if there were sin in the Virgin’s entire essence, she could nevertheless be made clean through faith for the purity of such a conception. But in this explanation every necessity of death and of any corruption or labor is plainly excluded from that man. [Note: Thu. 361 reads “from that name,” rather than “from that man.”] In the other, a question about this very matter appears to arise; but if it is carefully examined, it is dissolved by sufficient reasoning. [Note: Some manuscripts read “is solved”; Thu. 391 reads “will be dissolved.”]

Therefore, from both explanations it is clear that our Lord and Redeemer endured nothing except by a pious will in all that he suffered.

## CHAPTER XX

### That, born from the Virgin, he possessed original justice in place of original sin

As it seems to me, it has been sufficiently shown, as I proposed, how original sin could in no way descend from his parents to the man conceived from the Virgin; rather, reason required that he should be made just and blessed. [Note: “Just, blessed” in the manuscripts, without “and.”] Since, therefore, he was born just from a just Father according to divine nature and from a just mother according to human nature, just from his very origin, so to speak, he may not incongruously be said to possess original justice from his origin in place of the original injustice that all the other sons of Adam possess. [Note: The manuscripts of Thu, Gem, and Bec read “all the sons of Adam.”]

## CHAPTER XXI [elsewhere XX]

### Why he could not have personal injustice

But it is superfluous to discuss personal injustice, since it did not touch him. [Note: Thu. reads “which did not touch him.”] For human nature was never in him without the divine nature, nor was his soul ever weighed down against its will or in any way hindered by a corruptible body.

Since that soul—or rather, since the whole man and the Word of God, who is God—always existed as one person, he was never without perfect justice, wisdom, and power, which he always possessed from himself according to his person, as God, although he received from the divine nature what he possessed in the human nature. [Note: Thu. 546 reads “from the divine nature what he had received.”] [Note: The manuscripts of Cister, Thu, Gem, Bec, Saint Michael, and the Gothic Edition read “he possessed, having received it.”]

I do not deny that there may be some higher explanation, besides this one and the one I gave elsewhere (Book II, chapter 16), of how God assumed a man from the sinful mass without sin, as unleavened bread from fermented dough. [Note: The manuscripts of Cister, Gem, Bec, Victor 19, Saint Michael, Thu. 546, and the Gothic Edition read “from leaven.”] If such an explanation is shown to me, I willingly accept it; and if my explanations can be shown—which I do not think they can—to be contrary to the truth, I do not cling to them. [Note: The manuscripts of Cister, Thu, Gem, Saint Michael, and the Gothic Edition read “if they can be shown contrary to the truth”; Thu. 546 reads “if it can be shown contrary to the truth.”]

## CHAPTER XXII [elsewhere XXI]

### On the magnitude of original sin

Original sin can be neither greater than I have said nor less. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor, Gem, and Bec read “nor less, because.”] For when the infant has become rational, human nature does not possess in him the justice it received in Adam and ought always to have. Nor does inability excuse him for not possessing it, as has already been said above, in chapter 2.

Nevertheless, I do not consider it to be in every respect as serious as I stated above. For when I wished to show that it did not apply to the man conceived from the Virgin, I defined it as something to which nothing could be added, lest, as I said, because of the matter I was investigating I might appear to diminish its weight. I shall now briefly explain what I think about it. [Note: Thu. and Victor 19 read “I shall now briefly explain what I think.”]

Adam’s sin does not, I think, descend into infants in such a way that they ought to be punished for it as though each of them had personally committed it, as Adam did, although it did bring about the fact that none of them can be born without sin, which results in condemnation. [Note: Thu. 391 begins Chapter XXIII here.]

For when the Apostle says that “death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14), he seems clearly to signify that Adam’s transgression itself, or anything equally great, is not personally imputed to them. [Note: The manuscripts read “or anything else equally great.”] Yet in his writings he declares all the sons of Adam, except the Son of the Virgin, to be sinners and children of wrath.

For when he says, “even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” this can be understood as though he were saying, “even over those who did not sin as greatly as Adam sinned by transgressing.” And when he says, “the law entered in so that the offense might abound” (ibid., verse 20), we either understand the sin that existed before the law in those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression to have been less than Adam’s sin; or, if it was not less, sin abounded in them after the law beyond Adam’s sin. [Note: Thu. 546 reads “or we shall understand sin” and omits the repeated “sin.”] [Note: The manuscripts of Victor read “if it was not less.”]

I cannot understand this when I consider what I have explained, as you have already read, in *Cur Deus Homo*, concerning the weight and satisfaction of that sin (Book I, chapters 19 and 20). [Note: The manuscripts read “in the chapter *Cur Deus Homo*.”] [Note: Thu. 391 reads “concerning its meaning,” and elsewhere “concerning its sanctification.”]

Nevertheless, it is true that no one is restored to that for which man was made and for which the power of propagation was given to him, nor is human nature rescued from the evils into which it has fallen, except through satisfaction for that sin by which it cast itself into those same evils. [Note: The manuscripts of Thu. read “into which it fell,” rather than “into which it has fallen.”]

Someone may say: If individuals do not possess Adam’s sin, how can you assert that no one is saved without satisfaction for Adam’s sin? For how does the just God demand from them satisfaction for a sin they do not possess?

I answer: God demands from no sinner more than he owes. [Note: The manuscripts read “But God demands from no one.”] But since no one can repay what he owes, Christ alone pays more than all who are saved owe, just as I said in the aforementioned work. [Note: The manuscripts read “Christ paid”; some read “more than is owed.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII [elsewhere XXI]

### Why and how sin descends into infants

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Why and how sin descends to infants

In yet another way it must be considered for what reason sin is less in infants than in Adam, although it descends from him into all. For through one man—that is, through Adam—sin entered into this world, and through sin, death. But why it is less cannot be known unless both why and how it is present are understood.

[Note: At Col. 0453D, Vict. 19 and Thu. 546 begin Chapter 23 here, under the title: “Why and how it descends into infants.” In Gem., this is Chapter 25; in Thu. and Vict. 19 the preceding chapter continues.]

Although this has been said above as far as was needed for the question under examination, it will nevertheless not be superfluous if it is briefly repeated here.

[Note: Thu. and Vict. read “if this is briefly”; the printed reading is “if it is briefly repeated here.”]

Indeed, it cannot be denied that infants were in Adam when he sinned; but they were in him causally, or materially, as in a seed. In themselves they are present personally, because in him they were the very seed; in themselves they are each distinct persons; in him they were not other than he, while in themselves they are other than he. In him they were he; in themselves they are themselves. Therefore they were in him, but not themselves, because they did not yet exist as themselves.

[Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “naturally” (*naturaliter*) instead of “materially” (*materialiter*).]

Perhaps someone will say that the being by which other human beings are said to have been in Adam is something like nothing and a kind of emptiness, and ought not to be called being. Let him therefore say that the being by which Christ, according to the seed, was in Abraham, David, and the other Fathers was nothing, false, or empty; likewise, that the being by which all things that arise from seed were first in the seeds themselves was nothing; and that God did nothing when he first made in seeds all things which are generated from seed. Let him call nothing, or something empty, that which, if it did not truly exist, would entail that the things we see do not exist. For if it is not true that the things which nature produces from seeds were previously something in those seeds, they could in no way arise from them.

[Note: Vict. 19 reads “this which” (*istud esse quod*) for “this being by which” (*istud esse quo*).]

But if it is utterly foolish to say this, then the being by which all other human beings were in Adam was not false or empty, but true and substantial.
