Nor did God make something empty when he made them to be in him; rather, as has been said, in him they were not other than he, and for that reason were in him in a manner far different from that in which they are in themselves.

[Note: Thu. and Vict. 19 read “if these things” (*quod si haec*) rather than “if this” (*quod si hoc*). Vict., Gem., Bec., and Cister. read “it is not false” (*non est falsum*) rather than “not false” (*non falsum*).]

Although it is established that all were in him, the Son of the Virgin alone was in him in a manner greatly different from the others. For all the others were in him in such a way that they would come from him through the nature of propagation, which was subject to his power and will. This one alone, however, was not in him in such a way that he would be made from Adam through Adam’s nature or will. For, as regards the others, Adam, when he sinned, had received [the capacity] to be that from which they were to come and to be from him; but, as regards this one, he had received [the capacity] to be that from which he was to come, not, however, that this one should be from Adam, since it was not in Adam’s power that he should be propagated from Adam.

[Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic edition have *de aliis acceperat*, “as regards the others, he had received,” rather than *de aliis enim acceperat*, “for, as regards the others, he had received.” They omit only *enim*, “for.” Here *de aliis* introduces the comparison with the others; it does not mean that Adam received something from other people.]

When Adam sinned, he was such that there would be that from which the others were to come, and that they would come from him—that is, insofar as they are concerned. But in respect of this one, Adam was such that there would be that from which he was to come, but not such that he would come from Adam, because it was not in Adam’s power that he should be propagated from him.

[Note: Gem., Bec., Vict. 19, S. Mich., and the Gothic edition read “that he would come from him” (*ut de illo esset*) rather than “that they would come from him” (*ut de illo essent*). Vict. 19 reads “that they would come from him” for the singular in the clause concerning this one. Vict. 19, S. Mich., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read feminine *illa* rather than masculine *ejus*: “he was not in her power,” apparently referring to nature.]

Nor was it in Adam’s power that this one should be made from another essence or from nothing. Therefore he was not in Adam in such a way that he might exist by any means. For it was neither in the power of Adam’s nature nor in the power of his will that he should exist in any manner.

Yet in Adam there was the nature from which he was to be propagated—not by Adam’s power, but by God’s. For although, down to the Virgin Mother, will sowed in the parents and nature germinated, so that the Virgin herself was brought forth from Adam into her own existence partly by a natural and partly by a voluntary course, as were all others, yet in her neither the will of a creature sowed offspring nor nature germinated. Rather, the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High wondrously brought forth a man from the Virgin woman.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read plural *producerent*, “they brought forth,” for singular *produceretur*, “she was brought forth.” The manuscripts read *propagavit*, “propagated [him],” instead of *procreavit*, “brought forth.”]

Thus, with respect to the others, he was in Adam—that is, it was in Adam’s power that they should come from him. But with respect to this one, he was not in Adam in such a way that he should exist by any means. Just as he was not in the clay from which the first man was made so as to come from it wondrously, nor was he in the man so that Eve should come from him in the manner in which she did, so neither was he in any of those in whom he was from Adam down to Mary in such a way that he should exist.

[Note: Thu. reads “from which the first man was made”; other witnesses read “from which the first human being was made.”]

Yet he was in them because in them was that from which he himself was to be assumed, just as he was in the clay from which the first man was made and in that from which Eve was made: not by the will or power of a creature, but by divine power alone. But he was so present far more wondrously and with greater grace, inasmuch as they were mere human beings, whereas this one became God and man.

[Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “not in the will of a creature” rather than “not by the will of a creature.”]

Therefore this one was in Adam, when Adam sinned, in a manner greatly different from those who are generated by a voluntary and natural course. In a certain sense Adam makes those whom human will, by the power it has received, produces through sowing, and nature through germinating. But God alone made this one, although he was from Adam: for he was not made through Adam, but through God himself, as though from what was God’s own.

[Note: The Gothic and Venetian editions read “Adam made” (*fecit Adam*) rather than “Adam makes” (*facit Adam*). The manuscripts read singular “nature produces” (*germinando procreat*); the Gothic edition reads “nature produced” (*germinando procreavit*). Bec. reads “this righteous one” (*justum*) for “this one” (*istum*).]

What, then, could be more fitting for showing the greatness of God’s goodness and the fullness of the grace which he granted to Adam than that those whose existence lay in Adam’s power should be such that, as Adam was naturally, so they should be through him; and likewise that it should lie within the freedom of his choice to propagate them such as he himself was in righteousness and blessedness? This, therefore, was granted to him.

[Note: The Gothic edition omits *ad*, “for,” before “the fullness.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “the grace of Adam” rather than “the grace which he granted to Adam.” Thu. reads “that those” rather than “than that those.” Cister., Thu., Vict., Gem., and Bec. omit *in* in “he himself in righteousness.”]

Since, therefore, set upon so lofty a height of grace, he freely abandoned the good things which he had received to preserve for himself and for them, his children lost what their father could have given them by preserving it, but took away from them by not preserving it.

[Note: Vict., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read “the good things which he had received to preserve for himself and for them.” The fuller note reads: “What the Father could have given them by preserving it, he took from them by not preserving it.”]

This seems to me a sufficient explanation of why Adam’s sin and evils descend to infants, provided that the matter itself is carefully considered with our own will set aside, since it often and greatly obstructs the mind from understanding rectitude.

[Note: Thu., Vict., and Cister. read “seems sufficient” rather than “seems to me sufficient.”]

How this same sin seems to me to descend to them I shall explain briefly. There is sin arising from nature, as I said in Chapter 1; and there is sin arising from the person. Thus what arises from the person may be called personal; what arises from nature, natural—what is called original. And just as personal sin passes into nature, so natural sin passes into the person, in this way.

What Adam ate was demanded by nature, because nature was created so as to require this. But that he ate from the forbidden tree was done not by natural will but by personal will—that is, his own. Yet what the person did, he did not do without nature. For “Adam” designated the person; “man” designated the nature. Therefore the person made nature sinful, because when Adam sinned, man sinned.

[Note: Gem. and Bec. read “what was in Adam” (*quod apud Adam*) rather than “what Adam ate” (*quod Adam comedebat*). Vict. and the Gothic edition read “so that these things might be required”; Thu. and Cister. read “so that this might be required”; S. Mich. reads “created so that these things might be required.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “not this will” rather than “not this was done by will.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “Adam’s personal will, his own.”]

For he was not impelled to seize what was forbidden because he was human; rather, he was drawn by his own will, which nature did not demand but which the person conceived.

[Note: Vict. 19 reads “which nature did not demand.” The Gothic edition reads “because he did not do it,” with the gloss “which [nature] did not demand.”]

The reverse occurs similarly in infants. For the fact that they do not possess the righteousness which they ought to have was not brought about by their personal will, as in Adam, but by the natural lack which nature itself received from Adam. In Adam—for outside him there was nothing of that nature—nature was stripped of the righteousness which it possessed; and unless assisted it always lacks that righteousness. Because nature subsists in persons, and persons do not exist without nature, nature makes the persons of infants sinful.

[Note: Vict., Thu., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read “unless assisted, it lacked it” (*adjuta careret*) rather than “unless assisted, it lacks it” (*adjuta caret*). Vict., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read “nature made” (*fecit natura*) rather than “nature makes” (*facit natura*).]

Thus the person stripped nature of the good of righteousness in Adam; and nature, having become needy, makes all the persons which it generates from itself sinful and unjust through the same need. In this way Adam’s personal sin passes into all who are naturally propagated from him, and in them it is original or natural.

[Note: Vict. 19 reads “personally into all” (*personaliter in omnes*) rather than “personal into all” (*personale in omnes*).]

Hence it is clear that there is a great difference between Adam’s sin and theirs. He sinned by his own will; they sin by a natural necessity, which his own personal will deserved. Yet, since no one doubts that unequal sins are not followed by equal punishment, personal and original sin are alike in this respect: no one is admitted to the kingdom of God, for which the human being was made, except through the death of Christ. Without that death, what is owed for Adam’s sin is not restored, although not all deserve to be tormented equally in hell.

[Note: Vict. 19 reads “but it is clear.” Thu., Vict., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read indicative “no one doubts” rather than subjunctive “no one may doubt.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition read future “will not follow” rather than “does not follow.” Vict., Gem., Bec., S. Mich., and the Gothic edition read masculine *quo*, “without whom,” rather than feminine *qua*, “without which,” after “Christ.”]

For after the day of judgment there will be no angel or human being except either in the kingdom of God or in hell. Thus the sin of infants is less than the sin of Adam; yet no one is saved without that universal satisfaction through which both great and small sin are forgiven. Why salvation is not without that death, and how human salvation is through it, I investigated and explained in the book mentioned above, insofar as God granted me to do so.

[Note: Vict. 19 reads “through which great” rather than “through which both great.” Vict. 19 and the Gothic edition read “without any death” (*sine ulla morte*) rather than “without that death” (*sine illa morte*).]

## CHAPTER XXIV [elsewhere XXIII]  
### That the sins of parents after Adam are not reckoned in the original sin of their children

[Note: Vict. 19 and Thu. 546 have this as Chapter 24.]

I do not think that the sins of nearer parents belong to the original sin of their children. For if Adam had been unable to convey his righteousness to those whom he was going to beget, he could in no way have transmitted his unrighteousness to them. Therefore, since no one after Adam has been able to preserve his righteousness for his children, I see no reason why the sins of nearer parents ought to be imputed to the souls of their children.

[Note: Vict. 19 and the Gothic edition read “to bring forth his righteousness” (*suam producere*) rather than “to convey his righteousness” (*suam perducere*).]

Finally, no one doubts that infants preserve no rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself. In this respect, therefore, all are equally unjust, because they have none of that righteousness which every human being ought to have. This nakedness of righteousness descends to all from Adam, in whom human nature stripped itself of that same righteousness.

For even if some righteousness remained in Adam—that is, in human nature—so that it might preserve a right will in certain matters, it was nevertheless deprived of that gift by which it could preserve righteousness for posterity, so that it cannot propagate itself with any righteousness in any of them.

[Note: Cister., Thu., Vict., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read “that good” (*illo bono*) rather than “that gift” (*illo dono*).]

Thus it could not take more from infants than all righteousness and blessedness, which are given to no one who lacks the righteousness owed to him. But that the unrighteousness of nearer parents can increase this nakedness of righteousness, beyond which no greater deprivation can descend into infants from Adam the sinner, does not seem possible. For where there is no righteousness, no righteousness can be taken away. And where no righteousness can be absent, no unrighteousness can be added. Therefore unrighteous parents cannot add any unrighteousness to their infants beyond the aforesaid nakedness of righteousness.

[Note: Vict. reads “indeed” (*plus utique*) rather than “therefore” (*plus itaque*). The manuscripts read “given in some way”; the Gothic edition reads “given as though.”]

But where there is no righteousness, nothing prevents some righteousness from being introduced. Therefore it seems more probable and more possible that, if unrighteous parents are said to add some unrighteousness to their infants, righteous parents should be able to give some righteousness to theirs. If that happens, the infants of righteous parents have some righteousness.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “some unrighteousness may be found” (*aliquam invenire injustitiam*) rather than “some righteousness may be introduced” (*aliquam poni justitiam*). The manuscripts read “are said [to add] righteousness” rather than “unrighteousness.” Vict. 19 reads potential “could give” (*dare possent*) rather than “can give” (*dare possint*).]

If this is so, an infant of righteous parents who dies without baptism is condemned more lightly than an infant of unrighteous parents; or, if he is saved, he is chosen with some preceding merit of his own. But the Apostle Paul denies this in Romans 5, where, through Jacob and Esau, he proves that no one is saved except by grace preceding all merits.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “preceding grace” (*praecedente gratia*) rather than “grace preceding [all merits]” (*praeveniente gratia*).]

Therefore, since righteous parents give no righteousness to their infants before baptism, unrighteous parents surely add no unrighteousness to theirs. But if someone says, “Unrighteous parents do not add any unrighteousness to their infants, from whom they cannot take away any righteousness; rather, they make more serious in them the original unrighteousness which they have from Adam,” then righteous parents likewise make it lighter in theirs. Therefore, if infants of righteous parents are less unjust than infants of unrighteous parents, they ought to be rejected less than the latter. Let whoever dares say this and can show it do so. I, however, do not dare, since I see infants both of righteous and of unrighteous parents indiscriminately chosen for the grace of baptism and rejected from it.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “infants of the righteous” rather than “infants of the unrighteous” in the earlier comparison. Vict. 19 omits *suo*, “of his own,” in “some preceding merit of his own.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “the infants of the righteous” in the final clause.]

Nor can anyone who says this demonstrate it. For, in this respect, no one is more righteous than another unless he more greatly desires or avoids, by will, what he ought; and no one is more unjust than another unless he more greatly loves or despises what he ought not. Therefore, if it cannot be shown that infants, as soon as they have a soul, will more or less what they ought or what they ought not, no one can prove that one infant is born more righteous or more unjust than another.

[Note: Cister., Vict., Thu., and the Gothic edition read “greater or less” (*majus vel minus*); Gem. and Bec. read “more or less” (*magis vel minus*); the latter form is printed. The manuscripts read singular “what he ought or what he ought not,” rather than plural “what they ought or what they ought not.”]

Accordingly, righteous parents do not appear to make original unrighteousness lighter in their infants by their own righteousness, nor do unrighteous parents make it heavier in theirs by their own unrighteousness. Therefore, if unrighteous parents cannot increase original sin in their infants by their own sin either in number or in magnitude, it seems to me that the sins of parents after Adam do not enter into the merits of infants.

This does not mean that, because of the good merits of parents, many and great benefits of body and soul are not bestowed upon children; nor that, because of the sins of parents, children and grandchildren are not chastised by diverse tribulations in this life unto the third and fourth generation, and perhaps beyond, and lose even goods of the soul which they might perhaps acquire through their parents if those parents were righteous. Examples of these matters would take too long to insert here.

But I say that original sin is equal in all infants naturally conceived, just as Adam’s sin—which is the reason why they are born in him—belongs equally to all.

## CHAPTER XXV [elsewhere XXIV]  
### How the sins of parents harm the souls of their children

[Note: Vict., Thu., and the Gothic edition give the title “Sins, etc.” Vict. has: “How the sins of parents harm the souls of their children.”]

If the sins of parents sometimes harm the souls of their children, I think that this happens rather in the following way: not because God imputes those sins to them, or because he leads them into any sins on account of their parents, but because, just as he often rescues the children of righteous people from sins through the merits of their parents, so he sometimes leaves the children of unrighteous people in their own sins because of the merits of their parents.

[Note: Vict., Bec., and Gem. read “but just as often” (*sed sicut saepe*). Vict. 19, Thu., S. Mich., and the Gothic edition read “but because often” (*sed quoniam saepe*).]

For since no one is free from sin unless God frees him, when God does not free, he is said to lead into sin; and when he does not soften, to harden. Indeed, it seems more acceptable that God should leave in their sins, because of the sins of their parents, a sinful soul which owes him nothing except punishment, so that it may be punished for those sins, than that he should burden it with sins belonging to others, so that it may be tortured for them.

[Note: Vict. 19 reads an uncertain defective form, *susceptibilibus*; another reading is *susceptibus suis*. The printed *susceptibilius* means “more acceptable” or “more readily admitted.” The manuscripts read “that the soul” rather than “that God [should leave] the soul.”]

Thus, without contradiction, original sin is the same in all; the son does not bear the iniquity of the father; each bears his own burden and receives according as he has acted in the body, whether good or evil; and God repays the sins of parents upon children unto the third and fourth generation, even if this occurs in the soul; and whatever else is read which seems to signify that the sins of parents harm the souls of children.

[Note: Cister., Vict., Bec., Gem., and S. Mich. read “seems to signify that the sins of parents are imputed” (*imputari peccata parentum significare*) rather than “seems to signify that the sins of parents harm [them].”]

For the soul of the son does not die through the sin of the father, but through its own; nor does anyone bear the iniquity of his father when he is left in his own [iniquity], but his own; nor another’s burden, but his own; nor does he receive according to what his father did, but according to what he himself did in the body. Yet because he was not freed from his own evils on account of the sins of his parents, the evils which he bears are imputed to those same sins of his parents.

[Note: In Thu. 391, Chapter 26 begins at “For the soul of the son does not die …”]

## CHAPTER XXVI [elsewhere XXV]  
### How nevertheless no one bears the sin of his father, but his own

[Note: Vict., Thu. 546, and the Gothic edition have this as Chapter 26, under the title: “How nevertheless no one bears the sin of his father, but his own.”]

But if it is objected that all who are not saved through the faith which is in Christ bear Adam’s iniquity and burden, and someone wishes by this to prove either that infants ought likewise to bear the iniquities of other parents, or that they ought not to bear Adam’s, let him consider carefully that infants do not bear Adam’s sin, but their own.

[Note: Vict., Gem., Bec., and Cister. read “the faith which is in Christ”; a defective reading gives “which is in Christian.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition read simply “they do not bear sin,” omitting “infants.”]

For Adam’s sin was one thing, and the sin of infants another, because they differ, as has been said. The former was the cause; the latter is the effect. Adam lacked the righteousness owed to him, not because another abandoned it, but because he himself abandoned it. Infants lack it, not because they themselves abandoned it, but because another did.

[Note: Some manuscripts read merely “another [is] the sin of infants.” The manuscripts read “not as another, but as he himself” rather than “not because another, but because he himself.” In the next sentence they read “they lack it, not as themselves, but as another”; Cister. has a defective omission before *alius*, “another.”]

Therefore Adam’s sin and infants’ sin are not the same. And when the Apostle says what I quoted above, “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14), just as he signifies that the sin of infants is less than Adam’s, so he plainly shows it to be different.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “is plainly shown” (*aperte monstratur*) rather than “plainly shows” (*aperte monstrat*).]

Therefore, when an infant is condemned for original sin, he is condemned not for Adam’s sin, but for his own. For if he did not possess his own sin, he would not be condemned. Thus he does not bear Adam’s iniquity, but his own, although he is said to bear it because the iniquity of that sin was the cause of this one.

But this cause, which was in Adam so that infants might be born in sin, is not in other parents; because human nature does not have in them the power, as I said, for righteous children to be propagated. Therefore it does not follow that sin is in infants because of their sin as it is because of Adam’s sin.

## CHAPTER XXVII [elsewhere XXVI]  
### What original sin is, and that it is equal in all

[Note: Vict., Thu., and the Gothic edition have this as Chapter 27 under the title: “What original sin is, and that it is equal in all.”]

Therefore, I understand original sin as nothing other than what is in an infant as soon as he has a rational soul, whatever may previously have happened in the body before it was so animated—for example, some corruption of the limbs—or whatever may afterwards occur, whether in soul or body.

[Note: Gem. reads: “if there is some corruption of the limbs, or afterwards.”]

For the reasons stated above, I judge that it is equal in all infants naturally propagated, and that all who die in it alone are equally condemned. For whatever sin is added to it in a human being is personal. And just as the person is born sinful on account of nature, so nature is made more sinful through the person, because whenever any person sins, the human being sins.

[Note: Thu., Vict. 3, and the Gothic edition read “therefore because of the reasons stated above”; Vict. 9 and 19 read a defective repetition, “because of the reasons before those stated above.” The manuscripts, Thu., and Gothic edition read plural “are equal.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition place “personal” immediately after “is added.” The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “on account of the person” (*propter personam*) rather than “through the person” (*per personam*).]

I can understand this sin, which I call original, in these infants as nothing other than that nakedness of the righteousness owed to them, made through Adam’s disobedience, which I set forth above. Through it all are children of wrath, because the voluntary abandonment of righteousness, committed in Adam, accuses nature; nor does the inability to recover it excuse persons, as was said in Chapter 2. This inability is also accompanied by nakedness of blessedness, so that, as they are without all righteousness, so they are also without all blessedness. Through these two nakednesses they have been exposed in the exile of this life, open to sins and miseries which continually meet them everywhere and rush upon them from every side, except insofar as they are protected by divine providence.

[Note: Vict. 3 reads “unless by that righteousness”; Vict. 13 reads “unless righteousness itself.” The manuscripts read “placed” (*positi sunt*) rather than “exposed” (*expositi sunt*). Cister. reads “and their parents” (*et parentes*) rather than “and open” (*et patentes*).]

## CHAPTER XXVIII [elsewhere XXVII]  
### Against those who do not think infants ought to be condemned

[Note: Vict. and Thu. give the title: “Against all those who do not think infants ought to be condemned.” Bec. and Gem. give the same. S. Mich. and the Gothic edition read: “Against those who think that infants ought not to be condemned.”]

There are some whose mind refuses to accept that infants who die without baptism ought to be condemned on account of the sole unrighteousness which I have described. They argue that no human being judges them blameworthy for the sin of another person, and that, since at such an age they are not yet righteous and intelligent, they do not think God ought to judge the innocent more strictly than human beings judge them.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “wishes to accept” (*vult accipere*) rather than “does not wish to accept” (*non vult accipere*).]

To them it must be said that God demands one thing from infants concerning what they ought to do, and a human being another. For a human being ought not to demand from nature what he himself did not give and what is not owed to him. Nor does a human being justly rebuke another for being born with a guilt without which he himself is not born and from which he is healed only through another. But God rightly demands from nature what he gave it and what is justly owed to him.

[Note: Cister., Vict., Gem., Bec., and Thu. read “because God …”; Vict. 19 reads “how God …”; Thu. 391 reads: “that God requires from infants what they ought to do in one way, a human being in another way.”]

Yet the judgment by which infants are condemned is not greatly foreign from human judgment, if it is carefully considered. If a man and his wife, raised to some great dignity and possession not by any merit of their own but by grace alone, jointly commit a grave and inexcusable crime, and are therefore justly cast down and reduced to servitude, who would say that the children whom they beget after their condemnation ought not to be subject to the same servitude, but ought rather to be restored freely to the goods which their parents justly lost?

Such are the first parents and their children: the parents, justly condemned from blessedness to misery because of their fault, beget their children in that same exile. Like cases ought therefore to receive like judgment; but the judgment concerning the latter should be more severe in proportion as their offense can be shown to be more blameworthy.

[Note: Vict., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition read “as their offense” (*quantum delictum*). Some manuscripts read *improperabilius*, “more beyond reproach”; the printed *improbabilius* is “more blameworthy” or “more reprehensible.”]

Finally, every human being is either saved or condemned. Every human being who is saved is admitted to the kingdom of heaven, and every one who is condemned is excluded from it. Whoever is admitted is raised to the likeness of angels, among whom there never was nor will be any sin. But this cannot occur so long as any stain of sin remains in him. It is therefore impossible for any human being to be saved with any sin, however small. Therefore, if original sin is some sin, as I have said, every human being born in it must be condemned unless it is remitted.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “with one sin, however small” (*quamvis pro uno peccato*) rather than “with any sin, however small.” The manuscripts read “if what he said” rather than “if what I said.” They also read “born in it” rather than “born in it, unless it is remitted.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX [elsewhere XXVIII]  
### How inability to possess righteousness excuses them after baptism

[Note: Vict., Thu., Gem., Bec., and the Gothic edition have this as Chapter 29 under the title: “How inability to possess righteousness excuses us [that is, infants] after baptism.”]

I said that inability to possess righteousness does not excuse the unrighteousness of infants. Someone may therefore ask, saying: “If there is sin—that is, unrighteousness—in an infant before baptism, and inability to possess righteousness does not excuse it, as you say; and if in baptism no sin is remitted except what was previously present; since after baptism the infant remains without righteousness so long as he is an infant, and cannot understand the righteousness which he ought to preserve—for righteousness is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake—how is he not unjust even after he has been baptized?

[Note: Thu. 546 omits *ergo*, “therefore.” The manuscripts read “if [there is] an infant’s sin” rather than “if sin is in an infant.”]

“If, therefore, a baptized infant dies in infancy—not immediately after baptism, when he does not yet know how to repent—since he lacks the righteousness owed to him, and inability does not excuse him, he departs this life unjust, as he would have done before baptism, and is not admitted to the kingdom. But the Catholic Church does not hold this. And if, in baptism, the sin which would arise in infancy is remitted to infants, why are not also those sins remitted which occur in the following age?”

To this I reply that in baptism the sins which existed before baptism are wholly erased. Therefore the original inability to possess righteousness is not imputed as sin to those already baptized, as it was before. Just as, before baptism, inability to possess righteousness could not excuse the absence of righteousness because that absence itself was culpable, so after baptism it excuses him completely because he remains without all guilt.

[Note: The manuscripts and Gothic edition read: “therefore inability to possess righteousness could not previously excuse the absence of righteousness.” Thu. 391 reads: “therefore absence of righteousness could not previously excuse.” Vict. 19 reads “when it itself” rather than “because it itself.” Thu. 391 reads infinitive “to excuse completely” rather than indicative “excuses completely.”]

Hence it happens that the righteousness which was owed by infants before baptism is not required of them after baptism as though by debt, without any excuse. So long, therefore, as they lack righteousness solely through original inability, they are not unjust, because there is not in them an absence of righteousness owed to them. For what is impossible without any fault is not owed. Therefore, if those who are not unjust die in this condition, they are not condemned, but are saved as righteous through the righteousness of Christ, who gave himself for them, and through the righteousness of the faith of Mother Church, which believes for them.

[Note: Thu. 391 omits *non*, “not,” in “is not required of them.”]

These brief remarks concerning original sin I have made according to the capacity of my understanding, not affirming but conjecturing, until God reveals something better to me in some manner. But if anyone thinks otherwise, I reject no one’s opinion, provided it can be proved true.

[Note: Vict., Bec., Gem., and Thu. read “reveals something better at some time” (*aliquando melius revelet*). S. Mich.: “Here ends the Book on the Virgin Conception.” Vict. 3: “Here ends the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgin Conception and Original Sin.” Thu. 391: “Here ends the Book on the Virgin Conception and Original Sin, by Lord Anselm.” Thu. 546: “Here ends the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Virgin Conception.” Cister.: “Here ends the Book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on Original Sin.” “The declaration which follows does not occur in the aforesaid manuscripts.”]

[Col. 0463A]

107. DECLARATION OF A CERTAIN PERSON UPON THE SAME BOOK

[Col. 0463B]

Some criticize what is said here (above, chapter 7)—namely, that in the seed by which a human being is conceived there is no more any guilt, whether original or actual, than there is in spittle or blood if someone spits with evil intent or emits some of his blood. They assert that this is false because in the seed itself there is a certain tinder of sin and corruption of human nature, and hence the origin of original sin.

But if they are asked what they call the tinder of sin which is in it, and what they mean by the corruption of nature, I do not see what rational answer they can give. For no thing devoid of reason can either incite anyone to sin or urge anyone toward virtue, as Ambrose says in *On the Sacraments*, sermon 1. The Jew baptizes pitchers and cups as though insensible things could possess either guilt or grace. Therefore what can possess neither guilt nor praise cannot be the tinder of sin or of virtue.

[Col. 0463C] Such is the seed by which a human being is conceived, since it is insensible. Therefore that insensible seed, since there is no guilt in it, nor can there be, neither is nor can be the tinder of sin. As for the claim that the cause of the corruption of human nature is in that seed itself, this does not seem so—if by “corruption” they mean that which proceeded from sin and is present together with sin.

There is indeed a certain corruption of our nature which proceeded from sin; but this corruption is sometimes present together with sin and sometimes is not present together with sin. It is merely punishment, not sin: for example, the diseases of our bodies, other afflictions, and death itself. This corruption was in Christ’s body without sin, and it is present without mortal sin in holy people during this life; in sinners it is present together with sin.

This corruption has no cause in the seed or from the seed, although it passes into all who are begotten by paternal seed. But since it is the punishment of sin, it has its cause in the sin of our first parent, on account of which it was inflicted—not upon the insensible seed, but upon those who must feel and endure the hardship of affliction.

[Col. 0463D] From this corruption another corruption arises, which is indeed in the seed but does not have its cause from the seed. Thus, from diseased parents diseased seed is formed into diseased offspring, a matter considered by physicians. Yet in this there is neither original nor actual guilt. And I do not think that they are speaking of this.

[Col. 0464B] If, however, they call sin itself “corruption,” how can something be called the corruption of virtue? It is far removed from the seed mentioned above, as Ambrose’s authority cited earlier teaches.

What, then, do they call the tinder of sin, or the corruption of nature, which is in the seed? Perhaps they will wish to say that this authority is true, but that it cannot be true of the seeds from which human beings are produced, just as Ambrose did not say it concerning those seeds. For Augustine shows that there is sin in such seed in the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 8:

> “The nature of the seed [variant: of the human being],” he says, “has God as its author; in it, through the fault of disobedience, original sin is drawn along.”

For if the seed itself has no fault, what is meant by what is written in the Book of Wisdom?

> “Not unaware that their race was wicked, and their natural malice, and that their thinking could not be changed forever” (Wisdom 12:10).

For the seed was cursed from the beginning.

[Col. 0464C] Clearly, whatever people Augustine is speaking about here, he is speaking about human beings. How, then, is the malice of every human being natural, and the seed cursed from the beginning, unless reference is made to this:

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death” (Romans 5),

and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned?

And whose thinking cannot be changed forever, unless because it cannot do so by itself unless divine grace comes to its aid? Without that aid, what are human beings except what the apostle Peter says (chapter 2): “like irrational animals, naturally born for captivity and destruction”? This is Augustine’s statement.

“See,” they say, “you have in this authority proof that guilt is in the seed.”

To those who advance this argument, we reply first: let them say how they can show that Augustine understood this of the very seed by which a human being is generated. For “seed” is said equivocally, both of that which is a cause and of that which comes from a cause, as in: “We are the seed of Abraham” (John 8:33).

[Col. 0464D] Accordingly, “the seed is cursed” means that those are cursed who come from the seed or generation of those who persist in wickedness—provided that they themselves persist in the same wickedness.

“No,” they say. “Augustine plainly says this when he asks how the malice of every human being is natural, and the seed cursed from the beginning. ‘The malice of every human being,’ he says, ‘is natural, and the seed is cursed from the beginning.’ Just as the malice of every human being is natural, so the seed of every human being is cursed.”

[Col. 0465A] We reply that this zeugma—that is, repetition from what precedes—does not hold, nor did Augustine himself make that repetition. Therefore we are not compelled to agree with those who make it. Rather, we say this: the malice of every human being is natural, and the human being himself is the cursed seed—not that his seed is cursed, because there is no sin in it.

Or we may speak figuratively and say that the seed itself is called cursed because those who will be cursed will come from it. This is analogous to: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (Genesis 3:17), that is, “your works are cursed in the earth.” For the earth itself is not cursed, since elsewhere it is called holy, even though sinners work it: “The place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). Otherwise the same earth would be both cursed and holy.

So too the seed is cursed because those who come from the seed are cursed. In this sense our Anselm most excellently and truly explains that passage in Job concerning unclean seed, which nevertheless is neither unclean nor cursed in itself.

“But,” they object, “Augustine seems to be speaking of the seed that is the material of human flesh when he begins in this way: ‘For if the seed itself has no fault’—for why else would he make reference through the word ‘itself’? The discourse had preceded only about the seed.”

[Col. 0465B] Yet this pronoun often expresses not reference but a certain property of the thing that is the cause of the statement. Thus Palladius begins *On Agriculture*:

> “The first part of prudence is to assess the very person to whom one is going to give instruction.”

There is no reference through the pronoun “itself”; rather, it expresses the property of the person, as if he had said: “the person himself,” that is, the person’s virtue, knowledge, dignity, craft, profession, or something of that kind.

So here too “itself” is understood when the subject is the seed, as if he were saying: “The seed itself—that is, the condition of the seed—is such that it is not without fault.” For “if it is not at fault, if it has no fault, what is meant by what is written?” and so forth.

[Col. 0465C] We reply further: whatever may be the case concerning reference or the expression of a property through the pronoun “itself,” Augustine proves that there is no sin in the seed by raising another question against Jerome, who said concerning the origin of the soul that God creates new souls every day.

Augustine accepts this view without rejecting it, but, asking what Jerome might answer to the objections, puts to him the following question in his letter on the origin of the soul:

> “If the soul of this newly born infant was created by being infused, and infused by being created, when or how did it sin in Adam?”

That question could never have been raised by someone who said that there is original sin in the seed by which a human being is conceived. Such a person would have said to him:

> “Why do you ask what you yourself undoubtedly admit—that there is sin and fault in the seed, which is transmitted from the first human being to all his descendants? You are asking in vain how one sinned who proceeded seminally from Adam: the seed carries guilt with it.”

That, I say, is what would have been said to him. Therefore, if Augustine had held this view, he would never have put that question to Jerome. Jerome gave no answer to the question, nor did Augustine himself resolve it, since he produced no certain judgment concerning the origin of the soul.

[Col. 0465D] Let modern teachers see how they may resolve it.

Thus, through Augustine himself, we have established from the authority cited above that when he said there was fault in the seed, he did not understand this of the seed that is sperm. The judgment of Ambrose and our Anselm therefore stands, and it is to be understood generally that in a sensible thing there is neither grace nor guilt.

Nevertheless, they still object on the basis of the authority of John Damascene, who says that after the conception, or consent, of the blessed Virgin, the Holy Spirit came upon her and cleansed her of every sin and of all the tinder of sin. From this, I believe, they wish to derive the authority for saying that the virginal seed, although it did not arise from union with a man, nevertheless had to be cleansed from the tinder of sin through the working of the Holy Spirit.

To this we reply that we do not prejudge John Damascene in what he says, since we have read none of his writings except insofar as we have encountered them in many places, introduced by others as testimony.

[Col. 0466A] But we can readily produce against him the testimony of our most holy and learned Jerome, who says in his sermon on the Assumption of that same Lady and Queen of ours:

> “Blessed and glorious is the Virgin Mary. Although she was incomparable to all the virgins beneath the heavens, so that she might fittingly receive within herself the union of Divinity while both natures remained intact, nevertheless, when she is filled with grace, when she is suffused with the Holy Spirit, when she is overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, she becomes more precious in merits, higher in exalted dignity, more beautiful in holiness, and more glorious in the merits and prerogatives of her merits, so that she is no longer to be subjected to any uses except divine ones.”

[Cols. 0466A–B] I appeal to you, John Damascene—or whoever shares the opinion that the blessed Mother of God, after the annunciation of the holy angel, then first lost either sin or the tinder of sin through the coming of the Holy Spirit. I appeal to you, I say, by that same blessed *Theotokos* (θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”): desist; do not emulate the wicked; cease encrusting the most spotless vessel; take the sandals from your feet, which impede the progress of your right intention.

Indeed, you have zeal for God in this matter, but perhaps not according to knowledge. Perhaps you think that by this error you are rendering service to God. If you refuse to desist, know that this earth which you tread devours its inhabitants, exacting vengeance upon all the children of unbelief.

Listen further to what blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the organ of the Holy Spirit in our own times, says about this:

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Earlier she was called “full of grace,” and now how is it said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” and so forth? Could she have been filled with grace and not yet have the Holy Spirit, when he himself is the giver of graces? But if the Spirit was already in her, how is he still promised as though he had not come, as one who will come upon her?

Or perhaps he does not simply say, “He will come into you,” but adds, “He will come upon you,” because he was already in her through abundant grace, but is announced as coming upon her because of the more abundant fullness of grace which he will pour out upon her.

[Col. 0466C] But if she is full, how will she be able to receive anything more? And if she can receive something more, how are we to understand that she was previously full?

Or did the earlier grace fill only her mind, while the grace that followed and was to come had to suffuse her in such a way that the fullness of Divinity, which had previously dwelt spiritually in her—as it had in many saints—would also begin to dwell bodily in her, as in no other saint?

What does “the power of the Most High will overshadow you” mean? Let whoever can understand, understand. Perhaps it was said especially for this reason: “He will overshadow you,” because the matter was, of course, a sacrament; and what the Trinity alone wished to accomplish in the Virgin alone and with the Virgin alone was given to be known only to her, to whom alone it was given to experience it.

[Col. 0466D] We have introduced these words briefly against the objection they make from John Damascene. It would be presumptuous for us to impose a determination upon him, since we are entirely ignorant in what sense he spoke. But if he said here something contrary to Jerome and our authorities, we prefer in this matter to adhere not to him but to Jerome and our authorities.

An objection is also raised against our Anselm, because in this book he said that no truth and no understanding permits us to believe that, in a human being conceived from the Virgin alone, anything from the sinful mass could have or ought to have accrued—even if he were not God, although he had been taken from that mass.

For they say that Christ could not and did not wish to sin, not because he was the Virgin’s son, but because he was God.

“Christ,” they say, “neither wished nor could sin; therefore he was God.”

What, then, shall we say about the holy angels, who, through the grace of confirmation, neither wish nor can sin? Or if Adam, before he sinned, had begotten some who were confirmed in righteousness before him, what shall we say about them?

[Col. 0467A] Certainly, if those beings, although they neither wished nor could sin, would not for that reason be God or gods, then the same must be considered in Christ: whether the fact that he could not and did not wish to sin was caused solely by his Divinity united to the human being.

That his Divinity greatly and supremely assisted him is acknowledged by every believer. But it is one thing simply to be the cause; it is another to contribute assistance to a cause.

Perhaps they will say that, after Adam’s sin, no mortal flesh not united to Divinity could be or could have been without sin, however God might have created someone, male or female, without the seed of a man, provided that the person came from Adam.

But when they say this, they place the cause of sin, as above, in the seed. Yet just as God makes something arise from male and female, so he can make it arise from the female alone.

Let them therefore resolve what we have said above, both from authority and from reason, and we shall gladly listen.

[Col. 0467B] If they cannot do so, it will be clear to us—as it is established by Anselm’s irrefutable reasoning—that whoever is begotten in a manner other than Adam begot is not held under the prejudice of original sin, which descends from Adam by transmission, even though that person is not God, as Christ was.

[Col. 0468A] Thus, if such a person should wish not to sin, he will also be able not to will to sin, since he will be capable of not sinning—until confirming grace further adds the inability to will sin and the inability to sin.

Augustine agrees with us in the third book of *Against Julian*, chapter 5:

> “You think in vain,” he says, “that there is no wrongdoing in infants because wrongdoing cannot exist without the will, and there is no will in them. This is correctly said concerning each person’s own sin, but not concerning the original contagion [variant: wrongdoing] of the first sin [variant: of the parent]. For if that contagion did not exist, infants would be bound to no evil, and nothing evil—whether in body or in soul—would befall them under the authority of so just a God.”

Observe in these words, prudent reader, this maxim: from whomever the punishment of sin is removed, from that same person sin is also removed; the converse does not follow.

Therefore, from those infants whose punishment of sin in body and soul Augustine removes, he first teaches that all sin and the contagion of sin are removed. Those infants, then, would be neither God nor gods; and yet, if they wished, they could refrain from sinning, and once confirmed they could not sin.

Rightly, therefore, and most truly, Anselm—because truth is with him—and Augustine, the son of truth, held this view [variant: omit “held this view”].

[Cols. 0467B–C]

# SAINT ANSELM’S DIALOGUE ON TRUTH



## 109. PROLOGUE

I once composed three treatises pertaining to the study of Sacred Scripture, at different times. They resemble one another in this respect: they were composed in the form of question and answer. The person asking the questions is identified by the name “student,” while the person answering is identified by the name “teacher.” 

I have also published a fourth work in the same manner, which, as I think, is useful for introducing people to dialectic. Its beginning is: “Concerning the grammarian.” Since it concerns a field of study different from that of these three works, I do not wish to count it among them.

One of these three is *On Truth*: what truth is, in what things it is ordinarily said to exist, and what justice is.

Another is *On the Freedom of Choice*: what it is, whether a human being always possesses it, and what its various conditions are with respect to possessing or not possessing the rectitude of will for preserving which the rational creature was given it. In that work I showed only the natural strength of the will for preserving the rectitude it has received, not how necessary grace is to it for this very purpose, so that grace may follow. 

The third is *On the Question: What Did the Devil Sin, Since He Did Not Remain in the Truth?* God did not give him perseverance, which he could not have had unless God gave it. For if God had given it, he would have possessed it, just as the good angels possessed it because God gave it to them.

Although in that treatise I spoke about the confirmation of the good angels, I entitled it *On the Fall of the Devil*, because what I said about the good angels was incidental, whereas what I wrote about the evil angels arose from the purpose of the question.

Although these treatises are not joined together by any continuity of composition, their subject matter and the similarity of their argument require that they be written together in the order in which I have mentioned them. 

Although some hurried people wrote them down in another order before they were complete, I nevertheless wish them to be arranged in the way I have set them out here. 



[Col. 0468C]

## CHAPTER I

### That Truth Has Neither Beginning nor End

**STUDENT.** Since we believe God to be truth, and say that truth exists in many other things as well, I should like to know whether, wherever truth is spoken of, we ought to acknowledge that it is God.

For in your *Monologion* too (chapter 18, or 17), you prove through the truth of a proposition that supreme truth has neither beginning nor end. You say:

> “Let whoever can consider when this began, or when it was not true—namely, that something was going to exist; or when it will cease, and this will not be true—namely, that something will have existed.
>
> “But if neither of these can be conceived, and neither of these truths can exist without truth, it is impossible even to conceive that truth has a beginning or an end. 
>
> “Finally, if truth had a beginning or will have an end, then before it began it was true that truth did not exist; and after it had ended, it will be true that truth does not exist. 
>
> “But the true cannot exist without truth.  Therefore truth existed before truth existed, and truth will exist after truth has ended. This is entirely unacceptable.
>
> “Whether, then, truth is said to have or is understood not to have a beginning or an end, truth cannot be enclosed by either beginning or end.”

This is what you said in your *Monologion*. Therefore I expect to hear from you the definition of truth. 

**TEACHER.** I do not remember having found a definition of truth. But if you wish, let us investigate through the various things in which we say truth exists, and discover what truth is.

**STUDENT.** If I can do nothing else, I shall at least help by listening.

[Cols. 0469B–C]

## CHAPTER II

### On the Truth of Signification and on the Two Truths of a Proposition

**TEACHER.** Let us first ask what truth is in a proposition, since we often call a proposition true or false.

**STUDENT.** You ask, and whatever you discover I shall attend to.

**TEACHER.** When is a proposition true?

**STUDENT.** When what it states is the case, whether it states this affirmatively or negatively. I say that what it states is the case even when it denies that what is not the case is the case, because it states things as they are. 

**TEACHER.** Do you therefore think that the thing stated is the truth of the proposition?

**STUDENT.** No.

**TEACHER.** Why?

**STUDENT.** Because nothing is true except by participating in truth. Therefore the truth of what is true is in the true thing itself.  But the thing stated is not in the true proposition; hence it must not be called its truth but the cause of its truth.

Therefore it seems to me that its truth must be sought only in the proposition itself.

**TEACHER.** Consider, then, whether it is the proposition itself, or its signification, or something included in the definition of a proposition, that you are seeking.

**STUDENT.** I do not think so.

**TEACHER.** Why?

**STUDENT.** Because if that were so, it would always be true, since all the elements included in the definition of a proposition remain the same both when what it states is the case and when it is not. The proposition is the same, its signification is the same, and everything else is likewise the same. 

**TEACHER.** What, then, do you think truth is there?

**STUDENT.** I know nothing else except that when it signifies that what is the case is the case, then truth is in it and it is true. 

**TEACHER.** What was the affirmative proposition made for?

**STUDENT.** To signify that what is the case is the case.

**TEACHER.** Then is that what it ought to do?

**STUDENT.** Certainly.

**TEACHER.** Therefore, when it signifies that what is the case is the case, it signifies what it ought to signify.

**STUDENT.** Clearly.

**TEACHER.** But when it signifies what it ought to signify, it signifies rightly.

**STUDENT.** That is so.

**TEACHER.** And when it signifies rightly, is its signification right?

**STUDENT.** There is no doubt of it.

**TEACHER.** Therefore, when it signifies that what is the case is the case, its signification is right?

**STUDENT.** That follows.

**TEACHER.** Again, when it signifies that what is the case is the case, its signification is true?

**STUDENT.** It is truly right and true when it signifies that what is the case is the case.

**TEACHER.** Therefore, for it to be right and for it to be true are the same for it—that is, for it to signify that what is the case is the case. 

**STUDENT.** Truly, they are the same.

**TEACHER.** Therefore its truth is no different from its rectitude.

**STUDENT.** Now I plainly see that truth is rectitude.

**TEACHER.** The same is true when a proposition signifies that what is not the case is not the case. 

**STUDENT.** I understand what you are saying. But teach me what I could answer if someone said that even when reason signifies that what is not the case is the case, it signifies what it ought to signify.

For it has equally received the task of signifying that what is the case is the case and that what is not the case is the case. For if it had not received the task of signifying that what is not the case is the case, it would not signify it. Therefore, even when it signifies that what is not the case is the case, it signifies what it ought to signify.

But if, by signifying what it ought to signify, it is right and true, as you have shown, then the proposition is true even when it states that what is not the case is the case.

**TEACHER.** It is not ordinarily called true when it signifies that what is not the case is the case; nevertheless, it possesses truth and rectitude because it does what it ought to do.

But when it signifies that what is the case is the case, it does what it ought to do in two ways: it signifies both what it has received the task of signifying and what it was made to signify.

According to this rectitude and truth, by which it signifies that what is the case is the case, a proposition is customarily called right and true—not according to that rectitude by which it signifies that what is not the case is also the case.

For it has a greater obligation on account of what it received the task of signifying than on account of what it did not receive that task of signifying. It did not receive the task of signifying that a thing exists when it does not, or that it does not exist when it does, except because it could not at that time be given only the task of signifying that a thing exists when it exists, or does not exist when it does not. 

[Cols. 0470C–D] There is therefore one rectitude and truth of a proposition because it signifies that for signifying which it was made, and another because it signifies what it has received the task of signifying.  The latter is immutable in the proposition; the former is mutable.

For it always possesses the latter, but not always the former. It possesses the latter naturally, but the former accidentally and according to usage.

When I say, “It is day,” I rightly use the signification of this proposition to signify that what is the case is the case, because it was made for that purpose, and therefore it is then rightly said to signify.

But when, through the same proposition, I signify that what is not the case is the case, I do not use it rightly, because it was not made for that purpose. Accordingly, its signification is not then said to be right.

Nevertheless, in certain propositions these two rectitudes, or truths, are inseparable. For example, when we say, “A human being is an animal,” or, “A human being is not a stone.” The affirmative always signifies that what is the case is the case, and the negative that what is not the case is not the case.

Nor can we use the first to signify that what is not the case is the case, since a human being is always an animal; nor the second to signify that what is the case is not the case, since a human being is never a stone.

It was therefore the truth that the proposition possesses according to the way someone rightly uses it that we began to investigate, because, according to this truth, common linguistic usage judges it to be true. But we shall speak later about the truth which it cannot fail to possess.

**STUDENT.** Return, then, to what you began with, since you have sufficiently distinguished for me between the two truths of a proposition—provided that you show that it possesses some truth when it lies, as you say it does.

**TEACHER.** For the moment, let what we began to say about the truth of signification suffice. The same account of truth that we observed in a spoken proposition must be considered in all signs made to signify that something exists or does not exist, such as writing or sign-language made with the fingers.

**STUDENT.** Then move on to the other matters.

[Col. 0471C]

## CHAPTER III

### On the Truth of Opinion

**TEACHER.** We also call a thought true when what we think, whether through reason or in some other way, is the case; and false when it is not. 

**STUDENT.** That is how usage has it.

**TEACHER.** What, then, do you think truth is in thought?

**STUDENT.** According to the reasoning which we applied in the proposition, nothing more properly describes the truth of thought than its rectitude.  We were given the ability to think that something exists or does not exist for this purpose: that we should think that what is the case is the case, and that what is not the case is not the case.

Therefore, whoever thinks that what is the case is the case thinks what he ought to think, and for that reason his thought is right.

If, then, thought is true and right only because we think that what is the case is the case, or that what is not the case is not the case, its truth is nothing other than its rectitude.

[Col. 0471D]

## CHAPTER IV

### On the Truth of the Will

**TEACHER.** You are considering the matter correctly. But Truth itself also says that truth exists in the will, when it says that the devil did not remain in the truth (John 8:44). For he was not in the truth, nor did he abandon the truth, except in his will. 

**STUDENT.** I believe that. For if he had always willed what he ought to have willed, he would never have sinned, since he abandoned the truth only by sinning.

**TEACHER.** Tell me, then, what you understand truth to mean there. 

**STUDENT.** Nothing other than rectitude.

For as long as he willed what he ought to will—for that purpose he had received a will—he was in rectitude and truth. When he willed what he ought not to will, he abandoned rectitude and truth.

Nothing other than rectitude can be understood there as truth, since whether truth or rectitude, what existed in his will was nothing other than willing what he ought to will.

[Col. 0472A]

## CHAPTER V

### On the Truth of Natural and Non-Natural Action

## Textual apparatus

### Commentary on conception and original sin, cols. 0463C–0468B

These unassigned alternatives are marked *al.* (“another reading”) in the supplied text. No manuscript attribution is added.

- At “the tinder of sin which is in it,” *qui/quod* both mean “which,” with masculine/neuter relative forms.
- At “far removed from the seed,” *ea longe* means “it [is] far”; *alia est* means “it is different.” The latter is the supplied alternative at this point.
- In the Augustine quotation, *seminis*, “of seed,” is contrasted with *hominis*, “of a human being.”
- At “Augustine understood this,” *hoc*, “this,” is contrasted with *his*, “in/by these [things],” a different case and number form.
- At the preceding discourse, *praecessit*, “preceded,” is contrasted with the fuller *processit sermo de*, “the discourse proceeded concerning.”
- *Adhuc respondemus*, “we reply further,” has *Ad hoc*, “to this,” as an alternative to *Adhuc*.
- In the objection addressed to Augustine, *hoc*, “this,” has *hic*, “here,” as an alternative.
- *Videant moderni praeceptores*, “let modern teachers see,” has *Vide autem*, “but see,” as an alternative opening, which changes the grammatical construction.
- Near marker **108**, *generaliterque*, “and generally,” has *generaliter quae*, “which generally,” as an alternative. The narrative prints *in re sensibili*, “in a sentient thing,” despite the preceding argument about insentient things; a likely missing negative prefix is not silently supplied.
- In the appeal to John Damascene or another holder of the opinion, the supplied awkward *in tali sententia, quod putes*, approximately “in such an opinion, that you should think,” has *in sententia qui putas*, “in the opinion, you who think,” as an alternative.
- In Bernard's quotation, *aliquid*, “something,” has *aliud*, “something else,” as an alternative; *ante*, “previously,” has *autem*, “however.”
- Concerning the Trinity's work in the Virgin, *in sola*, “in her alone,” has *in solo*, “in [him/it] alone,” as an alternative masculine/neuter form.
- At what might accrue from the sinful mass, *aliquid*, “anything,” has *aliud*, “anything else”; *accedere*, “to accrue/be added,” has *accidere*, “to happen/befall.” The supplied clause is grammatically damaged (*de peccata massa peccatricis*); no additional sinful woman is inferred from it.
- At the comparison with Christ, *sic*, “thus,” has *sicut*, “just as,” as an alternative.
- Concerning the divinity's contribution, *adjuverit*, “has assisted,” has *adinvenerit*, “has devised/provided,” as an alternative.
- *Dicunt forte*, “perhaps they say,” has *dicent*, “they will say,” as an alternative verb.
- In the final Augustine citation, *primi peccati*, “of the first sin,” has *parentis*, “of the parent,” as an alternative to *primi*. *Originale contagium*, “original contagion,” has *delictum*, “offense,” as an alternative to *contagium*.
- At the close, one reading omits *senserunt*, “they held [this view].”

### Dialogue on Truth: prologue, col. 0467C

1. The *Dialogue on Truth* was collated with manuscripts from Bec and Jumièges, three Victorine manuscripts otherwise designated RR 3, CC 9, and EE 13, one Cistercian manuscript, one from the library of Saint Michael in the Mount, and the Gothic edition. The opening notices read: “Here begins the preface to the following treatises,” Gem., Bec. 2, and S. Mich.; “Here begins the preface to the following work,” Bec. 5; “Here begins the preface of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to the following work,” Vict. 3, Bec. 1, and Cister.; “Here begins the preface of blessed Anselm to the book On Truth,” Vict. 9.
2. *Nomine vocatur discipuli*, “is called by the name of student,” Bec. 2 and Vict.; *notatur nomine discipuli*, “is designated by the name of student,” the contrasting reading.
3. *Illi sit, sed ad hoc ut*, “it is for him, but for this purpose, that,” manuscripts; *illi fit ut*, “it happens for him that,” the contrasting reading. These are the apparatus's abbreviated forms of the clause concerning subsequent grace.
4. *Similitudo disputationis*, “similarity of discussion,” Vict. 9; *similitudo dispositionis*, “similarity of arrangement,” the contrasting reading.
5. *Ordine sint conscripti*, “have been written in [that] order,” S. Mich.; *ordine sint transcripti*, “have been copied in [that] order,” the contrasting reading.
6. “The preface ends,” manuscripts. The following title notices are: “Book On Truth,” Vict. 13; “Here begins the treatise On Truth composed by Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury,” Vict. 3; “Master Anselm's book On Truth,” Vict. 9; “Here begins Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury's treatise On Truth,” S. Mich.; “Here begins the treatise On Truth issued by Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury,” Bec. 6 and Cister.

### Dialogue, chapters I–II, col. 0469D

7. *Utrumque horum*, “each of these two things,” manuscripts; *utrumque hoc*, “both these things,” the contrasting demonstrative construction.
8. *Postquam finita, verum erit*, “after [truth has] ended, it will be true,” S. Mich. and the Gothic edition; *postquam finita erit, verum erit*, “after [truth] has ended, it will be true,” Bec. 6; *postquam finita erit veritas*, “after truth has ended,” the final contrasting citation. The abbreviated forms differ in their expressed verbs and subject.
9. *At quia verum*, “but because [it is] true,” Vict. and S. Mich.; *atqui verum*, “and yet [it is] true,” the contrasting reading.
10. *A te audire*, “to hear from you,” Vict., Bec., and Cister.; *a te discere*, “to learn from you,” the contrasting reading.
11. *Dico autem quod enunciat et quando*, “but I say what it states, even when,” manuscripts; the contrasting citation is *Dico enim esse quod enunciat, etiam quando*, “for I say that what it states is the case, even when.” Bec. 1 and Cister. omit *esse*, “to be/the being the case.”
12. *Et ideo veritas*, “and therefore truth,” manuscripts; *et ideo veri veritas*, “and therefore the truth of what is true,” the contrasting reading.
13. *Veritatis dicenda est*, “must be called [the cause] of truth,” manuscripts; *veritatis ejus dicenda est*, “must be called [the cause] of its truth,” the contrasting reading.
14. The note prints *semper esse vera*, “always to be true,” for Vict., S. Mich., Bec. 6, and the Gothic edition, then repeats exactly the same *semper esse vera* as its contrast. The narrative has *semper esset vera*, “would always be true.” No distinction is invented between the two identical apparatus quotations.
15. *Nisi cum significat*, “except when it signifies,” manuscripts; *nisi quia cum significat*, “except that, when it signifies,” the contrasting reading.
16. *Veram esse et significare*, “to be true and to signify,” manuscripts; *veram esse, id est significare*, “to be true, that is, to signify,” the contrasting reading.
17. *Similiter cum*, “similarly, when,” manuscripts; *similiter est cum*, “it is similar when,” the contrasting reading.
18. *Illi dare tunc*, “then to give it [the ability],” Bec., Gem., S. Mich., and Cister.; *illi dari tunc*, “then for it to be given [the ability],” the contrasting passive form.
19. *Quia significat quod accepit significare, et ad quod*, “because it signifies what it received [the ability] to signify, and that for which,” manuscripts; *quia significat ad quod*, “because it signifies that for which,” the contrasting reading. The latter continues “it was made to signify.” In the following distinction, the truth that a proposition has by signifying what it received the ability to signify is immutable and natural; the truth that it has by being used for its proper purpose is mutable and depends on use.

### Dialogue, chapters III–IV, col. 0471D

20. *Et falsum, cum*, “and false, when,” manuscripts and the Gothic edition; *et falsam, cum*, with the same English sense but feminine rather than masculine/neuter agreement.
21. *Quam in propositione*, “which in the proposition,” manuscripts; *quam de propositione*, “which concerning the proposition,” the contrasting preposition.
22. *Nisi voluntate*, “except by will,” manuscripts; *nisi in voluntate*, “except in the will,” the contrasting reading.
23. *Quid tu intelligas per veritatem*, “what you understand by truth,” manuscripts; *quid ibi intelligas veritatem*, “what you understand truth to be there,” the contrasting reading.

MAGISTER: You understand well. But truth must likewise be acknowledged in an action, just as the Lord said: “Whoever does evil hates the light,” and, “Whoever does the truth comes to the light” (John 3:20–21).

STUDENT: I see what you mean.

MAGISTER: Consider, then, what truth is present there, if you can.

STUDENT: Unless I am mistaken, it must also be contemplated in an action by the same reasoning by which we recognized truth above in other things.

MAGISTER: So it is. For if doing evil and doing the truth are opposites, as the Lord shows when he says, “Whoever does evil hates the light,” and, “Whoever does the truth comes to the light,” then to do the truth is the same as to do well. For doing well [Note: [Col. 0471D] “Doing well” and “doing evil” in one manuscript; “doing well and evil” in Béc. 6] is opposed to doing evil. Therefore, if doing the truth and doing well are identical in opposition, they are not different in meaning; rather, everyone agrees that whoever does what he ought does well and does what is right. Hence it follows that to do what is right [Col. 0472C] [Note: [Col. 0471D] “To do what is right.” D.; the manuscripts have simply “what is right”] is to do the truth. For it is established that doing the truth means doing well, and doing well means doing what is right. Thus nothing is clearer than that the truth of an action is its rightness.

STUDENT: I see no wavering at all in your argument [Note: [Col. 0471D] D. has “estimation” instead of “argument” in the manuscripts].

MAGISTER: Examine whether every action that does what it ought may appropriately be called “doing the truth.” There is a rational action, such as giving alms; and there is an irrational action, such as the action of fire, which gives heat [Note: [Col. 0471D] The manuscripts read “the action of fire which …”; Béc. 6 has “the action of fire, which …”]. See, then, whether it is appropriate to say that fire does the truth.

STUDENT: If fire received from the one from whom it has its being the power to give heat, then, when it gives heat, it does what it ought. Therefore I do not see what impropriety there would be in saying that fire does the truth and does what is right when it does what it ought.

MAGISTER: I do not see it otherwise either. From this it may be observed that the rightness, or truth, of an action is of two kinds: necessary and non-necessary. Fire necessarily does the truth and what is right when it gives heat; a human being does what is right and the truth non-necessarily when he does well. By “to do,” however, the Lord intended us to understand not only what is properly called doing, but every verb, when he said, “Whoever does the truth comes to the light” (John 3:21). [Note: [Col. 0473D] “What is properly called ‘doing’—‘doing the truth’ is understood not only in an act, but also in speech and in suffering; but he intended us to understand every verb when he said, ‘for whoever …’” in the manuscripts. Other manuscripts read: “What is properly called ‘doing,’ but he intended us to understand every verb when he said, ‘for whoever …’”]

For he does not exclude from this truth, or from this light [Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts of St. Michael and Béc. 6 read “truth without light”], the one who suffers persecution for righteousness, or the one who is where and when he ought to be, or the one who stands or sits when he ought to, and similar cases. No one says that such people are not doing well. And when the Apostle says, “Each will receive according to what he has done” (2 Corinthians 5:10), everything we are accustomed to call doing well [Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts read “to call doing, or doing well”; Victor, St. Michael, and Béc. 6: “to call doing well”] or doing evil must be understood there.

STUDENT: Common usage of speech also has this feature: it says that suffering, and many other things that are not doing, are nevertheless “doing.” Therefore, unless I am mistaken, we can also count a right intention among right actions—the truth of that intention we considered above, before the truth of action.

MAGISTER: You are not mistaken. For one who wills what he ought is said to act rightly and well, and is not excluded from those who do the truth. But since we are investigating truth, and the Lord seems to speak specifically of that truth which is in the will when he says of the devil that “he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44), I wanted to consider separately what truth in the will might be.

STUDENT: I am pleased that this has been done.

MAGISTER: Since it is established that the truth of an action is of two kinds, natural and non-natural, that truth of speech must be placed under the natural kind which we saw above (chapter 2) cannot be separated from it. Just as fire, when it gives heat, does the truth because it received this from the one from whom it has its being, so this statement—namely, “It is day”—does the truth when it signifies that it is day, whether it is day or not, because it naturally received the capacity to do this.

STUDENT: Only now do I see truth in a false statement.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Truth of the Senses [Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts have “On the truth of the senses”], and That the Falsity Thought to Be in the Sense Is in Opinion

MAGISTER: Do you think that, apart from the supreme truth, we have found every seat of truth?

STUDENT: I now remember a certain truth that I do not find among the matters you have discussed.

MAGISTER: What is it?

STUDENT: There is indeed truth in the bodily senses, but not always, for they sometimes deceive us. For when I occasionally see something through a pane of glass, sight deceives me: sometimes it reports to me that the object I see beyond the glass is the same color as the glass, although it is a different color; sometimes it makes me think that the glass has the color of the object I see beyond it, although it does not. There are many other cases in which sight and the other senses deceive us.

MAGISTER: It does not seem to me that this truth or falsity is in the senses, but in opinion. The interior sense itself is deceived; the exterior sense does not lie to it. This is sometimes easily recognized and sometimes with difficulty. When a child fears a sculpted dragon with its mouth open, it is easily recognized that this is not caused by sight, which reports to the child nothing other than what it reports to adults, but by the child’s interior sense, which does not yet know how to distinguish properly between a thing and the likeness of a thing.

The same occurs [Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts read “For the same occurs when”] when, seeing someone resemble another person, we think he is the person whom he resembles; or when someone hears a sound that is not a human voice and thinks that it is a human voice. This too is done by the interior sense.

As for what you say about the glass, the reason is that when sight passes through some body having an airy color, it is no more prevented from taking on the likeness of the color it sees beyond [Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts read “the likeness of the color which is seen beyond”; Béc. 6: “the likeness of the color which it sees beyond”] than when it passes through air—except insofar as the body through which it passes is denser or darker than air. This is the case when it passes through glass of its own color, that is, glass to which no other color has been added; or through very pure water, crystal, or something else having a similar color.
