But when the same sight passes through another color—for example, through glass not of its own color, but to which another color has been added—it receives the color that first meets it. Therefore, after having received one color, since it is affected according to that color, it receives any other color that meets it afterward either not at all or less completely [Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts read “receives completely” instead of “receives less completely”]. For this reason it reports the color it first received either alone or together with the color that subsequently meets it.

If sight is affected by the earlier color to the full extent of its capacity for color, it cannot at the same time perceive another color. But if it is affected by the earlier color less than it is capable of perceiving color, it can perceive another color. Thus, if it passes through some body—as through glass—that is so perfectly red that sight itself is wholly affected by its redness, it cannot at the same time be affected by a different color. But if the redness it first encounters is not as complete as its capacity for color, then, as though it were not yet full, it can still take on another color to the extent that its capacity has not been satisfied by the first.

Someone who does not know this thinks that sight reports that everything it perceives after taking on the first color is either wholly or partially of that same color [Note: [Col. 0473D] The manuscripts read “to report this, namely, that …” instead of “to report that …”]. Thus it happens that the interior sense attributes its own fault to the exterior sense.

The same is true when an unbroken stick, part of which is under water and part above it, is thought to be broken; or when we think that our sight finds our faces in a mirror; and in many other cases in which sight and the other senses seem to report things to us otherwise than they are. The fault is not in the senses, which report what they can, since they received the capacity to do precisely that, but must be attributed to the judgment of the soul, which does not properly distinguish what they can do from what they ought to do [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts read “what they could do, or what they ought to do”; Béc. 6: “what they can do, or what they deliberate”].

Since demonstrating this is more laborious than useful for our purpose, I do not think that time should be spent on it now [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts of Victor, Béc. 6, and Cistercian read “should be expended” instead of “should be spent”]. Let it suffice to say this: whatever the senses seem to report—whether they do so by their own nature or from some other cause—they do what they ought, and therefore they do what is right and the truth. This truth is contained under the truth that is in action [Note: [Col. 0475D] One manuscript of Victor: “whether they do this from another cause, they do what they ought, and therefore …”; Béc. 6: “whether from another cause, they do this because they ought, and therefore …”].

STUDENT: Your answer has satisfied me, and I do not want you to delay any longer over this question concerning the senses.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Truth of the Essence of Things [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts have “On the truth of the essence of things”]

MAGISTER: Now consider whether, apart from the supreme truth, truth should be understood to exist in any thing besides those we examined above.

STUDENT: What could that be?

MAGISTER: Do you think that anything ever exists, either at some time or somewhere, that is not in the supreme truth and did not receive from it what it is, insofar as it is what it is? Or that it could be other than what it is there?

STUDENT: That should not be thought possible.

MAGISTER: Whatever exists truly exists, insofar as it is what it is there.

STUDENT: You can conclude absolutely that everything that exists truly exists, since it is nothing other than what it is there.

MAGISTER: Therefore there is truth in the essence of all things that exist, because they are what they are in the supreme truth.

STUDENT: I see that truth is present there in such a way that falsity cannot exist there [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts read “falsity cannot exist”; the supplied text: “falsity cannot exist there”], since what exists falsely does not exist.

MAGISTER: You speak well. But say whether anything ought to be other than what it is in the supreme truth.

STUDENT: No.

MAGISTER: Therefore, if all things are what they are there, then without doubt they are what they ought to be [Note: [Col. 0475D] Béc. 6 continues the preceding chapter. The manuscripts read “all things are here” for “all things are this”; and “without doubt they are here” for “without doubt they are this”].

STUDENT: Truly they are what they ought to be [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts read “truly they are here” for “truly they are this”].

MAGISTER: Whatever is what it ought to be is rightly so [Note: [Col. 0475D] Béc. 6 reads “truly so” instead of “rightly so”].

STUDENT: It cannot be otherwise.

MAGISTER: Therefore everything that exists is rightly so.

STUDENT: Nothing follows more consistently [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts omit “Nothing follows more consistently”].

MAGISTER: Therefore, if truth and rightness are in the essence of things because they are what they are in the supreme truth, it is certain that the truth of things is their rightness.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Different Meanings of “Ought” and “Ought Not,” “Can” and “Cannot”

[Note: [Col. 0475D] In Béc. 6 and the Cistercian manuscript, chapter 8 begins at “But according to the truth of the matter …”]

STUDENT: Nothing could be clearer as far as the consistency of the argument is concerned. But according to the truth of the matter, how can we say that whatever exists ought to exist, when there are many evil deeds which certainly ought not to exist [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts of Victor and Béc. 6 read “ought not to exist”; the supplied text has “ought to exist” with “not” placed before it]?

MAGISTER: Why should it be surprising if the same thing ought both to exist and not to exist?

STUDENT: How can that be?

MAGISTER: I know that you do not doubt that nothing exists at all unless God either does it or permits it.

STUDENT: Nothing is more certain to me.

MAGISTER: Would you dare to say that God does or permits something unwisely or improperly?

STUDENT: On the contrary, I affirm that he does nothing except wisely and well.

MAGISTER: Would you judge that what such goodness and wisdom does or permits ought not to exist?

STUDENT: What intelligent person would dare think that?

MAGISTER: Therefore both what occurs through God’s doing and what occurs through his permitting ought equally to exist.

STUDENT: What you say is clear.

MAGISTER: Say also: do you think that the inclination of an evil will ought to exist?

STUDENT: That is the same as asking whether an evil deed ought to exist; no sensible person will concede that.

MAGISTER: Yet God permits certain people to do evil, because they will to do evil.

STUDENT: If only he did not permit it so often.

MAGISTER: Therefore the same thing both ought and ought not to exist. It ought to exist because it is permitted well and wisely by the one without whose permission it could not occur; and it ought not to exist insofar as it is conceived by the unrighteous will of the one who wills it.

In this way, the Lord Jesus, because he alone was innocent [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts of Victor and Béc. read “because the Lord Jesus alone …”], ought not to have suffered death, nor ought anyone to have inflicted it upon him; and yet he ought to have suffered it because he himself wisely, kindly, and beneficially willed to endure it [Note: [Col. 0475D] In the manuscripts of Béc., Gem., and Victor, this continues the preceding chapter].

For the same thing often receives contraries under different considerations, as happens in action—for example, in striking. A striking belongs both to the one who acts and to the one who suffers the action; hence it can be called both action and passion, although, according to the word itself, “action,” or “striking,” and words similarly formed from passive terms but used actively seem to belong more to the one who suffers than to the one who acts.

For according to what he does, the terms “acting” or “striking” seem more properly to be used; and according to what he suffers, “action” or “striking” [Note: [Col. 0475D] The manuscripts read “seem to be called”; Victor has “seems to be called”].

“Acting” and “striking” are derived from “agent” and “striker”—as “providence” from “one who provides,” and “continence” from “one who restrains”—and these, namely the agent, striker, provider, and restrainer, are active. “Action” and “striking,” however, are derived from “what is acted upon” and “what is struck,” which are passive.

But since, to say in one case what you should understand in the others, just as a striker does not exist without a striking, nor one who is struck without a striker, so striking and the striker cannot exist without one another—in fact, one and the same thing is signified by different names according to different aspects—therefore striking is said to belong both to the striker and to the one struck.

Consequently, insofar as the agent or patient is subject to the same judgment or to contrary judgments, the action itself will likewise be judged from both sides in the same way or in contrary ways.

Thus, when the one who strikes strikes rightly, and the one who is struck is rightly struck—as when a sinner is corrected by the one to whom correction belongs—the striking is right from both sides, because from both sides it ought to occur.

Conversely, when a righteous person is struck by an unrighteous person, since neither ought this person to be struck nor ought that person to strike, the striking is not right from either side, because it ought to occur from neither side.

But when a sinner is struck by someone to whom it does not belong to strike, since the sinner ought to be struck while the other person ought not to strike, the striking both ought and ought not to occur; and therefore it cannot be denied that it is both right and not right.

If you consider the judgment of supreme wisdom and goodness, whether the striking ought not to occur from only one side or from both—the side of the agent and the side of the patient—who would dare deny that what is permitted by such goodness and wisdom ought to exist?

STUDENT: Let whoever dares deny it do so; I, for my part, do not dare.

MAGISTER: What, moreover, if you consider the matter according to the nature of things—as when iron nails were driven into the Lord’s body? Would you say that fragile flesh ought not to have been penetrated, or that flesh penetrated by sharp iron ought not to have felt pain?

STUDENT: I would be speaking against nature.

MAGISTER: Therefore it can happen that an action or passion ought to exist according to the nature of things, although according to the agent or patient it ought not to exist, because the one ought not to act and the other ought not to suffer.

STUDENT: I cannot deny any of this.

MAGISTER: You see, then, that it can very often happen that the same action ought and ought not to exist, under different considerations.

STUDENT: You demonstrate this so clearly that I cannot fail to see it.

MAGISTER: But I want you to know that “ought” and “ought not” are sometimes used improperly [Note: [Col. 0477D] “Improperly; for example, ‘properly’” in Victor 3]. For example, when I say, “I ought to be loved by you.” If I truly ought to be loved, then I am a debtor who must return what I owe [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts of Victor read “if I owe, I am truly a debtor”; Béc. 6: “if I truly owe, I am a debtor”; another reading is “if, however, I owe, [I am] a debtor”], and I am at fault if I am not loved by you.

STUDENT: That follows.

MAGISTER: But when I ought to be loved by you, the demand is not to be made of me, but of you.

STUDENT: I must admit that this is so [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “I must so admit”; Béc. 6: “I must be so”].

MAGISTER: Therefore, when I say [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “when therefore I say that I am”], “I ought to be loved by you,” this is not said as though I owed something [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “as though I owed”], but because you ought to love me. Likewise, when I say, “I ought not to be loved by you,” nothing else is meant than that you ought not to love me.

The same manner of speaking occurs with power and inability, as when it is said: “Hector could be defeated by Achilles,” and “Achilles could not be defeated by Hector.” The power was not in the one who could be defeated, but in the one who could defeat; nor was the inability in the one who could not be defeated, but in the one who could not defeat.

STUDENT: I am pleased by what you say; I think it useful to know this.

## CHAPTER IX [elsewhere X]. That Every Action Signifies Either Truth or Falsity

[Note: [Col. 0477D] In the manuscripts this is chapter 9, with the title “That every action …,” as in the title of chapter 9 in the printed editions.]

MAGISTER: You think rightly. But let us return to the truth of signification, from which I began in order to lead you from what is more familiar to what is less familiar. Everyone speaks about the truth of signification; but few consider the truth that is in the essence of things.

STUDENT: It benefited me that you led me by this order.

MAGISTER: Let us see, then, how extensive the truth of signification is. For there is true or false signification not only in what we usually call signs, but also in everything else we have discussed. Since nothing ought to be done except what one ought to do, by the very fact that someone does something he says and signifies that he ought to do it. If he ought to do what he does, he speaks the truth; but if he ought not, he lies.

STUDENT: Although I seem to understand, since this has not previously been heard, show more clearly what you mean [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “although this seems to me …” instead of “although it has hitherto been unheard”].

MAGISTER: If you were in a place where you knew there were wholesome and poisonous herbs, but did not know how to distinguish them, and there were someone whom you did not doubt could distinguish them [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts of Victor read “that he could distinguish them”], and when you asked him which were wholesome and which poisonous he called some wholesome in words [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “but called others wholesome in words”] while eating others, whom would you believe more—the words or his action?

STUDENT: I would not believe his words as much as his deed.

MAGISTER: Therefore, by his action he would tell you more about which were wholesome than by his words.

STUDENT: That is so.

MAGISTER: Likewise, if you did not know that one ought not to lie, and someone lied in your presence, even if he told you that he ought not to lie, by his action he would tell you more that he ought to lie than by his words that he ought not to lie.

Similarly, when someone thinks about or wills something [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “something, or wills” instead of “thinks about or wills”], if you did not know whether he ought to will or think about it, but saw his will and thought, he would signify to you by the action itself that he ought to think about and will it [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts of Victor read “ought to think”; the supplied text has “ought to think about and will”]. If he ought to do so, he would speak the truth; but if not, he would be lying.

There is likewise true or false signification in the existence of things, because by the very fact that something exists, it says that it ought to exist.

STUDENT: Now I see clearly what I had not previously noticed.

## CHAPTER X [elsewhere XI]. On the Supreme Truth

[Note: [Col. 0477D] In the manuscripts this is chapter 10, under the title “On the supreme truth.”]

MAGISTER: Let us proceed to what remains.

STUDENT: Go ahead, and I will follow.

MAGISTER: You will not deny that the supreme truth is rightness.

STUDENT: On the contrary, I can acknowledge it as nothing other than that.

MAGISTER: Consider that all the rightnesses mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “that all the aforesaid rightnesses …”] are rightnesses because the things in which they exist either are or do what they ought. The supreme truth, however, is not rightness because it owes anything. Everything owes something to it; but it owes nothing to anyone, nor is it what it is for any reason except that it is [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscripts read “everything owes something; it …”].

STUDENT: I understand.

MAGISTER: Do you also see [Note: [Col. 0479D] Victor 3 reads “that this”; the supplied text has “how this”] how this rightness is the cause of all other truths and rightnesses, while nothing is the cause of it?

STUDENT: I see and observe that among the others some are effects only, while others are both causes and effects. Thus, the truth that is in the existence of things is an effect of the supreme truth, but it is itself also the cause of the truth that is in thought and of the truth that is in a proposition; these two truths, in turn, are the cause of no truth.

MAGISTER: You consider this well. Therefore you can now understand how, in my *Monologion* (chapter 18), I proved through the truth of a statement that the supreme truth has neither beginning nor end.

When I said, “At a time when it was not true that something was going to happen,” I did not mean that this statement, which asserted that something was going to happen, had existed without a beginning, or that this truth was God. Rather, because [Note: [Col. 0479D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “God, because”] it is impossible to understand a “when” at which, if this statement existed [Note: [Col. 0479D] The manuscripts read “when the statement …”; the supplied text: “when, if the statement …”], truth would be absent from it, it is understood from the fact that no time can be understood at which this truth could not exist, if there were a statement in which it could exist, that the truth which is the first cause of this truth existed without a beginning.

For the truth of a statement could not always exist unless its cause always existed. Indeed, the statement “Something is going to happen” is not true unless something really is going to happen; and nothing is going to happen unless it is in the supreme truth [Note: [Col. 0479D] The manuscripts read “something else is going to happen” instead of “something is going to happen”].

The same must be understood of the statement that says that something has happened in the past [Note: [Col. 0479D] The manuscripts read “the truth of the statement” instead of “the statement”]. For if, once this statement had been made, it could not lack truth under any understanding, it is necessary that no end can be conceived for that truth which is the supreme cause of this one.

Something is truly said to have happened in the past [Note: [Col. 0479D] The manuscripts of Victor read “something is truly said to have happened in the past”] because it is so in reality; and something has happened in the past because it is so in the supreme truth. Therefore, if it could never have been untrue that something was going to happen, and it can never become untrue that something happened in the past, it is impossible for the supreme truth to have had a beginning or to be going to have an end.

STUDENT: I see that nothing can be brought against your reasoning.

## CHAPTER XI [elsewhere XII]. On the Definition of Truth

MAGISTER: Let us return to the investigation of truth that we began [Note: [Col. 0479D] In the manuscripts, “Let us return …” continues the preceding chapter].

STUDENT: All of this pertains to investigating truth; nevertheless, return to whatever you wish.

MAGISTER: Tell me, then, whether it seems to you that there is any other rightness besides those we have considered.

STUDENT: None besides these, except the rightness that exists in bodily things, which is very different from these—for example, the straightness of a rod.

MAGISTER: In what way does it seem to you to differ from these?

STUDENT: Because it can be known by bodily sight, whereas those others are grasped by the contemplation of reason.

MAGISTER: Is not that rightness of bodies understood and recognized by reason, apart from its subject? Or if there is doubt whether the line of some absent body is straight, and it can be shown that it bends in no direction, is it not inferred by reason that it must be straight?

STUDENT: Yes. But the same rightness that is thus understood by reason is sensed by sight in its subject; whereas those other rightnesses can be perceived only by the mind.

MAGISTER: Therefore, unless I am mistaken, we can define truth as rightness perceptible only by the mind.

STUDENT: I do not see how one who says this could be mistaken. Indeed, this definition contains neither more nor less than is appropriate to the definition of truth, because the term “rightness” separates it from every thing that is not called rightness. The statement that it is perceived only by the mind separates it from visible rightness.

[Col. 0480B]

## CHAPTER XII [elsewhere XIII]. On the Definition of Justice

[Note: [Col. 0479D] In the manuscripts this is chapter 12. They have the title “On the definition of justice.”]

But since you have taught me that every truth is rectitude, and rectitude seems to me to be the same as justice, teach me also what I should understand justice to be. For it seems that everything which is right is also just, and conversely, that whatever is just is right. For it seems both just and right that fire should be hot, and that every human being who loves himself should love himself. For if whatever ought to be is right and just, and nothing else is right and just except what ought to be, then, as I think, justice cannot be anything other than rectitude. Indeed, although the supreme and simple nature is not right and just for the reason that it owes anything, nevertheless there is no doubt that rectitude and justice are the same.

[Note: Col. 0479D: The manuscripts read “nor is anything else right” (*nec aliquid recte*) for “and nothing else is right” (*nec aliud recte*).]

**MASTER.** You therefore have a definition of justice, if justice is nothing other than rectitude. And since we are speaking of rectitude perceptible by the mind alone, truth, rectitude, and justice define one another, so that whoever knows one of them and is ignorant of the others may arrive through the known one at knowledge of the unknown—or rather, whoever knows one cannot be ignorant of the others.

**STUDENT.** What then? Shall we call a stone just when it seeks what is lower from what is higher, because it does what it ought, just as we call a person just who does what he ought?

**MASTER.** We are not accustomed to call such a thing just by reason of this sort of justice.

**STUDENT.** Why, then, is a human being just rather than a stone, if both act justly?

**MASTER.** Do you yourself not think that the action of a human being differs in some way from the action of a stone?

**STUDENT.** I know that a human being acts voluntarily, while a stone acts naturally and not voluntarily.

**MASTER.** For that reason a stone is not called just: for one who does what he ought is not just if he does not will what he does.

**STUDENT.** Shall we therefore say that a horse is just when it wishes to graze, because it voluntarily does what it ought?

**MASTER.** I did not say that one is just who voluntarily does what he ought; I said that one is not just who does not voluntarily do what he ought.

**STUDENT.** Tell me, then, who is just.

[Note: One manuscript has “what is just” instead of “who is just”: Vict. 3 and S. Mich.]

[Note: Col. 0479D: At “who does what he ought,” S. Mich., Bec. 6, and Cister. read “when he does what he ought.” At “such a thing just,” the manuscripts read “by this sort of justice”; S. Mich. reads “this sort of justice,” and some witnesses have the accusative *huiusmodi iustitiam*. At “a human being just rather than a stone,” S. Mich., Bec. 6, and Cister. read “a just human being rather than a stone.”]

**MASTER.** As I see, you are asking for the definition of that justice to which praise is owed, just as its opposite, injustice, deserves blame.

**STUDENT.** That is what I am asking for.

**MASTER.** It is clear that this justice is not present in any nature which does not recognize rectitude. For whatever does not will rectitude, even if it possesses it, does not deserve praise because it possesses rectitude; but one who does not know rectitude cannot will it.

**STUDENT.** That is true.

**MASTER.** Rectitude, therefore, which earns praise for the one who possesses it, exists only in a rational nature, which alone perceives the rectitude of which we are speaking.

**STUDENT.** That follows.

**MASTER.** Since, then, every justice is rectitude, there is no justice which makes its possessor praiseworthy except in rational beings.

**STUDENT.** It cannot be otherwise.

**MASTER.** Where, then, does this justice seem to you to be in a human being, since he is rational?

**STUDENT.** It can be only in the will, or in knowledge, or in action.

**MASTER.** If someone understands rightly or acts rightly, but does not rightly will, will anyone praise him for justice?

**STUDENT.** No.

**MASTER.** Justice, then, is not the rectitude of knowledge or the rectitude of action, but the rectitude of the will.

**STUDENT.** Either that is so, or nothing is.

**MASTER.** Does the justice we seek seem to you to have been sufficiently defined?

**STUDENT.** You decide.

**MASTER.** Do you think that whoever wills what he ought thereby wills rightly and possesses rectitude of will?

**STUDENT.** If someone unknowingly wills what he ought—for example, when he wishes to close a door against someone who, without his knowledge, wants to kill another person in the house—whether or not he possesses some rectitude of will, he does not possess the rectitude we are seeking.

**MASTER.** What do you say about one who knows that he ought to will what he wills?

**STUDENT.** It can happen that someone who understands wills what he ought, but does not will that he ought to do so. For when a thief is compelled to return money he has stolen, it is clear that he does not will that he ought to return it; for he is compelled to wish to return it precisely because he ought to do so. Yet such a person is in no way to be praised for this rectitude.

**MASTER.** One who feeds a hungry poor person for the sake of empty glory wills that he ought to will what he wills. For he is praised precisely because he wishes to do what he ought. What, then, do you judge concerning him?

**STUDENT.** His rectitude is not to be praised, and therefore it is not sufficient for the justice we seek. But now show what is sufficient.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “what are sufficient”: Vict., Gem., Bec., Cister.]

**MASTER.** Every will, just as it wills something, also wills for some reason. For just as one must consider what it wills, so one must also see why it wills it. Indeed, it ought to be no more right in willing what it ought than in willing the reason for which it ought. Therefore every will has a “what” and a “why”; for we will absolutely nothing unless there is a reason why we will it.

**STUDENT.** We all recognize this in ourselves.

**MASTER.** Why, then, does it seem to you that each person must will what he wills in order to have a praiseworthy will? What ought to be willed is clear: whoever does not will what he ought is not just.

**STUDENT.** It seems no less clear to me that, just as each person ought to will what he ought, so he ought to will it because he ought, if his will is to be just.

**MASTER.** You understand well that these two things are necessary for justice in the will: namely, to will what one ought, and to will it because one ought. But tell me whether they are sufficient.

**STUDENT.** Why should they not be?

**MASTER.** When someone wills what he ought because he is compelled, and is compelled because he ought to will it, does he not in some way will what he ought because he ought?

**STUDENT.** I cannot deny it; but this person wills in one way, while the just person wills in another.

[Note: One manuscript reads “the just person wills in another way” and omits “this person wills”: Cister.]

**MASTER.** Distinguish these ways.

**STUDENT.** The just person, when he wills what he ought, preserves the rectitude of his will for no other reason, insofar as he is just, than for the sake of that rectitude itself. But one who wills what he ought only under compulsion or for an external reward—if he may be said to preserve rectitude—does not preserve it for its own sake, but for something else.

[Note: The manuscripts vary: “for something else, I say, the just person is”; “for something else, insofar as he is just”; and “for something else, insofar as he is to be called just.”]

**MASTER.** That will, then, is to be called just which preserves the rectitude of its will for the sake of rectitude itself.

[Note: Some manuscripts read simply “Therefore it is just”; another reads “Therefore that will is just”; Bec. 6 reads “therefore that will is just.”]

**STUDENT.** Either this is the only just will, or none is.

**MASTER.** Justice, therefore, is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake.

**STUDENT.** This is the definition of justice that I was seeking.

**MASTER.** Nevertheless, see whether something in it may perhaps need correction.

**STUDENT.** I see nothing in it that needs correction.

**MASTER.** Nor do I. For no justice exists which is not rectitude; and no rectitude other than that of the will is called justice in itself. The rectitude of an action is also called justice, but only when the action is performed with a just will. The rectitude of the will, however, does not lose the name of justice even if it is impossible for what we rightly will to be done.

But because it is said to be “preserved,” someone might say: if the rectitude of the will is to be called justice only when it is preserved, then it is not justice as soon as it is possessed; and we do not receive justice when we receive it, but make it justice by preserving it. For we receive and possess it before we preserve it. We do not receive it, nor initially possess it, because we preserve it; rather, we begin to preserve it because we receive and possess it.

We can answer this by saying that we receive it together with willing and possessing it. For we do not possess it except by willing it; and if we will it, by that very act we possess it. Just as we possess and will it simultaneously, so we simultaneously will and preserve it, since we do not preserve it except when we will it, nor is there a time when we will it and do not preserve it. As long as we will it, we preserve it; and as long as we preserve it, we will it.

Since, therefore, it happens at the same time that we will and possess it, and since willing and preserving it are not present in us at different times, we necessarily receive both possessing and preserving it together. Just as, so long as we preserve it, we possess it, so, so long as we possess it, we preserve it. No inconsistency arises from this.

Indeed, although the reception of this rectitude is by nature prior to possessing or willing it—for possessing or willing it is not the cause of receiving it, but receiving it produces willing and possessing it—nevertheless reception, possession, and willing occur at the same time. We begin simultaneously to receive, possess, and will it; and reception, possession, and willing are nevertheless simultaneous in time. As soon as it is received, it is possessed and willed.

Although possessing or willing it is by nature prior to preserving it, they are nevertheless simultaneous in time. Therefore, from the moment when we simultaneously receive, possess, will, and preserve the rectitude of the will, we receive justice; and as soon as we possess and will that same rectitude of will, it is to be called justice.

What we added—“for its own sake”—is so necessary that the same rectitude is in no way justice unless it is preserved for its own sake.

**STUDENT.** I cannot think of anything against this.

**MASTER.** Does it seem to you that this definition can be applied to supreme justice, insofar as we can speak about that reality of which nothing, or scarcely anything, can properly be said?

**STUDENT.** Although in it will is not one thing and rectitude another, nevertheless, just as we say “the power of divinity,” or “divine power,” or “powerful divinity”—even though in divinity power is not something other than divinity—so it is not inappropriate to say there “rectitude of will,” or “voluntary rectitude,” or “right will.” If we say that this rectitude is preserved for its own sake, it seems that this can be said of no other rectitude so appropriately. For just as it is not another thing that preserves it, but it preserves itself, and not through another, but through itself, so it is preserved not for anything else but for itself.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “so it is not preserved for anything else, but for itself.”]

**MASTER.** We may therefore say without hesitation that justice is rectitude of will, and that this rectitude is preserved for its own sake. And since the verb I use here, “is preserved,” has no present passive participle, we may use the passive past participle of the same verb in place of the present.

**STUDENT.** We have this usage very commonly: we use passive past participles for present participles that Latin does not possess, just as Latin has no past participles from active and neuter verbs and uses present participles in place of the past ones it lacks. Thus, if it is said of someone, “This man, having learned while studying and reading, teaches only under compulsion,” the meaning is: “He learned while he studied and read, but teaches only when compelled.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read “as if I were to say.”]

**MASTER.** We were therefore right to say that justice is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake—that is, rectitude which is preserved for its own sake. Hence just people are sometimes called “upright in heart,” that is, upright in will; and sometimes simply “upright,” without the addition “of heart,” since no one else is understood to be upright except one who has a right will. Thus we read: “Rejoice, all you upright in heart” (Psalm 31:11); and: “The upright will see it and rejoice” (Psalm 106:42).

**STUDENT.** You have satisfied even children concerning the definition of justice. Let us move on to other matters.

[Note: Col. 0483D: Some manuscripts read “You have also earlier satisfied [us] concerning …” (*etiam prius de*) for “You have also satisfied even children concerning …” (*etiam pueris de*).]

[Note: Additional apparatus for the preceding discussion. Col. 0481D: Bec., Gem., Vict. 3 and 9, and Cister. read “for he is therefore compelled” (*quoniam igitur*) where the text reads “for he is compelled precisely because” (*quoniam ideo*). Cister. reads “the just person wills in another way,” omitting “this person wills.” At “for no other reason, insofar as he is just,” the variants are: Bec. and Gem., “for something else, I say, [than that for which] he is just”; Bec. 6, Cister., Vict., and S. Mich., “for something else, insofar as he is called just.” At “that will … is to be called just,” the manuscripts read respectively “therefore [it] is just,” “therefore that will is to be called just” (Bec. 6), and “therefore that will is just.”

Col. 0481D: Gem., Bec., S. Mich., and Cister. add “but” in “but we do not receive justice”; the main text omits it. The manuscripts read “by that very act alone possess it” (*hoc ipso solo eam*) for “by that very act possess it,” or “by that very act possess it” with *illam* in place of *eam*. They also preserve the longer reading: “and thus, so long as we possess it, we preserve it; nor does any inconsistency arise,” instead of the shorter wording.

Col. 0483D: The witnesses vary in the repeated sentence about reception: some read, “reception makes us will and possess it; we begin simultaneously to receive, possess, and will it; yet reception, possession, and willing are simultaneous in time; and as soon as it is received, it is possessed”; others transpose these clauses, but retain the same point. Vict., Bec. 6, and Cister. read “to preserve it, [yet] simultaneously,” rather than “to preserve it, [they] nevertheless are simultaneous.” S. Mich. and Bec. 6 read “and as soon as we will and possess” for “and as soon as we possess and will.” At “so appropriately,” Vict., Bec. 6, and Cister. read “thus appropriately.”]


[Note: Some manuscripts read “You have satisfied them earlier as well concerning…”]

## CHAPTER XIII [elsewhere XIV]

### That there is one truth in all true things

[Note: In the manuscripts this is chapter 13.]

[Note: The manuscripts read: “That there is one truth in all true things”; Bec. 6 reads: “That there is one truth in all things.”]

**MASTER.** Let us return to rectitude, or truth. Since these two names signify one thing—for we are speaking of rectitude perceptible by the mind alone, which is the genus of justice—let us ask whether there is one single truth in all those things in which we say that truth exists, or whether there are as many truths as there are things in which truth is established.

**STUDENT.** I greatly desire to know this.

**MASTER.** It is established that, whatever thing truth may be in, it is nothing other than rectitude.

**STUDENT.** I have no doubt about that.

**MASTER.** If, then, there are several truths according to several things, there are also several rectitudes.

**STUDENT.** This is no less certain.

**MASTER.** If different rectitudes necessarily exist according to differences among things, then those same rectitudes have their own existence according to the things themselves; and just as the things in which they exist vary, so the rectitudes must also be various.

**STUDENT.** Show me in one thing in which we say that rectitude exists what I should understand in the others.

**MASTER.** I say that the rectitude of signification is different from the rectitude of the will because the one is in the will and the other in signification. Therefore the rectitude which exists by reason of signification has its own existence, and changes according to signification.

**STUDENT.** So it is. When what is is signified as being, or what is not as not being, the signification is right, and it is clear that rectitude exists, without which signification cannot be right. But if what is not is signified as being, or what is as not being, or if nothing at all is signified, there will be no rectitude of signification, which exists only in signification. Therefore it has existence through signification, and its rectitude changes through it, just as color has existence through a body, and ceases to exist when the body ceases to exist. For when a body exists, its color necessarily exists; and when the body perishes, it is impossible for its color to remain.

**MASTER.** Color does not stand in the same relation to body as rectitude stands to signification.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Color stands to body as rectitude stands to the likeness of significations”; another reads “color stands to body, and rectitude to signification.”]

**STUDENT.** Show the dissimilarity.

**MASTER.** If no one wishes to signify by any sign what ought to be signified, will there be any signification through signs?

**STUDENT.** None.

**MASTER.** Will it therefore not be right for what ought to be signified to be signified?

**STUDENT.** It will not for that reason be less right, nor will rectitude demand this any less.

**MASTER.** Therefore, even when signification does not exist, the rectitude by which it is right, and by which it is required that what ought to be signified be signified, does not perish.

**STUDENT.** If it had perished, this would not be right, nor would rectitude itself require it.

**MASTER.** When what ought to be signified is signified, do you think that the signification is then right because of this rectitude and according to this very rectitude?

**STUDENT.** Indeed, I cannot think otherwise. For if signification is right through another rectitude, then when that rectitude perishes nothing prevents signification from remaining right. But no signification is right if it signifies what it is not right to signify, or what rectitude does not require.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “would be right” instead of “is right.”]

**MASTER.** No signification, then, is right through any rectitude other than that which remains when signification perishes.

**STUDENT.** It is evident.

**MASTER.** Do you therefore not see that rectitude exists in signification, not because it then begins to exist when what is is signified as being, or what is not as not being, but because signification then conforms to a rectitude which always exists? Nor is rectitude absent from signification because it perishes when signification is not as it ought to be, or when there is no signification; rather, signification then falls short of rectitude, which does not fail.

**STUDENT.** I see this in such a way that I cannot fail to see it.

**MASTER.** Rectitude, therefore, by which signification is called right, does not have existence, or any alteration, through signification, however signification itself may alter.

**STUDENT.** Nothing could now be clearer to me.

**MASTER.** Can you prove that color stands in the same relation to body as rectitude stands to signification?

**STUDENT.** I am now more ready to prove that they are very dissimilar.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “I am now more prepared.”]

**MASTER.** I think it is already clear to you what is to be thought concerning the will and its rectitude, and concerning other things which ought to possess rectitude.

[Note: One manuscript reads “what is to be known.”]

**STUDENT.** I see entirely that by this same reasoning, however those things themselves may be, immutable rectitude remains.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “however the things themselves may be, immovable rectitude remains.”]

**MASTER.** What, then, do you think follows concerning the rectitudes themselves? Are they distinct from one another, or is the rectitude of them all one and the same?

**STUDENT.** Earlier I granted that if there are several rectitudes because there are several things in which they are considered, then they must exist and vary according to the things themselves. It has been demonstrated that this does not happen. Therefore rectitudes are not several because there are several things in which they exist.

**MASTER.** Do you have any other reason why they seem to you to be several, apart from the plurality of things themselves?

**STUDENT.** Just as I know that there is no such reason, so I judge that no other can be found.

**MASTER.** The rectitude of all things is therefore one and the same.

**STUDENT.** I must admit this.

**MASTER.** Furthermore: if rectitude exists in those things which ought to possess rectitude only when they are as they ought to be, and if this alone constitutes their being right, it is clear that the rectitude of them all is one and the same.

**STUDENT.** It cannot be denied.

**MASTER.** There is therefore one truth in all those things.

**STUDENT.** This too cannot be denied. Yet show me why we speak of the truth of this or that thing, as if to distinguish differences among truths, if they derive no diversity from the things themselves. For many people will scarcely concede that there is no difference between the truth of the will and what is called the truth of action, or of anything else.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “differences of truth” instead of “differences among truths.”]

**MASTER.** Improperly is truth said to belong to this or that thing, because it does not have its existence in the things themselves, or from them, or through them, in which it is said to exist. Rather, when the things themselves conform to that rectitude which is always present to things that are as they ought to be, then the truth of this or that thing is spoken of: for example, the truth of a word, an action, or a will.

[Note: Manuscripts variously read “the truth of a word, an action, and a will”; “the truth of the will and action”; “the truth of the will, action”; and “the truth of the will and of action.”]

It is like saying that time belongs to this or that thing, although the time of all things existing together at the same time is one and the same. Even if this or that thing did not exist, the same time would still exist. Time is not therefore called the time of this or that thing because time exists in the things themselves, but because the things themselves exist in time.

And just as time, considered in itself, is not called anyone’s time, but when we consider the things that exist in it, we call it the time of this or that thing, so supreme truth, subsisting in itself, belongs to no thing. But when something conforms to it, then its truth or rectitude is spoken of.

[Note: Manuscripts Vict., RR. 3, and Bec. 6 conclude: “Here ends the treatise On Truth, published by Anselm, archbishop.” Cister. has: “Here ends the treatise On Truth.”]

[Note: Additional apparatus for Chapter XIII. Col. 0485C: At “does not have existence, or any alteration,” Vict., Bec., Gem., and Cister. read “does not have being and non-being, or any …”; Vict. 9 reads “does not have being, so as to have any …”. The manuscripts read *promptior nunc* (“I am now more ready”) for *paratior nunc* (“more prepared”).

At “other things which ought to possess rectitude,” Gem., Bec., Vict. 3, and Cister. read “which ought to have rectitude”; Vict. 9 and 13 read “which ought [to possess] rectitude”; another reading is “which have rectitude.” Bec. 6 reads “what is to be known” (*sciendum est*) for “what is to be thought” (*sentiendum sit*). The manuscripts variously read “however those things themselves may be, immovable rectitude remains” and “however those things themselves may be, immutable rectitude remains.” At “Earlier I granted,” the manuscripts read “it was granted earlier.” At “I must admit this,” Vict., Bec. 6, and Cister. read “I must admit this to myself.”

At “differences among truths,” the manuscripts read “differences of truth.” At “the truth of a word, an action, or a will,” Gem. and Bec. read “the truth of a word, action, [and] will”; Vict. reads “the truth of will and action”; S. Mich. and Cister. read “the truth of will [and] action”; Bec. 6 reads “and the truth of will and action.”]

[Col. 0487]

# SAINT ANSELM’S BOOK ON THE WILL

116

[Note: See *On the Harmony of the Foreknowledge, the Predestination, and the Grace of God*, question 3, chapter 11, and *On Free Choice*, chapters 3 and 7.]

“Will” is said equivocally. For will means the instrument of willing, just as sight means the instrument of seeing. It also means an affection of that same instrument, such as a mother’s love for her son, which is always present in a mother’s will—that is, in the instrument of willing—which is always ready through that affection to will the son’s wellbeing, whether or not she is thinking about it.

Will also means the act of the instrument, when someone wills something by thinking about it. The will as instrument is natural to the soul.

There are two principal affections: namely, the affection of willing advantage, which can will something before possessing it, and the affection of willing justice. The affection of willing advantage is always and inseparably present in the instrument. The affection of willing justice is not always present, as is seen in an unjust person; nor, when it is present, is it always inseparable, as appears in just people during this life. Sometimes it is inseparable, as in the elect angels and in the saints—among the saints, after this life; but in the angels, always.

[Note: See *On Free Choice*, chapter 14.]

Through these two affections we will whatever we will. For we either will advantage or justice; and we will the one either for the sake of advantage or for the sake of justice.

The will that is called use or act of the instrument, just as vision is the act or use of the instrument of sight, exists only in one who is thinking; and it is simultaneously the act of the instrument and of the affection, just as sharp vision is the act of sight and of the sharpness of sight.

This will, then, is either for the thing which it is said to will—for example, when by thinking about wellbeing we will it—or for something else, as when we wish to ride for the sake of wellbeing.

There is also another division of this will: it either wills that something be, or wills that it not be—for example, willing that a human being exist and willing that a human being not exist.

[Note: He had promised to write about the multiple divisions of the will in *On the Harmony of the Foreknowledge, the Predestination, and the Grace of God*, question 3, chapter 11 [elsewhere 21].]

It also admits the division admitted by “to do.” For we say that “to do” exists in six modes, and correspondingly that “not to do” exists in six modes.

This will may also be called in one case efficient, in another approving, and in another permissive. I call efficient the will which effects what it wills, and which would effect it if it could. I call approving the will which approves what is, and which would approve it if it existed. I call permissive the will which permits what is said to be willed to exist, if it exists, and which would permit it if it existed.

The efficient will is also approving and permissive; the approving will is also permissive; but the permissive will alone can rightly be called neither efficient nor approving.

According to the efficient will it is said: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did” (Psalm 113:3). According to the approving will it is said that God wills every human being to be saved. For God approves and is pleased with all the just because they are just, so that they may be saved; and he would likewise be pleased with the unjust if they were just, so that they might be saved.

The meaning is as though it were said: God makes no one unjust; rather, each person has injustice from himself, so that he may be condemned. Therefore God cannot be said to be displeased if someone is just and is saved; nor can God be said to oppose anyone’s salvation, but rather to approve it if there is someone who may be saved.

According to the permissive will it is said: “He hardens whom he wills,” because he permits that person to be hardened. What precedes—“He has mercy on whom he wills”—was said according to the efficient will.

It is clear that of the two affections of the instrument of willing, that one is altogether better and altogether to be preferred which is directed to willing justice. Through it every just person is just, and no one can be blessed except through it. Even if the affection of willing advantage for the sake of justice did not exist in the soul at all, the soul would nevertheless be blessed through the love of justice alone, and would in no way be miserable through the absence of any other advantage, because it would not need something it did not will.

But the affection of willing advantage, through which all just people also wish to be blessed, if it exists alone, makes one miserable and nothing else, because without justice it never attains what it desires.

Power is aptitude for doing. Here I use “to do” for every finite or infinite verb, as common usage permits. For one who speaks when he ought, or sits, or stands; one who wills or undergoes what he ought; and one who is where and when he ought to be, acts well. But one who does not speak when he ought, or does not sit or stand; one who neither wills nor undergoes what he ought; and one who is not where or when he ought to be, acts badly.

One who does not do what he ought acts badly, while one who does not do what he ought not to do acts well. It is therefore clear that “to do” is used for every finite or infinite verb, including “not to do.”

Power is therefore aptitude for doing, and every aptitude for doing is power. Care must be taken, however, not to take “aptitude for doing” and “aptitude of doing” as entirely identical. Every aptitude for doing is also an aptitude of doing, but not every aptitude of doing is also an aptitude for doing.

For example, the aptitude for writing which is directed toward writing exists before writing takes place and is called the power of writing. But the aptitude for writing which exists in the act of writing, according to which we say that someone writes aptly, does not precede the writing itself. It is not the power of writing, but the effect of the power of writing. For because the power of writing aptly precedes, writing is done aptly—not because the writing is apt, therefore the writing can take place.

The definition says “aptitude for doing,” not simply “aptitude for something,” because an aptitude for something which is not an aptitude for doing is not power, as the aptitude of a garment for the body. A garment is said to be suitable for the body, but it is not therefore said to be powerful.

The definition of power is therefore rightly stated as “aptitude for doing”: by saying “aptitude,” it is separated from every thing that is not an aptitude; and by specifying “for doing,” it is distinguished from every aptitude, whether from one that is not for anything, such as the aptitude present in writing, or from one that is for something but not for doing, such as the aptitude of a garment for the body—which can more properly be called suitability for the body, since a garment is said to be suitable for the body.

This definition of power contains neither more nor less than it ought.

This is a definition of power according to usage, not according to the proper nature of power. For whatever can in any way do or undergo something can be said to have power according to this definition: a piece of wood can be cut, and a person can cut. The wood can be cut because it has an aptitude for being cut, and the person can cut because he has an aptitude for cutting.

[Col. 0489A]

Here begins the treatise On free choice, published by Anselm.”]
