## CHAPTER I

### That the power of sinning does not belong to free choice

**STUDENT.** Since free choice seems to conflict with grace, predestination, and God’s foreknowledge, I desire to know what freedom of choice itself is, and whether we always possess it. For if freedom of choice is the ability to sin and not to sin, as some commonly say, and if we always possess this, how is it that we sometimes need grace? But if we do not always possess it, why is sin imputed to us when we sin without free choice?

[Note: One manuscript reads “and if we ought always to possess this”: Vict. 3.]

**MASTER.** I do not think that freedom of choice is the power to sin and not to sin. For if this were its definition, neither God nor the angels, who cannot sin, would have free choice—which it is impious to say.

[Note: Some manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “if this were its definition”; others read “if this were its definition” with the neuter form instead of the feminine. Some read “neither the angel who cannot sin”; others, “neither the angels who cannot sin”: Vict., S. Mich., Cister., Bec.]

**STUDENT.** What if it is said that God and the good angels have one kind of free choice, and we have another?

**MASTER.** Although human free choice differs from the free choice of God and the good angels, the definition of this freedom, according to the name, must nevertheless be the same in all. For although one animal differs from another either substantially or accidentally, the definition according to the name “animal” is nevertheless the same for all animals. Therefore one must give such a definition of freedom of choice as contains neither more nor less than it should.

Since, then, the free choice of God and the good angels cannot sin, the ability to sin does not belong to the definition of free choice. Indeed, neither freedom nor a part of freedom is the power to sin.

To understand this clearly, attend to what I shall say.

**STUDENT.** I am here for that purpose.

**MASTER.** Which will seems freer to you: one that wills and can not sin in such a way that it cannot in any way be turned away from the rectitude of not sinning, or one that can in some way be turned toward sinning?

**STUDENT.** I do not see why the one which is disposed toward both should not be freer.

**MASTER.** Do you not see that one who possesses what is fitting and beneficial in such a way that he cannot lose it is freer than one who possesses that same thing in such a way that he can lose it and can be led to what is shameful and harmful?

[Note: One manuscript reads “cannot lose it”: Bec.]

**STUDENT.** I think no one doubts this.

**MASTER.** Will you likewise say, with no less certainty, that sinning is always shameful and harmful?

**STUDENT.** No sane person thinks otherwise.

**MASTER.** The will, then, which cannot turn away from the rectitude of not sinning is freer than one which can abandon it.

**STUDENT.** Nothing more reasonable seems capable of being asserted.

**MASTER.** Do you think that what diminishes freedom when added, and increases it when removed, is either freedom or a part of freedom?

**STUDENT.** I cannot think so.

**MASTER.** The power to sin, therefore, which diminishes the freedom of the will when added to it and increases it when removed, is neither freedom nor a part of freedom.

[Note: The Venetian edition of 1547, the Cologne edition, and the Gothic edition read “if it is divided”; the manuscripts read “if it is derived” or “if it is removed.”]

**STUDENT.** Nothing follows more consistently.

## CHAPTER II

### That the angel and the human being sinned through this power and through free choice; and although they were able to serve sin, sin nevertheless could not dominate them

[Note: In the manuscripts the chapter begins with the words: “It does not therefore belong to free choice.” Some manuscripts read “That only the human being and the angel sinned”; others read “That nevertheless the angel and the human being sinned.” Some read “and free choice” instead of “and through free choice.”]

Source preparation: Canonical local restored source checked directly; no foreign-text recoveries occurred in this chunk.

MAGISTER: Therefore it does not belong to free choice, since it is so extraneous to freedom. [Note: “It does not belong,” in the manuscripts; “therefore it does not belong.”]

DISCIPLE: I cannot in any way contradict your arguments. But I am considerably troubled by this: both the angelic nature and our own, at their beginning, possessed the power to sin; and if they had not possessed it, they would not have sinned. Therefore, if both of these aforementioned natures sinned through this power—which is so alien to free choice—how shall we say that they sinned through free choice? But if they did not sin through free choice, they seem to have sinned by necessity. For surely it was either voluntarily or by necessity: now, if they sinned voluntarily [Note: “Or if he sinned voluntarily,” in the manuscripts; “if he sinned voluntarily”], how was it not through free choice? [Note: “How, except through free choice?” in the manuscripts of Thu., Gem., and Bec.; “how was it not through free choice?”] Hence, if it was not through free choice, they seem certainly to have sinned by necessity.

There is also something else that troubles me about this power of sinning. For whoever can sin can be a slave of sin, since “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). But whoever can be a slave of sin can have sin rule over him. How, then, was that nature made free? Or what sort of free choice was it, over which sin could rule? [Note: “How was it free?” in the manuscripts; “how, then, was it made free?”] [Note: “Could rule?” in the manuscript of St. Michael; “could have ruled?”]

MAGISTER: Through the power of sinning, voluntarily, through free choice, and not by necessity, our nature and the angelic nature sinned at the beginning; and they could serve sin. Yet sin could not rule over them in such a way that they could therefore be called unfree, or their choice unfree. [Col. 0491D–0492A] [Note: “And voluntarily, through free choice,” in the manuscripts; the manuscript of Victorinus 9 reads, “and voluntarily and through free choice.”]

DISCIPLE: I need you to explain what you are saying, because it is obscure to me.

MAGISTER: The apostate angel, or the first human being, sinned through free choice because he sinned through his own choice, which was so free that nothing else could compel it to sin. He is therefore justly blamed, because, although he possessed this freedom of his choice, he sinned voluntarily—not because anything compelled him, nor from any necessity. He sinned through his own choice, which was free; but not through that by which it was free—that is, not through the power by which he could refrain from sinning and not serve sin—rather, through the power of sinning which he possessed [Note: “That is, through the power by which he could refrain from sinning and not serve sin; but through the power which he possessed not to sin,” in the manuscript of Gem. 54; “that is, through the power which he had of not sinning”]. Through that power he was neither assisted toward the freedom of not sinning nor compelled toward the servitude of sinning. [Note: “Which he had, of sinning,” in the manuscripts; “which he possessed, of sinning.”]

As for what seems to follow for you—that, if he could be a slave of sin, sin could rule over him, and therefore neither he nor his choice was free—this is not so. Whoever is in his own power so as not to serve another is not in another’s power so as to serve him, even though by his own power he may be able to serve. As long as he uses not the power of serving but the power of not serving [Note: “Which is not the power of serving,” in the manuscripts of Victorinus, Thun., and Gem.; “which is the power of not serving”], nothing can rule over him so as to make him serve.

Even if a free rich man can make himself the servant of a poor man, as long as he does not do this, he neither loses the name of freedom, nor is the poor man said to rule over him. Or, if this is said, it is said improperly, because the matter lies not in the power of the poor man but in the power of the other. Therefore, there is nothing to prevent the angel and the human being from having been free before sin, or from having possessed free choice.

## CHAPTER III

That after they made themselves slaves of sin they still possessed free choice; and what free choice is

DISCIPLE: You have satisfied me, since certainly nothing prevents this before sin. But after they made themselves slaves of sin, how could they preserve free choice?

MAGISTER: Although they had subjected themselves to sin, they could not destroy in themselves the natural freedom of choice. But they could bring it about that they were no longer able to use that freedom without another grace besides the one they had previously possessed.

DISCIPLE: I believe this, but I want to understand it. [Col. 0492D–0493A]

MAGISTER: Let us first consider what sort of freedom of choice they possessed before sin, when it is certain that they had free choice. [Note: “Let us therefore first consider what sort,” in the manuscripts; “let us first consider what sort.”] [Note: “They possessed freedom,” in the manuscripts; “they had freedom.”] [Note: “Because it is certain,” in the manuscripts; “when it is certain.”] [Note: “That they had free choice,” in the manuscript of Cistercian provenance; “that they had free choice beforehand.”]

DISCIPLE: I am waiting for this.

MAGISTER: For what purpose do you think they possessed that freedom of choice? Was it in order to attain whatever they wanted, or in order to will what they ought to will and what it was expedient for them to will?

DISCIPLE: In order to will what they ought to will and what it was expedient to will.

MAGISTER: Therefore they possessed freedom of choice for rectitude of will. For as long as they willed what they ought to will, they possessed rectitude of will.

DISCIPLE: That is so.

MAGISTER: There is still a question when it is said that they possessed freedom for rectitude of will, unless something is added. [Note: “Unless something else is added,” in the manuscripts; “unless something is added.”] I ask, then, in what sense did they possess that freedom for rectitude of will? Was it for acquiring it without a giver, when they did not yet possess it? Or for receiving it, though they did not yet have it, if it were given so that they might have it? Or for abandoning the rectitude they had received and recovering it after it had been abandoned? Or for always preserving it once received?

DISCIPLE: I do not think they possessed freedom for acquiring rectitude without a giver, since they could possess nothing that they had not received. As for receiving from the giver a rectitude that they did not yet possess, so that they might have it, it is not to be said that they possessed freedom for this, because they should not be believed to have been made without right will. Nevertheless, it must not be denied that they possessed the freedom to receive that same rectitude if they abandoned it and it were restored to them by that first giver himself. We often see this in human beings, who are brought back from injustice to justice by heavenly grace. [Col. 0493B–C]

MAGISTER: What you say is true: they can receive lost rectitude if it is restored. [Note: “Hence what you say is true,” in the manuscripts; “what you say is true.”] But we are seeking that freedom which they possessed before they sinned, when without doubt they possessed free choice [Note: “They had free choice,” in the manuscripts; “they possessed free choice”]—not that freedom which no one would need if he had never abandoned the truth. [Note: “Which no one would need,” in the manuscripts of Thu.; “which no one needs.”]

DISCIPLE: I shall continue, then, and answer the remaining points of what you asked. It is not true that they possessed freedom for abandoning that same rectitude, because to abandon the rectitude of will is to sin; and you showed above that the power of sinning is neither freedom nor a part of freedom (chapter 1).

As for recovering the rectitude they had abandoned by their own power, they did not receive freedom for this, since that rectitude was given so that it might never be abandoned [Note: “So that it might not be abandoned,” in the manuscripts; “so that it might never be abandoned.”] For the very power to recover what had been abandoned would generate negligence in preserving what had been received. Therefore, what remains is that freedom of choice was given to rational nature [Note: “To the rational creature or nature,” in the manuscripts; “to rational nature.”] for preserving the received rectitude of will.

MAGISTER: You have answered the questions well. But we must still consider why rational nature ought to preserve that rectitude [Note: “Rational creature,” in the manuscripts; “rational nature.”] Is it for the sake of rectitude itself, or for something else? [Note: “Or for something else,” in the manuscripts of Victorinus, Bec., and Thu.; “or for something else?”]

DISCIPLE: If that freedom had not been given to that nature so that it might preserve the rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself, it would not contribute to justice, since it is established that justice is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake. But we believe that freedom of choice contributes to justice. Therefore, it must be asserted without doubt that rational nature received it for no other purpose than to preserve the rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself. [Col. 0494B]

MAGISTER: Therefore, since every freedom is a power [Note: “Since every freedom is a power,” in the manuscripts; “therefore, since every freedom is a power.”], that freedom of choice is the power to preserve the rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself.

DISCIPLE: It cannot be otherwise.

MAGISTER: It is now clear, then, that free choice is nothing other than a choice capable of preserving the rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself.

DISCIPLE: It is certainly clear. [Note: “It is therefore clear,” in the manuscripts; “it is certainly clear.”] But as long as it possessed rectitude itself, it could preserve what it possessed [Note: “It could preserve what it ought,” in the manuscripts of Victorinus, Bec., St. Michael, and Thu.; “it could preserve what it possessed.”] After it abandoned that rectitude, how can it preserve what it does not possess? Therefore, when rectitude is absent—which could be preserved [Note: “Which it could preserve,” in the manuscripts; “which could be preserved”]—there is no free choice capable of preserving it; for it cannot preserve what it does not have.

MAGISTER: Even if rectitude of will is absent, rational nature does not thereby possess less of what belongs to it. For, as I think, we possess no power that is sufficient by itself for action; yet when those things are absent without which our powers cannot be brought into action, we are nevertheless said, insofar as it lies within us, to possess those powers. [Note: “That is sufficient for itself for action; yet when those things are absent without which our powers cannot at all be brought into action,” in the manuscript of Bec.; other manuscripts read, “that is sufficient for itself for action; and yet, when those things are absent without which our powers cannot at all be brought into action.”]

No instrument is sufficient by itself for carrying out its work; yet when those things are absent without which we cannot use an instrument, we truthfully admit that we possess the instrument for any work. To make this clear in many cases, I shall show it to you in one.

No one who possesses sight is said to be wholly unable to see a mountain.

DISCIPLE: Whoever cannot see a mountain certainly has no sight.

MAGISTER: Therefore, whoever possesses sight has both the power and the instrument for seeing a mountain. Yet if the mountain is absent and you say to him, “See the mountain,” he answers you, “I cannot, because it is absent; if it were present, I could see it.”

Again, if the mountain were present but the light absent, he would answer the person urging him to see the mountain that he could not see it because he could not see in the absence of light; but if light were present, then he could see it. [Note: “He would answer that he could not see the mountain because,” in the manuscripts of Victorinus, Bec., Thu., and Gem. 54; the manuscript of Cistercian provenance reads, “he would answer the person urging him to see the mountain that he could see it.”] [Note: “He could not in the absence of,” in the manuscript of Victorinus 13; “I cannot in the absence of.”] [Note: “Then he could,” in the manuscript of Victorinus 13; “then I can.”]

Again, if both the mountain and the light are present for someone who has sight, but something obstructs his vision—for example, if someone closes his eyes—he will say that he can see the mountain. But if nothing obstructed his sight, then without doubt he would possess the power to see the mountain. [Note: “If the mountain and the light were present, and something obstructed his sight, as if someone closed his eyes, he would say,” in the manuscripts; the manuscript of St. Michael reads, “and the mountain and the light are present, and something obstructs his sight, as in the other manuscripts.”]

DISCIPLE: All this is known to everyone.

MAGISTER: You see, then, that the power to see some body is one thing in the person seeing, another in the thing to be seen, and another in the medium—that is, in something belonging neither to the one seeing nor to the thing seen. [Note: “The same thing belongs neither to the one seeing nor to the thing seen,” in the manuscripts; “that is, it belongs neither to the one seeing nor to the act of seeing.”] And the power that exists in the medium is itself of two kinds: one is in what assists; the other is in what does not impede—that is, when nothing capable of obstructing actually obstructs.

DISCIPLE: I understand perfectly.

MAGISTER: There are therefore four powers. If any one of them is absent, the other three, neither individually nor all together, can accomplish anything. Yet, when the others are absent, we do not deny either that the person who possesses sight possesses sight [Note: “Or that the one who possesses sight possesses sight,” in the manuscripts of Thu., Gem. 54, and Bec.; “or that the person who possesses sight possesses sight.”], or that he possesses the instrument or power of seeing, or that the visible thing can be seen, or that light can assist sight.

119

## CHAPTER IV

How they can possess the power to preserve rectitude which they do not possess

MAGISTER: The fourth power, however, is improperly called a power. For that which customarily obstructs sight is not said to give the power of seeing for any other reason than that, when it does not obstruct, it does not take the power away. The power of seeing by light is found only in three things, because then the thing seen and the thing that assists are the same. Is this not known to everyone? [Note: “For this is known to everyone,” in the manuscripts; “is this not known to everyone?”]

DISCIPLE: It is certainly unknown to no one. [Note: “It is therefore unknown to no one,” in the manuscripts; “it is certainly unknown to no one.”]

MAGISTER: If, then, while the thing that could be seen is absent, we are placed in darkness and have our eyes closed or bound, we nevertheless possess, insofar as it concerns us, the power to see any visible thing [Note: “The power to see a thing,” in the manuscripts of Thu.; “a visible thing, then the power”]. What prevents us from possessing the power to preserve the rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself, even when rectitude itself is absent, as long as reason is present in us, by which we are able to know it, and will, by which we are able to hold it? For the freedom of choice mentioned above consists in these things.

DISCIPLE: You have satisfied my understanding: this power of preserving the rectitude of will is always present in rational nature, and this power was free in the choice of the first human being and of the angels, since rectitude of will could not be taken away from them against their will. [Note: “In the first place,” in the manuscripts; “in the first human being and in the angels.”]

## CHAPTER V

That no temptation compels one who is unwilling to sin

But now, how is the choice of the human will free in this power, when a person possessing a right will often abandons that very rectitude unwillingly, compelled by temptation?

MAGISTER: No one abandons it except by willing to do so. Therefore, if “unwilling” is said to mean “not willing” [Note: “Unwilling is said to mean willing,” in the manuscripts of Gem., Bec., Victorinus, and Cistercian provenance; “unwilling is said to mean not willing”], no one abandons it unwillingly.

A person can be bound unwillingly, because he can be bound while not willing it. He can be tortured unwillingly, because he can be tortured while not willing it. He can be killed unwillingly, because he can be killed while not willing it. But he cannot will unwillingly, because he cannot will while not willing to will [Note: “For a person can be bound even unwillingly, because he does not will it; he can be tortured unwillingly, because he does not will it; he can be killed; but he cannot will,” in the manuscripts]. For everyone who wills wills his own willing.

DISCIPLE: How, then, is someone said to lie unwillingly when he lies so as not to be killed, since he does this only voluntarily? [Note: “He does this only unwillingly,” in the manuscripts; the supplied reading has “voluntarily?”] For just as he lies unwillingly, so he unwillingly wills to lie; and whoever unwillingly wills to lie wills to lie while not willing to do so.

[Note: The manuscripts, including St. Michael, add: “He wills to lie while not willing to do so. M.: Perhaps that is why he is said to lie unwillingly: because, before he comes to this necessity, he does not want to lie, nor does he want ever to want this. Thus, when he lies on this occasion, he judges that he lies unwillingly because of the preceding necessity. M.: Perhaps that is why,” etc. This addition appears to have been inserted here by a copyist, since it is absent from the other manuscripts.]

MAGISTER: Perhaps that is why he is said to lie unwillingly: because, when he wills the truth in such a way that he would not lie except for the sake of life, he wills the lie because it is for the sake of life; yet he does not will the lie for its own sake, since he wills the truth. Thus he lies both willingly and unwillingly.

For one will is that by which we will something for its own sake, as when we will health for its own sake; another is that by which we will something for the sake of something else, as when we want to drink wormwood for the sake of health. Accordingly, it can perhaps be said, with reference to these different wills, that he lies both unwillingly and not unwillingly.

Therefore, when he is said to lie unwillingly because he does not will that act insofar as he wills the truth, this does not conflict with the proposition that no one abandons the rectitude of will unwillingly. For in lying he wills to abandon it for the sake of life; with respect to that will, he does not abandon it unwillingly but willingly. It is of this will that we are now speaking: the will by which he wills to lie for the sake of life, not the will by which he does not will the lie for its own sake.

Or certainly he lies unwillingly because he is unwilling either to be killed or to lie—that is, he is unwillingly placed in such a predicament that one of these must occur. For although it is necessary that he either be killed or lie, it is not necessary that he be killed, since he can avoid being killed by lying; nor is it necessary that he lie, since he can avoid lying by being killed. [Note: “Not to lie, but to be killed,” in the manuscripts; “nor is it necessary that he lie, since he can avoid lying by being killed.”]

Neither alternative is determined by necessity, because either is within his power. [Note: “Either is in his will or power,” in the manuscripts; “either is within his power.”] Thus, although he is unwilling either to lie or to be killed, it does not follow that he lies unwillingly or is killed unwillingly.

There is another reason, grounded in common usage, why someone is said to do unwillingly, while not willing, and by necessity what he nevertheless does willingly. Whatever we can do only with difficulty, and therefore do not do, we say that we cannot do, and that we abandon it by necessity or unwillingly. Conversely, whatever we cannot relinquish without difficulty, and for that reason do, we assert that we do unwillingly, not willingly, and by necessity. [Note: “To abandon, and what,” in the manuscripts; “to abandon, and what.”] [Note: “And therefore, when we do it,” in the manuscripts; “and for that reason we do it.”]

In this way, then, someone who lies so as not to die is said to lie unwillingly and while not willing to do so, and by necessity, because he cannot avoid the lie without the difficulty of death.

Therefore, just as someone who lies for the sake of life is improperly said to lie unwillingly, since he lies willingly, so he is not properly said to will to lie unwillingly, since he wills this only willingly. For just as, when he lies, he wills the act of lying itself, so, when he wills to lie, he wills the willing itself.

DISCIPLE: I cannot deny what you say.

MAGISTER: How, then, is the will not free when an external power cannot subject it without its consent?

DISCIPLE: By a similar argument, could we not say that a horse’s will is free, because it serves the appetite of the flesh only willingly?

MAGISTER: The cases are not similar. [Note: “It is not similar in this case,” in the manuscripts.] In the horse, it is not the will itself that subjects itself; rather, being always naturally subjected, it serves the appetite of the flesh by necessity. In the human being, however, as long as the will itself is right, it neither serves nor is subjected to what it ought not serve, nor is it turned away from that rectitude by any external force—unless it itself willingly consents to what it ought not consent to. This consent does not appear to arise naturally or by necessity, as in the horse, but plainly from the will itself.

DISCIPLE: You have satisfied my objection concerning the horse’s will. Return to where we were.

MAGISTER: Will you deny that everything is free from that by which it cannot be compelled or prevented except willingly? [Note: “From that by which it cannot be compelled unwillingly,” in the manuscripts; “from that to which it cannot be compelled except willingly,” in the manuscript of St. Michael.]

DISCIPLE: I do not see how I could deny it.

MAGISTER: Say also how a right will conquers, and how it is conquered.

DISCIPLE: To will that very rectitude perseveringly is for it to conquer; to will what it ought not will is for it to be conquered.

MAGISTER: I think, then, that temptation can either turn a right will away from rectitude or compel it toward what it ought not will only if the will itself wills this: that it not will the former and will the latter. [Note: “So that it wills the former and does not will the latter,” in the manuscripts; the supplied reading has the reverse.]

DISCIPLE: I see no reason why this should be false. [Note: “Nor do I see any reason,” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition.]

MAGISTER: Who, then, can say that the will is not free for preserving rectitude and free from temptation and sin, if no temptation can turn it from rectitude toward sin—that is, toward willing what it ought not will—unless it is willing? When it is conquered, then, it is conquered not by an external power but by its own.

DISCIPLE: What has been said demonstrates this.

MAGISTER: Do you not see, then, that it follows from this that no temptation can conquer a right will? For if it can, it possesses the power to conquer and conquers by its own power [Note: “It is conquered by its own power,” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition; “and conquers by its own power”]. But this cannot be so, since the will is conquered only by its own power. Therefore temptation cannot in any way conquer a right will; and when this is said, it is said improperly.

The meaning is only that the will can subject itself to temptation. Conversely, when a weak person is said to be capable of being conquered by a strong person, he is not said to be capable of being conquered by his own power but by another’s [Note: “He is said to be capable of being conquered by his own power, but,” in the manuscripts; “he is not said to be capable of being conquered by his own power, but”], since nothing else is meant than that the strong person has the power to conquer the weak.

120

## CHAPTER VI

How our will is powerful against temptations, although it seems powerless

DISCIPLE: Although you so subject to our will everything that assails it, and allow no temptation to rule over it, that I can find no objection to your assertions, nevertheless I cannot conceal that there is a certain powerlessness in that same will, which nearly all of us experience when we are overcome by the violence of temptation. Therefore, unless you reconcile the power which you prove with this powerlessness which we feel, my mind cannot come to rest in this question. [Col. 0498B–C]

MAGISTER: In what do you think this powerlessness of the will, of which you speak, consists?

DISCIPLE: In its inability to adhere perseveringly to rectitude.

MAGISTER: If it does not adhere through powerlessness, it is turned away from rectitude by an external force.

DISCIPLE: I grant it. [Note: “I believe,” in the manuscripts; “I grant it.”]

MAGISTER: What is this force?

DISCIPLE: The force of temptation.

MAGISTER: This force does not turn it away from rectitude if it does not itself will what temptation suggests. [Note: “Does not turn it away,” in the manuscripts; “does not turn it away from rectitude.”]

DISCIPLE: That is so. But temptation by its force compels it to will what it suggests.

MAGISTER: How does it compel it to will? Is it so that it can indeed refuse to will it, but not without grave distress; or so that it cannot refuse to will it at all?

DISCIPLE: Although I must admit that we are sometimes so pressed by temptations that we cannot without difficulty refuse to will what they suggest, I nevertheless cannot say that they ever so overwhelm us that we are altogether unable to refuse what they urge. [Col. 0498D] [Note: The manuscripts read “what they move [us to] … at all”; the supplied reading has “what they urge … at all.”]

MAGISTER: I do not know how that can be said. For if a person wills to lie so that he may not suffer death and may preserve temporal life, who will say that it is impossible for him to will not to lie, so that he may avoid eternal death and live without end? [Col. 0499A]

Therefore you should no longer doubt that this inability to preserve rectitude, which you say exists in our will when we consent to temptations, arises not from impossibility but from difficulty. For in common usage we say that we cannot do something, not because it is impossible for us, but because we cannot do it without difficulty. This difficulty, however, does not destroy freedom of the will: it can assail an unwilling will, but it cannot conquer an unwilling will. [Note: The manuscripts read, “It does not permit the freedom of the will to be conquered. It can assail …”]

I think that in this way you can see how the power of the will which the reasoning of truth affirms, and the powerlessness which our human condition experiences, are reconciled. For just as difficulty does not destroy the freedom of the will, so that powerlessness—which we say is in the will solely because it cannot retain its rectitude without difficulty—does not take from the will the power to persevere in rectitude. [Col. 0499B]

## CHAPTER VII

How the will is stronger than temptation, even when it is overcome by it

DISCIPLE: Although I am entirely unable to deny what you prove, I also cannot at all affirm that the will is stronger than temptation when it is overcome by temptation. For if the will to preserve rectitude were stronger than the force of temptation, it would resist more powerfully by willing what it holds than temptation would press upon it. I know of no other way to determine whether I possess a will that is stronger or weaker except by whether I will more or less strongly. [Note: The manuscripts read “less stronger”; the supplied reading has “less strong.”] Therefore, when I will what I ought to will less strongly than temptation suggests to me what I ought not will, I do not see how temptation is not stronger than my will.

MAGISTER: As I see it, an ambiguity concerning the will is deceiving you.

DISCIPLE: I would like to understand the ambiguity itself.

MAGISTER: Just as “sight” is used equivocally, so is “will.” We call sight the instrument of seeing itself—that is, the ray proceeding through the eyes by which we perceive light and the things that are in the light. We also call sight the operation of that instrument when we use it—that is, vision.

In the same way, “will” denotes the instrument of willing itself, which is in the soul and which we turn toward willing this or that, just as we turn sight toward seeing different things. “Will” also denotes the use of that will which is the instrument of willing, just as “sight” denotes the use of the sight that is the instrument of seeing.

Therefore, just as we possess sight, the instrument of seeing, even when we do not see, while sight as its operation exists only when we see, so the will—that is, the instrument of willing—is always in the soul, even when it wills nothing, as when it sleeps [Note: “It is always in the soul,” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition; “it is always in the soul”]. But the will that I call the use or operation of that same instrument exists only when we will something.

The will that I call the instrument of willing is therefore one and the same, whatever we may will. But the will that is its operation is as manifold as the things we will and as often as we will them. In the same way, sight, which we possess even in darkness or with closed eyes, is always the same, whatever we may see. Sight as its operation, however—which is also called vision—is as numerous as the things we see and as numerous as our acts of seeing.

DISCIPLE: I understand this clearly, and I appreciate this distinction of the will. [Note: “Distinction of the will,” in the manuscripts; “discrimination of the will.”] I now seem to perceive the deception I was suffering from through ignorance of it. But continue what you began.

MAGISTER: Since, then, you see that there are two wills—the instrument of willing and its operation—in which of these two do you understand the strength of willing to consist?

DISCIPLE: In the one that is the instrument of willing.

MAGISTER: Suppose you know a man to be so strong that, while he holds an untamed bull, the bull cannot move; and you see that the same man holds a ram in such a way that the ram tears itself from his hands. Would you think that he was less strong in holding the ram than in holding the bull?

DISCIPLE: I would judge him to be no less strong in each of those two operations [Note: “In both operations,” in the manuscripts of Bec., Victorinus, Gem. 54, Thu. 90, and of Cistercian provenance; “in each of those two operations”], but I would admit that he does not use his strength equally in both. For he acts more forcefully with the bull than with the ram. Yet he is strong because he possesses strength [Note: “He is strong who possesses strength,” in the manuscripts; “he is strong because he possesses strength.”]; his action is called strong because it is performed strongly. [Note: “Which is performed strongly,” in the manuscripts and the Gothic edition; “because it is performed strongly.”]

MAGISTER: Understand in the same way the will that I call the instrument of willing: it possesses an inseparable strength that cannot be overcome by any other force. [Note: “It possesses inseparable strength,” in the manuscripts; “it possesses an inseparable and by no other force conquerable strength” in Victorinus 9 and 13.] Through this strength it uses itself sometimes more and sometimes less in willing.

Hence, what it wills more strongly it never abandons when something it wills less strongly is offered. And when what it wills more strongly is offered, it immediately abandons what it does not will equally strongly. Then the will—which we can call the operation of this instrument, since it performs its work when it wills something—is called an action more or less strong according as it is performed more or less strongly. [Note: “This instrument performs its work,” in the manuscripts; “because it performs its work.”]

DISCIPLE: I must admit that what you are explaining is now clear to me.

MAGISTER: You see, then, that when a human being abandons a rectitude of will already possessed because of some temptation that has arisen, he is not drawn away by any external force; rather, he turns himself toward what he wills more strongly. [Note: “He turns himself,” in the manuscripts; “he turns itself.”]

## CHAPTER VIII

That not even God can take away the rectitude of will

88. **[Col. 0499D]** *Offertur fortior quod vult*, **mss.**: *offertur* means “is offered,” *fortior* “stronger” (a nominative adjective), and *quod vult* “what it wills.” The adjective makes the transmitted construction grammatically uncertain; the verb remains passive, and no stronger object or agent is supplied as certain. Printed *offertur quod vult fortius* means “what it wills more strongly is offered.”
89. **[Col. 0499D]** *Hujus, agit opus suum* — “of this [instrument], it performs its work,” **mss.**; printed *hujus, quoniam agit suum opus* — “of this, because it performs its work.”
90. **[Col. 0501D]** *Ipse convertit* — “he himself turns [it],” **mss.**; printed *ipsa convertit* — “it itself turns [it].”

**DISCIPLE.** Can even God take this rectitude away from it?

**MASTER.** See how He cannot. He can indeed reduce the whole substance that He made from nothing to nothing; but He cannot separate it from a will possessing rectitude.

**DISCIPLE.** I expect from you a substantial explanation of this assertion of yours, which I have never heard before.

**MASTER.** We are speaking of that rectitude of will by which a will is called just—that is, which is preserved for its own sake. Now no will is just except one that wills what God wills it to will.

**DISCIPLE.** Clearly, the will that does not will this is unjust.

**MASTER.** To preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude itself, therefore, is for everyone who preserves it to will what God wills him to will.

**DISCIPLE.** This must be admitted.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] The Vict., Gem., Bec., and St. Michael manuscripts read: “Disciple: This must be admitted, which …” The reading breaks off and is materially uncertain.]

**MASTER.** If God separates this rectitude from someone’s will, He does so either willingly or unwillingly.

**DISCIPLE.** He cannot do so unwillingly.

**MASTER.** If, then, He takes the aforesaid rectitude away from someone’s will, He wills what He does.

**DISCIPLE.** Without doubt, He wills it.

**MASTER.** Certainly, if He wills to separate that same rectitude from someone’s will, He does not will him to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude itself.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “from someone’s will”; another reads “from whose will.” Some manuscripts read “He does not will it” rather than “He does not will him.”]

**DISCIPLE.** That follows.

**MASTER.** But it has already been established that to preserve the rectitude of the will in this way is for everyone who preserves it to will what God wills him to will.

**DISCIPLE.** Even if this had not been established, it would nevertheless be so.

**MASTER.** Therefore, if God takes that oft-mentioned rectitude away from someone, He does not will him to will what He wills him to will.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “this rectitude” after “if God,” while others read “the oft-mentioned [rectitude].”]

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing could be more consequent—and nothing more impossible.

**MASTER.** Therefore nothing is more impossible than for God to take away the rectitude of the will. Yet He is said to do this when He does not cause that same rectitude not to be abandoned. Moreover, the devil, or temptation, is said to do this—either to overcome the will itself or to draw it away from the rectitude it holds—because, unless it promised or threatened to take away from the will something that it desired more than that rectitude itself, the will would in no way turn itself away from the rectitude that it desires to some extent.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “without the will” rather than “either to overcome the will”; others read “would not permit it” rather than “unless it promised.” Some read “he himself turns away from it” rather than “it turns itself away from it”; and “which it desires, it could turn away from” rather than “which it desires to some extent, it would turn away from.”]

**DISCIPLE.** What you say seems so clear to me that I do not think anything can be said against it.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “that nothing can be said in contradiction.”]

[Col. 0501D]

## CHAPTER IX. That nothing is freer than a right will

**MASTER.** You see, then, that nothing is freer than a right will, since no external force can take away its rectitude. Indeed, when we say that, when someone wishes to lie so as not to lose life or safety, he is compelled by fear of death or by torments to abandon the truth, this is not true. He is not compelled to will life more than truth; rather, because an external force prevents him from preserving both at once, he freely chooses what he prefers—not unwillingly, even though he has been placed under necessity, unwillingly, of abandoning either one.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “when he wishes to lie” rather than “when someone wishes to lie.” Others read “of torment” rather than “by torments,” and “both” rather than “both of them.”]

He is not less strong in willing truth than in willing safety; he wills safety more strongly. For if he were to see before him eternal glory, which he would attain immediately after preserving the truth, and the torments of hell, to which he would be consigned without delay after lying, he would plainly be seen at once to possess sufficient strength to preserve the truth.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “to which he would be assigned without delay.”]

**DISCIPLE.** This is evident, since he would display greater strength in willing eternal salvation for its own sake, and truth for the sake of the reward, than in preserving temporal safety.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “to display greater strength in this.”]

## CHAPTER X. How the sinner is a slave of sin; and how it is a greater miracle when God restores that rectitude to one who has abandoned it than when He restores life to the dead

**MASTER.** Rational nature, therefore, always possesses free choice, because it always possesses the power to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude itself, although sometimes with difficulty.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] The manuscripts vary between “rational human being” and “rational nature.”]

But when free will abandons rectitude because of the difficulty of preserving it, it thereafter becomes a slave to sin, through its inability to recover rectitude by itself. Thus it becomes a “departing spirit that does not return” (Psalm 77:39), because “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

For just as no will could grasp rectitude before it possessed it, unless God gave it, so, once it has abandoned the rectitude it received, it cannot receive it again unless God restores it.

I consider it a greater miracle when God restores to the will the rectitude it has abandoned than when He restores lost life to the dead. The body does not sin by dying necessarily, so as never to receive life again; but the will, by abandoning rectitude of its own accord, deserves that it should always need it.

And if someone voluntarily inflicts death upon himself, he does not take away from himself something he was never going to lose; but whoever abandons the rectitude of the will casts away what he was always bound to preserve.  
[Note: [Col. 0501D] Some manuscripts read “he does not take anything away from himself” rather than “he does not take away from himself something.”]

**DISCIPLE.** I see very clearly the truth of what you say about the slavery by which the one who commits sin becomes a slave of sin, and about the impossibility of recovering the abandoned rectitude except when it is restored by the one from whom it was first given. And all to whom it is given must consider that they are to hold it always and without interruption.  
[Note: [Col. 0503C] Some manuscripts read “that it had been given” rather than “from whom it was first given.”]

[Col. 0503A]

## CHAPTER XI. That this slavery does not take away freedom of choice

But this conclusion has greatly restrained my exultation, because I had already thought myself secure in the belief that a human being always possesses freedom of choice. Therefore I ask you to explain this slavery to me, lest it seem to conflict with the freedom just mentioned. For both—namely, this freedom and slavery—exist in the will, according to which a person is either free or a slave. If he is a slave, how is he free? Or if he is free, how is he a slave?

**MASTER.** If you distinguish the matter properly, when a person does not possess the aforesaid rectitude, he is, without contradiction, both a slave and free. For when he does not possess rectitude, it is never within his power to acquire it; but when he possesses it, it is always within his power to preserve it.

Insofar as he cannot return from sin, he is a slave; insofar as he cannot be drawn away from rectitude, he is free. From sin and its slavery he can return only through another; from rectitude, however, he can turn away only through himself, and from his freedom he can be deprived neither by himself nor by another.

For he is always naturally free to preserve rectitude if he possesses it—even when he does not possess what he is to preserve.  
[Note: [Col. 0503C] Some manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “what he preserves, he does not possess.”]

**DISCIPLE.** This explanation of freedom and slavery is sufficient for me, so that they can exist together in the same person in harmonious agreement.

[Col. 0503C]

## CHAPTER XII. Why, when a person does not possess rectitude, he is called more free because, when he possesses it, it cannot be taken away from him, than he is called a slave when he possesses it because, when he does not possess it, he cannot recover it by himself

[Note: [Col. 0503C] The manuscripts vary in the wording of this title. The St. Michael manuscript reads: “Why, when a person does not possess rectitude, he is rather called free, because, when he possesses it, it cannot be taken away from him, than, when he possesses it, he is called a slave, because, when he does not possess it, he cannot recover it by himself.” The Cistercian manuscript abbreviates the title after “when he possesses it, it cannot be taken away from him”; the Gem. 54 and 40 manuscripts also vary in the wording.]

But I very much wish to understand why, when a person does not possess rectitude, he is called more free—because it cannot be taken away from him by another when he possesses it—than, when he possesses rectitude, he is called a slave, because he cannot recover it by himself when he does not possess it.

Insofar as he cannot return from sin, he is a slave; insofar as he cannot be drawn away from rectitude, he is free. And just as he can never be drawn away from it if he possesses it, so he can never return to it if he does not possess it. Therefore, just as he always possesses that freedom, so he also always seems to possess that slavery.

**MASTER.** This slavery is nothing other than the inability not to sin. Whether we call it the inability to return to rectitude, the inability to recover it, or the inability to possess rectitude again, a person is a slave of sin for no other reason than that, because he cannot return to rectitude, recover it, or possess it, he cannot refrain from sinning.

When he possesses that same rectitude, he does not possess the inability not to sin. Therefore, when he possesses that rectitude, he is not a slave of sin.

He always possesses the power to preserve rectitude—both when he possesses rectitude and when he does not. And therefore he is always free. As for your question why, when he does not possess rectitude, he is called more free because it cannot be taken away from him by another when he possesses it than he is then called a slave when he possesses rectitude, the reason is that he cannot recover it by himself when he does not possess it.

This is like asking why a person, when the sun is absent, is said rather to have the power to see the sun because he can look at it when it is present, than, when the sun is present, to have the inability to see it because, when it is absent, he cannot make it present to himself.  
[Note: [Col. 0503C] Some manuscripts read “when the sun is present” rather than “when the sun is absent” in the first clause; others read “when the sun is absent” rather than “when the sun is present” in the second.]

For just as, even when the sun is absent, we possess within us sight by which we see it when it is present, so, even when the rectitude of the will is absent from us, we nevertheless possess within us the capacity for understanding and willing by which we can preserve it for its own sake when we possess it.

And just as, when nothing is lacking to us for seeing the sun except its presence, only then do we lack the power that its presence gives us, so only when that rectitude is absent from us do we possess the inability caused in us by its absence.

Thus a person always possesses freedom of choice, but he is not always a slave of sin—only when he does not possess a right will.

**DISCIPLE.** If I had carefully considered what was said above (chapter 3), when you distributed the power of seeing among four powers, I would not have doubted here. Therefore I acknowledge that this doubt of mine was my fault.  
[Note: [Col. 0503C] Some manuscripts read “I would not have doubted this.”]

**MASTER.** I shall now pardon you, provided that from now on, when necessary, you keep what we say so present to your mind that we do not need to repeat it.  
[Note: [Col. 0503C] Some manuscripts read “Nevertheless, I shall pardon you now”; others read “so that such things may be present.”]

**DISCIPLE.** I am grateful for your indulgence. But do not be surprised if what I am not accustomed to thinking about is not, merely from having heard it once, always entirely present in my mind for contemplation.  
[Note: [Col. 0505C] Some manuscripts read “what I am not accustomed to knowing” rather than “what I am not accustomed to thinking about”; another reads “for understanding” rather than “for contemplation.”]

## CHAPTER XIII. That the power to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude itself is the perfect definition of freedom of choice

**MASTER.** Tell me further whether you have any doubt about the definition of freedom of choice that we formulated.

**DISCIPLE.** There is one point that still troubles me somewhat. We often possess the power to preserve something, yet that power is not free in such a way that it cannot be hindered by an external force. Therefore, when you say that freedom of choice is the power to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude itself, take care lest something must be added to indicate that this power is so free that no force can overcome it.

**MASTER.** If the power to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude itself could ever be found without the freedom we have examined, it would be appropriate to add what you propose. But since the definition stated is so complete in its genus and differences that it includes neither less than it should nor more than the freedom we seek, nothing can be understood as needing to be added to it or removed from it.

“Power” is the genus of freedom. The addition “to preserve” separates it from every power that is not a power of preserving, such as the power of laughing or walking. By adding “rectitude,” we distinguish it from the power to preserve gold, or anything else that is not rectitude.

By the addition “of the will,” it is separated from the power to preserve the rectitude of other things, such as a rod or an opinion. By the words “for the sake of that rectitude itself,” it is distinguished from the power to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of something else, as when it is preserved for the sake of money or naturally.

For a dog naturally preserves the rectitude of the will when it loves its puppies or its master who treats it well. Since, therefore, there is nothing in this definition that is not necessary for comprehending the freedom of choice of rational will and excluding other things, it sufficiently includes the former and excludes the latter. Our definition is therefore neither excessive nor deficient. Do you see it this way?

**DISCIPLE.** It certainly seems perfect to me.

**MASTER.** Then tell me whether you wish to ask anything further about this freedom, on account of which the person who possesses it is held accountable, whether he does good or evil. For our discussion now concerns this freedom alone.

## CHAPTER XIV. The division of this same freedom

**DISCIPLE.** It remains for you now to divide this same freedom. Although, according to this definition, it is common to every rational nature, the freedom belonging to God differs greatly from that belonging to rational creatures, and the freedoms of rational creatures differ from one another.  
[Note: [Col. 0505C] The manuscripts vary between “rational nature” and “rational creature,” and between the singular and plural.]

**MASTER.** One kind of freedom of choice exists from itself: it was neither made nor received from another, and it belongs to God alone. Another kind was made and received from God, and it belongs to angels and human beings.

Among those that were made or received, one kind possesses rectitude to preserve, and another lacks it. Among those that possess it, one holds it separably and another inseparably.

The kind that holds it separably belonged to all the angels before the good were confirmed and the evil fell; and it belongs to all human beings before death who possess that same rectitude.

The kind that holds it inseparably belongs to the elect angels and human beings—to the elect angels after the fall of the reprobate, and to human beings after their death.  
[Note: [Col. 0505C] One manuscript reads “to the elect angels after the fall of the reprobate, and to human beings”; another reads “to the angels after the fall of the reprobate, and to human beings.”]

As for the kind that lacks rectitude, one lacks it recoverably and another irrecoverably. The kind that lacks it recoverably exists only in this life, among all human beings who lack it, although many do not recover it.

The kind that lacks it irrecoverably belongs to reprobate human beings and angels—to angels after the fall and to human beings after this life.  
[Note: [Col. 0505C] Some manuscripts read “namely, of the angels” rather than “of angels.”]

**DISCIPLE.** With God’s assent, you have satisfied me so fully concerning the definition and division of this freedom that I can find nothing I need to ask about them.

[Note: [Col. 0505C] The Cistercian and Bec. 1 manuscripts conclude: “Here ends the treatise on Freedom of Choice, composed by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.”]

[Col. 0507]

# SAINT ANSELM’S TREATISE ON THE AGREEMENT OF GOD’S FOREKNOWLEDGE AND PREDESTINATION, AS WELL AS OF GOD’S GRACE, WITH FREE CHOICE

[Note: [Col. 0507C] This little work was collated with the Gemmetic manuscripts and three Victorine manuscripts formerly marked CC 9, EE 13, and RR 3, one Cistercian manuscript, and the Gothic edition. The Gem., Victorine RR, and Cistercian manuscripts begin: “Here begins the book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Agreement of Foreknowledge and Predestination and the Grace of God with Free Choice.” The Victorine CC 9 reads: “The book of Master Anselm: How Free Choice Does Not Conflict with Foreknowledge, Predestination, and the Grace of God.” In the manuscripts there is no division into parts or chapters. In the other manuscripts and in the Gothic and Cologne editions there is a division, but no chapter divisions.]

[Col. 0507A]

Of those three questions in which free choice seems to conflict with God’s foreknowledge and predestination, as well as with grace, I shall endeavor, with God’s help, to show in writing what He deigns to reveal to me.

**123 QUESTION I. ON THE AGREEMENT OF GOD’S FOREKNOWLEDGE WITH FREE CHOICE**

## CHAPTER I. God’s foreknowledge does not conflict with freedom of choice, because God foreknows that what is not otherwise going to be by necessity will occur freely

[Note: [Col. 0507C] See above, Book I, *On the Fall of the Devil*, chapter 21.]

God’s foreknowledge and free choice do indeed seem to conflict, because the things God foreknows must be future, whereas things done by free choice come about without any necessity. But if they conflict, it is impossible both for God’s foreknowledge—which foresees everything—and for anything to be done through freedom of choice to exist simultaneously.

If this impossibility is understood to be absent, the conflict that seems to exist is completely removed. Let us therefore suppose that both God’s foreknowledge exists, which seems to be followed by the necessity of future things, and freedom of choice, through which many things are believed to occur without any necessity, and let us see whether it is impossible for these two to exist together.

If this is impossible, another impossibility follows from it; for something is impossible when, once it is posited, another impossibility follows. But if something is future without necessity, God, who foreknows all future things, foreknows this very thing. Whatever God foreknows is future by necessity, just as it is foreknown. Therefore something must be future without necessity.

Thus, to anyone who understands correctly, God’s foreknowledge, which is followed by necessity, and freedom of choice, from which necessity is removed, do not in fact seem to conflict. For it is necessary that what God foreknows be future, and God foreknows that something is future without any necessity.  
[Note: [Col. 0507C] Some manuscripts read “God foreknows something else to be future without necessity.”]

But you may say to me: “You do not nevertheless remove from me the necessity of sinning or not sinning, since God foreknows that I will sin or that I will not sin. Therefore, if I sin, I must sin; or, if I do not sin, I must not sin.”

To this I reply: You must not say simply, “God foreknows that I will sin” or “that I will not sin,” but rather: “God foreknows that I will sin without necessity,” or “that I will not sin without necessity.” It follows that, whether you sin or do not sin, either will occur without necessity, because God foreknows that what will occur will occur without necessity.

You see, then, that it is not impossible for God’s foreknowledge—which makes the future things He foreknows be said to exist by necessity—and freedom of choice—through which many things occur without necessity—to exist together. For if this were impossible, another impossibility would follow; but no impossibility arises from it.  
[Note: [Col. 0507C] Some manuscripts read “another impossibility follows” and “from this impossibility.”]

Perhaps you will say: “You have not yet removed the force of necessity from my heart when you say that I must sin or not sin without necessity, because God foreknows this. For necessity seems to imply compulsion or prohibition. Therefore, if I must sin by my will, I understand that I am compelled by some hidden force to will sin; and if I do not sin, I am prevented from willing sin. Consequently, if I sin, I seem to sin by necessity; or, if I do not sin, to refrain from sinning by necessity.”  
[Note: [Col. 0509D] Some manuscripts read “I seem therefore to sin,” and others add “and I” to the final clause.]

## CHAPTER II. How it is necessary that a thing be future when God foreknows it to be future, while the will nevertheless remains free; and concerning two kinds of necessity

It must therefore be understood that we often say that something must be, although it is compelled to be by no force, and that something must not be, although it is removed by no prohibition. For we say that God must be immortal and that God must not be unjust—not because some force compels Him to be immortal or prevents Him from being unjust, but because nothing can make Him not immortal or make Him unjust.  
[Note: [Col. 0509D] Some manuscripts read “or prevent Him from being unjust.”]

Thus, if I say that you must sin or not sin by will alone, just as God foreknows, this must not be understood to mean that anything prevents the will that will not sin or compels the will that will sin. God, who foresees something as future through will alone, foreknows this very thing: the will is compelled or prevented by no other thing. Thus what occurs through the will occurs through freedom.  
[Note: [Col. 0509D] Some manuscripts read “and thus it occurs through freedom.”]

If these matters are carefully understood, I think that nothing prevents God’s foreknowledge and freedom of choice from existing together. Finally, if someone considers the meaning of the word precisely, the very fact that something is said to be foreknown declares it to be future. For only what is future is foreknown, since knowledge concerns truth.

Therefore, when I say that if God foreknows something, it must be future, this is equivalent to saying: “If it will be, it will necessarily be.” But this necessity neither compels nor prevents anything from being or not being. It is because the thing is posited as existing that it is said to exist by necessity; or because it is posited as not existing, it is affirmed to be nonexistent by necessity—not because necessity compels or prevents the thing from existing or not existing.

For when I say, “If it will be, it will necessarily be,” necessity here follows the position of the thing; it does not precede it. The same is true if it is stated: “What will be will necessarily be.” For this necessity signifies nothing other than that what will be cannot at the same time not be.

It is equally true that something was, is, or will be without necessity, and that everything that was must have been, everything that is must be, and everything that will be must be future. For it is not the same thing for a thing to be past and for a past thing to be past; nor for a thing to be present and for a present thing to be present; nor for a thing to be future and for a future thing to be future. It is no more the same than for a thing to be white and for a white thing to be white.

Wood is not necessarily always white, because before it became white it could have failed to become white, and after it is white it can become nonwhite. But white wood must always be white, because neither before it is white nor after it is white can it become simultaneously white and nonwhite.

Similarly, a thing is not present by necessity, since before it was present it could have failed to become present, and after it is present it can become nonpresent. But a present thing must always be present, because neither before it becomes present nor after it is present can it be present and nonpresent at the same time.  
[Note: [Col. 0509D] Some manuscripts read “be simultaneously present and nonpresent.”]

In the same way, some thing, such as an action, is not future by necessity, because before it occurs it can fail to be future. But a future thing must be future, since the future cannot simultaneously be nonfuture.  
[Note: [Col. 0509D] Some manuscripts read “simultaneously future and nonfuture.”]

The same is likewise true of the past: a thing is not past by necessity, because before it was, it could have failed to be; and a past thing must always be past, because it cannot simultaneously not be past.  
[Note: [Col. 0509D] Some manuscripts read “simultaneously be past and not be past.”]

But there is something in a past thing that is not in a present or future thing. It can never happen that a thing that is past becomes nonpast, whereas a present thing can become nonpresent, and a thing that is not future by necessity can become nonfuture.

Thus, when “future” is said of a future thing, what is said must be so, because the future is never nonfuture—just as whenever we say the same thing of the same thing. For when we say, “Every human being is a human being,” or “If someone is a human being, he is a human being,” or “Everything white is white,” and “If something is white, it is white,” what is said must be so, because nothing can simultaneously be and not be.

Indeed, if it were not necessary for every future thing to be future, some future thing would not be future, which is impossible. Therefore every future thing is future by necessity; and if something is future, it is future when “future” is said of a future thing. But this is a subsequent necessity, which compels nothing to be.

[Col. 0511A]

## CHAPTER III. That things future freely are not necessary by a preceding necessity, but by a subsequent one
When, however, the future is predicated of a thing, the thing is not always future by necessity, although it is future. For if I say, “Tomorrow there will be a sedition among the people,” the sedition will nevertheless not occur by necessity. For before it exists, it can happen that it does not occur, even if it is future [Note: [Col. 0511D] “Even what is future” in the manuscripts, instead of “even if it is future”]. Sometimes, however, a thing is necessarily what is said to be future, as when I say that tomorrow the rising of the sun will occur. Therefore, if, when I declare something future with necessity, I say of a future thing in this way, “The sedition will occur tomorrow,” it will be future by necessity; or, “The rising of the sun will occur tomorrow,” it will be future by necessity. The sedition, which will not occur by necessity, is asserted to be future by the subsequent necessity alone, because it is said to be future of a future thing: for if it will occur tomorrow, it is necessarily future. The rising of the sun, however, is understood to be future by two necessities: namely, by the preceding necessity, which causes the thing to exist—for it will occur because it is necessary that it occur—and by the subsequent necessity, which compels nothing to exist, since it is future by necessity for this reason: that it is future.

Therefore, when we say that whatever God foreknows to be future must be future, we do not always assert that the thing is necessarily going to be future; rather, we assert that the future thing must be future [Note: [Col. 0511D] The manuscripts read “we do not assert”; Victorinus reads “it is not asserted”]. For the future cannot simultaneously not be future. The sense is the same if it is said in this way: “If God foreknows something,” without adding “future,” because the future is understood in “foreknows.” For to foreknow is nothing other than to know the future; and therefore, if God foreknows something, it is necessary that it be future.

It does not, therefore, always follow from God’s foreknowledge that the thing will be future by necessity; for although he foreknows all future things, he does not foreknow all future things as future by necessity, but foreknows some things as future through the free will of a rational creature. For it must be observed that, just as it is not necessary for God to will what he wills, so in many matters it is necessary for a human being to will what he wills; and just as whatever God wills must exist, so what a human being wills must exist in those matters which God has subjected to human will in such a way [Note: [Col. 0511D] The manuscripts read “to human nature and will, in such a way,” instead of “to human will, in such a way”] that, if a person wills, they occur, and if the person does not will, they do not occur [Note: [Col. 0511D] “And similarly it is necessary” in the manuscripts, instead of “and just as it is necessary”].

Since, therefore, what God wills cannot fail to exist, while he wills that the human will be compelled or prevented by no necessity either to will or not to will, and wills that the effect follow the will, then the will must be free, and what it wills must exist. In such a matter, therefore, it is true that the act of sin which a human being wills to perform occurs by necessity, although the person does not will it by necessity. But if the question concerns the sin of the will itself, when it sins by willing, whether that sin is necessary, the answer must be that, just as the will does not will by necessity, so the sin of the will is not necessary. Nor does the same will act by necessity [Note: [Col. 0511D] “The same will would act” in the manuscripts of Victorinus, instead of “the same will acts”]; for if it did not will spontaneously, it would not act, although what it does must occur, as I said above.

For since sinning there is nothing other than willing what one ought not to will, the sin of the will is not necessary, just as willing is not necessary. Nevertheless, it is true that if a person wills to sin, that person must sin—but by the necessity I described above (chapter 2), which compels or prevents nothing. Thus what the free will wills, it can will and cannot fail to will, and it must will [Note: [Col. 0511D] The manuscripts read “it is necessary for him to will,” instead of “it is necessary for it to will”]. For it can not will before it wills, because it is free; but once it wills [Note: [Col. 0511D] The manuscripts read “and when it wills,” instead of “and when it already wills”], it cannot not will, and it must will, since it is impossible for it simultaneously to will and not to will the same thing.

The act of the will, to which it has been granted that what it wills should exist and what it does not will should not exist, is voluntary or spontaneous, because it is performed by a spontaneous will. It is necessary in two ways, because it is compelled to occur by the will, and what occurs cannot simultaneously not occur. But these necessities are produced by the freedom of the will, which can avoid them before they exist.

All this God, who knows every truth and nothing but truth, sees as it is—whether things are spontaneous or necessary—and as he sees them, so they are. From this consideration it is therefore clear that, without any contradiction, God foreknows everything, and many things occur through free will which, before they exist, can fail ever to exist; and yet they are necessary in a certain manner. This necessity, as I have said, descends from free will.

## CHAPTER IV  
### If God’s foreknowledge imposes necessity upon the things he foreknows, he himself does nothing freely, but everything by necessity

It can also be recognized that not everything God foreknows occurs by necessity, but that some things occur through the freedom of the will. For when [Note: [Col. 0511D] The manuscripts read “by this, that when”; the Cistercian manuscript, “because when”] God wills or does something—whether it is spoken of according to eternity’s immutable presence [Note: [Col. 0511D] The manuscripts read, “According to eternity, he speaks of immutable foreknowledge,” instead of “whether it is spoken of according to eternity’s immutable presence”; Victorinus 13 and the Cistercian manuscript read, “according to eternity’s foreknowledge”], in which there is neither past nor future, but all things exist together without any motion, so that we do not say that he willed or will, did or will do something, but only that he wills [Note: [Col. 0511D] The manuscripts read “but nevertheless wills,” instead of “but only wills”] and does it—or whether it is spoken of according to time, as when we say that he will will or will do what we know has not yet been done—it cannot be denied that he knows what he wills and does, and foreknows what he will will and do.

Therefore, if God’s knowing and foreknowing impose necessity upon everything that he knows or foreknows, then he himself neither wills nor will do anything freely, whether according to eternity or according to any time, but does everything by necessity. But if it is absurd even to suppose this, then whatever God knows or foreknows to exist or not to exist does not exist or fail to exist by necessity.

Nothing, therefore, prevents something in our wills and actions from being known or foreknown by him as occurring or as future through free will, so that, although what he knows or foreknows must exist, many things nevertheless occur without necessity, but through free will, as I demonstrated above (chapter 1). Indeed, why is it surprising that something should be both from freedom and from necessity in this way, since many things receive contrary properties according to different considerations [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts read “and not from necessity, since many things are,” instead of “and from necessity, since many things are”]? For what is more contrary than approaching and departing? Yet when someone moves from one place to another, we see that the same movement is both an approach and a departure [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts of Victorinus read “is for it an approach,” instead of “is an approach”]. For the person departs from one place and approaches another.

Likewise, if we consider the sun under some part of the sky, while it continually hastens around the sky toward the same part, we see that the same place is both the place from which it withdraws and the place toward which it advances; at the same time and without interruption it approaches the place from which it recedes. Those who are familiar with its course also see that, if we consider the sky, it always passes from the western part toward the eastern. If, however, we attend to the earth, it always moves from the east toward the west, and thus it always moves contrary to the firmament, while moving, though more slowly, together with the firmament. The same is observed in all the planets.

Thus no contradiction arises if, according to the considerations stated above, we assert that something is necessarily future because it is future, and that it is not future by a necessity that compels it to be future, except by the necessity which, as I said above (chapter 3), is produced by free will.

## CHAPTER V  
### That many things are called necessary and immutable in Scripture by comparison with eternity, although in time they are free and could fail to exist

If, however, by what Job says to God concerning the human being—“You have appointed his limits, which cannot be passed” (Job 14:5)—someone wishes to show that no one could hasten or delay the day on which he dies, although at times it may seem to us that someone freely does something by which he dies, there is no objection [Note: [Col. 0513D] Victorinus reads “but there is no objection”] to this against what we said above. For since God is not deceived and sees only the truth, whether something occurs through freedom or through necessity, he is said to have immutably established with himself what, before it occurs, can be changed by a human being [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts read, “It occurs; it is said to have been established,” instead of “he is said to have established”; and “by human beings it can be changed,” instead of “it can be changed by a human being”].

The same applies to what the Apostle Paul says concerning those who are called saints according to the purpose: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:28–30) [Note: [Col. 0513D] “Paul also” in the manuscripts, instead of “the same applies to what the Apostle Paul says”].

For this purpose, according to which the saints are called, is immutable in eternity, in which there is neither past nor future, but only the present; yet in the human beings themselves it is at times changeable through free will. For just as, although in eternity nothing was or will be, but everything only is, nevertheless in time something was and will be without contradiction, so what cannot be changed in eternity is shown, without impropriety, to be changeable in time through free will before it exists.

Although there is nothing there except the present, that present is not temporal, as ours is, but eternal, in which all times are contained. For just as the present time contains every place and the things that are in each place, so the eternal present simultaneously encloses all time and the things that exist in each time [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts read “in whatever time,” instead of “in each time”].

When, therefore, the Apostle says that God foreknows his saints, predestines them, calls them, justifies them, and glorifies them, none of these things is earlier or later with God; rather, all are to be understood as existing together in the eternal present. Eternity has its own “togetherness,” in which are all things that exist together in place or time, as well as those that exist in different places or times.

To show that he did not use those words with temporal meaning, the same Apostle also expressed things that are future with a verb in the past tense. For those whom he foreknew, who were still to be born, he had not yet, in temporal terms, called, justified, and glorified. From this it can be understood that, because he lacked a verb signifying eternal presence, he used verbs with past-tense meaning, since things that are past in time are altogether immutable in the likeness of the eternal present.

In this respect temporal past things are more like the eternal present than temporal present things are, because what exists there can never fail to be present, just as what is past in time can never fail to be past. Temporal present things, however, all pass away and become non-present [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts read “the present things of time,” instead of “temporal present things”].

In this way, therefore, whatever sacred Scripture declares to be necessary concerning things that occur through free will, it speaks according to eternity, in which every truth—and nothing but truth—is present immutably [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts read, “Every truth immutably”].
