It does not speak according to time, in which our wills and actions do not always exist. For just as, while they do not exist, they do not have to exist, so it is often not necessary that they should ever exist.

For I do not always write or wish to write; and just as, while I am not writing or do not wish to write [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts of Victorinus read “do not wish to write” in a different order], it is not necessary that I write or wish to write, so it is not necessary that I should ever write or wish to write.

Since, therefore, a thing is recognized as being otherwise in time than in eternity [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts read “a thing to be otherwise,” instead of “a thing to be so otherwise”]—so that at some time it is true that something does not exist in time which exists in eternity, and that what existed in time did not exist there [Note: [Col. 0513D] The manuscripts read “and because what existed in time,” instead of “and what existed in time”], and that what will exist temporally will not exist there—it seems possible, with no logical objection [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts variously read “it seems possible likewise” and “it seems possible”], that something should likewise be changeable in time which is immutable there [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts read “is changeable in time,” instead of “should be changeable in time”].

For “changeable in time” and “immutable in eternity” are not more opposed than “not existing at some time” and “always existing in eternity,” or than “having existed” or “being future” according to time and “not having existed” or “not being future” in eternity.

I do not say that something never exists in time which always exists in eternity, but only that it does not exist at some particular time. For I do not say that my action of writing tomorrow exists at no time; I merely deny that it exists today, although it always exists in eternity.

And when we deny that something existed there or will exist there which existed or will exist in time [Note: [Col. 0515D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “And because,” instead of “And when”], we do not assert that what existed or will exist is in no way there. We merely say, in the past or future mode, that it is not there, although it exists there continually in its own present mode. In these matters no contradiction appears to arise.

Thus, without any contradiction, something is said to be changeable in time before it exists, while in eternity it remains immutable—not “before it exists” or “after it exists,” but continually, because nothing exists there according to time. For this very thing exists there eternally because temporally it both exists and, before it exists, can fail to exist, as I have already said [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts of Victorinus and the Cistercian manuscript read “something exists and before it exists,” instead of “it both exists and, before it exists”].

From what has been said, I think it is sufficiently clear that God’s foreknowledge and free will in no way conflict, owing to the power of eternity, which encloses all time and the things that exist in each time.

## 126. CHAPTER VI  
### Here the question concerns freedom with respect to the things that pertain to salvation, and what that freedom is

But since we do not have free will in every matter, we must examine where that freedom of will which human beings are believed always to possess is found, what it is, and what that will is. For will and the freedom called “free” are not the same thing.

Freedom and will are spoken of in many matters, as when we say that someone has the freedom to speak or remain silent, and that it is within his will which of these he wishes. In many other matters as well, freedom and will are spoken of similarly; yet these are not always present to us, nor are they necessary for the salvation of the soul.

The question here concerns only that will and that freedom without which a human being cannot be saved once he is able to use them. For many complain because they think that free will contributes nothing to salvation or condemnation, but that only necessity operates because of God’s foreknowledge.

Since, therefore, after reaching the age of understanding a human being is not saved without his own righteousness, it is there that the will and freedom under discussion must be investigated—where righteousness has its seat. First, therefore, righteousness must be shown; then this freedom and this will.

There is, indeed, a kind of righteousness, great or small, which is the rectitude of will preserved for its own sake. This freedom, however, is the power of preserving the rectitude of will for the sake of that very rectitude. I think I have demonstrated these definitions by clear arguments: the first in the treatise I wrote on Truth (chapter 12); the second in the work I published on this very freedom (chapters 3 and 13). In that work it was also shown (chapter 5) how this freedom exists naturally and inseparably in the human being, although he does not always use it, and (chapters 6, 7, and 8) that it is so strong that, for as long as a human being wishes to use this freedom, no thing can take away from him the aforesaid rectitude—that is, the righteousness—which he possesses [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts read “the strength, or elsewhere the certainty, aforesaid righteousness,” instead of “the aforesaid rectitude, that is, the righteousness”].

Righteousness, however, is not natural; rather, it was separable in the beginning, both in the angels in heaven and in human beings in paradise, and it still exists in this life—not by necessity, but by the own will of those who possess it [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts read “by necessity, or by the force of necessity impelling them, but by the own will of those who possess it,” instead of “not by necessity, but by the own will of those who possess it”; Victorinus 3 and 9 and the Cistercian manuscript read “in the angels,” instead of “in the angels in heaven”].

Since, then, the righteousness by which someone is righteous is established as the rectitude of will that I have described, and since this rectitude exists in someone only when that person wills what God wills him to will, it is clear that God cannot take this same rectitude away from someone unwillingly, since he cannot will to do so.

Nor can he will [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts and Gothic edition read “nor can it be brought about by any force,” instead of “nor can he will”] that someone who possesses it should abandon it unwillingly under any necessity; for he would thereby will that person not to will what he wills that person to will—which cannot be.

It follows, therefore, that God wills the right will to be free in willing rightly and preserving that same rectitude in this way; and when it can do what it wills, it freely does what it does. From this it can also be recognized most clearly that a free will exists together with its action without conflicting with God’s foreknowledge, as was demonstrated above [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts read “what it does, it wills. From this it can also be recognized most clearly,” instead of “when it can do what it wills, it freely does what it does. From this it can also be recognized most clearly”].

Let us now set forth an example in which right—that is, just—will [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscripts read “both right and just will,” instead of “right, that is, just will”], freedom of will, and the will itself may appear, as well as the way in which the right will is attacked so that it abandons its rectitude, and how it freely preserves that rectitude.

Someone has it in his heart to hold to the truth, because he understands that it is right to love the truth. He therefore already has a right will and rectitude of will. Will, however, is one thing, and the rectitude by which it is right is another.

Another person approaches and, unless he lies, threatens him with death. We now see that it is within his will’s power whether he abandons life for the sake of the rectitude of will, or rectitude for the sake of life.

This will—which can also be called judgment—is free, because reason, by which rectitude is understood, teaches that this rectitude must always be preserved for love of that same rectitude, and that whatever is brought forward as a reason for abandoning it must be rejected. It is the function of the will itself both to condemn and to choose, in the manner shown by the understanding of reason. For this purpose above all, will and reason were given to the rational creature.

Therefore, the will’s judgment is compelled by no necessity to abandon the same rectitude, although it is attacked by the difficulty of death. For although it is necessary to abandon either life or rectitude, no necessity determines which of the two it will preserve or abandon. Indeed, only the will determines what it holds there; the force of necessity does nothing where the choice of the will alone operates.

Since, therefore, there is no necessity for someone to abandon the rectitude of will that he possesses, it is clear that the power—or freedom—to preserve it is not lacking. This power is always free [Note: [Col. 0517D] Victorinus reads “for this power is always free”].

For this is the freedom which, as I said (Dialogue on Free Will, chapters 3 and 13), is the power of preserving the rectitude of will for the sake of that very rectitude. By this freedom of the rational nature, both the free will and the free will itself are so called.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Whether God’s foreknowledge is derived from things, and whether things derive their existence from his knowledge; and how evil things are from God

It remains for us now to consider, since God is believed to foreknow or know everything, whether his knowledge is derived from things, or whether things derive their existence from his knowledge [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “or whether things have their existence,” instead of “or whether things derive their existence”].

For if God derives his knowledge from things, it follows that those things exist before his knowledge, and thus they are not from God, from whom they cannot exist except through his knowledge.

But if whatever exists receives its essence from God’s knowledge, then God is the maker and author of evil works [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “and the agent of evil works,” instead of “and author of evil works”], and therefore does not justly punish the wicked [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “and therefore justly,” instead of “and therefore does not justly”]. We do not accept this conclusion.

The question can be easily resolved if it is first recognized that the good, which is righteousness, truly is something, whereas evil, which is injustice, is entirely without existence [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “entirely without existence,” instead of “without existence altogether”]. I demonstrated this most clearly in the treatise on The Fall of the Devil (chapters 9, 10, 15, and 16), and in the little book which I entitled On the Virginal Conception and Original Sin [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “I demonstrated most aptly,” instead of “I demonstrated most clearly”].

For injustice is not a quality, an action, or any essence, but only the absence of the justice that is owed; nor does it exist except in the will, where justice ought to be. By this will, whether just or unjust [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “justice or injustice,” instead of “whether just or unjust”], every rational nature is called just or unjust, and each of its actions is called just or unjust.

Every quality, every action, and everything that has any essence is from God, from whom all justice and no injustice come. God therefore makes everything that occurs through a just or unjust will—that is, good works and evil works. In good things he makes both what they are and that they are good; in evil things he makes what they are, but not that they are evil.

For to be just or good is for a thing to be something [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “to be just or good is to be something,” instead of “for a thing to be something”]; but for a thing to be unjust or evil is not for it to be something [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “to be something is to be unjust or evil”; Victorinus 13 reads “to be something, to be unjust or evil”]. To be good or just is to possess justice, and that is something. But to be evil or unjust is not to possess the justice that one ought to possess, and that is not something. For justice is something, whereas injustice is nothing, as I have said.

There is also another kind of good [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “there is also something,” instead of “there is also another good”], called a benefit, whose contrary is evil, namely, harm. This evil is sometimes nothing, as blindness, and sometimes something, as pain. But when this evil is something, we do not deny that God makes it, since it is written that he makes peace and creates evil (Isaiah 45:7). For he creates harms by which he exercises and purifies the just and punishes the unjust.

Thus, concerning only that evil which is injustice, by which someone is called unjust, it is certain that it is never something; nor is it the case that for anything to exist is for it to be unjust. And just as God does not make injustice, so he does not make anything to be unjust.

Nevertheless, he makes all actions and all movements, because he makes the things from which, out of which, through which, and in which they are made. Nothing has any power of willing or doing unless he grants it.

The willing itself, which is sometimes just and sometimes unjust, is nothing other than the use of the power of willing and of the will that God gives; insofar as it exists, it is good and is from God. When it is rightly directed, it is good and just; when it is not rightly directed, it is evil and unjust solely because it is not rightly directed.

To be rightly directed is something, and this is from God; not to be rightly directed is not something, nor is it from God. For just as, when someone uses a sword, a tongue, or the power of speech, the sword, tongue, or power is not one thing when its use is right and another when its use is not right, so the will which we use for willing, just as we use reason for reasoning, is not one thing when someone uses it rightly and another when he does not use it rightly. Nor is it more or less essentially what it is when it is just than when the will is unjust, the will through which a substance or an action is called just or unjust [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “Is it not something else?” instead of “is not one thing”].

Thus God makes, in all good wills and works, both what they essentially are and that they are good; but in evil things he does not make what they are as evil, only what they are in essence.

For just as the essence of things exists only from God [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts read “not the essence,” instead of “there is not the essence”], so rightness exists only from him [Note: [Col. 0517D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “so it is not right,” instead of “so rightness exists only from him”]. The absence of this rectitude of which I speak—which is injustice—exists only in the will of the rational creature, which ought always to possess justice.

Why, then, does it not possess what it ought always to possess? How does God make good things by his goodness alone, and evil things by the sole guilt of the human being [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “by goodness alone, and evil things not through its own guilt but through that of the human being,” instead of “by his goodness alone, and evil things by the sole guilt of the human being”] or the devil? How does the human being do good through free will under the guidance of grace, and evil through his own will alone? What does God have in evils without guilt on his part [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts of Victorinus read “with or without his guilt,” instead of “without guilt on his part”], and what does the human being have in good things together with his praise? How, nevertheless, good things done by a human being are evidently to be attributed to God, and evil things to the human being—when we treat of grace and free will, these matters will, I think, become clearer, God granting it [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “we are going to treat,” instead of “when we treat”].

For now I say only that the evil angel does not possess justice because he abandoned it and did not receive it afterward. The human being lacks it because he cast it away in his first parents and afterward either did not receive it or rejected it after receiving it.

I think that, with the help of God’s grace, we have shown that God’s foreknowledge and free will can coexist and, if what we have said is carefully considered, that this is not impossible; nor can anything be raised against it that cannot be resolved.

# QUESTION II  
## On the agreement of predestination with free will

[Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “On Predestination and Free Will.”]

Now, therefore, placing our hope in him who has brought us this far, let us undertake to resolve the disagreement that appears to exist between predestination and free will. Through what we have discussed above, as will become clear in what follows, we have already made considerable progress toward this.

## CHAPTER I [alternatively VIII]  
### The reason for doubt concerning the agreement of freedom and predestination

Predestination appears to be the same as preordination or pre-establishment (*praestitutio*) [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts of Victorinus 3 and 13 read *praedestitutio*, instead of *praestitutio*]. Therefore, when God is said to predestine, he is understood to preordain; and that means to establish that something will be future.

But whatever God establishes as future appears to be future by necessity. Therefore, whatever God predestines must be future. If, then, God predestines the good and evil things that occur, nothing occurs through free will, but everything by necessity.

But if he predestines only good things, then only good things occur by necessity, and free will exists only with respect to evil things—which is exceedingly absurd. God therefore does not predestine only good things.

If, however, free will performs certain good works through which people become just without predestination, then God does not predestine all the good works that make people just, and consequently he does not predestine those just people who become just through the works of free will. God therefore did not foreknow them, since “those whom he foreknew he also predestined” (Romans 8:29).

But it is false that God does not foreknow certain good works or certain just people. Therefore, certain good works of free will alone do not justify; only those works which God predestines do so [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “justified,” instead of “justify”].

If, therefore, God predestines everything, and predestined things occur by necessity, since nothing occurs through free will by necessity, it appears to follow either that there is no free will while predestination remains, or that, if we establish free will in some matters, predestination perishes in those matters.

## CHAPTER II [alternatively IX]  
### Predestination can be spoken of not only with respect to good things but also with respect to evil things

First, then, before answering the question, we must see that predestination is not only predestination of good things; it can also be spoken of with respect to evil things, just as God is said to do evils which he does not do because he permits them.

For he is said to harden a human being when he does not soften him, and to lead someone into temptation when he does not deliver him. It is therefore not inappropriate if in this way we say that God predestines the wicked and their evil works, when he does not correct them or their evil works [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “to predestine the wicked in this way, while he does not correct the wicked and their evil works,” instead of “if in this way we say that God predestines the wicked and their evil works, when he does not correct them or their evil works”].

He is said more particularly to foreknow and predestine good things because in them he makes both what they are and that they are good; in evil things, however, he makes only what they essentially are, not that they are evil, as was said above (Question I, chapter 7) [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “but in evil things,” instead of “in evil things, however”].

It must also be understood that, just as foreknowledge is not properly spoken of in God, so neither is predestination, because for him there is neither anything before nor anything after; rather, all things are present to him together.

## CHAPTER III [alternatively X]  
### Predestination is reconciled with freedom in the same way as foreknowledge

Let us now consider whether some things can be predestined as future through free will. It should certainly not be doubted that predestination and foreknowledge do not conflict, but that God predestines just as he foreknows [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts of Victorinus 3 and 13 read “It should therefore not be doubted,” instead of “It should certainly not be doubted”].

In the question concerning foreknowledge, we learned clearly that some future things occur through free will without any contradiction. Hence evident truth and reason likewise teach that certain future things are predestined through free will, without any impropriety.

For God neither foreknows nor predestines anyone as necessarily going to be just [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “just as necessarily going to be just,” instead of “as necessarily going to be just”]. For someone who does not preserve justice by free will does not possess justice.

Therefore, although what is foreknown and what is predestined must occur, certain foreknown and predestined things nevertheless do not occur by that necessity which precedes the thing and causes it, but by the necessity which follows the thing, as we said above.

For although God predestines them, he does not make them occur by compelling the will or resisting the will, but by leaving it in its own power. Although the will uses its own power, nevertheless it does nothing that God does not do: in good things by his grace, and in evil things not by his grace but through the guilt of that same will. As we promised, this will become clearer when we speak of grace.

And just as foreknowledge, which is not deceived, foreknows only the truth as it will be—whether necessary or spontaneous [Note: [Col. 0519D] The manuscripts read “but what will be,” instead of “as it will be, whether”]—so predestination, which is not changed, predestines only as things exist in foreknowledge.

And just as what is foreknown, although immutable in eternity, can nevertheless be changed in time before it exists, so it is in every respect with predestination.

From what has been said, if it is carefully considered, it is therefore clear that neither predestination excludes free will nor free will opposes predestination. For all the arguments by which we showed above that free will does not conflict with foreknowledge likewise show that it agrees with predestination.

It is therefore not reasonable, whenever something occurs through the action of a spontaneous will—as when one person inflicts an injury on another, as a result of which the latter kills him—for certain people to cry out, saying: “This was foreknown and predestined by God”; and therefore, “It happened by necessity and could not have happened otherwise.”

For neither the one who provoked the other by an injury nor the one who took revenge did this by necessity, but by will alone; for if he had not wished it spontaneously, neither would have done what he did.

# QUESTION III  
## On the agreement of grace and free will

[Note: [Col. 0521D] The manuscripts read “On Grace and Free Will.”]

It remains now for us to consider grace and that same free will, aided by the same grace.

## CHAPTER I [alternatively XI]  
### The difficulty proposed from Scripture concerning the agreement of grace and freedom
This question arises because divine Scripture sometimes speaks in such a way that free will seems to contribute nothing to salvation, but grace alone; at other times it speaks as though our entire salvation consists in our free will. For concerning grace the Lord says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); and: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6:44). The Apostle Paul likewise says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). And concerning God: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18); and: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” (ibid., 16). Many other passages likewise are read which seem to attribute our good works and our salvation to grace alone, without free will. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor and Cistercian read “works for salvation” instead of “good works and our salvation.”]

Many also claim that experience proves that a human being is in no way supported by free will, since they observe countless people striving with immense effort of mind and body—[Note: The manuscripts read “since many strive,” instead of “since they observe many.”] people who, weighed down by a certain difficulty, or rather impossibility, make no progress, or suddenly fall away irreparably after great progress. [Note: The manuscripts read “who strive to live well,” instead of “whom they observe striving.”]

Yet the same Scripture shows that we possess free will in this way. God says through Isaiah: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1:19). And David says: “Who is the man who desires life, who loves to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33:13–15). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28–29).

There are also many other innumerable passages which seem to rouse free will to do good; and, because it despises their admonitions, to reproach it. [Note: The manuscripts read “and those who despise the admonitions,” instead of “and because it despises the admonitions.”] Divine authority would certainly never do this if it recognized no freedom of will in human beings. Nor would there be any reason for God to repay the good or the wicked justly according to the merits of each, if no one did good or evil through free will.

Since, then, we find in sacred Scripture some passages which seem to favor grace alone, and others which are thought to establish free will alone, without grace, there have been arrogant people who judged that the entire effectiveness of virtue consists solely in freedom of will. [Note: The manuscripts read “virtue and effectiveness,” instead of “the entire effectiveness of virtue.”] In our own time, there are many who despair completely of free will’s being anything at all. Our purpose in this question, therefore, will be to show that free will exists together with grace and operates with it in many matters, just as we have found that it agrees with foreknowledge and predestination. [Note: The manuscripts read “This will be the purpose,” instead of “This will be our purpose.”]

## CHAPTER II [otherwise XII] — Concerning free will, without which no one merits salvation, and grace, without which no human being is saved

It must be understood that, just as the present question is not about a different free will, as I said above, but about that without which no one merits salvation after reaching the age of understanding, so it is not about a different grace, but about that without which no human being is saved. Every creature exists by grace, because it was made freely; and in this life God gives many good things by grace, without which a human being can be saved. [Note: The manuscripts read “without which a human being cannot be saved,” instead of “without which a human being can be saved.”]

In the case of infants who die after being baptized, before they are able to use their own free will, the concord that we seek does not appear, because in them grace alone works salvation, without their free will. For this too is grace: that others are given the will to assist them by their faith.

In those who have reached the age of understanding, therefore, what we are investigating must be demonstrated, because this question concerns them alone. It is beyond doubt that all of these who are saved are saved through righteousness. For eternal life is promised to the righteous: “The righteous will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord” (Wisdom 5:16).

That righteousness is the rectitude of the will is often shown by sacred authority. On this matter it is enough to offer one example. When David had said, “The Lord will not reject his people, nor abandon his inheritance, until righteousness is turned into judgment” (Psalm 93:14–15), in order to teach us what righteousness was, he asked: “And who is beside it?” [Col. 0523A] Answering himself, he said: “All who are upright in heart”—that is, all who are upright in will.

Although we believe and understand with the heart, just as we will with the heart, the Holy Spirit does not judge that person to have a right heart who believes and understands rightly but does not will rightly. For he does not use the rectitude of faith and understanding to will rightly, although that is why the rational creature was given the ability to believe and understand rightly. Nor should someone be said to possess right understanding if, according to that understanding, he does not will rightly. Nor is someone said to have faith except a dead faith if he does not will to act rightly according to faith; this is why faith is called faith and is given. [Note: The manuscripts read: “who does not will to act rightly according to that understanding; therefore he is not said to have faith except a dead faith, who does not will to act rightly according to faith; therefore faith is given.”]

We therefore rightly understand David to have spoken of those who are upright in heart, upright in will. But lest anyone suppose that divine authority calls someone just or upright who preserves rectitude of will only for the sake of something else, we say that righteousness is the rectitude of the will preserved for its own sake. For whoever preserves it only for the sake of something else does not love it, but loves that other thing for whose sake he preserves it; and therefore he should not be called just, nor should such rectitude be called righteousness.

When we were treating of foreknowledge and free will (Question I, chapter 6), we showed by a certain example that this rectitude—which I call righteousness—and free will can exist together. From this it is clear that the same is likewise true in many other cases. If, then, we can show that no creature can attain this rectitude except through grace, the concord between grace and free will which we seek, for the salvation of the human being, will be manifest.

## CHAPTER III [otherwise XIII] — The rectitude by which we attain salvation is obtained only through grace

There is no doubt that the will does not will rightly unless it is right. For sight is not sharp because it sees sharply; rather, it sees sharply because it is sharp. Likewise, the will is not right because it wills rightly; rather, it wills rightly because it is right. When it wills this rectitude, it unquestionably wills rightly. Therefore it does not will rectitude unless it is right; and for the will to be right is the same as possessing rectitude. It is consequently clear that the will does not will rectitude unless it possesses rectitude.

I do not deny that a right will can will a rectitude it does not yet possess, when it wills something greater than what it has. But I say that it cannot will any rectitude if it does not possess the rectitude by which it may will it. [Note: The manuscripts read “But I say that it cannot will that rectitude” instead of “But I say that it cannot will any rectitude.”]

Let us now consider whether someone who does not possess this rectitude can in any way possess it from himself. Certainly he cannot possess it from himself except either by willing or by not willing. By willing, no one can attain it through himself, because he cannot will it unless he possesses it. But that someone who does not possess rectitude of will could attain it through himself by not willing it—no mind can accept this. Therefore a creature can possess it from itself in no way.

Nor can a creature possess it from another creature. For just as a creature cannot save a creature, so it cannot give that creature what it ought to be saved by. [Note: The manuscripts read “what can save it” instead of “what it ought to be saved by.”] It follows, therefore, that no creature possesses the rectitude of will that I have described except through grace.

We have shown above that this rectitude can be preserved through free will. God, therefore, granting it, we find that his grace agrees with free will in saving the human being. Grace alone can save a human being, without any action of his free will—as happens in infants—and in those who do not understand, grace itself always assists the natural free will, which without grace is powerless for salvation, by giving the will the rectitude that it preserves through free will. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor and Cistercian read “and in those who understand,” instead of “and in those who do not understand.”]

Although God does not give this grace to everyone, since “he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18), he gives it to no one on account of any preceding merit, since: “Who has first given to God, that he should be repaid?” (Romans 11:35). [The printed text gives “Romans XI, 85.”]

If the will, by preserving through free will what it has received, merits either an increase of the righteousness received, or even the power to act for a good will, or some reward, all these things are fruits of the first grace and grace in return for grace. Therefore everything must be attributed to grace, because “it is not of him who wills” that he wills, “nor of him who runs” that he runs, “but of God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16). [The printed citation reads “Romans II, 16.”]

For everyone except God alone it is said: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

## CHAPTER IV [otherwise XIV] — The same rectitude is preserved only through grace

How the freedom of the will, which holds the rectitude it has received, is not overcome by any necessity that would force it to abandon that rectitude, but is attacked by difficulty, and yields to that difficulty not unwillingly but willingly, I think I have shown in the treatise on free will (chapters 5–9).

As for the ways in which, after receiving that same rectitude, grace assists free will so that it may preserve what it has received, although I cannot enumerate them all—for grace does this in many ways—it will nevertheless not be useless to say something about them. [Note: The manuscripts read “it will not be useless for me to say something” instead of “it will not be useless to say something about them.”]

No one certainly preserves this received rectitude except by willing it; but no one can will it unless he possesses it. And he cannot possess it in any way except through grace. Therefore, just as no one receives it except through prevenient grace, so no one preserves it except through the same subsequent grace.

Although this rectitude is preserved through free will, it must not therefore be attributed to free will as much as to grace when the rectitude is preserved, because free will possesses and preserves it only through prevenient and subsequent grace. Subsequent grace follows its gift in such a way that it never fails to grant it, whether it is small or great, unless free will, by willing something else, abandons the rectitude it received. This rectitude is never separated from the will except when the will wants something else that does not agree with it—for example, when someone receives the rectitude of willing sobriety and rejects it by willing the pleasure of drinking immoderately.

When he does this by his own will, and therefore by his own fault, he loses the grace he received. Grace also assists free will when it is attacked in order that it may abandon its received rectitude, either by softening or entirely removing the force of the temptation that attacks it, or by increasing its affection for that same rectitude.

Finally, since everything is subject to God’s ordering, whatever happens to a human being that assists free will in receiving or preserving this rectitude of which I speak must all be attributed to grace. [Note: The manuscripts read “must be attributed to his grace” instead of “must all be attributed to grace.”]

I have said that all righteousness is the rectitude of the will preserved for its own sake. It follows that everyone who possesses this rectitude possesses righteousness and is just, since everyone who possesses righteousness is just.

Nevertheless, I do not think that eternal life has been promised to all the just, but only to those who are just without any injustice. They alone are properly and absolutely called just and upright in heart. Someone may be just in one respect and unjust in another, as someone who is chaste and envious. [Note: The manuscripts read “who is chaste, envious” instead of “who is chaste and envious.”]

The blessedness of the just is not promised to such people, because just as true blessedness is without any need, so it is given to no one except one who is just without any injustice. Since the blessedness promised to the just will be a likeness to God’s angels, and since there is no injustice in the good angels, no one who has any injustice is joined to them.

How a human being becomes free from all injustice is not part of our present purpose to demonstrate. We nevertheless know that this is possible through holy Christian discipline [Note: The manuscripts read “through perfect Christian discipline” instead of “through holy Christian discipline”] and through the grace of God.

## CHAPTER V [otherwise XV] — The Scriptures which seem to attribute salvation to grace alone, and those which seem to attribute it to freedom alone, are explained

If what has been said is carefully considered, it is clearly understood that when sacred Scripture says something in favor of grace, it does not remove free will altogether; nor, when it speaks in favor of free will, does it exclude grace, as though grace alone or free will alone were sufficient to save a human being, as those who raise this question suppose.

The divine statements must therefore be understood in such a way that, except for what I said concerning infants, neither grace alone nor free will alone accomplishes the salvation of the human being. When the Lord says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), he does not say, “Your free will is of no benefit to you,” but “It can do nothing without my grace.” And when we read, “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16), free will is not denied any usefulness in the one who wills and the one who runs; rather, it is signified that what he wills and the course he runs must not be attributed to free will, but to grace. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor and Cistercian read “nor in the one who runs” instead of “nor in the one who wills and the one who runs.”]

When he says, “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs,” we should supply: “that he wills and that he runs.” It is like someone giving clothing to a naked person who owes him nothing and who cannot obtain clothing from himself. Although the recipient has the power to use or not use the garment he has received, if he uses it, it must not be attributed to the clothed person that he is clothed, but to the giver of the clothing.

Therefore it may be said: “It is not of the clothed person that he is clothed, but of the one who has mercy”—that is, of the one who gives the clothing. This would be said all the more if the one who gave the clothing had also given the power to preserve and use it, as God, when he gives a human being the rectitude mentioned above, also gives him the power to preserve and use it, because he first gave free will for preserving and using it. [Note: The manuscripts read “the rectitude often mentioned” instead of “the rectitude mentioned above.”]

But if clothing were not given to a naked person who owed nothing, or if he himself threw away what he had received, his nakedness would be attributed to no one except himself. Thus, when God gives to someone conceived and born in sin—someone who owes him nothing but punishment—to will and to run, it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy. Whoever does not receive that same grace, or rejects it after receiving it, is responsible—not God—for remaining in his hardness and iniquity.

The same understanding must be applied to the other passages in which Scripture speaks in favor of grace, so that free will is not excluded. Likewise, when divine statements speak in such a way that they seem to attribute human salvation to free will alone, grace must not be separated from them in any interpretation.

Just as natural generation does not produce offspring without a father, nor except through a mother, yet no interpretation removes either the father or the mother from the generation of offspring, so grace and free will do not disagree but cooperate in justifying and saving the human being.

## CHAPTER VI [otherwise XVI] — Why it is not superfluous to invite people to faith and to the things that faith requires

There is nevertheless a difficulty in those passages in which Scripture seems to invite free will to will and act rightly. It is asked why it invites a human being to will rightly, and why it reproves the one who does not obey, when no one can possess or receive that very rectitude except by grace giving it. [Note: The manuscripts read “For why does it invite a human being?” instead of “It is asked why it invites a human being.”]

It must be understood that, just as the earth produces innumerable herbs and trees without any human care—some of them sustaining human nature and others even destroying it—yet those plants which are especially necessary for nourishing us to life it does not produce without great labor, cultivation, and seeds, so human hearts, without instruction or study, spontaneously produce thoughts and desires that are of no use for salvation, or even harmful. But those things without which we do not progress toward the salvation of the soul they do not conceive and produce without the seed proper to them and laborious cultivation. Therefore the Apostle calls those people to whom such cultivation is devoted “God’s cultivation” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

The seed of this cultivation is the word of God—indeed, not merely the word, but the meaning perceived through the word. For a sound without meaning establishes nothing in the heart. Not only the meaning of the word, but every meaning or understanding of rectitude which the human mind conceives through hearing, reading, reasoning, or any other means, is a seed of willing rightly. [Note: The manuscripts read “is called the seed of willing rightly” instead of “is a seed of willing rightly.”]

No one can will what he has not first conceived in his heart. To will to believe what ought to be believed is to will rightly. Therefore no one can will this if he does not know what ought to be believed.

After the Apostle had said, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13), he added: “How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching? And how will they preach unless they are sent?” (ibid., 14). And shortly afterward: “Therefore faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (ibid., 17).

When he says that faith is from hearing, this must be understood to mean that faith arises from what the mind conceives through hearing—not in such a way that the mind’s conception alone produces faith in a person, but because faith cannot exist without conception. When the rectitude of willing is added to conception through grace, faith comes into being, because the person believes what he hears.

Hearing, however, comes through the word of Christ—that is, through the word of those who preach Christ. But preachers exist only if they are sent, and their being sent is grace. Therefore preaching too is grace, because what comes down from grace is itself grace; hearing is grace, understanding from hearing is grace, and the rectitude of willing is grace. [Note: The manuscripts read “preaching of grace is grace” instead of “preaching is grace.”]

Yet being sent, preaching, hearing, and understanding are nothing unless the will wills what the mind understands. The will cannot do this unless it has received rectitude, for it wills rightly when it wills what it ought.

Thus what the mind conceives from hearing the word is the seed of the preacher. [Note: The manuscripts read “it is the preacher’s” instead of “it is the seed of the preacher.”] Rectitude is the growth that God gives, without which neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:7).

Just as in the beginning God miraculously made grain and the other things that grow from the earth for human nourishment without a cultivator or seeds, so, without human instruction, he miraculously made the hearts of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists fruitful with salutary seeds. [Note: The manuscripts read “and the Gospels fruitful” instead of “and the evangelists fruitful.”] From them we receive whatever we sow beneficially in God’s cultivation for the nourishment of souls, just as we have only from the earth’s first seeds what we propagate for the nourishment of bodies.

Indeed, we preach nothing useful for spiritual salvation that sacred Scripture, made fruitful by the miracle of the Holy Spirit, has not produced or does not contain within itself. If we sometimes say something by reasoning which we cannot clearly show or prove from its statements, through Scripture we learn whether it should be accepted or rejected. If it is established by clear reasoning and Scripture contradicts it in no respect, since Scripture, just as it opposes no truth, so it favors no falsehood, then, because it does not deny what is said by reasoning, the statement is accepted on the authority of Scripture. But if Scripture unmistakably contradicts our understanding, then, although our reasoning may seem to us unassailable, it must be believed to rest upon no truth. [Note: The manuscripts read “although our reasoning may seem impregnable” instead of “unassailable.”]

Thus sacred Scripture contains the authority of all truth which reason gathers, whether it openly affirms that truth or in no way denies it.

Let us now see by examples how the word is a seed. When those to whom it is said, “If you are willing and obey me” (Isaiah 1:19), hear these words, they understand and think that what is meant by willing and hearing is obeying; for one who hears and does not obey is said not to hear. But they cannot obey unless they will; and to will to obey is to will rightly. No one can will rightly unless he possesses the rectitude of will, and no human being possesses this except through grace.

Yet the rectitude of willing something is given to no one unless he understands what he ought to will. We therefore see that the saying, “If you are willing and obey me,” is a seed. [Note: The manuscripts read “my word: now it is a seed” instead of “is a seed.”] By itself it does not germinate into fruit in anyone without the addition of rectitude, nor is rectitude itself given except through seeds.

Similarly, when God says, “Turn to me” (Isaiah 45:22; Joel 2:12; Zechariah 1:3), this is a seed without a sprout so long as God does not turn the human will toward willing the conversion that the person thinks about when he hears “Turn.” Without this seed, no one can will to turn.

Is “Turn” also said to those who have already turned? It is said either so that they may turn more fully, or so that they may preserve what they have become by turning. Those who say, “Turn us, O God” (Psalm 84:5), have already turned to some extent, because they possess a right will when they desire to turn. But by this prayer they ask that, through what they have already received, their conversion may increase, just as those who believed said, “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5). It is as though they and the others were saying: “Increase in us what you have given; perfect what you have begun.” What I have demonstrated concerning these passages must also be understood of similar ones.

Therefore, just as the earth does not naturally produce those things most necessary for the health of our bodies without seeds, and although God does not give growth to every seed, our farmers nevertheless do not cease sowing in the hope of at least some harvest, so the soil of the human heart does not produce the fruit of faith and righteousness without suitable seeds. Although God does not cause all such seeds to germinate, he nevertheless commands his farmers to sow his word most diligently in the hope of a harvest.

I think we have shown why it is not superfluous to invite people to the faith of Christ and to the things that this faith requires, although not everyone accepts this invitation. [Note: The manuscripts read “the things faith requires” instead of “the things that this faith requires.”]

## CHAPTER VII [otherwise XVII] — Those who resist the invitation are rightly reproved, although they cannot follow the invitation without grace

I also said that it could be asked why those who do not receive the word of God are reproved, when they cannot do this unless grace directs their wills. For the Lord says concerning the Holy Spirit: “He will reprove the world concerning sin, because they did not believe in me” (John 16:8). [Note: The manuscripts of Victor and Cistercian read “because they do not believe in me” instead of “because they did not believe in me.”]

Although it may perhaps be difficult to answer this, what I can answer with God’s help I ought not to keep silent. It must be noted that an inability arising from fault does not excuse the one who is unable, so long as the fault remains.

Thus, in infants, from whom God demands the righteousness which human nature received in its first parents, together with the power to preserve it for all their offspring, the inability to possess righteousness does not excuse them. They fell into this inability through fault. For the very fact that they do not possess what they cannot recover by themselves is their inability to possess it; and they fell into it because they willingly abandoned what they were able to preserve.

Since, therefore, they abandoned righteousness by sinning, the inability which they caused themselves by sinning is attributed to them as sin. Likewise, not only the inability to possess righteousness, but also the inability to understand it, is attributed as sin to the unbaptized, because it too proceeds from sin.

We can also reasonably assert that whatever has been diminished and corrupted from the original dignity, strength, and beauty of the human condition is attributed to it as guilt. For in this it diminished, as far as lay within it, the honor and praise of God. [Note: The manuscripts read “the praise due to God” instead of “the honor and praise of God.”] For the wisdom of an artisan is praised and proclaimed according to the excellence of his work. [Note: The manuscripts of Victor read “the wisdom of the maker” instead of “the wisdom of the artisan.”] Therefore, to the extent that human nature diminished and defiled in itself the precious work of God, by which God was to be glorified, it dishonored God through its own fault.

This is counted against it as so great a sin that it is erased only through the death of God. Indeed, sacred authority sufficiently shows that even the movements or desires by which, because of Adam’s sin, we are subjected like brute animals—movements which the Apostle calls “the flesh” and “desire” [Note: The manuscripts read “the desire of the flesh” instead of “the flesh and desire”]—are counted as sin. The Apostle makes clear that he endures them unwillingly when he says: “What I hate, that I do” (Romans 7:15), that is, “I desire unwillingly.”

For when the Lord says concerning the mere movement of anger, without deed or word, “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22), he openly shows that the guilt is not slight when so grave a condemnation, namely death, follows it. It is as though he said: “Whoever does what a human being ought not to do, and would not do if he had not sinned, must be removed from among human beings.”

And when Paul says concerning those who experience the flesh—that is, desires—unwillingly: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh” (Romans 8:1), that is, who do not consent by their will, he undoubtedly signifies that condemnation follows those who are not in Christ whenever they experience the flesh, even if they do not walk according to it. For the human being was made in such a way that he ought not to experience it, just as I said concerning anger.

Therefore, if anyone carefully considers what I have said, he cannot doubt that those who, because of their own fault, are unable to receive the word of God are rightly reproved.

## CHAPTER VIII [otherwise XVIII] — Every fault and culpable inability are removed in those reborn through baptism

To those who are given the grace of Christian faith, original injustice, with which they are born, is forgiven in baptism. Likewise, every fault consisting in the inability and entire corruption which they incurred because of the sin of their first parent, and through which God is dishonored, is forgiven. [Note: The manuscripts read “which they had incurred because of the sin of the first human being” instead of “which they incurred because of the sin of their first parent.”]

They are not reproved after baptism for any fault that was in them before baptism, although the corruption and desire which are the punishment of sin are not immediately removed in baptism. Nor is any transgression attributed to them after baptism except what they have committed by their own will.

It is therefore clear that the corruption and evils which were the punishment of sin and remain after baptism are not sins in themselves. Injustice alone is sin in itself; and those things which follow injustice are judged to be sins because of their origin, until injustice itself is forgiven. For if they were sins, they would be removed in baptism, in which all sins are washed away by Christ’s blood. Again, if they were properly called sins, there would be sins in brute animals, since the human nature subjected to these things because of our sins is like theirs.

There is also something else that must be greatly feared, which can be recognized in the first sin of human nature. Since the human being is “a spirit that goes and does not return” (Psalm 77:3), after he willingly falls—speaking now only of voluntary sins [Note: The manuscripts read “we speak only now” and the Cistercian manuscript reads “let him speak only about this”]—he can in no way rise again unless grace lifts him up. By his own merit he is plunged from sin into sin, down to the bottomless abyss of sins—that is, into a depth beyond reckoning—unless mercy holds him back. Thus even what is good is turned for him into hatred and becomes death to him.

Therefore the Lord says to the apostles: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John 15). And the Apostle says: “We are a good fragrance of God, to some indeed the fragrance of death unto death, but to others the fragrance of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2). For this reason it is said of God: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9).

Nevertheless, those on whom he has mercy do not all receive mercy equally, nor does he harden all whom he hardens equally.

## CHAPTER IX [otherwise XIX] — Why, when sin has been removed, its effect remains, and why those who are baptized and martyrs do not immediately become incorruptible
But why the penalty of sin should remain in us during this life after sin has been removed is another question. Although we have not proposed to deal with it now, I say briefly that, if the faithful were immediately changed into incorruption in baptism or martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “if into corruption”; Vict. 3, Vict. 9, and Cister. read “if into incorruption”; Vict. 13 also reads “if into incorruption”], merit would perish, and human beings [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “and human beings”; Vict. reads “so that human beings”], unless they were those who believed first, without an example, would be saved without merit [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “would in no way be saved”; the text reads “would be saved without merit”]. For faith and hope would fail, without which no rational human being can merit the kingdom of God: faith and hope are, after all, concerned with things that are not seen.

For when people saw those who converted to Christ immediately pass into incorruption [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “people who would be seen”; the text reads “when people saw those who”], no one would be so much as able to wish to withdraw himself from such great blessedness, which he would see. Therefore, so that we may attain more gloriously, through the merit of faith and hope, the blessedness that we desire [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “so that he may be glorious”; the text reads “so that we may attain more gloriously”], we remain, as long as we are in this life, in that condition which is no longer counted as sin, although it occurred because of sin [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “although sin occurred”; Vict. reads “although it occurred because of sin”].

Finally, through baptism and Christian faith, the blessedness that Adam had before sin in paradise is not promised to us, but the blessedness that he would have had when the number of human beings who were to be taken up to complete the heavenly city had been fulfilled—a city that is to be completed from both angels and human beings. There human beings will not beget children, as they would have done in paradise.

If, then, those converted to Christ immediately passed into that incorruption, there would be no human beings from whom that number could be gathered, since no one could fail to hasten toward the blessedness that they saw. I think this is what the Apostle says about them: “Those who through faith practiced righteousness”; and he says, “all these, having been approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected without us” (Hebr. XI, 33, 39–40).

If it is asked what better thing he provided for us [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “he asks what better thing God provided for us”; the text reads “it is asked what better thing he provided for us”], because they did not receive the promise, I see no answer that could be more fitting than what I said above: namely, that if the blessedness promised to the righteous had not been delayed until those approved [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “at least if those propagated”; the text reads “namely, if those approved”], merit would have perished in those who would know this not through faith but through experience. The propagation of human beings also, from which we have been born [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “for propagation”; the text reads “propagation also”], would have ceased, since everyone would hasten toward the incorruption that they saw present.

Thus God provided us with a great good when, for the saints approved by the testimony of faith, he delayed the reception of the promise, so that we too might be propagated [Col. 0532C], and faith might remain, through which we might merit the promise together with them, and be perfected together with them.

There is also another reason why the baptized and martyrs do not immediately become incorruptible. Suppose someone had a servant whom he intended eventually to enrich with great honors, but whom he severely flogged for an offense for which he could in no way make satisfaction by himself, intending, after this flogging, at an appointed time to thrust him into a horrible prison, where he would be tortured with the severest punishments. Suppose, however, that someone powerful with the master should exist who, making satisfaction on the servant’s behalf, reconciled him to his master.

Certainly, the wounds that the guilty man deservedly received before satisfaction, while he was still at fault, are not erased. But the greater torments into which he had not yet been thrust [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “into which he was to be thrust”; the text reads “into which he had not yet been thrust”; Vict. 13 reads “into which he had not yet been admitted”] are averted because reconciliation intervenes. The honors that he was to receive at the proper time, if he had not sinned, and of which he would have been deprived after the offense [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts read “after his offense”; Vict. and Cister. omit “his”], if he were not reconciled, are nevertheless conferred, in accordance with the perfect satisfaction, exactly as had previously been determined.

For if, before reconciliation, he had been disinherited from those honors, just as he would have been irrecoverably disinherited after the offense if he had not been reconciled [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “he had been disinherited”; the text reads “he was to be disinherited”], there would be no place for reconciliation to come to his aid. But since he could not have been disinherited from an honor that he did not yet possess and ought not yet to possess [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “which he did not have and ought not yet to have”; the text reads “which he did not yet have and ought not yet to have”], reconciliation can forestall this disinheritance and avert it.

If, then, while that servant lies in the sickness of flogging until it has passed, he vows and fulfills fidelity and amendment toward his master in heart and mouth, so it is between God and humanity. For when human nature first sinned, it was scourged by this penalty: that it should never naturally beget offspring except such as we see infants being born [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “such as we see”; the text reads “such as we see infants being born”], and that after this life it should be eternally exiled in hell from the kingdom of God, for which it had been made, unless someone reconciled it—something it could not accomplish by itself.

There is no one by whom it can be reconciled except Christ. Thus, in all infants naturally born, it is born with sin and scourged [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “in sin and scourging”; the text reads “with sin and scourged”]. When it approaches reconciliation [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “received reconciliation”; the text reads “approaches reconciliation”], the scourging that it deservedly received before reconciliation remains. The torments that it was going to suffer in hell, however, are remitted in those whom Christ has redeemed; and the kingdom of God, which it was to receive in due time after the transformation of the earthly paradise [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “the transformation of paradise”; the text reads “after the transformation of the earthly paradise”], is granted to it, provided that they persevere to the end in the faith that they promise in baptism [Col. 0533C].

## CHAPTER X [formerly XX]  
### That if some who strive make no progress or fall away, this does not happen because of impossibility

But the view that some think experience proves—that free choice is of no value because many strive with immense effort to live well and, because of some alleged impossibility, make no progress [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “accomplish nothing”; the text reads “make no progress”], or, after making progress, fall away irrecoverably [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “fall away unrecoverably”; the text reads “fall away irreparably”]—does not destroy what has been rationally demonstrated, namely, that free choice is effective together with grace.

That those who strive do not make progress, or fall away after making progress, happens, I think, not because of impossibility but because sometimes of a serious difficulty and sometimes of one that can easily be overcome. We very often assert that something is impossible for us when we cannot accomplish it without difficulty. For if each person carefully considers the movements of his will, he will understand that he never abandons the rectitude of will received through grace except by willing something else that he cannot will at the same time [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “unless by willing something”; the text reads “unless by willing something else”].

Certainly, he does not do this because the power to preserve that same rectitude has failed—the power that is itself free choice—but because the will to preserve it has failed. That will does not fail by itself; rather, another will expels it, as I have said.

## CHAPTER XI [formerly XXI]  
### In what sense there is in a just or unjust person a will to live rightly

Since this consideration is chiefly concerned with the will, I think it appropriate to say something further about the will which, as I believe, will not be useless.

Just as we have bodily members and five senses, each suited to its own use, which we employ as instruments—for example, hands suited for grasping, feet for walking, the tongue for speaking, and sight for seeing—so the soul also possesses within itself certain powers, which it uses as instruments for appropriate purposes [Col. 0534B].

There is reason in the soul, which it uses as its instrument for reasoning, and there is the will, which it uses for willing. For neither reason nor will is the whole soul; each is something in the soul [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “the rational will is the whole”; the text reads “neither reason nor will is the whole soul”].

Since, therefore, individual instruments possess both what they are and their aptitudes and uses, let us distinguish in the will—for this is why we are speaking of it—the instrument, its aptitudes, and its use. We can call these aptitudes in the will “affections.”

An affection, then [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “an affection, then”; Vict. 3 and Vict. 9 read “an affection”], is the instrument of willing together with its aptitudes. Hence the soul of a person is said, when it strongly wills something, to be affected toward willing it [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “to be affected toward it”; Vict. reads “to be disposed toward it”], or to will it affectionately [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “to be or to will affectionately”; Vict. 9 reads “to will pleasurably”].

Thus “will” appears to be used equivocally in three ways. One thing is the instrument of willing, another is the affection of the instrument, and another is the use of that same instrument [Note: [Col. 0533D] The manuscripts read “another is the affection, another the use”; the text reads “another is the affection of the instrument, and another the use”].

The instrument of willing is that power of the soul which we use for willing, just as reason is the instrument of reasoning, which we use when we reason, and sight is the instrument of seeing, which we use when we see.

The affection of this instrument is the disposition by which the instrument itself is affected toward willing something, even when it is not thinking about what it wills: for example, if that thing should come to mind, it will will it either immediately or at the proper time.

Thus the instrument of willing is affected toward willing health even when it is not thinking about health, so that as soon as health comes to mind it immediately wills it. Likewise, it is affected toward willing sleep even when it is not thinking about sleep, so that when sleep comes to mind it wills it at the proper time. It is never so affected that it should at some time will sickness or will never to sleep.

In a just person also, the same instrument is similarly affected toward willing justice even when he is asleep, so that when he thinks of justice he immediately wills it.

The use of that same instrument is something we have only when we think about the thing we will. “Will” is applied both to the instrument of willing, to its affection, and to its use.

We call the instrument “will” when we say that we turn our will toward different things: for example, sometimes toward willing to walk, sometimes toward willing to sit, sometimes toward willing one thing and sometimes another.

A person always possesses this instrument, although he does not always use it—just as he possesses sight, which is the instrument of seeing, even when he does not use it, as when he sleeps. When he uses it, he turns it sometimes toward seeing the sky, sometimes toward seeing the earth, and sometimes toward seeing something else.

Likewise, we always possess the instrument of reasoning, that is, reason, although we do not always use it, and by reasoning we turn it toward different things [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read “the mind turns”; Gem. reads “the mind is turned”; Vict. and Cister. read “we turn”].

The affection of the instrument of willing is called “will” when we say that a person always has the will for things to go well for him. Here we call “will” that affection of the same instrument by which a person wills that things go well for him [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read “we call this”; the text reads “we call this here”].

In the same way, a holy person is said to have, even when he is asleep and not thinking, an unceasing will to live justly [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read “the will to live is said; and when”; the text reads “is said to have an unceasing will to live justly”]. When we assert that one person has more of this will than another, we mean by “will” nothing other than the affection of that instrument by which he wills to live justly.

The instrument itself is not greater in one person and smaller in another [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read “the instrument, however, is not”; the text reads “the instrument itself is not”].

The use of this instrument is also called “will,” as when someone says, “Now I have the will to read,” that is, “Now I want to read,” or, “Now I have the will to write,” that is, “Now I want to write.”

For just as seeing is using sight, which is the instrument of seeing, and its use is vision—or “sight,” when “sight” signifies the same thing as “vision,” although “sight” also signifies the instrument itself—so willing is using the will, which is the instrument of willing, and its use is “will,” which exists only when we think about what we want.

The will that is the instrument is therefore one and only one: that is, there is only one instrument of willing in a human being, just as there is only one reason, that is, only one instrument of reasoning.

The will by which that instrument is affected, however, is twofold. For just as sight has several aptitudes—namely, for seeing light, through light for seeing shapes, and for seeing colors—so the instrument of willing has two aptitudes, which I call affections. One is for willing advantage, the other for willing rectitude.

The will that is the instrument wills nothing except either advantage or rectitude. For whatever else it wills, it wills either for the sake of advantage or for the sake of rectitude; and even if it is mistaken, it thinks that it refers what it wills to one of these.

Through the affection that is directed toward willing advantage, a person always wills blessedness and to be blessed. Through the affection directed toward willing rectitude, he wills rectitude and wishes to be upright, that is, just.

He wills something for the sake of advantage, as when he wishes to plow or work so that he may have the means to preserve his life and health, which he judges to be advantages.

For the sake of rectitude, however, he wills something when he wishes to learn through labor [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read “he wishes to labor or learn”; Cister. reads “he wishes to learn through labor”; another reading is “he wishes to learn by labor”], so that he may know how to live rightly, that is, justly.

The will that is the use of the aforementioned instrument exists only when someone thinks about what he wills, as has been said. This will has several divisions, which we will perhaps discuss another time.

“Willing” is also equivocal, like “seeing.” For just as someone is said to see both when he uses sight and when he does not use it but possesses the aptitude for seeing, so someone is said to will both when he uses the instrument of willing by thinking about what he wills and when he does not use it because he possesses the affection—that is, the aptitude—for willing.

This too makes it possible to recognize that the will that is the instrument of willing is one thing, its affection another, and the use of that same instrument another. For if a just person is said, even when he is asleep and thinking of nothing, to have the will to live justly, while an unjust person is denied, when asleep, the will to live justly, the same will is denied of the unjust person as is affirmed of the just person.

It is obvious, however, that when we say that an unjust person who is asleep does not possess the will to live justly, we do not deny that he possesses the will that I have called the instrument. Every person, asleep and awake, always possesses it [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read: “It is obvious that when we say that the sleeping unjust person does not possess the will to live justly, we do not deny that the will which I called the instrument exists in him, since he always has it.” Vict. 13 reads: “In the unjust person it is not denied that there is the instrumental will, since he has it.” Other manuscripts contain various abbreviated forms: “obvious … in the sleeping unjust person the will, etc., as in the printed editions.”].

Therefore, since the will that is declared to be in a good person in this way is not a different will from the one removed from the bad person, what is signified as being in the good person is not the will that is the instrument, but the affection by which the instrument is affected.

That the will which is the use of the instrument is not present in a sleeping person unless he is dreaming is beyond doubt. Thus, when the will to live justly is said to be in a sleeping just person [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read “in a sleeping just woman”; the text reads “in a sleeping just person”], the will that is the use of the instrument is not understood there [Note: [Col. 0535D] The manuscripts read “the will is not understood”; the text reads “the will that is the use is not understood there”].

Therefore, the will that is the affection is not the will that is the instrument or the will that is the use; moreover, no one is unaware that the will which is the instrument is not the will which is the use; for when I say, “I do not have the will to write,” no one understands me to mean that I do not possess the instrument of willing.

The will that is the instrument is therefore one thing, the will that is the affection another, and the will that is the use another.

The will that is the instrument moves all the other instruments that we use voluntarily, both those within us, such as the hands, tongue, and sight, and those outside us, such as the pen and the axe, and it produces all voluntary movements. It itself, however, moves itself by its affections; hence it may be called an instrument that moves itself.

I say that the will, which is the instrument, produces all voluntary movements. But if we consider carefully, the one who more truly is said to produce everything that nature or will produces is the one who produces nature and the instrument of willing together with its affections, without which that same instrument does nothing.

[Col. 0537B]

## CHAPTER XII [formerly XXII]  
### That all human merit, whether toward salvation or condemnation, proceeds from the will of rectitude or of advantage

From these two affections, which we also call wills, all human merit proceeds, whether good or evil.

These two wills also differ in this respect: the one directed toward willing advantage is inseparable, whereas the one directed toward willing rectitude was separable, as I said above (*Dialogue on Free Choice*, chap. 14), at the beginning in the angels and in our first parents, and still is separable in those who remain in this life [Note: [Col. 0537D] The manuscripts read “also differ in nothing”; the text reads “also differ in this respect”].

They differ in this respect as well: the will directed toward willing advantage is not the thing that it wills, whereas the will directed toward willing rectitude is rectitude itself [Note: [Col. 0537D] The manuscripts read “the one that is directed toward”; the text has the same wording].

No one wills rectitude unless he possesses rectitude; nor can anyone will rectitude except through rectitude. It is obvious that this rectitude belongs to the will that is the instrument.

We declare this when justice is defined as rectitude of will preserved for its own sake. This is also that truth of the will in which the Lord reproves the devil for not having stood firm, as I said in the treatise *On Truth* (chap. 4).

Now we must consider how these two wills, which I call aptitudes or affections, produce, as I said, human merits, whether toward salvation or toward condemnation.

Rectitude, insofar as it is concerned, is the cause of no evil and is the mother of every good merit. For it favors the spirit that desires against the flesh (Gal. V, 25), and delights together with the law of God according to the inner person (Rom. VII, 22), that is, according to that same spirit.

If evil sometimes appears to follow from it, it does not proceed from rectitude itself but from something else. Through rectitude the apostles were a good fragrance to God (II Cor.
