II, 16); but the fact that to some they were a fragrance of death unto death did not proceed from the apostles’ righteousness but from the wickedness of evil people.

The will directed toward willing advantage, however, is not always evil, but becomes evil when it consents to the flesh that desires against the spirit.

## CHAPTER XIII [formerly XXIII]  
### Whence the will is so vicious and so prone to evil

But so that this may be understood more clearly, we must investigate why this will is so vicious and so prone to evil. We must not believe that God made it such in our first parents.

When I stated that human nature had incurred corruption because of sin and that its appetites had become like those of brute animals, I did not explain how such a will arose in human beings. Vicious appetites are one thing; a vicious will that consents to those appetites is another. I therefore think we must ask about such a will: whence did it come to human beings?

But if we consider the original condition of rational nature, the cause of this kind of will will easily become clear to us.

God’s intention was to make rational nature just and blessed, so that it might enjoy him. But it could be neither just nor blessed without a will for justice and blessedness.

The will for justice is justice itself; the will for blessedness, however, is not blessedness, because not everyone who has the will for blessedness possesses blessedness.

Blessedness, according to everyone’s understanding, consists in an adequate sufficiency of advantages without any need, whether we understand angelic blessedness or the blessedness Adam had in paradise.

Although the blessedness of the angels is greater than the blessedness that human beings had in paradise, this does not mean that Adam should be denied having been blessed. For just as there can be great heat without any cold, while there can nevertheless be a greater heat, and just as there can be cold without any heat, while there can nevertheless be a greater cold, so nothing prevents Adam from having been blessed in paradise without any need, even though the blessedness of the angels was greater.

To have less of one thing than another is not always to be in need. Rather, to lack something when it ought to be possessed is to be in need [Note: [Col. 0537D] The manuscripts read “to have it”; the text reads “when it ought to be possessed”]. But where there is need, there is misery.

God did not, without a preceding fault, make rational nature miserable [Note: [Col. 0537D] The manuscripts read “make the rational creature miserable”; Vict. 3, Vict. 9, and Cister. read “make rational nature miserable”; Vict. 13 reads “make rational nature unto misery”], since he created it to understand and love him. God therefore made human beings blessed, without any need.

Thus rational nature simultaneously received the will for blessedness, blessedness itself, the will for justice—that is, rectitude, which is justice itself—and free choice, without which it could not preserve justice [Note: [Col. 0537D] The manuscripts read “the blessedness of justice, that is”; the text reads “blessedness and the will for justice, that is”].

God ordered these two wills, or affections, in such a way that the will which is the instrument should use the one that is justice for command and governance [Note: [Col. 0537D] The manuscripts read “for command and rule”; the text reads “for command and governance”], under the instruction of the spirit, which is also called mind and reason; and that the other should be used for obedience [Col. 0539A], without any disadvantage [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “for obedience without”; the text reads “for being obedient without”].

He gave human beings blessedness—for the moment I shall say nothing about the angels—for their advantage, and justice for his honor. But he gave justice in such a way that they could abandon it, so that, if they did not abandon it but preserved it perseveringly, they might deserve to be advanced into fellowship with the angels.

If they abandoned it, however, they could never afterward take it up again by themselves. They would neither attain the blessedness of the angels nor retain the blessedness they had possessed; instead, falling into the likeness of brute animals and becoming subject with them to corruption and to the aforementioned appetites, they would nevertheless retain the will for blessedness. Thus they would be justly punished with great misery through need of the goods they had lost.

Therefore, because he abandoned justice, he lost blessedness. And the will that he received as good and directed toward his own good, burning with desire for advantages [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “enjoying with desire”; the text reads “burning with desire”], which it cannot fail to will, because it cannot possess the true advantages suitable to rational nature that it lost, turned toward false advantages and toward the advantages of brute animals suggested by bestial appetites.

Thus, when it wills these things in an disordered manner, it either rejects rectitude so that it will not be received when offered, or drives it out after it has been received [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “it rejects or drives out what is offered”; the text reads “it rejects what is offered or drives out what has been received”]. When it wills them licitly [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “it licitly wills it”; the text reads “when it wills them licitly”], however, it does not act in this way.

In this manner, then, the will that is the instrument, created good [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “the good of the instrument”; the text reads “the instrument created good”] insofar as it has being, and just and strong for preserving the justice it had received, was made evil through free choice—not insofar as it exists, but insofar as it was made unjust through the absence of justice that it had voluntarily abandoned, although it ought always to possess it.

It was also made weak for willing the justice it had abandoned. For through free choice it cannot will justice in the way it can preserve it when it possesses it [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “to will it, although it does not possess it, in the way it can preserve it”; Vict. reads “to will it, when it does not possess it, in the way it can preserve it”; other manuscripts have “yet it does not possess it” and “it can preserve it”].

The will for advantage, likewise, created good [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “created good”; the text reads “created good”], insofar as it is something, was made evil—that is, unjust—because it is not subject to justice, without which it ought to will nothing.

Therefore, once the will that is the instrument has voluntarily become unjust, after abandoning justice it remains, insofar as it is concerned, necessarily unjust and a slave of injustice. For by itself it cannot return to justice, without which it is never free, since the natural freedom of free choice is idle without it.

It also became a slave to its own affection, the one directed toward advantage, because, once justice has been removed, it can will nothing except what that affection wills.

I say that both the instrument and its affection will, because both the instrument is called “will” and the affection is called “will.” Nor is it inappropriate to say that both wills will: the instrument wills the things that it wills by means of its affection, and the affection wills through which the instrument wills—just as both the human being who sees through sight and sight itself through which he sees are said to see.

Hence we may not absurdly say that the affections of that will which I called the instrument of the soul are, as it were, instruments of the same instrument, because it does nothing except through them [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “nothing except through these”; the text reads “the instrument itself does nothing except through these”].

Once the instrument of willing justice, that is, rectitude, has therefore been lost, the will cannot in any way will justice unless it is restored through grace.

Therefore, since it ought to will nothing except justly, whatever it wills without rectitude it wills unjustly.

The appetites that the Apostle collectively calls “the flesh” and “concupiscence” are not, insofar as they exist, evil or unjust. But because they are in rational nature, where they ought not to be, they are called unjust. In brute animals they are not evil or unjust, because they ought to be there.

## CHAPTER XIV [formerly XXIV]  
### Recapitulation and conclusion of the work [Col. 0540B]

From what has been said it can now be understood why human beings do not always possess the justice that they ought to possess without interruption: they cannot in any way attain or recover it by themselves.

It is also clear that God performs his good works solely through his goodness, because he creates the will together with free choice and gives it the justice through which it acts.

Human beings, however, perform evil works solely through their own fault, because they would not perform them if they did not wish to perform them. Yet God makes what these works are, because he created in human beings a will that they use without justice. Therefore the evil things they perform are evil solely through human fault [Note: [Col. 0539D] Vict. 13 reads “but God performs evil things”].

It is not God’s fault that he created in them, together with free choice, a will and conferred justice upon it, so that it would will nothing except justly. It is the fault of the human being, who abandoned the justice that he could have preserved.

God therefore has, in good things, both the fact that they are good in essence and the fact that they are good through justice. In evil things he has only the fact that they are good in essence, not the fact that they are evil through the absence of the justice that was owed, since that absence is not something.

The human being, however, has in good things the fact that they are not evil: although he could have abandoned justice and done evil, he did not abandon it, but preserved it through free choice, with grace giving and following after him [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “the human being ought”; Vict. 3 reads “the human being, however, ought”]. In evil things he has only the fact that they are evil, because he performs them through his own will alone—that is, through an unjust will.

I think I can now appropriately bring to an end the treatise on the three difficult questions, which I began in the hope of God’s assistance. If in it I have said something that ought to suffice for anyone who asks, I do not attribute it to myself, because it was not I but the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts read “I attribute it to the grace of God”; the text reads “I do not attribute it to myself, because it was not I but the grace of God”] that was with me.

I say this because, if someone had answered me, when I was asking about these same questions and my mind was wavering as it sought a reason, with what I have written, I would have given thanks because he would have satisfied me [Col. 0540D; Col. 0541A].

Since, therefore, what I came to know about these matters through God’s revelation greatly pleased me, and I understood that it would similarly please some others if I wrote it down, I wished to distribute freely to those who ask what I had received freely [Note: [Col. 0541D] MSS Gemm., chap. 19; Vict. 3 and Cister.: “The book of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, on the Harmony of Foreknowledge, Predestination, and the Grace of God with Free Choice, ends.”].

[Col. 0541A]

# Saint Anselm: On the Three Questions of Walerannus, and Especially on Unleavened and Leavened Bread

[Note: [Col. 0541D] The letter was collated with the Victorine manuscripts CC 9, EE 13, and Ef 20, the Corbie manuscript 307, and one Cistercian manuscript, as well as with the Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions. Vict. CC 9: “Letter of Master Anselm on Unleavened Bread.” Cister.: “Here begins the letter of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, on the sacrifice of unleavened and leavened bread.” Corb.: “Here begins the letter of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to Walerannus of Naumburg, on leavened and unleavened bread.”]

He first refers elsewhere the answer to Walerannus’s first question, which concerned the procession of the Holy Spirit. Then he refutes the error of the Greeks concerning the sacrifice made with leavened bread, while nevertheless indicating that the one who uses leaven also makes the body of Christ, although the one who consecrates with unleavened bread conforms more closely to Christ. Finally, he responds briefly to the third question, which concerned marriage.

[Col. 0541B]

### 135 Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to Walerannus, bishop of Naumburg

I speak briefly to one who understands. If I were certain that your wisdom did not favor the successor of Julius Caesar, of Nero, and of Julian the Apostate, against the successor and vicar of the Apostle Peter, I would most gladly greet you as a very dear and reverend bishop.

But since, in defending the truth that you seek against the Greeks who have come to you, we ought according to our ability to fail no one, I have sent you the little work that I published against them concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER I  
### That, without prejudice to the truth of the Sacrament, either unleavened or leavened bread may be used

[Col. 0541C]

As for the sacrifice, concerning which these same Greeks do not agree with us, it appears, for many reasonable Catholic reasons [Note: Vict. 9 and 13 read *rationabilibus catholicis* (“for reasonable Catholic [grounds]”); the note contrasts *rationibus catholicis* (“for Catholic reasons”).], that what they do is not contrary to the Christian faith. For one who sacrifices with unleavened bread also sacrifices, and so does one who sacrifices with leavened bread. And when it is read concerning the Lord, when he made his body from bread, that “he took bread and blessed it,” it is not added whether it was unleavened or leavened. It is nevertheless certain that he blessed unleavened bread; perhaps not because the thing being done required this, but because the supper at which this took place required it [Note: “Perhaps because” in the manuscripts; “but because the supper at which this took place required it” is omitted in the Gothic and Cologne editions]. And when elsewhere he called himself and his flesh “bread” (John 6:52), because just as a human being lives temporally by this bread, so by that bread he lives eternally, he calls it neither unleavened nor leavened, since each is equally bread. For unleavened and leavened bread do not differ substantially [Col. 0541D–0542B] (as some think), any more than the new man before sin and the old man, leavened with sin, differ substantially. For this reason alone, therefore, he appears to have called himself and his flesh bread, and to have made his body from bread: because just as this bread, whether unleavened or leavened, gives transitory life, so his body gives eternal life—not because it is leavened or unleavened.

Although in the Law, where nearly everything was done figuratively, it was commanded that unleavened bread be eaten at Passover (Exodus 12:15), so that it might be shown that Christ, whom they awaited, would be sincere and pure, and that we, who were going to eat his body, should likewise be warned to be pure from every leaven of wickedness and evil, now, after we have passed from the old figure to the new truth and eat Christ’s unleavened flesh, that old figure is not necessary for us in the bread from which we make that flesh.

## Chapter II. The Sacrament Is More Fittingly Made with Unleavened than with Leavened Bread

It is nevertheless most evident that the sacrifice is better made from unleavened than from leavened bread, both because it is performed far more fittingly, earlier, and more carefully, and because the Lord did this [Col. 0542C]. Hence this must not be left unsaid: when the Greeks anathematize those who use unleavened bread—for that is what they call us—they anathematize Christ. But if they say that we Judaize, let them likewise say that Christ Judaized. And if they dare to assert that Christ, on account of Judaism, made his body from unleavened bread in order that he might observe the commandment concerning unleavened bread [Col. 0542D–0543A; Note: Vict. 9 reads active *servaret* (“he might observe”); the note contrasts passive *servaretur* (“it might be observed”)], they are gravely mistaken, since they suppose that he infected so pure a newness with the leaven of antiquity [Note: MS. Vict. 20 reads “made the newness in leaven”; MSS. Vict. 9 and 19 and Corb. read “infected the will with leaven”; another reading is “infected the newness with leaven”].

It is therefore clear that, when he used unleavened bread for that act, he did not do so in order to observe the commandment concerning unleavened bread, but either to condemn the users of leaven, whom he foresaw, and approve those who use unleavened bread, or, certainly, so that, even if those who use leaven were approved, those who use unleavened bread might also be approved.

## Chapter III. Latins Who Make the Sacrament with Unleavened Bread Do Not Judaize

What they say—that we Judaize—is not true, because we do not sacrifice from unleavened bread in order to observe the old Law, but so that this may be done more carefully and so that we may imitate the Lord, who did this without Judaizing [Col. 0543B]. When we do something that the Jews did in order to preserve Judaism, we do not Judaize if we do it not for the sake of Judaism but for another reason.

For if someone eats unleavened bread during the days of Passover, either because he has no other bread or because he likes it better than leavened bread; or if someone, because of illness, is compelled to circumcise his foreskin; or if someone does not muzzle his ox while it is threshing, so that it may not go hungry—no one except a fool will judge the person doing these things to be Judaizing.

Therefore, when we sacrifice unleavened bread, we do not do so in order, by means of the figure of unleavened bread, to signify that the Lord Jesus would be such, but so that, by divine power at work, we may sacrifice that bread itself as his body, just as he did. In this we by no means preserve the antiquity of the Law, but celebrate the truth of the Gospel.

Finally, when he himself did this 136 and said to his disciples, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19), if he had not wished that we, to whom he commanded this through the apostles, should do this with unleavened bread [Note: The Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions read *si noluisset ut* (“if he had not wished that”); the note gives *si voluisset ut* (“if he had wished that”) as the unassigned contrast], he would have warned us through them and said, “Do not do this with unleavened bread.” Therefore, when he said, “Do this,” and did not exclude unleavened bread, who is there whose understanding dares to exclude what he did and to prohibit what he not only prohibited by no word but even commanded by his action?

Who, I ask, except one who is wiser than he ought to be, would trust so much in his own wisdom as to presume even to say that, when the Lord said, “Do this,” we may suitably understand the implied words, “as I do,” and yet confidently infer that it should be understood, “but not with this substance from which I do it”?

Again, if we ought to carry out divine things through those things that we recognize as more worthy, and if the sacrifice in question must be celebrated from the substance of bread, whether unleavened or leavened, what bread do we judge more worthy for making the truth of the Lord’s body [Col. 0543C–0544A] than that which both the old Law chose to signify and the Gospel to exhibit that same truth? If, therefore, we answer the Greeks that we do this with unleavened bread not because of the figure but for the reasons stated above, there is no intelligible reason why the Greeks should rightly judge us worthy of anathema, or at least of blame.

## Chapter IV. The Argument by Which the Greeks Prove That Latins Who Use Unleavened Bread Judaize Is Turned Back against the Greeks

But if they say that we cannot do this with unleavened bread without understanding the figure, by which we are proved to Judaize [Col. 0544B], then they likewise cannot use leavened bread for this same purpose without a figure. For the old Scripture also designates sin by leaven, when it curses the eating of leavened bread at Passover (Exodus 12:15), and the new Scripture, when it admonishes us to feast at our Passover not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness (1 Corinthians 5:8).

We also say that we do not Judaize if we retain the figure in unleavened bread, because we do not signify, like the Jews, that Christ will come without the leaven of sin; rather, as Christians, we show that he has come such. By this we are admonished to present ourselves as that which our Passover is, which we eat.

But they do not profess themselves either Jews or Christians in this matter, because by the figure of their leaven they signify neither that he will come without sin, as the Jews do, nor that he has come without sin, as Christians do. Rather, they seem to favor the pagans, who think that he, like other human beings, was fermented with sin [Col. 0544C].

If they say that Christians ought not to use figures because the old things have passed away (2 Corinthians 5:17), although figures were necessary in them, let them deny—as I leave other matters aside—that baptism is a figure of a certain death and burial, contrary to the Apostle’s words: “All we who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Romans 6:3–4).

Or if they grant that we use figures, but not in the same things in which the old Law used them, and therefore that unleavened bread should not be taken for any figure because it was taken for this purpose in that same Law, let them not baptize in water, since all our fathers “were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2), which cannot be denied to have occurred in figure. Let them also avoid water, lest they appear to baptize with the baptism of John, who baptized in water.

If, then, we irreproachably baptize figuratively in water, although that old baptism, which was a figure of this new one, took place in water, what wisdom is there in the Greeks which, because the old Passover by which ours was figured was celebrated with unleavened bread, detests our sacrificing the body of Christ, who is our Passover, from unleavened bread in a figure—either to commemorate that the one whose body we sacrifice was such, namely, without the infection of sin, or to admonish us that, because we eat his body, we ought to be such, according to the Apostle’s words [Col. 0544D–0545B]:

“Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:7–8).

## Chapter V. The Passages of Scripture Which the Greeks Misused against the Latins in the Controversy concerning Leavened Bread, Properly Explained; First, “The Letter Kills”

Whether, therefore, we sacrifice unleavened bread in a figure or without any figure at all, the Greeks are utterly unable to show us blameworthy. Either we alone act rightly and they do not; or, if they act rightly, we act better and more carefully.

They plainly show that they have no argument to support their own position or weaken ours when they bring against us something that is recognized as being in no way either against us or in their favor [Col. 0545C].

For, as I read in your letter, they object to us what the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6), and what the prophet Amos says: “Sacrifice praise from leavened bread,” or “Sacrifice praise with leaven” (Amos 4:5). From this they endeavor to show that the letter, which commands the old Passover to be celebrated with unleavened bread, kills us when we observe it by sacrificing unleavened bread, because we do not understand the Apostle’s words correctly.

The letter is said to kill when, by commanding us to turn away from sin, it reveals sin; for unless grace assists us so that what is commanded may be done, it makes the disobedient person a transgressor. The Apostle makes this equally clear in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: “I did not know sin except through the Law. For I would not have known coveting to be sin unless the Law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Exodus 20:17). “But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of coveting. For without the Law sin was dead. I was once alive without the Law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. And the commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me” (Romans 7:7 and following) [Col. 0545D–0546A].

Thus the letter kills without assisting grace, while the Spirit gives life, as the same Apostle says to Titus:

“When the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, he saved us—not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy—through the washing of regeneration and renewal [Note: “And renewal” is omitted in the manuscripts] of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:4 and following).

Therefore, after he had said, “Our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit” [Note: The manuscripts read “of the Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit”; then, “he added: for the letter…”], he says, “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:5–6). It is as though he said: God made us ministers of the New Testament, which is not in the killing letter, as the Old Testament was, but in the life-giving Spirit.

Both the killing of the letter and the giving of life by the Spirit are included in what he added:

“If the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was in glory—so that the children of Israel could not gaze steadily at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, a glory that was passing away—how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, the ministry of righteousness abounds much more in glory. Indeed, what was glorious in that respect is not glorified, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was passing away came through glory, much more will what remains be in glory.

“Therefore, having such a hope, we use great boldness, and not as Moses used to put a veil over his face so that the children of Israel would not gaze at what was passing away. But their minds were hardened; for to this day that very 137 veil remains unlifted in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is abolished in Christ. But to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But when one turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

“Therefore, having this ministry, according to the mercy we have received, we do not grow weary” (2 Corinthians 3:7–18; 4:1) [Col. 0546B–0547A].

Concerning the killing of the letter and the giving of life by the Spirit, it seems superfluous to me to add anything further here. It is therefore sufficiently clear that what they object concerning the letter that kills neither benefits the Greeks nor harms us.

## Chapter VI. How the Prophet Commands That Praise Be Sacrificed from Leavened Bread

As for what they take from the prophet—“Come to Gilgal and act impiously, and sacrifice praise from leavened bread” (Amos 4:5)—it must be understood either as spoken in approval of such a sacrifice or in condemnation of it.

But if the prophet commands this, speaking according to their interpretation, then the letter kills those who, by observing the letter, sacrifice from leavened bread. If, however, it was spoken as a reproach, with what face do they sacrifice what the prophet curses as a sacrifice, or by what reasoning do they claim this passage as an authority for themselves?

That the prophet said this not as a command but as a rebuke is beyond doubt, since he associated it with an impious action [Col. 0547B]. For he had said: “Come to Bethel and act impiously.” And shortly afterward, continuing his rebuke, he says: “And sacrifice praise from leavened bread.”

Let those who use leaven therefore either defend their position with as much reasoning as those who use unleavened bread strengthen theirs [Note: The manuscripts read “they defend”], or reject their leaven and become users of unleavened bread; or, if they can do neither the one nor the other, at least let them not blame those who use unleavened bread.

## Chapter VII. The Marriages of the Latins between Persons Related in Certain Separated Degrees, Wrongly Rejected by the Greeks

In the third question, as I understand it, you say that the Greeks detest our marriages in which relatives are joined to relatives from another kinship. I see no authority or reason for their doing this.

For if they forbid this in their own marriages, then either they do not extend kinship to the seventh generation, as we do, or what they command appears impossible to observe. There are often more than one hundred men and women within a single kinship who require marriage. It would therefore be necessary to find just as many kinships, from each of which individual men and women would be chosen, so that the individual members of one kinship might be joined individually to those of another [Col. 0547C–0548B].

Either, therefore, their marriages are unquestionably detestable if they occur within seven generations, and they ought not to criticize ours when relatives are joined to relatives from another kinship, since no authority or reason forbids this; or, as I have said, it is impossible to observe what they command—namely, that as many kinships be sought for the marriage of one kinship as there are men and women in it seeking marriage. [Note: The manuscripts and the Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions read passive *servari* (“to be observed”) for active *servare* (“to observe”) in the preceding statement that the command is impossible to observe.] But what is done without any authority or reason, contrary to reason, is without doubt judged reasonably to be rejected.

# St. Anselm: On the Diversity of the Sacraments, to Bishop Walerannus

## The Letter of Walerannus Which Provided Blessed Anselm with the Occasion for Writing

[Note: Walerannus’s letter was collated with MS. Vict. Ef. 20.]

He complains about the variety of ceremonies customarily observed in different ways by different people during the sacrifice at the altar—as though these touched the essence of the sacrament, whereas they rather concern its mystery and religious decorum [Col. 0547B–0547C].

To the most serene Lord Anselm, most reverend archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury: Walerannus, by the grace of God bishop of Newenburg, offers servile obedience, the urgency of his prayers, and himself, wholly devoted in every respect.

Since it is utterly unfitting to presume anything concerning the profession of letters in the presence of Minerva, the ability to establish credit by plausible reasoning among learned devotees of letters has not been granted to us [Note: The manuscripts read “the learned”; *edocumatos* is an evident corruption]. But when, sighing with the prophet, “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18), I raise my eyes with the greatest devotion toward the mountain of your highness, so that help may come to me from there—your help, help from the Lord, who made heaven and earth—“he who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17)—it may become clear that, from his fullness, you too search out the deep things of God, while our littleness hears his voice but is altogether ignorant of where it comes from or where it goes [Col. 0548C–0549A].

## 138. Chapter I. Walerannus’s Complaint about Such Great Diversity in the Celebration of the Sacraments

God is the indivisible Trinity, and whatever things are in God are one in him. Diversity in the Church is exceedingly opposed to unity. What is consumed by internal disagreement among its parts cannot long stand.

Regarding the sacraments of the Church, Palestine has one view, Armenia another, our Roman Church another, and Gaul, divided into three parts, another. The mystery of the Lord’s body is also handled one way by the Roman Church, another by the Gallican Church, and in a very different way by our Germany [Col. 0549A–0549B].

We have received from the ancient Fathers an order for making the sacrifice, and I greatly wonder where this novelty has crept into the house of the Lord: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8)—always one, always the same, tolerating no change. Whoever tends toward diversity dissents from Christ.

Christ is the bread of angels, which came down from heaven (John 6:41), and became the bread of human beings, the food of the poor, the satiety of those who reign with him, so that those who worthily eat may live forever and ever.

“One bread, one body, though many, we are all one in Christ, because we partake of one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). Christ is the way (John 14), by which we should walk and whom we should imitate. Whoever departs from Christ walks dangerously. Let us do, during the sacrifice, what Christ did:

“Whenever you do this, whenever you partake” (1 Corinthians 11:25–26) [Col. 0549B–0549C].

## Chapter II. Why Some Use Leavened Bread in the Mysteries

The Armenians indeed think that they sacrifice praise from leavened bread, but they do not walk with Christ in newness of life. Imitators of Christ ought to feast not in the old leaven but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5). Though it is small, leaven corrupts the whole mass.

The incorruptible body of Christ should, insofar as possible, be infected by no corruption. Let every such corruption be absent from the sacrifice of sincerity. Those who desire to be imbued with the incorruption of Christ’s body should strip off the old man through the sincerity of the new sacrifice.

In the making of Christ’s body, no substance is pleasing except that which he himself offered. And, if I may dare to profess it, the rule of sacrifice that he gave must be maintained [Col. 0549C–0549D].

## Chapter III. Why Most Form a Single, Not Multiple, Sign of the Cross over the Bread and Chalice

We bless the bread separately and the chalice separately. This is prescribed by the canons and by the ancient Roman Order: from the beginning of the canon we make separate crosses over the separate elements. We maintain this everywhere by public and long-established custom, from generation to generation, and we marvel at your strange diversity [Col. 0550A].

Christ did this, and commanded us to do it: “Do this whenever you partake” (Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; 1 Corinthians 11). Taking the bread, he blessed it separately, and likewise the chalice. He made separate crosses over each, as our—indeed, the Roman—Order prescribes. Thus our custom developed from him who is the same yesterday, today, and forever.

In the distinctness of the crosses, Christ’s authority agrees with us. But I greatly wonder by what reasoning diversity in the manner of sacrifice began. “There is one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5), and one Church, Christ’s beloved, bride, and dove. It greatly harms the unity of the Church to disagree in the sacraments and to make whatever one pleases lawful [Col. 0550A–0550B].

## Chapter IV. Why the Chalice Is Covered with a Veil or Pall from the Beginning

Moreover, during the consecration some cover the chalice from the beginning with a corporal, while others use a folded cloth in the manner of a napkin, which we read was found in the tomb—not placed with the linen cloths, but wrapped separately in one place [Col. 0550B].

Christ is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14); he is the way by which we walk in order to come to him. Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked (1 John 2:6). They do not come to life except as imitators of life.

The Paschal victim was sacrificed on the altar of the cross with his body uncovered. He who made known to his own everything that he had heard from the Father (John 15) wished to be offered with his body uncovered. In his sacrifice he manifested himself as he is. With unveiled face we shall contemplate his glory, transformed in every respect into his image and conformed to the body of his glory, so that he may be all things to us in eternal blessedness.

And, to use his own words (Matthew 27; John 19), “It is finished,” he said, so that we may not doubt that the old things have passed away and all things have become new. The veil of the Temple was torn from top to bottom, that veil which to this day lies over the hearts of the Jews, so that, though they have eyes, they do not see, and though they have ears, they do not understand.

But for us, to whom God has revealed these things through his Spirit, it is not fitting to wrap up the mysteries of the sacrifice; rather, following the example of the Lord Jesus, we should make them clear. Let us not, like the Jews with Moses, place a veil over them, but, offering with the Lord Jesus, let us strive to be transformed from glory to glory [Col. 0550C–0550D].

Jesus was naked on the altar of the cross; let him appear naked on the altar of our sacrifice. What we affirm in words, let us carry out in our deeds. That bread is truly Christ’s body, and as Christ’s body was sacrificed, so it ought to be sacrificed.

Christ’s body was uncovered on the altar of the cross, wrapped in linen cloths in the tomb, and in the devotion of the disciples it was wrapped for burial during the Passion. By burying him, as it is customary for Jews to bury, they showed their devoted reverence toward the Master, but they still did not know the truth of the sacrament.

The Jews bury him in a similar fashion as a Jew because they had not yet understood the mystery of the cross. “The Spirit searches everything, even the deep things of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). But the Spirit had not yet been given to them, because Christ had not yet been glorified after being crucified in weakness.

Once glorified, Jesus casts off the garments of corruption and removes corruptible things from himself. Clothed in incorruption, he leaves the tomb and reveals his glory to those who love him [Col. 0551A].

Why, then, do we seem to proclaim Christ’s weakness by wrapping him in an incorruptible napkin and wrap him in such darkness, when we most truly proclaim him to be the power of God and the light of the world? Let the light from light, which illuminates every human being (John 1), by no means be placed under the bushel of a napkin. Rather, just as the priest and victim himself offered himself, so let our sacrifice be offered to him, placed in the open air, so that it may shine for all in Christ’s house unto life [Note: The manuscripts read “I say, so that it may shine for all”].

Then our victim will be especially acceptable if it is like Christ’s victim. We too, however, wrap the living victim—not, as is your custom, from the beginning, but at the end, with Joseph and Nicodemus.

Since what is offered is offered not merely in appearance but in the truth of the thing, it ought not to differ in its sacrifice. Whoever differs in offering does not walk as Christ walked. But if sincerity in this matter of sacrifice is pleaded, it is very easy to observe cleanliness with us by means of a covering of sincerity, and yet not depart from the oldest rite of the Church and from the practice of sacrifice from the very beginning [Col. 0551B].

## Chapter V. He Notes His Own Return to Communion with the Church

Let your eyes see my imperfection, and, since you are joined together as though by the hands of virtues into the fullness of every kind of circumspection, have compassion on the excesses of our imperfection.

The Catholic Church glorifies God in me, because in our change the grace of divine goodness appears. By the grace of God I am what I am: from Saul, Paul; from an adversary of the Roman Church, an intimate of Pope Paschal and his most welcome 139 fellow secretary among the cardinals; and in all things I hope for successful outcomes in this matter [Col. 0552A].

Joseph was in Pharaoh’s house; I am in the palace of the emperor Henry. [The transmitted sentence is damaged:] “Neither iniquity nor my sin (God forbid), nor [anything] like Nero’s incest or Julian’s apostasy.”

Thanks be to God [Note: The manuscripts read “Grace to God”], because under the rule of your holiness the wolf and the lamb graze together, the lion and the calf lie down together, and a little child leads them. Because the rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom, we praise God’s power that, through ecclesiastical terror, untamed beasts are made gentle and harm no one on the mountain of the Lord.

“The lion has roared; who will not fear?” But because the righteous person is confident like a lion, and like David strong of hand, your heart does not tremble but triumphs in all things through God’s power.

May the Lord who anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions (Hebrews 1:9) crown you with mercy and compassion in the kingdom of blessedness [Col. 0552B].

# Anselm’s Response to Walerannus’s Complaints

[Note: MS. Cister. entitles this “Letter on the Sacraments of the Church.”]

To Lord Walerannus [Note: The Venetian edition reads Latin *Waleranno* (“Walerannus,” dative) for *Waleramo*, a variant spelling], venerable bishop of Newenburg by the grace of God: Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greeting, service, prayers, and the affection of love.

I rejoice and give thanks to God because, as you write, the Catholic Church glorifies him in you, since in your change the grace of divine goodness appears, and you have the friendship and intimacy of Lord Pope Paschal, so that I may now greet your holiness as a friend.

I do not take personally the fact that your lofty humility compares me to Minerva and calls me a mountain, because I understand nothing in myself that would justify this being said of me. Nevertheless, I ought not to be ungrateful for your kindness, since the abundance of your good will toward me causes this. [Note: The manuscripts read *vestrae erga me* (“your [kindness] toward me”); the note gives the fuller unassigned reading *vestrae benignitati, quoniam hoc facit abundantia vestrae erga me* (“to your kindness, because the abundance of your [good will] toward me causes this”).] We often judge those whom we love to be better than they themselves deserve. Thus my heart does not glory in praise that does not belong to me, but rejoices with gratitude in affection, which is always worthy of love [Col. 0552C].

## Chapter I. The Variety of Rites Is Consistent with Unity of Faith

Your reverence is asked about the sacraments of the Church because they are not performed everywhere in one way, but are administered in different ways in different places. [Note: Vict. 13 and the Gothic and Cologne editions read passive *quaeritur* (“is asked”); the note contrasts active *quaerit* (“asks”).]

Certainly, if they were celebrated throughout the Church in one way and harmoniously, that would be good and praiseworthy. Nevertheless, since there are many differences that do not disagree in the substance [Note: “In sum” in MS. Vict. 13] of the sacrament, nor in its power [Note: Vict. 13 omits only the preposition *in* from *neque in virtute* (“nor in [its] power”)], nor in faith, and since they cannot all be gathered into one custom, I think that they should rather be tolerated peacefully and harmoniously than condemned discordantly with scandal.

For we have received from the holy Fathers that, if the unity of charity in the Catholic faith is preserved [Note: The Venetian edition reads *quia si unitas* (“because if unity”); the note contrasts *quia ubi unitas* (“because where unity”)], differing custom does no harm [Col. 0552D].

But if it is asked from where these varieties of custom arose, I understand them to have arisen from nothing other than differences among human perceptions. Although people do not disagree in the truth and power of the matter itself [Note: MS. Vict. 13 and the Gothic and Cologne editions read “in the truth and unity of the matter”], they do not agree in the suitability and decorum of its administration [Note: The Venetian edition reads *et decentia* (“and decorum”); the note contrasts *et differentia* (“and difference”)].

What one judges more fitting, another often considers less fitting. I do not think that failing to agree in such variations departs from the truth of the matter itself [Col. 0553A].

## Chapter II. On the Complaint Concerning the Formation of a Single Sign of the Cross
