## Complete textual apparatus from the supplied source

Every printed note is represented below in source order. Latin forms are retained when English alone cannot show the wording, grammar, spelling, or punctuation. In the source’s apparatus syntax, the reading before a witness label belongs to that witness; a following form without a new label is recorded here as an unassigned contrast rather than assigned to the preceding witness.

### On the Eucharistic sacrifice, columns 0541D–0543A

- Vict. 9 and 13 read *rationabilibus catholicis* (“for reasonable Catholic [grounds]”) for *rationibus catholicis* (“for Catholic reasons”). The manuscripts read *forsitan quia* (“perhaps because”) for *forsitan non quia* (“perhaps not because”).
- The manuscripts read *vel quoniam* (“or because”) for *sed quoniam* (“but because”); the Gothic and Cologne editions omit the whole clause *sed quoniam coena in qua hoc factum est, hoc exigebat* (“but because the supper at which this was done required it”).
- Vict. 20 reads *propter hoc ergo solum videtur* (“therefore for this reason alone he appears”); Corb. reads *propter quod ergo et solum videtur* (“therefore because of which he also alone appears”); the note gives *propter hoc ergo videtur solum* (“therefore for this reason he appears alone”) as the unassigned contrast.
- Vict. 9 and 13, Corb., and the Gothic and Cologne editions read *at si audent* (“but if they dare”) for *et si audent* (“and if they dare”). Vict. 9 reads active *servaret* (“he might observe”) for passive *servaretur* (“it might be observed”).
- Vict. 20 reads *novitatem fecisse in fermento* (“made the newness in leaven”); Vict. 9 and 19 and Corb. read *voluntatem infecisse fermento* (“infected the will with leaven”); the note gives *novitatem infecisse fermento* (“infected the newness with leaven”) as the unassigned contrast.

### Chapter III, columns 0543B–0544A

- Cister. and Corb. read *quod aiunt* (“what they say”) for *quod autem aiunt* (“but what they say”). The manuscripts read *quia non* (“because we do not”) for *si non* (“if we do not”).
- The manuscripts read *ut per azymi* (“so that through the unleavened [bread]”); Cister. reads *non ut per azymi* (“not so that through the unleavened [bread]”); the note gives *ideo per azymi* (“therefore through the unleavened [bread]”) as the unassigned contrast.
- The manuscripts read *Dominum Jesum fuisse significemus* (“we may signify that the Lord Jesus had been [such]”); Corb. reads *Dominum Jesum futurum significemus* (“we may signify that the Lord Jesus would be [such]”); the note gives *Dominum significemus* (“we may signify the Lord”) as the unassigned contrast.
- The manuscripts read *vel ut ipsum* (“or so that that very [bread]”) for *sed ut ipsum* (“but so that that very [bread]”). Vict. 9 and 13 read *sanctificemus* (“we may sanctify”); Corb. reads *sacrificemus* (“we may sacrifice”); the note gives *significemus* (“we may signify”) as the unassigned contrast.
- The Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions read *si noluisset ut* (“if he had not wished that”) for unassigned *si voluisset ut* (“if he had wished that”). The manuscripts and those three editions read *quibus in* (“to whom in”) for *quibus hoc in* (“to whom this in”). The three editions read *hoc de azymo faceremus* (“we should do this with unleavened bread”) for *hoc non de azymo faceremus* (“we should not do this with unleavened bread”).
- Vict. 9 and 13 and Corb. read *praemonuisset in* (“he would have forewarned in”) for *praemonuisset nos in* (“he would have forewarned us in”). The Venetian edition reads *vel proferre* (“even to utter”) for *hoc proferre* (“to utter this”). Vict. 9 and 13 read *unde ego* (“from which I [do it]”) for *unde ergo?* (“from which, therefore?”).
- Vict. 13 has the scribal error *quem pacem* (“which peace”); the note contrasts *quomodo panem* (“in what way [the] bread”) at the place where the narrative has *quem panem* (“which bread”). The Venetian edition reads *Dominici corporis veritatem* (“the truth of the Lord’s body”) for *Dominici corporis varietatem* (“the variety of the Lord’s body”).
- Vict. 9 and 13 and the Gothic and Cologne editions read *quem vetus* (“which the old [Law]”) for *quem et vetus* (“which also the old [Law]”). Vict. 13 reads *intelligi valet* (“can be understood”) for *intelligimus* (“we understand”), and *cur nos* (“why us”) for *neque cur nos* (“nor why us”).

### Chapter IV, columns 0544B–0545D

- The Venetian edition omits *illi* (“they”) from *nec illi similiter* (“nor can they likewise”). It reads *cum execratur* (“when it curses”) for *quae execratur* (“which curses”). Cister. reads *nova dum* (“the new [Scripture], when”) for *nova lex dum* (“the new Law, when”). Vict. 13 reads *si figuram* (“if [we retain] the figure”) for *sed figuram* (“but [we retain] the figure”).
- The Venetian edition reads *non baptizent in aqua* (“let them not baptize in water”) for *quare baptizant in aqua?* (“why do they baptize in water?”). Vict. 13 and the Gothic and Cologne editions read *negari nequit* (“cannot be denied”) for *negare nequeunt* (“they cannot deny”). Vict. 20 and Cister. omit *vitent quoque aquam* (“let them also avoid water”) before *ne* (“lest”).
- Cister. reads *figurate baptizamus* (“we baptize figuratively”); the Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions read *figurate baptizatur* (“one is baptized figuratively”); the note gives *figuratur baptismus* (“baptism is figured”) as the unassigned contrast. The Venetian edition reads *nostrum figuratum est* (“ours was figured”) for *nostrum figurabatur* (“ours was being figured”).
- Vict. 9 and 13, Corb., and the Gothic and Cologne editions read *qui … detestantur* (“those who … detest”) for *quae … detestatur* (“which … detests”). Cister. reads *non quia corpus* (“not because [we eat] the body”) for unassigned *non qui corpus* (“not [those] who [eat] the body”).

### Chapters V–VII, columns 0545D–0548B

- The Venetian edition reads *sive itaque in* (“whether therefore in”); Vict. 9 and 13, Corb., and the Gothic and Cologne editions read *sive enim in Pascha sacrificari* (“whether indeed [it is] sacrificed at Passover”); the note gives *Pascha celebrari* (“Passover is celebrated”) as the unassigned contrast. The manuscripts read *nesciebam esse peccatum nisi* (“I did not know it to be sin unless”) for *nesciebam nisi* (“I did not know unless”).
- The manuscripts read *secundum magnam* (“according to [his] great [mercy]”) for *secundum suam* (“according to his [mercy]”), and omit *et renovationi* (“and renewal”). Corb. reads *ideo cum* (“therefore, when”); Vict. 20 reads *item cum* (“likewise, when”); the note gives *jam cum* (“now, when”) as the unassigned contrast.
- The manuscripts read *Testamenti, addidit: non littera sed spiritu; littera enim* (“of the Testament, he added: not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter”) for *Testamenti non littera sed Spiritu, ait: littera enim* (“of the Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit, he says: for the letter”). The quotation preserves *idipsum velamen* (“that very veil”) at printed marker **137**.
- Cister. reads *juxta quam* (“according to which [mercy]”); the editor marks *juxta quod* (“according to that which”) as the more correct construction.
- In the Amos discussion, the manuscripts read *cum impiae actioni associaverit* (“when he associated it with an impious action”); the Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions read *cum hoc impiae actioni associaverit* (“when he associated this with an impious action”); the note gives *cum hoc impie auctoritas sociaverit* (“when the authority impiously associated this”) as the unassigned contrast. The manuscripts read indicative *defendunt* (“they defend”) for subjunctive *defendant* (“let them defend”).
- In the marriage discussion, the manuscripts and the Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions read passive *servari* (“to be observed”) for active *servare* (“to observe”). The manuscripts read *ratione absque* (“without reason”) for the longer *ratione fit contra rationem, absque* (“is done contrary to reason, without”). The manuscripts read *reprehendendum judicatur* (“is judged worthy of censure”); the Venetian edition reads *repudiandum judicatur* (“is judged worthy of rejection”); the note gives *refutandum judicatur* (“is judged worthy of refutation”) as the unassigned contrast.

### Walerannus’s letter, columns 0547C–0552B

- Walerannus’s letter was collated with Vict. Ef. 20. The manuscripts read *edoctos* (“learned persons”) for the corrupt form *edocumatos*. They read present *attingit* (“touches”) for perfect *attigit* (“has touched”).
- In Chapter III the manuscripts read *E. Idem inolevit* (“E. The same became established”) for *idem est, nostra inolevit* (“he is the same; our custom became established”). The initial *E.* is transmitted but unexplained.
- In Chapter IV the manuscripts read *vitae via* (“the way of life”) for *vita, via* (“life, way”). The main sentence says that “we may be conformed to him in all things, configured to the body of his glory,” preserving *ut ei per omnia conformemur configurati corpori claritatis suae*.
- The manuscripts read *dico ut omnibus* (“I say, so that for all”) for *divo, omnibus* (“in the open air, for all”). In Chapter V the manuscripts read *gratia Deo* (“grace to God”) for *gratias Deo* (“thanks to God”).
- The sentence beginning *Neque iniquitas, neque peccatum meum* is syntactically damaged in the supplied source. It is rendered conservatively in the body as a transmitted fragment rather than expanded into an unsupported assertion.

### Anselm’s reply, columns 0551B–0553C

- Cister. titles the reply *Epistola de Sacramentis Ecclesiae* (“Letter on the Sacraments of the Church”). The Venetian edition reads *Waleranno* (“Walerannus,” dative) for *Waleramo* (a variant spelling of the name).
- The manuscripts read *vestrae erga me* (“your [kindness] toward me”); the note gives the fuller unassigned reading *vestrae benignitati, quoniam hoc facit abundantia vestrae erga me* (“to your kindness, because the abundance of your [good will] toward me causes this”).
- Vict. 13 and the Gothic and Cologne editions read passive *quaeritur* (“is asked”) for active *quaerit* (“asks”). Vict. 13 reads *in summa* (“in sum”) for *in substantia* (“in the substance”), and omits only *in* (“in”) from *neque in virtute* (“nor in [its] power”).
- The Venetian edition reads *quia si unitas* (“because if unity”) for *quia ubi unitas* (“because where unity”). Vict. 13 and the Gothic and Cologne editions read *in rei veritate et unitate* (“in the truth and unity of the matter”) for *in rei veritate et virtute* (“in the truth and power of the matter”).
- The Venetian edition reads *et decentia* (“and decorum”) for *et differentia* (“and difference”). Vict. 13, Cister., and the Gothic and Cologne editions read *quia enim unus* (“for because one”); the Venetian edition reads *quod enim unus* (“for what one”); the note gives *quod unus* (“what one”) as the unassigned contrast.

Indeed, some, when sacrificing the body and blood of the Lord, make individual crosses for the individual elements from the beginning of the canon; others make individual crosses only for the individual elements where bread or body is named separately [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “bread and body”; the Cologne and Venetian editions read “bread or body”], and likewise for the chalice or blood. But where the offering or sacrifice is named, they make one cross for both, because, just as there is one Christ who offered himself for us, so there is one offering and one sacrifice in the bread and wine that we offer. I do not see that these people disagree here with Christ any more than all those disagree who do not sacrifice the chalice after the Supper, as Christ did, nor always in the evening, as Christ did [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscripts of Victor 13 and the Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions omit “nor always in the evening, as Christ did”], and who call both together by one name, “offering” or “sacrifice,” which Christ did not do.

From this we can gather that, provided the truth of the matter is preserved [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 13 reads “the truth of God is preserved”], we may differ from one another in such an action without blame, since we differ from the author of the sacrifice himself without offense. When, however, we say, “These gifts, these offerings, these holy sacrifices,” whether individual crosses are assigned separately to the bread and wine, or one cross sanctifies both together, I do not see any blameworthy disagreement in this diversity [Col. 0553C], unless perhaps because it is more fitting for both to be marked with one cross, just as they are sanctified by one word of blessing [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 13 reads “sanctification”]. For when we bless several people or different things together, we do not give each one an individual cross, but believe that one cross is sufficient for all [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 13 reads “we bless together”].

## CHAPTER III. On covering the chalice during the sacrifice

As for the fact that some cover the chalice from the beginning—some with a corporal [Note: [Col. 0553C] The Venetian edition reads “some with a corporal”], others with a folded cloth—for protection against uncleanness [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 13 reads “cleanliness”], and do not leave the chalice uncovered, as Christ was crucified naked, so that, as they signify [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 20 reads “so that they signify”; the manuscripts of Cistercium and Victor 13 and the Gothic edition read “so that they thus signify”], he might show himself revealed to the world: I do not understand that they ought to be blamed on account of Christ’s nakedness, which they do not signify in the sacrifice, any more than because they do not demonstrate in that same sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0553C] The Venetian edition reads “in the sacrifice”] that he was crucified [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “that he is not crucified”] outside the city, outside a house, and beneath the open sky. Yet these matters are not without considerable reason.

For Christ, who suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps (I Peter II, 21), also gave us in these things an example of enduring, for the sake of righteousness, incomparable contempt and poverty. He was held in such contempt and judged so accursed that he was not considered worthy to die within any human dwelling; nor among human beings except accursed ones; nor beneath any roof, but under the sky, from beneath which he could not be expelled [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscripts and the Gothic and Cologne editions read “from which”], so that, according to the Prophet, he might be regarded as “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.”

He was so poor that, when he came into the world, he was born not in his own house but in another’s; and when born, because there was no room, he was placed in a manger for beasts [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 13 omits “for beasts”]. While living in the world [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscripts read “when he came into the world”], he had nowhere to lay his head (Psalm XXI, 7; Luke IX, 58); when dying, he had nothing with which to cover his nakedness; when dead, nothing in which to be wrapped; and no tomb or place [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 13 omits “or place”] where his body might be laid [Note: [Col. 0553C] The Gothic and Cologne editions read “his dead body”].

All these things are rather to be imitated in our manner of life through action, when reason requires it, than for Christ’s nakedness to be signified through the nakedness of the sacrifice. Nor can I conjecture why one should be more concerned that the sacrifice not be covered with a cloth [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscripts of Victor 13 and Cistercium read “that it should not be covered”] because Christ suffered naked, than that it should not take place beneath a roof or within a city [Note: [Col. 0553C] The Venetian edition omits “because Christ suffered naked, than that it should not take place beneath a roof or within a city.” The Gothic and Cologne editions read: “since Christ suffered naked, not beneath a roof or within a city, but under the open sky. But if…”], since Christ suffered under the open sky outside the city.

If custom does not permit the sacrifice to take place outside a roof because of disturbances in the weather, for a similar reason [Note: [Col. 0553C] The Gothic and Cologne editions read “for a similar reason”] it seems that the chalice should not be uncovered during the sacrifice, because of certain inconveniences that may occur. I therefore think it safer and more conscientious that the chalice be covered, lest a fly or something improper fall into it [Note: [Col. 0553C] The Gothic, Cologne, and Venetian editions read “should fall into it”], as we know has often happened; for, when uncovered, it is exposed to accidental impurities [Note: [Col. 0553C] The manuscript of Victor 13 reads “than that it should be uncovered. This…”].

This is my response according to my own understanding to your wisdom, rejecting no one’s better reasoning. Concerning those who sacrifice with leavened bread, I formerly sent you a certain letter [Note: [Col. 0553C] The Cistercian manuscript adds: “The letter of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, on the Sacraments of the Church ends.”].

[Col. 0555]

# SAINT ANSELM ON PRIESTS WHO KEEP CONCUBINES, OR THE OFFENSE OF PRIESTS

[Note: [Col. 0555C] “Offense” has been collated with the manuscripts of Bec E. 10 and Saint-Evroult.]

Concerning priests who, by an openly lustful way of life, show themselves rejected by God, one must altogether uphold what [Note: [Col. 0555C] Others read “that”] apostolic prudence established with ecclesiastical and righteous [Note: [Col. 0555C] Others read “with judgment and”] severity. Certainly, it is wholly inappropriate to stand there reverently [Note: [Col. 0555C] Others read “to stand”] where men stink with persistent, open, and shameless lust, despising the prohibition of God and the saints while ministering at the sacred altars—or rather, not ministering, but, so far as depends on them, polluting them. This does not mean that anyone should regard the things they handle as contemptible, but that the handlers themselves should be execrated. Thus, those who do not reverence the presence of God and the angels may at least, repelled by human abhorrence, not dare to contaminate the sacred rites.

Concerning those who have fallen while holding sacred orders, and who, of their own free will, secretly confess to those to whom they ought to confess, it must by no means be asserted that they can no longer use those same orders at all, if, by the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and a broken, humbled heart, they appease God and diligently [Note: [Col. 0555C] Others read “with diligence”] turn themselves toward progress in virtue. For neither is anyone’s office rejected before God because of a fault that God himself forgives; nor is the dignity of the sacred order discolored before human beings because of a person whose sin they themselves do not know.

For these two reasons, carnal falling prevents access and return to the sacred order [Note: [Col. 0555C] Others read “is prevented”]. But since it is almost always hidden whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered (Psalm XXXI, 1), and whose have not, it is always safer for someone conscious of guilt to abstain, through a humility pleasing to God, from those functions that require a person acceptable to God, than to presume upon them through culpable security. The former he can always do without God’s disapproval; the latter he ought not do unless God approves.

But whoever wishes to grant assent to this opinion—which permits the exercise of sacred-order office after a fall—only when it is supported by the authority of Scripture should read the letter of blessed Pope Calixtus addressed to the bishops of Gaul, and that of blessed Pope Gregory to Secundinus the recluse. There they confirm this opinion with such firm and almost identical arguments and authorities that it needs no proof from others.

But since the same blessed Gregory and other holy Fathers elsewhere seem deliberately to prohibit this very thing, it is to be understood that they prohibited it in the case of open offenses, but permitted it in the case of hidden offenses after worthy repentance. For a crime that is not imputed by God and is not considered to exist by human beings neither rejects nor discolors a person, although in such a matter it is safer for each person to fear more for himself before God than to trust himself.

I do not think that someone who voluntarily and secretly reveals a hidden crime through humble confession ought to be forced against his will to desist, lest the beneficial path of confession be closed to many who would prefer to hide themselves completely unto death rather than, on this account, be brought into certainty or suspicion of some crime [Note: [Col. 0555C] Others read “would prefer”]. Nor is sin imputed to the person to whom he confesses if he does not compel the penitent, without his consent, to cease from the office of his order; rather, he seems guilty of a great crime if he does compel him. For in this way he forces both the person confessing to repent of his confession [Note: [Col. 0555C] Others read “by confessing”] and many who have not yet confessed to dread confession.

Thus far the manuscript of Saint-Evroult.

Augustine: The Lord declared that, in one assembly of people receiving the same sacraments, the uncleanness of some cannot harm the clean; but the one who is a priest solely by the sacrament, as Caiaphas was, the persecutor of the one and true High Priest—

[Col. 0557]

# SAINT ANSELM ON THE MARRIAGES OF BLOOD RELATIVES

Whether marriages between blood relatives are forbidden, so that they cannot be remitted, and why they have been condemned.

[Col. 0557A] 141

## ANSELM OF CANTERBURY TO HIS BELOVED BROTHER: THE SPIRIT OF WISDOM AND UNDERSTANDING

### CHAPTER I. The reason for prohibiting marriages between blood relatives

I greatly rejoice in your studies, dearest brother, by which you exercise me, stirring me from the sleep of indolence while I lie dull and dream of no such matters, and challenging me with a question so that I may awaken. You ask me, a man whom you suppose to have read much, to write back to you carefully and clearly whether I remember having read anywhere in the decrees or treatises of the holy Fathers a prohibition against marriages between blood relatives; for what reason this prohibition has acquired such force in the Church of God that no indulgence at all can be granted for such a transgression unless the separation of the marriage itself precedes it; or why such a marriage is at least reckoned a sin.

And, as I see, you are not asking merely for an authority that recognizes the matter by a bare exercise of power, so to speak, but rather for a reason that teaches it rationally. I might say that the simple and pure reason is to obey the authority of those to whom it was said: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaks in you” (Matthew X, 20); and to follow the custom of the Church, for to wish to tear down its customs is a form of heresy. But so that you may know that I want to comply with your wishes in everything, even if perhaps I cannot, I shall nevertheless try not to fail you in this matter either.

### CHAPTER II. Why certain Jewish marriages among relatives were permitted

The canons are full of this command—that marriages are not to be contracted between blood relatives, or, if contracted, are to be dissolved—and there are many decrees of the Fathers. But the reason for the command that you demand, I confess, I do not remember ever having read. Nevertheless, this is how I habitually think about the matter when considering the sacred Scriptures.

Among that ancient people, marriages could not be contracted from tribe to tribe. When I asked myself why, I recalled the daughters of Zelophehad consulting Moses about marriage, and, through Moses, the Lord’s command that marriages not be contracted from tribe to tribe, in order to prevent the diminution of their inheritances (Numbers XXXVI). For that carnal people did not know how to possess its own heart; like an earthly creature clinging to the earth with its whole breast, it thought only of an earthly inheritance. Each tribe preferred to restrain itself within its own narrow limits by giving and receiving marriages among its members rather than, by giving marriages outside, dividing its inheritance outside as well. For such was their inheritance, and such is every earthly inheritance, that when divided it becomes smaller and does not come entirely to those who possess it.

Therefore, just as the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the granting of a bill of divorce (Matthew XIX), the response was suited to the carnality of their hearts.

### CHAPTER III. The reason for the contrary ordinance under the law of grace

Christian piety is not so. Since our inheritance is that of which it is said, “God is love” (I John IV, 8), just as they use a law suited to their inheritance, so we ought to claim a law suited to ours. For the more widely love is divided and spread, the more abundantly it remains with and increases in the one who distributes it.

Christian religion therefore decreed that, since the boundaries of blood relationship extend on every side up to the sixth degree according to the decrees of the holy Fathers and the canons, the affection due to birth should suffice for preserving love; even among barbarians, violating it is considered a sin. But where that affection fails, then, in order to bind love together, the marital bond should be added so that the boundaries of our inheritance—which is love itself—may be extended.

It therefore seems most just that, just as among them the transgressor of the law established for preserving their earthly inheritance was punished with a penalty, so among us the violator of the law established for expanding our heavenly bread and divine inheritance should not go unpunished.

[Col. 0558C]

### CHAPTER IV. Another reason for the same ordinance, common to most Jewish marriages among relatives that were likewise forbidden

There is still another consideration. Those who, like us, were forbidden to contract marriages outside their tribe were by the same law forbidden to approach their nearest blood relatives. For the law says: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relative” (Leviticus XVIII, 6); and it adds the authority of the one issuing the command: “I am the Lord” (ibid.). Then, as though a reason for the command were being demanded, it adds: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother, for it is the nakedness of your father or your mother” (ibid. V, 7). It then lists in order those nearest blood relatives whom one must not approach and whose nakedness must not be uncovered—brothers and sisters, and the others described there.

This reason can be common to us and to them, just as the command is common to us and to them.

### CHAPTER V. What the forbidden nakedness is; an explanation for understanding the proposed reason

Let us therefore ask what this nakedness is, the revelation of which makes the transgressor of the law deserving of death. It is shameful when one part does not fit another. But in the human body, before the first human being’s transgression, there was nothing shameful, nothing discordant. While that harmony, well and decorously arranged by the hand of the good Creator, still endured, each part fit the other, and the soul was wholly subject to God, while the body was wholly subject to its soul.

After the transgression of the commandment had made the soul disobedient to God, the lower body ceased to obey its superior, God’s rebellious creature. At once the transgressors’ eyes were opened. “And the eyes of them both were opened,” it says (Genesis III, 7)—namely, to desire one another. Although previously they had been naked and were not ashamed, as soon as they perceived that the parts of their bodies had become shameful, they hastened to cover them and made themselves loincloths.

It is easy to observe the same thing now in boys or infants: so long as they do not feel this desire, they have no shameful parts, because they do not know to be ashamed of any part of their bodies. But when they begin to experience that desire, they can no longer bear to have those parts uncovered.

Thus, once that most beautiful harmony had been dissolved in the first human beings, a considerable shame came into existence—an original punishment that would pass from them to their descendants along with original sin. From this, in our body, the body of sin, those members that serve this desire are called “shameful parts,” “nakedness,” or “dishonor,” naturally demanding the concealment and hiding of outward shame—that is, of desire.

This shame of desire is revealed when, as an indication of itself, it makes its members perform their function. It strives toward action while every power of the rational soul has been so dulled, confused, and cast down, and subjected to the flesh’s most shameful lust, that at that moment it may rightly hear: “Adam, where are you?” (ibid. 9)—that is, “You who wished to be like God, do you not see where you have come?”

And what is more shameful than this shame? What is more dishonorable than this dishonor? The Apostle points to it when he says: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against his own body” (I Corinthians VI, 18). That is, all sins injure the soul but do not defile the body; the fornicator, however, not only offends God and contaminates the soul, but also fouls and dishonors the entire beauty of the body itself.

For just as a mark of eternal disgrace is branded upon a thief caught in the act with iron or fire, so this is, in our nature, wholly corrupted by the fault of transgression, a mark of punishment for its sin through the one in whom the whole of our nature then existed and outside whom it did not exist. This shame would always have to be covered by the veil of modesty in everyone, unless it had become necessary for the propagation of the human race as a punishment for the first sin.

[Col. 0560A]

### CHAPTER VI. The proposed reason is concluded, and the marriages forbidden between certain blood relatives are explained by the reverence they owe one another

Yet no love connected with that propagation permits it to be revealed among those whom the law calls nearest in blood. By the right and instinct of nature itself, they owe one another such reverent affection that there can be no just reason for their bodies to be subjected to such insults toward one another, nor can anything honorable be brought forward that could conceal this dishonor.

I do not deny that holy marriages and an undefiled marriage bed, contracted lawfully and in the fear of God, cover themselves with such honor through the pious love of marriage—by which those who marry become one spirit, from which they become one flesh—and through holy love and the desire to beget offspring, and in a sense absorb that punitive shame of human generation, that, according to the Apostle (I Corinthians VII), those who marry are as though they did not marry.

Hence, in its catalogue of nakednesses that must not be revealed, the law also places the nakedness of one’s spouse among those not to be revealed. “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your wife,” it says (Leviticus XVIII, 17).

### CHAPTER VII. Why this prohibition is extended among Christians to more distant degrees than among the Jews

As has already been said, those who were forbidden to marry outside their tribe were by the same law not permitted to approach their nearest blood relatives. But among them that natural law of affection scarcely passed beyond the third degree of consanguinity. Among us, however, to whom the time of correction has come, for whom the Lord corrected the world—that is, brought it to perfection—which “shall not be moved” (Psalm XCV, 10), piety has grown, decency has overflowed, and, to signify the perfection of the Gospel, that number three has been doubled and extended into six, which is a perfect number and is composed of its own parts, just as the truth of the Gospel stands by itself and needs nothing to support it.

It is true that among the ancients even men worthy of praise, when certain honorable circumstances intervened, sometimes presumed to violate the first and second degrees. Before the law, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, recently separated from the other nations in order to avoid mingling with them, married their nearest blood relatives. Under the law, Caleb gave his daughter in marriage to his younger brother Othniel, after the city of Debir had been conquered, as a reward for victory (Joshua XV). Tamar too, when she was being assaulted by her brother, said: “No, brother; rather ask the king for me. He will not refuse me to you” (II Samuel XIII, 12–13). And certainly the king who was said to be about to give his sister in marriage to her brother was the father of both.

Although they presumed to do these things when certain circumstances intervened, Christian piety does not wish to judge honorable anything that acts against the honor of nature. This, then, is what seems to me to be the answer to your question. If it pleases you, so much the better; if it displeases you, I shall easily obtain pardon from you.

[Col. 0561]

# SAINT ANSELM’S DIALOGUE ON THE GRAMMARIAN

[Col. 0561A]

### CHAPTER I. 143

[Note: [Col. 0561C] The book *On the Grammarian* has been collated with the manuscripts of Bec, Gemmeticum, and the two Victorine manuscripts noted above, RR 3 and EE 13. The Victorine manuscript 2 explains how the Grammarian is substance and quality.]

Whether the grammarian is a substance or a quality: arguments are proposed on both sides.

**DISCIPLE.** I ask you to make me certain about the grammarian: whether he is a substance or a quality [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscript of Victor reads “a substance or a quality”], so that, once this is known, I may understand what I ought to think about the other things that are likewise called denominatively.

**MASTER.** First tell me why you doubt.

**DISCIPLE.** Because it seems that both alternatives can be proved by necessary arguments: both that he is and that he is not.

**MASTER.** Then prove it.

**DISCIPLE.** So do not hasten to contradict whatever I say, but allow me to bring my argument to its conclusion [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscript of Gemmeticum reads “my speech to its conclusion”; the manuscript of Victor 3 reads “my speech”]; then either approve it or correct it [Note: [Col. 0561C] Some manuscripts read “finally either”].

**MASTER.** As you wish.

**DISCIPLE.** To prove that the grammarian is a substance, it is enough that every grammarian is a human being and every human being is a substance. For whatever the grammarian has such that substance follows him, he has only because he is a human being [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscript of Victor 3 reads “with substance”]. Once, therefore, it is granted that he is a human being, whatever follows a human being follows the grammarian.

But that the grammarian is a quality is openly acknowledged by the philosophers who have treated this subject, and it would be presumptuous [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscripts read “imprudent”] to reject their authority in these matters. Moreover, since it is necessary that the grammarian be either a substance or a quality, so that, if he is one of these, he is not the other, and if he is not one, he must necessarily be the other [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscript of Victor 13 reads: “so that if one of these is, the other is not, and if one is not, the other must necessarily be”], whatever serves to establish one side destroys the other, and whatever weakens one strengthens the other [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscripts read: “Whatever establishes one side destroys the other, and whatever weakens one strengthens the other”; another manuscript reads only, “and whatever weakens one strengthens the other”]. Since, then, one of these is true and the other false, I ask you, by exposing the falsehood, to reveal the truth to me.

[Col. 0561C]

### CHAPTER II. The proposed arguments are refuted

**MASTER.** The arguments you have offered on both sides are necessary, except for your claim that if one is, the other cannot be. Therefore, you should not demand that I show one side to be false, which no one can do; rather, if I can, I shall explain how they do not contradict one another. But I would prefer first to hear from you what you think can be objected to these proofs of yours [Note: [Col. 0561C] One manuscript reads: “which no one can do. But I would prefer…”].

**DISCIPLE.** What you now demand from me is precisely what I was eagerly awaiting from you. But since you assert that these same proofs are irrefutable, it is my task to disclose what I doubt and what troubles me [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscripts read “what I doubt, to disclose what troubles me”]; yours, however, is to show the strength and compatibility of both sides.

**MASTER.** Then say what you think, and I shall try to do what you request.

**DISCIPLE.** I think that the proposition which says that the grammarian is a human being can be refuted in this way: no grammarian can be understood without grammar, whereas every human being can be understood without grammar. Again, every grammarian admits of more and less, whereas no human being admits of more and less. From these two constructions of two propositions a single conclusion is formed: no grammarian is a human being.

### CHAPTER III. The proposed arguments are strengthened against the objector

**MASTER.** That does not follow.

**DISCIPLE.** Why?

**MASTER.** Does the name “animal” seem to you to signify anything other than a substance? [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscripts of Bec and Gemmeticum read “anything else”].

**DISCIPLE.** Absolutely not. An animal is nothing other than an animate, sentient substance, and an animate, sentient substance is nothing other than an animal.

**MASTER.** So it is. But tell me, please [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscripts read “tell me also”], whether everything that is nothing other than an animate, sentient substance can be understood apart from rationality and need not necessarily be rational.

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny it.

**MASTER.** Every animal, then, can be understood apart from rationality, and no animal is necessarily rational.

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny that this follows from what has been granted, although I am very much afraid of what I suspect you are aiming at.

**MASTER.** But no human being can be understood apart from rationality, and every human being must necessarily be rational [Note: [Col. 0561C] The manuscripts read “either no human being … or every human being …”].

**DISCIPLE.** I am trapped on both sides [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “trapped on every side”]. For if I grant it, you conclude that no human being is an animal; if I refuse, you will say that I not only can be understood but truly exist without rationality.

**MASTER.** Do not be afraid; what you think does not follow.

**DISCIPLE.** If matters are as you promise, I willingly grant whatever you have proposed; otherwise, unwillingly.

**MASTER.** Then you yourself should arrange the last four propositions I made into two syllogisms.

**DISCIPLE.** They can certainly be arranged in this order:

Every animal can be understood apart from rationality, but no human being can be understood apart from rationality.

Again: no animal is necessarily rational, but every human being is necessarily rational.

From each of these arrangements of two propositions, the following conclusion seems to arise: therefore no human being is an animal—a statement nothing could be more false than, although I see no defect in the preceding propositions. For the two propositions whose subject term is “human being” are so self-evident that it would be foolish to prove them [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “which have only ‘human being’ as their subject”]. The two propositions that subject “animal,” on the other hand, seem so well proved that it would be shameless to deny them [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “seem to prove it, so that it would be shameless…”].

But I see that the connection of these two syllogisms is entirely like that of the two I presented shortly before. Therefore, I suspect that you introduced these only so that, when I plainly saw their conclusion to be false, I would reach the same judgment about the similar syllogisms I had constructed.

**MASTER.** That is so.

**DISCIPLE.** Then show where the deception is so great, both here and there, that although the propositions appear to be true and connected according to the nature of syllogisms, nevertheless the truth supports none of their conclusions [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscript reads “their conclusion”].

### CHAPTER IV. The flaw in the syllogisms proposed in Chapter II

**MASTER.** I shall do this with your syllogisms; if you wish, examine mine for yourself.

**DISCIPLE.** Let it be done according to your judgment.

**MASTER.** Repeat and connect the syllogisms you constructed.

**DISCIPLE.** Every human being can be understood without grammar.

**MASTER.** What do you mean by saying that a human being can be understood without grammar?

**DISCIPLE.** A human being.

**MASTER.** Then say in the proposition itself what you understand.

**DISCIPLE.** Every human being can be understood as a human being without grammar.

**MASTER.** I grant it. Proceed.

**DISCIPLE.** No grammarian can be understood without grammar.

**MASTER.** What cannot be understood without grammar?

**DISCIPLE.** A grammarian.

**MASTER.** Then state what you understand.

**DISCIPLE.** No grammarian can be understood as a grammarian without grammar.

**MASTER.** Join these two propositions as fully as you have just stated them.

**DISCIPLE.** Every human being can be understood as a human being without grammar; no grammarian can be understood as a grammarian without grammar.

**MASTER.** See, then, whether they have a common term, without which they accomplish nothing.

**DISCIPLE.** I see that they do not have a common term, and therefore nothing follows from them.

**MASTER.** Connect the other syllogism.

**DISCIPLE.** There is no longer any need for you to labor to demonstrate it, for I perceive its fallacy. I understood its propositions as though one were saying that no human being is more or less human, and every grammarian is more or less a grammarian. Since these two propositions have no common term, they accomplish nothing.

**MASTER.** Does it seem to you that nothing can be concluded from these connections of yours? [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “So it necessarily seems to you…”]

**DISCIPLE.** That is what I thought; but this question of yours makes me suspect that perhaps some efficacy lies hidden in them. Yet how can they accomplish anything without a common term?

**MASTER.** The common term of a syllogism must be considered not so much in its utterance [Col. 0564B] [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “in its proof”] as in its meaning. For just as nothing is accomplished if the common term is present in sound but not in sense, so it is no impediment [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “nor is it an impediment”] if it is present in understanding but not in utterance. Meaning binds a syllogism, not words.

### CHAPTER V. What can legitimately be obtained from the foregoing syllogisms is shown in one of them

**DISCIPLE.** I expect you to produce the effect of my propositions.

**MASTER.** They do produce something [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “something indeed”], but not what you expect [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscript reads “you expect. Disciple.”].

**DISCIPLE.** Whatever it may be, I accept it without gratitude.

**MASTER.** When someone says, “Every human being can be understood as a human being without grammar,” and, “No grammarian can be understood as a grammarian without grammar,” does this not signify that being a human being does not require grammar, whereas being a grammarian does require grammar?

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing is truer.

**MASTER.** Do these two propositions, which I have just said are signified by the other two, have a common term? [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “which I said are signified in those other two”]

**DISCIPLE.** They do.

**MASTER.** Therefore it follows that being a grammarian is not being a human being—that is, that the two do not have the same definition [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscripts read “the same definitions”].

**DISCIPLE.** Without doubt, I see that this is so and follows.

**MASTER.** Yet it does not therefore follow that a grammarian is not a human being, as you understood it. But if you understand “a grammarian is not a human being” as meaning “a grammarian is not the same as a human being,” that is, “they do not have the same definition,” the conclusion is true.

### CHAPTER VI. The other sophism is examined in light of what has been said
DISCIPLE. I understand what you say.

MASTER. If, then, you rightly understand what I have said, tell me how you would dissolve this syllogism, if someone constructed it as follows: Every grammarian is predicated in the category of quality; no man is predicated in the category of quality; therefore no man is a grammarian.

DISCIPLE. This seems to me equivalent to saying: [Col. 0565A] Every rational thing is predicated in the category of quality; but no man is predicated in the category of quality; therefore no man is rational. Yet no proof can make it true that “rational” is predicated of no man. Similarly, the syllogism you have just stated does not necessarily conclude that “grammatical” is not predicated of man. For its propositions signify this, if we understand them according to the truth, as though one said: Every grammarian is called “grammatical” in the category of quality; no man is called “man” in the category of quality. From these two propositions it by no means follows that no grammarian is predicated of man, because the term that is affirmed of the grammarian is not the same term that is denied of man.

There would also be a common term in those propositions, and they would produce a necessary conclusion, if, while the proposition remained as it had been stated, the assumption were made true in the same form: No man is called “grammatical” in the category of quality; or, while the assumption remained unchanged, one were to state the proposition truly in this form: Every grammarian is called “man” in the category of quality. For from these two combinations it would follow that “grammatical” is predicated of no man.

But if someone wishes to understand the statement “man is not a grammarian” as though it meant “man is not the same as grammarian”—as when I say “brightness is splendor,” or “brightness is not splendor,” that is, “brightness is the same thing as splendor,” or “brightness is not the same thing as splendor”—if, I say, someone understands “man is not a grammarian” in this way, then, if the force of those propositions is properly considered, it follows from them that no man is a grammarian. For, in order to prove that the essence of man is not the essence of grammarian, their signification has a common term.

[Note: “It would also be” in the manuscripts, instead of “there would indeed be.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “If, however, the proposition remains” in the manuscripts, instead of “if the proposition remains.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “As it was proposed” in the manuscripts, instead of “as it has been stated.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “So that it will have been true” in the manuscripts, instead of “so that it would become true.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “Every grammarian is called man” in Ms. Vict. 13, instead of “every grammarian is called man in the category of quality”; another reading is “every man is called grammarian.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “But no man is a grammarian” in the manuscripts, instead of “but no man is called grammarian in the category of quality.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “It has their signification” in the manuscripts, instead of “it has its signification.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “Or brightness is not the same thing” in the manuscripts, instead of “or brightness is not the same thing as splendor.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “But let him follow this sense” in the manuscripts, instead of “according to this sense it follows.”] [Col. 0565D]

145 **CHAPTER VII. The earlier argument proposed in chapter 2 is examined again.**

MASTER. You understood well what I said, but perhaps you did not consider it well.

[Note: “You considered what I said. DISCIPLE.” in the manuscripts, instead of “you considered it well. DISCIPLE.”] [Col. 0565D]

DISCIPLE. How did I understand it well and not consider it well?

MASTER. Tell me: if someone proposed the following: “No man can be understood without rationality; but every stone can be understood without rationality,” what would follow?

DISCIPLE. What else but this: therefore no stone is a man?

MASTER. How do you understand this? Is it because a stone is in no way a man, or because a stone is not the same thing as a man?

DISCIPLE. Because a stone is in no way a man.

[Note: “Therefore no stone is a man” in the manuscripts, instead of “what else but therefore no stone is a man?”] [Col. 0565D]

MASTER. Tell me, then, what difference there is between this syllogism and your syllogism, in which you say that a grammarian cannot be understood without grammar, whereas a man can be so understood, and therefore that a grammarian is not a man.

[Note: “Can be a non-grammarian; can be, and therefore is a grammarian” in the manuscripts, instead of “cannot be understood without grammar.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “For just as” in Ms. Vict. 3, instead of “for just as.”] [Col. 0565D]

DISCIPLE. As far as the force of the argument is concerned, I see no difference between this and that. For just as there it must be understood that a grammarian cannot be understood as a grammarian without grammar, whereas a man can be understood as a man without grammar, so here it must be understood that a man cannot be understood as a man without rationality, whereas a stone can be understood as a stone without rationality; and therefore, since the conclusion of this syllogism is valid—that a stone is in no way a man—you seem to me to have buried the conclusion of my syllogism, which is altogether like this one, beneath your clever explanations.

[Note: “Man without rationality; and therefore” in the manuscripts, instead of “and therefore.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “So now” in the manuscripts, instead of “therefore already.”] [Col. 0565D]

Now I understand what you meant when you said that I understood well but did not consider well: I understood well what you signified to me in speaking, but I did not properly consider the very thing you signified, because I did not know how it was deceiving me.

MASTER. Rather, you did not consider well in this respect: you did not know how it was not deceiving you.

[Note: “In this respect I did not consider well” in the manuscripts, instead of “rather, in this respect I did not consider well.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “How it was deceiving you” in Ms. Vict. 3, instead of “how it was not deceiving you.”] [Col. 0565D]

DISCIPLE. How so?

MASTER. If the syllogism I have just proposed is explained in the same way as I explained yours, so that it is stated thus: “No man can be understood as a man without rationality; but every stone can be understood as a stone without rationality,” it will have no other power of concluding than I said yours had.

[Note: “Every stone can be understood without rationality; it has no other” in the manuscripts, instead of “every stone can be understood as a stone without rationality, it will have no other.”] [Col. 0565D]

But since this syllogism can be understood in another way, in which yours cannot, it has this conclusion: that a stone cannot in any way be a man. For when I say that no man can be understood without rationality, and that every stone can be understood without rationality, this can—and indeed must—be taken as though one said: “No man can in any way be understood without rationality; but every stone can, in every way, be understood without rationality.” Hence it follows: “Therefore no stone is in any way a man.”

In your propositions, however, the truth by no means admits a similar implicit qualification. For it cannot be said that no grammarian can be understood in any way without grammar, or that every man can be understood in every way without grammar. Every man who is a grammarian can be understood as a man without grammar, and no man can be understood as a grammarian without grammar.

[Note: “It cannot be said, no grammarian” in the manuscripts, instead of “for it cannot be said that no grammarian.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “For every man who” in Ms. Vict. 3, instead of “for every man who is.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Note: “No man can” in the manuscripts and in Ms. Vict. 3, instead of “no man can be understood.”] [Col. 0565D]

Therefore they cannot establish that a grammarian is in no way a man.

[Note: “I cannot establish” in the manuscripts, instead of “they cannot establish.”] [Col. 0565D]

[Col. 0567A]

**CHAPTER VIII. Examination of the argument proposed in chapter 5.**

DISCIPLE. I have nothing to say against this position of yours. But since you have secretly admonished me not to be content merely to understand what you say, but to consider the very thing you say, it seems to me that your conclusion should be considered—the conclusion you showed to follow from my syllogism, namely, that being a grammarian is not being a man.

For if this is so, whoever has the essence of a grammarian does not thereby necessarily have the essence of a man. But if “man” follows “grammarian,” the essence of man follows the essence of grammarian. Yet this does not follow that; therefore neither does the former follow the latter. Not every grammarian, then, is a man.

But since all grammarians have one reason for being men, plainly either every grammarian is a man or none is. It is established that not every one is; therefore none is. It thus seems that, by taking away the conclusion from my syllogism—something you did cleverly—you have given it back even more cleverly.

[Note: “Therefore none seems; hence” in the manuscripts, instead of “therefore none. It thus seems.”] [Col. 0567D]

MASTER. Even if I secretly admonished you to consider what you hear, it was not, as appears, without benefit. For although you sophistically prove that no grammarian is a man by means of the claim that being a grammarian is not being a man, it will nevertheless be useful to you when you see the very sophism that deceives you under the cloak of true reasoning stripped bare in its own deceptiveness.

[Note: “That I prove no grammarian” in the manuscripts, instead of “although you prove no grammarian.”] [Col. 0567D]

[Note: “That being of reason” in the manuscripts, instead of “that being of man.”] [Col. 0567D]

DISCIPLE. Show me, then, that it deceives me, and where this proof I have just made concerning the grammarian deceives me.

MASTER. Let us return once more to animal and man, in which we, as it were, feel our way toward the truth so clearly that no sophism can persuade us—although it may compel us—to believe what is false.

[Note: “Thus we feel our way, as it were, toward the truth” in the manuscripts, instead of “in which we, as it were, feel our way toward the truth.”] [Col. 0567D]

Tell me, then, whether the being of each thing consists in its definition.

DISCIPLE. It does.

MASTER. Is the definition of man the definition of animal?

DISCIPLE. Certainly not. For if “rational mortal animal”—which is the definition of man—were the definition of animal, then whatever animal applied to, rational mortal would also apply to; and that is false.

[Note: “Rational, which is false” in the manuscripts, instead of “rational mortal, which is false.”] [Col. 0567D]

MASTER. The being of man, then, is not the being of animal.

DISCIPLE. That follows.

MASTER. Can you therefore prove from this that no man is an animal, by the same reasoning with which you just proved that no grammarian is a man?

[Note: “Animal with the same” in the manuscripts, instead of “no man is an animal by the same reasoning.”] [Col. 0567D]

Therefore, if you see that the falsity is evident in what your reasoning concludes here, do not believe that what it produces there is certain truth.

[Note: “That this reasoning of yours concludes” in the manuscripts, instead of “what this reasoning of yours concludes.”] [Col. 0567D]

[Note: “Certain truth” in the manuscripts, instead of “that it is certain truth.”] [Col. 0567D]

[Note: “What it concludes there” in the manuscripts, instead of “what it plays at there.”] [Col. 0567D]

DISCIPLE. You have now shown that it deceives me; show me also where.

MASTER. Do you not retain what I said shortly before, with your agreement: that “being a grammarian is not being a man” is the same as saying “the definition of grammarian is not the definition of man”—that is, “grammatical and man are not altogether the same”?

[Note: “Not to be the definition of man” in the manuscripts, instead of “the definition of grammarian is not the definition of man.”] [Col. 0567D]

For just as man ought not to be defined with grammar, so a grammarian cannot exist without grammar. Therefore your argument must be understood in this way: If being a grammarian is not simply being a man, then whoever has the essence of a grammarian does not thereby follow to have simply the essence of a man.

Similarly, it must be understood that man simply does not follow grammarian; that is, if he is a grammarian, it does not follow that he is simply a man. Thus nothing else follows except that no grammarian is simply a man.

DISCIPLE. Nothing could be clearer.

[Note: “Simply a man—which is true, but not simply; rather, such a man is a grammarian. DISCIPLE.” in the manuscripts, instead of “Nothing could be clearer. DISCIPLE.”] [Col. 0567D]

**CHAPTER IX. Whether there is a grammarian who is not a man.**

[Col. 0568B]

MASTER. But if it were proved—which, as I think, can easily be done—that being a grammarian is no more being a man than being white is being a man—for a man can exist without being white, and white without a man—then it would truly follow that some grammarian could be a non-man.

[Note: “Which, as I think, can be difficult to do” in the manuscripts, instead of “which, as I think, can easily be done.”] [Col. 0567D]

DISCIPLE. Why, then, are we laboring? If this can be proved, prove it, and let this question be settled.

[Note: “Why, then, are we laboring over whether it can be? If this...” in the manuscripts, instead of “Why, then, are we laboring? If this...”] [Col. 0567D]

MASTER. You ought not to demand this of me here. For in this question we are not debating whether such a thing can exist, but whether there is a grammarian who is not a man—which, as you see, cannot be demonstrated.

[Note: “And let this be firmly established” in the manuscripts, instead of “and let this question be settled.”] [Col. 0567D]

DISCIPLE. I do not yet see it, because I still have something to say against it.

MASTER. Say it.

DISCIPLE. Aristotle shows that a grammarian belongs among things that are in a subject; and no man is in a subject. Therefore no grammarian is a man.

[Note: “Because no grammarian is a man” in the manuscripts, instead of “therefore no grammarian is a man.”] [Col. 0567D]

MASTER. Aristotle did not intend this to follow from his statements. For the same Aristotle says that a certain man, and man, and animal are grammarians.

DISCIPLE. How, then, is this syllogism dissolved?

MASTER. Answer me: when you speak to me about “grammarian,” how am I to understand whether you are speaking of this name or of the things it signifies?

DISCIPLE. Of the things.

MASTER. What things, then, does it signify?

DISCIPLE. Man and grammar.

MASTER. Having heard this name, then, I will understand man or grammar; and, when speaking of “grammarian,” I will speak of man or of grammar.

[Note: “And you will speak of ... I speak” in the manuscripts, instead of “and, when speaking of ‘grammarian,’ I will speak.”] [Col. 0567D]

DISCIPLE. That is necessary.

[Note: “Therefore it is necessary” in the manuscripts, instead of “that is necessary.”] [Col. 0567D]

MASTER. Tell me, then: is man a substance or in a subject?

DISCIPLE. He is not in a subject, but is a substance.

MASTER. Grammar is a quality and is in a subject.

DISCIPLE. Both are true.

MASTER. What wonder is it, then, if someone says that “grammarian” is a substance and is not in a subject, insofar as it concerns man, while “grammarian” is a quality and is in a subject, insofar as it concerns grammar?

[Note: “And grammar is” in the manuscripts, instead of “while grammarian is.”] [Col. 0567D]

[Col. 0569A]

**CHAPTER X. Whether grammarian is a first or a second substance.**

DISCIPLE. I cannot deny it; but I will still say why grammarian is not a substance: because every substance is either first or second, whereas grammarian is neither first nor second.

[Note: “But I will still say, since...” in the manuscripts, instead of “but I will still say why.”] [Col. 0569D]

MASTER. Remember the statements of Aristotle that I mentioned shortly before, in which he says that grammarian is both a first and a second substance, because he testifies that a certain man, and man, and animal are called grammarians. But where do you prove that grammarian is not a first or a second substance?

[Note: “In which he says ‘grammatician’” in the manuscripts, instead of “in which he says that grammarian.”] [Col. 0569D]

DISCIPLE. Because it is in a subject, whereas no substance is; and because it is predicated of many, which is not true of a first substance. Nor is it a genus or species, nor is it predicated in response to “what is it?”—which belongs to a second substance.

[Note: “Because it is in a subject, because” in the manuscripts, instead of “because it is in a subject, whereas.”] [Col. 0569D]

MASTER. None of these points, if you remember what we have already said, removes substance from grammarian. For in one respect grammarian is not in a subject, and it is a genus and a species, and is predicated in response to “what is it?” For it is both man, which is a species, and animal, which is a genus; and these are predicated in response to “what is it?”

[Note: “What we have said, remove” in the manuscripts, instead of “what we have already said, removes”; “because in another respect” in the manuscripts, instead of “because in one respect.”] [Col. 0569D]

It is also an individual, just as man and animal are. For just as there is a certain man and a certain animal, so there is a certain grammarian who is an individual.

[Note: “But it is an individual” in the manuscripts, instead of “it is also an individual.”] [Col. 0569D]

For Socrates is both man and animal, and he is a grammarian.

DISCIPLE. I cannot deny what you say.

**CHAPTER XI. That man is not grammar.**

MASTER. If you have no other means by which you can prove that grammarian is not man, now prove that it is not grammar.

DISCIPLE. I can do this more easily with my finger than with an argument. For you broke all my arguments there when you disclosed that “grammarian” signifies different things, and that one must speak and understand “grammarian” according to those different things. Although I cannot deny this, it nevertheless does not satisfy my mind so that it can rest as though it had found what it was seeking: for you seem to me not so much to care about teaching me as merely about blocking my arguments. But just as it was my task to explain what drives me into ambiguity from both sides, so it was yours either to destroy one side or to show how the two sides do not contradict one another.

[Note: “I cannot deny it fully” in the manuscripts, instead of “although I cannot deny this.”] [Col. 0569D]

[Note: “You seem not to deal with me” in the manuscripts, instead of “you seem to me not so much to care about teaching me.”] [Col. 0569D]

MASTER. Why does it not seem sufficiently demonstrated to you that “grammarian” is a substance and “grammarian” is a quality are in no way contradictory, since one must speak and understand “grammarian” sometimes according to man and sometimes according to grammar?

[Note: “And that grammar is” in the manuscripts, instead of “and ‘grammatian’ is.”] [Col. 0569D]

DISCIPLE. Because no one who understands the name “grammarian” is unaware that “grammarian” signifies man and grammar. Yet if, relying on this confidence, I were to say in public, “A grammarian is a useful science,” or “This man knows a grammarian well,” not only would grammarians become angry, but even uneducated people would laugh. I will therefore never believe, without some other explanation, that writers on dialectic have so often and so carefully written in their books what they would be ashamed to say in conversation.

[Note: “Grammar is a science, or, properly speaking, this man knows grammar” in the manuscripts, instead of “grammatician is a useful science, or this man knows grammarian.”] [Col. 0569D]

For very often, when they wish to show a quality or an accident, they add “grammarian” and similar examples, although common usage among all speakers bears witness that “grammarian” is more properly a substance than a quality or accident.

[Note: “Although ‘grammarian’ is more ... bears witness” in the manuscripts, with the remainder omitted.] [Col. 0569D]

And when they wish to teach something about substance, they never put forward “grammarian” or anything of this kind.

[Note: “Or anything else of this kind” in the manuscripts, instead of “or anything of this kind.”] [Col. 0569D]

[Note: “Why is higher man not a quality?” in the manuscripts, instead of “why is man not similarly a quality?”] [Col. 0569D]

[Note: “Where anything else has been written” in the manuscripts, instead of “where anything has been written.”] [Col. 0569D]

[Note: “Has been proved as an example” in the manuscripts, instead of “is brought forward as an example.”] [Col. 0569D]

**CHAPTER XII. The various ways in which man and grammarian signify their significates.**

MASTER. You reject the explanation I gave—namely, why grammarian is both substance and quality—because it does not apply to the name “man.” You do this, I think, because you do not consider how differently they signify: the name “man” signifies the things of which man consists, whereas “grammarian” signifies man and grammar.

The name “man,” by itself and as one thing, signifies the things of which the whole man consists. Among these, substance holds the principal place, since it is the cause of the others and possesses them not as though it needed them, but as things that need it. For no difference of substance can be found without which substance cannot exist, and none of its differences can exist without it.

Therefore, although all these things together, as one whole, are called “man” under one signification and by one name, this name is nevertheless principally significant of and appellative for substance. Thus one may correctly say “substance is man” and “man is substance,” yet no one says “rationality is man” or “man is rationality,” but rather “that which has rationality.”

Grammarian, however, does not signify man and grammar as one thing. It signifies grammar by itself and man through something else. Although this name is appellative for man, it is not properly said to be significative of him; and although it is significative of grammar, it is not properly appellative for it.

[Note: “It is called its signified; and although it is signified” in the manuscripts, instead of “it is said to be significative of him; and although it is significative.”] [Col. 0571C]

[Note: “It is not properly” in Ms. Vict. 3, instead of “it is not properly appellative for it.”] [Col. 0571C]

By an appellative name of anything I now mean the name by which the thing itself is called in ordinary usage. For no ordinary usage says “grammar is grammarian” or “grammarian is grammar”; rather, it says “man is a grammarian” and “a grammarian man.”
