**CHAPTER XVI. How grammarian is a quality.**
**DISCIPLE.** It is clear what you are saying; but the mind does not accept without reservation that *grammaticus* is a quality, although it signifies a grammarian, or that a man alone—that is, without grammar—is a grammatician, even though it has been established that a man together with grammar is not a grammatician. Hence it follows that the man alone is a grammatician, since a grammatician cannot exist except either alone or together with grammar. For although the noun *grammaticus* is significative of grammar, it is nevertheless not a suitable answer to someone asking what a grammatician is to say “grammar,” or “a quality”; and if no one is a grammatician except by participating in grammar, it follows that a man is not a grammatician except together with grammar.

**MASTER.** What is said—that a man alone, that is, without grammar, is a grammatician—may be understood in two ways, one true and the other false, and is sufficient for resolving your question. A man alone, that is, without grammar, is a grammatician because he alone possesses grammar: grammar neither alone nor together with a man possesses grammar. But a man alone, that is, without grammar, is not a grammatician, because, in the absence of grammar, no one can be a grammatician. It is like someone who leads another by going ahead: he alone is “the one who goes before,” because the person who follows is not “the one who goes before,” either separately or as though one person who goes before were constituted from the two; and the one who goes before alone is not “the one who goes before,” because unless there is someone to follow, he cannot be the one who goes before. But when it is said that *grammaticus* is a quality, this is not correctly said except according to Aristotle’s treatise *On the Categories*.

*Note:* One manuscript of Victor 3 has “grammar is not” instead of “is not a grammatician.” Other manuscripts read “no one is grammar, or can be [a grammatician]” instead of “no one can be a grammatician.” The manuscripts variously read “he alone is first … is not first … one first is constituted … is not first … the first follows,” where the present text has “he alone is the one who goes before … is not the one who goes before … the one who goes before is constituted … is not the one who goes before … someone follows.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Aristotle’s Meaning in the Treatise *On the Categories*

**DISCIPLE.** Does that treatise say anything other than that everything that exists is either substance, or quality, or quantity, and so forth? If, therefore, a man alone is a grammatician, then substance alone is a grammatician. How, then, according to that treatise, is *grammaticus* more a quality than a substance?

**MASTER.** Even if what you say is understood there—that everything that exists is one of these things—Aristotle’s principal intention in that book was not to demonstrate this. Rather, since every noun or verb signifies one of these things, he intended to show that. He was not attempting to establish what individual things are, nor of what things individual expressions are appellative, but of what things they are significative. Since, however, expressions signify only things, in stating what it is that expressions signify, he necessarily had to state what things are.

For—to say nothing of other matters—the division he makes at the beginning of the *Categories* adequately demonstrates this. He does not say: “Of things that exist, each individual one is substance, or quantity, and so forth.” Nor does he say: “Of things said without combination, each individual one is called substance or quantity.” Rather, he says: “Of things said without combination, each individual expression signifies either substance or quantity.”

**DISCIPLE.** Your reasoning is persuasive.

**MASTER.** When Aristotle therefore says, “Of things said without combination, each individual expression signifies either substance, or quantity, and so forth,” which signification do you think he means: that by which the expressions themselves signify per se, and which is substantial to them, or the other, which is per aliud and accidental?

**DISCIPLE.** Surely only that signification which he himself assigned to those same expressions when defining a noun and a verb—the signification by which they signify per se.

**MASTER.** Do you think that he pursued the matter differently in the treatise from the way he proposed it in the division? Or that any of those who, following him, wrote on dialectic intended to hold a different view on this matter from his own?

**DISCIPLE.** Their writings in no way permit anyone to suppose this. Nowhere is any of them found to have introduced an expression in order to display something that it signifies per aliud; they always do so to display what it signifies per se. For when they wish to demonstrate substance, they do not introduce *white* or *grammaticus*; but when teaching about quality, they bring forward *white* and *black*, and similar examples.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That Dialecticians Call Expressions by the Names of the Things of Which They Are Significative

**MASTER.** If, then, after the aforesaid division has been proposed, I ask you what *grammaticus* is according to this division and according to those who follow it in their writings on dialectic, what am I asking—or what will you answer me?

**DISCIPLE.** Without doubt, the question can concern only either an expression or the thing it signifies. Since it is established that, according to this division, *grammaticus* signifies not a man but grammar, I shall answer without hesitation: if you ask about the expression, it is an expression signifying a quality; but if you ask about the thing, it is a quality.

**MASTER.** Are you unaware that, in the same book, Aristotle calls expressions by the names of the things of which they are significative, and not merely by the names of the things of which they are appellative? Thus, when he says that every substance seems to signify “this something”—that is, every expression signifying substance—he names, or rather points out, things by the expressions significative of them, and often not appellative expressions.

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot be unaware of this. 149 Therefore, whether the question concerns the expression or the thing, when one asks what *grammaticus* is according to Aristotle’s treatise and according to his followers, the correct answer is “a quality”; and yet, according to appellation, it is truly a substance.

**MASTER.** So it is. We should not be troubled by the fact that dialecticians write one way about expressions according as they are significative, and use them another way in speaking according as they are appellative—any more than we should be troubled when grammarians say one thing according to the form of expressions and another according to the nature of things. They say that *lapis* (“stone”) is masculine in gender, *petra* (“rock”) feminine, and *mancipium* (“slave”) neuter; that *timere* (“to fear”) is active and *timeri* (“to be feared”) passive. Yet no one says that a stone is masculine, or a rock feminine, or a slave neither masculine nor feminine; nor that “to fear” performs an action and “to be feared” undergoes one.

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether *Grammaticus*, Since It Designates One Possessing a Quality, Belongs to the Category of Having

**DISCIPLE.** Your clear reasoning leaves me no room to doubt what you have said; but there is still something about this question that I want to learn. If *grammaticus* is a quality because it signifies a quality, I do not see why *armatus* (“armed”) should not be a substance, since it signifies a substance; and if *armatus* is therefore *having* because it signifies *having*, I do not understand why *grammaticus* should not be *having*, since it signifies *having*. For just as *grammaticus* is proved to signify a quality because it signifies one possessing a quality, so *armatus* signifies a substance because it signifies one possessing a substance, that is, arms; and just as *armatus* is shown to signify *having* because it signifies one possessing arms, so *grammaticus* signifies *having* because it signifies one possessing learning.

**MASTER.** Once the matter is considered in this way, I cannot deny either that *armatus* is a substance or that *grammaticus* is *having*.

**DISCIPLE.** Then I would like you to teach me whether one thing can belong to several categories.

**MASTER.** I do not think that one and the same thing can be assigned to different categories, although there may be doubts in certain cases. I believe that this requires a fuller and more profound discussion than the brief conversation we have undertaken here. I see no reason, however, why one expression signifying several things, not as one thing, may not sometimes be placed under several categories—for example, if *albus* (“white”) is said to be both a quality and *having*. *Albus* does not signify quality and *having* as one thing, in the way that *homo* (“man”) signifies as one thing both substance and the qualities of which a man consists.

The thing called *homo* is one thing constituted from what I have mentioned. But the thing called *albus* is not one thing constituted from *having* and quality, because nothing is called *albus* except a thing that has whiteness; and that thing is in no way constituted from *having* and quality. Therefore, if one says “man is a substance” and “man is a quality,” the one and same thing signified and appellated by this name is said to be substance and quality, which seems incongruous.

When, however, we say that *albus* is a quality and *having*, we do not say that the thing appellated by this name is quality and *having*, but that these two are signified by this name; and no incongruity follows.

**DISCIPLE.** Why, then, is *homo*, according to Aristotle’s division, not both substance and quality, since it signifies both, just as *albus* is both quality and *having* because it signifies both?

**MASTER.** I think what I said above can suffice as an answer: *homo* is principally significative of substance, and that one thing which it signifies is substance, not quality but “qualified.” *Albus*, however, signifies quality and *having* equally and with no one thing arising from them that is more the one or the other, of which *albus* might be the significative.

## CHAPTER XX. How No One Thing Arises from the Things Signified by *Albus*

**DISCIPLE.** I would like you to explain more clearly how no one thing is produced from the things signified by *albus*.

**MASTER.** If something is constituted from them, it is either a substance or something belonging to one of the other categories.

**DISCIPLE.** It cannot be anything else.

**MASTER.** But nothing is produced from *having* and whiteness.

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot object.

**MASTER.** Again, one thing is not produced from several things except either by the composition of parts belonging to the same category, as an animal consists of body and soul; or by the agreement of one genus with one or more differences, as body and man; or by a species and a collection of properties, as Plato. But the things signified by *albus* do not belong to one category; nor is one the genus, difference, species, or collection of properties of the other; nor are they differences of one genus. They are accidents of the same subject. Yet *albus* does not signify that subject, because it signifies absolutely nothing other than *having* and quality. Therefore no one thing is produced from the things signified by *albus*.

**DISCIPLE.** Although reason seems to affirm what you say, I would nevertheless like to hear how you would answer someone who objected to your claim that *albus* signifies nothing other than *having* and quality as follows:

“*Albus*, being the same as ‘having whiteness,’ does not signify determinately this or that possessor, such as a body, but indeterminately something possessing whiteness. For *albus* is either that which has whiteness or that which does not have it. But that which does not have whiteness is not *albus*. Therefore *albus* is that which has whiteness. Since everything that has whiteness must be something, *albus* must be something that has whiteness, or something possessing whiteness. Finally, *albus* either signifies something possessing whiteness or nothing. But nothing cannot be understood as possessing whiteness; therefore *albus* must signify something possessing whiteness.”

## CHAPTER XXI. That *Albus* Does Not Signify Something Possessing Whiteness, but Merely “Possessing Whiteness”

**MASTER.** The question is not whether everything that is white is something, or whether there is something that possesses whiteness; the question is whether this name, by its signification, contains what is called “something,” or “that which possesses,” as *homo* contains *animal*. That is, just as *homo* is a rational mortal animal, so *albus* would be something possessing whiteness—or “that which possesses whiteness.”

For it is necessary that many things be true of any given thing, although they are not signified by the name of that thing. Every animal, for example, must be colored and either rational or irrational, yet the name *animal* signifies none of these things. Therefore, although *albus* is nothing except something possessing, or that which possesses, whiteness, it is not necessary that *albus* signify this.

Let us suppose that *album*, or *albus*, signifies something possessing whiteness. But something possessing whiteness is nothing other than something white.

**DISCIPLE.** It cannot be anything else.

**MASTER.** Therefore *albus*, or *album*, always signifies something white.

**DISCIPLE.** Let it be so.

**MASTER.** Wherever *albus* or *album* is placed, then, it is always correctly taken for “something white.”

**DISCIPLE.** That follows.

**MASTER.** Therefore, wherever “something white” is said, it is also correctly said twice: “something white”; and wherever it is said twice, it is said three times; and so on infinitely.

**DISCIPLE.** That follows, and it is absurd.

**MASTER.** Let *albus* also be identical with “that which has whiteness.” But “has” is nothing other than “is possessing.”

**DISCIPLE.** It cannot be otherwise.

**MASTER.** Therefore *albus* is nothing other than “that which is possessing whiteness.”

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing else.

**MASTER.** But when “possessing whiteness” is said, this expression signifies nothing other than *album*.

**DISCIPLE.** So it is.

**MASTER.** Therefore *albus* is the same as “that which is white.”

**DISCIPLE.** That follows.

**MASTER.** Wherever, then, *albus* is placed, it is correctly taken for “that which is white.”

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny it.

**MASTER.** If, therefore, *albus* is “that which is white,” then “that which is white” is also “that which is that which is white”; and if this is so, then “that which is that which is that which is white,” and so on infinitely.

**DISCIPLE.** This is no less a consequence and no less absurd than the claim that something is repeatedly something.

**MASTER.** If someone says that *albus* signifies either something possessing whiteness or nothing, and understands this as saying “*albus* either signifies something possessing, or signifies not something possessing,” where “not something” is an infinite name, the division is incomplete and not true, and therefore proves nothing. It would be like someone saying: “A blind person either sees something or sees not something.” But if it is understood to mean that *albus* either signifies something possessing whiteness or does not signify it, the division is complete and true, and does not conflict with what has been said.

**DISCIPLE.** It is sufficiently clear that *album* does not signify something possessing whiteness, nor one who possesses whiteness, but merely “possessing whiteness”—that is, quality and *having*. From these alone no one thing is formed. Therefore *albus* is both, because it signifies both equally. I see that this reasoning is valid for everything said without combination that likewise signifies several things from which no one thing is formed; and I do not think that any sound objection can be made to what you have established in this discussion.

**MASTER.** Nor does it seem so to me now. Yet you know how fiercely dialecticians in our time dispute the question you raised. I do not want you to cling to what we have said in such a way as to hold it obstinately, if someone should be able to destroy it with stronger arguments and establish a different position. If that should happen, you will at least not deny that these discussions have benefited us as an exercise in disputation.

# SAINT ANSELM’S BOOK ON THE WILL OF GOD

## CHAPTER I. What Is Called the Will of God

Since human reason must always treat of God and say something fitting in his praise, it does not possess names with which to speak of him properly. Instead, it adopts names given and imposed upon human beings, and through the effects themselves attempts, at least in a very feeble discourse, to disclose his omnipotence. It does this by gathering from these things the effect of God’s will according to his hidden justice, or according to his mercy, or according to the vengeance of his wrath; for it cannot aspire to the incomprehensible proper nature of divinity.

Therefore, when we too desire to say something about the will of God, we attend to the course of events, since we cannot reach the summit of his majesty. We call the will of God whatever he mercifully works in us, recalling us from error or piously strengthening us in righteousness. The punishment and rejection of certain people, carried out by God’s hidden strictness in accordance with justice, is also called the will of God.

The will of God is, to put it briefly, whatever occurs as it is found to occur in creatures. But someone may say: “If everything proceeds from the will of God, which is clearly always good and right, then everything is good and right. And if this is so, then it is useless for anyone to be judged wicked or condemned as impious”—a conclusion that is plainly contrary to the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER II. The Will of God Is Spoken of in Many Ways

It must therefore be explained that the will of God is understood in many ways, so that whatever objection is subsequently raised may be set forth more fully and without difficulty.

In Scripture, the will of God is sometimes understood as equivalent to his omnipotent foreknowledge and ordering, which wisely disposes all things. Hence it is said: “The Lord has done everything whatever he willed” (Psalm 113:3); that is, whatever God ordained from eternity that he would do, he left nothing unfulfilled.

The will of God is also understood according to a certain affection of God’s mercy, as in the statement: “God wills all to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4). This means that he causes the saints to will that all be saved. What God himself wills, however, is what he himself has ordained; but, by inspiring love, he causes the saints to will [what concerns] God and their neighbor [reading uncertain]. Through this love, it is not unfitting that prayers should be offered in the Church by the saints for schismatics and heretics, and also for Jews and gentiles.

Divine institution is not improperly called the will of God. God’s institution can be divided into two parts: the precepts of the divine Scriptures and the natural law implanted in human beings, which is: “What you would not have done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16), and so forth. Whoever opposes this does not observe the will of God.

The precepts of the divine Scriptures and the correct observances of the Churches are also rightly called the will of God. Whoever does not obediently submit to them is said to deviate entirely from the will of God, although no one is able to depart from the order of his foreknowledge.

## CHAPTER III. Clarification of Certain Ambiguities from the Preceding Statements

The will of God is understood by learned teachers in four ways: first, as God’s knowledge; second, as the will of the saints, who charitably desire even the unjust to be saved; third, as human reason; and fourth, as the divine commandments.

If anyone considers these ways attentively with the eye of the mind, he will no longer struggle in determining the will of God. Attending faithfully to the different senses of the expression, he will easily judge the meaning of the words.

Thus, when it is said that God wills or does not will adultery or homicide to occur, these propositions do not conflict or contradict one another. Both are true and indubitable if one faithfully attends to the multiple equivocation of the expression “wills.” For “God wills adultery” means that he foreknows and foresees it; no one doubts that he sees and foreknows everything. Likewise, “he does not will it” means that he does not command it, or that he does not inspire the minds of the faithful to will it.

Or “God does not will adultery” means that, by the power of reason in the soul—that is, by the natural law given by God—we have no ground for saying that anyone ought to offend against his neighbor in this or in any other matter. In accordance with these explanations, anyone may openly determine these meanings of the will of God.

## CHAPTER IV. Other Doubts Are Removed

But a subtler point arising in this discussion of the will of God must be considered. Human will often adheres to the will of God, and yet a person is condemned on that account. Human will also does not adhere to the will of God, and yet a person is rewarded on that account. Again, a person wills what God does not will and receives a reward from God for it; a person does not will what God wills and thereby receives praise. An intelligent person can investigate for himself the many other ways in which this will varies. 152

But let us now return to the explanation of what was said above. God wills what a person wills: if it is something destructive, such as homicide or adultery, God wills it in the sense that he foreknew it; but the person is also condemned for this will, since it was forbidden to him.

God wills that someone’s father should die, or wills the death of a particular person, while that person does not will it through natural affection or compassion for his neighbor; and the person is rewarded for this affection, provided that in other matters he has not exceeded the rule of right living. In all that he wills and does, however, he intends to agree with the divine will and plans to do nothing against it. For human will is good only when it wills what God wills it to will; and thus it agrees with the divine will, which is the teacher of the human will.

## CHAPTER V. The Divine Will as Effecting, Approving, Granting, and Permitting

The great will of God is incomprehensible, as God himself is, and a person wills contrary to it because he does not fully know it; this will become clear in the future. In the present, however, a person perceives certain of God’s dispositions through perception or prohibition, and obeys them.

In the matters stated above, it is not right to understand that anything false or superfluous has been said, or anything contrary to the authority of the saints. Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 100:

“Therefore his great will must be sought throughout all his wills, so that, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, nothing occurs contrary to his will—not even what occurs against his will, which would not occur if he did not permit it. Certainly he does not permit it unwillingly, but willingly; nor would he permit good to be done badly if he were not omnipotent and able to bring good even out of evil.”

There is another division of this will. One kind may be called effecting, another approving, another granting, and another permitting.

The effecting will in God accomplishes whatever he wills; in a human being, it effects what the person both can and wills through the act itself.

The approving will is that which approves something, and this belongs both to human beings and to God. In God, the approving will is that by which he wills all to be saved, since, as far as it depends on him, he prevents no one from being saved; indeed, if anyone labors for this, he approves it. What the approving will is in a human being is obvious.

The granting will is that which grants that something occur. By a granting will, God wills that a person who has not chosen the better course should marry.

The permitting will is that which permits something to occur, even though at times it displeases him. In this sense God is said to will evils, because he permits them to occur. Hence it is said: “He hardens whom he wills, and has mercy on whom he wills” (Romans 9:18).

Augustine, *On the City of God*: “When God is said to change his will, so that those toward whom he was gentle become, for example, objects of severity, it is they rather than he who change—just as the sun changes for wounded eyes, and from gentle becomes, in a certain sense, harsh, and from pleasing becomes distressing, while in himself he remains the same as he was.”

The will of God is also called that which he produces in the hearts of those who obey his commandments. Of this the Apostle says: “God who works in you both the willing” (Philippians 2:13). According to this will, something is also said to be willed which he himself does not will, but which he makes his own people will. Thus, inspired by him with a holy will, a person piously and devoutly prays for certain people, although God does not accomplish what they pray for.

According to his own will, which is eternal in his foreknowledge, he has done everything whatever he willed—not only past and present things, but also future things.

Gregory: “God wills all human beings to be saved,” that is, no one is saved except those whom he wills to save; or some are saved from every class of human beings; or, “he wills all to be saved,” meaning that he compels no one to be damned.

Likewise, concerning dismissing an unbelieving spouse, one must say: “He should not dismiss her,” because, although it is permitted, it is not expedient.

Again, in the book *On the Baptism of Infants*: “Just as it is evil to use a good thing badly, so it is good to use an evil thing well.”

# THE WORKS OF SAINT ANSELM, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, PART TWO: ASCETICAL AND PARAENETICAL WRITINGS

## HOMILIES AND EXHORTATIONS

### HOMILY I

**ON THE PASSAGE OF ECCLESIASTICUS:** “In all things I sought rest, and in his inheritance I shall dwell. Then the Creator of all things commanded and said to me; and he who created me rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclesiasticus 24:11).

Wisdom speaks—the Wisdom whom the Apostle attests to be Christ when he says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Wisdom, therefore, which is Christ—that is, the incarnate Wisdom of God—says: “In all things I sought rest.”

After labor, rest is ordinarily sought. The Lord, however, is himself tranquil and unchangeable; yet he testifies that he labors when he endures the harsh perversities of human beings, saying to any such person: “You have caused me labor in your iniquities” (Isaiah 43:24). And when he appeared in mortal flesh, he labored because of our weakness.

Therefore, after his resurrection, he sought rest in all things, so that he might rest in the faith and good works of all. He teaches in what things he sought rest by prefacing the statement: “Throughout every land I stood, and in every people and every nation I held primacy, and with power I trampled upon the hearts of all the excellent and exalted” (Ecclesiasticus 24:9). Immediately he adds: “And in all things I sought rest.”

Thus he sought rest among all the peoples and nations of the whole world, and among all the kings and rulers whose hearts he finally subjected to himself. He found rest in those who ceased to sin and lived holily and justly.

When he says that he sought rest among all peoples and nations and among the exalted—that is, among those placed in the eminence of dignities—he signifies that in every nation under heaven many can be openly seen living perversely, while only a few, like grains beneath the chaff, are found to act well. What is hidden and not possessed is what is sought.

Christ also seeks rest for himself in each person predestined to life: while that person is still sinning, Christ waits for him and strives to convert him and make him such, through commandments or admonitions, miracles, prosperity, and adversity, that he may be able to rest in him. But he denies rest in himself to the person who does not wish to cease from evil works and desires, so as to be able to provide God with a place of rest in himself.

## Textual Apparatus

The following omitted notes belong to the preceding text. Witness sigla and printed variant forms are retained; translations in parentheses give their sense where it differs materially.

### Chapters XVI–XXI, *De grammatico*

- At [Col. 0575A], “a man together with grammar is not a grammarian”: Vict. 3 reads *grammaticam esse* (“grammar exists/is [a grammarian]”) for *grammaticam non esse* (“grammar does not exist/is not [a grammarian]”).
- At [Col. 0575A], “except either alone, or together with grammar”: manuscripts read *nisi solus est* (“unless he alone is”) for *nisi aut solus aut* (“unless either alone or …”).
- “Although indeed”: manuscripts read *quamvis nunquam* (“although never”) for *quamvis namque* (“although indeed”).
- “The noun is significative”: manuscripts read *nomen significatum sit* (“the noun is signified”) for *nomen significativum sit* (“the noun is significative”).
- “Sufficient for resolving your question”: manuscripts read *quaestionem sufficit* (“the question suffices”) for *quaestionem solvendam sufficit*.
- “One true, the other false”: manuscripts read *uno modo vero, altero modo falso* (“in one way true, in another way false”).
- At [Col. 0575B], “alone, that is, without grammar”: manuscripts read *solus sine grammatica* (“alone without grammar”).
- “No one can be a grammarian”: manuscripts read *nullus est grammatica, vel potest esse* (“no one is grammar, or can be”).
- In the analogy of the person going before, manuscripts read *primus* (“first”) throughout: “he alone is first … is not first … one first is constituted … is not first … unless someone follows, [he] cannot be first,” where the printed text has *praevius* (“the one who goes before”).
- “At the beginning of the treatise of the *Categories*”: manuscripts read *principio Categoriarum* (“at the beginning of the *Categories*”).
- “Each individual one”: manuscripts read *singularium est* (“is of singular things”) for *singulum est*.
- “Nor does he say, ‘Of things …’”: manuscripts read *nec ait: quae secundum ullam* (“nor does he say: things which according to any …”) for *nec ait, eorum quae secundum nullam*.
- “Each individual is called”: manuscripts read *singulum aut* for *singulo aut*.
- “Either substance or quantity”: manuscripts add *aut qualitatem. D.* (“or quality. D.”).
- “Of which signification”: manuscripts read *et tunc de qua* (“and then of which”).
- “That by which”: manuscripts read *de illa quam per* for *de illa qua per*.
- “Or the other”: manuscripts read *aut de altera* for *an de altera*.
- “Any of those”: manuscripts read *an alium eorum* (“or another of those”); the Cologne edition reads *an aliud eorum* (“or another thing among those”).
- “Do not permit anyone to suppose this”: manuscripts read *hoc aliud opinari permittent* (“will permit another opinion of this”).
- “Introduced an expression in order to display something”: manuscripts read *eorum aliquam vocem ad ostendendum aliud quod* (“an expression of theirs to display another thing which”).
- “White or *grammaticus*”: Vict. 3 reads *album aut grammaticam* (“white [neuter] or grammar”).
- “They bring forward white and black”: manuscripts read *nigrum ponunt* (“they set down black”) for *nigrum profert* (“they bring forward black”).

### Chapter XVIII

- “The question can concern only”: manuscripts read *hoc non potest quaeri* (“this cannot be asked”) for *non hic potest quaeri* (“this cannot be asked here”).
- “Since it is established”: manuscripts read *quia constat*.
- “Of which they are significative, and not merely appellative”: manuscripts read *quarum voces sunt significativae, et non quarum sunt appellativae* (“of which the expressions are significative, and not of which they are appellative”).
- “When he says that every substance”: manuscripts read *dicit; omnis* (“he says; every”) for *dicit quia omnis*.
- “That is, every expression signifying substance”: manuscripts read *id est omnis vox significat* (“that is, every expression signifies”).
- “Which you remembered a little earlier”: manuscripts read *ante invenisti* (“you found earlier”).
- “It is truly a substance”: manuscripts read *vera est substantia* (“it is a true substance”).
- At [Col. 0577B], “if grammarians too”: Vict. 13 reads *sed et* (“but also”) for *si et* (“if also”).
- “According to the form of expressions, another according to the nature of things”: manuscripts read *formam aliud* (“form, another”) for *formam vocum, aliud*.
- “They say indeed”: manuscripts read *dicunt quidem*.
- “But *mancipium* is neuter; *timere* active, *timeri* passive”: manuscripts read *mancipiumque neutri, timere autem activum, timeri passivum*.
- “No one says that the stone is masculine”: manuscripts read *dicat lapidem* (“says stone”) for *dicat esse lapidem* (“says that a stone is”).
- The manuscripts’ corresponding continuation is: “or a rock feminine, or a slave neither masculine nor feminine, or that fearing …”; it differs only in arrangement from the printed wording.

### Chapters XIX–XXI

- “Leaves me no room to doubt”: manuscripts read *ratio in his quae dixisti dubitare non permittit* (“reason does not permit doubt about what you said”).
- “Something I want to learn”: manuscripts read *quod velim dicere* (“which I want to say”); Bec and Gembloux read *quod velim discere* (“which I want to learn”).
- “Whether one thing”: manuscripts read *utrum unum aliud* (“whether one other [thing]”).
- “Can be assigned”: manuscripts read *arctari posse* (“can be constrained”) for *aptari posse* (“can be assigned”).

- “Quality and having as one”: manuscripts read *et habere, quemadmodum* for *et habere ut unum, quemadmodum*.
- A manuscript repeats corruptly the preceding discussion of *armatus* and then reads “man signifies as one substance and the qualities of which man consists”; the printed text correctly continues, “The thing called man …”.
- “The thing called *albus*”: manuscripts read *album* (“white,” neuter) for *albus*.
- “Nothing is called white except a thing”: manuscripts likewise read *album, nisi res*.
- “Therefore, if it is said”: manuscripts read *quia dicitur* (“because it is said”).
- “When we say that *albus*”: manuscripts read *quia album est*.
- “We do not say that”: manuscripts read *non omnis, quia* (“not every, because”).
- “Is *homo* … just as *albus*”: manuscripts read *est album et qualitas* (“white is and quality”); the Cologne edition reads *est album est qualitas*.
- “Can suffice”: manuscripts read *satisfacere* (“satisfy”); the Cologne edition reads *facere* (“do”).
- “Principally significative”: manuscripts read *principaliter significatum* (“principally signified”).
- “Of which *albus* might be significative”: manuscripts read *sit album significatum* (“white might be signified”).
- In Chapter XX, manuscripts read *unum aliud ex* (“one other [thing] from”) for *unum aliquid ex* (“one thing from”).
- Before “If something is constituted”: manuscripts read *album. M. Si aliud* (“White. Master: If another [thing]”) for *albus. M. Si aliquid*.
- “Or something belonging to the other categories”: manuscripts read *aut aliud aliorum* (“or another of the others”).
- “It cannot be anything else”: manuscripts read *aliter esse* (“to be otherwise”) for *aliud esse* (“to be another thing”).
- “Except either”: manuscripts read *hoc est aut* (“that is, either”).
- “As Plato”: manuscripts read *ut propositio* (“as a proposition”).
- “The things which *albus* signifies”: manuscripts repeatedly read *album* for *albus*.
- “*Albus* does not signify”: manuscripts read *album non*.
- “Therefore no one thing is produced”: manuscripts read *quia non fit* (“because one thing is not produced”).
- “Although reason seems to affirm”: Vict. 13 reads *quae disseris* (“what you argue”) for *quae dicis* (“what you say”).
- “If someone”: manuscripts read *si quia ad*; Vict. 3 reads *si quis ad*.
- “*Albus* signifies nothing other than”: manuscripts read *album significat aliquid* (“white signifies something”) for *albus significat aliud* (“white signifies anything else”).
- “Would object: *albus*, since …”: manuscripts read *sic objiceres: album cum* (“you would object thus: white, since …”).
- “It is necessary that many things be true”: manuscripts add *aut qui habet albedinem* (“or that which has whiteness”) before *multa* (“many things”).
- “Although *albus*”: manuscripts read *licet album*.
- “It is not necessary that *albus*”: manuscripts read *ut album*.
- “*Albus*, or *album*, always signifies”: manuscripts read *sive album significat* (“or white signifies”).
- “Wherever *albus* or *album* is placed”: manuscripts read *vel album semper pro illo* (“or white always for that [thing]”).
- “And wherever twice, there three times”: manuscripts read *ibi ter, etc. et hoc* (“there [it is] three times, etc., and this”).
- “Let *albus* also be”: manuscripts read *album idipsum* (“white [neuter], that very thing”).

- The expanded manuscript reading of the infinite regress is *quicunque qui albus est, est, est* (“whoever who is white, is, is”), rather than the printed repeated *qui* (“that which/who”).
- Vict. 3 reads *non hoc minus consequens* (“this is no less a consequence”) for the manuscripts’ *non hoc minus inconsequens* (“this is no less inconsequent”).

- “Either signifies something possessing whiteness or does not signify”: manuscripts read *quia significat habens albedinem, aut non* (“that it signifies possessing whiteness, or not”).
- “Because it signifies both equally”: manuscripts read *quia per utrumque* (“because through each [of the two]”).
- “Several things”: manuscripts read *quaelibet plura* (“any several [things]”).
- “No sound objection can be made”: manuscripts read *te posse objicere existimo* (“I think that you can object”) for *objici recte posse existimo*.
- “How fiercely dialecticians”: manuscripts read *quam nostris* (“how [in] our times”) for *quantum nostris* (“how greatly [in] our times”).
- “I do not want you”: manuscripts read *volo te sic* (“I want you thus”) for *nolo te sic* (“I do not want you thus”).
- “Should be able to establish”: manuscripts read *velit astruere* (“should wish to establish”) for *valuerit astruere* (“should be able to establish”).
- “If that should happen”: manuscripts read *si contingeret* (“if it were to happen”).
- “As an exercise”: manuscripts read *ad excitationem* (“for arousal”) for *ad exercitationem* (“for exercise”).

And in his inheritance, he says, I shall dwell. “His” refers both to the rest and to what he had said above: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High,” so that this inheritance may be understood as belonging both to Rest and to the Most High—namely, the multitude of the elect, whom the Most High himself will possess, exalted in the heavenly kingdom to behold the glory of his majesty, and thus will cause to rest perpetually. He therefore says: “In his inheritance I shall dwell.” As though he were saying: “Indeed, I sought rest among all, although I did not find it enduring in all; but among those who are foreknown as God’s inheritance I shall dwell,” that is, I shall remain continually and not merely for an hour. [Col. 0586B] For God’s Wisdom does not dwell in those who believe for a time and depart in the time of temptation; rather, she dwells in those whom she makes persevere in goodness to the end. Hence he says concerning any such person: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

It follows: “Then the Creator of all things commanded and said to me; and he who created me rested in my tabernacle, and said to me: Dwell in Jacob, and inherit in Israel, and put down roots among my elect.” “Then,” he says, “when I was seeking rest among all, he who created all and has authority over all, desiring that no one should perish, commanded me what I should do among them; and he who also created me for their salvation according to my humanity himself rested in my tabernacle.” [Col. 0586C] He calls himself created because he became human, although earlier he had asserted that he was begotten by the Father before the ages, saying: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV, 5). The tabernacle of this Wisdom is the body assumed by him, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm XVIII, 6), that is, his body in the most manifest vision. In this tabernacle the Father rested, because he found no sin in it [Col. 0587A] that could offend him, but the fullness of all righteousness in which he might rest with delight. Hence he also says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew XVII, 5); and the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isaiah XI, 2).

Thus the incarnate Wisdom of God speaks, as was also said above, and, seeking the glory of the Father in all things, declares that he said to her: “Dwell in Jacob,” and so forth. Jacob, which is interpreted as “supplanter,” signifies wrestlers who, with labor, supplant and cast down vices. Israel, however, which is said to mean “most upright of God,” or “a man seeing God,” signifies those who, having subdued their vices, preserve the perfect uprightness of life insofar as is permitted and devote themselves to contemplation. 156 Therefore he dwells in Jacob, that is, in wrestlers, as the Apostle says to them: “That Christ may dwell [Col. 0587B] in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians III, 17), so that, strengthened by his power, they may become victors. In Israel, however, he is inherited—that is, he possesses as an inheritance those who are already perfect and will no longer be lost, those who, having quieted their vices, have chosen for themselves the better part, which shall not be taken away from them.

He himself also says this through Isaiah: “Assyria is the work of my hands, but Israel is my inheritance” (Isaiah XIX, 25). For “Assyria” is interpreted as “directing,” signifying one who, by wrestling, strives to overthrow the perversity of vices and to set himself straight. Such a person is the work of Christ’s hands, that is, his assistance, which remains in him; but Israel, already at rest, is possessed as an inheritance. The Savior also puts down roots among the elect, so that he can never be torn from their hearts, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Who [Col. 0587C] shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Romans VIII, 35.) For whoever can be separated from the love of Christ has not had Christ put down roots in his mind.

It follows: “From the beginning and before the ages I was created, and until the age to come I shall not cease; and in the holy dwelling-place I ministered before him. And so I was established in Zion, and likewise rested in the sanctified city, and my power is in Jerusalem. And I put down roots in the honored people, and his inheritance is in the portion of my God, and my abiding is in the fullness of the saints.”

From the beginning of the world, and before the ages, this Wisdom was predestined and created according to his humanity, because from the beginning of creation, and before the worldly times, [Col. 0587D] God had predestined in the secret of his counsel that his Word would become flesh—that is, that the Lord of all things would mercifully assume the form of a servant in order to redeem servants. And what he who made the future had most certainly determined to be done was already accomplished in his sight. Thus, before the ages, he created him according to his humanity, just as he “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians I, 4).

“From the beginning,” that is, from the time when the first human being was created, and “before the ages,” that is, from the time when the first age began, this Wisdom was created, as we have said. For when the human being was formed, and when the angel was created, it was foreseen that the Only-Begotten of God would mercifully become human and raise up the human race, which had been grievously cast down. [Col. 0588A] “And until the age to come I shall not cease,” because no temptations of the devil and no persecutions of tyrants will be able to prevent the Christian religion from enduring until the end of the world, for whose sake I was created before the beginning of the world. This is what is also said below: “I shall not cease among their generations, even unto the holy age” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV, 46). And likewise in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20).

“And in the holy dwelling-place I ministered before him.” By the holy dwelling-place he means the holy habitation of heaven, where he ministers before God, having been made high priest forever. Hence the Apostle says: “For Jesus did not enter a sanctuary made with hands, copies of the true ones, [Col. 0588B] but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf” (Hebrews IX, 24); and again: “We have such a high priest, who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle, which God fixed and not man” (Hebrews VIII, 1–2).

For what is said here, “in the holy dwelling-place before him,” is what the Apostle says: “into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf”; and what is added here, “I ministered,” the Apostle expresses as “a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle.” And lest such ministry be thought to contain anything degrading, he sits on the same throne with him before whom and for whom he ministers, and he sits at the right hand as an increase of honor. He also adds: “And so I was established in Zion.” Zion is interpreted as “watchtower” and “contemplation,” and signifies that homeland of the blessed [Col. 0588C] whose inhabitants never cease visibly to contemplate the glory of God. There, according to his humanity, Christ was established in the manner stated above—that is, sitting at the Father’s right hand and exercising the ministry of high priest, which consists in displaying before the Father, on our behalf, the scars of his passion. Concerning his establishment in the heavens, where he remains without end, it was said to the Father: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself” (Psalm LXXIX, 18). And in his own voice: “You established me in your sight forever” (Psalm XL, 13).

It follows: “And in the sanctified city I likewise rested.” Because in the Church, which is the city of God and has been sanctified by converted sinners, Christ found a rest like that which he found in the angels. Hence he taught [Col. 0588D] us to pray: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matthew VI, 10), that is, “as in the angels, so also in human beings.” “And in Jerusalem,” he says, “is my power.” In the heavenly Jerusalem, which is rightly called “the vision of peace,” because true peace is always seen there, is the power of our Redeemer, since there also he is able to do whatever he wishes. Hence he says: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew XXVIII, 18).

It follows: “And I put down roots in the honored people.” The root of wisdom is to fear God. The honored people are the multitude of the faithful, to whom Peter says: “Honor, therefore, to you who believe” (1 Peter II, 7). Wisdom, then, who is Christ, put down roots in this people, [Col. 0589A] because she gave believers the fear of God, by which they cease to sin, since “the fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclesiasticus I, 27); for “the one who is without fear cannot be justified.” Again, the honored people are the assembly of the religious. And in this people Christ put down roots in such a way that he could in no manner be uprooted from it. For he did what had earlier been said to him by the Father: “Put down roots among my elect.”

He also adds: “And his inheritance is in the portion of my God.” The portions of God are the Churches of the elect, the various orders of the saints, and the diverse actions of those who live well. Christ is also God, because Christ is human as well. His inheritance, therefore, extends into all the portions of God, because all the Churches of the righteous, and all who serve him commendably [Col. 0589B] in various vocations and actions, will be in his eternal inheritance. “And in the fullness,” he says, “of the saints he will be,” where none of them will be lacking, but when their number has been completed their entire assembly will be united. There too will be the abiding of incarnate Wisdom, because she will be held in them without end, delighting in their merits; and she will no longer go forth to the reprobate who will have been condemned, since she will no longer admonish them to be converted.

It follows: “Like a cedar I was exalted in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion.” Just as a cedar, surpassing in height all the heights of other trees, is lofty on Mount Lebanon—which is higher than all the other mountains of the promised land and is interpreted as “whitening”—so the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy II, 5), has been exalted above the height of the first [Col. 0589C] angels. Because of the brighter whiteness of the light with which they shine, these angels are rightly called “Lebanon,” that is, “whitening,” and they are higher than the others. The Apostle declares this exaltation of Christ, asserting that the Father established him at his right hand in the heavenly places, “above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things under his feet” (Ephesians I, 20–22). Thus he was exalted like a cedar.

This comparison is also appropriate because cedar is imperishable and gives off a wonderful fragrance: Christ, already immortal in the flesh, diffuses from himself an extraordinary sweetness of scent, by which the angels and spirits themselves are delighted. [Col. 0589D] Or, just as a cedar is exalted in Lebanon, that is, in the whitening of sanctification, so he surpassed all the saints in holiness as a cedar surpasses all the trees in Lebanon. For what he accomplished among human beings was so splendid and sublime that it transcends all the heights of the righteous, so that those who have advanced greatly in God can scarcely touch the traces of his works, even when they admire them from the summit of contemplation.

“And like a cypress on Mount Zion.” Mount Zion is the Church of the saints in the height of virtues and in the contemplation and vigilant discernment of spiritual things. 157 The cypress, however, puts forth evergreen leaves throughout the year like the pine, always bears fruit, and has a good fragrance. Thus Christ was exalted like a cypress on Mount Zion, because God gave him, as it is written, over all things to the Church, flourishing in unfading freshness, abounding in perpetual fruits, and spreading the fragrance of a good reputation. [Col. 0590A]

It follows: “Like a palm I was exalted in Kadesh.” Kadesh is interpreted as “holiness.” The palm, however, is rough below to the touch and wrapped, as it were, in dry bark, but above it is beautiful both in appearance and in fruit. Below, it is constricted by the layers of its bark; above, it expands in the breadth of its beautiful greenery. So too the life of Christ and of his members is despised below but beautiful above; in the lower regions it is wrapped, as it were, in many layers of bark while it is constricted by countless tribulations, but in the highest regions it expands, as it were, with the leaves of beautiful [Col. 0590B] greenery in the breadth of blessedness.

The palm, contrary to the nature of other trees, begins from below with lesser breadth and rises with greater strength toward its branches and fruit. What is slender as it begins below grows broader as it rises upward. So the conduct of the elect, who are members of Christ, accomplishes more by bringing things to an end than it proposes at its beginning; and they often begin their first efforts more sluggishly but complete their final works more fervently.

Thus Christ, whether in himself or in his own members, was exalted like a palm in Kadesh, that is, in holiness, because the saints continually advance toward higher things and expand in virtues; and those who emerge slender from the root of their beginning grow strong in the perfection of their summit. This appeared chiefly in the Head himself, because in the last three years he accomplished greater and more numerous things [Col. 0590C] than throughout all the preceding time of his life.

It follows: “And like a planting of a rose in Jericho.” A rose planting is thorny below but flowering above; so Christ below is surrounded by the thorns of tribulations, while above he is crowned with glory and honor. Jericho, which is called “moon,” usually expresses the decline of this world and of our mortality. Therefore, because the Lord, sent from heaven, assumed our mortality in this world, he was taken up, as it were, from elsewhere and planted in Jericho. In this respect also he was likened to a rose: humble and covered with the pricks of sufferings, but finally adorned above with the purple flower of royal dignity.

[Col. 0590D]

It follows: “Like a beautiful olive tree in the fields.” Anyone who has been all around it, whether far away or near, can see a beautiful olive tree in the fields and delight in its appearance. So anyone who looks faithfully and devoutly upon Christ can see him displayed to the whole world and delight in his appearance. Wherever an olive tree is found in the world, it is a messenger of peace; and Isaiah marvels at the feet of Christ announcing and preaching peace (Isaiah LII, 7).

His mercy can also be signified by the olive, which produces oil, because in Greek ἔλαιον (*elaion*) means “mercy”; and oil surpasses all liquids with which it is mixed, just as the Psalmist also testifies concerning the Lord’s mercies: “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm CXLIV, 9). Therefore the beauty of this olive is fittingly seen [Col. 0591A] in the fields, because those who have a field-like—that is, broad, uncultivated, and lowly—way of life chiefly need the Savior’s mercy and are accustomed to look toward it.

By oil, light is nourished to drive away the darkness of night, illnesses are relieved, and rest is granted to the weary. So the grace of our Savior’s mercy, nourishing in us the light of faith, charity, and knowledge, illuminates our darkness, heals the illnesses of our souls, and makes us, weary from the desires of the age, rest in spirit through contempt for the world. For it is a great labor to burn with earthly desires, and a great rest not to desire earthly things.

It follows: “And like a plane tree I was exalted beside water in the streets.” Although the plane tree is lofty [Col. 0591B] and pleasant in itself, it appears taller and more delightful by comparison with the lower water that lies near it. So the Lord Jesus, although he is incomparably exalted and beautiful in himself, appears yet more exalted and glorious in relation to the Christian people subject to him, who are signified by water, in the streets—that is, in the broad spaces both of the world and of a spacious way of life.

For if we consider the lowliness of our life and look toward the excellence of the life that Christ led among human beings, how lofty that life will be in our eyes! For just as the plane tree is exalted beside the lower water, that is, near and above the people of the faithful who are subject to it, so he is exalted. Hence the Psalmist had also said of him: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Psalm I, 6), [Col. 0591C] that is, through the mystery of the Incarnation he shall be placed beside the flow of peoples who pass by.

The streets usually signify breadths, that is, spacious ways of life in which those who are inferior and unstable in life roam, just as water signifies the broad regions of the world; for in Greek πλάτος (*platos*) means “breadth.”

It follows: “Like cinnamon and balsam giving fragrance, I gave forth a scent.” Cinnamon is so called because its bark is round and slender like a reed. It is a very small tree that produces extremely slender and precious branches. For what extends in thickness—that is, in bulk—is despised; but what grows more slender is excellent.

Cinnamon therefore seems to signify the humility of Christ, which is proclaimed by Scriptures made from a reed, that is, [Col. 0591D] a pen, and which produces extremely slender and precious branches: namely, saints made spiritually slender by discipline, who are his members. For spiritual people are precious in him, whereas carnal people are held in contempt.

Balsam too is exceedingly precious and is made into the consecrated chrism with which all Christians are anointed. It signifies both Christ and the anointing of his Spirit, concerning which John says: “You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things” (1 John II, 20). Both substances—that is, cinnamon and balsam—give off a wonderful fragrance, especially when someone is perfumed with them. Hence Christ is now compared to the fragrance of both aromatics as they give off their scent: for when he anoints believers in every people and nation with the gift of his Spirit [Col. 0592A], the fragrance of that anointing spreads more powerfully throughout the whole world, and he himself makes the sweet fragrance of his knowledge manifest everywhere through those whom he has anointed, so that everywhere it may be said to him: “We shall run after you, in the fragrance of your ointments.”

It follows: “Like choice myrrh, I gave the sweetness of fragrance.” Myrrh signifies the death of our Redeemer, whose flesh did not see corruption, because dead flesh preserved with anointing of myrrh cannot decay. Hence this myrrh is called “choice,” because the Lord’s death was uniquely chosen from among the deaths of all the saints, through which all might live. Therefore this death offers such a sweetness of fragrance as no one else could experience, so that the dead are brought back to life by its perfume.

It follows: “And like storax, galbanum, and onycha, [Col. 0592B] and fragrant resin, and like uncut Lebanon, I perfumed my dwelling, and my fragrance was like unmixed balsam.” Storax is said to be a fragrant tree, hollow inside like a reed and full of sap; and in Christ, who is the fragrant tree of life, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians II, 9).

Galbanum, they say, is compounded from aromatics. In Christ there is also the complete fullness of all spiritual virtues. Onycha is so called from *unguentum* (“ointment”), because it is especially suitable for anointing; it signifies the spiritual anointing of the Savior, concerning which John says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John II, 27).

The fragrant resin (*gutta*) is said to be a medicinal substance suitable for healing swelling and for suppressing and extinguishing poison. It signifies the Lord’s humility, which medicinally heals the swelling of our pride [Col. 0592C] and destroys all the poisons of the vices.

Lebanon is frankincense, or rather the frankincense tree, signifying Christ, who is the tree of life and produces fragrant fruit to be burned as a sacrifice to God. Uncut Lebanon produces frankincense of itself, and its fragrance is stronger; when cut, however, it is compelled to produce frankincense whose scent is not as great. Christ, like uncut Lebanon, freely brought forth everything he accomplished in the flesh and therefore gave off the better fragrance. We, however, are like cut Lebanon: often against our will we are compelled to do good, and what we do is of little worth and gives off little fragrance.

All these things that have now been mentioned—storax, galbanum, onycha, fragrant resin, and Lebanon—give off an excellent scent and fill the place where they are found. So Christ perfumes his dwelling with his fragrance and [Col. 0592D] warmth, because he fills the mind in which he dwells with the warmth of his love and the fragrance of his holiness. A mind that does not perceive this fragrance and warmth is not yet Christ’s dwelling.

Unmixed balsam gives off a stronger fragrance, because Christ’s holiness, into which no sin could ever be mixed, offers a sweeter fragrance than that of the other saints.

It follows: “Like a terebinth I spread out my branches, and my branches are branches of honor and grace.” The terebinth is a large tree, extending great numbers of huge branches in every direction. It produces an aromatic resin that is medicinal and superior to all other resins. Christ, therefore, like an immense tree, extended his disciples [Col. 0593A] as branches into every part of the world: Thomas and Bartholomew into India, Matthew into Ethiopia, John into Asia, Andrew and Philip into Scythia, Peter into Italy, Paul into Spain, and the others into the other regions of the world.

Or the branches that he extended are the works that he performed in the flesh. From these—whether from the works or from the disciples—he himself brings forth the resin of spiritual grace, which heals all things and is superior to all the preaching and deeds of the Old Testament. His branches are branches of honor and grace because both his disciples and his deeds are highly honorable and gracious: they are worthy of praise and bring the grace of the New Testament to human beings.

It follows: “Like a vine I brought forth the sweetness [Col. 0593B] of fragrance, and my flowers are fruits of honor and goodness.” A vine planted in the earth produces shoots from itself, and fruit from the shoots. Christ, planted in the land of the living through his resurrection and ascension, brings forth from himself the saints who are his members like shoots, and from these, as they remain in him, he produces the fruit of good works. Hence he says to them: “Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John XV, 4).

He therefore bears fruit in them, because whatever good they do, he does, and the fruit of their work rises from his root. He bears the sweetness of fragrance because the fruit of the works that he performs in them is the sweet fragrance of a good reputation, when those who see these things glorify the Father who is in heaven.

His flowers are fruits of honor and goodness, [Col. 0593C] because the works that he begins by proposing them to his members he brings honorably and rightly to completion; through them he grants them great honor and goodness. Flowers are vows and promises; fruits are the fulfillment of promises through the performance of works. Thus the flowers of the saints are fruits, because the members of Christ fulfill what they vow and do what they promise.

It follows: “I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope. In me is all grace of life and truth; in me is all hope [variant: way] of life and virtue.”

Wisdom, who is Christ, is the mother of beautiful love because she gives birth to love that is not shameful but beautiful, not indecent but honorable, not lustful but chaste. She is also the mother of fear [Col. 0593D]—namely, filial or chaste fear—because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm CX, 10); and beautiful love, whose mother is Wisdom, gives birth to the chaste fear of God.

She is the mother of knowledge, because “no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew XI, 27). He also said: “I shall announce the Father openly to you” (John XVI, 25). Thus Wisdom, who is the Son, is the mother of knowledge.

And she is the mother of holy hope, because only Christ gives birth to hope concerning holy things. Holy hope is the hope of attaining the kingdom of God and his righteousness. True Wisdom gives this hope, and in her is all grace of life and truth, because no one can attain everlasting life or the truth of unchanging blessedness [Col. 0594A] except through the grace that is in this Wisdom, that is, in Christ, since Christ himself is “the truth and the life” (John XIV).

Therefore all hope of life and virtue is in him, because only through him can anyone rightly hope for blessed life, find the power of his immortality, or possess any virtue of good conduct.

It follows: “Come over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations.” Some desire Wisdom, who is Christ, but are held back from coming to her and embracing her through a religious way of life by various obstacles of worldly affairs. For it often happens that when someone considers turning to the religious life and following Christ, an evil habit of the vices in which he usually delights stands in his way, as do the love of parents, spouse, [Col. 0594B] or children, possessions, the blandishments of carnal friends, and things of this kind.

Therefore true Wisdom commands all who desire her in mind to cross over all such obstacles, hasten to come to her while it is permitted, and, after they have come to her, not remain empty but be filled with her generations—that is, with the perceptions of understanding and prudence and with the virtues that she usually generates in those who come to her.

It follows: “For my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. My memory is for generations of ages.” We must therefore cross over to divine Wisdom, trampling underfoot the obstacles of difficulties, because her spirit, which she breathes into those who cross over [Col. 0594C] to her, is sweeter than honey; and the inheritance of eternal blessedness that she has prepared for them surpasses honey and the honeycomb in sweetness.

He says “honey” because of the souls of the righteous, which, released from their bodies, already stand before the sight of the Creator’s glory, and to each of which white robes have been given (Revelation VI, 11). He says “honeycomb” because of the elect who, after the resurrection, will be blessed in the heavenly kingdom both in body and in soul, when they will possess double things in their own land (Isaiah LXI, 7). The honeycomb is honey in wax, signifying the soul in the body, just as honey without wax signifies the soul without the body.

The memory of this Wisdom will also endure through the generations of the ages, because her praise will be sung perpetually by the elect, and she will make those who cling to her share in that same praise.

[Col. 0594D]

It follows: “Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst.” Those who taste with the mouth of the heart the sweetness of true Wisdom burn with desire for her in proportion as they perceive her taste; and the more they drink of this draught, the more eagerly they thirst for it. For spiritual delights, when possessed, are still desired; and the more they are eaten by the hungry, the more they are hungered for by the one who eats them.

It follows: “Whoever hears me will not be put to shame, and those who work in me will not sin.” Whoever obediently hears Christ will not be put to shame, that is, will not be disgraced, because he will be at Christ’s right hand with great honor in the judgment. And those who work in him will not sin, [Col. 0595A] because every work done according to him is free from sin.

It follows: “Those who make me shine forth will have eternal life.” They make Wisdom shine forth who explain the Scriptures in order to declare the knowledge of Christ beneficially, who piously preach Christ himself, and who glorify him by the light of their works. Therefore they will have eternal life—that is, Christ himself—for he is the true God and eternal life.

## 159. HOMILY II

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW: “When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up the mountain. And when he had sat down, he taught his disciples, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. (Matthew V, 1)

[Col. 0595B]

“Blessed are the poor in spirit,” those who live for God not from necessity but by devoted choice, having despised everything. This poverty has two aspects: the renunciation of possessions—even if they are retained, they are retained not for oneself but for works of piety—and contrition of spirit, so that one renounces oneself.

This virtue, poverty, is rightly placed first, since the virtues that follow cannot prevail without it. Although it does not make a person perfect without the virtues that follow, it nevertheless merits the blessedness that comes through the help of divine grace.

But because someone might despise his possessions and still, through the weakness of the flesh, be disturbed by some insult, he adds: “Blessed are the meek.” These are people whom anger or anything similar does not affect, but who endure everything with equanimity. Moses is praised for this virtue; Christ himself makes himself its teacher, as it were, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew XI, 29).

This virtue possesses the true land. Notice the fitting ascent. First is contempt for the world, to which eternal things are rightly promised. In second place is meekness, which preserves and protects true poverty so that it cannot in any way be disturbed. In third place follows: “Blessed are those who mourn.” After we have completely rejected the things of the world and tempered our evil habits through meekness, it remains for us to mourn over past sins. This is the lower watering-place; and mourning out of desire for the heavenly homeland is the upper watering-place. The lower washes away present filth, while the upper inflames those who love the life to come.

[Col. 0595D]

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.” Notice that righteousness is defined in three ways: when we preserve for our nature what belongs to it; when we do for our neighbor what we want done for us; and when we render to God what belongs to God. This righteousness is not fully accomplished in us until God is all in all. For this reason he says “to hunger,” not “to be satisfied.” Lovers of the true good always thirst, and the fact that they are righteous is never enough for them.

“Blessed are the merciful.” Mercy arises from the preceding virtues, because there is no true compassion for the wretched unless true poverty and true humility have come first, unless the mind subject to divine laws has become meek, unless it has begun to mourn the misfortunes of others and to hunger for righteousness. True mercy is generated from all these things.

Observe that justice precedes this virtue. The light of justice is mercy; the virtue of mercy is justice.

“Blessed are the pure in heart.” Purity of heart is placed sixth, so that the human being, created on the sixth day, may through this purity recover the image of God, which the darkness of the vices had erased; and so that, withdrawn from the noise of human thoughts, with a pure heart and the image of God restored, he may think only about the things of God and apply himself entirely to the divine commandments.

“Blessed are the peacemakers.” Peace is rightly placed seventh. For after a person has advanced to the point where, having despised all worldly things, he can love and contemplate only eternal things—which belongs to the contemplative life—nothing remains except that he should possess God, who is the true peace that he contemplated, as his reward.

[Col. 0596B]

These seven steps of the virtues correspond to the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, concerning which we read in Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah XI, 2).

But the passage in Isaiah begins from the summit, whereas this one begins from below. There the Son of God is taught as one who will descend to the depths; here the human being is taught as one who will ascend from the depths to the likeness of God.

In these steps the first is the spirit of fear, which rightly corresponds to the humble, concerning whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” This is filial fear, concerning which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm CX, 10). The fear of the Lord produces contempt for this world and causes the person who voluntarily becomes poor to be enriched with blessedness.

Hence supernal grace, providing for our salvation, gave us a prayer in which, through a sevenfold petition, we might obtain the sevenfold Spirit, so that by the assistance of sevenfold grace we might attain the seven virtues mentioned above and through them merit reaching blessedness. When in the final part of the Lord’s Prayer we ask, “Deliver us from evil,” we seem to be praying that through the spirit of the fear of the Lord every swelling of pride may depart from us and the humility of true poverty may take its place, so that the blessedness of heavenly life may be given to it.

The second is the spirit of piety, which corresponds to the meek. Whoever seeks to live piously meditates on Holy Scripture and does not criticize what he does not yet understand; therefore he does not resist it. This is to become meek. In order that this virtue may be preserved continually, he prays that he not be led into temptation. [Col. 0596D]

In third place is the spirit of knowledge, which corresponds to those who mourn, because they now know by what evils they are held bound. Before they read about them in the Scriptures they desired these things, and therefore they sigh for their homeland. And so that those tears may be beneficial, let them pray and say: “Forgive us our debts,” that is, the sins by which we are held, so that we may return free to our homeland.

In fourth place follows the spirit of fortitude, which corresponds to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because those who desire true joy labor to be refreshed by the true goods for which they hunger. But that hunger, in order to reach satisfaction, is supported by the spirit of fortitude, lest it grow weary on the way. Therefore we pray: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

[Col. 0597A]

In fifth place is the spirit of counsel, which corresponds to the merciful. For no one shows mercy unless he is guided by the spirit of counsel. Hence we pray: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth,” so that, consulting the will of God, we may show mercy to those whom we see ought to receive mercy.

In sixth place is understanding, which corresponds to the pure in heart—namely, those who, with the eye of the heart purified, see what the bodily eye could not see and the ear could not hear. This is said to be what the pure heart sees as the kingdom of God: not that kingdom which neither begins nor ends, but that which is in us when the vices and the power of the devil are excluded.

Hence we pray: “Your kingdom come,” that is, “grant that through the spirit of understanding we may be pure in heart and prepare a kingdom for you within us.”

[Col. 0597B]

The seventh is the spirit of patience, which is appropriate to the peacemakers, in whom there is no rebellious movement, so that they may not differ from one another in the sanctification of God’s name, but rather that the Father’s name may be displayed in his children through their life and conduct. Hence we are to pray: “Hallowed be your name.”

Or otherwise, observe the sequence of these virtues. The kingdom of heaven is promised to the poor—namely, to those who, through the spirit of the fear of the Lord, have despised all their possessions. An inheritance is promised to the meek, as to those who seek their father’s testament with devotion. Consolation is promised to those who mourn, knowing the evils in which they are entangled. To those who hunger and thirst, fullness is promised. Mercy is promised to the merciful, because they have extended to others the careful consideration of counsel. To the pure in heart is given the ability to see [Col. 0597C] God. To the peacemakers is given likeness to God, because they will be called sons of God. That person is supreme who is found worthy to be called a son. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10). All who possess whatever they desire are called blessed. For blessedness is the most perfect state, consisting in the gathering together of all good things. Thus there are seven things that bring perfection; the eighth is what glorifies. For perfection tests those who belong to God. Hence it is written: “Let the furnace be kindled, that the gold may be tested” (Wis. III, 6).

## HOMILY III

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

“Jesus ordered his disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait, until he had dismissed the crowds” (Matt. XIV, 22).

In this reading, according to its mystical meaning, the condition of the Church is described in summary, from the coming of the Savior to the end of the age. For the Lord ordered his disciples to get into the boat when he entrusted the Church to the apostles and their successors to govern. He likewise ordered them to go ahead across the strait—that is, to make for the harbor of the heavenly homeland—before he himself entirely departed from this world. For he is always here with his chosen and on account of his chosen, until the consummation of the age; and those go ahead of him across the sea of the world who daily pass from here to the land of the living. When he has sent all his own there beforehand, then, leaving behind the crowds of the reprobate—not exhorting them any further to conversion, but abandoning them to destruction—he will depart from here, so that he may be in the kingdom with his chosen alone.

Hence it follows: “Until he had dismissed the crowds.” For at the end of the age he will dismiss the crowds of his enemies, so that they may be seized by the devil for eternal condemnation. “And after dismissing the crowd, he went up the mountain by himself to pray.” He will not dismiss the crowds of the nations until the end of the world; but he dismissed the crowd of the Jewish people when, according to Isaiah, he commanded his clouds not to rain upon the unfruitful vineyard (Isa. V, 6)—that is, he ordered the apostles not to preach any longer to the Jews, but to go to the nations.
