Thus he dismissed that crowd and went up onto the mountain, that is, to the summit of the heavenly kingdom, concerning which it had been said: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Ps. XXIII, 3). For a mountain is a height, and what is higher than heaven? The Lord ascended that. And he ascended alone, because “no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13). Although, at the end, when he comes and gathers all of us, his members, and raises us into heaven, even then he will ascend alone, because the head with his body is one Christ. But now only the head has ascended: “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (I Tim. II, 5). And he ascended to pray because he went to the Father to intercede for us. For he did not enter a sanctuary made by human hands, copies of the true ones, “but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf” (Heb. IX, 24).

It follows: “When evening came, he was there alone.” Evening signifies the nearness of the end of the age, of which John also says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). When evening had therefore come, he was there alone, because, as the end of the world approached, he entered alone into the holy of holies as the true High Priest; and there he is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us (Rom. VIII, 34). Yet while he prays on high, the boat is troubled by waves in the depths. For since waves arise, this boat can be troubled; but because Christ is praying, it cannot sink.

For it follows: “The boat was being tossed by the waves in the middle of the sea, for the wind was against them.” The boat is the Church; the sea is the world; the waves of the sea are the swellings of the world and the tribulations of the world, or the surging assaults of temptations. The contrary wind is the spirit of demons, by which the powers of the world have been stirred up against the Church, and by which the world is frequently agitated against the saints, and by which vices and iniquities are continually suggested. Thus the ship was being tossed by waves in the middle of the sea while Jesus remained on the summit of the mountain, because from the time the Savior ascended into heaven, the holy Church has been shaken by great tribulations in this world, battered by various storms of persecution, harassed by the wickedness of evil people in many forms, and tested by vices in manifold ways. The wind was against it because the blast of evil spirits always opposes it, lest it reach the harbor of salvation; it strives to overwhelm it with the waves of worldly adversities, stirring up against it every opposition within its power.

[Col. 0599A]

It follows: “In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.” Since the night has twelve hours and four military watches, with three hours assigned to each watch, the fourth watch of the night is the last part of the night. Night signifies the darkness of tribulations and errors and vices, as well as the dangers of temptations. In the fourth watch of the night, therefore—that is, at the end of the persecution that had long raged under pagan kings, or around the end of any more serious adversity—Jesus came to his own. And he came walking on the sea, that is, trampling all the waves of tribulations, keeping all the swellings of the world beneath his feet, and pressing down all the heights of the age. For what is signified by the name “sea” except the bitterness of this world, raging in the destruction of the good? The Lord therefore walks upon the waves of the sea, because when the storm-clouds of persecution rise up, they are shattered by the amazement produced by his miracles. He who calms the swellings of human madness treads upon the waves as though they were raised into a heap. For when the pagan world saw that its customs were being destroyed by the preaching of a new way of life; when the deeds of the poor opposed the pride of the rich of this world; and when the wise of the age judged the words of the unlearned to be hostile to them, they swelled up into the storm of persecution. But those who, stirred by opposition in words, rush into the storms of persecution are restrained, as we have said, by their wonder at the signs. Thus the Lord set his feet upon as many waves as he displayed miracles to proud persecutors.

It follows: “When they saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, ‘It is a phantom’; and they cried out from fear.” Jesus passes by, trampling the waves; yet the tribulations are so great that even those who have believed in Jesus and strive to persevere to the end are often troubled and afraid that they may fail. When Christ, I say, is treading upon the waves—that is, when he is pressing down the ambitions and heights of the world—Christians become afraid. The disciples therefore rightly feared while the Lord was walking upon the waves, because Christians, although they have hope in the future age, are sometimes troubled by the crushing of human affairs when they see the height of this world being brought low; they do not think that this is done by God, but by the enemy.

They were therefore troubled, saying, “It is a phantom,” because when they see the glory of the world being brought low, the heights of worldly pride being cast down, and the waves of the world being trampled, they are often troubled by the blows inflicted upon the world. They do not yet understand that God is doing these things, but think that the phantom-like spirit of this world—that is, deceitful Satan—is carrying them out in the world; and in their fear they cry out in confusion to the Lord. But afterward, attending more carefully, they open the Gospel and open the divine Scriptures, and find all these things foretold there. They perceive that it is not that empty and shadowy spirit which has lost the truth of being, but the true Lord who does these things and depresses the heights of the age, so that he may be glorified by the humble.

Hence it appropriately follows: “Immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying: ‘Take courage; I am; do not be afraid.’” He speaks such things to his own either through inward inspiration, through the Scriptures, or through preachers. “Do not,” he says, “lose confidence, but take courage; do not be terrified, but be fearless. For I am the one who foretold these things, and now I am doing them for your benefit; therefore it is necessary that they should happen. I am the one who does not change, whose words do not pass away but remain and are fulfilled in events; the one who said to Moses, ‘I am who I am’ (Exod. III, 14), and commanded him, ‘Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: “He who is” has sent me to you’ (ibid.).”

For anything that is changeable does not truly exist. True being is not present where there is both being and non-being. Whatever can be changed, once changed, is no longer what it was. In truth, which remains, there is no change, neither past nor future, but only the present—and that incorruptibly. This is not found in creation. Examine the changes of things, and you will find: “it was” and “it will be.” Think of God, and you will find: “he is,” where “he was” and “he will be” cannot be. Rightly therefore Christ, who is eternal and unchangeable truth, says to those tossed about amid the tribulations of the world: “I am; do not be afraid.”

It follows: “Peter answered and said: ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.’ And he said: ‘Come.’” Peter signifies the order of preachers; the waters signify not only tribulations but also peoples. “If it is you,” he says—if you remain unchanging—“command me,” because your command is an effective power; command me to come upon the waters, that is, upon the waves of worldly tribulations and upon the peoples, to you, so that, adhering to you, the unchanging one, I too may become unchanging by sharing in your firmness.

He goes upon the tribulations who is not overcome or submerged by them, but tramples and conquers them, just as we read that the tribulation occurred under Stephen in which he was the first to lay down his life for Christ (Acts VII). He also goes over peoples to Christ who, by governing multitudes of believers, advances toward the kingdom of heaven.

It follows: “And Peter got down from the boat and walked upon the waters to come to Jesus.” This has been fulfilled and is being fulfilled whenever holy preachers are sent to foreign nations. Peter descended from the boat whenever a holy teacher, from the bosom of Mother Church where he had been nurtured, proceeded in compassionate condescension to those who were outside, in order to show them the way of salvation. He walked upon the waters when he both trampled down tribulations by overcoming them and subjected multitudes of people to himself by bringing them to faith in Christ.

He walked, I say, and did not stand still, because, continually fleeing farther from the things behind him, he advanced more and more toward the things before him and grew through daily increases in virtue. He did all this in order to come to Jesus, who is Savior and unchanging truth, so that, grasping him and adhering to him, he might hold in him true salvation and unchangeableness.

It follows: “But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: ‘Lord, save me.’” The strong wind is the violent effort of demons to stir up human hearts, like the waters of the sea, into the unrest of persecution against the faithful; or it is their powerful persuasion toward evil. This wind will blow strongly when, at the end of time, Satan is released in all his strength against the righteous.

This seems now to be indicated in this statement, because Peter, who is the order of preachers, is said to have been afraid when he saw the strong wind. For who, even among the perfect, will not be afraid when that monstrous persecution rages everywhere under Antichrist? In fear he will begin to sink somewhat, because, through horror at the cruelty of the punishments inflicted upon the saints and through amazement at the deceptive signs performed by the followers of Antichrist, wavering somewhat in his heart, he will feel something in the lower part of his soul by which, unless Christ’s right hand raises him, he could easily be submerged completely.

But because he will be among the chosen, he will cry out to Christ: “Lord, save me”; and thus, when Christ comes to his aid, he will be raised up. For then there will be “great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of creation until now, nor ever will be. And if those days had not been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the chosen, those days will be shortened” (Matt. XXIV, 21–22).

Hence it appropriately follows here: “And immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him: ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” The Savior will soon extend the hand of saving aid to each of his own, because he will not allow them to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear (I Cor. X). He will quickly seize each of them—that is, taking hold of them and holding them by a certain power of divine assistance, he will rescue them.

“You of little faith,” he says, “why did you doubt?” Whose faith will not falter in that tribulation, when the martyr who pours out his blood for Christ will be unable to perform any signs, while before his very eyes his torturer performs signs? Let us therefore consider what the temptation of the human mind will be then. Whose strength will not be shaken from the very depths of its thoughts when the one who torments with scourges flashes with miracles? For then Antichrist and his ministers will be driven against the righteous by such unrestrained iniquity and deceit that even the hearts of the chosen will be struck by considerable fear. Hence it is written: “So as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen” (Matt. XXIV, 24). This is said not because the chosen will fall, but because they will tremble amid great terrors as though they were about to fall.

It should also be noted that this disturbance of the waves, Peter’s wavering, and the beginning of his sinking are enacted daily even in our own time, according to the spiritual meaning. Each person’s desire is a storm. You love God: you walk upon the sea, and beneath your feet lies the swelling of the age. You love the world: it swallows you, for the world knows how to devour its lovers, not to carry them.

But when your heart is tossed by desire, call upon Christ’s divinity so that you may conquer your desire. You think that the contrary wind is present when adversity in this age arises, but not also when prosperity smiles. When there are wars, tumults, famine, pestilence, or even private calamity for individual people, then the wind is thought to be contrary, and God is thought to be invoked there. But when the world smiles with temporal prosperity, it is as though the wind were not contrary.

Do not therefore ask about the tranquility of the time; ask about your desire. See whether there is tranquility within you; see whether the inner wind is not overturning you. For it is a great virtue to struggle against prosperity, lest that prosperity entice, corrupt, or overturn you. Learn to trample the world; remember to trust in Christ. And if your foot is moved, if you waver, if you do not overcome something, if you begin to sink, cry out to Jesus: “Lord, save me.”

In Peter, therefore, the common condition of us all must be considered, so that if the wind of temptation attempts to overturn us in some way, or a wave to submerge us, we may cry out to Christ. He will extend his hand and rescue us from the depths.

It follows: “And when he had got into the boat, the wind ceased.” On the last day he will ascend into the boat of the Church, because then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty (Matt. XXV), and that throne is not inappropriately understood as the Church. For the one who now always dwells in the Church through faith and good works will then enter the Church through the manifestation of his glory. And then the wind will cease, because the demons will no longer have power to send against it the flames of temptations or the disturbances of tribulations. For then everything will be peaceful and quiet for it.

It follows: “Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Truly you are the Son of God.’” Those who faithfully come to him in the Church amid the storms of temptations will approach him joyfully; entering his kingdom with him, they will worship him and, praising him forever, will proclaim that he is truly the Son of God. For then what is said of the chosen raised from death will come to pass: “All flesh will come to worship before my face, says the Lord” (Isa. LXVI, 23). And again: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). For the one whom they believed in their heart for righteousness and confessed with their mouth for salvation (Rom. X, 10), they will see with their heart for life and praise with their mouth for glory, contemplating how he was ineffably begotten by the Father, with whom he lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IV

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

“After six days Jesus took Peter, and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain privately; and he was transfigured before them. And so forth” (Matt. XVII).

Because our Savior determined to lead his chosen, through the labors of this life, into that future life of blessedness which knows no labor, he describes in his Gospel now the sweat of temporal struggles and now the palm of eternal rewards, so that, when they hear of the necessities of the contest, they may remember that they must not seek rest in this life; and when they hear again of the sweetness of future blessedness, they may bear more lightly the passing evils which they hope will be rewarded with eternal goods.

For after he had shortly before foretold his own sufferings and those of his followers, he said: “For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his works” (Matt. XVI, 27). The disciples could have said in their thoughts: “You now say that slaughter and death are to come; but what you promise—that you will come in the glory of the Father with the ministry of angels and the power of a judge—will be deferred for a long time.”

Therefore, foreseeing what they might object, the knower of hidden things balanced present fear with a present reward. For he added: “Amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matt. XVI, 28). It was as though he said: “The kind of figure in which he will come at the end will, because of your unbelief, be shown in the present time to those who are standing here”—or, according to another reading, “living here.”

Since the time of the universal judgment is uncertain to all, and the hour of each person’s departure is uncertain to each, the present affliction could seem long to those who did not know when the promised rest would come. Therefore the gracious Teacher wished to show certain of his disciples, while they were still living on earth, a foretaste of the joys of the eternal promise, so that both those who had seen them and all who could hear about them might endure present adversities more lightly, frequently recalling to mind the reward of the future that they were awaiting.

“There are,” he says, “some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.” His disciples saw him coming in his kingdom when they saw him shining on the mountain in that glory in which, after the judgment had been completed, he will be seen by all the saints in his kingdom.

The Gospel narrative then follows with the passage about which we wish to speak: “And after six days Jesus took Peter, and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain privately.” That the Lord displayed his glory six days after promising his disciples the glory of his vision signifies that the saints will receive the kingdom on the day of judgment—the kingdom promised to them by God, who does not lie, before the times of the ages (Tit. I, 2).

For the times of the ages consist of six ages. When these have been completed, they will hear from the Lord: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34). The six days of the promised vision and glory of the Lord can also signify the perfection of good works, without which no one can reach the contemplation of the majesty of his Creator. Since the Lord formed the creation of things in six days and rested from his works on the seventh (Gen. I, 1–2), the six days rightly express the good works through which we must reach rest.

And because whoever desires to see God and attain the glory of the blessed resurrection must do the good things he knows, the Savior rightly displayed the glory of his kingdom, which he had promised to his disciples, after six days.

Luke, however, wrote as follows: “Now it happened about eight days after these words, that he took Peter, and John, and James, and went up the mountain to pray” (Luke IX, 28). According to Luke, therefore, the Lord manifested on the eighth day the glory of future blessedness promised to the disciples so that, by displaying the sweetness of heavenly life, he might warm the hearts of all who could hear of it, and teach through the number eight of the days that true joy would come at the time of the resurrection.

For he himself also rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the sixth day of the week, on which he ascended the cross, and the seventh day of the week, on which he rested in the tomb. And we, after the six ages of this world, during which we endure labors for the Lord, and after the seventh age of the sabbath-rest of souls, which is spent meanwhile in the other life, will certainly rise in the eighth age.

That Matthew, or Mark as well, says that the Lord was transfigured after six days does not differ either in chronological order or in mystical meaning from Luke, who gives eight days. Matthew relates only the intervening days, and therefore simply records that it happened after six days. Luke, however, includes both the first day, on which the Lord made this promise, and the last, on which he fulfilled his promise, and therefore, speaking more precisely, says “about eight days.”

In mystical interpretation, the one indicates that after the six ages of the world the saints will rest from all labor, while the other indicates that they will rise in the eighth age.

The Lord took three disciples with him to whom he would show his glorification, either because those who now preserve whole the faith of the Holy Trinity working through love will then rejoice perpetually in the revealed vision of it, or because there are three orders of believers in the Church who alone may deserve to reach this vision: superiors, those who practice continence, and married people. Whoever is not found in one of these three conditions will not share in the joy of this vision.

Peter, because of his primacy, signifies the leaders of the Church. John, who is said to have remained a virgin, represents the unmarried and those who despise the world. James, who is called “the supplanter,” signifies married people who use the world lawfully.

Thus the Lord leads these three disciples, through whom all the chosen are signified, up a high mountain in order to show his glory, so that he may teach all who desire to see it not to lie prostrate in lowly pleasures, not to serve carnal enticements, and not to cling to earthly desires, but always to be raised toward heavenly things by love of the eternal, and, insofar as is possible for mortals, always to imitate the life of angelic purity, devotion, peace, love, goodness, and righteousness, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven. From there also we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 20–21).

To display the glory of his majesty, he leads the disciples up the mountain, so that they may learn—and so that all who thirst to see it may learn—not to seek it in the depths of this age but in the kingdom of heavenly blessedness; and so that they may strive to become worthy to ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in his holy place.

The evangelist appropriately adds “privately” after saying that he led them up a high mountain. For the righteous, even when they are pressed by the proximity of the wicked, are nevertheless separated from them in their whole mind, intention, and execution of their works; and in the future they will be separated from them also in body and place, when the Lord will hide them in the secret place of his face from the disturbance of human beings and will protect them in his tabernacle.

According to Luke, he ascended the mountain to pray and was then to be transfigured, because he ascended into the secret height of heaven as the true High Priest, in order to intercede there for his own and manifest his glory to them; and also to show that those who await the blessed resurrection and desire to see the King in his beauty must dwell in heavenly things in their minds and persist in continual prayers.

It follows: “And he was transfigured before them. And his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow.” Luke says: “And it happened that, while he was praying, the appearance of his face became different, and his clothing was white and gleaming” (Luke IX, 29).

When the Lord was transfigured before the disciples and appeared with another form of face, he did not lose the form of his human body, but foreshadowed the glorification of himself and of his own. The appearance of his face became different—that is, it became the appearance of another glory—when it shone like the sun. The brightness of that splendor and glory belonged particularly to the nature of the humanity he had assumed.

For the ineffable and inaccessible vision of his divinity itself, which is reserved in eternal life for the blessed who are pure in heart, the disciples, still enclosed in mortal flesh, could in no way behold. In this transfiguration, therefore, the Lord both foreshadowed the glory of his body, by which it was to be illuminated through the resurrection, and foretold how great the brightness of the bodies of all the chosen would be after the resurrection.

For elsewhere he also says of them: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43). Here, as an example of his future glorification, his face shone like the sun. This does not mean that the brightness and glory of the Lord and of his saints can be equal; but because we know nothing brighter than the sun, the glory of the Lord and of the saints in the resurrection is compared to the sight of the sun. Nothing brighter than the sun could be found to provide an example for human beings.

We may also understand by his face the present and manifest knowledge of his humanity. His face therefore shone like the sun because, in the kingdom of heavenly blessedness, the contemplation of his humanity will shine upon all the saints with a single and singular brightness, just as the sun, with its unique and singular brilliance, surpasses all things that appear bright to bodily eyes.

His garments, which shone with the whiteness of snow, may appropriately be understood figuratively as his saints, since the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Gal. III, 27). These garments, while he himself lived among human beings on earth, appeared despised and like those of other people; but when he climbed the mountain, they shone with a new radiance. For, as John says: “Now we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2).

Hence Mark appropriately says of these same garments that they became shining, exceedingly white, like snow, “such as no fuller on earth can make white” (Mark IX, 3). For, as is evident to all, no one can live on earth without corruption and pain; no one can live on earth without touching some sin. But what a fuller—that is, a teacher of souls, or an exceptional purifier of his own body—cannot do on earth, the Lord will do in heaven, cleansing the Church, his garment, from every defilement of flesh and spirit, and, in addition, restoring it with the eternal blessedness and light of flesh and spirit.

It follows: “And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” Luke explained this more fully: “And behold, two men were speaking with him. They were Moses and Elijah, seen in glory, and they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem” (Luke IX, 30–31).

Moses and Elijah, who spoke with the Lord on the mountain and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem—that is, of his passion and resurrection—signify the oracles of the Law and the prophets. These were fulfilled in the Lord; they are now clear to the learned, and in the future they will become more manifest to all the chosen.

They are appropriately said to have been seen in glory, because then it will be seen more openly with what dignity of truth not only the meaning but also the wording of all the divine utterances was expressed.

We may understand his departure, in a particular sense, as the exaltation of his humanity, by which he surpassed all things, as the Apostle teaches when he says of the Father: “That you may know what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his mighty power, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things under his feet” (Eph. I, 18–22).

This is the departure, or surpassing exaltation, of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ. Although the Father worked this exaltation, the Son nevertheless worked and accomplished it no less according to the power of his divinity. For “whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John V, 19).

And he accomplished it in the Jerusalem above, where the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, is always seen (Phil. IV, 7). He will also accomplish a great departure, or exaltation, in his saints when, after the judgment, he raises them to the height of the Father’s vision.

Moses and Elijah spoke of this departure of the head and the members as something to be accomplished in the city of the great King, because the Law and the prophets continually foretold the glory of Christ’s and the Church’s exaltation.

At this point Luke alone adds: “Peter and those who were with him were weighed down with sleep. But when they awoke, they saw his majesty and the two men who stood with him” (Luke IX, 32). For he alone, who had mentioned the eighth day beforehand, now describes the likeness of the resurrection.

In Peter and his companions, as stated above, all the chosen are signified. They are weighed down by sleep while their bodies sleep in tombs until the end of the age; but on the day of the resurrection they will awaken and be raised up to see forever the glory of his majesty. They will also see the two men standing with him—that is, the truth of the meaning of the Law and the prophets, which foretold this glorification.

Alternatively, they were weighed down by sleep because the incomprehensible splendor of divinity presses upon the perception of our body like a heavy weight. And they awoke and saw his majesty because those who shake bodily sleep from their hearts and become watchful in mind are raised to the light of the heavenly vision.

[Col. 0607B]

Then Peter answered and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Luke too, when speaking of the two men, says: “And it came to pass, as they were departing from him, Peter said to Jesus, ‘Master, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tabernacles, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah’—not knowing what he was saying” (Luke 9:33).

The departure of Moses and Elijah from Christ is to be understood according to what the Apostle says: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be brought to an end” (1 Cor. 13:10). For the teaching of the law and the prophets will withdraw when the manifestation of the divine vision has appeared to the saints.

But Peter answered concerning what he was seeing: “It is good for us to be here,” and he wished to retain there the men who were already departing by constructing new tabernacles. For the more someone tastes the sweetness of heavenly life, the more he despises all that pleased him in earthly things. Therefore, having suddenly seen the majesty of the Lord and his saints, Peter deservedly forgets everything he had known on earth and delights in clinging only to what he was seeing. He desires to dwell there with Jesus, where he rejoices in the manifestation of his glory, saying: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.”

For truly the only good of a human being is to enter into the joy of his Lord and to stand forever in contemplation of him. Hence, someone whose guilt has required that he never behold the face of his Creator must rightly be thought never to have possessed any true good. But if blessed Peter, contemplating Christ’s glorified humanity, is so filled with joy that he wishes in no way to be separated from his vision, what do we suppose the blessedness of those must be who have deserved to see the height of his divinity? And if Peter considered it the greatest good to see, together with only two saints—namely Moses and Elijah—the form of Christ’s humanity transfigured on the mountain, what speech could explain, and what mind could comprehend, how great are the joys of the righteous when they have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels (Heb. 12:22), and have looked upon God himself, the architect and founder of that city, not through a mirror and in an enigma as now, but face to face (1 Cor. 13:12)?

Nevertheless, blessed Peter, in thinking that tabernacles ought to be made for the heavenly way of life, did not know what he was saying. In the glory of that heavenly life no house will be necessary, since the light of divine contemplation will pacify everything and no breath of adversity will remain to be feared. The blessed Apostle John bears witness to this when, describing the splendor of that heavenly city, he says among other things: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. 21:22).

He therefore did not know what he was saying because, carried beyond himself in mind, he did not know that in the house of the Father, which is in heaven, a house made by human hands would not be necessary. He did not know what he was saying because, wishing to retain Christ forever in that glory, he did not consider that the world could not be saved except through Christ’s death. He did not know what he was saying because he had forgotten that the kingdom had been promised by the Lord to the saints not somewhere on earth but in heaven; nor did he remember that he and his fellow apostles, still enclosed in mortal flesh, could not enter into the state of immortal life.

[Col. 0608A]

Next: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud said, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.’” Luke likewise says: “While he was saying this, a cloud came and overshadowed them; and they were afraid as they entered into the cloud. And a voice came from the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son; listen to him’” (Luke 9:34).

Because Peter was seeking to make tabernacles, he was admonished by the covering of the bright cloud that, in that dwelling of heavenly life, houses would not be necessary, where the Lord protects everything by the eternal shadowing of his light—he who dwells in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6:16). For this bright cloud, which now came upon the disciples and overshadowed them, is that inaccessible light in which God dwells. It is inaccessible to our powers, but one approaches it through divine gifts.

Moses approached the darkness in which God was (Exod. 20:21). That darkness, this cloud, and that light are the same. For every bodily light that cannot be looked upon because of the excess of its brightness can rightly be called darkness and inaccessible, as the dazzlement of our eyes proves when we look at the sun.

Concerning this cloud and light it is mystically said in Exodus: “The cloud covered the tabernacle of testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it; nor could Moses enter the tent of the covenant, because the cloud covered everything and the majesty of the Lord flashed forth” (Exod. 40:32–33). Similarly, it is written in the Third Book of Kings: “The mist filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the mist; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord. Then Solomon said: ‘The Lord said that he would dwell in the mist’” (1 Kings 8:10, 12).

Concerning this, the venerable Father Dionysius also says, as we have mentioned elsewhere:

“Divine darkness is the inaccessible light in which God is said to dwell. It is invisible because of its surpassing brightness, and inaccessible because of the supereminence of the superessential outpouring of lights. In this consists all knowledge and vision worthy of God: not seeing or knowing him, but becoming truly beyond vision and knowledge, knowing this very thing—that he is beyond all sensible and intelligible things and beyond prophetic vision. ‘Wonderful is your knowledge to me; it is strengthened, and I cannot attain it’” (Ps. 138:6).

The words of blessed Dionysius, so weighty, accord with David, who says of the Lord: “Darkness is under his feet; he mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds. And he made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:10–12).

Darkness is under his feet because he is not seen by those below with the same brightness by which he rules above. “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew.” Cherubim is said to mean “fullness of knowledge”; therefore he is declared to have mounted above the fullness of knowledge and to have flown, because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty. He flew because he carried himself far above our understanding. He flew upon the wings of the winds because he transcends the knowledge of souls. “He made darkness his hiding place” because, while we are darkened by the darkness of our weakness, he is hidden from us through our ignorance, so that we do not presently see him in eternal and intimate brightness.

He made darkness his hiding place because, in the knowledge of him, the edge of the mind of every rational creature grows dim, and whatever it can recognize concerning him seems little compared with what it perceives itself to be ignorant of. “Cloud and darkness are around him,” because he lies hidden in a certain obscurity of his incomprehensibility and cannot be known by a creature except insofar as he wishes to reveal himself.

Therefore the apostles feared as they entered this cloud, because whoever advances toward the contemplation of God so far as to see him in such a cloud of the mysteries of his obscurity does so with great reverent fear. Hence the seraphim, who know him first, veil his face and his feet and fly with their middle wings. By this we understand that even so exalted an order of blessed spirits is fearful in the presence of the higher and deeper things of divine visions and rises only moderately toward divine knowledge.

From the aforementioned cloud came the voice of the Father, saying concerning Christ: “This is my Son,” because from the immense obscurity of divine incomprehensibility there comes to us the lofty knowledge of the eternal generation of the Son of God. In that generation the Father is not earlier than the Son, nor is the Son later than the Father, because it is established that the Father eternally begot and that the Son was eternally born. But whose brightness the mind’s eye does not yet grasp—who will recount his generation? (Isa. 53:8.)

Because the apostles desired to see the shining face of the Son of Man, the Father was present in the voice, teaching that he was his beloved Son, so that they might learn to pass from the glory of his humanity, which they saw, to long to contemplate the presence of his divinity, which is equal and consubstantial with him.

When he says of the Son, “in whom I am well pleased,” this is what the same Son elsewhere testifies: “He who sent me is with me; he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John 8:29). For when he said concerning human beings, “It repents me that I made them” (Gen. 6:7), he was, as it were, displeased with himself in the sinners whom he had created.

But in the only-begotten Son he was well pleased, because he did not in any way regret creating him as a human being among human beings. In him he found no sin for which he might reproach himself, as though through repentance; rather, he found the fullness of all holiness, in which he was greatly pleased.

By adding, “Listen to him,” he indicated that he was the one concerning whom the aforementioned Moses warned the people to whom he gave the law: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him according to everything that he will speak to you” (Deut. 18:15).

For he does not forbid Moses and Elijah—that is, the law and the prophets—to be heard. Rather, he shows that the hearing of the Son, who came to fulfill the law and the prophets, must be preferred to all these, and he makes clear that the light of evangelical truth must be placed before all the types and enigmas of the Old Testament.

Matthew alone continues: “And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces and were very afraid.” Human frailty cannot endure the sight of greater glory; trembling in soul and body, it falls to the ground. All the saints, as they advance in the vision of God, recognize themselves to be nothing more the more deeply they behold the inner things of the divinity.

When Peter and his companions heard the voice of God, they fell upon their faces because, although a human being may be lifted up to understand sublime things, contemplation of God’s majesty nevertheless makes him understand the weakness of his condition. He is, as it were, without standing when he sees himself to be dust and ashes before God’s eyes.

They heard the voice of the Father because through his revelation they recognized the Son as wholly equal to him—holding all things, filling all things, encompassing all things, surpassing all things, sustaining all things, wholly present everywhere, unbounded, and incomprehensible. They fell upon their faces because they were so overwhelmed in their own thoughts by the greatness of what they were hearing. Considering the nature and excellence of God’s only-begotten Son, they were terrified and regarded themselves as contemptible in what they could comprehend, while directing their attention toward the heavenly things that they could not comprehend.

Hence Ezekiel also says concerning the winged creatures: “When there was a voice above the firmament that was over their heads, they stood and lowered their wings” (Ezek. 1:25). The creatures signify the saints. By the name “firmament” the incarnate Only-Begotten is expressed, because in him our nature has been established for eternity.

A voice therefore comes above the firmament when the Father says concerning Christ: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Then the creatures stand and lower their wings, because the saints attend to heavenly things with concentrated mind and humble their virtues. They stand when, in attentive contemplation, they consider him who is above their head—that is, above their minds. They lower their wings because their own virtues become contemptible to them when they look upon the heights of heavenly incomprehensibility.

Likewise, when it is said, “This is the Son in whom I am well pleased,” they lower their wings because, in his innocence and holiness, they see how greatly they themselves sin each day and how little of the perfection of holiness they possess; and they lay aside all presumption concerning their own strength.

[Col. 0611A]

Matthew continues: “Then Jesus approached, touched them, and said to them, ‘Rise, and do not be afraid.’” He approached the disciples lying in confusion at their weakness through grace, touched them through power, and commanded them to rise for strong deeds and to cast away the fear that love drives out. He approached and touched because he enlightened and helped.

He approaches but does not touch when we are enlightened by his grace but, because our merits demand it, are not helped. For often we see what ought to be done but are unable to accomplish it in deed. We strive and grow weak. The judgment of the mind sees what is right, but the strength of action gives way before it. Indeed, it is already part of the punishment of sin that one may see the good by gift but nevertheless be driven away from what one sees by one’s own merit.

But the Lord approached those who were prostrate, touched them, and commanded them to rise, because when we humbly lie prostrate, subtly recognizing our weakness, then we are touched by the power of the Holy Spirit and commanded to rise for vigorous works, which we perform not through fear but through love.

Matthew continues: “And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.” Luke too, while speaking of the Father’s voice, says: “A voice came from the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son,’ and so forth. And when the voice had come, Jesus was found alone” (Luke 9:35–36).

The servants disappeared so that we might recognize without doubt that Jesus alone is the natural and only Son of God, not Moses or Elijah. Those who, while lying prostrate, had fixed the eyes of their minds upon the consideration of their weakness now rose and lifted those same spiritual eyes toward the higher things of divine contemplation. Then they saw no one except Jesus alone, because no one is in the glory of God the Father except the Lord Jesus Christ, and in comparison with him none of the saints is anything. The voices of the law and the prophets cease where the Father declares his Only-Begotten with his own voice.

Next: “And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, ‘Tell no one of the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.’” Luke reports their observance of this command, saying: “And they kept silent, and in those days told no one anything of what they had seen” (Luke 9:36).

The Lord ordered the vision of his manifested majesty to remain silent for a time so that, if it were publicly proclaimed among the peoples, either those peoples might resist the rulers and impede the dispensation of his passion, thereby delaying the effect of human salvation that was to come through his blood, or else those who heard and believed the vision might be scandalized when they saw the disgrace of the cross.

After his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven had been completed, and after the apostles had been filled with the Holy Spirit, it was more fittingly proclaimed. In this way all who wished to be initiated into his sacraments could learn not only to believe in the effect of the resurrection but also to learn from those who had seen it the manner of that resurrection. They could likewise learn to believe and love together the eternity of the divine birth that the apostles had heard from the Father, and the apostles themselves could proclaim it to all.

Having said these things about the evangelical reading, it seems necessary to add that just as Moses and Elijah can signify the law and prophecy in it, so the Lord Jesus can signify the Gospel. Nevertheless, if the things contained in the reading can at some point be understood less openly as referring to the word of evangelical preaching, they should be referred to the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us.

He therefore says: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.” The Son of Man can not absurdly be understood as the evangelical word, because the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), generated it—that is, brought it forth from himself.

This word is seen in its kingdom when it appears clear and powerful, so that by its clarity it illuminates the minds of its hearers and by the power of the Holy Spirit’s virtue strengthens them, so that it may both be understood by them and fulfilled in their works. They do not taste death until they see it in this form: before they pay the debt of death, they are raised to a profound understanding of it and fulfill it through great power in their works.

This promise and gift was not given to all who stand with Christ—that is, who remain in the faith of Christ—but to some.

[Col. 0612C]

To this statement of the Lord’s words the evangelist adds: “And after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain privately.” Or, as Luke says: “It came to pass about eight days after these words, that he took Peter, John, and James and went up onto the mountain to pray” (Luke 9:28).

Jesus, that is, Savior and saving one, is the evangelical word, concerning which it is said: “Receive the implanted word, which is able to save your souls” (James 1:21); and: “I make known to you the Gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which you stand; through which also you are saved” (1 Cor. 15:1–2).

This saving and salvific word, containing within itself the grace of the Holy Spirit, took Peter, whose name is interpreted as “one who recognizes”; John, whose interpretation signifies “in whom there is grace”; and James, who is interpreted as “supplanter.” It took them after six days, or eight.

Because the works of the world were created in six days, by six days we understand the world and its works. And because the resurrection took place on the eighth day, by eight days the grace of the resurrection is expressed. Those who have risen above the world, transcended the works of this age, and awaited with a good conscience the immortal fruit of the future resurrection could be led by the Gospel word onto the mountain of sublime understanding and privately, removed from the turmoil of earthly thoughts, see the glory of the Word itself, transformed into a glorious appearance.

He ascended that mountain to pray because the Word of grace itself, while advancing before the eyes of our mind into the heights of a loftier and clearer understanding, intercedes for us in a certain sense, since it makes us spiritual and commendable to God.

Let us therefore ascend the mountain with the Word, so that it may appear to us in its form and beauty and advance prosperously and reign. For according to the measure of our capacity, the Word itself becomes smaller or greater for us. Unless we climb to the summit of higher understanding, wisdom does not appear to us, nor does knowledge of the mysteries, nor does the extent of the glory and beauty in the evangelical word appear to us. Rather, a certain baseness and contemptibility seem to be present in it.

“He was transfigured before them,” he says, “and the appearance of his face became different” (Luke 9:29), because the word of God itself is transformed into another appearance of wondrous beauty in the eyes of those whom it takes up—that is, whom it teaches—and leads onto the mountain of a higher understanding. It appears thus to those whom it leaves below in a weak understanding.

“And his face shone like the sun”: the splendor of the sight of his beauty shone forth with incomparable and singular brightness. For in comparison with it, the utterances of every particular teaching are nothing.

“His garments became white as snow, and his clothing was white and shining.” Christ’s garments are the words of the Scriptures. In the eyes of those endowed with lofty power, they become white as snow, and the words of the divine readings shine.

When snow has fallen, the birds of heaven have nowhere to dwell, and the grain harvest increases with greater abundance than usual—[a word is omitted here, perhaps *eget* or *annona*]. The words of the Scriptures are aptly compared to this: sent from heaven to earth, they have made fertile the barren fields of our breasts and left no place for aerial spirits, like unclean birds.

Next: “And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” Or: “Behold, two men were speaking with him. They were Moses and Elijah, seen in glory, and they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem” (Luke 9:30–31).

Moses and Elijah appeared on the mountain with the Lord, speaking with him, because the law and the prophets are seen with the Gospel on the height of a loftier understanding and agree with it in their statements.

They were also seen with him in glory because, to the wise and spiritual, they shine with him in the glory of divine excellence. They spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem, because they proclaimed the future exaltation of the evangelical word, by which it would surpass everything in dignity and power in the city of eternal peace and would remain without end.

Hence the Psalmist sang: “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven” (Ps. 118:89). The Lord also said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Luke 21:33).

Peter and those who were with him were weighed down by sleep because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks upon many things” (Wis. 9:15), making it sluggish as though by a kind of bodily sleep.

“And when they awoke, they saw his majesty and the two men who stood with him,” because when the mind has struggled vigorously against the torpor of negligence and overcome the sleep of ignorance, it can see the majesty of the meanings of sacred eloquence, and the law and prophecy remaining with the word of the Gospel’s grace.

Alternatively: Peter and his companions were weighed down by sleep. The saints are weighed down by sleep when they rest from earthly activity and from love of temporal things and close the eyes of the mind to the desire for visible things. They are said not simply to sleep but to be weighed down by sleep because such sleeping does not take place without the burden of labor.

Holy men, who are lulled to sleep by strength rather than by sluggishness in relation to the works of the world, sleep more laboriously than they could keep watch. For in abandoning and overcoming the activities of this age, they fight daily against themselves with strenuous conflict, lest the mind grow sluggish through negligence, lest the desire of the flesh prevail over it in anything, and lest they themselves become lazy regarding good works and heavenly desire.

“And when they awoke,” he says, “they saw his majesty,” because those who, as has been said, fall asleep with respect to external things and remain awake within penetrate the inner mysteries. Hence the bride says: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). It is as though she said: “While I lull my outward senses to sleep from the cares of this life, with my mind at leisure I come to know inner things more vividly.”

Such a soul acts so as to cast away from itself entirely the restless desire of this world and to abandon the noise of earthly thoughts; through devotion to quiet, it sleeps while keeping watch, intent upon the virtues. For one is not led to contemplate inner things unless one diligently withdraws from those things that entangle one outwardly.

Thus those who were weighed down by sleep awoke and saw his majesty, because those who fall asleep to the cares of this world and keep watch in heavenly pursuits contemplate the majesty of sacred eloquence and behold spiritual visions.

“Lord,” Peter said, “it is good for us to be here”—that is, to linger in contemplation of the majesty of the evangelical word and to behold together the law and the prophecies in the clarity of spiritual understanding. He called this word “Lord” and “Master” because he was ready to serve its commands out of love and wished to be instructed by its teachings.

But in seeking to make three tabernacles for the three, he did not know what he was saying, since there is one tabernacle of the Gospel in which the law and the prophets dwell. Even now, whoever wishes to make three tabernacles for the Gospel, the law, and the prophets is marked by ignorance, since these cannot in any way be separated from one another, possessing one tabernacle—that is, the Church of God.

Next: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud said, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.’”

Because Peter foolishly offered three tabernacles as though they were equal and divided, a bright cloud came—that is, the incomprehensibility of the mysteries, which both shines and overshadows. It illuminates the mind by revealing divine things, but it does not make God wholly manifest; rather, it conceals more about him than it reveals.

This kind of bright cloud came, I say, and overshadowed their minds with its obscure light. Entering it, they were afraid because of the incomprehensible judgments of God and because of the other things in Scripture that they were unable to comprehend with their minds.

From such great incomprehensibility of the mysteries came the voice of God, saying concerning the word of the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” For this word of grace proceeded from God and was given through God incarnate. It contains all the perfection of righteousness that mortals can grasp and declares all God’s good pleasure. Therefore he says of it, “in whom I am well pleased.”

Hence the Apostle says: “There is an annulment of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness, for the law brought nothing to perfection; but there is the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God” (Heb. 7:18–19). And again: “For if that first covenant had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second” (Heb. 8:7).

Therefore the Old Testament, which was given through a servant, retains in itself the lowliness of servitude; but the New, which was given through the Son, possesses the honor of sonship. Concerning it is said: “This is my beloved Son”; and it is added concerning him, “Listen to him,” because whatever the law of righteousness and the prophets proclaimed is contained in him, and much more besides.

For the Lord says there: “Whatever you wish that human beings should do to you, do likewise to them; for this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. 7:12). And concerning the greater righteousness that is in the New Testament than in the Old, he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matt. 5:33). Likewise: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, love your enemies and do good to those who hate you” (ibid. 5:43–44), and many other things of this kind.

Therefore, because the New Testament contains everything that the Old commanded, as well as many other things that are holier still, we are commanded to listen only to the New—that is, to obey its commands.

Next: “And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces and were very afraid.” For when we have heard the excellence of the divine word that is in the New Testament, we fall upon our faces—that is, we humble ourselves—and we are ashamed that we have not honored it as we ought by reverently obeying it in everything. For this reason we fear greatly lest we be condemned on that account.

“And Jesus approached, touched them, and said to them, ‘Rise; do not be afraid.’” The evangelical word itself, when we lie in repentance through knowledge of our guilt, becomes in a certain way closer to us. It touches us with the hand of its judgments, commands us to rise for good works, and thereafter drives away fear.

For why should one who is raised through repentance to courageous works of virtue fear any longer? “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

“When they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone”—that is, the New Testament. For when the cloud had been removed and Moses and Elijah had vanished, Christ alone was seen, because when the shadow of the law and the prophets has departed, the true light shines forth in the flashing grace of the Gospel.

Where the shadow of the law and prophecy, which covered human minds with its veil, withdraws, both are found in the Gospel. Though there were three, one has been made. Three were seen at the beginning; one at the end. For when the law, prophecy, and Gospel are considered according to the surface of the letter, they appear to be three; when they are examined according to their inner meaning, one appears.

According to spiritual understanding, the law and the prophets are nothing other than evangelical teaching.

From this point, when they are descending from the mountain—that is, returning from the height of loftier understanding and contemplation to the lowliness of ordinary life—they are commanded to tell no one this vision until after the Lord’s resurrection.

The clarity of sacred eloquence that has already been shown to the wise on this height of contemplation must not be recounted to anyone who has not yet believed that Christ has risen, because Christ himself did not open the disciples’ understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures until after the triumph of his resurrection.

Hence the Apostle concealed from certain people this glory of beautiful clarity, by which the divine word shines inwardly, saying: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). But to others who had already advanced he opened it, saying: “Among the mature we speak wisdom” (ibid. 2:6).

Smaller things must be preached to the lesser, and greater things to the greater; each person should be taught according to the measure of his capacity. Therefore the lofty vision of the clarification of the divine word should be spoken to those who possess great understanding and walk in newness of life.

Hence, as above, the word itself may be understood as the Son of Man. That word is, as it were, killed and counted among the dead by those who sin gravely against it; they are not afraid to transgress and trample upon it as though it did not exist.

While they remain such, we must not tell them of the clarification of that divine word, lest we be blamed for giving what is holy to dogs and casting pearls before swine (Matt. 7:6). But if that same word rises again in them through their repentance and improvement of life, then the vision of its glory may be proclaimed to them, since it again appears to those who reach toward the heights.

We have expounded this reading as it has been given to us from heaven and have disclosed its mysteries, so that all who have understood these things may, with the Lord’s help, strive to live and direct their attention toward heavenly things in such a way that they may deserve to rejoice in what has been said both in the present age and in the age to come, through Jesus Christ our Savior, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, before all ages, and now, and throughout all ages. Amen.

## HOMILY V

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

“The Lord Jesus said to his disciples this parable: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he had begun to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. And the rest’” (Matt. 18).

In this reading we are admonished to forgive our brothers when they sin against us, if we wish God to forgive us the sins that we have committed against him—or rather, if we wish him not to demand again from us what he has already forgiven us.

For behold, the servant who was a debtor of ten thousand talents is said to have obtained release from his entire debt from his lord. But because he later refused to forgive his fellow servant a hundred denarii, he was forced to repay everything that his lord had forgiven him.

He ought readily to have forgiven the lesser debt of his fellow servant, since he knew that greater debts had been forgiven him by his lord. But let us now examine the words of the sacred reading in order.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a king,” because, clearly, just as this king is described as acting, so it has been decreed that things will take place in the kingdom of heaven.

The kingdom of heaven is also called, in this age, the Church of the faithful, because while they strive, as far as they are able, to lead a heavenly life on earth, the Lord already reigns in them as in angels. And because of the distinction of their merit, the whole Church, whose members they are, is called the kingdom of heaven, although within it there are many who seek earthly things more than heavenly things and do not yet allow Christ to reign in their conduct as he ought.

The “king” to whom this kingdom is likened is understood to be the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return” (Luke 19:12).

He who wished to settle accounts with his servants, because he was pleased to demand in judgment an account of what each person had done. And when he began to settle accounts, one was brought before him who owed ten thousand talents.

He now begins to settle accounts, because, as Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God” (1 Pet. 4:17). He begins to settle accounts when, through the affliction of illness, he drags people to their beds and to death, so that, examining them in judgment concerning each of their acts, he compels them to render an account. Thus, when he had begun to settle accounts in this way—that is, to press various people toward death through sickness, so that they might already think themselves placed, as it were, before the tribunal in order to render an account to him—one was brought before him; that is, through the ministry of angels, one was compelled toward death who owed him ten thousand talents. This means that he was held liable for the perpetration of many grave sins.

The number ten signifies the fullness of the divine commandments, on account of the Decalogue of the Law. The thousand signifies consummate perfection. A talent, moreover, is said to be the greatest among all kinds of weights. Ten thousand talents, therefore, signify the perfection of many grave crimes, committed through the complete transgression of God’s commandments. Such a man was bound by so great a debt, and he is now said to have been brought before the king—that is, he was being driven toward death in illness by angels.

But since he had nothing with which to repay, the master ordered him to be sold, together with his wife, his children, and everything he possessed, and payment to be made. He had nothing with which to repay because, from himself, he had what enabled him to fall into guilt; but from himself he did not have what would enable him to rise again to forgiveness. And therefore the Lord ordered him to be sold—that is, to be handed over to demons for possession in eternal condemnation, and for punishments to be exacted from him. His wife means his carnal pleasure and desire; his children mean his wicked deeds; and everything he possessed means his words and thoughts.

A person is sold together with his wife, children, and everything he possesses in order to repay the debt when, through bodily death, he is removed from this life; and when, with the guilt of his carnal pleasure and desire, his deeds, words, and thoughts, he is handed over to evil spirits for eternal possession, so that, paying perpetual penalties, he may satisfy divine justice.

But that servant fell down and pleaded with him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” Then the servant fell before his master and, humbly entreating him, begged to escape being sold—that is, condemnation. This occurs when a person who fears, as one destined for condemnation, the death threatening him because of his sins humbly submits himself to divine mercy, and through true repentance and pure intention of heart turns to God, promising that thereafter he will repay God everything he owes him, if he escapes the sentence of death hanging over him.

For whoever corrects everything he has done wrongly and thereafter lives religiously repays the Lord everything he owed him. But the master had compassion on that servant, released him, and forgave him the debt. The servant humbly asked for a postponement, and the master mercifully granted forgiveness. For he released him—that is, he set him free to his own discretion, granting him again a period of life. And through this grant and through repentance, he forgave him the entire debt of his faults.

But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He seized him and began to choke him, saying: “Repay what you owe.”

While the servant was under the constraint of the aforementioned severity, he was in a certain sense standing before the face of his master. But when he was released, so that, according to the will of his free choice, he might still do good or evil, he went out from his master. For the Lord God is everywhere, and no one can go out anywhere where he is not present. But, as I have said, he went out—not spatially, but by his being released from his master to his own discretion—when he was again handed over to his own choice.

When he went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. This fellow servant was another human being who had resolved to serve Christ the King together with him. But he owed him a hundred denarii because he had sinned against him by committing some injury against him. A hundred denarii signify the sins that one human being commits against another, just as ten thousand talents signify what one does against God. For just as the quantity and number of a hundred denarii are small in comparison with ten thousand talents, so whatever a human being sins against us is small and rare in comparison with the faults we commit against God night and day and at every hour.

Although the number one hundred signifies perfection, the number one thousand nevertheless designates a much fuller consummation. A talent also surpasses the smallness of a denarius by an extraordinary magnitude. From these things it is clearly demonstrated that the sins we commit against God are great and numerous, whereas the sins human beings commit against us are small and few. Therefore, if God willingly forgives us the many and great evils we have committed against him, we ought much more readily to forgive people the few and small things in which they have offended against us.

But this servant did not wish to act in that way. For, as has been said, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii, and he seized him and began to choke him.

He seized him because he did not wish to forgive him what he had sinned against him. And he choked him—that is, he spiritually constricted him and tried to extinguish him in the guilt of the sin he had committed against him. A person holds a debtor fellow servant—that is, a brother who has sinned against him—when he does not forgive him what he has done against him, but preserves in his heart the memory of the injury he suffered from him. He also chokes him when he spiritually strangles his soul, oppresses it, and constricts it in the danger of sin, not forgiving him what he committed against him but binding him in guilt.

“Repay,” he said, “what you owe,” that is, “Now, without delay, pay me what is right for all the injuries you have done to me.”

And his fellow servant fell down and pleaded with him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you.” His fellow servant fell down and pleaded with him because he humbly asked him at least for a postponement, saying: “Have patience”—that is, “Wait for me patiently”—“and I will repay you everything,” that is, “I will correct everything in which I have sinned against you, and thereafter I will treat you well.”

But he refused. Instead, he went away and put him in prison until he should repay the debt. He did not wish to wait patiently for his fellow servant, so that he might be able to amend his ways; he did not wish to grant him a delay. Instead, disregarding his master, he went away and put him in prison.

He went away—that is, he proceeded by apostatizing and turning backward into worse things—and he put him in prison until he should repay the debt; that is, insofar as his malicious obstinacy was concerned, he plunged him into hell until he should pay everlasting penalties for his guilt.

There are, indeed, some people of wicked disposition, represented by this servant, who, forgetful of the grave sins they themselves have committed, become offended even by a slight fault of a brother who sins against them and burst into such obstinacy that—something which is also unspeakable—they would wish their brother to perish first in eternal punishments rather than forgive him what he had done against them.

When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were deeply grieved. And they came and reported to their master everything that had taken place.

His fellow servants here are understood as priests and religious men, who, seeing what he had wickedly done to his brother, were deeply grieved. And they came and reported all these things to their master because they returned to their own heart and, directing their attention there toward the divine presence, complained before him in their prayers about all these matters.

Alternatively, the holy angels may be understood as the fellow servants. When John wished to worship an angel in the Apocalypse, the angel said to him: “See that you do not do it; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Rev. 22:9). The angels, therefore, are fellow servants. They saw what was being done by the evil servant and were deeply grieved, because, assigned to watch over us, they carefully observe everything we do. They rejoice over our good deeds but grieve over our evil ones.

They cannot, however, be affected by sadness, because they are perfectly blessed; rather, the fact that our evil deeds displease them is called their sadness. Thus they were deeply grieved—that is, they were greatly displeased by what they saw being done unjustly.

And they came and reported to their master everything that had happened because they report to God all that we do, whether good or evil, so that they may know what he commands to be done concerning all these things.

Then his master summoned him and said to him: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me. Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?”

The Lord summons the ungrateful servant again and rebukes him for refusing to have mercy on his fellow servant after receiving mercy from the Lord. When a person who has received forgiveness from God forgets it and refuses to forgive his brother what he has done against him, the Lord recalls him to death through bodily illness and thus to judgment; and he again brings upon his head even those sins which, to his joy, had already been forgiven through repentance. “For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy” (Jas. 2:13).

Hence it is added: “And his master became angry and handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.”

Because he refused to forgive his brother and instead put him in prison on account of the debt, he deservedly lost the forgiveness he had received and fell into the hands of the torturers. For whoever, when asked, does not free a human being made in the image of God from sin, but through the hardness of his mind, insofar as it lies within him, hands him over to be punished in the prison of Tartarus, is hateful to God and undoubtedly acquires the same condemnation for himself.

His master therefore became angry—that is, he exercised against him the severity of just vengeance. God cannot become angry in his nature, since he always remains tranquil and unchangeable; but he appears angry to those to whom he renders punishment. Therefore the punishment itself is called his anger.

Thus, in his anger, he handed him over to the torturers—that is, to evil spirits, who would torment him in hell—until he should repay the entire debt, that is, without end. For whoever has once been handed over irrevocably to cruel angels, whose office it is to torment the rejected, is never afterward able to repay the debt, because he cannot correct through repentance and good works what he has done wrongly. Therefore he is compelled always to endure punishments.

But what this parable tends toward the Lord subsequently makes clear by adding: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.”

Just as he recalled from the servant everything he had forgiven and condemned him when he could not repay, because he had refused to forgive his fellow servant, so also my Father will again demand from each of you whatever he forgave you through repentance, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart every offense he has committed against you.

Thus my Father will recall each of you to judgment and will demand back what, moved by mercy, he first forgave; and he will hand you over to the angelic torturers if each of you does not forgive his brother every sin that brother has committed against you. You must forgive it not hypocritically, but truly from your hearts, so that, when you have forgiven it with your mouth, it does not remain in your heart.

The Father, however, will not carry out judgments of this kind by himself, but through the Son, because, as the Apostle testifies: “God will judge the secrets of human beings through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 2:16). The sin of your brother must therefore be forgiven from your hearts because God will judge the secrets of human beings, lest he see it now lying hidden in the secret places of our hearts and then inflict manifest condemnation for it.

Let us strive to have mercy and love toward our neighbor, mercifully forgiving him whatever he has done against us and loving him with a pure heart, so that we too may receive a similar return from our gracious Judge, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VI

## ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

“After the days of their purification according to the law of Moses had been completed, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.’” And so forth (Luke 2:22).

As we celebrate the splendid festival of this day, let us rejoice over the benefits divinely granted to us in it. For neither the Virgin, who was worthy to conceive from the Holy Spirit, nor the Son whom she thus bore had any need of purification. Rather, in their purification God prepared and prefigured our purification—we who, infected with many impurities, need purification of many kinds.

Therefore, what is now narrated historically about the Lord in the Gospel reading should be understood spiritually about us. For if we are his members or his body, he is in us; and what happens to us is rightly said also to happen to him. For the body of Christ, which is the Church, is also called Christ, as the Apostle says: “As the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Cor. 12:12).

It is therefore clear that all the faithful together with their head are Christ, as can also be proved from many other passages of Scripture. When, then, we speak of Christ’s purification, let us refer it to that part of him which needs purification, namely, the body.
