Thus what is now read historically about the head should mystically be referred either to the body or to any one of its members: “After the days of their purification according to the law of Moses had been completed, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord.”

The days of purification of the faithful people, or of the Church—that is, of the body of Christ—are indeed completed daily, while each of them continually strives to be purified and cleansed more and more; but they will not be completed entirely until the end of the age. Yet the end of the age for each individual is the hour of his death. Whoever is found cleansed from all sins at his death has completed the days of his purification according to the law of Moses.

For according to the Law this purification took place over forty days, and the number forty signifies either the period extending to the end of the age or the span of each one of our lives. When such a period of forty has been completed, the days of purification of the Church or of any one of the righteous will have been fulfilled.

Thus the Law says: “If a woman, having conceived seed, gives birth to a male child, she shall be unclean for seven days, as during the days of the separation of her menstrual flow; and on the eighth day the little child shall be circumcised. She herself shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. She shall touch no holy thing, nor enter the sanctuary, until the days of her purification have been fulfilled” (Lev. 12:2–4).

And who is this woman except the Church of the elect, or the person of the preachers? For, having received the seed of the word of God, she gives birth from it to a male child—that is, through preaching she spiritually generates a strong and new people of the elect.

Her forty days of purification, divided into seven and thirty-three, can, if explained separately, signify twice what they signify when joined together, on account of the confirmation provided by repetition. For this mother with her offspring is unclean for seven days because the holy Church, or the person of the preachers, together with those whom she has begotten in faith, is not without some stain of sin throughout the whole period of the present life, which is conducted in seven days.

For she sees “another law in her members warring against the law of her mind” (Rom. 7:23). And therefore she remains unclean according to the days of menstrual separation. For just as a menstruating woman is separated from the assembly of the clean during the days of her impurity, so this Church is separated from the assembly of the angels during the days of her mortality.

A menstruating woman is not touched by another’s flesh but is polluted by the flow of her own impurity; and she signifies the soul that is secretly defiled not by action but by a sordid thought. Likewise the Church of the saints, or the elect soul, while it lives in the flesh of sin, although not by deed, is nevertheless often defiled by sinful thought; and for this reason it is still judged unworthy of the fellowship of the blessed angels.

The eighth day, on which the little child is circumcised, is the day of baptism. On it every neophyte is stripped of the stain of his first generation, and, rising from the bath, becomes a participant in Christ’s resurrection, which illumined the world on the eighth day.

For this reason we have referred the eighth day, on which the child is circumcised, not to the time of the eternal resurrection of all, but to Christ’s resurrection—that is, to the baptism of each one of us. The child, after being circumcised, did not enter the sanctuary until the thirty-three days had been completed; likewise, although each of us has been baptized, we cannot enter the temple of heavenly blessedness until the period of mortal life, signified by the thirty-three days, has run its course.

For this entire number consists of threes and signifies the time of faith. Thus, with her son circumcised, the mother remains thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. For, together with each baptized elect person, holy Mother Church, as long as she walks by faith and not by sight, cannot be wholly cleansed from the blood of her purification—that is, from the sin from which she continually strives to purify herself but cannot attain perfection while she still bears a mortal body.

Hence the Psalmist says: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2). And Solomon says: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins” (Eccl. 7:21). And the disciple whom Jesus loved says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

It is therefore established that all who live in the flesh of sin cannot completely strip away the impurity of sin. Hence it is further said concerning Mother Church: “She shall touch no holy thing”—namely, that perfect purity possessed by the angels—“nor enter the sanctuary,” understood as the heavenly homeland, “until the days of her purification have been completed” (Lev. 12:4); that is, until the period of mortal life, during which she is continually purified but does not attain the perfection of purification, has been completed for her.

So great and so persistent is the pollution that the unclean spirit poured into the human race through Eve that it cannot be completely cleansed away until the end of mortal life or of the age arrives. But just as pollution came through Eve, so cleansing returns through Mary.

The perfection of purification and cleansing will come when the righteous, triumphing in the resurrection, say: “Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting? For the sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. 15:55–56).

In these ways, then, the days of purification of God’s people are fulfilled according to the law of Moses. But when the days of purification have been fulfilled in this way, the angels will carry him to the heavenly Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, where he will remain perpetually before him.

And this will happen because it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” For we know that the Law is spiritual; and, speaking spiritually, it signifies a spiritual womb and a spiritual male.

This male is the strong and new people of the elect Christians, or each one of them. And because the Church, according to Isaiah (ch. 54), had long been barren, this people, spiritually born from her, opened her womb—that is, her generative secret—since no one had previously been born in this way.

“Every” signifies universality. The word is placed here when it says “every male,” because this people is catholic and contains all the elect within itself. Thus he who opens the spiritual womb of the Church, as we have said, will be called holy to the Lord—that is, he will obtain the name and praise of holiness in the kingdom of heavenly blessedness, so that, made equal to the blessed angels in all holiness, he may stand perpetually before the presence of the Creator’s glory.

For this reason Christ the Lord and his most holy mother observed the purification prescribed by the Law, so that all those whom he knew would become his members might be purified in such a way as to be made worthy to attain this glory. Neither he nor, as has also been said above, his Virgin mother needed purification, because the Holy Spirit had already purified her from the beginning, and he created for himself in her womb flesh so pure that through it he might make the flesh of his own people as pure as the angels. He also assumed there a soul so holy that through it he might restore to the souls of all his people the holiness that remains in the angels.

But because he is in his people, what is done concerning his people is, as has already been stated, said to be done concerning him, because they are his body. Concerning this body it is subsequently added: “And to offer a sacrifice according to what was said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

For they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as we have explained, and to offer a sacrifice for him according to what was said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves, that is, equal purity of his body and soul; or two young pigeons (Lev. 12:8), that is, patience of his flesh and heart.

The turtledove is an exceptionally chaste bird, preserving unbroken fidelity to its living and dead mate; the dove, however, is without gall and bitterness. Therefore a pair of turtledoves signifies the chastity of the inner and outer person, while the two young pigeons signify patience displayed outwardly by the strong and preserved inwardly in the mind.

The angels therefore offer a sacrifice according to the Law—a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons—for the people of the saints, or for any elect person whom they present to God, when they represent to the Lord the merits of the chastity he preserved in body and heart, or of the patience he guarded inwardly and outwardly.

Chastity appears to pertain more especially to confessors, and patience more especially to martyrs. Since there is no elect person who is not counted either among confessors or among martyrs, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons is sufficient as the sacrifice of God’s people.

Patience is signified here by young pigeons rather than by adult doves because those who preserve patience as they ought are little and lowly in their own estimation, and continually grow greater by imitating those who are greater.

Thus, after the general resurrection has been completed, the angels will joyfully carry the entire people of the elect to the heavenly Jerusalem, together with the sacrifices of good works, to present them to the Lord. Since the Redeemer’s ascension, they have not ceased carrying each individual who migrates there when his days of purification have been completed.

And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel; and the Holy Spirit was in him. He had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he had first seen the Christ of the Lord. And he came in the Spirit into the temple.

This man signifies the holy people of the Israelite nation, who awaited the coming of the Redeemer for a long time and hoped to be freed by him from the miseries of this exile. Hence he is called Simeon, which means “hearing sorrow,” because that faithful people was accustomed through the Scriptures to hear of the sorrow of its expulsion from paradise and the loss of eternal goods. Therefore it awaited consolation concerning these things, believing that it would come to it from God.

Another interpretation of Simeon is “being heard,” because the Hebrew people used to hear God commanding so that God might hear them when they prayed. For the passage now concerns only its elect portion. For this reason he is also called a man, because he knew how to use reason in the knowledge of divine things and in seeking escape from this misery.

And he was in Jerusalem—that is, in the city of the great King, by which we are forbidden to swear; in the city of God, which is the Church. For, as we said above, Jerusalem signifies both the kingdom of heavenly blessedness and the Church of the righteous still journeying on earth.

In this Jerusalem—that is, in the number of the faithful—the Hebrew people had already long been present when the child was carried to the temple. This was at the beginnings of apostolic preaching, when, after the entrance into heaven had been opened through Christ, the new Christian people, in the persons of those among them who were migrating from this world, was already being carried there by angels.

For that elect people of the Hebrews persevered until the grace of the New Testament began to be preached everywhere through new teachers and many believers entered the homeland of eternal happiness by a blessed passage.

This man, through whom that holy people is mystically understood, was righteous because that people, serving God, gave God what belonged to God. Justice gives each person what is his; and human nature belongs to God, so that it may serve his will. Therefore every person who obeys God acts justly.

That people was also devout because it feared God either through fear of the Law or through the fear of love. It also awaited the consolation of Israel because, amid the pressures of this exile, it anxiously waited for the time when the Lord would deign to console his people through his coming.

The Holy Spirit was also in him because he could not have been justified through the Law unless the hidden grace of the Holy Spirit had justified him through faith in Christ.

He had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he had first seen the Christ of the Lord, because heavenly inspiration had revealed to his desires and prayers that he would live in faith and would not undergo the death of unbelief until he saw God, present in the flesh, anointed by God above his fellow participants; and they would demonstrate that participation even in their name, so that they would be called Christians from Christ.

And he came in the Spirit into the temple because he frequently came there in spirit through contemplation and prophetic vision—the place to which all the righteous will come after the resurrection in their bodies—entering, that is, the sanctuary of God and understanding the final things.

And when his parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he also took him in his arms and blessed God. And he said:

“Now you release your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel.”

The child Jesus, according to what was discussed above, should be understood in the new people of believers, because the Church is his body and all the saints are his members. Therefore what is narrated concerning the head should now be understood concerning the body or its members.

This is also the meaning of what he himself will say: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40). Thus “the child Jesus” should now be understood as though it said: “the new people of Christians.”

But who are his parents except the angels? They also show that they possess with us a kind of spiritual kinship, when they call us their brothers in the Apocalypse, saying: “The accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accused them before the presence of our God” (Rev. 12:10).

These parents therefore bring in our child, as was explained above, into the temple of the heavenly sanctuary, either at the death of individuals or at the resurrection of all. They do this in order to fulfill for him the custom of the Law, because, when purification according to the rite of the Law has been completed, they present him to the Lord with offerings of meritorious deeds.

Alternatively, these parents may be understood as the holy preachers. Because they received the keys of the kingdom of heaven in Peter, they open it to the new people of the faithful and bring them into the temple of that heavenly kingdom when they absolve, bless, and pray for them, asking that, when they depart from here, they may be received there.

They do this to fulfill the rite of the Law, because through their prayers they bring the people into that sanctuary of blessedness in such a way that, as the Law had decreed, when the days of purification have been completed at the end, they present them to the Lord with the offering of their merits.

This child who is brought into the temple may also now signify those who, coming to the faith, are brought into the Church. The holy Fathers carry out this bringing-in so as to observe the custom of the Law: when purification has been completed in baptism, they bring them to the holy altar to be consecrated as the divine Eucharistic victim.

Thus, when the new people of the faithful, like a child, began to be brought by their parents—that is, by angels or preachers—during the time of the radiant Gospel, as we have explained, into the temple of heavenly holiness and blessedness in the persons of those who were migrating from this light, or when those coming to the faith were brought into the Church, Simeon also took him in his arms. That is, the religious people of the Hebrews also embraced him in the arms of charity as their beloved.

Embracing signifies charity, and arms signify strong works. Therefore to receive someone in one’s arms is to embrace him with the strong works of love.

In this way he received him in his arms—that is, carrying him in his arms through the strong works of great charity—and blessed God, who had shown him present the people of the new grace, continually entering the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom. And he said:

“Now”—that is, after grace has been given—“you release, Lord, your servant in peace”; that is, “You release me from the prison of this present exile, which oppressed me under the servitude of the Law, so that I may now pass in peace to the homeland of the heavenly dwelling, with the prince of death bound through Christ’s triumph, according to the word you had spoken to me concerning the coming of grace.”

“For behold, now, either in himself or in his people, my eyes have seen, Lord, your salvation”—that is, your Jesus, whose name is interpreted as “salvation” or “Savior,” and who was sent by you to save the world.

This salvation you prepared before the face of all peoples, so that you might cause the Savior of the world to be seen by the eyes of faith by all the peoples who are in the world.

You prepared him, I say, as a light for revelation to the Gentiles, so that the darkness with which the hearts of the Gentiles were veiled, preventing them from being illumined by divine understanding, might be driven away by the splendor of his radiance; and as the glory of your people Israel, so that he himself might be the glory of the believing people of Israel, which has always been yours.

For it is a great glory for believing Hebrews that God assumed flesh from their race—he who also illumined the Gentiles through faith in him, saying: “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness” (John 12:46).

Hence the beautiful custom of the Church has arisen that the faithful carry candles or tapers in this celebration. Because Christ was offered in the temple today, they represent this very thing through their mystical offering when, each year as the feast returns, they carry candles to the house of God.

The taper or candle signifies Christ. And because each devout person who comes to this solemnity brings Christ, the true light, in his breast, he fittingly presents a candle in offering.

Three things are offered in a candle: wax, wick, and flame. The wax, which a virgin bee has made, signifies the flesh of Christ, which the Virgin Mary bore; the inner wick signifies the soul; and the upper flame signifies the divinity. Nothing can be found in creation by which Christ could be represented more fittingly.

The beauty of this festival is also increased by the fact that the glory of that great procession was appropriately redirected toward it. In this month, which is called February—that is, “the month of purification”—the ancient Romans used to hold that procession, purifying the city in the fifth year by going around it; and, as they thought, cleansing it from the sins they had committed during those five years.

For lustrare means both to go around and to purify. Our festival too is one of purification. Therefore the procession of purification has fittingly been transferred to it, although it is carried out by us in a manner very different from that of the pagans.

The Gospel reading, the festival, and its season all signify purification, so that through all these things we, who need purification, may deserve to be purified with the grace of Christ cooperating with us. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong all honor and glory, both before the world existed, now, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY VII

## ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

“His parents went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast; and when the days had been completed and they were returning, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.” And so forth (Luke 2:41).

[Col. 0628A]

The devout parents of the Savior went to Jerusalem every year, in accordance with the commandment of the law, in order to hear the law, participate in sacrifices, and attend the solemnities; they were still serving its shadow, whose reality they possessed. They signified the Jews, from whom the Lord assumed flesh, and who continually observed the rite of the old observance.

Mystically, he himself was twelve years old when his preaching had advanced to the point that it was entrusted to the twelve apostles, who through it would make known the knowledge of the supreme Trinity to the four parts of the world; for twelve is three times four. Then his parents went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, because the Jews, in accordance with the custom of festive rejoicing practiced by those who turn to God, [Col. 0628B] were raised to spiritual understanding and came by faith to the Church.

At last, when the days had been completed and the solemnity finished, as they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem. The solemnities of the Jews were completed when, after our Savior rose from the dead, the old things passed away and all things became new. And then, when the unbelieving Jews were returning to the things behind them, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace” and signifies the Church. Hence it is also said: “His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV, 2).

But his parents—that is, the Synagogue and the Jewish people—did not know this. Thinking that he was in their company, they traveled a day’s journey; by this is understood the period during which, after his resurrection, [Col. 0628C] they did not yet recognize that they were in error. For in their blindness they still thought that he was with them whom they had already killed and had heard saying: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 38); and in the Psalms: “Behold, I have gone far away, fleeing, and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV, 8).

But when they sought him among their relatives and acquaintances and did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him. This was fulfilled spiritually when, after Christ’s Passion, certain Jews, pierced in heart, came to the apostles. For this was to seek Christ and to return to Jerusalem. And they said: “What shall we do, brothers?” To them blessed Peter said: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (Acts II, 38).

Thus his parents signified these and the others who [Col. 0628D] believed at that time, because just as those parents had unknowingly lost him, so these had unknowingly killed him. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8).

And it came to pass that after three days they found him sitting in the temple, in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. Jesus is found in the temple after three days because, after the resurrection that took place on the third day, he is found in the Church by those who seek him. Before the three days he was not found, because people thought that he was not God but merely human.

But where is he found? In the temple, in the Church, in the assembly of the faithful, in the midst of the teachers, in the gathering of preachers. [Col. 0629A] There he is found listening to them and asking questions.

For us, listening is to lend an ear to a sound coming from elsewhere. But for God, to whom nothing is external, listening properly means perceiving our desires as they arise beneath him. He customarily questions us in three ways: either he strikes us with the severity of a scourge and shows how much patience we possess or lack; or he commands certain things that we do not want, thereby revealing to us our obedience or disobedience; or he discloses some hidden things to us and conceals others, making us aware of the measure of our humility. It is chiefly in this third way that he questions the teachers.

“All who heard him,” it says, “were astonished at his understanding and his answers.” Whoever still hears him with the ear [Col. 0629B] of the heart is astonished at his understanding, as was blessed Job, who had spoken wisely among human beings but, after hearing the words of God, declared that he had spoken foolishly.

His answers, too, are astonishing. For his answering means that he instructs by hidden inspirations the person who has recognized himself as humbly ignorant. He answers from the authority of inspiration and wonderfully teaches the minds of the humble. He answers, as it is also said elsewhere to him: “Call me, and I will answer you; or rather, I will speak, and you answer me” (Job XIII, 22).

God’s calling is to look upon us with love and election. Our answering, however, is to respond to his love through good works. We also speak when, through desire, we ask for his face. And he answers those who speak when he appears to us [Col. 0629C] who love him.

It follows: “And when they saw him, they were astonished.” His parents were astonished when they saw him sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers. To this day, whatever Jews come to the Church and are converted to the faith are astonished when they see there the Messiah, that is, Christ, whom in the Synagogue and among their relatives and acquaintances they were unable to see or understand through any of their interpretations.

And his mother said to him: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow.” We have said that the Lord’s mother signifies the Synagogue, from which the Lord took his origin according to the flesh. Whenever this Synagogue comes to the Church, understands the truth there, and marvels at its own ignorance [Col. 0629D] and at Christ’s absence, it says in astonishment: “Son, why have you treated us so? Why have you left us and passed over to the Church of the Gentiles? Behold, your father, the Jewish people, and I have been seeking you in sorrow.”

For this is what the Apostle says: “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X, 2). They seek Jesus and do not find him because they have not yet reached the temple and the Church.

And he said to them: “What is the reason that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” What does it mean, he says, that you were seeking me among the assembly of unbelievers and thought that I was outside the Church? Let the one who wishes to seek me seek me here. Or did you not know [Col. 0630A] that I must be in the things that belong to my Father, and among those who do the will of my Father?

And they themselves did not understand the word that he spoke to them. They did not understand because they had a blinded heart and did not recognize that Christ was in the Church of the Gentiles, since “a hardening has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel is saved” (Rom. XI, 25).

Since the Savior will return at the end of time to the remnant of Israel, it is appropriately added: “And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.” He will finally descend with the Hebrews and come to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, because with those who had believed from the circumcision he mercifully inclined himself toward the people of Israel. This, however, is still future, although we recount it as though it had already happened.

“And he was subject to them.” [173; Col. 0630B] As the Apostle also says concerning the Holy Spirit, “the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets,” so that it might do their will and not oppose their judgment. In this way, just as the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets, so the wisdom of preachers is subject to preachers. The wisdom of preachers, or teachers, is Christ.

“And his mother kept all these words in her heart.” The devout people of the circumcision carefully retained—or rather, will retain—the mysteries of Christ in their heart.

“And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and human beings.” Jesus advanced because the word of his preaching increased. He advanced in wisdom, because ever greater wisdom was found in [Col. 0630C] his teaching. He advanced in age, because the age of the advancing soul was continually found to be more mature in his speech. He advanced in grace, because by daily progress he gave greater grace to his own. This progress did not take place for himself but for his own.

He advanced with God and human beings because all these things were done both for the glory of God and for the salvation of human beings; and they became increasingly known to the angels who are with God, and to human beings as an example. Therefore praise and honor be given to that devout Savior, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout infinite ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VIII

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

“It came to pass, when all the people had been baptized, and Jesus had been baptized and was praying, that heaven was opened. And the rest” (Luke III, 21).

John baptized all the people who came to him. For if he had baptized the Lord alone, there would have been people who thought that John’s baptism was holier than Christ’s, as though Christ alone had been worthy to be baptized with John’s baptism, while the human race had received Christ’s baptism.

If Christ alone had been baptized with John’s baptism, people would have said: “What sort of baptism did John have? He had a great baptism, an ineffable sacrament. See: Christ alone was worthy to be baptized with John’s baptism.” Thus the baptism of the servant would have appeared greater than the baptism of the Lord.

Therefore others were also baptized with John’s baptism, so that John’s baptism would not appear better than Christ’s. The Lord was baptized so that, when the Lord received the servant’s baptism, the other servants would not disdain to receive the Lord’s baptism.

The Lord was baptized not in order to be cleansed by the waters, but desiring to cleanse the waters themselves. Washed through contact with his flesh, which certainly knew no sin, they would assume the right of baptism; and what so many baptisms under the law had been unable to accomplish, they would receive the power of regenerative sanctification against the evil of transgression.

Hence the evangelist rightly, when he said that all the people had been baptized, added nothing remarkable; but, after saying that Jesus had been baptized and was praying, he immediately declared that heaven had been opened. For when the Savior entered the waters of the river in the humility of his body, by the power of his divinity he opened for us the gates of heaven. And when he dipped his innocent flesh in the cold waters, he extinguished the fiery sword once placed before the gate of paradise against sinners.

For the whole mass of human nature had been expelled from paradise in our first parents, and from that time the heavenly gate had been closed to it. But the Lord mercifully deigned to become a participant in this nature, in order to plead the cause of the entire human race through it, as a true advocate.

This is why, after being baptized, he now began to pray. For just as he was baptized for us, so he also prayed for us. He is our high priest, and for us he opened heaven to his own humanity—a heaven that, as we have said, had been closed to the whole mass of the human race—and through that humanity he opened it to all who would become his members.

It follows: “And the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form, like a dove.” The Holy Spirit rightly descended in bodily form, because the Son, by assuming the reality of a body, had already descended.

And rightly the Spirit descended upon him like a dove, to make his gentleness known to us. He himself is the judge of the human race. But who could endure his justice if, before correcting us through gentleness, he had wished to examine our faults with the zeal of righteousness?

Therefore, having become human for human beings, he showed himself to be a gentle human being. He did not wish to strike sinners but to correct them. First he wished to correct them gently, so that he might have people whom he could save in judgment after they had been cleansed.

Thus the Spirit ought to appear above him in the form of a dove, since he had not come at that time to strike sins with zeal, but still to endure them with gentleness. The Holy Spirit did not then descend upon him because he was receiving the Holy Spirit for the first time; from the beginning of his conception he had always remained full of the Holy Spirit.

It follows: “And a voice came from heaven: You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.” The Father sent forth this voice, sounding physically through an angelic creature.

“You,” he says, “are my Son.” By this voice he was not teaching the Son himself, who had always known everything, but John and the others who were present, so that they might know who the one was whom they thought to be Joseph’s son. Hence Matthew preferred to report the Father’s voice as saying: “This is my Son.”

What he said, then, means this: “You are my Son, naturally begotten equal to me from my substance; and for this reason beloved, as the only-begotten. In you I am well pleased”—that is, I am pleased with everything that is in you and with everything that you have done, because I have never found anything in you except what always pleases me. For this reason it is pleasing to me that I have made you human.

But in those people I was in a certain way displeased with myself, concerning whom I once spoke in human fashion: “It repents me that I have made them” (Gen. VI, 7).

What we have said concerning the head must be referred to the members, or the body. For when Jesus had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened, because whenever one of his elect has been baptized and is not idle but occupied with devoted prayers and undertakes the path of virtues, then the gate of the heavenly kingdom is opened to him.

“And the Holy Spirit descended upon him,” because the gracious Spirit comes in bodily form upon the one who has been baptized and prays, to signify the firmness of his gift. “Like a dove,” to show that he brings innocence and simplicity to such people.

“And a voice came from heaven: You are my Son,” because each person is first a son of God when he rises from baptism. “And my beloved,” through my preceding grace, because you were previously hateful in your wickedness. “In you I am well pleased”: everything that I have brought about in you is pleasing, whereas until now whatever you yourself had done had been displeasing.

In the fact that the Father sounds forth in a voice, the Holy Spirit descends in a dove, and the Son is baptized as a human being, the Trinity is clearly declared. In its name and faith each one of us is baptized.

It follows: “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being thought to be the son of Joseph.” Jesus was baptized at the age of thirty, and only then began to perform signs and preach the Gospel, thereby showing the legitimate and mature period of life to those who think that any age is suitable for the priesthood or teaching.

Joseph, too, as a type of our Savior, was thirty years old when he took up the government of the kingdom; David began to reign at thirty, [174] and Ezekiel was of the same age when he began his prophecy. Therefore, those who become priests or teachers, or receive some such position of leadership, ought to have this age as an example from Christ.

The Savior’s age of thirty at baptism can also disclose the mystery of our baptism, namely, faith in the Holy Trinity [Col. 0630D] and the practice of the Decalogue of the law. The three decades that constitute thirty signify the faith and works of those who benefit from baptism: faith in the number three and works in the number ten.

For the Lord commanded those who are baptized to have these three decades when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

“Being thought,” he says, “to be the son of Joseph.” This was said on account of those who truly thought that he had been begotten carnally from Joseph’s flesh. And since his genealogy had to be recorded through Joseph, who was related to the Virgin Mary—for she conceived Christ from the Holy Spirit—it was necessary to do this because it is not the custom of the Scriptures [Col. 0633A] to construct genealogies through women.

For this reason Christ’s genealogy is appropriately recorded through Joseph, because he was born from Joseph’s wife, although she was always a virgin. When Joseph had been named, it was added: “Who was of Heli, who was of Matthan, who was of Levi” (Luke III, 23), and so forth.

Matthew, however, proceeding downward, says: “Matthan begot Jacob, and Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary” (Matt. I, 15). How does Joseph appear to have had two fathers, namely Heli and Jacob?

The difficulty of this question is resolved as follows. Matthan and Mathat each fathered a son by one and the same wife, named Esta. Matthan, who descended through Solomon, had taken her first as his wife; and after leaving behind one son, named Jacob, he died.

After his death Mathat, who [Col. 0633B] traced his lineage through Nathan, took her as his wife. He belonged to the same tribe, though not to the same family, and fathered by her a son named Heli. Thus Jacob and Heli became uterine brothers through different paternal lines.

One of them, namely Jacob, took the wife of his brother Heli, who had died childless, in obedience to the commandment of the law, and fathered Joseph by her. By nature Joseph was his own son, which is why it is written: “Jacob begot Joseph.” According to the commandment of the law, however, he became Heli’s son, since Jacob, being his brother, had taken Heli’s wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother.

Thus both genealogies are found to be valid and intact: the one Matthew reports, saying, “Jacob begot Joseph,” and the one Luke records, saying that he was thought to be the son of Joseph, who was of Heli. Joseph himself, with the same distinction [Col. 0633C] implied, was thought to be the son of Heli, who had been the son of Matthat.

The evangelist indicated this legal succession, which exists as a kind of adoption on behalf of the dead rather than through actual blood descent, with an entirely appropriate sign: he took care not to say that anyone had begotten another in such successions.

Nor should you be surprised that Luke placed more successions from David to Christ, and Matthew fewer—Luke forty-three and Matthew twenty-eight—since the descent of the genealogy proceeded through different persons. It can happen that some people live to an advanced age, while men of another generation die in the prime of life. We see some old men living together with their grandsons, while other men die immediately after their sons are born.

Luke does not [Col. 0633D] recount the generations from the beginning of his Gospel, as Matthew does, but from Christ’s baptism. Nor does he proceed downward, but upward, assigning him more particularly as a priest for the expiation of sins: there the voice from heaven declared him, and there John himself bore witness, saying: “Behold, the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

Proceeding upward, he passes through the generations and reaches from Abraham to God, to whom, once cleansed and expiated, we are reconciled. Appropriately, he also takes up the origin of adoption, because through adoption we become sons of God by believing in the Son of God.

He clearly demonstrated that he did not call Joseph the son of Heli because he had been begotten by Heli, but because he had been adopted by him. For he also called Adam the son of God, although Adam had been made by God; yet through the grace [Col. 0634A] that he later lost by sinning, he had been placed in paradise as a son. Nevertheless, it is believed that, having received forgiveness of his faults through Christ, he was counted among the sons of adoption.

Accordingly, Matthew’s generations signify Christ the Lord’s taking upon himself our sins; Luke’s generations signify Christ the Lord’s abolition of our sins. Therefore Matthew recounts them by descending, while Luke recounts them by ascending. Once our sins have been forgiven, we return and ascend to the Lord, from whom we withdrew by sinning in Adam and fell down to this condition.

For when the Apostle says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII, 3), this is the taking upon himself of sins. But when he adds, “and concerning sin he condemned sin in the flesh,” this is the expiation of sins.

Accordingly, Matthew descends from David through Solomon, whose mother David had sinned with; Luke, however, ascends to David himself through Nathan, the prophet of that name, through whom God expiated David’s sin.

We do not know, or know only imperfectly, [Col. 0634B] who the men were, or what their merits were, whom Luke placed from Joseph to Zerubbabel and from Salathiel to Nathan, the son of David, except that we do not doubt that they were of David’s lineage.

He says, among other things: “Who was of Rhesa, who was of Zerubbabel, who was of Salathiel, who was of Neri.” Matthew likewise reported: “Jechoniah begot Salathiel, Salathiel begot Zerubbabel, and Zerubbabel begot Abiud.”

Behold: according to the two evangelists, Salathiel also appears to have had two fathers, namely Jechoniah and Neri. But [Col. 0634C] something like what was said above concerning Joseph’s two fathers must also be understood concerning these two.

Among the Hebrews, the names of generations are reckoned sometimes according to nature and sometimes according to law. They are reckoned according to nature when they descend through the truth of physical seed; according to law when, after a man has died childless, another is substituted as his son under the name of the deceased brother.

The deceased man is not falsely called the father of such a son. Thus Salathiel is understood to have had one of his two fathers according to the flesh and the other according to the law, or according to adoption.

The practice of adoption was common among the Jews, and it is not inappropriate to say that someone begot the person whom he adopted, because he begot him by the benefit of adoption.

Furthermore, the fact that [Col. 0634D] Salathiel is the father of Zerubbabel according to both evangelists would appear to disagree with the Books of Chronicles, where it is written that “the sons of Jechoniah were Salathiel and Phadaiah, and from Phadaiah came Zerubbabel and Shimei” (I Chron. III, 17), unless the explanations already given were applicable.

Zerubbabel, naturally born from Phadaiah, is understood to have been called the son of Salathiel according to the law. For Zerubbabel himself was the firstborn, and the firstborn was commanded to be called by the name of his deceased brother.

It could also have happened that Salathiel adopted his brother Phadaiah’s son Zerubbabel as his own son, just as we read that Mordecai adopted Esther, his brother’s daughter, as his daughter (Esth. II, 7).

Again, Zerubbabel is shown here to have had sons named Abiud and Rhesa, although among the seven sons whom he fathered according to the Books of Chronicles none is called [Col. 0635A] by that name—unless perhaps some of them used two names. This often happened.

Or, if this was not the case, it is certain that these two were his sons either according to the commandment of the law or through the benefit of adoption.

Again, among other names it is said: “Who was of Sala, who was of Cainan, who was of Arphaxad.” But the name and genealogy of this Cainan are not found in Genesis according to the Hebrew text. Rather, it reports that Arphaxad begot Sala without anyone intervening.

For this is how we read: “Now Arphaxad lived thirty-five years, and begot Sala” (Gen. XI, 12). But the evangelist took this genealogy from the edition of the Seventy translators, where it is written that Arphaxad, at the age of 135, begot Cainan, and that Cainan himself, when he was 130 years old, [Col. 0635B] begot Sala.

Let no believer think that the translators of the Seventy erred in this passage. Let him believe without hesitation that they recorded what they knew to be true, and that they supplied what Moses had stated more briefly. For the Holy Spirit would not have placed this in the Gospel unless it were entirely true.

Those seventy elders had held the teaching office in the Synagogue from the time of Moses and had received it from the spirit of Moses; they had learned the law from Moses’ own tradition. Therefore, if anything had been omitted there that could be supplied, or that they knew how to interpret otherwise, they supplied or interpreted it.

For some reason known to God, Moses passed over the generation of Cainan and part of the years that elapsed under him and under his father. Perhaps, when he was describing the second age, he wished to place only ten generations from the Flood [Col. 0635C] to Abraham, and therefore omitted one generation.

Matthew likewise, wishing to place fourteen generations from David to the Babylonian captivity, omitted three when he said: “Joram begot Uzziah” (Matt. I, 8). Therefore, just as Joram is said to have begotten Uzziah with three placed between them, so Arphaxad is said to have begotten Sala with one Cainan placed between them.

That the sacred Scriptures sometimes include part of the years and omit part is shown by the Book of Kings, which says: “Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned over Israel for two years” (I Kings XIII, 1). Did he have only one year of age, he who was taller than all others from the shoulder upward? And did he reign only two years, he who held the kingdom for so long a [Col. 0635D] time?

Therefore, just as part of Saul’s years was omitted, so part of the years of Arphaxad and Cainan was omitted. Thus both Moses and our evangelist, together with the seventy elders, are truthful.

Again, it says: “Who was of Enoch.” Beautifully, the order of the generations, ascending from the baptized Son of God to God the Father, has Enoch at the seventieth degree. Enoch, whose death was postponed and who was transferred to paradise, signifies those who are regenerated by water and the Holy Spirit in the grace of adoption as sons and who, after the dissolution of the body, are destined in the meantime to receive eternal rest.

The number seventy, because of the seventh day, the Sabbath, most appropriately corresponds to signifying the rest of those who, with the help of Christ’s grace, have fulfilled the Decalogue [Col. 0636A] of the law. It shows that they are to be joined, at the time of the resurrection, to the contemplation of the immutable Wisdom of God throughout the ages.

Finally it is said: “Who was of Seth, who was of Adam, who was of God” (Luke III, 38). Because Christ joins us, expiated and cleansed from every sin, to his own righteousness and to that of the Father, so that what the Apostle says may come to pass: “He who adheres to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17), Christ himself, from whom the enumeration begins, and God, to whom it reaches, are included in this number of generations.

The number thus becomes seventy-seven, signifying the complete forgiveness and abolition of every sin. The Lord himself also clearly expressed this through the mystery of this number when he said that sins must be forgiven not merely seven times, but even “seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII, 22).

Nor does this number pertain without reason to the cleansing of all sins, if it is examined carefully. It consists of eleven and seven, since either eleven times seven or seven times eleven makes seventy-seven. Eleven signifies the transgression of ten. For ten, as the number of righteousness, is shown in the ten commandments of the law.

Sin, however, is the transgression of the law; and transgression of the number ten is fittingly represented by eleven. Hence eleven curtains of goat hair were commanded to be made in the tabernacle. Who would doubt that sackcloth signifies sin?

And therefore, because the whole span of temporal life revolves through the number seven of the days, all sins committed in time appropriately arrive at the number seventy-seven through eleven multiplied [Col. 0636B] seven times. In this number there is also complete forgiveness of sins: the flesh of our priest, from whom this number [Col. 0636C] now begins, expiating us, and God, to whom this number now reaches, reconciling us, through the Holy Spirit who appeared in the form of a dove at this baptism, where the number itself is mentioned.

But if perfection of blessedness is signified by ten—for all who were hired to work in the vineyard were rewarded with a denarius—then, when the sevenfold creature, that is, the inner and outer human being, is joined to the Trinity, which is God, it is clear that the transgression of ten signifies sin: the sin of one who, through pride, desires to possess [Col. 0636D] something more and loses integrity and perfection.

Eleven is multiplied seven times so that this transgression may be signified as taking place through the movement of the human being. The incorporeal part of the human being is designated by the number three, since we are commanded to love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind (Deut. VI, 5).

The body is expressed by the number four, because of its four principal members or because of the four elements of which it is composed. The human being, composed of these, is appropriately represented by seven.

Movement, however, is not expressed in numbers when we say one, two, three, four, and so forth, but when we say once, twice, three times, four times. Therefore it is not seven and eleven but seven times eleven that signifies transgression—the transgression produced through the movement of the human being [Col. 0637A] who sins, that is, who transgresses the stability of his perfection through the desire to possess something more.

Thus, because the transgression of the first human being and of all the others who proceeded from him is designated by the number seventy-seven, God appropriately came in the seventy-seventh generation to abolish all the sins of his faithful.

All who approach the baptismal font in the Christian manner are contained in the mystery of the seventy-seven generations. Therefore they obtain forgiveness of sins from the one who, cleansing so many generations, established the forgiveness of faults in this number and came at the end of so many generations to take away the sins of the world.

For he cleanses not only those who are baptized in the New Testament, but also those who, from the beginning of the world, rightly believed in his [Col. 0637B] future coming.

Hence the evangelist counts these holy generations by ascending, to show that Christ’s purifying and reconciling grace reaches all of them, and that all who now rightly observe the sacrament of baptism return to God.

For the grace of divine incarnation and purification ascends through all the generations of the past, so that we may understand that no age ever passed without Christ’s elect, who through him were freed from original sin.

For this reason Adam himself, whom the Wisdom of God—which is Christ—led out from his sin, as it is written (Wis. X, 2), is shown at the end of the account of the generations as a son of God through this grace of Christ.

And from there God the Father receives Christ, God and human, and through him all those who are his [Col. 0637C] members.

Let us then endeavor to interpret the names of the fathers backward in such a way that we always understand in them ascent and progress, and regard the sequence of their genealogy as a ladder reaching up to God, by which all the baptized must also ascend step by step.

For this genealogy, which extends from Jesus after his baptism to God, appears to us to be that ladder of which we read: Jacob placed a stone beneath his head and slept, and in a dream saw a ladder standing on the earth, its top touching heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder (Gen. XXVIII, 12).

The stone placed beneath the head, made as it were the foundation of the ladder, is Christ, who humbled himself in order to exalt all his own. Like a foundation, he supports everyone and is supported by no one. [Col. 0637D]

By this ladder of genealogy some ascend and others descend. Those who progress ascend; those who fail descend. The angels, [176] that is, the messengers of God, are so called because they speak of Christ.

Therefore, whoever has been baptized in Christ has heaven opened to him, and God is ready above to receive him. But he must ascend by the steps of the ladder that stretches from baptism to God, because, as Solomon says: “The path of life is above the instructed” (Prov. XV, 24)—the path by which the instructed person himself advances toward heaven.

The people of Israel, after crossing the Red Sea, did not stop there; rather, after long journeys and labors, they reached the promised land. Likewise, the person who has been baptized must not be sluggish, but must proceed by the way [Col. 0638A] of God’s commandments toward the heavenly homeland promised to him, and strive to ascend by the steps of the ladder of the generations if he desires to reach God, who is at its summit.

This ladder of genealogy is the road leading to heaven and to God. The more truly someone ascends it, the more powerfully he reaches that destination. One climbs it more strongly than another, and another more strongly or more perfectly still, according as it has been divinely given to each.

But woe to the one who climbs none of its steps, for he will remain in the lowest places.

Let us therefore proceed to these steps by interpreting the names of the Fathers. The most humble of all is found to be Jesus, as the foundation of the whole; his name is interpreted “Savior,” because he alone saves the human race, and salvation is found in no one else: “For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Each person begins to share in this salvation through baptism. But if he wishes not to lose what he has received freely, he must strive to grow in it through his own labor in holy action.

Hence Joseph is placed immediately afterward, whose name is interpreted “increase,” because the person who is not sluggish in doing good obtains an increase of grace after baptism. Next follows Heli, who is said to mean “ascending,” signifying the ascent of one who progresses from virtue to virtue. Then comes Matthat, whose name is interpreted “gift,” because whoever strives upward through the steps of the virtues receives the gift of still greater grace.

Next follows Levi, who is said to mean “taken up,” because God has taken him to himself for perpetual service, confirming him in constancy in good works. Melchi follows, whose name is interpreted “my king,” because it often happens that one who has already become such a person is made a ruler of the Church. Then comes Janne, who is said to mean “prepared,” because such a man is already prepared for every good work.

Joseph is added again, who, as was said above, is interpreted “increase,” because he always progresses and gains an increase of religion. Likewise comes Matthias, who is called “gift of God,” because the gift of divine grace is poured into him still more through new benefits. Then comes Amos, interpreted “honoring,” or “strong,” or “tearing away the people,” because by living well he honors God, is strong in enduring adversity, and by his teachings and examples tears the people’s heart away from the love of the world.

Naum also follows, who is called “comforter” or “comfort,” because he comforts those who have despised temporal things with the promise of eternal realities. Heli too follows, who is called “my neighbor,” because he becomes a neighbor to the one whom he soothes with consolation. Then comes Nagge, whose name is interpreted “solemnity,” because he himself becomes a solemnity of joy for the person whom he comforts.

Next comes Mahath, or Manat, who is said to mean “resting,” because he now rests in the secret place of divine contemplation, withdrawn from the labor of worldly desire; or because he has rest in the one whom he sees to have received his consolation and already to glory in tribulations for Christ. Matthias also follows, who, as we stated earlier, is called “gift of God,” because he perceives an even greater gift of heavenly grace on account of the foregoing good deeds, which he has diligently endeavored to perform.

For we are not speaking here of the ancient fathers whose names we are interpreting, although these things may perhaps also be understood of them; rather, we are speaking of any one righteous man whom we portray as ascending through these steps of the virtues from baptism to God. For through these steps the Church of the elect ascends, of which it is said: “God shall be known in her steps, when he receives her” (Psalm 47:4). Through these steps holy Job also ascended, saying: “I will declare him by my individual steps” (Job 31:37).

Let us therefore return to the order of the steps, so that we may consider the remaining ones. Semei follows, whose name is interpreted “hearing,” or may signify the hearing of obedience in a holy man. Joseph follows as well, who, as has already been said twice, is interpreted “increase,” because the righteous man always strives to acquire a new increase.

Juda also follows, who is called “confession” or “praise,” because he always renders to God a confession of praise. Joanna comes next, whose name is said to mean “to whom grace belongs,” or “the Lord is his grace,” because much grace is present in him, and that very grace is the Lord, so that, with the Lord God dwelling in him, he may be gracious.

Then comes Resa, interpreted “his head,” because the Lord, who is his grace, is also his head. Such a person is worthy to have Christ as his head. Zorobabel follows, interpreted “born in Babylon,” or “he himself is the teacher of Babylon,” because such a man is first born among the wicked and afterward teaches them how they may attain salvation.

Then comes Salathiel, whose interpretation is “God is my petition,” because this man now desires nothing but God, knowing that nothing except God is sufficient for his blessedness. Neri follows, who is called “my lamp,” because such a person can say to God: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Psalm 118:105); or we may say of him that the Lamb is his lamp (Revelation 21:25).

Melchi follows, interpreted “my king,” with “God” understood from what precedes, so that he may say, “God is my king.” Such a person has not any vice as king, but God alone. Or the Church may say of him: “Neri and Melchi,” that is, “my lamp, my king,” because he both illumines and governs her.

Addi follows, interpreted “strong,” because this man is exceedingly strong in the courage of his heart. Then comes Cosam, or Cusam, who is called “their Ethiopia,” because to those who think darkness is light and light darkness, such a man appears to be their blackness—the blackness by which many are darkened—since he illumines many.

Or he is called “their Ethiopia,” that is, “their blackening,” because by comparison with the light of his teaching and holiness he reveals them to be covered with the blackness of vices and errors.

Elmodach, or Elmadan [alternatively, Helmadam], follows, who is said to mean “the dwelling of God,” because this man always acts so regularly and moderately that he does not exceed the measure of the rule divinely given to him. Her follows, interpreted “watchful,” because, in accordance with the Gospel commandment, he is always watchful.

Then comes Jesus, who is called “salutary,” or “Savior,” because he effects the salvation of many by his words and examples. “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death” (James 5:20).

Eliezer follows, whose name is interpreted “the help of God,” or “God my helper,” because he becomes God’s help to many, and through him God helps many. Jorim comes next, who is called “the Lord exalting,” or “one who exalts,” because through him the Lord exalts others, and he himself does not cease to exalt those whom he can, raising them from lowly desires and saying: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:13).

Matthat follows again, whose name is interpreted “gift,” because the gift of heavenly grace overflows in him, and God has given him to many for their salvation. Levi also follows, who is called “taken up”; for God took him up, that is, made him one who served him in a more special way and persevered steadfastly.

Next comes Simeon, who is called “answer to prayer,” because such a man is the answer to the prayers of many, poured out before the Lord for a saving teacher. Simeon is also interpreted “hearing sorrow,” because, compassionately sharing in it, he hears the sorrow of penitents’ mourning.

Juda follows as well, who is called “confessing,” because the more he progresses in the virtues, the more and more abundantly he continually offers God a confession of praise. Hence Joseph is added, interpreted “increase,” so that an increase of merits may be signified as taking place in him through daily progress.

Eliacim follows, who is called “the resurrection of God,” because he himself becomes in many hearts the resurrection of divine grace, which had fallen in them through sin. Then comes Melca, interpreted “praising,” for he always praises the Lord.

Enam follows, who is called “their eye,” because such a man watches over others. Matthatha comes next, interpreted “his gift,” that is, “the gift of God,” because he himself is the gift of God, or because the gift of God is in him.

Then comes Nathan, who is called “he gave,” or “giving,” because God himself gave the aforesaid gift of God, and that gift belongs to the one who gives it. Or the man of God himself gave to others the gift of God that he had received.

David follows, whose name is interpreted “strong of hand,” or “desirable,” because he is strong in action and, on account of the merit of his holiness, is desired by many. Jesse also follows, who is called “the libation of the island,” because he is offered to God by the Church as a kind of sacrificial libation; and the Church, like an island, is battered on every side by the waves of the world, yet is not moved.

Obed likewise follows, interpreted “serving,” because he serves God with a pure conscience. Then comes Booz, who is called “in strength,” because in the strength of magnanimity he serves God out of the devotion of love.

Solomon follows, who is called “hanging,” or “perfection,” because, lifted above earthly things, he clings as far as he can to heavenly realities and is perfect to the extent of his ability. Nausson follows, interpreted “serpentine,” because he possesses the serpent’s cleverness and imitates the bronze serpent that Moses raised in the wilderness (Numbers 21)—that is, Christ.

Aminadab also follows, who is called “my spontaneous people,” because this same righteous man becomes God’s spontaneous and willing people when, through preaching, he produces abundant fruit in the multiplication of believers who willingly sacrifice to God.

Aram follows, called “exalted,” because the prophetic saying has been fulfilled in him: “I will raise you above the heights of the earth” (Isaiah 58:14); or: “I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms” (Jeremiah 1:10).

Esrom follows, interpreted “seeing the arrow,” because the higher he sits in the stronghold of the mind, the more freely he foresees the darts of the ancient enemy’s temptations. Phares comes next, called “division,” or “one who scatters,” because he divides and scatters the enemy’s arrows, which he foresees.

Judas follows, interpreted “confessing,” or “glorifying,” because he humbly confesses whatever human weakness may still befall him, or renders a confession of glory to God. Jacob also follows, who is called “supplanter,” because he supplants vices in himself or in others. For even after extensive exercises of virtue, certain stains of vice often assail the mind.

Isaac follows, who is called “laughter,” or “joy,” because he rejoices over the vices that have been supplanted. Abraham comes next, interpreted “the father seeing a people,” because such a man becomes the father of many and sees an immense people of his spiritual children, together with the army of virtues that he has begotten.

Through these steps of the virtues that we are describing, and which the interpretations of these names display, the righteous man, progressing daily, continually draws nearer to heaven. By means of them he builds his ascent into heaven; singing the Songs of Ascents, he arranges ascents in his heart; and he constantly progresses from virtue to virtue, so that at last he may see the God of gods in Zion (Psalm 83).

Therefore the evangelist, continuing to list the fathers and ascending beyond Abraham, passes onward until he reaches God himself, so that he may finally join to him the holy man ascending through this ladder of steps. For after Abraham, who is called “the father seeing a people,” comes the aforementioned Thare, interpreted “pasture,” or “feeding,” to signify one who nourishes with the food of the word those whom he has spiritually begotten.

Next follows Nachor, whose interpretation is “resting in light,” or “last supplication,” because this man seeks only to rest and to please God in the light of the living, and he makes supplication for those who are last.

Then comes Serug, or Sarug, who is called “perfect,” so that he may be shown to have attained perfection in the virtues. Ragau, or Reu, follows, who is called “ailing,” or “feeding,” or “pasture,” because he bears painfully the delays of the present life, and his bodily strength has withered through the exercises of spiritual virtues, while he feeds the Lord’s sheep.

Phaleg follows, interpreted “dividing,” or “he divided,” because by subtle discernment between virtues and vices he separated what was precious from what was vile. Heber comes next, called “passer-by,” because he did not fix his mind in love of the present world, but continually strives toward the world to come through desire and progress.

Sale follows, interpreted “peace,” because, with the vices already extinguished, he delights in great peace through the practice of the virtues. Cainan comes next, called “their possession,” because this man is now possessed by good things—that is, by the virtues—and no vice exercises dominion over him.

Arphaxad follows, interpreted “healing devastation,” because he heals and restores the devastation of the virtues that the ancient enemy has harmed and barbarously destroyed in many. Sen comes next, whose interpretation is “name,” or “named,” because one who is devoted to such things possesses a clear and renowned name.

Noe follows, interpreted “rest,” because, having conquered the ranks of vices through Davidic labor, he rests in the peace of Solomon.

After this comes Lamech, whose interpretation is “humbled,” “struck,” or “striking.” He appears to signify one who, after long exercises of virtue, reaches the glory of martyrdom and, humbled and struck by punishments, strikes his spiritual enemy more grievously.

Appropriately, Mathusale is added, who is interpreted “he is dead,” and “he questioned,” or “the release of death.” For each such person, having died for justice, questions and challenges the consciences of all by the example or memory of his death, asking whether they love justice and everlasting life or delight only in temporal things. He has completely expelled death from himself, so that death can no longer injure or touch him in any way, and he may live forever.

Henoch is beautifully added, who is called “dedication,” because one who has been perfected in this way is dedicated in the happiness of that world. Jarez follows, interpreted “descending,” or “strengthening,” because in pious condescension he bends down from above to us in order to strengthen our weakness.

Malaleel comes next, whose interpretation is “praising God,” because he devotes himself to divine praises in the heights. Cainan also follows, who is called “their possession,” because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are one God, possess him in the heavenly realms.

Henos follows, interpreted “violent,” because by the violence of his great virtue he seized the kingdom of heaven, which has suffered violence since the days of John the Baptist, and violent men seize it (Matthew 11:12).

Then comes Seth, whose interpretation is “placed,” or “having been placed,” because he is now placed in that kingdom of supreme blessedness from which he had long been an exile. He is also interpreted “seed,” or “resurrection,” because his natural body was sown, but that same body will rise spiritual.

Finally Adam is placed at the top, who is interpreted “man,” because every believer promoted through these steps of progress and renewed also through the resurrection of the body attains that highest perfection which man either possessed or can possess: then he is a perfect man, already capable of clinging inseparably to God.

Therefore God himself is placed at the highest summit above all, and the steps of the genealogical ladder are described as reaching him and ending there, because there is the end of our perfection, toward which we strive, so that in him we may rest without end. There is the sufficiency of all good things, because then God is all in all, and no one will need to seek anything further.

The passage previously mentioned, which we have just interpreted with reference to a martyr, may also be understood of a perfect person who does not depart from this life through the suffering of martyrdom—for not all the perfect are killed by the sword. Lamech, then, is interpreted “humble,” or “humbled.” Mathusale means “he is dead,” and “he questioned.” Henoch means “dedication,” and Jared “descending.”

It frequently happens that one who has long labored in praiseworthy works of virtue is stirred by the swelling of vainglory and begins outwardly to glory in his virtues. Therefore this person, after so many praiseworthy deeds, is now called humble, because the greater he is, the more he humbles himself in all things, becoming free from every vice of boasting or pride.

And the one who has so rejected the glory of the world proves himself to be dead to the world. By the example of such a death he questions the others, asking which of them desires to die to the world in the same way. From this comes dedication, because through contemplation he is now dedicated in the heavenly places.

Then he becomes one who descends, because, in order to raise others to the contemplation of those things that he himself is accustomed to contemplate above, he piously descends to their lowliness, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5:13).

The two names that follow—Malaleel, whose interpretation means “praising God,” and Cainan, who is called “their possession”—mystically indicate what takes place in that dedication to contemplation and descent toward one’s neighbors: there he praises God, and here he is possessed by those whose needs he serves.

Henos follows, whose interpretation is “despairing,” because he has disdained to place hope in temporal and perishable things, in accordance with blessed Job’s saying: “I have despaired; I shall not live any longer” (Job 7:16). For, being dead to the world, he no longer has hope in it.

Next comes Seth, who is called “position,” or “resurrection,” because he now lays down the body that will rise at the end. Then the perfect man will be restored to his former and better condition, as the succeeding Adam suggests; Adam is interpreted “man,” and the first man was created. Thus he is now joined to God, so that, clinging to him forever, he may live in him.

For this reason the Son of God mercifully humbled himself: to exalt to this height his own who had fallen, and to turn the steps of the generations through which they had fallen into steps of virtue by which they might ascend. As has been shown, these steps are designated in the names of the fathers. Each person who progresses ascends them according to his measure and attains something from each of the virtues; but he reaches God all the more strongly and gloriously the more truly and perfectly he has progressed in these things. Conversely, he reaches him all the more slowly and with greater difficulty the more laxly and negligently he has acted in them.

A lengthy discourse could be made concerning each step or name, but it was necessary to avoid weariness and to leave such matters to those who know how to say much from little, so that they too might undertake the interpretation. We have likewise omitted many interpretations of these names that we could have presented in the same way; and we do not doubt that many others still exist whose meaning we have not yet reached and which possess their own mystical senses.

Therefore the people of God can attain no perfection in the observance of justice that is not figuratively expressed in this genealogical ladder. The prize toward which they strive through it is God himself, placed above at its end.

The beginning, then, of the progress or ascent discussed here the Lord immediately indicated in himself, concerning whom it is written: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1). It does not say that he was “inspired by the Holy Spirit,” but “full,” because “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

For God does not give the Spirit to him—that is, to Christ—according to measure. To the other saints he gives him according to measure (Ephesians 4); but to this one he gives him immeasurably, that is, the whole immeasurable Spirit himself. Nor was he first filled with the Holy Spirit; rather, from the moment he began to be conceived in the Virgin’s womb, the Holy Spirit always remained wholly in him.

He is said now to have been full of the Spirit because he now began to declare through his works that the Spirit’s fullness remained in him. Thus he returned from the Jordan, because from his baptism onward he began to destroy the kingdom of the ruler of the world and to establish his new kingdom throughout the earth.

Every believer likewise returns from the Jordan after receiving the Holy Spirit in baptism, when, returning from the laver, he begins the struggle against the vices of the world in which he had previously lived. He returns from the Jordan who hastens from baptism to battle against the temptations of the world that he has renounced, so that, having conquered them, he may merit the crown of life through the Mediator between God and human beings, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: This was collated with the Corbie manuscripts 307 and S. 596, with one Becc manuscript, E. 10, and with one manuscript of the Church of Carcassonne; and with the Cologne and Gothic editions. Manuscript 596: “From the sayings of the Lord Archbishop Anselm.” The Carcassonne manuscript: “For the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.” It then gives the text as follows: “At that time Jesus entered a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.” And so forth. It then adds: “Homily of the venerable Archbishop Anselm.”]

## HOMILY IX

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE: “Jesus entered a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house,” etc. (Luke 10:38)

Many people are accustomed to ask what connection this reading has with the glorious Virgin, Mother of God [Note: “To the glorious Mother of God,” manuscripts 307; “to the blessed Mother of God,” manuscript E. 10; “to the glorious Virgin, Mother of God,” the Carcassonne manuscript; “to the blessed and glorious Virgin of God”; “Mother of God,” the reading of the Carcassonne manuscript; “Mother Mary,” another reading], so that it is read on her feast [Note: “Therefore, etc.” The Carcassonne manuscript omits the remainder of the preface.]. Therefore, what I thought about it I have already explained more than once, in the vernacular, as best I could, in the assembly of the brothers [Note: “I have explained more fully,” manuscripts E. 10 and 307; “I have explained more than once together,” another reading]. And because what I said pleased my hearers, I was ordered—indeed, compelled—to commit it to writing by those same men, and especially by the lords Abbots William of Fécamp and Arnulf of Troarn [Note: “And by those same lords,” manuscript E. 10; “William of Fécamp, Arnulf of Touarn,” manuscript E. 10; “William of Fécamp, Arnulf of Troarn.”].

I have said this beforehand [Note: “For that reason I said,” manuscripts; “for that reason I have said beforehand.”] so that this little exposition may not displease as something published by a presumptuous man; it was published not by presumption [Note: “Not presumption,” manuscript E. 10; “not this presumption,” another reading], but by obedience. Now, therefore, with the faith preserved and without prejudice to a better interpretation, I shall humbly undertake to write this little explanation [Note: “A little exposition,” manuscripts; “a little explanation.”] for the praise of the same Virgin and Mother of Jesus.

In [Note: [Col. 0643D] “The Gospel according to Luke. At that time: Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house,” etc. Homily on the same reading. Manuscripts: “Jesus entered a certain village.”], Sacred Scripture often presents one and the same thing as signifying different things, such as a lion, a goat, fire, water, or even the sun, as well as many other things. For there is “the Lion from the tribe of Judah” (Rev. 5), and there is the lion “who prowls around seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5). There is the scapegoat (*haedus emissarius*) who bore our sins (Lev. 16), and there is the goat on the left, which is condemned (Matt. 25). There is the fire that the Lord sent upon the earth and which he wishes to burn (Luke 12), and there is the fire that falls upon the impious so that they may not see the sun (Ps. 57).
