There is the water whose streams flow from the belly of the believer (John 7), and there is the water whose storm does not submerge us (Matt. 14). [Note: [Col. 0645D] “Does not submerge” (*non demergit*) in the Carcassonne and E. 10 manuscripts; “does not submerge us” (*non nos demergat*) in manuscript 307; “submerges us” (*nos demergat*) in the Gothic edition; “submerges us” (*nos demergit*) in another reading.] There is the Sun of righteousness that illumines us (Sirach 42), [Note: [Col. 0645D] The manuscripts read “usually illumines” (*illuminare solet*) instead of “may illumine” (*illuminet*).] and there is the sun that does not scorch us by day (Ps. 120). [Note: [Col. 0645D] The manuscripts read “scorches us” (*nos urit*) instead of “does not scorch us” (*nos non urat*).]

Although a village or fortress elsewhere signifies something evil, as in the passage, “Go into the fortress,” where it is added “which is against you,” [Note: [Col. 0645D] Manuscript E. 10 omits “where” and “what is added.” The Carcassonne manuscript reads “where it is added.” Manuscript Carcassonne reads *plane manifestat* (“plainly shows”); manuscript 307, *plane manifestans* (“plainly showing”); another reading, “where it is plainly manifested.”] clearly showing what it signifies, nevertheless here we understand the village into which Jesus entered, without violating the rule of Scripture, figuratively as the singular and undefiled Virgin Mary, the mother of that same Jesus.

A fortress is so called because it consists of any tower and the wall surrounding it. These two defend each other, so that enemies are kept away from the citadel by the wall, and from the wall by the citadel. The Virgin Mary is not inappropriately compared with such a fortress: her virginity of mind and body surrounded her everywhere like a wall, so that no one ever gained access to her through lust, nor were her senses corrupted by any enticement. And because, when lust is unable to overcome virginity, pride usually attacks it, there is in this same Virgin a tower of humility, which repels all pride from the wall of virginity. And because, when pride cannot overcome humility, lust usually attacks it, the wall of virginity repels all lust from the tower of humility.

Thus these two—the wall of virginity, that is, and the tower of humility—are fortified by each other, so that in the humble Virgin there was never proud virginity [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Cologne edition reads “nor pride of virginity” (*nec superbia virginitatis*) instead of “nor proud virginity.”], nor defiled humility; rather, in her there always remained both humble virginity and virgin humility. [Note: [Col. 0645D] The manuscripts read “and virginal humility” (*et virginalis humilitas*) instead of “and virgin humility.”]

Although what has been said is so true that the Christian faith can believe nothing truer, let us nevertheless set forth certain testimonies from the Gospel to her virginity and humility. For when the angel promised her a son, she replied: “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:54). If any betrothed virgin who was intending in her heart to marry were told, “You shall have a son,” she would not be astonished or ask how this would happen, since she knew herself to be betrothed and soon to marry, and expected by the ordinary course of nature to become pregnant by a man. But she was rightly astonished and asked how what was promised would happen, [alternative: the words “would happen” are omitted,] because although betrothed, she knew with complete certainty that she would never marry and would not know a man. [Note: [Col. 0645D] The manuscripts and the Gothic edition read “that she would marry” (*se nupturam*) rather than “that she would never marry” (*se nunquam nupturam*).]

This concerns virginity. Regarding humility, it must be said that when she was greeted by the angel, chosen to be the Mother of God, instructed how this could occur without violating her virginity—which she guarded so carefully—and proclaimed blessed above all women, she replied: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1:38); and in another passage: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). O exalted virgin and Mother of God! [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Carcassonne manuscript reads “O exalted mother” instead of “O exalted virgin and mother.”] O humble mother and handmaid of God! What could be more exalted? What could she think of herself more humbly? [Note: [Col. 0645D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read: “What could be more exalted? What could she think of herself more humbly? And so forth.”]

There are those who think that this village was Magdala, from which Mary Magdalene receives her surname. If this is true, it serves the interpretation given above. For *Magdalus* is said to mean “tower,” and it suits humility. [Note: [Col. 0645D] The manuscripts read “and is compared with humility” (*humilitati comparatur*) rather than “and suits humility.”]

Here, however, it is not named; only “a certain” village is mentioned, and we must not pass over this without examination. A certain village—that is, a singular fortress—was the Virgin Mary. Although many other women possess the wall of virginity and the tower of humility, that is, although they are both virgins and humble, nevertheless, while preserving their virginity, they cannot be mothers or bear children. She alone accomplished this. Therefore this village is rightly called “a certain,” that is, singular, because she alone was both virgin and mother—something no other woman could be or can be. [Note: [Col. 0645D] The manuscripts read “or will be able to be” (*vel esse poterit*) instead of “or can be.”]

But let us grant that some woman could be both virgin and mother, although this is impossible. Even so, Mary would be singular, because she bore the only Son of God, who, just as he is the only Son of the only Father, is likewise the only Son of the only mother. Therefore no other woman, even if she bears a child while remaining a virgin, will produce either that same Son or another like him. [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Carcassonne manuscript reads: “Therefore, even if a virgin gives birth, no one will produce either that same one or another like him.”]

Thus there is a certain fortress into which Jesus entered; and the door through which he entered is faith. Because she believed, what had been told her by the angel was fulfilled for her by the Lord, as Elizabeth said to her.

Nor was this fortress violated because Jesus entered it. Jesus saves; he does not violate. He repairs what is broken; he does not break what is sound. His work corresponds to his name.

“And a certain woman named Martha welcomed him into her house; and she had a sister named Mary.” These two sisters, as the holy Fathers have explained to us most fully, signify two ways of life in the holy Church: Martha, the active life; Mary, the contemplative life. The former labors to provide every human service to those in need; the latter is free for contemplation and sees that God is [Note: [Col. 0647C] Manuscript E. 10 reads “sees that God is”; the Carcassonne manuscript reads “sees that God is good and sweet”; another reading has “how God is.”]. The former is occupied with external matters; the latter contemplates what is within.

Just as the Mother of God was singular, so too the outcome of these ways of life, represented by these two sisters, was singular in her. Never in any other person did Martha work in this way; never did Mary elsewhere devote herself to contemplation in this way. Never did either of them elsewhere display in such a manner what belonged to her. When I speak of Martha or Mary, I mean the realities signified by them. [Note: [Col. 0647C] The manuscripts read “I mean what they signify” (*dico, eorum*) rather than “I mean the realities signified by them” (*dico, earum*).]

But let us now consider the action of this Martha, and then infer the contemplation of this Mary. To make the matter clearer, let us compare what others do as Martha with what she did.

Others receive any guest into their house; she received not just anyone, but the very Son of God, who has nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8:20), not into a house but into her womb. Others clothe any naked person with changeable and corruptible garments fashioned from whatever material; she clothed the Word of God, in a manner of speaking naked, with flesh, when that same Word assumed flesh in the same Virgin in the unity of his person—flesh that will remain forever unchangeable and incorruptible. [Note: [Col. 0647C] Manuscript Carcassonne reads “because it remains forever” (*quia sine fine permanet*) instead of “which will remain forever.”]

Others refresh whoever is hungry or thirsty with external food or drink; she nourished the God-man, who had human need, not only with external food and drink, but also with the inner milk of her womb. [Note: [Col. 0647C] The Cologne edition reads “with the inner [milk] of her womb” (*interiori uteri sui*) instead of “with her inner [milk]” (*interiori suo*).]

To pass briefly through the six works of mercy, which, when performed for one of Christ’s least ones, God acknowledges as performed for himself: she received as a guest in her womb not merely one of the least, but the supreme Son of God; she covered him, naked, with flesh and even with swaddling clothes; she fed him when he was hungry; she gave him milk when he was thirsty; and when he lay helpless in infancy, she not only visited him but continually attended to him by bathing, warming, soothing, and carrying him. Thus it is rightly said of her: “But Martha was occupied with much serving” (Luke 10:40).

When he had been seized and crucified, placed as though in prison, she stood by him, as it is written: “His mother stood near the cross of Jesus” (John 19:25). During these events she was anxious and troubled when she fled with him into Egypt from the face of Herod, who persecuted such a son of hers so fiercely that he killed many boys of the suspected age because of him. She was troubled when she recognized that the Jews were lying in wait for him and trying to inflict death upon him. At last she was greatly troubled, and, in accordance with Simeon’s saying, a sword pierced her own soul (Luke 2:35), when she saw such a son of hers seized, bound, scourged, spat upon, crowned with thorns, mocked, struck on the face, crucified, killed, and buried. [Note: [Col. 0647C] The manuscripts read “when she saw her son” rather than “when she saw such a son of hers.”]

Hence the saying rightly applies to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10:41). No one doubts that Blessed Mary wished her son to be freed from every tribulation and wished herself to be helped in her distress by the divinity which she knew to be present in that same son through contemplation, which is Mary’s portion. This is what Martha complains of: that her sister has left her alone to serve, and she demands her assistance in the service. [Note: [Col. 0647C] The Carcassonne manuscript reads “and demands her assistance in the ministry”; the Cologne edition reads “in the mystery.”]

This concerns Martha’s portion. But concerning Mary’s portion, which is proclaimed to be the better, who could speak worthily of how great or what kind it was in Blessed Mary? If Martha’s portion in Blessed Mary was such as we have described—or rather, because it was better than we have described—although it is not praised by the Lord, it is nevertheless not condemned, what was the portion that Mary chose as the better, a portion so praised that it is said it will not be taken away from her? (Luke 10:42). [Note: [Col. 0647C] The manuscripts read “which is not said to be taken away” (*non auferri dicatur*) rather than “which it is said will not be taken away.”]

O how great was the abundance of God’s sweetness in the Blessed Virgin when the Holy Spirit came upon her, the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke 1:35), and she conceived from that same Holy Spirit! What knowledge of God did she not possess, in whom the wisdom of God lay hidden [Note: [Col. 0647C] The Carcassonne manuscript reads “in whom wisdom lay hidden” rather than “in whom the wisdom of God lay hidden.], and in whose womb he fashioned a body for himself? [Note: [Col. 0647C] The Carcassonne manuscript reads “adapted himself” (*sibi coaptabat*) instead of “fashioned a body for himself.”] “Christ,” the Apostle says, “is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24); and “in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3). But Christ was in Mary. Therefore the power of God and the wisdom of God, and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, were in Mary. [Note: [Col. 0649D] The Carcassonne manuscript has the fuller wording: “And in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. But Christ was in Mary; therefore the power of God and the wisdom of God, and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, were in Mary.”]

She sat listening to the word from his mouth not only at his feet but also at his head. She preserved all the words of the angels, the shepherds, the Magi, and also of her own Son, pondering them in her heart (Luke 2:19). No one ever tasted as she did how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33:9). She was intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house and was given drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35:9). Nor is this surprising, since with her—indeed, within her—was the fountain of life (ibid., 10), from which flowed every perfection of both ways of life. [Note: [Col. 0649D] Manuscript 307 reads “so great a perfection” rather than “every perfection.”]

She was occupied with many things, like Martha; she delighted in the one thing, like Mary, because “one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:42). Many things are taken away; one remains.

Thus she singularly fulfilled Martha’s portion, and singularly chose Mary’s better portion. But Martha’s portion is taken away from her (ibid., 42). She will no longer be anxious to serve him as a child, since all the ranks of angels serve him as Lord. She will no longer be troubled while fleeing with him into Egypt from the face of Herod, because he has ascended into heaven, and Herod has descended into hell from before his face. [Note: [Col. 0649D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “she has ascended into hell from before his face” (*ipsa ascendit ad infernum a facie*) instead of “he has ascended into heaven, and Herod has descended into hell.” The Cologne and Gothic editions read “she has ascended into heaven, and Herod …” as in the manuscripts.] She will no longer be troubled about the many things that the Jews did to her son, because all things are subject to him (1 Cor. 15). Mary’s son will no longer be scourged or killed by Jews or soldiers, because “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

Martha’s portion, then, is taken away from her, but for her good; Mary’s portion, however, is perfected for her and will not be taken away from her. For she has been exalted above the choirs of angels; her desire has been filled with good things (Ps. 102:5); she sees God face to face, as he is (1 John 3:2); and she rejoices with her Son forever.

This is the better portion, which will not be taken away from her. May we too share in it through her merits and prayers, through Jesus Christ her Son, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0649D] Manuscript Carcassonne omits “with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit.” Manuscript 596 adds: “Amen. From the sayings of the lord Archbishop Anselm.”]

## 180. HOMILY X

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

“When Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, and they were watching him. And the rest.” (Luke 14:1.)

These events, which are now related as wondrous according to the historical sense, are known to be even more wondrous according to their spiritual meaning. For the Pharisees, whose name is interpreted as “the divided,” signify the Jews, divided from all other nations by circumcision and the Law. The ruler of the Pharisees mystically signifies the former high priest of the Jews. The house of this ruler is the Synagogue.

The Lord entered this house when, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber (Ps. 18:6), he was born among the Jewish people from the womb of the undefiled Virgin. He did this on the Sabbath, that is, when, in accordance with God’s will, the carnal works of the Law and the ordinances concerning those works had already ceased, since “the Law and the prophets were until John.” For according to the Law one ceased from external activity on the Sabbath; therefore the name “Sabbath” signifies the cessation of the carnal activities of the Law itself.

On such a Sabbath the Lord entered the house just mentioned, and he entered to eat bread, that is, to take food—meaning, to do the will of the Father. For he says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

“And they were watching him”: that is, even those to whom he had come were lying in wait for him. They signified that portion of the Jews, of which they themselves were a part, which was always envious of him, lay in wait for him, and sought opportunities to reproach or accuse him.

“And behold, there was a certain man with dropsy before him.” This man with dropsy, who was in the house of the ruler of the Pharisees, was a type of the people who were in the Synagogue of the Jews and suffered from the disease of avarice. For the more a person with dropsy drinks, the more he thirsts. So too, the more a miser increases his money, the more fiercely he burns with thirst for money; and his love of wealth grows as the wealth itself grows.

The Lord found the people of the Synagogue in this condition. They pursued only the killing letter of the Law and did not know the life-giving spirit. They expected from God, as the reward for their labors, the promises found there according to the letter—promises that were merely carnal—as though they were the greatest goods. Therefore they had poured themselves entirely into the desire for such things and thirsted only for the goods of the present life, which they thought were promised in the Law of God alone. Thus a badly understood letter was killing them.

Because of this spiritual sickness, the Lord, answering his plotters, said to the lawyers and Pharisees who wished to reproach him: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” That is: Is it just that, while the works of the Law have ceased—whose cessation is signified by the name “Sabbath”—this people should be healed of the disease of avarice with which it is swollen and inflamed?

And indeed it could be healed only on the Sabbath, because unless the activity of the carnal goods promised in the Law had ceased, [alternative: “unless the promises of carnal goods had ceased,”] the desire for them would not have been extinguished in the heart of the Jewish people.

But those who had been questioned about this remained silent, because they did not wish to speak about the abolition of the carnal observances, which they could no longer show, according to reason, ought to remain. From the time when they had conspired against the Savior, they had already closed their mouths to the confession of truth, so that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he would be expelled from the Synagogue (John 9:22). Their silence was represented by the silence of Zechariah, who did not believe.

The Lord, however, took hold of the sick man and healed him, because he took hold of the Jewish people, suffering, as has been said, from the disease of avarice, in those whom he chose, and freed them from every earthly desire. When they had sold everything they possessed and placed the proceeds at the feet of the apostles, they lived a poor and common life, united in love (Acts 4:32).

Thus Christ, through his grace, healed them of that whole plague of insatiable avarice. And so he dismissed them—that is, he released them from the yoke of the Law and set them free in the liberty of love, according to their own will—so that they would no longer do good under compulsion but willingly. For whoever burns with love does not need to be commanded, except that he should do whatever he wishes.

Then, refuting the envy of his rivals, the Savior said to them: “Which of you, if his donkey or ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath?” This saying both refutes the plotters and refers especially to the author of our liberation.

For according to the flesh he was one of the Jews, since he received flesh from their people. His donkey and ox fell into a well, because the Gentile and Jewish peoples, both of whom he himself had created, fell into the depths of vices. The donkey signifies the Gentile people, exceedingly brutish and burdened beneath every load of error; the ox signifies the Jewish people, subjected to the yoke of the Law.

Not only the donkey, that is, the Gentile people, but also the ox, that is, the Jewish people, fell into the depth of sins, because the latter too could not be justified by the works of the Law. But the Lord drew out both, because by justifying both through faith in him, he brought them into the liberty of love.

He did this “immediately,” that is, without delay, because in baptism he erased their offenses without postponement and gave them innocence. “On the Sabbath,” that is, in the clear light of faith and knowledge, when the works of the Law had ceased.

“And they could not answer him concerning these things,” because, after the two peoples had been drawn out of the depths of evils and called to the light of faith, God so made the wisdom of the world foolish that its wise men, who envy the Church of the Savior, could find nothing to answer or say against it rationally. Instead, with their mouths closed, they held their silence and wasted away inwardly with envy.

## HOMILY XI

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

“A certain man made a great supper, and invited many. And he sent his servant at supper time to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready. And they all began together to make excuses. The first said to him. And the rest.” (Luke 14:16.)

This man is “the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). His great supper is the new spiritual knowledge which, at the end of time, he graciously gave us abundantly through himself, through the apostles, and through the interpreters of Scripture, so that he might nourish our souls with spiritual delights.

He adds another course when he delightfully feeds our minds with his love. He adds a third when he grants us perpetually, among the angels, the vision of his divinity. This is his supper, which he prepared for his own and to which he invited many: Jews and Gentiles from the whole world—first the Jews, then the Gentiles.

This supper was signified by the banquet that Ahasuerus held in the third year of his reign for his nobles and friends; afterward he invited to it all the people found in his kingdom (Esth. 1:3, 5). For mystically Ahasuerus is Christ; the third year is the third period. The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. In this period the King of kings displayed his banquet. The nobles and friends are the apostles and those who first believed from among the Jews. The people invited from the whole city are the multitude of the Gentiles called from the whole world, since a city signifies either the world or the Gentile people.

Therefore this lord sent his servant at supper time to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready. The servant is the order of preachers. Supper time is the final age of the world, about which blessed John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (2 John 2:18). This hour is the period of time from the Lord’s coming until the end of the world, in which spiritual knowledge has been revealed, the grace of the Holy Spirit poured out, and the kingdoms of heaven opened. Therefore it is said: “Everything is now ready.”

Nothing remains except that each person prepare himself as one worthy, come, and enjoy all these things. The Lord first sent his servant to call those who had been invited when he said to his disciples: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:15). For the Israelites had already been invited to this supper by the patriarchs, Moses, and the prophets. Yet they were unwilling to come, either then or now; instead, they all began together to make excuses.

The first said: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it. I ask you to consider me excused.” This first person represents the powerful of the world, who claim farms and fortresses for themselves in order to exercise power over others and to be more honored and wealthier than the rest.

These people abandon their inner life and go out in mind toward external concerns. They are held back by certain bonds of necessity from returning to what is within; instead, they continually inspect their farms and possessions, think about them, and take pleasure in being held by them. Therefore they neglect God’s supper.

When preachers sometimes persuade such people to pursue better things, they promise that they will do what is commanded, but they raise obstacles and offer excuses, asking the preachers to pray to God on their behalf. What else is this than saying, “I ask you to consider me excused”?

Many such people existed in Judea when the Lord spoke these words. But those who are Jews now, because they cannot acquire farms, acquire money instead.

Another said: “I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them. I ask you to consider me excused.” This signifies those Jews who are more devoted to the carnal study of the Law. For the five yokes of oxen are the five books of Moses, which press down with heavy servitude those who are placed beneath them according to the flesh.

The Jews bought these books because of them they were circumcised, and because of them they offer tithes, firstfruits, and sacrifices. Yet they do not have them tested, because they do not yet understand them. For if they had understood them, they would have offered no excuse but would already have come to the supper.

But because they do not understand them, while pretending to honor them, they seek to establish their own righteousness and are not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3).

And another said: “I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.” By this are signified those who subject themselves entirely to the pleasures of lust and the flesh. They do not seek to be excused, because they love only this life and regard the other as insignificant.

In these three who were unwilling to come to the supper, all who neglect to come to it are represented; and in their type the Jews were unwilling to approach this supper.

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his master.” Hence Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 53:1).

Then the master of the household, becoming angry, said to his servant: “Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame.”

Because the Jews were unwilling to come, the Lord became angry with them. He no longer admonished them through his preachers to convert, but abandoned them entirely to their wickedness, commanding the clouds not to rain upon the unfruitful vineyard (Isa. 5:6), that is, ordering the apostles not to preach to Judea.

For it is a great anger of God not to call sinners to repentance, but to leave them in their sins until death. Thus he was angry with the Jews who were unwilling to come to the supper and believe, and he turned his merciful gaze toward the Gentiles.

Therefore Paul and Barnabas said to the Jews themselves: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

In this passage the city signifies the Gentile people, fortified by the walls of disputations, arguments, and worldly powers. Hence the Lord also says through the Psalmist: “Who will lead me to the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea?” (Ps. 59:11).

For the one who preaches among sinners leads Christ to sinners. Because such a person is rare, the Lord says: “Who will lead me?” For “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke 10:2).

The city, as we have said, is the Gentile people; and it is Idumea, that is, earthly. By the streets and alleys of the city, let us understand the broad and narrow places of the Gentile world.

Thus he said to the order of preachers: “Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame.” As though he were saying: Hurry to the foreign nations, and do not delay in bringing to life those whom you find there either enlarged by the breadth of their possessions or constrained by the narrowness of their resources.

The Gentiles were poor, weak, blind, and lame: they possessed neither the riches of the Law nor the strength of virtues by which they could resist the devil; they had neither the light of knowledge nor enlightened eyes of the heart; and they did not walk with upright feet on the way of righteousness.

Yet when invited to Christ’s banquet, they became spiritually rich and strong, were inwardly enlightened, and no longer wandered on the way of God but walked along a straight path.

And the servant said: “Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” “We have called,” he says, “the Jews and the Gentiles according to your command, and there is still room for those who wish to come.”

This place will be filled when this age comes to an end. For servants are still sent each day, and the faithful are still coming to the supper, some hastening through baptism, others through repentance.

[The surviving source ends here.]

The Lord therefore says to the servant: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to come in, so that my house may be filled.” For now neither roads nor hedges, nor any place—whether accessible or enclosed, visible or hidden—has been left unexplored by the servants of Christ. Therefore, whoever has failed or fails to attend this supper should attribute it not to the negligence of the servants, but to his own disobedience.

This third invitation pertains especially to our own time, in which the adversities of the world are increasing; and for this reason it says in it: “Compel them to come in.” At one time the world drew us away from God, but now it is so full of evils that it itself sends us to God. Hence it is also written concerning the waters of the Flood: “They prevailed exceedingly, and lifted the ark high above the earth” (Gen. VII, 17). For what are signified by the waters except tribulations, and what by the ark except the Church? When the waters therefore overflow, the ark is lifted high above the earth, because, when adversities rush upon it, the Church—or the faithful soul—is separated from earthly desires and brought near to heaven.

There are some who seek prosperity in this world but find adversity; they try to grasp temporal glory but cannot. The more eagerly they pursue pleasures, wealth, or honors, the more they experience stings, hardships, and humiliations. Adversity therefore compels them to come to God’s supper. But because, amid those very adversities, their minds have become so hardened through stupor that they cannot understand the evils they suffer, when the preacher explains to them the worldly evils by which they are afflicted, and by a certain force of reasoning and exhortation compels them to desire heavenly goods, he does what was said: “Compel them to come in.” Thus the number of the elect is completed and the heavenly house is filled.

Of those who had refused to come, it is then added: “I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.” None of those who were invited but refused to come shall taste the supper of inward sweetness; none of them shall enter with the saints into the banquet of the eternal feast. Hence through the prophet the Lord says to them:

“Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be ashamed. Behold, my servants shall praise because of the joy of their heart, but you shall cry out because of the sorrow of your heart, and because of the contrition of spirit you shall howl” (Isa. LXV, 13–14).

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst” (John VI, 35). The same sense is expressed in Exodus: “They saw the God of Israel, and they ate and drank” (Exod. XXIV, 11).

All these things ought either to make us afraid or to kindle our desire: to make us afraid, lest we should happen to hunger and suffer with the rejected; to kindle our desire, so that we may be worthy to feast and rejoice with the elect. Whoever is absent from this banquet will waste away eternally in hunger and misery and in the lack of every good. Whoever is present will be perpetually satisfied with an immeasurable fullness of every good. For the food of the righteous is the present face of God; while it is seen without failure, the mind is satisfied without end with the food of life. Hence it is also said: “Let the righteous feast and exult before God, and delight in gladness” (Ps. LXVII, 4).

There they rejoice in fellowship with eternity, those who have now escaped the snares of pleasurable temporality. There are the hymn-singing choirs of angels; there is the fellowship of the heavenly citizens. There is the sweet solemnity of those returning from the sorrowful labor of this pilgrimage. Let us therefore hasten to enter this banquet, where, together with the fellowship of all the elect, we may rejoice forever in festive gladness, through the bounty of him who lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XII

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

“Jesus told his disciples this parable: ‘There was a certain rich man who had a steward; and this man was accused before him of having squandered his possessions. And he called him and said to him…’ And so forth” (Luke XVI, 1).

This sacred reading, under the figure of a steward who first squandered his master’s possessions and afterward wisely provided for the needy from those same possessions, so that he might be praised by him, reveals the corruption and correction of any ecclesiastical superior who at first weakens discipline and religious observance, not only in himself but also in those subject to him, but later nobly reforms both himself and his subordinates.

“There was,” he says, “a certain rich man,” and so forth. This man is understood as the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Tim. II, 5). He is also rich, as Creator and Lord of all. The steward takes his name from the care of an estate and signifies one whose duty is to keep watch over and govern the Church, as it is written: “Unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it” (Ps. CXXVI, 1). The steward therefore represents the governor of the Church.

But it often happens that the person who has undertaken to govern the Church, longing for earthly advantages, neglects spiritual gains and, by living badly, destroys religious observance among those subject to him through his evil example. Such a person is accused before his Lord as though he were a squanderer of his goods, because the angels recount his works before God: by these works he dissipates the discipline of those whom he had undertaken to govern, offering them bad examples of himself.

For the angels announce all our works and prayers to God—not so that he may learn what he did not know, since there is nothing he does not know, but because it is necessary for a rational creature, in obedience to God, to refer temporal matters to eternal truth, whether by asking what may be done for oneself or for others, or by seeking counsel about what one should do. This is a pious disposition of mind, intended to build up the creature itself, not to instruct God. Indeed, it is also a kind of testimony by the rational creature that it does not itself possess the good by which it may become blessed, but that the good is unchangeable and that through participation in it the creature also becomes wise.

In this way, then, the steward was accused before his lord. The lord called him to give an account because he does not himself examine the deeds of superiors only at the end of time; rather, every day he judges the actions of those subject to them through the superiors themselves. He called him because, pressing him toward death through the distress of illness, he caused him to be brought before him by the angels, and said to him: “What is this that I hear about you?”—namely, that you seek not my gains from my goods, but your own, and that you harm those whom you ought to have benefited.

“Give an account of your stewardship.” For after death you will no longer be able to serve as steward. Considering that he was being hemmed in by such a severe reckoning, the steward anxiously began turning over thoughts of this kind in his heart: “What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship away from me?” That is, through death he removes me as unworthy from the position of authority that I held in the Church.

“To dig I am not able after this life”—that is, I cannot renew the soil of my heart with the mattock of contrition and the practice of discipline, so that, receiving the seed of the word, it may produce a harvest of good works.

“To beg I am ashamed”—that is, I am ashamed to seek in that age the food of life that I did not prepare here; as that lazy man who, according to Solomon, refused to plow because of the cold and therefore will beg in summer and receive nothing (Prov. XX, 4).

But seeing that some period of time was still being granted him for correction, and having now adopted a reasonable plan, he continued: “I know what I shall do”—that is, I have thought out what I ought to do—“so that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me, and the elect of God, who are now under my stewardship, may deign to have me as a fellow inhabitant in their houses,” that is, in the eternal dwellings divinely prepared for them.

Released from these thoughts and restored to health, he began to carry out in action what he had conceived in his mind, summoning the debtors of his lord—that is, all mortals, calling as many as he could to hear his preaching. For every human being is a debtor of God.

Although there are innumerable debtors, only two are mentioned, because the whole Christian people here is divided into two parts: sinners and righteous people. The first debtor represents that portion of the faithful which still serves sins and vices, since sins are properly called debts, as when we pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

This debtor confesses that he owes a hundred measures of oil because, in order to merit forgiveness, he confesses to the ecclesiastical steward the measures and quantities of his vices. The number one hundred signifies perfection; the measures signify quantities of sins; and oil signifies the favor shown to those same sins, when someone takes pleasure in his own vices or fondly flatters others who are sinning. Concerning this kind of oil it is said: “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. CXL, 5).

The oil of the sinner fattens the head when the favor of a flatterer caresses the mind. Since the favor and praise of vices, now signified by the name of oil, is especially damnable, this debtor, confessing the marrow of his faults, declares that he owes a hundred measures of oil, understanding that there are very many measures of the falsely sweet favor by which he pleased himself in his wickedness and soothed the vices of others. The steward therefore orders him, once he has accepted the bond—that is, once the impression of his former works has been retained and restrained—to sit; that is, to humble himself and repent.

That a bond signifies the form, impression, or number of works is indicated figuratively by the engravings that Solomon is reported to have made in the Temple. That sitting signifies humiliation is shown by Saint David in deed and word. When he had greatly humbled himself, he entered, as Scripture says, and sat before the Lord and said: “Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me to this point?” (II Sam. VII, 18). The king of Nineveh, repenting, put on sackcloth and sat in ashes (Jon. III, 6). This debtor is therefore ordered to sit, so that he may be humbled for repentance.

And because it is uncertain at what hour death will come, he is ordered to sit quickly, while time still permits. He is ordered to write fifty—that is, repentance. For whatever we do, we write as if in a book, so that it may be recited before Christ on the day of judgment. Hence Daniel says: “Judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII, 10).

The number fifty signifies repentance and the remission of sins, because David obtained forgiveness of sins while doing penance in the fiftieth Psalm. The fiftieth year was also established in the Law as a jubilee, in which remission took place. Instead of one hundred, therefore, he writes fifty: instead of the complete multiplicity of his vices, he demonstrates through works an evident repentance worthy of remembrance, by which he may also obtain the grace of forgiveness.

Just as the first debtor signifies either that portion of the faithful subject to sins or each individual sinner, so the second signifies either that portion of them which, as has been said, pursues righteousness, or each individual righteous person. For every righteous person is also a debtor of God, because he owes him all the good things he has received, so that he may return the same or their equivalent, if he can; but if he cannot, he should humbly acknowledge himself to be a debtor and, giving thanks, say: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV, 12).

The hundred measures of wheat that he declares himself to owe signify the perfection of righteousness and of the other virtues given to him according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Measures of wheat signify measures of the gifts of grace. That wheat signifies virtues and spiritual gifts by which the soul is nourished, Scripture teaches when it says: “The valleys shall abound with wheat” (Ps. LXIV, 14). Likewise: “The cloud desires wheat” (Job XXXVII, 41).

The valleys—that is, the humble—are filled with wheat, that is, with the grace of virtues, by which they live and are spiritually nourished. These virtues desire the clouds, that is, holy preachers, so that through them they may be watered by the rain of heavenly words.

This man therefore owed a hundred measures of wheat, because he had received, according to the measures divinely granted to him, the perfection of virtues. The steward ordered him to write eighty in his documents—that is, in his works—instead of one hundred; that is, instead of all that he owed, he was to show himself, through righteous deeds, worthy before God of the future resurrection.

The letters that we write are our actions, which we consign to the divine memory, whether good or evil. Hence the Lord himself says concerning every work that human beings have done: “Behold, it is written before me” (Isa. LXV, 6). The number eighty, like the number eight, corresponds mysteriously to the resurrection, because the Lord’s resurrection took place on the eighth day, and ours too will come after the seven days in which all time revolves—that is, on the day of judgment, which will be the eighth. Hence some Psalms are written “for the eighth.”

He therefore writes eighty in his documents, demonstrating through his works that he is worthy of that resurrection and of fellowship with the elect.

These, then, are the things in which the prudent steward endeavored to correct and improve both himself and the inhabitants of his estate, that is, the children of the Church he governed; and for these he deserved to be praised by the Lord. Let us therefore praise the one who is praised by divine judgment, and let us not dare to reproach him in anything before his correction, imagining that in what he did with the debtors he defrauded his lord. Rather, let us believe that in these matters he sought the profits of his lord by prudent counsel and fulfilled his will.

He is still called the steward of iniquity only because he had previously managed his stewardship wickedly, just as Matthew, because he had been a tax collector, is called a tax collector even in the catalogue of the apostles. But in all these matters the mercy of our most compassionate Judge is especially to be proclaimed. Although he had previously summoned this man and could have condemned him by a just judgment, he preferred to recall him from death by granting him another period of life, so that afterward, once corrected, he might count him among his friends. For he fulfilled what he had spoken: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 33).

To his statement that the steward of iniquity had acted prudently, he adds a judgment in which he indicates that many do similar things:

“For the children of this age,” he says, “are more prudent than the children of light in their own generation.” The children of this age are those who lead a worldly life. The children of light are called the righteous.

But there are some righteous people who, although they live justly and abstain from what is unlawful, nevertheless never perform great good works. There are others who first lived in a worldly and criminal manner, but afterward, returning to their senses and considering that they had done unlawful things, are pierced by the sorrow arising from that realization and burn with love of God. They exercise themselves in great virtues, seek every difficulty of the holy contest, and abandon all the world’s blandishments. They burn with desire and long for the heavenly homeland. Because they see that they have wandered from God, they compensate for their previous losses with subsequent gains.

These, then, in their own generation—that is, in the time in which they pass through the present life—are more prudent than those children of light who never depart from the mother of light, but perform the works of light more sluggishly and do not anxiously long for the homeland of eternal light.

After this judgment, the Lord adds an exhortation, so that those who previously acted badly may, following the steward’s example, turn toward the good and strive to act mercifully. It is as though he said:

“This steward, who had earlier managed his stewardship badly, afterward acted mercifully toward his subordinates, bestowing spiritual benefits from the goods of that same stewardship; for these he deserved to enter, together with the elect, the dwelling places of heavenly happiness. I too say and advise you: You who have mammon—that is, riches—of iniquity, meaning riches acquired through iniquity and hitherto unjustly dispensed or possessed, now, by dispensing them well to the saints who suffer want, make them your friends by means of them, so that, when you fail—that is, when you die—they may gladly receive you with themselves into the eternal tabernacles, that is, into everlasting dwellings, where you may rejoice with them forever. For ‘he who receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive the reward of a righteous person.’”

Some people, however, misunderstanding this judgment, seize other people’s property, give some of it to the poor, and think that they are doing what was commanded. They say: “To seize another’s property is the mammon of iniquity; to distribute something from it, especially to needy saints, is to make friends from the mammon of iniquity.” This interpretation must be corrected.

We must not acquire what we distribute as alms through robbery, usury, or fraud. But if it should happen that before our conversion we acquired wealth by such means, then after conversion we must not commit robbery or fraud; nevertheless, we should give generously from our wealth. Thus Zacchaeus is praised for having acted. He was chief among the tax collectors and was rich; but after receiving Christ into his house, he gave half of his wealth to the poor, and from the other half he repaid fourfold anyone whom he had defrauded.

Just as the steward is called the steward of iniquity even after his correction, because he had previously managed his stewardship wickedly, so riches that someone acquired, possessed, or dispensed unjustly before conversion are called riches of iniquity even after his conversion. But just as the steward acquired friends from that same stewardship after he had been corrected, so everyone should strive to make friends from his own resources, even if he had previously acquired them through lawful and unlawful means—provided only that he acquire nothing further through iniquity.

This entire reading therefore teaches correction and amendment, and exhorts everyone who lived badly and perversely managed the things entrusted to him to dispense to change his ways and overcome and erase his former evils by subsequent good deeds.

Nevertheless, all the riches of the world can be called riches of iniquity. Although they were created by God for everyone, some people gather them for themselves, even through just labor, yet with unjust desire; and because they give them to no one, they in a certain sense take them away from the needy, since they do not allow them to come into the needy’s use.

Thus, even if they were acquired through just labor, as was said, or received as an inheritance from religious parents, they are still riches of iniquity, because it is unjust—that is, contrary to the rule of equity—for one person to abound in wealth while another is in want. Whatever worldly riches are used to give alms, therefore, are riches of iniquity.

Let us therefore acquire riches no longer unjustly but justly; and from them, by making just almsgiving, let us gain the holy poor as friends, so that they may deign to receive us with themselves into the eternal tabernacles. Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XIII

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

“As Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee. And so forth” (Luke XVII, 11).

The present reading was fulfilled once in deed according to its historical sense, but according to its spiritual sense it is fulfilled every day. For in Adam we had withdrawn from the vision of peace, which is what Jerusalem means, and had fallen into the quarrelsome unrest of this exile; and we were hastening toward the punishments of hell, with no prospect of seeing anything peaceful thereafter.

But the Word of God, through whom all things were made, wishing mercifully to bring us back to the vision of his peace, in which we might rest forever, descended to us, who could not ascend to him. Having assumed our humanity into himself, he made his way toward the heavenly Jerusalem, where true peace is always seen, and opened the way there for us.

And because he made elect human beings his members, he still goes daily in his members to Jerusalem, when he leads his elect back from this exile to the homeland in which peace reigns without any disturbance of body or spirit. This homeland is designated here by the name Jerusalem, which, as has been said, means “vision of peace.”

As he went there, he passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee. Samaria means “watch” and signifies the diligence of the righteous, who keep God’s commandments, guard their hearts with all vigilance, and watch over their actions at every hour. Galilee, however, which is interpreted as “transmigration made,” designates the life of those who have migrated from evil works to religious conduct by the narrow way of repentance.

Going therefore to Jerusalem, he passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee, because every day he causes some who have been united to him to pass over to the blessed vision of eternal peace—both those who have not gone astray and those who have returned from error to truth.

He passes into Jerusalem in those whom, having made them his members, he rescues from the present wicked age and leads to the perpetual contemplation of the heavenly majesty. He passes through the middle of Samaria and Galilee—that is, by such a passage he divides Samaria and Galilee through the middle. By these, as has been said, we understand the righteous and the penitent, because from both the righteous and the converted he chooses some and leads them with himself to the land of the living, while he permits others among them still to struggle here.

The imperfect verb is used—“he was passing”—so that we may understand that this passage has not yet been completed but is still taking place. That portion of the elect which is retained amid the labors of this life is fittingly designated by the fortress of which it is then said that, as Jesus entered a certain fortress, ten leprous men met him.

For amid the dangers of the temptations of this age, the saints, like a fortress, guard themselves within the rampart of discipline by cautious vigilance. A fortress is fortified against enemies and carefully guarded; it signifies the Church, strongly closed and fortified on every side amid the dangers of this life against evil spirits, and preserved by ever-watchful care.

It is called “a certain” fortress so that its literal location may remain unknown while its spiritual meaning is understood. In this spiritual fortress—that is, in the Church—the Lord is always present, as he says to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). Yet he sometimes appears to be absent when he permits the wicked to multiply and does not openly grant his elect his help, but allows them to be afflicted by tribulations and adversities as though they had been abandoned by him. Hence also comes that cry: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why do you despise us in times of trouble?” (Ps. IX, 1).

When the Lord appears to be absent, those represented by the ten lepers then stretch outward. Many, broken by adversities, wish to depart from the faith and join themselves to unbelievers, as though saying: “Come, let us make a covenant with the nations that surround us” (I Macc. I, 12). Others, overcome by the temptations of vices, commit so many and such great evils that they become like the Gentiles in their conduct, stretching outward from the bosom of the Church toward worldly things through their desires.

These are spiritually leprous. They are said to be ten because those who act against God’s commandments are customarily understood through the number ten, on account of the Decalogue of the Law. Just as those who observe the heavenly commandments attain cleansing and health of soul, so those who act contrary to the commandments contract spiritual defilement and illness, becoming in soul what those who suffer from bodily leprosy are seen to be in body.

The more perversely they act, the farther outward they stretch. This is what happens while Jesus appears to be absent.

But it often comes about through the visitation of divine grace that the Lord Jesus himself appears openly to come to and enter this fortress of the Church: suddenly he stills the tribulations, turns his people away from their wickedness, and grants them a great increase in religious devotion.

Then spiritually what was said takes place: when he enters this fortress, ten leprous men meet him. He finds them moving against him—that is, walking along a path contrary to his own—while they are going outward and he is going inward. He stops them, makes them stand still, and causes them to cease, so that they may proceed no farther along the crooked path.

They stood, and they stood at a distance, because they could not immediately approach him. Standing far away, however, they turned to prayer and said with a great cry of the heart: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.”

They did not understand that he was the Savior who could heal every illness of sins, but they recognized that they had been made wretched because they had acted contrary to the commandments. Therefore they called him Jesus, that is, “Savior,” and Master, praying that he would have mercy on them.

When he saw them with a compassionate gaze, he said: “Go, show yourselves to the priests”—that is, through humble confession of the mouth, truthfully disclose to the priests all the stains of your inward leprosy, so that you may be cleansed.

What they asked was done for them as they went to the priests, because they were cleansed: sinners, although disfigured by the grievous leprosy of their crimes, are nevertheless purified as they go to confession, in that very confession, because of the repentance they are about to undertake.

They were cleansed as they went, because from the moment they enter upon this path they begin to practice righteousness; and the practice of righteousness is their cleansing. They were cleansed as they went, because from the moment they turn toward confession and repentance and, with the full deliberation of their minds, condemn and abandon their sins, they are freed from them in the sight of the inward Examiner.

Hence the Lord himself testifies through the prophet: “The wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12). Yet one must reach the priests and seek absolution from them, so that those who are already cleansed before God may also be shown clean to human beings by the judgment of the priests.

It follows: “One of them, when he saw that he had been cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice.”

The one signifies the one who perseveres in a good disposition among those who, after obtaining forgiveness through repentance, remain in humility and thanksgiving. When it is said “one,” this should be understood not as someone already divided among various wills, but as one who persists in the will to please God.

All the elect, because of this unanimity in goodness, may properly be called not only “one” but also “one person,” as the Apostle indicates when he speaks mystically of all, both good and evil, who are in the Church: “All indeed run, but one receives the prize” (I Cor. IX, 24).

All Christians, good and bad alike, run according to their capacity toward the prize; but one—that is, the unity of the elect—receives it, just as all these lepers were cleansed, but one gave thanks.

When this one saw that he had been cleansed from the leprosy of his crimes, he returned to the one who had cleansed him, offering thanks, humbling himself more deeply before him, becoming more devoted, and striving always to please him. This one, as has been said, signifies those who act in this way.

He did not wish to remain ungrateful, but returned, glorifying God with a loud voice. Rightly is it said “with a loud voice,” because he rejoiced that he had received great benefits from God. “A loud voice” should be understood as devoted rather than clamorous. He who rejoiced at having been magnificently delivered from such great evils did not wish to glorify God with a devotion of small voice.

Having received from Christ the healing of inward leprosy, he glorified God, so that the Father might be glorified in the Son.

“And he fell on his face at his feet,” because, ashamed of his former actions, he appeared despicable to himself and prostrated himself before Christ in devoted humility. He no longer possessed the rigid posture of pride, but, in complete consternation of mind, lay well at the feet of the Savior, giving thanks that he had been freed from such great misery.

And he was a Samaritan—that is, a guardian—because, lest he lose the benefits he had received, he preserved them through the guardianship of humility. He now carefully guarded himself, so as not again to incur the wound of spiritual leprosy, and he guarded his heart and actions from evil.

Jesus then answered and said: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” By the deeds of the one who returned thanks and of the others who were ungrateful, the Lord responded: “Were not ten cleansed? And ought they not all alike to have returned to give thanks?”

Ten were cleansed because the legitimate number was purified. But the nine are as though unknown to the Lord, because they preferred to distance themselves from him through sins rather than draw near to him through good works. Concerning them he says: “Where are they?” That is: Where are those who ought to be present in humility and thanksgiving? Where are those who ought to draw near to me through the merit of devotion and work? Where are those who ought to be in observance of my commandments?

Because the number nine contains three times three and pertains to faith in the Trinity, these nine signify those who, after being cleansed through repentance, become negligent and secure regarding their former faults and do not exercise themselves in good works, but think that faith alone is sufficient for them.

“No one was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner,” because no one is found who, after receiving forgiveness, remembers divine mercy and perseveres in good works while offering thanks to God with a devoted heart, except one who is not among the children of earthly Babylon but among the children of the heavenly Jerusalem.

And he said to him: “Rise, go; your faith has made you well.”

To the man who still lay humbly on the ground, repenting of sins now wiped away, he commands that he rise to do good and go—that is, advance and progress in good works. He who humbly acknowledged the weakness of his condition and understood himself to be dust and ashes is commanded to rise to vigorous works and to advance in the progress of righteousness.

To him it is also said: “Your faith has made you well.” He believed that thanks should be returned to him who had cleansed him [alternative reading: “to God, to him”], and that God had become known through the deed. He possessed the faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6), and through it he was saved from the former evils in which he had previously perished, because he did not, like the nine, suppose that faith alone, without works, was sufficient for him.

## HOMILY XIV

### ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

“There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. And so forth” (John IV, 46).

What we have heard in the Gospel reading as having happened individually to one royal official and his son, we shall see to correspond generally to the human race if, with careful attention, we fit the mystical meaning to the surface of the letter.

The fact that *regulus* derives its name from *rex*—“king”—is demonstrated both by the similarity of the words and confirmed by the meaning of the derivation. We also know that there were *reguli*, that is, lesser kings. Who would doubt, then, that the human being, made in the image and likeness of the most excellent King (Gen. I, 26), was a king when he ruled himself well and governed himself temperately?

The kingdom of this king was the paradise of God. In it blessed humanity was placed as a cultivator, as a worker, and as a king and lord, so that it might rule and preside over beasts, fish, reptiles, and birds, set upon a throne like a king.

But, alas, he who had been exalted as a great king and presided in this manner was driven from that kingdom through the swelling of disobedience and exposed to hardship and sorrow. Nevertheless, by the mercy of God, whose mercies are above all his works (Ps. CXLIV, 9), wretched humanity was not altogether cast into the abyss of destruction; for it neither lost free choice nor became alienated from the capacity for reason.

By himself, therefore, he lost something great; yet, through the mercy of the Creator, something small was left to him. In what he lost, he ceased to be a king; but in what was left to him above the other animals, he lived as a kind of lesser king. The very words of the Gospel seem to suggest this when they say: “There was a certain royal official.”

For by the word “was,” which is a verb of imperfect signification—having already passed away in part while in part seeming not yet to have passed away—and which possesses substantive force, the state of human existence is indicated. That existence had already partly passed away in death and was partly sick and wounded, so that the human being who had existed was almost nothing, since he was ill and beginning to die.

His proper name is withheld, and it is said: “There was a certain one,” because he was not worthy to hear: “I know you by name” (Exod. XXXIII, 17), nor was his name written in heaven, so that God might deign to name it. We too often omit the names of certain people, although we remember them well, out of disdain, when we are disgusted by remembering them.

His name was therefore contemptible to the Holy Spirit because he was a sinner, being only a lowly royal official.

Whose son was ill at Capernaum. The son is that in which the father takes particular delight with paternal affection, which he cherishes in the tenderest and wholly embracing embrace, as though it were himself. In the human being we understand this as the inner mind, which, from the first Creation until Christ, we do not doubt was afflicted beforehand by many forms of spiritual fever. Capernaum, however, is said to mean “the most beautiful field” [Col. 0665A], and this world, adorned with the ornaments of its creatures and made splendid by the ordering of the great Maker, can not incongruously be understood as the most beautiful field. Man is its tenant, being a stranger and sojourner; and the more freely he sinned, the more abundantly he became ill. The more precious part of man was sick—namely, the mind, which ought to be dearer to man, as a son.

When he heard that Jesus was coming from Judaea into Galilee, he went to him and begged him to come down and heal his son, for he was beginning to die. Judaea means “confession,” or “praise and glorification”; Galilee, however, is interpreted as “a transmigration that has taken place.” Jesus came from Judaea into Galilee when, from the confession and praise incessantly offered to him above by the holy angels [Col. 0665B], he deigned, by assuming flesh, to come to us who had transmigrated from paradise into this valley of misery. The ruler heard of this coming because he learned that through Zechariah Jesus had said: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord” (Zech. II, 10). When he had heard these and similar prophetic words about his coming, he went to him, intending to plead for his son, change his ways, and believe in him. He went to him because he began to approach his faith to some degree. And he begged him to come down and heal his son, whom we have said to be his mind, since through the Psalmist he said: “Lord, incline your heavens and come down” (Ps. CXLIII, 5); and: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” [Col. 0665C] (Ps. XL, 5). He begged him to come down—that is, mercifully to incline himself to the humility of his Passion—and to heal his son, that is, his more precious part. For the mind of man could not be healed from the sickness of sin unless the death of the physician himself became its medicine.

For he was already beginning to die from the sickness of sin. This is the wounded man whom, as it is said elsewhere, robbers left half-dead on the road. He lives in that part by which he can know God and distinguish what is right; but he is dead in that part by which he wastes away in sins and perishes in wickedness. He will be wholly dead if he is condemned to hell. Thus he was beginning to die: that is, he was being weighed down exceedingly by the sickness of vices and approaching the death of eternal condemnation. But lest he die completely [Col. 0665D], the father came to Jesus to plead for him, so that he who is life, physician, and medicine might confront death. After death no medicine could be found, because there is no redemption in hell. Whoever has once been handed over to eternal condemnation can never afterward obtain redemption.

The Lord answered the ruler who entreated him: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” There is this difference between signs and wonders: signs are so called because they signify something in the present; wonders are called, as it were, *porrodicia*, because they speak onward, signify onward, and point to something future. The Lord performed both signs and wonders, since some of his works signified something in the present, while others looked ahead to the future [Col. 0666A]. The ruler, then, was asking him to come down for the salvation of his son; but the Lord commended his own descent and subtly intimated it to the ruler, saying: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” It was as though he said: “My descent to death and to the underworld, which you desire, is a great sign, because it is the salvation of those who are feverish; and it is a great wonder, because it is the resurrection of the dead. Nor will the Christian faith be able to flourish among the nations unless it sees these signs and wonders.”

The ruler—one believer from among the nations, foreshadowed as the firstfruits of the nations—says to him: “Lord, come down before my son dies. Lord, since your descent is a great sign and wonder, and the uncircumcised cannot recover from his illnesses [Col. 0666B] unless he is found worthy to see these signs and wonders, come down, because it is better—as you ordained—that you should come down than that my son, that is, the mind of the Gentile people, should perish forever. Come down, therefore, from the incarnation to the Passion, because from your Passion my soul will obtain liberation.”

To such great faith and devotion the Lord replied only: “Go; your son lives.” For it is difficult to understand that he would have said to an unbelieving and faithless man, “Go; your son lives,” unless he had recognized the faith and devotion of the one pleading. Before performing the miracle, therefore, he foresaw the subtle and faithful response of the petitioner and proceeded to display the miracle, so that the faith of the one who was already believing might also advance [Col. 0666C] into manifestation. “Go,” he said—that is, transmigrate your thoughts toward perfection; and just as you have heard of my incarnation, await my Passion also. For already, from this spark of faith, your son—that is, your mind—lives. No one should be troubled by the fact that all these words are not found according to the historical account, as having been spoken by the ruler—that is, by the human race—to the Lord, and by the Lord to the human race. Such expressions are like those in the Song of Songs, where the bridegroom speaks to the bride and the bride to the bridegroom in words that are nowhere found historically. Such expressions are made not so much by words as by realities. “Go,” he says—that is, advance toward greater things in faith and progress toward spiritual understanding [Col. 0666D], because your son lives through this beginning of faith and through my predestination.

The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and he went. The human race believed that its mind lived inwardly through the grace of God, because it heard this from the Savior’s word, which it had learned to be truthful; and it went on, making progress in faith and conduct.

Now, as he was going down, his servants met him and announced that his son was alive. So he asked them at what hour he had improved. And they said to him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” As the man was descending—that is, returning to himself and examining his thoughts—his servants met him. These can not incongruously be understood as the rational senses of man, which ought to serve man as their master [Col. 0667A], announce what is pleasing, and give an account of the soundness of the whole inner man and mind, just as here they are said to have announced that the son was alive.

For a man to descend from God is for our humanity to be drawn away for a little while from that contemplation and to return somewhat to the things within us, carefully observing what we are and what we have done. For servants to meet their descending master is for all the senses of the whole human being to obey the Lord in his service and devoutly report to their householder what will please him. The man, now strengthened by converse with God and refreshed by the practice of Scripture, ought, like a most discerning investigator, to weigh the matter and, like servants and friends, consult his senses about the hour at which his son had improved, when his mind had recovered more freely [Col. 0667B]. This is what is meant by the statement that he asked them at what hour he had improved.

But let us hear what the servants answered: “Yesterday,” they said, “at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” “Yesterday” is past time. We too, while we are in this life, perceive two times and await a third. All the time from Adam until Christ’s Passion is past time. From Christ’s Passion until the day of judgment is the present time. From the day of judgment, when our bodies have been restored, there will be a third time that can have no end.

Yesterday, therefore, at Christ’s Passion, the fever left man, because Christ fastened to his cross the foreign and disordered heats of our vices and [Col. 0667C] the provocations of various desires, since he himself took our infirmities and bore our pains (Isa. LIII, 4). But this “yesterday,” so great and so long-lasting, had its hours, as one equal period of time succeeded another.

From Adam to Noah is the first hour, which was altered in the Flood. Extend it from Noah to Abraham, and observe the second hour in circumcision. The third runs from Abraham to Moses; take care not to omit the law. The fourth extends from Moses to David, and there you will see the kingdom of the Jews flourishing. The fifth runs from David to the time of the transmigration, and you will not deny that Israel’s glory withered. From there direct the sixth as far as the birth of Saint John, and understand that there the law and the prophets [Col. 0667D] came to an end. Measure the seventh from the birth of Saint John to the Savior’s Passion, and there recognize that the guilt of the whole world was crucified. This is the seventh hour, in which, while Christ taught and admonished, the fever left our mind as the ruler’s son.

And behold, we are already in the eighth, and we sing a psalm to the Lord for the eighth. For we are in a certain glory of resurrection, in a certain eminence of holiness, so that now there is nothing for us to grieve over unless, perhaps, after the washing of baptism we have voluntarily touched some corpse. Thus past time is completed in seven hours to show its imperfection. For if it had possessed a complete day, it would have been closed by twelve hours. Five hours are lacking from yesterday’s day, so that we may understand that neither the law nor that time brought anything to perfection [Col. 0668A]; and let us hear the Psalmist’s lamenting voice: “Your eyes saw my unfinished state” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 16).

But what was lacking from that day was supplied by our day, the eighth day, the day illuminating the day. For behold, we read the Pentateuch with Moses’ veil removed and his face unveiled; spiritually we reduce the Decalogue to the observance of our five senses; and we separate the five prudent virgins from the five foolish ones (Matt. XXV, 3). Our day, however, extends through twelve hours, because our city glories in twelve gates, is commended by twelve apostles, and the fullness of divine abundance and the health of the Church are carried in twelve baskets.

The father therefore recognized that it was the hour at which Jesus had said [Col. 0668B] to him: “Your son lives.” Everyone who, like a father, presides over his own mind ought to weigh the matter by reason and gather from the report of the senses serving him and from the testimony of Scripture that, in yesterday’s time—which is Christ’s Passion, the seventh hour—the mind of man began to live through faith; that is, by believing as one ought in Christ’s death, it immediately merited receiving life.

And he himself believed, and his whole household. The father believes because, with sin now emptied out, as though the fever of his son had been extinguished, he desires inexhaustibly and unfailingly to cling to the Lord. His whole household also believes, because all the movements of the soul that are within him obey his will and advance from virtue to virtue, so that by this very habit they are now almost compelled to do good.

[Col. 0668C]

Having examined these matters, we now wish briefly to repeat the whole reading in order, so that we may also disclose what we still understand about it in another way.

“There was a certain ruler,” and so forth. The Lord brought four people back to life in the Gospel: this ruler’s son, who was beginning to die and signified the spirit of man, which begins to die inwardly through the initial consent to a wrongful pleasure; the girl who was already dead but still shut inside the house, who signified the mind of man, dead inwardly through consent to an unrighteous pleasure and through the hidden commission of a wrongful deed; also the young man carried outside the gate, who signified the man whose spiritual death is publicly evident in his conduct; and Lazarus, dead and buried for four days and stinking, who signified [Col. 0668D] the sinner lying for a long time in the tomb of a deadly way of life and spreading from himself the stench of a sordid reputation.

Among these four degrees of death, the one who is now described as the ruler’s son struggling is the first. Unless I am mistaken, there is no death of the soul in this world that is not found in one of these degrees. Therefore the Lord is described as having raised all these people, to show that he restores all deaths of souls to life. But let us return to the reading.

“There was a certain ruler whose son was ill at Capernaum.” This ruler can appropriately be understood as reason; his son as the thought that is born from rational perception. “There was a certain ruler”—that is, a rational perception whose power was suffering decline [Col. 0669A], whose spiritual kingdom had been diminished. “Whose son was ill”—that is, whose thought and spirit were weakly resisting the pleasures of sin. He was ill at Capernaum.
