Capernaum is interpreted as “field of consolation” and “village of consolation”; it signifies this world, in which those have temporal consolation to whom it is said: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke VI, 24), and of which we read that “the field is the world” (Matt. XIII, 38). He was therefore ill at Capernaum because, amid the prosperity, riches, and blandishments of this age, he was losing his inner strength, so that he was no longer able to resist harmful pleasures.

When this ruler—that is, rational perception—heard from teachers that Jesus was coming from Judaea into Galilee, that is [Col. 0669B], that the Savior was coming from the confession of sins into the transmigration that had been carried out, namely, to those who had transmigrated into iniquity, he went to him—that is, he approached him spiritually through hope and devotion—in order to bring him down to himself. And he begged him to come down—that is, to incline his mercy—and to heal his thought from its weakness in resisting blandishments; for it was beginning to die, that is, to consent to sins.

Then Jesus said to him, rebuking the sluggishness of those who hesitate in faith: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” You do not believe the coming judgment, being stupefied by security, unless you are roused by marvels. For when such people see signs, their minds are accustomed to be terrified and to believe for a time. You do not believe my commandments because you do not do them; you do not believe my promises because you neglect to seek them. Signs and wonders are necessary for you so that through them you may be led to the faith that works through love.

The ruler, diminished in power, says to him: “Lord, come down”—that is, mercifully humble the benefit of your visitation or compassion toward me—“before my thought dies completely through the consummation of its consent to sin.”

Jesus says to him: “Go”—that is, cooperate with my grace, advancing in good works with my help—and thus the son of your heart lives through progress in righteousness. The man believed—that is, reason was obedient—to the word that Jesus spoke, and he went on, advancing along the way of righteousness.

[Col. 0669D]

Now, as he was descending—that is, humbling himself in penitence, afflicting himself, and returning from the height of contemplation to himself—his servants met him. This means that the members of his body served him in doing good, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. VI, 13). From this obedience they announced to him that his inner [188] son was alive. For the flesh cannot be ready to serve for good if its inner master is not living in a good will.

Alternatively, the servants are the bodily senses, which ought to serve reason; they met him when they offered themselves ready for service. Whether these servants are understood as the limbs of the body or as the bodily senses, it is necessary [Col. 0670A] that they announce to the ruler the life of his son, so that he may know with certainty that he is alive; for reason cannot truly recognize that its thought is alive unless good works have indicated its life to it with certainty. No one ought to believe whatever the mind tells him about the life of his thought without the testimony of works. For if the thought truly lives within, the external movements are immediately ordered in action.

So he asked—that is, investigated carefully—them about the hour at which his son had improved. For the works displayed through the members of the body could give this answer.

And they said—that is, they provided him with the reason for understanding—that “yesterday,” namely, in the recollection of past sins, “at the seventh hour,” that is, through the inspiration of the sevenfold Spirit, “the fever left him,” namely, the habitual, burning, and trembling weakness [Col. 0670B]. Or “yesterday,” that is, while he was before God in prayer, the fever left his thought. It was day for him while he stood before God in contemplation and prayer; but night came when he returned to himself. Then, when he vigilantly examined his works and senses in the clear light of his mind, a certain day shone upon him. Yet it was not on this day, but on the preceding day—that is, not when he was attentively observing himself, but when he stood before God as a suppliant—that the inner fever left his thought, as though it were the son of his heart.

And it left him at the seventh hour—that is, in the illumination of sevenfold grace. The father therefore recognized—that is, even after being admonished by the experience of his bodily senses and limbs obeying him for good, rational perception noticed—that this was the hour [Col. 0670C] at which Jesus had said to him: “Your son lives,” that is, the hour at which he first raised his hope for the salvation of his thought. And that rational perception, which previously had not believed fully, believed, and its whole household—that is, the entire multitude of the thoughts of its mind.

Let us also, therefore, recognizing this benefit of the Savior, strive, whenever necessary, to experience the same thing in ourselves. If anyone sees his thought, like a son, languishing amid the enticements of pleasures, let him not allow it to die completely, as did the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, through consent to pleasures and through action; rather, let him hasten to the Savior who seeks the salvation of sinners and obtain from him through devout supplication its life and salvation, by the grace of the Savior himself, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through [Col. 0670D] all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY XV

## ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. But the hired man, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep. The hired man flees because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep.” And the rest. (John X, 11.)

Because many people, paying no attention to themselves and not considering their own vices, take pleasure in hearing in this little exposition of the reading an attack on the life of the pastors of the Church, we have made another brief interpretation of it, one that may recall us to our innermost selves, so that no one may dare to bite at the life of superiors, which Christ himself will examine; rather, let each person strive to be such as the reading demonstrates by its approval and avoid the evils that it condemns [Col. 0671A].

The Lord is speaking to the Pharisees, who boasted that they were not blind; and in their type he denotes the blindness of all false religious people. Let us understand what he says now in such a way that it is referred not to the head itself but to one of its members. For very often in Scripture the Lord’s words are first referred to the Lord himself and then to the Church, which is his body, or to one of the elect, who is his member—as when he says: “Judge, Lord, those who wrong me; fight against those who fight against me” (Ps. XXXIV, 1), and similar passages.

[Col. 0671B]

We therefore wish these words to be understood as though one of his saints were speaking them. He says: “I am the good shepherd.” Each one of us ought to be a shepherd—not just any kind, but a good one—because he has a flock of sheep, that is, of pure and innocent thoughts and virtues, which he should nourish by feeding them in the pastures of Scripture and guard as one who will render an account of them to the Lord.

The holy David was a suitable shepherd of such sheep when he was anointed king, so that he who knew how to govern his own conduct and himself well might become the ruler of others. Saint Job possessed seven thousand such sheep, because he was perfectly enriched with the virtues of sevenfold grace. There are, however, some who do not feed the good things they do upon the meanings and rules of God’s utterances, but nourish them according to what seems [Col. 0671C] right to them. These are not perfectly good shepherds, because they do not feed the flocks of their actions well, since it is written: “Learn to do good” (Isa. I, 17).

The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep because he places his present life, designated by the term “life” (*anima*), in afflictions—that is, he voluntarily subjects it to suffering—for the benefit of his spiritual virtues and good works.

“But the hired man, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. And the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep. The hired man flees because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep.”

[Col. 0671D]

This was said of one who acts laudably; it is also said of one who lives sluggishly. I mean that it was said of the shepherd who does not refuse to lay down his life for the sheep, and it is also said of the hired man who does not dare to resist the wolf. A hired man is one who does good for the sake of temporal rewards, who does not worship God freely, and who, for the things he appears to perform religiously, seeks in this world either the reward of praise or of payment.

Such a person is not a shepherd, because he does not feed the sheep of his actions in the pastures of Scripture, acting according to the manner or devotion taught by the sacred utterances. “Whose own the sheep are not”: the virtues that he appears to guard in himself are alien to him, since he preserves them for a transient recompense and does not love them as his own. Let us therefore hear what this person, who acted in this way amid prosperity, does amid adversity.

[Col. 0672A]

“He sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep,” because, whether in a perverse person or in the storm of rising tribulations, he senses the beast that seeks to devour the sheep of good works—that is, the devil, who strives through the temptations of adversity to destroy the sheepfold of virtues.

The one who previously did good in order to receive a reward for it in the present now sees adversity threatening him because of those very deeds. He leaves the sheep, abandons the virtues he had been guarding, and forsakes the good things he was doing, so as not to suffer evil because of them; and he flees—that is, he withdraws from adversity. For he flees not so much by changing his location as by changing his works.

“And the wolf snatches,” because the devil takes away the good merits he appeared to possess. “And scatters the sheep,” because he dissipates the person’s actions, so that everything he has already done becomes disordered, incongruous, and discordant.

[189] The hired man does not resist the wolf as it devours his flock, but flees, because the one who guarded the sheepfold of virtues or religious actions not for the sake of the virtues themselves but for temporal profits withdraws from their protection and leaves them in the mouth of the devourer, so as not to experience the danger of adversity. He flees for this reason: because he is a hired man, that is, because he was accustomed to preserve works of virtue for the sake of the reward of bodily gains; and he has no concern for the sheep, because the virtues or actions he guards are not his, but the profits he seeks in exchange for them are. Their destruction does not touch his mind with grief, because he loves not them but the reward.

[Col. 0672C]

Up to this point the divine discourse has marked out, under the type of a single person, the perversity of those who, like the Pharisees, do good with a deceitful heart. After this it begins again to describe the purity of those who do good with a perfect heart, when it says through the voice of any such person: “I am the good shepherd.”

It is as though he said: “I feed well and, guarding with genuine care, nourish the sheep of good thoughts and virtues divinely entrusted to me. I know my sheep”—that is, I do not neglect my virtues but love them—“and my own know me”—that is, like those who are beloved by me, they cling to me and are not separated from me even in adversity. For virtues know the one who does not make himself unknown to them through the commission of vices.

[Col. 0672D]

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father”: just as that heavenly Father loved me for my own sake, that is, for my salvation, and not for anything else, so I love him for his own sake and not for anything else. For he sought nothing else through this love except me, nor do I seek anything else through this love except him.

Hence John also says in his epistle: “Because as he is, so are we in this world” (1 John IV, 17). Here “as” does not signify equality but likeness, since we are not speaking of the Redeemer, who according to his divinity is equal to the Father, but of the redeemed person, who is a member of the Redeemer.

The redeemed person accordingly adds: “And I lay down my life for my sheep.” That is, I humble my temporal life in labors and expend it so that I may not lose the sheep of my virtues and actions, but multiply and cherish them [Col. 0673A].

Since, after the labors of the active life, the righteous person usually advances to the sweetness of the contemplative life, he appropriately adds: “And I have other sheep that are not of this sheepfold”—that is, virtues of the sweetness of theoretical contemplation, which do not belong to the flock of virtues exercised in practice. For the righteous person has some virtues in the active life and others in the contemplative life.

“And those,” he says, “I must bring,” namely, those that belong to contemplation, “to the limits of my ability,” so that in my way of life I may join them to those that belong to action.

“And they will hear my voice,” because they will carry out the word of my will; that is, they will follow the inclination of my heart. For the heart too has its own voice and its own speech. “And there will be one sheepfold” made from the virtues of both lives, “and there will be one shepherd” of both—namely, my mind, which is watchful in guarding both.

If anyone attends carefully to these things and examines whether or not he himself has acted in this way, he will cease to tear apart the life of the Church’s pastors.

# HOMILY XVI

[Note: [Col. 0673D] From the Corbie manuscript, no. 596.]

## ON THE PASSAGE: “For it was fitting for him, for whom and through whom are all things,” etc. (Hebr. II, 10.)

Almighty God, even if he had created no creature at all, could have been fully blessed in himself, since he needed nothing and was entirely sufficient to himself. Wishing, however, out of his supreme goodness, for the creature to be blessed—a blessing that was to come solely from knowledge and love of him—he made the angelic creatures, by whom he would be praised; not so that anything might be added to him from their praise, but to them.

Moreover, by that same goodness, so that praise might not be imperfect, he created a corporeal creature and willed to bless it [Col. 0673C]. For this reason he placed a rational spirit in the body, so that by governing it well the spirit might be blessed in God together with the body, and thus the praise of God might be complete from every creature.

Hence all things are said to praise God: rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—marvel at and praise God’s wondrous power and goodness both in themselves and in the other creatures.

Thus the Apostle says: “For whom are all things,” namely, for the one who is to be praised and glorified; “and through whom are all things,” namely, nothing is superfluous. If this is true—and indeed because it is true—the human being must be led to glory. Yet this necessity proceeds from no other source than the great goodness of God that we mentioned above.

Man was lost through his sin; therefore he is not led to glory; therefore he does not praise. Consequently the corporeal creature does not praise either; therefore it was made in vain. And if that is so, then even the angels do not praise fully, since their number has been diminished. But in order to suppress all these absurdities at the very source from which they proceed, let us establish that lost man is led to glory. With the author’s help, let us examine the order of this glorious salvation.

God created man in the middle position in such a way that, if he remained obedient to God, then, once his obedience had been completed, he would pass from mortal to immortal without the intervention of death; but if not [Col. 0674A], he would fall from mortality into death.

Persuaded, therefore, by the devil, he became dead from mortal according to God’s terrible threat, and was justly possessed by the devil, to whom he had willingly consented (Gen. II, 17). Nevertheless, God willed to reclaim him, because although he had fallen willingly, he had fallen through another’s persuasion. The devil, however, ought not to have been reclaimed, because in the firmness of his own nature he had fallen by himself, without any external persuasion.

Therefore man needed to have an author of salvation through whom he might return to God by a just ordering. Let us see, then, who that author could have been. If he were simply God, he could indeed conquer the devil and rescue man; but this alone would be power, not the rationale of justice. It would not be just for him to take away from the devil—who, as the Apostle says, held the dominion of death (Hebr. II, 14)—the man who had willingly submitted to him, even though [Col. 0674B] the devil had invaded what belonged to another.

If he were simply man, how would he resist in a corrupted nature, when, placed in a better condition, he had fallen so easily? Here it must be noted that God’s grace does not impose force upon free will.

Again, if an angel undertook this combat, why would the devil’s defeat thereby entail the loss of the man? There would be no rational basis for it. Nor could the angel accomplish this in man, because if he were found weak in his own simple and strong nature, he would be found much weaker when joined to this lowly nature—namely, the human.

Therefore that author of salvation must be God in man, who, insofar as he is God, is able, and insofar as he is man, ought to act.

It was entirely fitting that, just as the devil first invaded [Col. 0674C] another’s property through an evil deception, so God should, so to speak, make the property his own through a good deception by grace; and just as that man fell through his own freedom, so this man should resist the devil through freedom of will.

He also had to suffer, so that the devil might sin against one in whom he found no fault by punishing him. For the devil attacked him, as he did the others, with every kind of temptation: first with flattering enticements, like a dragon; then with harsh ones, like a lion; and finally he killed him. Thus he most justly lost all his dominion over human beings, since he extended himself beyond what was permitted.

Hence the common law still holds that one who demands more than is owed loses what is owed. Therefore, just as he lost his right over the one who did not consent to him, so he lost it over all that one’s children who imitate his innocence.

Now this man ought not to remain in death, because [Col. 0674D] in that way he would have profited neither himself nor another. He therefore had to be perfected through suffering, so that in this way he might perfect his followers. This is what the Apostle says: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things.”

Mark each clause carefully. “It was fitting to lead many sons into glory”—namely, the Father, for whom—that is, for the purpose of being praised and glorified—all things were made, and through whom all things were made. This was accomplished by giving an author of salvation, namely Christ; by giving him over to suffering; and thus by bringing him to perfection.

If you carefully consider this order, you will see that man ought to have been saved even if no angel had fallen.

[Col. 0675]

# SERMON OF SAINT ANSELM ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD

(From manuscript no. 1697 of the Royal Library.)

[Col. 0675A]

Lord Jesus Christ, good shepherd, who deigned to die for your flock, acknowledge me among your sheep and draw me to your pastures; acknowledge your little sheep, so that I may deserve to be at your right hand. Make me a sharer in your glory, you who drank the bitter cup for me. Your punishment torments my conscience; your sufferings torture my memory. For I feared the potion which you drank [Note: [Col. 0675C] Read *confeci*, “I completed,” or another similar verb.] I sinned in what you bore; I, a disobedient servant, committed what you scourged; I [Note: [Col. 0675C] A verb such as *contraxi*, “I contracted,” is missing.] what you discharged. My wickedness was the cause of your death; my crimes inflicted your wounds.

Woe to my sins, which had to be expiated by so bitter a death! O my sins, how bitter you were, when you promised me sweetness and deceived me! O unhappy Eve, who bit the apple and brought death upon all [Col. 0675B]—indeed, who killed both God and man along with us! O unhappy man, who for a brief pleasure handed yourself over to the devil and destroyed both yourself and your descendants! Although God did not will it, forbade it, and threatened death, you consented to the devil; by God’s ordering, you found what was good and received grace.

O ineffable mercy! Where sin abounded, grace also abounded exceedingly (1 Tim. 1:14), so that, although no one but a human being ought to make satisfaction for the fault, no one but God could absolve it. He had sent [him] to become human, so that, owing nothing for himself, he might by dying for us release our sin. Therefore God is clothed in flesh; he who is is conceived, the Word is incorporated, the Eternal is born, bread is wrapped, placed in a manger, circumcised, baptized, hungers, and is tempted. God, as man, is sold, seized, held, bound, reviled, filled with insults, given vinegar and gall to drink, [Col. 0675C] crowned with thorns, counted among thieves, condemned to the most shameful death, and fastened to the cross.

Behold how God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us (Rom. 8:32). O grace of the one who hands him over! O compassion of his death! O good Jesus! O merciful Jesus! What shall I give you, what shall I endure for you, who endured so many and such great things for me? The performance of a work is proof of love. What, then, shall I do, who have received so much though utterly unworthy? What shall I return? What shall I repay?

Take what is yours; do with your servant what pleases you. I ought not to take away your right; I ought not to give your servant to another master. [Col. 0676A] Your right is my soul; my body is your servant. You made my soul your right when you gave your soul for it; you made my body your servant when you handed your body over to death for it. You gave your whole self for me and worked everything in me; you bought my spirit for yourself, you bought my body for yourself—both are your servants. Therefore I am yours in spirit and body; I ought to devote both to you.

Let me love you, then, with all my heart; let me serve you with my whole body. For me your eyes grew dim in death; may my wandering eyes be restrained, lest they see vanity. Your ears were open to insults and blasphemies; may my deaf ears be opened to the cry of the poor. [Col. 0676B] Your mouth was given gall and vinegar to drink; may my lying mouth speak truth and judgment. Your hands were stretched out upon the cross; may my contracted hands be stretched out toward the needy. Your feet were pierced with nails; may my crooked feet be directed into straight paths. Your side was opened by the lance; may I open my heart through confession, so that I may acknowledge my wound.

Your whole body endured the pangs of death, so that my putrid body might become your member. O good Lord, what shall I, a worthless slave, an unprofitable servant, repay you for such great benefits?

Shall I rejoice or grieve over your death? Certainly I shall do both. I shall rejoice at the grace of the one who hands himself over and at the love of the one who dies (These words are from Meditation II, *On Human Redemption*, p. 222, second edition). But first I shall grieve over the cause of your death—that is, over the consciousness of sin—and I shall grieve with the one who dies. If I do not rejoice, I am ungrateful; if I do not grieve, I am cruel. [Col. 0676C] But because it is a time for weeping before laughter, I walk sorrowfully with bowed head, and I shall be conformed to your Passion.

Let the iron of your Passion pass through my soul, and let your cross suspend my lust. Pierce my flesh with your fear, so that I may not follow my desires. Put to death in my flesh every stimulus of the flesh and every lustful movement, and grant me true and perpetual chastity and eternal life. Amen.

[Col. 0677]

## Saint Anselm’s Exhortation to Contempt for Temporal Things and Desire for Eternal Things (G)*

[Col. 0677A]

What are you doing, O man? Why do you move about in the world like an animal? The Lord created you wise and discerning. Do not wish to be like those who lack prudence. Keep watch, O pitiable one; have mercy on yourself. Be wise. For your sake the exalted God came from heaven, to raise you from earthly things to heaven.

You have been invited, O man, to the wedding feast of the heavenly Bridegroom. Why do you despise it and show yourself unworthy? Tell me, how will you enter the wedding feast without a precious garment or a shining lamp? Hate the world; make God your meditation. Abhor wickedness and sin, and love your gracious Redeemer.

Keep yourself pure on earth; like an angel, hold chaste and holy thoughts continually. Correct yourself from perverse [Col. 0677B] thoughts, lest you become entangled in the deeds of the world. Free your soul entirely from the vain affairs of this world, so that you may be crowned by Christ above the heavens. Be like a cloud bringing forth a rain of tears, so that you may extinguish the flames of sins.

Remember that dreadful day; apply remedies to the wounds of your soul. Walk courageously in the law of the Lord; continually make progress through sincere faith and charity. Grow daily through discipline in self-restraint, holding a sure hope of seeing the Lord in his splendor, kingdom, and glory. Beware of an idle word, lest you depart from Christ’s command. Plant a good planting in your heart and soul—namely, the virtues, the ways of the holy Fathers, and of priests who please God [Col. 0677C].

Remember, pitiable one, that you walk amid the snares of the devil. Wake up, lest you fall into the abyss of death. Do not suppose that you will live long on earth; do not therefore linger longer in evil deeds. Pray always to Christ, so that your whole affection may bear fruit; so that your life, like good and excellent soil, may be fruitful and most acceptable to God.

Keep the day of your departure before your eyes. Hasten to be found without sin at that hour, so that on the day of your calling your soul may ascend to God, borne upward by the ministrations of angels. Hate this world; love your Redeemer with the whole desire of your mind. Do not neglect your soul, nor let it take pleasure in the deadly sweetness and pleasantness of the devil’s snares, lest, weighed down by sins and immense confusion [Col. 0678A], it tremble and waste away in that hour from excessive fear.

Be ever ready, senseless one; keep watch, free from every earthly impurity. Take care to be delivered from every scandal and most shameful thought. Be prudent, senseless one; awaken from the sleep of wickedness. If you wish to be heavenly, continually abhor and despise earthly things. Follow the examples of the perfect, so that you may reach the paradise of delights and the desired homeland of the priests.

Why do you hate your life, pitiable one? What do you seek more precious than your soul, most faithless one? Draw near, hurry, before the door of repentance is closed. Gladden the heavenly host by your manner of life.

The physician awaits seeing your tears. Draw near, [Col. 0678B] do not be afraid. Show your wound, and offer the medicine of tears and weeping. Behold, the door of repentance is open. Hurry before it is closed.

Pour out tears while there is time, lest in the other age you weep without profit. Here there is mercy; there, judgment. Here pleasure; there, torments. Here laughter; there, weeping. Here singing; there, eternal fire. Here adornment of clothing; there, the torment of worms. Here exaltation; there, humiliation. Humble yourself, therefore, in this life, lest you be condemned in the outer darkness. Let no earthly delight please you here, lest bitter lamentation await you there.

Who would not weep for us, and who would not mourn? Hating life, we love death. What is higher and more magnificent than to exercise the mind and bring the flesh into servitude, so that it obeys the command of the spirit, submits to its counsels, and diligently carries out the spirit’s purpose and will? What food, moreover, is more delightful than to do the will of God and overcome the devil’s assaults by strength of mind?

Let each person conquer himself, restrain anger, and not be softened by any enticements. Let him not be disturbed by adversity, nor lifted up by prosperity, nor carried about as if by a wind through the changing conditions of various things. Consider, dearest, within yourself what is better: to weep for sins in the present age and pray more frequently, or to weep in eternal fire without any profit.

Why does the strength of your spirit waste away through affection for and desire of the perishing world? Lift your mind to the immeasurable splendor of eternal happiness, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, which God has prepared for those who love him [Col. 0679A] (1 Cor. 2:9). Maintain restraint in your tongue, restraint in your gaze, in food, clothing, thought, and laughter, so that you may be shown in all things to be God’s most perfect athlete. Strive above all not to have any enemy except the devil.

What benefit can a gift bring you if you are bound by its concerns? What do you gain from concern for costly clothing except eternal punishments? Why are you puffed up with swelling pride? Who would not tremble, lament, and mourn when our hidden things are revealed in the sight of angels and human beings? Why do you grieve your most loving Father by your evil deeds, senseless one, the one who deigned to count you among his children?

Restrain your tongue from evil, seek peace, and pursue it (Ps. 33:14), lest the Lord, angered by your evils, hand you over as a most wicked servant to perpetual punishment if you refuse to follow him to glory. If you are to serve the eternal King as a soldier, renounce your own wills. Be content with every lowliness and extremity. Declare with your tongue that you are lower than all; believe in the innermost affection of your heart that you are more worthless. Do, while there is opportunity, what will profit you forever.

Rise during the night for prayers and tears to God, so that you may be delivered from all the snares and scandals of the passions. For if your soul is suddenly taken from you, it will be found sinful and most foul, without time for final repentance. What will you say to death at the hour of your separation, when you will no longer be granted even a moment of one hour to live? Keep the day of death before your eyes. Consider how you will have to stand before [Col. 0679C] the judgment seat. Continually prepare your lamp in the best preservation; hurry so that it may always be burning.

Despise temporal and perishable things, so that, like an outstanding warrior abandoning the pomp of the world, you may deserve the prize after victory. Return, pitiable one, to your conscience; unload yourself from the burdens of earthly concerns. Let contention not rule in you, nor contradiction, nor any iniquity at all. Reject earthly things; desire heavenly things; abandon temporal things; love eternal blessedness.

Awaken for a little while from your pitiable sleep, open your mouth, entreat God, and cast the burdens of sins from you. Pray frequently; pour out tears without ceasing. Flee softness of spirit; abhor negligence [Col. 0679D]; detest wickedness. Love gentleness; cherish self-restraint; meditate on psalmody.

Hurry to pray while there is time for repentance. Love God with all your soul (Matt. 22:39), as he loved you. Fear the day of judgment. For Christ’s love, deny yourself to yourself. Guard the acts of your life at every hour. Make yourself a stranger to the deeds of the world, so that you may become heir to the kingdom of God.

Listen, soul, to what I say; hear what I speak; attend to what I admonish. Let no impurity pollute you any longer; let no lust stain you. Withdraw yourself from every corruption of the flesh; extract yourself from every corruption of the flesh. Let wantonness no longer prevail; let lust no longer enslave you. For it is better to die than to be stained by lust. [Col. 0680A] It is better to pour out the soul than to lose it through lack of self-restraint.

Chastity makes a human being close to God; chastity makes God close to a human being; the kingdom of heaven is promised to the chaste. But if you are still touched by the goads of the flesh, if you are still struck by the suggestion of lust, set the remembrance of death before yourself; put the day of your departure before yourself; place the end of life before your eyes. Set before yourself the future judgment and future torments; set before yourself the perpetual fires of hell; set before yourself the horrible punishments of Gehenna.

Pray continually with tears; pray always; persist frequently in prayer. Entreat God by day and night; devote yourself constantly to prayer; always groan and weep. Rise at night for prayer; spend the night in prayer [Col. 0680B] and supplication; devote yourself to nightly vigils; pray again, closing your eyes for a little while.

Frequent prayer drives away the devil’s darts; the frequency of prayer expels unclean spirits; the persistence of prayer conquers unclean spirits; demons are overcome by prayer; prayer prevails over all evils.

Take away from yourself, too, the satiety of bread; discipline your body by frugality. Devoted to fasts and abstinence, wear a pale face and carry a lean body. Hunger and thirst; abstain and grow thin. Unless you are trained by fasts, you cannot overcome temptations.

Be humble; be founded in humility; humble yourself; make yourself least. Put yourself before no one; consider yourself superior to no one. Regard everyone as superior to you. Consider yourself the least of all; reckon yourself lower than everyone [Col. 0680C]. However great you are, hold to humility. For the humbler you are, the greater height of glory will follow you.

Beware of boastfulness; beware of the desire for display; beware of pursuit of empty glory. Do not arrogate anything to yourself; do not boast. Do not lift yourself up insolently; do not spread the wings of pride. Do not raise the feathers of exaltation; presume nothing about yourself; attribute no good to yourself.

Do not be proud of the virtue of justice through any elation; do not be lifted up by good deeds; do not glory in a good work. Humble yourself so that you may be exalted, lest, once exalted, you be humbled. For whoever lifts himself up is humbled; whoever is exalted is cast down; whoever is raised up is thrown prostrate; whoever is puffed up is dashed to the ground.

Pride cast down the angels; swelling pride dissolves kingdoms; arrogance humbled the lofty. Humility knows no fall; humility does not know a lapse. Recognize, pitiable one, that the humble God has come. Walk as he walked; follow his example; imitate his footsteps.

Consider yourself worthless, rejected, despised; be displeasing to yourself; be despised in your own eyes. For whoever is worthless in his own eyes is great before God. Whoever displeases himself pleases God. Be little in your own eyes, therefore, so that you may be great in God’s eyes. For you will be more precious to God the more despised you are among human beings.

Always bear shame upon your face from remembrance of your offense; bear embarrassment in your countenance from memory of the sin committed. Blush to raise your eyes because of the shame of sin [Col. 0681A]. Walk with lowered face, downcast countenance, mournful mouth, beaten breast, and sorrowful clothing; wrapped in sackcloth, with your body covered by haircloth; always mourning, always sorrowful, always groaning, always sending forth sighs from your heart. Let there be contrition in your heart and lamentation in your breast; let weeping and mourning always delight you.

Always be ready for tears. Never abandon mourning and tears. Let nothing make you secure about sin; let hope and fear continually remain in your heart. Hope for mercy in this way, and fear justice; let hope of forgiveness raise you up in this way, and let fear of Gehenna always afflict you.

Do not be saddened by your weaknesses; give thanks to God in your illnesses. Desire to be healthy in spirit rather than in body; desire to be healthy in mind rather than in flesh. Illness wounds the flesh but chastens the mind.

If prosperity smiles upon you, do not be lifted up; if adversity occurs, do not be cast down. If calamity befalls you, do not become fainthearted. Maintain moderation in prosperity; maintain patience in adversity. Recognize that you are being tested in suffering, lest you be exalted.

Be even-tempered in all things; let your mind be changed neither by joy nor by sorrow. Bear everything with equal resolve; do not be changed toward any insolence. Let no misfortune find you unprepared; let there be no misfortune which your meditation has not anticipated.

Set before yourself that nothing is impossible. In favorable circumstances, consider how you will bear adversity; always imagine future miseries. Misfortune yields to prudent counsel; forethought breaks the force of assaults when they come [Col. 0681C]. Prepare your heart, therefore, for good things and for bad; bear good and bad as they occur; tolerate adversity and prosperity as they come; whatever happens, endure it with a free mind.

If anger arises beforehand, restrain it; if it has seized you, calm it. Temper fury; temper indignation; restrain the movement of your spirit; curb the attack of anger. If you cannot avoid anger, at least temper it; if you cannot guard against fury, at least restrain it. Learn to bear evils rather than to return them; learn to tolerate evils rather than to commit them.

Be gentle, patient, mild, and restrained. Preserve patience; preserve moderation. Despise the insults of inflicted abuse. Break the arrows of insult with the shield of patience [Col. 0681D]. Prepare the shield of patience against harsh words; offer the shield of patience against the sword of the tongue. However much anyone incites, provokes, insults, abuses, accuses, challenges you to litigation, speaks insult, does injury, or treats you abusively, be silent, keep quiet, disregard it; overlook the injury; do not answer; do not return the insult. By keeping silent you will conquer more quickly.

Learn endurance from Christ; learn moderation. Look to Christ, and do not grieve over injuries. Temper grief through consideration of justice. Pacify enemies with every moderation; overcome the evils of others by your good.

Therefore, when you are disparaged, pray; when you are cursed, bless; oppose a blessing to the one who curses you [Col. 0682A]. Calm the angry person with patience; dissolve the fury of the enraged with gentleness; conquer wickedness by kindness; conquer malice by goodness. Meet even insults inflicted on you with a tranquil mind. Open the pain of the injury with a calm heart, for an enclosed wound greatly consumes the spirit.

If you have saddened your brother in anything, do penance before him. If you have offended against your brother, reconcile him through prayer. Quickly ask forgiveness for your offense, with the swiftest affection of love; invite him to forgiveness through humility; beg forgiveness with a suppliant spirit; prostrate yourself in affection.

Pleasantly forgive the one who asks forgiveness; immediately embrace the one who returns; promptly receive the one who comes back with kindly love. Forgive so that you may be forgiven; pardon so that you may be pardoned [Col. 0682B]. You will not have forgiveness unless you give it. Even if he does not plead, does not ask to be forgiven, does not possess the humility to beg, and does not acknowledge his sin because of a bad conscience, release him from your heart; forgive him in your spirit; freely pardon him; grant forgiveness of your own will.

Do not retain resentment and grief in your heart; remove your brother’s offense from your heart; do not preserve sorrow over another’s wickedness. Hatred separates a person from the kingdom of God, withdraws him from heaven, and casts him out of paradise. Hatred is removed neither by suffering nor expiated by martyrdom.

What shall I say of the fires of jealousy? Envy burns up every seedling of virtue; envy devours every good thing with its pestilential heat. It first harms itself, first bites itself, and first gnaws at its own author. Envy is the moth of the soul [Col. 0682C]; it eats away understanding, burns the breast, afflicts the mind, and, like a plague, consumes the human heart.

Let goodness therefore confront jealousy; let charity be prepared against envy. Love peace; cherish peace; preserve peace with everyone; embrace all in gentleness and charity. Do not be unfaithful in peace. Be ready in affection, and always preserve the bond of steadfastness. Have tranquility of mind and kindness of spirit.

Be agreeable in speech; appear to all with a grateful spirit; flee quarrels; avoid lawsuits; beware of contentions; remove occasions of litigation. Despise strife; live always in peace; do not strive to contend in any action. Contention gives birth to lawsuits, produces quarrels, kindles the torches of hatred, extinguishes peace of heart, and breaks concord.

[Col. 0682D]

If your enemy falls, do not rejoice; do not be lifted up at the ruin of your adversary. Rather, let a humane feeling toward his humiliation be yours. Satisfy yourself with tears at the sorrows of others. Let your breast not be iron, nor your heart hard. Mourn another’s misery as though it were your own. Weep with those who weep; join your affection of mind to those who mourn.

In all your actions, in all your work, and in your entire manner of life, imitate the good and emulate the saints. Let the examples of the Fathers be incentives to discipline. Let no one be scandalized by disgrace in life; let no one be saddened by an adverse report. Learn, O man, to burn with praise; possess a good testimony. Let your reputation be darkened by no foulness; let it be torn by no reproach.

[Col. 0683A]

Beware of popular glory; avoid the admiration of the crowd; despise favors. Strive to be good rather than to appear good. Let favor not seduce you, nor blame break you. Whoever does not seek praise does not feel insult. Judge yourself by your own judgment, not by another’s. Measure yourself by your own mind, not by that of others.

Be what you wish to be considered. Demonstrate your profession both by your clothing and by your conduct. Do not make a spectacle of yourself; do not give others an opportunity to disparage you. Avoid the wicked; beware of the unjust; desire the company of the good; seek the fellowship of the good; cling inseparably to the holy. It is better to hate the wicked than to associate with them.

Restrain your tongue even from idle speech; repress your tongue from an idle word. Reject immodest conversations [Col. 0683B]; flee dishonorable words. Do not chatter empty words, for vain speech quickly pollutes the mind, and what is gladly heard is easily done. Let that proceed from your lips which does not pollute the ears of the hearer. Avoid small things, lest you reach greater ones. Let what you say be worthy and laden with instruction.

Let your speech be irreproachable and useful to the expectation of those who hear. Discern what you should say and what you should keep silent; be skilled both in speaking and in silence. Deliberate at length beforehand about what you should say; contend in nothing. Put a seal upon your lips; impose the bars of silence; surround your tongue with the fortification of watchfulness. Let a question open your mouth.

Let your words be few. Much speaking does not avoid sin. A talkative person is unlearned; the wise use few words [Col. 0683C]. To speak much is foolishness; knowledge makes speech brief. The unlearned makes enough noise and says nothing meaningful. The voice of the foolish lies in multiplying speech. Always moderate your words; let measure remain in your word and a balance in your speech.

Do not tear apart another’s life; do not defile your mouth with another’s evil. Do not slander the sinner, but grieve with him. Fear in yourself what you disparage in another. Slander is a grave crime; slander is a grave condemnation. Nothing is fouler than this; this is the height of disgrace. It is the practice of dogs to tear apart, to exercise their tongues, and to bite with a deadly tooth.

When you slander another, examine yourself; when you bite another, rebuke your own sins. If you wish to slander, turn yourself back toward your own sins [Col. 0683D]; look not at another’s offenses but at your own. Attend to your own vices, not those of another.

You will never slander another if you have examined yourself well. Therefore, concerned with your own correction and intent upon your own salvation, do not lend an ear to whisperers. Slanderers and those who listen are held liable by the same guilt. Correct your own vices with as much care as you observe those of others.

193 Beware of lying in everything; speak falsely neither by accident nor deliberately. There is no just lie; every lie is sin. For everyone who lies kills the soul. And: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7); and: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19:5). Flee deceit, therefore; avoid lying [Col. 0684A]. Beware of falsehood; never lie. Be truthful in speech; deceive no one by lying.

Prohibit oaths; remove swearing. Let “it is” be in your mouth; let “it is not” be in your mouth. Do not be easy in words and difficult in deeds. Change your resolution concerning a shameful vow.

Sin there where you do not know the Lord to be. The one who made hidden things sees what is hidden; and if public reputation does not condemn you, let your own conscience nevertheless condemn you.

In all your work, ask God’s help; ascribe everything to divine grace and divine gift; attribute nothing to your merits; presume nothing upon your own strength.

Promise nothing without consideration of your abilities. Those who have not fulfilled what they promised are counted among the faithless. Hide your virtues lest you become elated [Col. 0684B]. Conceal your good deeds out of humility; avoid being seen as what you have deserved to be.

Reveal the vices of your heart; immediately make your perverse thoughts known. If a fault is exposed, it becomes small from being great; if it is hidden, it becomes great from being small.

Deliberate for a long time over a doubtful decision. Investigate at length what you intend to do. Let sluggish laxity be absent from good things; let sluggish negligence be absent. Delaying what is expedient obstructs it. Sloth cools the intellect; negligence and torpor dissolve the spirit.

Nothing is better than wisdom; nothing sweeter than prudence; nothing more pleasant than knowledge; nothing worse than folly; nothing uglier than cowardice. The uneducated is easily deceived; the foolish quickly slips into vices.

[Col. 0684C]

Fulfill in deed what you promise with your mouth; let your words precede your works. Beware lest, while raising others by teaching them, you yourself sink through desire for praise.

Yield quickly to truth; remove contention from debate; remove obstinate defense. Love hearing more than speaking; listen first and speak last. Be the first to keep silent; speak last.

Render honor to each person according to his dignity. Yield to the authority of elders; obey their will. But if ordered to do evil, do not comply. If ordered to do evil, do not consent.

Keep measure in every work; keep discretion in every matter. What you wish to be done to you, do to another. Be toward others as you wish others to be toward you. Beware of honors you cannot sustain. The height of honors [Col. 0684D] is the magnitude of crimes.

Why do you delay until tomorrow? You can gain today as well. For you must beware lest you fail to retain that day also and lose this one. Even a single hour is no small loss.

Therefore pray to God by day and by night, and restrain your eyes from wantonness. Remove the occasion; take away the material for sinning. Arrange everything not with a troubled spirit but with a tranquil heart; judge no one more strictly than yourself.

Brief is the happiness of this world; limited is the glory of this age. Temporal power is fleeting and fragile. Say: Where are the kings? Where the princes? Where the emperors? Where the wealthy in worldly possessions? Where the powerful of the age? [Col. 0685A] Where the rich of the world? They passed away like a shadow and vanished like a dream.

The cares of worldly affairs disturb the mind; the concerns of affairs harass the mind. If you wish to be tranquil, desire nothing of the age. You will always possess rest of mind if you cast the cares of the world away from you. Whoever entangles himself in earthly concerns separates himself from the love of God.

No one can embrace the glory of God and the world at the same time. No one can embrace Christ and the age at the same time. Renounce everything, therefore, for God’s sake. Strive to serve God without the world’s impediment.

Share with everyone; give to everyone; provide for everyone. Let goodwill be greater than the thing obtained; let favor be greater than the thing given. There is no mercy where there is no goodwill. Your work will be such as your intention has been.

[Col. 0685B]

Be a temple of God, and the exalted God will dwell in [Col. 0686A] you. From your just labors provide for the poor; do not take from one in order to give to another.

Whatever you do, do it for the future reward, in expectation of eternal recompense. Future reward, not present reward, is promised to the saints. Reward is promised to the righteous in heaven, not on earth. What is to be given elsewhere is not to be awaited here.

Be dead to the world, and let the world be dead to you. Look upon the glory of the world as one dead; like one buried, have no concern for the age. As one deceased, deprive yourself of every earthly occupation. While alive, despise what you cannot possess after death.

Strive for nothing on account of praise, nothing on account of temporal opinion, nothing on account of reputation, but for eternal life—which may he grant you who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0685B]

## Saint Anselm’s Admonition to One Dying and Excessively Afraid of His Sins (G)*

[Note: [Col. 0685C] This has been compared with the Beccian manuscripts E. 10 and O., one Vatican manuscript (1237), and one manuscript of the Library of Saint-Germain. Vatican manuscript: “Admonition of Blessed Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.” Manuscript Bec. E. 10: “Whoever, near death, has spoken with a contrite and confessed heart shall not see death for ever.” Manuscript Bec. O.: “Blessed Anselm the archbishop to a certain dying man, excessively afraid of his sins.” “Admonition to one dying.”]

[Col. 0685C]

194 **Question.** [Note: *Interrogatio*; manuscript Vict.: *magister*, “master”; the other manuscripts omit this.] Brother, do you rejoice that you are dying in the Christian faith?  
[Note: *Morieris*, “you will die,” in the Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts, instead of *moreris*, “you are dying.”]

**Answer.** [Note: Vatican manuscript: *Discipulus*, “disciple.”] I rejoice.  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts add *etiam*, “indeed.”]

**Question.** Do you rejoice that you are dying in the monastic habit?  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts read “in the habit of religion” and “in the monastic habit.”]

**Answer.** I rejoice.  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts add *etiam*, “indeed.”]

**Question.** Do you confess that you have lived so badly that eternal punishment is due to you by your merits?  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts read: “Do you confess that you have not lived well, as you ought?” Another reading is: “Do you confess that you have lived so badly that eternal punishment is due to you by your merits?”]

**Answer.** I confess.  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts add *etiam*, “indeed.”]

**Question.** Do you repent of this?  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts read: “Do you repent of having offended God?” and “Do you repent of this?”]

**Answer.** I repent.

**Question.** Do you have the will to amend your life, if you had time?  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts read: “If you had time to live?” and “If you had time?”]

[Col. 0686C]

**Answer.** Indeed.  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts read *habeo*, “I have [it],” and *etiam*, “indeed.”]

**Question.** Do you believe that the Lord Jesus Christ died for you?  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts read: “Do you truly believe that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, died for you?” and “Do you believe that the Lord Jesus Christ died for you?”]

**Answer.** I believe.

**Question.** Do you give him thanks?  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts read: “Do you also give thanks for his Passion and death?” and “Do you give him thanks?”]

**Answer.** I do.  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts add *etiam*, “indeed.”]

**Question.** Do you believe that you can be saved only through his death?

**Answer.** I believe.  
[Note: The Beccian and Saint-Germain manuscripts add *etiam*, “indeed.”]

Interrogation. Come, then, while breath still remains in you; place all your trust in this death alone; have confidence in nothing else; commit yourself wholly to this death; cover yourself entirely with this death alone; envelop yourself wholly in this death; and if the Lord God wishes to judge you, say: “Lord, I set the death of our Lord Jesus Christ between myself and your judgment; otherwise I do not contend with you.” And if he says to you that you are a sinner, say: “Lord, I set the death of the Lord Jesus Christ between you and my sins.” If he says to you that you have deserved condemnation, say: “Lord, I place the death of our Lord Jesus Christ between you and my evil merits; and I offer his merit in place of the merit which I ought to have had but do not have.” If he says that he is angry with you, say: “Lord, I oppose the death of the Lord Jesus Christ to your anger against me.” When this has been completed, say again: “Lord, I place the death of our Lord Jesus Christ between you and me and your anger.” Having done this, let the sick man say three times these words: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit. You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth.” Again, the verse: “You have broken my bonds, Lord; to you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord.” The verse: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name; the righteous await me until you repay me.” Afterwards let him say: “Mary, mother of grace, mother of mercy, protect us from the enemy and receive us at the hour of death. Therefore, O Virgin, through your Son, through the Father and the Holy Spirit, be present at my death, because my departure is near. Amen.”

[Note: At col. 0685C: “Come, then, always while breath is in you; place your trust in Christ, and establish your faith in this death of Jesus Christ alone, and hope in no other thing.” The manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read *sperans hujus morti*, “hoping in this death.”]

[Note: At col. 0685C, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “Commit and entrust yourself; cover yourself wholly with this death”; alternatively: “commit yourself, cover yourself wholly with this alone.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “Say to him thus: Lord.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “And if he says that you deserve it.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “And if he says to you that you are a sinner, say: Lord, I set the death of the Lord Jesus Christ between you and my sins. If he says to you that you have deserved it.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “Answer him thus: Lord.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “Between me and you, my evil merits, and his death; I offer the merit.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “between you and my evil merits; I offer his merit.” The manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer also read: “between me and you, my evils; I offer his death.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “and do not have it.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “And say again: Lord, I place the death of the Lord Jesus Christ between you and me and your anger. Having completed this, let him say.” Alternatively: “If he says that he is angry with you, say: Lord; I oppose the death of the Lord Jesus Christ to your anger. Having completed this, let him say.”]

[Note: At col. 0687B, the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer read: “Three times these words: ‘Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.’” In the manuscripts of Bec and Saint-Germer this admonition ends here.]

[Note: The manuscript omits the passage beginning “Again, the verse: ‘You have broken…’” through “Let the priest begin and say.”]

After these words and responses have been spoken by the sick man, let the priest say the following psalms on behalf of the sick man: Psalm: “Save me, O God, by your name.” Psalm: “I believed.” Psalm: “O God, come to my assistance.” Psalm: “With my voice.” Psalm: “In you, Lord, I have hoped.”

[Col. 0688A]

If he is a layman, the priest must question him in the following manner.

First question. Do you believe those things which belong to the Christian faith, insofar as they have been determined by the Church?

Response. I believe.

Question. Do you rejoice because you are dying in the Christian faith?

Response. I rejoice.

Question. Do you acknowledge that you have gravely offended God?

Response. I acknowledge it.

Question. Do you grieve that you have offended your Creator?

Response. I grieve.

[Note: The manuscripts omit the passage beginning “Question. Do you grieve…” through “At the end make her say.”]

Question. Do you propose that, if God prolongs your life for you, you will avoid offending him?

Response. I propose it.

[Col. 0688B]

Question. Do you hope and believe that you will attain eternal salvation, not through your own merits, but through the merits of the passion of Jesus Christ?

Response. I hope so.

Then the assurance follows, and he should say to himself: “If anyone presents himself against you and brings a charge against you, set the merits of Christ’s passion between yourself and him.” At the end make him say these verses: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend…” and so forth, as above.

Note carefully: You who wish to enter into eternal life, consider the words written below every day throughout your life, and thus you will never offend God. First, the brevity of life. Second, its instability. Third, the uncertainty of death. Fourth, the rewards of the righteous. Fifth, the punishments of the wicked.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “eternity” instead of “instability.” When these things are finished, Anselm says that he will undoubtedly be saved. The manuscripts have further material at the end.]

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “Here end the admonitions of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.”]

[Col. 0687B]

# SAINT ANSELM’S POEM ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD (G)*

[Note: This has been collated with manuscripts Bec, O, and K 10, Gembloux C 70, and the manuscript of the Greater Monastery 593. The manuscripts Bec, O, and the Greater Monastery have neither a title nor the author’s name. Manuscript K 10 has: “The verses of Roger of Caen, monk of Bec.” Manuscript C 70 begins here: “Claudianus to the monks.”]

195 What befits a monk, or what kind he ought to be—

[Note: Manuscript 593 reads *qui jubet*, “he who commands”; the alternate reading is *quid jubet*, “what commands.”]

let him who commands me to speak extend his hand.

Holy flock, monks, we write these things to you; these things instruct you, and this page of life opens the way.

Nor should you, beloved brothers, despise us if our admonitions urge anything pious, if they urge anything beneficial.

Often a small light drives away immense darkness,

and a little stream often supplies sweet waters.

[Note: Manuscript 593 reads *aemulus*, “a rival,” instead of *rivulus*, “a little stream.”]

It is not the tonsure that makes a monk, nor the rough garment,

but strength of spirit and unremitting severity.

A humble mind, contempt for the world, a chaste life,

and holy moderation: these make the monk.

These things, monks, will raise you to heaven like a four-horse chariot;

these things will grant the highest rewards after this life.

The tonsure is of no help, nor the most wretched garment,

if you are a wolf, however much you appear to be a sheep.

For human beings can both be deceived and deceive; but no one can deceive Christ,

who deceives no one.

[Note: Manuscript 593 reads *simulator*, “the pretender,” instead of *simulatae*, “of feigned.” The manuscripts also read *fallere*, “to deceive,” rather than *sed fallere*, “but to deceive.” They further read *hominum nemo potest*, “no human being can,” instead of *fallere nemo potest*, “no one can deceive.”]

He condemns the sham of feigned religion and cannot dwell in reprobate ways.

You have made vows, brothers; you have made vows. We ask you: live anxiously to repay your vows to God.

He sins greatly against divine majesty, whoever makes vows which he does not wish to repay.

You have vowed to change your ways for the Lord:

from now on let there be an end to sins and vices.

Let the man who formerly lived proudly now live humbly;

let whoever was lustful now be chaste.

One person sought wealth, another grasped at honors;

now let wealth and honor become worthless to him.

He used to rejoice in feasts, he used to rejoice in a rich table;

now a sober supper will provide a modest meal.

He used to be happy in his successes;

now let him wash away his faults with his own tears.

Conspicuous in purple, distinguished by jewels and gold,

now let him cover his limbs with a cheap, shabby garment.

Let the talkative man be silent; let the passionate man’s anger grow gentle.

Let the envious man vomit out the bitter poisons of envy.

Whoever formerly delighted in slaughter and robbery,

now let him be pious and gentle, a lover of peace.

Whoever used to swell with the inflated praise of flatterers,

now let him consider the praises of men to be nothing.

And whoever voluntarily was wicked and used to harm others without cause,

now let him wish to be useful even when he has been injured.

This man was quick to quarrels and headlong into disputes;

now let him bear another’s insults bravely.

[Note: Manuscripts C and K read *maledicta ferat*, “let him bear insults”; the printed reading in the other witness is *maledicta feret*, “he will bear insults.”]

[Note: Manuscript 593 omits this couplet.]

Let neither contempt nor injury break him;

let him bear all annoyances with a steadfast heart.

Let peace and tranquility of mind endure amid insults;

for no storm of circumstance moves the strong man.

[Note: The manuscripts read *fontem*, “spring,” instead of *fortem*, “strong”; and *procella monet*, “the storm admonishes,” instead of *procella movet*, “the storm moves.”]

This true conversion, brothers, deserves forgiveness;

this life is able to please an offended God.

[Note: The manuscripts read: “A life which has offended God is able to appease him.”]

[Col. 0690A]

Let this brief and false pleasure not entice you;

let these perishable goods not deceive you.

Why should one desire anything who has abandoned everything?

Why should one who has resolved upon good return to evil?

Despise the earth, you who seek to possess heaven;

if these things please you because they endure, flee them because they are fleeting.

[Note: The manuscripts read: “if you desire things that endure,” instead of “if enduring things please you.”]

While it is permitted and time for this life is granted,

always live prepared for every good work.

Do every good thing you can while you live for a brief time;

you will reap much if now you cast a few seeds.

Purchase everlasting rest with a little labor,

and balance long joys with brief weeping.

Let your mind not cling to earthly and perishable things:

whatever you see in the world slips away and passes.

[Note: The manuscripts read *ubi quae vides*, “whatever you see there,” instead of *in orbe vides*, “whatever you see in the world.” Manuscript 593 inserts many verses here concerning prelates, absent from the printed editions and from the other manuscripts consulted; they are not relevant here.]

What is the present life? A temptation, a troublesome struggle;

here there is always a battle-line, and the enemy is always present.

But when the burden of the flesh is no longer yours,

then there will be rest without end and everlasting peace.

Envy and ambition, gluttony, deceit, dangerous lust,

anger, swelling of mind, schisms, love of praise—

and the other thousand things belonging to Satan’s camps—

surround us on every side and continually press upon us.

While the feeble mind is held among these plagues,

it fluctuates and seethes in wondrous ways;

and although it may never fall, it always seems about to fall,

shaken as it is by such great evils.

Who could withstand so many storms of vices

if divine help did not come to his aid?

Let monks avoid these things with the whole effort of their minds;

let them cleanse past sins by weeping and groaning.

Let them read, work, and pray at appointed intervals;

let no time be vacant from sacred studies.

Let them always devote themselves to useful and honorable things:

idleness is an exceedingly destructive condition.

The fuel of lust is an incentive to evils;

it prepares a place for wicked spirits.

When the deadly enemy suggests something evil to a monk

and tries to deceive him in a thousand ways,

let him believe that God is always present everywhere;

let him not suppose that he can remain hidden if he sins.

He knows and sees everything, and nothing escapes him;

all things are naked and open to his eyes.

When someone does something shameful which he would blush to do while I watched,

why does he not blush even more while God watches?

If he knew that his country’s judge knew his deeds, he would be afraid.

The Lord knows all things; why, then, does he fear nothing?

But he is silent and delays, and does not yet punish crimes:

he will punish, and as a just judge he will be equitable according to their merits.

[Col. 0691A]

Monks, preserve the severity of your way of life.

Nor should you be reluctant to endure hardships for a short time.

But beware of the world’s vanities, however much they delight you;

things sweet to the taste often kill.

[Note: Manuscript 593 reads “often harm” instead of “often kill.”]

Nor love whatever pleases the bodily senses:

the things which delight the flesh themselves harm the mind.

Worldly joys produce everlasting sorrows,

and brief life takes away eternal life.

The labor is slight, but the reward of the labor is great;

196 the labor quickly passes, but the rewards have no end.

Therefore, if you recognize that nothing is better than God,

or rather, if you believe that he is the highest good,

then, having despised these fleeting things of the world,

let your joys now be in God alone.

Nothing that can be lost seems anything to me;

I do not think that whatever passes away is lasting.

For what are honor, wealth, glory, or youth?

Beauty, lineage, strength, a woman, clothing, a field,

a jewel or silver—what are royal scepters, or gold,

purple, a broad estate, and a spacious house?

Great power, much knowledge, false pleasure—

and what is life itself, or the health of our body?

[Note: The manuscripts read “What is life?” instead of “What is it?”]

I do not love what plague, thief, or enemy snatches away,

and what death takes even if all the rest should spare it.

There are people whom false honor and perishing power please;

they think themselves somebody because they occupy lofty places.

And just as though from a lookout they saw fields and plains,

so also from the summit of their minds they avoid everyone.

[Note: The manuscripts read “from the summit of the mountain” instead of “from the summit of their minds.”]

While they do not attend to the human condition,

they do not know what it is to see, but only what they possess.

But while they bear scepters, kings shine beneath their diadems,

and rejoice in the breadth of their dominion;

while they are distended with feasts and glow with nectar,

and earth and sea serve their tables;

while fine linen and costly purple clothe them,

and royal majesty is at leisure amid pleasures;

and while flattering lust caresses their softened bodies

and drags them under its authority through its enticements;

while these men shamefully serve a shameful mistress,

whom the world falsely calls kings,

they turn away their eyes and refuse to see clearly

that they themselves are human beings and flesh destined to die;

that worldly power passes more quickly than smoke;

that a human being is a glass vessel or an earthen vessel;

that mortal flesh grows old like a garment,

and bent old age comes with swift decline;

that the span of our lives is always diminishing,

and that a man’s days flee like smoke and shadow;

that life is brief, death uncertain,

and at every moment some trouble presses upon us.

You are called a king: why do you rejoice in an empty name,

when, driven by vices, you lie defeated and overcome everywhere?

You who shine with so great a name, tell me:

why does reason serve, while lust rules kingdoms?

Why does the man who commands kingdoms serve his vices,

and not blush to be the slave of his vile body?

O lovers of the world and false possessors of power,

do you really think that earthly riches are anything?

And what of the worldly honors you pursue,

whose constant companion is anxiety?

All lofty things fear a headlong fall;

and alien force always harms the great.

The tall tree more often falls beneath the blasts of the winds;

the lowly myrtle and tamarisk remain safe.

When a military engine overturns lofty towers,

it does no harm to the poor man’s little hut.

And when the violence of a river carries away obstacles,

it passes easily over the level ground with gentle course.

The wave of the savage sea overwhelms mountains and cliffs,

but a gentler wave reaches the peaceful shore.

We know that the lofty Alps grow white with snow,

and are oppressed by cold and perpetual ice.

There the violence of the winds rages most fiercely;

the nearby valley enjoys agreeable weather.

So, powerful men, adversities never fail you.

You have no peace at all, no rest at all.

[Col. 0692C]

O how many tumultuous feelings the hearts of kings endure!

How they themselves roar with stormy agitation

amid royal banquets and varied preparations,

wasting away through cares and anxious fear.

Power feared by many fears not a few;

it scarcely trusts anyone while guarding against plots.

[Note: The manuscripts read “while he fears ambushes” instead of “while guarding against plots.”]

Surrounded by a thousand bodyguards and the weapons of his own men,

it cannot drive fear from its trembling heart.

Again, what good does abundant money do its master?

Listen to what care and what fear it contains.

Sleep becomes brief and rare for those who possess gold;

for all unrestrained desire remains awake.

Neither ivory nor purple gives secure sleep;

poverty lies safely on cheap straw.

The possessor of gold is always afraid,

and regards every noise as a plot being made.

He fears weapons and poisons, fears theft and robbery;

anxiously he guards whatever he has long acquired.

[Col. 0693A]

While this man seeks wealth, wretched greed torments him;

once he begins to possess what he has sought, fear torments him.

Thus the poor man is wretched while he seeks to possess;

and the rich man is wretched while he fears losing what he has acquired.

While he lies on feathers covered with silk and purple,

he is gnawed by cares and keeps watch against schemes.

He burns to extend his poor neighbor’s field over his own,

and knows no limit in pursuing crime.

[Note: Manuscripts O and K read: “He considers a limit”; the printed reading is “he does not know how to have a limit.”]

He drives orphans from their ancestral homes,

persecutes widows, and oppresses them through the courts.

Although he has been kindled by the unjust torches of avarice,

he cannot satisfy himself with unjust profits.

[Note: Manuscripts C and 593 read: “He cannot satisfy himself with unjust profits.” Manuscript K reads: “to associate himself with just lights.”]

Thus he makes many poor; rich through robbery,

he serves luxury, but once stripped, he is needy.

This man enjoys delicacies and the possessions of the poor;

but he will groan, unworthy as he is, over these goods when they are lost.

For him varied banquets and costly clothing are prepared;

but the poor man scarcely has bread and a coarse garment.

Yet, once he has entered Tartarus amid flames, he will ask

for a little water from the poor man’s fingertip.

And when the order of things has been reversed, the one who abounded in wealth will be needy;

the poor man who is needy here will possess abundance there.

But why, whoever you are, do you hoard these riches, you miser?

Perhaps they will cause you to perish more quickly.

Tell me: has an enemy ever been lacking for the rich?

A grievous downfall often crushes and shatters them.

Good fortune is accompanied by envy, and never

does that changeable thing remain sufficiently faithful to anyone.

Therefore exclude the causes of anxiety and fear;

if you wish to be poor, you will at once be safe.

Nothing has ever been happier than poverty;

nothing can be safer than poverty.

These things are not your support, but a great burden,

which always presses you, wretched man, down to the depths.

No one will climb the mountains of justice and the heights of virtues

while he is laden with the things of the world.

Fool, why do you pursue these things? Why do you cling so to fleeting things?

Mortal man, what do you want with riches, since you are destined to die?

When, after the cares of the world and vain labors,

the things which you hold in evil possession have passed away from you,

Tartarus will swallow you, terrified, with a dreadful opening,

and, wretched, you will be tortured in various ways.

When the terrible exactor, commanded by the just judge,

plunges you into the depths of a lake of sulfur,

then, then, unhappy man, you will repent too late over these things,

because you placed your hope in these false goods.

[Col. 0694A]

Neither silver nor gold will descend there with you;

the world’s glory, which quickly falls, will not be present.

Perhaps another spendthrift will one day scatter

all the riches which you, a thrifty man, now gather.

Then he will be happy alike in your possessions and in your wife,

while you are a little ash or a corpse.

You have a great name; your fame is renowned throughout the world;

the world praises you, but you will nevertheless die.

Vain praises are of no use whatsoever to the buried;

has anyone, once turned to ash, ever felt them?

You enjoy the people’s fame and eagerly draw their favor to yourself;

you do not know what divine judgment has in store.

197 Smoke and a light shadow is all this glory of the world;

the savage realms of Tartarus torture those who were famous.

[Col. 0694B]

Both color and face, and the youth once so pleasing,

and the voice that formerly knew how to utter sweet sounds,

at last flee when wretched old age arrives;

the well-combed hair which once adorned him flees.

The mouth is disarmed when the teeth have fallen out;

then it scarcely produces imperfect sounds.

Strength fails, and the old man’s wrinkle now appears;

on the exhausted body the rough skin bristles.

Now, now he bends; now saliva flows from his mouth;

his color is bloodless, and his very breath is heavy.

Thus the charm of his pleasant appearance gradually perishes,

and none of the many things that once pleased remains.

Things once tasted now have less flavor; he scarcely perceives odors.

He scarcely hears even loud sounds with his ear.

His eyes grow dim; of the whole body only

skin and bones bound together by their sinews remain.

[Col. 0694C]

Now he can scarcely steady his tottering steps with a staff,

and scarcely can he hold anything with his trembling hand.

If he once possessed any wisdom, it has all departed:

he praises only what has a childish flavor.

Thus each wretched old man loses himself each day;

he is taken away from himself.

And although old age itself is a sufficiently serious illness,

it is nevertheless afflicted by countless evils.

This useless age, I say, is tormented in many ways,

and every old man always has some reason to complain.

Eating is difficult, and fasting becomes burdensome;

sleep is oppressive to him, and wakefulness harms him.

He hates summer, blames winter and cold;

he thinks autumn is a cause of pain.

[Col. 0694D]

Even the mildness of spring injures him in some small way,

and nothing can please the complaining old man.

[Col. 0695A]

Amid all these troubles which the old man feels,

itching torments him, and breathless coughing shakes him.

Unwelcome to his own people, exhausted by illness and years,

he complains that the span of his life is long.

Beauty is a fleeting good; appearance is hostile to modesty

and often delays the useful path of the virtues.

Now it inflates the foolish, now it advises shameful things;

often it also causes the strong to fall headlong.

Death, illness, and sorrowful old age seize it;

it perishes through a thousand causes and does not remain long.

[Note: The manuscripts read “it does not remain for a single day” instead of “it does not remain long.”]

It is not beautiful form but a sincere mind that merits God;

a blessed life is granted to justice alone.

You recall royal ancestors and great parents,

and swell with the empty nobility of the flesh.

You do not know that the origin of all is common:

birth and death are the same, and flesh is one.
