[Note: The manuscripts add material here. One reading is: “Origin. Not otherwise do Davus and the fierce master emerge. Birth and death and the famous name of ancestors, if he is a slave to vices…” Another is: “Origin. One birth and one death, and one flesh. What good is the nobility and illustrious name of ancestors to you, if you are a slave to vices…”]

What good are nobility and the illustrious name of ancestors to you,

if you yourself have become the slave of your vices?

Noble is anyone who shines with the virtue of his spirit;

degenerate is he alone who delights in an evil life.

It is not lineage but character that the court of heaven reveres;

the just man, not the highborn man, possesses heaven.

[Note: Manuscripts O and K read *ne genus aut*, “not lineage or,” instead of *nec genus at*, “not lineage but.” Manuscript C omits this and other material through “but when you see yourself overcome…”]

Nor does the officer set over death, the minister of punishments,

torment the condemned mind more mildly.

No honor is preserved for him, no reverence;

nor is he any safer because of his nobility.

But you boast of strong shoulders and sinewy arms,

and of the outstanding strength of your body.

You recount wars, conquered commanders, and subdued peoples,

and the greatest kingdoms subjected to your rule.

[Col. 0695C]

You are no stronger than an ox or an ass; nevertheless,

you see those animals themselves bought at a sufficiently cheap price.

[Note: The manuscripts read *attamen illas*, “nevertheless those [feminine things],” instead of *attamen illos*, “nevertheless those [masculine animals].”]

Thus, whatever you see that you share with animals,

do not marvel at it excessively or regard it as precious.

But if you wish to consider the senses and powers of the flesh,

many beasts surpass us in both.

Swift horses beat us in speed,

and a dog hears and smells better than we do.

Who would wish to test an angry lion in wrestling,

or dreadful bears and boars swift as lightning?

Only the virtue of the mind is what places us above them;

in all other respects our abilities are sufficiently inferior.

Fast for three days, and see what becomes of all your pride:

now, as a man about to die, you scarcely draw a thin breath.

[Note: The manuscripts read “you scarcely draw your breath heedlessly” instead of “you scarcely draw a thin breath.”]

[Col. 0695D]

But if an igneous fever should scorch you even lightly,

you will immediately wither and at once become nothing.

[Note: The manuscripts read “if it should scorch you gently” instead of “if it should scorch you lightly.”]

But when you see yourself overcome by vices and yielding beneath them,

I wonder that you call yourself strong and think yourself so.

Lust commands war; you yield at the first blows,

and offer your neck to be pressed beneath its shameful yoke.

So you serve avarice; so you serve the stirrings of anger;

so you obey the shameful commands of burning gluttony.

Woman is a sweet evil; by her enticements

she deceitfully breaks masculine mind and strength.

Woman, Satan’s torch, adorned with radiant jewels, gold,

and clothing, comes arrayed so that she may destroy.

Whatever wise nature gave her, she reshapes;

whatever she received, she thinks it disgraceful.

She pricks her eyes with a needle and makes her livid eyes bright with pigment:

“Thus,” she says, “the beauty of the eyes will be greater.”

There is also someone who pierces tender ears, so that from them

either gold or a precious stone may hang.

Another wretchedly fasts and diminishes her blood,

and brings about precisely the pallor she desires.

For whatever woman is not pale seems rustic to her;

“This is fitting, this is the true color of a lover,” she says.

She also stains her face with various foul substances.

But why? A better color is sought through art.

By art she thins her eyebrows, and by art again

she gathers her breasts into the smallest possible space.

By art, indeed, you may see black hair turned blond;

she strives to move her limbs from their natural position.

Thus she paints every part of her body with fragile artifice,

so that you would think she disliked everything she was born with.

[Note: Manuscript C omits the passage beginning “Thus she paints every part…” through “in a thousand ways.”]

O what postures the soft woman twists herself into,

and how she pleases with her deceitful tongue’s lisping sounds.

Often she sings sweetly, but diligently composes her steps,

so that you might believe she moves her feet with some art.

[Note: The manuscripts read “and you might believe” instead of “so that you might believe.”]

Often her eloquence torments her listeners;

now by laughing, now also by weeping, she pleases.

In a thousand ways woman attacks our minds,

and it is a great gain to her to destroy many.

There is nothing in the world more harmful than a harmful woman,

and the deadly enemy has nothing by which he may capture more people.

Nor do we cast accusations upon the entire sex;

but in our time a chaste woman is rare.

But the holy prophet declares that flesh is hay;

keep that flame far away from your hay.

Flee soft laughter, nods, and sweet words,

and women’s jokes; they contain poison.

The poison of feminine love gradually creeps in;

if you do not watch for it, you will at once be captured.

Flee women’s conversation, holy man; beware

of women’s flatteries, if you wish to conquer.

[Col. 0696D]

For the mind captured by feminine love is bound

and can never rise to the heights of the virtues.

What useful purpose does conversation with these women serve?

You came as a monk; you leave as a shameful lover.

[Col. 0697A]

Therefore, unless you avoid the poisonous serpent,

unless you go far away, you will certainly be infected.

[Note: Manuscript O reads “unless you avoid the troop” instead of “unless you avoid the serpent,” and “unless you make far away” instead of “unless you go far away.”]

Every woman kindles the fires of lust,

and, when she has come near even holy men, she harms them.

When Andreas, great bishop of the city of Fundana,

wavered, a woman was the cause.

[Note: The manuscripts read “changed”; the printed reading “wavered” is uncertain.]

If you turn over the books of the ancients and the writings of the Fathers,

you will grieve that holy men have fallen in this way.

[Note: Manuscripts K and O read “if you grieve”; manuscripts C and 593 read “how many holy men you will grieve to have fallen in this way.”]

Nor can you be wiser than learned Solomon,

nor holier than holy David.

If a woman cast down Lot, Samson, David, and Solomon,

who will now be safe?

Did not a woman expel a human being from his blessed place

and become the origin of our death?

[Note: Manuscript C 70 has much material here which is absent from the printed editions and the other manuscripts; I therefore judge it to have been added by Claudianus.]

198 But if her face is sufficiently bright and her form attractive,

and her whole milk-white appearance pleases you greatly,

[Note: The manuscripts read “her face is bright” for “with a sufficiently bright face,” and: “Outward things please; inwardly she is discordant.”]

if her entrails were exposed, and the rest of her flesh as well,

you would see what filth her white skin conceals.

If shining purple covered vile dung,

would any sane person love the dung because of this?

A woman sufficiently adorned enters the enclosure of the cells,

sighing, she says: “I wish to learn holy things.”

“I approach the monks as a sinful woman, for these men

give admonitions and instruction in the holy way.”

“You come adorned, and holy things please you: who could believe it?

I regard you with suspicion; I believe you have come to cause harm.

Your wanton laughter, the nodding of your ardent eyes,

and your loquacity have displeased me.

Shepherds, keep watch; drive ravening she-wolves away

from your flocks; let the enclosures be closed to them.

[Note: The manuscripts read “from our flocks” instead of “from your flocks.”]

They kill souls and send many to Tartarus;

no plague is more dangerous for monks.

Woman is death to the soul; let her never dare

to approach monks; let her remain far from the sacred choir.

Let woman remain far from the assembly of the holy; for even

if she cannot conquer, she nevertheless begins a battle.

But perhaps you will say that there are married men,

and that you praise the bonds of chaste marriage.

Believe me, brother: whoever is a husband is wretched.

Shall I tell you how grievous this burden is?

If someone has an ugly wife, he despises and hates her;

if she is beautiful, he himself anxiously fears adulterers.

For you see how greatly beauty and modesty oppose one another,

and how rarely a beautiful woman can be chaste.

You will fear losing the woman for whom many sigh and whom many desire,

or that she may not be possessed by you alone.

[Col. 0698A]

If she becomes pregnant, another concern is added;

your multiplied troubles increase.

On one side you fear that an adulterer may corrupt her

and that she may bear children whose father you yourself will not be.

On the other, your resources are too limited and your money too scant;

she forces the whole unfortunate household to live in poverty with you.

There is also the talkative woman who creates perpetual quarrels

and becomes troublesome to her husband night and day.

And a drunken wife is exceedingly harmful to her husband:

what was acquired over a long period she squanders in a short time.

She gives soft embraces and presses sweet kisses,

but she keeps poisons in her silent heart.

[Note: The manuscripts read “she fashions sweet kisses” instead of “she presses sweet kisses.”]

[The supplied source ends here, mid-section.]

## Complete textual apparatus (source order)

1. **[Col. 0685C]** Bec and Saint-Germain manuscripts read: *Age ergo… Sperans, hujus morti* — “Therefore do these things while breath remains in you… hoping, [cling] to this death”; the printed wording is *Age ergo… huic morti* — “therefore… to this death.”
2. **[Col. 0685C]** Bec and Saint-Germain: *Committe, et immitte; hac morte te totum contege* — “Commit and entrust [yourself]; cover your whole self with this death”; printed: *commit te, hac sola te totum contege* — “commit [yourself], cover your whole self with this death alone.”
3. **[Col. 0687B]** Bec and Saint-Germain have *Dic ei sic; Domine* — “Say to him thus: Lord”; printed *dic: Domine* — “say: Lord.”
4. **[Col. 0687B]** Bec and Saint-Germain read *Et si dixerit quod mereris* — “And if he says that you deserve [it],” followed by the longer plea that one sets Christ’s death between God and one’s sins; printed: *Si dixerit tibi quia meruisti* — “If he says to you that you have deserved [it].”
5. **[Col. 0687B]** Bec and Saint-Germain: *Responde ei sic: Domine* — “Answer him thus: Lord”; printed *dic: Domine* — “say: Lord.”
6. **[Col. 0687B]** Bec and Saint-Germain: *Inter me et te, mala merita mea, ipsiusque mortem: meritum offero* — “Between me and you I offer my evil deserts and his death as merit”; Vatican: *inter te, et mala merita mea: ipsiusque meritum offero* — “between you and my evil deserts I offer his merit”; printed: *inter me et te, mala mea, ipsiusque mortem offero* — “between me and you I offer my evils and his death.”
7. **[Col. 0687B]** Bec and Saint-Germain *Et non habeo* — “and I do not have”; printed *nec habeo* — “nor do I have.”
8. **[Col. 0687B]** Bec and Saint-Germain give the longer direction: “Say again: Lord, I set the death of the Lord Jesus Christ between you, me, and your wrath… If he says he is angry with you… when this is finished, let him say”; printed has the shorter *Et iterum dicito… Hoc facto, dicat* — “and say again… when this is done, let him say.”
9. **[Col. 0687B]** Bec and Saint-Germain: say three times *In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum* — “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit”; in those manuscripts the admonition ends here. Printed: *Ter haec verba: in manus tuas etc.* — “three times these words: into your hands, etc.”
10. **[Col. 0687B]** “Again the verse ‘you have broken [my bonds]’ etc., through ‘let the priest begin and say’”: the manuscript omits this whole span.
11. **[Col. 0687B]** Vatican *sacerdos dicat* — “let the priest say”; printed *Incipiat sacerdos et dicat* — “let the priest begin and say.”
12. **[Col. 0687B]** Vatican *destinata* — “ordained/intended”; printed *determinata* — “determined.”
13. **[Col. 0687B]** The manuscripts omit from the question *Doles te* — “Do you grieve that…?” through *in fine fac eam* — “at the end make it….”
14. **[Col. 0687B]** Vatican *aeternitas* — “eternity”; printed *lubricitas* — “slipperiness/inconstancy.” Vatican continues: “When these things are finished Anselm says that he will without doubt be saved”; its ending reads *etc.*

16. **[Col. 0687B]** Collated with Bec, O, K.10, Gem., C.70, and Major Monastery 593. Bec, O, and Major Monastery have neither title nor author; K.10 calls it “Verses of Roger of Caen, monk of Bec”; C.70 begins “Here begins Claudianus to monks.”

113. **[Col. 0697D]** Manuscripts: *Exteriora placent, dissonat interius* — “outward things please; inwardly she is discordant”; printed *Et tibi non minimum lactea tota placet* — “and her whole milk-white appearance pleases you greatly.”

Whether he boasts of his appearance or his nobility,

And thinks his hand worthy of holding a scepter.

Many men have perished through the deceitfulness of wives; [Col. 0698B] a woman shrinks from nothing and thinks everything permissible.

She dares whatever imperious lust commands her;

Fear, reason, and even modesty yield.

She despises sacred laws and every right.

Whatever is shameful or savage, so long as it serves her purpose, she loves.

Delilah destroyed Samson, and Clytemnestra the son of Atreus.

Each man experienced women’s deceit in his own case.

But why, I ask, should an ancient story now be told to you,

When you see many such things happening in our own time?

What filth, what fears and anxieties husbands endure—

Who could count them all?

You see now how burdensome a wife’s burden is,

And how heavily she presses the necks subjected to her harsh yoke.

Are we therefore condemning the bonds of the marriage bed?

No; but we do not attribute these things to perfect men. [Col. 0698C] Married couples do not receive a hundredfold fruit, nor that which

They return multiplied tenfold through six successive stages;

Yet they are not deprived of the light of the eternal kingdom;

They will receive rewards worthy of their merits.

Soft byssus clothes you, and shining purple; [Col. 0697D]

And every kingdom of the world weaves its separate products for you.

What precious skin does not yield to your use?

What kind of garment, what color, is absent?

Nor are you ashamed to add to indecorous adornment [Col. 0697D] whatever

The skilled hand of the craftsman knows how to forge. [Col. 0697D]

Your fingers and arms alike gleam with gems,

And you can scarcely bear the weight of your own gold.

O how empty is such human madness! Fool, [Col. 0698D] what good does it do to wish to shine with outward goods?

If you are filthy with vices, what benefit is a gleaming garment?

No purple will wipe away your stains. [Col. 0699A]

The brilliance of gems and so much gold does not make

Your blind mind free of its own darkness.

But holy conduct, not clothing, makes a person honorable;

And integrity alone makes great men.

Preserve intact what nature has given: does the image of God need

To be adorned with these worthless things? [Col. 0699D]

Certainly boastful pride compels these things to be done;

A sober life alone pleases righteous God.

You seek to extend the long boundaries of your fields, [Col. 0699D]

And desire many harvests and full granaries.

You know what the evangelical saying threatens the miser—

That in this night, fool, he will lose his soul:

“It says: You have possessions—whose will all that you have prepared be?”

Wicked man, now restrain your desires and fear to die.

So many crops, so much gold and wine, so many fields— [Col. 0699B]

What need has brief life for so much?

You seek fertile farmland, human being, for yourself; yet you never

Look back at your own barren life.

Everywhere, swollen with pride, you despise God’s farmer,

And wish to yield no fruits of righteousness.

But the thorns of crimes choke the seeds of life,

And a bitter crop of sins rises.

Uproot the thistles of your mind and tear out its thorns;

Sow Christ’s wheat in the fields of your heart.

Let the fallow ground of your heart bear fruit for God,

And let the harvest of virtues crush the seeds of wickedness.

What, do you think, are silver, gems, gold,

And estates? What are all the riches possessed by the world?

A Jew possesses these, a Gentile, a bloodstained robber;

Believe me, God often gives such things in anger.

Consider small whatever the wicked happen to possess.

Consider small whatever a thief and adulterer possess; [Col. 0699D]

Whatever a prostitute or adulterer possesses, do not consider it great:

The Almighty gives far better things to his own.

But the eye of the mind is blinded by the dust of earth,

So that you cannot see the light of righteousness.

Alas for you, to whom virtue does not shine, but gold does shine, [Col. 0699D]

And you prefer the lowest things to the highest goods.

Nor do I regard as great the evils with which God’s friends are afflicted,

Nor as goods whatever God’s enemies are known to possess.

But whenever the righteous man is in need and the criminal abounds,

Is not the abundance of the wicked a great good? [Col. 0699D]

The wise man is sick, but the unrighteous man flourishes in health:

Is bodily health, when confined to such limits, not a great good?

The Lord’s beloved dies, but the adulterer lives: [Col. 0700A]

Is a short-lived existence not among great goods?

Therefore, son, gather the rest in a manner resembling this,

And, being prudent, despise the worthless gifts of earth.

Leave the worthless earth behind; desire the heights of heaven:

There you will receive the blessed gifts of God.

Purple does not make anyone precious merely because it is precious, [Col. 0699D]

Nor do bestowed scepters change wicked character.

If, piously, you see these things given by God to his enemies,

You will see that the impious portion of humanity rules almost everywhere.

If honor were given to virtue, if rewards to the deserving,

And if each thing occupied its proper place according to its merit,

You would now see human affairs, believe me, blessed and peaceful,

And restraining themselves within a proper order.

But because kingdoms are given to the wicked, and power to crime, [Col. 0699D] [Col. 0700B]

Lust holds the reins owed to virtue.

The world is thrown into confusion; the order of things is overturned;

And a great chaos entangles everything together.

Violence suppresses laws, crimes overthrow morals,

And virtue, shaken by the violent storm, lies hidden.

Lebanon gives you its timber; Paros sends its marble;

Arabia supplies gold; India provides ivory.

With foreign cedar and marble you build your houses;

A marvelous structure rises, and you pour out your wealth.

199. Your doorposts gleam with silver, your ceilings, covered with much

Gold, clothe carved ivory distinguished by their workmanship.

You enclose your halls with elaborate porticoes: what chambers,

And how many, do you think this labyrinth contains? [Col. 0699D]

There you may gaze in astonishment at whatever an artist’s mind and hand can paint and carve. [Col. 0700C]

There are many doors indeed, and a thousand windows of varied form;

The house is supported by a thousand marble columns. [Col. 0699D]

Why, doomed man, do you prepare such a massive construction? Why

Do you devote your mind to empty things and take pleasure in what will perish?

Why do you build spacious structures when you will be enclosed in a narrow tomb?

Your brief lifespan will run out. [Col. 0699D]

What need have you of such great buildings? How much happier you yourself would be

If you were a living temple and the living house of God.

Be the house of the Lord, and adorn it with holy conduct;

As a worshiper of religion, love virtue.

How happy is the soul in which the Spirit of the Most High himself

Deigns to establish his dwelling.

Every earthly power has a sudden end, [Col. 0700D]

And swiftly flees, abandoning its own.

Therefore fear, whoever climbs to lofty honors:

Remember that you stand in a place destined to collapse. [Col. 0701A]

Caesar was great and more powerful than the whole world;

Now an urn contains him whom the world itself could not contain.

So too Alexander, that exceedingly mighty Macedonian,

Is enclosed in a narrow place as dust and bones.

He had been greater than the world; now a poor patch of sand

Covers the noble body of an exile and a defeated man.

Babylon fell, and mighty Troy also fell:

Once mistress of the world, behold, Rome lies fallen.

Behold, nothing long remains for mortals; behold,

No honor prevents death, no glory prevents it.

Aristotle, supreme and acute investigator of logic,

Published many discoveries produced by his own intellect.

It was not accomplished by a syllogism or an enthymeme

That the Fates should spare such a great man.

What benefit was it for Plato to penetrate nature’s secrets, [Col. 0701B]

And to devote so much study to the world?

He knew the course of the sun, the regions of heaven, the moon’s paths,

And the wandering stars or those fixed at the highest pole,

And many other sufficiently difficult matters; yet now

The philosopher is ash: only an empty name remains.

While Hippocrates investigates things and their causes,

While he debates their natures and inserts [Col. 0701D] them

Into his books, while he reveals many hidden matters, [Col. 0701D]

While he preserves bodies through medical skill,

The man’s immense fame spreads throughout the whole world;

And he enjoys the fruits of the favor he has earned.

Yet no herbs or roots could bring it about

That he would not have to undergo the law of death as a physician.

And Christ grants rewards to the righteous, not to philosophers;

You are a peasant: be righteous, and you will be blessed. [Col. 0701C]

The philosopher Varro, Peter the fisherman: and behold,

Peter possesses heaven, while Varro holds Tartarus.

The former rejoices in the varied sweetness of pleasures,

And everywhere serves his own desires.

Whatever a prostitute, cook, or actor considers supreme, he considers so;

He prefers nothing to these, nor judges any good equal to them.

Whatever the sea, earth, or air nourishes for food,

The man’s luxurious hunger seeks and obtains.

And the vast world scarcely suffices for his moderate belly.

Therefore the palace roars with the voices of servants.

Dishes are set out on silver, Bacchus in gold,

And a great deal of jeweled nectar fills the drinking vessel.

A long line of attendants shines in clothing and appearance,

A crowd ready to respond to their master’s slightest nod. [Col. 0701D]

Both sexes sing; citharas and lyres resound,

And instruments there produce sweet melody.

At last, made happy by lavish banquets and a full belly,

The swine enjoys the pleasures of the night with prostitutes.

O splendid virtue of a man! O blessed life! [Col. 0702A]

Fed on delights, he lies with a prostitute.

Why should I recount his garments, beds, and wealthy houses?

Wasteful luxury knows no limit.

For him, bright channels carry fountains along their length;

Green grass grows enclosed by marble columns.

The garden produces every kind of fruit-bearing tree,

And white privet is mingled with blood-red roses.

Nor are violets absent; indeed, there is also whatever flower and plant

Thrives in beauty or fragrance.

Now he is carried on the backs of richly caparisoned horses,

Now a boat bears him, well fed, with slow-moving oars.

Now he delights in being beneath tents, and now

He seeks pleasant shade beneath the leafy branches of trees.

Now he delights in crowds and the applause of the city; [Col. 0702B]

Now he wishes to live as a private man in the countryside.

Whatever softness pleases, whatever is pleasing to the eye and beautiful,

And whatever is ordinarily sweet to bodily senses—

Alas for the wretch! He turns it all to shameful uses, [Col. 0701D]

And the filthy beast avoids nothing disgraceful.

Thus he spends all the time of his life blessed by jokes, sex, wine,

And sleep.

And now, entirely flesh, he does not know how far astray he wanders. [Col. 0701D]

His mind, weighed down and dulled by the heavy burden of flesh, [Col. 0701D]

Does not know that the body, which it cares for and nourishes in so many ways,

Feeds a perpetual fire.

What kind of life do you think mortals have?

It is both brief and burdened with many evils.

For all who are born, their first cry is one of pain: [Col. 0702C]

Whoever is human begins to live with weeping. [Col. 0701D]

Look at the blows with which misfortunes strike us from every side: how many,

And how great, are the public evils mixed with private ones.

Now excessive cold harms us, now excessive heat;

Hunger torments us, and bitter thirst afflicts us. [Col. 0701D]

A fly and even a tiny flea trouble kings themselves;

Royal scepters do not make their possessors safe.

One man grieves over exile; another grieves over a friend’s death;

Another, deprived of a beloved spouse, wishes to weep.

One lies disgraced; another mourns miserably in prison;

Fear of the enemy terrifies one; another is in want.

One groans over the incest of a corrupted spouse; [Col. 0701D]

Another, deceived by a false suspicion, lives in fear. [Col. 0702D]

Someone laments vines stripped by hail;

Another that his ships have perished on the vast sea.

One complains that seed entrusted to barren soil has been lost; [Col. 0701D]

Another fears his master’s violence and threats.

One has lost a just case under an unjust judge;

Thieves seize the possessions of some; fire consumes those of others. [Col. 0703A]

And who does not have something to mourn, and who is wounded

By no sorrow, everywhere possessing exactly what he desires?

Fortune does not favor prosperous circumstances so gently [Col. 0703D]

That wickedness fails to mix some sadness with their joys; [Col. 0703D]

Nor is the lesser part of evil absent: vices waste people away,

And they carry burning torches in their captive breasts.

Greed blazes; an evil mind is kindled by anger;

And at times it seethes with mad love, as though

It had long ago enclosed all of Etna within itself; [Col. 0703D]

In its blind frenzy it sees nothing that is fitting.

Often evil envy rouses heavy goads against it;

Often desire for honor generates fear and hope.

Luxury devastates one person, pride another;

A savage storm of sadness also shakes this one. [Col. 0703D]

These things, and more, weigh upon us in this period of life; [Col. 0703D]

None of them remains certain even for a moment.

One perishes from hunger, fungus, fever, serpent, or arrow,

From waves, flames, an enemy, or a robber. [Col. 0703D]

A thousand diseases corrupt our health;

No sickness is absent from the human body.

If you now examine all the other animals,

You will find none subjected to such great evils.

Headache, pain in the sides, and fever fatigue us;

Leprosy destroys the whole person, gout the hands,

Grievous podagra the feet; ophthalmia blinds the eyes;

Asthma obstructs the passages of the constricted chest.

The bladder, injured by urination, closes its own channels; [Col. 0703D]

The viscera are tortured, as is the lower bowel. [Col. 0703D]

200. A tooth or the neck aches; the mouth grows numb; the tongue is bound;

The spleen swells; the lung is sick; the liver labors. [Col. 0703C]

The heart withers; the kidneys suffer; the bowels are loosened;

The arms can do nothing; the weakened legs lie still.

Each individual part is subject to not a few diseases,

And the whole unhappy human being lies exposed to evils.

Therefore this does not seem to me health, nor does this seem life.

Disease has the power to take away what death extinguishes. [Col. 0703D]

So it is: public error judges these matters wrongly;

What fools consider precious is worthless.

Let us therefore, brothers, seek better things,

Things worthy of a good and wise man.

Why, Lord of all things, why, image of divinity,

Do you desire little things? As a great man, desire the greatest.

It is not fitting that the marvelous creation of so great an artificer

Should admire all things inferior to its own goods.

The moon shines for you; for you the sun’s orbit revolves, [Col. 0703D]

And for you the stars are scattered throughout the whole sky.

The day is yours, the night is yours, the fiery ether is yours,

And for you all the seasons exchange their turns.

The globe of the earth is yours, and whatever it encloses [Col. 0704A]

Is wholly subjected to your will.

Indeed, the parent of all things, sent down from high heaven,

Descending to you, became human for your sake.

The brightest palace of the star-bearing kingdom awaits you;

You too are the image of your eternal king. [Col. 0703D]

Therefore you, so great, who surpass all other things by so much,

And are inferior only to God, who created everything:

Do not subject yourself to the kingdom of sin; do not

Pursue these transient things, which flee more swiftly.

Let your mind strive to rise above the lowly earth,

And bravely seize the narrow path to heaven.

Life, health, and all else belonging to human beings are smoke and shadow.

Everything passes away; you see that nothing remains.

Do not let the lowest things that perish delight you; do not let

Earth stain your heavenly nature with its dust. [Col. 0704B]

Let not the ill-advising pleasure of the flesh cast you down,

Nor let food and Venus draw you on with their enticements.

Let virtue and ardor be your perpetual study;

Let your mind burn continually with love of the good. [Col. 0703D]

Seek the fountain of virtues by your steps, and let you

Be warmed by the streams of that fountain.

Let no burden of the world delay you as you run:

Turn away from everything that is accustomed to harm you.

When you, a joyful and happy traveler, arrive,

And the abundance of the life-giving fountain is granted,

You will become eternal, wise, and truly blessed.

Everything will be prosperous for you; nothing will be sad.

And you will see the King himself in his own splendor,

And you will be light from his blessed light. [Col. 0703D]

There will be no darkness of mind; once night has been banished,

Within there will be perpetual day without a cloud.

Then the causes of things, closed within Scripture, will be opened;

Everything will be clear to you and full of light.

Then, in the joyful region of the living, you will see

What the Lord’s goods are, and how great are God’s gifts.

Death, disease, toil, enemy, anxiety, and old age will be absent;

That blessed heavenly house has none of these.

Fear will not afflict the saints, nor the sensation of pain;

There is no heat and no cold in those places.

Here no one hungers, no one is naked; rather, one

Good will become everything to all, and God will be so.

This city will need neither the moon nor the light of the sun;

It will always be serene in the great Sun, God.

Finally, each of the righteous will shine like the sun: [Col. 0704D]

This will be the glory of restored flesh.

The grace of the King will make the spirit equal to the highest beings,

For whose sake he willingly endured the bitterness of the cross.

Led back from the valley of death to the mountain of life, [Col. 0703D]

The wretched exiled human being will become a blessed citizen. [Col. 0705A]

For God is the commonwealth of that city; and there

There is abundant provision for all, and no one is in need.

Therefore the king’s gifts will not be lacking for you; [Col. 0705D] nor will he,

Who enriches the deserving with great things, allow you to be in want.

For when you taste from the perennial fountain of life,

And are granted participation in the supreme good,

Great knowledge, abundant power, and marvelous pleasure

Will be restored to your life and your service.

Who will be able to speak, who write, who imagine

What rewards, Christ, you will give your own in heaven?

Let us, monkish brothers, pursue these things with our whole minds:

Let no cause delay the journey that brings salvation.

That I may be granted to behold the Lord of majesty, [Col. 0705B]

That I may be permitted to possess such beauty and such a great good,

I count the treasures of Arabia, the tables, and the feasts of kings—

Whatever the world possesses—as worthless mud.

Whoever therefore is journeying toward these joys of paradise,

Now diligently act and learn the narrow way,

Lest you loosen the reins of your narrow mind through vices;

Always hold the reins of divine fear.

Await the Lord, dread the judge’s anger,

And love as a soldier what the King promises you.

Be little; see to it that you lay aside your mind’s swelling pride;

The narrow gate of God admits no one who is swollen with pride. [Col. 0705D]

We avoid bulls threatening with horn and neck;

You will be neither lion, bull, nor horse, but a lamb. [Col. 0706A]

Be a lamb; no sacrifice pleases Christ more than a lamb:

Through your simplicity you will be a lamb for Christ.

A turtle dove and a simple dove are offered to the Lord:

Be chaste as a turtle dove, and a gentle, mourning dove.

Blessed are those who have castrated themselves for the Lord; [Col. 0705D]

Tartarus, flame, and death await the unchaste. [Col. 0705D]

The highest virtue of a monk is certainly to obey his superior;

To bear the yoke of the rule and deny oneself.

Whatever he commands, immediately and without murmuring observe:

Consider only sin to be disgraceful.

Let neither a poor garment nor your lowly position distress you;

These things often move the foolish in your order.

But if we understand soundly, if we acknowledge the truth,

Virtue undertakes difficult things and proves what is hard. [Col. 0706B]

He who is worthless in his own eyes, who considers himself nothing,

Both fears and flees the unstable heights of the world,

That man is wise and close to heaven;

Not without reason does he bear the empty name of monk.

But if he wishes to become rich and seeks empty honors, [Col. 0705D]

He has put on a wolf hidden beneath a sheep’s skin.

But the pious judge who sees everything

Knows the sheep and also knows the silent wolves.

Let a monk repeat these things with lips and heart. [Col. 0705D]

“Give me yourself, and yourself alone, God, and that is enough.”

O truly happy possession, and the one that alone makes a person blessed!

Everything else has the weight of misery.

[Col. 0705B]

## ANOTHER POEM ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD (G)*

[Col. 0705C]

What are integrity and nobility except the death of souls?

Why does a man boast, when it is certain that he will die?

For mortal flesh, and whoever serves it,

Perishes by a double death, because after death he is tormented.

What does it profit a man if he lives a hundred years,

When, dying, he thinks that life has passed like the wind?

What does it profit a man if his purse is stuffed with interest,

If through it he consumes himself in punishment without end?

Why does a man rejoice in the prosperity of the world,

Which is exceedingly brief and possessed amid anxiety?

The prosperity of the world quickly passes and is annihilated:

Thus it is sufficiently clear that it is proved to be nothing.

All the things of this world that nature has created

Are like the flower of the field, which cold and wind have scorched,

For just as autumn flowers, born in their season, [Col. 0705D]

Wither in the cold, ready to be carried away by the winds,

So the precious things the world possesses quickly fail,

Though the unhappy human mind busies itself with them.

The things of this world are carried along toward their own end,

And fall without law, governed by no rational order. [Col. 0706C]

201. Just as in rivers the wave flows irreversibly,

So human times flee, together with every favorable circumstance.

The things of this world are unstable like an hour;

All beautiful things ought to be counted as nothing.

Therefore, wretched man, while you live, labor without end;

Do not lose for nothing those things that are better.

Hold to them so that you may prevail over future death:

Give what you have, so that you may possess what is free from care.

Speak, mortal flesh; speak, worm of putrefaction;

Why, wretched one, are you mad? What profit is there in the glory of flesh?

Speak, man; speak, dust; why, putrefaction, are you proud?

Say what you are and what you will be; remember that you will die.

After death you will return as a worm into ashes. [Col. 0705D]

Despise what you pursue; recognize the path of reason.

Do you not know the laws of the human condition? [Col. 0705D]

The body is made from earth:

From the body, seed:

From seed, blood:

From blood, the body:

Thus the human body grows together in the womb of its mother: [Col. 0706D]

Thus the human body rots in the womb of the earth:

From the body, decay:

From decay, a worm:

From the worm, ash:

From dust, earth.

Thus the human body is created from mother earth:

Thus the human body will return to earth.

Therefore, sorrowful man, by the reins of true reason

Restrain your heart and mind by fleeing the world.

Strive in this way to obtain perpetual life for yourself.

## GOD ALONE IS TO BE LOVED, IN WHOM AND FROM WHOM ARE ALL GOOD THINGS

All human things hang by a slender thread,

And those that have had power collapse through a sudden accident.

Divine power plays with human affairs,

And scarcely does the present hour possess any assured stability.

How exceedingly and excessively gentle the Lord is above all,

And how wrong it is to deny him ready forgiveness.

Do you wish to recognize the merciful one? Look at yourself; look back at what you are,

What you have been, what you will be—what are flesh, earth, and God?

Heaven serves you with the sun, the sun with its light, and the air

With its breezes; the waves with food, and the earth with a thousand good things.

But what are you? From where do you have what you possess, and what does he provide?

The sweet and abundant kindness of God freely does both.

He is the fountain from which every good flows, a fountain that cannot be emptied,

A fountain open without end—and God without end.

For you ought to measure sin not by the brevity

Of time, but by its own impiety.

For no impiety is greater than to despise without cause

Himself, who freely granted you existence.

He gave you yourself, promising himself to you, and God himself

Had nothing better to give than himself.

Whatever you are, whatever you have, and whatever you may be able to have,

What, after all, are these things together in comparison with God’s merit?

Despising him, and subjecting himself in every way

To the service of the devil, what punishment does a man deserve?

Add that whoever rushes into vice himself

Often imposes upon himself the shameful necessity of falling.

For virtue becomes a servant to vice and to vices;

It does not possess within itself the power to release what it has admitted.

Therefore perpetual punishment necessarily awaits him

Who willingly makes the necessity of sinning perpetual for himself. [Col. 0707D]

Let undeserved grace be removed; let deserved punishment follow—

Pressing death, and remaining without end.

O how sweet the honor, how true the power, what glory,

What stable gain it is to love God!

Abraham, loving him, is more than a guest among citizens, and alone

More than a soldier among the people; thus he is more powerful than a king.

For virtue in the love of God provides what is true and everlasting [Col. 0708A]

And makes a person love that which truly is.

He alone truly is, who remains one and the same

[long lacuna]

Who possesses eternal being, without beginning and without end,

Always the same, if anyone strives to love him.

If it is not so solid, it nevertheless deserves to be solid:

For blessed life follows the good life.

If you look at the rest, how utterly nothing all things are,

The end reveals it; consult the Assyrian—he is a witness.

What do honor, wealth, beauty, weapons, or extensive

Power, alas, profit? It profited to have loved God.

But since God is true salvation, and is held by love,

For his sake I desire you to love him.

He himself is worthy to be loved; by loving, you will learn

What fruit, what honor, what it means to love God. [Col. 0708B]

Virtue truly deserves God, or an honorable life;

What a good it is always to love God.

How merciful he is, how ready he is, how greatly, finally, he benefits—

Whoever loves him can know this better.

If another person’s deeds teach you, you are taught honorably

To conceive hope or fear from your own merits.

O what a loss it is to place anything before God!

If someone possesses him well, I ask: what does he lack, what does he possess?

For if you seek great things, God is great above all;

If good things, no one can say how good he is.

If you desire beautiful things, who is more beautiful than he? Perhaps you seek

Wealth: he gives wealth, while he himself remains rich. [Col. 0708C]

If lofty and noble things please you, how noble,

How exalted he is, no one can express.

If perhaps power and goodness please you, behold: power

Is from him, or goodness is power without end.

What of character? He himself is the maker of heaven, earth, and sea, and of all things;

Whatever was, is, or will be, he remains the source of goodness.

Serving and obeying him, the Hebrew rules;

He serves and is free; he is subject and is powerful.

Fleeing subjection to him, he is wickedly subjected to Satan, the enemy;

He is subjected to him, and subjected to countless vices.

But at last, seeing where and from what point he had fallen,

He was sick at heart, his breast gnawed by anxieties,

And, revolving many thoughts, the conviction settled upon him

That God must be sought courageously as a refuge for the fallen.

Thus the guilty man longs for the one he injured; he prays to the one he had despised; [Col. 0708D]

He finds the one he fled; he loves the one he had rejected.

He returns to him and seeks forgiveness, weeping over his crime,

And draws much joy of hope from his mercy.

And what is comparable to this sweetness, this everlasting sweetness—

God, sweetly ordering all things?

What did powerful sweetness and sweet power accomplish?

It accomplished what this sweetness habitually accomplishes; the sweet one does sweet things.

[Col. 0709]

# THE BOOK OF THE MEDITATIONS AND PRAYERS OF SAINT ANSELM (G)*

202. ## PROLOGUE [Col. 0709C]

The meditations or prayers written below, since they were composed to arouse the reader’s mind to love or fear of God, or to self-examination, are not to be read amid turmoil, but in quiet; not rapidly, but gradually, with attentive and prolonged meditation. Nor should the reader make it his aim to read any one of them through in its entirety; rather, he should read as much as, with God’s help, he feels will be useful to him for kindling the desire to pray, or as much as gives him delight. Nor is it necessary always to begin any one of them from the beginning, but wherever it may please him more. [Col. 0709C] For this very reason they have been divided into paragraphs, so that he may begin or end wherever he chooses, lest length or frequent repetition of the same passage produce boredom; rather, let the reader derive from it some of the devout feeling for which they were composed. [Col. 0709B]

## FIRST MEDITATION: On the dignity and misery of the human condition

### Editorial and textual notes

- [Col. 0697D] For “Whether she boasts”: *Haec et de* in MSS K and O; *haec vel de* in the printed text. For “Whatever”: *quicquid iam* in the manuscripts. MS C omits from “She despises sacred laws” through “If you are filthy with vices.” For “should ... be told”: *narrat* (“relates”) in the manuscripts.

- [Col. 0697D] “Soft byssus ... shining purple”: the manuscripts read *te mollis purpura* (“soft purple clothes you”). “Indecorous adornment”: *indecoris cultus* (“of indecorous adornment”) in the manuscripts. “Knows how to forge”: *novit plurima* (“knows very many [things]”) in the manuscripts.

- [Col. 0699D] “But holy conduct”: *et sancti* (“and holy”) in the manuscripts. “Does not need these”: *non eget ista* in the manuscripts. “You seek to extend”: *extendere quaevis* (“you may wish to extend”) in the manuscripts. “Many harvests”: *multas messis* in the manuscripts. “You know”: *sicut evangelicus* (“as the evangelical [saying]”) in the manuscripts; MS C has *scit evangelicus* (“the evangelical [saying] knows”). “Wicked man”: *improba* (feminine) in MSS K and O. “So many crops, so much gold”: the manuscripts read *fruges auxi, tantum*; the printed reading is *fruges, auri tantum*.

- [Col. 0699D] “And with Christ’s wheat”: MS O has *e tritico*. “Whatever a thief and adulterer possess”: the manuscripts have *adulter habet* (“an adulterer possesses”). “Whatever a prostitute or adulterer possesses”: the manuscripts have *moechus habet* (“an adulterer possesses”). “Do not consider it great”: MS C has *ne magna* (“do not [consider] great”). “So that you cannot”: MS O has *et nequeas* (“and that you may not be able”). The manuscripts read *nec tibi cui virtus non lucet et auro*; the printed text reads “Alas for you, to whom virtue does not shine, but gold does shine.”

- [Col. 0699D] “But whenever”: MSS O and K read *an quoties vir iustus eget, scelerosus abundat* (“or whenever the righteous man is needy, does the criminal abound?”); MS 593 reads *quo vir iustus eget, numquid scelerosus abundat?* (“in that in which the righteous man is needy, does the criminal abound?”). “Purple does not make anyone precious”: the manuscripts read *nec pretiosa: quendam*. “Nor do ... change”: the manuscripts have *nec mutent mores* (“nor may ... change character”). MS C omits from “If honor were given to virtue” through “Behold, nothing long remains.” “Blessed and peaceful”: MSS O and K have *et pace beasse*.

- [Col. 0699D] “Power to crime”: MSS O and K read *scelera donata potestas*; MS 593 has *sceleri est donata potestas*; another reading is *sceleris donata potestas est* (“power has been granted to crime”). “The reins owed to virtue”: the manuscripts have *debita virtutum* (“owed to virtues”). “This labyrinth”: the manuscripts read *haec domus intus habet* (“this house has within”). “Supported by a thousand marble columns”: the manuscripts have *marmor: fulta*.

- [Col. 0699D] After “Why do you build spacious structures when you will be enclosed in a narrow tomb?” MSS K and O read: “Whom the confines of a pious pygmy mother bore”; MS 593 reads: “The few spans of your life will fail”; another reading is “Small spans are owed to your life.” The printed text reads: “Your brief lifespan will run out.”

- [Col. 0701D] In “While he debates their natures and inserts them,” the manuscripts have *infert* (“brings in”) for *inserit*. “Many hidden matters”: the manuscripts have *multa libentia*, an uncertain corrupt reading, for *multa latentia*. “Dishes are set out”: the manuscripts read *ridet quoque* (“there also laughs/smiles”). “Whatever is pleasing to the eye and beautiful”: the manuscripts have *cumque decorum* (“and whatever is beautiful”).

- [Col. 0701D] The manuscripts variously read *haec misero totum miseros*; MS O has *heu misero totum turpes*; the printed reading is “Alas for the wretch! He turns it all to shameful uses.” “How far astray”: the manuscripts have *quam clivius*, an uncertain corrupt reading, for *quam devius*. “Dulled by the burden of flesh”: the manuscripts read *carnis haeret*; MS O, *carnis habet*. “Which it cares for and nourishes”: the manuscripts have *curat aliique*.

- [Col. 0701D] “Begins to live with weeping”: the manuscripts have *incaepit a fletu*. “How great, public evils mixed with private”: the manuscripts read *quanta privatis*. “Bitter thirst”: the manuscripts have *amara sitis*. “One groans”: the manuscripts read *iam gemit* (“now groans”). “Of a corrupted spouse”: the manuscripts have *corrupta coniugis*. A manuscript instead gives: “That noisy and royal boy fears his father”; the printed reading is “One complains that seed entrusted to barren soil has been lost.”

- [Col. 0703D] “Fortune does not favor”: MS O has *nunc sic blanda* (“now thus gently”). “Nor is the lesser part”: MS O has *non pars*. “It had enclosed”: MS O has *conceperat* (“had conceived”). “A savage storm of sadness”: the manuscripts have *tristitia saeua*. “In this period of life”: MS 593 has *tempora vitae* (“periods of life”). MS O adds the couplet: “One perishes from hunger, fungus, fever, serpent, or arrow; from waves, flames, an enemy, or a robber.” “No sickness is absent from the human body”: the manuscripts have *corpora languor*.

- [Col. 0703D] “If you now examine”: the manuscripts have *sic nunc* (“thus now”). “The bladder, injured by urination”: the manuscripts have *lithia vesica* (“a stone-afflicted bladder”). “The viscera are tortured”: the manuscripts have *viscera torrentur*. “The lower bowel”: MSS O have *colon* (“colon”) for *colus*. “What death extinguishes”: the manuscripts have *mors extinguis*.

- [Col. 0703D] “You too are the image of your eternal king”: MS 593 has *imago tui*; another reading is *imago Dei* (“image of God”). The manuscripts give an expanded couplet after “Let your mind burn continually with love of the good”: “Let your mind continually burn with love of goodness: thus the burning flame of the eternal pyre perishes.” The printed text has the two preceding lines only. “Seek”: the manuscripts have *quare boni* (“why [seek] the good?”). The note after “you will be light from his blessed light” states that in MS 593 this poem ends here, and several hexameter verses follow it.

- [Col. 0703D] “From the valley of death”: MS O has *de noctis valle* (“from the valley of night”).

- [Col. 0705D] “The king’s gifts”: the manuscripts have *regia tibi* (“a royal gift for you”). “Who enriches the deserving”: MS O has *merito magnis* (“rightly with great things”). “Great knowledge, abundant power”: the manuscripts have *summa potentia* (“supreme power”). “Will be restored”: the manuscripts read *reddetur* (“will be restored,” singular). The note on “Let us, monkish brothers” says that MS C, no. 70, ends Claudianus here, although other poems occur there as well.

- [Col. 0705D] “Who is swollen with pride”: MS K has *qui timet* (“who fears”). “How many”: MS K has *quam sunt*. “Death await”: MS O has *morsque manebit* (“and death will await”). “Seeks empty honors”: MSS O and K have *quaerit honores*. “With lips and heart”: MSS O and K read *et corde frequenter* (“and frequently with the heart”); another reading is *hoc corde frequentet* (“let him repeat [these things] with this heart”).

- [Col. 0705D] MS Bec. O has a leonine poem on the same subject beginning “Speak, moral flesh,” rather than “Speak, mortal flesh”; there it is followed by the verses “The body becomes man,” etc., which had not previously been printed. For “After death you will return as a worm into ashes,” the manuscript has *vilis post* (“base after”) for *vermis post* (“worm after”). The note on “Despise what you pursue” says that the manuscript places this verse before “Do you not know the laws ...?” “Do you not know the laws”: the manuscript has *an casus* (“do you not know the chances/events”) for *an leges*.

- [Col. 0709C] The Prologue was collated with the Bec manuscripts O; Thuanus 267; Victorine manuscripts RR. 3 and KK. 16; Corbie 160; Saint-Germain 345; the Carthusian manuscript at Porta; one manuscript of St Martin of Tournai; one of Vallis Lucentis; one of St Benedict of Fleury; and Sommalius’s edition. The St Benedict of Fleury manuscript begins: “The Prayers or Meditations of Lord Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, begin.” MS Thuanus 267: “The Prologue of St Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his Prayers or Meditations begins.” MS Vallis Lucentis: “The Prologue of Lord Anselm, Archbishop, begins.”

- [Col. 0709C] “Since [they were composed] to”: MSS Corbie, Victorine 16, Vallis Lucentis, and Fleury read *quae ad* (“which [were composed] to”). “Not rapidly, but gradually”: Bec and Thuanus read “not even rapidly, but gradually, with”; Corbie 160, Victorine 16, Vallis Lucentis, and Fleury read “not hurriedly and rapidly, but with.” “Wherever it may please him more”: the manuscripts have *illi placet* (“pleases him”). “They have been divided into paragraphs”: the manuscripts have *paraphis sunt distinctae*; another reading adds *per partes* (“into sections”).

- [Col. 0709C] Thuanus and Vallis Lucentis end: “The Prologue ends.” Victorine RR reads: “Meditations of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.” Victorine KK. 16 and Corbie 160 read: “The Prayers or Meditations of Lord Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, begin.” Vallis Lucentis adds: “very useful for arousing the reader’s mind to love or fear of God.” It also reads: “The Prayers or Meditations published by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, begin.”

# I. That we have been made in the image and likeness of God

[Note: [Col. 0709C] I found the First Meditation, which begins “Awake, my soul,” etc., in none of the manuscripts I had.]

Awake, my soul, awake; exercise your spirit, rouse your understanding, drive away the sluggishness of your deadly torpor, and seize concern for your salvation. Let the wandering of useless thoughts be banished; let laziness withdraw, and let diligence take its place. Apply yourself to sacred meditations; cling to divine goods; attend to eternal things, abandoning temporal ones.

What, then, could you think about that would be more useful or more salutary in so divine an exercise of the mind than to recall, in the sweetest reflection, the immeasurable benefits of the Creator? Consider, therefore, at the very beginning of creation, what sublimity and dignity he bestowed upon you, and weigh with what love and reverence he ought to be worshiped. [Col. 0709C]

Certainly, when he had decided to create and order the whole universe of visible and invisible things, he deliberated with supreme wisdom about the dignity of your condition, since he intended to honor you above all the other creatures that are in the world. [Col. 0710A] Behold, therefore, the sublimity of your creation, and recall the love you owe in return.

“Let us make man,” God said, “in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). If you do not awaken at this saying of your Creator; if, in the face of such ineffable kindness and condescension toward you, you do not burn wholly with love for him; if you are not inflamed with all your innermost being by desire for him—what shall I say? Shall I consider you asleep, or rather dead?

Attend, then, carefully to what it means that you were created in the image and likeness of God. Here you have a sweet pledge for pious meditation, in which to exercise your thoughts. Recognize, therefore, that likeness is one thing and image another. For example, a horse, an ox, and other similar creatures can have a certain likeness to a human being, [Col. 0710B] but no creature has the image of a human being except another human being.

A human being eats, and a horse also eats: here is a certain likeness and commonality between different natures. But the image of a human being is imitated only by another human being of the same nature as the one whose image it is. The image, therefore, is more worthy than the likeness.

We can therefore have likeness to God in this way: if, considering him good, we strive to be good; if, recognizing him to be just, we contend to be just; if, contemplating him as merciful, we devote ourselves to mercy.

But how are we made in his image? Attend. God always remembers himself, understands himself, and loves himself. Therefore, if you, according to your measure, remember God without weariness, understand God, and love God, you will be in his image, because you strive to do what God always does.

To remembering, understanding, and loving the highest good, a human being ought to refer everything that he lives for. Every thought and every movement of the heart should be turned, sharpened, and conformed to this end, so that with indefatigable devotion you may remember God, understand God, and love God, and may profitably express the dignity of your creation, by which you were created in the image of God. [Col. 0710C–0711A]

Why do I say that you were created in the image of God, when, according to the Apostle, you yourself are the image of God? “A man,” says the Apostle, “ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (I Cor. XI, 7).

# II. That we were made for this purpose: to praise God without end

Are these immeasurable benefits of the Creator not sufficient for you to return continual thanksgiving and the debt of uninterrupted love, when you consider that, from nothing—or rather, from clay—his goodness raised you at the very beginning of your creation to such exalted dignity? Turn, therefore, the saying of the saints toward your own life, and attend to what is said of the holy man. [Col. 0711B]

What is the praise of the holy man? “With all his heart he praised the Lord.” Behold for what you were created; behold the work of your service. Why, indeed, would God raise you up with so splendid a privilege of creation unless he wished you to devote yourself continually to his praises?

You were therefore created to praise your Creator, so that, occupied with his praises, you might both continually advance here toward him through the merit of righteousness and live well in the future. For his praise grants righteousness here and blessedness there.

But if you praise him, praise him with your whole heart; praise him with love. This is the rule proposed to the saints for praising: “With all his heart he praised the Lord; and he loved God who made him” (Eccli. XLVII, 10). Praise, then, and praise with your whole heart, and love the one whom you praise, because you were made for this: to praise and to love.

For one praises, but does not praise with his whole heart, when prosperity caresses him into blessing God, while adversity restrains him from the duty of blessing. One also praises, but does not love, when in praising God he seeks something other than God himself. [Col. 0711C]

Praise, therefore, and praise worthily, so that, insofar as strength is given you, no concern, no intention, no thought, and no anxiety of mind may be vacant from the praise of God. Let no prosperity of this life call you back from his praise; let no adversity restrain you. Thus you will praise the Lord with your whole heart.

But when you have praised him with your whole heart, and have praised him with love, seek nothing else from him but himself: let him himself be the end of your desire, the reward of your labor, the comfort of this shadowy life, and the possession of that blessed life.

You were made for this purpose: to praise him without end. You will then understand this more fully, when, raised up by his blessed vision, you see that solely and freely by his goodness you, who did not exist, were created, called, justified, glorified, and made so blessed and destined for such ineffable blessedness. [Col. 0711D]

Such contemplation will give you tireless love for praising him without end, and you will rejoice that through him, from him, and in him you have been blessed with such great and immutable goods.

# III. That wherever we are, in him we live, move, and exist, while we have him within us

But, turning your contemplative gaze for a little while from that future happiness, consider also the greatness of the grace with which he has enriched you even in this fleeting life.

He who dwells in heaven and reigns among the angels, before whom heaven and earth, with all that is in them, bow down, has offered himself to you as a dwelling place and made his presence ready for you. [Col. 0712A] For, as the Apostle Paul teaches, “in him we live and move and exist” (Acts XVII, 28).

Sweet life, lovely movement, desirable existence! What is sweeter than to have life in him who is himself blessed life? What is more lovely than to direct every movement of our will and action toward him and in him, who continually strengthens us with stability? What is more desirable than to be continually in him through our desire and way of life, in whom alone—or rather, who alone is true existence, without whom nothing can exist well?

“I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14). And rightly so. He alone truly exists whose being is immutable. Since, therefore, his being is so excellent and singular that he alone truly is, and since, in comparison with him, all being is nothing, where did he establish you when he created you for such exalted dignity that you cannot even understand the glory of your condition? What dwelling place did he prepare for you? [Col. 0712B]

Hear him saying in the Gospel: “Remain in me, and I in you” (John XV, 4). O immeasurable condescension! O blessed dwelling! O glorious exchange! How great is the Creator’s condescension, that he wishes his creature to dwell in him! How incomprehensible is the creature’s blessedness, to remain in its Creator! How great is the glory of a rational creature, to be joined to its Creator in so blessed an exchange, so that he dwells in it and it in him!

He therefore mercifully willed that we, created so excellently, should remain in him: above all things, as the governor of all, existing without anxiety; sustaining everything, as the foundation of all, without labor; surpassing everything, as superior to all things, without pride; embracing everything, as the one who contains all things, without diffusion; filling everything, as the fullness of all things, without constraint upon himself. [Col. 0712C]

Since he is absent from nowhere, he has chosen for himself a delightful kingdom within us, as the Gospel declares: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21). But if the kingdom of God is within us, and God dwells in his kingdom, does he not himself remain in us, whose kingdom is within us?

Certainly. For if God is wisdom, and the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom, then whoever is truly just has God dwelling within him. “For the temple of God is holy, which you are,” says the Apostle (I Cor. III, 67).

Devote yourself, therefore, without weariness to holiness, lest you cease to be the temple of God. He says of his own: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Cor. VI, 16). [Col. 0712D] Do not doubt that wherever holy souls are, he is in them.

For if you yourself are wholly present everywhere in all the members that you give life to, how much more is God wholly everywhere, since he created both you yourself and your body?

We must therefore consider with the utmost care how rationally and reverently we ought to move our senses and the members of our body, over which Divinity itself presides. Let us therefore give, as is fitting, complete authority over our hearts to so great an inhabitant, so that nothing in us may resist him; but let all our thoughts and movements of the will, all our words and all our deeds, attend to his command, serve his will, and be directed according to his rule of righteousness. [Col. 0713A]

Thus we shall truly be his kingdom; he will remain in us; and, remaining in him, we shall live well.

# IV. That all who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ

Awaken yourself, I beg you, my soul, and let the fire of heavenly love burn within your inmost being. Wisely understand the beauty bestowed upon you by the Lord your God; understanding it, love it; loving it, venerate it through the duties of a holy way of life.

Did not he who granted you a dwelling in himself and condescended to dwell in you clothe, fortify, and adorn you with himself? “All of you,” says the Apostle, “who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III, 27).

What praise, then, what thanksgiving, can you worthily offer to him who clothed you with such beauty and raised you to such honor that, with the sweetest rejoicing of heart, you can say: “The Lord clothed me with the garment of salvation; he wrapped me in the robe of gladness” (Isa. LXI, 10)? [Col. 0713B]

For the angels of God it is the highest joy to contemplate Christ; and behold, in his immeasurable condescension he stoops so far toward you that he wishes you to be clothed with himself.

With what garment, unless with that of which the Apostle glories, saying: “Christ was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification” (I Cor. I, 30)? With what marks of clothing could he adorn you more greatly than by making you radiant with the garment of wisdom, the ornament of righteousness, and the beauty of satisfaction?

# V. That we are the body of Christ

And why should I say that Christ made himself your garment, when he united himself to you so completely that, in the unity of the Church, he willed you to be of his flesh? [Col. 0713C]

Hear the Apostle explaining the testimony of Scripture: “The two shall be one flesh. But I speak,” he says, “of Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 32).

Consider also with what great union he has joined you to himself. The Apostle confirms that you are the body of Christ: “You are the body of Christ,” he says, “and members from the members” (I Cor. XII, 27).

Guard, therefore, your body and its members with the dignity that is fitting, lest, if you treat them insultingly through any frivolous pursuit, you should be subjected to a punishment greater by as much as the reward with which you would have been crowned had you treated them worthily would have been more excellent. [Col. 0713D]

Your eyes are the eyes of Christ. You may not therefore direct Christ’s eyes toward the contemplation of any vanities, because Christ is truth, and every vanity is contrary to him.

Your mouth is the mouth of Christ. You ought not to open the mouth that you should keep open only for the praises of God and the edification of your neighbor—not merely for slander, not merely for lies, but not even for idle talk.

Understand the same concerning the other members of Christ entrusted to your keeping.

# VI. That we are one in Christ, and with him one Christ

But recognize still more deeply how closely you are joined to him. Hear the Lord himself praying to the Father for his own: “I will,” he says, “that as you and I are one, so they also may be one in us” (John XVII, 21). [Col. 0714A]

I am your Son by nature; let them also be your sons and my brothers by grace.

How exalted it is for a Christian person to advance in Christ so far that he himself may in a certain sense be called Christ! This was understood by that truly faithful steward of the ecclesiastical household who said: “All Christians are one Christ in Christ.”

Nor is this surprising, since he is the head and we are his body; he is the bridegroom, and he is also the bride: the bridegroom in himself, the bride in the holy souls whom he has joined to himself by the bond of eternal love.

“As a bridegroom,” he says, “he placed a diadem upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament.”

Turn over these benefits of his toward you, therefore, my soul; kindle yourself in love for him; burn with desire for his blessed contemplation. Cry out boldly, with that most ardent affection of inward love, and, wholly melted into desire for him, break forth in the voice of the faithful bride: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 1). [Col. 0714B]

Let every delight that is outside him depart from my soul. Let no affection of the present life, no comfort, flatter me while his blessed presence is denied me. Let him embrace me with the arms of charity; let him kiss me with the mouth of that heavenly sweetness; let him speak to me with that ineffable word by which he reveals his secrets to the angels.

Let this be the reciprocal exchange of words between bridegroom and bride: that I may pour out my whole heart to him, and he may reveal to me the secrets of his sweetness.

Strengthened by these and similar meditations, strive with the full affection of holy desire to follow your bridegroom, and say to him: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I, 3).

Say it faithfully—not with a passing sound, but with tireless desire. Say it so that you may be heard; desire to be drawn so that you may be able to follow.

Say, then, to your Redeemer and Savior: “Draw me after you.” May the sweetness of the world not draw me; may the sweetness of your most blessed love draw me. My vanity once drew me; but now may your truth draw me after you.

Draw me, because you have drawn me; hold me, because you have seized me. You drew me by redeeming me; draw me by saving me. You drew me by showing mercy; draw me by making me blessed. You seized me when, appearing among human beings, you became human for us; hold me now, exalted in heaven and ruling above the angels. [Col. 0714C]

Your word, your promise, is this. You promised, saying: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32).

Draw, therefore, now that you are powerfully exalted, the one whom you mercifully drew when humbled. You have ascended—let me perceive it; you reign above all—let me acknowledge it.

Do I not acknowledge that you reign? Certainly I do, and I give thanks. But let me perfectly acknowledge by loving what I piously acknowledge by believing concerning you. Let me acknowledge by seeing what I acknowledge by believing. [Col. 0714D]

Bind to yourself, with indissoluble bonds of love, the desires of my heart, where the first fruits of my spirit are with you. May the unity of charity join us, whom the charity of redemption has united.

For you loved me and gave yourself for me. Let my intention therefore be continually with you in heaven, and may your protection continually be with me on earth.

Help me, who burn with desire for your love, you who loved me when I despised you. Give to me who seek, you who gave yourself to me when I did not know you. Receive me when I return, you who called me back when I fled.

May I love in order to be loved; rather, because I am loved, may I love more and more, so that I may be loved more.

May my thought be united with you; may my intention with you be one and undivided, where our blessed substance, mercifully received by you, already reigns with you. [Col. 0715A]

May I cling to you inseparably, adore you without weariness, serve you perseveringly, seek you faithfully, find you happily, and possess you eternally.

With these words, my soul, appeal to God; kindle yourself, set yourself aflame, burn, and strive to become wholly fire in desire for him.

# VII. Reconsideration of our sins, for which our conscience reproaches us most, and through which we lost all these things

When you consider to what and how many good things you have advanced through his grace, also reconsider what and how many good things you lost through your own fault, and into what evils you fell under the burden of your sins.

Turn over with sighs the evils you wickedly committed, and recall with groans the good things you miserably lost because of those same evils. [Col. 0715B]

What good did your most excellent Creator fail to bestow upon you in his goodness? And what evil did you not repay him, strengthened by accursed wickedness?

By losing good things, you deserved evil; rather, by throwing away good things, you chose evil. Having lost—or rather, cast away—the grace of the Creator, you miserably incurred his anger.

You have no grounds on which to prove yourself innocent, since a multitude of your evils surrounds you like an immense army: on one side exposing the disgrace of wicked deeds; on another bringing forward an immense heap of useless words and, what is more condemnable, harmful ones; elsewhere displaying an infinite mass of evil thoughts.

These are the things because of which you lost immeasurable goods; because of these you were deprived of the Creator’s grace.

Recall these things with groaning; groan over them by renouncing them; renounce them by condemning them; condemn them by changing your life for the better. [Col. 0715C]

Struggle with yourself in your heart, lest from now on, even for a moment, you give assent to any vanity, whether in heart, in tongue, or—what is most deserving of condemnation—in deed.

Let there be a daily, indeed continual, quarrel in your heart, so that you retain no pact with any vice. Always examine yourself strictly; scrutinize what is hidden; and whatever you find in yourself to be reprehensible, strike, overthrow, crush, uproot, cast out, and reduce to nothing by stern judgment.

Spare yourself nothing; flatter yourself not at all. But “in the morning”—that is, in contemplation of the final judgment, which follows the night of the present life like the morning light—“destroy all the sinners of the earth,” that is, the sins and offenses of earthly conduct, so that you may “destroy from the city of the Lord,” which you ought to build for him within yourself, “all those who work iniquity”: that is, diabolical suggestions, pleasures hateful to God, deadly consents, and perverse deeds. [Col. 0715D]

You must be cleansed from all these things as the city of God, so that the Creator may find, establish, and possess in you a dwelling pleasing to himself.

Do not be among those whose stubbornness God himself seems to lament, saying: “There is no one who considers in his heart and says, ‘What have I done?’” (Isa. LVII, 1).

If they are rejected because they were unwilling to blush for their past evils and rebuke themselves, will you neglect to confront, judge, and correct yourself with severe discipline, so that you may run among the number of the elect?

Revolve, therefore, carefully in your thoughts the immeasurable benefits of the Creator, by which he raised you up without any merits intervening; and recall the countless evils by which your wickedness unworthily answered those same benefits. [Col. 0716A]

Then, giving birth to great sorrow, cry out: “What have I done? I have provoked God; I have aroused my Creator to anger; I have repaid his immeasurable benefits with countless evils. What have I done?”

As you say these things, crush your heart bitterly, utter groans, and shed tears. If you do not weep here, when will you weep? If the turning away of God’s face from you, caused by your sins, does not awaken you to compunction, let the enormity of the punishments of hell, which those same sins have brought upon you, at least break your hardness.

Return, then, return to your heart, transgressor, and withdraw your foot from hell, so that you may escape the evils you deserve and recover the good things of which you have been justly deprived. [Col. 0716B]

For if you consider your evils, you have lost every good thing that was bestowed upon you by him. You must therefore always turn your eyes toward those evils, especially those of which your conscience accuses you more gravely, so that he may turn his eyes away.

For if you turn away from your sins with the intention of making satisfaction, he turns away from them the gaze of vengeance. If you forget, he remembers.

# VIII. Reconsideration of the Lord’s incarnation, through which we recovered all these things

To be freed from these evils, then, consider the mercies of your Redeemer toward you.

Certainly, by the guilt of original sin you had been blinded and could not see the sublimity of your Creator. Surrounded by clouds of sins, you were hastening toward darkness, and, driven by the swift currents of vices, you were rushing toward eternal darkness. [Col. 0716C]

And behold, your Redeemer applied the eye-salve of his incarnation to your blinded eyes, so that, although you could not see God shining in the secrecy of his majesty, you might behold God appearing in human form; by beholding him, recognize him; by recognizing him, love him; and, loving him, strive with the greatest zeal to attain his glory.

He became incarnate to recall you to spiritual things. He became a sharer in your mutability so that he might make you a sharer in his immutability. He bowed down to your lowliness in order to raise you to his heights.

He was born from the integrity of virginity in order to heal the corruption of transgressing nature. He was circumcised to teach that human beings ought to cut away from themselves everything superfluous belonging to sins and vices.

He was offered in the temple and received by a holy widow, to admonish his faithful to frequent the house of God and to devote themselves to holiness so that they might deserve to receive him. [Col. 0716D]

He was received and praised by the old man Simeon, to show that he loves the gravity of life and maturity of conduct.

He was baptized to sanctify the sacraments of our baptism. In the Jordan, bowing beneath the hand of John for baptism, he heard the voice of the Father and received the coming of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, teaching us that we ought to remain in humility of mind—which is signified by the Jordan, for Jordan is interpreted as “their descent”—and that there we should be honored by the conversation of the heavenly Father, of whom it is said, “His conversation is with the simple” (Prov. III, 32), and exalted by the presence of the Holy Spirit, who rests upon the humble.

This occurred beneath the hand of John, whose name is said to mean “the grace of God,” so that we might attribute whatever we receive from God to that same grace, and not to our own merits. [Col. 0717A]

When the forty-day fast was completed, he overcame the devil with his temptations and was glorified by angelic ministry, teaching us, throughout the whole period of the present life, to avoid the pleasures of temporal things, to trample the world and its prince beneath our feet, and thus to be fortified by angelic protections.

By preaching the kingdom of God, he spent his days among the people and edified the gathered crowds by miracles and words. At night he frequented the mountain and devoted himself to prayer, admonishing us that, according to the suitability of the time, we should at one moment demonstrate life to our neighbors, among whom we live, by words and examples suited to our measure; and at another enter the solitude of the mind, ascend the mountain of virtues, long for the sweetness of heavenly contemplation, and direct our intention upward with tireless devotion. [Col. 0717B]

On the mountain he was transfigured before Peter, James, and John, signifying to us that, if, like Peter—whose name is interpreted as “one who recognizes”—we humbly strive to recognize our weakness; if we strive to become overthrowers of vices—which is signified by the name James; and if we faithfully submit ourselves to the grace of God—which is indicated by the name John—we shall happily ascend that heavenly mountain to contemplate the glory of Jesus, with our same King as guide.

In Bethany—which is interpreted as “house of obedience”—he raised Lazarus, showing that all who, through zeal for good will, die to this world and rest in the bosom of obedience will be raised by him to eternal life. [Col. 0717C]

At the mystical supper he gave his body and blood to his disciples and humbly washed their feet, teaching that sacred ministries must be celebrated with pure works and pious humility of mind.
