As he was about to be exalted by the glory of the holy Resurrection, he endured the mockery of the faithless, the harshness of words, the disgrace of the cross, the bitterness of gall, and finally death. He admonished his own that those who strive to reach glory after death should not only endure with an even spirit the hardships and labors of the present life and the oppressions of the wicked, but should love, seek, and gladly receive all the harshness of this world in exchange for eternal rewards.

If you strive to think worthily about, devoutly embrace, and imitate with fervent love these so splendid and immeasurable benefits of your Creator toward you, you will not merely recover the good things lost through the first parent, but will eternally possess far greater ones through the ineffable grace of your Savior. [Col. 0717D]

For your God himself, through the mystery of the Incarnation, became your brother. What inexpressible joy this has caused you, when you see human nature exalted in him above every creature!

# IX. That we must pray to be rescued from the lake of misery and from the mire of filth

What, then, remains except that, having worthily considered all these things, you should kindle your mind in every way toward the inheritance of such great goods, and continually beseech him who created you to possess other things also, so that he may rescue you from the lake of misery and from the mire of filth, and make you a possessor of such blessedness?

What is the lake of misery except the depth of worldly desire? And what is the mire of filth except the stench of carnal pleasure? [Col. 0718A]

For these are the two restraints by which the human race is, to its pitiable oppression, prevented from tending toward the blessed freedom of heavenly contemplation: namely, desire and pleasure.

For worldly desire is truly a lake of misery. It subjects the mind to its dominion and, through countless desires, drags it into the depths of vices as though by chains, permitting it no rest.

The mind oppressed by the yoke of desire is scattered outside itself through love of visible things and is carried away through various passions of the soul. Labor in acquiring devastates it; anxiety in multiplying; joy in possessing; fear of losing; grief when it has lost. These things do not allow it to see at all amid how many dangers it exists. [Col. 0718B]

This is the lake of misery, which worldly desire never ceases to fill with such evils. Blessed David rejoiced that he had been rescued from this lake when, giving thanks, he said: “He brought me out of the lake of misery and from the mire of filth” (Ps. XXXIX, 3).

What is the mire of filth? The unclean delight of pleasure. Cry out, therefore, boldly with blessed David, and say to your Creator: “Rescue me from the mire, so that I may not become fixed in it” (Ps. LXVIII, 15).

Cleanse your heart from every defilement of carnal pleasure; exclude unclean thoughts from your mind if you wish to escape the filth of this mire.

But when, by repenting, confessing, weeping, and diligently introducing holy thoughts into your heart, you have escaped, do not fall back from it. Sigh with all your heart before God, beseeching his mercy to set your feet upon a rock—that is, to make the affections of your heart firm through the virtues of Christ—so that your mind may be placed upon the firm foundation of righteousness, clinging steadfastly to Christ, of whom it is said that he was made for us by God “wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification” (I Cor. I, 30). [Col. 0718C]

Pray also that he may direct your steps, so that they do not turn back toward vices, but advance with unbending stability in the heavenly commandments and hasten with complete intention toward the blessed homeland of the angels.

But, raised up by such direction, do not be lazy in praising the Creator. Beg his mercy to place a new song in your mouth, so that with worthy devotion you may sing a hymn to our God. For it is fitting that, joined to God through the newness of your life, you should resound with a new song in his praises, despising temporal things and desiring eternal things alone, and obeying the divine law no longer from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness. [Col. 0718D]

For this is to sing a new song to God: to crush the practices of the old person and to walk with all the effort of the heart, desiring only enduring life, in the ways of the new person that the Son of God showed to the world.

He also sings a hymn who retains in the pure memory of his mind the joys of the heavenly homeland and strives to reach them, supported by the conscience of a holy life and strengthened by the gift of heavenly grace.

# X. Consideration of the miseries of this life

Amid these things, weigh the miseries of the present life and reflect with vigilant heart how cautiously you must live in it.

Consider that you belong to the company of him of whom Scripture says: “The way of the man is hidden, and the Lord has surrounded him with darkness” (Job III, 23). [Col. 0719A]

For you are truly surrounded by the deep blindness of ignorance: you do not know how God weighs your deeds, and you are unaware of what end awaits you. “A person does not know,” says Solomon, “whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but everything remains uncertain until the end” (Eccl. IX, 1).

Imagine in your heart that you see a certain deep and dark valley, containing every kind of torment at its bottom. Imagine above it a single bridge extending a great distance, only one foot wide.

If someone were forced to cross this bridge—so narrow, so high, and so dangerous—with his eyes bound so that he could not see his steps, and with his hands tied behind him so that he could not guide his path even by feeling it with a staff, what fear and distress do you think he would carry in his mind? [Col. 0719B]

Would there be any place in him for joy, pleasure, or wantonness? I do not think so. All pride would be removed; empty glory would be driven away; and the dark shadow of death alone would occupy his mind.

Consider further the monstrous birds flying around the bridge and wishing to drag the traveler into the depths. Would not fear increase? What if, as he crossed, the boards were continually removed from behind his heels? Would this not impose even greater anxiety upon the one crossing?

Recognize what such an example signifies, and bind your mind anxiously with divine fear.

Understand the deep and dark valley as hell, immeasurably deep and horribly dark with gloomy obscurity. Every kind of torment converges there. Everything that delights is absent there; everything that terrifies and tortures, and everything capable of causing distress, is present. [Col. 0719C]

The dangerous bridge, from which anyone who crosses badly is thrown down below, is the present life. Whoever lives badly in it falls from it and descends into hell.

The boards removed after those who cross are the individual days of our life. They pass in such a way that they never return; by their continual diminishing they press us toward the end and compel us to hasten toward our appointed limit.

The birds flying around the bridge and lying in wait for those who cross are evil spirits, whose whole endeavor is to cast human beings down from the stability of the right path and hurl them into the depths of hell.

We ourselves are those who cross: blind with the darkness of ignorance and bound, as though by a heavy chain, by the difficulty of doing good, so that we cannot direct our steps freely toward God in a holy life. [Col. 0719D]

Consider, then, whether in so great a danger you ought not to cry out to your Creator with the utmost zeal, so that, fortified by his protection, you may sing confidently amid the ranks of your adversaries: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. XIX, 1).

Light, namely, against blindness; salvation, against difficulty. These are the two evils into which the first parent cast us: ignorance and difficulty. Thus we neither see where we are heading nor what must be done; and even when we see something in part, hindered by difficulty we cannot fulfill what we rightly know.

Meditate on these things, my soul; think on them. Let your mind exercise itself in them daily. Attentive to these things, let it withdraw from the cares and thoughts of useless matters, and let it kindle itself wholly with the fire of holy fear and blessed love, both to flee these evils and to grasp eternal goods. [Col. 0720A]

# XI. Concerning the body after the soul’s departure

Now I return to you, sweetest Creator and most merciful Redeemer, my maker and reformer, humbly imploring your goodness with my prayers: teach my heart, through life-giving fear and salutary trembling, to consider how foul and how mournful will be the condition of my flesh after death, when deprived of the spirit by which it is presently animated, it is handed over to decay and worms to be consumed.

Where then will its beauty be, if it now possesses any of that which it boasts? Where will be its carefully sought delights, with which it now overflows, and its delicate limbs? [Col. 0720B]

Will that prophetic saying not then truly be fulfilled in it: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL, 6)?

Its eyes, which I often delighted to let wander through vain and harmful things, will be closed and turned inward toward the depths of the head. Covered with horrible darkness, they will lie there—those which now rejoice to drink in vanities as though they were light.

Its ears, soon to be filled with worms, will lie open—those which now receive the voices of detraction and worldly rumors with damnable pleasure.

Its teeth will be miserably clenched and fastened together—those which gluttony once loosened.

Its nostrils, which now delight in various scents, will decay.

Its lips, which often delighted to burst into foolish laughter, will shudder beneath foul filth.

Its tongue, which often uttered empty tales, will be bound by putrid corruption.

Its throat will be constricted, and its belly will be filled with worms—those limbs which are now frequently distended with various foods. [Col. 0720C]

Why should I mention each part individually? The entire structure of that body, for whose health, comfort, and pleasure almost all care is devoted, will dissolve into decay, into worms, and finally into the most despised dust.

Where will be the upright neck? Where the boasting of words, the adornment of clothing, and the variety of delights? Like a dream they have vanished; everything has passed away, never to return, and has left behind its most wretched lover.

## XII. On the soul separated from the body

Good God, what is this that I behold? Behold, fear meets fear, and sorrow meets sorrow. After its separation from the body, will not the soul be surrounded by a multitude of demons pressing around it, magnifying its accusations, and investigated concerning everything down to the slightest negligence? The prince of this world will come with his attendants, raging with fury, skilled in entrapment, inclined to lying, malicious in accusation, bringing forward against it whatever true charges he can from the evils it has committed, while fabricating many false ones. O dreadful hour, O terrifying examination! On one side a strict judge for judgment; on the other, shameless adversaries for accusation.

The soul will stand alone, without a comforter, drawing its only consolation from the fact that the conscience of good works defends it. But in such strict judgment, when everything will appear naked, who will boast of having a pure heart? If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear? (1 Peter 4:18.) Then the lips of those who praise will fall silent; the tongue of flatterers will be of no avail; vain glory will be proved to have been deceptive. Foolish joy will flee; the pomp of rank will be driven away; the ambition for honor will be seen to have been full of deception.

Blessed is that soul whom, in such a crisis, the conscience of innocence protects and the memory of holiness defends; whom, while it was still placed in the flesh, the wave of devout remorse repeatedly washed, the diligence of confession adorned, and meditation on sacred law enlightened; whom humility made gentle, patience tranquil, obedience free from its own will, and charity fervent for the practice of every virtue. Such a soul will not fear that dreadful hour, nor be put to shame when it speaks with its enemies in the gate (Psalm 126:6). For it will be joined to those of whom Scripture says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (ibid., 4).

## XIII. Recollection of the day of judgment, when the goats will be placed on the left

Who, now, could say anything about the terror of that final judgment, when the sheep will be placed on the right and the goats on the left? What trembling there will be when the powers of heaven are shaken? What confusion of all things, what groaning, what cries of those howling, when that terrible voice is directed against the negligent: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire!” (Matthew 25:41.)

Truly, that day will be a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and blast. Truly then the voice of the day will be bitter; there the mighty man will be afflicted. For those who, with proud minds, now despise the divine will and boast of pursuing their own will—then perpetual fire will envelop them, fire that will never be extinguished; and the worm will devour them, the worm that will not die; and the smoke of their torment will rise forever and ever.

## XIV. Recollection of joy, when the sheep will be placed on the right

But while these are mourning and uttering dreadful groans of the heart because of the anguish of their spirit, what do you think the joy and exultation of those blessed ones will be who, placed at God’s right hand, are to hear that most joyful voice by which it will be said to them: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”? (Matthew 25:34.)

Then truly the voice of exultation and salvation will dwell in the tent of the righteous. Then the Lord will raise up the head of the humble, who now do not disdain to be lowly and rejected for his sake. He will heal those broken in heart and console with everlasting joys those who mourn in this pilgrimage out of desire for him. The ineffable reward of those who, for love of their Creator, rejoice that they have cast aside their own wills will appear.

On that day a heavenly crown will encircle the heads of the obedient, and the glory of the patient will shine with indescribable splendor. There charity will enrich its soldiers with the fellowship of angels, and purity of heart will bless its lovers with the happiest vision of their Creator. Then God will show himself to all who love him and exalt them forever in eternal security. Then all the elect will truly sing:

> Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord;  
> forever and ever they will praise you.  
> (Psalm 83:3.)

May he deign to make us participants in that praise, God who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# MEDITATION II

[Note: It was collated with the manuscripts previously mentioned: Vict., Thuan., Bec., Corb., Val-luc., and Flor. “On the terror of judgment, to instill fear”; elsewhere entitled “The Book of the Misery of Man” (manuscript Corb. 160), “Meditation for arousing the fear of God” (other manuscripts), and “Prayer for stirring up fear.”]

## On the terror of judgment, to arouse fear within oneself

My life terrifies me [Note: “My life” in manuscripts Vict. 16 and Corb. 166; “my whole life” in manuscripts Vict. 16, Bec. O, Corb. 160, Val-luc., and Flor.; “my life wearies me”]; for, carefully examined, it appears to me to be either entirely sin [Note: “To me, either sin” in manuscripts Bec., Vict., Thu., Val-luc., and Flor.] or almost entirely fruitlessness. And if any fruit seems to appear in it, it is either so feigned, or imperfect, or corrupted in some way, that it can either fail to please God or displease him.

Therefore, O sinner, your life is now not almost entirely, but certainly entirely either in sin [Note: “Your life is now almost entirely in sin” in manuscripts Bec. and Thu.; “your life is not now almost entirely, but certainly entirely in sin” in manuscript Corb.; “your life is now not almost entirely, but certainly entirely in sin” in manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor.] and damnable [Note: “Or damnable” in the manuscripts], or fruitless and contemptible. But why do I separate the fruitless from the damnable? Surely, if it is fruitless, it is also damnable. For it is established and true what Truth said: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10) [Note: The manuscripts read, “It is true that the truth of God said: Every tree” or “It is true that truth said: Every tree”]. Finally, if I do anything useful, it in no way compensates for the bodily nourishment that I abuse. But who feeds an animal that is not as useful as what it consumes? And yet you, merciful God, nourish and await your useless worm and foul-smelling sinner [Note: The manuscripts read “worm and”; manuscripts Vict. 16, Corb. 160, and Flor. read “your sinner, foul-smelling with sins”; the text reads “your foul-smelling sinner”].

How much more tolerably does a rotten dog stink to human beings than a sinful soul to God; how much more unhappily does this soul stink to God than that dog to human beings! Alas, not a man but a reproach of men [Note: “A reproach of man” in manuscripts Vict. 3, Corb. 160, Val-luc., and Flor.; manuscript Vict. 16 omits “of man”], baser than cattle, worse than a corpse. My soul is weary of my life; I am ashamed to live, I fear to die. What, then, remains for you, O sinner, except to weep through your whole life over your whole life, so that your whole life itself may weep over itself entirely?

But in this too my soul is miserably marvelous and marvelously miserable [Note: “In this my soul” in the manuscripts], because it does not grieve as much as it knows itself to deserve; rather, it lies torpid in security, as though it did not know that it was suffering. O fruitless soul, what are you doing? Why are you torpid, sinful soul? The day of judgment is coming; the great day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift: a day of wrath, that day; a day of tribulation and distress; a day of calamity and misery; a day of darkness and gloom; a day of cloud and storm; a day of trumpet and blast. O bitter voice of the day of the Lord! Why do you sleep, lukewarm soul, worthy of being vomited out? Why do you sleep? Whoever does not awaken, whoever does not tremble at such thunder, is not asleep but dead.

Fruitless tree, where are your fruits? Tree worthy of the axe and fire, worthy to be cut down and burned, where are your fruits? Surely, piercing thorns and bitter sins—which, would that they pierced you through repentance [Note: “Pierced you through by pricking” in manuscript Vict. 16], so that they might be broken [Note: “So that they might rise up” in the manuscripts]; so that they might become bitter and disappear.

Perhaps you think some sin is small. Would that the strict Judge considered any sin small! But alas for me! Does not every sin dishonor God through transgression? What then? Will the sinner dare to call sin small [Note: “Therefore, what sin” in manuscripts Vict. 16, Corb. 160, and Flor.]? When is it a small thing to dishonor God? O dry and useless wood, worthy of eternal fires, what will you answer on that day, when every moment of life granted to you will be demanded from you, and it will be asked how you spent it?

Then whatever work or idleness [Note: “Or idle conduct” in manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.], speech or silence is found in you will be condemned, down to the smallest thought—even the fact that you lived—if it was not directed according to God’s will. Woe! How many sins will burst forth there unexpectedly, as though from ambush, which you do not see now? Certainly more, and perhaps more terrifying, than those you now see. How many things that you think are not evil, how many things that you now believe to be good, will appear there, stripped bare, as the blackest sins [Note: The manuscripts vary: “which you do not now see; and things you think are not evil”; “which you now see; how many things you think are not evil”; “which you yourself can see”; and other arrangements of the same clauses].

There, without doubt, you will receive according to what you did in the body; then, when there will no longer be a time of mercy [Note: “When punishment is received and no delay is granted”; another manuscript reads: “then, when repentance will no longer be received and amendment will no longer be promised”]; then, when repentance will not be accepted and amendment will not be promised.

Here [Note: The manuscripts add or vary: “When punishment is received and no delay is granted”; “here”; manuscript Corb. 160 reads: “then, when repentance will no longer be accepted and amendment will not be promised. Here”], consider what you have done and what you ought to receive. If there are many good deeds and few evil ones, rejoice greatly; if many evil deeds and few good ones, mourn greatly.

O useless sinner, are these things not enough for an immense groan [Note: “For a vain groan” in the manuscripts]? Are they not enough to draw blood and marrow out into tears [Note: One manuscript reads “into tears?”; another, “in tears”]? Wondrous hardness, to break which such heavy hammers are light! Insensible torpor [Note: “Unconquerable torpor” in manuscript Flor.], to awaken which such sharp goads are blunt! O deadly sleep [Note: “Prophetic sleep” in the manuscripts], to awaken which such terrifying thunder is hoarse!

Useless sinner, these things ought to be enough for you to continue your mourning; they can be enough for you to swallow unceasing tears. But why should I conceal anything by keeping silent about the weight and magnitude of the misery that threatens, and steal it from the eyes of my soul [Note: “Enjoy it” in the manuscripts]? Is it so that sudden pains may rush upon me unexpectedly, so that an intolerable storm may suddenly break upon me [Note: “And suddenly a storm may break upon me” in the manuscripts]? Certainly this is not advantageous for the sinner. But if I say whatever I can imagine, it still cannot be compared with what the reality is [Note: “It may accomplish” in the manuscripts]. Therefore let my eyes pour out tears day and night and not be silent.

Increase, then, O sinner, increase the burden upon your former afflictions; add terror to terror, howling to howling [Note: Some manuscripts read simply “terror, howling”]. For he himself will judge you, he who gave me good for evil, to whom I returned evil for good [Note: Manuscript Flor. reads “for good I returned”]. He who is now most patient [Note: “Most wise” in manuscript Flor.] will then be most strict; now most merciful, then most just.

Alas for me, alas for me! Against whom have I sinned? I have dishonored God; I have provoked the Almighty. Sinner, what have I done? To whom have I done it? How badly have I done it? Woe, woe! Wrath of the Almighty, do not rush upon me [Note: “May it not rush upon me” in the manuscripts]. Wrath of the Almighty, where could you be contained in me? There is nothing in all of me that could endure you [Note: “That could endure you” in the manuscripts].

O anguish [Note: “Anguish for me” in the manuscripts]! Here will be accusing sins; there, terrifying justice; beneath, the dreadful abyss of hell lying open; above, the angry Judge; within, a burning conscience; outside, a blazing world. The righteous will scarcely be saved; in what direction will the sinner, caught in this condition, press himself [Note: “The sinner, reproved, where will he press himself?” in the manuscripts]? Hemmed in, where will I hide? How will I appear? To hide will be impossible; to appear, intolerable. I will desire that, and it will be nowhere; I will curse this, and it will be everywhere. What then? What will there be then [Note: “Whatever then, whatever will there be then” in the manuscripts]? Who will rescue me from the hands of God? Where will I find counsel? Where salvation?

Who is he called the angel of great counsel, who is called Savior, so that I may cry out his name? It is he himself, it is he himself: Jesus himself is also the Judge, between whose hands I tremble.

Breathe now, O sinner, breathe; do not despair—hope in him whom you fear. Flee to him from whom you fled. Call insistently upon him whom you arrogantly provoked.

Jesus, Jesus, for the sake of your name, deal with me according to this name of yours [Note: “According to the name” in the manuscripts]. Jesus, Jesus, forget the proud man who provokes you; look upon the wretched man who invokes your sweet name, your delightful name [Note: The manuscripts read: “the beloved name, the delightful name”; or “look upon the wretched man invoking the sweet, delightful name”], the name that strengthens the sinner and is a name of blessed hope.

For what is “Jesus” except “Savior”? Therefore, Jesus, for your own sake, be Jesus to me: you who formed me, lest I perish; you who redeemed me, do not condemn me [Note: The manuscripts read variously: “You who created me, do not destroy me; you who redeemed me, do not condemn me”; “you who formed me, lest I perish; you who redeemed me, do not condemn me”; “you who saved me, lest I perish; you who redeemed me, do not condemn me”]. You who created me by your goodness, do not let your work perish through my iniquity [Note: “Do not destroy your work” in the manuscripts]. I ask you, most merciful one: let my iniquity not destroy what your omnipotent goodness made.

Recognize, most kind one, what is yours, and wipe away what is alien. Jesus, Jesus, have mercy while it is the time for mercy, lest you condemn me at the time of judgment. For what profit is there for you in my blood, if I descend into everlasting corruption? “For the dead will not praise you, Lord, nor all those who descend into hell” (Psalm 113:17).

If you admit me within the broad bosom of your mercy, it will not become narrower because of me, Lord [Note: “You will not become narrower” in the manuscripts]. Admit me, therefore, O most desired Jesus, admit me into the number of your elect, so that with them I may praise you, enjoy you fully, and glory in you among all who love your name. You who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, are glorified throughout endless ages. Amen.

# MEDITATION III

[Note: It was collated with the previously designated manuscripts Vict., Thu., Bec., Corb., Val-luc., and Flor. The manuscripts title it “Lamentation for Lost Virginity” (Vict., Thu., and Bec.); “Lamentation for Virginity Badly Lost” (Corb. 160 and Val-luc.); “On Torpor: How to Awaken the Soul to Correct Its Sins” (Flor.); and “Lamentation over Lost Virginity.”]

## Lamentation for virginity badly lost

My soul, my sorrowful soul, my soul, I say, the wretched soul of a wretched little man: shake off your torpor, examine your sin, and shake your mind. Bring that enormous crime back to your heart, and bring forth from your heart an immense groan. Attend, unhappy soul, attend to the horror of your crime; extend [Note: “And display” in manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor.] the dreadful terror [Note: “Horror” in manuscript Flor.] and the terrifying sorrow.

You, I say, who once, washed white in the heavenly bath [Note: “Once white” in manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor.; “since you were made white” in another reading], endowed with the Holy Spirit, sworn to the Christian profession, were a virgin betrothed to Christ [Note: “You served as a virgin” in the manuscripts]. O, how I remember [Note: “O, I remember too much” in the manuscripts]! O, whom have I named! Certainly no longer the kind bridegroom of my virginity, but the terrifying judge of my impurity [Note: “How terrifying” in the manuscripts].

Alas, memory of lost delight! Why do you thus heap weight upon the burden of my present misery? What a miserable lot for a disgraceful person, for whom both good and evil alike become torment [Note: “Of disgraceful things, for whom” in the manuscripts]! The evil conscience torments me, and its sufferings, in which I fear that I will burn; the memory of a good conscience torments me, and of its rewards, which I know I have lost and will no longer recover.

Woe to the miserable loss! It is grievous to lose irrecoverably what ought to be preserved without end [Note: “Miserable to lose, grievous to lose” in the manuscripts]. Alas, the inconsolable loss of what is not only the loss of good things but also, in addition, the gain of torments!

O virginity, no longer my beloved but my lost possession; no longer my joy but my despair [Note: “But my despair” in the manuscripts], where have you gone? Into what foul, what bitter mire have you left me [Note: “Into the mire of the road you left me”; “into the mire of the road you left me” in manuscripts Vict. 3, Val-luc., and Flor.]?

O fornication, defiler of my mind, destroyer of my soul, from where did you steal upon me in my misery? From what a clean, what a joyful state did you cast me down? Here you burn me, O bitter grief, because that has been lost [Note: “That has been dismissed” in the manuscripts]; here you distress me, O grievous pain, and the fear of a worse pain, because this has been committed [Note: Some manuscripts read: “Pain and the fear of a greater pain, because this has been lost”; manuscript Corb. 160 reads: “Serious pain and fear, because that has been committed”]. Here is inconsolable loss [Note: “Incomparable” in manuscript Flor.]; here, intolerable torment. Woe from this side, and woe from that.

Thus, thus alike [Note: “But if alike” in the manuscripts], good and evil alike justly punish the wretched wrongdoer while he still lives. Deservedly, certainly deservedly. For you, my soul, faithless toward God, perjured against God, adulterous toward Christ, willingly descended miserably from the height of virginity [Note: “From the exalted state of virginity” in manuscript Thu.] into the abyss of fornication [Note: “Were lowered into” in manuscript Vict. 16, Val-luc., and Flor.].

You, once betrothed to the King of heaven, have ardently [Note: “Boldly” in the manuscripts] become the harlot of the torturer of Tartarus. Alas, rejected by God, cast to the devil—or rather, rejecting God and embracing the devil. O most wretched [Note: “O wretched and more than wretched” in manuscript Flor.] exchange!

Alas! From how exalted a place have you fallen, into what depth have you plunged! Woe! How kind a one have you despised, and with how evil a one have you joined yourself! What have you done, madness of the mind, senseless impurity, filthy wickedness—what have you done?

In heaven you abandoned your chaste love [Note: “Your love” in the manuscripts; “your lover” in manuscripts Vict. and Thu.], and into hell you followed your hateful corrupter; and in the abyss you prepared for yourself not a bridal chamber but a brothel. Astonishing horror—how perverse the will! Horrible marvel—how voluntary the perversity!

Whence, O God, can correction of such depravity come to me [Note: “Corruption of depravity?” in manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.; “correction of depravity” in manuscript Flor.; “reproof of depravity” in another reading]? Whence can satisfaction for such a great crime come to you, O God? Plunge yourself, wretched little man, into the dark and deep realm of boundless sorrow, you who willingly plunged yourself into the abyss of dreadful wickedness.

Bury yourself, unhappy one, beneath the weight of terrible pain [Note: “Bury yourself beneath the mass of wickedness” in manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor.], you who willingly fell into the mire of infernal foulness. Wrap yourself, criminal, in the dreadful darkness of inconsolable mourning [Note: “Sorrowful, in dreadful darkness” in the manuscripts; “sorrowful” in manuscripts Vict. 3 and Val-luc.], you who willingly rolled yourself into the chasm of such filthy luxury. Roll about in the whirlpool of bitterness, you who delighted in the mire of shamefulness.

Horrible terror, terrible pain, inconsolable grief: gather over me, rush upon me, overwhelm me, trouble me, wrap me, possess me [Note: “Destroy me” in the manuscripts]. It is just; it is just. With shameless boldness I despised you, and with stinking pleasure I provoked you—indeed, I provoked God, not you—and now, with miserable repentance, I desire you.

Torture the guilty one; avenge God [Note: “To avenge God” in the manuscripts]. Let the fornicator experience the torments of hell [Note: “Infernal torments” in manuscript Vict. 3; “torments of hell” in manuscripts Vict. 16 and Flor.] that he has deserved; let him taste beforehand what he has prepared; let him become accustomed to what he is to suffer.

Extend and prolong, immoderate sinner, your mournful repentance, you who prolonged the impurity of your crime so far. Turn over and over in the same whirlwind of bitterness, you who so often turned over and over in the same abyss [Note: “Vertigo” in manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.] of lust.

Comfort, security, joy—I do not want you; I reject you, unless forgiveness of sin brings you back. Stay far away, stay far away [Note: “Stay far away” in manuscripts Vict. 3 and Val-luc.] before death, if perhaps indulgence may recall you to me [Note: Manuscripts vary: “unless perhaps indulgence might recall you”; “if perhaps indulgence recalls you”].

Let continual bitter repentance be the companion of my life; let continual, insatiable pain be the torturer of my life [Note: “Unhealable pain, the torturer” in manuscripts Vict. 3, Val-luc., and Flor.]; let grief and bitter mourning be the tireless persecutors [Note: “Tribulations” in manuscript Flor.] of my youth and old age. Would that it were so! Would that it were so! I desire, pray, and long for it to be so.

For if I am not worthy to raise my eyes to heaven in prayer [Note: “To pray while raising them” in the manuscripts], certainly I am not unworthy to blind them even with weeping. If my mind is ashamed to pray because of the shame of conscience, it is fitting that it should be confounded by the whirlwind of mournful pain and sorrow. If it fears to be displayed before the sight of its God, it is just that it should have before its sight the torments of its crime.

Let my heart, therefore, think and think again what it has done and what it has deserved. Let my mind, I say, descend, descend [Note: “Before it descends” in the manuscripts] to the dark land covered by the shadow of death, and consider what awaits my criminal soul [Note: “Who await there” in the manuscripts]; let it attend and contemplate, see and be terrified.

What is this, O God? What is it that I perceive in the land of misery and darkness? Horror, horror. What is it that I behold, where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells? (Job 10:22.) Alas, a confusion of howlings, a tumult of weeping, a gnashing of teeth, a disordered multitude of groans. Woe, woe [Note: The manuscripts vary: “A confession of howling ones, a tumult of those gnashing with their teeth, a disordered multitude of those groaning, woe, woe”; “a confusion of howlings, a tumult of those gnashing with their teeth, a disordered multitude of groans, woe, woe”]. How many, how many, how many woes—woe, woe!

Sulfurous fire, Tartarean flame, and shadowy coils: with what terrifying roar I see you rolling about. Worms living in the fire [Note: One manuscript reads “rolling worms”; another, “rolling? worms”], whose wondrous eagerness to gnaw thus sets you aflame [Note: The manuscripts read variously “dreadful eagerness to return … approaches” and “wondrous eagerness to gnaw … sets aflame”]—you whom that fire of fires does not burn!

Demons, scorched and groaning with heat, gnashing their teeth in fury: why are you so cruel to those who roll about among you? O torments of every kind [Note: “O convenient torments” in the manuscripts], governed by justice, immoderate to endure—will no limit, no remedy, no end temper you [Note: “Moderate justice, immoderate to endure; will no end temper you?” in the manuscripts]?

Are these, great God, the things prepared for fornicators and for those who despise you, of whom I am one? I—I am indeed one of them.

My soul, be terrified; my mind, faint; my heart, be torn apart [Note: “Tear yourself apart” in manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.]. Where are you dragging me, exactors of my crime? Where are you thrusting me [Note: “Where are you handing me over?” in the manuscripts], my sin? Where are you handing me over, my God?

If I acted so as to become your guilty one, could I have acted so as not to be your creation? If I deprived myself of my chastity, could I have destroyed your mercy? Lord, Lord, if I committed the act by which you can condemn me, have you lost that by which you are accustomed to save? [Note: “If I lost” in the manuscripts.]

Do not, Lord, do not consider my evil in such a way that you forget your goodness [Note: Manuscript Vict. 16 reads “so that you do not forget”]. Where is it, O truthful God—where is it: “As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live”? (Ezekiel 33:11.)

Lord, who do not lie, what does “I do not desire the death of the sinner” mean, if you bury in hell the sinner who cries out to you? Is thrusting the sinner into Gehenna what “I do not desire the death of the sinner” means? Is this what “I desire the sinner to turn and live” means?

I am a sinner, Lord; I am a sinner. Therefore, if you do not desire the death of the sinner, what compels you to do what you do not desire—to hand me over to death? If you desire the sinner to turn and live, what prevents you from doing what you desire, turning me so that I may live? Does the enormity of my sin compel you to do what you do not desire and prevent you from doing what you desire, although you are omnipotent God?

Far be it from you, omnipotent God; far be it! Lord God [Note: “Far be it, my God. Far be it, Lord my God” in manuscript Flor.; “Far be it, omnipotent God; far be it, Lord God” in another manuscript], let the wickedness of a sinner who confesses and grieves not prevail against the sentence of the Almighty [Note: The manuscripts vary: “my God, so that it may prevail”; “my God. May it not prevail”; “may it not prevail”].

Remember, just, holy, and good God; remember that you are merciful, and that you are my creator and re-creator. Therefore, good Lord, do not remember your justice against your sinner, but remember your goodness toward your creature; do not remember wrath against the guilty, but remember mercy toward the miserable.

It is true that my conscience deserves condemnation and that my repentance is not sufficient for satisfaction, but it is certain that your mercy surpasses every offense. Spare me, therefore, good Lord, to whom salvation belongs and who do not desire the death of the sinner; spare my sinful soul.

For, terrified, it flees from your terrifying justice to your comforting mercy, so that since the reward of virginity lost is, alas, irrecoverable [Note: “Since virginity is corrupted, alas, irrecoverable”; “since virginity is corrupted, alas, irrecoverable” in manuscripts Vict. 3 and Val-luc.; “since virginity is corrupted, alas, irrecoverable” in another reading], at least the punishment of fornication may not be unavoidable for the penitent—for this is neither impossible to your omnipotence, nor inconsistent with your justice, nor unfamiliar to your mercy—since you are good and since your mercy is forever, you who are blessed throughout the ages. Amen.

# MEDITATION IV

[Note: It was collated with manuscripts Vict., KK. 16, Corb. 160, Flor., and Val-luc. The manuscripts title it “The Awakening of the Sinful Soul to Correct and Abandon Sins” (Vict. and Val-luc.); “On the Sinner: How He Should Awaken His Soul to Correct His Sins” (Corb.); and “On the Body: When He Should Awaken His Soul to Correct His Sins.”]

## How the sinner should awaken his soul to correct his sins

My soul, wretched and foul soul, carefully gather back inwardly to yourself all the senses of your body, and look more carefully and see how grievously you have been wounded and cast down within.

While the immense goodness of your Creator still grants you life, while his ineffable mercy patiently and with great gentleness awaits your correction and fitting satisfaction, do not be lazy or slow to heal your wounds, correct your sins, reconcile yourself to your offended Creator, and make all his saints favorable to yourself—saints whom, by offending their Creator and yours, their Lord and yours, you have made your adversaries [Note: The manuscripts read “to reconcile again”; manuscript Val-luc. reads “to make favorable again”].

If you had always remained upright and pure, just as your Creator made you upright and pure, and if you had clung unfailingly to his will, as you could have done had you wished, you would now be passing your present life joyfully and happily; and when it had passed and ended, with the help of him who created you, you would possess life and happiness without end.

But now, because you, wretched and miserable, set aside the will of your Creator [Note: The manuscripts add: “and unhappily and miserably clung to your carnal pleasures, if deliberately”] and unhappily and miserably clung to your carnal pleasures, if deliberately and with great diligence, neither flattering nor sparing yourself, you examine how deeply you are entangled in evils and iniquities, and, examining and repenting, resolve to return to satisfaction and amendment [Note: The manuscripts read “but deliberately”], first cast this out from your inner self—namely, the will to sin [Note: “Cast it out and expel it from your inner self, namely” in the manuscripts]—and embrace and do those things that you understand to please your Creator in every respect.

But perhaps, when you look upon the enormity of your crimes and despair of pardon and forgiveness because of the continual foulness of your sins, you say to yourself: “How can I now amend myself any further, since I have acted against God’s will for nearly my whole life? I am always intent upon every wickedness, every evil desire, and every evil deed [Col. 0730C], and I lie hardened in my sins like a stone which neither iron can cut nor fire soften.”  

Therefore, when I examine more carefully the justice of my Creator, and with no less diligence consider the evil deeds I have continually committed [Note: [Col. 0729D] “The evils which I have continually committed,” manuscripts; “the evil deeds which I have continually committed,” the edited text], I know that, since he will render to each according to his deeds, I shall receive the torments and punishments deserved by evil deeds. It is true what you say: God, the just Judge who loves equity, inflicts torments for evil deeds and sins. Yet, by that same justice with which he punishes those who persist in wickedness, he rewards with an eternal recompense those who turn back from evil and do good works [Note: [Col. 0729D] “Is rewarded,” manuscripts: “rewards,” in the edited text].

For this reason I warned you above to inspect more carefully all your inward parts, and the things you do before him [Note: [Col. 0729D] “The things you do before God,” manuscripts: “the things you do before him”], and to see with no less diligence what end each of them will reach [Col. 0730D] [Note: [Col. 0729D] “Are going to reach,” manuscripts; “will reach,” manuscript Flor.; “will reach” (singular), another Flor. reading]. And I believe that, if you do this constantly, and continually beat down the hardness of your heart with the recollection of these things as with iron hammers, then—unless you are insane—you will do those things from which you may receive happiness and joys [Note: [Col. 0731D] “You will receive joys,” manuscripts: “you may receive joys”], and you will abandon those things by which you deserved torments and sorrow.

For this reason [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Besides this,” manuscripts; “besides these things,” manuscript Val-luc.; “for this reason”], I warn you again and again to remember without interruption how sweet and good your Creator is toward you, how great his goodness has been: that, when you did not exist, he created you; and that he made you not an animal or an insensible creature, but a creature capable of understanding and loving him, and of possessing his eternity with him, eternally and happily [Note: [Col. 0731D] “quod non posses” (“that you could not”), manuscript Victor. 3; “quae eum posset” (“which could understand him”)]. He loved you so greatly that, although he knew you would do many things against his will, he did not refuse to create you, but willed that you should be made and exist; [Col. 0731B] and that he still endures you with such gentleness, as one who is pious and merciful, awaiting your amendment.

Your Creator waits—he waits, as I have said—for your correction, because he who was pleased to make you when you did not exist does not in any way ever desire to destroy you. Rather, he desires that you return to his most tender mercy and that, once purified and amended through true repentance, he restore to you the happiness of eternal life which you had lost through sin [Note: [Col. 0731D] “You had lost; he will restore,” manuscripts: “you had lost, that he might restore”].

Therefore think, and think again, of such great kindness on the part of your Creator toward you, and raise yourself, as is right, together with all your senses, toward his ineffable love. For his love [Note: [Col. 0731D] “But his love,” manuscripts: “for his love”] tolerates no foulness of vices and consents to no pleasure of carnal desires existing alongside it. Where his love dwells, there are perfect peace, perfect tranquility, and great ease [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Great happiness,” manuscripts: “great ease”] in doing and thinking all those things by which eternal happiness is acquired.

In all your actions and in all your thoughts, know [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Know in your actions,” manuscripts: “know in your actions and in all your thoughts”] for certain that two are present [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Always two,” some manuscripts; other manuscripts omit “always”]: one your friend, and the other your enemy. Your friend is your Creator, who rejoices in your good works; your enemy is the devil, who grieves over those same good works.

Conversely, the devil, always lying in wait for you, rejoices if he sees you doing evil deeds and devoting yourself to vain and foolish thoughts [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Vain thoughts,” manuscripts: “vain and foolish thoughts”], by which he can accuse you before the heavenly Judge, and, once accused and condemned, drag you with himself to destruction. The devil, always desirous of the destruction of the faithful, not only accuses them of the evil deeds they commit, but also attempts to stain, by accusing them unjustly [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Thoughts unjustly,” manuscripts: “even their good deeds and good thoughts, by accusing them unjustly”], their good deeds and good thoughts.

But against his subtle deceptions, and against his wiles, which are full of many deceits, be cautious; be watchful. Invoke your Creator and most sweet Lord [Col. 0732A], that he may not permit you to be led astray by the devil’s frauds and deceptions. Flee beneath the shadow of his wings from the face of the wicked who afflict you (Psalm 16:8), who strive to drag you, afflicted and overthrown, to death and destruction. Your Creator and your Lord is more compassionate and merciful than can be said or even imagined; therefore he destroys no one except through that person’s own great fault and great iniquity.

A father and mother according to the flesh usually have great compassion for those whom they have begotten. If they see them afflicted by some pain or bodily distress, they willingly spend themselves and their possessions, if necessity demands it, to restore their health [Note: [Col. 0731D] “But if they see any of them afflicted by some pain,” manuscripts: “and if they see them afflicted by some pain”]. Many animals, too, are often unafraid to face death for their offspring; in order that their young may escape death, they themselves incur it.

From where, then—from where comes that natural compassion in them, except from him who is the fountain of compassion, who does not desire anyone to perish and does not rejoice in the destruction of those who die? Our Creator, therefore, the fountain of compassion, the fountain of mercy, sweeter and more lovable than all else, when he sees us, his creatures, stained by some contagion of sin or even wounded almost to death by great and numerous crimes, applies far greater care to us—to curing our sins, healing our weakness, cleansing the leprosy and filth of our crimes, and purifying the vanities and dust of our thoughts—than a human father or an animal applies to caring for his children or young.

Nor is it enough for him merely to heal our weakness and then dismiss us. Once healed, he makes us most intimate with himself and afterward tenderly embraces us as his dearest children. Embracing and kissing us, he soothes and consoles us for every sickness and leprosy of sin into which we have fallen through folly; and he completely forgets all the injuries we have inflicted upon him by scorning him in his commandments.

[211] He honors us in the present life and crowns us in the future; he makes us kings and makes our soul a queen. Therefore, having already made us kings, he admonishes us in the Psalm: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10). We are truly kings if we rule our disordered impulses and recall them to reason and to the will of our Creator.

We are instructed when we judge the earth—that is, when we see that our heart desires earthly things, and compel it to despise earthly things and love heavenly things [Col. 0732D] [Note: [Col. 0731D] “If it desires the earth,” manuscripts, Victor. and Val-luc.: “if it desires earthly things”]. Our soul becomes a queen because, clothed in various garments—that is, adorned with various gifts of virtue—it is joined, through enduring thought, action, and conduct, while it dwells on earth, to Christ its Bridegroom, who is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0731D] “But the soul becomes a queen,” manuscripts, Victor. and Val-luc.; “the soul becomes a queen” in the edited text; “which is adorned with various…” manuscripts, Victor. 3 and Val-luc.: “because, adorned with various…”].

It was not enough for our Creator to create us, govern us once created, and send his angels to defend us whenever we needed them. He himself, taking our form and assuming our nature, in compassion for his creature, descended to us; he carefully examined our wounds and death, and, examining them, handled and touched them. Moved by compassion for the misery he saw us enduring, he groaned in sympathy. After this, making a kind of plaster from the very flesh he had assumed for us and applying it to our pains, he healed our entire infirmity. And, to show in this way how greatly he loved us, he gave us for food the very flesh which he had assumed for us; and even now he does not cease to minister it in the sacrifice of his altar [Col. 0733B].

But you, my soul, enlivened and consoled by the sweet remembrance of all these things, pray to your Lord, pray to your Creator, invoke all his saints, that they may come to your aid. Thus, helped and consoled through their intercession, may he who made you grant you to live in the present conduct of your life in such a way that you may cleanse your iniquities through true repentance and confession, so that, when your temporal course is finished, you may deserve to ascend to eternal joys—through him who lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## MEDITATION V

[Note: [Col. 0733D] Compared with manuscripts Victor. KK. 16, Corb. 160, Val-luc., and Floriacensis. It is not found in the other manuscripts. “Whence the soul lives … they leave the body,” manuscripts; “whence the soul may live … they depart from the body,” manuscript Val-luc. “Prayer: Whence the soul may live, and whence the flesh may live; and concerning the glory of the good soul and the unhappiness of the evil soul when they leave the body.”]

### Whence the soul lives and whence the flesh lives; and concerning the glory of the good soul and the unhappiness of the evil soul when they leave the body

While the soul remains in the body, a human being lives according to the flesh. When the soul abandons the flesh, the person dies according to that same flesh [Note: [Col. 0733D] “When it abandons the flesh, it dies,” manuscript Victor.; “when it abandons the flesh, it dies”]. But just as the soul gives life to the flesh while it remains in the flesh, so the flesh gives life to the soul while that flesh performs works of righteousness.

Thus, in this way, they seem to give life to one another: the soul to the flesh, and the flesh to the soul. And so, while the flesh works together with the soul, they acquire for one another the life of perpetual life. Yet the soul, once separated from the flesh, immediately receives the life which the flesh, together with the soul, will receive at the resurrection on the last day.

Therefore, my soul and my flesh, exult in the living God (Psalm 83:3) [Note: [Col. 0733D] “Exulting in,” manuscripts: “exult in”]; draw near to God your Creator; draw near and be enlightened (Psalm 33:6); and do no longer do anything for which you should be ashamed. Rather, always strive to do those things in which you may rejoice forever [Note: [Col. 0733D] “Forever,” manuscripts: “for eternity”].

I exhort you; I warn you: do not receive the grace of God at present in vain (2 Corinthians 6:1) [Col. 0734A]. Although now he patiently endures many things being done by you which greatly displease him, do not think that he will always endure them in this way [Note: [Col. 0733D] Some manuscripts omit “endure”]. For without doubt he is a patient recompensor and a diligent examiner of heart and kidneys.

Now he endures many things, awaiting our correction, like the gentlest of beings [Note: [Col. 0733D] “Awaiting correction, like…” manuscripts: “awaiting our correction”]. But if we do not correct ourselves now, he will condemn us as the most just of judges. And he who is now so sweet toward us that he calls us his brothers and friends will then, at the final examination, regard us as people unknown to him [Note: [Col. 0733D] Manuscripts Victor., Val-luc., and Flor.: “not knowing us”] and not known to him through good works—as his enemies.

My soul and my flesh, wake up at last, always and everywhere thinking about your final destiny. Perhaps, if you do this, you will not easily sin. If you do now as I warn you, be secure; for when many will mourn—those who now laugh and rejoice miserably—you will exult and rejoice with indescribable joy.

Attend carefully to your works [Note: [Col. 0733D] Manuscripts omit “now”]. If they are upright and pleasing to God, rejoice; if they are crooked and not accepted by God, correct them quickly. Do not let your eyes sleep; do not let your eyelids slumber. The pit of destruction is open. The one who does not now guard himself carefully slips into it easily. Sin and iniquity, folly and vanity, easily drive one into it now; once immersed there, one does not rise again forever.

Just as eternal destruction is open to those who always do wicked and evil things [Note: [Col. 0733D] Manuscripts: “wicked and evil things”], so the entrance to paradise is open to the good and to those who persevere in good works. Once admitted there, a person will remain forever and eternally rejoicing and happy. Thus good works raise the good person upward to the heights [Col. 0734C] [Note: [Col. 0733D] Manuscript Victor. 3 omits “to the heights”], while evil works plunge the evil person downward into the depths.

But now let us carefully see, if we can, in what order good works lead the soul of one who has lived well into heaven, and evil works drag the sinner’s soul into hell.

As soon as the pure soul departs from the body, it sees all its works. And because it sees all of them as good, it rejoices with indescribable joy. Immediately the angel receives it—the angel who held back its eyes so that it would not see vanity [Note: [Col. 0733D] Manuscripts: “so that they would not see vanity”]. The one who stopped up its ears so that it would not hear iniquity [Note: [Col. 0733D] Manuscripts: “so that they would not hear”] embraces it; the one who guarded its mouth so that it would not speak falsehood protects it; the one who protected it from sinning through the sense of smell or touch rejoices with it. Thus, glad and cheerful, he surrounds it on every side and places it before the throne of divine glory, where it may rejoice without end.

Other angels and other saints who stand there before the presence of the divine majesty come to meet it. Recognizing it as their companion and friend through its good works, they joyfully welcome it in the arms of the purest charity. Speaking to it in this manner, they display to it, as it were, the individual joys of all who dwell there:

“Behold, our friend; behold, our companion. Because you served God faithfully and labored bravely by carrying out his commandments, at last rest from your labor, and from now until eternity enjoy everlasting joys with us.”

But, on the other hand, when the sinner’s soul is compelled to leave the body, the angels of Satan immediately receive it. Binding it tightly with fiery chains and driving it with still greater force from every side toward the torments of hell, they drag it away to the place where Satan himself lies plunged downward into the depths.

There are weeping and the gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12); there are fire, the snare, and the spirit of storms as the portion of the sinners’ cup (Psalm 10:7) [Col. 0735B]. Then Satan himself seizes it and spits upon it a fire full of stench [Note: [Col. 0735D] Manuscripts: “a stench-filled fire upon it”; “full” in the edited text]. He orders his ministers to constrict it on every side and, once constricted, to throw it into the torments themselves. There it is tormented with them without end and dies ceaselessly amid those pains without end.

Then the unhappy soul, tormented in those punishments and hemmed in on every side by those infernal furies, finally comes to itself. Seeing all the evils it has committed, it cries out in misery:

“Alas, wretched me, wretched me! Why did I ever come into life? Wretched me, who am tortured on every side by so many kinds of torment! Worms, worms, who gnaw me so cruelly, spare me, I beg you; spare me, wretched as I am, while I suffer so many other monstrous torments. Alas, wretched me, wretched me!” [Note: [Col. 0735D] Manuscripts: “Wretched me, wretched me, wretched me, and I desire to die”; “wretched me, wretched me, and I desire to die”].

[212] “I desire to die, and yet, though dying, I cannot die. Now, wretched as I am, I receive whatever I sinned through sight, through taste, through hearing, through smell, and through touch.”

Yet it does no good to the unhappy soul, suffering such misery, repenting so late, and crying out so wretchedly, that it is then afflicted by such great sorrow. Rather, what it earned while it was alive, it now receives amid the very pains of hell, wretched and sinful as it is.

Behold, my soul and my flesh, attend carefully. While attending, judge with true judgment, and discern what is better and more useful to follow: to do good and receive good, or to do evil and receive evil. Unless you are of unsound mind, you will answer nothing other than: “To do good and possess good” [Note: [Col. 0735D] “bene facere et bonum habere” (“to do good and possess good”), manuscripts Victor.; “bonum facere et bonum habere” (“to do what is good and possess good”), manuscript Corb.; “bona facere et bona habere” (“to do good things and possess good things”)].

Therefore do good, so that you may possess that good from which every good comes—the good of every good—which can be nothing other than good. Our Creator has given us many good things and placed many things under our power. But no good is so precious, so desirable to every wise person, as that good to which no evil can approach.

That good is our Creator himself, who is never anything but good. If, by his grace bestowing it, you are able to possess this good, you will possess all other good things in him. But if you possess other good things and do not possess him, you labor in vain; and, foolishly following the wind, you will find at the end not truth but vanity.

The glory of the present life, as you see if you consider it rightly, is like a bladder filled with air. While it is held full in the hands, it appears beautiful and bright. But if by chance the smallest puncture is made in it, there remains in the hands not brightness but emptiness and wind.

Take heed, therefore, and, as I warned you at the beginning of this meditation, always think about your final destiny. For by thinking in this way, and always fearing your departure, you will not easily sin [Note: [Col. 0735D] Manuscript: “you will not sin easily”]. And thus, living to the very end, when temporal joy is finished—the joy which, while you feared it in this way, flew around your eyes like wind—you will find not vanity but the truth, which is Christ. May he who created you lead you to that truth. Amen.

## MEDITATION VI

[Note: [Col. 0735D] Compared with manuscripts Victor. KK. 16, Corb. 160, and Val-luc. “To strengthen the spirit, so that we may not despair,” manuscripts Victor. and Val-luc.; “Prayer: that we may not despair, because if we do true…” in the edited texts; manuscript Corb.: “Consideration of sins, whence fear arises; and concerning the never-failing fountain of mercy.”]

### To strengthen the spirit, so that we may not despair; for if we do true repentance, we shall without doubt find true mercy for all our sins

When I look back upon the sins I have committed [Note: [Col. 0735D] “Which I have committed,” manuscript Victor.; “which I have committed,” manuscripts Corb. and Val-luc.], and understand the punishments and torments I must suffer for them, I am not a little afraid [Col. 0736C]. Therefore, very anxious and very fearful for my destruction, I search to see whether I may find consolation somewhere [Note: [Col. 0735D] Manuscripts Victor. and Val-luc.: “I shall find”; manuscript Corb.: “I might find”; another manuscript: “to find”].

But alas, wretched that I am, I find none; for I am certain that I have offended not only my Creator but also him and every creature of his [Note: [Col. 0735D] Manuscripts: “I am certain that I have offended him”; “I am certain that I have been offensive”]. My Creator, therefore, together with all his creation, gravely offended by my sins, condemns me. My conscience, certain of its evil deeds, accuses me on every side. And so I find no consolation, nor do I easily think that I can obtain it from anyone [Note: [Col. 0735D] One manuscript: “nor from another”; printed reading: “nor from anyone”].

What, then, shall I do? Where shall I turn, thus desolate, thus entangled in the wickedness of my sins? If I wish to return to him who made me upright, and beg his ineffable compassion to have mercy on me, I am very much afraid that, because of such presumption, I may rather move him to anger against me, and that for this reason he may punish more severely the crimes by which I was not afraid to provoke his gentleness.

What, then? Shall I remain, as one despairing, without counsel and without help? My Creator still permits me to live. He still does not cease to provide me with the things necessary to sustain this life. And, as I discover by the facts themselves, my sins cannot overcome his goodness, so that he should now wish, as I have deserved, to put me to shame and destroy me utterly. It is therefore most certain that he is compassionate toward me, since he bestows such great blessings upon me and still does not seek to avenge himself upon me for my iniquities.

I have heard—and, as those who have experienced it themselves testify, what I heard is true—that the fountain of mercy itself, which began to flow from the beginning of the world, still flows.

He was, as they say, exceedingly merciful and compassionate toward our first parent Adam when he committed that sin concerning the forbidden fruit. He did not immediately condemn him to eternal destruction, as he had deserved, [Col. 0737B] but patiently awaited his amendment and mercifully helped him to return to the grace of the one whom he had offended.

For this purpose he sent to him, and often to all those who sprang from him, his angels, warning them to return and do penance for their iniquities, because he would still gladly receive them if they repented of their sins with all their heart. But they, persisting in their sins and scorning his warnings, added sin to sin. Becoming, as it were, insane and abominable in their iniquities, although they had been made honorable through the likeness of God, they began against nature to imitate the ways of beasts.

Moreover, he sent patriarchs and prophets. Yet even then they were unwilling to abandon their crooked and perverse ways. Some of those who gave them warnings of salvation they killed; others they tortured with various and unheard-of torments.

Nevertheless, he sometimes chastised them, like a merciful father—not as one angered by their evil deeds and seeking vengeance for the insults they inflicted upon him, but so that, corrected, they might return to the mercy of the one who in no way desires the destruction of those whom he created by his goodness.

But when, though visited by him repeatedly through warnings and correction, they still did not return, the fountain of compassion could no longer restrain itself. Descending from the bosom of the Father, assuming true humanity and the likeness of sinners, he began gently to warn them to do saving penance for their sins at that time and to recognize that he was the Son of God [Col. 0737D].

For their salvation he had come, and for this reason they should not despair. Rather, they should most certainly believe that they would still obtain forgiveness for all their sins, if only they abandoned them and did penance [Note: [Col. 0737D] Manuscripts: “but only if…”; printed reading: “if only…”]. For no sin is so serious that it cannot be abolished through repentance, so completely that not even the devil himself could thereafter recall it.

When sinners saw such sweetness in their Creator [Col. 0738A], they too began eagerly to run to the fountain of mercy, to the fountain of compassion, and to wash their sins in it. The fountain of compassion himself also began to eat with sinners and to disclose to them the sacraments of holy confession, through which every burden of sin is lightened; for in true confession every stain of transgression is cleansed.

After this, when the time approached in which he was to suffer for the redemption of sinners, the Jews, from whose lineage he was descended according to the flesh, driven by envy, crucified him because he was compassionate and merciful. Yet even in death he did not forget his compassion. He prayed to his Father for his executioners, asking him to forgive them this sin: “For they do not know what they are doing,” he said (Luke 23:34) [Col. 0738B].

[213] The Lord’s most sweet compassion excuses them. He does not desire the death of the sinner, but that the sinner should turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Whose heart, then, is so hard and so stony that such gentleness on the part of our Creator could not soften it?

Although his creature, whom he had created from nothing in his own image and likeness [Note: [Col. 0737D] Manuscripts: “in his own likeness”; printed text: “in his own image and likeness”], dishonored him in many ways, he did not avenge himself. Rather, though dishonored and provoked by their many evil deeds, he endured patiently and gently warned them to return to him without hesitation.

Therefore our pious and sweet Lord Jesus Christ, as it is said through the prophet, does not desire the death of the sinner, but that the sinner should abandon his evil ways (Ezekiel 18:23), and, doing penance for his iniquities, return to the grace of his Creator.

How merciful he also is toward the sinful soul, he says through another prophet, exhorting it to return to him even after sin and to find mercy:

“You have committed fornication with many lovers” (Jeremiah 31:1)—that is, “You who promised me faith in baptism, by defiling your chastity with many lovers you violated it” [Note: [Col. 0737D] One manuscript omits “by defiling it with many lovers”]. “Nevertheless, do penance, return to me, and I will receive you.”

Let no sinner, therefore, despair. When one who has committed fornication with many lovers is received, the fountain of compassion and mercy, Jesus Christ, is exhausted by no one’s iniquities and polluted by no one’s crimes [Note: [Col. 0737D] Manuscripts: “by no iniquities … by no crimes”; edited text: “by no one’s iniquities … by no one’s crimes”]. Rather, always pure and overflowing with the sweetness of grace, he receives all the weak and sinful who return to him and washes them, whatever sins may stain them.

And so that all sinners and wicked people may be certain that they receive forgiveness of their sins if they take care to abandon those sins and do penance, the fountain of compassion himself, because of the love he had for them [Note: [Col. 0737D] Manuscripts: “Therefore us”; printed text: “the love he had for them”], allowed the same flesh which he had assumed for them, as I explained above, to be crucified. Thus those who were dead through sins, and could not otherwise return to life unless redeemed by the price of his blood, should in no way despair [Note: [Col. 0737D] Manuscripts: “should not have despaired”; printed text: “should in no way despair”], seeing the price that was given for their sins [Col. 0739A] [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscripts Victor. 3 and Val-luc.: “which was to be given”; manuscript Corb.: “which was to be given”; printed text: “which was given”].

Since, then, I see such great compassion in my Lord Jesus Christ, and so many sinners and wicked people running to the fountain of compassion, with no one excluded and all received, should I alone despair, thinking that the fountain of compassion, which washes others, cannot wash away my sins?

I know—yes, I know with certainty, and truly believe—that he who washes others can also wash me and, if he wills, because he is all-powerful, forgive me all my sins.

But there is a great difference between sinner and sinner—that is, between the one who sins more and the one who sins less. Therefore, considering how greatly I have sinned and by how many iniquities my unhappy soul has been polluted, I understand that I am not merely equal to other sinners, but more than any other sinner [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscripts: “more than any other”; printed text: “more than any sinner”], a sinner beyond all sinners [Col. 0739B].

Many have sinned and then stopped. Some, although they sinned frequently, nevertheless at some point put an end to their wickedness. Others, although they did many evil things, did not fail to do many good things as well. By these they either earned the complete remission of those evils or acquired for themselves a more tolerable punishment in Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscript: “that they might abandon them”; manuscript Victor. 3: “that they might abandon them”; printed text: “that those evils might be forgiven”].

But I, wretched as I am, more wretched than all the wretched and a sinner and miserable beyond all sinners, understood and knew to what destruction sin and the delight of sin were dragging me, yet I never took care to cease from sins and evil deeds. I continually added sin to sin and, thus, willingly and knowingly plunged myself wholly into the destruction of sin. Unless the Lord’s immeasurable goodness had still endured me, I ought long ago to have been devoured by Gehenna itself.

How, then, shall I, who have lived in this way, who have committed such great evils, who have entangled myself in such great iniquities, dare to run with other sinners who have not committed such great evils to the fountain of mercy? I fear that, because of the stench of my crimes, he may be unwilling to wash me as he washes other sinners, whose stench is more tolerable [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscripts: “Because of the stench of my crimes, may he not wish…”; printed text: “because of the stench of my crimes, he may not wish…”].

Help, therefore, Lord Jesus Christ; help your creature. Though you see me buried beneath the enormity of my sins, nevertheless, seeing that I was created by you, help me not to despair. For, as we believe, no enormity of crimes can overcome you, provided only that the sinner does not despair of your mercy.

Permit me, therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, permit me to contemplate your ineffable compassion and to proclaim how sweet and good you are toward sinners and the wretched. I said this above as well, but it greatly delights me, whenever a suitable occasion presents itself, to remember how great is the grace of your sweetness toward sinners.

For the love and redemption of sinners—not only of those who sin less or more, but also of those who sin beyond measure, provided only that they repent—you descended from the bosom of the Father, entered the Virgin’s womb [Col. 0740A], assumed true flesh from her, lived in the world, called all sinners to repentance, and finally endured the cross for them. Thus, having died according to the flesh, you restored to them the life which they had justly lost on account of their sins.

Therefore, when I look upon the evil deeds I have committed, if you wish to judge me according to what I deserve, I am certain of my destruction. But when I look upon your death, which you suffered for the redemption of sinners, I do not despair of your mercy [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscripts: “And therefore”; printed text: “therefore”].

That thief who was crucified with you for his crimes remained in sins until the very departure of his soul [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscript Victor. 3: “until the sobbing of his soul”; printed text: “until the departure of his soul”]. Yet, in the very hour of his expiration, because he confessed his evils and acknowledged his guilt, he found mercy and was with you that same day in paradise (Luke 23:43).

Seeing that you died for the redemption of sinners; seeing your hands and feet pierced with nails, your side opened by the soldier’s lance, and a stream of blood and water flowing from that same side, should I despair?

There is only one thing you desire, without which no sinner can be saved: namely, that we repent of our evils and take care to amend them as far as we can. If we do this, we are secure [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscript Val-luc.: “If we do this, let us be secure”; printed text: “if we do this, we are secure”]. For if the last day finds us acting in this way—and we have the example of the thief, who deserved to be saved in his final hour—we can, trusting in the ineffable compassion of our Lord Jesus Christ, fear the accusation of the enemy either little or not at all.

Therefore, keeping before our eyes the price of our redemption, namely the death and blood of our Redeemer, which was poured out for the remission of our sins [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscripts: “was made”; printed text: “was poured out”], and also keeping before us the example of the thief and of many who were entangled in many great sins, whom Jesus Christ, the fountain of compassion, mercifully absolved, let us not despair. Rather, let us run confidently to that same fountain of compassion for the forgiveness of sins. In it we already see and recognize so many great sinners washed [Note: [Col. 0739D] Manuscripts: “absolved”; printed text: “washed”], and let us be certain that we too shall be washed by the same fountain of mercy, if we abstain from our wickedness and sins and thereafter take care, as far as we can, to do good.

Yet we cannot abstain from evil and do good by our own strength without his help. Let us therefore implore his ineffable mercy. He took care to create us when we did not exist; may he grant us to amend our sins in this life, before we depart from it, and thus cleanse them through continual compunction, so that, when this life is ended, we may be able to reach him by a straight course, with no impediment, and be joined with him in perpetual glory, together with the angelic choirs and all the saints who already enjoy that glory, rejoicing without end.

[Col. 0741A]

## MEDITATION VII

[Note: [Col. 0741C] Compared with the manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai and with the *Book on Contrition of Heart* in the Appendix to Saint Augustine, vol. IX. “That nothing is stable in the world,” manuscript; “Concerning the dangers of this life,” another manuscript.]

# I. That Nothing in the World Is Stable

## 214. Nothing Is More Certain Than Death, Nothing More Uncertain Than the Hour of Death

[Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript omits these words. They were doubtless the title of the Meditation.]

Let us consider, then [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript omits “then”], how brief our life is, how slippery the way, how certain death, and how uncertain the hour of death. Let us consider how many bitter things are mingled with whatever sweetness or pleasure in the journey of this life plays before us by its passing. How deceptive and suspect, how unstable and transitory is whatever the love of this world produces [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “whatever life has produced”; the edition of Saint Augustine reads “whatever life disturbs,” while the present text reads “whatever the love of this world produces”]; whatever temporal appearance or beauty promises; whatever the pleasure of the flesh extends before us.

Let us also consider what sweetness or delight, serenity and loveliness belong to the heavenly homeland; and let us weigh from where we have fallen and where we lie, what we have lost [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads: “Whatever appearance promises is deceptive and all is vanity; let us also consider what sweetness, delight, serenity, and loveliness belong to the heavenly homeland; and let us attend to where we have fallen, where we lie, and what we have lost.” The edition of Saint Augustine reads: “Whatever appearance promises; whatever the hope promises; whatever the pleasure of the flesh extends before us. Let us consider and weigh where we have fallen, where we lie, and what we have lost.”]; and what we have found, so that from both we may understand [Col. 0741B] how much we ought to mourn in this [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript and the edition of Saint Augustine read “how much there is in this,” rather than “how much we ought to mourn in this”] exile.

Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiasticus 1:18), because the more a person understands the evils of his soul [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript and the edition of Saint Augustine read “his evils”], the more he sighs and groans.
