Meditation indeed produces knowledge, knowledge produces compunction, compunction commends devotion, and devotion commends prayer. Through constant meditation a person is enlightened unto knowledge of himself. In compunction, through consideration [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscripts read “and through consideration”] of his evils, the heart is touched with deep [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “with inward pain”; the edition of Saint Augustine reads “with intense pain”] sorrow.

## II. On the Many Benefits of God

Miserable man that I am [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “Therefore miserable man”; the edition of Saint Augustine reads “O miserable man”], how greatly ought I to love my Lord [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript and the edition of Saint Augustine read “my Jesus Christ, who”], who made me when I did not exist and redeemed me when I had perished. I did not exist, and he made me from nothing. Among all the other creatures lacking reason, he did not make me—that is, not a tree, not a bird, not one of the animals—but he willed me to be human. He gave me life [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript and the edition of Saint Augustine read “gave me the ability to live”], sensation, and movement [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “and discernment”]; I had perished, and he descended to the mortal; the immortal assumed mortality [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads: “He had perished, and the immortal descended to the mortal and assumed mortality”], endured suffering, conquered death, and thus restored me [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “restored me to life”; the edition of Saint Augustine omits “restored me” and reads “to life”].

Thus, thus, his grace [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “May his grace thus be”] and his mercy have always gone before me [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript and the edition of Saint Augustine read “his mercy went before me”]; my liberator also delivered me from many dangers [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript and the edition of Saint Augustine read “and my Lord Jesus Christ,” which the present text omits]. When I was wandering, he led me back [Note: [Col. 0741C] Saint Augustine reads “he rebuked me”]; when I was ignorant, he taught me; when I was sinning, he rebuked me; when I was sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript and the edition of Saint Augustine read “when I was sad”], he comforted me; when I was despairing, he strengthened me; when I fell, he raised me up; when I stood, he upheld me; when I went, he guided me; when I came to him, he received me.

These and many other things my Lord Jesus Christ did for me [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “my God did for me”], and for these it will always be sweet for me to give thanks [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript reads “It is always sweet for me to give thanks”; the edition of Saint Augustine reads “It will always be sweet for me to speak, always to think, always to give thanks”], so that for all his benefits I may be able to love him and always praise him. For all these things I have nothing to repay him except to love him with all my heart. Nothing better or more fitting than love has been given [Note: [Col. 0741C] The manuscript of Tournai ends here; the remainder has been restored from the Appendix to Saint Augustine].

## III. Here the Sinner Rebukes Himself for Ingratitude toward the Divine Benefits

Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, [Col. 0742B] Father of mercies, would I dare to come and appear before your saints, most unhappy and most wretched, so ungrateful for so many and such great benefits, so shameless and detestable an abuser of your gifts? I who so often and for so long was not afraid to attack you with those very benefits of yours; who so often and for so long was not ashamed to serve as a soldier for the devil against you with your pay; who was not afraid to turn your very gifts into diabolical weapons; who presumed to abuse myself so abominably, and dared to present myself as a servant to the devil and to make my members his, with which I attacked you, their Creator, Maker, and Giver.

Am I not, Lord my God, the one who so often offered myself as a sharp sword to the ungrateful devil, for devouring souls? How often did I arm myself against you for another’s death? How often did I present my tongue as a bow of falsehood, when I shot arrows of detraction and flattery at others? I am not able, most merciful and sweetest Father, to enumerate the wicked abuses of my members, by which I both armed the devil and attacked you, most kind and most gracious.

## IV. Recognition of Sin

I am that utterly senseless man whom you created from nothing, whom you chose from the mass of sin and perdition to be a son of your grace, and whom you adopted as a coheir with your most beloved only-begotten Son, our God and Lord Jesus Christ. You filled me with the honor and glory of your kingdom and with such abundant and undeserved grace. Yet I forgot the abundance of this great sweetness of yours; and, seeing so many good things entrusted to me by you, I despised the honor of the heavenly kingdom and your glory, turned myself into an illegitimate and degenerate son, and surrendered myself to the devil to be dragged through the dungheaps of lust and the thorny thickets of greed, to be battered amid the scandals, waves, and storms of pride.

I am that blind merchant who, with the most precious riches of your talents, miserably purchased such poverty, nakedness, and eternal sighs: with the dungheap of lust and the thorns of riches, the most delightful and sweetest peace; with the storm of pride, the safest harbor; with the darkness of eternity, eternal light; with eternal pains, eternal joys; with eternal disgrace, eternal glory; and with diabolical servitude, your kingdom.

I am that utterly feeble man who exposed myself, like a target, to be pierced by the arrows of sins and torn by wounds. I am that man who, like a corpse to be cut apart and mangled by infernal dogs and all unclean birds, cast out from your holy city—which is the city of your holy friends—and from the holy, most delightful fellowship of the heavenly holy spirits, surrendered myself to be eaten by the worms of vices.

How abominable I appear before your holy eyes: unclean and soiled with the foulest and most horrible filth of lust, half-burned by the fire of anger and greed, my members infested with the worms of hatred and envy, swollen with the wind of pride, wholly monstrous, ulcerated, and pierced through, sealed with the diabolical marks of so many and such great sins and shameful acts.

I know, merciful Lord, that you can rightly and most justly deny me and refuse to acknowledge me—not only as your son, but even as your creature—insofar as I am such a one. For that dreadful and monstrous appearance of every kind of shame is not the work of your creation or re-creation; this abomination is not your image and fitting likeness. You created me otherwise. Truly this likeness of diabolical shame shows me [Col. 0743D] to have been the devil’s son and an heir of unbelieving torments until now.

This is the bargain and exchange: blind and utterly senseless, I exchanged the glory and honor of your likeness for the most abominable and worthless filth.

It was not for this reason, holy Father, that you entrusted those precious talents of yours to me: that I might make you receive this horrible abomination as interest. It was not for this reason that you sowed so many and such great benefits in me: that you might gather from me the stench, thorns, and thistles of sins. It was not for this reason that you filled and enriched me with so many and such great benefits: that I might turn them against you. It was not the intention of your kindness to arm me against you, nor to arm diabolical power [Col. 0744A] with your gifts.

Behold, I am covered with so many wounds, yet I am tortured by no sense of pain. Pierced through by so many and such great wounds, I do not suffer. I see myself blind, since I am not ashamed of so many and such great disgraces and of my nakedness.

Truly I am insensible and dull of heart, since I do not grieve over my many and such great losses and cannot mourn my death. Truly I have been hardened with a heart of stone, since I do not even fear the eternal punishments that threaten me. Truly I have a heart frozen altogether, which the fires of the benefits brought near to me cannot warm with love for the most merciful Father. Truly I rebuke myself abundantly, yet neither the trumpet of preaching nor the thunder of your threats is sufficient to rouse me.

Where is the piercing pain, the pain of compunction, [Col. 0744B] with which I ought to crush and destroy all that diabolical hardness and break into pieces the entire stone of that hardness and obstinacy? Where is, my God, that shame with which I ought to be confounded before your eyes and before the whole heavenly court? Where is that fear of your vengeance with which I ought to tremble entirely before your presence? Where is that love and desire for recovering your peace, love, and grace, with which I ought to burn? Where is that torrent of tears with which I ought to wipe away my filth before you? Where is the devotion of prayer by which I ought to make you favorable and propitious toward me?

Where shall I turn, merciful and compassionate Father, when I offer your majesty nothing worthy of the regard of your mercy? Where shall I flee, most loving Father, when I appear before the presence of your saints and the armies of the heavenly holy hosts empty of every good and even full of every evil?

I know, Lord God, ruler of my life, that every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father and fountain of lights (James 1:17). I know that I can offer you nothing acceptable and pleasing unless I have first drawn it from the fountain of your goodness—and this, certainly, with you enlightening and teaching me. I know that this pledge of your mercy goes before me.

I know, sweetest Father, that just as I cannot seize or take away your good things from you by any fraud, so also I cannot obtain by any merits of mine all the things by which I may return to you and please you. For what can be owed to my merits [Col. 0744D] except the punishment of eternal death? I know that it lies in your holy good pleasure either to destroy me according to the multitude of my disgraces, crimes, negligences, and omissions, or to reform me and make me acceptable to you according to the immeasurable riches of your mercy—you who alone are the reformer of the creature whom you alone formed.

Now, merciful Father, I flee to you, knowing that I have no flight from you except to you. Who can free me from your hands except you alone? Your mercy can free me—the mercy which by so many and such great iniquities I have not only failed to merit but have even attacked—from your most just anger, which I, most wretched and most ungrateful [Col. 0745A], have provoked.

Therefore deign to receive me, Lord, returning to you. I beseech you, turn your holy eyes away from my ingratitude and filth. Look, I beg you, upon yourself, to whom no one ever prays without hope of pardon. In yourself you will find the reason and cause to pity me, according to the abundance of your sweetness and the immensity of your mercy. Do not, I beg you, look upon me, because you will find in me nothing except reasons for anger—or someone most deserving of eternal death.

Turn away, I beg you, Lord, your holy eyes from the sight of my disgraces and abominations. If I myself clearly and fully saw and perceived them, I could not endure them because of the excess of horror; rather, I would loathe and flee from myself. Turn away, I beg you, your nostrils from my stench [Col. 0745B], and turn them toward yourself.

I know, Lord of mercy, that your holy eyes are pure and that they cannot look upon the horror of my deformity unless you give me the good things by which I may please you. I know that your whole heavenly court turns away its eyes and closes its ears, unable to endure my abominations. But you, merciful Father, turn toward that fountain of mercy whose mercy has neither number nor end, and look upon me, your creature, with a compassionate and serene face. I am your creature, Lord, and the work of your hands.

Reform, then, I beg you, what you have made in me, and destroy what I have made in myself against your commandments. Destroy, then, what you hate in me and what you certainly did not make, but I, miserable man, did. Reform and restore what you yourself made and formed. For this is yours, Lord my God: to hate what cannot be. You hate none of the things that you have made (Wisdom 11:25). Destroy in me what is mine, what you certainly did not make—that is, the shamefulness of my abominations. Do not destroy me. Destroy this, merciful and compassionate Lord; for you hate this, and you have granted me to begin hating what you hate.

# Meditation VIII. The Penitent’s Elevation to the Father

Look, I beg you, holy Father, almighty eternal God, upon that overflowing abyss of your mercy, through which, like a flood of cleansing, the most precious and life-giving blood of your most beloved only-begotten Son overflowed for the cleansing of the world; by his death your goodness was pleased also to give us life and wash us in his blood. You also gave your most beloved Son to the world as the shield of your good will (Psalm 5:13), so that they might protect themselves from your anger, and so that he himself, setting the shield of his righteousness against your most just anger, might receive the death which they feared.

There you deigned to show how much good you desired for us, when you deigned to set your most beloved Son before your anger like a shield. And it pleased your mercy that he should receive both your anger and our death—the anger and death which we had deserved. Your only-begotten Son alone bore our death.

Remember your compassion, Lord, and your mercies, which are from eternity (Psalm 25:6), and stretch out your right hand to your creature striving toward you. Help the weakness of one striving toward you. Draw him—you know that he cannot come to you unless you, Father, draw him by your love and desire (John 6:44).

Make me a servant acceptable and pleasing to you, since you know that I cannot please you otherwise. Give me, I beg you, those holy gifts by which alone I may please you—you who give good things to those who ask you. Grant, I ask, that you alone may be my love and my desire; that you alone may be my love and my fear. Claim me wholly for yourself, since I know that I owe to you alone the whole of what I am, the whole of what is in me, indeed the whole of what I understand and the whole of what moves me.

Turn me wholly into your praise and glory, since I owe my whole self to your praise. Do not hand over, I beg you, your creature to your enemies; retain it for yourself, since it belongs wholly and solely to you. Complete in me, piece by piece, what you began, and strengthen what you have wrought.

Hear, I beg you, my prayer, whose giver and inspirer you are before I called upon you. Look upon one who supplicates you—you who deigned to look upon me in this way while I was wandering. Merciful Lord, you did not deign to inspire this prayer in vain, nor did you give it to me without purpose. You deigned to give it to me for this very reason: that you might hear me. You gave it to me so that I might plead with you to have mercy on me, a sinner, and, since you have already granted me the pledge of your mercy, to bestow what remains.

Recover me, Lord [Col. 0746C] my God, and rescue me from the hands of my enemies, since they too are yours and are subject to your omnipotence. They hate nothing in me except what you have given me in all good actions. They hate nothing in me except that I love you. With all their efforts and strength and with every deceit they strive to prevent me from loving you, glorifying you, or seeking you at all.

Therefore let the enemies of your glory not prevail against me; rather, let them be confounded by the abundance of your mercy when they see me wholly converted into your praise and glory, seeking your peace and glory against those lying in wait for me and aiming at my transformation. Do not, I beg you, allow their so unjust and detestable will concerning me and against me to be fulfilled.

Magnify, then, my soul, my God, so that it may proclaim your praise and the heralds of your glory, so that henceforth I may live wholly according to the greatness of your glory and my whole life may glorify you. By my example invite and summon many of the predestined to glorify you. May the glorious presence of the radiance and sweetness of your glory, which they cannot endure, draw away from me, I ask, the most vile, unclean, and abominable spirits of darkness.

Break my bonds, lead me out of confinement and from a horrible, dark, and most loathsome prison, from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, from the depths of death and darkness, into your freedom and marvelous light.

Illuminate me with your most saving faith; gladden me and strengthen me with your most delightful and certain hope. Give me life through your strongest and most righteous love. Depress and humble me, and guard me with your strongest, safest, and most invincible fear. Profitably confound me with your most beautiful and glorious shame.

Whenever I bring before your eyes anything that offends them, torment me and afflict me with womanly grief and with the sweetest manner of the most effective medicine of your compunction, so that I may not depart from the face of your mercy empty and confounded, but may obtain whatever, at your command, by your gift and inspiration, I ask, and whatever you have promised to those who ask you.

Let me feel, merciful and compassionate Lord, that no one flees to your mercy in vain, that you are present to those who seek you in order to find you, and that I shall not fail at the fountain of your mercy—you who rescued me from the depths and bestowed upon me such things, and as great and as many things, as you know. By the same power of your omnipotence, wisdom, and goodness by which you spoke and all things came to be, you can, with the same ease of your mercy, speak, and all that has been deformed in me will be reshaped.

Behold, almighty and merciful Father, I have enumerated so many and such great benefits of yours that I have received; I have recounted so many and such great evils that I have returned to your goodness. I am unhappy and ungrateful: after so many and such great evils that await me and threaten me, I still stand before you with a cold, hard, shameless, dead, and stupid heart, and I am not ashamed.

Caught in so many and such great robberies and awaiting only an infernal gallows, I am neither shaken by fear, nor tortured by sorrow, nor confounded by shame, nor inflamed by love for your peaceable and enduring goodness. Do you, sweetest Father, wait and delay looking upon me and having mercy on me until I appear worthy before you according to your mercy and offer before you something worthy to be asked for and heard by you?

Behold, as a dead corpse, swarming with worms and stinking after three days, I come to you, the Giver of life, and have brought myself to you. Behold, I offer the blind to your almighty mercy to be illumined, the sick to be healed, one bound by so many and such great debts to be released, and the utterly naked and impoverished to be enriched—before whose eyes it is easy suddenly to make the poor honorable [Col. 0747D].

I can offer you nothing else, most merciful God, except myself as I am, and to show you my death and wounds, my nakedness and poverty, and my debts, because of which I fear the prison of eternal death. Show, therefore, the eyes of your mercy, if in any way you will turn toward me, forgive me, and pour the grace of your blessedness over me.

For I cannot turn myself toward you, weighed down and rendered powerless by so many and such great wounds and illnesses, and by death itself. But you, merciful Father, turn me, and I shall turn to you. Turn me, Lord, to yourself, crush and humble my heart, and send into me the perceptions of living pain.

There is no fountain of good things except you. There is no one from whom I may receive love, fear, sorrow, and shame—by which I may be found worthy of your mercy—unless you pour out, from your overflowing mercy, grace upon me, utterly unworthy. Lord, if you grant this to me, I shall be blessed. If you deign to punish my disgraceful acts and crimes according to your judgment and justice, I am happy—not, however, if according to your anger, which at the end overtakes rebels and those who resist your mercy.

And this is your justice and your judgment, merciful Father: that fear, love, shame, and sorrow are produced in the hearts of those who truly repent and return to your goodness, so that they may obtain mercy.

Nail this robber, then, with your holy fear, and burn this apostate with the fire of your love and charity. Nail, Lord, this evildoer with your life-giving and most salutary sorrow; confound this shameless transgressor with your glorious shame. Fasten this criminal to the cross of penal labor, and make him acceptable through your mercy. Make me hunger for you with all my heart and thirst for you with all my inward being; make me embrace you with my whole desire.

Make me serve you alone with all my inward being and seek with all my zeal what is pleasing before you. To you, with your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, your most holy gift and Paraclete, belong all honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Meditation IX

[Note: [Col. 0747D] Compared with the manuscript of the Oratory of Paris and with the Gothic edition. Also, On the Humanity; elsewhere entitled “The Spur of Love” or “Mirror of Evangelical Discourse.” The manuscript is entitled “The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the World, according to Blessed Anselm, Archbishop.” In the Gothic edition the work is divided into nineteen chapters.]

## On the Humanity of Christ

Let us Christians honor Jesus the Nazarene, innocently condemned by the Jews and fastened to the cross by the Gentiles, with divine acts of devotion [Note: [Col. 0747D] The manuscript omits “we Christians” and reads simply “us”]. It is worthy, salutary, and honorable that we who belong to Christ reverently venerate the frailties of our Savior [Note: [Col. 0747D] The manuscript omits “our”], lovingly embrace them, and courageously imitate them.

For these are the strongest instruments by which the almighty power and unsearchable wisdom of God powerfully and wonderfully accomplished, and still accomplishes, the restoration of the world. Christ the Lord was made a little lower than the angels [Note: [Col. 0747D] The manuscript reads “he is a little lower than the angels”], so that he might make us equal to the angels; and who would not humble himself for Christ?

Christ the Lord was crucified for our sins, and made the bitterness of the cross sweet to those who love him; he died and slew death, so that we might live through him. And who would not love Christ the Lord? Who would not suffer for Christ? [Note: [Col. 0747D] The manuscript reads “for him”].

Christ passed through the shame of the cross to the glory of heavenly brightness, and for his reverence God the Father gave him all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), so that all the angels of God might adore him and every knee might bow at his name [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “at the name of Jesus”], in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2:10).

Where, then, is your glorying, O Christian [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript also reads “O Christian”], except in the name of your crucified Lord [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “of our Lord”] Jesus Christ—in the name that is above every name, in which the one who is blessed on earth will be blessed in heaven?

Glory in his holy name, children of redemption; give honor to your Savior, who has done great things in you, and magnify his name with me, saying:

We adore you, O Christ [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “You, Jesus”; it omits “Jesus” here], King of Israel, prince of the kings of the earth, light of the nations, Lord of hosts, strongest power of almighty God. We adore you, precious price of our redemption, peace-offering, which alone, by the marvelous sweetness of your fragrance [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “immeasurable sweetness”], inclined the Father who dwells in heaven [Note: [Col. 0749D] Other manuscripts read “in heaven”] to look upon the lowly, and you alone made him propitious [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “and [to] the children of wrath,” whereas the present text reads “and you alone [made] him himself”].

We proclaim your mercies, O Christ; with abundance we pour forth the memory of your sweetness [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “the memory of your mercy”]; to you, Christ, we offer the sacrifice of praise for the abundance of your goodness, which you showed to us, a wicked seed and criminal children [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript adds “and lost [children]”].

For while we were still your enemies, Lord, and ancient death exercised dominion over all flesh [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “exercised unjust [dominion]”; the present text omits “unjust”]—the whole seed of Adam being subject to it under the law of primordial sin—you remembered your overflowing mercy and looked down from your exalted dwelling upon this valley of weeping and misery [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “this valley of misery and weeping”].

You saw, Lord, the affliction of your people; touched inwardly by the sweetness of charity, you set your thoughts upon us—thoughts of peace and redemption. Indeed, although you were the Son of God, true God, coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, dwelling in inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16) and sustaining all things by the word of your power (Hebrews 1:3), you did not disdain to bend your height into the prison of our mortality, where you both tasted and absorbed our misery and restored us to glory.

It was not enough for your love, to complete the work of our salvation, to send a cherub, a seraph, or one of the angels: you yourself deigned to come to us [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “he deigned to come”] at the command of the Father, whose excessive love for us we have experienced in you.

You came, I say, not by changing your place, but by displaying your presence to us through the flesh [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “through love”]. You descended from the royal throne of your exalted glory into a maiden humble and lowly in her own eyes, first sealed by a vow of virginal continence.

In her sacred womb [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “most holy”], the ineffable power of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript omits “alone”] caused you both to be conceived and to be born in the true nature of humanity, so that the event of your birth violated neither the majesty of divinity in you nor the integrity of virginity in your Mother.

O lovable, O wondrous condescension! You did not disdain, God of immeasurable glory, to become a contemptible worm; Lord of all, you willed to appear as a fellow servant of servants. It seemed too little to you to be our Father [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “our Father to us”]; you also, Lord, deigned to be our brother.

And you, Lord of all, who have no need of anything [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “having no need of anything”], did not shrink, from the very beginning of your birth, from tasting the hardships of the most abject poverty. For, as Scripture says, when you were born you had no place in the inn (Luke 2:7), nor did you have a cradle to receive your tender body. Instead, you who enclose the earth within a span were wrapped in little cloths and laid in the filthy manger of a squalid stable (ibid.); and your mother borrowed lodging—that is, a manger—from brute animals [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “and this very lodging, namely the manger”].

Take comfort, take comfort, you who are nourished amid the filth of poverty, because God is with you in poverty. He does not lie amid the luxuries of a splendid bed, for he is not found in the land of those who live softly.

Why do you glory further, O rich man, earthen thing [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript reads “in an earthen thing”], wallowing in a painted and luxurious bed, when the King of kings preferred by his lying down to honor the bedding of the poor? Why do you despise hard bedding, when the tender infant, in whose hand all things are, preferred the hard straw of animals to your silks and feathers?

But even your tender infancy, Christ, was not safe from the swords of persecutors. For you were still hanging at your mother’s breast, sucking amid its sweetness, when an angel appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying:

“Rise, and take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod is going to seek the child to destroy him” (Matthew 2:13).

From that time onward, good Jesus, you began to suffer. Nor did you bear in yourself only that persecution of your infancy; you also endured death in your little ones, many thousands of whom Herod’s savagery slaughtered for your sake between their mothers’ breasts.

Having passed through the more tender years of childhood, you offered us an example of learning the truth humbly [Note: [Col. 0749D] The manuscript has “of humility” instead of “humbly”]. For you did not sit with the council of vanity (Ps. 25:4), but in the midst of the teachers, questioning them and listening to them [Col. 0750D], although you were yourself the Lord of knowledge (1 Sam. 2:3), indeed the very Wisdom of God the Father. You also gave us a pattern of obedience, when you, the ruler of the world, humbly submitted to the authority of your parents.

But when the fullness of a more vigorous age arrived [Col. 0751A], intending to stretch out your hand toward mighty deeds, you went forth for the salvation of your people, like a strong giant to run the whole road of our misery (Ps. 18:7). First, so that in every respect you might be made like your brothers, you approached your servant, who was baptizing sinners for repentance, as though you were a sinner; and you, innocent Lamb of God, whom no stain of sin had ever defiled [Note: [Col. 0751D] Or “no contagion”; the manuscript omits this], asked to be baptized by him.

You were baptized, not sanctifying yourself in the waters, but sanctifying the waters in yourself, so that through them you might sanctify us. From baptism you went forth into the desert in the Spirit of strength, so that in you there might also be an example of the solitary life. You patiently endured solitude and a fast of forty days, the bitterness of hunger, and the temptations of the deceiving spirit, in order to make all these things bearable for us.

At last you came to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel (Matt. 10:6), openly raising the lamp of the divine word for the illumination of the world and announcing the kingdom of God to all. You became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey (Heb. 5:9), and you confirmed the word [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript reads: “announcing the word of God to all, you became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey, confirming the word”] by the signs that followed it [p. 218]; you displayed the power of your divinity in all who were ill, freely providing everyone with whatever was suitable for their salvation, so that you might win them all.

But their foolish heart was darkened (Rom. 1:21), Lord, and they cast your words behind them (Ps. 50:17). They paid no attention to all the wonders that you performed among them, except for a very few nobler athletes [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript has “noble ones”], whom you chose from among the lowly and despised things of the world, so that through them you might magnificently overthrow the lofty and mighty (1 Cor. 1:27).

Nor were they merely ungrateful for your freely bestowed benefits: they also heaped insults upon you, Lord of lords, and did to you whatever they wished (Matt. 17:12). When you were performing the works of God—works that no one else had done—what did they say? [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript reads simply: “what did they say?”] “This man is not from God” (John 9:16); “He casts out demons by the prince of demons” (Matt. 11:18, 19). “He has a demon; he misleads the crowds; he is a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Luke 10:15).

Why do you weep? Why do you sigh, O man of God, while you endure insults in words? Do you not hear how many reproaches, because of you, fell upon the Lord your God? If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household? (Matt. 10:5.)

These and similar blasphemies, and at times attacks with stones, you patiently endured, good Jesus. You became before them like a man who does not hear, and who has no words of reproof in his mouth (Ps. 37:15) [Col. 0752A]. Finally, they valued your righteous blood [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript reads: “your blood, good Jesus”]—your blood, which had been appraised by your disciple, the son of perdition—at thirty pieces of silver (Matt. 27:9), so that they might plunge your soul into death without cause.

The treachery of your utterly wicked betrayer did not escape you when, at the supper, for the sake of washing, you knelt and bowed down even before him [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript reads: “even before washing, before him”], and deigned with your most holy hands to touch, wash, and wipe his accursed feet, swift to shed your blood (John 13:5). And still you walk with your neck extended, O earth and ashes; still pride lifts you above yourself, still impatience agitates you!

Look upon the teacher of humility and gentleness [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript has “mirror” instead of “teacher”], the Lord Jesus Christ, maker of every creature [Col. 0752B], the awesome judge of the living and the dead, bending his knees before the feet of his human betrayer [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript has “of the human betrayer”]. Learn that he is meek and humble of heart (Matt. 11:29), and be confounded by your pride; blush for your impatience [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript has “blush at your impatience”].

This too belonged to your gentleness, Lord Jesus: you did not wish openly to expose and shame that treacherous man in the gathering of the brothers, but, after gently admonishing him, ordered him to hasten what was being prepared [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript has “what he was preparing”]. In all these things his fury was not turned away from you; but, going out, he was busily engaged in his repeated wickedness.

How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning (Isa. 14:12) amid the delights of paradise! [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript omits: “How, then, were you reckoned among the sons of darkness?”] You appeared glorious, a companion of the citizens of heaven and a guest at the banquet of the divine Word. You who were nourished among saffron-colored things—how have you embraced dung? (Lam. 4:5.) [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript omits “how.”]

Then your household, Christ, was glorified in the likeness of an angelic company; then at last that blessed gathering was refreshed from your mouth by the most abundant outpouring of the divine word [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript omits “sacred”]. For that corrupted wineskin [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript has “that other wineskin”] had been sent outside, whom you knew to be unworthy of being filled with this limpid liquor.

After giving the commandment of the Savior’s charity and patience [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript has “of saving charity”], and assigning the kingdom of your Father to the brothers, you went with them to a place known to your betrayer, knowing all that was going to befall you. There you did not blush to confess in the hearing of the brothers the sorrow of your soul, which you had freely assumed because of the passion that was approaching, just as you confessed the other things that you suffered, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38).

Then, with your knees placed [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript reads: “with your knees therefore placed upon the ground”], you fell on your face, praying in agony and saying: “Abba, Father, my Father [Note: [Col. 0751D] The manuscript reads: “My Father, if…”], if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., 39) [Col. 0753A]. The anguish of your most sorrowful heart was also revealed by that bloody sweat, which, during the time of prayer, flowed drop by drop from your most holy flesh onto the ground.

Lord Jesus Christ, ruler of all, whence came this vehement sorrow of your soul? Whence such anxiety of sweat [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript has “such anxiety of sweat”], and such anxious supplication? Did you not offer yourself wholly as a voluntary sacrifice to the Father, and did you suffer nothing unwillingly? Indeed, Lord.

We think, however, that you assumed this also for the consolation of your weak members, lest anyone despair if weak flesh should murmur, while the spirit is nevertheless ready for suffering. Certainly, too, so that we might have greater incentives to love and gratitude toward you, you expressed in yourself the natural weakness of the flesh by such signs [Col. 0753B], teaching us that you truly bore our infirmities, and that you traversed the thorns of suffering not without the sensation of pain.

For that saying seems to have been the voice of the flesh, not of the spirit, since you added: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). How willing your spirit was, good Jesus, to suffer, you clearly showed when men of blood came with your betrayer, seeking your life by night with lanterns, torches, and weapons. You went out to meet them willingly, and revealed yourself by the sign that they had received from the leader of the crime (John 18:3, 4) [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “after the sign had been given, which…”].

You did not shrink from the bloodstained beast as he approached to kiss your mouth [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “the kiss of your most holy mouth”]. Rather, you gently applied the mouth in which no deceit was found (Isa. 53:9) to the mouth overflowing with wickedness (Matt. 26:49) [Col. 0753C].

O innocent Lamb of God, what have you to do with that wolf? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? (2 Cor. 6:15.) Yet this too belonged to your kindness, Lord Jesus: that you should offer him everything that might have softened the obstinacy of his wicked heart.

For you also reminded him of your former friendship, saying: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:50.) And you wished to strike the impious man’s heart with horror at his crime when you said to him [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “When you said”] (Luke 26:48): “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?”

“And behold, the Philistines are upon you, Samson” (Judg. 16:14, 16). They were not deterred from you by the fact that, at the hour of your arrest, you struck them to the ground with your almighty arm—not indeed for the sake of defense, but so that human presumption might learn that it could do nothing against you except insofar as you permitted it [Col. 0753D].

And who could hear without a groan how, at that hour, they laid murderous hands upon you? Binding your innocent hands, good Jesus, with chains, they dragged you, the gentlest Lamb, saying nothing in protest [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript has “speaking”], like a robber, shamefully to the sacrifice [Col. 0754A].

Yet even then the honeycomb of your sweetness did not cease to let your mercy drip upon your enemies, Christ. For you healed the ear of your enemy, mutilated by your disciple [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript omits “by him”], and restrained your defender’s zeal from injuring those who were dragging you [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “touching the enemy’s ear, you healed it”]. Cursed is their fury, because it was obstinate; neither the majesty of the miracle nor the kindness of the benefit could break it.

You were brought before the council of the priests who plotted evil against you, and, having confessed the truth as was fitting [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “as you taught”], you were condemned to death as though for blasphemy.

Most loving Lord Jesus, how many unworthy things did you endure there from your own people? Your honorable face, upon which the angels desire to gaze, which fills all the heavens with joy, and which all the rich among the people entreat (Ps. 45:13) [Col. 0754B], they defiled with the spittle of their polluted lips, struck with sacrilegious hands, covered with a veil in mockery, and, treating you, Lord of all creation, as a contemptible slave, they struck you with blows.

And further, they handed your soul over to an uncircumcised dog to swallow. Having bound you, they led you before Pilate the governor [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “before Pilate the Governor”], demanding that you, who knew no sin, be put to death by crucifixion, while a murderous man was given to them (Acts 3:13, 14), preferring the wolf to the Lamb and clay to gold [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “the Lamb to the wolf, and placing gold behind clay”].

O unworthy and wretched exchange! That impious man indeed knew that this was being done to you out of envy, yet he did not restrain his rash hands from you; rather, he filled your soul with bitterness [Col. 0754C] without cause. He sent you to Herod to be mocked, received you when you had been mocked, and made you stand naked in the sight of those who laughed [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “ordered you to stand”]. Nor did he spare tearing your virginal flesh with the most bitter scourging, cruelly heaping bruise upon bruise.

Chosen youth of my Lord [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “beloved youth of the Lord my God”], what had you committed worthy of such bitterness, such disgrace [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript omits “what such disgrace”]? Absolutely nothing. I, the lost man [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript reads: “I, I the lost man”], became for you the cause of all contrition and all disgrace [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript omits “your”]. I ate the sour grape, and your teeth were set on edge, because you were then paying what you had not taken by force (Ps. 68:5).

In all these things the impiety of the treacherous Jews was not satisfied [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript has “the impiety of the treacherous was satisfied”; it omits “healed”]. Finally, you fell into the hands of uncircumcised soldiers, to be consumed by a most shameful death [Col. 0754D].

It was not enough for these sacrilegious men to crucify you unless they had first filled your soul with mockeries as well (Ps. 37:8). For what does Scripture say?

“They gathered the whole cohort around him into the praetorium; and, stripping him of his garments, they clothed him in a purple tunic and placed a scarlet cloak around him. Weaving a crown of thorns, they put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand; and, bending the knee before him, they mocked him, saying: ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ They struck him with blows, and, spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head. And after they had mocked him, they clothed him in his garments and led him away to be crucified, carrying his own cross. They brought him to Golgotha and gave him wine mixed with myrrh and gall to drink; but when he had tasted it, he would not drink” (Matt. 26:27–34).

Then they crucified him, and two robbers with him, one on either side, with Jesus in the middle. But Jesus was saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Col. 0755B] (Luke 23:33, 34).

Afterward, knowing that everything had already been accomplished so that Scripture might be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript reads: “knowing that everything was accomplished”], Jesus said: “I thirst.” One of them ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him to drink. When he had received the vinegar [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript reads: “When he had therefore received it”], he said: “It is finished” (John 19:28–30). And, crying out with a loud voice, he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46); and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30). Then one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out (ibid., 34).

Awaken now, my soul; shake yourself [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript omits “and”] from the dust, and contemplate more attentively this memorable man whom, in the mirror of the Gospel word, you behold as though present. Pay attention, my soul: who is this who enters bearing the likeness of a king and yet is filled with the disgrace of a most despised servant [Col. 0755C]?

He walks crowned, but his crown itself is his torment, and a thousand punctures tear his beautiful head. He is clothed in royal purple, but in it he is despised rather than honored. He carries a scepter in his hand [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “the scepter is carried by his hand”], but with that very scepter his revered head is struck. They adore him, bending their knees to the ground before him [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “on the ground”], and proclaim him king; yet immediately they leap upon his lovely cheeks to spit upon them [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “leap upon them”], strike his jaws with their palms, and dishonor his honorable neck [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “dishonor”].

See other things as well [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “See, my soul”]: how in every respect this man is constrained, spat upon, and scorned [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript omits “and scorned”]. Under the burden of the cross he is ordered to bend his back and carry his own shame. Led to the place of punishment, he is given myrrh and gall to drink. He is lifted up on the cross [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “onto the cross”], and says: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

What sort of man is this, who in all his distresses did not once open his mouth to utter against those accursed dogs a word either of complaint, excuse, threat, or curse, and finally poured over his enemies a word of blessing such as had never been heard from the beginning of the world? What is gentler than this man? What have you seen, my soul, that is kinder?

Look upon him still more attentively [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “more intently”], for he appears worthy both of profound wonder and of the most tender compassion. See him naked and torn by scourges, shamefully fastened to the cross with iron nails in the midst of robbers, given vinegar to drink upon the cross, wounded in the side by a lance after death, and pouring abundant streams of blood from the five wounds of his hands, feet, and side.

Draw out tears, my eyes [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript omits “and”]; melt, my soul, in the fire of compassion over the brokenness of that beloved man whom you see afflicted by such pains in such gentleness.

[Col. 0756B]

And now, my soul, have you seen his weakness and pitied him [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript reads: “and pitied him”]? Now attend to his majesty, and you will marvel [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript omits “and more”]. For what does Scripture say?

“From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “over the whole earth”] until the ninth hour, and the sun was darkened; and the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has “from the top”]; and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split; and the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose” (Luke 23:44, 45; Matt. 27:51, 52).

What sort of man is this, since heaven and earth suffer with him whose death gives life to the dead? Recognize, my soul, recognize: this is the Lord Jesus Christ, your Savior, the only-begotten Son of God, true God and true man, who alone beneath the sun was found without stain.

And behold how he was reckoned among the wicked (Isa. 53:12), and was regarded as though he were a leprous man and the least of men (ibid. 3, 4). And like an abortion cast from the womb, so he was cast out from the womb of his unhappy mother, the Synagogue (Job 31:16). He who was beautiful beyond the sons of men—how disfigured he was made beyond the sons of men! For he was wounded because of our iniquities and crushed because of our crimes (Isa. 53:5).

And he became a holocaust of sweetest fragrance in your sight, Father of eternal glory, so that he might turn away your indignation from us and make us sit with him in the heavenly places.

Look, holy Lord Father, from your sanctuary and from the lofty dwelling of the heavens, and behold this most holy victim, which our great High Priest, your holy child Jesus [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript reads: “your Lord Jesus Christ”], offers to you for the sins of his brothers [Col. 0756D]; and be appeased toward the multitude of our wickedness.

Behold, the voice of the blood of our brother Jesus cries to you from the cross. For what is it, Lord, that hangs upon it? It hangs, I say, because past things are present before you [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript reads: “it hangs, I say, upon it, because…”]. Recognize it, Father: this is the tunic of your son Joseph [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript reads: “of your true Joseph”]. A most savage beast [Col. 0757A] devoured him; in its fury it trampled his garment and defiled all the beauty of the rest of his body [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “with remnants of blood”], and behold, it left five grievous tears in him.

This is the garment that your innocent child Jesus left in the hand of the Egyptian prostitute for the sins of his brothers [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript reads: “See, Lord, the cloak that the modest young man left in the hand of the adulteress of the generation, that is, the Egyptian prostitute”], judging the loss of his cloak better than the loss of chastity [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “of the garment rather than of holy innocence”; the present text reads “of the cloak rather than of chastity”], and choosing rather, stripped of the garment of his flesh, to descend into the prison of death than to consent, for the glory of the world, to the adulterous voice—that voice, I mean, which said: “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9)—which would indeed have been to sleep with the adulteress.

And now, Lord Father, we know that your Son lives and rules over the whole land of Egypt (Gen. 45:26), indeed, in every place of your dominion [Col. 0757B]. For, brought forth at your command from the prison of death and the underworld, and having cut off the hair of mortality, with the garment of the flesh changed [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript reads: “with the flesh of the garment changed”], he blossomed again in the beauty of immortality, and you received him with glory.

He weakened the rule of cruel Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “the rule of the reason of plunder”], and with triumph, by his noble strength, he entered the heavens. And behold, crowned with glory and honor, he stands at the right hand of your majesty before your face for us. For he is our brother and our flesh (Gen. 37:27).

Look upon the face of your Christ (Ps. 83:10), who became obedient to you even unto death (Phil. 2:8); and may the scars of his wounds never depart from your eyes, so that you may remember how great a satisfaction you received from him for our sins.

Would that, Lord, you would place in the balance the sins by which we deserved wrath [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript omits “our”], and the calamity that your innocent Son suffered for us. Surely, Lord, the latter will appear weightier and more worthy that you should pour mercy itself upon us [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “so that through it…”] than that you should contain your mercies in anger against them or against their sins [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “for our sins”].

May every tongue give thanks to you, holy Father [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript reads: “Lord Father”], for the abundance of your kindness [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “for your superabundance of kindness”], who did not spare the one Son of your heart, but handed him over to death for us, so that we might have such a great and faithful advocate in heaven before you.

And to you, Lord Jesus, strongest zealot, what thanks, what worthy recompense can I, a human being, dust and ashes and a worthless creature, render? What could you have done for my salvation that you did not do? From the sole of your foot to the crown of your head, you plunged yourself wholly into the waters of suffering [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “into the waters”], so that you might draw me wholly out of them; and the waters entered into your soul (Ps. 68:2).

For you even gave up your soul to death [Col. 0758A], so that you might restore my lost soul to me. And behold, you have bound me by a double debt: I am your debtor both for what you gave and for what you lost because of me. For my life, given to me twice by you—once in creation, once in redemption—I have nothing more just to return to you than that very life itself. But for your precious soul, so deeply afflicted, I cannot find what could worthily be repaid by a human being.

For if I could repay heaven and earth and all their adornment for it, surely even then I would in no way reach the measure of the debt. But that I may return to you, Lord, even what I have [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript reads: “even what I owe”] and am able to offer [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript reads: “and what is possible for me”] is itself your gift.

You must therefore be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, the whole mind, and the whole strength; and your footsteps must now be followed [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript reads: “your footsteps must be followed by me”], since you deigned to die for me. And how will this happen in me except through you? May my soul cling after you (Ps. 62:9), because all its strength depends upon you.

And now, Lord Jesus, my Redeemer, I adore you as the true God; I believe in you, I hope in you, and with whatever desires I can, I sigh toward you. Help my imperfection. Before the glorious insignia of your passion, in which you wrought my salvation, I bow down completely.

In your name, Christ, I adore the royal standard of your victorious cross; your crown of thorns; the nails reddened by your blood; the lance plunged into your holy side [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “imprinted, immense” instead of “plunged”]; your wounds; your blood; your death; your burial; your victorious resurrection and glorification. I adore and glorify them suppliantly, Christ [Col. 0758C].

For the fragrance of life breathes for me in all these things. By their life-giving fragrance, Lord, raise my spirit from the death of sin. By their power guard me from the cunning of Satan and strengthen me, so that the yoke of your commandments may become sweet to me, and the burden of the cross, which you command me to carry after you, may be light and bearable upon the shoulders of my soul (Matt. 11:30).

For what is my strength, that, according to your command, I should endure so many pressures of the world with unconquered spirit? Are my feet like those of deer (Ps. 17:34), so that I might swiftly follow you as you run through the thorns and rough places of suffering [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “a swift runner”]?

But hear, I beg you, my voice, and bend over your servant [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript has “over me, your servant”] that sweet cross, which is the tree of life for those who seize it, so that I too, as I hope [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscript reads: “and so that in spirit I may…”], may run eagerly. I will carry tirelessly after you the cross that comes from enemies.

That most divine cross, I say, place upon my shoulders, whose breadth is charity, extending over every creature [Col. 0759A]; whose length is eternity; whose height is omnipotence; whose depth is inscrutable wisdom. Nail my hands and my feet to it, and clothe your servant in the whole form of your passion [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript reads: “clothe me, your servant”].

Grant me, I beg, to refrain from the works of the flesh, which you hate, and to do the justice that you loved; and in both to seek your glory [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript has “seeking your”]. I shall regard my left hand as fastened to that lofty cross by the nail of temperance, and my right by the nail of justice.

Grant that my mind may continually meditate on your law and continually cast every thought [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript has “my thought”] upon you; and fasten my right foot to that same tree of life with the nail of prudence.

Grant that the wretched prosperity of passing life [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript has “of the present life”] may neither weaken the sensuality that serves my spirit [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript has “the servant of my spirit”], nor that fortunate misfortune disturb the rewards of eternal life; and let my left foot also be held upon the cross by the nail of fortitude [Col. 0759B].

But so that some likeness of the thorns of your head may also appear in me, grant, I beg, to my mind both the compunction of salutary repentance, compassion for another’s misery, and the spur of zeal that emulates what is right before you; and let me turn to you in my affliction while a threefold thorn is fastened into me (Ps. 31:4).

I desire that you should extend a sponge on a reed to my mouth and apply the bitterness of vinegar to my taste. I desire that through your Scriptures you should grant my reason to taste and see how this flourishing world is like an empty sponge, and all its desires more bitter than vinegar.

Thus, Father, let it happen in me that the golden cup of Babylon, intoxicating the whole earth (Jer. 51:7) [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript omits “golden”], may neither seduce me with empty splendor nor intoxicate me with false sweetness, as it does those who consider darkness light and light darkness, bitterness sweet and sweetness bitter (Isa. 5:20).

The wine mixed with myrrh [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript omits “mixed with gall”] is suspect to me because you refused to drink it, perhaps because it signified the excessive bitterness [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript omits “of envy and wickedness”] of those who crucified you.

Conform your servant also to your life-giving death [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript reads: “your servant to death”], making me die to sin according to the flesh but live to righteousness according to the spirit.

But so that I may glory in bearing the complete image of the Crucified One, I ask that you also reproduce in me the likeness of what the insatiable malice of the wicked exercised against you after your death [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript omits “of the Jews”]. Let your living and effective word, sharper than every most piercing lance, and reaching to the innermost parts of my soul (Heb. 4:12), wound my heart and bring forth from it, as though from my right side, love of you [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript omits “Lord”] and of my brothers, in place of blood and water.

Finally, wrap my spirit in the clean shroud of the first robe, in which I may rest as I enter to you into the place of the marvelous tabernacle (Ps. 41:5), and hide me until your fury has passed (Isa. 26:20).

On the third day, after the day of labor, after the day of simple glory, on the morning [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript omits “and”] of the first Sabbath of eternity, raise me, unworthy as I am, among your children, so that in my flesh I may see your glory and be filled with the joy of your countenance (Ps. 15:11).

O my Savior and my God, may the time come—may it come, I pray—when I shall finally behold with lifted eyes what I now believe; when I shall grasp what I now hope for and greet from afar; when I shall embrace and kiss with the arms of my soul what I now desire with all my strength [Col. 0760B], and be wholly absorbed into the abyss of your love [Note: [Col. 0759D] The manuscript reads: “and into the love…”].

O my Savior and my God! But now, in the meantime, bless your Savior, my soul; and magnify his name, which is holy and filled with the holiest delights.

O how good and gracious you are, Lord Jesus, to the soul that seeks you: Jesus, redeemer of captives [Note: The manuscript reads “of the lost”], Savior of the lost [Note: The manuscript reads “of the redeemed”], hope of exiles, strength of those who labor, breadth of the anxious spirit [Note: The manuscript reads “of the distressed spirit”], sweet consolation and gentle refreshment of the tearful soul that runs after you in sweat, crown of the triumphant, the sole reward and joy of the citizens above [Note: The manuscript omits “of all”], most abundant fountain [Note: The manuscript reads “most abundantly, O fountain”] of all graces, illustrious offspring of the Most High God.

Most High God, may all things that are above in heaven bless you, and all things that are below on earth [Note: The manuscript reads “and all things that are on earth below”]; for you are great, and great is your name. O unfading beauty of the exalted God, and purest brightness of eternal light, life that gives life to every living thing, light that illumines every light and preserves, in perpetual splendor, a thousand times a thousand [Note: The manuscript omits the second “thousand”] shining lights [Note: The manuscript reads “lights before”] before the throne of your divine majesty [Note: The manuscript reads “divinity”] from the first dawn.

O eternal and unceasing, bright and sweet outpouring of the hidden fountain, concealed from mortal eyes [Note: The manuscript reads “from our eyes”], whose wave has no origin, whose depth has no bottom, whose height has no limit, whose breadth cannot be circumscribed, whose purity cannot be disturbed. The heart of the Most High God pours you forth from the impenetrable abyss of its depth: Life from Life, Light from Light, God from God, Eternal from Eternal, the Boundless from the Boundless, wholly coequal with himself; and from your fullness we have all received (John 1:16).

You, therefore, most generous fountain of every good, precious light of sevenfold grace [Note: The manuscript reads: “Light: You, I say, etc. You send forth from the treasury a stream whose sweetness may deign to mitigate the bitter saltness of the weakness of this our sea, in which we are tossed; a stream of the oil of gladness, a stream of purest wine. A torrent of fiery strength, the Paraclete Spirit, equal to each, is poured forth from you and the Father over the world, filling all things and containing all things. The Spirit from you, the Spirit from the Father, one from both, uniquely both, as the indivisible union of both, life-giving bond, indissoluble embrace, and peace surpassing all understanding. Hence is the torrent of your delight, Lord, by which you continually water and cause to surge in joyful drunkenness that delicate and glorious city, Jerusalem which is above, so that those bright and fiery instruments may chant to you an unceasing hymn, in a voice of exultation and confession and the sound of feasting. With its desirable drops refresh the dry throats of your exiled people, Lord, who continually await you. Allow, I pray, even the little dogs to drink of the drops that fall from their masters’ table. Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One: that by which, Lord, you made the illustrious firstfruits of your people glow in the notable solemnity of ours; with that fiery dripping, I pray, Lord, cleanse, illumine, inflame, gladden, strengthen, and unite the hearts of those who believe in you, so that they may be one, think one thing, unanimously seek one thing, attain, see, possess, and bless you, God of gods, in Zion. And to you, illustrious Jesus, highest and best Jesus, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit—to the holy and undivided Trinity—be glory, thanksgiving, honor, and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”]—I beseech you, most merciful Spirit, that if through my frailty I have understood anything less than I ought in the truth of your majesty, and have neglected through the wantonness of the flesh what I understood in the Lord’s commandments, you may deign to enlighten me by your visitation. Grant that I may correct these things properly and as is necessary for me, and through you obtain mercy for my error, so that through you, whom I have called upon for help amid the dangerous sea of this life, I may be brought without shipwreck to the harbor of everlasting rest.

Therefore I ask you, most merciful Father, who first created me and restored me through the passion of your Only-Begotten Son, to make me think about and love whatever pertains to your praise. But because I am frail and cannot bring anything to completion, nevertheless grant that through constant confession I may strive, so that I may obtain the grace of your redemption [Col. 0761B] and salvation.

Grant that whatever work I undertake from now on may wholly proceed from your grace, through your grace, and in your grace, to your praise; and henceforth protect me from sins, command that I become stronger in good works, and grant that, so long as I live in this body, I may always offer you some service. After my soul’s departure from the body, grant me to obtain forgiveness of all sins and to receive eternal life. Through him who lives and reigns with you forever and ever. Amen.

## MEDITATION X. On the Passion of Christ

[Note: From the Vatican Library.]

Sweet is Jesus in the inclination of his head and in his death; sweet in the extension of his arms; sweet in the opening of his side; sweet in the fastening of his feet with a single nail.

Sweet in the inclination of his head: for, inclining his head upon the cross, he seems to say to his beloved: “O my beloved, how often you have desired to enjoy the kiss of my mouth, announcing to me through my companions, ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth’” (Song of Songs 1:1). I am ready: I bow my head, I offer my mouth; kiss as much as you wish. Do not say in your heart, “I do not seek that kiss, which is without outward form and beauty, but that glorious one which the angelic citizens always desire to enjoy.” Do not err in this way, for unless you first kiss that mouth, you will not be able to reach the other at all. Therefore kiss this mouth, which I now offer you; for although it is without outward form and beauty, it is not without grace.

Sweet in the extension of his arms: for by extending his arms he intimates to us that he himself desires our embraces, and seems to say: “O you who labor and are burdened, come and be refreshed” (Matthew 11:28) between my arms, within my embraces. See, I am ready to gather you into my arms. Come, then, all of you; let no one fear being rejected, for I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). For my delight is to be with the children of men (Proverbs 8:31).

Sweet in the opening of his side: for that opening revealed to us the riches of his goodness, namely, the love of his heart toward us.

Sweet in the fastening of his feet with a single nail; for through this he speaks to us, as it were, in the following words: “Behold, if you think that I ought to flee and therefore delay approaching me, knowing that I am exceedingly swift, like a fawn, see that my feet have been fastened with a single nail, so that I cannot flee from you at all, because mercy holds me completely bound. Nor will I flee from you as your sins have deserved, because my hands have been fastened with nails.”

Kind Jesus, humble Lord, gracious Lord, sweet in mouth, sweet in heart, sweet to the ear, ineffably and indescribably lovely, kind and merciful, powerful, wise, generous but not wasteful, exceedingly sweet and gracious. You alone are the supreme good, “fairer in form than the children of men” (Psalm 44:3), beautiful, comely, and chosen from among thousands (Song of Songs 5:10), and altogether desirable (ibid., 5:16). Beautiful things befit the beautiful.

O my Lord, now my whole soul desires your embraces and kisses. I seek nothing except yourself, even if no reward were promised; even if there were neither hell nor paradise, nevertheless, because of your sweet goodness, because of yourself, I would wish to cling to you. You are my continual meditation, my word, my work. Amen.

## MEDITATION XI. On Human Redemption

[Note: This text has been collated with the manuscripts Vict., Thuan., Bec., Corb.; one manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai; one of Saint Médard of Soissons; one Val-luc.; one of Fleury; and one Cistercian manuscript; with Sommaius’s edition and the Gothic edition. The manuscripts Vict. 16 and Corb. 160 title it “On Human Redemption.” The Thuan. manuscript calls it “A Supplicatory Meditation from the Recollection of the Lord’s Passion.” The Bec. manuscript calls it “A Contemplation of Human Redemption.” The Cistercian manuscript calls it “Anselm’s Meditation on Human Redemption.” The Val-luc. manuscript calls it “A Meditation on Human Redemption, Published by Anselm the Archbishop.” The Gothic edition calls it “On the Redemption of the Human Race.”]

Christian soul, soul raised from a grievous death, soul redeemed and liberated from miserable slavery by the blood of God [Note: The manuscripts of Bec., Val-luc., S. Med., and Flor. read “by the blood of Christ”], stir up your mind; remember your restoration to life [Note: The manuscripts Vict. 16 read “your resurrection”; the Tournai manuscript reads “your raising up”]. Reconsider your redemption and liberation. Recall where and what the power of your salvation is; turn it over in meditation; delight in its contemplation. Shake off your weariness; exert yourself upon your heart; direct your mind to this. Taste the goodness of your Redeemer; kindle yourself in love of your Savior. Chew the honeycomb of words; draw in a flavor sweeter than honey; swallow a health-giving sweetness. Chew by thinking, draw in by understanding, swallow by loving and rejoicing. Rejoice as you chew, give thanks as you draw in, take delight as you swallow.

Where, then, and what is the power and strength of your salvation [Note: The manuscripts read “of your Savior”?]? Certainly Christ restored you to life [Note: The manuscripts read “raised you up”]. That good Samaritan healed you [Note: The Tournai manuscript reads “saved you”]; that good friend redeemed and liberated you by his own life [Note: The manuscripts read “liberated you”]: Christ, I say.

Therefore the power of your salvation is the power of Christ [Note: The manuscripts read “Your salvation is the power of Christ”; the Tournai manuscript reads “Your Savior’s power”]. Where is this power of Christ [Note: The manuscripts read “Where is the power”; the Tournai manuscript reads “Where, then, is the power”]? “Indeed, the horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Habakkuk 3:4). The horns are indeed in his hands [Note: The manuscripts read “In his hands, there”], because his hands have been fastened to the arms of the cross.

But what strength is there in such weakness? What height in such humility? What is venerable in such contempt? Yet it is certainly hidden for this reason: because it is in weakness [Note: The Tournai manuscript reads “entirely hidden”]; concealed for this reason: because it is in humility [Note: The manuscripts Vict. 16 and Val-luc. read “and therefore concealed”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “concealed for this reason”; the Tournai manuscript reads “entirely concealed”]; and hidden for this reason: because it is in contempt [Note: The manuscripts Vict. 16 read “hidden for this reason”; the Tournai manuscript reads “entirely hidden”].

O hidden strength! A man hanging upon a cross suspends the eternal death weighing upon the human race; a man fastened to wood [Note: The manuscripts of Bec., O., and Thu. read “fastened to the wood”; other manuscripts read “fastened to the wood of the cross”] nails down the world that is affixed to everlasting death.

O concealed power! A condemned man, together with thieves, saves condemned men together with demons. A man stretched out upon the gibbet draws all things to himself.

O hidden power! One soul, sent forth amid torment, draws countless souls out of hell; a man undergoes bodily death and destroys the death of souls.

Why, good Lord, gracious Redeemer, powerful Savior, why did you conceal such great power beneath such great humility? Was it in order to deceive the devil, who by deceiving man cast him down from paradise? But surely truth deceives no one. Whoever does not know the truth deceives himself; whoever does not believe the truth deceives himself; whoever sees the truth and hates or despises it deceives himself. Truth, therefore, deceives no one.

Or was it so that the devil himself might deceive himself? Yet just as truth deceives no one, so it does not intend that anyone deceive himself, although it is said to cause this when it permits it. For you did not assume humanity in order to conceal yourself, who were known, but to reveal yourself, who were unknown. You declared yourself true God and true man, and demonstrated this by your works.

The reality was hidden in itself, not deliberately hidden [Note: The manuscripts read “hidden by design”]; it was not made in such a way that it should be concealed, but in such a way that it should be accomplished in its proper order; nor was it made in order to deceive anyone, but in order that it might happen as it ought.

And if it is said to be hidden [Note: The manuscript of Corb. reads “concealed”], this means nothing other than that it was not revealed to everyone [Note: The Tournai manuscript reads “not revealed to us”]. For although truth does not manifest itself to everyone, nevertheless it denies itself to no one.

Therefore, Lord, you did not act in this way either to deceive or so that anyone might deceive himself; rather, in order to do what had to be done, and in the manner in which it had to be done, you remained wholly in the truth [Note: The Florentine manuscript reads “you accomplished everything in truth”]. Whoever, then, deceived himself in your truth should complain not of you but of his own falsehood.

Did the devil justly possess anything against God or against man, on account of which God ought first to act against him on behalf of man in this manner rather than with open strength: so that, while he unjustly killed that just man [Note: The manuscripts read “while he ensnared that man”], he might justly lose the power he held over the unjust?

But certainly the devil was owed nothing by God except punishment, nor by man except a return [Note: The manuscripts read “except victory, so that”]: so that, just as man had easily allowed himself to be conquered by him through sinning, he might conquer him with difficulty through death, preserving complete justice.

Yet man owed even this only to God. For he did not sin against the devil but against God; and neither man nor devil belonged to the devil, but both man and devil belonged to God. Moreover, the devil did not afflict man out of zeal for justice but out of wickedness; nor at God’s command, but by his permission; not because the devil’s justice demanded it, but because God’s justice demanded it.

There was therefore nothing in the devil on account of which God ought to conceal or postpone his strength for the salvation of man.

Did some necessity compel the Most High to humble himself in this way, and the Almighty to labor so greatly in accomplishing something? But every necessity and impossibility is subject to his will. Whatever he wills must exist; whatever he does not will cannot exist.

By will alone, therefore—and because his will is always good—he did this by goodness alone [Note: The manuscripts read “he did this by will”; the Tournai manuscript reads “he did this by goodness”].

God was not acting so that he might save man in this manner; rather, human nature needed to satisfy God in this manner [Note: The manuscripts Vict. 16, Val-luc., Flor., and Cister. read “to satisfy the Lord God in this manner”; the Corb. manuscript reads “to satisfy God”]. God did not need to endure such laborious suffering; man needed to be reconciled to God in this manner [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads “so that men might be reconciled to God”]. God did not need to be humbled in this way; man needed to be rescued in this way from the depths of hell.

The divine nature neither needed nor could be humbled or subjected to labor. All these things had to be done by human nature so that it might be restored to the purpose for which it had been made; but neither human nature nor anything that is not God could suffice for this.

For man is not restored to the purpose for which he was established unless he is advanced to the likeness of the angels, in whom there is no sin [Note: The manuscripts Vict. 16 and Flor. read “unless he is truly advanced without sin”]. This is impossible unless he receives remission of all sins [Note: The manuscripts of Gem., Bec., Vict. 16, Val-luc., and Flor. read “of all commandments”], and this does not occur unless complete satisfaction precedes it.

That satisfaction must be such that the sinner, or someone on his behalf, gives God something of his own that was not owed, something that surpasses everything that is not God. For if sinning is to dishonor God, and man ought not to do this—even if everything that is not God had to perish—then immutable truth and manifest reason demand that the one who sins should render something to God for the honor that was taken away, something greater than that for which he ought not to have dishonored him.

Since human nature did not possess this by itself, and could not be reconciled without due satisfaction, lest God’s justice leave disordered sin in his kingdom, God’s goodness came to its aid. The Son of God assumed human nature into his own person, so that in that person there might be one who was both God and man, possessing what surpassed not only every essence that is not God, but also every debt that sinners ought to pay.

And this he paid for others, although he owed nothing for himself, while those who owed the debt had nothing with which to repay it. The life of that man is more precious than everything that is not God, and surpasses every debt that sinners owe as satisfaction.

For if his killing surpasses the multitude and magnitude of all sins that can be conceived outside the person of God [Note: The manuscripts read “if the killing of the Son surpasses…”], it is clear that his life is more good than all the sins outside the person of God are evil.

This man, since he did not owe death as a debt—for he was not a sinner—freely gave this life of his own to the honor of the Father, when he allowed it to be taken from him for the sake of justice.
