In this way he gave an example to all others that God’s justice must not be abandoned on account of the death which they must at some time undergo out of necessity: for he, who did not owe death and could avoid it while preserving justice, freely endured it when it was inflicted upon him for the sake of justice [Note: The manuscripts read “when he did not owe death”].

Thus human nature, in that man, freely and not from debt gave God what belonged to it, in order to redeem itself in others, who had no means of returning what was exacted from them as a debt.

In all this the divine nature was not humbled, but human nature was exalted; the divine nature was not diminished, but human nature was mercifully assisted.

Nor did human nature in that man suffer anything from necessity, but solely from free will. It did not yield to any violence, but, through spontaneous goodness [Note: The manuscripts read “through spontaneous will”], for the honor of God and the benefit of other human beings, laudably and mercifully endured what was inflicted upon it by an evil will; nor did it do so under any coercive obedience, but under wisdom that ordered all things powerfully.

The Father did not compel that man to die by forcing him to do so. Rather, what he understood would please the Father and benefit humanity, he freely did. The Father could not compel him to do what he ought not to demand of him; nor could such great honor fail to please the Father, when the Son freely offered it with such good will.

Thus he displayed free obedience to the Father, when he freely wished to do what he knew would please the Father. Finally, because the Father gave him this good will, although it was free, it is not improperly said that he accepted it as though it were the Father’s command [Note: The manuscripts read “he accepted it as though…”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “he, through it, as though…”].

In this way, therefore, he was obedient to the Father even unto death. And just as the Father gave him a command, so he did. And he drank the cup that the Father gave him [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “because he drank the cup”].

For this is the perfect and utterly free obedience of human nature: when it freely submits its free will to the will of God, and when, without any compulsion [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “without any coercion”], it accomplishes by spontaneous freedom the good will it has received.

Thus that man redeems all others, when he counts what he freely gave to God as payment for what they owed. By this price man is redeemed from sins not only once, but also whenever he returns with worthy repentance [Note: The Florentine manuscript reads “with fitting repentance”]; yet such repentance is not promised to the sinner [Note: The manuscripts read “repentance for sin”].

Because this was accomplished upon the cross, our Christ redeemed us through the cross. Those who approach this grace with a worthy disposition are saved; those who despise it, because they do not repay the debt they owe, are justly condemned [Note: The Corb. manuscript reads “will be justly condemned”].

Behold, Christian soul: this is the power of your salvation [Note: The manuscripts read “this is the power”; that is, “this is the power” rather than “this is the…”], this is the cause of your freedom [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “the cause of your liberation and freedom”], this is the price of your redemption [Note: The Florentine manuscript reads “this is the price,” feminine in Latin]. You were captive, but in this way you have been redeemed. You were a slave, and in this way you have been liberated [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “and thus you have been made free”]. Thus you, an exile, have been brought back; lost, restored; dead, raised to life.

This is what your heart should command, O man [Note: The manuscripts read “Man commands this”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “Eat this, O man”]; it should chew this, draw in this, swallow this, while your mouth receives the flesh and blood of the same Redeemer [Note: The manuscripts read “when your mouth received…”]. Make this your daily bread and food and provision for the journey in this life; for through this, and only through this, both you will remain in Christ and Christ in you. And in the life to come it will be your complete joy [Note: The manuscripts read “and in the future…”].

But, O Lord, you who accepted death so that I might live [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “you made yourself dead”], how shall I rejoice in my freedom, which comes only from your bonds? How shall I give thanks for my salvation, when it comes only from your sufferings? How shall I rejoice in my life, which comes only from your death?

Shall I rejoice in what you suffered, and in the cruelty of those who inflicted these things upon you? For unless they had done these things [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “unless they had done them”], you would not have suffered; and if you had not suffered, all these good things [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “these good things”] would not exist.

Or if I grieve over what they did, how shall I rejoice in those things for the sake of which they happened, and which would not exist unless those things had happened? Yet certainly their wickedness could do nothing except because you freely permitted it, and you suffered only because you mercifully willed it.

I ought, therefore, to curse their cruelty; to imitate your death and sufferings by sharing in them; to love your merciful will by giving thanks; and thus to rejoice securely in the good things bestowed upon me.

Therefore, little man, leave their cruelty to God’s judgment [Note: The manuscripts read “leave it to God”], and deal with what you owe your Savior. Consider what you were and what has been done for you, and weigh how worthy of love is the one who did this for you.

Look upon your need and his goodness [Note: The manuscripts read “his kindness”], and see what thanks you should give and how much you owe to his love [Note: The manuscript Vict. 16 omits “and see”].

You were in darkness, on slippery ground, descending over an impassable chaos of hell [Note: The manuscripts of Tournai, Bec., Gem., and S. Med. read “immersed beneath an impassable, immense chaos, and as though…”]. An immense, almost leaden weight hung from your neck and dragged you downward; an unbearable burden pressed upon you from above; invisible enemies pushed you with all their strength.

Thus you were without any help [Note: Some manuscripts read “without any counsel”], and you did not know it, because you had been conceived and born in this condition. O what you then were—and where these things were carrying you! Be terrified as you remember; tremble as you think.

O good, O Lord Jesus Christ [Note: The manuscripts of Tournai, Gem., Bec., S. Med., and Cister. read “O good Lord”; the Val-luc. manuscript reads “O Lord, O good Jesus Christ”], when I was in such a state, neither asking nor expecting anything, you shone upon me like the sun and showed me what I was [Note: The manuscripts read “and showed me how I was”].

You cast away the lead that dragged me downward; you removed the burden that pressed upon me from above; you repelled those who were pushing me, and set yourself between them and me for my sake [Note: The Florentine manuscript reads “and offered yourself to them for my sake”].

You called me by a new name, which you gave me from your own name, and raised me, bent down as I was, to behold you, saying: “Take courage; I have redeemed you; I have given my soul for you. If you cling to me, you will escape the evils in which you were, and you will not fall into the depth toward which you were hastening. Rather, I will lead you to my kingdom and make you an heir of God and my co-heir.”

From then on you took me into your protection, so that nothing might harm my soul against its will [Note: The Thuan. manuscript reads “against your will”]. And behold, although I had not yet clung to you as you advised, you nevertheless had not allowed me to fall into hell; you still wait for me to cling to you, and to do what you promised [Note: The manuscripts read “although I still have not…”].

Certainly, Lord, this is what I was, and this is what you did for me [Note: The manuscripts read “and this you did”; the Tournai manuscript reads “and thus you did”]. I was in darkness because I knew nothing, not even myself; on slippery ground because I was weak and fragile with respect to falling into sin; descending over the chaos of hell because in our first parents I had descended from righteousness into unrighteousness, through which one descends to hell, and from blessedness into temporal misery, from which one falls into eternal misery [Note: The manuscripts Vict. 16, Gem., Bec., Tournai, Val-luc., and Flor. omit “misery”].

The weight of original sin dragged me downward; the unbearable burden of God’s judgment pressed upon me; and my enemies, the demons, pressed hard upon me insofar as they could, so as to make me more deserving of condemnation through additional sins.

Thus, when I had been deprived of all help, you shone upon me and showed me what I was. For even when I could not yet know this, you taught others who would know it for me [Note: Sommaius’s edition reads “who would be for me”], and later taught me myself, before I asked, all these things [Note: The manuscripts read “taught me all these things”].

You cast away the lead that dragged me down, the burden that weighed upon me, and the enemies that pushed me, because you removed the sin in which I had been conceived and born, together with its condemnation, and prevented the evil spirits from doing violence to my soul.

You made me be called a Christian, from your name; through this I confess you, and you recognize me among your redeemed. You raised and lifted me to knowledge and love of you; you made me trust in the salvation of my soul, for which you gave your soul, and promised me your glory if I followed you.

And behold, although I do not yet follow you as you advised, but have even committed many sins that you forbade, you still wait for me to follow you and grant what you promised.

Consider, my soul [Note: In the Florentine manuscript this title is prefixed here: “To the Holy Cross”]; attend, all my inmost parts, how much my entire being owes him [Note: The manuscripts and Sommaius’s edition read “how much my entire being owes him”].

Certainly, Lord, because you made me, I owe myself wholly to your love; because you redeemed me, I owe myself wholly; because you promise so much, I owe myself wholly [Note: The manuscripts read “because you promise so many things, I owe myself wholly”; the Tournai manuscript reads “because you endured so much for me, I owe myself wholly”; Sommaius omits this sentence].

Indeed, I owe your love more than my whole self by as much as you are greater than I, for whom you gave yourself and to whom you promise yourself.

Grant, I beseech you, Lord, that through love I may taste what I taste through knowledge; that through affection I may feel what I feel through understanding. I owe more than my whole self, but I have neither more than this [Note: The manuscript Vict. 16 reads “neither more nor even this”] nor the ability to repay even this whole self by my own power.

Draw me, Lord, into your love—or rather, this whole self of mine. Everything that I am is yours by creation; make it wholly yours by love. [Note: The Bec., O., Vict. 16, Gem., S. Med., Cister., and Val-luc. manuscripts read: “to repay it wholly. Draw me, Lord, into your love, and this whole self. Everything that I am”; the Thuan. manuscript reads: “to repay it wholly. Draw you, Lord, into your love, or this whole self. Everything that I am”; the Tournai manuscript reads: “to repay it wholly. Everything that I am”; another reading is: “to repay it wholly. Draw me, Lord, into your love, or this whole self. Everything that I am.”]

Behold, Lord, my heart is before you. It strives, but by itself it cannot; do what it cannot do. Admit me into the chamber of your love. I ask, I seek, I knock.

You who make me ask, make me also receive. You give me to seek; grant me to find. You teach me to knock; open to the one who knocks. To whom do you give, if you deny the one who asks? Who finds, if the one who seeks is frustrated? To whom do you open, if you close against the one who knocks? What do you give to one who does not pray, if you deny your love to one who prays?

From you I have the desire; from you may I have the obtaining. Cling to him, cling insistently, my soul. Good, good Lord [Note: The manuscripts read “Good Lord, gracious Lord, do not”; the S. Med. manuscript reads “Good, good Lord, do not”; the Tournai manuscript reads “Good Lord, do not”; Val-luc. reads “O Lord, O good Jesus Christ”], do not reject her. She languishes from hunger for your love; refresh her. May your love satisfy her; may your affection enrich her; may your love fill her, occupy me wholly, and possess me wholly, because you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, are the one blessed God forever and ever. Amen [Note: The manuscripts of Thu., Rec., and 160, and Val-luc. and Cister. read “possess me wholly. Amen. My God. Amen.”; the Tournai manuscript reads “possess it wholly. Amen.”].

## MEDITATION XII. On the Humanity of Christ

The most holy birth and infancy of our Savior overflow completely with joy, piety, and usefulness: with joy insofar as they bring exultation, with piety insofar as they concern the Passion, and with usefulness insofar as they have significance.

For what is more joyful than to see the very one whom we know to be the creator of humanity as a human being? And what, again, ought to appear more pious to that same human being than to see with a clear eye that in this mediator between God and humanity, our Lord Jesus Christ, eternity begins in a marvelous and ineffable way, and sublimity is humbled?

He is conceived in the womb of a mother who is eternal in the bosom of the Father. Born eternally from the Father without a mother, he is born in time from a mother without a father. He is wrapped in swaddling clothes, he who clothed the earth with shrubs and trees, adorned the heavens with lights, and filled the sea with fish.

He whom the heavens of heavens cannot contain is enclosed within the narrowness of a manger and nourished with his mother’s milk. He advances in wisdom, whose wisdom neither begins nor ends; he who is also the wisdom of God the Father advances in age, although his eternity, just as it does not increase toward anything greater, so does not diminish toward anything less. He advances in grace, although he himself is the author, preserver, and rewarder of all grace.

He is subject to his parents, while every creature adores him and every knee is bowed before him. Let us add, if you please, that he is baptized—and indeed, the Lord by a servant, God by a human being, and the King by a soldier.

He is tempted by the devil, while angels minister to him. The food hungers, the fountain thirsts, the way grows weary, the height is brought low, power is weakened, strength is enfeebled, glory is insulted, joy mourns, delight suffers, majesty is humbled, and life dies.

Good Jesus, how sweet you are in the heart of one who thinks of you and loves you! And certainly I do not know—for I cannot fully comprehend it—why this is so: that you are far sweeter in the heart of one who loves you inasmuch as you are flesh than inasmuch as you are the Word; sweeter inasmuch as you are humble than inasmuch as you are exalted. Indeed, it is far sweeter for the memory of one who loves you to see you born in time from the Virgin Mother than generated by the Father before the morning star in splendor; to see you emptying yourself and taking the form of a servant than to see you, in the form of God, equal to God; sweeter to see you die on the wood before the Jews than to rule over the angels in heaven; to behold you subject to all things than set over all things; to see you, as a human being, endure human things than to see you, as God, perform divine things; to see you as the redeemer of those who are perishing than as the creator of things that did not exist.

O how sweet it is, good Jesus, to call you back in the secret of the heart: conceived for us in the Virgin without defilement, born without injury to her virginity, wrapped in swaddling clothes, laid in a manger, enduring insults, silent before reproaches, washing the feet of your disciples and wiping them with a linen cloth, praying at greater length through the night, emitting a sweat of blood, sold for thirty pieces of silver, handed over with a kiss, seized with swords and clubs, bound, judged, condemned to the scourging, led to execution like an innocent lamb, not opening your mouth when you were mistreated, not answering when you were accused on many charges, struck on the head, suffering blows on the face, beaten with scourges, livid with wounds, smeared with spittle, clothed in a scarlet cloak, crowned with thorns, worshiped in mockery, struck on the head with a reed, mocked in a white robe, condemned to death, carrying your cross and fastened upon it, praying for your crucifiers, given vinegar to drink and gall to eat, reviled by a robber, pouring out your blood through the five wounds of your body, bowing your head, giving up your spirit, commending your beloved soul into the hands of the Father, and enduring all these things for us. All these things shape and increasingly enlarge exultation, confidence and consolation, love and longing.

For who would not rejoice and exult? Who would not delight and give thanks beyond measure, seeing that his creator not only became human for him, but also endured things so harsh and so unworthy? What is ruminated upon in the mind more sweetly? What is tasted more deliciously? What is thought of more joyfully? Who will take away from me a place in the kingdom where he who is almighty is my brother and my flesh? What outcome can bring me any desolation, when so great a hope confers such certainty? How could any sadness find a place in one in whom this thought is continually active? Nor does it produce lesser confidence when it is itself carefully kindled toward the Creator. Certainly, consideration of Christ’s humanity forms a confidence secure in every respect, and in no way a presumptuous rashness.

How could I not hope to reach the lot of the elect, when I see the very Creator of all things dead for me? He poured out his blood for me from his side: how could I not presume myself redeemed, when I know that so great and so precious a price was given for me? He also poured out water for me: how could I not trust that I have been cleansed from all my defilements, since it is clear that the one cleansed by the water flowing from Christ’s inmost being has been cleansed? He was poured out, I say, and she was poured out: he for the redemption, she for the washing of the redeemed; he to redeem me, a captive, she to wash me, unclean.

The Son was handed over for me, a servant, so that by his death he might purchase an inheritance for me. How could I not believe myself an heir—indeed, an heir of God and coheir of Christ? (Romans 8:17.) When I was an enemy, I was reconciled to God through the death of his Son. How, now justified by his blood, shall I not be saved from wrath through him? The gracious Father did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for me. How, then, would he not also give me all things with him? (Romans 8:32.) Who will accuse me, when his love covers a multitude of sins? (1 Peter 4:8.) His blood cries from the earth more powerfully than Abel’s—and will so great and such a sound of crying not move the Father’s heart?

[Col. 0771D]

Far be it—again and again far be it—from me to lack the inward compassion of one who looks upon you, good Jesus, dying for me! You are crucified before my eyes, and no emotion touches my heart? Your sword appears to me, and it will not pass through my soul? Sweet Jesus, what benefit is there for me in sympathizing with you? Yet it is no less useful. How could it be less useful, when it is certain—if the one in whom you were speaking truly saw and felt it—that “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him”? (Romans 8:17.) And elsewhere: “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him.” (2 Timothy 2:12.)

For this compassion of which we speak to remain vigorous in the mind, it is necessary that love burn ardently within it, because the one whom we embrace with fervent love we certainly both pity in adversity and congratulate in prosperity. Jesus, neither my mind can contain nor my tongue express how worthy you are of being loved by me, since you have deigned to love me so greatly. You loved me and washed me from my sins in your blood (Revelation 1:5). For if I love you greatly, you certainly loved me first—and more. “In this,” says the Apostle, “the love of God is revealed: not that we loved God, but that he first loved us.” (1 John 4:10.) He loved when I did not love, because unless you loved one who did not love you, you would not make him one who loves.

I love you above all things, O most sweet Jesus, but far too little, because I love you far less than you deserve, most beloved, and therefore less than I ought. And who could do this? Someone can love you, by your gift, as much as he is able, but never as much as he ought. Who will return to you your innocent blood, of which not a drop but a flood flowed through the five parts of your body? You created me when I did not exist; you redeemed me when I was lost. But the sole cause of both my creation and my redemption was your love. Therefore, O Jesus, sweetness of my life, what did you see in me for which you would give so great a price? Absolutely nothing, except that it was thus pleasing before you. You gave much as Creator, but far more as Redeemer.

O how beautiful you are, Lord Jesus, and how gracious! Beautiful to those who see you; gracious to those who taste you. You are not known unless you are seen; you do not become sweet unless you are tasted. Make me seek you, find you when sought, hold you when found, so that you alone may be sweet, relished and pleasing to me. Make me recognize you, fear you, love you, desire you. Do not let me fall into love of temporal things. Alas, my Lord, for I cannot continually taste how gracious and sweet you are!

I am a sinner, O most merciful Jesus. Have mercy on me, you who came not to call the righteous but sinners (Matthew 9:13). O open fountain for the house of David (Zechariah 13:1), appear, pour yourself out, and wash me. For you are open to all who thirst for you, and you wash away all the filth of all who truly repent, O most sweet Jesus, giving them good in place of evil, a gift in place of iniquity, merit in place of sin, righteousness in place of crime, and grace in place of guilt.

King David experienced this. In his repentance he heard from your messenger: “The Lord has taken away your sin from you; you shall not die.” (2 Samuel 12:23.) In you he was washed with tears of repentance and cleansed from the stains of grave guilt. Your purity in him washed away the crime of adultery, and your mercy wiped away the cruelty of murder.

In you that prince of the apostles was cleansed, who wept bitterly for having denied what he had denied through fear. In you also that renowned sinful woman was made white, O purest and sweetest fountain; she merited such intimacy that she was the first to see the new glory of your resurrection and to announce it to the apostles. In you also was cleansed the man who, hanging beside you on the cross, acknowledged that he had received what his deeds deserved and asked you to remember him in your kingdom; he immediately merited to hear from you: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:45.)

And how many are daily enlightened and washed in you, gracious Jesus, from darkness to light and from filth to purity! Receive me, long exiled from you.

Sweetness of life and unfailing health, O good Jesus: if I have sown in the flesh, what shall I reap from the flesh except corruption? And if I have loved the world, what fruit shall I gain from it? Threefold tribute I used to pay to the Babylonian king in his wicked service. What is his service except sin? The tribute, moreover, is threefold: delight, consent and habit. This tribute was paid from the heart, mouth and deed.

See with what fires this cauldron was kindled, whose face was turned toward the face of the north, whose coals the enemy’s suggestion made to burn, scorching the thoughts of my mind. See the merciful God; see the threefold cord violently binding mind, tongue and body. “There was no soundness in me, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head.” (Isaiah 1:6.) Heal my soul, therefore, because I have sinned against you (Psalm 40:5). Do your work, then, gracious Jesus, and save me. For you are called Jesus for no other reason than that “you will save your people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21), you who live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## MEDITATION XIII. On Christ

A secret word is addressed by me to you, my Lord, King of the ages, Jesus Christ. The work of your hands presumes, in the boldness of love, to address you, desiring your beauty and longing to hear you. Desire of my heart, how long shall I endure your absence? How long shall I groan, and my eye shed tears after you? Beloved Lord, where do you dwell? Where is your lodging, in which you happily recline among your dearest companions and satisfy them with the manifestation of your glory? How happy, how illustrious, how holy—and with what avidity to be desired—is that place of divine delight, that place of everlasting pleasures!

My eye has not reached it, nor has my heart drawn near to the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden inwardly for your children. By its fragrance alone I am somehow sustained outside. The breath of your sweetness comes to me from afar; it is more to me than the scent of balsam and the fragrance of frankincense and myrrh, and of every kind of sweet-smelling perfume. It produces pure desires in me, whose burning is sweet, though scarcely bearable.

“For what have I in heaven?” (Psalm 72:25.) Who is my treasure in that heavenly chamber? What is my inheritance in the land of the living? Is it not Christ, my Lord, my only salvation, my entire good, my complete joy? And how shall I restrain my heart, Lord, so that it does not love you? If I do not love you, what shall I love? If I transfer my love away from you, where shall I place it worthily? Desirable Lord, where could my desires find rest outside you?

If my love extends its foot anywhere beyond you, it will be polluted; if my desires turn away from you, they will be empty. Are you not lovable and desirable above all that can be loved and desired? From you comes whatever beauty and worth every creature possesses. And what wonder if you alone surpass everything? You clothed the sun among the stars with its exceptional brightness, and you are brighter than the sun. Indeed, what is the sun, what is all created light in comparison with you, except darkness?

You adorned heaven with stars, the empyrean with angels, the air with birds, the waters with fish, and the earth with grasses, flowers and shrubs. But none of all these has beauty or loveliness beyond comparison with you, O fountain of all beauty, Lord Jesus. You gave honey its sweetness, and you are sweeter than honey. You gave oil its pleasantness, and you are more pleasant than oil. You bestowed on all spices their fragrances, and your fragrance, O Jesus, is sweeter and more pleasing than all spices.

Gold, precious and beautiful among all metals, was created by you in singular excellence. And what is this compared with the priceless Lord and the immense splendor into which the angels desire to look? Every precious stone is the work of your hands, desirable to behold: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, amethyst, sapphire, carbuncle and emerald. And what are these except straws compared with you, O King exceedingly beautiful and greatly to be loved?

Your work are the living and immortal gems with which, O wise Architect, at the beginning of the ages you beautifully differentiated the heavenly palace, to the praise and glory of the Father.

Through you thousands upon thousands continually move between heaven and earth in eager activity, to complete the Father’s mysteries, like busy bees arranging everything sweetly between their hives and flowers: an armed people who know neither stain nor delay in obedience. Through you hundreds of times ten thousand times ten thousand stand in the sanctuary of the heavenly temple, gazing upon the face of majesty with clear and unwavering sight, and sounding the harmony of an unceasing hymn to the glory of the triune and simple divinity. Through you the seraphim burn, through you the cherubim shine, through you the thrones judge.

You, our Lord, are an innocently burning fire, and through the immediate approach of your divinity the sacred order of the seraphim is wholly kindled with love and clothed in fiery radiance. It also scatters the abundance of its sweet burning among the other ranks that serve you, from whose fullness we taste—and do not [fully taste].

You, our God, are the true light, and the mountains receive light for your people, while through you yourself you pour abundantly upon the nearby eyes of the cherubim the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in you, and cause them to flow down to illuminate the subordinate chosen lamps of your wondrous tabernacle, which shine unquenchably before your face, Lord.

You, King of kings and great and awesome Judge of judges, sit upon lofty thrones, having above them only your own height: living and gracious seats, most peaceful and compacted in the uniformity of supreme tranquility. Through you they discern the paths of truth; through you they judge judgments of equity.

Lord and Ruler, the holy sublimity of the dominions adores you, extending its spirit toward divine things with singular generosity and, among the most noble heroes of your court, exercising through you the primacy of lofty rule without the height of arrogance.

Noble ornament of the principalities, through you, Lord my God, the exalted order of the principalities rules over the army of heaven without envious superiority. To fulfill the divine mysteries, in accordance with the disposition perceived inwardly in your heart, it provides the guidance of sweet instruction.

Yours is the power, Lord of the powers, of those who press down with a flaming weapon the necks of the infernal princes; and they fear you in this, that they cannot accomplish as much evil as they wish for our destruction.

Yours, O power of the Father, is all the marvel-working of the blessed virtues. Through their ministry it comes about that every age wonders at you and, falling silent before your marvels, cries out and says: “All that the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths.” (Psalm 135:6.)

Yours, O sweet Jesus, is the magnificence of the archangels, in whom your kindness performs a work of great condescension, since you do not disdain to send such glorious satraps of your palace into the weakness of this world, to assist our lowliness—we who are compared with clay and likened to dust and ashes.

Through them, at your command, the highest affairs of our salvation are administered, and the highest secrets of heavenly counsel are conveyed to us. Through them the healths of mortals are produced; through them the kingdoms and empires of the world stand. Among them we know your chief, Michael, the noble standard-bearer, citizen of heaven, who stands before the army of the living God, extending the sword of defense and thundering in a terrifying voice, “Who is like God?” against those who oppose him.

And is not that lovable innocence of the blessed angels also the precious work of your fingers, O Wisdom of God? Therefore you adorned them as though with incorruptible clothing on the day when you created them for the work of your sacred ministry. These are the living stars of the higher heaven, the lilies of the inner paradise, roses planted beside the water of Siloam, which flows in silence; they cling immovably to you through the roots of their minds.

O river of peace, O fragrance of the field of delights, O Wisdom alone encircling the circuit of heaven: from you they shine, gleam white and glow red—in abundant wisdom, in virginal purity, in everlasting fires of love.

This flowering youth, Lord, faithfully serves you in our weakness: in the darkness of this world it guides our steps with pedagogical leading by the hand; it repels hostile attacks from us; it announces to us the secrets of your will; it strengthens our minds when they have grown slack toward every good; it carries the incense of our prayers to the golden altar; and it continually pleads before the face of the gracious Father for us.

Thus, gracious Father, you still have some concern for us, though we remain far away. And if the tenth drachma, once slipped from your bosom and at last sought in your labors, has any worth, this is the work of your merciful gift, good Jesus. If this tenth string of divine praise has any sweet-sounding voice, your pleasant touch produces it in her, while on the ten-stringed psaltery you sing the Father’s glory.

Sing, Lord, as you sing; play a sweet melody to the Father with the swift movements of manifold graces. Touch those nine pure strings in heaven, which have never sounded anything sad. Touch also this heavy tenth string, whose upper part, already drawn out toward you, sounds joy, while its lower part, still bound to the earth, knows how to resound mournful sounds. [The final verb is uncertain in the supplied text: *roboare* may reflect an OCR corruption.]

As I consider attentively all the works of your power, O Only-Begotten of God, I am stunned and tremble with awe, because you appear glorious in them in every way. They are great, beautiful and exceedingly good, but compared with you they are regarded as almost nothing and emptiness.

Heaven and earth, and all their adornment, subsist through you as their author and governor; and all things proclaim you powerful and awesome, wise and beautiful, good and lovable. As light surpasses darkness, so you alone surpass all things.

And you are preserved in heaven, my God, as the reward of your servant; you yourself are both the giver and the gift of the salvation that my soul awaits from you. “And what has it desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm 72:25.) Why do I roll down from heaven to the center? What did I consider better or more lovable than you upon earth, so that I might draw my heart away from you to desire something in the world apart from you?

Why did I love, why did I desire, throughout my life, anything except you, Jesus my God? Why did I delay, why did I at any time cease to turn you over in my heart, embrace you with my whole mind, and delight all the inward parts of my spirit in your sweetness? Where was I when I was not with you in mind? Where did my desires flow when they did not have you alone?

God of my life, how vainly were my times consumed, how fruitlessly did they pass—times you gave me to do your will, and I did not do it! How many years, how many hours have perished for me, in which I lived before you without fruit? And how shall I stand? How shall I be able to lift my eyes to your face at that great examination of yours, if you command all my sins to be recalled, or my times, and require the fruit of each?

Most patient Father, let this not happen. Rather, let those times I lost—alas, far too many—be forgotten before you. And if I have usefully preserved any with your help, though their number, Lord, is small, make them remain in eternal memory. Beloved Father, at least let this remnant of my time be fruitful and sanctified in your grace, so that it may find a place in the days of eternity and be counted before you.

From this moment on, let all my desires grow hot and flow toward the Lord Jesus. Run—is it not enough that you have delayed until now? Hurry where you are going; seek the one whom you seek. “You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified.” (Mark 16:6.) “He has ascended into heaven; he is not here.” (Ibid.)

He is not where he was; he is not where he could not lay his noble head to rest; he is not where he walked amid tribulation, filled with contempt; he is not where he stood to be judged before Pilate; he is not where he stood rejected and mocked before Herod; he is not where he hung, spat upon, beaten, wounded and covered in blood, among criminals; he is not where he lay enclosed by a stone and guarded by the army of the nations.

Where, then, is the most loving Lord? He dwells in confidence, and no scourge approaches his dwelling. He ascended by his own power above the heights of heaven and above every excellence of the angels, to the throne of singular glory at the right hand of the Father, with whom, coeternal and consubstantial, he sits. Clothed in divine light and crowned with glory and honor, as befits the Only-Begotten of God, serene in joy and full of omnipotence, he is Lord in heaven and on earth.

There all the angels of God adore him, as does the entire multitude of the citizens of heavenly Zion. In him the hearts of all rejoice together; in his desirable face the eyes of all the good are nourished. The desires of all the saints flow toward him from every side. The entire heavenly city sings to him, applauds him and magnifies him, glorious in every way in his splendors.

“Exult and praise, dwelling-place of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 12:6.) Rejoice in your noble son, illustrious patriarchs, for all your expectation has been fulfilled in him. He is exceedingly exalted, and in him—that is, in your offspring—all nations shall be blessed; for so the divine word promised.

Rejoice in Jesus, the great prophet, you truthful prophets, for you see wonderfully and gloriously fulfilled everything that you announced about him in the Holy Spirit, and through him you have been found faithful in all your words.

Rejoice in the Lord Jesus, your teacher, illustrious leaders of heaven, blessed apostles; rejoice in him, and again I say, rejoice with Christ in familiar joy. For behold: the one whom you saw among you hungry and thirsty, weary and enduring the weaknesses of the flesh, rejected by all and reckoned among criminals—how he has conquered, how he reigns, how all things are beneath his feet, how gloriously he shines in the light of his dominion and his joy. He now has you as companions of his ineffable glory, you who once remained with him in his trials and shared his afflictions.

Adore now those sweet knees that bent before you to the ground while you sat at the most holy supper. Adore now those most sacred hands with which the King of kings deigned to wash and wipe the dust from your feet.

Rejoice in Jesus, the prince of your army, victorious martyrs, who handed over your souls to death for him; you possess as the reward of your struggle that very one for whom you gave yourselves to death—Jesus, the Son of God.

Rejoice in Jesus, supreme teacher of truth, venerable confessors and teachers, because the one whom you once confessed before human beings through sacred teachings and righteous works now confesses you before his Father and his holy angels.

Rejoice in Jesus, virgin and sanctifier of virgins, virgins who dwell in paradise, you who are like angels. Behold: the one whom you loved, whom you desired, whom you sought with burning desires, for whose love you rejected earthly bridegrooms and all the adornment of the world—you now see and now hold, the Son of the supreme King; now you rest in his chaste embraces, and no deceitful plotter can separate you from him.

But among all the inhabitants of heaven, let the richest joy be yours, O Mary, singular Virgin of virgins, rose of heavenly loveliness, brilliant star among the primordial lamps receptive of divine light.

In your sweetest son Jesus, rejoice alone above all others with great joy, because the one whom you bore as a human being and nourished at your own breasts, you adore with the angels and all the citizens of heaven as the living and true God.

Rejoice, happy mother, because the one whom you saw hanging on the wood of the cross, you see reigning in heaven with great glory. You see all the height of heavenly, earthly and infernal beings bowed before his majesty, and all the strength of his enemies crushed.

The fullness of the saints is a joy of joys for you. Blessed Jerusalem, our mother, who are above, celebrate a joyful and unceasing festival in the peaceful vision of your Jesus, the author of your freedom.

And now, my soul, raise yourself once more with whatever effort you can, and join the holy multitudes rejoicing in the Lord Jesus. Travel there in the vehicle of faith and hope; dwell there through the ardor of love, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3:1). Direct the eye of your mind toward the light of his face. Examine and kiss, with joyful devotion, each place of his blessed wounds, from which those precious streams of holy blood flowed—the blood by which the Only-Begotten of God valued you and sanctified you for eternal life.

Jesus: let whoever does not love you be accursed. Let whoever does not love you be filled with bitterness. Your love, Lord, is chaste and admits no impurity. The taste of your love is sober and alienates no mind from what is right. Your love is sweet and contains nothing bitter; indeed, it sweetens the world’s bitter things and makes its sweet things bitter.

It is not constricted amid straits or compressed amid pressures. It does not perish in poverty or contract through sorrow. Amid the labors of the hands it remains even-tempered; amid threats it is secure; amid flatteries incorrupt; amid torments unconquered; in death it is always alive.

As a miser rejoices in a treasure, and as a mother delights in the love of her only son, so the joy and delight of your love, sweet Jesus, is pleasing to the soul that loves you. The sweetness of honey, the pleasantness of milk, the intoxicating taste of wine, and all delights do not please the throats of those who taste them as your love pleases the minds of those who love you.

[Col. 0778D]

O sweet Jesus, most desirable living bread, sweet cluster of grapes, blended oil, gentle lamb, strong lion, beautiful panther, innocent dove, swift eagle, morning star, eternal sun, angel of peace, fountain-light of everlasting lights: may every good sense attuned to your praise love you, delight in you and admire you, O God of my heart and my portion, Jesus Christ.

May my heart fail through its spirit, and my flesh through its desires; may you live in me; may the living coal of your love grow hot in my spirit and rise into a perfect fire. May your grace warm and nourish that fire in me, so that it burns continually on the altar of my heart; may it glow in my marrow and blaze in the hidden places of my soul; and on the day of my consummation may it be found consummated before you.

On the day when you see me snatched away from this mortal tunic that I now wear, May your love surround me and be for my soul like a garment of beauty, so that it may be found not naked but clothed, and may have something with which its weaknesses can be hidden from your eyes.

May the fervor of your love keep far from me the alien fire, the fire that burns through your adversaries; may it lift my soul to you, its Creator, and immerse it sufficiently in your divine light.

Lord Jesus, may all who love you be filled with your blessings. May those who approach you be inscribed in heaven, so that there may be peace for them beneath the shelter of your wings forever (Psalm 63:8). To you, Only-Begotten of God, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, be unfailing praise, inviolate honor and enduring kingship, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0779B]

## MEDITATION XIV

[Note: It has been collated with the Somnium edition and with volume IX of Augustine; for it is not found in our manuscripts. The work is entitled *The Book of Blessed Anselm on the Salvation of the Soul*, which may also be called the *Enchiridion*, or manual; elsewhere it is entitled *A Little Book on the Contemplation of Christ*, or *On the Word of God, by Which the Dormant Memory of Heavenly Desire May Be Renewed*. In the *Somnium*: *Manual of Saint Augustine*, or *A Little Book on Contemplation*, etc., as in Raynaldus’s edition.]

### PROLOGUE

Since we are placed amid snares, we easily grow cold toward heavenly desire. Therefore we continually need a reminder [variant: protection], so that, awakened to our true and highest good, God, we may return to him whenever we have drifted away.

For this reason, not through the rash presumption of self-confidence but through great love of my God, I have devoted myself to this little work in his praise, so that from the more elegant sayings of the holy Fathers I might always have with me a brief, manual word about my God; and whenever I grow lukewarm, I might be kindled to his love by the fire of its reading [variant: love].

### I

[Note: “Now be present,” etc. In the *Somnium* the Prologue continues.]

Now be present to me, my God, whom I seek, whom I love, whom I confess with heart and mouth, and whom with all the power I possess I praise and adore.

My mind, devoted to you, kindled by love of you, breathing toward you, longing for you, desiring to see you alone, finds nothing sweet except to speak of you, hear of you, write of you, converse about you, and frequently turn your glory over beneath its heart, so that the sweet memory of you may be some rest for me amid these storms.

Therefore I call upon you, most desired one; I cry to you with a great cry from my whole heart. And when I call upon you, I call upon you within myself, since I would not exist at all unless you were in me; and unless I were in you, you would not be in me.

You are in me because you remain in my memory. From it I came to know you, and in it I find you when I remember you; and in you, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are, I delight because of you.

[Col. 0779D]

You, Lord, fill heaven and earth, bearing all things without burden, filling all things without being enclosed.

[Note: “You, Lord, fill heaven,” etc. In the *Somnium* chapter 1 begins here, under the title “On the Wonderful Essence of God.”] Always active, always at rest. Gathering and lacking nothing. Seeking, although nothing is lacking to you. Loving, yet not burning with agitation [variant in the *Somnium*: “and not estimating”]. Jealous, yet secure. You repent, yet do not grieve. You grow angry, yet remain tranquil. You change your works, yet do not change your purpose. You receive what you find, yet have never lost anything.

Never needy, yet rejoicing in gains. Never greedy, yet demanding interest. You give more than is owed to one to whom you owe nothing, or more is always given to you so that you become a debtor. And who has anything that is not yours? [Variant in the *Somnium*: “And who has anything?”]

You repay debts while owing nothing to anyone. You give debts away while losing nothing. You who are everywhere and wholly everywhere. You can be sensed but cannot be seen. You are absent nowhere, yet you are far from the thoughts of the wicked. You are absent neither even where you are far away, because where you are not present by grace, you are present through punishment.

You are present everywhere and can scarcely be found. We follow you as you stand, but cannot seize you. You hold all things, fill all things, embrace all things, surpass all things, sustain all things. You teach the hearts of the faithful without the noise of words. You are not extended through places, nor varied by times, nor do you have approaches and withdrawals.

You dwell in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see (1 Timothy 6:16). Remaining at rest in yourself, you encircle the whole everywhere. For you cannot be split or divided, because you are truly one; nor are you made into parts, but, wholly, you hold the whole, fill the whole, illuminate the whole and possess the whole.

If books filled the entire world [Note: In the *Somnium*: “If books filled the entire measure” (*modum*). Here begins chapter 2, under the title “On the Unspeakable Knowledge of God”], your ineffable knowledge could not be expressed. Since you are unspeakable, you cannot in any way be written down or confined.

You are the fountain of divine light and the sun of eternal brightness. You are great without quantity [Note: In the *Somnium*: “without quality,” rather than “without quantity”], and therefore immeasurable. You are good without quality, and therefore truly and supremely good; and no one is good except you alone.

Your will is your work, and your willing is your ability. Whatever you created from nothing, you made by will alone. You possess your entire creation without any need, govern it without labor, and rule it without weariness; there is nothing that disturbs the order of your government, either in the highest or in the lowest things.

You exist in all places without being located, contain all things without spatial enclosure, and are present everywhere without position or movement. You are not the author of evil, which you cannot do. You can do everything, and you have never regretted having done anything.

By your goodness we were made; by your justice we suffer punishments; by your mercy we are liberated. Your omnipotence governs, rules and fills all that it has created. We do not say that you fill all things so that they contain you; rather, they themselves are contained by you.

Nor do you fill all things piecemeal, nor should it in any way be thought that each thing receives you according to the size of its portion—that the greatest receives more and the smallest less—since rather you yourself are wholly in all things, and all things are in you.

Your omnipotence encloses all things, and no one will be able to find an avenue by which to escape your power. For whoever does not have you as propitious will by no means escape you as angry.

[Col. 0781A]

## II  
[Note: [Col. 0781D] Chapter 2. In Som[nalius], Chapter 3. On the desire of the soul thirsting for God.]

Therefore I invoke you, most merciful God, into my soul, which you prepare to receive you through the desire that you inspire in it. Enter it, I beg you, and fit it to yourself, so that you may possess what you made and remade; so that I may have you like a seal upon my heart. I beseech you, most merciful one, do not abandon me as I call upon you; for before I invoked you, you called and sought me, so that I, your servant, might seek you, find you by seeking, and love you once found. I sought and found you, Lord, and I desire to love you. Increase my desire and grant what I ask; for even if you gave me everything that you made, it would not suffice your servant unless you gave yourself also. Give yourself, then, to me, my God; restore yourself to me. Behold, I love you; and if that is too little, let me love you more powerfully. I am therefore held by love of you, I burn with desire for you, I delight in the sweet memory of you. Behold, while my mind sighs for you and meditates upon your ineffable mercy, the burden of the flesh itself weighs less, the tumult of thoughts ceases, and the weight of mortality and miseries does not dull me as usual; all things are silent, everything is tranquil. The heart burns, the spirit rejoices, memory is vigorous, understanding shines, and the whole spirit, kindled by desire for the vision of you, sees itself carried away by love of invisible things.

May my spirit assume wings like an eagle’s; may it fly and not grow weary; may it fly and reach the beauty of your house and the throne of your glory. There, upon the table of refreshment of the citizens above, may it feed upon your eyes in a place of pasture beside streams overflowing. Be our exultation, you who are our hope, salvation, and redemption. Be our joy, you who will be our reward. May my soul always seek you, and grant that it may not grow weary in seeking.

## III  
[Note: [Col. 0781D] Chapter 3. In Som[nalius], Chapter 4. On the misery of the soul that does not love or seek our Lord Jesus Christ.]

Woe to the wretched soul that does not seek or love Christ: it remains dry and miserable. Whoever does not love you, God, loses what gives life. Whoever is concerned to live not for you, Lord, is nothing and exists for nothing. Whoever refuses to live for you is dead. Whoever does not find wisdom in you is foolish.

Most merciful Lord, to you I commend, surrender, and yield myself, through whom I exist, live, and understand. In you I trust, hope, and place all my hope, through whom I shall rise again, live, and rest. I desire, love, and adore you; with you I shall remain, reign, and be blessed.

The soul that neither seeks nor loves you loves the world, serves sins, and is subject to vices; it never rests [Note: [Col. 0781D] “It never rests” in Som[nalius]: “never tranquil”], is never secure. May my mind always serve you, most merciful one. May my pilgrimage always sigh for you; may my heart burn with love of you. May my soul rest in you, my God; may it contemplate you in ecstasy of mind, sing your praises with jubilation, and may this be my consolation in this exile of mine. May my mind flee beneath the shadow of your wings from the heats of this world’s thoughts. May my heart rest in you—my heart, a great sea swelling with waves.

O rich provider of every good banquet, most generous God who lavishly grants heavenly satiety, give food to the weary, gather the scattered, free the captive, and restore what has been torn apart. Behold, he stands at the door and knocks. I beseech you, by the bowels of your mercy with which, rising from on high, you visited us (Luke 1:78), command that the miserable man who knocks be allowed to enter, so that with free steps he may come to you, rest in you, and be refreshed by you with heavenly bread. For you are the bread and fountain of life; you are the light of eternal brightness; you are everything by which the righteous who love you live.

## IV  
[Note: [Col. 0781D] Chapter 4. In Som[nalius], Chapter 5. On the soul’s desire.]

God, light of the hearts that see you, life of the souls that love you, strength of the thoughts that seek you, grant that I may cling to your holy love. Come, I beg you, into my heart, and intoxicate it with the abundance of your delight, so that I may forget these temporal things. I am ashamed and weary of suffering such things as this world does. What I see is sad to me; everything I hear about transitory things is burdensome. Help me, Lord my God, and give joy to my heart; come to me, so that I may see you.

But the house of my soul is narrow until you come to it and enlarge it through yourself. It is ruinous; rebuild it. It contains many things that offend your eyes—I confess and know this—but who will cleanse it, or to whom besides you shall I cry? Cleanse me from my secret faults, Lord, and spare your servant from those of others (Psalm 18:13). Make me, sweet Christ, good Jesus, make me, I beg you, through love and desire for you, lay down the burden of bodily desires and earthly cravings. Let the soul rule the flesh, reason rule the soul, and your grace rule reason; subject me inwardly and outwardly to your will.

Grant me that my heart, my tongue, and all my bones may praise you. Enlarge my mind and lift the gaze of my heart, so that my spirit, even in swift thought, may reach you, eternal Wisdom abiding above all things. Release me, I beg you, from the bonds by which I am held fast, so that, abandoning all these things, I may hasten to you [Note: [Col. 0781D] “May hasten to you” in Som[nalius]: “may hasten to serve you”], cling to you alone, and attend to you alone.

## V  
[Note: [Col. 0781D] Chapter 5. In Som[nalius], Chapter 6. On the blessedness of the soul released from its earthly prison.]

Blessed is the soul that, released from its earthly prison, seeks heaven in freedom; that sees you, sweetest Lord, face to face; that is troubled by no fear of death but rejoices in the incorruption of everlasting glory. It is tranquil and secure; it no longer fears either the enemy or death. It possesses you, its gracious Lord, whom it sought for so long and always loved; joined to choirs that sing hymns, it eternally sings songs of the perpetual festival, sweet as honey, to the praise of your glory, good King Christ Jesus. For you give it drink from the abundance of your house and from the torrent of your delight (Psalm 35:9).

Blessed is the fellowship of the citizens above, and glorious the solemn assembly of all who return to you from the sad labor of our pilgrimage to the loveliness of beauty, the splendor of every brightness, and the dignity of all elegance, where your citizens continually behold you, Lord. There one hears nothing at all that could disturb the mind.

What songs, what organs, what melodies, what harmonies are sung there without end? There the melodious instruments of hymns always resound, together with the sweetest melody of angels and the wondrous songs of songs, which the citizens above sing to your praise and glory. Bitterness and every harshness of gall have no place in your realm. There is neither evil nor wickedness; neither adversary nor assailant; nor any enticement to sin. There is no want, no disgrace, no quarrel, no reproach, no accusation, no fear, no unrest, no punishment, no uncertainty, no violence, no discord. Rather, there are supreme peace, perfect love, eternal jubilation and praise of God, secure rest without end, and joy always in the Holy Spirit.

O how fortunate I shall be if I hear the most delightful songs of your citizens, honey-sweet verses bringing forth praises to the supreme Trinity with due honor! But I shall be exceedingly blessed if I myself should deserve to sing to the Lord Jesus Christ a song from the sweet songs of Zion.

## VI  
[Note: [Col. 0783D] Chapter 6. In Som[nalius], Chapter 7. On the joy of paradise.]

O life that truly lives, eternal life, eternally blessed life! Where there is joy without sorrow, rest without labor, dignity without trembling, riches without loss, health without sickness, abundance without decline, life without death, perpetuity without corruption, blessedness without calamity; where all good things exist in perfect love [Note: [Col. 0783D] “All good things in” in Som[nalius]: “all things in”]; where there are form and vision face to face; where there is complete knowledge in all things and through all things; where the supreme goodness of God is seen and the illuminating light is glorified by the saints; where the present majesty of God is contemplated, and the minds of those who gaze are satisfied without weariness by this food of life.

They always see and desire to see; they desire without anxiety and are satisfied without disgust. There the true Sun of righteousness refreshes all by the wondrous vision of its beauty, and so illumines all the citizens of the heavenly homeland that they themselves shine—light, that is, illuminated by God; light [Note: [Col. 0783D] “Through God, light” in Som[nalius]: “through divine light”] shining beyond all the splendor of our sun and the brightness of all the stars. Clinging to the immortal Godhead, they thereby become immortal and incorruptible [Note: [Col. 0783D] “Incorruptible” in Som[nalius]: “incorporeal”], according to the promise of the Lord Savior: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory; that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, and they also may be one in us” (Job 17:22–24).

## VII  
[Note: [Col. 0783D] Chapter 7. In Som[nalius], Chapter 8. On the kingdom of heaven.]

The kingdom of heaven, the most blessed kingdom, a kingdom without death and without an end, to which no periods of time succeed throughout the ages; where the unbroken day without night does not know how to possess time; where the victorious soldier, after his labor, is heaped with unspeakable gifts.

“Noble, with an everlasting crown embracing his head.”

Would that, once the burden of my sins had been removed, divine mercy should command me, the least of Christ’s servants, to lay down this burden of flesh, so that I might pass into the eternal joys of his city and rest there; that I might take my place among the holiest choirs above and stand with the blessed spirits before the glory of the Creator; that I might see the face of God; that no fear of death might touch me; that, secure in the incorruption of perpetual immortality, I might rejoice; that, joined to the one who knows all things, I might lose all the blindness of ignorance; that I might regard all earthly things as of little worth and no longer deem myself worthy to look upon or remember this valley of tears, where life is laborious, life corruptible, life full of every bitterness, life mistress of evils and servant of hell.

Humors swell it; pains wear it down; heats dry it; the air makes it sick; foods bloat it; fasts emaciate it; amusements loosen it; sorrows consume it; anxiety constricts it; security dulls it; riches make it boastful; poverty casts it down; youth exalts it; old age bends it; sickness breaks it; grief depresses it; the devil lies in wait for it; the world flatters it; the flesh delights it; the soul is blinded; the whole human being is troubled! And after so many and such great evils comes furious death, bringing such an end to empty joys that, once they have ceased to exist, they seem never to have existed.

But what praises, what thanks can we render to you, our God, who even amid these great sorrows of our mortality never cease to console us through the wondrous visitation of your grace? Behold me, a wretched man full of many sorrows: while I fear the end of my life, while I consider my sins, while I dread your judgment, while I think upon the hour of death, while I shudder at the punishments of Tartarus, while I do not know with what strictness and scrutiny you will weigh my works, while I utterly do not know by what end I shall close them, and while I turn these and many other matters over within my heart, you are present, Lord God, ready to console me in your accustomed goodness.

Amid these complaints, these excessive tears, and the deep sighs of my heart, you take my sorrowful and anxious mind over the high ridges of the mountains to the beds of spices, and place me in a pasture beside streams of sweet waters. There you prepare before my eyes a table furnished with many things, to give rest to my weary spirit and gladden my sad heart. At last refreshed by these delights and forgetful of my many miseries, lifted above the height of the earth, I rest in you, true peace [Note: [Col. 0783D] “I rest in peace.” Som[nalius] adds here: “Chapter 27.”].

# MEDITATION XV  
[Note: [Col. 0783D] Saint Anselm wrote this for his sister.]

On the memory of Christ’s past benefits, the experience of present benefits, and the expectation of future ones

What excites love of God ought never to weary anyone who hears it. It is read in the Gospel that two sisters loved the Lord with intense love; and although both loved God and their neighbor, Martha was especially occupied with serving her neighbors, while Mary drew love from the divine fountain (Luke 10:39–42).

Two things belong to love of God: the feeling of the mind and the feeling expressed in works. The latter consists in the practice of virtues; the former, in the sweetness of spiritual taste. The practice of virtues is commended in an established manner of life, in fasts, vigils, work, reading, prayer, silence, poverty, and other such things; the feeling of the mind is nourished by salutary meditation.

Therefore, so that that most sweet love of Jesus may grow in your affections, you need a threefold meditation: on the past, the present, and the future—that is, on remembrance of past things, experience of present things, and consideration of future things.

When your mind has been cleansed of the tumult of thoughts through the practice of virtues, turn your purified eyes backward. First, enter with blessed Mary into the chamber, unfold the books in which the Virgin’s childbirth and Christ’s coming are foretold, and await the angel’s arrival. See him enter and hear him greet her. Then, filled with wonder and ecstasy, greet your most sweet Lady Mary together with the greeting angel, crying out: “Hail, Mary” (Luke 1:27), and so forth.

Repeating this frequently, contemplate and marvel at what this fullness of grace may be, from which the whole world borrowed grace; and what sort of Word became flesh. Contemplate and marvel at the Lord who fills earth and heaven, yet was enclosed within the womb of one young woman whom the Father sanctified, the Son made fruitful, and the Holy Spirit overshadowed.

O sweet Lady, with what sweetness were you intoxicated, with what fire of love were you kindled, when you felt in mind and womb the presence of such majesty; when he took flesh for himself from your flesh and fashioned from your holy members the members in which the whole fullness of divinity would dwell bodily (Colossians 2:9)! All these things happened for you, O Virgin, so that you might love the Virgin whom you resolved to imitate, and the Son of the Virgin to whom you were betrothed.

Now climb with your sweetest Lady into the hill country. Behold the embrace of the barren woman and the Virgin, and the service of their greeting, in which the servant recognized and greeted with unspeakable joy the Lord, the herald the Judge, the voice the Word—while he was enclosed within the aged woman’s womb and the latter within the Virgin’s womb.

Blessed are the wombs in which the Savior of the whole world arose and, once the darkness of sorrow had been driven away, everlasting joy was foretold. Run, I beg you, run; mingle with such great joys; prostrate yourself at the feet of both; embrace your bridegroom in the womb of one and venerate his friend in the womb of the other.

From there follow the Mother with complete devotion to Bethlehem. Turn aside with her into the lodging, stand beside her, and assist her as she gives birth. When the little child has been placed in the manger, burst into a cry of exultation, shouting with Isaiah: “A little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:7), and embrace that sweet manger. Let love soften your modesty and affection drive away fear, so that you may press your lips to the most holy feet and kiss his knees.

Then consider inwardly the shepherds’ night watches, marvel at the army of angels, join your prayers to the heavenly melody, singing together in heart and voice: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14).

Do not pass over the gifts of the Magi in your meditation, nor leave the one fleeing into Egypt without company. Let the eye of devotion behold little Jesus sweetly suckling the sweet breasts of the glorious Virgin Mother, handling his mother’s breasts in a child’s manner, and smiling at his mother. What is more pleasing to see? What more delightful?

Behold him who is boundless, hanging by his little arms around his mother’s neck, and say: “I am blessed, and more blessed still, while I see him whom kings desired to see and did not see” (Matthew 13:17). He is worthy to be seen, for he is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3).

Think and think again with what feeling and what thoughts that sweetest Mother of his was filled when, rejoicing and glad, she held in her arms the Lord so great and yet so little; when, as he delighted in infancy, she shared his joy with frequent kisses; when she consoled him as he wept upon her knees by whatever means she could; and when, finally, with one care and then another, to which maternal affection instructed her, she diligently caressed him according to his changing needs.

Suppose that what is said is true: that he was seized by robbers on the road and rescued through the assistance of a certain young man. This man, they say, was the son of the chief of the robbers. Having obtained his booty, when he saw the little child in his mother’s lap, such majesty of splendor appeared in his exceedingly beautiful face that, certain he was more than human, the young man, growing warm with love, embraced him and said: “O most blessed of little ones, if another occasion for mercy toward me should present itself, remember me then, and do not forget this moment.”

They say that this was the robber who, crucified at God’s right hand, rebuked the other who was blaspheming, saying: “Do you not even fear God?” (John 23:40), and so forth. Then, turning to the Lord and seeing in him the majesty that had appeared in the child, mindful of his pledge, he said: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (ibid., 42). Thus, as an incentive to love, I think it not unhelpful to use this opinion, while removing all rashness of affirmation.

Moreover, do you not think that something sweet will come to you if you contemplate him at Nazareth as a child among children [Note: [Col. 0785D] Perhaps “among his parents”], if you behold him obeying his mother and assisting his foster father at his work [Note: [Col. 0785D] Perhaps “marveling”]? What if, when he was twelve years old, you follow him with his parents as they go up to Jerusalem, and, when they return without knowing that he has remained in the city, seek him with his mother for three days? O what a flood of tears will flow when you hear the Mother striking her Son with a kind of sweet reproach: “Son, why have you treated us so?” (Luke 2:48).

But if you delight in following the Virgin Bridegroom wherever he goes (Revelation 14:4), examine his higher and more hidden things, so that in the river Jordan you may hear the Father in the voice, see the Son in the flesh, and see the Holy Spirit in the dove. There, invited to a spiritual wedding, you receive the Bridegroom given by the Father, purification from the Son, and the pledge of love from the Holy Spirit.

After this, beloved Jesus consecrated to you the secrets of solitude and sanctified for you the fast that had to be undertaken, teaching you the struggle with the cunning enemy. Carefully attend to the things done there, done for you, and the manner in which they were done. Love him by whom they were done, and imitate what was done.

Now let that woman caught in adultery come to mind, and remember what Jesus did and said when he was asked to pronounce judgment. He cast his eyes upon the ground, lest by looking at the accused he should perhaps overwhelm her with shame. For, by writing on the ground, he showed that they were earthly, not heavenly, when he said: “Let the one among you who is without sin first cast a stone at her” (John 8:7).

O wondrous and unquenchable kindness of Christ! Consider how piously and cautiously he freed the woman whom he could justly have condemned. When his sentence had crushed them all and driven them from the temple, imagine how gently he raised his eyes upon her and how sweetly and tenderly he pronounced the sentence of her absolution. Suppose that he sighed and wept when he said: “Woman, has no one condemned you?” (ibid., 10), and so forth.

Blessed, so to speak, is this adulterous woman, who is absolved from the past and made secure concerning the future. Good Jesus, when you say, “Neither will I condemn you” (ibid., 11), who will condemn? “It is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns?” (Romans 8:33–34.) Let your voice be heard thereafter: “Go, and from now on do not sin anymore” (John 8:11).

Now enter the house of the Pharisee. Observe your Lord reclining there. Approach with the most blessed sinful woman to his feet; wash them with tears, wipe them with your hair, caress them with kisses, and cherish them with ointments. Are you not already drenched in the sacred fragrance of that liquid? If he still denies you his feet, persist, pray, lift your eyes heavy with tears, and by your sighs and inexpressible groans wrest from him what you ask.

Struggle with him, like Jacob (Genesis 32:24), so that he may rejoice at being overcome. At times it will seem to you that he turns his eyes away, closes his ears, and hides the feet you desire. Nevertheless, persist, in season and out of season (2 Timothy 4:2), and cry: “How long shall I cry, and you will not hear?” (Habakkuk 1:2.) “Restore to me, good Jesus, the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 50:14), because “my heart has said to you: I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will seek” (Psalm 26:8). Surely he will not deny a virgin the feet that he offered to be kissed by a sinful woman.

Nor will you pass by that house where a paralytic is lowered through the roof tiles before his feet, where mercy and power meet. “Son,” he says, “your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2). O wondrous clemency! O unspeakable mercy! The blessed man received forgiveness of his sins, which he had not requested, which confession had not preceded, which satisfaction had not earned, and which contrition had not demanded. He asked for bodily health, not that of the soul, and received health of both body and soul.

Truly, Lord, life is in your will. If you have determined to save us, no one can prevent it. If you have determined otherwise, no one dares say: “Why do you act so?” Pharisee, why do you murmur? “Is your eye evil because he is good?” (Matthew 9:15.) Surely he has mercy on whom he wishes (Romans 9:18); let us weep and pray that he may wish it.

Let prayer also grow rich through good works; let devotion increase and love be awakened. Let pure hands be lifted in prayer—hands not stained by the blood of impurity, not defiled by illicit touch, not embittered by greed. Let the heart also be lifted, without anger or disputation: a heart calmed by tranquility, composed by peace, and washed clean by a pure conscience.

Yet this paralytic is not recorded to have undertaken any of these things beforehand, and nevertheless he is recorded to have earned forgiveness of all his sins. Such is the power of his ineffable mercy: just as it is blasphemous to detract from it, so it is utterly foolish to presume upon it. He can effectively say to anyone he wishes the same thing he said to the paralytic: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:5). But whoever expects this to be said to him without his own labor, contrition, confession, or even prayer will never have his sins forgiven.

But we must leave this place and come to Bethany, where the most sacred bonds of friendship are consecrated by the Lord’s authority. For “Jesus loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus” (John 11:5). No one doubts that this was said because of the special privilege of friendship, by which they clung to him with a more intimate affection. Those sweet tears are witnesses—tears with which he wept together with those who were weeping, and which the whole people interpreted as a sign of love: “See how he loved him” (John 11:36).

“And they made him a supper there, and Martha served; Lazarus was one of those reclining at table. Mary took a pound of ointment” (John 12:2–3), and so forth. Rejoice, I beg you, to be present at this banquet. Distinguish the duties of each person. Martha served; Lazarus reclined at table; Mary anointed. The last is your part: break open there the alabaster of your heart, and whatever devotion, whatever love, whatever desire, whatever affection you possess, pour it all over the head of your Bridegroom, adoring God in the man and the man in God.

If the traitor grows angry, murmurs, and envies; if he calls devotion waste, do not be concerned. “Why this waste?” he says. “This ointment could have been sold for much” (Mark 14:4), and so forth. The Pharisee murmurs, envying the penitent woman; Judas murmurs, envying the outpouring of the ointment. But the Judge does not accept the accusation; he absolves the accused: “Let her alone,” he says, “for she has done a good work” (ibid., 6), and so forth.

Let Martha labor, serve, and prepare hospitality for the stranger, food for the hungry, drink for the thirsty, clothing for the cold. I belong to Mary alone, and she to me. Let her give everything she has; from me let her await whatever she desires. Why, then, do you advise Mary to leave the feet she sweetly kisses, turn her eyes away from that most beautiful face she contemplates, and withdraw her hearing from his sweet speech by which she is refreshed?

But now let us rise and leave this place. “Where?” you ask. Certainly to accompany the Lord of heaven and earth as he sits upon a donkey, marveling at all that is done for you, and to join your voice to the praises of the children, crying: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matthew 21:9), and so forth.

Now ascend with him into the large upper room, furnished and prepared (Mark 14:15), and rejoice to take part in the delights of the saving supper. Let love overcome modesty and affection exclude fear, so that at least from the crumbs of his table he may give alms to the beggar.

Or stand at a distance, and, like a poor person looking toward a rich man, stretch out your hand to receive something; reveal your hunger through tears. When he rises from supper, girds himself with a towel, and pours water into a basin (John 13:4–5), consider what majesty and power wash and wipe human feet, and what kindness touches the traitor’s footprints with sacred hands.

Look and wait, and finally offer your own feet to him to be washed, because whoever is not washed by him will have no part with him (ibid., 8). Why are you now hurrying to leave? Wait a little. Do you see, I ask you, who that person is who reclined upon his breast (ibid., 25) and rested his head in his bosom? Blessed is whoever he is. O indeed, now I see! His name is John.

O John, what sweetness, grace, and delight, what light and devotion, were you drawing from that fountain? There surely are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). There is the fountain of mercy, the dwelling place of compassion, the honeycomb of eternal sweetness.

Whence came all these things to you, O John? Were you more exalted than Peter, holier than Andrew, or more beloved than all the apostles? This is the special privilege of virginity: because you are a virgin, chosen by the Lord and more beloved than the others.

Now rejoice, virgin; draw nearer, and do not delay to claim some portion of this sweetness. If you cannot have the greater portion, leave to John the breast where he intoxicates himself with the wine of joy in contemplating the Godhead; run to the breasts of the humanity and draw out the milk by which you may be nourished.

Meanwhile, when he commended his disciples to the Father in that most holy prayer, saying, “Father, keep them in your name” (John 17:11), bow your head, so that you may deserve to hear: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (ibid., 24).

It is good for you to be here, but we must leave. He will go ahead to the Mount of Olives; follow him. Although he withdrew into solitude with Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, observe from a distance how he took our need upon himself. See how he whose all things are began to be afraid and troubled. “My soul is sorrowful,” he says (Matthew 26:38), and so forth. Whence is this, my God?
