You show such compassion toward me by presenting yourself as man that you seem, in a certain way, not to know that you are God. You pray prostrate upon your face, and sweat came to be (Luke 22:44), and so forth.

Why do you stand still? Run, lick those sweetest drops, and lick the dust from his feet. Do not sleep with Peter, lest you deserve to hear: “Could you not watch with me one hour?” (Matthew 26:40.)

But behold, the traitor goes ahead, followed by a crowd of impious men. Judas offers a kiss, and they lay hands upon Jesus; they seize their Lord and hold him bound, and bind those sweet hands with cords. Who could endure it? I know that compassion now occupies your heart and zeal inflames all your inward parts. Let the one who suffers for you endure, I beg you. Why do you desire a sword? Why do you grow angry? Why are you indignant?

If, like Peter—or anyone else—you cut off an ear, if you remove an arm with the sword, if you sever a foot, he will restore everything. Even if you kill someone, he will undoubtedly raise him up. Rather, follow him to the courtyard of the high priest, and wash with your tears his most beautiful face, which they smear with spittle.

Observe with what compassionate eyes, how mercifully and effectively, he looked upon Peter when he denied him three times, and how Peter, turning and coming to himself, wept bitterly. Would that your sweet eye, good Jesus, might look upon me, who so many times have denied you at the voice of an insolent servant—namely, my flesh—through my worst deeds and desires.

But now, at daybreak, he is handed over to Pilate. There he is accused and remains silent, because he was led like a sheep to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7; Acts 8:32). See and attend to how he stands before the governor, head bowed, eyes lowered, face peaceful, speech restrained, ready for insults and prepared for blows.

I know that you will no longer be able to endure seeing his sweetest back worn by scourges, his face struck with slaps, his tender head crowned with thorns, or his right hand—which rules heaven and earth—dishonored with a reed.

Behold, he is led out, scourged, bearing a crown of thorns and a purple garment, and Pilate says: “Behold the man” (John 19:5). Truly he is a man—who could doubt it? The wounds of the rods, the bruising of the injuries, and the foulness of the spittle bear witness.

Now recognize, Zabule, that he is a man. “Truly this is a man,” you say. “But what is this?” you ask. What is it, then, that amid so many insults he does not grow angry as a man, is not moved as a man, and does not resent his torturers as a man? Therefore he is more than a man. But who recognizes him? He is certainly recognized as a man enduring the judgments of the impious on earth, but he will be recognized as God when he executes judgment.

You noticed it too late, Zabule. What did you think you could accomplish through the woman, so that he might be released? You spoke too late. The judge sits at the tribunal; the sentence has been pronounced. Now, carrying his own cross, he is led to death.

O spectacle! Do you see? “Behold, the principate is upon his shoulder” (Isaiah 9:6). This is the rod of his equity, the rod of his kingdom. Wine mixed with gall is given to him; his garments are removed and divided among the soldiers. His tunic is not torn but passes to one man by lot. His sweet hands and feet are pierced with nails, and, stretched upon the cross, he is hung among robbers.

The mediator between God and human beings, hanging midway between heaven and earth, unites the lowest with the highest and joins earthly things to heavenly ones. Heaven is astonished; earth has compassion [Note: [Col. 0785D] Perhaps “the parents”].

What about you? It is no wonder if, when the sun is darkened, you are saddened; if, when the earth trembles, you tremble; if, when the rocks are split, your heart is split; if, when the women beside the cross weep, you cry out with them.

Throughout all these things, consider how that sweetest breast preserved the tranquility of compassion. He does not attend to his own injury, does not reckon the punishment, does not feel the insults. Rather, he has compassion upon those by whom he suffers; he heals those by whom he is wounded; he procures life for those by whom he is killed.

With what sweetness of mind, with what devotion of spirit, with what fullness of charity he cries: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34)! Behold me, Lord, an adorer of your majesty, not an executioner of your body; a worshiper of your death, not a mocker of your passion; a contemplator of your mercy, not a despiser of your weakness. Therefore let your sweet humanity intercede for me; let your ineffable compassion commend me to your Father. Say, then, sweet Lord: “Father, forgive him.”

But you, virgin, whose confidence with the Son of the Virgin is greater than that of the women standing far away, approach the cross with the Virgin Mother and the virgin disciple, and look closely upon his face covered with pallor.

What, then? Most loving one, will you see your Lady’s tears without tears of your own? Will you remain with dry eyes while the sword of sorrow pierces her soul? (Luke 2:35.) Without a sob will you hear him say to his Mother, “Woman, behold your son,” and to John, “Behold your mother”? (John 19:26–27.)

Likewise, when he entrusted his Mother to the disciple and promised paradise to the robber, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance (ibid., 34). Hurry; do not delay. Eat your honeycomb with your honey (Song of Songs 5:1). Drink your wine with your milk (ibid.). Blood is changed for you into wine, so that you may be intoxicated; water is changed into milk, so that you may be nourished.

For you, rivers have been made in the rock, wounds in his limbs, and a cavern in the wall of his body. Hiding and kissing each of them like a dove, may your lips, from his blood, become like a scarlet ribbon, and may your speech be sweet (Song of Songs 4:3).

But wait a little longer, until that noble decurion comes and, removing the nails, releases his hands and feet. See how he embraces the body with his blessed arms and presses it to his breast. Then that most holy man could say: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh” (Song of Songs 1:12), and so forth.

Follow that most precious treasure of heaven and earth. Either carry his feet, or support his hands and arms, or at least carefully collect the drops of his most precious blood as they fall one by one, and lick the dust from his feet.

Moreover, behold how sweetly and carefully the most blessed Nicodemus handles his most holy limbs with his fingers, cherishes them with ointments, and, together with Saint Joseph, places them wrapped in a linen cloth in the tomb (Luke 19:38–42).

Do not, moreover, abandon the company of Mary Magdalene; but remember to visit with her the Lord’s tomb, with spices prepared. O that, as she saw with her eyes, so you may deserve to see in spirit [Col. 0792A]—now the angel sitting upon the stone rolled away from the entrance of the tomb (Mark 16:3–5); now within the tomb one at the head and one at the feet, proclaiming the glory of the Resurrection (John 20:12); now Christ himself restoring the weeping and sorrowful Mary with so sweet a glance and such a gentle voice, saying, “Mary” (ibid., 16). At that voice all the cataracts of the head burst open; tears are drawn forth from the very marrow; sobs and sighs are pulled up from the deepest entrails.

“Mary.” O blessed woman, what was your mind, what your spirit, when at this voice you prostrated yourself and, returning the greeting to the one who greeted you, cried out, “Rabboni” (ibid.)? With what affection, I ask, with what longing and ardor of mind did you cry, “Rabboni”? Now tears prevent further speech, when affection excludes the voice and excessive love absorbs [Col. 0792B] every sense of soul and body.

But, O sweet Jesus, why do you thus drive away the lover from your hallowed and most desired feet? “Do not touch me,” you say (ibid., 17). Why, Lord? Why should I not touch those desired footprints of yours, pierced for me by nails and drenched with blood? Why should I not touch and kiss them? Are you more hostile than usual because you are more glorious? Behold, I will not let you go, nor depart from you; I will not spare my tears. My breast will burst with sobs and sighs unless I touch you.

And he says: “Do not fear. This good will not be taken from you because it is delayed; nevertheless, go and announce to my brothers that I have risen” (ibid.). She ran quickly, eager to return quickly. She returned—but with the other women, whom Jesus himself encountered, raising the fallen with a gracious greeting and consoling the sorrowful [Col. 0792C] (Matthew 28:9). Observe: then what had earlier been delayed was granted. For they approached and took hold of his feet (ibid.).

Here, virgin, remain as long as you can. Let not your sleep interrupt these delights; let no outward disturbance hinder you. But because in this wretched life nothing is stable, nothing eternal, and a person never remains in the same condition, it is necessary that, while we live, our soul be nourished by a certain variety. Therefore let us pass from the recollection of past things to the experience of present things, so that from these also we may understand how greatly God ought to be loved by us.

## MEDITATION XVI  
### Or, the second part of the fifteenth meditation—On God’s present benefits

**233** I do not consider it a small benefit that God [Col. 0792D], making good use of the evil of our parents, created us from their flesh and breathed into us the breath of life, distinguishing us from those who were either cast from the womb as miscarriages or, suffocated within their mother’s womb, seem to have been conceived for punishment rather than for life. He also created our limbs whole and sound, so that we would not be a source of grief to ourselves or of reproach to others. This is certainly a great thing.

But how, and with what measure of goodness, shall we judge the fact that he willed us to be born at that time and among such people through whom we came to his faith and sacraments? We see this denied to countless people, although we rejoice that it has been granted to us, with whom we share the same condition. They were abandoned through justice; we were called through grace.

Let us proceed, recognizing [Col. 0793A] that it was his gift that we were raised by Christian parents: that flame did not harm us, that water did not swallow us, that we were not devoured by a demon, not struck by beasts, not killed by a precipice, but nourished in his faith and good will until a suitable age. Thus far, sister, we have reviewed those things in which our condition was the same: those whom the same father begot, whom the same womb contained, whom the same maternal entrails brought forth.

Now, sister, turn your attention to me and see how much God has done for your soul. For he divided between you and me as between light and darkness, preserving you for himself and leaving me to myself. My God, where did I go? Where did I flee? Where did I escape? Cast away from your face like Cain, I dwelt as a wanderer and fugitive in the earth, and whoever found me would kill me [Col. 0793B]. What could the wretched creature do, abandoned by its Creator? Where could the wandering sheep go, or where could it hide, deprived of its shepherd?

O sister, a savage beast devoured your brother. In me, therefore, see how much he bestowed there who preserved you unharmed from such a beast. As miserable as I am, having lost my chastity, so blessed are you, whose virginity divine mercy protected. How often, though tempted and attacked, was your chastity preserved for you, while I willingly advanced into every shameful thing, piling up for myself fuel for the fire in which I would be burned, fuel for the stench by which I would be destroyed, fuel for the worms by which I would be consumed?

Recall, if you please, those foul deeds of mine for which you wept and often reproved me—when you were a girl correcting a little boy, a woman correcting a man. But Scripture does not deceive when it says: “No one can correct the one whom God has despised” [Col. 0793C] (Ecclesiastes 7:14). O how greatly he ought to be loved by you, who, when he rejected me, drew you to himself; and although our condition was equal, nevertheless despised me and loved you.

Recall now, as I said, my corruptions, when the cloud of lust rose up from the wanton desire of the flesh, and there was no one to rescue and save me (Psalm 7:3). For the words of the wicked prevailed against me (Psalm 64:4), and in the pleasant cup of love they offered me the poison of lust. The sweetness of affection and the impurity of desire, coming together, carried my still-weak age away along the precipices of vice and plunged it into the whirlpool of wickedness.

Your anger and indignation came upon me, O God, and I did not know it [Col. 0793D]. I went farther from you, and you allowed it. I was tossed about, poured out, and drained away through my uncleanness, and you were silent.

Come, sister, carefully attend to all those shameful and abominable things into which my own will plunged me; and know that you would have fallen into them if Christ’s mercy had not preserved you. I do not say this as though he bestowed no good upon me, since, apart from the things mentioned above that were bestowed upon both of us, he endured my iniquities with marvelous patience.

To whom do I owe the fact that the earth did not swallow me, that heaven did not strike me with lightning, that the rivers did not drown me? How could creation have endured such an outrage against its Creator, unless he himself who made it had restrained its assault—he who does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live? (Ezekiel 33:11.)

How great a grace it was [Col. 0794A] that he pursued the fugitive, spoke gently to the fearful, raised one utterly despairing into hope, overwhelmed the ungrateful with his benefits, drew and enticed one accustomed to filthy pleasures by a taste of inward sweetness, dissolved the unbreakable bonds of evil habit, and kindly received one withdrawn from the world!

I am silent about many things and about the works of his great mercy toward me, lest any portion of his glory—which belongs wholly to him—seem to pass over to me. Even according to human judgment, the grace of the giver and the happiness of the recipient are so joined that not only is the giver praised, although he alone ought to be praised, but the recipient also. For who possesses anything that he has not received? But if he received it freely, why is he praised as though he had earned it?

To you, therefore, be praise, my God [Col. 0794B]; to you glory; to you thanksgiving; but to me shame of face (Daniel 9:7), for I have done so many evils and received so many good things.

“What, then,” you say, “have you received less than I?” O sister, because the one whose ship, full and laden with merchandise and riches, was brought safely back to harbor by the winds is happier than the one who suffered shipwreck and escaped death naked. You therefore rejoice in the riches that divine grace preserved for you; upon me falls the greatest labor, to restore what was broken, recover what was lost, and mend what was torn.

Nevertheless, I wish you to imitate me and to consider it a matter of profound shame if, after so many crimes, I should be found equal to you in that life; for the glory of virginity is often diminished by intervening vices, and the reproach of an earlier preservation is erased by imitation of evil conduct and by virtues succeeding vices [Col. 0794C].

But now look at those gifts of yours of which you alone are conscious before divine goodness: see with what joyful face Christ met you when you renounced the world, with what delights he fed you while you hungered, what riches of his mercies he displayed, what affections he inspired, and with what cup of charity he intoxicated you.

For if he did not leave a fugitive and rebellious servant, recalled solely by his mercy, without experience of spiritual consolations, what sweetness should I believe he bestowed upon a virgin? If you were tempted, he sustained you; if you wavered, he steadied you. How often did the pious Comforter stand beside you as you withered from fear? How often, when you burned with love, did he pour himself into your innermost being? How often did he illuminate you, singing psalms or reading, with the light of spiritual understanding [Col. 0794D]? How often, when you prayed, did he carry you away into an ineffable desire of his own? How often did he lift your mind from earthly things and transport it to heavenly delights and the beauties of paradise?

Turn all these things over in your mind, so that your entire affection may turn toward him. Let the world become vile to you; let every carnal love be foul; do not know yourself to be in this world, because you have transferred your purpose to those who are in heaven and live for God. “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matthew 6:21).

Do not enclose your soul with silver images in your worthless purse, for you will never be able to fly to heaven with the weight of money. Consider yourself to be dying every day, and do not think about tomorrow. Let not the barrenness of the future terrify you; let not fear of future hunger cast down your mind [Col. 0795A], but let all your confidence depend upon him who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies.

Let him be your granary, your storeroom, your purse, your riches, your delights; let him alone be everything to you in all things. For the present, let these things concerning present benefits suffice.

## MEDITATION XVII  
### Or, the third part of the fifteenth meditation—On God’s future benefits

But who grants his own such great things in the present as he reserves for them in the future? The beginning of future things and the end of present things is death. Whose nature does not shrink from it? Whose feelings do not dread it? For beasts avoid death by flight, by hiding places [Col. 0795B], and by a thousand other means; they protect their lives.

Now attend carefully to what your conscience answers you, what faith presumes, what hope promises, and what your affection expects. If your life is a burden to you, if the world is wearisome, if the flesh is painful, then death is surely your desire, since it lays down the yoke of this burden, removes weariness, and takes away the body’s pain.

This alone surpasses all the delights, honors, and riches of this world: not to fear death because of a clear conscience, firm faith, and certain hope. He will experience this most fully who, having sighed for some time under this servitude, escapes into the freer air of conscience.

These are the saving first fruits of your future blessedness: when death arrives, faith overcomes natural horror, hope moderates it, and a pure conscience drives it away [Col. 0795C]. Thus, in a certain sense, death becomes the beginning of rest, the goal of labors, and the destruction of vices. For it is written: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Revelation 14:13).

Therefore, distinguishing the death of the rejected from that of the elect, the prophet says: “All the kings slept in glory, each one in his own house; but you were cast out from your tomb like a useless shoot, polluted and wrapped up” (Isaiah 14:18–19). Those whose death a good conscience commends slept in glory, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:15).

They truly slept in glory at whose passing angels stand by, the saints come to meet them, offering aid and sharing consolation with their fellow citizen. They oppose their enemies, repel those who resist, refute the accusers, and thus accompany the holy soul to Abraham’s bosom, placing it in a place of peace and rest [Col. 0795D].

Not so the wicked—not so. Evil spirits drag them from the body as from a foul tomb, with infernal instruments; polluted by lust and wrapped in greed, they cast them into fires to be burned, to be torn by birds, and to be suffocated by everlasting stenches. Truly, “the expectation of the righteous is joy, but the hope of the wicked will perish” (Proverbs 10:28).

What that rest is, what that peace and joy in Abraham’s bosom are—what is promised to those who rest there and what joy they await—because experience has not taught us, no style of writing can explain. The blessed await the fulfillment of the number of their brothers, so that on the day of resurrection they may enjoy perpetual blessedness in a double garment, namely, of body and soul [Col. 0796A].

Now contemplate the terror of that day, when the powers of heaven will be shaken, the elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire, the underworld will be opened, and all hidden things will be laid bare. The Judge will come from above in anger, his fury burning, and his chariot like a storm (Jeremiah 4:13), to repay vengeance in anger and destruction in a flame of fire. Blessed is the one who is prepared to meet him.

What will happen then to the wretched souls? How wretched will those be who are now defiled by lust, scattered by greed, and exalted by pride? The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous (Matthew 13:49), placing some on the right and others on the left.

Imagine yourself now standing before Christ’s tribunal between these [Col. 0796B] two communities, not yet separated into one side or the other. Turn your eyes now to the Judge’s left and contemplate that miserable multitude. What horror is there, what shame, what stench, what fear, what pain? The wretched and unhappy stand there, gnashing their teeth, trembling with their sides bare, dreadful in appearance, disfigured in face, cast down by shame and confounded by the disgrace and nakedness of their bodies.

They wish to hide, but are not allowed; they attempt to flee, but are not permitted. If they lift their eyes upward, the Judge’s fury threatens them; if they lower them, the horror of the infernal pit is thrust upon them. No excuse for their crimes is available, nor can there be any accusation against God of an unjust judgment, since their own conscience will not be unaware that whatever is decreed is just.

See now how greatly he ought to be loved by you, who by predestining you distinguished you from this condemned company, by calling you separated you from it, and by justifying you purified you [Col. 0796C].

Now turn your eyes to the right and observe into whose company he will insert you by glorifying you. What beauty is there, what honor, what happiness, and what security? Some are exalted upon judicial thrones; others shine with the crown of martyrdom; others are radiant with the flower of virginity; others are fruitful through generosity in almsgiving; others are distinguished by teaching and learning. They are joined together in one covenant of charity.

The face of Jesus shines upon them, not terrifying but lovable; not bitter but sweet; not frightening but gracious.

Stand now as though in the midst, not knowing to which side the Judge’s sentence will assign you. O harsh expectation! “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” [Col. 0796D] (Psalm 54:6). If he joins me to those on the left, I will not call it unjust; if he enrolls me among those on the right, this must be attributed to his grace, not to my merits.

Truly, Lord, “life is in your will.” You see, therefore, how greatly your soul ought to be extended in his love: although he could have turned against you the sentence pronounced upon the unjust, he preferred to insert you among the just in order to save you.

Now imagine that you have been joined to that holy company and hear the decree of that voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). Then, with the wretched hearing the Lord’s word full of anger and fury: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (ibid., 41). “Then,” he says [Col. 0797A], “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (ibid., 46).

O harsh separation! O miserable condition! For once the wicked have been removed, lest they see the glory of God, while the righteous have each been inserted into the angelic orders according to their rank and merit, that glorious procession will take place: Christ our head going before, all his members following, and the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that he himself may reign in them and they in him, receiving that kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

The condition of that kingdom cannot even be imagined by us, much less spoken or written. This I know: nothing at all will be absent that you could wish to be present.

There, therefore, will be no mourning, no weeping, no pain, no fear. No sadness, no discord, no envy [Col. 0797B], no tribulation, no temptation, no change or corruption of the air, no suspicion, no ambition, no flattery, no slander, no sickness, no old age, no death, no poverty, no night, no darkness, no necessity of eating, drinking, or sleeping, and no weariness.

What good, then, is there? Where there is neither mourning, nor weeping, nor pain, nor sadness, what can there be but perfect joy? Where there is no temptation or tribulation, no change of seasons or corruption of the air, no excessive heat or harsher winter, what can there be but a supreme moderation of all things and true, complete tranquility of mind and flesh?

Where there is nothing to fear, what can there be but perfect security? Where there is no discord or envy, what can there be but the highest and truest love? Where there is no deformity [Col. 0797C], what can there be but the highest and truest beauty? Where there is no poverty, what can there be but complete abundance? Where there is no labor or exhaustion, what can there be but perfect rest and strength? Where there is nothing to burden or weigh one down, what can there be but complete happiness? Where old age is not awaited and illness is not feared, what can there be but true health? Where there is neither night nor darkness, what is there but perfect light? Where death and all mortality have been swallowed up, what is there but eternal life?

What more is there for us to seek? Certainly, that which surpasses all these things: the vision, knowledge, and love of the Creator.

He will be seen in himself; he will be seen in all his creatures, ruling all things without anxiety [Col. 0797D], sustaining all things without labor, imparting himself in some manner to each according to its capacity, without diminution or division. That lovable and desirable face will be seen upon which the angels desire to gaze. Who can speak of his fullness, his light, or his sweetness?

The Father will be seen in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. For he will be seen as he is, when his promise has been fulfilled: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

From this vision proceeds the knowledge of which he himself says: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God” (John 17:3). From these things will arise such love, such ardor of holy affection, such sweetness of charity, such abundance of enjoyment, and such intensity of desire, that neither satiety will hinder desire nor desire satiety [Col. 0798A].

What is this? Certainly, it is what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart: what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

These seeds of spiritual meditations concerning the memory of Christ’s past benefits, the experience of his present benefits, and the expectation of future benefits I have taken care to sow in you, sister, so that from them a richer fruit of divine love may arise and grow: so that meditation may awaken affection, affection may produce desire, and desire may wring out tears; so that your tears may be your bread day and night (Psalm 41:4), until you appear in his presence, are received into his embraces, and say what is written in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is mine, and I am his; he will dwell between my breasts [Col. 0798B]” (Song of Songs 1:12).

May he deign to grant this to you, the God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## MEDITATION XVIII  
### Thanksgiving for the benefits of divine mercy and petition for divine assistance

My hope, Christ God, sweet lover of humankind,

My light, life, salvation, peace, and every glory of your own,

For the salvation of all those for whom you willed to bear

Flesh, bonds, cross, wound, death, and tomb.

After three days, rising again and conquering death,

You appeared to your disciples, restoring their wavering hearts;

Then, after forty days, you sought the heights of heaven;

You live forever, and now and through the ages you reign. [Col. 0798C]

You are my living God, my holy Christ, my merciful Lord, my great king, my good shepherd, my truthful teacher, my timely helper, my most beautiful beloved, my living bread, my priest forever, my leader to the homeland, my true light, my holy sweetness, my upright life, my splendid wisdom, my pure simplicity, my peaceful harmony, my safe protection, my good portion, my everlasting salvation, my great mercy, my strongest patience, my spotless victim, my holy redemption, my firm hope, my perfect charity, my holy resurrection, my eternal life, my exultation and most blessed life, destined to endure without end.

I beseech, implore, and entreat you to complete in me the work of your mercy that has begun. For I [Col. 0798D], the least of your servants, not forgetful of the benefits of your compassion bestowed upon me, a sinner, give you thanks because, solely through your clemency, you caused me, unworthy as I am, to be born of Christian parents; through the water of holy baptism and the renewal of the Holy Spirit you released me from the bonds of original sin and gathered me among the sons of your adoption.

For you gave me the right faith and have deigned continually to increase and confirm it in my heart through the illumination of your grace and through the teachings of holy Mother Church. I beseech and humbly ask you, Lord, always to increase this faith in me: true faith and holy faith, catholic and orthodox faith, most prudent and unconquerable faith, adorned with all good things [Col. 0799A] and every virtue, which may work in me through love what pleases you; which cannot be conquered amid disputatious words in a time of persecution or on the day of need and death.

God, source and origin of all things, giver and preserver of virtues, increase, I ask, in me right faith, unshaken hope, perfect charity, profound humility, unconquerable patience, and perpetual chastity of body and soul. Give me prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, discretion in all things, and an ever-watchful understanding, so that I may wisely distinguish between good and evil, between the right and the left.

Make me, therefore, rich in holy virtues, through which I may serve you and by which I may truly please you; for by your grace I have become a lover of their beauty [Col. 0799B]. Give them to me for the honor and glory of your name. Join them to my faith, so that they may be its inseparable companions throughout the whole time of my life.

Therefore, I ask, by your grace make me always steadfast in faith and effective in every work, so that the faith my tongue speaks and my hand bears witness to in writing may be acknowledged by a credible life of good conduct.

I give you thanks, Lord, because you filled me, an empty and useless vessel and an ignorant fool, with knowledge and understanding; and you have always given me humble knowledge that builds up. Give me also gentle and wise eloquence, which does not know how to become inflated or to exalt itself over the brothers because of your gifts.

Place in my mouth, I ask, a word of consolation, edification, and exhortation through your Holy Spirit [Col. 0799C], so that I may exhort the good toward better things and recall those who walk contrary to the line of your righteousness by word and example.

Let the words you give your servant be like very sharp arrows and burning shafts, piercing and kindling the minds of those who hear them to fear and love of you.

You are the shepherd and ruler of all, Christ God, who, not because of any merits of mine but solely through the favor of your mercy, called my littleness to this pastoral office. For your sake and for the sake of your name, make me fit for this ministry, so that I may govern your household wisely and may be able to feed your flock in all things according to your will.

Grant, in your piety and goodness, that I may become in your house a burning and shining lamp. Grant, for the honor and glory of your name [Col. 0799D], that with much good fruit for the fellowship of the brothers I may deserve to reach your glory. For nothing is difficult for you; nothing is impossible. Your willing is doing; your will is the work itself.

And therefore I believe with my heart and confess with my mouth (Romans 10:10) that you can and will magnificently accomplish that work through me, so very small. I know and am certain that you can bring forth good and abundant fruit from your flock through me, insignificant and weak.

For I am little and a man of no virtue, possessing nothing in myself that is suitable or worthy of so great an office. Therefore, despairing entirely of my littleness, I breathe only in your mercy.

But although you are great in great things, you work great things more gloriously in the least [Col. 0800A]. Certainly your praise will be sweeter and more abundant in the mouths of people when you deign to accomplish great things from your flock through me, so very small.

Send, therefore, your holy angel from heaven to my aid (Psalm 19:3), so that, assisting me in all things, he may cause this work to prosper in my hands, so that your blessed name may be glorified in me, a miserable sinner.

Rich in mercy and generous in gifts, you who give everything to everyone and lose nothing, give me heavenly and earthly assistance sufficient for every need, so that I may have the means to feed and sustain your flock both spiritually and bodily, to receive those who come in your name without any hesitation, and at the same time to arrange and prepare the places entrusted to me for the rest and salvation of the brothers, as is fitting and necessary [Col. 0800B].

All these things I ask from you, Lord our God, because all our good things are your gifts. For we cannot serve or please you from anywhere else except from what you bestow.

But if it should perhaps not be in the plan of your eternal will that through me you bring forth good and abundant fruit from your sheep, I beseech and humbly ask you to release me from the bond of so great an office, in whatever way seems good to you and in whatever order pleases you. For you know all things and can do all things.

What am I doing here? Why do I remain amid these tumults if, through your grace, I am not going to accomplish anything good for the salvation of the brothers? I ask two things of you; in your clemency, do not deny me one of them. By all your mercies I ask you: give me your heavenly consolation amid my many tribulations.

For I cannot bear this exceedingly heavy burden [Col. 0800C] that has been placed upon my shoulders, yet I fear to lay it down. Troubles surround me on every side, and I do not know what to choose. God, helper of all who hope in you, let your goodness not abandon me; let your grace not forsake me.

God, who helps those who hope in you and trust solely in your mercy, help me, because without you I cannot please you. Who has ever hoped in you and been forsaken? (Sirach 2:11.) “It has never been heard since the beginning of the world” (John 9:32). You are the supremely good God of infinite mercy and immeasurable goodness, who have never been accustomed to abandon those who hope in you.

Show, I ask, your mercy toward me, because I have fled to you, so that those who hate me may see and be confounded; for you, Lord, have helped me [Col. 0800D] and comforted me (Psalm 83:17).

I give you thanks, Lord, because you have separated me from the vain fellowship of this world and brought me to your holy office, not because of any merits of mine but solely through the favor of your mercy.

I bless you, Lord our God, who grant me, unworthy as I am, the enjoyment of the fellowship and charity of your servants. Give me rest and the salvation of body and soul, together with suitable leisure for you.

For the advancement of my soul, free me from the most vain entanglements of this world, for the honor and glory of your name. For it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2:4). You separate from all the tumult of cares the souls of those who serve you, so that they may be free for you alone, the Lord, day and night.

Give those who renounce the world fruitful and spiritual leisure [Col. 0801A], so that with the palate of their heart they may taste and know that you are sweet and gracious (1 Peter 2:3), as your Scripture admonishes, saying: “Be still and see that I am God” (Psalm 54:11). And elsewhere: “Learn wisdom in a time of leisure, and the one who is less occupied with activity will attain it” (Sirach 38:25).

Moreover, your most sacred sentence, spoken by your gracious mouth, instructs us more fully and absolutely forbids worldly cares, saying: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13). And again: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62). Elsewhere, too, you deign to turn us back by an evident example, saying: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32).

[Col. 0801B]

I give you thanks, most merciful Lord, because from the beginning, from my cradle, you have patiently and kindly awaited the repentance of me, a miserable and exceedingly negligent sinner, running through nearly every vice and sin, unwilling to destroy me together with my sins, vices, faults, and negligences.

For if you had wished to deal with me according to my sins, Lord, the earth ought long ago to have swallowed me alive. But I ask you, merciful Lord, do not let your waiting for me be empty—or, God forbid, fruitless.

You who do not desire the death of the sinner (Ezekiel 33:11), grant me forgiveness for my past evils; grant amendment in the present; and for the future continually bestow protection and caution. Give me time and opportunity to produce worthy fruits of repentance (Luke 3:8).

Open [Col. 0801C] the eyes of my heart through your Holy Spirit, so that I may see and mourn all my sins. Lord, now is the acceptable time, and these are the days of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Have mercy on me, Lord, and do not destroy me together with my sins (Psalm 25:9); do not reserve my evils for punishment in that future life, in those infernal torments, in that dreadful judgment of yours.

Because of your great clemency, loosen the bonds of all my sins before I depart from this life. Give me a contrite and humbled heart; give me the grace of tears. Give light to my heart and strength to my body, so that I may see what must be done and may grow strong enough to accomplish what I see throughout all the days of my life.

Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy on me (Psalm 56:2). Do not permit this sinful soul [Col. 0801D], for which you deigned both to be born of a Virgin and to die upon the cross; do not command, I ask, that it be separated from this mortal body before you make me fully and perfectly repent and mourn all my sins, whatever I have committed since baptism and from my very cradle, whether knowingly or unknowingly, whether proudly or negligently.

Grant that on the day of my departure, when all my sins have been cleansed and my conduct rightly corrected, I may securely and joyfully see your most sweet and beautiful face, with gladness and exultation, because of your immeasurable mercy and goodness.

I give you thanks again and again, almighty and merciful Christ, because, for your sake and for the sake of your holy name, you have deigned until now to free my unworthy littleness from many [Col. 0802A] anxieties, tribulations, calamities, and illnesses; from many pits, snares, scandals, and sins; from many plots of visible and invisible enemies; and from many evils and most grave dangers.

You have directed my life wondrously and mercifully amid adversity and prosperity, so that neither adversity cast me down nor prosperity exalted me. For you placed your bridle upon my jaws and did not abandon me entirely to the power of my own will, caring for me with fatherly kindness and not permitting me to be tempted beyond what I could bear (1 Corinthians 10:13). Where there was an opportunity for sinning, sometimes there was no will; and when there was a will, there was no opportunity.

Let there be praise for you, blessing, and thanksgiving, Lord my God, for all your gifts and endowments, [Col. 0802B] 237 and for all your benefits, which you lavish upon my soul and body and have always lavished from my very cradle, through your mercy and goodness, though none of my merits demanded them—indeed, despite my gravest sins. But I beg you, Lord, I beg you: do not allow me to be ungrateful for such great benefits and unworthy of so many mercies. Let neither I, nor the devil, nor the world, nor any created thing, nor any human being be able to overturn your gifts within me, since everything that strives to oppose you is fragile.

Place your bridle more and more firmly, I beg you, in my jaws, and draw me after you like a tame animal, resisting none of your commands, but carrying you, my Lord, with an even and measured gait, [Col. 0802C] and obeying your will in all things. Awaken my sluggishness, Lord, with your goads, and make me seek your face with all my heart and all my strength throughout all the days of my life. Draw me to yourself, God, the strength of our salvation, with the bridle of your mighty grace, and do not allow me to wander according to my own will under my own power. Do not allow your image in me to grow dim; if it is defended by your aid, it is always excellent, noble, and clear.

Have mercy, Lord, on me, your most wretched and unworthy servant, for I am not like the innumerable and many servants of yours who have served you most devotedly from their very cradles; nor am I like those who, after public crimes, deserved through repentance to become devoted to you. I am not like certain Christian women [Col. 0802D] joined to husbands, who serve you in acts of mercy with the greatest devotion. Nor am I like many of those who seem, in the eyes of men, to be wicked and perverse, but are very different in your sight: for you alone know the hearts of the children of men (II Chronicles 6:30).

Yet if I do, or shall do, anything good, granted by your grace, I do not know for what end I do it, or with what strictness it is weighed by you. Therefore, O God terrible in your counsels concerning the children of men (Psalm 65:5), I humbly and tremblingly implore your holy and immeasurable mercy: since you desire no one to perish but to save all (I Timothy 2:4), do not abandon me to the power of my own counsel, nor to the judgment of my own free choice, nor to the power or temptation of demons, nor to the erring [Col. 0803A] judgment or harmful counsel of men. Rather, according to your goodness and mercy, and in accordance with your most gracious providence—which cannot be deceived in its ordering—dispose here and everywhere, now and always, the days of my life according to your good pleasure. Direct my heart, tongue, and actions through your Holy Spirit according to your will and in your mercy, so that, with you as my ruler and guide, I may always strive to think, speak, and do what pleases you in truth, through your grace; and may these things finally lead me to eternal life, through your mercy and gift, you who are the giver of every good thing, and who are God, blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# MEDITATION XIX

[Note: [Col. 0803D] It has been collated with the manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai. § I. Astonishment at the remembrance of God and man’s forgetfulness. Manuscript: Astonishment at the ineffable goodness of the Creator and the great misery of created man.]

## On the sweetness of the divine majesty and many other matters

[Col. 0803B]

### I. Astonishment at the ineffable goodness of the Creator and the great misery of created man

When I consider what God is—how sweet a nature, how lovable, how good, how ineffable, how admirable, and how worthy of reverence and worship by every creature—and when again I see and understand what man is, whom God himself made in his image and likeness, and whom he further created in such a way that, just as he would always express within himself the image of his Creator, so he would always retain in his memory the will and love of the one who created him in such a way [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *quamque propterea* (“and therefore”) for *quemque praeterea* (“and whom further”); it reads *quia eum* (“because he”) for *qui eum* (“who him”)], I am greatly amazed and astonished both at the immeasurable goodness of God the Creator and at the great misery of created man.

I marvel at the ineffable goodness of God because, although he is almighty and most just [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *quod cum sit* (“that, since he is”) for *qui cum sit* (“who, although he is”)], he permits man to live even for an hour [Col. 0803C]—man whom he therefore wished to create so honorable [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “to create honorably” instead of “to create so honorable”] that, just as man himself would be more honorable than the other creatures, so he would always live more honorably than the other creatures [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *esset cunctis* (“would be than all”) for *esset caeteris* (“would be than the others”)], according to the will of his Creator. Yet he, most wretched and unhappy, acts in the opposite way: although all the other creatures always agree with the will of their Creator, he always, or almost always [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “always almost, or always” instead of “always, or almost always”], resists that will.

But at the immense misery of man I marvel: how can he have his understanding so lost [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *sic sensum* for *sensum sic*], and live almost like an animal [Note: [Col. 0803D] “Like an animal” in the manuscript instead of “so, almost like an animal”], which has no understanding [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *non habet ut* for *non habet, vivat ut*], that he ever forgets his Creator, who cannot forget himself [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *sui, sicut non sui* for *sui, qui sui ipsius*]?  Unless he is insane, I think he is never forgetful of himself [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “he will be forgetful” instead of “he is never forgetful”], so that he understands that he exists, lives, and understands. Yet although man understands that he possesses all these things, it is astonishing and greatly to be wondered at that he should ever forget the one who was pleased to give him all these things.

### II. How much one man is loved by another, and why God ought to be loved more than any human being

[Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript’s heading reads: “How much one man is loved by another, and why the Lord is loved more than any human being.” The Anselmus manuscript omits this.]

A man [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *homo namque* (“for a man”) for *homo itaque* (“therefore a man”)] to whom another man gives some benefit in this world usually loves the one who did him this good so fervently [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads simply “fervently”] that he continually presents himself in the benefactor’s service [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *quia sibi* (“because to him”) for *qui sibi* (“who to him”)] [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “in his services”], and, if the cause of that benefactor should require it, he often does not fear to incur death on his behalf [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “does not fear to die, and …”]. Yet whatever any human being can ever possess in this world, or whatever one person can give another [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads *vel alius* (“or another”) for *vel quod alius* (“or what another”)], there is no one so dull-witted that he does not understand that he cannot retain it forever, but must relinquish it either before his end arrives or, if not before, at least when his end has come [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript omits: “it will be necessary to relinquish it.”].

But what God gives to man in this world is either something he will never lose and which no one will ever take from him, or something which, even if he loses it, can nevertheless enable him, when this present life has ended, to merit being with his Creator in blessed life forever [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads: “He gives something such that it is never lost and no one can ever take it from him. It is, I say, such that …”]. God often gives man the ability to live according to reason in this world, to love his Creator as he commands and as is just, and to obey all his commandments without contradiction; and no human being can take this good away unless the person himself abandons it by his own will. Temporal money, whether he wishes it or not, man must relinquish; but while he possesses it, if he distributes it as his God has commanded, by doing so he will merit [Col. 0804C] reaching eternal life [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “he can thus provide for the members” instead of “by doing so he will merit reaching …”].

O immense goodness of our Creator! O immeasurable mercy! Although he has never needed man in any way, he nevertheless created man solely out of his goodness, and in creating him adorned him with reason [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “he adorned him in creating him”], so that he might be able to share in his happiness and eternity, and thus possess joy [number 238] and gladness with him forever [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “might possess” instead of “possess”].

Even now, although man is opposed to him in many ways and knowingly and willingly does many things that displease him [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “although they displease him”], he nevertheless urges him to return and seek the mercy of his Creator, and does not allow him to presume to despair over any offense, however grave. For he is a fountain of mercy and compassion, and desires to cleanse all who are defiled by any stain of sin [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “whoever is defiled by any stain”], and, once cleansed, to restore to them the joy of everlasting life [Col. 0804D] [Note: [Col. 0803D] The manuscript reads “the joy of everlasting glory”].

[Col. 0805A]

### III. That God made all good things, and that he alone is good essentially

[Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript has no title: “§ III. That all good things, etc.” The Anselmus manuscript omits this.]

Most sweet and sweetest [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “Most sweet Lord” instead of “Most sweet and sweetest Jesus Christ”] Jesus Christ, who are the merciful lover of mankind and the most gracious Redeemer of sinners [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads *peccator te adorat* (“a sinner adores you”) for *peccatorum, te adoret anima mea* (“of sinners, may my soul adore you”), and omits *et pius* (“and merciful”)], may my soul adore you, may my whole life serve you, and may all my inmost being desire you. My wretched soul wishes, most merciful Lord [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “My wretched soul wishes for mercy”], wishes to think about you, contemplate your wonders, and understand how good and merciful you are toward sinners, so that, despairing because of my sins, I may not—alas, wretch that I am!—wish to separate myself from your goodness, but that by thinking in this way and believing in you, who are truth, I may at last be able to cease from iniquities and reform my mind, which has been bent down by evil works and sins, so that it may do what is right [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “stained” instead of “bent down”].

Behold, Lord, I know that you made everything that exists from nothing [Col. 0805B]—that is, they did not exist, and you made them. But you yourself, who made them, always existed, and there was never a time when you came to be; rather, you have always been [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “and you will never cease; but you have always been good, always” instead of “and there was never a time when you came to be; rather, you have always been”] good, always almighty. Therefore everything you made, whatever it was, you made good.

You, then, who always were, and are, and will be, and who did not come from nonbeing into being [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “and who did not come from …”], just as being always belonged to you, so goodness and omnipotence always belonged to you. For this reason your essence is not something other than goodness and omnipotence; rather, what is your essence is the same as your goodness and omnipotence [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript omits this sentence]. Therefore you cannot be anything except good and almighty, and the same is true of all those things that are similarly said and believed about you.

You truly are, and there is nothing other than you; and for you there is only one [reality], because you are not what now is and now is not, but what you now are, you always are [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads: “You are truly something else, and for you there is only one [reality]; because you are not what now is and now is not, but what you are, you always are.”].

But a creature, for which being did not always exist, but which came from nonbeing into being through you and from you, for whom being always existed [Col. 0805C] [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “came, created by you, for whom …”], does not have an essence identical with goodness and power. Rather, whenever it is good and whenever it can do good, it is good from you and can do good from you [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “and can do good”], who are good and almighty essentially.

You made every creature good; yet, although every creature was made good by you, you did not give every creature the capacity to understand you. And although every creature praises you and proclaims you to be its Creator and governor [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “repays” instead of “proclaims”], nevertheless not every creature understands you, but only the rational creature, which you made [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “which you made for …”] in your image and likeness.

[Col. 0806A]

### IV. That every creature praises its Creator

[Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript omits this heading.]

That creature also praises you to which you did not give the gift of understanding, whenever a rational creature sees that you created it good and beautifully ordered. This is its praise of you: that it is understood by the rational creature that you made it good and beautifully ordered it [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “that it itself praises you, being rational”].

But human nature, which you made rational, and that nature to which you did not give the gift of understanding, you distinguished in such a way that human nature, for whose sake you made the other creature, would arrange it according to your will and, with your permission, receive from it the nourishment by which it might sustain itself [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “so that it would arrange human nature”].

But because man consists of two natures, namely soul and flesh, he receives from the creature the nourishment by which he lives according to the flesh; but from the Creator he receives that by which he lives according to the soul—yet both come from the Creator. [Col. 0806B] In the meantime man lives according to the flesh while he is nourished by human foods; but he lives according to the soul while he keeps the will and commandments of his Creator [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “he receives nourishment according to the flesh” instead of “he receives from the creature the nourishment …”].

And just as he dies according to the flesh if he is not sustained by human foods, so he dies according to the soul when he does not obey the divine commandments. Thus man, who consists of soul and flesh, lives in flesh and soul by doing what God commands, because by doing this he earns the right to live happily with his Creator in eternal life.

But if he tries to turn away from doing what his Creator commands [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “what he who commands”], and instead desires to live according to the desires of the flesh—which is truly not to live, but unhappily to take life away from himself—if anyone were to observe him carefully, [Col. 0806C] he would see in him not the image of that man who was made in the image of God, but the image of an animal, whose ways he strives to imitate. Then it can truly be asserted that he is dead [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “that he is to be declared dead”], and will undoubtedly undergo eternal death if he persists in this and dies in that state.

### V. In what way man is like his Creator

[Note: [Col. 0805D] In the manuscript, as in the printed edition, “§ V.”]

[The manuscript omits this heading.]

God the Creator made man in his image [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript omits “and likeness”] and likeness because he made him rational [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “he made him rational”]. And just as God is good by his will, so man, made in his likeness, is good by his will [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript reads “voluntarily good”]. In this he is like the Creator: the Creator is good by his will, and man is good by his will [Note: [Col. 0805D] The manuscript omits “man is good by his will”]. But he differs in this, that the Creator is eternally and essentially good from himself, whereas man is good because he imitates the one who is eternally and essentially good from himself [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “he is good because he imitates the one who is eternally good from God”].

As I have said, the Creator is good by his will, and man, made in the likeness of the Creator, is good by his will [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript omits “man, made in the likeness of the Creator, is good by his will”]. But they differ in this: the Creator neither wishes nor can be or wish to be anything other than good, for will and power are his essence.

For man, however, will and power are something other than essence. Yet if he agrees with the will of God and wills what God wills, he expresses the image of God in himself. And if he perseveres in this to the end [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “remains to the end”], through the working of divine mercy he merits afterward to cling eternally to the will of his Creator, never again to be separated from it. And just as afterward he will always be what he will be, so whatever he wills will always be [Col. 0807B].

And just as for the Creator essence is not something other than will, nor will something other than essence [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads: “For him will is not one thing and essence another; likewise …”], so for man, already existing in that blessed state, his will will, according to his mode of being, be as unchangeable by the gift of his Creator as his essence. Just as he will undoubtedly be able to do whatever he wills, so, existing happily, he will undoubtedly be a happy essence.

Then man will have free choice truly liberated completely from every evil [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “liberated from every evil”], insofar as here in the meantime, while he lives, through the working of God’s grace he wills to do what God commands and to abandon what he forbids [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “he wills with it and establishes the good things that God …”].

### VI. That man exists in two natures, one of which is raised to the heights and the other weighed down toward the depths

[Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads: “That man, existing in two natures, has one directed toward the heights and the other weighed down toward the depths.”]

Man consists of two natures: [Col. 0807C] the nature of the soul and the nature of the flesh. The nature of the soul, because the soul is spiritual [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “the soul is a spiritual thing”], naturally tends toward higher things. But the nature of the flesh, because flesh proceeds from desire into carnal appetites [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “because carnal appetite proceeded”], tends, as it were naturally, toward lower things.

Between these two natures, of which man consists, there is the will, as something intermediate, possessing free choice. If, by this free choice, it joins itself to the soul—which naturally tends toward higher things [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “to the soul, which naturally tends toward higher things; then the soul and will …”]—then the soul [number 239] and will, with divine grace assisting, raise the flesh upward with them to lofty things [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “with grace, and the soul, raise the flesh …”] and establish it in eternal happiness, where it will live without end, so that there will no longer be any conflict between flesh and soul, but always the same love and the same will.

Then the will of the Creator and that of created man, whom he made in his image and likeness, will be one, when God is all in all (I Corinthians 13:28) [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “in his likeness; at last God …”].

But if by that same free choice it joins itself to the desires of the flesh, which tends, as it were naturally, toward lower things [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “because it …”], then the will, making bad use of free choice, and the flesh drag the soul, deprived of heavenly assistance, down toward lower things. The sins of man plunge the whole man—that is, soul and flesh—into destruction, so that he has nothing further except evil, or that which he suffers, namely torment [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “through which he suffers”].

### VII. Here man prays that God not permit him to misuse free choice

[Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads: “Here man prays to God that he not permit him to use either evil or free choice.”]

O sweetest Lord [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “Lord Jesus Christ, O”], O most merciful God, my Creator, my salvation, my life, my hope and consolation, my refuge, govern and sustain my free choice through your grace and your most merciful compassion. Do not let me, by using it wrongly, offend you, my sweetest Creator. Whenever evil pleases me, before I carry it out, destroy [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “destroy it itself”] and confound every evil desire of mine.

I would rather be dragged to you, sweetest Father [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “sweetest Lord and Father”], even unwillingly, or even be bound in chains and thrown into some corner of your house, than be separated from you. There, although because of my sins I might not be able to look upon your most merciful face, at least I might be able to hear the joy and gladness of those who serve you [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “I would rather be dragged to you, whatever you may will”].

Who, O sweetest Creator [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “Creator of all”] of mankind, can estimate your ineffable goodness, by which you loved human nature so greatly that you not only created it [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “caused it”] when it did not exist, but you yourself, its Creator, became a creature for love of it?

Whose heart could be so hard, so iron-like, that, knowing and understanding such great love of yours for the man whom you created, it could not be softened and wholly dissolved in love and reverence for your sweetness?

Truly, my soul, truly, my heart and all my inmost being, it is astonishing if you can ever forget such great love and such great mercy of your Creator. Behold, wretched man, what your Creator has done, what your Lord has done. He, for whom being always is and always has been [Note: [Col. 0807D] The manuscript reads “For he is always being and always has been”], immutable [Col. 0809A] and invisible, immeasurable and incomprehensible [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript reads “unchangeable”], in a wondrous and ineffable manner, without relinquishing his own being, emptied himself for you [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript reads “without relinquishing himself for you”], when for your sake he willed to become a creature.

He did this so that he might reconcile more familiarly to himself you, who came from nonbeing into being, with him who did not come from nonbeing into being, but for whom being always existed; and so that, once reconciled and completely restored to your former dignity, he might bring you back to his own being, so that you, happy and joyful, might rejoice with him forever in his eternal glory [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript reads “and, once reconciled, might restore you …”; “and happily” instead of “so that you, happy …”].

Behold, my God and my Creator, behold where I have arrived by thinking; and yet, while thinking about this, behold to how many vanities and follies my unhappy soul is still subject. If at some time, looked upon by your grace, I begin to think about how this may contribute to some benefit for my soul, my unstable mind, almost empty of every good thing, quickly slips into empty and harmful things, like straw that the lightest breath of wind blows away from the threshing floor [Col. 0809B].

Therefore, seeing, my Creator, such inconstancy in my mind, so sluggish and indolent in thinking about useful things, yet so ardent and diligent in things that are harmful, do not look upon the fact that I am a sinner. I confess, I confess, I am a sinner [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript reads “I confess: a sinner”]; I am unworthy; I am unclean [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript omits “I am unclean”]. Yet I do not withdraw from you, sweetest Jesus [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript reads “Lord Jesus”], Christ. Whether you wish it or not [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript reads “whether you will what you will”], I do not let go of you, even if I hold you with a weak hand; nor will you depart from me until you release me from every thought of sin.

Strike me, correct me, and rebuke me, and chastise your servant [Note: [Col. 0809D] The manuscript omits “Lord”] for as long as necessary, until through your ineffable goodness you lead me to the glory of contemplating you.

[Col. 0809C]

# MEDITATION XX

## A Complaint about the Absence of God

(From manuscript codex no. 167 of the Thuanean Library.)

It is not enough, Lord—not enough for my sinful soul that, from the abundance of your ineffable clemency, it hopes that its sins will be forgiven, unless, by laying before you at least its complaint about the grief it suffers from the absence of your countenance, it strives somehow to obtain relief from that grief. For it is exiled from you, and this because of its iniquities. Whenever, then, an occasion for speech presents itself to me, I intend to console my grief, yet I observe that it increases through the consolation obtained. The very search for consolation brings the memory of grief before the mind. For I would not seek consolation from grief unless I remembered that I was grieving; from the memory of grief, a refuge of consolation is sought, and from the desire for consolation, the memory of grief is increased; and the more often grief is brought before the mind, the more greatly it is accumulated. What, then, shall I do? Does the very expression of grief provide some sort of benefit of consolation? I shall therefore unfold before your mercy, Lord, the bitterness of my soul, with which it has been surrounded by the abundance of its iniquities; for on account of those same iniquities it suffers the bitter absence of your most beautiful face.

From this, then, my God, comes the summit of my grief: I recognize that by my iniquity I have gravely offended your clemency, and that, because of that same iniquity, the eyes of my heart have been blinded, so that they cannot behold the light of your desired splendor. You made me so that I might rejoice in you, and I have made myself so foul that I am ashamed to appear before you. For my iniquities have risen above my head, and, like a heavy burden, they weigh heavily upon me (Psalm 37:5); my mind has been drunk with the gall of wickedness, my soul has been bent beneath the weight of its crimes, my spirit has been befouled with the mud of vices, and my heart has been filled with the corruption of injustice; my soul has been entangled in the bonds of sins, and my entire substance has been crushed beneath the mass of crimes.

Who, then, will assist me, placed as I am in so great a depth of misery? Who will stretch out a hand to me? Or have I—what is true—exasperated God alone by such great iniquity that neither he himself nor any of his creatures ought henceforth, by right, to look upon me? Alas for me! Why was I permitted to remain in this world even for one hour after I was born, so that such evils should be committed by me against God? Why is life granted to me for so long, when it is all squandered in vicious desires?

But why do I lament the prolongation of life, when I recognize that through it I am being invited by God to repentance? “Or do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment?” (Romans 1:4–5.) Life, then, is granted to me for this purpose: that it may be amended. Why, then, does this not happen? If life is prolonged for the sake of repentance, why is repentance itself feigned? If God spares my soul by allowing it to continue for a time, why does it not spare itself by abandoning its sins?

O senseless hardness of my heart! Death is delayed so that life may be improved, yet while life is prolonged, a worse death is acquired. Distress is present on both sides. While I am in the body, I am exiled from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6); and, lest it be worse for me outside the body because of my sins, I fear departing from the body. I grieve at being deprived of God’s presence, and I fear undergoing the absence of this corruptible body, without which I cannot be joined to God’s presence.

What is it, Lord—what is it that the heart of this sinner perceives but cannot sufficiently explain in words? Certainly, good Jesus, to be dissolved and to be with you is far better. Why, then, is what is proved to be best not desired? To be dissolved from the mortal body and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23) is blessedness; to be bound to the body and to be absent from Christ is misery. Why, then, is misery feared to be lost, while blessedness is not desired to be possessed?

But this is why we do not desire to be dissolved from the body: because it is uncertain whether, after our dissolution, we shall be with Christ. And so remaining in the flesh is judged useful for this reason: while one lives in it, improvement of life is hoped for. Woe to the sins of human beings, by whose merit it comes about that the very misery of human life is judged useful! Is not the whole of the present life misery? And yet this misery is sometimes useful even to the just, because it increases good merit; but to the unjust it is especially necessary as a remedy of repentance.

This same misery, however, seems particularly to be mourned by good minds when it is loved too dangerously by the foolish. For when one perseveres in love of it, through that very misery one reaches eternal misery, and in a pitiable manner there is a passage through misery to misery: the present misery is spent in the labor of desires, and the eternal misery that follows is endured in everlasting pain.

But eternal misery itself will be all the sharper as punishment in proportion to the length of time that the misery of the present life has been prolonged by merciful Christ for the sake of repentance. O Father, who truly are, because you supremely are, because you yourself are, and your years do not fail (Psalm 101:28), come to the aid of me, oppressed by misery. If the misery I suffer is delayed, by your merciful ordering, so that a greater misery may be avoided—as ordinarily happens through the practice of repentance—why, then, is that very misery loved? Why do I love what I must soon lose, and not desire what could make me blessed once the misery of the present life has ended?

If I cannot love, as it would benefit me, the blessedness that you promise to those who love you, why at least do I not fear the punishments that you threaten to those who despise you—punishments of which, alas, I am one? For if I feared them, I would amend myself to some degree, and, by your mercy, it would come about that through fear and correction I might eventually arrive at love.

Why do I not fear your judgments, except because I neglect to think about them? Yet, lest I be able to think about them more frequently, my vices do not cease to obstruct me, flattering me with deadly pleasures and delights.

O Lord, Lord, behold, I am your servant and the son of your handmaid (Psalm 115:16)—for although I am a sinner, I am nevertheless a son of your holy Church. But what have I said? With what audacity have I presumed to call myself your servant, when I know that I am a servant of sins? For everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin (John 8:34); but I do not cease sinning without interruption. I am therefore a servant of sin. How, then, have I dared to call myself your servant?

I would certainly not say this unless I had presumed upon your ineffable compassion, which gave me the courage to say it. For although I am a servant of sin because of the weakness I suffer from iniquity, I am nevertheless your servant through the desire that, by your venerable goodness, I rejoice has been granted to me. I am therefore your servant, Lord, if not in deed and conduct, at least in affection and will.

But in this I am miserable and greatly to be lamented: that, although I know myself to be your servant, I do not strive to render you, my Lord, the honor that would be fitting. For if I did so, there would certainly be nothing to call me back from remembering you, from desiring you with understanding, or from the blessed sweetness of your love.

My Lord, my Lord, since you are my Lord, why do I not live as your servant ought to live? I recognize you as my God, and I desire to be your servant. Why can I not maintain the life of your servant through true conduct? But why do I seek the cause of this misery of mine, when I do not doubt that my iniquity has deserved it?

Alas for me! Why am I alive? Why do I live so long when I live so badly? I am permitted to live so that death may be escaped; yet life itself is found to be worse than death. You grant me, my most wise creator, the opportunity to prepare myself to contemplate your beauty, while I do not cease to make myself uglier day by day. What, my God, is more beautiful than your indescribable splendor, and what is uglier than my iniquity?

O my whole heart, delight in sighs, through whose practice you may be illuminated by your beauty and your inward eye may more easily be raised to contemplate the splendor of the heavenly light! O my entire soul, now lay aside all your wanderings; direct yourself toward the divine radiance alone; pour forth, from desire for it, abundant rains of tears, by whose flood both the innumerable muddy guilt of your own self may be washed away and the natural beauty that the good Maker of all bestowed upon you may, under the guidance of his compassion, be restored to you!

O, I say, all my inmost parts, take strength; exert all your effort to seek that sincere, simple, eternal, and only blessed good, whose light may drive away your darkness; whose clearest fountain may wash away your defilements; whose freedom may loose the bonds by which you are bound beneath the dominion of vices; whose strength may reinforce your weakness; whose wisdom may empty out your folly; whose life may rescue you from eternal death and unite you to its immortality!

O good that surpasses all goods, because from you and in you are all goods—for you are every good! I confess that my evils are excessive, that my sins are too many and too grave, and that my vices have multiplied beyond measure, because my soul has until now remained pitiably intent upon them.

O my evils, why have you rushed upon me so cruelly that you have made me alien to every good? O my sins, how do you hold me so mercilessly entangled in your bonds that you do not permit me to approach any freedom of justice? O my vices, why do you fasten my mind to yourselves with deadly enticements, as a dormouse is accustomed to overcome its reed with clinging tenacity, so that, wherever I am placed on the road—even if I crawl—you do not allow me to proceed?

My mind, be troubled; my heart, faint; my soul, shudder; my eyes, fail from weeping. For what can be found more miserable than I in every condition? All things inviolably preserve the order appointed for them; I violate it every day.

But will he who tolerates the sinner for so long not receive the repentant? It cannot be that, while he permits me to live, he will not receive me. I shall therefore approach my father, although an unworthy son. I shall approach him after dissipating the innocence he gave me, after the long hunger for heavenly speech that I endure. And I shall say to him: “Father, I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:19). I do not presume to compete in dignity with sons; I seek mercy among servants. Therefore, “make me as one of your hired servants” (ibid.).

Your clemency, merciful Father, will thereby be proclaimed, and your riches will not be diminished if you come to meet me as I desire to return to you; if you embrace me in the arms of your mercy; if you command that I be clothed with the ring of faith and the robe of righteousness; if you deign to say of me to your angels: “We ought to rejoice, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (ibid., 24).

But who, O best and wondrous Father, will give me to eat, with a fitting devotion of faith and holiness, of that fattened calf whom you commanded to be sacrificed on the altar of the cross for my redemption? And what is this calf, so gentle for sacrifice and so health-giving for food, except your own only-begotten Son, whom you did not spare but handed over for us all? (Romans 8:32.)

This is he, Lord, this is he whose sweetness my heart desires for its refreshment; he is the one whom my mind longs to love above all. This is he from whose absence my soul complains that it is separated, not without great sighs [Note: [Col. 0813D] Manuscript: *est, cujus* (“is, whose”).].
