But while I desire the Son, do I neglect the Father? Far be it!

For how could this happen, since the Father who begot is not something other than the Son who was begotten, but the Father is what the Son is, although the Father himself is not the Son? Nor can I desire the Father and the Son while removing the love of the Father and the Son, which is not something other than what the Father and the Son are, even though it is distinct from the Father and the Son. There is no possible way.

Say, then, my soul, say to your Maker, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God: “I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek” (Psalm 26:8). Behold, Lord, behold, I seek, I ask, and I knock. When shall I find? When shall I receive? When shall it be opened to me?

The secrets of my heart are open to you, Lord; you see that the only hope of my consolation is the presence of your face. Alas for me! How far I have been cast from the ineffable joy of that presence! How, then, shall I be consoled? Is it not only when that beauty of your face appears, Lord, upon which the hope of all my consolation depends?

Let my eyes, then, my God, fail while awaiting your word, saying: “When will you comfort me?” (Psalm 118:82). Attend, then, my God, to the singular desire of my soul; attend to the groaning of my heart, and place my tears in your sight (Psalm 55:9), tears that I pour out from the grief with which my soul is afflicted because of the absence of your face, as it faints [Note: [Col. 0813D] Another reading: “of benefit”]: “For my life is exhausted in sorrow, and my years in groaning” (Psalm 30:11).

Have mercy on me, Lord, have mercy on me. At a suitable and unsuitable time I shall cry out to you, nor shall I abandon you until you have gladdened me with the presence of your face. I shall deny myself every consolation; I shall avenge myself only through mourning over the absence of your face.

O radiant face! O luminous countenance of God! As long as I do not see you, my soul will remain in darkness [Note: [Col. 0813D] Manuscript: *videro*, “I shall see”]. O harsh, O bitter absence of the face of God, how long will you torment me? O troublesome life of this vain age, how long will you keep my unhappy soul, through your habitation, enclosed in your vanities as in a prison?

O my soul, what delights you in this mortal life? Why do you not hasten to reach the happiness of the divine vision, from which you are separated by the merit of guilt? Why do you not shudder at being exiled from the face of God and entangled in the bright bonds of this life? Why do you not desire with such ardor to share in the joys of that blessed life and to be absent from the filth of this obscene life? Why do you not flee from this life and run toward that one?

If this life is granted to you as a postponement, why do you delay? Why do you delay to render God such prompt repentance that he may forgive your sins and mercifully take you to himself? [Note: [Col. 0813D] Perhaps the reading is: “Why do you delay to render such repentance?”]

But my conversion is toward you, so that your mercy may look upon me, confirm my mind in desire for your face, and make me persevering through your clemency [Note: [Col. 0813D] Manuscript: “its clemency”]. For I believe that I shall not be excluded from blessedness if I am not wearied in desiring you.

May my soul continually desire the glory of your face; may my mind love it; may my thought be directed toward it; may all the affection of my heart sigh for it; may my tongue speak of it; may my entire substance be occupied in its love. Only let your goodness command that, while I bear this mortal body and endure the bonds of my exile, I remain grounded in your fear, magnanimous in your love, instructed in your law, devoted to your commandments, most fervent in desiring your promises, a trampler of vices and a cultivator of virtues—so that, adorned with these, I may always please you and reach you happily and as quickly as possible, where glory without end, praise without limit, and honor belong to you forever. Amen.

# MEDITATION XXI  
[Note: [Col. 0813D] This meditation is collected from the *Proslogion*.]

## Stirring the soul to seek and find God

Now, little man, withdraw for a while from earthly occupations; hide yourself briefly from your tumultuous thoughts; cast aside your burdensome cares [Note: [Col. 0813D] Another reading: “your”], and postpone your laborious disputes [Note: [Col. 0813D] Another reading: “dissensions”]. Give yourself for a little while to God, and rest for a little while in him. Enter into the chamber of your mind; exclude everything except God and whatever helps you to seek him; and, with the door shut, seek him. And now say, my whole heart, say now to God [Note: [Col. 0813D] Another reading: “about God”]: “I seek your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek.”

Come, then, now, my Lord and my God, teach my heart where and how it should seek you [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “I should seek”], where and how it should find you. Lord, if you are not here [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “I shall find. Where, Lord, are you, if…”], where shall I seek you in your absence? But if you are everywhere, why do I not see you as present? Yet surely you dwell in inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “within light”]. And where is this inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “this light”]? Or how shall I approach inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “that light”]? Or who will lead me into it, so that I may see you in it [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “so that I may see it”]?

Finally, by what signs, with what face, shall I seek you? I have never seen you, Lord my God; I do not know your face. What shall this distant exile of yours do, Most High Lord? What shall your servant do, anxious with love for you and cast far away from your face? He longs to see you, yet your face is far from him. He desires to approach you, yet your dwelling is inaccessible. He longs to find you, yet he does not know your place. He desires to seek you [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “Why?”], yet he does not know your face.

You are my God and my Lord, and I have never seen you. You made me and remade me, and you bestowed upon me all the good things I possess [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “and displayed them”], yet I still do not know you. Finally, I was made to see you, and I have not yet done what I was made for [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: omitted].

O miserable lot of humanity, when a human being has lost that for which he was made! O hard, O dreadful fall! Alas, what did he lose, and what did he find? What departed, and what remained? He lost the blessedness for which he was made, and found the misery for which he was not made. That without which nothing is happy departed, and what in itself is nothing but miserable remained. Then man was eating the bread of sorrows, which he did not know at that time [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: *manducavit*, “ate”].

Alas, the common mourning of humanity [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “of all human beings”], the universal lamentation of the children of Adam! He belched forth abundance [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “belched forth from satiety”]; we sigh from hunger [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “from hunger”]. He abounded [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “abounded”]; we beg. He held possession happily and abandoned it miserably; we lack unhappily and desire miserably—and alas, we remain empty!

Why did he not preserve for us, when he could easily have done so, what we now lack so grievously? Why did he thus bar the light from us and cover us with darkness? Why did he take life away from us and bring in [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “inflict”] death? Wretched ones, from where have we been expelled, and where have we been driven? From where have we been hurled down, and in what have we been buried? From our homeland into exile; from the vision of God into our blindness; from the joy of immortality into the bitterness and dishonor of death. Miserable change! From how great a good into how great an evil!

A grave loss [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: omitted], grave sorrow, everything grave. But alas for me, miserable as I am, one among the other children of Eve, miserable and separated from God! What did I begin? What did I do? Toward what was I heading? Where have I arrived? What was I aspiring to, and over what do I sigh?

I sought good things, and behold, confusion (Job 14:19). I was reaching toward God, and stumbled against myself. I was seeking rest in my secret place, and found tribulation and sorrow (Psalm 114:3) in my inmost being. I wished to return from the joy of my mind, and I am forced to roar from the groaning of my heart (Psalm 37:9). Joy was expected, and behold, sighs grow dense [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “from where they grow dense”].

And, O Lord, how long? How long, Lord, will you forget me? How long will you turn your face from me? (Psalm 12:1.) When will you look upon me and hear me? When will you enlighten my eyes and show me your face? When will you restore me to myself?

Look upon me, Lord, and hear me, and enlighten me; show me yourself. Restore yourself to me, so that it may be well with me, since without you I am in such misery. Direct, Lord, my labors and my efforts toward you, because without you I can do nothing. You invite me; help me, I beg you, Lord, lest I despair while sighing [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “while obtaining”], but let me breathe again in hope [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “in love”].

I beg you, Lord: my heart has been embittered by its desolation; sweeten it with your consolation. I beg you, Lord: hungry, I began to seek you; do not let me cease [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “do not let me desist”] from you while fasting. Famished, I approached; do not let me depart unfed. Poor, I came to the rich [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “to you, the rich”]; miserable, to the merciful; do not let me depart empty and despised [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “or let me depart”]. And if I sigh before I eat, give me, after my sighs, something to eat.

Lord, I have been bent down; I can look only below. Raise me up, so that I may be able to direct my gaze upward. My iniquities have risen above my head (Psalm 57:5); they envelop me, and, like a heavy burden, they weigh me down (ibid.). Unwind me; unload me; do not let their pit press its mouth over me (Psalm 68:16).

Let me behold your light from afar, or from the depths. Teach me to seek you, Lord, and show yourself to the one who seeks you; for I cannot seek you unless you teach me, nor find you unless you show yourself to me [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “I cannot, unless…”]. Let me seek you by desiring; let me desire you by seeking; let me find you by loving; let me love you by finding [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: omitted].

I confess, Lord, and I give you thanks, because you created me as your image [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “into this image of yours”], so that, remembering you, I might think of you and love you. But it has been so erased by the abrasion of vices and so darkened by the smoke of sins that it cannot do what it was made for, unless you renew and reform it [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “instruct it”].

I do not attempt, Lord, to penetrate your height, for in no way do I compare my understanding with it; but I desire to understand to some degree your truth, which my heart believes and loves. For I do not seek to understand in order to believe; rather, I believe in order to understand [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “to believe”].

Truly, Lord, this is the inaccessible light in which you dwell. Truly, there is nothing that can penetrate it so as to see you there [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “see you in it”]. Truly, I do not see it because it is too great [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “too great for my weakness”]; and yet whatever I see, I see through it, just as a weak eye sees whatever it sees through the light of the sun, though it cannot look upon that light within the sun itself [Note: [Col. 0815D] Another reading: “because—or, which—is unable to look into the sun itself”].

My intellect cannot approach that light; for it shines too brightly, and therefore cannot contain it, nor is the eye of my soul strong enough to gaze upon it for long. It is dazzled by the brilliance, overcome by the vastness, overwhelmed by the immensity, and bewildered by its own capacity.

O highest and inaccessible light, O holy [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “entire”] and blessed truth [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “unity”], how far you are from me, though I am so near to you! How remote you are from my sight, though I am so present to your sight! You are wholly present everywhere, and I do not see you. In you I move, and in you I am, yet I cannot approach you. You are within me and around me, and I do not perceive you.

You still lie hidden, Lord, from my soul in your light and blessedness, and therefore it still moves about in its own darkness and misery. For it looks, but does not see your beauty. It listens, but does not hear your harmony. It smells, but does not perceive your fragrance; it touches, but does not feel your gentleness; it tastes, but does not recognize your flavor.

For you possess these things in yourself, Lord my God, in your ineffable manner, just as you gave them to created things in their sensory manner [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: omitted]. But the senses of my soul have grown stiff and numb through the ancient sickness of sin. What are you, Lord? What are you? What does my mouth understand of you? Certainly, you are life, you are truth, you are goodness, you are blessedness, you are eternity, and you are every good.

Awaken now, my soul, and raise up your entire intellect; consider how great, how excellent, and what kind of good that is. For if individual goods are delightful, consider attentively how delightful that good must be which contains all goods and the delight of all goods—not such as we have experienced in created things, but differing from them as much as the Creator differs from the creature.

If created life is good, how good is the life that creates? [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “the Creator’s life”]. If created salvation is pleasant [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “good”], how pleasant is the salvation that made every salvation? If wisdom in knowledge of created things is lovable, how lovable is the wisdom that created everything from nothing? Finally, if there are many and great delights in delightful things, how great and what kind of delight is there in the one who made delightful things?

O whoever will enjoy this good, what will be his condition, and what will not be his condition? Certainly, whatever he wishes will be, and whatever he does not wish will not be. For there will be there the goods of body and soul such as no ear has heard, no eye has seen, and no human heart has imagined.

Why, then, do you wander through many things, little man, seeking goods for your soul and body? Love the one good in which all goods are found, and it is enough. Desire the simple good, which is every good, and that is sufficient.

What do you love, my flesh? What do you desire, my soul? There is there whatever you love, whatever you desire. If beauty delights you, the righteous will shine like the sun (Matthew 13:43). If speed, strength, or bodily freedom delights you—freedom such that nothing can resist it—you will be like the angels of God (Luke 20:36), because “the natural body is sown, the spiritual body will rise” (1 Corinthians 15:44), with respect to power, certainly, not nature.

If long and healthy life delights you, there is healthy eternity and eternal health, because “the righteous will live forever” (Wisdom 5:16), and “the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Psalm 36:39). If satiety, “they will be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16:15). If melody, there the angels sing together to God without end. If drunkenness, “they will be drunk from the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35:9). If any pleasure that is not unclean but pure, “you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight, Lord” (ibid.).

If wisdom, the Wisdom of God itself will show itself to them. If friendship, they will love God more than themselves, and God will love them more than they love themselves, because they will love him and one another through him, and he will love himself and them through himself.

If harmony, they will all have one will, because they will have no will except the will of God. If power, they will be omnipotent in carrying out their will, as God is in carrying out his. For just as God will be able to do whatever he wishes through himself, so they will be able to do so through him. For just as they will not wish anything other than what he wishes, so he will wish whatever they wish, and what he wishes cannot fail to be [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “What he will not wish cannot be”].

If honor and riches, God will set his good and faithful servants over many things. Indeed, they will be called sons of God and gods; and where the Son is, they too will be—heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ (Romans 8:17).

If true security, they will certainly be assured that they will not lose it of their own accord; nor will the Lord who loves them take it away from those who love him; nor will anything more powerful than God separate God and them against their will.

But what and how great is the joy where such a great and excellent good exists? Human heart, needy heart, heart acquainted with hardships, indeed overwhelmed [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “subject”] by hardships—how greatly would you rejoice if you abounded in all these things! Ask all your inmost parts whether they can contain their joy at such blessedness.

But certainly, if someone else whom you loved altogether as yourself possessed the same blessedness, your joy would be doubled, because you would rejoice for him no less [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “for himself”] than for yourself. If two, or three, or many more possessed the same thing, you would rejoice for each one as much as for yourself, if you loved each one as yourself.

Therefore, in that perfect charity of innumerable blessed angels and human beings, where no one loves another less than himself, each person will rejoice for every other person no differently than for himself.

If, then, the human heart can scarcely contain its joy over its own such great good, how will it be able to contain so many and such great joys? And certainly, to the extent that anyone loves another, to that extent he will rejoice in his good [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another reading: “someone else”]. So also in that perfect happiness, each person will love God incomparably more than himself and all others together. Thus he will rejoice beyond measure in God’s happiness more than in his own and that of all others together.

But if they love God with all their heart, all their mind, and all their soul, so that their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul are insufficient for the dignity of that love, then surely the righteous will rejoice in that heavenly happiness with all their heart, all their mind, and all their soul, so that their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul are insufficient for the fullness of their joy.

My God and Lord, my hope and the joy of my heart, tell my soul whether this is the joy of which you speak to us through your Son: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full” (John 16:24). For I have found a certain joy that is full, and more than full. Even when the heart is full, life is full, the soul is full, and the whole human being is full of that joy, joy beyond measure will still remain. For that entire joy will not enter into those who rejoice; rather, those who rejoice entirely will enter into that joy.

Tell me, Lord—tell your servant within his heart—whether this is the joy into which your servants will enter, those who will enter into the joy of their God. But certainly, that joy with which your elect will rejoice is something that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not entered the human heart in this life (1 Corinthians 2:9).

I have not yet, then, said [Note: [Col. 0819B] Another reading: “said to you”], Lord, nor have I considered, how greatly those blessed ones of yours will rejoice. Certainly, they will rejoice as greatly as they love [Note: [Col. 0819B] Another reading: omitted], and they will love as greatly as they know.

How greatly will they know you then, Lord, and how greatly will they love you? Certainly, no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart in this life has imagined how greatly your saints will know and love you in that life.

I ask you, my God, that I may know you, love you, and rejoice in you; and if I cannot do so fully in this life, may I at least advance day by day until that fullness comes [Note: [Col. 0819B] Another reading: “until I reach it here”]. May knowledge of you progress in me here, and there become complete. May your love grow here, and there become full, so that here my joy may be great in hope, and there may be full in you.

Lord, through your Son you command—or rather, counsel—and promise that we should ask and receive, so that our joy may be full [Note: [Col. 0819B] Another reading: “your joy”]. I ask, Lord, what you counsel through your wondrous Counselor, so that I may receive what you promise through your Truth, so that my joy may be full.

Meanwhile, may my mind meditate upon you; may my tongue speak from that meditation; may my heart love it; may my mouth speak about it; may my soul hunger for it; may my flesh thirst for it; may my entire substance desire it, until I enter into the joy of my Lord, who is the triune and one God, blessed forever and ever. Amen.

# MEDITATION ON THE *MISERERE*

## Notice concerning the following little work

(Edited by His Eminence Cardinal Angelo Mai, *Nova Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. I, p. 505; Rome, 1852.)

Among the published works of Leo Allatius, bibliographers include a certain supplement attributed to Saint Anselm of Canterbury. Not without reason: for Theophilus Raynaud, in his edition of Anselm, Lyon, 1630, admits on page 248 that he gratefully received from Leo Allatius, a priest of distinguished learning and integrity—Raynaud is mistaken, for Allatius was never a priest—some additions to Saint Anselm transcribed from Vatican manuscripts.

Gerberon, the last editor of Anselm, occasionally notes in his censures of the works which of these Meditations, specifically, had been received by Raynaud from the Vatican Library. But I have now observed in Allatius’s papers at the Vallicelliana a lengthy Meditation by the same Anselm, in the form of a little book, which I had not seen printed even in Gerberon’s edition, much less in Raynaud’s.

It necessarily follows that Allatius discovered this work after the other Meditations had been sent to Raynaud and after the Lyon edition had been published. As a result, this distinguished Meditation on the hundred-and-fiftieth Psalm, far longer than all the others, remained at that time in Rome and thereafter remained unpublished for as many as one hundred and seventy years—that is, until the copy preserved at the Vallicelliana and kindly supplied to us by the learned librarian Theiner was handed over. Thus even the principal bibliographers—Trithemius, Possevinus, Bellarmine, Labbe, Fabricius, Oudinus, Cavaeus, Cellerius, Mazzuchellius—were entirely unaware of it.

We now present this most noble writing of Anselm.

# MEDITATION ON THE *MISERERE* BY SAINT ANSELM, BISHOP OF CANTERBURY (G)*
1. Most powerful God of all spirits and of all flesh, who cannot be conquered, because you are omnipotent and a mighty king; who cannot be deceived, because you are wise, God who searches hearts and reins; who cannot be corrupted, because the Lord is just, and you have always loved justice; who will not spare on the day of vengeance, nor yield to anyone’s prayers, nor accept many gifts as a ransom: I, a guilty and wretched sinner in the presence of your divine majesty—before which the one who truly confesses is absolved—acknowledge that I have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea, and that my iniquities have multiplied.

I have been bent down through the long course of my iron will, and there is no respite for me. And because, from the disorderly course of the business of my life, I perceive that your justice must plainly weigh heavily upon me at your final judgment, nevertheless, from that very merit of mine which I rightly suspect, I flee and appeal to your mercy. And lest, while this appeal is pending, you enter into judgment with your servant, may your mercy rather go before me and follow me; and, submitting my perceptions, acts, thoughts, affections, and works to its protection, and asking for that mercy rather than demanding judgment, I say to you humbly, with a contrite heart:

2. **(V. 3.)** Have mercy, because it is the time for mercy, not for judgment; because you said in your holy Gospel that you did not come to judge the world, but to save the world. And I trust in your goodness that you ought to give heed to my appeal, which I—now trembling and afraid before your justice—interpose, as from a lower to a higher tribunal, before the seat of your mercy, knowing that mercy exalts itself above judgment, and that your mercy has been established above all your works. Therefore, my appeal ought not unjustly to receive your consideration.

Nor should your clemency be indignant against me, O God, if, seeing the danger of my soul impending from you when you are angry, I have dared to appeal wholly to you when you are appeased, since you bore with equanimity the fact that your apostle Paul, fearing that he might be physically oppressed by the governor Festus, appealed to Caesar. Therefore, with confidence in your grace, I approach the throne, so that I may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help. And because I am wretched and pitiable, I therefore say to you again, groaning in spirit: Have mercy.

For your mercy is the cord of the wretched, by which they are drawn out of the pit of filth and misery. Since, then, the sufferings are not proportionate to the future glory that I await, and since your mercy regards not merit but misery alone, from the deep waves of inward and outward misery, in which the image of God is affirmed [thus the manuscript], I cry out to your mercy within myself, tearfully saying to you: Have mercy on me.

3. I suppress my name. For if I told it to you, perhaps you would not recognize me by it; and I have withdrawn, in great thoughtlessness, from that sweet intimacy of yours which, after I had once recovered, as I hope, baptismal innocence, I formerly enjoyed when I sometimes ascended the mountain of prayer to you, intending to speak familiarly with you as a friend with a friend, and you repeatedly wished to receive me sweetly.

Then you knew me by name, as you knew Moses, and I rejoiced in you with your other servants, whose names are written in heaven; and my name was honorable before you. But now, because my sins have erased my name from the book of the living, and it is not written with the righteous, I do not dare to name it or recall it to your memory—like that blessed man whom you found to be a man after your own heart, who confidently commended both his name and his gentleness to your blessed memory, saying: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness.”

These words, whether flattering you or myself, I dare to say to you as he did: “Give authority to your boy,” or “to your servant,” or “to the son of your maidservant.” For these names of intimacy would accuse me, a guilty man making petition, even more. But pursuing my appeal, touched inwardly by grief because I have aroused anger against myself, sighing, I say to you again and again: Have mercy on me, O God.

4. I do not dare to say “my.” I acknowledge you only as God, but I cannot call you mine. For when a child had been born to me, and the little Son of God had been given to me—given, I say, by the Father, who so loved the world that he gave you, his only-begotten Son; given by the mother, who, like another Samaritan woman, in order to nourish us, cooked you, her Son, in the fire of suffering (IV Kings 2:29), and gave you to us to eat in the sacrament of the altar; given, moreover, by you yourself, who gave yourself for us in order to redeem and cleanse us from all iniquity—when, I say, you had thus been given to me by all those whose concern this was, and therefore were properly and peculiarly my God, I, unhappy because of my sins, lost you.

For I truly acknowledge that you are mine, since, complaining of me and of other sinners, you say: “Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me.” And if I lost you, I lost everything, and myself as well. But you, O God, who were imprudently made by me like a lost vessel, and who, by your great mercy, permitted yourself to be found by your sorrowing mother, who had lost you in the temple, so that she would not lose you again but would carefully guard you—

5. So you too, O God, have mercy on me according to your great mercy. I do not say, according to my misery, but according to your great mercy, which is far greater than my exceedingly great misery. I do not ask according to my merit, or according to your justice or mine, or according to my works, by which I, wretched man, went astray from you, but according to your great mercy.

I seek great mercy, because it is not fitting for your great magnificence to give little things. Indeed, I would not be worthy to be heard if I were to ask a great one for little things. For I esteem you—not that great Alexander, but one infinitely greater—who do not consider what I ought to receive, but what it is fitting for you to give. And in asking for great things I do not presume upon my merits, but trust in your great mercy, which, like your sister, grew up with you from infancy and came forth with you from your mother’s womb.

I therefore ask for your great mercy. I would be greatly troubled if I did not know your mercies, O Lord; but by experience I perceive in myself that you possess three mercies.

The first is that you did not immediately consume me and other sinners for every offense by which we offend the eyes of your majesty, just as we too, when our fellow servants offend us, immediately wish to shame and punish them. Rather, you suspended the sword of vengeance for so long that we can truly say with the prophet: “It is the Lord’s mercy that we have not been consumed.”

And this first mercy of yours would indeed be small; nor, if it stood alone, would it suffice for my salvation. Rather, while piling up judgment and condemnation, it would make me a despiser of your divine goodness, patience, and long-suffering; and according to my hardness and impenitent heart I would store up wrath for myself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of your just judgment, in which, reproaching me with all my evils, you would bring against me the words: “You did these things, and I was silent.”

Therefore you extended to me your second mercy, greater than the first, by which you recalled me, a wretched sinner, to repentance, so that thanksgiving and a voice of praise might be offered to you for it. For when I was dead in sins, I could not move the foot of my affection in order to turn to you in repentance, unless your mercy had helped me. But when I said, “My foot was shaken,” your mercy, O Lord, was helping me.

6. Nor am I content with these two mercies. For although they are great in themselves, they are nevertheless small in comparison with that great mercy of yours which I seek. I could abuse the patience of your first mercy, and my foot—which is moved by the second so that it may turn to you—could slip again, and my last error could be worse than the first.

Therefore I know, O supreme Wisdom, taught by you; I know what I ask, because I ask for your great mercy, by which you may so strengthen and confirm the earth of my heart and body—melted from the stability of the virtues into various desires—through the Spirit of your strength, that I may not offend your clemency hereafter; that I may not lose you again, but always hold you and never let you go, until you bring me into the house of that heavenly Jerusalem, my mother.

Then I shall glorify your name forever and say: “For your mercy is great over me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell.” This is that great mercy of yours which I ask: by it you not only await sinners for repentance, and not only give them the grace to repent, but you clothe and strengthen the repentant with power from on high, so that their foot may not slip thereafter.

It is plainly a difficult thing, impossible to man but possible to you alone: namely, to cast from one’s neck the yoke of sin once taken up, in such a way that it cannot be done without the help of your great mercy. In this manner that mercy confirmed the angels in heaven and will confirm human beings in the resurrection, when you will make them equal to the angels.

Therefore I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing a psalm to you among the nations: “For your mercy has been magnified up to the heavens,” indeed, above the heavens; and thus, according to your great mercy, you will save me, unworthy as I am.

7. And according to the multitude of your mercies, which you displayed in the bestowal of benefits upon the fathers of old, and in which you never failed sinful humanity.

When that stubborn and rebellious people—whom you led terrifyingly out of Egyptian slavery by signs and wonders, whom you conducted through the midst of the Red Sea on dry ground, for whom you descended from heaven onto the mountain in order to speak—[manuscript: “spoke”]; for whom you miraculously provided bread from heaven containing every delight, without labor; for whom you most abundantly brought forth water from the rock when they were thirsty; whom you brought into a land flowing with milk and honey, as you had promised—when, I say, that hard-hearted people, after so many great deeds, so many wonders, so many terrifying benefits of their salvation and welfare, which you had mercifully bestowed upon them, had forgotten you and, acting proudly against you, hardened their exceedingly stiff neck;

and lest that ungrateful people should worship you, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt, when, despite Aaron’s resistance, they sought foreign gods, rose in the morning, and offered sacrifices to a cast calf amid threats and terrors; and, departing from you, cast behind their backs the law and ceremonies that you had given them; and brutally killed your prophets, who urged them to return to you; and heaped great blasphemies upon you, provoking you to anger; and because of these things you had delivered them into the hands of their enemies—

after all this, when they cried out to you in the time of their tribulation and distress, you, O merciful God, rich in mercy and true, heard them from heaven according to your many mercies.

And when you again left them, perverse as they were, in the hands of their enemies, and they cried out to you again and again, you delivered them from heaven by your many mercies; and in your abundant compassions you did not destroy them, because you are a God of compassions and are gracious.

Since, then, I am less than all your mercies, remember me, O God, and spare me according to the multitude of your mercies, which surpass every multitude of sins. For I do not cast my prayers before your face in my own justifications, but in your many mercies.

Remember, therefore, O Lord, your mercies, which you effectively bestowed upon the sinners of old through deeds of mercy equal to mine, and your compassions naturally implanted in you, which are from eternity.

8. And lest what you began from the beginning of the world fail in the case of a wretched sinner, according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity, because it has itself erased me, alas, from the book of life.

Thus you, O God, who erased the names of the ungodly like the mud of the streets, erase it as tablets are usually effaced and erased, so that, once it has been effaced and erased, my name may be rewritten with the righteous in the book of the living, from which that iniquity had erased it.

Blot out, I beg you, O most omnipotent one, the record of the decree that stands against me. For you had decreed, Father, that if I wished to escape death, I should not sin. And because I, unhappy man, acted recklessly in body and heart against your decree, to my great folly, you wrote for me a record of memory in your knowledge and in my conscience, so that, when your great and terrifying judgment should sit, these books of your knowledge and my conscience would be opened, along with that other book which the enemy, the accuser of the human race, holds against me; and from what was found in these records I would be judged.

But lest iniquity then be found in me, O God who love humanity, blot out my iniquity. You have always hated the unrighteous, because you are not a God who desires iniquity. But, O Lord, who do not despise the groans of the contrite, you know that, just as some ugliness remains from the erasure itself upon erased writing, by which the traces and meaning of the erased letters can be discerned unless the letters and the erasure are completely scraped away, so too the iniquity erased by you through repentance has left a certain deformity in my soul.

By this deformity my iniquity can still be discerned by you, who alone inspect hearts and know secrets, and by him who is the wicked accuser of souls—how great it was—unless, after your erasure, it is washed away more completely by you.

9. **(V. 4.)** Therefore I humbly ask: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity,” O most pure and radiant washer of us, who for this purpose sent the water of the grace of your divinity into the basin of your most pure flesh, so that you might wash us from our sins in your blood.

Wash me from my iniquity, and wash me so perfectly—you who know no imperfect works—that you leave no trace of sin in me. O humble sublimity, O sublime humility, who, to signify that inward washing of the soul which I seek, bent your height down even to the washing of your disciples’ feet: wash me, so that I may have a share with you forever.

Wash not only the feet of my affections, but also the hands of my works and the head of my perceptions. And because my soul has become vile and repeats its worst paths, wash its heart from wickedness, so that harmful thoughts may not dwell in it.

Wash with the warm and bitter lye of tears the bed of my conscience through every night. Wash my feet and the inner person with the butter of devotion; wash and renew me through the sacraments.

And because some things are sometimes washed in such a way that after washing they still remain impure and unclean, wash me in such a way that you cleanse me, and cleanse me from my sin.

Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed, except you alone? O most kind and good physician, Jesus Christ, who restore all things by a single word, I know—truly I know—and I confess this to your goodness: you can cleanse me in this way.

Therefore, good God, good man, good Lord, by your great mercy say to my soul, infected with the leprosy of many sins: “I will; be clean.” And so that I may be healed and cleansed here, burn me here, cut me here; here let my expiation take place, here my cleansing, so that when you come in your strict examination to winnow and cleanse your threshing floor, you may find my soul purified and adorned by the brooms of true repentance.

Meanwhile, I will not spare my mouth, but I will go and show myself to the priests, so that it may also happen to me that, while I live, I become cleansed. For I cannot truly show the leprosy of my soul to a priest unless I have first shown it to you, and you have [Note: [Col. 0825D] Testimony concerning confession to be made to a priest, and indeed with due preparation.]

10. **(V. 5.)** Therefore I truly show myself to you, the supreme and eternal Priest, saying: “For I acknowledge my iniquity.”

I acknowledge my iniquity, O Lord, but I know it only in part, and not as you know it, nor as I am known by you, whose eyes are far brighter than the sun, observing the ways of human beings and the depth of the abyss, and looking upon human hearts.

But my heart, O God, is perverse and inscrutable. I myself do not know it, but you, O Lord, who knew our formation, and who behold the abysses, behold and know it, and know my iniquity which is in it, exactly as it is.

If I had known it so nakedly and openly as you know it, before whose eyes all things are naked and open, surely tears would have burst from the innermost veins of my heart, and I would not have been able to restrain myself. I would have wept, as though I were weeping over myself, lest you, O God of patience and consolation, should again weep over me.

For formerly, in the days of your flesh, under the figure of that material Jerusalem, seeing the city of my soul and recognizing my iniquity, you wept over it in compassion. And as your words were interrupted by tears and sobs, you uttered a half-completed statement, saying: “Because if you too had known”—as I think you wished to say to me, unless your many groans and the deep sighs of your compassion had cut short your words: “You too would weep over your iniquity if you had truly known it as I do.”

You added how long I ought to weep over myself, when you subsequently said to me: “And indeed in this present day,” in which you act according to your will, not mine, and seek what belongs to your peace, not mine.

O Word, who are Truth, how truly you search the innermost depths of my heart! Truly, if I had known as you do, I would ask you—from whom everyone who asks worthily receives—to open the floodgates of my head and make the deluge of my tears overflow, so that my whole soul would be dissolved in tears and my iniquity—which has filled the earth of my body and heart—would be erased in this flood.

But now evils have been hidden from my eyes, and I have not been able to see them, because the days have come upon me which you, who opened the mouths of all the prophets, foretold prophetically.

For my spiritual enemies have surrounded me with a rampart of worldly occupations that tear my mind apart, so that they do not permit me to go outward to useful action or inward to contemplation. They have surrounded me, I say, and confined me on every side with so many anxieties and pressures that the bed of my conscience has been so narrowed and compressed that one of two must necessarily fall: either you, O God, who are the rightful bridegroom of the soul, or the adulterous world, which I have introduced alongside you into the same chamber, although I knew you to be a jealous God, so that with it, before your eyes, I might sin—O excessively bold sinner and thoughtless fornicator!

And they have thrown me to the ground through love of earthly things, and my children—that is, my thoughts and affections, which are within me—so that I may rightly lament that mournful song of Jeremiah: “My liver has been poured out upon the earth.”

And whereas I ought to have been like a stone placed in a heap of testimony beside the road, so that I might point it out by my example to travelers, there has not remained in me a stone of good example upon the stone of strength or virtue.

All these evils have flowed together in me because I did not recognize—by returning to you the thanks due—my time of visitation, when you, rising from on high, visited me beneficially by assuming flesh and delightfully by illuminating my mind, and your visitation guarded my spirit.

And from that tiny portion of the Spirit which your visitation preserved in me, I recognize my iniquity, so that you, O God, who alone forgive sins, may forgive it to me.

11. And my sin is always against me. O possessor of heaven and earth, you know what I learned in my youth: that “mine” and “yours” are possessive names. Therefore, if my sin is mine, I possess my sin. But alas, how wretched is the possession of my sin, which makes its possessor wretched!

O my sin, how did I possess you? Or rather, how did I tolerate you? How did I remain silent? How did I conceal the matter, so that you might possess me instead?

For my sin is not mine in the same way that my cloak is mine; nor do I possess you as I possess my cloak, whose possession and ownership I can completely cast off from myself in one act. But you have possessed me so unhappily that, even when abandoned by me, you do not wish to cease possessing my soul.

Nevertheless, if consent is given to you, you seek my soul for yourself, follow it, and pursue it even through the narrowest gate of death, so that you may deliver it to everlasting flames and torments.

How, then, are you mine, my sin, except because I made you? And therefore you are mine as a work belongs to its maker, or rather as a defect which I, God’s creature, committed against God.

Alas, then, my horrible and abominable deed! My sin, why did I make you? Why, through you, did I kill my soul? Why did I infect it with such deadly poison? What madness was leading me? What frenzy was compelling me?

For I knew that “the wages of sin is death.” And I knew that when sin is completed it gives birth to death—not only the momentary death of this body, which entered the world through sin, but also the death of the soul through the withdrawal of the life of grace in the present, the deprivation of glory, and the imposition of everlasting punishment in the future.

And I had learned this too, taught by you, because “the soul that sins shall die.” O eternal Life, set before the face of my soul that eternal death by which the immortal soul dies through sin, so that my soul may always see it before you and flee that death as from the face of a serpent.

For I heard from one of your intimate friends, to whom you, my God, who reveal hidden things, had revealed the duration and bitterness of this death, that it is death without death, an end without end, destruction without destruction: for that death always lives, its end is always beginning, and its destruction cannot be destroyed.

This is the worst death of sinners. Of this death, O most merciful one, you said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner.” But alas, I and other wretched sinners, against your will, desire our own death.

Yet you, my God, who did not make the soul’s death, saw and remained silent for as long as I cast all my sins behind me so that I would not see them and repent of them.

12. But now, O most omnipotent one, my sin is the consequence of my sin, namely eternal death, always against me; and for this I offer many thanks to you, the bestower of all good, because you did not leave me any longer opposed to you on account of my sin. As long as my sin was with me, it was not against me.

But now, because it is no longer with me, it is always against me, and I wish to be forever against it, because when I committed it—**(V. 6.)**—I sinned against you alone, because you alone are without sin.

And when all others have existed one after another, you alone, my God, my only Lord, will remain without sin; and you alone can release me from my sin and condemn me, because against you alone I have sinned and done evil before you.

Alas, alas for me, O Lord, alas for me! When I did evil before you, I made myself evil—though you, who alone are good, had made me good in baptism.

But now fear and trembling have come upon me, because I heard your truth crying out in the Church that you will destroy evil people through evil, among whom you will not spare me unless you are appeased concerning my wickedness, O God.

Hear me, then, O Lord; be appeased, O Lord; attend to me, and show me your great mercy. For even when I did evil before you, I was exceedingly bold: I did before you what I would not have done before human beings.

But those, O Lord, who are found righteous before you will rejoice before you, like those who rejoice at harvest. But I, unrighteous, who displayed my injustice before human beings and did evil before you, am now ashamed before you of my evils.

Therefore spare me, my God, spare me, as I bring forth the bitterest groans of repentance and deep sighs from the bottom of my heart. May you, who said through your Holy Spirit: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will not remember any of his iniquities that he has committed,” be found just and true, as you are, in your words; for your word is truth.

May you show those who say that you will not spare me when I groan to be liars, and conquer them when they judge you, whose proper work is always to have mercy and to spare, to be without mercy.

Consider, O merciful God, the substance of my weakness and poverty. Display over me the greatness of your goodness, lift me into the boundless ocean of your mercy, and in your kindly clemency forgive all my sins—those that clung to me from original sin and those that later came upon me from my own perversities.

And, O Lord, cleanse me mercifully from these, and grant everlasting joys to all my ancestors.

13. **(V. 7.)** For behold, I was conceived in original and actual iniquities. [Note: [Col. 0829D] Let theologians observe the extensive doctrine of Anselm that follows concerning original sin; it may usefully be compared with the same saint’s book *On the Virginal Conception and Original Sin*.]

And do not understand this, my God, who gave understanding to the rooster (Job 38:36), as though I meant that I was conceived in the original and actual sins of my parents, since I believe that you erased their original sins in baptism, and that I was an imitator of their actual sins; for you said that “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”

Rather, this is my meaning, O God, when I say that I was conceived in original and actual iniquities: I mean that I was conceived in that diseased law of my origin in which we are all conceived and born in the womb and from the womb as children of your wrath; and through the transmission of the lust of the flesh, even before we actually sin, we are constituted sinners and made more inclined toward actual sins.

But since there is only one original sin, which is drawn from our parents and for which unbaptized infants are condemned, do not accuse me in anger, O Lord, if I have used the plural number here by saying that I was conceived in original and actual iniquities.

I have used these words because that one original sin has many effects, and because many things can be understood in that one original sin if it is divided, as it were, into individual parts. Especially because in this plural number I understand a singular thing, just as you yourself, O God, understand it.

Thus, when your angel appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying, “Take the child and his mother and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s life are dead,” you said through the angel “those who are dead” in the plural, not “the one who is dead,” although you meant singularly Herod, who alone at that time sought the child in order to destroy him.

Similarly, when Moses stood in the breach before you, in order to turn away your anger, he designated a singular thing by the plural number when he said: “This people has sinned a great sin; they have made golden gods for themselves,” although they had cast only one calf. Concerning that one calf also, they added a plural expression.

14. By saying that I was conceived in original and actual iniquities, I mean that I was conceived in that one and singular original sin in which all sinned in Adam, as in a material mass.

For seminally all were in him when he corrupted human nature; and from that one man, who was the matter and origin of us all, all descended through concupiscence; and through the succession of propagation and the lust of the flesh, that corruption secretly passed over into his descendants.

Yet propagation did not cause this, but lust; not the fruitfulness of human nature, but the foulness of lust, which human beings possess as a result of the just condemnation by you, O God, of that first sin.

For we are not held by original sin merely because we descend from Adam through the propagation of the flesh, since you yourself, Lord Jesus Christ, who were entirely free from original and actual sin, descended from the same Adam, for the medicine of our wound, without the work of concupiscence, through bodily matter alone and by the divine conception and the reason of the Creator.

But because we were conceived according to that diseased law of conception, which came to us secretly and miserably through the sin of the first man, we are therefore guilty of original sin by your most just judgment, O God.

For just as you, almighty God, knower of hidden things, secretly infuse the most hidden grace of your Holy Spirit into your faithful, even into infants at baptism, so that man through whom original sin entered the world secretly infected all those who were to come from his stock with the hidden stain and foulness of his lustful desire.

Thus the soul, infused by you, O God, when it is created and joined to the body, is so weakened, stained, polluted, and defiled, just as wine poured into an impure vessel, even if it is excellent wine, becomes tainted and sour.

And in that infusion the soul itself, receiving within itself the just sentence of condemnation, contracts guilt and liability, and is bound to everlasting punishment.

15. But, O Lord, what shall I say? What shall I answer when my sensuality is questioned by my reason as to how this can be: that a child born of baptized parents is born with original sin, when they cannot pour into him what they do not possess?

Behold, O Lord, you who taught me from my youth to stand upon my ways and to inquire about the ancient paths, walking simply along those same ancient paths. I think that it is in the same way as a child once was born with a foreskin, although his parents, who generated him, had been circumcised.

And just as every day a naked grain, carefully separated from the chaff by human labor and then sown, nevertheless is born and rises together with the chaff, so I confess that I too was born with original sin, although you, almighty God, had cleansed my parents from it in baptism.

For they generated me carnally from what they had contracted from the old sinful man, and not according to that generation by which they had been born again, but rather because they themselves had been generated carnally.

Remembering this, I poured out my soul before you, O God, so that I might miserably understand in myself what that first man, when he was in honor, did not understand: what you, in your most just judgment, were to do in him.

But you, O God, who are rich in mercy, forgiving original and actual sins—not because of our merit, but because of the exceeding love with which you loved us—when I had been conceived in these iniquities and was dead even before I had been born, made me alive together with you through your grace in baptism.

You cleansed my soul from the oldness of guilt, released it from its liability, and freed it from everlasting punishment. Therefore I will always confess to you, O Lord, in the psalms.

16. Nevertheless, even after baptism, O Lord, I still constantly feel in my flesh that lust of the flesh which is the fuel of sin, the weakness of nature [the manuscript reads *langor*, archaically], the tyrant of the flesh, the goad of death, the law of the members resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin.

It exercises such violent dominion over me that, groaning beneath this heavy burden, I must cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Since I cannot free myself from this cruel dominion of the flesh, who will deliver me from this body of death?”

Certainly not the law of Moses, not the prophets, not my own powers, but your grace, O God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom your mercy, Father, gave to me so that through him I might receive the remission of sins.

In this I consider and lament your most just sentence of condemnation, O God, which you pronounced upon Adam and his descendants because of that disobedience: namely, that there is no one who has lived in this flesh even after baptism who is not afflicted by this hostile concupiscence—unless, perhaps, by an ineffable miracle of your omnipotence, O God, the law of sin that is in his members is entirely extinguished in him. This is a very great privilege granted to few.

Nevertheless, I give thanks to you, the bestower of all good, because although this domestic enemy of mine, this goad, this tyrant, remains in me after baptism, it does not dominate and reign to the same extent as before. After the grace of baptism it is weakened; the enemy is pacified, so that it cannot dominate me unless I receive your grace in vain, O God, and follow my desires, thereby restoring strength to the enemy and subjecting myself to it through unlawful consent.

17. But alas for me, miserable sinner, my fearful Lord! Although I knew that you rejoice to watch me struggle, to help me when I fail, to lift me when I fall, and to crown me when I conquer, behold, Lord, you saw how this enemy suddenly sprang upon me, driven on by him whose breath makes burning coals glow, and disturbed the quiet of my heart and body. How often he shamefully blasphemed me with obscene, unclean, and empty thoughts! How often, morning and evening, he shouted against the ranks of my heart, urging me to descend into single combat against him, and taunted me with the battalions of my affections! You also saw, Lord, how, on the other side, I did not fight him like a faint-hearted man, or fought him unlawfully like an unbeliever, or altogether dishonorably broke the bond of my military service before the adversity of the battles had yielded to him.

Moreover, you saw—Lord, do not be silent and therefore finally depart from me—how, when he had been humbled and, not by my strength but by yours, had fallen silent and left me in peace, I myself aroused him against me for battle; I restored to him the forces of my guilt, which he had lost through my baptism and my former repentance; and thus—woe is me!—I lost the crown which you had prepared only for those who fight lawfully.

But if, with your help, I have at some time bravely resisted, or shall hereafter resist, the vicious desires of this aforementioned enemy, and with your aid have overcome, or shall overcome, him—even though in this miserable life I cannot altogether drive this enemy, this domestic tyrant, from my flesh, like another Jebusite—you have nevertheless provided for me that, if I do not consent, he remains in me only with respect to the act and not with respect to guilt after baptism. For I trust in your goodness that you ought not to impute to me as sin what I unwillingly and resistingly suffer from this enemy.

And here too, my God, you chiefly manifest your omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy: just as other evils pass away in us with respect to the act but remain with respect to guilt—murder, adultery, and the like—so, conversely, your omnipotence works wondrously in us, O God, so that carnal concupiscence, whose vicious desires are not consented to, passes away with respect to guilt in baptism, while it remains with respect to the act as a punishment for sin.

18. And this is the heavy yoke which was created over the children of Adam from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all. Beneath this most grievous yoke all who feel its weight groan; beneath it Tobias groaned, and Susanna also groaned. Indeed, every creature groans and labors beneath this yoke until now.

I too groan, feeling it within myself, because the sighs of death surrounded me, and torrents of alien and my own iniquity troubled me. For these reasons I can tearfully say with the prophet: “Many are my groanings, and my heart within me has become sorrowful.”

Moreover, when I am at times oppressed by this yoke and recall, my God, that in baptism you blotted out the original sin in which I was conceived—for from it comes grace—I groan and sigh within myself, asking why in that same baptism you did not likewise remove the penalties that I suffer because of that original sin. Yet, among these penalties and pressures, I confess that your wondrous providence, by a supreme dispensation, willed them to remain in me, so that your arrows, Lord, might be in me, teaching me that my humiliation should be in the midst of me.

Also, so that your terrors might wage war against me daily and instill in me both your fear and your love. Also, so that affliction might give me understanding, teaching me that evil comes from us, not from you. Also, so that Adam might be my example from my youth, and I might avoid the sin of disobedience. Also, so that you might draw me to yourself, O God, with the cords of Adam and the bonds of charity, so that I might understand that you, Father, admonish and chastise me as your son whom you love.

Also, so that I might always have the practice of fighting against spiritual wickedness and exercise myself in sacred virtues; and especially so that, if I had been freed from these penalties in baptism, I and other human beings might think that this was the price or reward of baptism, rather than the glory of your kingdom. Therefore, although guilt was loosed from my soul, your providence, O God, nevertheless willed temporal punishment to remain in me during this life, so that I might seek more earnestly another life, which will be free from every punishment.

19. Rise, therefore, Lord, and help me. Clothe me in the breastplate of righteousness and gird my loins with strength, so that amid so many assaults of enemies I may stand secure in the battle line, and, girded [cod. *accensus*, “set aflame”] with the virtue of patience and long-suffering across the open fields of humility, may steadily overcome those who attack me. By dispersing the whirlwind of presumptuous warfare with wise moderation, may I be able, through innocence of life and the support of devout prayer, to continue in your grace, O God.

From that point I shall not lay aside Joshua’s shield until you, O God, who obey the voice of a human being, prolong the day of my life unto triumph. Nor shall I withdraw from the battle line until the contest begun has brought me both victory and a crown. Otherwise, whatever I do without you turns to my ruin.

For even now I remain held by the stain of original sin; and therefore, as I said before, I am more inclined toward actual sins. I do not say this, my God, to make excuses by which I may rightly be accused by you of my sins, or because I wish to cast my guilt back upon my parents—since I have never believed that it is guilt or sin when married couples unite carnally for the procreation of offspring—but so that you, O God, who know what is in a human being, may more readily incline to pity me if I confess before you that I am a sinner from my very root.

For in everyone iniquity, the bond of sin, and the propagation of death are drawn from Adam, with you alone excepted, Lord Jesus Christ, who, while nature marvels, were conceived from the Holy Spirit. “And in sins my mother conceived me”; that is, through the concupiscence of lust, which is sin unless it is excused by the goods of marriage.

And although that act bore no guilt in either of my parents, who feared you, Lord, and begot me not in adultery but in chaste marriage, nevertheless the origin of sin brought with it its due punishment into their offspring. Do not therefore remember, Lord, my sins or those of my parents. Do not take vengeance for my sins if, as a sinner before you, who know all things, I confess to you the whole truth that I know.

20. (V. 8.) “For behold, you have loved truth.” You are truth, never deceiving; the way, never wandering; the life, never failing. O true charity and not merely cherished truth, you were born for this and came into the world for this: to bear witness to the truth. In your truth, Lord, hear me, in your righteousness!

And because I know that you will judge the peoples in truth and destroy all who speak falsehood, I first judge myself here in truth before you, so that when you, my God, have taken the appointed time and judge acts of righteousness themselves, you may not enter into judgment with me, your servant—to you be thanksgiving for this and a voice of praise!—to whom I have already revealed the truth: the truth of your blessed incarnation, which through your wisdom is still uncertain and hidden from unbelievers; and the truth of the remission of my sins, concerning which it is likewise uncertain and hidden whom you will pity and whom you will judge.

Yet you have revealed these two things, uncertain and hidden in your wisdom, to me. The first, through faith, as though through the two witnesses Isaiah and Gabriel, wonderfully agreeing and saying to me: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.” The second, through hope, as though through another prophet, Nathan, saying to me as to David truly repentant: “The Lord has taken away your sin, and you shall not die.”

And when, with a contrite and humbled heart, I said, “I confess,” you mercifully forgave me. Because I wish to remain in your word and truly be your disciple, I have therefore come to know this twofold truth, hidden from ages in your wisdom, because you have revealed it.

You, O God, who resist the proud and give grace to the humble in the present, and whose glory will receive humble hope in the future, since you have confidently revealed your aforesaid hidden and concealed things to me, I trust that you will not leave this gift of yours half-complete.

21. (V. 9.) “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop.” Your saints, Lord, through whom you have willed us to learn your figures and parables, tell us that hyssop is a humble and medicinal herb, whose root is said to cling to rock and to restrain and cleanse swollen lungs. Therefore, when you spoke here, Lord, of hyssop, you are understood to be speaking to us of humility, which, when it considers itself, is a small virtue but is esteemed greatest in your sight and in that of the whole heavenly court.

To this humility you, O God, the supreme physician, have imparted a great remedy against the swelling of pride. When you, O God, who from the lofty throne of your glory regard the lowly and set the humble on high, though you were immense and exalted, bowed the heavens and descended to earth, taking the form of a servant, you offered the human race an example of humility, so that your humility, Christ, might be medicine for human swelling.

For where your majesty, Lord, emptied itself, it is disgraceful that a little worm should be puffed up and swollen by the wind of pride. What is more wondrous, what more detestable, what deserves heavier punishment than that, seeing the Son of God supreme in the kingdom of heaven and made the least in the kingdom of human beings, a human being should still magnify himself above the earth?

O teacher and Lord—and rightly do we say this—you showed us the book and instruction of your humility when you read to us that lesson which we were to commit to memory, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.”

O humble height! If you had wished, you could truly have said: “Learn from me to make the moon and the sun, or the whole structure of this world; learn from me to raise the dead who have lain three days.” But because the most solid humility is more powerful than the most windy height, you, the outstanding teacher of humility, preferred to say: “Learn from me, who was born, died, preached, and worked miracles, because I am gentle and humble in heart.”

O that you would sprinkle the innermost parts of my heart with hyssop! Then surely I would cling to you, Christ, the firmest rock, with all my heart and from my roots, so that I would be one spirit with you and cry out for joy that it is good to cling to you, my Lord.

And because this hyssop is necessary for all of us who are swollen with pride, I therefore humbly and devoutly beseech you, whose pleasure has always been in the prayer of the humble and meek, that you would deign to sprinkle me inwardly and outwardly with this hyssop, and I shall be cleansed—thoroughly cleansed—from the greatest sin, which is pride, a sin that among great sins is not merely greater but the first and greatest.

Through this cleansing, wash me by your holy grace, renewing through repentance in the baptism of blood my soul, which you have already washed in the baptism of water and of the Spirit—to you be praise and jubilation for this! “And above snow I shall be made white.” From this I dare to say confidently, because you, Lord, have said: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow in repentance; and though they be red as a worm, they shall be white as wool.” Thus, through mercy, the works of blood will be changed into your garment, Lord, so that from me, together with your other saints whom you will clothe in glory as in a splendid garment, you will make your garment—whose wondrous whiteness you signified when, at the Transfiguration, your clothes became white, such as no fuller on earth could make them.

22. And if you should ever permit me, together with those who saw you naked and clothed you, to hear that joyful voice of yours: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (v. 10), you will give my hearing joy and gladness.

O voice of exultation and salvation, which will give those who hear you eternal joy in Christ, sound in my ears! You are a very sweet voice, and the face of the one who sounds it is beautiful. Sound, so that with the hearing of my ear I may hear you, and with my eye see you—for to see you is the same as to possess you.

Meanwhile, out of reverence for you, O God, I will listen in silence to what your Holy Spirit speaks within me, since he now speaks in me only peace. However much the world outside may disturb and clamour, and as I listen, an unspeakable truth melts into my heart—which, if you are not that truth, I do not know what it is.

O most secret bridegroom of my soul, make me hear this voice inwardly in silence, so that, like a friend of the bridegroom, I may not fall through excessive talking, but may rejoice with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. Thus may my soul, which is still like snow frozen on the mountain of pride, melt in the heat of your utterance, which is fiercely burning, and descend swiftly and gladly into the valley of humility.

“And the humbled bones shall exult.” The bones of my soul, Lord, are the virtues by which it is supported inwardly, just as the body is supported outwardly by bones, so that it can stand before you upon the feet of its affections and not slip.

But you, O God, who know all things, know—and I neither wish, dare, nor am able to deny it to you—that you have often scattered these bones of my soul, which sought to please human beings to such an extent that the remedy [*medella*, an archaic form in the manuscript] of devotion, from which they derive all their strength, is dry and withered. Thus I can say with the prophet: “My bones have dried up like a cinder.”

But because you are the God of virtues, whose bone—or strength—was not crushed on the cross when the bones of the other two were broken, I therefore implore your ineffable goodness to send the fire of your love from on high into my bones. For I desire henceforth to please you alone through deeds pleasing to you, so that I may offer you marrow-filled holocausts.

Thus may the aforesaid humbled bones of my soul, through the sprinkling of hyssop and the joy of your voice entrusted to my hearing, exult in you, Lord, with exceedingly great joy.

23. (V. 11.) And so that this exultation may not henceforth be turned into sadness, “turn your face away from my sins.” Until now, Lord my God, I have spoken to you of one iniquity and one sin, namely pride and great arrogance, which I greatly fear, considering that you did not spare even the angels who became proud, but dragged that Cherub who was the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, from the delights of paradise into hell because of pride.

Therefore, Lord, I asked you so urgently to blot out, wash, and cleanse this iniquity and my sin, because it has made a deeply clinging stain in my soul. But now, because I understand that from this sin of mine, as from a poisonous root, many other sins and iniquities have sprouted in me—for all pride is the foundation and beginning of sin, and made both angel and human being apostatize from you with extreme folly—I humbly implore your ineffable mercy, O God, lest the joy and exultation that you have poured into my hearing and my humbled bones be changed into lamentation or the voice of those who weep.

Turn your face away not only from that sin of mine, pride, but also from all my sins—yet do not turn your face away from me, since in this life I wish to seek your face, that is, your joyful presence, always.

For I know, Lord, that your face is contemplated in jubilation, and if you show it, I shall be saved. But if you turn your face away from me, I shall be troubled beyond consolation. Therefore, my God, do not turn your face away from me; turn it away from my sins, lest, taking notice of them in me, you punish me for them. Turned away from them, I shall turn my face toward you; and from the sins that I have and shall henceforth have, with your help, I shall always flee.

And blot out all my iniquities from your knowledge, O God—their root, offspring, and shoot—just as you utterly blotted out the memory of Amalek from beneath heaven.

24. (V. 12.) “And when my iniquities and sins have been blotted out, create a clean heart in me, O God.” O God of my heart, who gives understanding to little ones, grant me to understand this. Inwardly I ask that you create a clean heart in me, O God, lest, if I ask for what I do not know, you say to me what you said to the mother of the sons of Zebedee: “You do not know what you are asking.”

For behold, the heavens are not clean in your sight, and you find perversity even in the angels. How much less can a human being, corruption, and his child say, “My heart is clean”? Nor ought I to have a heart and have it clean before I see you, whom only the pure in heart—those who have been pure of heart—will see.

But now, O intelligible light, whose invisible things are perceived through the things that have been made, I understand, with you as my inward teacher teaching me intimately in the school of my breast, that just as my body receives life, taste, joy, and sorrow from its fleshly heart and, when separated from that heart, is deprived of all these things, so—indeed, more truly and more vividly—you, O God, are the heart and life of my soul.

As long as you dwell within it, it lives by your grace and spiritually tastes sweet and bitter things: heavenly things and virtues are sweet to it, while earthly things and vices are bitter. And, as one member of your mystical body, if another member rejoices in prosperity, it rejoices with it; and if that member suffers adversity, it is troubled and grieves through a kind of sharing in compassion.

Thus I perceive that my soul has a heart. But when you are separated from my soul because of my iniquities, it neither feels nor possesses life, taste, joy, or sorrow concerning any of your promises. Rather, like a dead thing without a heart, it lies in the coffin of its body, and then it can truly say with the prophet: “My heart has forsaken me”; and that it has become “like a deceived dove without a heart.”

And truly every human being who loses his soul because of the lack of so great and such a heart is miserably deceived. For this is to be for nothing; this is to be for sin, which is truly nothing, for which nothing the heart of the impious sinner perishes.

25. And alas for me, my Lord God, without whom all things were made: by me this nothing was made, and for this nothing I perished, and I was reduced to nothing and did not know it.

But you, God, creator of all, who created everything from nothing, create a clean heart in my soul, returning to it in mercy as it sighs and cries out to you: “Hear me quickly, Lord; my spirit has failed.” Therefore do not turn your ear away from my sobbing, but for your own sake, O God, and for the sake of your holy name, return to my soul so that it may live. For you are truly its own heart and life.

Therefore, most merciful, most secret, most inward one, who keeps covenant and mercy with your servants; you who promised that you would give us a new heart and place a new spirit within us if we returned to our heart, and would plant us [cod. *plorantes*, “weeping”] in your heart and in your whole soul—give yourself alone to me, plant yourself in my soul, and I am full.

I, however, a transgressor, wish to return at your call to the heart—that is, to you, who are the heart by which my soul lives, tastes, rejoices, sorrows, knows, and understands, O God. And this is the clean heart that I ask you to create in me, O God.

Nevertheless, Lord, attend to what I mean. For it is not my intention, my God, to ask you—who are always creating all things and are not created—to create yourself in me, since no creation can occur in your eternal essence. Rather, I ask you to send your Holy Spirit into me, so that, if I do not have charity, he may create me from this nothing into you, who truly are the true, living, and pure heart of my soul; and who wash and cleanse this clean heart from all its defilements.

And for the sake of reverence toward you, the life-giving and pure heart of my soul, grant me through your ineffable goodness that I may so preserve a clean, sincere, and pure heart from unclean, empty, and harmful thoughts that, because of the purity of my heart, I may have you, the King of glory, as my friend.

26. And because, while my soul was without you, its heart, I became wretched and was bowed down, and the uprightness of my spirit was bent toward earthly things, therefore renew a right spirit within me also.

For you are the righteous Lord our God, who willed to make the human being upright for this purpose: so that, while all living creatures look down toward the earth, the uprightness of this external bodily form might remind that inner human being, made in your image, of his spiritual uprightness; and so that the uprightness of the body might expose the crookedness of the soul if it saw that the soul was crooked within an upright body.

And because the innocent and upright cleaved to you, since they love you, and because you are good to those who are upright in heart, I therefore humbly implore your uprightness, O God, that you would renew a right spirit in my breast, so that my prayer and intention may be directed before you like incense.

And renew me not only in spirit but also in my inward parts, from which the sin of the uncleanness of my flesh came forth.
