For in the inward parts of the kidneys is the seat of pleasure, except only for those blessed inward parts that bore you, God and Lord, in the virginal chamber that you had chosen.

And because the devil’s strength is in his loins and in the navel of his belly, he has often tried through illusions to fill my loins, so that by his strength he might bind my weak flesh. But because of the poverty of my heart and the effeminate sadness of my mind, I unhappily consented. And the devil himself, whom the archer did not drive away, shot his fiery and burning arrows—shot by him and by his evil angels—into the inward parts of my kidneys and fixed them there, and thus cast and drove me, miserable sinner that I am, down from the lofty throne of virginity and chastity.

Therefore, woe, woe is me! I lost that honor, that dignity, that wreath, that diadem, that golden crown—or rather, that aureole—which only souls destined to be established in earthen vessels, their bodies, acquire by utterly restraining unlawful impulses and likewise curbing the incitements of the flesh.

But alas, miserable man that I am! When I lost my virginity, why did I not consider that every defilement is unworthy of a continent soul? Why, unhappy man, did I not know its value? Why did I not gird my loins with strength together with the strong woman? And you, Lord Jesus Christ, coming from afar, from the furthest bounds of heaven, to the estate [cod. *pretium*, “price”] of my virginity, would have crowned it as a reward from yourself, who are the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.

O good Jesus, crown of virgins, if only virgins, men and women, follow you wherever you go and sing before you the new song which no one else can sing, where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face, I who have lost my virginity? For if I do not follow you, I shall walk in darkness; and what shall I sing except lamentations, having lost and abandoned the song of joy?

27. Therefore, my deceived soul, my wretched soul, my suffering soul, take up the hymn of confession. Harlot surrendered to oblivion, shake off your torpor, disperse your sin, and shake your mind. Bring back to your heart the enormity of your guilt and lead yourself to the heart’s monstrous roar. Attend, unhappy soul, attend to the error of your crime, and therefore to its horrific terror and terrifying grief.

You, I say, O my soul, once made white in the heavenly bath, betrothed through faith, endowed with the Spirit, redeemed by Christ’s blood, marked with the image of God, and instructed in the Christian religion—you were a virgin betrothed to Christ the Lord.

O, how I remember! O, what have I named! Certainly I have named not so much the kind bridegroom of my virginity as the terrifying judge of my uncleanness. Alas for the memory of lost joy! Why do you thus heap pressure upon the unhappiness that possesses me? How wretched is my condition, for which both good and evil are alike sources of torment!

An evil conscience torments me, together with its anguish, in which I fear that I shall burn. The memory of a good conscience and its rewards also torments me, for I know that I have lost them and shall not recover them again.

Woe, woe! A grievous loss: to lose, to lose that which should have been preserved by me without end, to lose it irrecoverably. O my virginity, no longer my beloved but my lost virginity; no longer my joy but my despair—where have you come to? Into what foul, into what bitter mire have you left me? O fornication, defiler of my mind and destroyer of my soul, whence did you, wretch, arise? From what snowy and delightful state did you cast me down?

For you, my soul, faithless toward God, forsworn before God, adulterous toward Christ, have been miserably plunged from the height of virginity into the abyss of fornication, rejected by God and cast to the devil—or rather, rejecting God and embracing the devil. By devoting yourself to fornication, you first offered a bill of divorce to the Creator and most loving God, and of your own will gave yourself over to your ambushing demon.

O miserable and more than miserable exchange! Woe, because you despised the kind one and clung to the wicked one! What have you done, O madness of mind, mad uncleanness, illegitimate wickedness—what have you done? In heaven you abandoned your chaste lover, and you followed into hell the hateful corrupter.

Consolation, security, joy—I do not want you; I reject you. If forgiveness of sin should bring you back to me, stay far away; stay far away before death, if indulgence should perhaps recall you, or after death. But let bitter repentance continually accompany my life; let continual pain and unsatisfied sadness be the condition of my life; let grief and bitter mourning be the tireless afflictions of my youth and old age.

Would that it were so, would that it were so! I desire, I pray, I long for it to be so. For if I am not worthy to raise my eyes to heaven in prayer, surely I am not unworthy to blind them with weeping.

28. Consider, therefore, consider and reconsider what you have done and what you have deserved. Let your mind descend to the dark earth covered by the shadow of death, and let it consider what awaits my criminal soul there. Let it attend and contemplate; let my soul see and be troubled.

Tremble, my soul; faint; rend yourself, my heart. O good Jesus, our redemption, if you have permitted me to weep my grief a little this far, henceforth, good God, permit me to call upon your help. For if I have made myself guilty, I can never make myself not your summoned one.

If I deprived myself of virginity, I never destroyed your mercy, Lord, Lord. If I committed what enables you to condemn me, have you then lost what you are accustomed to use in saving? Do not, Lord, do not regard my evil in such a way that you forget your goodness.

Where is it, O truthful God—where is “I do not desire the death of a sinner”? If you bury in hell a sinner crying out to you, is that “I do not desire the death of a sinner”? Is it not rather, “I do not desire that he should be converted and live”?

I am a sinner, Lord; I am a sinner. If, therefore, you do not desire the death of a sinner, who compels you to refuse what you do not desire, since you are almighty God? Far be it, Lord, far be it, O God, that the wickedness of a confessing sinner should prevail, and that he should erase the sentence of the Almighty.

Remember, righteous God, who are merciful and my creator and re-creator; and do not remember, good Lord, only your justice against your sinner. Do not remember your anger against the guilty, but your mercy toward the miserable.

It is true, and I confess, most merciful one, that my conscience deserves condemnation and that my repentance is insufficient for satisfaction. But it is certain that your mercy surpasses every offense. Therefore the abyss of my misery calls upon the abyss of your mercy.

Spare me, then, Lord, who are salvation. Spare my sinful soul, which, worn down by fear of your terrifying justice, flees toward your comforting mercy.

And since the reward of virginity has been lost—O irreparable grief!—at least let punishment not be unavoidable. This is not impossible for your omnipotence, nor unbecoming to your justice, nor unfamiliar to your mercy, for you are good and your mercy endures forever.

Finally, because I sinned in soul and body alike, and do not wish to commit anything of this kind again, I therefore ardently desire to be purified by you, most merciful Lord God, who heal together both the soul and the body.

Moreover, if I have sinned—indeed, because without doubt I have sinned—and for this reason my eye remains in the bitterness of repentance, nevertheless I hope for pardon, knowing that your goodness is greater than my iniquity, which is exceedingly great.

29. (V. 13.) Nevertheless, if I have done evil before you and did not blush before your face, as I ought, “do not cast me away from your face.” Just as you cast Cain, for the fratricide he committed, from your face and from the face of the earth—and no wonder, since he had cast away his inmost self and, despairing of pardon, refused to repent, saying that his iniquity was greater than he could deserve forgiveness—so, Lord, do not cast me from your face.

Do not cast me away like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth. Rather, through your overflowing and ineffable goodness, make me one of those simple people whom you do not cast away. Cast all my sins behind your back, and cast all my iniquities into the depths of the sea. But do not cast me, a human being, from your face; instead, make me attain that blessedness in which, not as in this life through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face, we shall see you, the end of our desires—whom we shall see without end, love without weariness, and praise without exhaustion.

This gift, this effect, this act will certainly be without faith for all who shall there see you with unveiled face.

And do not take your Holy Spirit from me—the Spirit through whom I recognize, confess, and repent of my sin; the Spirit whom, from the moment I grow angry with myself, I confess my former evils, mourn them, and resolve not to commit them again. I trust that I already possess him as a pledge of glory, knowing that I cannot possess these things entirely from myself.

Therefore, O God, whose anger no one can resist, do not be angry with me forever. Do not merely refrain from taking your Spirit from me; also (V. 14), “restore to me the joy” that I once had but lost through sin—the joy, I mean, not of the world, which rejoices when it has done evil, but of your saving Christ, my Savior, who is my joy, who will be my reward, who is my hope, my light, my praise, my home, my homeland, my life, my salvation, and my saving deliverance.

Our fathers who lived before us looked toward this saving deliverance as something yet to come, and in the expectation of this faith they were saved. In that saving deliverance there is and will be eternal joy for them. And because through the same faith—though in the case of a thing already accomplished, not yet to be accomplished, with the times changed—I expect to be saved by the same Savior, who wills all human beings to be saved and wills no one to perish, therefore, Father and Lord of my life, restore to me also the eternal joy that I lost through my sins.

30. “And confirm me with a principal spirit.” O God, who are the greatest Spirit, the greatest realm of blessed spirits in which the souls of the saints rest, I first invoked you above as the right spirit, then as the Holy Spirit, and here, thirdly, as the principal spirit, intending to invoke the whole Trinity for my help, so that [*ita cod.*, “thus in the manuscript”] the Lord our God is upright and there is no iniquity in him.

By the Holy Spirit I understand the Spirit by his proper name. Here I take you, the Father, as the principal spirit, because power is principally attributed to you to confirm the good of grace that you have worked in me.

Confirm it, therefore, Father. And if you confirm me, as I desire and as your surpassing knowledge knows that I need, I shall not be confirmed in vain, but I shall teach.

In this, my God, you will appear wondrous and worthy of praise as you teach me what is useful, because you will suddenly have made me a teacher from one who was weeping; from a wolf, a lamb; from another Saul, a Paul.

And other sinners, seeing that you have spared me, will advance through my example. Thus, by word and example, I shall teach the wicked who, while remaining in the faith, mortify their faith through their sins like apostates. I mean those apostatizing people who have departed from you, whom you yourself, Lord, came to call to repentance, not the righteous.

I shall teach your ways, not mine, but yours: your ways, which are mercy and truth, by which you come to us and by which we can reach you. And those impious sinners themselves will be converted to you, and through you, Lord, who turn rock—that is, the hardness of the heart—into pools of water, that is, into streams of tears.

For your law, Lord, is immaculate, converting souls. I am ready to offer my heart, tongue, and lips for the execution of your ministry. I most devoutly beseech you—my God and Lord Jesus Christ, who in the days of your flesh spoke the words of eternal life so wondrously, when everyone marveled at the words of grace that proceeded from your lips—to open my heart, teach my tongue, and surround my lips, so that through you the impious may turn from the error of their life and return to you through my example and ministry.

May my soul thus be saved in death, and may you cover the multitude of my sins, so that henceforth they may be recognized neither by you nor by the devil.

31. So that this may be granted to me more effectively, (v. 16) “deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation.” Holy Spirit, God, who for this purpose wished to appear to your disciples in divided tongues of fire, so that you might make us understand that you knew every kind of language: hear effectively and heed the new and ancient grammar of my tongue, in which, as though amid the sorrows of my sins, I ask you to deliver me from bloods.

For you know, O God of knowledge, that in our Latin, according to the grammarians, *sanguines* is not said in the plural, but *sanguis*. Yet, in confessing your name, O Most High, I intend more properly and explicitly to ask you, my God, to deliver me not [Col. 0843C] from *blood* but from *bloods*: that is, from all carnal sins, which are many, and especially from my carnal parents, to whom I am so joined and bound by love that I may not fall into what those fall who “build Zion in bloods,” or who “build a city in bloods.” If by your grace I am delivered from these, I shall not gather their assemblies—that is, the associations of the wicked—“from bloods,” lest, moved and unnaturally softened by carnal feeling toward them, I should be unable to break the bonds of ungodliness or loosen the bundles that weigh me down.

For I know that “flesh and blood will not possess the glory of your kingdom,” and that nothing is more unjust than what flesh and blood has devised. For it was not flesh and blood that revealed to blessed Simon Bar-Jonah that Christ was the Son of the living God; rather, flesh and blood so blinded him at the voice of a single maidservant that he denied having any knowledge of him. But you, Lord, revealed this to him—you who are my strength, my refuge, and my deliverer, who delivered Daniel from the lions’ den and Susanna from a false accusation.

Therefore, from you, my deliverer, I humbly ask and entreat that you deliver me from the aforesaid bloods and from every corruption of punishment and guilt. Instead, grant me incorruption, which you will give your faithful in the future, O God, giver of my salvation—the salvation which you, the Savior, worked in the midst of the earth. That salvation will be found in that incorruption, when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality.” Then you will truly say to me, “I am your salvation,” when you have granted me complete, certain, secure, and everlasting happiness and salvation. [Col. 0844A]

32. O when shall I come to that incorruption and thus be saved! Truly, then I shall be satisfied, when that salvation and happiness is revealed to me—happiness which I cannot attain unless I have first been delivered by you from the aforesaid bloods. If I am delivered from them, and by no other deliverer, then my tongue “will proclaim your righteousness with exultation,” that is, with rejoicing and joy.

I do not mean that righteousness—whose preceding designation is textually uncertain—because it will not permit my mistress, mercy in which I hope, to sit with it in your final judgment. For I could not recall that righteousness of righteous deeds with exultation, since my heart trembles greatly in fear of it. Rather, my tongue will proclaim with exultation and gladness that righteousness of yours by which, through the power of your present righteousness, you now receive me as I confess; for the sacred laws of your righteousness in this life do not disdain to imitate the sacred canons of your mercy, however fiercely they may have to rage against unrepentant sinners in the future.

But if you, my God and deliverer, should not deliver me from bloods, as I desire—which God forbid!—with what presumption would my tongue, while my conscience rebuked me, dare to exult in your righteousness or proclaim it with rejoicing of spirit? Surely it would rather fear that you, God, might say to me, a sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my covenant upon [Col. 0844C] your mouth?” But since these two things—mercy and righteousness—are always joined in your judgment, from the moment I confess concerning the bloods and offer you acceptable repentance, I have no doubt of my deliverance.

33. (V. 17.) Why, O Lord, will you open my lips, which until now have been closed because of my sins—you who opened the mouth of the prophet Zechariah, which no one could shut before it blessed you as its Lord; and who, conversely, so closed the mouths of the lions in the den that no one could open them to harm Daniel?

You, I say, who open and no one shuts, who shut and no one opens, open my lips, O God—not only the lips of my body, so that I may confess you, but also the teeth and lips of my heart, which are its desires and will. For just as no food can enter my bodily mouth and become nourishment for the body unless, after the lips have been opened, it is chewed and ground by the teeth, so the great multitude of your sweetness cannot enter my heart unless the will itself—like lips and teeth, virtues and desires—is first opened entirely to you. Thus, through the open lips of the will, you may enter my heart and soul, and, as food for the soul, give it spiritual nourishment among the teeth of fervent virtues and desires.

For you, worn down because of our crimes, draw me powerfully, so that by frequently turning over your benefits I may remember them. Thus my soul, having tasted through such lips and teeth the sweetness of your unspeakable goodness, may be able to sing of you, as of another, that song of songs: “His throat is most sweet, worthy of the beloved for drinking, and of lips and teeth for chewing.”

And if you open my lips in this way—you who opened the understanding of your disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures—then the mouth of my heart and body will proclaim your praise, for it will no longer be able not to praise you for the good things and benefits which it confesses that it has received and continues to receive from so good a Lord and God: namely, that you created me; that you did not abandon me when I sinned; that you did not forgive me together with my sin; that you urged me to confess; that you justified me when I turned back; that you cleansed me from my iniquities; that you visited me through your grace; and that, when I persevere, you will crown me with the crown of righteousness which you have prepared for those who persevere.

These are the praises which my inner and outer mouth will proclaim concerning you, who dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel, who are greater than every praise. And so that your praise may always be in my mouth, I ask that you fill my mouth with praise. For if you do not fill my mouth with your praise, desire will not burn, nor will praise be beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.

But since praise of your ineffable goodness is pleasant and beautiful, I, with your help, will enlarge my mouth as far as I can, so that you may fill it—you “from whose fullness we have all received.” My mouth will speak your praise, so that I may praise you in my present life and equally in the life to come. And because you said that “the sacrifice of praise honors” you, I now know that at this time—namely, in the fullness of the time of grace—you no longer seek sacrifices of cattle. [Col. 0845B]

(34. V. 18.) For if you had desired a legal sacrifice, which in accordance with the law of Moses the ancients confidently offered you for the expiation of their sins, and which has now been changed into a sacrifice of praise, I would certainly have given it; I would gladly have spent all my possessions in offering bulls and rams to you.

But because I heard you, Lord, crying out in the Church: “I did not desire the holocausts of rams and the fat of fattened animals, nor the blood of calves, lambs, and goats,” and because you would not accept calves from my house or goats from my flocks—so that you would not accuse me concerning sacrifices of this kind, since you do not eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats—I therefore did not offer this sacrifice, knowing that you take no pleasure in such holocausts.

You reject, Lord, the holocausts of bulls, goats, and other animals, which had their appointed time while they promised something still to come. But after the fullness of time came and you sent your Son into the world, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself to you, the living God, as an immaculate victim and cleansed our conscience from dead works, from that time onward you rejected the holocausts and sacrifices of animals, since no offering can compensate for the price of Christ’s sacrifice.

But when I ask you what I should offer you, I hear you answering concerning yourself as though concerning another: (V. 19) “The sacrifice of sinners which pleases God is a contrite spirit”—that is, a spirit afflicted with patience. It is a spirit which, although the furnace of tribulation outwardly afflicts and burns it, is inwardly soothed and softened by patience. For just as an angry man stirs up quarrels, so one patient in peace calms those that have been stirred up, so that a spirit afflicted with patience may be offered as a sacrifice to you, Lord, who govern spirits. [Col. 0846A]

35. This is that sacrifice which, among the other holocausts offered to you by sinners, is always especially pleasing to you. For while other offerings and sacrifices are offered from outside, this one is offered from the innermost depths and marrow of the heart itself.

When the spirit is shaken by tribulations and provoked by insults, yet is wholly kindled by the fire of charity and preserved inwardly intact in the sinner through the virtue of patience, without thinking of revenge, then it is held, restrained, and slaughtered for you, Lord, who are the God of patience and consolation, amid the injuries inflicted upon it. Then incense is placed in your anger; then marrow-filled holocausts are offered to you with the incense of innocent rams.

Then, when savage ferocity has been destroyed in the human being, oxen of complete stubbornness, together with goats of wantonness, are offered and sacrificed. Therefore, I think, you wished to teach through a certain wise man that “the patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities.”

For countless men have held cities and peoples in their power, but very few have held themselves. And when someone fights against peoples or cities, the whole inner and outer person fights at once. If he conquers, he does not seem to have earned a great crown from such a victory, since what is conquered is outside him. But whoever fights against his own spirit within himself by the virtue of wisdom does not fight as a whole person, but as less than half a person.

If by his patience he conquers and rules the spirit that resists him, striking down without weapons or hands the enemy of anger, which had already entered his fortress and climbed with him into the citadel, that man is truly better than a capturer of cities, and this triumph is far more glorious. Thus it is clear that patience, the greatest of virtues, conquers unarmed and is accustomed always to conquer armed men.

Therefore you, God, chosen among thousands, have chosen this sacrifice of a contrite spirit above all others. I too, your sinner, have chosen to sacrifice this same offering to you gladly from my inmost being, if you would give me the means to offer you this sacrifice. [Col. 0846D]

36. But behold, my spiritual and bodily enemies who afflict me will rejoice if I am moved by impatience and anger. Yet I trust in you, who are my patience, that when I am afflicted you would give me patience, if then, returning to myself, I should humbly consider with Joseph’s brothers: “I rightly suffer these things, because I once sinned against my brother.”

And if I should say with Micah: “I will bear the anger of God, because I have sinned against him,” then I would bear the insult inflicted upon me lightly, when in the secrecy of my mind I recalled the evils I had committed. For just as a patient man bears the surgeon’s iron more patiently the more putrid he sees the thing being cut, so, the more I recognized the weight of my guilt, the more lightly I would endure the punishment of tribulation and the more fervently sacrifice to you, my Lord and God, a spirit afflicted with patience.

But O strong and patient God, who are life to those whose hearts are afflicted, so that, if they wish, they may receive from you lessons in patience: how often, in the furnace of tribulation in which you test your laws, have I cracked and failed through anger? How often, forgetting that you were with me in my tribulations, have I flared up against my brothers through impatience? How often have I lost my heart in fury, and, blinded by tribulations, been unable to find the door by which I might return to myself and contain my afflicted spirit inwardly, lest outwardly, through words or blows, it should bellow like thunder and flash like lightning?

And if, at times—although rarely—you granted patience to my afflicted spirit amid adversities or insults, it seemed to me, Lord [Col. 0847B] my God, that your angel who descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, shook the flame of fire out of the furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew, had descended into my heart and, amid my tribulation, inwardly fattened my afflicted spirit in that inner sacrifice by your grace, just as a donkey is outwardly fattened with thistles.

Then the fire of anger did not touch me at all, nor did it grieve me or cause me any trouble. Rather, I proved by experience in myself that, although persecutors fight, afterward they do not sweeten life for themselves, but for the patient person.

For this reason David, setting himself forth as an example in order to invite me to patience, says of his persecutors: “They surrounded me like bees.” For although bees inflict the pain of a sting, they are nevertheless loved because they provide the sweetness of honey.

So I too wish to love my persecutors, Lord, and to endure with an afflicted spirit the stings which they inflict through their bitter efforts, so that a honeyed delight may follow. For from a certain wise man I heard you say, Lord, that “the patient man will endure for a time, and afterward there will be a return of delight.”

37. Therefore, good Lord, good God, who crushed the heads of dragons in the waters and do not reject the prayer of the afflicted, crush the head of my poisoned pride in a flood of tears, so that I may sacrifice to you my spirit afflicted with patience, and also a contrite heart—that is, a heart ground down or constrained by your grace.

For many people, without your grace, God, are worn down and constricted in their hearts by various pains and anxieties; yet you despise and reject their hearts, because contrition and misery are in their ways, and therefore, on account of their affliction of spirit, they howl.

But a heart contrite through repentance for sins—a heart which Judas ploughs by confessing and Jacob follows by breaking through the hardness of the furrows, whose contrition is great like the sea—and a heart humbled, not exalted by excusing its sins, you will not despise, God, for you do not despise the speech of a groan but regard the humble in heaven and on earth.

To whom, then, will you look, Lord my God, if not to one who is humble, contrite, and trembling at your words? My soul too, sorrowful over the greatness of its evil, walks bowed down and, though disgraced, desires to give glory to you.

And so that I may be able worthily and continually to sacrifice these two offerings—the spirit and the contrite heart—to you, my Lord and God, kindly God, whose kindness leads us to repentance, (V. 20) “deal kindly, Lord, with Zion”—that is, with that higher part of my soul represented by the citadel of Zion, once situated in an elevated place of that material Jerusalem. From its summit, keeping watch like a sentinel, it would cry out when it saw enemies.

May that higher part of reason likewise be established on an elevated throne in my soul, foreseeing the spiritual wickednesses that come to attack my inner Jerusalem and crying out against them from the walls. Do not let this Zion in me, Lord, sleep or grow drowsy, since it ought to guard my city together with you. [Col. 0848B]

38. Deal kindly with it, Lord, good God, in your good will—not in my dead will, which lies beside me, that is, lies paralyzed beside the side of my soul. Deal kindly, I say, with the aforesaid Zion, which already observes something of what it hopes for; and in your good will make it so that I may always possess your good will and do it, and discern what your will is—good, pleasing, and perfect: good in you, pleasing in its affections, well-pleasing to those who enjoy it, and perfect for the perfect who seek nothing further.

And truly, Lord, if you deal kindly with me in this way, I shall reckon that you have given me greater benefits than if you gave me all the prebends and dignities of the entire Church militant. For your good will itself, if you, my God, grant it to me as I desire, would not allow my Zion to grow drowsy from weariness. Rather, it would make it stand continually at its watch.

Then, as it kept watch, seeing spiritual enemies rushing against my inner Jerusalem and seeing that city—which it guards—lying open on every side, without the encircling protection of walls of virtue, it could not keep silent because of the dangers it saw approaching. Instead, it would cry with me on high and say: “Deal kindly, Lord; deal kindly in your good will with Zion, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built”—namely, of that inner Jerusalem which is my soul.

For this is that Jerusalem which is built as a city, for which I plead with you, most kindly lover of souls. I know that you are kind, Lord, and yielding concerning evil, and that your mercy is kind, Lord. Therefore deal kindly, and in your good will—which your kindness will give me freely and without my merits—so that the walls of my soul may be built, walls established principally upon living faith, certain hope, and sincere charity.

Make also the walls of the worldly Jericho in me collapse utterly, never to be rebuilt again. For through Joshua you pronounced a sentence of cursing upon those who would raise the walls of this Jericho. The devil builds these walls from the clay of pleasure, the straw of vanity, and the bricks of greed. [Col. 0848D]

39. Through you, therefore, Lord, may the walls of this Jericho be destroyed in me, and may the aforesaid walls of Jerusalem be built. Unless you yourself build them, those who think they are building them labor in vain.

For you alone, Lord, pour faith into these walls as their foundation; you raise hope like a wall; and you construct and bestow charity as impregnable defenses which never fail. This is that impregnable wall which the desires of my heart long to have built through you, who are the builder and guardian of Jerusalem, the heavenly city, and they cry: “Surround us, Lord, with your impregnable wall, and always protect us with the arms of your power.”

And this, Lord my God, is absolutely necessary for me: that you build the aforesaid walls in me. For before they have been built, you will not accept anything from my hands as pleasing or acceptable. But when these walls have been firmly built in my inner Jerusalem, then you will accept it, because before that you will not regard as acceptable the sacrifice of righteousness in which I punish myself.

Through repentance I will sacrifice myself to you. For what is more just than that I should be angry with my own iniquities and sins and perform righteous works through repentance and lamentation? Truly it is just that I should pass from my old life into a new life, so that, once the old person has been extinguished through repentance, I may sacrifice to you, Lord my God, a sacrifice of righteousness according to the regeneration of the new person in myself.

You will also accept, Lord, offerings of alms given to you by me through the hands of the poor, since you consider it specially done to you when something is bestowed or offered by me to one of the least of those whose angels always see the face of the Father.

Let this offering not be made from injustice—that is, from something wrongly acquired or wrongly retained. For you did not wish to look upon Cain or his gifts, because he offered you corrupt gifts. You do not look upon the offerings of the unjust; rather, you consider worthy and acceptable those offerings made from that good substance in whose possession there is no sin in the conscience. These offerings you require of me through the Wise Man, saying: “My son, if you have possessions, do good to yourself, and offer to God worthy thanks and offerings.” [Col. 0849C]

40. (V. 24.) Then you will also accept holocausts—my holocausts, that is, made not only from what is mine but from my whole self. This is because my spirit is afflicted with sorrow, my body with labor, and all that is mine, inward and outward, is equally kindled and consumed by the fire of charity.

For I understand these to be those holocausts concerning which you say to me, Lord: “Your holocausts are always pleasing and acceptable in my sight.” After the aforesaid walls have been built in me, then, with the assistance of angels and the counsel of prelates—whom, together with the perfect Zion, I have appointed as sentinels and guardians upon those walls—the powers of my soul will make their offering upon your altar and mine.

You, who are the high priest of future good things, wish this altar to be dedicated uniquely to you. On it, whatever goodness, devotion, and inner sweetness I possess, I receive from you and offer to you, and you offer to me. Concerning this altar your Wisdom says: “The offering of the righteous makes the altar rich.”

This is the altar which Noah spiritually built for you in himself. Taking from all his animals—that is, from bodily creatures—and from spiritually purified and clean birds, he offered a holocaust to you upon that altar.

This is the altar of your holy temple, which I am. Beside it stands the angel appointed for its guardianship, holding a golden censer in his hand, so that he may present before you, Lord, with much incense, the prayers poured out with tears.

This is the hollow and empty altar, emptied of every earthly affection, which you commanded to be made for you for placing upon it the ashes of the memory of our mind. Concerning this altar, beloved friend, whose speaking is doing, you said that the fire of your love should always burn upon it, and that the priest should nourish it by laying upon it each day the desired wood of my heart.

You came to cast this fire upon the earth so that it might burn. Come, then, and kindle the fire of your love upon this altar of my heart. [Col. 0850B]

41. O supreme priest forever, and high priest of future good things, come and nourish this fire so that it may not fail in Zion. Until a furnace is made in that Jerusalem above, our mother, place upon it the kindling and nourishing wood of this fire.

First, place yourself there—yourself who are, for those who apprehend you, the tree of life: the tree, I say, of life, planted in the middle of paradise, so that those who run toward you from every side may apprehend you as their life and the life of lives.

You are also the tree of life that brings forth each month its fruits, awakening the fruits of our affections through desire—most sweet, peaceful, and pleasant fruits by which the souls of the saints are refreshed without weariness and rejoice.

As the second wood, place there your life-giving cross: that sweet wood through which bitter waters were changed into sweetness; the blessed wood through which justice was wrought against the evil one; the small wood to which faithful people entrusted their souls, and to which I too entrusted mine. It was found faithful, since through this wood all the souls that have been saved were made safe.

These, then, are the two woods that nourish the saving fire of your love upon the altar of my heart. Therefore you alone, priest without the stain of sin, must place these woods each day upon the altar of my heart, so that I too, with the woman of Sarepta, may gather these two woods and enter the altar of God, and from them make bread of life and understanding for myself and for my son—that is, for my affection—so that we may eat and die, and, lest we die, may see and know you alone, the living and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.

Upon this altar all the powers of my soul have placed calves of prayers and praises, thanksgivings and blessings, charity and honor, strength and virtue. Thus, as long as I live, I shall render to you the calves of my lips, freed and released from the yoke of sin by your grace.

And because you are the Lord of hosts, my king and my God, and because you still have other altars, I humbly ask your omnipotence to command that all these things mentioned above—namely, the sacrifice of righteousness, the offerings, the holocausts, and the calves—having been placed upon the altar of my heart, be carried by the hand of your holy angel to your sublime altar, in the presence of your divine majesty.

There there is perpetual praise; there the blessed who dwell in your house, Lord, will praise you forever and ever. May Christ Jesus, your Son, our Lord, bring us to their fellowship. He is God, blessed above all, forever. [Col. 0851A]

42. Finally, since, through you, Lord, who do all things well, your servant found the opportunity to pray to you with this prayer, glory be to the unbegotten Father, the Father of the age to come, the Father of the poor, the Father of orphans, the Father of mercies, the Father of spirits, the Father of lights, the just Father, the holy Father, who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all.

He alone and truly is our Father, whose name is from eternity.

Therefore attend, Father and Lord; attend from heaven, from your holy dwelling place, and from the throne of your glory. Look upon and visit the vineyard of my soul, which you fashioned in baptism.

Where is your zeal, Lord, and my strength, which do not violently and completely draw me back from sin? Alas for me, Lord: the multitude of your mercies has been restrained over me. Why have you made me wander from your ways? Why have you hardened my heart so that it would not fear you?

And now, Lord, you are our Father; we are all clay. You are our maker, and we are all the work of your hands, O God. Do not be angry, Lord, beyond measure, and do not remember my iniquities forever.

Behold, all my desirable things have been turned into ruins. Will you restrain yourself over these things, Lord? Will you remain silent and afflict me exceedingly?

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. But because of your ineffable goodness, make me like one of your hired servants.

For this reason I bend my knees before you, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, asking that, according to the riches of your glory, you grant me steadfastness and strengthen me with power through your Holy Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell in my heart through faith, which works what is pleasing to you through love.

To you, Father, who are able to do for us abundantly beyond all that we ask or understand—indeed, beyond what we understand or ask—be glory in Christ, in the Church, and throughout all generations forever and ever.

And to your only-begotten Son, whose glory we have seen, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father. Although no one has ever seen God, the Only-begotten Son himself, who is in the bosom of the Father, has seen him.

In him I firmly believe with all my heart, and I plainly confess that whoever does not believe in him has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. For in this the love of the Father was revealed among us: God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him, who was obedient to him even unto death.

43. Therefore, only-begotten Son of the living God, Redeemer of the world, God, have mercy on me. For the Father has given you power to exercise judgment. But I beg you to forgive my sins as a sinner before you come to judge me. Then judge me, God, in such a way that you distinguish and separate the cause of my soul from an unholy nation.

For you are the One whom God the Father begot in heaven before the morning star, the Only-begotten; and whom the blessed Virgin Mary, your happy mother, bore on earth as her firstborn, after whom there was no other. At your birth the multitude of the heavenly host came forth praising and saying: “Glory to God in the highest.”

And glory be to the Holy Spirit—not made, not created, not begotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son; who in the beginning was borne over the waters; who is the God of the spirits of every creature; who spoke through the prophets; who is the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and salvation; who filled the world; who makes us ask with unutterable groanings; who filled the disciples of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ with himself and appeared over them in tongues of fire.

O Holy Spirit, God, who are fire not consuming but shining, not burning up but setting aflame, burn my reins and my heart, so that I may serve you with a chaste body and please you with a pure heart.

O divine fire, who are love that affects and an unfailing ardor, my God, Charity, kindle me. Who will grant me that you may come into my heart, intoxicate it, make me forget all my evils, and embrace my one and highest good, which you are?

Have mercy on me, Lord, so that I may speak, though I am dust and ashes. What am I to you, that you command yourself to be loved by me, and, if I do not do so, become angry with me and threaten me with immense miseries? Is my misery small if I do not love you?

O love, Holy Spirit, God, you promise me many good things if I love you. Give yourself alone, for you are love, and that is enough for me. Give what you command, and command what you will, for love of your love. These things I ask of you, who are the Spirit sweeter than honey.

Therefore, to you, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the triune and one God, great, universal, eternal, most almighty, and exalted, let there be, from this entire prayer, glory and jubilation, praise and thanksgiving, honor and everlasting dominion.

As it was in the beginning—indeed, before the beginning—for before the mountains were made or the earth and the world were formed, from eternity and unto eternity you are God, worthy of supreme praise and supreme glory throughout all ages.

And now also you have been glorified in us in the present, you who are always glorious in yourself with the glory which you had with yourself before the world was made. From that glory, which is in me through faith, may glory be given to you.

And in this present moment I desire to follow you with my whole heart and in fear, and to seek your face. Do not put me to shame in my expectation, but deal with me according to your gentleness and according to the abundance of your mercy. Rescue me from the furnace of sin through your wonders, and now give glory to your name, because you alone are the glorious Lord God over the earth and forever.

For all wisdom is from you, Lord God; it has always been, and it is before the age. Your power and divinity are likewise eternal. Although they could consign me to everlasting disgrace, I implore your everlasting omnipotence to grant me everlasting joys instead.

For you are the eternal God who created the ends of the earth, who neither begins nor ceases, but to whom glory belongs now and always and forever and ever.

[Col. 0853A]

44. O King of the ages, immortal and invisible, how many generations have fallen, how many ages have passed, and how many are still to come! You will change them, and they will be changed.

But you, who said, “I am who I am,” are yourself eternally immutable and omnipotent, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning. For although all things are from you, through you, and in you, they are nevertheless not what you are—you who change but are not changed, who make and move while remaining.

And since your blessed apostle says that we are those “upon whom the ends of the ages have come,” I beseech your eternity, my God, to fulfill this apostolic word in me in such a way that the age or worldliness which makes me, a canon or monk, so worldly that this adjective wholly absorbs and destroys its substantive in me, may come to an end in me in such a way that worldly affairs no longer drag me away or disturb me.

Having been exempted from the jurisdiction of this wicked age, make me think of those infinite ages and afterward, with those who live and give confession, bring me to attain them. They are parts of the holy age, the ages of ages.

For I have learned, Lord, that “the ages of ages” is used by the Latin translator in place of “eternal,” and that the repetition in the phrase “the ages of ages” directs the mind of the one who thinks upon it toward eternal things.

These are those eternal, immortal, infinite covenants—the ages of ages—which the righteous will obtain immutably after these present and changeable ages. In them, to you, their author, may there be everlasting glory alone.

45. Amen. O God of the Hebrews, you wished me to know [Col. 0853C] that “amen” is neither Greek nor Latin, but Hebrew; and, on account of its excellence, it was neither translated nor altered by interpreters, so that it might designate your name, which is wonderful and immutable. [Col. 0854A] Accordingly, you wished this word to have three meanings.

First, “amen” is understood substantivally: it is a noun, and it signifies your holy and terrible name, as when it is read in the Apocalypse (3:14): “Thus says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation.” Therefore, from you, Lord my God, who alone are designated by this name, I ask and entreat with all the affections of my heart that, out of reverence for this holy name of yours, you may write my name again in the book of life; and that, with those who have kept your Sabbaths, chosen what you willed, and held fast your covenant, you may give me in your house and within your walls a place, and a name better than that of sons and daughters, an everlasting name that will not henceforth perish.

Second, “amen” is understood adverbially. When you, my God, appeared on earth and lived among human beings, whenever you wished to assert some truth, you frequently added: “Amen I say to you”—that is, “I say to you truly, truthfully, or infallibly: it is as I say.” And sometimes you repeated “amen, amen,” so that the repetition itself might be a greater expression of truth. Therefore I humbly beseech you, who are true truth and beloved love that does not deceive, that your truth may always shine in my heart and that every worldly and diabolical falsehood may be destroyed.

Third, “amen” is understood verbally: it is a verb, as when, in response to every expression of desire, “amen”—that is, “let it be done”—is answered by those who ask and desire what is requested. The psalmist is also read to have repeated it at the end of certain psalms, where it is said: “Let it be done, let it be done.” In this sense, at the end of the present prayer, which contains my vows and desires, I say: “Amen”—that is, “So let it be.” Namely, to you, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the triune and one God, be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0853C] Thus far Anselm of Canterbury. For we have given in the *Spicilegium Romanum*, vol. VI, the summaries or chapters of the entire canonical work of Anselm of Lucca, from complete manuscripts. Indeed, Niccolò Alemannus (*De parietibus Lateranensibus*, chapter 12), a competent judge of such matters, suspects that Anselm’s collection was perhaps drawn from an equally extensive work by Pope Leo III. Moreover, in another Vatican manuscript, no. 325, which belonged to Queen Christina of Sweden, I read the following title: *An authentic and concise collection of the rules and sayings of the holy Fathers and of authoritative councils, made in the time of Gregory VII, most holy pope, by the blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, his diligent imitator and disciple, who, at his command and instruction, eagerly completed this work. Here begins the first book, on the power and primacy of the Apostolic See.* Yet nothing else follows in the aforementioned manuscript except forty-seven brief excerpts from the decrees of synods, pontiffs, and others. Finally, we shall later present, among the poems, a little flower of a certain monk named Anselm.]

[Col. 0855]

# The Prayers of Saint Anselm (C, G)*

## Prayer One. To the Holy Trinity

Be present, holy Trinity, one almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who desire not the death but the repentance of sinners. Do not repel me, wretched and sinful, frail and unworthy, from your mercy. Do not look upon my crimes, impurities, and shameful thoughts, by which, lamentably, I am separated from your will; instead, pour out upon me the abundant clemency of your goodness. Do not allow my enemies to rejoice over my destruction in hell, where no one will confess you; rather, have mercy on me, oppressed by the weight of my crimes and polluted by the stain of every wickedness.

Grant me, I beg you, wretched as I am, your grace, and free me from all evils, past, present, and future; from sudden and everlasting death; from every plague and calamity; from every scandal and danger; from evil desire, perverse action, and every sin. Wipe away all my crimes, iniquities, offenses, and negligences. Be gracious to me in all my anxieties and tribulations, in my necessities and temptations, in all my dangers and infirmities.

Holy and undivided Trinity, unfailing goodness, attend to my supplications. Just as you have made me a participant in your sacraments—not through any merits of mine, but solely through your freely given goodness—so make me persevere in faith, hope, and charity until that hour when I shall depart from here. Protect and defend me from every evil; grant me everything that will benefit me; free me from eternal punishment; and bring me into everlasting joys. In your mercy, most merciful one, cause now to cease that deadly and diabolical temptation which I fear may prevail over me because of my sins.

Triune and one God, receive now the prayers of your humble little servant. Grant me, Lord, diligence that seeks you, wisdom that finds you, a soul that recognizes you, eyes that see you, a way of life that pleases you, perseverance to the end, a perfect end, and an eternal reward.

Hear me as I pray, just as you heard Jonah from the belly of the whale; free me, as you freed Susanna from a false accusation. Hear me as you heard Peter on the sea and Paul in chains. Help me, I beg you, Lord, and continually free me from every evil. Snatch me from the jaws of demons; withdraw me from everlasting death; fill me with the abundance of your grace. Fortify my breast with protecting power; purify my mind; sanctify my life; correct my conduct; illuminate my heart with heavenly wisdom; temper the heat of the flesh; extinguish anger; restrain my tongue from empty talk. Let words of truth and mercy, goodness and concord proceed from my mouth.

Direct me completely in every uprightness of conduct, and, lest I be reproved in anger, strengthen me, most merciful one, in every good work. To you, Lord, I lay open the secrets of my heart; to you I confess all my sins; to you I uncover the foulness of my heart; to you I reveal the filth of my shame. For I have sinned more gravely than Sodom and transgressed more seriously than Gomorrah. I owe you not merely ten thousand talents on account of my crimes, but I owe you an account of my entire life. For I have become a transgressor of your law, utterly negligent, disobedient, and a violator of all your commandments throughout my life.

Therefore I now come before your face in confession, [Col. 0856B] entreating you with excessive anguish of heart and the contrition of weeping and tears, that in this acceptable time you may hear me and in these days of salvation help me. Order all my actions according to your good pleasure, so that I may progress from day to day and advance from virtue to virtue. To you, Lord, I pour out supplicating prayers; to you I pour out the weeping of my heart. You, pardon me as I confess, so that, with your help, I may lament my sins in this mortal life in such a way that I may escape the sentence of condemnation on the day of judgment.

You, eternal light, open my eyes from every human blindness; preserve in me the purpose and habit of religious life. Defend my heart from every impediment of the world and from worldly desire. And just as I wear the habit of innocence, so grant me an increase of virtues, that I may deserve to put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man with righteousness and holiness. Thus, fortified in every way by the help of your protection, may I always remain in your love, receive the heavenly blessing, and, by your gift, rejoice in the supports of the present life and of the eternal one. Amen.

I again entreat your immense mercy, merciful and compassionate God. Forgive me all offenses arising from slippery presumption, so that my soul may be filled with the sweetness of your goodness; and, once pardon and complete forgiveness have been granted, wipe away and cleanse, through your ineffable goodness, everything I have tasted through my own guilt. May the mercy of your clemency not be far from me; rather, whatever, contrary to your will, I have contracted through the devil’s deception and through my own iniquity and frailty, wash away by forgiving it, gracious and merciful as you are.

Heal my wounds and forgive all my sins, so that, separated from you by no iniquities, but always here and everywhere fortified by the help of your protection, I may be able always to cling to you, Lord, and at some time receive a share in perpetual glory, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart,” which you have prepared for those who love you (1 Cor. 2:9). Amen.

O blessed light of the Trinity and principal unity, increase faith in us, increase hope, increase charity. Deliver us, save us, justify us. O blessed Trinity, dissolve crimes, forgive sins, drive away miseries, remove anxieties, look upon tribulations, drive away adversities, and, granting the fulfillment of our petition, mercifully hear us, so that, stripped of all the evils we suffer, we may always delight to rejoice in your judgments.

Come, I beg you, merciful Lord, and stand among us, so that we may feel you present in our hearts. Gladly receive the confession of our lips, and grant that we may possess the fruit of freshness, so that, watered by your rains, we may deserve to please you with an abundance of sweet fruits, be kindled by the illumination of your love, and be enlightened by the fire of true charity. And just as you wondrously illuminated your servant Moses with splendor, so deign to enlighten our hearts and minds, that, purified from the stain of sins, we may deserve to come to you, who are eternal life.

Grant the rewards of joys; grant the gifts of graces; dissolve the bonds of strife; bind fast the covenants of peace. Illuminate the human heart; wipe away the filth of minds; loosen the bond of guilt; overturn the masses of crimes.

We have sinned against you, Lord; have patience with us, and rescue us from the evils that daily increase over us. Our iniquities, Lord, have multiplied over our heads (Ps. 39:13); our offenses have grown up to heaven. Spare us, Lord, [Col. 0857C] and incline your mercy over us. Lord, today we have been diminished because of our sins; but may we be received with a contrite heart and a humble spirit, and deal with us according to your gentleness, because there is no shame for those who trust in you (Dan. 3:40), Lord.

There is no other God besides you, Lord (Ecclus. 36:5), and you care for everything (Ecclus. 42:4), because you are Lord of all. Spare your people (Joel 2:17), who grant abundance to those who pray, so that evil may be turned into goodness. Hear, Lord, the supplication of your servants, and have mercy on your people, so that all nations may know that you are the God of the ages (Baruch 2:15). Have mercy, Lord our God, on the city of your sanctification (Ecclus. 36:15). Have mercy on your people, Lord, over whom your holy name has been invoked (ibid., 14), so that all who dwell on earth may know (ibid., 19) that you are the God who protects your peoples. Forgive, Lord, the sins of your people according to the abundance of your mercy (Ps. 105:45). Just as you were gracious to our fathers, be gracious also to us, so that your glory may be fulfilled throughout the whole earth.

Hear, God, our supplication, and be gracious to your people; turn our tribulation into joy, so that, while living, we may bless you, Lord. We beseech you, Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and anger may be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned. Incline your ear, Lord, and hear (Ps. 85:1); look down from heaven and see the affliction of your people (Ps. 79:15). Hear, Lord; be gracious, Lord; attend, do not delay, because your holy name is invoked over us (Ecclus. 36:14).

Many are our sins, Lord; we have sinned against you, patience of Israel. Free us, Lord, in the time of our distress. We have sinned, Lord, and you are angry with us (Isa. 64:5), and there is no one who can escape your hand (Tob. 13:2); but we beg that your mercy may come upon us (Ps. 118:41). You who spared Nineveh, have mercy on us. Remember your mercies, Lord (Ps. 24:6), and pierce with repentance those whom you have tolerated until now.

Be gracious, Lord, to all living and departed Christians. Help the best, so that they may always remain in goodness. Have mercy on the good and the middling, so that they may become better. Come to the aid of those acting wickedly and of sinners, so that they may quickly correct themselves. Be gracious also, Lord, to heretics and schismatics, Jews and pagans, so that they may turn back from their evil ways and acknowledge you, the living and true God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. Have mercy on all the faithful departed, giving them blessed life because of your goodness.

Remember us, Lord, in this heavy body; may your goodness convert those whom your long-suffering has sustained. [Col. 0858C] Have mercy on us, God of all, look upon us, and show us the light of your mercies (Ecclus. 36:1). We are wretched; we are your works, which you gave to your Son as an inheritance for himself (Ps. 32:12). Do not close your ear to our prayers, but mercifully relieve the affliction of your people, recalling what you promised when you said: “Turn back to me, and I will return to you” (Mal. 3:7).

Remember us, Lord, remember us, so that we may become heirs of your kingdom; and, seeing your glory, may we worship your goodness and say together, when we behold your immeasurable beauty: “Glory to the Father, who made us; glory to the Son, who saved us; glory to the Holy Spirit, who renewed us,” through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0858D]

## Prayer II. To God the Father through the Merits of the Incarnate Son

[Note: [Col. 0857D] Compared with Sommal’s edition, the Gothic edition, and the Paris edition of Saint Augustine, where it appears in volume IX of the *Book of Meditations*, page 335. The title is “To God the Father through the merits of the incarnate Son.” Sommal notes that in the Gothic edition it is invoked without a title and follows the preceding prayer immediately.]

I invoke you, my God; I invoke you, because you are near to all who invoke you, but to those who invoke you in truth (Ps. 144:18); for you are truth. Teach me, I beg you, through your clemency, holy truth; teach me to invoke you in truth, because I do not know how this ought to be done, but I humbly implore you, blessed truth, to teach me.

[Note: [Col. 0857D] Augustine omits the words “but to those who invoke you.”]

For to be wise without you is to be foolish; but to know you is to know perfectly.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] For *abs te sapere*, etc., Sommal reads *abs te enim sapere*. Sommal and Augustine read *perfectum est scire* (“it is perfect knowledge”) rather than *est perfecte scire* (“is to know perfectly”).]

Instruct me, O divine Wisdom, and teach me your law. For I believe that the one whom you instruct and teach from your law will be blessed.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Another reading is: “I truly believe that the one whom you instruct is blessed, and whom you teach from your law.” Sommal reads: “For I believe, the one whom you instruct and teach from your law will be blessed.”]

I desire to invoke you; may this, I beg, be done in truth. What is it to invoke truth in truth, except to invoke the Father in the Son?

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read: “What is it to invoke truth in truth?”]

Therefore, holy Father, your Word is truth; the beginning of your words is truth. For this is the beginning of your words: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1).

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “Holy, the Word,” rather than “Holy Father, your Word.”]

In that Beginning I adore you as the highest Beginning; in that Word of truth I invoke you, O perfect Truth. In that very Truth, direct me and teach me in truth.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal reads: “In that same truth at last direct me and teach me in truth”; Augustine reads: “In that same truth, direct me in truth and teach me.”]

For what is sweeter than to entreat the Begetter in the name of the Only-Begotten, to bend the Father toward mercy by recalling the Son, and to soften the King by naming his most beloved offspring?

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “to invoke the Only-Begotten” rather than “to entreat the Only-Begotten.” They also read “to bend the Father by recalling him” and “to soften the King by naming his beloved offspring”; the supplied text reads “to bend the Father toward mercy by recalling the Son” and “to soften the King by the designation of his offspring.”]

Thus are criminals accustomed to be snatched from prisons; thus are those bound delivered from chains; thus do those receiving a sad sentence of death not merely obtain acquittal but also gain an extraordinary favor, provided that, before angry rulers, they have made known the love of their beloved offspring.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “not merely life, but …” rather than “not merely obtain acquittal, but …”; and “angry fathers” rather than “angry rulers.”]

Thus guilty little servants escape the punishments of their masters when the sweetness of sons intervenes on their behalf.

Thus I ask you, almighty Father, through the love of your almighty Son: lead my soul out of prison to confess your name. Through him who was born co-eternal with you, I implore you: free me from the bonds of sins. Restore me placated to life, although my own merits threaten me with a lethal sentence, through the intercession of your most precious offspring, who sits at your right hand.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “a joyful sentence” and “your precious offspring,” rather than “a lethal sentence” and “your most precious offspring.”]

For I do not know what other intercessor I should direct to you on my behalf except him who is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2), who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us (Heb. 7:25).

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read: “who is the propitiation for our sins”; and “who also, in the glory common to him, intercedes with your goodness for us.”]

Behold my advocate with you, God and Father; behold the high Priest, who does not need to be purified by another’s blood, because he shines, drenched in his own blood. Behold the holy victim, pleasing and perfect, both offered and accepted as an odor of sweetness. Behold the spotless Lamb, who remained silent before those shearing him, who, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, and subjected to insults, did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7). Behold him who committed no sin, bore our sins, and healed our sicknesses by his bruising (ibid., 4).

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “shines, poured forth” rather than “shines, drenched”; and “struck with blows” rather than “struck with slaps.”]

Look, merciful Father, upon your most merciful Son, who suffered such impious things for me. Look, most clement King, upon the one who suffers, and remember graciously for whom he suffers. Is this not that innocent one, my Lord, whom you handed over as a Son in order to redeem a servant? Is he not the author of life, who, led like a sheep to the slaughter and obedient to you unto death (Phil. 2:8), did not fear to undergo the most atrocious kind of death? Recall, dispenser of all salvation, that this is the very one whom, although you begot him from your own power, you nevertheless willed to make a participant in my weakness.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “most clement Father, the one who suffers” rather than “most clement King, upon the one who suffers”; “the most atrocious death” rather than “the most atrocious kind of death”; “disposer” rather than “dispenser”; and “from one power” rather than “from your own power.”]

Truly this is your divinity which, having put on my nature, ascended the gibbet of the cross, and in the flesh it had assumed endured a grievous punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Augustine reads “having put on” rather than “which, having put on”; Sommal and Augustine read “in the assumed flesh” rather than “in the flesh it had assumed.”]

Turn back, my God, the eyes of your majesty toward this work of ineffable goodness. Look upon the sweet-born one stretched out with his whole body; see the innocent hands streaming with pious blood, and, placated, forgive the crimes my hands have committed.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “beloved offspring” rather than “sweet-born one,” and “harmless hands” rather than “innocent hands.”]

Consider the unarmed side pierced by a cruel spear, and renew me in the sacred fountain which I believe flowed from it. See the immaculate feet, which did not stand in the way of sinners (Ps. 1:1), but always walked in your law, fastened with dreadful nails; and perfect my steps in your paths (Ps. 16:5). Make me hate every way of iniquity (Ps. 118:128); in your mercy, remove from me the way of iniquity (ibid., 29); and, being gracious, make me choose the way of truth (ibid., 30).

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “pierced by a spear” rather than “pierced by a cruel spear”; “the holy and sanctified fountain” rather than “the sacred fountain”; and “make me hate, graciously, all the ways” rather than “make me hate every way.”]

I beseech you, King of the ages, through this Redeemer of mine, make me run in the way of your commandments (ibid., 32), so that I may be able to be united in spirit with him who did not shrink from clothing himself in my flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal and Augustine read “King of the saints” rather than “King of the ages”; and “through this holy Holy-of-Holies, through this Redeemer” rather than simply “through this Redeemer.”]

Do you not see, merciful Father, the beloved head of your youthful Son, bent with his snow-white neck lowered, and his most precious life dissolved in death? Look, gentlest Creator, upon the humanity of your beloved offspring, and have mercy on the weakness of your frail creature.

[Note: [Col. 0859C] Sommal reads “the beloved head … its precious life dissolved in death”; Augustine reads “the most beloved head … the precious life dissolved in death.”]

His bared breast gleams white; his bloodied side glows red; his stretched entrails are dry; his beautiful eyes grow dim; his royal face is pale; his tall arms stiffen; his marble-like legs hang down; a stream of sacred blood waters his pierced feet. Behold, glorious Begetter, the mangled limbs of your most beloved offspring, and remember graciously what my substance is. Look upon the punishment of the God-man, and release the misery of the created human being. See the suffering of the Redeemer, and forgive the offense of the redeemed.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal and Augustine read “Look; raise up” rather than “Look upon … and release”; and “Forgive the sin of the redeemed” rather than “forgive the offense of the redeemed.”]

This is he, my Lord, whom you struck on account of the sins of your people, although he is himself the beloved one in whom you were well pleased. This is that innocent one in whom no deceit was found, and yet he was numbered with the wicked.

What did you commit, sweetest child, that you should be judged in this way? What did you commit, most loving young man, that you should be treated so?

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal reads “that you should be treated so harshly.”]

What was your crime, what your offense, what the cause of your death, what the occasion of your condemnation? For I am the wound of your pain; I am the guilt of your killing. I am the bruise of your suffering; I am the labor of your torment. I am the merit of your death; I am the crime deserving your vengeance.

O wondrous condition of judgment, and ineffable ordering of the mystery! The wicked sins, and the just is punished; the guilty transgresses, and the innocent is beaten; the impious offends, and the devout is condemned; what the evil one deserves, the good one suffers; what the servant perpetrates, the master pays; what the human being commits, God endures.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal reads “the guilty transgresses” as “the guilty person transgresses,” while the supplied text has “the guilty one has transgressed.”]

Where, Son of God, where has your humility descended? Where has your charity burned? Where has your goodness advanced? Where has your kindness grown? Where has your love reached? Where has your compassion arrived?

For I acted unjustly, and you are punished; I committed the crime, and you are chastised; I produced the offense, and you are subjected to torture; I was proud, and you are humbled; I swelled up, and you are weakened; I was disobedient, and you, obedient to the Father, pay the penalty for the crime of disobedience; I obeyed gluttony, and you are afflicted by hunger; desire dragged me into the heat of illicit passion, while perfect charity leads you to the cross; I presumed upon what was forbidden, and you underwent the rack; I delight in food, while you labor on the gibbet; I enjoy delicacies, while you are torn by nails; I taste the sweetness of the fruit, while you taste the bitterness of gall.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal and Augustine read “disobedient to the Father, you pay the penalty for the crime” rather than “you, obedient to the Father, pay the penalty for the crime”; and “desire dragged me into illicit passion” rather than “into the heat of illicit passion,” with corresponding differences in the following verbs.]

For me, the guilty one, Eve laughs and rejoices; for you, the devout one, Mary weeps and suffers with you.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal and Augustine read “May Eve laugh and rejoice for me, the guilty one; may Mary weep for you, the devout one.”]

Behold, King of glory, behold my impiety, and your goodness shines forth; my injustice and your justice are made clear. What, my King and my God, what shall I repay you for all that you have repaid me? (Ps. 115:12.) For nothing can be found in the human heart that can worthily be offered in return for such rewards. Can human ingenuity devise anything comparable to divine mercy? Nor can a creature undertake any service by which it might justly repay the protection of the Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] The repeated wording “for such rewards” is found also in Sommal and Augustine.]

Yet, Son of God, in this your wondrous dispensation there is something by which my frailty can in some measure assist: if, pierced by your visitation, the mind crucifies its flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24). And if this is granted by you, it begins already, as it were, to suffer with you, since you too deigned to die for my sin. Thus, under your guidance, through the inner victory of the human being, it will be armed for an outward triumph, so that, once spiritual persecution has been defeated, it may not fear to submit to the material sword for love of you.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal reads “to which my own [frailty] may contribute”; “if this is done by you”; “to suffer—or to live—with you, since you died for sinners”; and “through the inner victory” rather than “through the inner victory of the human being.”]

In this way the smallness of the creature, if it pleases your goodness, will be able, according to its strength, to respond to the greatness of the Creator. And this, good Jesus, is the heavenly medicine, this is the antidote of your love.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal reads “of the Creator” where the supplied text reads “of the Creator”; the editions also have “this is the heavenly medicine of the Creator,” rather than “this is the heavenly medicine.”]

I beseech you, through your ancient mercies, pour into my inmost being what, when the venom of the serpent’s contagion has been rejected, may restore me to my former soundness; what, once I have tasted the nectar of your sweetness, may make me despise with my whole affection the enticing prosperity of the world and fear none of its adversities for your sake; and, mindful of perpetual nobility, may make me always disdain the winds of this passing fear.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Augustine reads “pour into my wounds” rather than “into my inmost being”; Sommal reads “so that, when the serpent’s contagion has been rejected,” “the stain” rather than “the venom,” and “once your nectar has been tasted.” Augustine and the Gothic edition likewise vary between “contagion of thought” and “contagion.” Augustine reads “tumor” rather than “fear.”]

Let nothing, I beg you, be sweet to me without you; let nothing please me, let nothing be precious, let nothing beautiful smile upon me apart from you. Let everything without you become worthless to me, I beseech you; let all things be filthy. Whatever is contrary to you, let it be grievous to me; and let your good pleasure be my unfailing desire. Let me be weary of rejoicing without you, and let me delight in being sorrowful for you.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal and Augustine read “let nothing smile upon me apart from you”; one reading has “let nothing without you be pleasing to me.” They also read “and let it be grievous to me,” rather than “let it be grievous to me.”]

Let your name be my refreshment, and your remembrance my consolation. Let my tears become my bread day and night (Ps. 41:4), as I seek out your ordinances. Let the law of your mouth be good for me, above thousands of gold and silver (Ps. 118:72). Let obeying you be lovable to me, and resisting you detestable.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal and Augustine read “let obedience to you be lovable to me, and resistance to you detestable.”]

I ask you, my hope, through all your mercies, to be gracious to all my impieties. Open my ears to your commandments, and, I beg you by your holy name, do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins (Ps. 140:4). I also ask you, through your wondrous humility, that the foot of pride may not come against me and that the hand of the sinner may not move me (Ps. 35:12).

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Sommal reads “all my iniquities” rather than “all my impieties.”]

Behold, almighty God, Father of my Lord, graciously determine how you may have mercy on me, since whatever I found most precious I devoutly offered to you, and whatever I discovered most dear I presented in supplication; I have left nothing for myself without laying it before your majesty. Nothing now remains for me to add, because I have entrusted my entire hope to you.

[Note: [Col. 0863C] Sommal and Augustine read “how, whatever I found …” rather than “since whatever I found”; and “whatever I found again” rather than “whatever I discovered.”]

I sent you my advocate, your beloved Son; I sent the glorious offspring as mediator between me and you. I sent, I say, an intercessor through whom I trust in forgiveness. I sent the Word in words, whom I said was sent in deeds because of my deeds; and I recounted to you the death of your most holy offspring, which I believe he endured for me.

[Note: [Col. 0863C] Sommal reads: “I sent the Word in words, because I said that he was sent in deeds for my sake; I recounted to you the death of your most holy offspring.” Augustine reads “the passion of your most holy offspring” rather than “the death.”]

I believe that our Godhead, sent by you, assumed humanity, in which it deemed it worthy to endure bonds, blows, spittle, and mockery, and also to receive the cross and nails. This humanity, once worn down by the cries of infancy, bound in the swaddling clothes of childhood, wearied by sweats, weakened by fasts, afflicted by vigils, and exhausted by journeys, he later subjected to scourges, tore with punishments, numbered it among the dead, but then endowed it with the glory of resurrection, led it into the joys of heaven, and placed it at the right hand of your majesty.

[Note: [Col. 0863C] Sommal and Augustine read “bound in the swaddling clothes of childhood, wearied by the sweats of youth” with differing word order; the supplied text has “wearied by sweats” without an explicit “of youth.” Sommal and Augustine also read “afterward afflicted by scourges,” “tore it with punishments,” “placed it among the dead,” “endowed it with the glory of resurrection,” and “placed it at your right hand”; the supplied text reads “appointed it a place among the dead” and “placed it at the right hand of your majesty.”]

You are my appeasement [Note: Som. Aug.: “This appeasement”] and my propitiation. Here attend, graciously, to the Son whom you begot [Note: Som. Aug.: “My propitiation, here attend graciously to how you begot him”; “your propitiation. Here attend graciously to the Son whom you begot”], and to the servant whom you redeemed; here look upon the Maker, and do not despise what he made. Embrace serenely the Shepherd, and receive mercifully the sheep borne back on his own shoulders [Note: Aug.: “Receive”; “look upon”].
