This is that most faithful Shepherd who, not long ago, had sought the wandering sheep through mountain crags and valley precipices with many and varied labors [Note: Som.: “He had sought through the valley precipices with many and varied labors, who now … to the dying one”; “He had sought through the valley precipices with many and varied labors. And now, to the dying one …”; Aug. omits the relevant words]. When at last he had found it, rejoicing, he placed himself beneath it [Note: Aug.: “places himself beneath it”] as it was already dying and failing through prolonged exile, and with a wonderful effort of love he lifted it from the deep abyss of confusion [Note: “leaning upon it from the abyss of confusion … bound … he carried the one sheep …”; Som.: “straining from the deep abyss of confusion … fastened … he brought back the one [sheep] to the ninety-nine”; Aug. omits “straining”]. After clasping it in pious embraces, he brought back the one sheep that had perished to the ninety-nine sheep (Luke 15:4).

Behold, Lord, my King, almighty God; behold, the Good Shepherd returns to you what you entrusted to him [Note: Som. Aug.: “to you the sheep which you entrusted to him”]. At your command he received, for the salvation of humanity, the one whom he restored to you free from every stain. Behold, your most beloved Son reconciles to you your creature, which had strayed far from you [Note: Aug.: deviavit, “strayed,” rather than deviaverat, “had strayed”]. Behold, the gentle Shepherd reforms for your flock what the violent robber had carried away. He returns before your sight the servant whom his own conscience had made a fugitive [Note: Som.: “his own conscience had made him a fugitive”], so that the one who deserved punishment through himself may, through the Maker of the world, deserve pardon [Note: Som.: “through his satisfaction”; Aug.: “through his making”]; and the one for whom hell remained because of his sins [Note: Som. Aug.: “for whom he expected hell”] may now, with so great a guide, confidently hope to be recalled to his homeland.

I could offend you, holy Father, through myself, but through myself I could not appease you for myself. My helper became your beloved Son, my God [Note: Som. Aug.: “my helper, your beloved [Son]”; “my helper. My God, your beloved [Son]”], sharing in my humanity in order to heal my weakness, so that from the very place from which the guilt of offense had arisen [Note: Som. Aug.: “from which he had brought forth guilt”], he might offer you a sacrifice of praise, and through this make me acceptable again to your piety, since, seated at your right hand, he would always show himself to be a sharer in my substance [Note: Som. Aug. and the Gothic edition: “show himself to be a sharer in my substance”].

Behold my hope; behold my complete confidence. If, as I deserve, you despise me because of my iniquity, at least look upon me in pity because of the love of your beloved offspring [Note: Som. Aug.: “look upon my salvation in pity for me”; “look upon me, at least, mercifully, because of”]. Look upon the Son, through whom you may be propitiated toward the servant [Note: Som. Aug.: “Look upon the Son; consider what you may be propitiated toward in the servant”; “attend to the Son, through whom you may be propitiated toward the servant”]. See the mystery of the flesh, and remit the guilt of the flesh. Recall what the good Son endured, and forget what the evil servant did [Note: Som. and Aug. omit this sentence]. Whenever the wounds of your blessed offspring are displayed before you [Note: Som. Aug.: “Whenever the wounds of the wounded one are displayed before you”], let my crimes, I beseech you, remain hidden [Note: Som.: “my wounds”; Aug.: “my crimes”]. Whenever precious blood reddens from his gracious side, I beg you, let the stain of my pollution be wiped away [Note: Som.: “let the corruption be wiped away, I beg”; Aug.: “let my stain be washed away, I beseech you”]. And because flesh provoked you to anger, may flesh, I pray, bend you toward mercy; so that just as flesh seduced me into guilt, flesh may lead me to pardon [Note: Som.: “into guilt, so may flesh”].

For indeed my wickedness deserved much [Note: Som. Aug.: “much indeed”; Gothic edition: “much, for”]; but far greater is what the piety of my Redeemer demands by right [Note: Som. Aug.: “the piety demands”; “my Redeemer’s piety demands by right”]. For my injustice is great, but much greater is the justice of my Redeemer [Note: Aug.: “injustice, but greater indeed”]. For as much as God is superior to humanity, so much is my wickedness inferior to his goodness, both in quality and in quantity [Note: Som.: “in quality and also in quantity”; Aug.: “both in quality and quantity”]. For what could a human being do wrong that the Son of God, made human, did not redeem [Note: Som. Aug.: “What could a human being do wrong that the Son of God, made human, would not redeem”; Aug.: “what did humanity do wrong that the Son of God, made human, did not redeem”]? What pride could swell that such great humility could not bring low? What power of death could there be that the punishment of the cross of the born God would not destroy [Note: Som. Aug.: “What such great thing could there be”; “What great power could there be”]? Surely, my God, if the sins of the offending human being and the grace of the redeeming Author are weighed on an equal scale [Note: Som. Aug.: “If the injustice of the offending human being and the grace of the redeeming Author are freed”; “are weighed”; Gothic edition: “is weighed”], piety surpasses the sinner’s wickedness by as much as the east is distant from the west, or the lower underworld is separated from the highest vault of heaven [Note: Som. and Aug. omit this clause].

Now, best Creator of light, forgive my sins because of the immense labors of your beloved Son. Now, I ask, let my wickedness be forgiven because of his piety, my perversity because of his gentleness, and my savagery because of his meekness [Note: Som.: “And let savagery be forgiven because of his meekness”; “and may my savagery be forgiven because of his meekness”]. Now let his humility [Note: Som.: “his humility”; “your humility”] profit against my pride; his patience against my impatience; his kindness against my harshness; his obedience against my disobedience; his tranquility against my restlessness; his sweetness against my bitterness; his pleasantness against my anger; his charity against my cruelty [Note: Gothic edition: “against my cruel obstinacy”].

Who with you … [Note: Som., Aug., and the Gothic edition here append an invocation of the Holy Spirit: “Now, O divine love …”].

## ORATION III [Note: Compared with manuscripts Vict., KK. 16, Corb. 160, Val-luc., and Flor. In particular, “vain glory, envy, pride”; the manuscripts omit these words.]

### To God: Against the three enemies who very often assail the sinner more grievously and, unless God’s mercy protects him, frequently wound him unto death—namely, vain glory, envy, and pride

Lord, my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all who persecute me and deliver me (Psalm 7:2). In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me not be put to shame forever. In your justice deliver me and rescue me (Psalm 70:2). Lord, my God, my Creator and my Governor, as I have said and shall always say [Note: the manuscripts: “and I always say”], I have hoped in you, and in you I hope; and as long as there is breath in my nostrils, I shall not despair of your mercy.

But as for myself, if I carefully examine all my actions, I always despair, because I am always occupied with evil works. Yet when I look toward my sweetest Creator and my most patient Lord, who sees me living badly and nevertheless awaits my correction—awaiting and enduring, he listens to see whether I might in some respect undertake [Note: the manuscripts: “whether I might undertake”] to amend my life—I recover breath and invoke the mercy of my Creator, who endures me with such sweetness.

My enemies attack me from every side and now almost from every side pierce and break into the interior of my heart. Unless that most compassionate Lord of mine, who created me, comes to my aid and, coming to my aid, terrifies my enemies who so afflict me and drives them back [Note: the manuscripts: “drives back my enemies who”], my soul, already unhappily bound in their chains, will soon be led away captive. Therefore deliver me, Lord, from all who pursue me (Psalm 141:7)—and, if not for my sake, at least for your own.

For my sake, I confess, sweetest Lord my God, you have no reason to deliver me, because I am almost always pleased to do evil and to persist in evil works. But deliver me for your own sake, because it is a disgrace to you for your enemies to mock your creature in this way, to mistreat one whom they have so mocked and defiled with their most filthy vices—one whom you created so nobly, adorned with so great an honor of reason, and fashioned in your image and likeness [Note: the manuscripts: “your handiwork”].

Behold, my sweetest God, behold my unhappy spirit, corroded on every side by evil works. It has scarcely been torn from the teeth of its enemies, by which it was unhappily mangled, and now implores your help and sighs for the visitation of your grace; for unless you come quickly to its aid, exhausted by their pursuit, it will soon be unable even to breathe toward you.

My enemies are many, as you see, most merciful Creator. I am grievously battered by their savagery, and, struck and mocked, I endure no small pains. But one among the others always attacks me more grievously and always strives, without any compassion, to cast me down unto destruction. For often, when my other enemies, as though wearied by pursuing me, rest, one more audacious than the others brandishes his weapon more forcefully: namely, vain glory, which not only stains the wretched human being with evil works [Note: the manuscripts omit “openly”], but also, unless he carefully guards himself, slays him through the very good works that he appears to perform.

This plague was born from that pride which first overthrew the human being and drove the overthrown and wounded one from the happiness he possessed. And, to overthrow more forcefully the wretched person whom it attacks, it summons envy to its aid—envy through which death entered the world (Wisdom 2:24). Envy therefore burns the wretched person whom it seizes; by burning him, it makes him go about sorrowful and as though possessed by sickness [Note: the manuscripts: “makes him go about”; manuscript Vict.: “makes him fall into it”]. But vain glory, as though restoring him, exalts him on account of the very good works that he pretends to do.

Yet, so that vain glory, once it has seized the wretched person [Note: the manuscripts omit “once”] may lead him away more unhappily as a captive and leave him no hope of escape, it turns back to its mother, pride. Animated by her deadly counsel, it cuts away from him the virtue of loving God and neighbor. For when the unhappy person infected by vain glory desires to appear superior to everyone else, if he sees someone whom he cannot deny to be better than himself in good works and to walk more uprightly [Note: the manuscripts: “if he considers someone who is better in good works”], he suppresses that person and everything he does, if he can. If he cannot, because those actions are plainly right, he at least strives by every means to obscure them so that they may not be believed to have been wholly rightly performed.

Thus the wretched mind possessed by this captivity does not act rightly, even if it seems to do something right, because it neither loves his neighbor, whom it is commanded to love as itself (Matthew 19:19), nor loves God; by acting in this way it is shown not to love him [Note: Corb. 160: “Nor does he act rightly, even if he seems to do something right, because he neither loves his neighbor, whom he is commanded to love as himself, nor loves God; by acting in this way he is shown not to love him.” Manuscript Vict.: “Nor does he act rightly, even if someone seems to act rightly, because he neither loves his neighbor, whom he is commanded to love as himself, nor loves God; by loving him in this he is shown not to love him.” Val-luc. and Flor.: “Nor does he act rightly, even if he is commanded to do something right; nor does he love God, whom by doing this he is shown not to love.”].

For whoever does not love his neighbor, and does not help him insofar as he is able to advance in goodness, is neither loved by God nor regarded by him in his works, even if those works appear good before human beings. What, indeed, what could be more wretched than a person who exalts himself because of a good work? While he thinks he is rising, he falls from the heights to the depths. For pride always naturally lies in the depths of hell, whereas humility always dwells in heaven and remains in heaven. And the one whom vain glory casts down from the heights is received by its mother, pride, into the arms of eternal perdition. Conversely [Note: manuscript Corb.: “Thus there is contrition”; manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor.: “as is the case conversely”], God, who regards the humble and recognizes the exalted from afar (Psalm 137:6), raises to the heavens the one whose humble way of life is on earth.

I confess, most gentle God, I confess that I have been grievously overthrown by these three evils—or rather, these three infernal furies—and wounded in soul almost unto destruction; and unless your most indulgent mercy quickly comes to my aid, I must be condemned still more grievously. Woe to me, woe to me, always and everywhere—woe to me! What captivity the wretched human being is in!

If he lives badly, condemnation is open and clear. If he appears indeed to live rightly but, failing to guard himself carefully, takes glory in it, once again certain death and eternal condemnation await the wretched man. O God, our refuge; O our Creator and our strength against those who persecute us—if they see that you abandon us because of our sins, they are always lying in wait—help us, merciful Lord, who always need your mercy and who ask, more sluggishly than would be useful to us, for the help of your compassion.

And if you despise us because we are entangled in many iniquities [Note: Corb.: “you despise us because we entangle ourselves in many iniquities”; Vict., Val-luc., and Flor.: “you despise us because we are entangled in iniquities”], at least turn your merciful eyes back toward us, because we are your creature. And just as it is most true that you are always our Creator, so may we always and everywhere experience you as our defender and unfailing protector against our enemies, so that, defended and aided by you throughout the present life, when our temporal course is ended we may come to you, our Creator and Lord, cleansed and absolved from all sins. Amen.

## ORATION IV [Note: Compared with manuscripts Thu. 267, Vict., KK. 16, and Val-luc. “He strips bare and spreads out”; the manuscripts omit “he strips bare and.”]

### To God: When the sinner is greatly troubled by his iniquities and spreads them openly before God, setting aside all shame

Most High and most gentle God, lover of humanity, Creator and Governor of all creatures, I confess to your immeasurable goodness all my sins—whatever I have committed, in whatever manner—from the hour when I was able to sin until this hour, in which you still allow me to live by your mercy.

I cannot remember them all, because they are many and cannot easily be enumerated. But you, most compassionate and most merciful God, to whom all things are known before they happen, who are the true examiner of thoughts [Note: the manuscripts omit “are”] and the most just scrutinizer of heart and kidneys (Psalm 7:10), you know all my sins, whatever I have done or am still doing, whether inwardly in my soul through hidden thoughts or outwardly through manifest actions.

And because you understand that I truly committed all these things against your will [Note: the manuscripts: “which I truly understand against your will”], I confess before your majesty and before all your saints [Note: manuscript Thu.: “before all your saints, [I confess] myself”; “before your blessed angels and all saints, [I confess] myself”] that I am guilty and blameworthy. Unless your most indulgent mercy comes to my aid first, after the death of the flesh I shall be condemned to eternal death and tortured eternally by everlasting torments [Note: manuscript Thu.: “eternal tortures”; manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.: “eternal torments”].

I know, my sweetest God, I know that you created me, and that you mercifully loved me once created; and that you created me for this purpose: that I too should love you, my Creator, as was fitting, and obey all your commands. You did all this for my good, not so that you might become better through me or in any way richer [Note: manuscript Thu.: “for me”].

For you need no good, because you are essentially goodness itself, and every good thing—or person—that is good is from you. Therefore you cannot be either better or richer [Note: the manuscripts: “either greater or richer”; manuscript Val-luc.: “greater or”]. You cannot do this, not through a false incapacity, but through true power. For whoever can and does evil can and does it through his own evil, because through this power he is not happily raised upward to the heights but unhappily dragged downward to the depths.

Deceived miserably by this power—or rather, incapacity—and, like a swelling bladder, vainly puffed up, placed outside reason and made like a foolish beast of burden (Psalm 48:13), struck and overthrown most wretchedly by the weapon of pride, I despised you, my Creator and most merciful Lord, in your commandments, which you gave me for my good if I should observe them. Despising them [Note: manuscript Thu.: “and despised”], and as though bereft of mind, while I am borne proudly here and there, having lost true solidity, I rush into the ways of perdition and death and foolishly and senselessly follow vanity and the wind of vain exaltation [Note: manuscript Thu.: “the poison of vanity, foolishly”].

I confess, most merciful God, I confess before your omnipotence that I am excessively proud, vain, and full of every kind of elation. And I think that, if I possessed any power in this world [Note: the manuscripts: “I think that if”], no one would be able to endure my pride.

But although this pride, by which I am so grievously afflicted before human beings, is execrable and very dangerous [Note: manuscript Thu.: “and dangerous”], there is nevertheless another pride which, when I carefully search the secret recesses of my mind, without flattering myself [Note: manuscript Thu.: “the recesses of my mind”; manuscript Vict.: “without flattering me”], greatly troubles and scatters my unhappy soul [Note: manuscript Thu.: “scatters the soul”].

Sometimes, if it happens—which nevertheless happens rarely—that I, unhappy as I am, do something [Note: the manuscripts: “if something happens”] which, according to human judgment, appears to possess some likeness of goodness, I take no small pride in that very thing. And if no one speaks of it or takes care to praise me in any way [Note: the manuscripts: “does not take care to praise”], I despise him as though he were foolish and knew nothing. Or even if, as though unconcerned, I shun human praise as vain and useless, I nevertheless glory in it greatly within my inmost self, where God alone sees; and, astonishingly, while I avoid praise, I desire praise and vain glory all the more [Note: manuscript Thu.: “while I avoid praise, I seek praise and more”].

Behold, my God and my Creator, behold, you see me doing this, living this way, and squandering my whole life. Behold, you see and execrate it, and for such a life you promise nothing but punishments and torments. Help me, therefore, my Creator; help me, helper in times of need; help and aid my soul. Through your ineffable mercy destroy and confound my pride.

Behold, my God and my Lord, behold, I confess to your immeasurable goodness that I am wholly infected, corrupted, and destroyed by the poison of this evil, and now have almost been reduced to nothing unless your mercy comes to my aid. But before your majesty I acknowledge my guilt; guilty and blameworthy, I ask pardon and forgiveness from you, merciful Creator, for this and for all my sins—you who do not desire the death of the sinner and do not rejoice in the destruction of those who are dying (Ezekiel 18:23).

There are also many other things that spring from the root of this plague, and I likewise confess that I possess them and am greatly disturbed by their annoyances and very often worn down by them. Likewise, I seek pardon and forgiveness for all these things. They are, namely: anger [Note: the manuscripts: “these: anger”], impatience, discord hostile to God and hateful to all the saints [Note: manuscript Thu. omits “hateful”], indignation, resentment of spirit, weariness of mind, voracity of the belly, grumbling, avarice, rapacity, and many similar things. I see my unhappy soul vexed and afflicted, torn and mangled by these.

Besides these there is one evil, an evil surpassing all evils, by which I feel my soul so much more grievously and miserably torn and afflicted because it has always been with me from my very cradle, grew with me, clung to me throughout infancy, adolescence, and youth [Note: manuscript Thu. omits “always”], and even now, when my limbs are failing through old age, does not abandon me.

This evil is the desire for pleasure, the delight of the flesh [Note: manuscript Vict.: “carnal delight”], the storm of lust, which has tormented and dissolved my unhappy soul in many varied ways and, depriving it of every virtue, has made it empty and weak. I confess, sweetest and gentlest God, I confess before your omnipotence that I have often been polluted by unclean recollections of this wicked act—of this wicked deed [Note: the manuscripts: “by the unclean recollections of this wicked deed”; “by the unclean recollections of this wicked deed”]—and inflamed, suffering no small and dishonorable ardors [Note: the manuscripts: “immoderate ardors”]. And not only do the evil memories and foolish recollections of my own pleasures harm me; the misdeeds of others, told to me and recalled to memory through filthy recollections, also stain my heart with no small blemish of iniquity [Note: manuscript Thu.: “with no small poison”].

Behold, my God, my most compassionate and merciful Lord: although I have suffered no little shame, I have spread my iniquities before you. I have shown my wounds and sins; I have shown my soul stained by evil works, infected by the pleasures of evil works, and defiled by recollections of evil pleasures.

My God, my mercy, look upon my repentance; look upon your piety [Note: manuscript Thu.: “look upon my piety”; manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.: “look upon your piety”]. Receive my confession and deal with me according to your mercy. If you should observe iniquities, Lord—Lord, who could endure it? (Psalm 129:3) Or who could be freed without your mercy by his own justice [Note: manuscript Vict.: “by your justice”]?

Be propitious toward me, Lord [Note: manuscript Vict. omits “my Lord”; manuscript Val-luc.: “toward me, Lord”]; be propitious toward me, a sinner (Luke 18:13). Spare my sins and iniquities, so that through your mercy I may be cleansed and purified from all vices and mercifully absolved from all sins; and when my temporal life has ended [Note: the manuscripts omit “life”], may I deserve to be led to the kingdoms of heaven, where, with all the saints, I may be able to praise, bless, and glorify you forever and ever. Amen.

## ORATION V. TO GOD

### For obtaining compunction of heart in prayer

Forgive, Lord; forgive graciously; forgive and have mercy. Spare my ignorance and my many imperfections. Do not reject me as presumptuous because I, a servant—if only a good one, and not also useless and evil, and therefore very evil—dare to praise, bless, and adore you, our almighty God, terrible and greatly to be feared, without contrition of heart and a fountain of tears, without due reverence and trembling.

For if angels who adore and praise you tremble, filled with wondrous exultation, why, when I, a sinner, stand before you, utter praises to you, and offer sacrifice, do I not tremble in heart, grow pale in face, quiver in lips, and shudder with my whole body, and thus, when tears have arisen, mourn continually before you?

I wish to, but I cannot, because I am unable to do what I desire. For this reason I am greatly astonished within myself when, with the eyes of faith, I behold you as exceedingly terrible.

But who can do this without the help of your grace? For our entire salvation is your great mercy. Woe to me: how has my soul become so senseless that it is not seized by overwhelming terror while it stands before God and sings his praises? Woe to me: how has my heart become so hardened that my eyes do not continually produce rivers of tears while a fellow servant speaks before his Lord—while a human being speaks with God, a creature with the Creator, one made from clay with the one who made everything from nothing?

Behold, Lord, I place myself before you, and I do not keep silent from your fatherly ears about what I perceive in secret concerning myself. You are rich in mercy and generous in rewards. Give me from your good things, so that from them I may serve you. For we cannot serve or please you from anywhere else except from your gift.

Pierce my flesh, I beseech you, with your fear (Psalm 118:120). Let my heart rejoice so that it may fear your name (Psalm 85:11). Would that my sinful soul feared you as that holy man who said: “For I have always feared God as though waves were swelling over me” (Job 31:23).

God, giver of all good things, grant me amid your praises a fountain of tears together with purity of heart and exultation of mind, so that, loving you perfectly and praising you worthily, I may feel, taste, and savor with the palate of my heart how sweet and pleasant you are, Lord, as it is written: “Taste and see that the Lord is pleasant. Blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Psalm 35:9). “Blessed is the people that knows rejoicing” (Psalm 88:16). “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has established ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which he appointed” (Psalm 83:6). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

## ORATION VI [Note: Compared with manuscripts Vict., KK. 16, Val-luc., and Corb. 160, in which the beginning of this prayer has been torn away.]

### To God: That the sinner ought not to despair on account of any sin, because the Lord is gracious and merciful and does not desire the sinner’s death but life

Have mercy on me, God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity (Psalm 50:3).

We believe that the Holy Spirit dictated this prayer. Moved by his inspiration, the sinful but also faithful human being asks God to have mercy on him [Note: manuscript Vict.: “to have mercy on him”], and asks that his iniquities be blotted out according to the multitude of God’s compassions, believing him to be both the most almighty God and the most merciful Lord.

It is the work of the Holy Spirit that the sinner is displeased with his crimes and strives to do those things that please his Creator. Yet he cannot do this by his own strength unless he is enlightened by the grace of that same Holy Spirit [Note: manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.: “inspired by grace”]. When the Spirit visits his heart through his grace, he immediately cleanses it from every stain of vices.

The Lord is sweet and gracious toward his creature, which he created in his own image and likeness (Genesis 1:27); and, having endowed it with so great an honor, he in no way allows it to perish except through its own great iniquity. Indeed, the Creator of the universe is altogether kind and gentle and rich in mercy toward all who call upon him (Psalm 85:5), toward all who call upon him in truth. He fulfills the desire of those who fear him [Note: manuscript Vict.: “he will fulfill”], hears their prayer, and through his great mercy leads them safe to eternal glory (Psalm 148:18).

For he has mercy on all and hates none of the things he has made; he overlooks human sins for the sake of repentance and spares them, because the Lord is gracious (Ecclesiasticus 2:13). The Lord is merciful toward sinners who cease from their wickedness, cleanse their evil deeds through true repentance and the good works of true repentance, and through true confession and the sacrifice of true confession slaughter themselves [Note: manuscript Vict. omits “themselves”].

True repentance and true confession consist in mourning the evils that have been committed and not committing again the evils that ought to be mourned. As a father has mercy on his children, and much more than a fleshly father has mercy on his children, so the gracious and merciful Lord has mercy on all who fear him.

For he knows our formation; he also knows from what he made us—our clay [Note: manuscript Vict.: “from what he made us, our light”; “from what he made us, our clay”]. For he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 102:13–14), and ashes, yet made in his image. Therefore, when we contemplate and truly confess such great mercy of our Creator toward his creature, let us not despair of the remission of our offenses. For if we repent with our whole heart and pursue our iniquities with worthy tears, we shall unquestionably obtain his most indulgent piety.

But perhaps someone who has lost his senses and is already immersed in the very chasms of eternal damnation, considering the enormity of his crimes and despairing of God’s mercy, dares to say to himself:

“What remedy for recovering salvation can I find any longer, or what consolation can I hope for that promises some pardon for my crimes? From the time when I was able to sin, I have never ceased from sins and evil works. I have always heaped sins upon sins, and the sins that I was at some point unable to fulfill in deeds I never ceased to complete through evil wills and evil desires. Enveloped, therefore, in such evils and iniquities [Note: manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc.: “and wills”], surrounded by such crimes and sins, what can I now expect except eternal destruction and the eternal condemnation of eternal destruction?

“Sometimes, if by God’s mercy I made a confession of sins and, receiving penance for my sins from a priest, promised some amendment of my evils, immediately—or after a short delay—I committed the same evils or worse sins. Like a dog, I returned to my vomit: what I had vomited out through confession, with mouth and heart [Note: the manuscripts: “with mouth and heart”], I took up again in a still filthier manner.

“I have also sworn many times that thereafter I would cease from sins, entirely abandon the way of iniquity, and follow the way of justice. But neither fear of that very perjury could hold me back from sins, nor fear of God, who sees everything from on high.”

Behold, you see, O God, most sweet lover of humanity; behold, from your sanctuary you see and from the lofty dwelling-place of the heavens you look upon the wretched human being who turns his back upon you [Note: [Col. 0873D] *Promentem*, “turning forth,” in the manuscripts; *ponentem*, “placing,” in the reading adopted here], despises you in your commandments, and, because of his great sins, despairs of your great mercy. Although he is exceedingly wretched and sinful [Note: [Col. 0873D] “And sinful” in the manuscript of Victor; “and sinning” in another reading], you nevertheless look upon him and see that he was created by you and, while he exists in this life, is sustained by your benefits.

Send, good God [Note: [Col. 0873D] “Send, good Lord” in the manuscripts], your fear into his soul, and remove from his heart the harmful fear. Look upon him and illumine his blinded heart, so that he may see and understand how great and how lovable is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden from those who despair of you, but have perfected for those who hope in you (Psalm 30:20). Let neither the storm of water overwhelm him, O most sweet God, nor the deep swallow him up, nor the pit close its mouth over him (Psalm 68:16)—that is, the abyss of his iniquities and the despair of your mercies.

We believe, O most merciful Creator and God of humanity, that you are omnipotent and do everything whatever you will. For the Prophet says of you [Note: [Col. 0873D] “The Prophet says of you” in the manuscripts; “For the Prophet says of you” in the reading adopted here]: “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Psalm 134:6). We know, however, that you do not wish to destroy sinners, but that they cease from sins [Col. 0874B] and live. If, then, you are omnipotent, as you truly are, because you can do whatever you will; and if you do not wish to destroy sinners, but wish them to turn back from evil and live, we ought not to despair of the abundance of your mercies, but, secure in the hope of pardon, to await your mercy. It is altogether true that our sins are many and great, but we are certain that your mercy is also great and abundant.

We know, omnipotent and merciful God, we know that you are the supreme Spirit, unchangeable and eternal, living by your own life, which you yourself are, and by your eternity; while we are your creation, created by you through your goodness and mercy. But when we sin—that is, when we do not do what you command and do what you forbid—we die through our sin [Note: [Col. 0873D] “Because of our sin” in the manuscript of Victor; “through our sin” in the reading adopted here], although, even while dead, we continue to exist in a certain kind of life granted to us by your mercy.

But if we again exist obedient to you, and, aided by your grace, restrain ourselves from evil works, and are joined through good works to you, who are the living Spirit and our Creator, we come to life again; and after death we shall live with you in eternal glory, if thereafter, for as long as we live, we remain persevering in right works [Note: [Col. 0873D] “Perseverable” in the manuscripts; “persevering” in the reading adopted here]. When the prophet Elisha had died and been buried, and a dead man was touched by his bones, he rose alive and, through the merits of the prophet and the touch of his body, was permitted to live again (2 Kings 13:21) [Note: [Col. 0873D] “The prophet, when he had died” in the manuscript of Victor; “the prophet, as though dead” in another reading]. If, then, one who was dead rose again through the touch of a dead prophet, much more shall we come to life again if we are joined through good works to you, our Creator, who are the living and immortal Spirit.

Have mercy, then, upon us, our Creator; have mercy upon us according to your great mercy, and according to the abundance of your mercies blot out our iniquity (Psalm 50:3). Raise us up in this present life from death to [Col. 0875A] life [Note: [Col. 0875D] “To life” in the manuscript of Victor; “into life” in another reading]—that is, from the death of sin to the life of righteousness—and at the end of the age, justified through your mercy, raise us up to eternal glory. May you deign to grant this to us, you who live and reign through eternal ages. Amen.

## 251. PRAYER VII. TO GOD

With confession of sins and humble petition for grace.

Most gracious God, merciful and compassionate God, be favorable to our sins, and grant that the sins which we have committed either at the instigation of the author of death or by our own will you may not reserve for examination at your judgment, but that, through the grace granted, we may rejoice solely in pardon. For if, Lord, we compare before your eyes the faults we have committed with the scourges we endure [Col. 0875B], what we suffer is less than what we deserve.

We feel the punishment of sin, yet we do not avoid the persistence of sin. Under your scourges our weakness is broken, but our iniquity is not changed. The sick mind is tortured, but the stiff neck is not bent; life sighs in pain, yet does not amend itself in its conduct. If you wait, we are not corrected; if you punish, we do not endure. In correction we confess what we have done; in visitation we forget what we have wept over. If you press your hand upon us, we promise what must be done; if you suspend the sword, we do not fulfill our promises. If you strike, we cry out that you should spare; if you spare, we again provoke you to strike. If distress comes, we ask for time to repent; if mercy looks upon us, we abuse the patience that spared us.

The wound inflicted has scarcely passed, and already the ungrateful mind does not remember what it endured. If you hear us quickly, we grow insolent through mercy; if more slowly, we murmur through impatience. We want you to keep what you have promised, yet we do not fear failing to observe what you have commanded. You therefore have us before you as confessed offenders, Lord; spare us, because you are compassionate. We know that, unless you forgive, you will rightly punish us; but with you there is abundant mercy and overflowing propitiation. Grant, therefore, without merit, what we ask—you who made out of nothing those who would ask.

Have mercy upon us who cry out to you, Lord. May a faithful and tearful voice move your compassion, and may that mercy in which we place all our hope not reckon what we have offended in, while it looks upon what we ask. And although it is a great misery for us to be guilty, may it be a greater clemency for you that we are miserable.

As suppliants for your help, we lay before you both the evils and the pains of our crime, and by praying we await from you the mercy which by sinning we rejected. Grant, therefore, most holy Father, that we may mourn what we have committed, and that throughout all the hours of day and night you may permit us, freed from every assault of evil, to serve your compassion. May what you are asked to receive be granted to us through your indulgence, for you recognize that we have no confidence in our own righteousness. Raise us up, Lord our God, and lift us in your mercy, so that, while we desire to be saved by your gift, we may also rejoice in the faith and peace of all nations.

## PRAYER VIII. TO GOD

God of immeasurable mercy, God of boundless compassion, God, creator and restorer of the human race, who cleanse the hearts of those who confess to you and absolve those who accuse themselves before the sight of your divine clemency from every bond of iniquity: with all my sighs I implore your power, that, according to the abundance of your mercies, you may grant me to make before you a pure confession concerning all my iniquities of which my conscience accuses me, and may grant me true and worthy repentance for all these things: whatever I have sinned in evil thoughts, in evil consent, in wicked counsel, in lust and unclean pleasure, in idle words, in malicious deeds, in sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

For you, in your mercy, gave me the individual members of my body, fitted for human use, so that I might work out the salvation of my soul; but I, most wretched of all and a sinner, despised you, the lover of eternal salvation, and consented to the eternal fires prepared for me by the enemy. I fell into sins, collapsed into offenses, exceeded proper measure in each of my members, and made myself liable to impious labors.

In saying these things I do not blaspheme your creature in me, Lord, but I ask from you, most holy God, medicine for what is mine, because I understand myself to be guilty beyond measure, because I recognize that my offenses are innumerable, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea. Moreover, there are anger, sadness, acedia, boastfulness, and sloth. Therefore I confess that I am subject to the principal vices; but you, who do not desire the death of a sinner, look upon me and have mercy upon this wretched person.

## PRAYER IX [Note: [Col. 0875D] Compared with the two Victorine manuscripts noted above, with Thuaneus 267, Bec O., Corbie 160, one manuscript of Vallis Lucentis, one of Fleury, and the edition of Sommaius. “To God the Father, for obtaining pardon and virtues” in Victorine manuscript 16. “Prayer to God the Father” in the manuscripts of Thuaneus and Bec. “Prayer to God” in Victorine manuscript 3. “For oneself” in the Corbie manuscript. “The prayer of Lord Anselm to God” in the manuscript of Vallis Lucentis. “Good prayer” in the Fleury manuscript. “Supplicatory meditation from remembrance of the Lord’s passion”]. TO GOD.

Omnipotent God, merciful Father, good Lord, have mercy upon me, a sinner. Grant me pardon for my sins; grant me to avoid and overcome every snare, temptation, and harmful pleasure; perfectly to avoid in mind and deed [Note: [Col. 0875D] “And perfectly” in the manuscripts; “perfectly” in the reading adopted here] what you forbid [Note: [Col. 0875D] “And to avoid in deed” in the manuscripts; “to avoid in mind and deed” in the reading adopted here], and to do and observe what you command; to believe, hope, love, and desire what and as much as you know and will [Note: [Col. 0875D] “To live what” in the manuscripts; “to desire what” in the reading adopted here]; contrition of humility and devotion, disciplined abstinence and mortification of the flesh; a pure, sober, and devoted mind for loving, praying to, praising, and meditating upon you, and for every action and thought according to you; a truthful and effective knowledge, love, readiness, and practice of your commandments [Col. 0877A] [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Delight and practice” in the manuscripts; “love, readiness, and practice” in the reading adopted here]; always, Lord, to advance humbly toward better things and never to fail.

Do not entrust me, Lord, to my own will [Note: [Col. 0877C] The manuscripts omit “to my own will”], nor to human ignorance or weakness, nor to my merits, nor to anything other than your compassionate ordering [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Nor to anything else” in Victorine manuscript 16; “nor to anything whatsoever else” in the reading adopted here]. But mercifully order me yourself, and all my thoughts and deeds [Note: [Col. 0877C] “My deeds and words” in the manuscripts; “my deeds” in the reading adopted here], according to your good pleasure, so that in me, by me, and concerning me your will alone may always be done [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Alone” in the Fleury manuscript; “only” in another reading]. Free me from every evil and lead me into eternal life. Amen.

## 252. PRAYER X [Note: [Col. 0877C] It is included among the works of Saint Augustine in Book IX of the *Meditations*. Compared with manuscript Thuaneus 267, the edition of Sommaius, the Gothic edition, and the Paris edition of Saint Augustine. “To God, for cutting away vices, etc.” in one manuscript. “Prayer to God the Father” in another. In the edition of Sommaius it occurs among the *Meditations* of Saint Augustine, where it is also divided into sections]. TO GOD

For cutting away vices and obtaining virtues.

Lord my God, grant my heart to desire you [Col. 0877B] [Note: [Col. 0877C] “By desiring you” in one manuscript and in Sommaius; “to desire you, desiring” in the reading adopted here], to seek you by desiring, to find you by seeking, to love you by finding, and by loving to redeem my evils, and, once redeemed, not to repeat them. Grant, Lord my God, to my heart repentance [Note: [Col. 0877C] “The compunction of repentance” in one manuscript and in Sommaius], to my spirit contrition, to my eyes a fountain of tears, and to my hands generosity in almsgiving.

My King, extinguish in me the desires of the flesh and kindle the fire of your love [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Kindle the strength of your love” in Sommaius; “kindle the fire of your love” in the reading adopted here]. My Redeemer, drive from me the spirit of pride and graciously grant me the spirit of your humility [Note: [Col. 0877C] “The treasure of humility” in one manuscript and in Sommaius]. My Savior, remove from me the fury of anger and kindly bestow upon me the shield of patience [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Grant me the understanding of patience” in one manuscript; “kindly bestow upon me the shield of patience” in Sommaius]. My Creator, tear from me the rancor of my soul [Note: [Col. 0877C] “The rancor of my soul” in Sommaius; “the rancor of my own soul” in another reading], and gently grant me sweetness of mind [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Grant me sweetness of mind” in one manuscript; “gently grant me sweetness of mind” in Sommaius]. Grant me, most merciful Father, firm faith [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Grant, most merciful Father, firm faith to me” in the manuscript and in Sommaius], fitting hope, and continuous love [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Perfect love” in the manuscript and in Sommaius].

[Col. 0877C]

My Ruler, turn away from me the vanity of the soul [Note: [Col. 0877C] The manuscript omits “of the soul”], inconstancy of mind, wandering of heart, vulgarity of speech, haughtiness of the eyes, gluttony of the belly, insults against my neighbors, the crimes of slander, the itch of curiosity, desire for riches [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Desire for riches” in Sommaius; “greed for riches” in another reading], the plundering of positions of power, the appetite for empty glory, [Col. 0878A] the evil of hypocrisy, the poison of flattery, contempt for the needy, oppression of the weak, the burning of avarice, the rust of envy, and the death of blasphemy.

Cut away in me, my Maker, rashness, wicked obstinacy [Note: [Col. 0877C] “In me, the rashness of my deeds and wicked…” in the manuscript and in Sommaius; Sommaius reads “iniquity”], restless idleness [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Restlessness and idleness” in the manuscript; “restless idleness” in the reading adopted here], sleepy sluggishness [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Sleepiness and sluggishness” in the manuscript; “sleepy sluggishness” in the reading adopted here], dullness of mind, blindness of heart, stubbornness of perception, savagery of behavior, disobedience to the good, resistance to counsel [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Resistance” in the manuscript and in Sommaius; “contradiction” in the reading adopted here], unbridled speech, the plunder of the poor, violence toward the powerless, the slander of the innocent, negligence toward subordinates, cruelty toward members of my household, impiety toward those close to me, and hardness toward my neighbors [Note: [Col. 0877C] The manuscripts read: “violence, the slander of the innocent, negligence toward subordinates, severity toward subjects, impiety toward members of the household, hardness toward neighbors.” Sommaius has the same text as the edition, except that instead of “impiety toward members of the household” he reads “impiety toward those close to me.”]

My God, my mercy, I beseech you through your beloved Son: grant me works of mercy, devotion to compassion, to suffer with the afflicted, to assist the needy, to help the miserable, to advise the wandering, to console the sorrowful, to relieve the oppressed, to refresh the poor, to support those who weep, to forgive debtors, to spare those who sin against me, to love those who hate me, to return good for evil, to despise no one but to honor all [Note: [Col. 0877C] “But to honor” in the manuscript; “but to honor all” in the reading adopted here], to imitate the good, to avoid the wicked, to embrace virtues, reject vices, to have patience in adversity, restraint in prosperity, and guardianship over my mouth—“and set a door of restraint upon my lips” (Psalm 140:3)—to trample earthly things underfoot and desire heavenly things [Note: [Col. 0877C] “To thirst for heavenly things” in the manuscript; “to desire heavenly things” in the reading adopted here].

Behold, my Fashioner, I have asked for many things, although I have deserved not even a few [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Although he deserved not even a few” in Sommaius]. I confess—alas, I confess!—that not only are the gifts I ask not owed to me [Note: [Col. 0877C] “The good things are not owed” in Sommaius; “the gifts are not owed” in the reading adopted here], but many and carefully devised punishments are owed to me. Yet publicans, prostitutes, and thieves encourage me [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Yet publicans, prostitutes, and thieves encourage me” in the manuscript; “nevertheless they encourage me” in Sommaius], people who, snatched from the jaws of the enemy by the humility of momentary repentance [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Snatched by momentary repentance” in the manuscript; “snatched from the jaws of the enemy by the humility of momentary repentance” in the reading adopted here], are received into the bosom [Note: [Col. 0877C] “Are received into bosoms” in the manuscript; “are welcomed into the bosom” in Sommaius] of the Shepherd.

For you, God, Maker of all, although you are wondrous in all your works, are believed to be more wondrous still in the depths of your compassion [Note: [Col. 0877C] The manuscript and Sommaius read: “For you, God, Maker of all, although you are wondrous in all your works, are believed to be more wondrous in the depths of compassion.” Sommaius also has “in works of compassion”]. Therefore you said concerning yourself through one of your servants: “His mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144:9) [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscript and Sommaius read: “Therefore, speaking concerning yourself through one of your servants, you said: ‘His mercies…’”]. And, as though speaking of an individual, we confidently believe that you said concerning your entire people: “But I will not scatter my mercy from him” (Psalm 88:34) [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscript and Sommaius read: “Speaking, you confidently said concerning your entire people: ‘I will not scatter my mercy…’”].

For you despise no one, cast no one away, and shudder at no one—unless perhaps at one who, madly, has shuddered at you [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscript and Sommaius read: “You cast away no one, shudder at no one, unless perhaps one who, madly, has shuddered at you”]. Therefore not only do you refrain from striking when angry [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscript reads: “You strike, being not merely angry”; Sommaius: “you do not strike merely when angry”; Augustine’s edition: “you do not strike when angry”], but, if those who provoke you seek them, you bestow good things upon them, my God, horn of my salvation and my protector (Psalm 17:3).

Unhappy that I am, I provoked you; I did evil before you (Psalm 50:6), stirred up your fury, and deserved your anger. I sinned, and you endured it; I offended, and you still bear with me. If there is repentance [Note: [Col. 0879C] Sommaius reads “if I repent”; the reading adopted here is “if there is repentance”], you spare; if I return, you receive me; moreover, while I delay, you wait for me. You call back the one who wanders, invite the one who resists, awaken the one who is sluggish [Note: [Col. 0879C] Sommaius reads “you await the sluggish one”], embrace the one who returns, teach the ignorant, soothe the sorrowful, raise up the fallen, restore after the fall, give generously to the asker, let the seeker find, and open to the one who knocks (Luke 11:10).

Behold, Lord God of my salvation, I do not know what to set against this, nor do I know what to answer; no refuge from you [Note: [Col. 0879C] “No refuge” in Sommaius; “no refuge from you” in the reading adopted here], no hiding place from you is open [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscript reads “the hiding place lies hidden”; the reading adopted here is “the hiding place is open”]. You showed me the way of living well, gave me knowledge of how to walk, threatened me with Gehenna, and promised me the glory of paradise [Note: [Col. 0879C] “You promised me paradise” in Sommaius]. Now, Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Corinthians 1:3), pierce my flesh with your fear (Psalm 118:120), so that by fearing what you threaten I may escape it, and graciously restore to me the joy of your salvation (Psalm 50:14), so that by loving I may receive what you promise [Note: [Col. 0879C] “That I may share in what you promise” in another reading].

My strength, Lord, my firm foundation and refuge [Note: [Col. 0879C] “My God and refuge” in the manuscript; “my firm foundation and refuge” in the reading adopted here], and my deliverer (Psalm 17:2–3), suggest to me what I should think about you [Note: [Col. 0879C] “Suggest what I should think” in the manuscript], teach me with what words I should invoke you [Note: [Col. 0879C] “With what words” in the manuscript and Sommaius; “with what words I should invoke you” in the reading adopted here], grant me by what works I may please you [Note: [Col. 0879C] “By what works I may please you” in Sommaius; “by what works I may please” in the manuscript].

For I know—indeed I know—one thing: that you are appeased; and another: that you do not despise. A troubled spirit is truly a sacrifice to you, and you accept a contrite and humbled heart (Psalm 50:19). Enrich me, my God, [Col. 0880A] my Redeemer [Note: [Col. 0879C] “My helper” in the manuscript; “my Redeemer” in the reading adopted here], with these gifts. With these protections fortify me against the enemy; grant me this refreshment from the flames of vices [Note: [Col. 0879C] “Grant refuge” in the manuscript and Sommaius], and in your goodness open this refuge from the passions of desires.

Make me, Lord, the strength of my salvation (Psalm 139:8), so that I may not be among those who believe for a time and withdraw in the time of temptation [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscript and Sommaius read: “among the number of those who believe in favorable times and withdraw in the time of temptation”] (Luke 8:13). Shelter my head on the day of battle (Psalm 139:8); be my hope on the day of affliction and my salvation in the time of tribulation [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscripts and Sommaius add “of my affliction” and “of my tribulation,” and continue: “Behold, God is illumination”; another reading has “Lord, my illumination”].

Behold, Lord, you are my illumination and my salvation (Psalm 26:1). I have asked for what I need; I have disclosed what I fear. But my conscience gnaws at me; the secrets of my heart rebuke me; what love supplies, fear disperses; zeal urges, dread reproves. My deeds inspire fear [Col. 0880B] [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscript reads: “The firmness of my deeds of life reproves”; Sommaius: “the narrow way reproves fear”; another reading: “My deeds inspire fear, but…”], but your compassion introduces confidence. Your goodness encourages; my wickedness holds me back [Note: [Col. 0879C] “Discourages” in the manuscript; “holds me back” in Sommaius]. And, to speak more truly, images of vices [Note: [Col. 0879C] “Images of sins” in the manuscript and Sommaius; “images of vices” in the reading adopted here] come to mind, and they strike back at the boldness [Note: [Col. 0879C] “Edge” is found in one reading; Sommaius omits the word] of presumptuous spirits.

For when someone deserves hatred, with what face does he seek forgiveness of sins [Note: [Col. 0879C] “Seek grace” in the manuscript; “seek the grace of sins” in the reading adopted here]? When punishment is owed [Note: [Col. 0879C] The manuscripts read “when punishment”; Sommaius “for when there is punishment”; another reading “to whom punishment”], with what audacity is glory demanded [Note: [Col. 0879C] Sommaius reads “he demands glory”]? He provokes the judge who, setting aside satisfaction for his offense, seeks to be honored with rewards [Note: [Col. 0879C] “He seeks to be honored with rewards” in the manuscript and Sommaius]. He insults the king who is subject to punishment, demanding to be given an undeserved prize [Note: [Col. 0879C] “An undeserved reward” in the manuscript and Sommaius]. And the foolish son exacerbates the sweet affection of his father [Note: [Col. 0879C] “The beloved father” in the manuscript and Sommaius], who, after insults have been inflicted, arrogates the dignity of an inheritance before repentance.

What do I remember having done, my Father? I deserved death, and I ask for life. I provoked my King, whose protection I now shamelessly invoke [Note: [Col. 0879C] “I invoke help” in the manuscript and Sommaius]; I despised the Judge [Note: [Col. 0879C] “The judgment of the Judge” in the manuscript and Sommaius] whom I rashly ask to be my helper; insolently I refused to listen to the father whom I now presume to have as my guardian.

Alas for me! How late I come; alas, alas! How slowly I hasten; alas for me, because I run after the wounds, disdaining [Note: [Col. 0879C] “Having disdained” in the manuscript] to guard against the arrows while unharmed. I neglected to watch for the weapons; now I am anxious about approaching death. I inflicted wounds upon wounds, because I did not fear adding crimes to crimes. I sprinkled scars with fresh corruption [Note: [Col. 0881C] “With fresh blemish” in the manuscript], because I answered ancient crimes with modern iniquities [Note: [Col. 0881C] “Pollutions” in the manuscript and Sommaius], and my frenzied itching dissolved what divine medicine had made firm [Note: [Col. 0881C] “Grace” or “medicine” in the manuscript; Sommaius omits the expression “grace or”].

The skin that had grown over the wounds and concealed the disease rotted when the pus burst forth, because repeated iniquity emptied out the mercy that had been granted. For I know what is written: “On whatever day the righteous person sins, all his righteousnesses will be forgotten” (Ezekiel 33:13). If the righteousness of a falling righteous person is erased, how much more the repentance of a sinner who returns to the same things [Note: [Col. 0881C] The manuscript and Sommaius read: “how much more the repentance of a sinner who falls into the same things”]?

How often I returned like a dog to its vomit, and, like a pig, sought again the mire’s wallow [Note: [Col. 0881C] The manuscript and Sommaius have: “and, like a pig, sought the wallow?”; Augustine omits “of the mire”]. It is difficult for me to confess, and impossible even to remember how many mortal people I taught to sin while they were ignorant [Col. 0881B] [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius: “It is impossible for me both to confess and to remember how many mortal people I taught to sin while ignorant.” The manuscript: “I confess that it is impossible for me to remember what mortal people ignorant of sin I taught.” Augustine’s edition: “I confess, because it is impossible to remember anything. How many mortals…”], persuaded those unwilling to offend, compelled those who resisted, consented to those who wished, laid a snare for how many who were walking [Note: [Col. 0881C] The manuscript reads “how many walkers I led into a snare”; Sommaius: “how many walkers I led into a snare”; another reading has “what…”], uncovered a pit for those seeking the way, did not shrink from committing evils, and did not fear forgetting God’s gifts [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius: “I did not shrink from committing evil so that I might forget…”; Augustine’s edition: “I did not fear forgetting so that I might not shrink from committing…”].

But you, just Judge, sealed up my sins as though in a purse [Note: [Col. 0881C] “My sins as money in a purse” in the manuscript and Sommaius; “my sins in a purse” in the reading adopted here] (Job 14:17), watched all my paths, and counted all my steps (ibid., 16). You were always silent, you kept silence, you were patient. Woe to me! At last you will speak like a woman in labor (Isaiah 42:14).

God of gods, Lord, exalted above wickedness [Note: [Col. 0881C] “Toward iniquity” in the manuscript and Sommaius; “toward wickedness” in the reading adopted here], I know that you will come openly [Note: [Col. 0881C] “Coming openly” in the manuscript; “you will come openly” in the reading adopted here] (Psalm 49:3). I know that you will not always remain silent, when fire blazes before you and a mighty storm rages around you, when you summon heaven from above [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius reads “heaven from above”], and the earth, to distinguish your people (ibid., 14).

Behold, before so many thousands of peoples all my iniquities will be stripped bare; before so many ranks of angels all my crimes will be revealed [Note: [Col. 0881C] “They will be revealed before the ranks” in Sommaius; “before the ranks of angels they will be revealed” in the reading adopted here], not only those of my actions but also those of my thoughts and words [Note: [Col. 0881C] “And likewise of my words” in the manuscript and Sommaius]. I shall stand destitute before as many judges as there were people who preceded me in good works [Col. 0882A] [Note: [Col. 0881C] The manuscript and Sommaius read: “I shall stand destitute, and as many as preceded me…”; the Gothic edition: “I shall stand destitute before as many as…”]. I shall be confounded by as many accusers as gave me examples of living well [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius reads “holy examples of living”]. I shall be convicted by as many witnesses as admonished me [Note: [Col. 0881C] The manuscript and Sommaius read “moved me”; the Gothic edition also reads “admonished me”] with profitable words and gave themselves to me for imitation through righteous actions [Note: [Col. 0881C] The manuscript reads “and often gave themselves to me for imitation”; the reading adopted here is “and gave themselves…”].

Lord, my God, I have nothing to say; no answer comes to me [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius reads “what I should say…what I should answer”]. And whether I am already present at that danger, conscience presses me [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius: “And behold, I am already present at that danger; it presses me,” and another manuscript: “and when I am already present at that terrible danger, it torments me”; the reading adopted here is “and whether I am already present at that danger, conscience presses me”]. The secrets of my heart also torment me; avarice constricts me; pride accuses me; envy consumes me; lust inflames me; luxury pollutes me; gluttony dishonors me; drunkenness confounds me; slander tears me apart; ambition supplants me; rapacity binds me [Note: [Col. 0881C] The manuscript reads “rapacity rebukes me”; one witness omits the expression]; discord scatters me; anger disturbs me; levity casts me down [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius reads “levity casts me down”; Augustine’s edition reads “levity dissolves me”]; torpor oppresses me; hypocrisy deceives me; flattery breaks me; favor lifts me up; calumny [Col. 0882B] pierces me.

Behold, my deliverer from angry nations (Psalm 17:48); behold those with whom I have lived since the days of my birth [Note: [Col. 0881C] “Since the day I lived” in the manuscript; “since the days…” in the reading adopted here], with whom I have studied and to whom I have kept faith [Note: [Col. 0881C] “Whom I studied, to whom I kept faith” in the manuscript]. The very pursuits I had loved condemn me; those I had praised censure me. These are the friends to whom I listened, the teachers whom I obeyed, the masters whom I served, the counselors whom I trusted, the citizens with whom I dwelt, and the members of my household with whom I grew old [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius reads “with whom I consented”].

Woe is me, my King and my God, because my sojourn has been prolonged (Psalm 119:5). Woe is me, my illumination, because I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar (ibid.)! And since holy David said “much,” how much more can unhappy I say: “My soul has been a very long sojourner!” (ibid.)

My firm foundation, God, no living person will be justified [Col. 0882C] in your sight (Psalm 142:2) [Note: [Col. 0881C] “My firm foundation, no living person will be justified” in the manuscript and Sommaius; “my firm foundation, God, no living person…” in the reading adopted here]. My hope, among the children of men there is no one whom, if you judge him with mercy removed, you would find just [Note: [Col. 0881C] “You will find him just” in Sommaius; “you will find him to be just” in another reading]; and unless you anticipate the ungodly with mercy, there will be no one whom you may glorify as godly [Note: [Col. 0881C] Sommaius reads “for there is no one whom you may glorify as godly”; Augustine’s edition: “there is nothing which you may glorify as godly”].

For I believe, my salvation, what I have heard [Col. 0883A] [Note: [Col. 0883C] “What I have heard” in Sommaius; “who I have heard” in another reading], namely, that your kindness leads me to repentance (Romans 2:4) [Note: [Col. 0883C] The manuscript and Sommaius read “How your kindness…”]. Tower of strength, your lips have sounded what was necessary for me [Note: [Col. 0883C] Sommaius: “The necessary things have sounded from your lips”; Augustine’s edition: “Your nectar-like lips have sounded to me from your mouth”]: “No one can come to me unless my Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

Indeed, because you have instructed me thus [Note: The manuscript reads “because you instructed me”; Som. reads “because you did indeed instruct me.”] and, in your graciousness, have formed me through such great instruction [Note: Som. reads “instruction”], with all the marrow of my heart and with all the effort of my mind I beseech you, omnipotent Father, together with your most beloved Son [Note: The manuscript reads “with the striving of my mind”; Som. reverses the order, “with the effort of my mind I beseech you”; Augustine’s edition omits “I beseech you.” The manuscript and Som. read “together with your sweetest Child”], and I invoke you, O sweetest Offspring, together with the most serene Paraclete. Draw me after you, so that, running after you, I may delight in the fragrance of your ointments [Note: The manuscript reads “so that it may delight in running after you, in the fragrance of your ointments”; Som. reads “so that, running after you, I may delight in the fragrance of your ointments”; Augustine’s edition reads “so that I may run after you, sweetly, in the fragrance of your ointments”] (Song of Songs I, 3).

How great, O Lord, my God [Note: From “How great, O Lord God” through “I invoke you, my God,” this passage is absent from Sommalio and also from the Book of the Meditations of St. Augustine, vol. IX. After the words “in the fragrance of your ointments, sweetly,” it proceeds without interruption to “I invoke you, my God”; thus the words inserted here in Anselm are not found in Augustine or in Sommalio], is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you! (Psalm XXX, 20.) You have hidden it because you have preserved it, not because you have concealed it. You have taken it away, while multiplying it all the more [Note: The manuscript reads “while multiplying her all the more.”] What is hidden is sometimes sought more diligently, and, once found, loved more closely; delays do not diminish desires for you, but make them grow still more. Your love, therefore, is not transitory but eternal. Those who love you do not grow lukewarm but become fervent.

Your love is not idle. The remembrance of you is sweeter than honey, and meditation upon you is more pleasant than food [Note: The manuscript reads “sweeter than honey, meditation.”] To speak of you is complete refreshment; to know you, perfect consolation; to cling to you, eternal life; to be separated from you, everlasting death. You are a living fountain for those who thirst for you, unfailing nourishment for those who hunger for you. You are glory for those who seek you, joy for those who find you. Your fragrance raises the dead; your regard heals the sick; your light drives away every darkness; your visitation dispels all sadness.

With you there is no sorrow; far from you there is every pain; with you there is no grief and no want. Where you are, there is no necessity [Note: The manuscript reads “no want, no necessity wherever you are”; another reading is “and no want; where you are, there is no necessity.”] No good is difficult to obtain; there darkness never exists, nor is the terror of Gehenna named; with you there is no blindness of dreadful night [Note: The manuscript reads “the dreadful blindness of night”], no tumultuous wickedness, no poverty of hunger or thirst. Want caused by cold or heat does not remain around you; there is no bodily illness, and certainly no corruption of mind; no jealousy, contention, or ambition whatsoever. There anxiety over the end is absent, as are the care of death, the toil of old age, and the weariness of sickness. There one knows neither the suffering caused by the air nor the changing conditions of the seasons.

For this is the great abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you, but perfected for those who hope in you [Note: The manuscript omits “but perfected for those who hope in you”] (ibid.).

O how good is the concealment that becomes perfection! For this concealment is not judged to be loss, but rather preservation, which becomes perfection. O glorious King, how true are your judgments, justified in themselves, truly more desirable than gold [Note: The manuscript omits “indeed”] and much precious stone, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb! (Psalm XVIII, 10–11.)

O my life, my God, I beseech you, by the name of my beloved Redeemer [Note: The manuscript reads “my only-begotten Redeemer”] your Son, graciously grant that I may keep them. For I have learned that there is a great reward in keeping them (ibid., 12).

My glory, my God, you hide your treasure in order to stir up the greedy; you conceal the pearl in order to increase the love of the seeker; you delay giving in order to teach us to ask; you pretend not to hear the one who asks in order to make him persevere. Finally, you promise to those who begin to seek [Note: The manuscript omits “to seek”]; but you grant salvation only to those who truly persevere [Note: The manuscript reads “so that you grant salvation only to those who truly persevere”; another reading is “so that you grant salvation.”]

This is clearly shown by that weeping woman who sought your Christ in the tomb—or rather, sought you in Christ—while the darkness still lasted [Note: The manuscript reads “the living Christ born among the dead, while the darkness still lasted.”] You had kindled her so that she might seek; yet, when she sought, you withdrew from her so that she might persevere. She persevered while hoping, and hoped while persevering; and because she persevered in hope [Note: The manuscript reads “because she persevered in you”], she deserved to see you.

O blessed vision [Note: The manuscript reads “blessed vision”], and complete exultation! O supreme joy and desire brought to fulfillment! O desirable face and delightful appearance [Note: The manuscript reads “desirable face, delightful”]! O blessed hope [Note: The manuscript reads “O hope”] and happy perseverance! For if she had not hoped, she would not have persevered; and if she had not persevered, she would not have received the fruit of hope.

Thus, my God, my mercy, you are hidden from those who fear you so that you may be found by those who hope in you; thus you withdraw from those who seek you [Note: The manuscript reads “you withdraw from those who seek”] so that you may draw near to those who persevere: “Those who distance themselves from you shall perish” (Psalm LXXII, 27); “but those who wait for you shall be put to shame” (Psalm XXIV, 3). “Let those who fear you hope in you, for you are their protector and helper” (Psalm CXIII, 11).

Through fear one comes to love [Note: The manuscript reads “one comes to.”]. You are to be feared as Lord and loved as Father. Your holy fear endures because it makes holy those whom it possesses. Nothing is lacking to those who fear you, because your eyes are upon them and your ears are attentive to their prayers (Psalm XXXIII, 16).

My mercy and my refuge, my protector and my deliverer, instill fear in me in such a way that you may introduce love [Note: The manuscript reads “so that I might love.”]; impose fear in such a way that you may increase my desire for you. Thus make me a companion of those who fear you, so that you may also make me one of those who keep your commandments (Psalm CXVIII, 63), and so that through the servitude of fear I may deserve to attain the grace of love, through which at last I may reach your glory. Amen.

## 254. PRAYER XI. TO GOD.

Lord God, omnipotent Father, and good God Jesus, have mercy on me, a sinner, and grant me forgiveness of my sins. Grant me the ability to avoid and overcome all the snares of my enemies, and all harmful temptations and pleasures; perfectly, in mind and deed, to avoid doing what you forbid; to serve you and love you as much as you know and will; and to live according to your will.

Grant me, O Lord, contrition of heart, exercise of devotion, the virtue of humility, prudent abstinence, mortification of the flesh, a right approach to you for praying and loving, meditating and praising, and for every action according to you; grant me perfect, sober, and truthful thought, and a vigorous and effective mind.

Grant me, O Lord, knowledge, love, and delight in your commandments; facility and effectiveness in keeping them; and constant perseverance in advancing toward better things, progressing with humility and never failing.

Do not abandon me, O Lord, to human weakness or ignorance, to my merits, or to anything else except your disposition. O Lord, mercifully dispose me, and all my thoughts and actions, according to your good pleasure, so that your will alone may always be done by me, in me, and concerning me [Col. 0885C].

Deliver me, O Lord, from every evil, and grant me every good—that is, yourself—so that my joy may be in you, who are eternal life. Amen.

## PRAYER XII. TO GOD. The praise of God, with devoted thanksgiving.

I offer you praise and thanks, my God, my mercy, who have deigned to lead me to the thought of you and, through the cleansing of holy baptism, to number me among the children of adoption.

I offer you praise and thanks, who, from the very beginnings of infancy until this hour, while I have been flowing onward through many sins, have patiently awaited my amendment through the immeasurable endurance of your goodness.

I praise and glorify you, who by the arm of your power have often delivered me from many straits, calamities, and miseries; who until now have rescued me from eternal punishments and from the torments of this body.

I praise and glorify you, who have deigned to grant me health of my limbs, tranquility of the seasons, love, affection, and charity from your servants toward me—gifts of your compassion.

Holy of holies, who sanctify all things, I bless you, I glorify you, I adore you, I give you thanks. May all your creatures bless you; may all your angels and saints bless you. Thus may we bless you during my life.

May all my inner and outer being adore, glorify, and bless you. My salvation, my light, my illumination: may my eyes bless you, eyes which you made and prepared to contemplate the beauty of your serenity.

My sweetness, my delight: may my ears bless you, ears which you made and prepared to hear the voice of your joy.

My fragrance, my refreshment: may my nostrils bless you, nostrils which you made so that they might live and delight in the fragrance of your ointments.

My praise, my new song, my exultation: may my tongue bless and magnify you, tongue which you made and prepared so that I might recount your wonders.

My wisdom, my meditation, my counsel: may my heart, which you prepared and gave me for discerning your immeasurable mercies, always adore and bless you.

My life, my blessedness: may my soul, though sinful, bless you—the soul which you made and prepared to enjoy your blessings.

O you worthy of adoration, awe, and reverence, Father worthy of fear, I bless you, whom I have loved, whom I have sought, whom I have always desired. My God, my lover, I thirst for you, I hunger for you, I desire you, I beseech you, I long for you with all my inmost being and all my sighs.

And just as the mother of an only son, deprived of his presence, sits beside the place of his tomb, always weeping and lamenting, so I too—though not as much as I ought, but as much as I can—remembering your passion, remembering your blows, remembering your scourges, remembering your wounds, remembering how you were killed for me, how you were laid away, how and where you were buried, sit with Mary weeping beside the tomb of my mind.

There faith buried you; hope seeks you in order to find you; love, in order to anoint you. Most kind, most serene, sweetest Lord, who will grant me to find you outside and kiss you, and sprinkle with tears the places of your wounds, the holes of the nails? “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love” (Song of Songs V, 8). May he appear to me; may he show himself to me; may he call me by my name and restrain me from my grief.

For my grief cannot contain itself within me as long as I am a pilgrim away from you, my God. Come now, O Lord, reveal your face; show your mercy to those who entreat you. We know that the resurrection has been accomplished; declare before our eyes the blessed incorruption.

Wonderful, immeasurable, incomparable one, you were the one I wanted, the one I hoped for, the one I sought. Behold, you yourself are coming, clothed in purple; your garment is red (Isaiah LXIII, 2). “You washed your robe in wine, and your cloak in the blood of the grape” (Genesis XLIX, 11). “You struck the head of the house of the wicked, going forth for the salvation of your people” (Habakkuk III, 13).

Remain with us, O Lord—remain, or at least remain until morning. Meanwhile, let us enjoy your presence. Let us rejoice and delight in your resurrection. Darkness is closing in; evening presses upon the day. May our sun, our light, Christ our God, shine his face upon us (Psalm LXVI, 2).

But what are you doing, alas, my Lord? Alas, my soul! What shall I say, or what shall I do, or where shall I go? Now, now you are raising your hands. Behold, you yourself are entering upon your ways. The heavens come to meet you; the firmaments are spread beneath you; a cloud is prepared for the one who is about to ascend. I shall offer you only the tears of my bereavement as you depart.

“My tears shall be my bread day and night” (Psalm XLI, 4). I shall feed upon my weeping; I shall give my soul drink from my sorrows. “My life fails in sorrow, and my years in groaning” (Psalm XXX, 11). “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm LXII, 25.) “My soul longs for you in the night, and my spirit within me will watch for you from early morning” (Isaiah XXVI, 9).

Meanwhile, come to us, O Lord, for you are good, and you will not delay (Hebrews X, 37), because you are compassionate. To you be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## 255. PRAYER XIII. TO GOD. For father, mother, relatives, and friends.
