Sovereign Lord God, who wonderfully established all things and created everything by your ordering; who ordained that the propagation of offspring should come from man and woman, and commanded that love be shown toward father and mother, hear me, merciful God, as I cry to you for the salvation of my father and mother, whom in your providence you have deigned to prepare for me, most lowly as I am; and for my brothers and sisters, and for all who are joined to me, a sinner, by bodily kinship, familiarity, promise [Col. 0887C], or commission, both the living and the dead, whose names and merits are known to you, Lord God of all.

Grant that you may deign to bestow eternal life upon the dead, defend the living from every evil, and direct them into the way of salvation, so that through true confession and true amendment of all their sins you may forgive their offenses, and, when they have put off the flesh, make them heirs through participation in heaven.

Hear me, most merciful God, miserable as I am, as I supplicate you for the souls of your male and female servants who wish me well, do good to me, and serve me; who have bestowed their alms upon me, and from whom I have received alms; whose names are known to you, Lord God of all; and who have commended themselves to my prayers. Grant that you may bestow upon them the benefits of your mercy and deign to place them in the dwelling of those who please you, O Savior of the world, who live and reign with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

## PRAYER XIV [Note: Compared with the Thuanus manuscript (for it is not found in the other manuscripts), with Somma­lius’s 1637 edition, with Augustine’s edition in the Book of Meditations, chapter 9, p. 337, and with the Gothic edition]. TO THE HOLY SPIRIT.

Now also [Note: The manuscript reads “O divine”; Som. reads “Now, O divine”; the Gothic and Augustine editions read “Now, O divine”], O omnipotent Spirit Paraclete, holy communion of the divine love of almighty God the Father and of the most blessed Offspring, most merciful comforter of the sorrowful, glide by your powerful might into the innermost chambers of my heart. As a gracious inhabitant, make every dark hiding-place of my neglected dwelling [Note: The manuscript reads “every neglected hiding-place of the dwelling”; the Gothic edition reads “the neglected hiding-places of the light.”] joyful with the radiance of your shining light [Note: The manuscript and Augustine’s edition read “a gracious habitation”; Som. reads “I, a gracious inhabitant”; the Gothic edition reads “I shall be an inhabitant”]; and, by visiting me, make fruitful through the abundance of your dew those places that have withered in the long dryness of desolation.

Wound the hidden places of the inner person with the arrow of your love. Penetrate the marrow of my sluggish liver and set it ablaze with saving flames [Note: The manuscript and Gothic edition read “of the tepid liver”]. Enlighten with the fire of holy fervor, and, illuminating, consume all the innermost parts of mind and body [Note: The manuscript reads “illuminating all the inmost parts of the mind”; Som. reads “illuminating the mind.”].

“Give me drink from the torrent of your delight” (Psalm XXXV, 9), so that I may no longer wish to taste anything worldly beside the sweetness worthy of veneration. Judge me, O Lord [Note: The K manuscript and the Gothic edition omit “O Lord”], and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation (Psalm XLII, 1); teach me to do your will, because you are my God (Psalm CXLII, 10).

I believe, therefore, that whoever you inhabit, you establish as the dwelling-place of the Father [Note: The Gothic edition reads “the Father in him”] and likewise of the Son. Blessed is the one who deserves to have you as a guest, for through you the Father and the Son will make their dwelling with him (John XIV, 23) [Note: Augustine reads “make,” rather than “make their dwelling.”]

Come now, come, most merciful comforter of the sorrowful in times of need and helper in tribulations (Psalm IX, 10) [Note: The manuscript reads “protecting”; Augustine’s edition reads “promptly”; the Augustine and Gothic editions omit the following word]. Come, cleanser of crimes, healer of wounds. Come, strength of the weak, lifter of those who fall; come, teacher of the humble, destroyer of the proud.

Come, gracious father of orphans, gentle judge of widows. Come, hope of the poor, restorer of the failing. Come, guiding star of those at sea [Note: The manuscript reads “of those shipwrecked”], harbor of the shipwrecked [Note: The Gothic edition reads “of shipwreck.”]. Come, singular glory of all the living, the sole salvation of the dying.

Come, most holy Spirit; come and have mercy on me. Make me suitable for yourself, and graciously condescend [Note: The manuscript reads “and grant”; Som. retains “and condescend”; the Gothic edition reads “and descend”] to me, so that my smallness may please your greatness, and my weakness your strength, in accordance with the multitude of your mercies, through Jesus Christ my Savior, who lives and reigns with the Father in your unity for ages of ages. Amen.

## PRAYER XV. TO CHRIST, With remembrance of his benefits and of human misery.

To you, sweetest and most gracious Lord Jesus Christ, who are the fountain of compassion and mercy, I turn above all. For I confess that through the power of your divinity, by which with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, you made all things from nothing, I was created; and I know that through your incarnation, which you assumed in the distinctness of your person, though with the cooperation of the Father and the Holy Spirit, I was restored and renewed.

Therefore I pray your sweetest mercy, most holy and gracious Lord Jesus: by your holy annunciation, have mercy on my unhappy soul. Sweetest Lord Jesus Christ, by your holy incarnation and birth, have mercy on my soul. Sweetest Lord Jesus Christ, by your circumcision, have mercy on me. Sweetest Lord Jesus, by your holy infancy, have mercy on me. Sweetest Lord Jesus, by your youth, have mercy on me. Sweetest Lord Jesus, by your baptism, have mercy on me. Sweetest Lord Jesus, by your fasting, hunger, and weariness, have mercy on me.

Sweetest Lord Jesus, by your miracles, through which, although you were truly human, you were recognized as truly God, have mercy on me. Sweetest Lord Jesus, by the scourges, spittle, and blows that you endured for us, have mercy on me. Sweetest and most merciful Lord Jesus, by the crown of thorns that you bore upon your head, in order to remove the thorns of our sins, have mercy on me.

Have mercy on me, sweetest Lord Jesus, by your cross and the death that you suffered upon that cross, in order to redeem us from death. Have mercy on me, Lord Jesus, by your tomb in which you lay according to the flesh, and by your most gracious descent into hell, where you visited the faithful and your friends who had long awaited you there as their sweetest Redeemer.

By visiting them, you mercifully rescued them from demonic dominion in glorious triumph. The infernal furies were vigorously accusing their prince because he had unjustly killed you, in whom he had found nothing belonging to him; and because of that unjust killing they were then justly losing those whom they had held captive for so long and unhappily bound in their chains.

Have mercy on me, sweetest and most gracious Lord Jesus, by your glorious resurrection, through which, on the third day after you were killed for sinners, you appeared alive and immortal to your disciples and friends, who were grieving and deeply distressed at your death; and by your sweetest conversations with them during the forty days after your resurrection.

During that time, appearing to them with many proofs and speaking about the kingdom of God, comforting and strengthening them, and often eating with them (Acts I, 3), you removed all doubt from their hearts through the clearest signs and through the truth of your flesh, in which you had suffered death, and established them in faith and belief in your resurrection.

Have mercy on me, sweetest Lord Jesus, by your wondrous ascension, through which, while your disciples and your Virgin Mother watched, you went to heaven and placed at the right hand of the Father the human nature that you had mercifully assumed for sinners, in which you had suffered death and destroyed death.

Have mercy on me, sweetest Lord Jesus, by the coming of the Holy Spirit, whom, as you had promised, you sent to your disciples on the day of Pentecost. Filled with him and greatly strengthened, setting aside all fear, they announced the truth of your resurrection to all nations and taught them that, if they believed in you and obeyed your commands, then, putting aside all doubt, they would ascend after the death of the flesh to the kingdom of heaven and happily reign with you in eternal glory.

Have mercy on me, sweetest Lord Jesus, by your return to judge the living and the dead. In that judgment you will separate the wicked from the good and condemn the wicked to eternal destruction; but you will lead the good with you to heaven and place them in eternal happiness.

Strengthened by these sweetest remembrances and devout recollections, sweetest Lord Jesus, as I gently and with great wonder turn over and over in the secret chamber of my heart these great benefits that you have mercifully bestowed upon the weak and sinful, I sometimes reject, with the help of your goodness, the weak memories and recollections of sin that drag one toward condemnation and the destruction of condemnation; and I look upon, venerate, and embrace those things that savor of the divine and ordinarily raise up my weak and sinful soul.

But alas for my unhappy soul, sweetest and most gracious Lord! Alas for the great destruction that so grievously torments my unhappy soul, which, unless it is sustained by your most merciful compassion, descends in an instant to hell!

For behold, when I carefully examine the secret place of my heart, I find that unhappy soul of mine—which I had thought would stand clean and spotless before your divine majesty—not a little infected with the poison of malice and iniquity.

Often, moreover, when I begin speaking with someone, even for the sake of some useful matter, I immediately—or after a brief interval—fall into detraction, or murmur shamelessly about some matter, or yield to the fault of foolish curiosity, or endure within my innermost self the foulness of evil thoughts and unlawful, immodest impulses.

Again and again, alas, for such great misery and such great destruction! I confess, sweetest Jesus, and I spread before you the iniquities that my wretched soul suffers within.

For while I wish, forgetting what lies behind, to stretch myself toward what lies ahead, and while I desire, if I could [variant: if I can], to delight longer in these sweetest recollections that I have mentioned above, and, gathering all my thoughts as though into a bundle, with every disturbance of mind removed, desire to cling to God in continual perseverance, suddenly I see myself, through some unknown misery, slipping back into empty and harmful things.

And, like a death that suddenly kills—or like a mad dog that, even when driven back by a blow, does not restrain itself from tearing a person apart—so carnal pleasure disturbs and destroys all tranquility of mind and all the uprightness of justice that I thought I possessed.

And though I thought I was standing in the citadel of the virtues because of their sweet fragrance, I feel the unbearable and most dreadful stench of vices.

What, then, shall I do, sweetest Lord Jesus, lover and creator of human beings, reformer and Redeemer of sinners? Where shall I turn, surrounded by such evils, wrapped in such darkness of the worst pleasures?

“Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? But who, except the grace of my Lord Jesus Christ?” (Romans VII, 24.)

Have mercy, therefore, sweetest Lord Jesus; have mercy on your creature; have mercy on my sinful soul. Attend, sweetest Lord Jesus, attend to its misery and deliver it; for the sake of its enemies, rescue it (Psalm LXVIII, 19).

Enlighten its eyes, lest it ever sleep in death, lest its enemy at some time say, “I have prevailed against it” (Psalm XII, 4). Judge those who harm it, Lord; fight against those who attack it. Take up arms and shield, and rise to its aid [Col. 0891A] (Psalm XXXI, 1).

I believe, sweetest Lord Jesus, I believe that if you take up your weapons for its defense and defend with the shield of your good will (Psalm V, 13) the soul that you created, then no enemy, no dart of the adversary—even if they attack it from without or attempt to rage within—will in any way be able to overcome the soul that you defend.

Sweetest and most merciful Lord Jesus, heal it, overwhelmed by many evils, overcome by many iniquities, stained by many crimes. Helper of the poor, defender of orphans, heal and assist the soul that you created, that you redeemed, and that through you was cleansed.

Sustain its striving, strengthen its desire, and grant it to pass through this span of life, during which it must live in this world, in such a way that, through your ineffable mercy, it may amend all its iniquities and, through true repentance and true confession, cleanse, correct, purify, and wipe them away.

Thus, by your most indulgent compassion, may it, cleansed, purified, corrected, and wiped clean of every stain of vice after the death of the flesh, be able to reach you, its sweetest Creator and most merciful Lord, and possess your ineffable glory with all your saints in eternal happiness for ages everlasting. Amen.

## 257. PRAYER XVI [Note: Compared with chapter 36 of Som­ma­lius and Augustine’s edition in the Book of Meditations, chapter 36, p. 347. “To Jesus Christ, for obtaining the grace of tears from remembrance of sins,” in Som. “A most devout prayer for offering praises.”]. TO CHRIST. For obtaining the grace of tears from remembrance of sins.

Christ the Lord, Word of the Father, who came into this world to save sinners, I beseech you, by the most indulgent depths of your mercy: amend my life, improve my actions, order my conduct, take away from me whatever harms me and displeases you, and grant me what you know pleases you and benefits me.

Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed, except you alone? (Job XIV, 4.) You are the omnipotent God of infinite compassion, who justifies the ungodly and gives life to the dead because of sin, who changes sinners, and they are no more.

Take away, therefore, from me whatever in me displeases you. For your eyes see my many imperfections (Psalm CXXXVIII, 16). Send, I beg you, the hand of your compassion into me, and take away from me whatever in me offends the eyes of your compassion.

Before you, O Lord, are my health and my sickness. Preserve the one, I pray; heal the other. “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” (Jeremiah XVII, 14)—you who heal the weak and preserve those who have been healed, you who by a mere nod restore what has been ruined and collapsed.

For if you deign to sow good seed in the field of my heart, it is necessary that the hand of your compassion first uproot the thorns of my vices.

Sweetest, kindest, most loving, dearest, most desired, most lovable, most beautiful one, pour, I beseech you, the abundance of your sweetness and your love into my breast, so that I may desire or think of nothing earthly, nothing carnal, but love you alone and have you alone in my heart and on my lips.

Write with your finger upon my breast the sweet remembrance of your honey-flowing name, never to be erased by any forgetfulness. Write your will and your ordinances upon the tablets of my heart, so that I may always and everywhere have before my eyes the Lord of immeasurable sweetness and your commandments.

Set my mind ablaze with that fire of yours which you sent upon the earth and wished to be intensely kindled, so that each day I may offer you, with tears arising, “the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite heart” (Psalm L, 19).

Sweet Christ, good Jesus, as I desire, as I ask with all my mind, grant me your holy and chaste love, which may fill me, hold me, and possess me entirely.

And grant me a clear sign of your love: a watered spring of tears, continually flowing, so that these very tears in me may bear witness to my love for you; may themselves reveal and declare how greatly my soul loves you [Note: Som. reads “how greatly my soul may love you”], while, because of the excessive sweetness of your love, it cannot restrain itself from tears.

I remember, gracious Lord, that good woman Hannah, who came to the tabernacle to pray for a son. Scripture reports of her that, after her tears and prayers, her face was no longer changed in different directions (1 Samuel I, 18).

But as I remember such great virtue and steadfastness, I am tortured by grief and overcome by shame, because I see myself lying very far below her. For if the woman who sought a son wept in this way and persevered in her lamentation, how ought my soul to mourn and persist in mourning, since it seeks and loves God and desires to reach him?

How ought such a soul to groan and weep when it seeks God day and night and wishes to love nothing besides Christ? Surely it is astonishing if its tears have not already become its bread day and night (Psalm XLI, 4).

Look upon me, therefore, and have mercy on me (Psalm XXIV, 16), for the sorrows of my heart are multiplied. Grant me your heavenly consolation, and do not despise the sinful soul for which you died.

Grant me, I beg you, inward tears arising from my whole heart, tears able to loosen the bonds of my sins and continually fill my soul with heavenly joy; if not with the true and perfect monks, whose footsteps I cannot imitate, then at least grant that I may obtain some small portion in your kingdom with devout women.

The wondrous devotion of another woman also comes to mind: she sought you, lying in the tomb, with pious love. When the disciples departed from the tomb, she did not depart; she sat there, sad and grieving, and wept long and bitterly. Rising, she repeatedly explored the deserted chambers of the tomb with watchful eyes and many tears, to see whether she might perhaps find you somewhere—whom she sought with fervent desire.

Certainly, she had already entered the tomb once and again and had seen it, but for one who loved so greatly, that was not enough. For the virtue of a good work is perseverance.

And because she loved you more than the others, and in loving wept, and in weeping sought, and in seeking persevered, she therefore deserved to find you first of all, to see you [Note: Augustine omits “to see you”], and to speak with you.

Nor was this all: she also became the herald of your glorious resurrection to the disciples themselves, at your command and gracious instruction: “Go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me” (Matthew XXVIII, 10).

If, then, the woman who sought the living among the dead (Luke XXIV, 5), who touched you with the hand of faith, wept in this way and persevered in weeping, how ought the soul to mourn and persist in mourning when it believes in its heart that you, its Redeemer, now preside in heaven and reign everywhere, and confesses you with its mouth? (Romans X, 10.)

How, then, ought such a soul to groan and weep when it loves you with all its heart and longs with all its desire to see you?

The sole refuge and the only hope of the wretched, Lord, to whom no one ever supplicates without hope of mercy: grant me this grace for your sake and for the sake of your holy name, so that whenever I think of you, speak of you, write of you, read about you, converse about you; whenever I remember you, attend upon you, offer praises, prayers, and sacrifice to you—at every such moment, with tears welling up, I may weep copiously and sweetly in your presence, so that my tears may become my bread by day and by night (Ps. XLI, 4).

You indeed, King of glory and teacher of every virtue, have taught us by word and example to groan and weep, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5). You wept over your deceased friend and lamented greatly over the city destined to perish. I beg you, good Jesus, by those most precious tears of yours and by all your mercies, by which you graciously deigned to come wondrously to the aid of us who were lost: grant me the gift of tears, which my soul greatly desires and longs for, because without your gift [Note: Augustine omits *tuo* (“your”) after *dono* (“gift”).] I cannot possess it—but through your Holy Spirit, who softens the hardened hearts of sinners and pierces them with compunction for weeping.

Grant me the gift of tears, as you granted it to our fathers, whose footsteps I ought to imitate, so that I may mourn over myself throughout my whole life, as they mourned over themselves night and day. For the merits and prayers of those who pleased you and served you with the greatest devotion, have mercy on me, your most wretched and unworthy servant, and grant me the gift of tears.

Grant me an upper spring and a lower spring, so that my tears may be my bread by day and by night, and so that in your presence, my God, through the fire of compunction, I may become a rich and marrow-filled burnt offering; may I be wholly sacrificed upon the altar of my heart and, like the richest burnt offering, be offered up to you as a pleasing fragrance. Grant me, O sweetest Lord, a well-watered and crystal-clear spring in which this defiled burnt offering may continually be washed.

For although, with the help of your grace, I have offered my whole self to you, nevertheless I offend daily in many ways because of my excessive weakness. Grant me, therefore, the gift of tears, blessed and loving God, especially from the great sweetness of your love and from remembrance of your mercies. Prepare this table for your servant in your presence, and grant it to me as my possession [Note: Augustine: “grant me possession of it”], so that whenever I wish I may be satisfied from it. In accordance with your piety and goodness, grant that this cup of yours, intoxicating and splendid, may satisfy my thirst (Ps. XXII, 5), so that my spirit may long for you and my mind burn with love of you, forgetful of vanity and misery.

Hear me, my God; hear me, light of my eyes; hear what I ask, and grant that I may ask what you will hear. Merciful and easily entreated Lord, do not become inexorable to me because of my sins, but because of your goodness receive the prayers of your servant, and grant the fulfillment of my petition and desire through the prayers and merits of the glorious Virgin Mary, my lady, and of all the saints. Amen.

## PRAYER XVII

[Note: Compared with Sommalius, chapter 8, among the *Meditations of St. Augustine*, and with the edition of St. Augustine. It is found in volume IX of the *Meditations*, p. 346. It is not found in the manuscripts of St. Anselm. Sommalius’s prayer is the same in its ardent desire to love Christ alone and to enjoy the object of that desire. The prayer is highly moving toward devotion and divine love.]

### TO CHRIST

With an ardent desire to love Christ alone.

Jesus, our redemption, love and desire, God from God, be present to me, your servant. I call upon you; to you I cry out with a great cry from my whole heart. I call you into my soul; enter it and fit it to yourself, so that you may possess it without wrinkle and without stain. For a dwelling place is owed to the most spotless Lord that is itself clean.

Sanctify, therefore, your vessel, which you have made; empty it of wickedness, fill it with grace, and preserve it full, so that I may become a temple worthy of your dwelling, here and forever. O sweetest, kindest, most loving, dearest, most powerful, most desired, most precious, most lovable, most beautiful one—you sweeter than honey, whiter than milk and snow, more pleasant than nectar, more precious to me than gems and gold, dearer to me than all the riches and honors of the earth. What am I saying, my God, my one hope, your mercy so great? What am I saying, blessed and secure sweetness? What am I saying while saying such things? I say what I can, but I do not say what I ought.

Would that I could say such things as those angelic choirs, makers of hymns, say! O how gladly I would pour myself out entirely in your praises [Note: Sommalius and Augustine read “myself in your praises”]! O how devoutly I would proclaim those songs of heavenly melody, to the praise and glory of your name, in the midst of the Church, tirelessly [Note: Sommalius: “unbreakably”]!

But since I cannot say such things, shall I remain silent? Woe to those who are silent about you, who loosen the mouths of the mute and make the tongues of infants eloquent (Wis. X, 21). Woe to those who are silent about you, for when they do not speak your praises, they are talkative mutes. Who can worthily praise you, O ineffable power and wisdom of the Father?

And since I find no words by which I can sufficiently express you, almighty and all-knowing Word, I shall meanwhile say what I can, until you command me to come to you, where I may say what becomes you and what is fitting for me. Therefore I humbly beg that you look not only at what I now say, but at what I desire to say. For with great longing I desire to speak about you what is fitting and becoming, because praise becomes you, a hymn becomes you (Ps. LXIV, 2), and all honor is owed to you.

You know, therefore, God who knows hidden things, that you are dearer to me than not only the earth and all that is in it, but also heaven itself [Note: Augustine omits *coelo* (“heaven”)]; and all that is in it, you are more acceptable to me [Note: Augustine reads “more lovable to me”]. For I love you above heaven and earth and all the other things that are in them; indeed, unless they are loved for love of your name, transient things ought certainly not to be loved [Note: Augustine reads “rather, for love of your name”].

I love you, my God, with great love, and I desire to love you still more. Grant me to love you always as much as I wish and as much as I ought [Note: Sommalius and Augustine: “as much as I ought”], so that you alone may be my entire attention and my every meditation. May I meditate upon you throughout the days without ceasing; may I feel you during sleep at night; may my spirit speak to you and my mind converse with you. May my heart be enlightened by the light of your holy vision, so that, with you as my ruler and guide, I may walk from virtue to virtue and at last see you, God of gods, in Zion—now through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face, where I shall know you as I am known (1 Cor. XIII, 12).

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

I therefore ask you, Lord, by all your mercies, through which we have been freed from eternal death: soften my hard, stony, rocky, and iron heart with your most sacred and powerful anointing, and make me, through the fire of compunction, become before you at every hour a living sacrifice. Make me always possess in your sight a contrite and humbled heart, with an abundance of tears.

Make me, through desire for you, be utterly extinguished to this world and forget transient things because of the greatness of fear and love of you, to such an extent that, as regards temporal things, I may neither mourn nor rejoice, neither fear nor love anything temporal; that I may neither be corrupted by flatteries nor shaken by adversities. And because your love is as strong as death [the printed text reads *ditectio*, apparently an OCR error for *dilectio*], may the fiery and honey-sweet power of your love absorb my mind from all that is beneath heaven [Note: Sommalius and Augustine: “fiery”], so that I may cling to you alone and feed only upon the memory of your sweetness.

Descend, Lord, descend, I beg; descend into my heart. May your sweetest fragrance enter, and may your honey-sweet love come in. May the wondrous and unspeakable fragrance of your savor come to me, awakening eternal desires within me and bringing forth from my heart streams of living water springing up into eternal life (John IV, 14).

You are boundless, Lord, and therefore you ought to be loved and praised without measure by those whom you have redeemed with your precious blood. Most kind lover of human beings, most merciful Lord, and most just judge, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John V, 22): in the most wise judgment of your justice, you discern that this is right and just—that the children of this age, of night and darkness, should love and seek perishable riches and fleeting honors with greater desire, strength, and zeal than we, your servants, love you, our God, through whom we were made and redeemed.

For if one human being loves another with such love that each can scarcely endure the other’s absence; if a bride is so joined to her bridegroom by the ardor of her mind that, because of the greatness of her love, she can enjoy no rest, bearing the absence of her beloved with immense sorrow—then with what love, with what zeal, with what fervor ought the soul whom you have betrothed to yourself by faith and mercies to love you, the true God and most beautiful Bridegroom, who have loved and saved us in this way, who have done so many, such great, and such extraordinary things for us?

Although these lowly things have their pleasures and their loves [Note: Sommalius and Augustine: “the lowest things”], they do not delight in the same way as you, our God. For the just person delights in you, because love of you is sweet and peaceful; you fill the hearts that you possess with sweetness, gentleness, and tranquility.

By contrast, love of the world and of the flesh is anxious and troubled; the souls it enters it does not permit to be at peace. It continually harasses them with suspicions, disturbances, and various fears. You, therefore, are the delight of the upright, and rightly so; for with you there is strong rest and an undisturbed life. Whoever enters into you, good Lord, enters into the joy of his Lord (Matt. XXV, 21), and will fear no more, but will be perfectly secure in the best place, saying: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it” (Ps. CXXXI, 14). And also: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has set me” (Ps. XXII, 1).

Sweet Christ, good Jesus, continually fill my heart, I beg, with your unquenchable love and with continual remembrance of you, so that, like a burning flame, I may wholly burn in the sweetness of your love, which many waters can never extinguish within me [Note: Augustine: “which many waters can never extinguish”].

Make me, sweetest Lord, love you, and through desire for you lay down the burden of all carnal desires and the heaviest load of earthly cravings, which attack and weigh down my wretched soul, so that, running freely after you in the fragrance of your ointments (Song I, 3) and being effectively satisfied at the vision of your beauty, I may, with you as my guide, deserve to reach you as quickly as possible [Note: Sommalius: “free, in the fragrance”].

For two loves—one good, the other evil; one sweet, the other bitter—cannot be held together in a single heart. Therefore, if anyone loves anything besides you, your charity, O God, is not in him: love of sweetness and sweetness of love, love that does not torment but delights; love remaining sincerely and chastely forever and ever [Note: Sommalius: “chastely and remaining”]; love that always burns and is never extinguished.

Sweet Christ, good Jesus, charity, my God, kindle me wholly with your fire, your love, your gentleness and sweetness, your joy and exultation, your delight and desire—which is holy and good, chaste and pure, tranquil and secure—so that, wholly filled with the sweetness of your love and wholly set ablaze with the flame of your charity, I may love you, my God, with all my heart and with all the marrow of my innermost being, having you always and everywhere in my heart, on my lips, and before my eyes, so that no place in me may remain open to adulterous loves.

Hear me, my God; hear me, light of my eyes (Ps. XXXVII, 11); hear what I ask, and grant what I may ask, so that you may hear me. Merciful and most compassionate Lord, do not become inexorable to me because of my sins, but because of your goodness receive the prayers of your servant, and grant the fulfillment of my petition and desire, with your glorious virgin Mother Mary, my lady, interceding, praying, and obtaining it, together with all your saints. Amen.

## PRAYER XVIII

[Note: Compared with Sommalius, chapter 37, and with the edition of St. Augustine in the *Meditations*, p. 248. “So that you may make fruitful use of the time granted by grace and reach true peace.” Sommalius: “In this prayer the human mind is more abundantly pierced with compunction if it is said in quiet.”]

### TO CHRIST

Whom the Christian soul alone hungers and thirsts for.

Lord Jesus, devout Jesus, who deigned to die for our sins and rose again for our justification, I ask you by your glorious resurrection: raise me from the tomb of all my vices and sins, and grant me each day a share in the first resurrection, so that in your resurrection I may truly deserve to receive my portion.

O sweetest, kindest, most loving, dearest, most precious, most desired, most lovable, most beautiful one, you ascended into heaven in the triumph of your glory and sit at the right hand of the Father. Most powerful King, draw me upward to yourself, so that I may run after you in the fragrance of your ointments (Song I, 3), run and not grow weary, with you drawing me and guiding me as I run [Note: Augustine: “with you drawing me as I run”]. Draw upward the mouth of my soul, which thirsts for you, to the heavenly streams of eternal satisfaction; indeed, draw me to yourself, the living fountain, so that from it I may drink according to my capacity, from the source by which I may live forever, my God, my life.

For you said with your holy and blessed mouth: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII, 37). Fountain of life, grant the thirsty soul always to drink from you, so that, according to your holy and truthful promise, waters of life may flow from my belly. Fountain of life, fill my mind with the torrent of your delight (Ps. XXXV, 9), and intoxicate my heart with the sober intoxication of your love, so that I may forget what is vain and earthly and continually have you alone in my memory, as it is written: “I remembered God, and I was delighted” (Ps. LXXVI, 4).

[Col. 0898B]

Grant me your Holy Spirit, whom those waters signified—the waters which you promised to give to the thirsty. Grant me, I beg, to strive with all desire and zeal toward the place to which we believe you ascended after your resurrection on the fortieth day, so that in the present misery I may be held only by the body, but may always be with you in thought and longing; so that my heart may be where you are, my desirable, incomparable, and most beloved treasure (Matt. VI, 21).

For in this great flood of the present life, where we are tossed amid surrounding storms, no trustworthy station or higher place is found where the foot of the dove might in some measure rest: nowhere is there safe peace, nowhere secure repose; everywhere there are wars and quarrels, everywhere enemies, outward conflicts and inward fears (2 Cor. VII, 5). And because we are partly of heaven and partly of earth, the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul (Wis. IX, 15).

Therefore my mind, my companion and friend, weary from the road, grows faint as it comes and lies there, torn apart and lacerated by the vanities through which it has passed. It is very hungry and thirsty, and I have nothing to place before it, because I am poor and a beggar (Ps. XXXIX, 18). You, Lord my God, richest in all good things and most abundant giver of the food of heavenly satisfaction, give food to the weary, gather up what is scattered, restore what is torn.

Behold, he stands at the door and knocks (Rev. III, 20). I beseech you, by the innermost mercies with which, rising from on high, you visited us (Luke I, 78): open to the wretched one who knocks the hand of your kindness, and command in your merciful condescension that he enter into you, rest in you, and be refreshed by you, the living and heavenly bread. When he has been satisfied by it and recovered his strength, may he climb to the heights and, carried on the wing of holy desire from this valley of tears, fly toward the heavenly kingdoms.

[Col. 0898D]

May my spirit, Lord, assume—assume, I beg—wings like an eagle, and fly without growing weary; may it fly and reach the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells (Ps. XXV, 8), so that there, upon the table of refreshment of the citizens above, it may feed upon your hidden things in the place of your pasture (Ps. XXII, 2), beside overflowing streams.

May my heart rest in you, my God—my heart, a great sea swelling with waves. You who commanded the winds and the sea, and there came a great calm (Matt. VIII, 26), come and walk upon the waves of my heart, so that everything within me may become tranquil and serene. Then may I embrace you, my one good, and contemplate you, the sweet light of my eyes (Ps. XXXVII, 11), without the blind darkness of tumultuous thoughts.

May my mind flee, Lord, beneath the shadow of your wings (Ps. XVI, 8) from the heats of this world’s thoughts, so that, hidden in the temperate coolness of your refreshment, it may rejoice and sing and say: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV, 2).

[Col. 0899B]

Let my memory sleep, I beg, Lord my God, let it sleep concerning all things [Note: From “let my memory sleep concerning all things” through “let it love righteousness”: these words are absent from Sommalius and Augustine, where the text reads: “Let my memory sleep concerning all evils; let it hate iniquity and love righteousness.” The words beginning “For what…” belong to the following prayer.] that are beneath heaven, while remaining awake to you, as it is written: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V, 2).

May my soul, my God, be safe and always secure beneath the wings of your protection. May it remain in you and always be cherished by you. May it contemplate you in an ecstasy of mind and sing your praises with rejoicing. May these sweet goods of yours meanwhile be my consolation amid these storms, until I come to you, true peace, where there is no bow, shield, sword, or war, but supreme and upright security; secure tranquility, tranquil joy; joyful happiness, happy eternity; eternal blessedness; blessed vision of you; and praise forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER XIX

### TO CHRIST

When one desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ, according to the Apostle’s saying.

Christ the Lord, power and wisdom of the Father, who make the cloud your ascent, who walk upon the wings of the winds, who make your angels spirits and your ministers a burning fire (Ps. CIII, 4): I beseech and humbly ask you, give me swift wings of faith; give me rapid wings of the virtues, by which, carried aloft, I may contemplate eternal and heavenly things.

May my soul cling to you, I beg, and may your right hand receive me (Ps. LXII, 9). May it lift me above the height of the earth and feed me with that heavenly inheritance for which my pilgrimage sighs day and night. And because my dying limbs dull the vigor of my soul:

> Scatter the clouds and weights of the earthly mass,  
> Halt the wandering mind, rushing through many byways,  
> And grant a heavenly mind to climb the heavenly seat,

so that, irradiated by the highest light, it may look down upon earth, look up to heaven, hate sins, and love righteousness.

For what is more beautiful, or sweeter, than amid the darkness of this life and its many bitter things to long for divine sweetness and sigh for eternal blessedness, and there to be held in mind where it is most certain that true joys are possessed?

O sweetest, most loving, kindest, dearest, most precious, most desired, most lovable, most beautiful one, when shall I see you? When shall I appear before your face? When shall I be satisfied with your beauty? When will you lead me out of this dark prison, so that I may confess your name and thereafter suffer no more compunction? When shall I pass into that wondrous and most beautiful house of yours, where the voice of joy and exultation resounds in the tents of the righteous? (Ps. CXVII, 15.)

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). Blessed—and truly blessed—are those whom you have chosen and taken into that heavenly inheritance (Ps. LXIV, 5).

Behold your saints, Lord, flourishing before you like the lily. For they are filled with the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the torrent of your delight, because you are the fountain of life, and in your light they see light (Ps. XXXV, 9), to such an extent that they themselves—light illumined by you, the God who illumines—shine before you like the sun.

O how wondrous, how beautiful, how desirable are the dwelling places of your house, Lord of hosts! My sinful soul longs to enter them. “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. XXV, 8). “One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. When shall I come and appear before your face? (Ps. XLI, 2–3.) When shall I see my God, for whom my soul thirsts? When shall I see him in the land of the living? For in this land of the dying he cannot be seen by mortal eyes.

What shall I do, wretched as I am, bound by the heavy fetter of my mortality? What shall I do? “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord” (2 Cor. V, 6); here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come (Heb. XIII, 14). Our citizenship, however, is in heaven.

Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a very long sojourner (Ps. CXIX, 5). Who will give me wings like a dove, so that I may fly away and rest? (Ps. LIV, 7.) Nothing is as sweet to me as being with my Lord. “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28).

Grant me, Lord, while I remain attached to these fragile limbs, to cling to you, as it is written: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. VI, 17).

Grant me, I beg, wings of contemplation, clothed in which I may fly upward to you. And because everything sinister lies below, hold my mind so that it may not fall into the depths of the dark valley; so that, when the shadow of earth intervenes, it may not be separated from you, the true Sun of righteousness; and so that, when a cloud of darkness has been drawn over it [alternative reading: “when a cloud of darkness has been brought upon it”], it may not be prevented from looking upward.

Therefore I reach upward toward the joys of peace and the delightful, most serene state of light. Hold my heart in your hand, because without you it cannot be snatched up to higher things. I hasten there where supreme peace reigns and perpetual tranquility shines.

Hold and govern my spirit, and take it according to your will, so that, with you as its guide, it may ascend into that land of abundance where you feed Israel forever with the pasture of truth; so that there, even by a swift movement of thought, it may reach you, supreme Wisdom abiding above all things, passing beyond all things, and governing all things.

But as the soul flies toward you, many things make a noise against it. At your command, Lord, let everything fall silent for me. May my soul itself be silent to itself; may it pass beyond everything; may it transcend within itself all created things and reach you; and in you alone, Creator of all, may it fix the eyes of faith. May it long for you, attend to you, meditate upon you, contemplate you, set you before its eyes, turn you over within its heart as the true and highest good, and as joy that will endure without end.

There are, finally, many forms of contemplation by which the soul devoted to you is wondrously nourished; but in none of them does my soul delight and rest as it does in you, when it thinks of and contemplates you alone. How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you wondrously breathe into the hearts of those who love you! How marvelous is the gentleness of your love, which those enjoy who love nothing besides you, seek nothing, and desire even to think of nothing else!

Happy are those for whom you alone are hope and whose every work is prayer. Blessed is the one who sits alone and is silent, and continually stands upon his watch day and night, so that, while still placed in this fragile little body, he may in some measure taste your sweetness.

I ask you by those saving wounds of yours, which you suffered on the cross for our salvation, from which flowed that precious blood by which we were redeemed: wound this sinful soul of mine, for which you also deigned to die; wound it with the fiery and most powerful arrow of your immense love. For “the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV, 12).

You are the chosen arrow and the sharpest sword, which by your power can pierce the hard shield of the human heart. Fix my heart with the arrow of your love, so that my soul may say to you: “I have been wounded by your love,” so that from the very wound of your love abundant tears may flow day and night.

Strike, Lord, strike, I beg, this exceedingly hard mind of mine with the tender and powerful dart of your love; penetrate more deeply into its innermost places with your mighty power; and thus draw from my head an immense quantity of water and from my eyes a true fountain of tears continually flowing, from the excessive affection and desire for the vision of your beauty.

Let me mourn day and night, receiving no consolation in the present life, until I deserve to see you in the heavenly bridal chamber, my beloved and most beautiful Bridegroom, my God and my Lord. There, seeing your glorious, wondrous, and most beautiful face, full of every sweetness, may I humbly adore your majesty with those whom you have chosen; and there, at last, filled with heavenly and ineffable jubilation, may I cry out with those who love you in eternal exultation, saying:

“Behold, now I see what I desired; now I possess what I hoped for; now I have what I longed for. I have been joined in heaven to the one whom, while placed on earth, I loved with all my strength; whom I embraced with all my love; to whom I clung with complete affection. Him I praise, bless, and adore.”

He lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER XX

[Note: Compared with the manuscripts Thu. 267; Vict. RR. 3 and KK. 16; Corb. 160; Bec. O.; Val-luc.; Flor.; and the Carthusian manuscripts of the Portae; and with Sommalius, chapter 41, among Augustine’s *Meditations*. “To Jesus Christ, with meditation on his Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension.” Manuscript Thu.: “Here begins a prayer or meditation for kindling the love of God in oneself.” Manuscripts Vict. 16, Corb., and Flor.: “A meditation for kindling the love of God in oneself.” Manuscript Vict. 3: “A prayer to Christ.” Sommalius: “A devout prayer on remembrance of Christ’s Passion.”]

### TO CHRIST

For kindling the love of God and desire for Christ within oneself.

Lord Jesus Christ, my redemption, my mercy, my salvation, I praise you and give you thanks. Although these praises and thanks are very unequal to your benefits, greatly lacking in worthy devotion [Note: Vict., Carthusian, Val-luc., and Flor. read “lacking in devotion,” omitting “worthy”], and exceedingly lean in the desired richness of affection for you, most sweet Lord, nevertheless my soul renders you whatever praises and whatever thanks it can—not such as I know I ought to render, but such as it is able to endeavor to render [Note: The manuscripts read “although lean,” omitting “exceedingly”; some read “nevertheless whatever thanks”; manuscript Thu. reads “nevertheless whatever praises, whatever thanks”; one witness omits these words.].

Hope of my heart, strength of my soul, help of my weakness, may your most powerful goodness complete what my very tepid weakness endeavors [Note: The manuscripts read “help of my weakness, may it complete”; they also read *dignitas, quo* (“dignity, which”) for *benignitas, quod* (“goodness, what”); the Carthusian manuscript reads “goodness and kindness, what”]. My life, the end of my intention—and if I have not yet deserved to love you as much as I am bound to love you, at least I desire to love you as much as I ought [Note: The manuscripts read *merui tamen* (“but I have deserved”) for *merui te tantum* (“I have deserved you so much”); they also read “to love you as much as I ought.”].

You are my illumination (Ps. XXVI, 1); you see my conscience, for, Lord, every desire of mine is before you, and you grant whatever my soul desires rightly [Note: The manuscripts read “whatever my conscience desires”]. If what you inspire is good, Lord—indeed, because it is good that I should wish to love you—grant what you make me wish for. Grant that I may deserve to love you as much as you command.

I give you praise and thanks for the desire that you have inspired. I offer praise and prayers, lest your gift, which you freely gave [Note: The manuscripts read “which you gave by your spontaneous will”], prove fruitless for me. Complete what you have begun, and grant what, by graciously going before me, you have caused me, though unworthy, to desire.

Turn, most kind Lord, my tepidity [Note: The manuscripts read “my torpor”] into the most ardent love of you. To this end [Note: The manuscripts add “for this end”; one witness omits the phrase], most merciful Lord, this prayer of mine, this remembrance and meditation upon your benefits, is directed: that you may kindle your love in me [Note: Manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read “that I may kindle your love in myself”].

Your goodness, Lord, created me; your mercy cleansed me, once created, from original sin; your patience, after that cleansing in baptism, has until now tolerated, nourished, and awaited me, though I have wallowed in other filth of sins [Note: The manuscripts read “entangled in other filth”; the Carthusian manuscript reads “of pleasures”]. You, good Lord, await my correction [Note: The manuscripts omit “my”]; my soul awaits the inspiration of your grace, so that it may repent sufficiently and live well [Note: The manuscripts read “for repenting”].

My God [Note: Manuscript Flor. reads “My Lord, my God”; another reads “My Lord, my Creator”], my Creator, my sustainer and nourisher, be my helper (Ps. XXVI, 9). I thirst for you, I hunger for you, I desire you, I sigh for you, I long for you [Note: The manuscripts read “and I long for you”].

And just as an orphan deprived of the presence of a most kind father, weeping and lamenting, continually embraces with all his heart the beloved face of that father, so I too [Note: The manuscripts read “so I”], not as much as I ought but as much as I can, remembering your Passion, remembering your blows, remembering the scourges, remembering your cross, remembering your wounds [Note: The manuscripts read “remembering the cross, remembering your wounds”], remembering how you were killed for me, how you were laid away, how you were buried, and likewise remembering your glorious resurrection and wondrous ascension—I hold these things by unwavering faith, mourn the hardships of my exile, hope for no consolation except your coming, and burn with desire for the glorious contemplation of your face [Note: The manuscripts read “I ardently desire”; manuscript Vict. 16 reads “I burn, desiring your face”].

Woe is me, for I could not see the Lord of angels humbled to share the life of human beings, so that he might exalt human beings to share the life of angels, when the offended God willingly died so that the sinner might live [Note: The manuscripts read “when the offended one died”]. Woe is me, for I was not worthy to stand present and be astonished at such wondrous and immeasurable compassion [Note: The manuscripts read “at such compassion”].

Why, O my soul, did the sword of the sharpest sorrow not pierce you while you were present [Note: The manuscripts read “does not especially pierce you” (*te praesertim non transfigit*)], when you could not endure the side of your Savior to be wounded by a lance, when you could not bear to see the hands and feet of your Maker violated by nails, when you shuddered to see the blood of your Redeemer poured out [Note: The manuscripts omit “to see it poured out”]? Why were you not intoxicated with the bitterness of tears when he was made to drink the bitterness of gall? Why did you not suffer with the most chaste Virgin, his most worthy and most gracious Mother, your Lady [Note: The manuscripts read “his most worthy Lady”; another reads “most gracious Lady”]?

[Col. 0903D]

My most merciful Lady, what fountains shall I say burst forth from your most chaste eyes when you saw your only innocent Son bound, scourged, and slaughtered before you? [Col. 0904A] What tears may I believe drenched your most devout face when you received that same Son—your God and your Lord—stretched upon the cross without guilt, and flesh from your flesh cruelly cut apart by the wicked?  With what sobs shall I imagine your most pure breast afflicted when you heard: “Woman, behold your son”; and the disciple: “Behold your mother”? (John 19:26.) When you received a disciple as a son in place of the Teacher, a servant in place of the Lord? Would that, with blessed Joseph, I had taken my Lord down from the cross, anointed him with spices , placed him in the tomb—or at least  had followed him —so that my service might not have been lacking from so great a funeral! [Col. 0904B]

Would that, with the blessed women, I had been terrified by the radiant vision of angels and had heard the announcement of the Lord’s resurrection, the announcement of my consolation, an announcement so awaited, so desired! Would that, I say, I had heard from the angel’s mouth: “Do not be afraid, you; you seek Jesus who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here!” (Matthew 28:5.)

Most kind, most gentle, most serene Lord, when will you restore me, since I did not see that blessed incorruption of your flesh ; since I did not kiss the places of the wounds and the piercings of the nails ; since I did not sprinkle with tears of joy the scars that bear witness to the true body ? [Col. 0904C]

Wondrous, immeasurable, incomparable Lord, when will you console me (Psalm 118:82) and restrain me from my sorrow?  For my sorrow cannot find room within me as long as I am a stranger to my Lord. Alas for me, Lord; alas for my soul! You have departed, O consoler of my life; nor did you bid me farewell . Entering upon your ways, you blessed your own, and I was not there. With hands raised, you were received by a cloud into heaven, and I did not see you. The angels promised that you would return, and I did not hear them. [Col. 0904D]

What shall I say? What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where shall I seek him; where or when shall I find him ? Whom shall I ask? Who will announce to the beloved that I am faint with love? (Song 5:8.) The joy of my heart has failed; my laughter has been turned into mourning (Lamentations 5:15). My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart, and my portion forever (Psalm 72:26). My soul refused to be comforted (Psalm 76:3), except by you, my sweetness. [Col. 0905A] For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth? (Psalm 72:25.) I desire you, I hope in you, I seek you; my heart has said to you: “I have sought your face, your face, O Lord ; I shall seek it. Do not turn your face away from me” (Psalm 26:8). [Col. 0905D]

Most kind lover of humankind, to you the poor man has been abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan (Psalm 10:14). My safest advocate, have mercy on me, an abandoned orphan ; I have become a fatherless child (Lamentations 5:3); my soul is like a widow. Look upon the tears of my bereavement and widowhood, which I offer to you until you return. Come now, Lord, come; appear to me, and I shall be consoled. Show me your face, and I shall be saved (Psalm 79:4) . Show me your presence, and I shall attain my desire. [Col. 0905B] Reveal your glory, and my joy will be complete. My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you (Psalm 62:2). My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain. When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord  (Psalm 41:3)? [Col. 0905D] When will you come, my consoler, whom I await ? Oh, if only I could one day see my joy, which I desire! Oh, if only I might be satisfied when your glory appears  (Psalm 16:15), for which I hunger ! Oh, if only I might be filled with the abundance of your house (Psalm 35:9), for which I sigh; if only you would give me to drink from the torrent of your delight (ibid.), for which I thirst!

Meanwhile, Lord, let my tears be my bread day and night, until it is said to me: “Behold your God” (Psalm 41:4); until I hear: “Behold, your bridegroom” (Matthew 25:6). [Col. 0905C] Feed me meanwhile with my sobs; give me to drink meanwhile from my tears; refresh me with my sorrows. In the meantime, perhaps my Redeemer will come, for he is good; he will not delay, for he is merciful. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen. 

## PRAYER XXI



**To Christ. Prayer of a servant of God who thinks humbly of himself.**

I know, Lord Jesus Christ , I know and confess that I am not worthy for you to love; but certainly you are not unworthy for me to love. Indeed, I am unworthy to serve you, but you are not unworthy of the service of your creature. Therefore give me what is worthy of you, and I shall be worthy in that wherein I am unworthy. Make me  cease from sins in whatever way you wish, so that I may serve you in whatever way I ought. [Col. 0905D]

Grant me, through your most devout mercy, so to guard, govern, and complete my life that I may sleep in peace and rest (Psalm 4:9) in you. Grant me, Lord, that at the end my soul may receive sleep with rest, rest with satisfaction, satisfaction with eternity, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen. 

## PRAYER XXII

**To Christ. Prayer of a penitent humbly asking for divine help.**

Lord Jesus Christ, my Redeemer, my mercy, my salvation, my consolation, my life, I praise you and give you thanks. Your goodness created me; your mercy cleansed me from original sin. After that cleansing, your presence has thus far tolerated, nourished, and awaited me amid the other filth of pleasures. [Col. 0906A]

Lord God, my Creator, my Sustainer, my Nourisher, and my Helper, I thirst for you, I hunger for you, I desire you, I sigh for you, I long for you. Most kind, most gentle, most serene Lord, I wish, seek, and hope to see you. My soul refused to be comforted (Psalm 72:26), except by you, my sweetness. [Col. 0906B]

Come to me, Lord; appear to me, and I shall be consoled. Show me your face, and I shall be saved (Psalm 79:4). Show me your presence, and my desire will be fulfilled. Reveal your glory, and my joy will be complete. My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you (Psalm 62:2). When will you come to me, my consoler? Oh, if only I could one day see my joy, which I desire! Oh, if only I might be satisfied when the glory of him whom I hunger for appears (Psalm 16:15)! Oh, if only I might be filled with the abundance of his house (Psalm 35:9), for whom I sigh! Oh, if only you would give me to drink from the torrent of your delight (ibid.), for which I thirst! [Col. 0906C]

Give me, Lord, in this exile, the bread of sorrow and tears, which I hunger for above every abundance of delights. Meanwhile, Lord, let my tears sometimes be my bread day and night, until it is said to me: “Behold your God” (Psalm 41:4); until I hear: “Behold your bridegroom.” Feed me meanwhile, Lord, with my sobs; refresh me with my sorrows. Amen.

## PRAYER XXIII



**To Christ. For friends.**

Sweet and kind  Lord Jesus Christ, who displayed the charity than which no one has greater, and equal to which no one can possess; who owed nothing to death, yet laid down your devout soul for your servants and sinners , and prayed for those who killed you, so that you might make them your brothers and righteous, and reconcile them to your merciful Father and to yourself. [Col. 0906D–0907A]

You, Lord, who showed such great charity toward your enemies, yourself commanded charity toward your friends . Good Lord, with what feeling shall I contemplate your immeasurable charity? What shall I repay for your immense benefit? The sweetness of your kindness surpasses every affection; the greatness of your benefit surpasses every repayment.

What, then, shall I repay to my Creator and Restorer ? What shall I repay to my merciful Lord and Redeemer? Lord, you are my God; you have no need of my goods (Psalm 15:2). For the world is yours, and its fullness (Psalm 49:12). What, then, shall I, a beggar and poor man (Psalm 39:18), I, worm and ashes, repay to my God (Psalm 115:12), except that I obey his command from my heart? And your command is that we love one another (John 15:12). [Col. 0907B]

Good man, good God, good Lord, good friend, O complete Goodness, whatever you are: your humble and contemptible servant desires to obey this command. You know, Lord, that I love the love you command; I love love; I long for charity. I ask for this, I seek this; for this your poor and beggar knocks and cries at the door of your mercy.

And insofar as I have already received the sweet alms of your free generosity—loving every human being in you and for your sake, though not as much as I ought or as much as I desire—I implore your mercy for all. Yet there are many whose love your love has impressed upon my heart as especially intimate and familiar; so I desire good for them more ardently [Col. 0907C] and wish to pray for them more devotedly.

Your servant wishes, wishes, O merciful Lord, to pray to you for his friends; but your guilty servant is called back by his beloved. For I am not capable of pleading pardon for myself: with what boldness do I presume to ask your grace for others? And I anxiously seek intercessors: with what confidence do I intercede for others? What shall I do, Lord God, what shall I do? You command me to pray for them, and love desires it; but while my conscience cries out that I should be concerned for my sins, I tremble to speak for others. [Col. 0907D]

Shall I therefore abandon what you command because I have done what you forbid? No; because I presumed upon what was forbidden, I shall embrace what was commanded—if perhaps obedience may heal presumption, if perhaps charity may cover the multitude of my sins.

[Col. 0907D]

I therefore pray to you, devout and good God, for those who love me for your sake, and whom I love in you; and more devotedly for those whose love toward me, and my love toward whom, you know to be more sincere . I do not do this, my Lord , as though I were righteous and secure  concerning my sins, but as one concerned, with whatever charity I possess, for others. [Col. 0908A]

Therefore love them, O fountain of love, you who command and grant me to love them. And if my prayer does not deserve to benefit them because it is offered to you by a sinner, let it benefit them because it is made at your command, with you as its author. For your sake, therefore—you who are the author  and giver of charity—for your sake, not for mine , love them. Make them love you with all their heart, all their mind, and all their soul, so that they may will, speak, and do only what pleases you and is beneficial to them.

My prayer, my Lord, is far too lukewarm, because my charity is too little fervent. But do not measure your benefit to them, rich in mercy, according to the coldness of my devotion. Rather, just as your kindness surpasses all human charity, so may your hearing of my prayer transcend the feeling of my supplication. [Col. 0908B]

Do for them and concerning them , Lord, what is beneficial to them according to your will, so that they may always and everywhere be governed and protected by you, and thus attain both glorious and eternal security. You who live and reign.

## PRAYER XXIV



**To Christ. For enemies.**

Almighty and devout Lord Jesus Christ, whom I desire to be favorable toward my friends: before you there is also something that my heart earnestly desires for my enemies . For you, God who searches hearts and reins (Psalm 7:10), penetrate the secrets of my mind . It is open to you whether you have sown anything in the soul of your servant that ought to be offered to you; nor can it be hidden from you if I and the hostile man have sown anything there (Matthew 13:28) that must be burned by fire. [Col. 0908C]

Do not despise, most kind God, what you have sown, but cherish it, increase it , perfect it, and preserve it. For just as I could begin nothing good without you, so I can neither complete nor guard it without you.

Do not judge me, merciful God, because of what displeases you in me; rather, take away what you did not place there and save the soul you created. For I cannot correct myself without you, because when we are good, you yourself make us, and not we ourselves (Psalm 99:3). Nor could my soul endure it if you judged it according to its wickedness.

Therefore, Lord, who alone are powerful, you who alone are merciful, whatever you yourself make me desire for my enemies, grant it to them and repay it to me. And if I ever desire anything for them beyond the rule of charity, whether through ignorance, weakness, or malice, good Lord, do not grant it to them, nor repay it to me. [Col. 0908D–0909A]

You who are the true light, illumine their blindness. You who are supreme truth, correct their error. You who are true life, give life to their souls. For you said through your beloved disciple that whoever does not love remains in death (1 John 3:14). I therefore pray, Lord, that you grant them the charity toward you and their neighbor that you command should be possessed, so that they may not have sin before you against their brother . [Col. 0909D]

Far be it, O devout Lord, far be it that I should be an occasion of death to my brothers, that I should be for them a rock of stumbling and a stone of offense! (1 Peter 2:8.) It is enough, and more than enough, for me, Lord, that I myself am a scandal to myself; my own sin is sufficient for me. [Col. 0909B]

Your servant pleads with you for his fellow servants: may they not offend the kindness of so great and so good a Lord because of me, but may they be reconciled to you and be at peace with me, according to your will, for your sake.

This is the vengeance that the secret of my heart wishes to exact from my fellow servants , enemies, and fellow sinners. This is the punishment that my soul asks for my fellow servants and enemies: that we may love you and one another, as you wish and as is beneficial for us; that we may make satisfaction to the good Lord, as for ourselves so also for one another; and that we may serve the common Lord harmoniously for the common good, with charity as our teacher . [Col. 0909C]

This sinner of yours asks that this retribution be prepared for all his ill-wishers and wrongdoers.  Prepare it, most merciful Lord, for your sinner.

Act, therefore, good Creator and merciful Judge of mine; act through your immeasurable mercy. Forgive me all my debts , as I also  forgive before you all my debtors (Matthew 6:12). And if I have not yet done this perfectly—in fact, because I have not yet done it perfectly—but my spirit wishes to do so before your judgment, and by forcing itself, through you, accomplishes what it can , I offer this very effort to you, so that you too may wish perfectly to forgive me my sins  and, as you are able, pardon my soul.

Hear me, hear me, great Lord and good Lord: my hungry soul desires to feed upon the affection of your love, but cannot satisfy itself with you; when my mouth calls upon you, it cannot find a name sufficient for my heart. For no word tastes to me like what my feeling receives concerning you by your gift. [Col. 0909D–0910A]

I have prayed, Lord, as I could, but I desired more than I could. Hear me, hear me yourself, as you can—you who can do whatever you will. I prayed as a weak and sinful person; hear me, hear me as the powerful and merciful one. And not only grant to my friends and enemies what I have asked, but distribute the remedies of your mercy to all the living and the dead, as you know is beneficial to each and does not conflict with your will. Hear me always, Savior of the world—not as my heart wishes, nor as my mouth asks, but as you know and will that I ought to wish and ask. You who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign as God forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER XXV



**To Christ. When a priest greatly fears that the altar-service he performs may harm him more than benefit him, and what counsel he should take about this.**

Most sweet and kind Lord Jesus Christ , highest Son of the Most High Father, who with that same Father and the Holy Spirit exist as Creator of the universe; to whom all things are known before they come to be: you know my foolishness; you know also how weak and fragile my soul is, and its sins and offenses are not hidden from you. [Col. 0910B]

I acknowledge that you are my Creator, and I confess that you provide everything necessary for me to sustain this present life . You made me when it pleased you, and I shall remain in this life as long as it pleases you; no force can drive me from here until it pleases you.

And because I am utterly certain that this is so, above all I entreat your immeasurable goodness that, however things may turn out for me while I live, at least my end may be good, and that, with all my iniquities forgiven through true repentance, I may be able to attain the glory of your vision, for which you created me. [Col. 0910C]

I confess, most sweet Lord Jesus, that you gave me all the good things I possess, and that  you gave them to me so that I might love you above all things, as is fitting, and willingly do everything that pleases you, while I should in no way dare to do what displeases you.

But among the other good works that you commanded me in your service, I do not know by what hidden judgment of yours you permitted the burden of the priesthood to be imposed upon me . When I carefully consider with what reverence this service must be performed, how pure the conscience must be, and how cleansed from every contagion of sin the mind must be that undertakes to handle so awesome a ministry; and when, on the other hand, I consider no less carefully who I am, that I dare to handle this, I fear my presumption considerably, and I fear most vehemently  that it will bring me to a greater judgment and to the condemnation of a greater judgment, since I, so unworthy, dare to approach so worthy a matter. [Col. 0910D–0911A]

I know for certain, and have no doubt about this, that if I lived as the one ought to live who performs this ministry, I could do no service of God that would be more beneficial and salutary for me. But just as it would be beneficial if a worthy life existed, so a greater danger and greater condemnation threaten the weak soul burdened with its sins, which dares, unworthily, to handle so worthy a matter.

It is truly so: this matter is useful and salutary to a good priest beyond what can be said, and it is dangerous beyond what can be said for one who handles it unworthily.

What, then, will this priest of yours do, most sweet Lord Jesus—or rather, what will this sinner do—burdened by the weight of this service of yours? [Col. 0911B] I am exceedingly uncertain what is more beneficial for me: to abandon it or to perform it. Yet if I abandon it altogether, I again fear greatly that, under the pretext of this fear, I may dare to begin, or even commit, many evils and many sins that, because of fear of this service, I previously did not dare even to think about.

For I confess that many times, when I prepare myself for the service of this office and recognize the evils I have committed , I grieve over them more painfully and strictly within myself; and I reject more readily the vain thoughts and vain pleasures that then disturb me . After the service has been completed, I receive more timidly, because of fear of that same service, the many evils and sins that rise up again . [Col. 0911C]

When this happens, I draw some consolation from my presumption in undertaking that service, because I understand that through fear of its reverence I cease somewhat from my sins. But, O most gentle and merciful Jesus, as you perceive, so often my heart is full of every evil and blinded by the darkness of every iniquity , that, putting aside all these fears and knowingly scorning your commands , like a torrent that draws with it all the filth flowing into it and rolls it now upward, now downward, my heart, together with my wretched soul, receives all the uncleanness of carnal pleasures ; and, like a pig in mud, wallows and rolls again in those same uncleannesses . [Col. 0911D]

I confess, O most merciful Jesus, before your majesty my iniquities; I confess my uncleannesses; I confess my monstrous pride and my filthy thoughts, which my wretched soul unhappily embraces within after casting aside your fear . As you see, most merciful Lord Jesus, so often—again and again—I act in this way, and in such a filthy vessel, or rather in such a filthy heart , I receive your body and blood. I speak the truth; I do not spare myself! [Col. 0912A]

So often, full of sins and iniquities, I approach the service of your altar. Hence I greatly fear  that this presumption may be more to my destruction than to my salvation: that, foul and corrupt as I am, I presume to touch such pure sacraments.

Now let some faithful person come, one who is filled with the Spirit of God, and instruct the wretched priest by spiritual counsel about what is better or worse for him: whether to abandon the altar-service because of such impediments, or to perform the service because it restrains the many iniquities that are often repressed by fear of that same service. [Col. 0912B]

There is, as it seems to me, a clear and salutary counsel about this: to cease from sins and to render the service that we owe to God. Although we are unworthy to serve God, God is not unworthy of the service of his creature. I do not know what others themselves may choose; concerning myself, I know that I would rather serve God—even if I cannot wholly restrain myself from evil—than abandon his service through fear of sin and lie more securely in the condemnation of sins.

It is better that he should strike us because of some offense committed in his service, while we nevertheless perform his service, than that he should condemn us because, through fear of sin, we are unwilling to perform his service.

For immeasurable is his kindness, immeasurable his mercy. Even if he sees us walking along the path of his righteousness while limping, even if we often stumble and fall again, provided that we do not wish to turn away from the straightness of that path, if we do not grow weary , he cannot long hold himself back; he will assist our effort and direct our steps onto the way of salvation. [Col. 0912C]

Nevertheless, if a priest’s sins are criminal, it is more beneficial for him humbly to abstain from offering the sacrifice than, by presuming to offer it, to incur a greater condemnation, until, after beginning or completing repentance, he can approach the service of the altar more securely.

But behold, most sweet and merciful Lord Jesus, I confess to your immense goodness that I am a very great sinner, doing many things that displease you, yet presuming to perform the service of your altar. [Col. 0912D]

For I cannot despair of your mercy; I cannot, nor is it beneficial for me, abandon the service of your altar and not receive your body and blood—your body and blood which accepted death for my redemption, and which came forth from your pierced side, opened by the soldier’s lance, with water, for the forgiveness of sins (John 19:34). [Col. 0913A]

If I am unworthy, as I am—and I confess it—strike me, correct me, and rebuke me. Chastise your priest, or rather your sinner, until all the rust of sin departs from me, rust that through such a long period has hardened from great negligence upon the sides of my soul.

I confess, I confess: I am a sinner; I am unclean; I am unworthy. Yet I do not withdraw from you, most sweet Jesus Christ. Whatever you may will, I will not let you go; though my hand is weak, I will hold you. You will not depart from me until you free me from every contagion of sin. And thus, as I eat your flesh daily and drink your blood, continually cleaving to your will and constantly doing your commandments, may you lead me after the death of the flesh to true salvation—namely, to you, the true Priest. There, with the other priests, your members, may I too then be not a sinner but a worthy priest and a worthy member of your body, praising and glorifying you throughout eternal ages. Amen. [Col. 0913B]

## PRAYER XXVI



**To Christ. When a priest carefully contemplates how mercifully our Redeemer assumed for us the nature of our clay, from which he made us.**

Supreme Priest, and Lord greater than all other priests, Jesus Christ, to whom every priest cleaves—indeed, every Christian who walks before you in truth—with the ears of your compassion hear my voice, and, if I pray rightly, grant my prayer. For I do not wish, most sweet Father, to ask you for anything that could justly offend you in the asking. [Col. 0913C]

And if through any ignorance , or through a carnal will , I wish to ask you for something contrary to the salvation of my soul, this above all I beg of you, most merciful Lord: never be willing to hear me in such petitions.

You know—and you know well —most kind God, by how many delusions, how many vanities, how many pleasures of carnal desires, and how many appetites for worldly ambitions  my unhappy spirit is wounded every hour and without interruption.

And it often happens, as you yourself, most gentle Lord, perceive , that if you permitted me to go according to my most evil will , I would plunge my entire self into a great abyss of sins. [Col. 0913D–0914A]

Therefore, most sweet Father, I ask you because I know that I am far too great a sinner and have scarcely any strength at all against sin: through your great mercy restrain my fury, which drags me toward sin, and confound and destroy every evil desire that perverts within me every sense of righteousness .

## Textual apparatus

Entries follow the supplied notes in order. Witness labels apply only to the reading assigned to them; unassigned contrasts and apparent corruptions are retained. Abbreviated quotations mark the scope of variants, not additional missing text.

### Col. 0903D: the Passion and longing for Christ
