1. *Quos fletus credam*, “what weeping shall I believe [you shed]?” Vict. 16; *quos fluctus lacrymarum dicam*, “what floods of tears shall I speak of?” Val-luc.; *quos fluctus credam*, “what floods shall I believe [you shed]?” the unassigned contrast.
2. *Acciperes discipulum*, “you received the disciple,” manuscripts; *acciperes in filium discipulum*, “you received the disciple as a son,” the contrast.
3. *Condidissem*, “I had laid away/preserved,” manuscripts; *condiissem*, “I had seasoned/embalmed,” the contrast. The narrative prints *condivissem*, likewise “I had embalmed,” with spices.
4. *Ut saltem*, “that at least,” manuscripts; *aut saltem*, “or at least,” the contrast.
5. Vict. and Val-luc. omit *vel consecutus*, “or having followed.” The narrative at the corresponding point prints *prosecutus*, “having accompanied.”
6. The apparatus prints *mihi, qui non*, “to me, who did not,” both as the manuscripts' reading and as the contrast. The narrative instead has *mihi, quia non*, “to me, because I did not.” No difference is invented between the identical cited forms.
7. *Illum beatae*, literally “that [masculine] of the blessed [feminine],” manuscripts, is apparently corrupt here; *illam beatam*, “that blessed [incorruption],” the contrast.
8. *Fixuram*, “the piercing/nail-hole,” manuscripts; *et fixuras*, “and the piercings/nail-holes,” the contrast.
9. *Cicatrices corporis veri*, “the scars of the true body,” Corb., Vict., Carth., and Val-luc.; *cicatrices testes veri corporis*, “the scars, witnesses of the true body,” the contrast.
10. *Inaestimabilis, quando*, “immeasurable [Lord], when,” manuscripts; *inaestimabilis, incomparabilis quando*, “immeasurable, incomparable [Lord], when,” the contrast.
11. *Consolaberis et*, “will you console, and,” manuscripts; *consolaberis me et*, “will you console me, and,” the contrast.
12. *Cadit a me*, “[my sorrow] falls away from me,” manuscripts; *capit in me*, “[my sorrow] finds room in me,” the contrast, within the negative sentence.
13. *Animae meae nec valedixisti*, “of my soul, and you did not say farewell,” manuscripts; *vitae meae nec valedixisti mihi*, “of my life, and you did not say farewell to me,” the contrast.
14. *Ubi eum quaeram, vel quando inveniam*, “where shall I seek him, or when shall I find [him]?” manuscripts; *ubi et quando eum quaeram, ubi vel quando inveniam*, “where and when shall I seek him, where or when shall I find [him]?” Val-luc.; *ubi cum quaeram, ubi vel quando inveniam*, literally “where, when I seek, where or when shall I find?” the damaged unassigned contrast, with *cum* where the narrative has *eum*, “him.”

### Col. 0905D: longing for Christ and Prayers XXI–XXIII

15. *Quaesivi vultum tuum, Domine*, “I sought your face, Lord,” manuscripts; *quaesivi vultum tuum: vultum tuum, Domine*, “I sought your face: your face, Lord,” the contrast with the repetition.
16. *Miserere mei orphani*, “have mercy on me, an orphan,” manuscripts; *miserere orphani*, “have mercy on the orphan,” the contrast.
17. *Ero. Exhibe*, “I shall be. Show,” manuscripts; *ostende mihi faciem tuam et salvus ero. Exhibe*, “show me your face and I shall be saved. Show,” the fuller contrast.
18. *Ante faciem Domini*, “before the face of the Lord,” manuscripts; *ante faciem Dei mei*, “before the face of my God,” the contrast.
19. *Quem exspectabo*, “whom I shall await,” manuscripts; *quem exspecto*, “whom I await,” the contrast.
20. *Gloria mea*, “my glory,” manuscripts; *gloria tua*, “your glory,” the contrast.
21. *Quem sitio*, “for whom I thirst,” manuscripts; *quam sitio*, “how I thirst,” the contrast.
22. *Audiat anima mea, ecce*, “let my soul hear: behold,” manuscripts; *audiam. Anima ecce*, “let me hear. Soul, behold,” the contrast.
23. *Meis, refocilla*, “with my [sobs], revive,” manuscripts; *meis, pota me interim fletibus meis, refocilla*, “with my [sobs], meanwhile give me my tears to drink, revive,” the fuller contrast.
24. *Veniet fortasse*, “perhaps he will come,” manuscripts; *veniet interea fortasse*, “perhaps meanwhile he will come,” the contrast.
25. Prayer XXI was collated with Sommal., chapter 10 of the *Meditations of Saint Augustine*. Sommal.'s heading is “Prayer of a servant of God humbling himself”; the contrast is “Prayer of a servant of God thinking humbly of himself.”
26. Som. omits *Jesu Christe*, “Jesus Christ,” in *Domine Jesu Christe*, “Lord Jesus Christ.”
27. *Fac me Domine quoquo modo vis*, “make me, Lord, in whatever way you will,” Som.; *fac me quomodo vis*, “make me as you will,” the contrast.
28. Som. has *Recipiat anima mea summum cum requie, requiem cum saluritate, saluritatem cum aeternitate, per J. C. D. N. Amen*: “May my soul receive the highest [thing] with rest, rest with ‘saluritas,’ and ‘saluritas’ with eternity, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.” The printed *summum* and *saluritate/saluritatem* are damaged or uncertain here; “sleep” and “security” are plausible intended senses but are not silently substituted. The contrast is *me excipiat somnus cum requie, requies cum securitate, securitas in aeternitate. Amen*: “May sleep receive me with rest, rest with security, security in eternity. Amen.”
29. Prayer XXIII was collated with the previously identified Bec., Gem., Corb., Vict., Thu., Val-luc., Floriacens., and Carthus. manuscripts. Their heading is “Petition for charity, and prayers for friends”; the contrast is “Prayer for friends.”
30. *Et benigne*, “and kind [Lord],” manuscripts; *et benignissime*, “and most kind [Lord],” the contrast.
31. *Servis et*, “for servants and,” manuscripts; *servis tuis et*, “for your servants and,” the contrast.

### Col. 0907D: Prayers XXIII–XXIV

32. *Domine, qui tantam charitatem praecepisti*, “Lord, who commanded such charity,” manuscripts; *Domine, qui tantam charitatem fecisti inimicis tuis, tu ipse charitatem praecepisti*, “Lord, who showed such charity to your enemies, you yourself commanded charity,” the fuller contrast.
33. *Creatori et Redemptori meo? Domine etc.*, “to my Creator and Redeemer? Lord, etc.,” manuscripts; *recreatori meo? Quid retribuam miseratori et Redemptori meo? Domine*, “to my re-creator? What shall I repay to the one who has mercy on me and to my Redeemer? Lord,” the fuller contrast.
34. *Reclamante*, “crying out in protest,” manuscripts; *clamante*, “crying out,” the contrast, of conscience.
35. *Synceritatem*, “sincerity,” manuscripts; *synceriorem*, “more sincere,” the contrast. The narrative has *sinceriorem*, referring to love.
36. The note cites *ago Domine mi*, “I do [this], my Lord”; Vict. 16 and Val-luc. omit *mi*, “my.” The note does not say that they omit the preceding narrative *non*, “not.”
37. *Quasi justus, securus*, “as though righteous, secure,” Thu.; *quasi justus, quasi securus*, “as though righteous, as though secure,” the contrast.
38. *Tu auctor*, “you, author,” Vict. 16; *tu actor et*, “you, agent/doer and,” the contrast.
39. *Propter te ergo, non*, “therefore for your sake, not,” manuscripts; *propter te, non*, “for your sake, not,” the contrast.
40. *Fac illis et de illis*, “do for them and concerning them,” Carth.; *fac illis, et da illis*, “do for them, and give to them,” the contrast.
41. Prayer XXIV was collated with the previously designated manuscripts. Their label is *Faculae ad Deum pro inimicis*, literally “Little torches to God for enemies,” an unusual expression retained as printed; the contrast is “Prayer for enemies.”
42. *Coram te est quid*, “before you is what,” manuscripts; *coram te est etiam quid*, “before you is also what,” the contrast.
43. *Mentis tuae*, “of your mind,” manuscripts; *mentis meae*, “of my mind,” the contrast.
44. *Quod tibi sit*, “which may be for you,” Vict. 3; *quid tibi sit*, “what may be for you,” the contrast. This is the source's attribution, not its reverse.
45. In *fove et auge*, “cherish and increase,” Vict. 16 omits *et auge*, “and increase.”

### Col. 0909D: forgiveness and Prayer XXV

46. *Nec habeant*, “and may they not have,” manuscripts; *ne habeant*, “lest they have,” the contrast.
47. *Satis est mi*, “it is enough for me,” Vict. 16 and Val-luc.; *satis est mihi*, the same sense with the full form *mihi*.
48. In *de conservis*, “concerning fellow servants,” Vict. 16 omits *de*, “concerning.”
49. *Domino: et commune*, “to the Lord: and the common [good],” manuscripts; *Domino in commune*, “to the Lord for the common [good],” the contrast.
50. *Consequamur*, “may we attain,” manuscripts; *obsequamur*, “may we serve,” the contrasting reading; *exequamur*, “may we carry out,” Thu.
51. In *hanc etiam*, “this also,” manuscripts omit *etiam*, “also.”
52. *Debita mea*, “my debts,” Vict. 16 and Flor.; *delicta mea*, “my offenses,” the contrast.
53. *Si et ego*, “if I also,” manuscripts; *sicut et ego*, “just as I also,” the contrast.
54. *Pro te quod*, “for your sake what,” Victorin. 16 and Flor.; *per te, quod*, “through you, what,” the contrast.
55. *Perficere dimittere*, literally “to complete to forgive,” manuscripts, an awkward construction; *perfecte dimittere*, “to forgive perfectly,” the contrast.
56. Prayer XXV was collated with Thu. 267, Vict. KK. 16, Corb. 160, and Val-luc. The cited heading is: “For a priest when he greatly fears that the ministry of the altar which he performs may harm him more than benefit him, and what counsel he should take in such perplexity.” Thu. and Vict. have “Prayer when a priest greatly fears … and what counsel he should take from this.” Corb. has “A priest's confession from the remembrance of benefits, and whether it is better to serve the altar or to refrain through fear of sins.” Val-luc. has “Prayer when a priest greatly fears that the ministry of the altar which he performs may harm him more than benefit him, and what counsel he should take concerning this.” The source abbreviates the intervening words in the shorter title citations.
57. Corb. omits *et benignissime*, “and most kind,” from *et benignissime Domine*, “and most kind Lord.”
58. *Ad praesentem vitam sustentandam necessaria sunt*, “are necessary to sustain the present life,” manuscripts; *ad praesentis vitae necessitatem*, “for the needs of the present life,” the contrast.
59. *Omnia quae habeo, et scio tu mihi dedisti, et docuisti, et quia*, “all that I have and know you gave me and taught me, and because,” manuscripts; *omnia bona quae habeo, tu mihi dedisti, et quia*, “all the good things I have you gave me, and because,” the contrast.
60. *Imponi permisisti*, “you allowed [the burden] to be imposed,” Corb.; *imponi praecipisti*, “you commanded [it] to be imposed,” the contrast.
61. *Cum altera*, “with the other [part],” manuscripts; *ex altera*, “from the other [part],” the contrast in the comparison of the two alternatives.

### Col. 0911D: the priest's confession

62. *Sed vehementissime*, “but most intensely,” Vict. and Val-luc.; *et vehementissime*, “and most intensely,” the contrast.
63. *Animae peccatis*, “of the soul [burdened] with sins,” manuscripts; *animae, et peccatis*, “of the soul, and with sins,” the contrast with the conjunction.
64. *De malis*, “concerning evils,” manuscripts; *et de malis*, “and concerning evils,” the contrast.
65. *Cogitationes, expeditius*, “[vain] thoughts, more readily,” Vict. and Val-luc.; *cogitationes vanasque delectationes expeditius*, “[vain] thoughts and vain pleasures more readily,” the fuller contrast.
66. *Servitium mala*, “the service, evils,” Vict.; *servitium multa mala*, “the service, many evils,” the contrast.
67. *Ita est*, “so it is,” Thu.; *ita et*, “so also,” the contrast.
68. *Obcaecatum, omnes*, “blinded, all [these things],” manuscripts; *obcaecatum, ut has omnes*, “blinded, so that all these [things],” the contrast.
69. *Postponens … contemnens*, “setting aside … despising,” Vict.; *postpones … contemnes*, “you will set aside … you will despise,” the contrast. These differ in grammatical construction; the dots abbreviate the intervening words.
70. *Voluit, omnes*, “he wished, all,” manuscripts; *voluit cor meum cum misera anima mea, omnes*, “he wished, my heart with my wretched soul, all,” the unassigned fuller citation. Both print *voluit*, ordinarily “wished,” where the narrative has *volvit*, “rolls,” in the image of flesh dragging the heart downward. A possible typographical confusion is marked rather than glossing *voluit* without explanation as “rolled.”
71. *Recipit*, “receives,” manuscripts; *recipiat*, “may receive,” the contrast.
72. *Volvit et revolvit*, “rolls and rolls again,” manuscripts; *volvat et revolvat*, “may roll and roll again,” the contrast.
73. *Meas fateor*, “my [iniquities]; I confess,” manuscripts; *meas, fateor immunditias meas, fateor*, “my [iniquities]; I confess my uncleannesses; I confess,” the fuller contrast.
74. Vict. omits *vel potius in tam sordido corde*, “or rather in so filthy a heart.”
75. Corb. omits *sic multoties*, “thus so often.”
76. *Formido, quod*, “I fear that,” Thu.; *formido ne*, “I fear lest,” the contrast.
77. *Non lassemus*, “may we not weary [ourselves],” Vict. and Val-luc.; *non lassemur*, “may we not grow weary,” the contrasting active/passive form.

### Col. 0913D: Prayer XXVI

78. This prayer was collated with Vict. KK. 16, Corb. 160, and Val-luc.; it is not found in the other manuscripts. The cited title reads: “When a priest diligently contemplates how mercifully our Redeemer assumed for us the nature of our clay, from which he made us.” Vict. agrees with the printed editions. Corb. has “Prayer of a priest in consideration of his own indignation and the dignity of this office, and concerning the reception of the Lord's Body and Blood.” The printed *indignationis*, “indignation,” may be corrupt for a word meaning “unworthiness,” but that is conjectural.
79. *Et si aliquando inscitia*, “and if at some time through ignorance,” Corb.; *et si aliqua inscitia*, “and if through some ignorance,” Val-luc.; *et si aliqua inscientia*, “and if through some lack of knowledge,” the contrast.
80. *Vel etiam carnali*, “or even through carnal [weakness],” manuscripts; *vel carnali*, “or through carnal [weakness],” the contrast.
81. In *nosti Domine*, “you know, Lord,” Corb. and Val-luc. omit *Domine*, “Lord.”
82. *Saecularium cupiditatum et Ecclesiasticarum dignitatum appetitionibus*, “by desires for worldly objects of craving and ecclesiastical dignities,” manuscripts; *saecularium voluptatum appetitionibus*, “by desires for worldly pleasures,” Val-luc.; *saecularium cupiditatum appetitionibus*, “by desires for worldly objects of craving,” the contrast.
83. *Perspicis*, “you see clearly,” Corb.; *prospicis*, “you look ahead/foresee,” the contrast.
84. *Meam malam*, “my evil [will],” manuscripts; *meam pessimam*, “my utterly evil [will],” the contrast.
85. In *pervertit in me*, “perverts in me,” manuscripts omit *in me*, “in me.”

At times, God, lover of humankind [Note: [Col. 0913D] The manuscripts read *amator hominum*, “lover of humankind”; the text has *plasmator hominum*, “fashioner of humankind”], when I think more diligently [Note: [Col. 0913D] The manuscripts read *cum studiosus*, “when [I am] more diligent”; the text has *cum studiosius*, “when I think more diligently”], and recall to mind the evil things [Note: [Col. 0913D] The manuscripts read *cogito mala*, “I think evil things”; the text has *cogito et mala*, “I think, and evil things”] that I have often done and still, wretched and sinful, do not cease to do, and carefully consider [Note: [Col. 0913D] The manuscripts read *diligenter qualiter*, “carefully, how”; Val-luc. reads *diligenter intueor qualiter*, “I carefully consider how”; the text has *diligentius intueor qualiter*, “I consider more carefully how”.] how I live, how I may lament the very evils that I have done and still do: that I am called a priest, yet do not fulfill the priestly office by worthy works. Although I greatly fear many other things that I have done, I fear greatly above all the dignity of this office, which I bear unworthily, and whatever else may happen to me [Note: [Col. 0913D] The manuscript omits *valde*, “greatly”].

[Col. 0914B]

The dignity of this office is, in fact, exceedingly great—greater than can be estimated—and incomparably dear to God and human beings, if the priest lives as one ought to live who bears the care of this office. I bear the name of this dignity, but my unhappy life, in almost everything, contradicts the dignity of this name by evil conduct. My heart is unclean, all the senses of my body are unclean, and thus I am wholly unclean within and without [Note: [Col. 0913D] The manuscripts read *interius et foris*, “inwardly and outwardly”; the text has *intus et foris*, “within and without”]. I find nothing clean in my whole self in which I might honorably and fittingly place the Lord’s body.

Thus placed in great distress, and not knowing what I ought chiefly to do, I carry myself here and there, thinking now of this, now of that, and examine my entire conscience more carefully, in case I might find some wholesome counsel [Col. 0914C] which I might understand to afford some salvation to my soul [Note: [Col. 0913D] The manuscripts read *ad salutem*, “for salvation”; the text has *ad aliquam salutem*, “for some salvation”]. Considering, therefore, all that concerns me, and finding almost nothing or very little good in my whole self, I scarcely discern this tiny bit of good there—if indeed that should be called good: that in another, when he possesses it, I love the good which I do not have, and, since I do not have it, humbly acknowledge that I do not have it [Note: [Col. 0913D] Corb. reads *dici quod bonum ego cum habeo*, “to be called good which I, when I have it …” [incomplete reading]; Vict. and Val-luc. read *dici, quod ego non habeo*, “to be called that which I do not have”; the text has *dici quod bonum, quod ego non habeo*, “to be called good, which I do not have.”]. I believe myself more sinful and wretched than any other person, and yet I do not despair of the mercy of almighty God.

For I believe that he who cared to make me when I did not exist, and still cares in his mercy to provide me with what is necessary for the use of this life, will in his compassion care also to grant me to do some good work—or at least, if I cannot do all things wholly [Col. 0914D], to begin some good; and, if not wholly, to cease at least somewhat from evils.

[Col. 0915A]

For God is gracious [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *est enim pius*, “for he is gracious”; the text has *est enim Deus pius*, “for God is gracious”] and merciful, and in no way wishes to destroy his creature; rather, he mercifully admonishes it by every means to return to his compassion [Note: [Col. 0915D] Vict. reads *movens*, “moving,” for *monens*, “admonishing”]. He truly shows how greatly he loves his creature and how unwillingly he destroys it, when [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *ostenditur, cum*, “is shown when”; the text has *ostendit cum*, “shows when”] he descends from heaven to earth; when he who existed without beginning chose, for love of his creature, to have a beginning; when he assumed for our redemption the clay from which he made us; and when, after that very clay—that is, his flesh, which he assumed for us—had been thoroughly baked through the passion of the cross upon the altar of that cross, he offers it to us to eat, and, while giving us to drink the blood of that same flesh pressed out in the winepress of the cross, quenches the thirst of our soul.

[Col. 0915B]

When we eat this flesh of our Redeemer and drink his blood, we mix it with our own clay, and, making from it, as it were, a plaster [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *de hoc quoque*, “from this also,” for *de hoc quasi*, “from this, as it were”], and applying it to the infirmities of our soul [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *nostrisque infirmitatibus*, “to our infirmities,” for *nostraeque animae infirmitatibus*, “to the infirmities of our soul”], if we receive it worthily, we immediately cast out from the inner parts of our soul everything that draws us toward the danger of condemnation.

O immeasurable compassion of our Lord Jesus Christ! O wondrous and ineffable mercy! If some powerful man, traveling with a great retinue, happened to see beside the road along which he was passing a poor man immersed in some muddy pool, unable by any means to pull himself out of the mud in which he was submerged, and, moved by pity, himself pulled that poor man out of the mud, no one would doubt that such great mercy and compassion would be proclaimed by everyone and exalted with great praise by all who possessed sound judgment [Col. 0915C]. The more mercifully he acted toward the poor and needy man, the more compassionate and merciful he would appear to all pious and truly Christian people.

What, then, should be thought of the great compassion, the ineffable mercy and love of our Lord Jesus Christ? He himself existed without beginning, yet for the sake of the poor—and of one exceedingly poor and needy—he took upon himself a mortal beginning and mortality, in order to draw him out of the most filthy mud of sin into which the wretched and unhappy man had immersed himself [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *immiserat*, “had put himself in,” for *immerserat*, “had immersed himself”]. Besides this [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *propter hoc*, “because of this”; the text has *praeter hoc*, “besides this”], the wretched man endured such great unhappiness and lay so miserably immersed in the very abysses of eternal destruction. He was oppressed by great anguish [Col. 0915D] and by the great pains of hunger and thirst. On the one side, he suffered the intolerable stench of the mud in which he was immersed; on the other, finding no one to sympathize with his misery and pain, he was afflicted with intolerable suffering both by the stinking mud in which he lay and by despair of the consolation which no one removed from him [Col. 0916A]. And if it were delayed any longer that mercy might at some time be mercifully bestowed on him by someone, he would already die irreparably amid the very miseries of eternal destruction.

The merciful Creator came [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *venit ergo*, “therefore came,” omitting *ergo* in the text], possessing ineffable compassion for this sinner lying in the mire of sins; without stripping himself of the garment of his glory, he put on the rags of our misery. He came like the purest Sun through those very stenches, suffering no contamination from their foulness, all the way to the wretched sinner himself; wiping him clean of those very stenches, he took him by the arm and pulled him out onto solid ground.

After he had been drawn out of the pit of misery and the mud of filth (Psalm XXXIX, 3), he fed him with the bread of saving wisdom (Ecclesiasticus XV, 3). After this, he fed and gave him to drink his own flesh, which he had assumed for the man’s redemption, and his own blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins; and thus, refreshed, he soothed him from the very pains by which he had been so grievously tormented.

This flesh, which he gave him to eat, was of the nature of that same clay from which he had fashioned the first human being, whom he created in his image and likeness. That likeness, which the first man himself disfigured through his fault [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read “which the man first…”], he restored completely through the eating of his flesh [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read “through feasting”] and through right faith. After Christ had suffered on the cross and risen on the third day, he carried this flesh—or the nature of this clay—to heaven and placed it at the right hand of the Father, granting it dominion over angels and archangels.

Behold, the clay that by its nature always clings to the earth has been carried by our Redeemer into heaven, and holds heaven itself and everything in it under its dominion [Col. 0916C] [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts read *portatus ipsum*; one reads *portatur, ipsum* (“is carried, [and] it itself”)]. No faithful person can or will ascend to that clay unless he first takes care to eat it beneficially on earth and drink its blood.

I, however unworthy, am a minister and priest of this flesh and blood. When I behold such great compassion and the sweetness of such compassion shown by our Redeemer toward his creature, I do not distrust his immeasurable goodness. Come to my aid, therefore, Lord Jesus Christ; come to the aid of your priest. Forgive his sins and offenses, so that I may worthily celebrate the mystery of your body and blood, and, celebrating it worthily, may worthily eat and drink the truth of your body and blood. Thus, persevering continually to the end, may I be able after the death of the flesh to reach you, where—not at intervals, as now, but without interruption—I may eat and drink you yourself, who are truth and life, together with all the saints [Note: [Col. 0915D] The manuscripts add “Amen”]. Amen.

[Col. 0916D]

[Col. 0917A]

## PRAYER XXVII

[Note: [Col. 0917D] Compared with the manuscripts Vict. KK. 16, Corb. 160, and Val-luc. The manuscripts of Vict. and Val-luc. title it: “Preparatory prayer when the priest is about to celebrate, and how, while holding the body and blood of Christ in his hands, he should sweetly remember the sufferings he endured in his heart on the cross for us.” The manuscripts also read: “Prayer of the priest, when he holds the body and blood of Christ in his hands, and while holding them sweetly remembers what sufferings he endured for us on the cross.”]

### TO CHRIST

When the priest holds the body and blood of Christ in his hands, and while holding them sweetly remembers what sufferings he endured for us on the cross.

Most sweet, and desirable above all things, and most gracious Jesus Christ, attend to my supplication and give heed to the voice of my prayer (Psalm V, 3). Through your great mercy cleanse my soul from every stain of sin, so that I may be worthy to approach the service of your altar and worthily handle the mystery of your body and blood.

I confess, most sweet Lord, before your omnipotence that I am exceedingly guilty, committing many evils almost every hour, and yet not despairing of your ineffable goodness [Col. 0917B]. You are good, Lord, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances (Psalm CXVIII, 68), so that, understanding them and continually practicing them as is fitting, I may receive your mysteries with a pure heart and a clean soul.

Behold, my soul: prepare the lodging of your heart to receive the body and blood of your Creator through pure thoughts and pure works. Purge from all your inner parts whatever could offend a guest of such immeasurable majesty. For he cannot remain in that soul or in that heart possessed by any contamination of evil; and unless the highest peace and the highest charity are there, judging that lodging unworthy of the manner of life proper to his dwelling and unable to endure for long so great a disturbance of disorder, he quickly departs from that lodging [Col. 0917C].

Woe to that mind which Christ abandons because of its iniquities and, abandoning it, permits it to be led astray by the temptations and deceits of the enemy!

Therefore, my soul, examine yourself carefully; carefully gather all the senses of your body inwardly back to yourself [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts read *interius recollige*, “gather inwardly”]. Whatever sordid or unclean thing you find among them, cast it out. Having expelled every malice and iniquity, carefully close the entrance of your breast against them [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts read *peccatis interclude*, “bar it against sins”], lest they ever be able to return to you or further defile your inner parts.

When everything that pertains to the consecration of this venerable mystery has been completed, and everything that usually stains the secret place of the mind has been expelled, you, my wretched soul, look with great care upon all your negligences, all the evils and sins that you were accustomed to commit [Col. 0917D]. And while you hold the body and blood of your Redeemer in your hands, plead with him as sweetly as you can for his ineffable mercy, so that through his great compassion he may forgive all your sins and may grant that you be unable to commit these or other sins again.

Above all—and I warn you as you would your own destruction—beware lest in such recollections you fall into any snares of the devil, into which many unwary people repeatedly fall. While they bring their evils back before the eyes of their minds as though weeping over them, through those very recollections they foolishly fall again into delight in those evils [Note: [Col. 0917D] Vict. reads *in ipsorum*, “into their [evils],” for *in ipsas*, “into them”].

Remember, as sweetly as you can, the ineffable compassion of the body of Christ that you hold [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts read “the ineffable compassion of Christ,” rather than “of the body of Christ that you hold”], and its sweetness, more wondrous than can be estimated. For your redemption it endured many insults and was finally crucified.

Also think and rethink, pain by pain, the passion that he endured on the cross [Col. 0918B]: with how great a pain his feet and hands were fastened to the gallows of that cross [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts read “with the pain of his cross”]; how his side was pierced by the soldier’s lance; how, there before the cross, even by those for whom he was suffering [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts variously read “by those for whom,” “by those from whom,” “by those and for whom,” or “even by those for whom”], he was mocked and ridiculed as though he were a criminal, enduring such dreadful insults; and how, like the gentlest Lamb, he displayed immeasurable patience.

Though he could easily have taken vengeance on his executioners, he did not do so, but prayed to the Father for them [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts read “but prayed to the Father that he might forgive them this sin”], asking that he forgive them this sin.

When [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts read *cum ergo*, “when therefore,” for *cum vero*, “when indeed”] you have begun to rest as though satisfied by such recollections, and yet, while resting, have not ceased to ruminate on them sweetly and with deep feeling, speak to that sweetest body of the sweetest Lord which you hold in your hands, and, as though speaking with him present, disclose your needs to him [Col. 0918C] [Note: [Col. 0917D] Vict. reads *de quo hoc*, “concerning which, this”; Corb. and Val-luc. read *de illo haec*, “concerning it, these things”; the text has *de illo hoc*, “concerning it, this”]. Believe faithfully concerning it that this body truly is that body which was born of the Virgin, which was crucified, which was placed in the tomb, which rose from the dead on the third day, which ascended into heaven, and which sits at the right hand of the Father.

Nor should you doubt that, at the hour of the sacrifice of the body and blood of your Redeemer, angels are present before their Creator and render ineffable service, with great reverence, to the flesh and blood of their Creator.

What, then, should be thought of all the saints? What can be imagined when they see the price of their redemption being celebrated on earth, while they, rejoicing in the eternal vision of the one by whom they were redeemed, already possess great joy in heaven? You, however, my soul, faithfully believing all these things and sweetly embracing the flesh of your Creator, signify your need in those embraces of his compassion [Note: [Col. 0917D] The manuscripts read “in the embraces of his compassion”], and plead as sweetly as you can for his mercy, so that through his ineffable mercy he may cleanse all your foulness [Col. 0919A].

Throw your whole self into the Christ whom you hold, and, first adoring him [Note: [Col. 0919D] The manuscript of Vict. reads “adoring him afterward”], present your needs to him again and again [Note: [Col. 0919D] The manuscript of Corb. reads “present your needs again and again”].

## PRAYER XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0919D] Compared with the manuscripts Vict. KK. 16, Corb. 160, and Val-luc. In the manuscript of Val-luc. it is not separated from the preceding prayer and therefore has no title. The manuscripts have no title here.]

### TO CHRIST

To be made by the priest before the consecration of Christ’s body.

O most sweet Lord Jesus Christ, who for my redemption were crucified and died, before you is all my desire, and my sighing is not hidden from you (Psalm XXXVII, 10). Behold, most gracious God, my misery is before you, and your mercy is in my hands: the misery of my sinful soul, the mercy of your redemption [Note: [Col. 0919D] The manuscripts of Corb. and Val-luc. read “your redemption”; the manuscript of Vict. reads “my redemption”].

Therefore have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity (Psalm L, 1–3), and from this hour to the end preserve my life. Defend my soul from every iniquity, so that I may no longer be able to do anything that would offend the eyes of your majesty.

Grant me, most gracious God, to love you above all things, as you command and as is right; and then to love my neighbor no less than myself, as you again command. For [Note: [Col. 0919D] Vict. reads *est autem*, “but it is,” for *est enim*, “for it is”] it is most just and altogether reasonable that we should love you above all things, and even more than ourselves, because you loved us before we existed, creating us in love and caring to bring us, once created, to knowledge of your most holy name. We, however, do not have from ourselves even this very fact—that we love you or anything good—but have it from you.

You also rightly command us to love our neighbor as ourselves, and we do not rightly love him as you command, because you created all of us with equal love, assumed the passion for all with equal love, and prepared eternal life equally for all.

Grant to all, most merciful Father, who possess the right faith, to live rightly and holily and not to deviate in any way at all from what you command [Note: [Col. 0919D] Corb. reads *nec in nulla*, “and not in no [matter]”; Vict. reads *nec nulla*, “and no [matter]”; the text has *nec ulla*, “and not in any [matter]”]. But to those who do not yet believe in you, grant, before they depart from this life, to receive faith in and love for your most holy name, and, having received them, to preserve them right and inviolate to the end.

May the sacrifice of your body and blood be, for all the living and the dead, the remission of all sins: for the living, namely, those who live rightly and those who, if they do not yet live rightly, at least desire sometime to live rightly; and for the dead, those who hope through this sacrifice to receive from your mercy the remission of their iniquities and afterward to attain eternal glory and the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0920A]

We believe concerning you, Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0919D] The manuscripts read “We believe, Lord”; the text has “We believe concerning you, Lord”], that you are the very same person who is the Son of God and the Son of the Virgin; the very same person who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and through whom all things were made (John I, 1–3). Begotten by the Father before all ages [Note: [Col. 0919D] One manuscript reads “begotten before all things”; the text has “before all ages”], in time you were born of the Virgin. Although you are of a different nature from the Father [Note: [Col. 0919D] The manuscript of Vict. reads “a different person”], after you became the Son of the Virgin and dwelt among us, you existed with a different nature, according to which you are the Son of God; yet, in one person and in two natures, you exist as God and human being, equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity.

Because you are the very same God who is human and the very same human who is God, the most holy Virgin who bore you is proclaimed and believed by all the faithful to be Θεοτόκος—that is, “Mother of God” [Col. 0920B]. And because you are not one Son of God and another son of humanity, but are the very same Son of God who is the Son of humanity and who assumed suffering and death for the salvation of the human race—not in the nature of divinity, but in the nature of humanity—you are the very same person, not another on account of the distinction of natures, just as you are not one nature on account of the unity of person.

There is still something else that we can and ought to consider concerning the ineffable love with which you love us, and which you show to us wretched sinners as a sign of your great love in this mystery of your body and blood.

When one person loves another as much as possible, he may perhaps, because of the force of love, die for him if love demands it. Yet it rarely happens that anyone wishes to suffer this for someone he loves. If ever a friend does this for a friend, it turns all who hear of it to great wonder and astonishment [Note: [Col. 0919D] The manuscripts read “it turned”; the text has “it turns”].

But you, most sweet Lord Jesus, wished to die not only for friends but also for enemies. Not only this: you did what no one wishes to do for a friend, and you still do it—namely, when you give yourself, who endured death for us, to be eaten and drunk in this mystery of your body and blood. We eat your body and drink your blood, the price of our redemption.

Grant me, therefore, Lord Jesus, henceforth to live chastely [Note: [Col. 0919D] The manuscripts read *Domine Jesu, amodo sic vivere sic caste*, “Lord Jesus, henceforth thus to live, thus chastely”] and to perform the service of your altar holily, so that by thus living, thus acting, thus eating your flesh [Col. 0920D] and drinking your blood, I may, after the death of the flesh, absolved from all sins, reach you, my Creator and Redeemer, by the straight path. There may I praise and bless you without end, together with all the saints, in eternal happiness.

[Col. 0921A]

## PRAYER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0921C] Compared with the manuscripts Vict. KK. 16, Corb. 160, Carthus. a Porta, Val-luc., and Flor. Victorinus: “Of the priest who is about to celebrate.” Corb.: “A useful prayer to be said by the priest before Mass.” “Prayer of the priest before Mass.”]

### TO BE MADE BY THE PRIEST BEFORE MASS

Most High Priest and true Pontiff [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “Pontiff Jesus Christ”; the text omits “Jesus Christ”], who offered yourself to God the Father as a pure and spotless victim on the altar of the cross for us wretched sinners [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “for us wretched and sinful people”], and who gave us your flesh to eat and your blood to drink, and established this mystery by the power of your Spirit [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “of your Holy Spirit”], saying, “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 19).

I ask through your precious blood, the great price of our salvation [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “your great precious blood”]. I ask through that wondrous and indescribable love by which you deigned to love us wretched and unworthy people so greatly that you might wash us from our sins in your blood (Revelation I, 5). Teach me, your unworthy servant, whom you also deigned to call to the priestly office among your other gifts [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “among your gifts also,” omitting “other”], not because of any merits of mine but solely through the gracious favor of your mercy [Col. 0921B], teach me, I ask, through your Holy Spirit to handle so great a mystery with the reverence and honor, the devotion and fear that are necessary and fitting.

By your grace make me always believe and understand, perceive and firmly hold, say and think concerning so great a mystery whatever pleases you and benefits my soul. May your good Spirit enter my heart, sounding there without sound and speaking, without the noise of words, the whole truth of such great mysteries. For they are exceedingly profound [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “the truth: profound indeed”] and covered with a sacred veil.

Because of your great clemency, grant me to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass with a pure heart and clean mind. Free my heart from unclean and abominable, empty and harmful thoughts. Fortify me with the loving and faithful guardianship and strongest protection of the blessed angels [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscript of Carthus. reads “fortify me, I ask, with the…”], so that the enemies of every good may depart in confusion.

Through the power of so great a mystery and through the hand of your holy angel, drive away from me and from all your servants the most harsh spirit of pride and vainglory, envy and blasphemy, fornication and uncleanness, doubt and distrust. Let those who persecute us be confounded; let those perish who hasten to destroy everything [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “who hasten to destroy us”].

King of virgins, lover of chastity [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read *virginum et amator*, “of virgins and lover”; Corb. reads *castitatis et integritatis*, “of chastity and integrity”; the text omits *et integritatis*, “and integrity.”], O God, extinguish with the heavenly dew of your blessing in my body [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts of Corb. and Flor. read “from my body”; the manuscript of Vict. reads “in my heart”] the tinder of burning lust [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscript of Val-luc. reads “the whole tinder”; the manuscript of Flor. reads “the whole tinder-source”], so that the constancy of chastity of body and soul may remain in me [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts of Val-luc. and Flor. read “the constancy of complete chastity”].

Put to death in my members the goads of the flesh and every lustful stirring, and grant me true and perpetual chastity, together with the other gifts that truly please you, so that with a chaste body and pure heart I may be able daily to offer you the sacrifice of praise [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “with a pure heart may I be able”; the text has “with a pure heart daily may I be able”].

With how great a contrition of heart and fountain of tears, with how great reverence and trembling, with how great chastity of body and purity of soul must this divine and heavenly sacrifice be celebrated, Lord—where your flesh is truly received, where your blood is truly drunk, where the lowest things are joined to the highest [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read *terrena divinis*, “earthly things to divine things”], where the presence of the holy angels is present, where you are wondrously and ineffably both sacrifice and priest [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read *mirabiliter et ineffabiliter constitutus*, “wondrously and ineffably constituted”]?

[Col. 0922B]

Who can celebrate this worthily [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “who will be able to celebrate”; the text has “who can celebrate”], unless you, almighty God, make the one offering worthy? I know, Lord—I truly know—and I confess this to your goodness [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “to your compassion”] that I am not worthy to approach so great a mystery because of my excessive sins and my countless negligences.

But I know, and I truly believe with all my heart, and confess with my mouth, that you can make me worthy—you alone can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed (Job XIV, 4); you alone make the worthy from the unworthy, the clean from the unclean, and the just and holy from sinners [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read: “from seed; and from sinners…”; another reading is “you alone make the worthy from the unworthy, the clean from the unclean, and the just from sinners”]. By this omnipotence of yours I ask you [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read *te rogo, Deus meus, ut concedas*, “I ask you, my God, that you grant,” for *te rogo, concede*, “I ask you: grant”]: grant me, a sinner, to celebrate this heavenly sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “this sacrifice”] with fear and trembling, with purity of heart and a fountain of tears, with spiritual joy and heavenly gladness.

May my mind feel the sweetness of your most blessed presence and the watchful guardianship of your saints [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “of your holy angels”] around me.

For I [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts add *Domine*, “Lord”] , remembering your venerable passion, approach your altar, though a sinner, to offer you the sacrifice that you instituted and commanded to be offered in remembrance of you for our salvation (Luke XXII, 19). Receive it, therefore, I ask [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “receive it, I ask”], most high God, for your holy Church and for the people whom you acquired with your blood [Note: [Col. 0921C] The manuscripts read “for your people whom…”].

And since you wished me, a sinner, to stand between you and this people of yours, although you recognize in me no testimony of any good work [Col. 0923A], at least do not reject the ministry of the stewardship entrusted to me; nor, through me, though unworthy, let the price of their salvation perish, for those for whom you deigned to become a saving victim and redemption [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read *victima salutaris*, “a saving victim,” for *victima factus salutaris*, “having become a saving victim”].

Therefore I bring forward, Lord—if you deign to look upon them favorably—the tribulations of peoples, the dangers of nations, the groans of captives, the miseries of orphans, the needs of travelers, the poverty of the weak, the despair of the sick, the failings of the old, the sighs of the young, the vows of virgins, and the lamentations of widows.

For you have mercy on all, Lord, and hate nothing that you have made (Wisdom XI, 24–25). Remember what our substance is, because you are our Father, because you are our God. Do not be angry beyond measure, nor hold back from us the multitude of your mercies. For we do not cast down our prayers before your face on the basis of our righteousness [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “our prayers”; the text has “prayers”], but on the basis of your many mercies.

Take away our iniquities from us, Lord, and mercifully kindle in us the fire of the Holy Spirit. Take the heart of stone from our flesh and give us a heart of flesh (Ezekiel XI, 19), one that may fear you, love you, cherish you, delight in you, follow you, and enjoy you [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read *te timeat, te timet, te diligat*, “may fear you, fears you, may love you,” for *te timeat, te amet, te diligat*, “may fear you, love you, cherish you”; *et honorificet* (“and may honor you”) is omitted.]

We beseech your clemency, Lord, that you may deign to look with a serene face upon your household awaiting the duties of your holy name; and, so that no one’s vow may be fruitless and no one’s petition empty, suggest to us the prayers that you yourself may graciously desire to hear and answer [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “that you may deign to hear and answer”].

We also ask you, holy Father [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “Lord, holy Father”], for the souls [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “for the spirits”] of the faithful departed, that you may be for them salvation, healing, joy, and refreshment—this great sacrament of compassion [Col. 0923C].

My God [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “Lord, my God”], let there be for them today a great and complete banquet of you, the living bread who came down from heaven and give life to the world (John VI, 33); of your holy and blessed flesh, namely, that of the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John I, 29); of the flesh taken from the holy and glorious womb of the blessed Virgin Mary and conceived from the Holy Spirit; of that, I say, fountain of compassion [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “and of that fountain of compassion”], which flowed through the soldier’s lance from your most sacred side [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts of Corb., Val-luc., and Flor. read “from the side of our crucified Lord”], so that, refreshed and satisfied, cooled and comforted [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “and from then on refreshed, satisfied, cooled, and comforted”; the manuscript of Val-luc. reads “so that from then on, healed, cooled, refreshed, and comforted”; another manuscript has “so that from then on. The rest as in the printed edition”], they may rejoice in your praise and glory.

I ask your clemency, O God, that the fullness of your blessing and the sanctification of your divinity may descend upon it [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read *super panem tibi sacrificandum*, “upon the bread to be sacrificed to you”; the text has *super illud*, “upon it”]. May that invisible and incomprehensible majesty of your Holy Spirit also descend, as once it descended upon the sacrifices of the fathers. May it make our offerings your body and blood, and teach me, an unworthy priest, to handle so great a mystery with purity of heart and the devotion of tears, with reverence and trembling, so that you may graciously and kindly receive the sacrifice of praise [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “receive the sacrifice”; the text has “receive the sacrifice of praise”] from my hands for the salvation of all, both living and dead.

I ask you [Note: [Col. 0923C] At the opening “I also ask you, etc.,” the Corbie manuscript prefixes the heading “Prayer of the Priest before the Body and Blood of the Lord.” The manuscripts omit *etiam*, “also.”], Lord, by the very sacred mystery of your body and blood, by which we are daily nourished and given drink in your Church, washed and sanctified, and made participants in the one and supreme divinity [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read *unius summae*, “of the one supreme [divinity],” for *unius summaeque*, “of the one and supreme [divinity].”], grant me your holy virtues. Filled with them, may I approach your altar with a good conscience, so that these heavenly sacraments may become salvation and life for me.

For you said with your holy and blessed mouth: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts omit: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” The Carthusian manuscript adds: “And whoever eats me will himself live because of me, for he remains in me and I in him. And again: ‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven.’”]. “If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:52).

Most sweet bread, heal the palate of my heart, so that I may perceive the sweetness of your love. Heal it [Note: [Col. 0923C] The Carthusian manuscript reads “heal me”; the Val-luc manuscript, “heal him”] of every sickness, so that it may perceive no sweetness apart from you [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts of Corbie, Victor, and Val-luc read “so that I may perceive no sweetness apart from you”], seek no love apart from you, and love no beauty apart from you.

Most radiant bread [Note: [Col. 0923C] The Carthusian and Florus manuscripts read: “sweetness; may I seek no lover apart from you, nor love any beauty apart from you; most radiant bread”], possessing every delight and every flavor of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0923C] The Victor manuscript reads “every flavor”] (Wisdom 16:20), who always restore us and are never exhausted in yourself, may my heart eat you, and may the inmost parts of my soul be filled with the sweetness of your flavor. The angel eats you with full mouth; may the pilgrim human being eat you according to his measure, lest, refreshed by such a provision for the journey, he be unable to fail.

Holy bread, living bread, beautiful bread [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “living bread, pure bread”; another reading is “living bread, beautiful bread, pure bread”], pure bread, who came down from heaven and give life to the world, come into my heart and cleanse me from every pollution of flesh and spirit (2 Corinthians 7:1); enter my soul and sanctify me within [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “heal and cleanse me within”] and without. Be the protection and continual salvation of my soul and body. Drive away from me the enemies lying in wait for me; let them withdraw far from the presence of your power [Note: [Col. 0923C] The Victor manuscript reads “the presence of your majesty and power”], so that, defended by you within and without [Note: [Col. 0923C] The manuscripts read “defended within and without by you”], I may reach your kingdom by the straight path, where we shall see you face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12), not in mysteries, as is done at this time, when you will have handed over the kingdom to God the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24), and God will be all in all (ibid., 28) [Note: [Col. 0925D] The Carthusian manuscript reads: “I may reach the kingdom, where we shall see you face to face, not in mysteries, as is done at this time, when you will have handed over the kingdom, etc.” It also reads: “I may reach the kingdom, where I may see you face to face. Meanwhile, you commended to the Church that this be done, indeed be frequently observed, until you come at the end of the age; that will be the saints’ rest, now still in the sacrament in which your members are joined in this time, as long as that which flowed from your side is drunk. This will be in the very perfection of eternal salvation, when you will have handed over the kingdom to God and Father, so that in that clear contemplation of your unchangeable truth we need no mysteries: for then you will satisfy me, etc.”].

Then you will satisfy me with marvelous satisfaction from you, so that I shall neither hunger nor thirst forever [Note: [Col. 0925D] “Forever. You who, with the same God the Father and the Holy Spirit, live and reign forever and ever. Amen.” The manuscripts read: “Forever. Amen. Nor shall I thirst forever, you who, with the same God the Father…” The Val-luc manuscript reads: “Nor shall I thirst forever. Amen.”].

### 269. Prayer XXX. For a Priest Who Is to Celebrate

The duty of ministry urges me, Lord God, to offer saving sacrifices for the people’s offense; conscience concerning an unworthy priesthood terrifies me because of my own guilt. If sacrifice is offered by me, the offscouring of all priests, the crime of polluted conscience is increased; yet [if] it is not offered to the majesty of the Judge of all flesh, the guilt of negligence is imputed. [The second conditional “if” is supplied from the parallel sense; the source prints only “yet … is not offered.”]

Amid these things I implore the balance of your mercy, almighty God. I dread the day of your vengeance, with conscience accusing me, lest you judge unworthy of your mercy one whom you do not exclude from the time of repentance. Suspend, Lord, the axe until the cultivator of the vineyard, the Holy Spirit, brings a basket of manure to the root of the barren tree.

Spare me, Lord; spare me, most merciful one, who kindly recalled David to pardon after his fall; who, merciful toward Peter, looked upon the tears of one weeping bitterly; who illumined by divine grace the thief guilty of so great a crime, to whom confession immediately obtained the vision of the Son of God, faith obtained a reward, punishment obtained pardon, and lamentation obtained everlasting joy—while, after the cross, he who confessed on the cross became its possessor [i.e., of paradise].

But because my words need the forgiveness of your mercy, and the works of an unworthy priest do not commend them, at least receive the prayers of those standing here, so that by their prayers before you I may obtain pardon, and by their merits the sacrifices for our wounds may beneficially confer medicine upon us.

And because, almighty God, you became a victim for all of us on account of sins, be our satisfaction in the sacrifice for offenses, you who live and reign, etc.

### Prayer XXXI. For a Priest Who Is About to Celebrate

Although trembling in conscience, almighty God, I approach your altar; yet I am held by confidence in the mercy of your kindness. And although I am always found unworthy to celebrate sacrifices for you, nevertheless, if I withdraw, I fear being condemned for disobedience.

For this reason deign, most loving Father, to look upon me with fatherly kindness and a reconciled countenance, and meanwhile cleanse the mouths of my heart. And if I am constrained by the weight of my sins and by guilt, nevertheless, through the favor of my prayers, may the mysteries to be consecrated be pleasing to you in all things, I ask, Lord. Through our Lord, etc.

### [Col. 0926A]

### Prayer XXXII. For the Same Purpose

With a guilty conscience, trembling and anxious in life, taken captive by the cords of crimes, I beseech you, Lord, my only refuge and singular remedy for the wretched: have mercy on me, your unworthy priest, and forgive me because I presume to consecrate with sinful lips and to handle with polluted hands that saving sacrament which is feared and adored by angels, archangels, and all the heavenly powers.

But as I approach by myself, I confess, Lord, I presume upon you, remembering my evils and your goods that have existed from eternity. Again, Lord, I presume to ask you that your most holy sacrifice may be neither for judgment nor for condemnation to me, but rather for the liberation of my sins and distresses, and for the perpetual salvation of my soul.

I repeat this same petition, Lord God, not with an arrogant presumption, as you yourself see, but with a prostrate and fearful presumption, because, wretched and unclean, I dare to consecrate the sacrament of your holy flesh and precious blood with unclean hands.

I humbly entreat and beseech you, Lord: look upon your ministry and have mercy on me, your wretched minister; purify the sacrificer and sanctify the sacrifice. God the Father, hear me. Whatever is in me against me, mercifully remove from me. Make me fit for your holy service, make me an able minister for you, and grant that I may ask, amid these holy mysteries, for whatever is pleasing to you; and whatever I ask, may I receive from your most gracious mercy, I beg, Lord.

To you be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

### Prayer XXXIII. For the Same Purpose

If we think only of the guilt of our transgression, we do not fulfill the ministry entrusted to us. For it is grievous that we do not come to your table with a pure heart and innocent hands; but it is more grievous if, while we fear our sins, we also fail to offer the sacrifice.

Therefore, let it be permitted to stand here on account of disobedience, to ask for forgiveness, to minister on account of duty, to sacrifice for healing, and to intercede for the people. I ask you, therefore: strengthen in me what trembles, heal what is weary, reconcile what is at odds, empty what corrupts, and humble what is proud.

Let your just judgment be merciful correction; let it never swallow up the sinner, but rather reconcile the penitent. Give discipline for salvation, not a sentence for death. Hear the prayer of the sinner—you who visit one groaning in sorrow. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

### [Col. 0927A]

### 270. Prayer XXXIV [Note: [Col. 0927D] Compared with manuscripts Thu. 267 and Bec. O. The manuscripts title it “Prayer before receiving the Body and Blood of Christ”; “Prayer for receiving the Lord’s Body.”] To Christ: Before Receiving the Body and Blood of Christ

Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the Father’s ordering and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, by your voluntary death mercifully redeemed the world from sin and eternal death, I adore and venerate, as far as I can—with however lukewarm an affection and humble a devotion—giving thanks for so great a benefit, this holy body and this blood of yours [Note: [Col. 0927D] The manuscripts read “your holy Body and your blood”; “this holy Body and this holy blood”], which I desire to receive for cleansing and defense against sins.

I confess, Lord, that I am exceedingly sinful (Luke 5:8) and unworthy to approach their touch. But trusting in that mercy by which, for sinners to become righteous, you laid down your soul and gave it, and willed to be slain as a devoted sacrifice to the Father, I, though a sinner, presume to receive them, so that through them I may be justified.

Therefore I humbly beseech you, compassionate lover of humankind: let what you gave for the wiping away of sins be for me not an increase of sins, but forgiveness and protection.

Make me receive them with mouth and heart, and perceive them by faith and affection, in such a way that through their power I may be deemed worthy to be grafted into the likeness of your death and resurrection, through the mortification of the old human being and the renewal of a just life; so that I may be worthy to be incorporated into your body, which is the Church, and may be your member, with you as my head; and may I remain in you and you in me, so that at the resurrection you may reform the body of my lowliness, conforming it to the body of your glory, according to the promise of your Apostle (Philippians 3:21), and may I rejoice forever in you in your glory, you who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

### Prayer XXXV. To Christ: Before Receiving the Body of Christ

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who, by the Father’s will and with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, gave life to the world through your death, I adore and venerate this holy body of yours and this blood of yours, which was handed over and poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28).

I beseech your mercy, most merciful Lord: through their power, make me one of those many, and make me perceive this through faith and affection in such a way that I may perceive it through the effect of salvation.

Absolve and free your male and female servants—me and all who have confessed their sins to me, for whom I have promised or am bound to pray, and those who hope or ask to be helped before you by my prayers—from every sin and from the punishment of sin. And make your Church rejoice through your continual protection and consolation.

### Prayer XXXVI. To God and All the Saints

Almighty, eternal, ineffable Lord God, without end or beginning, whom we confess as one in Trinity and triune in unity: you alone I adore as God; you I praise, you I bless, and you I glorify. I give you thanks; I entrust myself wholly to you in devotion. Attend to the voice of my prayer (Psalm 5:3), Father, God from heaven, my King and my God.

Son, Redeemer of the world, God, have mercy on me; do not destroy me with my iniquities (Psalm 25:9), nor in anger reserve my evils for the end.

Holy Spirit, kindly God, breathe into me the breath of your grace and direct me in the way of eternal salvation. Teach me to do your will (Psalm 142:10). Whatever displeases you in me, remove from me.

Triune and one, almighty, kind and merciful Lord, look upon me (Psalm 118:132), turn my tribulation into joy, and, O Most High, do not give your inheritance over to destruction (Joel 2:17).

Ruler of all and protector of those who hope in you, Lord, receive my prayer. Through the intercessions of the glorious virgin Mary, take your anger away from me (Psalm 84:5), Lord God of my salvation, and do not receive my soul from my body before you have forgiven all my sins.

O glorious Mother of God, mother of mercy, ever-virgin Mary, who were worthy to bear the Lord of all and, as a virgin alone, to nurse the King of angels, help me in the day of my tribulation, so that, supported by your patronage, I may be worthy to reach the heavenly kingdoms.

O holy Michael, archangel of God, guardian of paradise, come to my aid and defend me from the evil enemy at the hour of my death; lead my soul into the paradise of eternal joy.

All holy angels and archangels of God, all the powers of heaven and all the orders of holy spirits, restrain the forces of hostile damnation; overcome those who attack me (Psalm 34:1); powerfully defend me from the savagery of the roaring enemy; guard me at every hour, day and night, as I faithfully walk in the way of truth; and at the hour of my departure receive my soul in peace with yourselves.

Holy John the Baptist, all holy patriarchs and prophets, I beseech you with an obligated prayer: extend your hand to me; offer me help in all my needs and weaknesses. Ask God for me forbearance, patience, perseverance, justice, obedience, self-control, and holy steadfastness.

### [Col. 0928D]

Holy Peter, most blessed prince of the apostles, and all holy apostles and evangelists, princes of the Churches and triumphant soldiers of the heavenly court, grant me an honorable life, greatness of virtues, a praiseworthy completion, and eternal blessedness. Through you, may peace, virtue, and perpetual salvation flow to me.

### 271.

Most sweet priests of Christ, renowned teachers, and all holy confessors, who increased the talent entrusted to you through the unfading fruit of good works, may God’s ineffable mercy grant me through you forgiveness of sins, an abundance of every good, desire for heavenly things, grateful goodwill among brothers, reverence in conduct, and observance of God’s commandments.

I beseech you, blessed N., with most devoted prayer: deign to acknowledge me among your own when, powerful in judgment, you sit with the Lord to judge the world.

All holy virgins, who, clinging with perpetual devotion to the heavenly Bridegroom, trampled the luxury of the world, and all holy widows, obtain for me, foul as I am, the gift of perpetual grace, holiness of life, purity of body, innocence of heart, steadfastness of faith, and the charity of brotherhood.

Intercede for me, all saints, whoever pleased God from the beginning of the world. Fit me to carry out God’s will in every good work, so that, dead to sins, I may live for God; and, with your merits assisting, may I fulfill with complete affection the vows I have made to God, so that I may be worthy to reach the harbor of eternal salvation and rejoice with you without end in eternal happiness. Amen.

### Prayer XXXVII. To God

*(From the Corbie manuscript.)*

Most gracious Lord Jesus, fountain of life, fountain of mercy, from whom all the saints drink, drinking and becoming intoxicated with ineffable sweetness, living in eternal satisfaction: grant me, through their merits, so to thirst for you always in this present life that in the age to come I may be able to be eternally satisfied with you together with those same saints.

Therefore I pray your sweetest mercy, most loving and gracious Lord Jesus: feed my wretched soul with remembrance of your benefits, lest it fail, wearied on its pilgrimage by the great burden of its sins.

Your goodness created me, Lord, and restored me through your baptism; until now it has patiently awaited me, sinning daily. The power of your divinity made me; the humility of your humanity restored me.

Behold, Lord Jesus Christ, by your grace, you who are my Lord and my God: behold, I remember that, as you foretold through your saints from the beginning of the world, born of the holy Virgin you truly received flesh from her, and truly sucked the breasts of your virgin mother. Feed my sinful soul with your holy flesh; satisfy it with your sweetness.

Placed in a manger and wrapped in swaddling clothes, wrap my soul in the swaddling clothes of your mercy, lest it remain naked before you. Shepherds and Magi coming from the East adored you lying in the manger; make me, Lord, faithfully adore you now seated in heaven.

You permitted your flesh to be circumcised; circumcise my mind from every sin. You were presented in the temple, and Simeon received you in his arms—that is, in his embrace. Present me to your holy majesty, so that I may embrace you with the arms of my soul.

You were subject to your parents in your purity; make me subject to you and to all to whom your ordering subjects me. You were baptized by John; in infancy you baptized me. After your baptism I have often been polluted; baptize me through true confession and repentance.

You commanded sinners to do penance and promised forgiveness to those who repent worthily. Make me repent for my sins in such a way that I may deserve to obtain their pardon from you.

You taught truth, gentleness, and justice; teach and enlighten my heart, so that I may deserve to be one of those whom you taught and inwardly illumined.

You performed miracles, mighty deeds, and healings in the bodies and souls of human beings, as much as pleased you. Heal the sicknesses of my soul, because I have sinned against you.

You fasted for my sake; make me abstain from every sin for love of you. You hungered for my sake; make me truly hunger for you, who are the true bread. You grew weary for my sake; strengthen me and restore the weariness of my soul.

Most sweet and merciful Lord Jesus Christ, while you were dining with your friends, you washed their feet and fed them with your body and blood. Wash my body and soul from every defilement, and strengthen me with that same body and blood of yours, lest I fail.

What more shall I say, Lord Jesus Christ? You are my life, my salvation, my sweetness, my strength, my gladness, my joy, my redemption, and my resurrection.

You were handed over for my sake; do not hand my soul over to beasts. You were bound for my sake; loose the bonds of my sins. You were mocked for my sake; free me from the mockeries of demons.

Most sweet Lord, you alone, a human being without sin, were scourged for my sake; free me from the scourges deserved by my iniquities. Most merciful Lord, you were crowned with thorns for my sake; take away from me the thorns of my sins.

Most gracious Lord Jesus, you carried your cross upon your holy shoulders; make me follow you and carry my soul after you. Most high Lord, exalted upon the cross, you drew all things to yourself; draw me to yourself.

Most sweet Lord, you permitted your hands and feet to be pierced by iron nails, your side to be opened by a lance, and your blood to be poured out for sinners. Through that blood of yours wash my soul from all sins, and remove every pain from it through the anguish you endured for us.

Most sweet Lord, you received the thief’s petition; receive the prayer of me, a sinner. You were given vinegar to drink for my sake; intoxicate my soul with the honey of your sweetness.

Good Shepherd, you laid down your soul for your sheep; do not allow my sinful soul to perish and die. You freed the souls of the devout from hell; free my soul from the condemnation of the impious.

Most mighty and powerful Lord Jesus Christ, after you conquered death, rising from the dead alive and immortal, you appeared to your disciples. You gladdened them, sorrowing over your death, and, eating and drinking frequently with them, strengthened their hearts in faith in your holy resurrection. Gladden and strengthen my soul, the soul of your servant, in faith in your holy resurrection.

### Prayer XXXVIII. To Christ

*(From the Corbie manuscript.)*

Most sweet, most gracious, most beautiful, most lovely, most desired Lord Jesus Christ, my Lord and my God, after your resurrection, on the fortieth day, in the sight of your most holy mother, the Virgin, who rejoiced ineffably, and in the sight of your friends the apostles, who rejoiced ineffably in your glorification, you blessed them, ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father.

Bless us also and make us participants in so great a rejoicing as they had in the glory of your exaltation. Through these benefits of yours, and through the countless others by which you recalled fallen humanity to salvation, refresh and strengthen my wretched soul while I remain detained in this life, so that, when it has departed from the body, nourished and refreshed by such pious recollections and memories, it may, under the wings of your mercy, at the feet of your holy apostles, at the feet of your most glorious witness Stephen, and at the feet of your other children who are with you in your holy chamber, rest—through your mercy and your gift, Savior of the world, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign as God forever and ever. Amen.

### Prayer XXXIX. To Christ and All the Saints

*(From the Corbie manuscript.)*

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, my Lord and my God, you are my life and my salvation, without whom I cannot live well or be well; for even before I existed and lived, I was with you and lived in you, and before I knew myself, you knew me.

Most gracious, most pleasant, most sweet Lord, make me remember the mercies that you mercifully bestowed upon the human race; make my heart, through remembrance of them, continually burn and blaze with the fire of your love.

Most powerful Lord, you first formed me in my mother’s womb; by your power I was born of my mother, and you sanctified me through your baptism. You inspired my parents to give me over to the study of letters and to the fellowship of monks, and you gave me an aptitude for learning letters, as much as pleased you, though I was ungrateful.

You have patiently awaited me until now, though I sin daily. I beg and beseech your most gracious mercy, most benign Lord: never allow me to return to the former filth of my sins, but make me persevere with your servants in your service.

I know, Lord, that I am not worthy to be heard because of my sins; but grant me the consolation and intercession of your saints, whom I dare to call upon before you, so that what I do not deserve because my sins oppose me, I may obtain with their merits assisting, and so that you may not exclude me from their fellowship.

All you saints, children of mercy, children of the Lord Savior, now resting with him in eternal rest, whom charity itself has begotten from its own depths: I, a sinner, call upon you. Raise my prayer to the ears of your mother, the highest charity.

First, I dare humbly to pray to you, who are nearer to our salvation, who gave birth to our life and brought a remedy to the lost world, blessed among women, virgin mother of mercy herself, holy Mary, Lady of the world, Queen of heaven. I entrust my prayer, whatever it may be, to your most holy kindness, so that you may offer it to your beloved Son, our Lord.

You also, holy angels and archangels—holy Michael, holy Raphael, holy Gabriel—and all the holy orders of the heavenly powers, I presume to call upon you to raise my prayers to God.

All you holy patriarchs and prophets, who came before and announced the coming of our Savior, be helpers to my prayers.

Holy John, Baptist of the Lord, friend of the supreme Bridegroom, be a helper to my prayers.

Holy Peter, to whom the supreme Shepherd entrusted the feeding of his lambs. Holy Paul, chosen vessel of the Lord Jesus Christ, teacher of the nations. Holy Andrew, holy James, holy James, holy John, beloved of the Lord Jesus, holy Thomas, holy Philip, holy Bartholomew, holy Matthew, holy Simon, holy Thaddeus, holy Matthias, holy Mark, holy Luke, holy Barnabas.

All holy apostles and evangelists, pray for me, a sinner; I entrust my prayers to your merits.

Holy Stephen, first martyr of our Lord Jesus Christ, friend of God, I commend myself to your merits.

Holy martyrs Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John, Paul, Cosmas, Damian, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Vincent, Sebastian, and all martyrs who shed your blood for love of the Savior, pray for us.

Holy Vedast, Remigius, Benedict, Martin, Ambrose, Augustine, Hilary, Basil, Nicholas, Amandus, Gregory, Germanus, and all holy confessors who pleased God through the holiness of your lives, pray for us.

Holy Mary Magdalene, who were worthy to touch the feet of the Lord Savior by kissing them, to bathe them with tears, and to see him risen from the dead first; holy Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Agnes, Cecilia, Lucia, Anastasia, and all holy virgins, widows, and continent women, pray for us.

### Prayer XL [Note: [Col. 0931D] Compared with manuscripts Corbie 160 and Victor KK 16]. Hymn to God and All the Saints

God the Father of believers,

salvation of those who hope in you,

hear the prayers of your little servant,

which he pours out with a suppliant heart.

Most holy Son of God,

who deigned to be born of a Virgin,

hear the sacrifice of my heart,

seated at the Father’s right hand.

Holy Spirit of them both,

finger of God’s right hand,

visit the secret place of my mind [Note: [Col. 0931D] The Corbie manuscript reads “the secret places of the mind”; the Victor manuscript, “the secret place of the mind”]

and fill it with your grace.

Holy Trinity in persons,

but Unity in divinity,

be present to my prayers,

favoring my suppliant vows.

Increase faith, O Trinity;

increase hope, holy Unity,

so that your charity, O God,

may strengthen me in worshiping you.

You who are called God-human

and are known as true human,

remember me, a human being,

when you come to judge.

In that which remains divinity,

erase the burdens of my guilt,

so that in that which is humanity

your mercy may bend toward me [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads “may still bend”; the Victor manuscript reads “may bend toward me”].

You swore the kingdom to the Fathers;

you promised it to your followers.

So that the promise may be kept,

grant the kingdom to your servant.

May your mercy grant

what humanity asks [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads “humanity”; the Victor manuscript, “humility”],

so that what charity promised,

the heir may obtain.

Mary, virgin of virgins,

door of redemption,

unbroken gate of salvation,

lift up the neck of the fallen.

Extend your hand to the powerful [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads “to the powerful”; the Victor manuscript, “to the one asking”],

grant the help of rest,

and through your assistance

strive to appease your Son.

Queen of heaven, daughter [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads “daughter”; the Victor manuscript, “Lady”],

most chaste Mother of God,

help, so that the hand of your Son
may grant what the servant asks.

You, Michael the archangel,

prince of the heavenly army,

shake the dragon’s jaws,

lest he harm me in my wound.

Gabriel, interpreter of God,

and Raphael, healer,

together with cherubim and seraphim,

destroy the enemy’s heresy.

All spirits of heaven,

divided into nine ranks,

present before the face of God,

favor my words.

Twenty-four elders,

offer these things that I ask,

you who pour out prayers

with lyres and bowls.

O dignity of the patriarchs,

O sublimity of the prophets,



before the presence of your King,

utter [the prayer] at the petitioner’s word [Note: [Col. 0933] Corbie has *verbo peccantis*, “at the sinner’s word”; Victor has *verba peccantis*, “the sinner’s words,” an accusative object for “utter.” The printed *verbo precantis* is “at the petitioner’s word,” and its construction is irregular].

John, forerunner of Christ,

renowned Baptist of the King,

hasten; do not delay

to cut away the stain of the wound.

Him whom, enclosed in your mother’s womb,

you reveal by bodily movement,

whom you indicated with your finger,

make him come to the aid of the wretched.

Key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom,

standard-bearer of the apostles,

Peter, first in rank,

look upon human frailty.

Through you may your mind see

what the human lot is worth;

and while you remember your own,
