remember the condition of humanity.

When you ask for mercy,

may he extend his right hand to me,

he who held you up upon the waters

when he said to you, “O you of little faith.”

[Loose] the bonds of guilt,

with the power given for this purpose,

you who call him the Word of God,

by whom you are called Bar-Jonah.



[The supplied *Salve*, “Hail,” gives a disrupted construction with “bonds”; “Loose” tentatively reads *Solve*.]

Paul, teacher of the nations

and witness of Christ,

while you preach throughout the whole world,

strive to bring help.

John, by the grace of God,

subtle like an eagle,

satisfy me from that very fountain

whose streams you drank.

He who joined his mother to you

and opens the closed gates of heaven,

may spare my misery

through the gift of your prayer.

The rest of the apostles,

the other evangelists,

the hosts of disciples,

help these prayers.

You innocent children,

who are slaughtered for Christ,

give your assistance,

you who cry, “Avenge us.”

And first martyr Stephen,

you first in the struggle,

heir of the sacred name,

be present to my desires.

You bare your head to the stones;

the entrance to heaven lies open.

You behold Jesus standing;

secure, you endure your enemies.

You prayed on bended knees,

bowed down for your enemies.

For the suppliant servant

intercede, I beg you.

You, most unconquered martyr,

[lacuna]

be gracious to the servant [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads: “You, unconquered martyr, be gracious”; the Victor manuscript reads: “You, unconquered martyr, Albanus, most gentle man, be gracious”]

who earnestly beseeches you.

You who thirsted for martyrdom,

dried up the river by prayer,

seeking the heavenly kingdoms

by a capital sentence,

dissolve the bonds of crimes,

through Jesus Christ the Lord,

so that with you among the heavenly

I may be joined to the company of the saints.

Vincent, renowned martyr,

your blood made the coals blossom,

holding heaven as your reward,

strive to pray for me.

Lawrence, steadfast soldier,

piously obstinate in faith,

you who serve in the fire,

strive to pray for me.

Assembly of all martyrs,

spurning concern for your bodies [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads “perceiving”; the Victor manuscript has “supnentes,” apparently to be read “serpentes”],

for whom you shed your blood,

render him propitious.

Admirable Sylvester,

noble in confession,

made head of the Church,

look upon my prayer.

Placed in Peter’s seat,

indeed his vicar,

sharing his glory,

rejoicing at heaven’s summit,

attend to my sighs,

helping through your prayers,

you who multiply the talent

so as to please your King.

Gregory, excellent bishop,

flower of the whole Church,

lampstand of God’s house,

ask the Lord to spare.

Martin, star of Gaul,

burning with the gift of virtues,

whom you rule [lacuna]

make the Lord come to his aid [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads “Make the king”; the Victor manuscript, “make the king’s catechumen”].

Priestly confession,

prayer of confessors,

offer to the sight of the supreme King

the servant’s prayers [Note: [Col. 0933] The Corbie manuscript reads “of the servant”; the Victor manuscript, “of the little servant”].

Truly happy Felicity,

who, first among the others,

because of the merit of charity,

hold this privilege:

when you behold Christ in your mind,

you despise all earthly things.

Help us before him

in whose glory you rejoice.

O Mary Magdalene,

hasten to offer help

to the one to whom Christ first appeared

when he overcame death.

Simple dove in spirit,

be present to the one praying, I beseech you,

you who seek the embrace of the Lord,

the crown of martyrdom.

All consecrated virgins,

carrying lamps for the Bridegroom,

holding oil in vessels,

seek my welfare.

Holy assembly of holy ones,

one communion,

come to my aid,

and intercede with Christ for me.

Be favorable, Christ,

behold the sighs I pour out.

Free from every evil

the one whom your right hand created.

You who wished to be born,

to die, to rise,

to ascend into heaven,

and who send the Holy Spirit,

cleanse me from the filth of sins.

When you come as Judge of the world

to give reward to your servants,

place me with the sheep at your right hand,

not with the goats.

Prepare bread for the Church;

protect it by governing it.

Although it is partly divided,

in the end it is believed to be one.

Deign always to govern

the lord of the Roman see

and the flock subject to him,

whom you redeemed with your blood.

Preserve the bishop of this place,

steadfast in your faith,

for your people,

armed with the shield of the cross.

For the souls of the faithful

who lack this light,

prepare eternal rest

for the perpetual praise of you.

Most gentle Lamb of God,

who cleanse the world from crime,

hear, spare, help,

have mercy, and free.

Christ, way, light, truth,

splendor and charity of God,

*Sōtēr* [Greek: “Savior”] and *ousion* [Greek: “being, essence”],

Alpha and Omega, *eleyson* [Greek: “have mercy”]. Amen.

### Prayer XLI [Note: [Col. 0935C] Compared with manuscripts Thu. 267, Corbie 160, Victor KK 16, Bec. O, Saint-Germain-des-Prés 345, Val-luc, and Flor. The manuscripts Thu. and Corbie title it “For adoring the holy cross”; Victor, Val-luc, and Flor.: “Prayer for adoring the holy cross”; Bec. and Saint-Germain: “Prayer concerning the Holy Cross.”] To the Lord’s Cross
Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 0935C] “Holy Cross,” according to the Thuane manuscript; “O holy Cross,” according to another], through which that cross is recalled to our minds on which our Lord Jesus Christ, by his death, raised us from the eternal death toward which we were all miserably hastening [Note: [Col. 0935C] “On which we were all hastening,” in the manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Val-luc, and Florence; “toward which we were all hastening,” in the text], to eternal life [Note: [Col. 0935C] The manuscripts read “life”], which we had lost by sinning [Note: [Col. 0935C] “And the mercy,” which the manuscripts omit], I adore, venerate, and glorify in you that cross which you represent to us, and in it that same most merciful Lord of ours, together with what he mercifully accomplished through it. O lovable cross, in which are our salvation, life, and resurrection! O precious wood, through which we have been saved and liberated! O venerable sign, through which we have been marked as belonging to God! O glorious cross, in which alone we ought to glory!

[Col. 0935B]

[Note: [Col. 0935C] The Saint-Germain manuscript omits the passage from “For you are not …” through “How, then …”]

For you are not to be understood according to the utterly foolish impiety of the cruel men who prepared you for the most gentle one [Note: [Col. 0935C] The manuscripts read “prepared you for the most gentle Lamb”; they omit “Lamb”], but according to the most wise piety of the one who willingly accepted you. For they could do nothing except with his wise permission; nor did he endure anything except by his merciful will. They chose you in order through you to perpetrate the crime of their impiety; he chose you in order through you to complete the work of his piety. They chose you in order through you to hand over the just man to death; he chose you in order through you to rescue sinners from death. They chose you in order to kill life; he chose you in order to destroy death. They chose you in order to condemn the Savior; he chose you in order to save the condemned. They chose you in order to put to death the one who gives life; he chose you in order to give life to the dead. They acted foolishly and cruelly; [Col. 0936A] he acted wisely and mercifully. Therefore, O wondrous cross [Note: [Col. 0935C] “O holy cross,” in the manuscripts; they omit “O holy cross”], you are not to be judged according to the intention of cruel folly, but according to the effect of merciful wisdom.

How, then, shall I praise you [Note: [Col. 0935C] The manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Val-luc, and Florence omit “cross”]? In what manner shall I exalt you? With what affection shall I pray to you? With what joy shall I glory in you? Through you hell is despoiled and shut against all those redeemed through you. Through you the demons are terrified, restrained, conquered, and trampled underfoot. Through you the world is renewed and adorned, with truth shining in it and justice reigning. Through you sinful human nature has been justified, the condemned has been saved, the slave of sin and Tartarus has been liberated, and the dead has been raised. Through you that blessed city in heaven is restored and perfected. Through you God the Son of God willed to be obedient to the Father for us unto death (Philippians II, 8, 9); [Col. 0936B] therefore, having been exalted, he received the name that is above every name. Through you he prepared his throne (Psalm IX, 8) and restored his kingdom.

O cross, chosen and prepared for such ineffable blessings, not so much the human or angelic mind and tongue as the works accomplished through you praise and exalt you! O you in whom and through whom are my salvation and life! O you in whom and through whom is all and every good of mine [Note: [Col. 0935C] The manuscript of Saint-Germain omits “of mine”], far be it from me to glory except in you! (Galatians VI, 14.) For what benefit is it to me to be conceived, born, live, and enjoy all the goods of this life [Note: [Col. 0935C] The manuscripts omit “is it beneficial”; the Thuane manuscript reads “to enjoy would have been beneficial”], and afterward descend into hell? Certainly, if that were my lot, it would have been better for me never to have been conceived. [Col. 0936C] And that would indeed be my condition if I had not been redeemed through you.

[Col. 0937A]

With what affection, then, shall I glory in you, without whom [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscripts have sine quo (“without which”) for sine qua (“without whom”)] I would have had not only no glory, but infernal mourning [Note: [Col. 0937C] Saint-Germain reads “infernal torment and mourning”; it has aeterna me for aeterne me, “would possess me eternally”] and misery would have possessed me eternally? With what delight [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscripts read “with what love”; another reads “with what delight”] shall I rejoice in you, through whom, instead of slavery to Tartarus, the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven has been given to me? With what joy shall I rejoice in you, without whom I would have been destined to dread even existing for a moment, and through whom I hope that I shall rejoice in being well forever? For although I still serve God between hope and fear, I am nevertheless certain that, if by giving thanks, loving, and living I glory in you [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscripts read the present in te glorior (“I glory in you”) for the future in te gloriabor (“I shall glory in you”)], I shall reach these blessings through you.

Let my glory, then, be through you and in you; let my true hope be through you and in you. Through you may my sins be blotted out; through you may my soul be put to death with respect to its former life and raised to a new life of righteousness. I ask you: grant, grant that just as in baptism you cleansed me from the sins in which I was conceived and born, so you may cleanse me anew from those which I contracted after I was reborn, so that through you I may reach those blessings for which humanity was created. May this be granted by that same Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever. Amen.

## PRAYER XLII

[Note: [Col. 0937C] This prayer was collated with the manuscript of Saint-Germain 345.] TO THE HOLY CROSS. Reinserted here from the Appendix of Gerberon.

Hail, most glorious cross, most precious and most splendid of all woods, sanctified by the touch of our Creator and stained with his most precious blood. You remain blessed, and shall remain so forever. Although you did not arise from the soil of paradise [Col. 0937C], nor through the beauty of your own foliage, nor through the loveliness of your leaves [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “through the loveliness of your flowers”], nor almost through the dignity of your fruit, yet you were honored by the most chaste limbs of the eternal King, which you sustained while he redeemed the whole world. Now not only does your power shine, but your name also is most precious to the whole world [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “your name is precious”]. You gleam over earth and ether, fill the world, and illuminate hell [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript omits this passage]. The angelic powers marvel at you; the rulers of the world adore you; the servants of demons fear you. [Col. 0938A] You restore what has been lost, preserve what has been restored, sanctify what has been consecrated, repair what has been destroyed, strengthen the weak and broken [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “strengthen the weak and shattered”; another reads “heal the weak”], gladden the sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “the things that are to be mourned”], and save those injured by demonic arts. [Note: [Col. 0937C] After “save,” the manuscript reads: “you give life to the dead and build all good things. At …”]

At your presence hell groans, the demons tremble and flee, death quakes, and every hostile power, hearing your holy name, fears [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “the demon flees, death is terrified, and every…”; another reads “the hostile power fears to hear you”]. For just as the mighty deeds of Jesus Christ, who is the living victim [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “who hung upon you”], are preeminent, great, and incomprehensible [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “remain great and incomprehensible”], so no mortal tongue can ever express your praise and power [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “no mortal tongue”]. For in you is Christ, your sweetest fruit, himself your most beautiful flower, your most fragrant scent, your most precious adornment. Sweet wood, sweet fruit, sweet burden. Blessed are you: alone you bore the weight of the world. Therefore there is no purchase-price in you [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript omits the passage beginning “Therefore there is no purchase-price in you” and ending “Therefore”], no price for you, no valuation above you. Compared with you, gold is straw, gems are ashes, and every glory is dung. The sun and clouds, moon and stars, and all things that pass away are not equal to you. The four regions of the world do not bear so blessed a tree in root, fruit, leaf, flower, and holy shoot.

Therefore I, your useless servant [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “we, your useless servants”], singing, groaning, and lamenting [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript omits “and lamenting”], prostrate myself before your presence [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “we prostrate our prayers before”], and pray to you [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “and we adore you”] and confess to you [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript omits “and confess”], venerable cross, through whose wood I have been redeemed [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “we have been redeemed”], whose sign has confirmed me, whose banner has fortified me, whose name has defended me, [Col. 0938C] and by whose power I have been saved until now. I adore you, invoke you, and implore you [Note: [Col. 0937C] The note records sum firmatus (“I have been strengthened”) … sum munitus (“fortified”) … sum defensus (“defended”) … salvatus (“saved”) …; the manuscript instead has plural forms throughout: “we have been strengthened … fortified … defended and protected … saved … we adore, invoke, and implore you”]. You are my salvation [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “May you be salvation”], my strength, my protection, my wall [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “our unconquerable wall”], my defense [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “our defense”], my joy [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “our joy”], and my consolation [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “our consolation”]. Save me, placed in this life; revive me in distress [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “our light, way, life, unconquerable weapon, liberation, redemption, and resurrection. Save us who are placed in the span of this life, in distress…”]; strengthen me in adversity; fortify me in weakness; at death free me from demons; withdraw me from eternal death [Note: [Col. 0937C] The manuscript reads “from everlasting death”; another reads “At death free us from demons; rescue us from death”]. Open the gate of paradise, and [Col. 0939A] join me after this miserable life [Note: [Col. 0939D] The manuscript reads “most wretched life”] to my Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, who hung crucified upon you [Note: [Col. 0939D] The manuscript reads “fastened upon you”], [Note: [Col. 0939D] The manuscript reads “our Lord, who…”]. Amen.

## 275 PRAYER XLIII [formerly XLII]

TO THE LORD’S CROSS. Concerning the holy cross, the blessed Virgin, and the good thief.

Hail, holy cross, my salvation and life. Hail, cross, which the army of angels adores and desires. Hail, cross, which every choir of saints adores and invokes. O truly holy and venerable cross! Behold, a sinful and unhappy man stands before you and before the one crucified upon you, though unworthy; but he is so anxious on account of his sins that he scarcely knows what he ought to do. For he desires to adore you, but dares not raise his eyes to you. He has a good desire toward you, but feels no merit in himself by which he may have confidence in you. I therefore remain trembling and uncertain in your presence, so that I am ashamed to stand before you and fear to withdraw from you. The memory of divine and your own compassion urges me to stand before your presence; but my miserable conscience and my long-standing iniquity dissuade me. I am grievously constrained by these two things and scarcely know what to choose. Yet I have chosen to remain, even importunately, before your most opportune presence, though you should kill me. For it is better for me to die beside you than to live far from you (Jonah IV, 8), because no death is worse for a human being than to be far from you.

I therefore humbly implore you, dear majesty and great charity, who hang upon the cross, not to receive my importunity in an untimely manner, but to look mercifully and opportunely upon my need. For you are my hope, my refuge, and my mercy. Therefore have mercy, have mercy on me, and teach me how I ought to adore you and how I may be able to love you. Although, because my sins demand it, I do not know how I ought to adore and love you, nevertheless this is my desire: to adore and love you. I beseech you, Jesus, truly ready to hear the devout, by all the love that you have for humanity while you hang upon the wood, to grant this special favor to your servant: that I may never grow weary or reluctant to stand in your presence and before your cross, but rather may delight in it and find it pleasing. May it delight my soul faithfully to remain in your presence, and may it please the eyes of your divinity to look mercifully upon me. May it delight me to mourn my misery, and may it please your omnipotence to turn my sadness into joy.

May it also delight me to remember what, while hanging upon the cross, you said to your blessed virgin mother: “Woman, behold your son” (John XIX, 26). And now, I ask you, most gracious Lord, say to me, your servant: “Man, behold your God; behold your Redeemer.” I also beseech you, virgin blessed among all women, to say to me: “Man, behold my son; behold your Savior.” For I see your son, venerable lady, lying in the manger; I recognize your son teaching in the temple; but nowhere do I know him more certainly than hanging upon the cross. For there he himself bears witness concerning himself, saying: “Woman, behold your son” (ibid.). Therefore, blessed mother, worthy of all praise, intercede here for me, miserable as I am, with the one who, while naming himself your son, in some way binds himself as your debtor, so that he may receive your prayers with love. Say to him, then: “Son, this sinner cries to me and tearfully begs me to intercede for him with you, so that you may forgive him his sins, which he foolishly committed against you.” It is true, my Lord; it is certainly true. I, the guilty one, confess before you, God, and before your Mother, that from my childhood until now, coming before your glorious cross and the presence of your holy majesty [Col. 0940B], I have not come and pleaded as I ought, nor have I adored you. But you, whose proper nature is to spare and have mercy, do not regard my weakness and my most wretched uncleanness; rather, forgive whatever I have done wrong through negligence, because you alone are my true and only hope, and I have no confidence in anyone other than you, the living and true God.

That devout and sweet prayer which you offered to the Father for those who crucified you gives me great confidence, O my supreme Redeemer, when you said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). For if you thus pleaded for those who crucified you, will you not pray for those who adore you? And if upon the cross you remembered forgiveness, have you forgotten mercy in heaven? Have mercy, I beg you, Lord, [Col. 0940C] have mercy on me, your servant; either forgive me yourself, or intercede with the Father that he may forgive. For this is why I remain before you and adore your holy cross, through which you redeemed the world. For I believe and confess that by the elevation and extension of your body upon the wood you drew to yourself all who rightly love you. Draw me, therefore, most sweet Lord, draw me and my desire after you (Song of Songs I, 3), so that I may feel the power of your cross within me.

May I feel, my Savior, the power and fragrance that come from your cross, as did that thief who said: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (John XXIII, 42). Perhaps that thief had previously seen you giving sight to the blind or raising the dead [Col. 0940D], and had not adored you. But then, when he sees you hanging upon the wood, he adores you, saying: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Your cross accomplished in him what your miracles could not accomplish. He knew you more truly and perfectly hanging upon the cross than teaching in the temple or working miracles. O how great is the power of your cross, how great the glory of the one hanging upon the wood! As soon as that thief saw your wood, he recognized your kingdom; and where he saw you hanging, there he understood that you reigned. O what fragrance issued from the cross, driving all unbelief from him! O how rightly he called you [Col. 0941A] his Lord, knowing truly that he was your servant, because with his own eyes he saw the price by which you were redeeming the whole world.

But what did you answer the thief praying to you, good Jesus, what did you answer, most sweet Lord? “Today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid. XXIII, 43). And what does this mean, O desirable King? You are fastened with nails, yet you promise paradise. You hang upon the wood, yet you say to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” And, O desire of souls, where is paradise, since you say to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise”? Is paradise with you, and wherever you will, is paradise? Or are you undoubtedly paradise, since you promise so confidently: “Today you will be with me in paradise”? I believe, Lord, indeed I believe, that wherever you will and wherever you are, there is paradise; and to be with you [Col. 0941B] is to be in paradise. For that venerable confessor and glorious martyr was with you throughout that entire “today,” and afterward for all time. O how good it is to be with you! O how blessed are those who are with you! Those who are with you in faith and love are truly in paradise, truly in the kingdoms.

Your cross, Lord, promises paradise and grants paradise. Therefore I humbly adore your cross; I adore you on the cross, and the cross in you. Finally, I adore the cross because of the one hanging upon the cross. I adore the one whom the thief adored, and I pray as he prayed: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Recognize in me, Lord, this prayer, as you recognized it in the thief. Receive this prayer from your servant, as you received it from your servant. [Col. 0941C] Remember me from your kingdom, as you remembered him from the wood. Say, then, say, I beg you, Lord; say to your servant, say to my soul: “Today you will be with me in paradise,” so that, strengthened by your desirable promise, I may faithfully remain in your faith and love, my Redeemer, mediator of God and humanity, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign as God forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER XLIV [formerly XLIII]

TO THE LORD’S CROSS. Praise of the holy cross.

Hail, holy cross, our strength. Hail, adored cross, our praise and glory. Hail, cross, our help and refuge. Hail, cross, consolation of all who mourn; hail, cross, our victory and hope; [Col. 0941D] hail, cross, our defense and life. Hail, cross, our redemption and liberation. Hail, cross, sign of salvation and unconquerable wall against every power of the enemy. May the cross always be the hope of my Christianity. May the cross be the resurrection of my death. May the cross be my triumph against the demons. May the cross be the mother of my consolation. May the cross be the rest of my tribulation. May the cross be the staff of my old age. May the cross be the medicine of my sickness. May the cross be the protection of my nakedness. May the cross be the consolation of my life. May the cross be comfort for me in all my distress. May the cross be a remedy in my tribulations. May the cross be medicine in my weaknesses, [Col. 0942A] and protection against every adversity. Amen.

## PRAYER XLV [formerly XLIV]

TO THE LORD’S CROSS. Elevation to the holy cross.

Save me, holy cross, which was consecrated in Christ’s body and adorned, as with pearls, by the structure of his limbs; you were worthy to bear our price and brought eternal life to us. Good Jesus, grant me that through the sign and restoration of the holy cross you may free me from all attacks of my enemies and preserve me by your goodness, forgive my sins, and grant me the pardon of indulgence—you who live and reign as God, and so forth.

## PRAYER XLVI [formerly XLV]

TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY. With remembrance of her merits and of our evils.

O most blessed and most holy ever-virgin Mary, behold, I stand grieving before your compassionate presence, and I am deeply ashamed because of the abominations of my sins, by which I have been made deformed and dreadful before God, before you, before his angels, and before all the saints. I am exceedingly afraid of the final judgment of condemnation, when each person will be repaid divinely according to what he has done, whether good or evil (II Corinthians V, 10). And because on account of this fear and trembling have come upon me and darkness has covered me (Psalm LIV, 6), because of my evil deeds, I see myself leprous and unclean. Therefore I know myself worthy to be separated from the fellowship of the faithful, from whom the brightness and purity of chastity distinguish me. For this reason, weeping and wailing, I beg you, Lord, not to turn your face away from me, who am dead for four days and already full of intolerable stench [Col. 0942C]; but rather look upon how grievous a wound has struck me, and consider how you may heal me with heavenly medicine and restore me, cleansed, to your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, whose mother you are and who was born from you.

For you know, most merciful Queen, that you were born for this purpose: that our same Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true man, in whom I most truly believe and in whose mercy I do not despair, might be born through you; so that he who was the Creator of humanity might also become its Savior, and might have you as such a mother that, intervening for sinners, you might obtain perfect salvation for him. But you, his lady and mother, were a virgin in childbirth, a virgin before childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth. In you chastity remains untouched, modesty unblemished, and steadfastness firm. You rejoice that you conceived as a virgin, that you carried the Lord of heaven in a chaste womb, that you gave birth while remaining a virgin, and that you were greeted by the angel and overshadowed by the Holy Spirit (Luke I, 35). What angelic purity announced, ineffable divinity accomplished, and you were worthy to give birth to that God who by his will granted all things to be born.

You, lady, marveled both at the integrity of your body and at the fruitfulness of conception, and you rejoiced that you were about to give birth to your parent, our Lord Jesus Christ; for you rejoiced in two gifts. You marvel that you gave birth as a virgin and rejoice that you brought forth the Redeemer [Col. 0943A] of the world, Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Therefore, Queen of ineffable mercy, I believe that you are not empty of compassion, since you gave birth to the very source of all things. And since you nursed the Angel of great counsel, you can also be an angel of great counsel for me, if you intercede for me with the Son of God, who appeared to the world in the flesh through you, so that the world might recognize him, previously hidden and unknown with the Father, when he appeared in the flesh; and, having recognized him, might believe; and by believing in him might be saved through faith. By his indescribable gift he ensured that human nature, created in the likeness of its Creator, but made unlike him through sin and death, should not perish in eternal condemnation; rather, through you, he restored it by his immense mercy, and made you, a new and undefiled virgin [Col. 0943B], atone for the crime of the ancient woman.

277 O wondrous operation of divine dispensation! You, blessed among all women, did not know a man; yet you are a mother and remained a virgin after the Son was born. After I accepted this holy faith, lady, I have not always kept to the straight path, because I did not obey its commandments. If I had striven to obey them, you would readily hear me crying to you, knowing that I desired to please your Son. But because the ancient enemy led me astray, wounded me with his arrows, stripped me of my white garments, and clothed me in black, tear-stained, and half-burnt garments, scorched by the fire of my sins, I shall therefore appear to you clothed in deformed garments. For this reason, most merciful Queen and Lady, do not despise me; but remembering human frailty, grant that I may not flee in despair, but await your consolation. I shall know that it has come when I feel that the fires of crimes and iniquities within me—especially those by which I am ceaselessly consumed—gradually fail through your power and are extinguished in my heart and body by the rain of your intercessions.

O my lady, what shall I say, or what shall I do? I am in darkness and do not see the light of heaven. Where shall I go, or where shall I flee from the face of your judging Son? (Psalm CXXXVIII, 5.) I have no escape in the east, the south, the west, or the north, nor in the depths of the abyss; everywhere your Son is, everywhere wholly present, everywhere discerning and judging all things, and dwelling above the heavenly realms. If he judges me justly according to my deeds, it would have been better for me not to have been conceived, or to have died immediately after being born. Yet that would not have helped me, because, conceived and born in sins and dying without baptism, I would certainly have perished. For I was conceived of sinners and born a sinner; baptized and saved, I became a sinner again. And not as before, but filthier and more monstrous; for I am such a person as the world has none worse. Therefore I seek such a helper as the world cannot find more powerful or better after your Son. The world has apostles, patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, confessors, virgins, good and excellent helpers, whom I long humbly to pray to. [Col. 0944A] But you, lady, are better and higher than all those helpers, because you are lady over them and over all the other saints, even angelic spirits, as well as over the kings and powers of the world, the rich and the poor, masters and servants, greater and lesser; and whatever all these can do with you, you alone can do without all of them. Why can you do this? Because you are the mother of our Savior, the bride of God, the queen of heaven and earth, and of all the elements. Therefore I seek you, I flee to you, and I humbly ask that you help me in everything. If you are silent, no one will pray; no one will help. If you pray, all will pray; all will help.

A hundred million people cry out to you, most gracious Queen, and all are saved; shall I cry out to you and not be helped? Perhaps not, because I am worse and most wicked of them all. What follows from that? For this very reason I shall not be silent. Crying out, therefore, I call to you. Excellent virgin and most devout lady, spare me and hear me. Hear the wretched and comfort the grieving; gather up the wanderer and warm the despairing. Heal in me the wounds you see, through your holy medicines; remove my filthy garments and provide me with green and splendid clothing, in which you may present me, renewed, to your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. Be for me against the devil a tower of strength, an unconquerable wall, an arm of defense. Receive him when he rages against me, and lest he pierce me, weak in strength, with his cunning, oppose him invincibly. He is crafty and deceitful and is not afraid to fight against the strong, but he brings a greater force of temptation against the powerful than against the weak. You, however, heavenly helper, who know his deceptions, so crush his strength [Col. 0944C] that no cunning suggestion of his may deceive me through temptation; but when he tries to deceive, may he depart confused and overcome by your power, while I, poor as I am, protected by your defense, never cease praising you and your Son.

Grant, O blessed lady, worthy of all praise, that I, your servant, who throughout the long course of my days have miserably fallen over the precipices of sins, may now, placed in the final days, do penance for all my sins—whatever I have committed in thought, will, action, and negligence. And although for a very long time, that is, from the beginning of my life [Col. 0944D] until this hour, I have persisted in the sins I began, nevertheless obtain from your most merciful Son, O queen of heaven, that iniquity may no longer reign in me, but the power of divinity. May an abundance of virtues and prayers justify, cleanse, and fortify me, and, leading me along the paths of righteousness, bring and advance me to the good of perseverance. When I am at the end of life, may no forgetfulness dull me, nor any defect of illness impede the service of my tongue. When the number of my days has been completed and the holy ministry of the Church has been fulfilled in me, may I deserve to be received by the angel of light, freed from the angel of death, and carried before the tribunal of the most merciful Judge, where through you, lady, I may receive the peaceful rest of eternal life. Amen.

[Col. 0945A]

## PRAYER XLVII [formerly XLVI]

TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY.

Most blessed Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary, sanctuary of all virtues, by giving birth to Christ, the Lord of virtues and King of glory, through that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, whom you merited to bear for your eternal glory and our eternal salvation, I pray you through your clemency to aid me, unworthy of every mercy, before the divine majesty, and, Lady, do not delay to show yourself responsive to the prayers of so great a sinner; from you both the happiness of blessedness and redemption have come to us. For although, most holy God-bearer Mary, I am altogether unworthy to approach you in prayer, the remembrance of many who denied Christ [Col. 0945B] and you, but who at last, having converted, through your intercessions deserved the restoration of the integrity of their former mind, grants confidence to my hope. I am a greater sinner than my tongue can confess; alas, my sins are more numerous than can scarcely be counted. And although after baptism I have not observed the profession of Christianity very rightly, nevertheless I have never fallen into the pit of denial in heart or mouth. Thanks be to almighty God, who has upheld me through your holy prayers. God made you, as we hope, his mother for this purpose: that you should become the mother of all who believe in him whom he commanded us to call Father.

What could ever be judged more worthy than that you should be the mother of those whose father and brother Christ deigns to be? For, because of his extraordinary goodness, he will offer paternal benefits to all if he perceives that you, lady, do not refuse maternal affection. How could you not have mercy on me, Mother of Mercy? Where is my hope except in God and in you? Therefore, without you there is no compassion and no goodness, because you are the mother of virtue and of all virtues. Accordingly, help me, lady, I beg you; for I know that I am nothing and shall come to nothing unless you deign to help me. Help me, then, and do not deny to one person the benefit you grant to all, even without being asked. I have nowhere to go in search of the consolation of life except to her to whom all the guilty flee. I flee to you, because your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, provided you as our refuge after himself. Receive me, and pray to him that he may make me such as he commands me to become; and let him no longer permit me to be deceived by the suggestions of demons, but by his mercy and through your intercession let him make me enjoy temporal life in such a way that I may attain eternal life, with the help of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0946A]

## PRAYER XLVIII [formerly XLVII]

TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY.

Holy and glorious Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, who merited to give birth to the Savior for the world, hear me and have mercy on me now and always, for the honor of your holy and most excellent virginity. I humbly beseech you: be my savior and helper with almighty God, so that he, the merciful shepherd and prince of peace, may cleanse me from the stains of my sins, rescue me from the darkness of hell, and lead me to eternal life. May he who through you, most chaste virgin, came into this world, saved the human race by his blood, destroyed the prison-bars of hell, and opened the gates of the heavenly kingdom deign by his mercy to save and preserve me; and after the end of this fleeting life, through your prayers may he grant me some share of eternal blessedness in the fellowship of the saints.

## PRAYER XLIX [formerly XLVIII]

[Note: [Col. 0945D] This prayer was collated with manuscript 345 of the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where it is found among various prayers without the author’s name, and with the Val-luc manuscript, where it appears under the name of Maurilius, Bishop of Rouen.] TO THE SAME MOTHER OF GOD.

Singular in merit, alone without example, mother and virgin Mary, whom God so preserved inviolate in mind and body [Note: “He preserved her in body”; one manuscript reads “preserved her inviolate in body”], that you might be worthy to be the one from whom the Son of God fashioned for himself a body as the price of our redemption: I beseech you, most merciful one, through whom the whole world has been saved, intercede for me, most wretched [Note: One manuscript reads “wretched sinner”], and defiled by every iniquity [Note: One manuscript reads “most foul”; another, “defiled”; the Val-luc manuscript, “foul”; manuscripts that read “weighed down by the entire burden of sins” omit this passage], so that the Lord may at least now grant my unhappy soul a love of purity, an inclination toward cleanliness, and steadfastness in chastity. For I—I, unhappy that I am, have lost the grace of all innocence and all [Col. 0946C] holiness; I have repeatedly violated God’s holy temple. But what am I doing, recounting my obscenities to undefiled ears? I shudder, mistress, I shudder; and, with my conscience accusing me, I blush shamefully, naked before you. To whom, dying as I am, shall I offer my wound? To whom shall I go, and before whom shall I lament my pain, or from where else shall I hope for the benefits of healing, if that one refuge of eternal mercy is closed to me?

Hear, therefore, mistress; hear graciously; hear and answer a banished citizen of the portion of your inheritance [Note: The manuscripts read “of his inheritance”], returning after long exiles, after long sighs, after cruel mockeries, after many punishments [Note: One manuscript reads “after cruel mockeries, after many crimes”; another, “after long sighs, after many punishments”; the Val-luc manuscript, “after cruel mockeries, after many punishments”], to the breasts of your consolation.

I remember—and it is a delight to remember—how, to commend your sole protection to the wretched [Col. 0946D] [Note: The manuscripts omit “to us wretched ones”], you revealed your memorable name to one of your servants who was at the point of death. For when you appeared to him as he was in distress and asked whether he recognized you [Note: One manuscript reads “whether he recognized you alone”], and when he tremblingly replied, “Not at all, mistress,” you, in accordance with your kindness, said to him most gently and most familiarly [Col. 0947A] [Note: One manuscript omits “you, mistress”]: “I am the mother of mercy.”

Before whom, then, should we wretched and desolate more rightly groan, lamenting the evils of all our calamity and misery, than before you, the true and undisputed mother of mercy? Holy mother, only mother, immaculate mother [Note: One manuscript reads “holy, immaculate mother”; another, “holy, only mother, immaculate mother”; the Val-luc manuscript, “incorrupt mother, mother of mercy”], incorrupt mother, mother of mercy, mother of compassion and pardon, open the bosom of your compassion and receive the one dead in sins.

Behold, mistress, your prodigal son, barefoot, naked, and worn out [Note: One manuscript reads “naked and worn out in his feet”], sighs, cries out, and calls from a place of terror, from a cloud of filth and stench, upon his mother—remembering how often you have cherished him, covered him, and excused him before the Father. And indeed, he is the most compassionate and kind father, and you so sweet and gracious a mother. Recognize, blessed one, your children, whom your uniquely beloved only-begotten Son did not blush to call his brothers [Col. 0947B]. And if, for the sake of that innocent crucified Son of yours, a sword passed through your soul (Luke 2:35), how can you restrain yourself over your orphaned children who are dead in sin [Note: The Val-luc manuscript reads “how could you ever restrain yourself over your children who are dead”]; how could you ever restrain yourself, mistress, from maternal weeping and tears [Note: The manuscripts read “how could you restrain yourself from maternal…”; another reading is “how could you ever…”]?

We are dragged away, plundered, and taken captive; there is no one to rescue [Note: The Val-luc manuscript reads “there is no one to rescue, no one to redeem”; another, “there is no one to rescue who will redeem”], no one to redeem [Note: One manuscript reads “who will snatch away”], no one to rise early and stand surety [Note: The Val-luc manuscript reads “and answer for us”] on our behalf. Rise, compassionate one; rise, gracious one; enter the sanctuary of being heard, and spread your immaculate hands before that golden altar of human reconciliation. Through you it will be possible to obtain what we bring forward through you; through you what we fear will be excusable [Note: The manuscripts read “certainly excusable”]. Nor will the one whom you so often consoled, sweet mother, as he wailed in infancy, be able for long to withstand your supplication on our behalf.

Who, then, is more powerful in merits for appeasing the Judge’s anger than you, who were worthy to be the mother of that same Redeemer and Judge? Do not doubt [Note: The manuscripts read “Do not doubt”], my mistress; for he himself is my mouth and my flesh, my salvation and my glory [Note: The manuscripts omit “my salvation and my glory”]; he himself is our head; he knew our frame (Psalm 102:14).

Adornment of virgins, mistress of nations, queen of angels, fountain of gardens, cleansing of sins, holy and perpetual virgin Mary, help the wretched, assist the lost; so that he who now, alas, does not dare hope for that angelic virginal robe may, through your glorious merits [Col. 0948A] [Note: The manuscripts read “through your glorious merits”], at least receive some wedding garment.

Finally, even if I shall not be worthy—or rather, because I shall not be worthy—to approach more closely and take part in the flower-bearing and fragrant choirs of your glory, may I at least, placed at a distance and standing far away, be worthy to see and hear your processions, your drums, your harmonies [Note: The manuscripts omit “and” before “your harmonies”], and whatever glory and rejoicing there will be, when you dance for joy, following the Lamb wherever he goes.

Unique virgin, supreme and perpetual virgin, alone mother and virgin, holy Mary, at the end of my prayer, at the conclusion of this foolish supplication [Note: The Val-luc manuscript reads “of my supplication”; the manuscripts read the feminine “unworthy” (indignae), rather than the masculine “unworthy” (indignus)], I, unworthy, ask, beg, and beseech this one thing [Note: The manuscripts read “I ask, beg, and entreat”; another reads “I ask this one thing, I beg”; the Val-luc manuscript reads “I ask this one thing, I beg, and beseech”]: in the name of your beloved Son, grant me a constant and enduring remembrance of your most sweet name [Col. 0948B]. Let it be the sweetest food, the most delightful nourishment of my soul. May it be present to me in dangers, present in distress, present at the beginning of my joy. For if by this gift of God and of yours I am worthy [Note: The manuscripts read “If by God’s gift, and by yours, I am worthy of this”] to obtain this, I shall certainly never fear utterly perishing. Your grace will always be with me; your compassion and protection will be with me. And if I am plunged into hell [Note: The manuscripts read “in hell”], you will seek me there, draw me out from there [Note: The manuscripts read “draw me out from there”; one omits “me”], and restore me to your Son, who redeemed me and washed me in his blood, Jesus Christ our Lord [Note: The manuscripts read “Jesus Christ our Lord”], who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit [Note: The Val-luc manuscript reads “and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen”].

## PRAYER L [formerly XLIX]

[Note: This has been compared with manuscripts Vict. KK. 16 and RR. 3, Bec. O, Corb. 160, Thu. 267, Carthus., Val-luc., and Flor. In the Vict. 3 manuscript: “To the blessed virgin Mary, with remembrance of sins”; in manuscripts Vict. 16 and Flor.: “To the holy Virgin, Mother of God”; in the Corb. manuscript: “Prayer to holy Mary”; in the Thu. manuscript: “Here begin the prayers of blessed Mary”; in the Val-luc. manuscript: “First prayer to holy Mary, when the mind is weighed down by sluggishness,” without a title.]

### To the Holy Virgin Mary, with remembrance of sins, to rouse sluggishness

Holy Mary, and singularly holy among the saints after God, admirable mother of virginity, lovable virgin of fertility, who gave birth to the Son of the Most High, who bore the Savior for the human race that had been lost, mistress shining forth in such holiness, surpassing in such dignity [Note: The manuscripts read “surpassing” rather than “surpassing in such dignity”; other manuscripts read “surpassing in eminence”], whom it is certainly clear to possess power and compassion no less great [Note: Some manuscripts read “not to die” rather than “no less great”], endowed [Note: Some manuscripts read “to be excellent” rather than “endowed”] with both.

To you, O mother of life, O mother of salvation, O temple of compassion and mercy, my miserable soul strives to present itself—sick with the diseases of vices, torn by the wounds of crimes [Note: One manuscript reads “ulcers of crimes”], rotten with the ulcers of scandals [Note: One manuscript reads “wounds of scandals”]. To you, as far as a dying soul can, it strives to plead that, through your powerful merits and your pious prayers, you may deign to heal it.

For it has been so alienated from itself by the brutality of its stupor [Note: One manuscript reads “alien”] that it scarcely has any awareness of its monstrous sickness. It is so defiled by filth and stench that it fears your merciful countenance may be turned away from it; it wastes away in despair of winning your regard, so that even its mouth falls silent [Note: The manuscripts read “now falls silent”] for prayer.

My sins, my wickedness: if you have killed my soul with your poison, why do you make it so horrifying through your foulness that mercy cannot look upon it? If you overwhelm its hope of being heard by your mass, why do you block its voice of prayer through your shame? If you have made its mind insane through love of you, why do you render its understanding senseless through your torpor [Col. 0949B] [Note: The manuscripts vary considerably here: “The voice of prayer through your shame? If you have made its mind insane through love of you, why have you blocked its voice of prayer through your shame? If you have made its mind insane through love of you, why do you render its understanding, through your torpor, not serving?” Another manuscript reads: “The voice of prayer through your shame? If you have made its mind insane through love of you, why do you render its understanding senseless through your torpor?”]?

Alas, the shame of defiling iniquity in the presence of shining holiness [Note: The manuscripts read “monstrousness” and “in the presence of shining health”]! Alas, the confusion of an unclean conscience in the sight of radiant purity! O you blessed among women, who surpass the angels in purity [Note: The manuscripts read “who surpasses the angels”], and surpass the saints in compassion: my dying spirit pants for the regard of such kindness, but blushes at the sight of such brilliance.

I desire, mistress, to ask you to heal the wounds and ulcers of my sins through the regard of your compassion; but before you I am confounded by their stench and filth. I shudder, mistress, to appear before you in my uncleanness and horrors, lest you should shudder at me because of them; and, woe is me, I cannot be seen without them.

O disturbed [Note: The manuscripts read “O disturbance”], O confused condition of sinning [Note: The manuscripts read “condition to be avoided”]! Behold, my sins, how you tear me apart by rending me, corrode me by tearing me apart, and torment my inward parts by corroding me. For these same sins of mine, mistress, desire to be known by you for the sake of healing, but flee from appearing before you [Note: Some manuscripts read “shrink from appearing before you”; the Val-luc and Flor. manuscripts read “flee from being seen by you”] for fear of condemnation. For they are not healed [Note: One manuscript reads “they are not healed”; Vict. 16 and Flor. read “for they are not healed”] without confession, nor are they exposed without shame [Note: One manuscript reads “nor are they destroyed without…”]. If they are concealed, they are incurable; if they are seen, they are detestable. They burn me with pain, terrify me with fear. They overwhelm me by their mass, press upon me by their weight, and confound me by shame.

O you, Mary, piously powerful and powerfully pious, from whom the fountain of mercy arose, I beg you not to withhold such true mercy where you recognize such true misery. If I am confounded by the obscenity of my iniquity before the radiance of your holiness, will you, mistress, blush at the miserable man because of the compassion inherent in you [Note: The manuscripts read “because of the effect inherent in you”; other manuscripts read “through the compassion inherent in you”]? If I confess my wickedness, will you then deny your kindness? If my misery is greater than is good for me, will your mercy be less than befits you? For the more my sins stink in the sight of God and in your sight, mistress, the more they need his healing [Note: The manuscripts read “the more they need healing”] and your assistance.

Heal, therefore, most merciful one, the infirmity; and you will wipe away the foulness that offends you. Remove, most kind one, the sickness, and you will no longer perceive the stench at which you shudder. Make it so, most compassionate one, that there may be nothing to grieve over [Note: The manuscripts read “that grieves”], and there will be nothing that soils your purity [Note: The manuscripts read “that soils your purity”]. Do so, mistress; hear me, mistress. Heal the soul of your sinful servant through the power of the blessed fruit of your womb, who sits at the right hand of his almighty Father, supremely praiseworthy [Col. 0950B] and supremely glorious forever (Daniel 3:53).

## PRAYER LI [formerly L]

[Note: Compared with the manuscripts mentioned above. In the Thu. manuscript: “Alternately to the Mother and to the Son.” In the Bec. manuscript: “Second prayer to holy Mary, when the mind is troubled by fear.” In the Val-luc. manuscript: “Prayer to the same, when the mind is troubled by fear.” Another title is: “Prayer to the blessed, glorious, and perpetual Virgin Mary, Mother of God.”]

### To the Holy Virgin Mary, when the mind is oppressed by fear

Virgin venerable to the world, mother lovable to the human race, woman wondrous to the angels, most holy Mary, by whose blessed virginity all integrity is sanctified, by whose glorious childbirth all fertility is saved. Great mistress [Note: The Flor. manuscript reads “My mistress”], to whom the joyful assembly of the righteous gives thanks, to whom the terrified crowd of the guilty flees [Note: The manuscripts read “the hideous crowd”].

To you, most powerful and merciful mistress, I, a sinner and indeed a very great sinner [Note: The manuscripts read “a sinner of very great sin”], flee in anxiety. For when I see myself, mistress, before the omnipotent justice of the strict Judge, and consider the intolerable violence of his anger, I weigh the enormity of my sins [Col. 0950C] and the monstrousness of the punishment I deserve. Therefore, troubled by such horror and terrified by such fear, whose intervention shall I implore more earnestly than hers whose womb nurtured the world’s reconciliation? From where shall I hope more securely for swift help in need than from where I know that propitiation came forth for the world? Or whose intercession will obtain pardon more easily for the guilty than that of the woman who nursed him who is both the universal and particular just avenger and merciful pardoner?

For just as, most blessed one, it is impossible that you should forget merits so singular to you and so necessary to us, so, most gentle one, it is incredible that you should not have compassion on wretched suppliants [Note: One manuscript reads “on you, wretched suppliants”]. The world knows this well, and we sinners of the world cannot in any way conceal it [Note: Vict. 3 and Val-luc. read “cannot in any way be concealed”]: we know well enough, I say, mistress, who the Son of man was, or whose son he was, who came to save what had perished (Luke 19:10) [Note: One manuscript reads “the Son of man, that is, your very own son, came”].

Will you then, my mistress, mother of my hope, will you, out of hatred for me, forget what has been so mercifully announced to the world, so joyfully proclaimed, and so lovingly embraced? That good Son of man came of his own will to save the lost; and can the mother of God fail to care for the lost person who cries out? That good Son of man came to call the sinner to repentance (Luke 5:32) [Note: The manuscripts read “the good mother” or “the mother of God”]; and will the good mother despise one who prays in repentance [Note: The manuscripts read “one who sins in repentance”; the Flor. manuscript reads “one who prays into repentance”]? That good God, gentle man, merciful Son of God, I say, came to seek the wandering sinner; and will you, his good mother, powerful mother of God, repel the wretched man who prays?

[Col. 0951B]

Behold, woman from whom God was born, God who became man so that sinful man might be saved: behold, before your good Son and before his good mother [Note: The Carth., Val-luc., and Flor. manuscripts read “before you, his good mother”], sinful man repents and confesses, groans and prays. I beseech you, therefore, good Lord and good mistress; I beseech you, pious Son and pious mother [Note: The manuscripts read “pious mother”], I beseech you by this very truth, by this unique hope of sinners: just as you truly are his Son, and you truly are his mother, so that the sinner may be saved, so may this sinner be absolved [Note: The manuscripts read “so may he be absolved”; other manuscripts read “if he is indeed absolved”] and healed [Note: Some manuscripts add “here”; others read “be healed, cured, and saved”], cured and saved here.

Let your sinner prove it in himself; let him prove here that you truly are what you are; let him feel in himself that, for the salvation of sinners, you are Son and you are mother. Certainly he is the sinner of you both [Note: The manuscripts read “he is apparently…”]. For when I sinned against the Son, I provoked the mother; nor did I offend the mother without injury to the Son.

What, then, will you do, sinner? Where, then, will you flee, sinner? Who will reconcile you to the Son when the mother is hostile? Who will appease the mother when the Son is angry [Note: One manuscript reads “Who will appease me…”]? But even if both of you are offended alike, are you not both compassionate? Let the guilty man, therefore, flee from the just God to the pious mother of the merciful God. Let the guilty man flee from the offended mother to the pious Son of the kindly mother. Let the guilty man thrust himself between both, place himself between the pious Son and the pious mother.

Pious Lord, spare the servant of your mother; pious mistress, spare the servant of your Son; good Son, appease your mother for the sake of your servant; good mother, reconcile your servant to your Son [Note: The manuscripts read “your Son to your servant”; another reads “your servant to your servant”; the Val-luc. and Flor. manuscripts read “your servant to your Son”]. I who cast myself between two such immense mercies [Note: The manuscripts read “between two such powerful…”; other manuscripts read “into two such powerful…”] shall not fall between two such powerful severities. Good Son, good mother, may it not be in vain for me that I confess this truth about you, nor may I blush at hoping for this compassion in you. For I love the truth that I confess about you, and I implore the compassion that I hope for in you.

Tell me, Judge of the world, whom will you spare? Tell me, reconciler of the world, whom will you reconcile [Note: One manuscript reads “To whom shall I pour out my prayers? Tell me, reconciler of the world”; other manuscripts read “whom will you spare? Tell me, reconciler of the world”], if you, Lord, condemn, and you, mistress, turn away [Note: One manuscript reads “turn away”] from a little man who confesses your good things with love and his own evils with sorrow [Note: The manuscripts read “with fear”]? Singular Savior, tell me whom you will save. Mother of salvation, tell me for whom you will pray. If, at your command, Lord, and with your consent, mistress [Note: The manuscripts read “and with the mercy proceeding from you, mistress”], torments afflict the sinner who curses himself and beseeches you; if hell swallows the guilty man who accuses himself and entreats you; if Tartarus devours the poor man who despairs in himself but hopes in you.

God, who became the son of a woman out of mercy; woman, who became the mother of God out of mercy [Note: The manuscripts read “through mercy”]: either have mercy on the wretched—by sparing, you; by intervening, you—or show me to whom I may flee more safely, more merciful beings, and show me in whom I may trust more surely, more powerful ones [Note: The manuscripts read “to more powerful ones”].

For if my iniquity is so great—or rather, because it is so great—and my faith so small [Note: Vict. 16 omits “my”], my charity so lukewarm, my prayer so foolish, and my satisfaction so incomplete that I do not deserve pardon for my sins or the grace of salvation, this is precisely what I entreat: where you see that my merits are insufficient for me [Col. 0952C] [Note: The manuscripts read “where you see that merits are insufficient for me”], there may your mercies deign not to fail.

I beg, therefore—I beg: hear me, but for your own sake, not for mine; through the compassion in which you overflow, through the power in which you abound—so that I may escape the deserved pains of the condemned and be worthy to enter the joys of the blessed, there to praise you, God, who are blessed and supremely praiseworthy forever (Daniel 3:52) and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER LII [formerly LI]

[Note: Compared with the manuscripts noted above. In the Corb. manuscript: “To the same Virgin, with meditation on and praise of her merits.” In the Thu. manuscript: “Prayer to holy Mary.” In the Val-luc. and Bec. manuscripts: “Third prayer to holy Mary, for obtaining love of her and of Christ.” Also: “Prayer to holy Mary.”]

### To the Holy Virgin Mary, with meditation on and praise of her merits

Mary, you great Mary, you greatest of blessed [Col. 0953A] Marys [Note: The manuscripts read “the greater of blessed Marys”; the Val-luc. and Flor. manuscripts read “Mary, you the greater”] [Note: One manuscript reads “Mary, you”], you greatest of women. You, great and exceedingly great mistress, you my heart wishes to love, you my mouth longs to praise, you my mind desires to venerate, you my soul yearns to entreat, because my entire being entrusts itself to your protection.

Strive, inward parts of my soul; strive as much as you can, if you can do anything at all [Note: The manuscripts read “whatever you will be able to do”], all my inner faculties, to praise her merits, to love her blessedness [Note: Vict. 16 and Val-luc. read “and her blessedness”], to admire her loftiness, to implore her kindness [Note: Vict. 16 and Val-luc. read “and her kindness”], whose patronage you need daily; needing it, you desire it; desiring it, you implore it; imploring it, you obtain it [Note: The manuscripts read “you may implore…you may obtain”]. And if not according to your desire, nevertheless beyond—or certainly contrary to—your merit [Note: The manuscripts read “or certainly contrary to our merit”].

Queen of angels, mistress of the world, mother of him who cleanses the world, I confess that my heart is far too [Note: The manuscripts read “I confess, my heart is…”] unclean to look upon one so pure without good reason for shame, nor can it worthily touch one so pure by gazing upon her [Note: One manuscript reads “touch her worthily”].

Therefore all my innermost being beseeches you, mother of the illumination of my heart, nurse of the salvation of my mind. Hear me, my mistress; be present graciously; help me with your great power, so that the filth of my mind may be cleansed, my darkness illuminated [Note: One manuscript reads “and my darkness illuminated”], my lukewarmness kindled, and my sluggishness awakened. Thus, just as your blessed holiness has been exalted above all things after your supreme Son [Note: The manuscripts read “above all things, the supreme…”], through your all-powerful Son, for the sake of your glorious Son, by your blessed Son [Note: The manuscripts read “You are your Son”], so may my heart understand, venerate, love, and entreat you above all things after my Lord and God and your Son [Note: The manuscripts read “above all things, my true Lord and God, and the Lord, your Son”], with that affection—not as I, imperfect as I am, desire, but as I ought, having been made and saved, redeemed and restored by your Son [Note: The manuscripts read “but as it ought”; the Val-luc. and Flor. manuscripts read “but as I ought”].

O mother of the life of my soul [Note: The manuscripts read “O mother of my life”], foster-mother of the restorer of my flesh, nurse of the Savior of my entire being! But what shall I say [Note: The Thu., Bec., and Val-luc. manuscripts read “What shall we say?”]? My tongue fails me because my mind is insufficient. Mistress, my mistress, all my innermost parts are anxious [Note: Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read “my innermost parts are anxious”] to repay you thanks for such great benefits [Note: The manuscripts read “to repay thanks for such benefits”]; but they cannot even conceive worthy thanks, and they are ashamed to utter unworthy ones [Note: The manuscripts read “unworthy” rather than “not worthy”].

For what worthy thing can I say to the mother of my Creator and Savior, through whose holiness my sins are cleansed, through whose integrity incorruptibility is given to me, [Col. 0954A] through whose virginity my soul is loved by its Lord and betrothed to its God? What, I say, worthy thing shall I recount to the mother of my God and Lord, through whose fertility I, a captive, have been redeemed [Note: One manuscript omits “a captive”], through whose childbirth I have been rescued from eternal death, through whose offspring I, who was lost, have been restored and led back from the exile of misery to the homeland of blessedness? Blessed among women (Luke 1:28): the blessed fruit of your womb (ibid., 42) gave me all these things in the regeneration of his baptism—some in hope, some in reality—although I myself, by sinning, have so taken all these things away from myself [Note: The manuscripts read “so, behold, by giving, I have taken away”] that I possess neither the reality and scarcely retain the hope.

What then? If they have vanished through my fault [Note: The manuscripts read “if my fault should make them vanish”], shall I be ungrateful to her through whom so many good things freely came to me [Note: The manuscripts read “through whose grace so many good things came to me freely”]? Far be it from me to add this iniquity to my iniquity [Note: The Carth. manuscript reads “far be it from me to add”]. Rather, I give thanks because I had them; I grieve because I do not have them; I pray that I may have them. For I am certain that just as through the Son’s grace I was able to receive them, so through the mother’s merits I can receive them again.

Therefore, mistress, gateway of life, door of salvation, path of reconciliation, entrance to restoration, I beseech you through your life-giving fertility: obtain for me both pardon for my sins and the grace of living well, and preserve this servant of yours under your protection until the end [Note: The manuscripts read “so that this servant of yours may remain until the end”; the Val-luc. and Flor. manuscripts read “and so that he may remain until the end”].

The world, wrapped in darkness, lay subject to the snares and oppressions of demons [Note: The Corb., Vict. 3, Carth., Val-luc., and Flor. manuscripts omit everything from “The snares…” through “O hall”; it is nevertheless found in Vict. 16 and Bec. O.]. But when the sun rising from you had illumined it, the world both avoids their snares and tramples down their power.

You, hall [Note: The Carth., Val-luc., and Flor. manuscripts read “O hall”] of universal propitiation [Note: The manuscripts read “piety”], general cause of reconciliation, vessel and temple of the life and salvation of all: I diminish your merits excessively when, as a vile little man, I recount individually your benefits to me, which the world, loving them, rejoices and, rejoicing, proclaims to be its own.

For you, admirable mistress, singular in virginity, lovable in saving fertility, venerable in inestimable holiness, showed the world its Lord and its God, whom it did not know; you presented to the world its visible Creator, whom previously it did not see; you gave birth for the world to its restorer, whom the lost world needed; you bore for the world its reconciler, whom the guilty world did not possess.

Through your fertility, mistress, the sinful world has been justified; the condemned world has been saved; the exile has been brought back. Your childbirth, mistress, redeemed the captive world [Note: Vict. 16 omits “the captive”], healed the sick, and raised the dead [Note: In the Corb., Thu., Val-luc., and Flor. manuscripts, the material beginning “The snares…” above, which was omitted earlier, is placed here].

Heaven, the stars, earth, rivers, day, night, and whatever things are subject to human power or usefulness rejoice, mistress, in some way to have been restored through you to their lost splendor and endowed with a new and ineffable grace. For all things seemed dead when, having lost their innate dignity of serving dominion [Note: The manuscripts read “having lost their innate dignity of ruling and serving”], or of serving the uses of those who praise God, for which purposes they had been made, they were overwhelmed by oppression [Note: The manuscripts read “were held by oppression”] and discolored by the abuse of those who served idols [Note: The manuscripts read “by the use of idols”], for whose sake they had not been made.

But now, as though raised to life again, they rejoice, since they are governed by the dominion and adorned by the use of those who confess God. And they seemed to exult in a new and inestimable grace when they saw—not only invisibly sensing the very God, their Creator, ruling them above themselves, but also visibly seeing him within them, sanctifying them by using those same things [Note: The manuscripts read “using them within”]. These great benefits came through the blessed fruit of the blessed womb of blessed Mary.

But why do I speak only of the world as filled with your benefits, mistress? They penetrate the regions below and surpass the heavens. For through the fullness of your grace, those things that were in hell rejoice that they have been liberated, and those that are above the world rejoice that they have been restored. For through that same glorious Son of your glorious virginity, all the righteous who died before his life-giving death exult in the breaking open of their captivity, and the angels rejoice [Col. 0955C] in the restoration of their half-ruined city.

O woman wonderfully unique, and uniquely wondrous, through whom the elements are renewed, the regions below are remedied, demons are trampled underfoot [Note: The manuscripts read “the regions below are remedied, human beings …”; Vict. 16 reads “the regions below are remedied, demons are trampled underfoot, human beings …”; Flor. reads “the regions below are reclined, human beings …,” as in the printed text], human beings are saved, and angels are restored! O woman full and more than full of grace, from the overflowing abundance of whose fullness all creation, sprinkled with it, flourishes anew!

O blessed and more-than-blessed Virgin, through whose blessing all nature is blessed—not only nature created by the Creator, but also the Creator by the creature! O one exceedingly exalted, whom the affection of my soul strives to follow: where are you fleeing from the sight of my mind? O beautiful to behold, lovable to contemplate, delightful to love: where are you escaping the capacity of my heart? Wait for the weak soul that follows you; do not hide yourself, mistress, from the soul that sees you only faintly and seeks you [Col. 0956A]. Have mercy, mistress, on the soul that languishes, panting after you [Note: The manuscripts read “on the soul…that languishes”].

What a wondrous thing: how sublimely I contemplate Mary as having been placed [Note: “Placed.” The manuscripts read “placed. Everything, etc.” There is nothing equal to Mary; nothing is greater than Mary except God. God loved His Son—His only Son, begotten from His heart, equal to Himself, whom He loved as Himself—and gave Him to Mary; and from Mary He made Him His Son, not another, but the same one (the Val-luc manuscript reads: “not another, but the same one himself”), so that naturally He might be one and the same common Son of God and Mary. “Everything, etc.” The manuscripts Vict. 16, Carth., and Flor. omit the words “and from Mary He made Him His Son, not another, but the same one.”].

Nothing is equal to Mary; nothing is greater than Mary except God. God gave His Son to Mary—the Son whom alone, begotten from His heart equal to Himself, He loved as Himself—and from Mary He made Him His Son, not another, but the same one, so that naturally He might be one and the same common Son of God and Mary. All nature was created by God, and God was born from Mary [Note: “And all God’s nature was born from Mary,” according to the manuscripts Thuan., Corb., Vict., and Flor.; “and God’s nature was born from Mary,” according to Bec., O., Carth., and Val-luc.; “and God was born from Mary,” according to the printed text.]. God created all things, and Mary gave birth to God. God, who made all things [Note: “Who made or created all things”; some manuscripts omit “or created.”], made Himself from Mary; and thus He remade everything that He had made. He who was able to make all things from nothing did not wish to restore them, once violated, without Mary. God, therefore, is the Father of created things [Note: “Of created things,” in the manuscripts Thu., Vict., and Carth.; “of recreated things.”], and Mary is the mother of recreated things. God is the Father of the establishment of all things, and Mary is the mother of the restoration of all things. For God begot Him through whom all things were made, and Mary gave birth to Him through whom all things were saved. God begot Him without whom absolutely nothing exists, and Mary gave birth to Him without whom nothing at all is good. O truly, “the Lord is with you,” to whom the Lord granted that all nature should owe so much to you together with Him.

Mary, I beseech you by the grace through which the Lord so willed that He should be with you [Note: “That He should be God with you,” according to the manuscripts.] and that you should be with Him: for that very grace, and according to that same grace, show your mercy toward me; cause the love of you always to be with me, and care for me always to be with you. Cause the cry of my need, for as long as that need persists, to be with you; and may the regard of your compassion, for as long as I endure, be with me. Cause the rejoicing in your blessedness always to be with me, and compassion for my misery, insofar as it is good for me, to be with you [Note: The manuscripts read “and suffering” instead of “and compassion.”].

For just as, O most blessed one, everyone turned away from you and despised by you must necessarily perish, so everyone turned toward you and regarded by you cannot possibly perish. For just as, Lady, God begot Him in whom all things live, so you, O flower of virginity [Note: The manuscript Vict. 16 reads “and you, O flower.”], gave birth to Him through whom the dead also revive [Note: The manuscripts read “the dead revive” or “the dead are revived.”]. And just as God preserved the blessed angels from sin through His Son, so you, O adornment of purity [Note: The manuscripts read “so you, adornment,” without “O.”], will save wretched human beings from sin through your Son [Note: The manuscripts read “saved.”]. For just as the Son of God is the blessedness of the righteous, so, O salvation of fruitfulness, your Son is the reconciliation of sinners. For there is no reconciliation except that which you, chaste one, conceived; there is no justification except that which you, undefiled, cherished in your womb; there is no salvation except that which you, virgin, gave birth to. Therefore, O Lady, you are the mother of justification and of those justified; you are the parent of reconciliation and of those reconciled; you are the mother of salvation and of those saved.

O blessed confidence! O secure refuge! The Mother of God is our mother. The mother of Him in whom alone we hope and whom alone we fear is our mother; the mother, I say, of Him who alone saves and alone condemns is our mother.

But, O blessed and exalted one, not for yourself alone but also for us, how great and how lovable is what I see happening to us through you—what I rejoice to see, but, rejoicing, do not dare to say. For if you, Lady, are His mother, are not your other sons His brothers [Col. 0957B]? But what brothers, and whose? Shall I speak of what makes my heart rejoice [Note: The manuscript Vict. 16 reads “let him speak of what makes…”], or shall I remain silent, lest my mouth be accused of elation [Note: The manuscripts Thu. and Val-luc. read “lest elation,” omitting “of”]? But if I believe it through love, why should I not confess it in praise? I shall therefore speak, not in pride, but in thanksgiving.

For He who made Himself, through maternal generation, a sharer in our nature [Note: The manuscripts read “a sharer in nature.”], and made us, through the restoration of life, sons of His mother [Note: The manuscripts read “sons of His own mother.”], Himself invites us to confess that we are His brothers [Note: The manuscripts read “not fathers.”]. Therefore our judge is our brother; the Savior of the world [Note: The manuscripts Thu. and Corb. read “our Savior.”] is our brother; finally, our God has become, through Mary, our brother.

With what confidence, then, ought we to hope, and with what consolation can we fear, when both our salvation and our condemnation depend upon the will of a good brother and a pious mother [Note: The manuscripts read “upon the goods of the brother”]? With what affection ought we to love this brother and this mother? With what familiarity shall we entrust ourselves to them? With what security shall we flee to them? With what sweetness shall we who flee to them be received [Note: The manuscripts read “we who flee,” omitting the prefix meaning “to seek refuge”]?

Therefore, may the good Brother forgive us what we have done wrong [Note: The manuscripts read “what we do wrong”]; may He Himself turn away what we have deserved by doing wrong; may He Himself grant what we, repentant, ask. May the good Mother pray and intercede for us; may she ask and obtain what is useful for us [Note: The manuscripts read “what may be useful to us.”]. May she ask her Son for His sons, the Only-Begotten for those whom He adopted, the Lord for His servants. May the good Son hear His mother on behalf of His brothers, the Only-Begotten on behalf of those whom He adopted, the Lord on behalf of those whom He freed.

O Mary [Note: The manuscripts rearrange the close of the preceding sentence: “for the brothers; the Only-Begotten for those whom He adopted; the Lord for those whom He freed. Mary…”]! How much we owe you, Lady and Mother, through whom we have such a brother [Note: The manuscripts read “Lady, through whom…”]!
