What thanks, what praise shall we return to you [Note: “Shall we give you?” in some manuscripts; “shall we return to you?” in the printed text.]?

## [Col. 0958A]

Great Lord, you are our greater Brother; great Lady, you are our better Mother. Teach my heart with what reverence it ought to think of you. Good are you, and good are you; sweet are you, and sweet are you. Tell and grant my soul the affection with which, remembering you, it may delight in you, delighting may rejoice, and rejoicing may grow rich. Enrich it and kindle it with your love; may my heart languish in your continual love, may all my bones melt [Note: The manuscripts read “may my soul melt.”], and may my flesh fail. Would that the inward parts of my soul should burn with such a sweet fervor of your love that the inward parts of my flesh might wither! Would that the depths of my spirit should be so enriched by the sweetness of your affection [Note: The manuscripts read “your effect”], that the marrow of my body might be dried up!

Lord, Son of my Lady; Lady, Mother of my Lord [Col. 0958B]: if I am not worthy to be blessed by your love in this way, certainly you are not unworthy to be loved in this way—indeed, you deserve to be loved more [Note: Some manuscripts read “perhaps you,” and others “indeed, more.”]. Therefore, most kind ones, do not deny me, when I ask, that which I confess myself unworthy of, lest you be deprived of that of which you certainly cannot deny yourselves worthy. Give, then, most merciful ones—give, I beseech you, to my suppliant soul, not because of my merit but because of yours, your love, in the measure worthy of you. Give me, I say, what I am unworthy of, so that what you are worthy of may be returned to you [Note: The manuscripts read “give me, who am…” and “to you, who are…”; one manuscript reads “what you are worthy of.”]. For if you do not wish to give me what I desire to have, at least do not refuse me the means of returning to you what I owe.

Perhaps I shall speak presumptuously, but surely your goodness makes me bold. I shall therefore speak still to my Lord and my Lady, although I am dust and ashes (Gen. XVIII, 27). Lady and Lord, is it not much better when you freely give the petitioner what he himself does not deserve than when what is justly owed to you is withheld from you [Note: The manuscripts read “when you give thanks” instead of “when you freely give”]? The former is a matter for proclaiming mercy; the latter is unspeakable injustice.

Therefore, most merciful ones, extend grace so that you may receive what is owed. Show me your mercy, which is useful to me and fitting for you, lest I do to you my injustice, which is useful to no one and fitting for no one. Be merciful to me, as I beseech you, lest I be unjust toward you, which I abhor [Note: The manuscripts read “I beseech you not…”]. Give graciously, you gracious ones, lest you be difficult to persuade [Note: Some manuscripts read “and may you not be…”]. Give my soul the love of you [Note: The manuscripts read “to give my soul…”], which it rightly asks and which you rightly demand; lest it be ungrateful for your good gifts [Col. 0959A]—something it rightly dreads [Note: The manuscripts read “which it rightly prays for”] and you justly punish.

Certainly, Jesus, Son of God, and you, Mary, Mother, both wish—and it is right—that whatever you love should be loved by us. Therefore, good Son, I ask you by the love with which you love your mother [Note: The manuscript Vict. 16 reads “with which you so love…”]: just as you truly love her and wish her to be loved, so grant me that I may truly love her. Good Mother, I ask you by the love with which you love your Son: just as you truly love Him and wish Him to be loved [Note: The manuscripts read “just as He may be loved”], so obtain for me that I may truly love Him.

For behold, I ask for something whose fulfillment truly lies within your will [Note: The manuscripts read “within the will of both of you.”]. Why, then, should it not come to pass because of my sins, when it lies within your power as well [Note: The manuscripts omit “as well”]? Lover and merciful one of humankind, you have caused your guilty ones to love even unto death; can you deny love of yourself and of your mother to one who asks you [Col. 0959B]? Mother of this Lover of ours, you who deserved to carry Him in your womb and to nurse Him at your breast—can you or will you not obtain for the one who asks it love of Him and of yourself? Therefore, may my mind revere you as you deserve; may my heart love you as is right; may my soul cherish you as is beneficial for it; may my flesh serve you as it ought. And may my whole being be brought to completion in this: that it may sing psalms forever [Note: The manuscripts read: “May my mind love you as you deserve; may my heart love you as is right; may my soul cherish you as is beneficial for it; may my flesh serve you as it ought; and may my flesh be consumed in this, that it may sing forever.” Other manuscripts read: “May my mind love you as you deserve; may my heart cherish you as is right; may my soul serve you as is beneficial for it; may my flesh serve you as it ought; and may my life be brought to completion in this, that it may sing forever.” The manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor. read “may they be brought to completion.”] with all my substance. Blessed be the Lord forever; so be it, so be it [Note: The manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor. add “amen,” which is omitted here.].

## ORATION LIII [formerly LII]. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY AND TO SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST

O undefiled and eternally blessed, singular and incomparable Virgin, Mary, Mother of God, most beloved temple of God, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, gate of the kingdom of heaven, through whom, after God, the whole world lives: incline the ears of your compassion and those merciful eyes of yours toward my unworthy supplications, and be for me, a sinner, a pious helper in all things.

And O most blessed John, familiar friend of Christ, chosen by that same Lord of ours Jesus Christ and loved more than the others, instructed above all in heavenly mysteries, made His most illustrious apostle and evangelist, and inseparable guardian of His mother: I invoke you together with the mother of that same Savior, so that you may deign to bring me your aid with her.

O two heavenly gems, Mary and John! O two lights divinely shining before God! By your rays drive away the clouds of my crimes. You are those two in whom God the Father specially built Himself a house through His Son, and in whom the Only-Begotten Son of God, because of the merit of your most sincere virginity, confirmed the privilege of His love, hanging upon the cross and saying to one of you: “Woman, behold your son” (John XIX, 26). Then to the other: “Behold your mother” (ibid., 27).

In the sweetness, therefore, of this most sacred love, by which you were then joined by the Lord’s own words as mother and son, I, N., a sinner, commend my body and soul to you two, so that you may deign to be for me at every hour and moment steadfast guardians within and without, and pious intercessors before God. For I firmly believe and confess without doubt that your willing is God’s willing, and your refusal is God’s refusal. Hence whatever you ask, you obtain without delay.

By this most powerful virtue of your dignity, therefore, ask for me the health of body and soul [Col. 0960B]. Act, I beg you, act through your most glorious prayers, so that the Holy Spirit, the gracious Paraclete, may deign to visit and inhabit my heart; may cleanse me from all the filth of vices, adorn me with sacred virtues, make me stand and persevere perfectly in the love of God and neighbor, and, after the course of this life, lead me to the joys of His elect—that most kind Paraclete, bestower of graces, who, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, lives and reigns with them and in them as almighty God, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## 283. ORATION LIV [formerly LIII]. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY

O holy, O blessed one, deign to be present in our necessities as our counsel and aid—you who are more ready, more powerful, more effective, more lovable, more gracious, and sweeter than all others. You are sweet on the lips of those who praise you, in the hearts of those who love you, and in the memory of those who pray to you. You are glorious among every sex, every age, every condition, among tribes, peoples, and languages.

You are the moon in the midst of the firmament, the lampstand in the midst of the world, the tree of life in the midst of paradise; you are chosen myrrh, the pool in Heshbon, a column of smoke from spices, a bundle of myrrh and frankincense between the breasts of the bridegroom, a terebinth extending branches of grace and salvation. Among the blessed, you are more blessed; you are more chosen, more beautiful, more gracious, more glorious than all others—the mother of Him who grants grace, glory, honor, and eternity.

Rise, most blessed Virgin, and mercifully pray for us [Col. 0960D]. Rise, and embrace the mercy of the Redeemer; continually offer prayers for us, whom you see grievously offending before the eyes of the Creator. Through you, glorious Lady, may we deserve to ascend to Jesus your Son, who through you deigned to descend to us [Col. 0961A]. Through you, blessed Virgin, may we be able to come into the glory of Him who through you came into our misery. Through you may we gain access to your Son, who through you redeemed the world.

O blessed discoverer of grace, mother of life, mother of salvation, may He who was given to us through you receive us through you. Most pious Lady, Virgin Mary, may your integrity excuse before your most pious Son the guilt of our corruption, and may your humility, pleasing to God, obtain pardon for our vanity. May your abundant charity confer upon us the glorious fruitfulness of merits. In general, hear all who invoke you, glorious Virgin Mary; be present to all, help all; may all who believe you to be the Mother of God feel you to be their helper in their distress and necessities.

## [Col. 0961B]

In particular, may your daily and constant prayer defend those whose frequent devotion serves you; and whoever remembers you on earth, remember them before your most pious Son, our Lord, in heaven. Our Lady, our mediator, commend us to your Son; reconcile us to your Son; present us to your Son. O blessed one, by the grace that you found, by the prerogative that you merited, by the mercy that you brought forth, cause Him who through you deigned to become a sharer in our misery and weakness, through your intercession also to make us sharers in His glory and eternal blessedness.

## ORATION LV [formerly LIV]. TO THE SAME HOLY VIRGIN MARY

O gracious Virgin Mary, you are more glorious than all the spirits of the angels and all the souls of the elect throughout the entire inheritance of your Son Christ our Lord, to the extent that you merited to be made more blessed by Him. We therefore beseech you with tearful sighs to incline now the ears of your magnificent compassion to the groaning of our sorrow.

We sinners, bowed down beneath innumerable offenses, have deserved infernal punishment, where there is no place at all for repentance, because we once promised faith to God but by our evil lives have hitherto lied. O holy Mother of God, most worthy and purest of all creatures, wipe the eyes of blind hearts and show us the paths of justice. By praying, remove vices from us and plant within us the nurseries of sacred virtues [Col. 0961D]. Obtain for us the course of eternal dancing, which the heavenly prize continually follows.

Thus, I beg you, most pious Lady, pray for us in heaven, so that you may erase whatever we have done wrong on earth. For there is nothing so small in us that prayer, if you are pleased to grant it, cannot erase. O most holy Virgin Mary, may we who believe that you are Virgin and Mother of God, by believing, experience that you pray for us. And may we who confess that you gave birth to God and man rejoice that salvation comes to us through you. And may we who acknowledge that you are better than all human beings rejoice to receive happiness through you. Whenever your divine mercy comes to us, may your protection be present, lest we become puffed up. And if tribulation or temptation comes, may your holy prayer be present, lest we fall [Col. 0962A]. Thus, I beg you, merciful Lady, pour out prayers for our salvation in heaven, so that after death we may deserve to enjoy the joys of paradise.

O blessed Mother of God, Virgin Mary, temple of the living God, court of the eternal King, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. You are the branch from the root of Jesse, the cedar of Lebanon, the purple rose of Jericho, the cypress on Mount Zion; you who, by a singular privilege, just as you know no comparison in all things, likewise surpass even the dignity of the angels. To you, by a new and unheard-of miracle, it was granted that the Word whom God begot before the ages should become your Son, God and man.

You gave birth to Him at the end of the age, so that He might be the true and perfect Son of God, possessing a twofold nature but one person: God and man, one Emmanuel. O glorious mother in childbirth, in whom alone fruitful virginity is found, you brought forth the Son of God with undefiled inward parts, so that the integrity of unviolated chastity might increase and desire might not violate the seal of virginal integrity.

While you were conceiving, the Holy Spirit overshadowed you—not, God forbid, so that He Himself might become the seed of offspring in your most holy womb, but rather by the virtue and power of the Creator. From you our High Priest took the offering of His body, which He offered as a sacrifice upon the altar of the cross for the salvation of the whole world.

You are the rising light of Nazareth. You are the joy of Israel. You are the glory of the world. You are the nobility of the Christian people. O queen and Lady of the world, ladder of heaven, throne of God, gate of paradise, hear the prayers of the poor; do not despise the groans of the wretched [Col. 0962C]. Through you may our vows and sighs be brought before the Redeemer, so that although our merits exclude us, through you we may obtain access to the ears of your compassion. Erase sins, release crimes, raise the fallen, free the shackled. Through you may the brambles and shoots of vices be cut away, and may the flowers and ornaments of virtues come forth.

Appease by your prayers the Judge whom, in a singular childbirth, you gave birth to as Savior, so that He who through you became a sharer in our humanity may through you also make us sharers in His divinity. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## 284. ORATION LVI [formerly LV]. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY. On Her Nativity

## [Col. 0962D]

Deign to let me praise you, consecrated Virgin; give me strength against your enemies and against the enemy of the whole human race. Give me strength humbly to pray to you. Give me strength fervently to praise you with prayers, by the merits of your most sacred nativity, for you were born into the world as joy, hope of life, and consolation for all Christianity.

When you were born, most holy Virgin, then the world was illuminated. Blessed stock, holy root, and blessed is your fruit: you alone merited, as a virgin full of the Holy Spirit, to conceive God, to carry God, to give birth, and to remain a virgin after childbirth. Therefore have mercy on me, a sinner, and help me, Lady, so that just as your glorious nativity, arising from the seed of Abraham, born from the tribe of Judah, and shining from the stock of David [Col. 0963A], announced joy to the whole world, so it may fill me with true joy and cleanse me from every sin.

Pray for me, most provident Virgin, so that the very joyful joys of your most health-giving nativity may confer the veil of pardon upon all my sins. Holy Mother of God, blooming like a lily, pray to your sweet-born Son for me, a wretched sinner. Amen.

## ORATION LVII [formerly LVI]. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY. On Her Annunciation

I beseech you, sweetest Virgin, by the merits of your most health-giving annunciation and by that angelic “Hail” which you received from Saint Gabriel, the messenger of your salvation, the messenger of the Incarnation of the divine Word, the messenger of eternal life, and the messenger of our salvation through you, that you receive our prayers.

Most merciful Lady, my sins are great, but your grace is greater, because you are full of grace and the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. Mother of all grace, pray for me so that, just as your annunciation was an approaching end to the old guilt, but the hope of promised grace and, for all who awaited it in truth, the source and way of future grace, so the remembrance of that same annunciation of yours—recalled in my heart and proclaimed by my mouth in honor of your joy—may become in me the end and abolition of all my old and new guilt, and the grace of continual saving chastity.

Help me, my Lady, hope of the living, consolation of the sorrowful, support of the needy, merciful helper of all, so that I who recognize my guilt through the very scourges of sorrow, sadness, and weakness [Col. 0963C] may, through the joys of your most holy annunciation, deserve by your mercy to obtain a remedy for weakness and joy from sorrow; so that henceforth I may strive to please God in useful sorrow, in purity of heart and body, in humility of mind, in integrity of faith, and in every goodness, and so that my spirit may rejoice in God my Savior throughout all the time of my life.

Holy Mother of God, come to my aid and intercede with your sweet-born Son for me, a sinner. Amen.

## ORATION LVIII [formerly LVII]. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY. On Her Childbirth

Most holy Virgin, give me strength, through the merits of your most holy virginal childbirth, against your enemies [Col. 0963D]. For blessed are you, Mary, who carried the Lord, Creator of all ages. You gave birth to Him who made you, and you remain a Virgin forever.

Blessed is the womb that carried the Son of the eternal Father. Blessed are your breasts, which nursed Christ the Lord. Blessed and venerable are you, Virgin Mary, full of the blessedness of every good. Blessed is the mother who alone gave birth without pain, because you alone gave birth as a virgin.

Blessed and blessed among women are you, because Christ our God, born from you the Virgin, by His most holy nativity, cancelling the curse of the first parent and of the first woman giving birth painfully as a punishment, granted through you to the woman giving birth without pain, once the old guilt had been dismissed, the honey-sweet blessing of new grace and eternal salvation.

Through the joys of your most holy virginal childbirth, have mercy on me, my Lady, and hear my prayer. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins (Ps. L, 6).

I was born in sins, and I have lived in sins throughout the whole time of my life. But you, my Lady, without any violation of modesty, were found to be the mother of the Savior. Have mercy on me, unclean as I am, conceived and nourished in sins; and help me by your holy prayers, most serene Virgin.

Thus, just as the nativity of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, was the downfall of dreadful sorrow and His birth was new exultation for all the faithful, so may these same joys of the Lord’s Nativity be for me the beginning of a religious life and saving continence, the downfall of all unjust grief and wrongful sadness, and the birth of spiritual joy and exultation, as well as love and desire for the heavenly homeland and sublime gladness.

Holy Mother of God, come to my aid and intercede with your sweet-born Son for me, a sinner. Amen.

## 285. ORATION LIX [formerly LVIII]. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY. On Her Purification

O most serene Virgin, by the merits of your most pious purification give me strength against your enemies. Most holy Virgin, most chaste in body, most beautiful in conduct. Virgin of virgins, never defiled in heart or mouth, but wholly beautiful, wholly without stain.

Undefiled virgin in body, undefiled virgin in mind, owing nothing to the laws and touched by no excesses, you fulfill the rite of purification established for polluted mothers, so that you might show in yourself an example of humility. You brought to the temple with you for purification Him who, born human, increased the glory of your integrity.

Undefiled Mother, you brought to the temple with you for purification Him who, understanding our sins—for all things are naked and open to Him—cleanses His servants daily from our hidden faults through confession and repentance, and spares them from the faults of others through the spirit of continence (Ps. XVIII, 14).

You brought to the temple with you for purification Him whose blood, washing us from original contagion in the passion of His cross, daily also through the sacred mysteries upon the altar of the cross cleanses us, repentant and confessed, from our crimes.

You brought to the temple with you for purification Him who, made High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, daily sympathizes with our weaknesses, is merciful toward us, and is a faithful High Priest before God in making propitiation for the sins of the people. Daily He reconciles us to God the Father through what He, God from God, offers to God the Father, if we turn back and confess our sins. God, faithful, just, and patient, will forgive and absolve us.

In His name, most perfect Virgin, I flee to you. In His most sweet name and love, therefore, receive me, my most merciful Lady, fleeing to you, and help me by the merits of your most chaste purification, so that I may perceive and rejoice that I am continually purified from the filth of conscience in such a way that henceforth I may never grieve at being defiled by any contagion or perpetration of crime [Col. 0965A].

Holy Mother of God, receive me and intercede for me, a sinner, with your sweet-born Son Jesus Christ, the blessed fruit of your womb, and have mercy on me.

## ORATION LX [formerly LIX]. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY. On Her Assumption

Most serene Virgin, holy Mother of God Mary, by the merits of your glorious assumption and by the love of your sweetest Son, by whom you were assumed into heaven, give me strength against your enemies and [grant me] entrance into the eternal kingdom.

For you are blessed, sacred Virgin Mary, and worthy of all praise, because from you has arisen Christ our God, the sun of justice, like a cedar exalted in Lebanon and like a cypress on Mount Zion, like chosen myrrh giving the sweetness of fragrance (Ecclus. XXIV, 17, 20). Exalted above the choirs of angels, rejoicing and glorious forever as Queen of heaven, you help all who glorify you as Lady and frequently invoke your holy name with humble prayer.

Therefore, blessed and venerable Virgin Mary, who are kind to all who cry out to you with devout hearts, be pious and willing to hear me, a sinner, who humbly invoke you. Under your protection I flee, where, though weak, I have received strength. With your protection, cause me to receive that strength of soul and body, so that, freed through you from sins and sinful desires, and without fear delivered from the hand of visible and invisible enemies, I may be able at all times to bless your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and always have His praise in my mouth [Col. 0966A].

O glorious Virgin, you underwent death but could not be held down by the bonds of death, because you alone, a Virgin, gave birth to Him who was the death of death and the sting of hell. Help me through your death and through the joys of your assumption into heaven, so that I may lead the remainder of my life with sincere faith and your help, and happily bring my life to its end: prostrate on the earth in ashes and sackcloth with tears; in confession and repentance for my sins; and, what is greater, in confession of the name of Christ, in receiving His body and blood, and in commending my spirit into the hands of His mercy.

Pray for me, holy Mother of God, so that although, conscious of many sins, I tremble and dread the tribunal of your Son, through your venerable intercession I may rejoice to be cleansed from all my crimes, with contrition of heart watering me and the dew of most pious confession presented by you [Col. 0966B]. May no stain of sin henceforth defile my soul; but with a pure heart and chaste body, through the merits of your most health-giving nativity, annunciation, and most holy virginal childbirth, and of your most chaste purification and most glorious assumption, may I be presented in the lofty palace of heaven, where you rejoice and reign gloriously as Queen of angels and human beings, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Come to the aid of my crimes, Mother of mercy, obtaining pardon for me through your virginal prayers before your sweet-born Son Jesus Christ our Lord. He lives and reigns, blessed, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## 286. ORATION LXI [formerly LX] [Note: From manuscripts 160, Vict., and KK. 16, collated together]. A RHYTHMUS TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY AND TO ALL THE SAINTS

Mary, temple of the Lord,

sanctuary of the Paraclete,

glory of sacred virgins,

consolation of the sorrowful.

To you I sigh, Lady;

receive my tears;

deign to open for me

the bosom of mercy.

Illustrious Queen of heaven,

starry lamp of the world,

wipe away my tears

and the clouds of my sins.

Whatever the Only-Begotten Son wishes,

He will grant to you;

for whomever you wish,

you will obtain pardon and glory.

But woe to the sins of human beings

who dwell in darkness.

My conscience terrifies me,

[lacuna]

so that I may hide like Adam [Note: The manuscript Vict. reads: “My conscience terrifies me because of the consciousness of guilt.” The manuscript Corb. reads “so that I may add.”],

or flee like Cain [Note: The manuscript Cister. reads “as her”; the manuscript Vici. reads “like Cain.”].

My crimes compel me,

because they are many and grave.

But amid such clouds

and the burdens of sins,

remembering the Father of lights,

I do not despair of help.

I considered nothing worse

than to despair of anything,

nothing more perverse,

especially when you, Lady,

carry my prayers.

When I consider the angels,

prophets, and apostles,

victorious martyrs,

and exceedingly chaste virgins,

none seems to me more powerful,

none more merciful—

let me say this with due respect to them—

than the Mother of the Lord.

Therefore, to make her especially

my patroness

seems to me nothing more religious,

nothing more healthful.

Therefore, honey-sweet Mother

and most chaste Virgin,

may I now, in the present,

experience

what I express about you.

I first lay upon you

the complaint of my groaning;

may you carry it to the Lord,

to your true Son.

Mary, heavenly light,

that you may carry my prayers,

I humbly ask in mind,

prostrate at your feet.

My former contagions

of sins have putrefied,

but the physician is wise;

the Lord is almighty.

He is effective

at lifting me out

of evil habit,->____
Who raised Lazarus,

dead for four days.

After Peter’s fall, he looks upon him,

and shakes him with great weeping,

nor does he, being gracious,

refuse the prayers of the Canaanite woman.

David repented of such monstrous

crimes,

and afterward deserved to be praised

by the mouth of the Lord himself.

Therefore I confidently believed

that I could quickly be freed

from the bonds of sins,

if only you should ask it.

Mother of mercy,

can you despise one so affected,

you who call the impious,

and do not reject the unbelieving?

What you accomplished in Mary—

I mean that Egyptian woman—

the Church knows fully,

and rejoices in the grace.

Theophilus, given over to the devil

by his own written contract,

as though from the bottom of the abyss,

was able to be brought back by you.

But who could comprehend in words  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “comprehend,” or “carefully write out”; ms. Vict.: “would comprehend,” or “arrange the writing.”]

or set down in writing,

how many you free each day

and reconcile to God?

Warned by these things long ago,

I have fled to you in faith,

lest you reject me in your goodness;

I humbly beg you to delay.  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “that you delay”; ms. Vict.: “or delay.”]

Obtain for me as soon as possible

tears of devotion,

so that they may be sufficiently capable

of washing away my filth.

Let shameful desire

not defile body or mind,

which I have now placed,

Lady, under your protection.

For the authority of Scripture,

and sacred truth, cry out

that the body is subject to sins

and hates the holy spirit.

Let fury and indignation

be far from the soul

which it has chosen

to entrust to the most holy protection.  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “it has chosen”; ms. Vict.: “I have chosen.”]

Let hatred not exasperate it,

boasting not exalt it,

gnawing envy not sharpen it;

but let true peace possess it.

If the world laughs, I shall flee it;

or if it rages, I shall mock it;

for whoever loves the world

ceases to stand with Christ.

But let diligent reading

and compunctionate prayer

satisfy the one who applies himself,

and intoxicate the one who clings.

In you let me turn

the gaze of my mind;

let me turn the sting of death,

and, if it is so much the more suspect

the more it remains concealed.  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “and if it is so much”; ms. Vict.: “and if it is thus so much.”]  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “more concealed”; ms. Vict.: “more hidden.”]

### 287. O Jesus, most high King,

O fountain of mercy,

make the terrible hour of death

easy through good hope.

A secure conscience

does not tremble greatly there,

for, strengthened by the hope that has been formed,

it passes on much more confidently.

Let there be no other joy,

nor any other desire of mine,

than that, once divested of the body,

I may be able to stand before you.

O inhabitants of heaven,

citizens of the heavenly homeland,

who enjoy God,

have compassion on us also.  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “who enjoy God”; ms. Vict.: “who now enjoy God.”]

Michael, among heavenly beings,

who shines before the ranks,

grant us consolation

for the sake of your special glory.

Angels whom the very heavy

burden of flesh does not weigh down,

pray for human beings

who labor beneath it.

John, greatest of the prophets,

receive the words of those who pray,

and summon to this task

a companion from the company of the prophets.

Peter, fisher of human beings,

and Paul, teacher of the nations,

with the other apostles,

help us with swift aid.

Stephen, together with Lawrence,

leaders distinguished by great merit,

with the great throng of martyrs,

bring us great protection.

You illustrious confessors,

endowed with eternal life  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “having lost the unconquered”; ms. Vict.: “endowed with unconquered faith,”]

we do not at all forget,

but earnestly beseech you:

since you passed through

temporal and fragile things,

stand all the more readily

for those still fighting.

Agnes, Thecla, Cecilia,  
[Note: Ms. Cister.: “Cecilia also”; ms. Vict.: “Cecilia, Lucia also.”]

and likewise Scholastica,

and all holy virgins,

stand in prayer for us.  
[Note: Ms. Vict.: “Here end the Prayers or Meditations of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.”]

### ORATION LXII [formerly LXI]. TO THE GUARDIAN ANGEL

I beseech you, angelic spirit, to whose care I have been entrusted by God, that you may guard me continually and protect me, visit me, and defend me from every assault of the devil, whether I am awake or asleep. By night and by day, at every hour and moment, cherish me; wherever I go, accompany me. Drive away from me every temptation of Satan, and obtain by your prayers from the most merciful Judge and our Lord—who appointed you as my guardian and entrusted me to you—what my merits do not demand, so that no admixture of the contrary power may find a place in me.

And whenever you see me straying through the precipices of vices, strive to lead me back by the paths of righteousness to my Redeemer. In whatever distress you see me, may I feel that, through your intercession, the help of almighty God is upon me.

I therefore pray, if it can be done, that you make known to me my end; and when I have been led forth from this body, do not allow the evil spirits to terrify or mock me, nor to lead me into the pit of despair. Do not abandon me until you bring me to the vision of my Creator, where, through your intervention, I may deserve to rejoice forever with all the saints, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0969A]

### ORATION LXII [formerly LXIII]  
[Note: Compared with mss. Vict. KK. 16 and RR. 3; Thu. 267; Bec. O; Corb. 160; Saint-Germain 345; Carthusian “a porta”; and Vallis-Lucentis and Floriacensis. “To Saint John the Baptist, with remembrance of sins.” Mss. Vict. 16, Vallis-Lucentis, and Floriacensis: “Prayer to Saint John the Baptist.” Ms. Saint-Germain: “On Saint John the Baptist.” Ms. Corb.: “To Saint John the Baptist.”]

### TO SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST  
With remembrance of sins

Holy John, you are that John

who baptized God,

you who were praised beforehand by the archangel

before you were begotten by your father;  
[Note: “Who was begotten,” according to the manuscripts; “before you were begotten,” according to the printed text.]

you were filled with God

before you came from your mother;

you knew God before you were known  
[Note: “Before you were born,” according to mss. Vict. 16, Saint-Germain, and Vallis-Lucentis.]

in the world.

You, before your birth, showed the pregnant Mother of God to your mother, before your pregnant mother could call you [the reading *te dici* is uncertain].

You are the one of whom God said:

“Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater” (Matt. 11:11).  
[Note: Ms. Vict. 16: “You are the one of whom”; “you are the one,” according to another manuscript.]

To you, Lord, so great, so holy, so blessed,

there comes a criminal worm,

a sorrowful little man,

hardly feeling pain because his senses are already dead,

yet, with a dead soul, a sinner greatly to be pitied by himself.

To you, so great a friend of God,  
[Note: Ms. Saint-Germain: “who made such a friend of God”; “who made such a blessed one,” according to another manuscript.]

comes one greatly afraid,

uncertain of his salvation

because certain of his great guilt,

but hoping in your greater grace.

For your grace, Lord, is greater than my guilt,

because you have more power with God than my guilt has to erase my crimes.

To you, therefore, Lord,

whom grace made such a friend of God,

the one whom iniquity made so guilty before God

flees in anxiety.

To you, whom grace made so blessed,

I come, whom wickedness made so wretched.

Truly, Lord, I confess:

my iniquity made me such;

but you became such—not through yourself,

but through the grace of God with you.

Remember, therefore, Lord,

that just as the grace of God raised you so high,

so may your mercy lift up

the one whom his guilt so humbled.  
[Note: “Your mercy may lift up the one whom his guilt so humbled”; some manuscripts omit “so.”]

Alas for me—what have I made myself?

What kind of person was I?

O God, what sort of person did you make me,

and what sort have I made myself again?  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “What sort was I, O God?”; another manuscript: “For what sort of person, indeed, O God?”]

I was conceived and born in sins;

but you washed me,

you sanctified me,

and I defiled myself with worse things.

I was then born amid necessities;

now I have wallowed in voluntary sins:

in the former I was conceived without knowing it,

in the latter I am willingly full and covered;

from the former you mercifully led me out,

into the latter I miserably led myself;

from the former you piously redeemed me,

in the latter I impiously destroyed myself.

You had healed, merciful God,

the soul wounded by its parents;

I, impious, killed it after it had been healed.

You had stripped me, merciful Lord,

of the old rags of original sin,

and clothed me in the garment of innocence,

promising another garment of incorruptibility.

But I, having rejected the one you gave me,

covered myself with the filth of wickedness;

despising the one you promised,

I chose instead the sufferings of eternal misery.  
[Note: “And having despised it,” according to the manuscripts.]

You made a son of your wrath

a son of your grace;

but I, having despised that grace,

made myself a son of your hatred.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “You made me a son of wrath”; another: “You made me a son of your wrath,” omitting “me.”]

You restored in me your lovely image,

and I stamped over it a hateful image. 288

Alas, alas! Whose?

Whose image, wretched and mad little man,

did I stamp over the image of God?  
[Note: “I stamped over it,” according to ms. Vict. 16; “you stamped over it,” according to ms. Vallis-Lucentis; “you stamped over it,” according to another reading.]

Why was I not ashamed to do

what I am so terrified to say?

Why did I not hate the imitation

of the one whose name I so dread?

He fell voluntarily;

I willingly made myself filthy.

But he sinned in pride

without any punishment for sin preceding;

I, having seen his punishment,

hurried contemptuously into sin.

He was established in innocence once;

I was restored to it.

He acted against the one who made him

and remade him;  
[Note: “Remade and redeemed him,” according to the manuscripts; some manuscripts omit “and redeemed.”]

he abandoned God who was promising;

I fled from God who was pursuing me.

He persists in wickedness

while God rejects him;  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “He prevails in wickedness.”]

I ran into wickedness

while God was calling me back.

He was hardened against the one punishing;

I was hardened against the one entreating.

Although both acted against God,

he acted against one who did not even seek him,

while I acted against one who was dying for me.

O unhappy, most unhappy little man,

if indeed all humanity has not departed

where such monstrous wickedness has entered!

Behold: the image whose horror I dreaded—

in many respects I see myself more horrifying.

Flee, flee, you horrible, nameless substance,  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “some unknown pride.”]

flee from yourself, terrified of yourself.

But alas, you cannot flee from yourself.

Do not, then, look at yourself,

because you cannot endure yourself.

For if you can endure yourself

without the horror of pain,

do not endure precisely this—

that you can endure yourself.

For to the extent that you can do this,

you are more like the first sinner

and more intolerable to God.

This is not strength,

but dullness of mind;  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “habit of death.”]

it is not health,

but hardened wickedness;

it does not arise from consolation,

but from condemnation.

Therefore do not endure,

without the empty groaning of your heart,

the horror of your inward face.

Since, then, you cannot flee from yourself,

at least do not look at yourself,

because you cannot endure yourself.

But behold something worse:

if I do not look at myself,

I deceive myself.

O excessively grievous distress!

If I look into myself,

I cannot endure myself;

if I do not look,

I do not know myself.

If I consider myself,

my face terrifies me;

if I do not consider myself,

my condemnation deceives me.

If I see myself,

the horror is unbearable;

if I do not see myself,

death is unavoidable.

Evil on this side, worse on that;

evil everywhere.

But excessively evil on this side,

exceedingly worse on that,

and exceedingly evil everywhere.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “Exceedingly worse on that side”; another: “exceedingly evil on that side.”]

Exceedingly wretched is the one

whom his conscience torments

and from which he cannot flee.

Still more wretched is the one

whose condemnation awaits him

and which he cannot avoid.

Exceedingly unhappy is the one

who is himself horrifying to himself.

Still more unhappy is the one

for whom death will be eternally perceptible.

Exceedingly sorrowful is the one

whom continual horrors of his foulness terrify.

Still more sorrowful is the one

whom eternal pains for his wickedness will torment.

This is evil, and this is evil;

but this is exceedingly evil,

and this is exceedingly evil.

To sin—what an evil and bitter thing you are!

Sins—how easy your entrances,

how difficult your exits!

Sinners, where are you bringing yourselves?

Within what bars are you shutting yourselves?  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “Among what things?”]

Understand, understand

how evil and bitter it is

to have abandoned the Lord.

You who have sinned, make restitution;

you who wish to sin, do not.

Do not, I say—do not.

Truly it is evil and bitter;

I have experienced it,

I am in it myself.  
[Note: Some manuscripts repeat: “Do not sin. It is evil and bitter. Do not. Truly it is evil and bitter. I have experienced it.” Ms. Carth.: “Do not sin. It is evil and bitter; do not—truly it is evil and bitter: I have experienced it.”]

For either continual pains

will torment my penitent life,

or eternal punishments

will afflict my soul when it is punished.

In either case it is certainly evil and bitter.

And surely the one guilty before God

is justly distressed between evil and worse—

exceedingly evil,

between exceedingly evil and exceedingly worse.  
[Note: Ms. Flor.: “between less evil and exceedingly evil.”]

It happens justly;

it happens rightly;

my judge is just.

But surely you yourself are God,

and Lord,

and my Creator.

Therefore, Creator, take away,

take away so great an evil

from your creature,

if it gives thanks because it is your work.

Rescue, Lord, rescue your servant

from such great evils,

if he rejoices to confess you as his Lord.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “who rejoices.”]

Spare, God, spare your sinner,

if he does not despair of your goodness.

For even if I judge myself

to have sinned more wickedly

than that first sinner,

I do not hate you as he did,

nor do I detest your goodness.

Therefore, through the merits of your great Baptist,

renew in me the grace of your baptism.

Let your grace precede me,

and let your mercy follow me.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “May your grace precede me.”]

Grant through the lament of repentance

what you gave through the sacrament of baptism.

Give to one who asks

what you gave to one who did not know.  
[Note: Corb. and Vict. 16: “Give to the penitent.”]

Restore the face that I defiled;

restore the innocence that I violated.

You who took away the sins

that I brought with me at birth,

take away the sins

that I acquired by living.

You who take away the sins of the world,

take away these sins,

the sins of the world

that I carry from my life in the world.

You who take away the sins of the world,

through the merits of the one

who showed you to the world by this testimony,

take away the sins

that I acquired in the world.

Take from me what is not from you,

because I hate what is from me,

and I still hope in you.

And you, holy John,

who showed to the world

the one who takes away its sins,

through the grace given to you,

grant me this mercy:

that he may take away my sins.

You, God, take away the sins of the world;

you, his friend, say:

“Behold, this one takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “You who are his friend.”]

Behold, before you is one burdened

with the sins of the world.

You take them away,

and you say:

“Behold me, the one from whom you should take away

what you yourself say you take away.”

Behold the physician,

and his witness;

and behold the sick person,

the physician’s servant and his work,

asking the physician

and his witness.

Truly, physician, I beg you:

heal me.

Truthful witness of the physician,

I beseech you:

pray for me.

Prove yourself to me in me:

your deed,

your word.

Let me experience what I hear;

let me feel what I believe.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “Let me know what I believe”; ms. Carth.: “Let me feel what I may believe.”]

Good Lord Jesus,

if you perform what he bears witness to,

let your work be accomplished in me.

John, proclaimer of God,

if you bear witness to what he performs,

let your word be fulfilled in me.

Heal me, Lord,

whose work it is to heal.

Obtain this for me, Lord,

you who can obtain it.

For you are a great Lord,

and you are great before the Lord.

You are supremely powerful through yourself,

and you are very powerful with him.

You are the supremely good God,

and you are his very good friend—

he who is forever merciful

and blessed God.

Amen.

### ORATION LXIV [formerly LXIII]  
[Note: Compared with mss. Thu. 267; Vict. RR. 3 and KK.; Corb. 168; Bec. O; Carthusian “a porta”; Saint-Germain 345; Vallis-Lucentis; and Floriacensis. “To Saint Peter the Apostle, with lamentable mourning over sins.” The manuscripts: “Prayer to Saint Peter the Apostle.”]

### TO SAINT PETER THE APOSTLE  
With lamentable mourning over sins

Holy and most kind Peter,  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “And kind Peter”; Vict. 3: “and kind.”]

faithful shepherd of God’s sheep,

prince of the apostles,

prince of so many princes,

you who bind and loose whatever you wish,

who heal and raise up whomever you wish,  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “whatever you wish.”]

who give the kingdom of heaven to whomever you wish:

great Peter, great—

so enriched with so many and such great gifts,  
[Note: Ms. Saint-Germain omits “so enriched with so many and such great gifts.”]

so exalted with so many and such great dignities,  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “exalted with gifts.”]

behold, I, the poorest and lowest little man,

surrounded by many grievous distresses,

miserably need the help of your great power.  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “marvelously need”; ms. Vict. 16: “the help of your kind power.”]

Yet my mouth has no words

with which to express my need as it truly is,

nor does my heart possess a devotion

that can rise from such lowliness

to your such great sublimity.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “to your holiness.”]

Again and again I try

to stir up my sluggish mind,

and to restrain it from empty things,

now that it has been scattered;

but, gathering all my strength,

it can neither break through

the darkness of its dullness,

which it has contracted from the filth of its sins,

nor remain for long in the same concentration.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “nor can it break out.”]

Alas for me, wretched beyond misery!

It is truly so;

there is no pretense;

it is so.

Who, then, will help the wretched one,

who can neither produce the voice of one in distress  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “the voice of one who is in distress.”]

nor the mind of one who grieves?

O great Peter,

if the cry of my distress

does not ascend as far as you,

may the gaze of your compassion descend as far as me;

may it break my hardness,

tear apart my darkness,

and look upon my distresses.

Look, kind shepherd,

upon the sheep of the flock entrusted to you;

have pitiful mercy on one who suffers miserably,

and on one who prays—not as much as his evils require,

but as much as they permit.

For behold, before the faithful shepherd

lies and groans a diseased sheep

before the Lord of shepherd and sheep.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “and gives birth.”]

The fugitive has returned

and asks pardon for error and disobedience.

To the compassionate physician  
[Note: “To the compassionate physician,” according to Bec., Vict., Vallis-Lucentis, and Floriacensis; ms. Thu.: “to the compassionate and physician”; another: “to the compassionate physician.”]

and shepherd she reveals

the bites of wolves,

the tearing wounds she incurred by straying,

and the ulcers she nourished through long neglect.

While she still draws breath,

she implores him to have mercy on her,

displaying her misery before the merciful shepherd

more by laying it bare than by pleading.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “by observing”; ms. Thu.: “by cursing.”]

Good shepherd Peter,

do not be difficult to persuade;

do not turn away your merciful eyes.  
[Note: Ms. Saint-Germain: “and do not turn them away.”]

Look upon the penitent, I beg you;

do not reject her.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “and do not reject her”; ms. Saint-Germain: “and do not despise her.”]

Do not delay hearing the suppliant.  
[Note: Ms. Saint-Germain: “and do not delay.”]

Because she rejected the life-giving pastures,

she languishes from lack of strength;

because she indulged in pestilential things,  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “deadly things.”]

she is tormented by the touch of diseases.  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “by attraction”; ms. Vict. 16: “by touch”; ms. Flor.: “by the touch”; another reading: “by contact.”]

Mature ulcers and battered wounds,

made worse by rotting,

quickly drag her toward death.

The wolves, having already tasted her blood,

lie in ambush,

waiting for her to be cast away.  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “waiting for her to be cast away there”; “already waiting to cast her away,” according to another reading.]

Her enemy, like a roaring lion,

prowls around seeking her to devour her (1 Pet. 5:8).

Faithful shepherd,

turn your eyes toward her

and recognize her as entrusted to you.

For even if she has strayed,

she has not denied the Lord and shepherd.

Look into her face

and notice the sign of your Lord and of his sheep.

If, beneath such squalor,

you do not recognize the face

washed and made radiant

in Christ’s font,

recognize the voice of confession

under the name of Christ—

the one who, after asking you three times

whether you loved him,

said to you, when you confessed three times:

“Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).  
[Note: The manuscript reads: “in the name.”]

Surely he is a lover of the sheep

who, before entrusting them,

so carefully examines the shepherd’s love.

Behold, you confess yourself to be his lover,

and she confesses herself to be his sheep.

Why, then, do you despise Christ’s sheep,

his shepherd?  
[Note: Mss. Vict. 3, Vallis-Lucentis, and Floriacensis: “Christ’s sheep, his shepherd”; ms. Vict. 16: “the sheep, the shepherd of the sheep.”]

Peter, shepherd of Christ,  
[Note: The manuscripts of Thu., Corb., Bec., Vict. 16, Vallis-Lucentis, and Floriacensis read: “Peter, lover of Christ.”]

gather Christ’s sheep again.

Your Lord, rejoicing,

placed the sheep he had sought and found upon his shoulders (Luke 15:5).

Do not drive her away as she returns

and begs.

Your Lord bought her with his blood

before she was born;

do not despise her, her shepherd,

now that she has been born again

and entrusted to you with such care.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “now born again.”]

Alas! How long will she fail to feel

that she has been received,

healed,

and refreshed?

[Col. 0974A]

O holy Peter,

if the name of shepherd and sheep

does not move you,

let the name of apostle,

of prince of the apostles,

and the name of a Christian soul

move you.  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “Prince of the Apostles.”]

For this is the sheep

I offer to you:

my soul,

regenerated by Christ’s baptism.

These wounds of which I spoke,

these ulcers,

these tears,

are not wounds of sheep’s flesh,

but of a rational spirit.

This hunger,

this lack of strength,

these torments,

are not afflictions of a sheep’s belly,

but of the human mind.

These wolves and these lions

are not four-footed animals,

but demons.

These great evils

are poverty of virtues

and heaped-up sins.

Since, therefore, I do not yet feel

that I have been heard,

and since distress presses upon me,

I shall repeat my account from the beginning  
[Note: “My account, and I shall multiply my prayer.” Ms. Thu.: “I shall set forth my petition”; ms. Corb.: “my account. I shall set forth.”]

and multiply my prayer.

Before the doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven

and the prince of the apostles,

I shall present a faithful but wretched soul

under the kingdom of sins,

gaping toward the kingdom of heaven,  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “inhabiting.”]

and for this reason invoking Peter,

the doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven

and prince of the apostles.

Behold, therefore, merciful Peter,

before you I present my soul:

loosened from the sinews of virtues,

bound by chains of vices,

weighed down by the burden of sins,

defiled by the filth of offenses,

torn apart by the wounds of demons,

putrid and foul with the ulcers of crimes.

As you see,

it is overwhelmed, oppressed,

surrounded, and enveloped

by these and other grave evils,

which you see better than I do,

and it is deprived of every support of good things.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “which you see better than I do”; ms. Vict. 16: “of every relief”; ms. Vict. 3: “of every covering.”]

Behold the wretched soul,

and the merciful apostle Peter,

before the merciful God,

who showed mercy to the apostle Peter,

commanded him to show it,

and gave him the power to do so.  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “who commanded him to show mercy and gave him the power to do so.”]

Behold misery,

and behold mercy:

the mercy of God

and of his apostle Peter;

the misery of a soul confessing God

and invoking God and Peter.

Will misery, then,

continue to oppress the soul

that looks toward God and Peter,

and will the mercy of God and Peter see this?  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “and will you see this through mercy”; ms. Vict. 16 omits “of God and Peter.”]

O God—and you, greater among his apostles—

what is this enormity of my misery,

if the immensity of your mercy

cannot prevail against it?

Or if it can, but does not wish to,

what is this enormity of my guilt,

which exceeds the multitude of your mercies?

Is it because I do not confess

everything I have sinned?

Behold, I confess that everything

you know me to have sinned

is true.

Is it because, neither by sufficient repentance

nor by repaying evil with good,

I do not make satisfaction?

Indeed it is so;

I confess it.

But this is precisely the misery

by which I am tormented.

Will mercy, then,

be slower the more misery constricts me?

O unheard-of word

from the merciful toward one who begs!

But I understand, just God;

I understand what you answer my soul:

“She rightly suffers what she voluntarily undertook,

and she is deservedly not heard,

because she did not obey.”

Alas, the bitterness of despair!

I recognize it;

I recognize that this sentence belongs to justice,

not to mercy.

Who summoned justice

to my case?

My speech was with mercy,

not with justice.

My sorrowful soul

begs bread of mercy from you, O God,

in its distress and misery.

Why do you crush its bones

with the stone of justice?  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “Why do you break them?”; ms. Bec.: “my bones.”]

May your mercy, merciful God,

through the merits  
[Note: Ms. Thu. omits “through the merits.”]

and intercession of your blessed apostle Peter,

hasten to rescue it

by forgiving its sins.  
[Note: Ms. Saint-Germain: “rescue my soul from every evil and every tribulation, and lead it to eternal life.”]

Holy Peter, prince of the apostles,

through the mercy shown to you

and the power given to you,

loose its bonds

and heal its wounds.

Free it from the misery

of the kingdom of sins;  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “from the misery of sins.”]

lead it into the blessedness

of the kingdom of heaven,

so that, rejoicing with you

and giving thanks,

it may praise God

forever and ever.

Amen.

### ORATION LXV [formerly LXXII]  
[Note: Compared with mss. Vict. KK. 16 and RR. 3; Thu. 267; Corb. 160; Bec. O; Saint-Germain; Vallis-Lucentis; and Floriacensis. The manuscripts: “Prayer to Saint Paul the Apostle.”]

### TO SAINT PAUL THE APOSTLE  
With fear of the final judgment and of sins

Holy Paul, great Paul,

you are that one who,

one of the great apostles of God,

following all the others in time,

surpassed them in labor

and effectiveness

in God’s cultivation.  
[Note: Ms. Saint-Germain reads: “Apostle of Christ, who are one who…”]

You who, while still burdened by mortality,

were caught up to the third heaven,

and, caught up into paradise,

heard things that it is not permitted

for a human being to speak.

Among Christians you were not merely

like a nurse nurturing her children,  
[Note: Ms. Vict. 16: “nurturing your children.”]

but also, with astonishing concern,

you were again in labor with your children.  
[Note: Ms. Thu.: “but in your concern”; the manuscripts: “astonishing in affection.”]

You became all things to all people,

so that you might win all.

To you, Lord—to you,

known to the world through these

and many other words and deeds

as possessing great power with God

and boundless compassion toward human beings—

to you comes one who is certainly

an exceedingly great sinner,

one exceedingly accused

before the powerful  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “before the almighty.”]

and severe Judge, God,

charged not with one,

not with a few,

but with countless crimes;

not merely small,

but also immense;

not doubtful,

but certain;  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “but also certain.”]

not with a brief accusation,

but one as long as his life;

not by a single accuser,

but by as many as know his offenses.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “as many as his offenses are.”]

For the severe Judge himself

is my accuser,

and I am his manifest sinner.

All good and evil spirits also

accuse me before God with him:

the good, because they owe God justice;

the evil, because they preserve my wickedness;

the good, because they testify to the truth

which they contemplate;

the evil, because they seek my punishment

which they desire.  
[Note: Ms. Vict. 16: “which they await.”]

They also judge my wickedness in this matter,

because they know

that I deserve to be condemned

according to justice.

Alas! How many judges,

how many accusers

against one wretched man!

How severe they are against the weak!

How strict against the exposed sinner!

Alas! Whom will he have to excuse him

when he has God as his accuser?

Who—even one—will be his intercessor,

if all are his accusers and judges?

But I myself also,

compelled by conscience,

am my own accuser and judge.

For I confess

that I have sinned excessively,

and therefore deserved

a severe condemnation.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “and therefore a great condemnation.”]

O even irrational

and senseless things,

if I am not myself senseless,

confound me.  
[Note: Other manuscripts read: “All irrational things,” or “O other irrational things.”]

For I understand

that I ought to blush before every creature,

because I sinned against the one

who is so powerful that he could make it,

and so good that he wished to make it.

I am also confounded by myself,

because I too was made by him.

Woe! From where do so many

and such great evils rush upon me

that they overwhelm this wretched man?

My evil sins,

from you all these evils flow upon me.

You attract accusers;

you remove those who might excuse me;

you bring the condemner;

you exclude the intercessor;

you provoke the avenger;

you turn away the pardoner;

you lead the understanding

into fear and confusion;

you cut off from it

hope and consolation;  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “you hide from it”; others: “you cut it off.”]

you drive it into eternal destruction;

you repel every aid.

And, to make still more miserable

whatever you miserably do to me,

you add this to heap up my misery:

although the matter truly is so,

it seems to me as though it were not so.

Truth shows that it is so,

and yet feeling does not perceive it.

Reason teaches it,

and the heart does not grieve.

I see that it is so,

and, alas, I cannot dissolve entirely

into tears because it is so.

If I could do this,

perhaps I would hope;

by hoping, I would pray;

by praying, I would obtain.

But since feeling and sorrow

are not in me in proportion

to my distresses,  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “are not,” plural.]

how shall I hope?

How shall I pray without hope?

What shall I obtain without prayer?

[Col. 0976D]

Unhappy little man,

what has become of your prayer?

Where have your hope and confidence vanished?

I had begun to pray

with the confidence of presumption,

but despair arising from an understanding of the truth

came upon me,

and prayer failed

through despair of any compassion toward me.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “prayer failed,” or “prayer has failed.”]

For if everything that exists

is justly against me,

whose compassion is with me?

If everything that exists

is rightly hostile to me,

whose mercy will turn toward me?

If the Creator and the creature

rightly despise me,

whose gaze looks upon me?

Wretched sinner,

if this is so,

nothing remains for you

except to grow numb away from hope,

to be silent away from prayer,

and always to lie

in your misery.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “and always to lie”; another reading omits “so.”]

Surely, since you voluntarily

made yourself wretched,

you must justly remain wretched forever.

Indeed, miserable sins,

this is how you repay your promises.

While you attract,

you promise sweetness;

when you drag one completely in,

you drench your possession in bitterness.

While you persuade,

you anoint;

after you have persuaded,  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “after you persuade.”]

you prick the soul unto death.

While you call it into your pit,

you show repentance’s pain

as though it offered an easy return;

but when you hurl it down,

you bury what you have hurled down,

blind what you have buried,

harden what you have blinded,

and close every exit

for the one you have hardened.  
[Note: One manuscript reads: “you harden every exit.”]

And thus you make your wretched victim—

deceived, captured, and bound—

despair,

be silent,

and lie senseless,

as though lost to God

and forgetful of God.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “forgetful of himself.”]

You do this until you sell him

to the merchants of hell,

who carry their merchandise

into the lake of death.

You have done all this to me;

I have experienced all of it,

except that I have not yet

been handed over to those merchants.

Yet I too await this,

miserably and fearfully,

while they await it

with malicious delight.  
[Note: The manuscripts read: “I have experienced it, except that I have not yet been handed over to those merchants; this too I await.”]

Alas! how evil it is thus to despair, thus to be silent, thus to lie! And alas! how vain [Note: [Col. 0977D] “How vain,” manuscript of Victor 3; “how evil”] it is to cry out without hope, to strive without hope! O God, whose goodness is not exhausted, whose mercy is not emptied, whose knowledge does not fail, whose power accomplishes whatever he wills, where can I draw breath, compelled as I am by my sins thus to despair? For although you are angry with sinners, yet, gracious Lord, you are accustomed to give counsel to those who ask [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Counsel to those who ask,” manuscripts; “counsel to the penitent”]. Teach me, Lord, from where I ought to hope, so that I may be able to pray. For I wish to pray to you; but I neither know how, because of my ignorance, nor can I, because of my hardness, and I am prevented by despair, because of my wickedness. I seek something that might excuse me, and there is nothing that does not accuse me. I seek one who will pray for me, and I find that everything is against me. I seek one who will have mercy on the wretched, and everything that exists opposes the wretched man.

[Col. 0978A]

Jesus, good Lord, why did you come from heaven? What did you do in the world? Why did you give yourself over to death, except to save sinners? Holy Paul, what else did you teach as you travelled through the world? To this faith you and his apostles, and especially you, invite us sinners; you show us this alone as a safe refuge. How, then, shall I not hope, if I believe this and ask in this faith? Or how will this hope deceive me, if the faith from which it arises does not deceive me? Jesus, God, and you, his apostle, I, a sinner, believe this faith at your instruction [Note: [Col. 0977D] “At your instruction I yield,” manuscripts; “at your instruction I believe”]; upon it I throw myself—indeed, long ago I threw myself. Led by this faith, I have approached you to pray [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Led, I approached you,” manuscripts of Corbie, Thuanus, and Val-luc; “led, I approached you,” manuscripts of Bec, Victor, and Florence; “clothed, I approached you”]. In this faith I ask, in this faith I seek, in this faith I knock: have mercy on the sinner [Note: [Col. 0977D] “That you may have mercy on the sinner,” manuscripts]; you by sparing, you by interceding; you by saving, you by praying. In this faith I wrap myself before you, so that I may lie hidden from the inquisitors and exactors of my sins, and from the blow of your, O God, strict judgment. At your counsel the sinner asks this concealment; I beseech you, do not expose him [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Beseeching that he not be exposed,” manuscripts] to your judgment for condemnation.

But alas! behold, another grave evil presents itself [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Another evil presents itself,” manuscripts; “and another evil presents itself”]. I had hoped to obtain hope through faith [Note: [Col. 0977D] “I hoped to obtain hope,” manuscript of Victor 16; “I hoped”], and behold, I see that I do not even possess faith. I thought that I was wrapped in this faith, and I recognize that I have been stripped of it [Note: [Col. 0977D] “That I was stripped of it,” manuscripts; “stripped of it”]. I trusted that I was hiding in it, and I feel that I am exiled from it; for faith without works is dead (James 2:20); but dead faith is not faith. Therefore whoever has dead faith does not have faith. Woe! The fruitfulness of evil works prevented me from having hope, and the barrenness of good works proves that I lack faith. Woe to the one who acts wickedly! Woe to the one who neglects what is good! For just as it is necessary to displease God through evil works, so it is impossible to please God without faith, which is nothing without good works [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Without good works,” manuscript of Thuanus; “without works”].

[Col. 0978C]

Indeed, if the just man lives by faith, then the one who has no faith is dead. But if the one barren of good works is dead [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Dead of good works,” manuscript of Bec; “dead of good works”], how much more dead is the one fruitful in evil [Note: [Col. 0977D] “How much more,” manuscripts of Victor, Bec, Val-luc, and Florence; “how much,” manuscripts]? For if the tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down as dry, then surely the one that produces evil fruit is uprooted [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Will be cut down … will be uprooted,” manuscripts; “is cut down … is uprooted] as harmful. This death is not of the flesh, but of the soul. How much greater, and how much worse, is that death by which one dies than the death by which one dies in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0977D] “How much greater,” manuscript of Thuanus; “how much more detestable than the evil is this death”; “how much greater,” manuscripts of Victor, Bec, Val-luc, and Florence]. For all human flesh, once dead, will at some time rise again, but not every dead soul rises again. And that death which perhaps takes away a life that will never return destroys more than the death which takes away a life that must eventually return [Col. 0978D]. And the one who loses the life of righteousness, through which he loses blessed life, dies worse than the one who loses this wretched life. Finally, much more grievously and miserably perishes the one who abandons the life which, if preserved, restores a better bodily life even when that life has been lost [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Restores the lost,” manuscripts; “restores the lost life,” manuscript of Val-luc], and without which it is better not to have been born, than the one who abandons that life without which nothing prevents the soul from being blessed.

I live this wretched life, and I am dead to that blessed life. I live in what is lesser in me; I am dead in what is better [Note: [Col. 0979D] “I am dead in that,” manuscript of Victor 3; “and I am dead in that”]. Therefore I am more dead than alive; and I am dead more miserably than I shall die in the flesh. For that death would not be evil for me, except because this one already precedes it [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Than I am dead in the flesh: for that death,” manuscripts of Bec, Victor, Corbie, Val-luc, and Florence; “than I shall be dead in the flesh: for that death,” manuscript of Thuanus; “than I am dead in the flesh, than I shall be dead in the flesh”].

Holy Paul, I came to you as a sinner in need of reconciliation, and behold, I have been found dead before you, in need of resurrection [Note: [Col. 0979D] “I came to you as dead,” manuscripts; Victor omits “as”]. I came as a guilty man needing an intercessor, and I have been found wickedly dead, in need of one who would raise me. I came as a wretched man, and I found myself most wretched. I approached as one accused yet alive, and behold, before you I am dead and condemned. For although I have not yet been handed over to death that torments, I have already been abandoned to the death that draws it to itself. For although I have not yet been thrust into the prison of torments [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Although I am not yet,” manuscripts of Victor 3 and Val-luc; “although I have not yet been”], I have already been shut up in the pit of sins. For although I am not yet buried in hell [Note: [Col. 0979D] Manuscript of Victor 16 omits “for”], yet I am already as one destined to be buried, wrapped in sins.

This, certainly, was why I could neither pray nor knew how to pray. This truly was the case [Note: [Col. 0979D] “This certainly was the case,” manuscripts of Victor 3, Bec, and Thuanus; “this truly was the case”], because I understood myself to be hateful to every being, and, like one without sensation, I did not grieve. I understood through the rationality of nature; I did not feel through the insensibility of death [Col. 0979C]. Truly I was dead, and I came dead, and therefore I found myself dead.

O God, who will pray for this dead man? Holy Paul, I have brought him to you; do not turn him away [Note: [Col. 0979D] Manuscript of Thuanus omits “do not turn him away”]; pray for him. Lord, Elijah [Note: [Col. 0979D] “To him, O God, Elijah,” manuscripts; “to him, Lord Elijah”] and Elisha, when they raised the dead, joined themselves to the dead, and fitted living limbs to dead limbs. Lord, the living made contact with the dead and gave them life [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Lord Paul, the living,” manuscripts; “Paul” omitted], while the dead brought the living nothing but glory [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Nothing but,” manuscript of Thuanus omits]. Lord, you too say that you made yourself all things to all people, so that you might win them all.

Friend of God, the examples of others make me presume; your words urge me to trust. Therefore I shall speak, Lord, I shall speak; Lord, Lord, descend to this dead man, spread yourself over this dead man, make yourself not dead, but as this dead man. Let this dead man, warmed by the touch of your compassion [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Compassion,” manuscript of Victor 16; “passion”], be rekindled; let this dead man live again through the effect [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Effect,” manuscripts; “affection”] of your power [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Let your power bring him back to life,” manuscript of Thuanus; “let him live again through your power], so that, alive, he may glorify God, and, as this dead man, glorify you. Lord, you are not powerless to raise this dead man, since, as God testifies, God’s grace is sufficient for you. For if it was sufficient for you while you lived on earth, surely it has not failed you while you dwell in heaven [Note: [Col. 0979D] “It does not fail,” manuscripts; “it has not failed”]. Why, Lord, should this dead man, offered to you, lie any longer without life, when God testifies to your power and you yourself testify to your compassion?

Lord God, you say to Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Holy Paul, you say to us: “I have become all things to all people” (1 Corinthians 9:22). And behold, this dead man, brought to you in this hope, awaits the fulfillment of your words [Note: [Col. 0979D] “The fulfillment of your word,” manuscript of Victor 16]. You speak, and the dead man, hearing, hopes. You promise, and the dead man, praying, waits. You speak, and what has been proclaimed has come from you; I beseech you, let me experience through your action [Col. 0980B] what the world rejoices has been made known through you [Note: [Col. 0979D] “The fulfillment, which,” manuscripts; “the effect, which”]. If you do not deny what you have said, why do you deny its fulfillment to one who asks? Or to whom can a dead man more securely be carried to be raised, if, brought by you, he is returned dead by you [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Dead by you,” manuscript of Victor 16; “dead by us”]? Where are you sending him, if you dismiss him thus? Where will he go, if he departs from you? O God, who raises him if God does not raise him? From whom may he hope, if he despairs of God? From whom can lost life be recovered [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Life is recovered,” manuscript of Victor 16; “life is restored], except from him from whom it was first received?

Holy Paul, who will be compassionate toward one in need and pain, if the one who promises to be weak with the weak is harsh? Who will deign to pray for the wretched [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Deign for the wretched,” manuscript of Victor 16; “may deign for the wretched”], if the one who proclaims himself all things to all people disdains him? Or who will even be heard [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Or even hears,” manuscript of Thuanus; “or is even heard”], if the one for whom God’s grace is sufficient is not heard [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Is not heard,” manuscript of Thuanus; “does not hear”]? Does compassion or power fail him for whom God’s grace is sufficient?

O you two, what moves you, if these things do not move you? From where shall I take, except from you, what I may present to you to stir your mercy? What can a dead soul present about itself except that it is sinful and wretched? Yet, repentant and grieving, it prays. If only the one who came from heaven to call sinners to repentance [Note: [Col. 0979D] “To repentance,” manuscripts; “into repentance”], and the one who laboured more than all others for this very purpose after him, were to despise the repentant soul because it is sinful! If the one who came forth from the bosom of the Father to bear our sorrows, and the one who says that he is weak with the weak [Note: [Col. 0979D] “With the weak,” manuscripts; “with those who are weak”], were to despise the grieving because she is wretched [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Because he is wretched,” manuscripts of Victor and Val-luc; “because she is wretched”]! If the one who made himself dead in order to raise dead souls, and the one who declares that he made himself all things to all people, were to reject the one who prays [Col. 0980D] because she is dead [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Because he is dead,” manuscripts of Victor 16; “because she is dead”]! God forbid; let it not be so [Col. 0981A]. If it is so, compassion has perished. If it is thus, mercy is dead.

Soul cast out and rejected: when you sinned, you were cast out; when you plead, you are rejected. Where will you turn? Turn to persistence. They seek one who grieves importunately; they want the wretched one to be insistent; they love one who mourns without ceasing [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Without ceasing,” manuscripts of Victor, Val-luc, and Florence; “unceasing”]. Seek, then, still [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Seek still,” manuscripts; “seek, then, still”] something in them that you may press against him, something indefatigable [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Indefatigable,” manuscript; “indefatigable”] that you may bring forward.

O holy Paul, where is that famous nurse of the faithful, cherishing her children? Where is that loving mother who everywhere proclaims that she gives birth to her children again? Sweet nurse, sweet mother, what children do you give birth to or nurse, except those whom, teaching and training in Christ’s faith, you beget and educate [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Giving birth by teaching and educating,” manuscript of Victor 16; “you beget by teaching and educate,” manuscripts of Val-luc and Florence; manuscript of Florence adds “you beget by teaching and instructing”]? Or what Christian, after your teaching, was not born and strengthened in the faith? For although this blessed faith was born and nourished for us also through the other apostles, it was so especially through you, because you laboured and accomplished more than all in this matter [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Who laboured more,” manuscripts; “because you laboured more”]. Since they are mothers to us, then, you are more truly our mother.

Therefore, holy Paul, this dead man is your son. Mother, this dead man is surely your son. Sweet mother, recognize your son from the voice of confession; let him recognize his mother from the feeling of compassion. Recognize your son from his confession of Christianity; let him recognize his mother from the sweetness of your mercy. Offer, mother—you who give birth to your children again—offer your dead son to him who by his death raised your servants. Offer, mother, your son to him who by his undeserved death recalled his guilty ones from their deserved death; offer him your son, so that he may restore his lost life to him.

For through baptism he was led out of death; through barrenness and perversity he has been led back into death [Col. 0981C]. Mother of renowned affection, let your son feel the bowels of maternal compassion. Present him to him who raised you and preserved you alive. Pray to him for your son, because he is his servant; pray to him for his servant, because he is your son [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Pray to him for his son, because he is your son,” manuscripts; “pray to him for your Son, because he is his servant. Pray to him for his servant, because he is your son”].

But you also, Jesus, good Lord—are you not also a mother? Are you not a mother, you who are like a hen gathering her chicks beneath her wings? Truly, Lord, you too are a mother. For what others brought forth and gave birth to, they received from you. You first died in labour for them and for those whom they brought forth [Note: [Col. 0981C] “You first for them, and what they brought forth,” manuscripts of Thuanus and Florence; “you for them, and those whom they brought forth”]; labouring, you died, and by dying you gave birth. For if you had not laboured, you would not have died [Note: [Col. 0981C] “You would not have endured death,” manuscripts of Victor 16 and Florence; “you would not have died”]; and if you had not died, you would not have given birth. From desire to beget children unto life, you tasted death, and dying [Col. 0982A] you gave birth. You did it through yourself; they did it at your command and with your help. You as author [Note: [Col. 0981C] “You as author,” manuscript of Victor 16; “you as author”], they as ministers. Therefore you, Lord God, are more truly a mother.

So you are both mothers. For although you are fathers, you are also mothers [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Yet mothers,” manuscripts; “yet also mothers”]. For you brought it about [Note: [Col. 0981C] “You brought him about,” manuscripts]: you through yourself, you through him, so that we who had been born unto death might be reborn unto life.
