You are therefore fathers by what you accomplish, mothers by your affection; fathers by authority, mothers by kindness; fathers by protection, mothers by compassion. Therefore you too are a mother [Note: [Col. 0981C] “And you are a mother,” manuscripts of Corbie and Victor 16; “and you are Father,” manuscript of Florence; “and you are both mother and father”], and you too are a mother; although unequal in the quantity of affection, you are nevertheless alike in quality. Although you do not equal one another in the greatness of kindness [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Although the greatness,” manuscripts of Victor 16, Val-luc, and Florence; “although in the greatness”], you agree in will; although you do not coincide in the fullness of compassion, you do not disagree in intention.

Why should I be silent about what you say [Note: [Col. 0981C] “What do you say? What is it that you say?” manuscript of Victor 16; “what you say?”]? Why should I conceal what you proclaim [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Why do I conceal,” manuscript of Thuanus; “why should I conceal”]? Why do I hide what you do [Col. 0982B]? You proclaim yourselves mothers; I confess myself your son. I give thanks: you gave birth to me when you made me a Christian [Note: [Col. 0981C] “You gave birth … you made,” manuscripts; “you gave birth … you made”]; you through yourself, and you through that same one; you through the teaching made by you, and you through the teaching inspired in you; you through the grace granted to me by you, and you through the grace received from him. Paul, mother, he himself gave birth to you [Note: [Col. 0981C] “He himself, as mother, gave birth to you,” manuscripts; “he himself gave birth to you”].

Place, then, your dead son before the feet [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Before the feet,” manuscript of Thuanus; “before his sight”] of Christ, your mother, because he is her son. Rather, cast him into the bosom of her compassion, because she is more truly a mother. Pray that she raise the dead son, not so much yours as her own. Pray for your son, because you are a mother [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Because you are a mother,” manuscript of Victor 16; “who is a mother”], so that she may give life to her son, because she is a mother. Do, mother of my soul, what the mother of my flesh would do. Surely, if she had hope, she would pray as much as she could, nor would she cease until she obtained her request, if she could. Certainly, if you wish, you cannot despair; and if you pray, you can obtain. Persist, then, so that the dead soul whom you gave birth to alive may be restored to life; and do not cease until she is returned alive to you.

You too, dead soul [Note: [Col. 0981C] “My dead soul,” manuscripts omit “my”], run beneath the wings of Jesus, your mother, and complain of your sorrows beneath her feathers. Ask her to nurse your wounds and, once nursed, to restore life [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Let life return,” manuscript of Florence; “let her restore life”]. Christ, mother, you who gather your chicks beneath your wings [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Chicks beneath your wings,” manuscript of Thuanus; “chicks beneath your feathers”], this dead chick of yours [Note: [Col. 0981C] Manuscript of Victor omits “yours”] submits itself beneath your wings [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Beneath your wings,” manuscript of Thuanus; “beneath your feathers”]. For by your gentleness the terrified are warmed [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Are strengthened,” manuscript of Florence; “are warmed”], and by your fragrance those who despair are restored. Your warmth gives life to the dead; your touch justifies sinners.

Recognize, mother, your dead son, either through the sign of your cross or through the voice of your confession. Warm your chick [Col. 0983A], raise your dead one, justify your sinner. Let your terrified one be consoled by you; let the one despairing of himself be strengthened by you; and let him be restored through you to your complete and inseparable grace. For from you flows the consolation of the wretched. Blessed are you unto ages of ages. Amen.

## PRAYER LXVI [formerly LXIV] [Note: [Col. 0983C] Collated with the manuscripts Thuanus 267 and San-Germanensis 345. For it is not read in the other manuscripts.]

### TO SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

Holy and devout Andrew, brother of the chief of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0983C] The manuscripts omit “brother of the chief of the apostles” through “at the door of your compassion”], most devout of the apostles, gentlest of the saints; you, John’s disciple and diligent hearer; you, eager pursuer of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world and careful investigator of his dwelling; you, eager guide to Jesus of your brother Simon and your fellow citizen Philip; you, I say, preacher and lover of the cross, and through it a devout imitator of the good Master, at the door of your compassion [Note: [Col. 0983C] “At the door of your famous compassion,” manuscripts; “at the door of your compassion”] my soul sits and cries out as a beggar.

Lend the ear of your mercy, open the door of your compassion [Note: [Col. 0983C] “The door of your great compassion,” manuscripts; “the door of compassion”], and admit [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of Thuanus: “and dismiss”] the cry of the poor man fleeing to you: you whose compassion was so great that you were surnamed the compassionate Andrew by all [Note: [Col. 0983C] “You were to be surnamed,” manuscripts; “you are surnamed”].

There is no intercessor to plead my cause with you; there is no one to bring before you the urgency of my need. Therefore let your own compassion plead for me with you, and make you favorable [Note: [Col. 0983C] “Let it plead with you and make you favorable,” manuscripts; “let your compassion plead for me with you; there is no one to bring before you the urgency of my need [manuscript of Thuanus: ‘to carry it before you’]. Therefore let your compassion plead for me with you, and make you favorable”] toward me.

If my wretched and pitiable soul turns away from you, if it does not receive from you the bread of mercy, to whom will it go [Note: [Col. 0983C] “If it turns away, to whom will it go,” manuscripts; “if it turns away from you, if it does not receive from you the bread of mercy, to whom will it go”]? Whom will it entreat? Shut out by others, it flees to you, whom it had heard to be renowned [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscripts: “so renowned”; “so” omitted] for immense compassion. Completely consumed by hunger, it will utterly fail, because, coming from far away, it has nothing to eat [Col. 0983C], nor is there anyone who will have mercy on it, 290 and give it something good.

Moreover [Note: [Col. 0983C] “Which also,” manuscripts], it has fallen among robbers who stripped it of love of God and of every virtue, wounded it even with the deadly weapons of vices, and left it—not half-alive, I say, but almost wholly extinguished [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of San-Germanensis: “leaving it, I do not say half-alive, but wholly extinguished”; manuscript of Thuanus: “leaving it half-alive”; “leaving it, I do not say half-alive, but almost wholly extinguished”].

At last let that compassion come to your mind which that fountain of all compassion, from whom you drew such compassion, showed toward people like these. “I have compassion,” he said, “on the crowd, because they have remained with me now for three days and have nothing to eat” (Matthew 8:2). You heard and were present and took part when, in compassion for them, he fully satisfied more than five thousand people with five loaves [Col. 0984A]. Will you therefore restrain the bowels of your compassion from a soul already failing from hunger, seeking from you the bread of mercy, and now waiting for you so long [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of San-Germanensis omits “therefore”; “failing? Will you restrain the bowels of your compassion from a soul already failing, seeking from you the bread of mercy, and waiting for you so long?”; “failing? Will you restrain …”]? Will you be impious toward me alone? Or because I have sinned too greatly, have I deserved that mercy be entirely denied me [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of San-Germanensis: “Or because I have sinned too greatly, have I deserved that mercy be entirely denied me”; manuscript of Thuanus: “Or because I have sinned too greatly”; “Or because I have sinned too greatly”]?

Certainly mercy and compassion are not needed where there is no misery or want. And the greater the need that presses, the more renowned is the mercy. Who, then, will imitate the master of compassion in carrying out the command of compassion, if you do not imitate him who are proclaimed compassionate above all others?

Are you troubled by my persistence [Note: [Col. 0983C] The manuscript of San-Germanensis omits from “You are troubled by my persistence” through “Behold, he lies before you”]? But what am I to do? For if I do not cry out, I am dead, because I shall fail and perish. But if I do not cease crying out, I fear that I shall be troublesome to you [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of Thuanus: “I wish to cry out; woe to the wretched man who is troublesome”; “but if I do not cease crying out, I am troublesome”]. Good teacher, teach my heart what to pray for, and how it ought to entreat you with some effectiveness.

Good teacher [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of Thuanus: “I ought to entreat you, so that I may be able to obtain what I ask. Good teacher”], taught by him who does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that he be converted and live [Note: [Col. 0983C] “May he live, taught,” manuscript of Thuanus; “may he live, having been taught”], look with the gaze of compassion upon a sinful soul which desires to be converted and return to its Creator. Submerged in the mud of vices, she struggles and strives to rise, but lacking the strength by which she might lift herself up, she is already failing from pitiable weariness [Note: [Col. 0983C] “She does not have it; she failed,” manuscript of Thuanus; “not having it, she failed”].

For a long time now, labouring, she has cried out and waited for you. Her eyes have failed while she hopes in her God (Psalm 68:4). Where, then, is your compassion, where your goodness [Note: [Col. 0983C] “Your compassion, where your mercy,” manuscript of Thuanus; “compassion, where goodness; where your mercy”], where your mercy? So that she may not perish utterly in despair, stretch out your hand to the one who asks; lift her up, hold her, support her, until she reaches him whom she thirsts for and desires—namely, the mercy of her Creator.

Shepherd of the Church, admit the wandering sheep that longs to return, seeks and implores [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of Thuanus: “and weeps”] to deserve admission. Will you exclude one wishing to enter, whom you would call back if she did not wish to return, and carry on your shoulders? If you exclude her, the supreme shepherd will perceive the loss of his flock. For the lion prowls [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of Thuanus: “the lion prowling”], seeking someone to devour—a lion whom you yourself perhaps feared to be devoured by when you cried out from the cross in devout and merciful prayer [Note: [Col. 0983C] Manuscript of Thuanus omits “from the cross”]:

“Lord, do not permit your servant to remain separated from you any longer [Col. 0985A] in error, like a sheep [Note: [Col. 0985D] Manuscript of Thuanus: “Lord, any longer”; “Lord, your servant, any longer”; “to remain separated like a sheep”] without a shepherd.”

Then the supreme shepherd heard and answered your cry, and at once took you with him and placed you in heaven. Hear, then, now, the cry of the lost sheep, which returns from far away and begs to be admitted. Show her the same merciful aid that the compassionate shepherd showed you when you underwent the same necessity.

Receive her, wishing to return to the fold, longing with all her heart to be joined to her flock from which she had strayed. Of that wounded man whom the Samaritan healed, when the Lord had recalled the story, what did he finally add [Note: [Col. 0985D] “What did he add?” manuscript of Thuanus]? “Go, and you do likewise” (Luke 10:37) [Note: [Col. 0985D] The manuscripts omit: “Mercy itself commands and invites you to become merciful”].

Behold, before you lies my soul, wounded and badly torn. Pour in the oil of compassion; apply the aid of your intercession [Note: [Col. 0985D] “Of your devout intercession,” manuscript of San-Germanensis], if in any way she may escape the danger of eternal death [Col. 0985B]. He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, will gladly hear you supplicating for us (Romans 8:32) [Note: [Col. 0985D] “His Son,” manuscripts; “the Son”].

You too, my soul, sick animal, lost sheep through your own fault, return to the shepherd. And because you do not deserve to be admitted by yourself, ask devout Andrew to admit you into the shelter of his protection, so that through his intercession the compassionate Saviour, who came to seek what had strayed and save what had perished (Luke 19:10), may heal the sick, save the lost, bring the erring one back to the fold, and join her to the flock—he who is blessed forever. Amen [Note: [Col. 0985D] Manuscript of Thuanus adds: “He handed him over. To whom be honour and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.” It then repeats: “You too, my soul, sick animal, lost sheep through your own fault, return to the shepherd. And because you do not deserve to be admitted by yourself, ask devout Andrew to admit you into the shelter of his protection; so that through his intercession the compassionate Saviour, who came to seek what had strayed and save what had perished, may heal the sick, save the lost, bring the erring one back to the fold, and join her to the flock—he who is blessed forever. Amen.”]

## PRAYER LXVII [formerly LXV] [Note: [Col. 0985D] Collated with manuscripts Victor KK. 16 and RR. 3; recension O; Corbie 160, Thuanus 267, San-Germanensis 345, Val-luc, and Florence. “To blessed John the Evangelist, for fear of condemnation,” manuscripts Thuanus, Bec, and Carthusian. “To Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, for the forgiveness of sins,” manuscripts Corbie, Victor, and Florence. “To Saint John the Evangelist,” manuscript Val-luc. “Prayer to Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist.”]

### TO SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST [Col. 0985C]

For fear of condemnation.

Holy and blessed [Note: [Col. 0985D] “Holy and most blessed,” manuscripts; “holy and blessed,” manuscript of Florence] John, highest of God’s evangelists [Note: [Col. 0985D] Manuscript of San-Germanensis omits “of God”], most beloved of God’s apostles; you so especially beloved by God among those especially beloved by him that surpassing love is your distinctive sign among them; you, that John who was accustomed to recline upon the glorious breast of the Most High [Note: [Col. 0985D] “Upon that,” manuscripts of Victor, San-Germanensis, and Val-luc]; you whom God appointed as a son to his mother in his own place, when by dying bodily he departed from her:

To you, blessed one, so much the friend and beloved of God, this little man, guilty before God, approaches to entreat you, so that through an intercessor so beloved he may escape the anger of God threatening him. For his necessity, Lord, compels the guilty man to seek an intercessor, and that famous intimacy of yours with the one whom he fears as avenger comes to mind [Col. 0986A]. Therefore, Lord, assured through that same intimacy of your power—for you will accomplish with him whatever you wish [Note: [Col. 0985D] “For what you wish with him,” manuscripts; “whatever you wish with him”]—and hoping in your compassion, because you will not despise the wretched man crying out to you in distress, I turn to you, though tepidly, yet with all the affection of my mind, and I dare to ask for that powerful intercession of yours on behalf of my sinful soul, so that through you she may be drawn back from the torments to which my many iniquities are dragging her.

But alas for me, wretched man! How contrary to this do my sins promise me [Note: [Col. 0985D] “For they promise me contrary things,” manuscripts; “how contrary”]! For while I try to take courage through your intimacy with God, I am compelled even more to be frightened by that same intimacy, because of my perversity against God [Col. 0986B]. For, O Beloved of God, since I sinned against the one you love, I am certain that I have deserved your hatred also.

O immeasurable guilt! Guilt against God, which not only offends him, but also those who can intercede with him. For it is truly the case that the one guilty before God is deservedly hateful to God’s friends—and not only to his friends, but certainly also to himself and to every creature of his.

Sins, sins, how much more you are feared the more you are considered! For you—where do you lead, and to where do you bring the wretched little man whom you deceive [Note: [Col. 0985D] “You—whence,” manuscript of Victor 16; “you—whence do you lead us”]? From where does the unhappy soul that follows you fall, and where is it hurled headlong [Note: [Col. 0985D] “That follows you,” manuscript of Victor 16; “that will follow you”]? What does that miserable soul lose, and what does it acquire, when through your wickedness it is thrust from the love of God—which it could have retained through innocence—into hatred of God and of all his creatures?

If sins therefore bring such universal abhorrence upon the one whom they draw away from God, where will the little man hide himself, to whom will he show himself, carrying about the burden of his sins, which he cannot himself lay down, dreadful and foul with the wounds and ulcers of his sins, which he cannot himself heal? Such does my soul approach before you, beloved John of God; indeed, this is my soul, this wretched soul of mine [Note: [Col. 0985D] “My wretchedness,” manuscript of Thuanus; “my misery,” manuscript of Florence; “my wretched soul”], which, making herself a friend of this world and overwhelming herself with the multitude of her sins, has made herself an enemy of God. Alas! the name accursed by every being—the name “enemy of God”! Alas, how wickedly I have drawn it upon myself, how justly it has been charged to me!

Distress! The truth of the matter proves me an enemy of God, and the enormity of the horror prevents me from confessing it. Distress! I have provoked God and all things to vengeance, and I have left nothing unoffended to intercede for me. Sorrows, pains, groans, roars—where are you, if you are absent here? Where do you burn, if you are lukewarm here? Tear apart my frame by tormenting it; consume my inner parts by burning them; rage within my heart [Note: [Col. 0987C] “Tumulamini” (“make tumult”), manuscripts of Bec, Thuanus, Victor, and Corbie; “tumultuamini” (“make tumult”)], if perhaps some mercy may look upon my misery [Note: [Col. 0987C] “My misery,” manuscript of Florence; “my soul”].

O merciful friends of God, have mercy on one so needy, by that mercy which God has shown you. Come to my aid, lest God’s anger overwhelm me together with his enemies. I do not wish, I detest and abominate being, or being called, his enemy, although I confess that I am his sinner. Come to my aid, at least one of you [Note: [Col. 0987C] Manuscripts: “at least one of you”].

[Col. 0987B]

You, that disciple whom Jesus loved—if you recognize your sign—I ask you, by this very love, that in such great need I may recognize your help. John, John, if you are that disciple whom Jesus loved, I beg you, by this very thing [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscript of Saint-Germain reads “through this one” instead of “through this very thing”], that through you I may be that sinner whom Jesus may forgive [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscript of Saint-Germain reads “I, the sinner, through you” instead of “I, the sinner”]. If that glorious breast of yours was a familiar resting place, I ask that through you it may likewise be for me a saving place of propitiation. I confess, my Lord, beloved of God, that you were also justly angry with the God who loves you when he sinned; but certainly the Lord is accustomed to be reconciled through a friend to a supplicating servant. Therefore, blessed John, who possess such great love with God, his guilty servant beseeches you to reconcile him to God. Beloved of God, it is not contrary to the love of God if you assist his guilty servant—not by defending him, but through intercession. I do not put forward a defense of my iniquity, nor do I seek a defender, since I offer a confession [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscripts read “nor do I put forward a descendentem (‘one descending’) if I bring forth [a confession]”; or “nor do I seek a descendentem, but I set forth [a confession]” instead of “nor do I seek a defender, since I offer”], and I seek one who will intervene. Friend of God, do not count as an enemy of God—or of you—the man who, insofar as he can, believes and confesses through love that your God is his friend. If I believe, confess, and wish to love the love of God granted to you in such abundance, I ask you, by this grace given to you, to turn away from me the hatred of God that is due to me [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscripts read “the hatred not due to me” instead of “the hatred due to me”]. Do this, Lord, for the sake of that very lover of yours; do it because I am his work, his servant, and his redeemed one. Do it, therefore, for his sake with him, so that he may not lose what he made, or destroy what he redeemed. Do it, as you truly love his work and the confession of his blessed name.

[Col. 0988A]

Jesus, against whom I have sinned wickedly; Lord, whom I have contemptuously despised; almighty God, whose anger I have arrogantly provoked; lover of John, your blessed apostle: your terrified guilty servant, your sinner, your offender [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscripts read “your hater” instead of “your offender”], however criminal, however shameful, flees to him [Note: [Col. 0987C] Bec, Victor 3, Corbie, and Val-luc read “flees to you”; Victor 16 reads “flees to him, to you”; Thuanus reads “flees to you yourself”; another reading is “flees back to him”], placing the name of your beloved between himself and the sentence of your just judgment. By that blessed love, spare the man who seeks his protection. Lord, by whose name you show mercy to your sinner, will you condemn one who prays through the name of your beloved? Lord, under whose shelter is he protected [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscripts read “protection” (protegmine) instead of “shelter” (tegmine)]—will he be struck down under the name of your beloved? Where is refuge, if there is danger under your beloved? Let him who flees to your beloved not experience your hatred, Lord. Lord, Lord, let my wickedness not have greater power for condemnation than his grace has for mercy. Good one, good one [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscripts of Corbie, Bec, Victor, and Val-luc read “Good Lord”], let my hatred not have greater power to destroy the work you made than his love has to spare the servant whom you redeemed.

Most gracious Lord, who hate nothing that you have made, behold the one whom you made and remade [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscripts read “Behold what you made”]. Why, then, will you condemn one who accuses himself and invokes you, if you hate nothing that you have made? [Note: [Col. 0987C] Victor 16 and Florence read: “If you hate nothing that you have made, do [this].”] Therefore, good Lord, for the sake of him whom you loved more intimately among your disciples, do not be my condemner, since you alone are Savior. Blessed are you forever. Amen.

## PRAYER LXVIII [formerly LXVI]

[Note: [Col. 0987C] Compared with the manuscripts Victor KK, 16; Thuanus 267; Bec O; Corbie 160; Val-luc and Florence. The heading is “To the same Apostle, for obtaining the twofold love of God and neighbor.” Victor 3 reads “Prayer to the same”; Bec, “Prayer to Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist”; Thuanus, “Prayer to the same, for obtaining Charity”; Val-luc and Florence, “Also, a prayer to the same.”]

### TO THE SAME APOSTLE

For obtaining the twofold love of God and neighbor.

Saint John, you are that John, one of the great apostles of God, one of the great princes of the kingdom of God; one, I say, of those richest in the love with which God loves and is loved [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscripts of Bec and Victor 3 read “in the love with which God loves and with which he is loved, and richest in the love with which God is loved”; Thuanus reads “in the love with which God loves and is loved, and richest in the love with which God loves”; Victor 16 and Florence read “in the love with which God is loved, and richest in the love with which God loves”; Val-luc reads “in the love with which God loves and is loved, richest in the love of those whom God loves”; another manuscript ends incompletely with “in the love with which he loves”], and richest in the love of those whom God loves.

Behold, O man wealthy in such blessed riches, and rich in such blessed wealth: behold this sorrowful but Christian soul, poor and destitute of those riches in which you abound so abundantly. Hungry, it approaches the door of your clemency, humbly begging an alms from your wealth, so that from what can suffice without diminution for you and for many, you may at least impart to it enough by which it itself may live [Note: [Col. 0987C] The manuscript of Thuanus reads “from which it may live”]. Therefore extend your hand, rich friend of God; extend to the soul of the poor servant of your beloved God, from that rich chamber of your mind, this alms—small for you, great for me; easy for you, vital for me—so that my Lord, who was pleased to enrich you in order to enrich many, may through you deign at least to refresh it for the preservation of life.

[Col. 0989A]

Certainly, my Lord, beloved of our Lord, my soul is poor—poor in the twofold love of God, as I am compelled and ashamed to confess—because it loves God far less than it ought, and is loved by God far less than it needs. In the one respect I confess myself very unjust; in the other, I confess God just. In both respects I feel myself exceedingly wretched, by the just judgment of God. I have not forgotten this when I say it, O just and merciful God; nor am I ungrateful for the many benefits of your love toward me from the beginning of my creation. Yet until it is satisfied with both your loves, my hungry soul always cries out that it is poor and needy.

[Col. 0989B]

For this very reason is one of your greatest and most welcome benefits to me [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts read “most grievous” instead of “most welcome”]: through the sweet taste of you, you have aroused in me such eagerness that my soul refuses to be consoled (Psalm LXXVI, 3), except by its being satisfied. Since the supplication of your less-beloved sinner is insufficient to obtain this, I invoke the merits of your much-beloved lover [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts of Victor 16 and Florence read “to implore it” instead of “to obtain it”]. Therefore, O good sweet one, and sweet good one, from whom every good comes, make him favorable to me and make you favorable to him—or rather, make both him and you favorable to me—so that through him I may attain the desired good of this satisfaction.

I know, Lord, I know and confess that I am not worthy for you to love me; but certainly you are not unworthy for me to love you. Therefore, Lord, through his merits give me that by which you are worthy, and I shall be worthy of that by which I am unworthy. But let your beloved one, the Lord Jesus, pray for me instead, because he can do so more effectively [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts read “But let him also pray” instead of “But let him pray”]. Let that loving breast of his, his sweet resting place, pray to you for me; and hear my desire through him, for your sake.

Saint John, beloved of Jesus Christ, my Lord, your friend’s servant asks you, for the sake of the name of your beloved Lord, to obtain for him the mutual love of God. Obtain it, therefore [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts of Corbie, Victor 16, and Thuanus read “Obtain it, I beg you”], for me, so that I may be loved by him in such a way that I too may worthily love him. Certainly, beloved of God, if he loves us for your sake, you show us mercy; and if we love him through you, you repay him with grace. Certainly, Lord, if you turn him toward loving us, you make us debtors to you for so great a good; and if you kindle us to love him, you make yourself the one who repays his debt to him. Certainly, blessed one, however much you cause him to love more people, you take nothing away from yourself; and the more people you cause to love him, the more you repay him. Therefore, Lord, show this mercy to your suppliant: thereby make me your debtor for so great a good, and make yourself the one who repays God for one soul.

[Col. 0990A]

Do this, I beg you, Lord; do it; do not refuse it: no one will suffer harm from it; rather, salvation will come to your servant, grace to you, and glory to God. Most-beloved disciple of compassion, why will you deny the needy, though you are rich, and the asker, though you are powerful, something that harms no one and is bound up with so many goods? For if his sins hinder him when he wishes, why should your merits not rather assist him when he prays? Are my sins powerful for harming [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts of Victor, Val-luc, and Florence read “for asking” instead of “for harming”], while your merits are powerless for helping? Far be it, Lord, that I should be forced to feel what I shudder to say.

Why, finally, should one be denied because of his sins when, by confessing them, he seeks nothing through his own merits but everything through yours? Why, I say, when the merits set before him are more powerful than the offenses brought against him? For I am certain, Lord, that if your grace is more powerful with your beloved God than my sins are, he will dismiss my sins and, by loving me, make me his lover.

Therefore, blessed John, make the one who loves you love me also, through that breadth of charity which you taught and possess, and which you begrudge no one, but wish to be a common good in which you rejoice. In exchange for the love you owe him, repay him my love as well, together with your own [Note: [Col. 0989D] Victor 16 reads “repay him my love together with yours”; the other reading is “when you repay him” (cum illi solvas)], to the one to whom, for his love alone, you owe not only your own love but many loves [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts read “for his alone” instead of “for his love alone”].

Indeed, blessed John, you have learned through your own blessedness that just as no one can give anything to God before giving what he owes, so no one can repay more than he owes. Therefore, if all who through you love God, their lover, cannot make a sufficient return [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts read “cannot make a return”], I beg you, Lord, do not reject the one who asks to be counted among them. Kindle the one who is lukewarm with love for him [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts of Victor 16 and Florence read “kindle his love”], and make him fervent. Help the one who strives; hear the one who prays.

Jesus, Lord, whom I desire as my hearer; John, whom I ask as my intercessor: my desire compels me to desire that my heart compel you [Note: [Col. 0989D] The manuscripts read simply “my desire, that”], not unwillingly, but willingly [Note: [Col. 0989D] Victor 3 reads “not as those invited” instead of “not unwillingly”]; not reluctantly, but gladly. Therefore endure me and spare me; and if my heart devises anything, direct it toward love [Note: [Col. 0989D] Corbie reads “If love devises anything in order to extort love”; Thuanus reads “And if my heart devises anything, let it be tormented toward love”]. Endure me, I say, because the love of the love of God compels me.

Lord and Lord, I believe and know that you love each other. But how shall I myself experience this, if you do not grant what I ask for the sake of each other? Jesus, how shall you prove to me—or I to anyone—that you love him, if you do not grant me, who ask for his sake, either to be loved by you or even to love you? John, how shall I know that he loves you, if you do not obtain for me that he should love me also [Note: [Col. 0991D] Thuanus and Florence read “that he should love me also”]? Or how shall I know that you love him, if you do not help me to love him also? Excuse my excess; your love of God compels me to speak in this way [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts read “Let him excuse my excess”].

Therefore, O God, and you, his beloved, do not love each other only for yourselves, who are blessed, but also for us who are wretched. Let us rejoice with you; suffer with us. Do not close this great good within yourselves alone by enjoying it together [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts of Victor, Val-luc, and Florence read “within us”]; but let something flow over upon us, which, poured out within us [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts of Victor, Val-luc, and Florence read “among us”], may fatten and gladden our souls.

Beloved of the lover of God, John, who confidently glory in that blessed fullness of your mutual love, be all the more generous to the poor man who begs from you the mutual love of God, the more you sense yourself to possess it abundantly and see me to be in greater need. For you know, Lord—you know him who decreed in his epistle that if anyone possesses the world’s goods and sees his brother [Note: [Col. 0991D] Victor and Florence include “his”] in need, he should not close his heart against him (1 John III, 17). What, then, if someone possessing the substance of eternal life sees his neighbor’s soul in need [Note: [Col. 0991D] Corbie, Val-luc, and Florence read “sees the soul”]? Will he close his heart against him?

Merciful teacher, if you wished the heart of one possessing the substance of the world not to be closed against one suffering need, surely much more should the heart of one possessing the better substance not be closed against one suffering greater need [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts read “many more” instead of “much more”]. Behold, I hear you command that hearts be opened [Note: [Col. 0991D] Victor and Val-luc read “perceive” instead of “command”], and I see that you possess the substance of loving God and of being loved by God [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts read “of loving the Lord and of being loved by one’s neighbor”]. And you see that my soul is in need. Behold: the one who commands and the one who possesses, and the one who is needy in his presence, look upon one another.

Therefore, Lord, if your seeing [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts read “your command” instead of “your seeing”] is more compassionate than my devout prayer, let your seeing be my prayer. For you did not write, “If anyone sees his brother praying, and closes his heart against him,” but, “If anyone sees his brother in need.”

Come, then, Lord, see my need—or rather, behold, you see it. My soul, my soul, gather all your feeling and thrust yourself into his sight; cry out and repeat with inward feeling in his presence: “You see me.” Repeat it there alternately and persistently: “You see me,” and “See me.” John, certainly you see me; you see me. Therefore see me, Lord: you see me by knowing me; see me by showing mercy. You see and know; see so that I may know. You see and know my need [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts of Victor 3, Val-luc, and Florence read “You see and know; see so that I may know; you see and know my need”], see so that I may know your compassion. See, see me [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscript of Bec reads “You see, you see me”]. See me because you see me. I have long known it; now let me feel that you see me. I know it; let me feel it.

O what does my understanding hear being brought against me! I concede, Lord [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts read “Grant, Lord”], that you commanded a brother’s heart to be opened. But whether I am a brother or a neighbor, I dare not assert what I desire, nor do I wish to concede what is not advantageous to me.

Jesus, his teacher, look upon us. Lord, my soul is anxious with thirst before a stream; but there is nothing for it to drink unless it flows from a spring. Spring of mercy, let it flow from you into him, so that I may drink of you in him. Good Lord, answer for me [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts read “Good Lord, answer”]. I return to the spring; I can go no farther. Let a soul so parched not perish beside the living spring; let the drink not be blocked for the thirsty one. Let your satisfied one hear your judgment, and let your thirsty one draw your compassion from him.

Say to him: “John, who do you think was neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?” (Luke X, 36). Answer, blessed John, as the human race answers concerning its Samaritan, giving him thanks: “The one who showed mercy to him” (ibid., 37). Come, good Jesus; you have begun to assist my prayer [Note: [Col. 0991D] Victor reads “my reason” instead of “my prayer”]. Now I commend it into your hands (Psalm XXX, 6); since you are perfectly good, perfect it. Say, I beg you, to your beloved John, and present me to him as your servant. “Go, and do likewise” (Luke X).

Hope and rejoice; rejoice and love, my soul. The very one whom, in doubt, you desired as your hearer, is preparing an intercessor for you. You begged through another because you did not trust yourself to approach him directly [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscripts read “who did not trust yourself through you”]; and behold, he hastens forward and pleads where you were failing [Note: [Col. 0991D] The manuscript of Carthusian origin reads “where you will plead”; the manuscripts read “where you trusted”]. O goodness, O compassion, O lover! Behold how greatly he shows you that he loves you, and how greatly he kindles you to love him. Therefore persevere and hope—not in yourself, but in him—for he will hear your desire, the one who thus completes your prayer.

My heart and my flesh, exult in him (Psalm LXXXIII, 3), love him, and let all that is within me bless him (Psalm CII, 1). Amen.

## 293 PRAYER LXIX [formerly LXVII]

[Note: [Col. 0991D] Compared with the manuscripts Victor KK, 16; Thuanus 264; Bec O; Corbie 160; Saint-Germain 345; the Carthusian manuscript of Porta; Val-luc and Florence. The manuscripts title it “To blessed Stephen, with a reconsideration of his charity and falling asleep,” or “To Saint Stephen, the protomartyr.”]

### TO SAINT STEPHEN

With a reconsideration of his charity and falling asleep.

Saint Stephen, blessed Stephen, gracious Stephen, strong soldier of God, first in the blessed company of God’s martyrs, powerful prince, one of the great princes of heaven: I have learned, believed, and gladly embrace the truth that, while still placed on earth, you shone with such a light of holiness that your venerable face gleamed with angelic dignity; that you glittered with such purity of heart that your blessed eyes saw God in his glory; that you burned with such compassionate charity [Note: [Col. 0993D] Victor 16 reads “you burned with the compassion of such great charity”] that your loving mouth prayed piously for the impious who were killing you.

So it was, good Stephen; so it was. I rejoice that it was so [Note: [Col. 0993D] Thuanus reads “So you were, good Stephen; so I rejoice that you were so”], and I rejoice, delight, and exult that I have come to know it. For, fearing the strict sentence of the just Judge—fearing, I say, as a sinner and guilty man, the punishment I deserve—I need a helper, and I have the pleasant and safe course of sending you as an intercessor, so that you may reconcile to me my almighty friend, the Lord and my Creator and yours [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts read “so that you may make peace for me”]. For I know, Lord, and am certain from your great merits that you can; I trust, from your abundant charity, that you will; I hope, from the immeasurable mercy of the Judge, that he will not refuse. Therefore the anxious and trembling sinner, conscious of his evil, flees to you.

[Col. 0993B]

See, then, compassionate Stephen, my anguish, and spread your charity over it [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscript of Saint-Germain reads “over me”]. Behold, the guilty man stands before the terrifying Judge. He is accused of many and great offenses. He is convicted by the witness of his own conscience and by the eyes of the Judge himself. He has done no good deeds to counterbalance his evil deeds. By offending everyone, he has earned no familiar friend of the Judge through any past service, but has earned only accusers. The Judge is terrifyingly strict, intolerably severe, immeasurably offended, vehemently angry. Once pronounced, his sentence is unchangeable; the prison that admits no return is open. In the prison immense torments have been prepared, and torturers stand ready to drag the condemned man to punishment once sentence has been given. The torments are without end, without respite, without mitigation; the torturers are dreadful, never growing weary and never showing mercy. Fear disturbs the guilty man, conscience confounds him, his thoughts reproach him, and he cannot flee. Thus he stands suspended before the gravest sentence.

Behold a wretched man in narrow peril, in perilous anguish. Behold a man in need of swift assistance. Where is he now? Let the one who had compassion on those stoning him beneath the pressure of their stones now come to his aid. Let the one who stood as an advocate before this same Judge for his own murderers now pray for him [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts read “Let him pray for him”]. Stephen, Stephen—and truly Stephen, because truly crowned. Stephen, I say, Stephen: behold the place of compassion, behold the time of mercy [Note: [Col. 0993D] Victor 3 omits “of mercy”; Victor 16 reads “the place of mercy”], behold, certainly, the occasion for showing charity. For I remain continually in this danger, except that I do not always think about it [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts read “except that I do not always think this”]; and I am more wretched and more pitiable when I am able to forget it.

[Col. 0993D]

For God always sees me, and my sins; his strict justice always threatens my sinful soul. Hell is always open, and its torments ready; invisible ambushers are always ready to drag my wretched soul there [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts of Victor, Val-luc, and Florence read “to drag it there”].

[Col. 0994A]

This is how I am when I am awake; this is how I am when I sleep, when I laugh, when I joke; this is how I am when I am proud, when I slander; so I am when I grow angry, when I avenge myself; so, so I am when I wretchedly embrace the delights of the body. In short, this is how I am always and everywhere. Therefore hasten, compassionate one, I beg you, hasten, before I am condemned, before the torturers—the enemies of the human race—drag me away, before the infernal prison swallows me, before the torments of Gehenna consume me.

But O you, my sins—O you, my sins—you are exceedingly great, you are exceedingly many, so that pardon for my soul is rightly refused because of you [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts of Victor, Val-luc, and Florence read “But you, sins”]. I know it; yes, certainly, it is so [Note: [Col. 0993D] Victor reads “I know; certainly it is so”; Val-luc reads “I know also; certainly it is so”; Florence reads “It is certainly known”]. I confess: it is so. But the heavier my unhappiness, the narrower my need, the more wondrous will be the compassion of the one who pardons, and the greater will appear before him the grace of the intercessor.

[Col. 0994B]

I know well, Lord, beloved of God Stephen, that I have offended God, and that I have offended you and all his saints as well. But my need is so great [Note: [Col. 0993D] Victor 16 reads “My need is such”; the manuscripts of Victor 3, Saint-Germain, and Val-luc read “My offense is such”; another reads “My need is such”] that it forces me to seek help even from those from whom I have deserved punishment. And you and the other saints are so filled with that abundant, immeasurable fountain of compassion that you delight even to free mercifully those whom you may justly condemn [Note: [Col. 0993D] Thuanus reads “whom you might justly condemn”].

Great are your merits, great Stephen [Note: [Col. 0993D] Saint-Germain reads “Great are they, holy one”]; they are great enough to suffice for you and for me, and if they benefit me, nothing will be diminished from you. Behold, before God and before you, blessed Stephen, are all my sins—the sins that terrify, trouble, and burden my soul. Say, therefore, O compassionate one, to your most compassionate and beloved lover [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts of Victor, Saint-Germain, Carthusian, Val-luc, and Florence read “to your most beloved lover”], say, Lord, “Do not hold these sins against him” (Acts VII, 59) [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts read “this sin” or “his sin”]. Say, I repeat, for the needy man who supplicates you, what you said for the people who were killing you. Let your compassionate charity say only this, and I am certain that the most gracious God will forgive all my evils. For he is merciful and my Creator; I am wretched and his work; you are his beloved friend. Blessed is he forever. Amen [Note: [Col. 0993D] Thuanus adds: “Amen. Reconsideration of the charity of blessed Stephen.”]

### Reconsideration of the Charity of Saint Stephen

When your mad enemies were crushing you, their friend, as truthful Scripture bears witness, you knelt and cried out in a loud voice: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII, 59) [Note: [Col. 0993D] The manuscripts of Victor 16 and Florence read “Thus Scripture”; Victor 16 also reads “that you knelt and cried out”].

O heart rich with the fatness of charity, from which, while you were being afflicted, such abundant mercy overflowed! O mind intensely burning with love, richly anointed with charity, from which, while you were being persecuted, sparks both sweetly burning and ardently sweet flashed forth! O honeycomb rich with the honey of love, from which, while you were being pressed, drops so rich and so delightful trickled down!

“Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

Blessed man, what hope you give to your sinful friends when they hear that you were so solicitous for your impious enemies! Vessel of charity overflowing with fullness: with what abundance will you water those who desire to receive you within their hearts, when you thus drench those who were casting you outside their city [Note: [Col. 0995D] Victor 16 and Florence read “pour over” instead of “drench”]?

When you thus offer drink to those panting with fury as they rush upon you, how will you refresh those panting with fear as they flee to you?

“Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

How kindly will the one who is invoked answer, since, when provoked, he thus rebuked [Note: [Col. 0995D] Victor 16 reads “who thus will rebuke the one who provoked him”]? How benevolently will the exalted one cherish the humble, since he thus assisted the proud when he was humbled [Note: [Col. 0995D] The manuscripts read “the humble exalted”]? With what speed will the one powerfully delivered free the afflicted, since he thus helped those afflicting him when he himself was afflicted?

They hastened to take your life; you strove to restore their lives to them. They raged with stiff necks and great fury to destroy you; you knelt and prayed in a loud voice that they might not perish. In a loud voice, certainly, because with great charity; kneeling, because with true simplicity.

Pride was grinding humility beneath the whetstone of tribulation [Note: [Col. 0995D] Thuanus reads “was grinding beneath the whetstone”; Victor 16 reads “grinds beneath the whetstone”], and the fragrance of charity arose from it. Charity was struck by hatred together with the stone, and the ringing of compassion was returned. Impiety was pressing down compassion with a stone, and the oil of mercy was boiling over.

## 294

O if I should ever be found worthy through prayers to draw from Stephen’s charity the oil that they were able to press out with stones! For my soul languishes with an exceedingly grave languor [Note: [Col. 0995D] The manuscripts of Victor 16 and Florence read “For it is languishing”], which is healed only by the oil of mercy. Would that he might even once suggest to God on my behalf and on behalf of all my sin:

“Lord, do not hold this sin against him.”

Teach me, blessed soul of blessed Stephen, with what flavor you rejoiced, with what fullness you burned, when your heart poured forth a word so good (Psalm XLIV, 2). How sweet your utterance is to the throat of my soul (Psalm CXVIII, 103), sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Psalm XVIII, 11) to my mouth [Note: [Col. 0995D] The manuscripts read “to his mouth”]. As it is chewed, it grows sweeter and sweeter; as it is sucked, its most pleasant flavor flows more and more abundantly. The more it is seen, the more brightly it shines; handled in every way, it always increases in delight.

It bears the form of faith; it possesses the firmness of patience. It gleams with the purity of simplicity; it shines with the color of kindness. It tastes of charity, smells of compassion, conveys gentleness through touch, and represents mercy through sound.

Say, therefore, blessed Stephen, what did you cherish within, from which such a mixture of delights burst forth? Surely you were full of all these things; you were adorned with all these things; you were kindled with all these things. By all these virtues in which you abounded, I beg you, O charitable Stephen [Note: [Col. 0995D] Victor 19 reads “O charity” (O charitate); another reading is “O dear one” (O chare)], pray that my dry soul may be filled with the fatness and richness of charity (Psalm LXII, 6). Help my hungry soul to be satisfied with the bread of charity. Make my cold soul burn with the fire of charity, through the one who created it [Note: [Col. 0995D] Thuanus adds: “He who created it. Reconsideration of the falling asleep of blessed Stephen.”]

### Reconsideration of the Falling Asleep of Saint Stephen

“And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord” (Acts VII, 59).

O, he fell asleep! O sleep with rest, rest with security, security with eternity! You rest, O fortunate one, in joy; you rejoice in rest. You glory, O secure one, in fullness; you are satisfied in glory. Your joy will not change; your light will not fail. Whatever you do not wish for is far away; whatever you wish for is present according to your desire.

Your soul thirsted for God, the living fountain (Psalm XLI, 3). You came to him, and you drink from the torrent of his delight as much as you wish, in whatever manner you wish, for as long as you wish. Always satisfied, you always drink, because it always delights you to drink, and you never grow weary of it. You do not drink so that satisfaction may come to you as though you did not yet possess it; rather, you always drink so that the satisfaction you already possess may always endure [Note: [Col. 0995D] The manuscripts read “may abound”]. For you always desire what you always possess, and you are always secure that you will always possess it.

Indeed, without ceasing and with delight you desire the very delightful desire [Note: [Col. 0995D] The manuscripts read “the desirable desire”]; and you always drink, with delightful ardor, that very desire, with abundant satisfaction. O sufficient blessedness, and blessed sufficiency! How happy it is to fall asleep—to fall asleep in the Lord! With what peace those who fall asleep in the Lord fall asleep!

For the burdens of the flesh will no longer weigh them down; the pains of corruption will no longer afflict them. The goads of temptation will not attack them; the consciousness of sins will not terrify them. No need will trouble them. God has wiped away every tear from their eyes (Revelation VII, 17) [Note: [Col. 0995D] The manuscripts read “from the eyes of the saints”].

O rich and blessed peace, how far I am from you! Behold, while I try even faintly to taste the saliva of another’s happiness, I am forced to swallow abundantly the bitter draughts of my unhappiness. These move me to be silent about goods that I cannot even contemplate, and to weep over grievous evils that I can touch by enduring them.

Woe to me, wretched man! Where I am not, and where I am—when I do not know where I shall be [Note: [Col. 0995D] Thuanus reads “and where I am, and where I shall be”]. For my soul is wretchedly at odds with my flesh, joined to it: it does not wish to follow it, nor can it do so without fear; it does not dare, nor is it able, to leave it without pain; it wishes to drag it behind itself, and cannot do so even with labor.

[Col. 0997A]

Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? (Romans VII, 24). I beg you, blessed Stephen, have compassion on me, wretched and needy, though I rejoice with you in your blessedness, even though you are not needy. By your merits, may the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, free me from this body of death, so that one day I may sleep and rest in peace in the same place (Psalm IV, 9), in the Lord, who lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER LXX [formerly LXVIII]

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Compared with the manuscript of Thuanus 267; it is not found in the other manuscripts.]

### TO SAINT LAWRENCE
Most blessed martyr and most ardent lover of the Savior, Laurence, crowned with the laurel of true happiness: you are that precious vessel of the house of God; you are that faithful steward [Col. 0997B] of the heavenly treasure, and most kindly provider for Christ’s poor. I invoke you to aid me, who desire to pray before God’s face but, because of the magnitude of my sins, do not dare to lift my face to him. Come, therefore, most valiant witness to Christ’s power; show me your goodwill, attend to my need, and carry my prayer before him. By your devout intercession empty out my sins; by your merciful assistance uproot my vices, so that, once torn away from them, my soul may somehow kindle within itself that love with which you, in blessedness, burned wholly with desire for Christ.

For this reason, most precious Lord, I approach you above all, because I contemplate in you the marvelous flame of this love. For who would be capable of thinking, what mind of estimating, what understanding of grasping with what ardor, [Col. 0997C] with what heat and holy feeling you held his love fixed in your heart [Note: [Col. 0997D] “With what heat and holy feeling, his love”: manuscript reading, “with what heat of the holy one, his love”], or rather, had fixed your heart upon his love, when you were inwardly so filled with his sweetness [Note: [Col. 0997D] “With his sweetness”: manuscript reading, “with that sweetness”] that you regarded as nothing the flames pressing upon you outwardly?

Enter, my soul, into the inner regions of spiritual contemplation, and, if you can, penetrate the secret of the blessed breast of so fiery a lover of your Lord. Consider how happily his soul was bound by the nectar-like bond of divine love, while a cruel fire tortured his flesh outwardly and his inner affection, exulting, sent praises heavenward. Attend, I say, and wonder; marvel and rejoice; rejoice and love; love and praise. However intensely you devote yourself to contemplation, that sweetness with which he himself delighted through his affection and was made blessed through its effect far surpasses your understanding [Col. 0997D] [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Far surpasses”: manuscript reading, “surpasses yours”]. Yet by thinking about it you make progress toward this end: that you hunger to be satisfied by it [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Hunger to be satisfied”: manuscript reading, “desire to be satisfied”], and, so long as satisfaction is absent, suffer its hunger. For assuredly, the more you are affected by hunger, the more abundantly you will rejoice when satisfaction is received.

Therefore do not cease crying out; do not be ashamed to beg at the door of this rich treasurer whose help you implore. Pray humbly that, just as he distributed the Church’s treasures to the poor as a faithful [Col. 0998A] and prudent steward, so he may allow at least so much to drip for you from the treasure of love that, day by day, you may become hungrier with desire for it, and may always long for its satisfaction.

To you, therefore, most powerful and precious witness of the Savior of the world, Laurence, this hungry and starving poor man cries at the door of your compassion—not that you may remove his hunger, but that, having refreshed it with whatever taste of love, you may kindle it more intensely; by pouring even the smallest drop of its sweetness into my thirsty soul, increase its thirst within me. Let every sweetness be burdensome to me that does not flow from its fountain—if indeed that may rightly be called sweetness which has no taste of it.

Therefore, most kind lord, do not permit any worldly pleasure to empty the hunger of my heart, however lukewarm, which this starvation endures [Col. 0998B]. Let no carnal delight extinguish its thirst; rather, let it increase day by day in the mind of your humble lover. Let my soul be greedy for this hunger and disgusted by all earthly things, so that, failing through them and advancing toward it, it may reach through spiritual hunger that blessed satisfaction by which you, rich in distinguished merits, deserved to be satisfied and made blessed.

Let other poor people approach the doors of the rich, so that, satisfied in body by earthly feasts, they may drive away the discomforts of bodily hunger. I knock at the doors of your compassion so that I may deserve to escape the satisfaction of earthly pleasure and obtain an unfailing hunger for heavenly sweetness. For this I burn: to hunger for it, thirst for it, groan toward it, and sigh for it.

Counsel me, most glorious martyr. Behold, perhaps indiscriminate [Col. 0998C] verbosity says: “Enough has been prayed,” while the affection of desire cries: “Persist in prayer still more ardently.” Is this, most sweet lord and most fervent lover of Christ, the character of genuine devotion in prayer—that the more one devotes oneself to prayer, the more one is inflamed? Is it thus that the incomparable fragrance of love attracts those who pray in spirit and truth, so that, when the prayer is said to its conclusion, they delight in praying longer? Indeed it is. Blessed is that soul which such a true fire inflames.

But, so that my inadequate prayer may now be concluded, I beseech you, most blessed martyr and foremost pillar of God’s Church, Laurence, who deserved to hear happily from the most kind Jesus: “Come, good beloved; my angels will receive you, because, when roasted, you did not deny me; when tested, you confessed me.” You, I say, I beseech: by your exalted and most powerful merits lift up my prayer, so that, through your intercession and with the good Lord Jesus favoring me, I may deserve to obtain what I desire above all—namely, that all iniquity may be uprooted from me and that true love may advance within me all the way to the end. May the same Lord and our Redeemer grant this, he who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, life and kingdom, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0999A]

## PRAYER LXXI

[Note: [Col. 0999C] Compared with manuscripts Thu. 267; Vict. KK. 16 and RR.; Corb. 160; Bec. O, where it is read twice; Thu. 267; San-Germ. 345; Carth.; Vallis-luc.; and Flor. “To Saint Nicholas,” or “To Saint Martin,” “for a man existing in the abyss of sins”: manuscripts Vict. 3 and Val-luc.; “prayer to Saint Martin, or to Saint Nicholas”: manuscripts Vict. 16, Corb., and Flor.; “prayer to Saint Martin”: manuscript Bec.; “most devout prayer to the most blessed and most glorious Nicholas”: manuscript San-Germ.; Likewise: “Prayer to Saint Nicholas.” Manuscript Thu.: “prayer to the most blessed Nicholas.” Manuscript San-Germ.: “Of Saint Nicholas the Confessor.” In the prayer’s text, the name Nicholas is nowhere read in manuscripts Vict., Corb., and Flor., but only Martin; in manuscripts Thu. and Bec., the name Nicholas is always present, and Martin nowhere appears.]

### TO SAINT MARTIN

For a man existing in the abyss of sins.

Sinful little man, you who are greatly needy, you who have grievously saddened God: rouse your mind, attend to your need, and invoke mercy upon your misery. My soul, awake! My miserable self, awaken! My guilty self, cry out to your angry God, if perhaps he may turn his face toward you. But he is most high, and I am most low. How will my voice reach him? I will raise my soul above myself, so that it may attend to him who is above it, if perhaps, when called, he may hear it [Note: [Col. 0999C] “To him who is above it”: manuscripts Vict. 16, Val-luc., and Flor. read, “to him who is above him”]. But assuredly he is most just, and I am exceedingly unjust. How will he hear my cry [Note: [Col. 0999C] “How will he hear”: manuscripts read, “How do you hear”]?

I will enter within myself; I will exclude everything [Col. 0999B] except him [Note: [Col. 0999C] “Except him”: manuscripts Vict. read, “after him”] and myself; and I will pour out before him my soul and all that is within me. I will rouse my feeling, both sorrowful and deserving of sorrow; I will spread my troubles before him, if perhaps his great compassion may move him.

But my sins are exceedingly immense, exceedingly boundless; my prayer is not sufficient without an intercessor [Note: [Col. 0999C] “Without an intercessor”: manuscript Vict. 16 reads, “without intercession”], nor is my prayer acceptable [Note: [Col. 0999C] “My prayer”: manuscript Thu. reads, “my prayer without an assistant”].

I will ask one of those great familiars of God whether God may perhaps hear him on my behalf. I will call upon that great confessor Martin, whose name is glorified throughout the world.

Martin! Oh, if only you too would hear me [Note: [Col. 0999C] “Oh, if only you too”: manuscripts read, “Oh, if only you”]. You are that great Martin [Note: [Col. 0999C] “You are that great Martin”: manuscript Thu. reads, “He himself will hear me! You are that great one”; “hearing me yourself, you great one”]. But if God despises me [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts read, “If my God despises me”], who will regard me? If God turns his face away from me, who will turn his face toward me? Or if God hates me, whom will he hear on my behalf?

Merciful and compassionate God, do you so abhor one who returns to you that you cannot endure any one who clings to you having mercy on him? Or do you so utterly detest one of your grieving ones that, because of him, you will not hear any of your friends? You, I say, who are called “kind and merciful, patient toward evil” (Psalm II, 13): do you burn so fiercely against a repentant sinner that you forget what you are?

For your own sake, either hear me, or permit someone to hear me whom you may hear on my behalf. Lord, if you withhold your hearing from a sinner because you are just, do not at least prevent another from hearing the wretched petitioner, because you are compassionate. Kind one, you are more merciful than I can think; may I feel this no less than I presume to hope for it.

Your servant, created and recreated by you, Lord, trusts so greatly in your compassion that your accused servant dares to ask you to be his intercessor [Col. 1000A]. For no one will regard me [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts read, “No one will reject me”] unless you command it; no one will benefit me unless you consent. Yet I hope that what you deny me because of my sins, you may grant because of the merits of one of your familiars.

Good Lord, do not show yourself as an avenger when I ask you to be an intercessor; if you do not give a stone for bread, a serpent for a fish (Matthew VII, 9), or a scorpion for an egg (Luke XI, 12) [Note: [Col. 0999C] The manuscripts vary between “if you do not give” and “but do not give”]. Give me, therefore, Lord, as intercessor that great confessor Martin, whose blessed name you have glorified throughout the whole world.

Holy Martin, by him I beg you [Note: [Col. 0999C] In manuscript San-Germ. the prayer here begins, “Holy Nicholas, by him I beg you”], who causes your name to be venerated throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts Vict. 16, Val-luc., and Flor. read, “who causes your name to be venerated throughout the whole world,” rather than “who causes the whole world to venerate your name”]: do not deny your help to one who is needy and supplicating.

Why, lord, are you called upon by everyone throughout the world, if not so that you may be the advocate of all who ask? Why does this sound on everyone’s lips: “My lord is Saint Martin; my lord is Saint Martin,” if not so that they may be able to say: “My helper is Saint Martin; my helper is Saint Martin” [Col. 1000B]? Why is your name spread everywhere, if not so that through it some great good may be poured into the world?

Your fame calls me to you; your miracles send me to your intercession; your works draw me to your help. But why should I recount your miracles, when your power is greater? Why should I rehearse your works, when your grace before God surpasses them? Why should I recite the aids you have given to many, when the spiritual things you can do are better than the bodily things you do while dwelling in heaven and did while journeying on earth?

For you cannot do only these things and not those. No, I say: you are not powerful only in things that come to nothing [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts read, “that will come to nothing”] and powerless in things that attain eternity [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “that reach eternity”]. Surely you did not advance [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc. read, “you did not perfect”] only to perform these things; you did not ascend only to bestow these gifts. Impart the spiritual gifts in which you glory; make joyful with eternal things in which you rejoice; pour in the heavenly things in which you dwell [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts read, “in which you persevere”]. Through you, let us, who are needy, feel the overflowing abundance of those things whose perpetual flood you receive in fullness [Note: [Col. 0999C] Manuscripts read, “more fully”].

O the abundance of your good things, and the abundance of my evil things! How great is the distance between them? How powerfully the former makes you happy; how exceedingly the latter makes me unhappy! The former descends from God’s fullness [Col. 1001A]; the latter rises from my need. The former flows from God’s wealth; the latter rises from my poverty.

Oh, if only the overflow of that flood would inundate me, so that it might wash away the abundance of my evils [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts read, “the abundance”]! Oh, if only the fullness of that satisfaction would fill the emptiness of my destitution! I do not doubt, lord, that you can obtain this for me, if only you are willing to entreat on my behalf my beloved judge, your beloved lover [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “my beloved lover,” rather than “my beloved judge, your beloved lover”; manuscript San-Germ. reads, “my beloved one, your beloved one”].

Do not wait, Lord, to hear my importunity, for you know how long my weakness is in praying. I am quick to fail; but be you quicker to help [Col. 1001D]. Certainly, if my heart is contrite, if my inward parts are stirred, if my soul is melted, if streams have long flowed from my eyes, then I shall hope that Martin is present with my prayers.

Therefore, holy Martin, shake my spirit; rouse my heart; move my mind toward the feeling that its need requires, so that I may experience the effect of your compassion according to your power [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts Bec., Vict., Carth., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “the feeling of your compassion,” rather than “the effect of your compassion”].

But alas! For how long has my mind languished? With what stupor has my heart been hardened? With what torpor is my soul overwhelmed? Holy Martin, what is it that so impedes me? What is it that so weighs upon my neck? Why is my vision so darkened? Why is my circuit so closed?

My soul wishes, Lord—it wishes—to raise its face toward God and toward you, but, bent down beneath a leaden weight, it is burdened. It longs to direct its vision toward you, but it is obscured by murky darkness. It tries to free itself, but is bound with iron chains. It attempts to escape, but is shut within a bronze prison.

What are these things, God? What are these things that so darken and burden my soul, close and bind it? Perhaps they are my sins. Indeed, they truly are my sins. Certainly they are.

Carnal affection has dulled my taste for spiritual things; attention to lowly things has bent my soul away from contemplation of heavenly things; love of earthly things has extinguished in me delight in heavenly things; through the practice of vices, the perception of true goods has vanished from me [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts read, “the practice of vices has emptied me”].

I have been distanced from those good things and occupied with these evils; shut out from the former and shut in by the latter; rolled away from the former and wrapped up in the latter. Hence comes that prison and those chains. Hence come that darkness and those weights.

My sins, for whom do you keep me in these chains and this prison, beneath these darknesses and this weight [Col. 1001D]? For whom, if not the strict Judge, your torturers, and eternal torments? For whom, if not hell’s prison and everlasting chains? For whom, if not the darkness of perpetual night and the weight of unending death?

Certainly you keep me for these evils; you drag me toward these evils. Certainly I shall be wrapped up in them if I am not first released by you. Truly I shall be their unfree servant [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “their unprofitable servant,” rather than “their unfree servant”] if I am not first freed from you. Surely that day is near—near, I say—and unknown [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts read, “near, I say, and unknown to everyone”]. It comes suddenly, and perhaps it will be today [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts read, “it comes today”].

My sins, were you going to be so harmful when you watered my soul with your sweetness, when you anointed my heart with your pleasure? Why did you conceal these things from me? Why did you betray me? No—you did not betray me; I betrayed myself, because I trusted you [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts read, “because I entrusted myself to you”]. You did not deceive me; I deceived myself, because I received you within me.

O unheard-of madness! I knew that there was no faithfulness in you, yet I placed faith in you [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts Vict. read, “I applied faith to you”; manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor. read, “I had faith in you”]. No—I neither had faith nor trusted you; but, in some horrible manner, although seeing, I handed myself over to you. I was seeing, because I knew you and knew what evils followed you; I was blind, because I did not guard myself against things I knew.

Alas, sin—a dreadful name [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “my dreadful name”], a detestable reality, incomparable to any evil! The blind person does not see the pit into which he falls; the mad person thinks he ought to do what he does. But whoever sins willingly, seeing and knowing, hands himself over to destruction.

Death and every kind of torment are only torments; nor are they intrinsically ugly, because they are ordered. Sin possesses its own ugliness and draws eternal unhappiness along with it. It was therefore better to choose eternal torment, which in itself does not draw eternal ugliness [Col. 1002C], than sin, which joins eternal pains to its own ugliness.

And certainly, wretched man, you ought to have avoided the ugliness of sin alone more than any enormity of torments [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscript Vict. 3 reads, “which alone was to be feared”]. For in sinning, with the most shameful perversity, you placed yourself before God your Creator—nothing is more unjust than this. In enduring torments, in a most beautiful order, the work would subject itself to its maker—nothing is more just [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts Vict. 3, Val-luc., and Flor. read, “to his maker”; manuscript Vict. 16 omits “his”].

O man, where has your humanity vanished? You had learned that whoever commits sin is the slave of sin (John VIII, 34); and, in order to be the slave of so great an evil, you committed sin. You knew that you were a spirit going away and not returning (Psalm LXXVII, 39); yet you cast yourself into an irreversible and bottomless abyss of sin.

Truly, my sins are an abyss, because they are incomprehensible in weight and depth, and beyond reckoning in number and vastness. That abyss is irreversible, because no one returns from it [Note: [Col. 1001D] Manuscripts read, “from where he returns”] unless he is drawn back by grace; and it is bottomless, because whoever sins willingly deservedly falls into infinity if he is not held back by mercy [Col. 1003A] [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscript Vict. 16 reads, “because, if he sins willingly”].

“Abyss calls to abyss” (Psalm XLI, 8)—my sins! The torments as well by which you keep me are an abyss, because they are infinite and utterly incomprehensible [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscripts read, “O abyss that calls to abyss—my sins! Torments”; other manuscripts read, “Abyss calls to abyss! My sins; torments”].

Alas, the prison and chains, the darkness and weights of sins terrified me; but I have become the slave of an evil incomparable with any evil. Thus I have been plunged into the abyss, and with this lamentable slavery and abyss I am to be buried in another abyss. Woe upon woe, fear upon fear, sorrow upon sorrow. Behold a third abyss, itself exceedingly terrifying: “the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Psalm XXXV, 7). Perhaps, in the voice of these cataracts, my abyss calls to abyss (Psalm XLI, 8). The cataracts are hidden; the judgments of God are hidden [Col. 1003B]. The abyss is driven to call to abyss in the voice of God’s cataracts, because the abyss of sins deserves the abyss of torments, as God’s judgments declare.

Even if my sins were not an abyss, the great abyss of God’s judgments would nevertheless be greatly to be feared, since its hiddenness lies beyond human understanding.

Now, therefore, the judgments of God are an abyss; my sins are an abyss; the torments owed to me are an abyss; the mouth of the abyss of judgments is over me [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscripts Vict. 16 and Val-luc. read, “the abyss of God’s judgment is above me”]; the abyss of hell is beneath me; the abyss of sins in which I am is also within me.

I fear the one that threatens from above [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscripts read, “the one that always threatens”; manuscripts Vict., Carth., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “the one that threatens from above”], lest it rush upon me and overwhelm me, together with my abyss, in that other abyss which lies open below, where torments will never erase sins, but sins will always hold the torments.

Wretched man—against whom have I sinned [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscript Carth. reads, “Wretched man, why have I sinned?”]? What have I become? Where have I gone away from God? Where have I been lost from him? Who will seek me, lost in an abyss amid abysses? Or who will find God’s lost one? Or who, outside the abyss of sins, hears one crying from their depths?

But, O Lord, you who behold the abysses, where have I gone from your Spirit, and where have I fled from your face? Certainly you are not absent from where I still am, because even if I descend into hell, you are there (Psalm CXXXVIII, 8). Even if I wickedly fled from you and damnably hid myself in my abyss, you see me there also.

For who but you moves my soul to repentance? Or how do you move it if you do not see it in its abyss? Good Lord, you knocked and awakened it in the abyss of its sins, as though it were sleeping in a bed. You shook it when it was numb; you troubled it when it was negligent; you made it repent over what had delighted it [Col. 1003D] and grieve over what had pleased it. You advised it to seek an intercessor [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscript Corb. reads, “to repent”]; you provided that intercessor for it.

Good God, you did all these things in the abyss; and do you not hear one crying from the abyss? Going before your fugitive [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscripts read, “your fugitive servant”], you did these things; will you not follow one who wishes to return to you, so that you may complete what you began?

Good Lord, thanks be to you. Truly you sought your lost one in the abyss, and you found him by terrifying him in this way through his sins. Through the merits of your beloved Saint Martin, bring back from the abyss of sins the one you sought and found, your lost one. Do not lose what you have found again; do not lose your sought-and-found servant in the abyss of hell, where you find no one.

I hear, Lord, that you command me to return, but, miserably bound and weighed down by too great a burden, I cannot escape.

But, holy Martin, why then do I pray to God through your merits [Col. 1004B], when you, who are before him, can do this better? I beseech you, lord [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscripts Vict., Carth., and Val-luc. read, “I beseech you, holy one”], by his name: do not turn away from one whom he has already regarded [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscript Vict. reads, “from one whom he has regarded”], even though he is his guilty servant. Be present for me before God, I ask—not to defend me, but to pray for me.

For I do not defend my sins before him, but display them; I do not excuse them, but accuse them. I am guilty; I myself am beneath him, and on his behalf I am my own accuser.

[297] Let him who made me not accuse me. I alone was sufficient for sinning; I alone shall be sufficient for accusing myself. Finally, if he is Judge for judging his guilty servant, he is also Lord for protecting his servant; he is also Creator for preserving his work; he is God for saving his believer and baptized servant.

Or how will he judge as contemptuous the sinner who recognizes and confesses himself wretched and repentant because of his sins? Or how will he condemn as an adversary the sinner who grieves that he has sinned and flees to so intimate an intercessor of his?

God, in you I place my hope. Holy Martin, to you I entrust my prayer. Upon both of you I cast my care; rather, upon you I cast my soul—that is, what you demand from me most: you by commanding, you by advising. Receive it, cast before you [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscript San-Germ. reads, “Receive it, therefore, within you”]; hold it prostrate before you. Bring it back from the abyss of sins: you sought it and found it lost; do not lose it now that you have found it.
