Guard it when I sleep; preserve it when I do something else; watch over it when I think of something else: you through permission [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscripts San-Germ. read, “preserve me… watch over me… you through consent,” rather than “preserve it… watch over it… you through permission”]; you through intercession; you because of the merits of your so beloved confessor [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscript San-Germ. reads, “because of the merits of so beloved a one”]; you because of the name of your Creator and mine [Col. 1004D], who are blessed forever [Note: [Col. 1003D] Manuscript San-Germ. reads, “because of God, who is”]. Amen.

[Col. 1005A]

## PRAYER LXXII

[Note: [Col. 1005C] Compared with manuscripts Thu. 267; Vict. KK. 16 and RR. 3; Bec. O; Corb. 160; San-Germ. 345; Carthusian manuscripts from Porta, Saint Martin of Tournai, Vallis-lucensis, and Floriacum. “To Blessed Benedict,” or “N.”: manuscripts Vict. 3 and Bec.; “proper prayer of monks”: manuscripts Vict. 16, Bec. 2, Carth., and Flor.; “prayer to Saint Benedict”: manuscript San-Germ.; “prayer to Blessed Benedict”: manuscript Torn.; “proper prayer of monks to Saint Benedict”: manuscript Val-luc. In all the manuscripts, “or N.” is omitted.]

### TO SAINT BENEDICT

Holy and blessed Benedict, whom heavenly grace enriched with so abundant a blessing of virtues that it not only raised you to the glory you desired, to blessed rest, and to a heavenly seat, but also drew countless others to that same blessedness through your admirable life, urged them on through your sweet admonition, instructed them through your gracious teaching, and summoned them through miracles: to you, I say, Benedict of God, whom God blessed with so lavish a blessing, my distressed soul, fleeing to you, prostrates itself before you with as humble a mind as it can; it pours out prayers to you with as much feeling as it can; it implores your help with as much desire as it can.

For its need is exceedingly great [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts read, “its desire is humble; its need is exceedingly great”] and unbearable [Col. 1005B]. I profess by name and habit the life of holy conduct that I promised as a monk; yet, by living far away in exile from that life, my own conscience convicts me of lying to God, to angels, and to human beings [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts read, “with my conscience as witness”; manuscript Torn. reads, “my own conscience”].

Be present, merciful Father; be present to the supplicant. I ask you not to shudder at one so full of faults and so false, but to regard one who trusts, and to have mercy—more than I deserve—on one who grieves [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscript San-Germ. reads, “have mercy on the grieving one,” rather than “have mercy on one who grieves”].

Indeed, illustrious leader among the great leaders of Christ’s armies, I have placed myself under your command, although I am a feeble soldier. I have submitted myself to your instruction, although I am a cowardly disciple. I have vowed to live according to your rule, although I am a carnal monk.

For my perverse heart is stony and dry when it comes to mourning the sins I have committed [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Torn., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “past sins”; manuscript Vict. 16 reads, “my sins that I have committed”]; but, when it comes to resisting present attacks [Col. 1005C], it is soft and muddy [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscript Torn. reads, “present temptations, it is soft”].

My depraved mind is swift and tireless in carrying out useless and harmful things [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Bec., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “in handling”], but, when it comes even to thinking about beneficial things [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscript Bec. reads, “any things”; manuscripts Vict. 16, Torn., and Flor. read, “things to be thought about”], it is disgusted and immobile.

My blinded and distorted soul is ready and eager to plunge and roll itself in vices, but difficult and sluggish even to remember virtues. It would take far too long, dearest Father [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Corb., Vict., Torn., Val-luc., and Flor. read, “most holy Father”; manuscript Bec. reads, “dearest Father”], to recall each thing.

It is far too long, I say, to enumerate gluttony, sleepiness, frivolity, impatience, vainglory, detraction, disobedience, and the other vices [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts read, “and earth”], through which my unhappy soul has become a daily mockery [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Torn. and Vict. read, “a mockery for demons”; manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor. read, “a mockery of demons; it”]. These vices now draw him to themselves and pull him apart in turn [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Vict. 16 and Flor. read, “hand it over in turn”] in order to make sport of this wretched and almost ragged little man [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts read, “and ragged”]; now, together with their mob, they insult him by trampling him, and trample him while insulting him.

Behold, blessed Benedict, how vigorously this soldier of Christ fights under your command; behold how effectively this disciple of yours advances in your school; behold the good monk who, with vices and the pleasures of the flesh so mortified, burns and lives only through virtues! Rather, behold one so ruled by a crowd of vices [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Vict. 16 and Carth. read, “one whose virtues have been extinguished and who is so ruled by a condemned crowd of vices”; manuscript Torn. reads, “one whose virtues have been extinguished and who is so ruled by a crowd of vices”; manuscript Flor. has the same reading], so pressed down by the mass of sins [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts read, “so reveals the mass”].

Shame upon me [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts read, “Alas, grief”]!

O shameless monk, with what face do you dare to be called a soldier of Christ, a disciple of Saint Benedict? False professor [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Vict., Carth., Torn., and Val-luc. read, “false professor” in the masculine plural or “professor of falsehood”]. With what shamelessness can you endure having upon you the tonsure and clothing of a profession whose life you do not possess?

Alas, grief! O anguish that surrounds me on every side! If I deny my supreme King, my good Master, and the profession I have made [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts read, “the promise I have made”], it is death for me. But if I profess myself their soldier, disciple, and monk while my life accuses me of falsehood, it is judgment for me.

My spirit is anxious within me; my heart is troubled within me. Break out and cry, my soul: Jesus, good Lord, see my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins (Psalm XXIV, 18). Be my helper, Lord; do not forsake me, nor despise me (Psalm XXVI, 9), but teach and help me to do your will (Psalm CXLII, 10) [Col. 1006C], so that my life may testify to what my heart and mouth gladly confess [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscript Vict. 16 reads, “teach and help me to do”; manuscript San-Germ. reads, “teach me to do”; “and life” is found in one manuscript rather than “so that my life”].

Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God (Psalm V, 3), through the merits and intercession of your devout Benedict, my beloved, my leader, and my teacher [Note: [Col. 1005C] Manuscripts Corb., Bec., and Val-luc. read, “your beloved, my sweet master”; manuscript San-Germ. reads, “your beloved, both sweet and my master”; manuscripts Torn. and Flor. read, “your beloved and my master”].

O my good leader, O gracious teacher, O sweet Father [Col. 1007A], Benedict, I pray and beseech you [Note: [Col. 1007D] Manuscript San-Germ. reads, “O my good leader, O gracious teacher, O sweet Father Benedict, or N., I pray and beseech you”; it also has, “Come, my good Father, sweet Father Benedict, I beseech you”], by the mercy you showed toward others and by the mercy God showed toward you: have compassion on my misery, for I rejoice in your happiness.

Come to the aid of one crying out for you as his patron [Note: [Col. 1007D] Manuscript San-Germ. reads, “calling upon you as patron”]. Relieve one overwhelmed by the mass of sins; release one bound by the ropes of offenses; free one entangled in crimes; raise the one who lies fallen; support the one who totters; equip with spiritual weapons—that is, virtues—the one who is unarmed; teach and protect the one who fights; defeat those who fight against me (Psalm XXXIV, 1); raise up victory for me [Note: [Col. 1007D] Manuscripts read, “raise me to victory”], and lead me to the crown.

Come, advocate of monks. Through the love with which you were concerned about how we ought to live [Note: [Col. 1007D] Manuscripts vary: Vict. 16, “how we ought to live”; Flor., “how we live”; others, “how we might live”], be concerned that we may sufficiently desire and effectively be able to live as we ought [Note: [Col. 1007D] Manuscript Flor. reads, “that we may be able to live as we ought”], so that you may glory before God in our discipleship, and we in your instruction [Col. 1007B]—God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER LXXIII

[Formerly LXXI]

### TO SAINT DUNSTAN

With remembrance of his miracles.

Saint Dunstan, sweet to invoke and kind in hearing, compassionate in helping; for those who flee to you, you are never an uncertain refuge; for those who cry to you, never an unprepared aid. Holy, kind, and compassionate Dunstan, look upon the misery of my soul: for if you look upon it, if you attend to my calamity and misery, surely you will not restrain the depths of your mercy. My soul is tormented by fear, trembling, and horror; it fears, trembles, and dreads the monstrous punishments it deserves; and [Col. 1007C] there is nowhere for it to flee, since it stands before the Judge. It stands alone; there is no one to act on its behalf. Its life is examined and found condemnable. For good deeds are sought; scarcely any, or none, are found. Its offenses are brought forward; such numerous and such grave offenses cannot be denied, offenses that exclude every hope of pardon. The Judge, by demanding an account, displays the long-suffering patience he has shown toward it; this soul displays nothing but obstinate impenitence. Accusers surround it; they repeat and repeat, recite and explain the accusations brought against it. It is accused from every side and excused by no one. Cruel and dreadful torturers stand by and wait, so that once the sentence of condemnation has been pronounced they may immediately drag it away to be tortured. Overwhelmed by so great a mass of miseries, the wretched soul searches and looks around; and behold, it sees no one who will rise and answer on its behalf. [Col. 1007D]

Therefore, compassionate, merciful, and gracious Dunstan, rise—rise! Display your customary help of pity, offer the depths of your compassion, and extend the assistance of intercession. The works of mercy that are proclaimed about you invited and encouraged me to cry to you; but the works of impiety committed by me repel and silence them, works that you abominate and curse with intolerable horror. [Col. 1008A] Behold misery, behold anguish: here the guilty person is condemned, and every bosom of God’s mercy and compassion is closed; conscience, acting as accuser, argues, confounds, and overwhelms her so completely that she dares neither entreat the Judge nor find anyone to entreat him for her. But you, compassionate and merciful one—where is pity, where compassion, where mercy, if not where there is misery? Toward whom will you be compassionate and merciful, if not toward the miserable? I acknowledge it, I acknowledge it; and, acknowledging it, I fall silent. I am setting before you the enormity of my crimes; nevertheless, the greater the misery, the more worthy of proclamation does mercy become. Nor will my misery be so great that the power of your virtue fails. Is my misery magnified to such a degree that your mercy is narrowed? Will my weakness outweigh your all-powerful merits? No: may the surpassing grace of your merits lift up, lighten, and empty the weight of my wickednesses. [Col. 1008B] The Judge himself will most willingly grant you whatever your deeply beloved and cherished intimacy with him requests. He will not refuse you the salvation of one miserable person, he who is salvation itself and with whom you are so familiar; he will readily restore to you the life of one dead person, he who is life itself and with whom you possess such great favor.

May the generosity of your kindness not fail in my one case, when its benefits overflow upon so many, indeed upon countless others. Through you may I obtain pardon, so that all may proclaim and magnify the mercy of your so beloved and loving God and Lord. O how clearly God demonstrated, by signs worthy of proclamation, how pleasing and familiar you were to him! O immeasurable purity of your heart, with which the angels of God so often conversed! [Col. 1008C] O immeasurable familiarity with God, to whom the dignity of the angels was so familiar! O glory and reward of virginity, which the angelic nature so rejoices to honor! You were carried into heaven; you entered among their blessed ranks; you delighted in angelic melodies, singing with them the song that only the virginal choir sings. Again, when you celebrated hymns on earth, heavenly melody in turn attended and harmonized with you; the ranks of virginity sang together—the supreme dignity of the heavenly city. Powerful and all-powerful grace, whose dignity was so obedient to the power of the angels! Excellent and surpassing eminence of merit, which divine transcendence showed to be so acceptable and so precious to itself! [Col. 1008D] Therefore, he will never reject the prayer of one so beloved and so familiar to him, so as not to grant pardon to one guilty person. Indeed, he himself bears witness that he does not desire the sinner’s death (Ezek. 33:11); therefore he will gladly give salvation to a sinful soul whose death he testifies that he does not desire.

Again, the signs of your intimacy with the Judge himself bring forward hope and confidence in my deliverance. For what heralds, what attendants did he send ahead to you when he decreed that your blessed soul, already about to depart from the flesh, should approach him and remain with him? So that you would not be terrified by fear, disturbed by astonishment, or troubled by uncertainty, the day was foretold, the dwelling of eternal blessedness was promised, and the leadership of the heavenly court was brought forth, so that you might be led onward by joyful security and secure joy.

With what—and O with what—exultation is one received who is led forth with such and so great an apparition? How greatly does he rejoice and receive glory when welcomed, whose arrival is so honored? Finally, with what veneration and with what display of glorification is the announcement of your departure made? In a vision, while you were sitting in your pontifical chair, a multitude of angels stood before and around you, [Col. 1009B] the court of the heavenly citizens. It asked you how long you wished to remain in this flesh. It delivered the message and announced the desire of the entire heavenly assembly, which wished, prayed, and entreated that you should now sing with them in heaven before the eternal High Priest, the Holy One. You replied that you could not yet depart, because the feast of the Lord’s Ascension was at hand, on which you were to address and communicate with the people entrusted to you. A concession was made to your just and charitable excuse; a day was appointed on which no reason for delay would arise. O remarkable and astonishing grace of intimacy, to whose single will the desire and will of the entire heavenly dignity yields! It grants a postponement of its own desire, lest your wish remain unfulfilled; it prefers that what it does not wish should happen rather than that what you wish should not happen. With what love, then, is his presence loved and embraced, whose absence is so desired and awaited? What gift of grace did he receive in heaven, to whom he granted so great a gift of glory on earth? Resplendent in the robe of virginity, he is received with reverence at the marriage feast of the Lamb. He reclines among the first, because he is clothed with the beauty of integrity and the virtue of humility; endowed with the grace of charity and every virtue, he follows the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14:4). How, then, will you, so loved and so familiar to the very author of salvation, mercy, and compassion, fail to obtain the salvation of one sinner? If there is willingness, it is certain that possibility is not lacking; nor may willingness be absent, since it is not lawful for you to be contrary to his will—he who desires all human beings to be saved. Obtain, therefore, what you wish, and obtain what you can: by your intercession may my soul be freed and live, for whom, that it might live, the blessed Life, God himself, my mercy, who is blessed forever, wished to die. Amen.

[Col. 1010A]

## 299–301. PRAYER LXXIV [formerly LXXIII]

[Note: [Col. 1009D] Compared with manuscripts Vict. KK. 16 and RR. 3, Thuan. 267, Corb. 160, Becc. O, in which the reading is *San-Germ.*, 345, *Carthus.*, *a Porta*, *Floriacensis*. “To Blessed Mary Magdalene, with a reconsideration of love for Christ.” The manuscripts read: “To Saint Mary Magdalene”; manuscript S. Ger.: “Of Saint Mary Magdalene.”]

### TO SAINT MARY MAGDALENE, with a reconsideration of love for Christ

Saint Mary Magdalene, who came with a fountain of tears to Christ, the fountain of mercy, from whom, thirsting ardently, you were abundantly refreshed; through whom, though a sinner, you were justified; by whom, grieving most bitterly, you were most sweetly consoled. You, my dearest lady, learned through your own experience how a sinful soul is reconciled to its Creator, what counsel may help a miserable soul, and what medicine may restore health to one who is sick. For we know well, dear friend of God, to whom many sins were forgiven, that she loved much (Luke 7:47). I, most wicked sinner that I am, most blessed lady, do not recall your sins by reproaching you; rather, I dwell upon the immensity of the clemency by which they were erased. Through it I breathe, lest I despair [Note: [Col. 1009D] “I breathe, lest I perish, and I sigh for the same, lest I despair,” according to the manuscripts; the printed text reads, “I breathe, lest I despair, and I sigh toward it again” (manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor.: “toward the same”), “lest I perish”]; and toward that same clemency I sigh, lest I perish—I, I say, miserably cast down into the depths of vices, weighed down by the excessive burden of crimes, thrust by myself into the dark prison of sins, and wrapped in the darkness of torpor [Note: [Col. 1009D] “In the darkness of the body,” according to manuscripts Vict., San-Ger., Val-luc., and Flor.; the printed text reads, “in the darkness of torpor.”]

Therefore, chosen lover and beloved electress of God, I, miserable, entreat you, blessed one; I, dark, entreat you who were illumined; I, a sinner, entreat you who were justified; I, unclean, entreat you who were cleansed. Most kind one, remember what you were and how greatly you needed mercy, and ask indulgence for me, just as you wished it to be given to you. Obtain for me the compunction of compassion, the tears of humility, desire for the heavenly homeland, distaste for earthly exile, the bitterness of repentance [Col. 1010C] [Note: [Col. 1009D] “Bitternesses,” according to the manuscripts; the printed text reads, “bitterness”], and fear of eternal torments. May the familiar companionship [Note: [Col. 1009D] The manuscripts variously read “your dearest familiar companionship,” “dearest one, familiar companionship,” and Corb. and Thu. “most reverend one, familiar companionship”] that you had and still have with the fountain of mercy benefit me, dearest one. Draw from it for me what will wash away my sins; pour out for me from it what will satisfy my thirst; infuse into me from it what will water my dryness. For it will not be difficult for you to obtain whatever you wish from your most beloved [Note: [Col. 1009D] Manuscript San-Ger. reads “from your most beloved”; another manuscript reads “from your sweetest”] and most gracious Lord and friend [Note: [Col. 1009D] Manuscript San-Ger. reads “Lord and friend”; another reads “Lord, friend”] [Note: [Col. 1009D] The printed text continues: “your Lord, who reigns with God.” Some manuscripts omit “who reigns with God”; manuscript San-Ger. reads “your Lord, who reigns forever and ever.” Other manuscripts omit the remainder, which follows in the printed editions. Manuscript Flor. omits “who lives and reigns with God.”]

For who could explain, O blessed bride of God, with what kindly intimacy and intimate kindness he opposed those who slandered you, answering on your behalf; with what compassion he defended you when the proud Pharisee was indignant at you; how he excused you when your sister complained about you [Note: [Col. 1009D] The manuscripts read “he himself excused you,” rather than “how he excused you”]; how he praised your deed when Judas raged against you? Finally, what shall I say—or rather, how shall I speak—when, burning with love for him, you sought him at the tomb, weeping, and sought him while weeping? How affably [Note: [Col. 1009D] Manuscripts Vict. 16 and Flor. read “how ineffably,” rather than “how affably”], how amicably, did he come to console you, and yet inflame you more [Col. 1011A], while he concealed himself from you who saw him and revealed himself to you who did not see him; while he himself, present, whom you were seeking [Note: [Col. 1011C] Manuscripts Becc. and Flor. read “when he himself was present, whom you were seeking”; the printed text reads “while he himself was present, whom you were seeking”], asked whom you were seeking and why you were weeping [Note: [Col. 1011C] Manuscript Vict. 16 reads “and when you were weeping,” rather than “and why you were weeping”]?

But you, most compassionate Lord, why do you ask what she is weeping for [Note: [Col. 1011C] Manuscripts Becc., Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read “why do you ask?” rather than “why do you ask what she is weeping for”]? Had not her heart seen you, the sweet life of her soul, cruelly slaughtered? O astonishing compassion! Alas [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “But alas,” rather than “alas”], horrendous impiety! When you hung stretched out on a certain piece of wood [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “on the wood of the Cross,” rather than “on a certain piece of wood”], fastened with iron nails, like a robber, as a mockery to the impious, you say: “Woman, why are you weeping?” (John 20:19). And because she could not help [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “and since she could not help”] prevent them from killing you [Note: [Col. 1011C] Manuscript Becc. reads “help, lest they kill you,” rather than “help prevent them from killing you”], or because she wished to preserve your body for a long time with ointments, lest it decay, so that, since she could not speak with you while you were alive, she might at least weep over you when dead, and might recite beside the dead man, in broken words, the life-giving teaching she had heard from you alive, having hated life. [Col. 1011B] Now, moreover, she believes that the very body—which, however little, she rejoiced had been left to her—has been lost; and you say: “Woman, why are you weeping?” O provocation [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read: “The body has been lost. O provocation,” rather than “O provocation” alone] to grief! Her own eyes had seen—if indeed she could look upon it—what the cruel had cruelly done to you; and she had lost, as she thought, the remains of their hands. Every hope concerning you had now fled, since she could not even preserve your remains as a memorial of you; and someone asks what you are seeking and why you are weeping? At least you, O her singular joy, why do you stir up her sorrow [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “You, singular joy,” rather than “you, O singular joy”]? For you yourself knew, and so wished it to be, that she could recount the cause of such weeping only by repeatedly interrupting her words and bursting out in repeated groans. You did not fail to recognize the love that you yourself inspired. Surely you knew, O gardener, what you had planted in the garden of her soul. [Col. 1011C] I suppose that what you had planted, you watered. You watered it—shall I say, or did you test it? But, to speak more truly, you both watered and tested it.

But, O good Lord, O kind teacher, behold your faithful handmaid [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “your handmaid and,” rather than “your handmaid”] and your disciple, so recently redeemed by your blood: behold, she burns and is anxious with desire for you; she looks around, asks questions, and nowhere does the one she desires appear. Whatever she sees displeases her, because she does not see you alone, whom she longs to behold. What then? Would my beloved Lord endure this for long [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “Would my Lord endure this?”]? Or have you lost compassion because you have found incorruption? Have you lost pity because you have acquired immortality? Far be it, Lord! You do not despise us mortals [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “He does not despise us,” rather than “You do not despise us”] because you became immortal [Col. 1012A] for us, for whom you became mortal in order to make us immortal. Indeed, loving compassion cannot tolerate for long either that she should groan or that he should remain hidden from her. The sweetness of the lover breaks forth, lest the bitterness of the weeper break forth. The Lord speaks the handmaid’s familiar name, and the handmaid recognizes the Lord’s familiar voice. I suppose—or rather, I affirm—that she sensed the accustomed sweetness with which she had been accustomed to being called: “Mary.” O delightful voice! O how much tenderness! How full it was of love! It could not have been expressed either more briefly or more quickly [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “nor more quickly,” rather than “either more briefly or more quickly]. I know who you are and what you desire [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “and what you desire,” rather than “and what you wish”]. Behold me; do not weep [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “nor weep,” rather than “do not weep”]. Behold me, whom you are seeking. Immediately the tears were changed. I do not believe that they were at once restrained; rather, the tears that the contrite heart had previously wrung from itself by tormenting itself, the rejoicing heart afterward poured forth in exultation. O how [Col. 1012B] unlike are “Rabboni!” and “If you have carried him away, tell me!” O how discordant are “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him,” and “I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me!” (John 20:13).

But what am I, miserable as I am, presuming without feeling to express the feeling of God and of the blessed friend of God? How can a good heart pour forth a good fragrance when it does not possess the flavor within? Yet you are my witness, O Truth; you are my witness, my sweetest Lord Jesus, that I do this out of love for your love [Note: [Col. 1011C] The manuscripts read “out of love for you,” rather than “out of love for your love”]. I desire to kindle your love in myself, because I desire to love you alone and what you command; and to sacrifice to you a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50:19). Give me, Lord, in this exile the bread of sorrow and tears, which I hunger for more than an abundance of delights. [Col. 1012C] Hear me for the sake of the love and dear merits of this beloved Mary of yours, and of your most blessed mother, the greatest Mary. Do not, most compassionate Redeemer Jesus, do not despise the prayer of your unworthy sinner; rather, help the effort of your weak lover [Note: [Col. 1011C] Manuscripts Becc., Vict., and Val-luc. read “your weak sinner,” rather than “your weak lover”]. Shake the lukewarmness from my heart, and through the fervor of your love grant me to reach the eternal contemplation of your glory, you who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, live and reign as God forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER LXXV [formerly LXXIV]

[Note: [Col. 1011C] Compared with manuscripts Vict. KK. 16 and RR. 3, Bec. O, Corbeiensis 160, Carthus. a Porta, Val-luc., and Flor. “Of a prelate to any saint, the patron of his church.” Manuscripts Vict. 3 and Bec. read: “Prayer of a bishop or abbot to the saint under whose name the church is governed.” Manuscript Corb.: “Likewise, to Saint Martin.” In manuscripts Vict. 16 and Flor. this prayer is the final part of the prayer to Saint Vedast. Where the printed editions have “N.,” manuscript Corb. has the name Martin; manuscripts Vict. 16 and Flor. have the name Vedast. In those manuscripts, where the printed editions have “bishop,” the name “abbot” is used, as also in manuscript Vict. 3, in which “bishop” is written only in the margin. In manuscript Carth. only the name “abbot” is given. In manuscript Val-luc. the name Albanus is given, and “abbot” appears in place of “bishop.”]

### OF A PRELATE TO ANY SAINT, THE PATRON OF HIS CHURCH

Holy N., compassionate N., blessed N., one of God’s glorious apostles [Col. 1013A] [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscripts Vict. 16, Corb., Carth., and Flor. read “apostles of God”; manuscript Bec. reads “confessors of God”; others read “apostles of God, or martyrs, or confessors”], one of God’s blessed friends: this sinner, this needy man, this man who is yours—though unworthy, though inept, though a most unsuitable vicar—returns again and again to you, uncertain, ignorant, and anxious about your people, about your congregation [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscript Vict. reads “about your people, about the congregation”; manuscript Bec. reads “about the congregation”; the manuscripts specify: “if he is a bishop, about your people; if an abbot, about the congregation”], and about his own danger.

I, that is, an useless person adorned with no good qualities, darkened by profound ignorance, disfigured by countless vices, weighed down by immense sins—I, I say, whom God—and you after God [Note: [Col. 1013C] The manuscripts read “you, compassionate Lord,” rather than “you after God”]—I do not know whether you commanded or permitted to be called rector [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscript Bec. reads “to be called rector”; manuscripts Vict., Corb., Carth., and Flor. read “to be called rector, bishop, or abbot”; manuscript Val-luc. reads “to be called abbot”; other manuscripts read “bishop or abbot”] in the church established under your advocacy, under your protection, and in your name, anxious about myself and about those entrusted to me: I ask you to be my counselor, I beg you to be my helper, and I await you in every respect as the one who acts on my behalf.

For I am called a teacher, but I do not know how to be one; I am named a shepherd, but I cannot be one; I am called a bishop [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscript Bec. reads “I am called a bishop”; manuscripts Vict., Corb., Carth., and Val-luc. read “I am called a bishop or abbot”; manuscript Val-luc. also reads “I am called an abbot”], but I am not one. They see me sitting where a bishop sits, but I see that I do not do what a bishop does; they see me proceeding as a bishop, but I see that I do not live as a bishop; they show me the honors due to a bishop, but I do not display the conduct of a bishop to them. I have not yet lived the life of a good layman, and they expect from me to learn how clerics should live [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscript Bec. reads “how clerics should live”; manuscripts Corb., Vict., Carth., Val-luc., and Flor. read “how monks should live”].

What have I done, little man, worm, and corruption? What have I done? What have I presumed to do? To what have I consented? Rather, you, God, and you, N., his apostle [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscript Val-luc. adds “and you, N., martyr”; manuscript Bec. reads “his apostle, martyr, or confessor”], what have you done [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscript Bec. reads “his apostle, what have you done”; other manuscripts read “his apostle, martyr, or confessor”]? For you have done this, whether by commanding or by permitting it. Therefore you who have done this in whatever manner, do what is needed—you by praying, you by giving—that what you have done may harm neither me nor anyone else [Note: [Col. 1013C] The manuscripts read “may harm neither me nor them,” rather than “neither me nor anyone”], but may benefit me and many others. You who have made an ignorant teacher, a blind guide, and an erring rector: teach the one whom you appointed as teacher; guide the one whom you set in place as guide; govern the one whom you permitted to be rector [Note: [Col. 1013C] The manuscripts read “whom you established,” rather than “whom you permitted”]. Teach me, I beg you, what I should teach; guide me where I should guide; govern me so that I may govern. Rather, teach them [Note: [Col. 1013C] The manuscripts read “teach them in me,” rather than “rather, teach them”], and me in them; guide them, and me with them; govern them, and me among them.

Good Lord Jesus, they are not mine but yours, because I too am not my own but yours. I am yours, Lord, and they are yours, because you made both me and them by your wisdom, and purchased them with your soul [Note: [Col. 1013C] The manuscripts read “with your blood,” rather than “with your soul”]. Therefore we are yours, good Lord; we are yours, whom you made so wisely and purchased at so great a price. If, then, you entrust them to me, Lord, do not therefore abandon either me or them. You entrust them to me; I entrust myself and them to you. The flock is yours, Lord, and the shepherd is yours [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscripts Vict., Val-luc., and Flor. read “the shepherd is yours”; they omit “is”]. Be the shepherd of your flock [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc. read “of your flock”; the printed text reads “your flock’s shepherd”] and of its shepherd.

Lord, through the merits of blessed N., your friend, hear the prayer of your sinner. Make him concerned for us, Lord, whom you have given us as an advocate; let us feel him praying for us, through whom we daily demand your help [Note: [Col. 1013C] The manuscripts variously read “your help for us,” or omit the repeated “us”]. May we obtain your grace through him, through whom we daily implore your majesty. Lord, we confess him to be our advocate; through him may we experience you as our Savior. May our demerits not prevail, Lord, over his merits [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor. read “Lord, may our merits,” rather than “Lord, may our demerits”]; rather, may our sins be erased by his prayers.

And you, O blessed and holy N., you are my advocate; be my intercessor with the Lord. I ask you: entreat him. I ask you: obtain from him. Carry my prayer to him, and bring back his hearing of it to me. Through you let my distress be reported to him, and through you let his consolation be restored to me. Show him my danger, and present his help to me.

For I have undertaken to govern God’s Church under your protection, although I have not yet begun to govern my own soul. Therefore, timid about myself, I am compelled to be concerned about others. Weighed down by the burden of my sins, I am ordered to raise up others; bent beneath the weight of my crimes, I am required to straighten others. Therefore, holy, blessed, and compassionate N., recognize me as your vicar, whatever kind of vicar I may be, so that your counsel may always precede me and your help follow me [Note: [Col. 1013C] Manuscripts Vict. and Val-luc. read “your counsel, and may your help follow”] in governing myself and the flock entrusted to me. They were entrusted to you before they were entrusted to me; and when they were entrusted to me, they were not dismissed by you [Col. 1014C] but I was entrusted more fully.

Therefore, whatever has been imposed upon me concerning them, do concerning me and them. Do for me what has been imposed upon me to do for you. Do, Lord, what has been imposed upon me to do for you; do, Lord, do for me, because you see that I neither know nor can do anything for you; rather [Note: [Col. 1013C] The manuscripts read: “What has been imposed concerning them, do concerning me and them; do for me what has been imposed upon me to do for you (Carth.: ‘through you’); do, Lord, do for me, because you see that I neither know nor can do anything except through you.” Manuscripts Val-luc. and Flor. omit “except”], act yourself, not I, for yourself; for this pertains first and more to you than to me; and if anything pertains to me, it is after you and under you.

Therefore you, Lord—you owe more, know more, and can do more than I—you should act rather than I. Let the care of them that I have undertaken not burden me, Lord, since the burden of my sins has burdened me sufficiently. Let them not burden me, since I myself am too heavy a burden for myself; indeed, I burden myself excessively, and there is no need for others to burden me. But let neither my burden burden them, nor my sin impede them, nor my evil harm them. Let my evils not harm those whom my goods ought to benefit; let them not impede me, concerning whom I ought to make progress [Note: [Col. 1015A] The manuscripts read “from whom I ought to make progress,” rather than “concerning whom”]; and let me not harm those whom I ought to benefit. My offenses are more than sufficient for me; let the offenses of others not drag me down with them. It is more than enough for me if my sins condemn me; let them not involve others with me.

But you, O holy N., apostle of God [Note: [Col. 1015A] Manuscript Bec. adds “martyr or confessor”], you who can, lift me and them up; carry me and them; excuse me and them; help us both [Note: [Col. 1015A] The manuscripts read “help them; excuse me and them; help,” rather than the printed wording]; govern and protect us both. Thus may I, rejoicing together with them in their salvation, and they, rejoicing together with me in mine, always praise our good Lord Jesus Christ with you—he who is blessed God, and you who are his blessed apostle [Note: [Col. 1015A] Manuscript Bec. adds “martyr and confessor”; manuscript Val-luc. reads “martyr, his apostle”—]—forever. So be it, so be it. Amen.

[Col. 1015A]

# SAINT ANSELM’S TREATISE ON PEACE AND CONCORD

*(From a manuscript codex of Leuven.)*

## CHAPTER ONE. [Col. 1015B] How we ought to preserve peace with our neighbor

It is exceedingly necessary to have peace and concord with our brothers, to obey the prelate, and to offer God purity of heart. For with our neighbors we ought to think the same thing, so that with one mind and one voice we may honor God.

It is fitting to obey the prelate, as the Apostle says: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them. For they keep watch as those who will have to render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning. For this would not be beneficial to you.” We ought to prepare purity of heart for God, because “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Let us therefore see how these three things may be preserved.

To preserve concord with our neighbors, let us strive to anticipate them in honor. Someone anticipates his brother in honor when he subjects his own will to the other’s will. People devoted to the world commonly love their own will, act according to it, and desire that everyone else should obey them. Each person covets this; each proclaims it in word and deed. If they do not carefully consider what they want, their wills will certainly never be harmonious.

Nevertheless, they possess a certain concord in this: all desire to be honored, all wish to be loved, and all desire others to agree with their will. But in this—that each seeks what is his own and no one seeks what belongs to another—they disagree in many ways. For in this matter, one wishes submission and honor to be shown to him, while another seeks the same thing for himself with no less zeal; neither will be able to agree with the other. [Col. 1015D] One says, “I want this or that to be done for me”; the other says, “I absolutely do not want it to be so.” By disagreeing in this way, they dissolve the bonds of peace and concord.

But those who desire to please God by guarding peace and charity should establish for themselves such a rule of life that whatever they perceive to be pleasing to their neighbors, they too should wish to have done for them. And since, as the blessed Apostle testifies, it is more blessed to give than to receive, to honor than to be honored, and to serve than to be served, does not the one who serves out of charity acquire more than the person being served?

Indeed, the one who offers another a service of charity already possesses that by which God is pleased with him. The one who receives the service does not possess this in the same way. What thanks does God owe me if you, or anyone else, loves me? Since, then, it is greater to possess something for which God will make a good repayment than something for which he will make none, it is clear that the one who ministers out of charity possesses something greater than the one to whom the ministry is rendered.

Moreover, the one served by another’s charity receives from it some temporary gift—namely, honor, a meal, or any other benefit. The other, who served out of charity, not only retains charity for himself but makes it greater than it was by sharing in it. For material things diminish when dispersed, but the more charity is spread, the more it increases. Through its administration, love has greatly increased in you who displayed it; and this will certainly add to your merit, since through you love for you itself has grown within me.

And although the service of charity has passed through me for this reason, your charity’s reward—which never passes away—will always remain there. From this too it may be concluded that it is better to serve than to be served. Thus, in all things, let them desire more to give than to receive as God’s justice requires, and let them strive more to obey another’s will than their own. Whoever wishes to conduct himself in this way will be a partner in the other’s will. Thinking the same thing and being of one mind, he will otherwise be unable to have concord. For how will he have it unless he diligently seeks it? He cannot seek it in order to possess it in any other way; seeking it in this manner, he will possess it.

[Col. 1017A]

## CHAPTER TWO. On the obedience to be shown to the prelate
We must preserve submission and obedience to our superior from the heart; otherwise we do not keep the rule we profess. For he is truly subject—and a monk or canon—who rejoices that, for God’s sake, he is not his own. Whoever obeys not from the heart but only under the law of subjection will have no reward for his obedience unless he corrects himself; for nothing is good unless it is voluntary. Therefore he must hold to the law of obedience out of love, lest he lose the reward of possessing it. As long as he does not obey willingly, so far as he is concerned he remains in his own will; and insofar as he has that will, he belongs to himself, not to another. And if he belongs to himself, let him see with what power, weapons, or strength he can defend himself against those attacking him. [Col. 1017B]

It is astonishing how the adversary, who goes about seeking whom he may devour, does not attack this man and that man—attacking, swallow him; swallowing, destroy him. He travels along a road where robbers are found: if he is not recognized by them, they attack him, beat him, and strip him. If, however, he is recognized but has no lord or advocate whose reverence and fear enable him to escape the robbers’ hands, observe how they treat him, as though they loved and valued him. If he is a king, or the son of a king, or some powerful person, he is spared out of fear, greeted with reverence, and proceeds unharmed on the journey he has begun; but otherwise he is stripped and beaten.

Thus, brothers, thus without doubt it happens in our souls. Almighty God has prepared his kingdom for us; if we are willing to obey him, we shall be called—and shall be—his friends and sons, not slaves. [Col. 1017C] Therefore we shall obey him if, whenever we are able to know what he wills, we strive to carry it out of our own good will. Our will will be good and obedient if we submit it to his will and take care to obey him voluntarily. If in good will we agree with the Lord’s will, we shall be called friends and become sons of God. Once this has been accomplished, a man will be able to go and pass safely wherever he wishes. For he will not fear the hands of powerful robbers and demons, nor dread evil encounters, since he will be a king’s son.

Therefore let each person beware of willing anything except what, with God or his spiritual father as author, he may licitly be able to will. Yet permission is accustomed to deceive; for obedience and disobedience are [Col. 1017D] opposites. Permission lies between them. Whoever wills what he ought not to will, yet does not intend to carry out that will unless an act has first been authorized, will be excused for the deed by the obedience he embraced in this matter. But willing what he held contrary to obedience will be dangerous for him unless he repents. Some, paying insufficient attention to this, are often deceived by permission. Let us therefore take care not to rely on permission beyond measure, since although permission diminishes punishment, it does not remove it altogether.

He should know that the devil fears to approach no one so much as the person who never wishes to depart from the will of his superior. For just as a thief undoubtedly often suggests evil to one who conceals himself from the knowledge of his superior, so he does not venture confidently against one who shows his superior what he is and who, for no reason, wishes to disagree [Col. 1018A] with his will. Whatever evil he may suggest turns to his own shame, since the person to whom it is suggested either almost completely disregards the suggestion or, if he consents to it for a time, corrects himself through confession and worthy satisfaction.

Therefore the subject must obey God in all things and through all things, and undertake the command of his superior while preserving fidelity to God. If the superior orders his subject to commit perjury, theft, fornication, or anything of this kind, he must in no way obey, because God forbids such acts. Let him therefore obey God in all things; let him obey his superior in all things while preserving God’s will; and, insofar as it lies within him, let him preserve the will of God and of his master and remain at peace with all human beings.

Whoever is subject in this way [Col. 1018B] to the will of God and of his superior will then obey God. When he has obeyed his superior in God, he will confidently be able to declare that he belongs not to himself but to God. When his soul is at the moment of leaving the body, he will not fear the powerful hand of the demons who come to meet him, because he will have Christ the Lord as a powerful advocate.

Behold how much good obedience acquires. When a man is brought to account—whose man he is, from where he comes, where he is going, and whom he seeks—if he has obeyed the will of God, he will be able to say that he belongs to God. But if he remains in his own will and for that reason has stood opposed to the will of God and of his superior, he lies if he says that he belongs to God; for while he lived, he lived according to his own will, not God’s. What advocate, then, will he have? To whom will he go? Who will help him? What will he plead? [Col. 1018C] Certainly he will not be able to flee; he must go through the midst, and he will have or follow a road either to life or to death. I ask: by what power, with what strength, will he escape the hands of his attackers? The wretched man will be tortured if he has not made God and his superior the authors of his will and action.

Indeed, all who are estranged from the will of their superior are shaken by storms of vices and assaults of demons, just as ships are tossed in a shallow place during a violent storm. For if a post is set in a shallow full of rocks, with ships fastened to it by ropes, the farther they are from the post, the more violently they will be struck as the storm bears down upon them. But the closer they are bound to it, the less they will feel the storm’s violence.

Thus, whoever is estranged from the just will of his superior [Col. 1018D] is undoubtedly endangered in the pursuit of his own will; nor will he agree with God’s will as long as he disagrees with the will of God’s vicar. For whoever assumes the position of superior authority in God’s Church undertakes to act in God’s place; in whatever manner he assumes it, let him look to that himself. It is not mine to judge him, but to obey his command, provided it is not unjust, as the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ chair. Therefore, whatever they tell you, do; but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:2–3). And the Apostle says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls by his own master” (Romans 14:4); and: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Romans 13:1–2). And elsewhere: “Brothers, do not make yourselves many teachers, lest you fall under judgment” (James 3:1).

[Col. 1019A]

A man becomes a teacher when he indiscreetly censures the actions of his own rector. Thus he falls under God’s judgment, because he has improperly usurped the role of teacher. This must be avoided with the greatest care, since it is exceedingly dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. If the Father’s actions have been worthy of reproach, let him be entreated gently, modestly, and with reverence. For it is written: “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father” (1 Timothy 5:1).

## CHAPTER III. On the Purity of Heart to Be Offered to God

We have said that purity of heart must be preserved for God. He alone is the examiner of the heart, since he is the creator of mind and body. A human being cannot see another human being’s heart, because no one knows what belongs to a human being [Col. 1019B] except the human spirit that is in him (1 Corinthians 2:11). But God, from whom no sins are hidden, freely sees the human heart and its intention. Whoever keeps his heart pure will be able to see God; whoever does not keep it pure will unquestionably be unable to see God in any way.

Therefore whoever desires to have God dwelling within him must possess purity of heart. No one can possess him unless he has emptied his heart of earthly desire and striven to burn with the love of Christ. To the degree that someone loves the world, to that degree he will be empty of heavenly love. And the more someone sins and withdraws from God’s justice, the more he abandons Christ.

For what benefit is it to anyone to be baptized if he is not justified? Indeed, the one who said, “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not [Col. 1019C] enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), also said: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20). Why, then, do many hasten to be baptized out of fear of the former, yet, because they do not fear the latter, take no care to be justified?

Certainly God wishes a person to be justified by observing his commandments and to be loved by that person, in whose heart he himself ought to dwell. For just as incense longs for the heat of fire so that it may give off fragrance, so God longs for the warmth of love so that he may dwell within us. Whoever desires God to dwell within him should sincerely embrace the discipline of abstaining from what is unlawful. For the Spirit of God, the Spirit of discipline, will flee what is feigned, and is driven away by iniquity when it arrives. Iniquity and the Spirit of God, who is also love, cannot dwell together.

Wherever the love of God has taken up residence, if the person who has given it a place also gives in himself a place to iniquity, [Col. 1019D] he is undoubtedly rebuked, and the love or Spirit of God is driven out by the iniquity that has arrived. It will not remain unless he reforms, for the benefit of his host. Indeed, the love of God and iniquity do not come together.

Whoever wishes to become the Lord’s dwelling place must maintain purity of heart and drive carnal desires far away. Just as a chaste woman, a faithful bride, disdains speaking with an adulterer and rejects his secret words, consenting neither secretly nor openly to anything he desires, so [Col. 1020A] the faithful soul must not consent to its own appetite in its will, must not accept its permission, must disregard its words, and must admit none of its blandishments.

If it does this, it establishes itself unmistakably as God’s beloved bride. But if it consents to unlawful desires, it will be called not a bride but an adulteress. Therefore let our will be pure, so that it may be called—and may be—God’s bride; let it not be corrupted by the stain of any impurity, lest it become an adulteress. As long as it consents to God’s will, it is pure and a bride; but when it dissents from his will, it is corrupted, stained, and commits fornication.

It often happens that, while someone wishes to cultivate purity of heart, he frequently has impure and detestable thoughts. Because he pays too much attention to them, he severely reproves, judges, and condemns himself for the fact that such a thing has entered his mind. [Col. 1020B] Thus the wretched man torments himself, saying:

“What did I think? What did I do? What did I feel? Alas, how will I be cleansed from such impurity, from so wicked a thought? I am afraid to conceal it; I am afraid to reveal it. I would wish not only not to say such a thing, but not even to hear it from anyone. How, then, shall I name such filth?”

While he is distressed and considers what he would not wish to see, he is attacked and troubled more and more, and is not set free. But he must not behave in this way if he desires to be liberated. What, then, should he do? Pay attention.

When what he detests seeing has attacked him and has become excessively persistent, let him despise it, pay it no attention, give no assent to it, turn his thought to something else, and devote himself to doing some task. Let him care no more [Col. 1020C] about involuntarily experiencing something than he would if a butterfly were fluttering before his eyes.

When a traveler is harassed by a dog, if he stops and tries to defend himself from its persistence, he immediately finds the dog becoming more persistent. But if he disregards its barking, passes on, and pays no attention, that canine attack soon comes to an end, and the traveler proceeds freely.

So whoever strives to possess purity of heart should despise empty, fruitless, or impure thoughts, turn his heart away, and consider the entire attack he suffers within to be nothing. He should not repeatedly ponder what he has thought, but utterly disregard whatever evil he has considered with insufficient care. For those who are in the faith of the Lord Jesus and do not live according to the flesh are not yet condemned (Romans 8:1).

If we live in this way, if we cultivate this discipline, and if we present ourselves in this manner before [Col. 1020D] God, we shall be able to become his dwelling place and his guests. If, as long as we live, we strive to love and honor him, he will undoubtedly repay us, as long as we live, with the return of his love and honor. For by the same measure with which we have measured, it will be measured back to us by him who gave himself for us and freed us from the abyss of death, who will crown us with immortality in the eternal homeland. To him be honor and glory forever. Amen.

## [ASCETICAL TREATISE]

[Col. 1021]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULUM

*(In Acherius, Spicilegium, vol. I, p. 443.)*

I attribute the *Ascetical Treatise* to blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, more by association than with certainty. For when I came upon a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Évroult containing various works of that same holy Doctor, this *Ascetical Treatise* was found inserted among them.

But I would hesitate to assert that this little work is Anselm’s, since Eadmer’s *Life* compels such hesitation, as does the chronicler of Bec, who, in carefully and minutely reviewing Anselm’s writings, makes no mention whatsoever of this ascetical treatise. Moreover, it does not breathe Anselm’s style or character. Whether it is Anselm’s or not matters little, however, since it is composed with learning and piety and is exceedingly suitable for the instruction of the ascetical life.

Nevertheless, I do not think it should be concealed that Anselm himself—or some other writer—borrowed or collected the greater part of this treatise from Cassian’s *Conferences of the Fathers*. I do not deny, however, that I have read in Anselm some passages found in this treatise, especially in chapter 2 the comparison with mills, which was especially familiar to that Father.

[Col. 1021]

## SAINT ANSELM’S ASCETICAL TREATISE

### CHAPTER I. On the Monk’s Purpose or End

All arts and disciplines have a certain *scopos*, that is, a purpose, and a *telos*, that is, their proper end. Looking toward this, the diligent practitioner of each art willingly and calmly endures all labors, dangers, and losses.

Thus the farmer, now not avoiding the scorching rays of the sun, now not avoiding frost and ice, repeatedly subdues the stubborn clods of the field with the plow, while keeping his purpose in view: by cultivating it, he will reduce it to earth cleared of all thorns. He confidently expects thereby to attain the end—that is, the receipt of abundant crops. He also willingly empties granaries filled with grain and entrusts it to the furrows, not feeling the present diminution because he is considering the future harvest. [Col. 1021B]

Merchants do not dread the uncertain hazards of the sea or any dangers; soldiers do not regard the exile of journeys or the dangers of war, while the former are driven forward by hope toward the end of profit, and the latter toward the honor they have set before themselves.

So too the end of our purpose is, according to the Apostle, eternal life, as he declares: “You have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Romans 6:22). Our *scopos*, however, is purity of heart, which he rightly called sanctification, without which the aforementioned end cannot be attained. It is as though he had said in other words: “You have your purpose in purity of heart, and the end—that is, the *telos*—is eternal life.”

Whatever can direct us toward this purpose—that is, [Col. 1021C] purity of heart—must be pursued with all our strength. For its sake we do and endure everything; for its sake parents, homeland, honors, riches, and every pleasure are rejected, so that purity of heart may be preserved forever.

With this purpose, therefore, set before us, our actions and thoughts must always be directed toward attaining it, as toward a fixed [Col. 1022A] line. If it is not continually established before our eyes, it will not only make all our labors equally varied and unstable, causing them to be poured out in vain and without fruit; it will also arouse thoughts that are diverse and opposed to one another.

For a mind that has no place to which it may return or to which it may principally cling must change from hour to hour and moment to moment according to the variety of assaults, and, as a result of external events, be continually transformed into whatever condition first presents itself.

This is why we see some people who have despised the greatest resources of this world later become agitated over a stylus or a needle, retaining their former attachment in matters of little importance. If they held contempt for the world firmly fixed in their hearts, [Col. 1022B] they would never admit, over small things, what they preferred entirely to cast away lest they incur it over great riches.

Our principal effort, therefore, must be that the mind always cling to divine things and to God, judging fornication to be even a momentary departure from the contemplation of Christ. Everything depends upon withdrawal within the soul. Once the devil has been expelled and vices no longer reign in it, the kingdom of God is consequently established within us, as the Evangelist says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:22).

Within us there can be nothing other than knowledge or ignorance of the truth, and either friendship with vices or with virtues; through these we prepare a kingdom in the heart either for the devil or for Christ. The Apostle also describes the character [Col. 1022C] of this kingdom, saying: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).

For it is said of someone: “This world will rejoice” (John 16:20); and: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn” (ibid.). Therefore, if the kingdom of God is within us, and the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy, whoever dwells in [Col. 1023A] these things is undoubtedly in the kingdom of God.

Conversely, those who live in injustice, discord, and sorrow that produces death are established in the kingdom of the devil, in hell, and in death. Whoever is there cannot praise God, according to the Prophet’s saying: “The dead will not praise you, Lord, nor all those who descend into hell” (Psalm 113:17), because of sin. “But we,” he says, “who live”—not in vices or in this world, but for God—“will bless the Lord from this time forth and forever.”

“For there is no one in death who remembers God. But in hell, who will confess to the Lord?” (ibid., Psalm 6:6)—that is, no one. For no one, even if he professes a thousand times that he is a Christian or a monk, confesses God when he sins; nor does he truly profess himself to be the servant of the one whose [Col. 1023B] commands he contemptuously and rebelliously disregards.

The kingdom of heaven must be understood in three ways: either as meaning that the heavens—that is, the saints—will reign over others who are subject, according to the saying: “You, be over five cities, and you, over ten” (Luke 19:19), and that which is said to the disciples: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28); or as meaning that the heavens themselves begin to be ruled by Christ, when, with all things subjected to him, God begins to be all in all; or certainly as meaning that the saints will reign with the Lord in heaven.

Therefore, while he is still established in this body, let each person know that he will be assigned to that region or ministry of which he has shown himself a participant and worshiper in this life. Let him have no doubt that in that everlasting age he will also be a [Col. 1023C] companion of the one whose servant and associate he has now preferred to show himself, according to the Lord’s saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my servant will be” (John 12:26).

### CHAPTER II. On Thought

It is impossible for the mind not to be disturbed by thoughts; but, by the grace of God, it is possible for anyone who strives to receive or reject them. This exercise of the heart is aptly compared to mills, which a rushing current of water drives and carries forward by its whirling force. Driven around by the force of the water, they cannot [Col. 1023D] cease from their work. But it lies within the power of the person in charge to decide whether wheat, barley, or darnel should be ground. What is fed into the mill by the one entrusted with responsibility for its work is what must be ground.

So too the mind, driven on by the assaults of the present life and by torrents of temptations pressing upon it from every side, cannot be empty of the flood of thoughts; but its diligent care will determine what kinds of thoughts it should admit or prepare for itself.

If we continually return to meditation on the Holy Scriptures, raising our memory to the recollection of spiritual things, to the desire for perfection, and to hope of future blessedness, then the thoughts that arise from these things [Col. 1024A] must cause the mind to linger upon what we have meditated. But if, overcome by laziness or negligence, we occupy ourselves with vices and idle conversations, or become entangled in worldly cares and needless anxieties, then what is generated from them, like a kind of weed, will also supply our heart with harmful activity. According to the Lord Savior’s saying, “Where the treasure of our deeds and intention is, there our heart must necessarily remain” (Matthew 6:21).

Above all, we must know that there are three sources of our thoughts: from God, from the devil, and from ourselves.

Thoughts are from God when the illumination of the Holy Spirit deigns to visit us, raising us toward more sublime progress and correcting us with most salutary remorse for what we have [Col. 1024B] acquired insufficiently or in which we have been overcome through acting negligently. This is also so when he discloses heavenly mysteries to us and turns our purpose toward better actions and our will toward better things.

Thus, when King Ahasuerus, chastised by the Lord, is prompted to consult the annals in which he remembers Mordecai’s services, he exalts him immediately to the highest rank of honor and at once revokes the most cruel sentence concerning the destruction of the Jewish people.

A series of thoughts arises from the devil when he attempts to overthrow us both by the struggle of vices and by hidden ambushes, displaying evil deceitfully under the appearance of good with the subtlest craft and transforming himself into an angel of light.

So the Evangelist reports: “When supper had taken place, the devil had already put it into the heart of Simon [Col. 1024C] Iscariot that he should betray the Lord” (John 13:2); and again: “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (ibid.). Peter also said to Ananias: “Why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5:3). And Solomon says: “If a spirit having power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes 10:4).

Thoughts arise from ourselves when we naturally remember what we are doing, have done, or have heard. Blessed David says of these: “I considered the days of old, and I kept the eternal years in mind. I meditated at night in my heart; I was exercised and sifted my spirit” (Psalm 76:6). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are empty” (Psalm 23:11). [Col. 1024D] And: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Proverbs 12:15).

We must therefore continually observe this threefold account and examine every thought that emerges in our heart with wise discernment, first investigating its origins, causes, and authors, so that we may consider how we ought to respond to it according to the merit of those who suggest it. Otherwise some intellectual beast—a passing lion or dragon—may have secretly left harmful tracks there, by which, through negligence concerning our thoughts, access may also be given to the hidden recesses of our hearts to other such creatures.

Thus, plowing the soil of our heart at every hour and moment with the Gospel plow—that is, by continual remembrance of the Lord’s cross—we shall be able to destroy either the lairs of harmful beasts born from ourselves or the hiding places of venomous [Col. 1025A] serpents.

This figure of the perfected mind is beautifully represented by the Gospel centurion. His strength and firmness, by which he was not carried away by thoughts rushing upon him indiscriminately but, according to his judgment, admitted good thoughts or drove away contrary ones without difficulty, are described in this figurative sense:

“For I also am a man under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Matthew 8:9; Luke 7:8).

Therefore, if we too fight manfully against disturbances and vices and can subject them to our authority and discernment, or bring the unstable cohort of our thoughts under the command of reason, we shall be advanced to the rank of this [Col. 1025B] spiritual centurion. We read that he was also represented in Exodus through Moses: “Appoint for yourself chiliarchs, centurions, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten” (Exodus 18:21).

Thus, raised to the summit of this dignity, we too shall possess the power of command, so that we may say to evil suggestions, “Go away,” and they will go; and to good ones, “Come,” and they will come. We shall likewise impose upon our servant—that is, our body—the duties of chastity and continence, and it will serve without any contradiction, no longer raising against us the goads of desire but offering complete service to the spirit.

Hear the Apostle [Col. 1025C] proclaiming what weapons this centurion has and for what exercises of battle they are prepared: “The weapons of our warfare,” he says, “are not carnal, but powerful through God” (2 Corinthians 10:4). If we wish to wage the Lord’s battles with these weapons and serve among the evangelical centurions, we must continually go about armed:

“Take up,” he says, “the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16).

Faith, therefore, receives the burning darts of lust and kills them through fear of future judgment and belief in the heavenly kingdom.

“And the breastplate of love” (ibid., 6:14). It is love itself that surrounds and protects the vital parts of our breast and does not permit the devil’s darts to penetrate our inner person. For love “bears all things, suffers all things, endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7).

“And the helmet of the hope of salvation” (Ephesians 6:17). A helmet is a protection for the head. Since [Col. 1025D] Christ is our head, we must always fortify him in every temptation and persecution with the hope of future blessings as with an unconquerable helmet, and above all preserve his faith unharmed and entire. For although someone may be truncated in other limbs, it is possible for him, though weakened, to survive somehow; but without a head no one is granted even a brief span of life.

“And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (ibid.). For it is sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Hebrews 4:12)—that is, dividing and cutting away whatever it finds in us that is carnal and earthly.

[Col. 1026A]

Whoever is equipped with these weapons and always defended against the darts and plundering of enemies will not be led away as a captive and subject to the hostile land of thoughts, bound by the chains of plunderers. Nor will he hear the Prophet say: “Why have you grown old in a foreign land?” (Baruch 3:11). Instead, as a victor, he will remain in whatever region of thoughts he chooses.

Do you wish to recognize the strength and power of this centurion, by which he carries the weapons we have mentioned—non-carnal weapons, but powerful through God? Hear the King himself gathering strong men for spiritual warfare, marking and testing those he has chosen:

“Let the weak say, ‘I am strong’” (Joel 3:10); and let the one who is patient be a fighter.

You see, therefore, that the Lord’s battles cannot be fought except by those who are patient and weak—by that weakness, [Col. 1026B] undoubtedly, in which our Gospel centurion was established when he spoke confidently: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). And again: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (ibid., 12:9).

One of the Prophets speaks of this weakness: “The one who is weak among them will be like the house of David” (Zechariah 12:8). The patient person will also fight these battles, with that patience of which it is said: “You need patience, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the reward” (Hebrews 10:36).

Concerning an evil thought, we must know that as soon as it has been disclosed through confession, it withers. Before judgment by discernment is pronounced, the most dreadful serpent, as though drawn from a dark subterranean cavern into the light by the power of confession, and [Col. 1026C] in a certain sense exposed and disgraced, withdraws.

Its harmful suggestions dominate us only as long as they are concealed in the heart. We read this same meaning represented in Ecclesiastes: “If the serpent bites without hissing, there is no advantage to the enchanter” (Ecclesiastes 10:11). This indicates that, if a diabolical suggestion or thought is not disclosed through confession to some enchanter—that is, a spiritual man accustomed to heal the wound immediately with the words of Scripture and draw the serpent’s harmful poisons from the heart—he will be unable to come to the aid of one who is in danger and about to perish.

God, moreover, is not only the suggester of good things but also their supporter and instigator, so that at times he draws even the unwilling and ignorant toward salvation. It is therefore established that no one can be deceived by the devil unless he has chosen to offer him the assent of his own will.

[Col. 1026D]

### CHAPTER III. On the Desire of the Flesh and of the Spirit

“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Galatians 5:16).

At this point the Apostle appears to name three things: the desire of the flesh against the spirit, and the desire of the spirit against the flesh. Their struggle against one another seems to have this cause and rationale: “so that,” he says, “we are unable to do the things we wish.” [Col. 1027A]

A fourth cause therefore remains—namely, that we do what we do not wish.

Let us now consider each point. Here we must understand “flesh” not as the human being, that is, the substance of the human being, but as his worst desires. Nor should we understand “spirit” as some substantial entity; rather, it designates the soul’s good and spiritual desires.

Since both of these—the desires of the flesh and of the spirit—are in one and the same person, an internal war is waged within us every day. The desire of the flesh, which rushes headlong toward vices, rejoices in pleasures belonging to present rest and delights in luxuries. By contrast, the desire of the spirit, opposing it, wishes to cling entirely to spiritual pursuits, so that it even desires to exclude the necessary uses of the flesh.

The flesh desires to be satisfied with sleep, filled with [Col. 1027B] food, and enriched with every abundance; the spirit is nourished by vigils and fasts and glories in poverty. The flesh seeks to shine through baths and to be surrounded by daily crowds of flatterers; the spirit rejoices in the squalor of filth and recoils from the presence of all mortals. The flesh is cherished by honors and human praise; the spirit glories in the insults and persecutions inflicted upon it.

Between these two desires, therefore, the will of the soul, standing in a certain blameworthy middle position, is delighted neither by the crimes of vices nor content with the pains of virtues. It seeks to be restrained from carnal passions in such a way that it does not wish to endure the necessary pains without which the desires of the spirit cannot be possessed.

It wishes to acquire bodily [Col. 1027C] chastity without chastising the flesh; purity of heart without the labor of vigils; the grace of patience without anyone’s provoking insult; to practice the humility of Christ without surrendering worldly honor; the simplicity of religion while pursuing worldly ambition; to serve Christ with human praise and favor; to proclaim the strictness of truth without causing even the slightest offense to anyone. Finally, it wishes to attain future blessings without losing present ones.

Such a will would never bring us to true perfection but would place us in a certain most dreadful tepidity, making us like those whom the Lord rebukes and corrects in the Apocalypse:

“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, [Col. 1027D] I will begin to remove you from my mouth” (Revelation 3:15).

This most lukewarm condition would remain unless the wars rising from both sides tore it apart. For when, serving this will of ours, we gradually wish to relax ourselves into such ease, the goads of the flesh immediately rise up. Wounding us with their vices and passions, they do not allow us to remain in the quality of purity in which we delight; instead, they drag us toward the cold road, full of the pleasures and thorns that we dread.

Again, if, kindled by spiritual fervor, we attempt to extinguish the works of the flesh and, without any regard for human frailty, devote our whole selves with elated heart to immoderate zeal for the virtues, the weakness of the flesh intervenes, and recalls and restrains the spirit from that blameworthy excess. Thus it happens that the two desires, each resisting the other in such alternating struggle, temper the soul’s will by a certain just moderation: for the soul neither wishes to surrender itself wholly to carnal desires nor to sweat through the labors of the virtues. This contention between the two excludes the more destructive inclination of the soul and places, as it were, a balance of equity upon the scales of our body, which fairly distinguishes the boundaries of spirit and flesh, permitting neither the mind, kindled by the ardor of the spirit, to prevail on the right, nor the flesh, weighted with the goads of vice, to prevail on the left.

And while this struggle is usefully stirred up within us day after day, we are salutarily compelled to come to that fourth state which we do not desire: namely, to acquire purity of heart not through leisure or security, but through continual toil and contrition of spirit, and to preserve bodily chastity through strict fasts, hunger, thirst, and vigilance. We would therefore be utterly and hopelessly lukewarm, without any continual indication of our negligence either in our body or in our own consciences; nor would we ever strive to attain the fervor of perfection, or even maintain the discipline of moderation, unless at least the irritation of the flesh and its increasing fluidity humbled and blunted us, and made us anxious and attentive also to the cleansing of spiritual vices.

This condition, namely lukewarmness, descending from the carnal state becomes the animal state, which is the worse degree. It is this condition that, passing from coldness to lukewarmness, is marked by the Lord’s most detestable word [Col. 1028C].

For there are three states of souls: the first is carnal, the second animal, and the third spiritual. We read that these are designated in the Apostle as follows. Of the carnal state it is said: “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, and indeed even now you are not able.
