For you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:2); and again: “For where there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” (ibid.). The animal state is likewise mentioned: “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Cor. 2:14). Of the spiritual person, however: “The spiritual person examines all things, but is himself judged by no one” (ibid.); and again: “You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1).

Therefore we must hasten, once we have renounced and ceased to be carnal—that is, once we have begun to withdraw from worldly conduct and to cease from that manifest pollution of the flesh—to strive immediately to grasp the spiritual state. We must not imagine that the conversion of the outward person, which we mentioned above, is sufficient for our perfection if we become slower in cleansing the remaining passions. Otherwise, if we are found in that lukewarm state which is judged most detestable, we may know that, according to the Lord’s sentence, we shall be vomited out of his mouth. He says: “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to spit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3:15).

And not without reason does the Lord declare that those whom he had already received into the entrails of his love, but who have been harmfully warmed into lukewarmness, must be expelled with a kind of convulsion of his breast. Although they could in some manner have offered him a salutary substance, they preferred to be torn away from his entrails. They have thus become far worse than those who were never brought to the Lord’s mouth as food, just as what we cast out under the compulsion of nausea is more detestable than anything else.

Whatever is cold, once received even into our mouth, is turned into warmth and perceived with salutary sweetness. But what has once been presented through the fault of pernicious lukewarmness we cannot, under the compulsion of great horror, bring near even to our lips—indeed, we cannot look upon it from a distance.

It is therefore rightly declared to be worse, because a carnal person—that is, a worldly or pagan person—more easily approaches salutary conversion and the summit of perfection than one who, having professed to be a monk yet not taking up the way of perfection according to the rule of discipline, has once departed from that fire of spiritual fervor [Col. 1029B]. The former, humbled at least by bodily vices and shuddering at that most icy state of unbelief in which he stands, will more easily fly toward perfection, kindled by the ardor of the spirit.

But the latter says in his heart: “Because I am rich and lack nothing” (Rev. 3:17). To him the following words also appropriately apply: “But you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3:17). He has become worse even than a worldly person because he does not recognize himself as wretched, blind, naked, or worthy of cleansing, nor acknowledge that he needs anyone’s admonition or instruction. He does not understand that, simply by the name of monk, he is burdened and weighed down in the opinion of many, since, while everyone believes him to be holy and honors him as a servant of God, it is necessary that in the future he be subjected to a more severe judgment and punishment [Col. 1029C].

## CHAPTER IV. On Chastity

There are six degrees of chastity.

The first degree is that a monk, while awake, not be struck down by carnal assault.

The second is that his mind not linger over pleasurable thoughts.

The third is that he not be moved toward desire even slightly by a woman’s appearance.

The fourth is that, while awake, he not endure even a simple movement of the flesh.

The fifth is that, when the memory of human generation has been introduced either by the discussion of its nature or by the necessity of reading, the subtlest assent to pleasurable action should not touch the mind; rather, he should contemplate it with the tranquil and pure gaze of his heart as a simple work and service necessarily contributed to the human race, conceiving no more from its recollection than if he were considering in his mind the making of bricks or the operation of any other workshop.

The sixth degree of chastity is that, even while asleep, he not be deceived by seductive images of women. Although we may not believe this deception to be subject to sin, it is nevertheless an indication that desire still lies hidden in the marrow of the soul. Gradually, according to the measure of chastity toward which each person strives, the mind—even when lulled by sleep—must be turned to hatred of that which it previously experienced as pleasurable. Then the promise made through the prophet to strong men as the highest reward of their labors may be granted to him by the Lord: “I will shatter bow, sword, and war from your land, and I will make you sleep securely” (Hos. 2:18).

Only then will he reach the state in which he is found by night as he is by day; in bed as he is in prayer; alone as he is when surrounded by crowds of people. Finally, the unavoidable eye will never detect in him anything that he wishes to conceal from human sight.

This will happen when the flesh, ceasing to desire against the spirit, has consented to its desires and virtue, and they have begun to be joined to one another by the firmest peace. Then, according to the Psalmist’s saying, “The brothers will dwell together as one” (Ps. 132:1), possessing the blessedness promised by the Lord, of which he says: “If two of you agree on earth about anything whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:19).

Whoever, therefore, has surpassed the degree of that intellectual Jacob—that is, the supplanter—will ascend, with his heart perpetually directed, to the status of Israel. He will have passed beyond the struggle of self-restraint and the supplanting of vices, with the sinew of his thigh struck numb.

Blessed David also distinguished this order by a prophecy of the Holy Spirit. He says first: “God is known in Judah” (Ps. 75:1), that is, in the soul which is still held under confession of sins, for Judah is interpreted as “confession.” But in Israel—that is, in the one who sees God, or, as some interpret it, “the most upright of God”—his name is not merely known, but is great.

Then, calling us to higher things and wishing also to show the very place in which the Lord takes delight, he says: “His place has come to be in peace” (ibid.)—that is, not amid the conflict of struggle and contention with vices, but in the peace of chastity and the perpetual tranquility of the heart.

If someone deserves to possess this place of peace through the extinction of carnal passions, then, progressing from this degree and consequently becoming a spiritual Zion—that is, a watchtower of God—his dwelling too will be there. For the Lord does not dwell amid the struggle of self-restraint, but in the continual watchtower of the virtues. There he no longer blunts or restrains the powers of the bows, but has broken them forever—the fiery darts of lust that were once shot against us from those bows [Col. 1030D].

You see, therefore, that just as the Lord’s place is not in the struggle of self-restraint but in the peace of chastity, so also his dwelling is in the watchtower and contemplation of the virtues. Hence the gates of Zion are rightly preferred to all the tents of Jacob: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Ps. 87:1).

In order, therefore, that the law of the body may correspond with the law of the mind, excess must also be curbed in the drinking of water itself. The daily accumulation of moisture should flow so sluggishly into members dried out by inactivity that it makes the movement of the body not only very rare but also slow, and kindles, so to speak, a lukewarm and cold fire—a flame moist with dew and without the heat of any burning—after the pattern of that marvelous vision of Moses, so that the bush of our flesh, surrounded by harmless fire, may not be consumed.

Or it should be like the case of the three young men, for whom the flame of the Chaldean furnace was scattered by the Spirit’s dew, so that not even the smell of fire touched their hair or the fringes of their garments. Thus we may begin already in this body to possess what the prophet promises to the saints: “When you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you” (Isa. 43:2).

Let us inquire more carefully what the blessed Apostle thought about this purity of chastity. “Put to death,” he says, “your members that are upon the earth”—not, certainly, the members of our body, but the body of sin, which consists of members and which, in his zeal for perfect holiness, he desires to be destroyed as quickly as possible. Concerning this body he says elsewhere: “That the body of sin might be destroyed” (Rom. 6:6). He then explains its destruction: “So that we may no longer serve sin” (ibid.).

From this body he also asks to be delivered with a cry, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24).

This body of sin is proved to be constructed from many members of vice, and whatever is sinned by deed, word, or thought belongs to its portion. Its members are rightly said to be upon the earth. For those who employ their service cannot truthfully profess: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

Describing the members of this body in the present passage, the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5).

In the first place, therefore, he thought fornication should be named, which is accomplished through carnal intercourse. As the second member he named impurity, which sometimes steals upon people, whether asleep or awake, without contact with a woman, through the negligence of an unguarded mind.

For this reason it is marked and prohibited in the Law. The Law not only deprived the impure of participation in sacred flesh but also commanded that they be separated from the assembly of the camp, lest by their contact they pollute holy things. It says: “Any person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of well-being that belongs to the Lord while impurity is upon him shall be cut off from his people” (Lev. 7:20). And: “Whatever the impure person touches shall be impure” (Lev. 22:3).

In Deuteronomy also: “If there is among you a man who is unclean because of a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp; he shall not come inside the camp until evening, and he shall wash himself with water. After sunset he may come back into the camp” (Deut. 23:10–11).

Next he set down lust as the third member of sin. It grows in the hidden recesses of the soul and can occur to someone even without bodily passion. There is no doubt that lust is so called from the fact that something is pleasing—*libido*, from *libet*, “it pleases.”

After this, descending from greater sins to lesser ones, he introduced the fourth member, evil desire. This can refer not only to the passion of impurity mentioned above but also generally to every harmful desire. It is the sickness of a corrupted will, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

It is a much greater achievement to restrain the desire of a slippery mind precisely when the opportunity for seductive sight is presented. These words most clearly prove that, for the perfection of purity, bodily chastity alone cannot suffice unless integrity of mind is added to it.

After all these, he names the final member of that body: greed. He undoubtedly shows that the mind must be restrained not only from desiring what belongs to others but also from its own possessions, which must be despised with generosity.

The multitude of believers is said to have done this in the Acts of the Apostles: “The whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul,” and “they distributed to each as any had need” (Acts 4:32, 35). And lest this perfection seem to belong only to a few, he testifies that greed is the service of idols.

Not without reason. Whoever does not share with the needs of the poor, and who postpones the commands of Christ for the sake of money that he preserves with faithless hoarding, incurs the crime of idolatry: he prefers love of worldly matter to divine love.

The blessed Apostle is so confident that fornication or impurity can be uprooted from our members that he declares they should not merely be put to death but should not even be named among us: “Fornication and every impurity or greed must not even be mentioned among you, as is fitting among saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or vulgar joking, which are not fitting” (Eph. 5:3–4).

He teaches that these are likewise harmful and exclude us equally from the kingdom of God, saying: “Be sure of this: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—that is, an idolater—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (ibid., 5:5).

And again: “Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with men, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10).

We should be certain, however, that although we undergo every severity of self-restraint—hunger and thirst, vigils, continual labor, and unceasing devotion to reading—we cannot attain the perpetual purity of chastity as the reward of these labors unless, sweating constantly in them, we are taught by the discipline of experience that incorruption is granted by the generosity of divine grace.

We should also know that to the degree in which someone progresses in gentleness and patience of heart, he will progress in bodily purity. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are the gentle, for they will possess the earth” (Matt. 5:5).

We shall not otherwise possess our earth—that is, this rebellious earth of the body will not be subjected to our rule—unless our mind has first been established in the gentleness of patience: “The gentle shall possess the earth” (Ps. 37:11).

They will not only possess it; they will also delight in an abundance of peace. No one whose flesh is still stirred by wars of desire will enjoy that peace securely. Such a person must necessarily be harassed by the fiercest battles of demons and, wounded by the fiery darts of lust, be cast down from possession of his earth, until the Lord removes wars to its furthest boundaries, breaks the bow, shatters the weapons, and burns the shields with fire (Ps. 46:9)—the fire, namely, which the Lord came to cast upon the earth.

When the Lord, having crushed the wars, has freed him from the heat of every incitement, he will reach that state of purity in which, having laid aside the shame by which he hated himself—that is, his flesh—while it was under attack, he will begin to delight in it as in a most pure tabernacle. “No evil shall befall you, and no scourge shall come near your tent” (Ps. 91:10).

Until we deserve to possess this peace as something firm and perpetual, we must be tested by many assaults, and we must often repeat this verse with groaning and tears: “I am utterly miserable; all day long I go about mourning, for my loins are filled with burning, and there is no health in my flesh” (Ps. 38:7–8).

This must continue until, strengthened by God’s grace in the purity that he desires, he may effectively say: “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined toward me” (Ps. 40:1).

## CHAPTER V. On Spiritual Knowledge

It is impossible for a soul that is occupied even slightly by worldly distractions, or that devotes itself to reading with the purpose and zeal of acquiring human praise, to deserve the gift of true knowledge, or to become generative of spiritual perceptions or a faithful keeper of sacred readings.

For it is one thing to possess ease of speech and polish of expression, and another to enter into the veins and marrow of heavenly words and contemplate their deep and hidden mysteries with the purest eye of the heart. This is obtained not at all through human teaching or worldly learning, but solely through purity of mind illumined by the Holy Spirit.

“Blessed are the pure in heart,” says the Lord, “for they will see God” (Matt. 5:8).

You must therefore hasten, whoever you are who wish to attain the true knowledge of the force of the Scriptures, first to acquire steadfast humility of heart. Through the perfection of love, it will lead you not to the knowledge that puffs up but to that which illumines.

Then you must strive with every effort to expel all worldly anxiety and thought and to offer yourself continually, or rather without interruption, to sacred reading, until constant meditation permeates your mind and forms it after its own likeness. It will make of it, in a certain sense, an ark of the covenant, containing two stone tablets—namely, the perpetual firmness of the two Testaments.

It will also contain a golden urn, that is, a pure and sincere memory, preserving within itself with perpetual tenacity the manna stored there: namely, the enduring and heavenly sweetness of spiritual perceptions and of that angelic bread.

It will also contain Aaron’s rod, that is, the saving standard of our supreme and true High Priest Jesus Christ, ever putting forth leaves with the green freshness of immortal memory. This is the rod which, after being cut from the root of Jesse, revives with greater vitality after having been made dead.

All these things will be protected by two cherubim, that is, by the fullness of historical and spiritual knowledge. For *cherubim* is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” They will continually protect the mercy seat of God—that is, the peacefulness of your heart—and will overshadow it against every assault of spiritual wickedness [Col. 1034B].

Thus your mind, raised not only into the ark of the divine covenant but also into a priestly kingdom, absorbed, as it were, in spiritual disciplines through an undissolving love of purity, will fulfill the priestly command prescribed by the lawgiver: “He shall not go out of the sanctuary, nor profane the sanctuary of his God” (Lev. 21:12)—that is, his heart, in which the Lord promises that he will dwell continually, saying: “I will live in them and move among them” (2 Cor. 6:16).

For it is impossible for an impure soul to attain spiritual knowledge. No one pours noble perfume, the finest honey, or any precious liquid into a foul and corrupted vessel. A jar once saturated with dreadful odors more easily contaminates even the most fragrant myrrh than receives any sweetness from it, because clean things are corrupted far more quickly than corrupted things are cleansed.

Thus the vessel of our heart, unless it has first been cleansed from every most foul contagion of vice, will not deserve to receive that anointing of blessing of which the prophet says: “It is like precious oil on the head, running down upon the beard, upon the beard of Aaron, running down over the collar of his robe” (Ps. 133:2).

Nor will it preserve undefiled that spiritual knowledge and those words of Scripture which are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. “What partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial?” Wisdom comes to rest in a good heart.

## PRAYER

To be said before receiving the body and blood of the Lord, published by Anselm, archbishop [Col. 1035].

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who, by the will of the Father and with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, gave life to the world through your death: I adore and venerate this holy body of yours and this holy blood of yours, which was handed over and poured out for many for the remission of sins.

I beseech your clemency, merciful Lord: through their power, make me one of those many, and make me perceive these things by faith and devotion in such a way that I may experience them through the effect of salvation.

Absolve and free your servants and handmaids—me and all who have confessed their sins to me, and for whom I have promised or am bound to pray, and those who hope or ask to be helped by my prayers before you—from every sin and punishment for sin.

Grant that our Church may rejoice in your continual protection and consolation. You who, with God the Father, and so forth.

## [SALUTATION TO JESUS CHRIST]

### A NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING VERSES

*(From Levis,* Anecdota sacra, *p. 33.)*

In a certain parchment manuscript in quarto format, as librarians call it, from the twelfth century, which was presented to us by the brothers Joseph and Jacob Reycends and which already contained several works published both by Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and by Saint Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, as well as by others, and so forth, we discovered among them these few verses, not yet published. We transcribe and issue them to the light of day.

### ST. ANSELM’S SALUTATION TO THE LORD JESUS CHRIST

Hail, body of Christ, born of a holy virgin,

Living flesh, complete divinity, true human being.

Hail, true salvation, way, life, redemption of the world;

May your right hand free us from every evil.

Hail, blood of Christ, holiest drink of heaven,

Saving stream washing away our sins.

Hail, blood poured from Christ’s side through the wound,

Hail, saving stream, hanging upon the cross.

## HYMNS OF SAINT ANSELM AND PSALTER OF THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY

### 303. Hymn at Matins

Light that shines in darkness,

Born from the Virgin’s womb,

Strip us of our night,

And clothe us in your day.

Mary, bridal chamber of God,

Ask that those who venerate you

May shine with virtues,

They whom guilt darkens.

Glory to you, Lord,

Born of the holy Virgin,

Reigning after conquering death,

With the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Amen.

### At Lauds

Most radiant sun of righteousness,

Risen from the holy Virgin,

With your brilliance illumine

Our harmful darkness.

Most chaste mother of the Dawn,

Make us, Lady,

So that the old life may wholly fall away

And the new may advance.

Glory to you, Lord, and so forth.

### At Prime

O Christ, offspring of the Virgin,

Equal to the Most High Father,

By the merits of your mother

Erase our sins.

O Virgin mother,

Venerable throughout the world,

Wonderful Mary, full of grace,

Pray for us, Lady.

Glory to you, Lord, and so forth.

### At Terce

O gracious Lord,

Whom we believe was born of the Virgin,

May this confession be for us

The remission of sins.

You who gave birth to the Son

Begotten by the Most High Father,

Through these your merits

Free us from the fall of death.

Glory to you, Lord, and so forth.

### At Sext

Supreme King, born

From Mary’s virginal womb,

Cleanse us from vices

And adorn us with holy merits.

Mother of God, O Lady,

Exalted by such great grace:

Make your exaltation

Our restoration.

Glory to you, Lord, and so forth.

### At None

Son of the Virgin Mary,

Grant us, by her merits,

To rise from our sins

And reach life.

You who became her Son,

God, for sinners:

Grant that those who proclaim this in faith

May experience salvation.

Glory to you, Lord, and so forth.

### At Vespers

Sun rising from a chaste womb

As the world grows evening,

Illumine us forever,

And do not decline at evening.

Mother of the eternal sun,

Bring it about by your holy merits

That perpetual morning may remain for us

And never fall away.

Glory to you, Lord, and so forth.

### At Compline

Day without end,

Rising for us from a chaste mother,

Foster us with perpetual light

And remove the night of guilt.

Mother of everlasting day,

Stand against our darkness,

Lest it scatter the light from us

And entangle us in sins.

Glory to you, Lord, and so forth.

### Supplicatory Salutation to Be Said before the Psalter of the Blessed Virgin

Hail, Queen, mother of mercy; our life, our sweetness, and our hope, hail. To you we cry, exiles, children of Eve; to you we sigh, groaning and weeping in this valley of tears.

Come then, our advocate, turn your merciful eyes toward us; and after this exile show us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb. O merciful, O loving, O sweet and glorious Lady, intercede for us.

# THE PSALTER OF OUR LADY

## PART I

Hail, mother of the Advocate,

Who, blessed in counsel,

Proceeded from the chamber

Of an incorrupt womb, as from a bridal room.

“Blessed is the man who has not walked,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

Asked the God and Father

And received as an inheritance

The nations whom he redeemed.

“Ask,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

Falling asleep through suffering,

Having slept in the tomb,

Conquered death by rising again.

“Glory to you,” and so forth.

“I slept,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

Gave himself to us in blood,

So that the baptized person

Might be marked with the light of divinity.

“Glory to you,” and so forth.

“It has been marked,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose Son

Mercifully clothes us

With the shield of good will,

The light of immeasurable majesty.

“With the shield of good will,” and so forth.

Hail, throne of the Godhead,

On which God of majesty

Deigned to become human.

From there he rescued our souls

By grace;

And those whom he made free,

He made safe in glory.

“Turn back,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

By his righteousness makes it so

That in us the just aids

Of his Father may be present.

“My just help is from the Lord.”

Hail, our advocate

And restorer of life,

Whose offspring is Lord

Above the thrones of heaven.

“For she has been exalted,” and so forth.

Hail, Zion, in whom God

Dwelt, having become human;

In whom those who know his name

Hope with greater effort.

“And let them hope in you,” and so forth.

Hail, singular Virgin,

Pleasing virginal chamber,

Whose Lord is in the temple

And whose seat is in heaven.

### 304. “The Lord is in the temple,” and so forth.

Hail, she whose Son

The Father appointed as salvation,

In whom, as in the only one,

He established our faith.

“I will place him in salvation,” and so forth.

Hail, she in whose Son,

The saving gift of God the Father,

We rejoice in the Lord,

Who grants us good things.

“My heart exulted,” and so forth.

Hail, our advocate,

Deliverer of captives,

From whom Emmanuel of Zion

Becomes salvation for Israel.

“Who will give,” and so forth.

Hail, she whose Son is the mountain

Of the one God and Father,

In whom the saints rest,

Those who love the truth.

“Lord, who will dwell,” and so forth.

Hail, Queen of virgins,

Virgin mother after her Son,

Whose offspring’s inheritance is splendid

Among joys.

“The measuring lines have fallen,” and so forth.

Hail, mother whom our mortality

Proclaims in you,

Because your offspring magnifies

His mercies.

“He magnifies his mercies,” and so forth.

Hail, whom the spirits praise,

To whom every virtue sings,

From whose heaven the Lord thundered

Through the cloud of flesh.

“And he thundered,” and so forth.

Hail, she from whose virginal

Bridal chamber God proceeded,

Offering himself to us

In bridal grace.

“In the sun,” and so forth.

Hail, Zion, from whom God,

Incarnate, watches over us,

Mindful of our offering

In the peace of his body.

“May he remember,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

The heavenly Father, his only one,

Gives to the nations forever

In blessings.

“For he will give,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

Made for us the bread of life,

The fat ones of the earth live from him,

Eat him, and adore him.

“They ate,” and so forth.

Hail, our advocate,

Whose offspring is the table of the Father;

For us he is consolation,

Lest tribulation break us.

“You have prepared in the sight,” and so forth.

Hail, Queen of grace,

Whose offspring, the King of glory,

Is the King, the Lord of virtues,

Christ God, light from light.

“Who is this?” and so forth.

Hail, she from whose virginal

Sanctuary proceeded

The one salvation of the whole world,

Sweet God, upright human being.

“Sweet and upright,” and so forth.

Hail, our advocate

And restorer of the fallen,

From whom God became human.

He alone stood upright.

“My servant,” and so forth.

Hail, mother whose bridegroom

And creator and son,

God, is illumination,

Salvation, and protection.

“The same,” and so forth.

Hail, mother of the Redeemer,

Whose flesh blossomed forth

When, having suffered the taste of death,

He rose from the tomb.

“And it blossomed again,” and so forth.

Hail, mother of chastity,

From whom the God of majesty

Rained down the voices of Scripture

And thundered forth virtues.

“The voice of God is over the waters,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

Having risen again, became for us

The joy of morning;

He is our hope and glory.

“Until evening,” and so forth.

Hail, heavenly Lady,

Whose offspring, righteousness,

Is our liberation

And protection with God.

“Be to me as God,” and so forth.

Hail, singular mother,

Whose fecundity is this:

Through it, for blessed men,

All iniquity is forgiven.

“The same,” and so forth.

Hail, virginal star,

Whose singular offspring

Taught us from the lyre

When he died upon the cross.

Then we sing psalms to him well

On the ten-stringed psalter;

When we refer to him

The mystery of the Decalogue.

“Give thanks to God with lyres,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

Was made the food of life

And gave our minds to taste

How sweet the Lord is.

“I will bless the Lord,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

Has become salvation for us;

A sword is poured forth,

Which cut apart our wounds.

“Pour out the sword,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

The torrent of supreme delight,

The Word of the Father made human,

Is the fountain of life and splendor of light.

“You intoxicated me,” and so forth.

Hail, heavenly gate,

Through which Emmanuel proceeded,

Whose light is righteousness,

And whose judgment is midday.

“And he will bring forth as,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, who gave birth

To the joy of the faithful,

Before whom stands the desire

Of those who love him.

Through her, he who was born for us

Is not hidden from the Father,

As he makes himself an advocate,

Mercifully granting a hearing.

“Lord, before you,” and so forth.

Hail, mother from whom

Our expectation proceeded,

In whom our substance

Sat upon the Father’s throne.

“And now what is,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

God made flesh,

Made himself a holocaust for us,

Our sole remedy.

“A holocaust of reproach,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

Healed our souls,

The sole powerful advocate,

Conducting cases and releasing sins.

“I said, Lord,” and so forth.

Hail, mother of chastity,

Whose praises become the sound of one feasting,

The sweet foods of Scripture,

In the voice of confession.

“In the voice of exultation,” and so forth.

Hail, mother of compassion,

Whose offspring is the altar of God the Father,

Making joyful the gaze

Of the youth of our mind.

“And I will enter,” and so forth.

Hail, she who gave birth

To the arm of the Father,

Jesus Christ,

Whose illumination

Makes the face of God visible.

“But your right hand,” and so forth.

Hail, she from whose womb

God the unbegotten Father

Brought forth the good Word,

Namely, the only-begotten Son.

“The same.”

Hail, she whose Most High One

Consecrated the tabernacle,

The ray of the Father’s light,

Made our remedy.

“Of the river,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring

Has become our salvation;

Therefore the Psalm cries to us:

“Clap your hands, all peoples.”

“The same.”

Hail, heavenly dwelling,

From the middle of whose temple

We received the incarnate

Mercy of God.

“We received,” and so forth.

Hail, entrance of heaven,

Divine dwelling,

Whose Son is for us

Brother and redemption.

“A brother did not redeem,” and so forth.

Hail, glorious Zion,

From whom the face of the Word,

Made manifest to us in flesh,

Becomes visible in the beauty of God.

“From the rising of the sun,” and so forth.

Hail, heavenly gate,

Through which the only one of God the Father,

Given back to us,

Proceeded as saving joy.

“Restore to me,” and so forth.

## PART II OF THE PSALTER OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

Like a fruitful olive tree,

Having suffered the cross’s gibbet,

Flowed forth wholly in grace.

“But I,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

The one who was without sin,

Was born from the Virgin

And did not derive guilt from his origin.

Hail, mother, whose offspring,

The only one of the heavenly Father,

Was made for us

A voluntary sacrifice.

“Voluntarily,” and so forth.

Hail, she from whom Christ arose;

In the evening of Passover he taught,

In the morning he was led to Pilate

And proclaimed the truth.

At midday he was crucified

And was heard by the Father;

Dying, he conquered death,

He who rose from death.

“In evening and morning,” and so forth.

Hail, Queen of virgins,

Joy of the faithful,

Who gave birth to joy

In the light of the living.

“For you have rescued,” and so forth.

Hail, she whose Son

Has been exalted above the heavens,

And whose glory is

Throughout all earthly things.

“Be exalted above the heavens,” and so forth.

Hail, she from whom

The just fruit was certainly born,

Judging those on earth,

So that he may exalt them to eternal things.

“And the human being will say,” and so forth.

Hail, she in whose mysteries

The Word of the Father became incarnate,

And ran without sin,

And directed his course toward glory.

“Nor is there iniquity,” and so forth.

Hail, she from whom the Word of the Father,

For our sake made flesh,

Extended his sandal

Into Idumea of the nations.

“Into Idumea,” and so forth.

Hail, mother, whose only one,

God and human being, Son,

Cries out from the ends of the earth,
While it calls us members of itself.

“From the ends of the earth,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

God spoke once,

while the Father’s only Word

is truly your son.

“He spoke once,” etc.

Hail, heavenly star,

bearing the light of the nations,

whose child we adore

while we keep vigil from the light.

The same.

Hail, joy of the righteous,

in whose son they hope,

and the upright in heart are praised,

so that they may rejoice in rest.

“The righteous man shall rejoice,” etc.

Hail, that Zion of peace

in which a hymn to God is fitting,

the hall of your chastity

which he made his bridal chamber.

The same.

Hail, from whose son

we rejoice to God the Father;

we offer psalms and praise,

and in the Psalms we rejoice.

The same.

Hail, earth, which gave

the fruit of confessing God,

whose blessing is

the true knowledge of itself.

“So that we may know,” etc.

Hail, temple of Jerusalem,

possessing a heavenly appearance,

from whose sanctuary

the vision of the Father proceeded.

“Confirm this, O God,” etc.

Hail, through whom

our confessing Zion is saved,

and those to whom grace is given

shall dwell in it.

“For God will save,” etc.

Hail, through whose son

God the Father, hastening

to the aid of the nations,

turns his attention to helping them.

The same.

Hail, secret of the Virgin,

through which the light of light proceeded,

and Jesus Christ added

praise above all others.

For the Father of power,

creating all things, made himself known;

but the Father of sweetness

was made clear to us in Christ.

“But I shall always hope,” etc.

Hail, fleece of purity,

in which God of majesty,

pouring down like rain,

distilled in grace.

“He shall descend like,” etc.

Hail, whose son is

the good God to the upright in heart;

whoever turns toward him

attains fullness of days.

“Therefore he shall turn,” etc.

Hail, virginal earth,

in whose midst God

worked the mysteries

of salvation in the Son.

“But God is our King,” etc.

Hail, powerful in virtues,

whose Son, exulting on the cross,

broke the horns of sin

and its bonds.

“And all the horns,” etc.

Hail, whose Son,

God known in Judea,

has a great name in Israel

for those who rightly believe.

The same.

Hail, mother, from whom

the Father made his hand known,

and with his arm

redeemed the peoples through the Only-begotten.

“You made your hand known,” etc.

Hail, mother, from whom

the bread of angels was born for us;

he recalls us, restores us,

and perfects us in himself.

“The bread of angels,” etc.

Hail, Queen of joy,

whose heavenly Son’s people

are the Christians,

and whose sheep are the sheep of his pasture.

“But we are your people,” etc.

Hail, from whom the Most High God,

the Only-begotten in the Father’s bosom,

who sits above the Cherubim,

appears before Ephraim.

“He who sits,” etc.

Hail, from whom Christ,

who is not a recent God for us,

was born; he is the Son

eternally coeternal with God the Father.

“Hear, O people,” etc.

Hail, whose son is

God, Lord of gods,

the only God who judges,

and who makes blessed in himself.

The same.

Hail, star of paradise,

mother of that Son

who alone is Most High,

whose name is Lord.

“And let them know,” etc.

Hail, virginal star,

whose child, bearer of the law,

is in the bosom of God the Father,

the giver of blessing.

“For indeed a blessing,” etc.

Hail, blessed earth,

sanctifying the mysteries,

whose sacred fertility

is the truth of God the Father.

“Truth,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

all nations adore

and glorify as the true God,

confess and magnify.

“I bow down,” etc.

Hail, heavenly city,

whose fertility is God.

Hail, Zion, in which

your very founder was born.

“Can it be that Zion,” etc.

Hail, mother of the true God,

who died for us,

broke the gates of hell,

and was the only free one among the dead.

“I have been counted,” etc.

Hail, heavenly lily,

through whose single flower

the eternal covenant

has been established for the faithful.

“I have arranged,” etc.

Hail, whose son

became a refuge for us

through the fellowship of the flesh,

which is the remedy of life. [Col. 1043]

The same.

Hail, singular splendor,

whose virginal power

made the Most High God

our refuge and Father.

“He says to the Lord,” etc.

Hail, virginal goodness,

which we confess to the Lord,

when we profess that, with the Virgin,

the true God was born.

The same.

Hail, virginal beauty,

which the Father’s Word put on

when, from the fountain of chastity,

he girded himself with our flesh.

The same.

Hail, mother, whose child,

the Lord, King of retribution,

fully enacted liberty

when he rose from the dead.

The same.

Hail, mother in childbirth,

whose royal son

we celebrate in thanksgiving

to God our Savior.

The same.

Hail, from whose son

we sing a new song,

through whose exchange of flesh

salvation was made for the nations.

The same.

Hail, glorious mother,

solar light, bright star,

from whom the righteous one, the light,

has arisen as joy for the upright in heart.

“The light has arisen,” etc.

Hail, mother, from whom he proceeded

who performed wonders,

whose right hand did not save itself

by its own power.

“He saved,” etc.

Hail, sanctuary of the King,

whose honor is judgment,

whose footstool

is the garment of the flesh he assumed.

“Exalt,” etc.

Hail, whose fertility

is divine sweetness,

whose mercy

endures forever.

“Praise his name,” etc.

Hail, mother of graces,

who bore the Lord;

to him we sing

of mercy and judgment.

The same.

## PART III

Hail, through whom

our Zion will be seen in glory,

whose child is the work

of all creation together.

“For the Lord has built,” etc.

Hail, from whose sanctuary

that Son proceeded,

whose dominion is wondrous

in every place.

“Bless the Lord, all his works, in all places,” etc.

Hail, from whose inmost parts

God put on beauty,

and clothed himself

in the garment of our faith,

as in light.

“Confession,” etc.

Hail, star of Paradise,

whose light we adore,

while we sing Alleluia

in praise of your Son.

Title of the Psalm: “Alleluia.”

Hail, heavenly star,

Alleluia of the faithful,

through whom all praises of God

are proclaimed among the nations.

Again, “Alleluia” in the title.

Hail, mother, for whom the redeemed,

rescued from the hands of the enemy,

clothed in a double robe,

sing a double Alleluia.

Double “Alleluia” in the title.

Hail, mother, from whom God,

incarnate, is led

into a fortified city,

strengthening the faith of the Church.

“For he will lead,” etc.

Hail, from whose son

the Father did not withhold praises,

and whom he raised

from the dead out of the tomb.

The same.

Hail, daughter of David,

from whom our substance,

Jesus Christ in glory,

sits at the Father’s right hand.

The same.

Hail, Queen of virgins,

who bore the Son,

who was made redemption,

sent by the Father to the people.

“Redemption,” etc.

Hail, mother of true light,

from whom was born in darkness

the light, God,

merciful and just to the upright in heart.

“The light has arisen,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

is exalted above the nations,

regarding the humble

both in heaven and on earth.

“Who is like the Lord,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

they shall not praise in hell;

but we ourselves, who live,

bless the Lord.

“The dead do not,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

is accepted by God the Father

in the land of the living,

where they live through his death.

“I shall please,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose crucified child

obtained us through the cup of salvation,

through water together with blood.

“The cup,” etc.

Hail, through whom

God’s mercy was confirmed,

and he opened

the truth of prophecy and grace.

“For his mercy was confirmed,” etc.

Hail, mother, from whom God,

the Son of God, shone forth,

conceived by the Holy Spirit,

and rising from death.

“Blessed is he who comes,” etc.

Hail, mother, through whom

the spotless way was revealed,

he who, from God the flower,

caused virginity to blossom.

The same.

Hail, mother of this child,

to whom we cry out in faith,

that he may be a gracious hearer

and the oppressor may have no power.

The same.

Hail, mother, from whom proceeded

Jesus Christ Emmanuel,

who does not sleep but keeps watch,

the true protector of Israel.

“Behold, he neither sleeps,” etc.

Hail, mother of this King,

whose thrones of judgment

will sit in judgment

to praise the Lord.

“For there,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

is God dwelling in heaven,

while in the minds of the saints

he reigns through his sweetness.

The same.

Hail, whose son

the faith of the martyrs proclaims;

unless God had helped,

the persecutor would have swallowed them.

“When they rose up,” etc.

Hail, in whose Son

those who trust wholeheartedly

become like Mount Zion for God,

in which there is a vision of peace.

The same.

Hail, in whose Son

we have been made comforted

and are filled with joy,

freed from captivity.

The same.

Hail, heavenly Lady,

whose fruit is our reward,

because through his precious death

we received life.

“When he gives,” etc.

Hail, singular mother,

whose child is Emmanuel,

through the exchange of his flesh

made the peace of Israel.

“So that you may see,” etc.

Hail, mother of the Most High King,

whose blessing is

everlasting life,

eternal possession.

“And they did not say,” etc.

Hail, in whose Son

this mercy is found:

that abundant redemption

may be made for his people.

“For with the Lord,” etc.

Hail, in whose Son

true Israel now hopes,

which, not lifted up in conduct,

has humbly regarded itself.

“Let Israel hope,” etc.

Hail, mother, pure Virgin,

whose child, God and man,

sits at the Father’s right hand,

God and son of David.

The same.

Hail, in whose Son’s

sheepfold we dwell,

like that brotherhood

which one charity governs.

The same.

Hail, in whose Son’s

courts we dwell,

when, in his faith,

we are enlarged by charity.

“You who stand,” etc.

Hail, mother, in whom God,

blessed from Zion,

dwells in Jerusalem,

possessing the vision of peace.

“Blessed is God from Zion,” etc.

Hail, in whose Son

we confess the Father God,

for his mercy

endures forever.

The same.

Hail, blessed earth,

in which the song is sung

that may not be sung

in a foreign land.

“How shall we sing,” etc. [307]

Hail, whose son,

the true temple of God the Father,

we adore as is fitting,

while confessing in faith.

“In the sight of,” etc.

Hail, whose child,

laid asleep in the tomb,

made night like day

when he rose from the night.

“For darkness,” etc.

Hail, whose son’s

Father is the saving power,

acting on the day of battle

with the force of our redemption.

“Lord, Lord, power of my salvation.”

Hail, mother, whose child

made a singular way,

until he completed the passage

through which he gave us life.

“They shall fall into the snare,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

all the righteous awaited,

until the Father gave

our race over to his death.

“Lead me out of prison,” etc.

Hail, mother of this child,

whose spirit leads us

into the land of righteousness,

the land of resurrection.

“Your good Spirit,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child,

while he flashed forth his powers,

scattered the unbelieving powers

by his death.

“Flash forth,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

is the Lord worthy of praise,

and of whose greatness

there is neither end nor limit.

“Great is the Lord,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

truly frees the fettered,

because his faith alone

enlightens blind minds.

“The Lord sets free,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

builds Jerusalem,

while mercifully gathering us

to its vision.

“He who builds,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

that Jerusalem praises,

and for whom it sighs forever,

whose boundaries he gave peace.

“He who established its boundaries,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

the angelic citizens praise

out of due justice,

and every creature praises.

“Praise him, all his angels,” etc.

Hail, from whose son

the daughters of Zion exult,

while the souls of the saints

rejoice in his fellowship.

“The saints shall exult,” etc.

Hail, mother, whose child

the saints praise with the drums

of their merits, by grace,

putting vices to death.

“Praise the Lord with the drum,” etc.

## CONCLUSION OF THE SALUTATIONS

Hail, singular jewel,

bearing written mysteries,

placed in the breastplate

of the eternal Pontiff.

Hail, golden tablet,

you yourself circumscribed,

the propitiatory name,

which is ineffable.

Hail, sole virginity,

whose fertility is God,

through whose divine power

our shoulder-piece is made divine.

Afterward the antiphon is to be said:

“Hail, Queen of heaven,” etc.

After it comes this other one:

Rejoice, Virgin, immaculate Mother of God;

rejoice, you who received joy from the Angel;

rejoice, you who bore the love of the eternal light;

rejoice, mother of piety and mercy;

rejoice, holy Virgin, Mother of God;

you alone, unwedded mother;

all creation praises you

as the Mother of light;

be, we beseech you, a gracious intercessor for us.

Prayer: “O God, who from the blessed,” etc.

## HYMN I IN PRAISE OF THE HOLY MOTHER OF GOD

O Mary, good name,

memorable name:

O name better

than many riches!

A balsam giving fragrance,

incense of wondrous perfume,

an eternal flower, a rose of old age,

an ever-green tree.

A star surpassing

the sun’s radiance

with its own brilliance,

always a mother, because never

will you be without offspring.

Beautiful and gracious,

a song of joy;

to be proclaimed and praised

privately and publicly,

not here only, but throughout

the breadth of the world,

and in the heavens,

with the sweet melody of the angels.

No one can refuse

to love you without guilt;

to please you, stand firm in faith,

and live for God.

While we commend ourselves to you,

receive our vows;

while we prostrate ourselves

to salute you,

although this is very rarely done,

hail you before your image,

speaking to you,

incorrupt and fruitful;

do not despise me.

Heaven of heavens, house of God,

vessel of mercy,

you are assuredly ready

and wholly able to send angels

to whatever uses you wish,

as many examples prove,

which it would be lengthy to set out.

Therefore send to us

holy Gabriel,

who fittingly saluted you

as the mother of his God,

and proclaimed that you were to be made pregnant

by the holy Spirit,

without the generation

of natural intercourse.

Grant him, therefore, to us

as an advocate before you,

so that he may deign

to present our prayers to you.

May he tend our hearts

with heavenly medicine,

for they are excessively

subject to vanity.

But you, glorious mother,

have compassion on the wretched,

and, if anyone asks,

stretching forth your hand,

to loose his chains;

not disdaining

to attend to the hardships of the miserable,

but ready to aid

anyone who calls upon you.

O patroness of sinners,

turn toward us here;

illumine our lands

with the star of your face.

And from that seat of yours

look upon this house,

and commend this place

unceasingly to the Savior.

And, kindly mindful of us,

rescue us from evils,

and continually refresh us

with your benefits.

We who commend ourselves to you

with sufficient necessity,

imploring your help

to descend upon us:

for on account of our sins

we are afflicted on every side,

and the plots of the enemies

have prevailed against us.

They do not cease

to gnaw us with their native tooth.

Alas, wretched ones! Why was I born

to behold such evils?

Pious mother, star of the sea,

comfort me in this,

and grieve with the great friend of God,

Nicholas.

And grieve with the pious handmaid of God,

Cunegund,

whose honor in the commonwealth

has now almost failed.

By her intercession,

be the guardian of this vineyard,

surrounding it with a wall

against those who tear away

the branches from the fire.

Bless and protect

the shoots I have produced;

for she loved you

most devotedly,

always burning

with zeal for your Church’s welfare.

Therefore love her servants

in turn.

Comfort the abandoned,

stretch out your hand to the fallen,

and lead us out of the mud of filth

and the pit of misery. [308]

May the darkness of everlasting death

not seize us,

but may the heavenly light of grace

illumine our minds.

By the gift of which

we can escape such filth,

by which the world

pollutes our members wickedly.

For you are the mother of Christ,

of sweet remembrance;

because of you

the gates of paradise are open to us.

You are so powerful

in every work of goodness

that it is altogether blessed

to recognize what you are.

“Blessed is his name,

holy and terrible,”

he who made your name

celebrated throughout the world,

through whom he could forgive

his guilty ones their sins.

I beg you, pious Virgin,

always remember me.

And always obtain for me

the gifts of truth,

so that he may protect me

with his holy governance.

By your prayer,

may he be the consoler

of my soul,

and pour oil

into the lamp of the sinner,

so that, prepared,

it may be able to meet

the heavenly Bridegroom.

Hail, singular Virgin,

kindly accepting this;

hail, temple of all graces,

capable of receiving them all;

hail, whose alms

feed sinners.

Rejoice, blessed one,

and grant me one of those alms,

so that, by removing through it

all fear of the enemies,

I may be able without end

to give thanks to God.

May the angelic powers

bless you forever,

and may all the saints

bless you at every moment

to the praise of the Creator;

and may you bless me,

and I you.

## HYMN II, TO BE SUNG ON VARIOUS SOLEMNITIES OF THE BLESSED MOTHER OF GOD

Hail, unwedded bride,

through whom the rescue

of the utterly fallen world

was accomplished;

hail, through whom

the redemption of Eve,

the first mother, was accomplished;

holy Mary, pray for us.

Hail, bride, etc.

You are inaccessible

in the height of thought,

an invisible depth

to the eyes of angels.

Χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη  
Θοτόκος παρθένε

Rejoice, highly favored one;

Mother of God, Virgin.

Holy Mother of God, pray for us.

Hail, bride, etc.

Bearing the One who bears all things,

you are the throne of empire;

you are the star showing the sun,

the sun of the mystical day;

the star of the world’s setting,

of conspicuous light.

Holy Virgin of virgins, pray for us. [Col. 1049]

Hail, bride, etc.

You became the womb

of the divine Incarnation.

Through you every form

of creation is renewed,

and with you the Maker

and Origin of all things is adored.

Lady of angels, pray for us.

Hail, bride, etc.

You stand forth as the initiator

of the hidden counsel,

the first fruits of Christ’s true

and wondrous works;

you are the fountain and beginning

of his doctrines.

Queen of heaven, pray for us.

Hail, bride, etc.

You are the heavenly ladder

by which God himself descended,

leading earthly things,

as his bride, above heavenly things.

You, unwedded mother,

are superior to all honor;

ever-virgin, pray for us.

Hail, bride, etc.

You are the strong lament

and grief and sadness of demons;

but of the good angels,

praise, honor, and glory.

You satisfy

the joy of all the elect.

Temple of the Lord, pray for us.

Hail, bride, etc.

Generating perpetual

and inaccessible light,

surpassing the knowledge

of all the wise,

you are the splendor

and prudence of holy souls.

Sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, pray for us.

Hail, bride, etc.

Germinating the civic crown

of life through the fruit of your womb;

possessing divinity

and flourishing in it;

nurturing humanity

and cultivating it,

you alone, without equal, pray for us.

That virginity whose seals remain intact,

yet which is fruitful,

may grant us sweet help.

[Col. 1049]

## VERSES OF ST. ANSELM ON HIS PREDECESSOR LANFRANC

[Col. 1049A]

Lanfranc undertook neither the wealth

nor the honors of an archbishopric,

but cares and labors.

Born in Italy,

from the region of Pavia,

of distinguished citizens

and honorable condition,

he was a monk and prior of Bec,

then abbot of Caen;

afterward, a prelate,

primate and archbishop of Canterbury.

He was the restorer

of the whole Church of the English,

and likewise a helper

of the Normans.

Most of the world

had experienced his teaching;

and he was a common comfort

to widows and to the world,

to the lame, crippled, leprous,

possessed, deaf, and blind,

and also to others afflicted by vices.

After exhortation,

he did not refuse to bring help;

but while he lived,

he was hope and relief to everyone.

And although delicious meals

with drink,

and soft and costly garments,

were available to him, [Col. 1049B]

he himself was clothed

in the garment of austerity,

always living on meager

and poor fare.

A true, not false,

cultivator of justice in his office,

he was a most upright

and pious avenger of wickedness.

Harsh toward the proud,

begging no one for a reward,

and never two-faced

toward the innocent and good.

Chaste, he helped

by sparing the unchaste;

just, he corrected

by tolerating the unjust.

Thus caring for others,

he performed the work of a shepherd;

thus preserving himself,

he pleased the Lord in all things. [Col. 1050A]

This man, so wise

and strong in this struggle,

could not finally escape

the snares of death.

O how many sorrows

the wretched then experienced!

And how many honors

the English people lost!

With what groaning did the clergy pray,

with what weeping the monk!

And how great the sorrow

with which both sexes suffer!

If anyone trusts that he can

say everything,

I affirm that he does not know

how to say everything.

And whoever judges himself

comparable to Lanfranc

is rightly made blameworthy

by his presumption.

When the sun was entering

the eleventh day,

the final boundary

of his blessed life was set.

Eternal God, King of kings

and Creator of all things,

be his perpetual defender

and helper.

Most holy Virgin,

mother of the Redeemer of the world,

preserve him,

lest the dark spirit wear him down. [Col. 1050B]

All you elect,

help Lanfranc

with your prayers and merits,

and join him to yourselves.

You also who still gladly retain life

and possess hope of what is to come,

as long as you remain,

I exhort and admonish you

to assist him,

so that what you have done

you may receive after death.

For whoever prays for him

as a suppliant and diligently,

he himself works for that person

as a suppliant and diligently.

Amen.

[Col. 1051]

## WORDS OF THE VENERABLE ANSELM

(Edited by Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, p. 987, from a manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden.)

[Col. 1051A]

### [LETTER]

The venerable Father Anselm, while he was still abbot of Bec, was one day meditating deeply in his mind and, by thinking excessively, was almost disturbed by his own thoughts. A certain monk of his who happened to be present said to him:

“Lord Father, for God’s sake, tell me what you are thinking, because I see you disturbed by your thoughts.”

“I shall tell you,” he replied. “This is what I was thinking. Suppose there were a rich man who had a flock of sheep and summoned a boy so weak and small that, if a wolf came, it could more easily carry him away than any sheep, and entrusted his sheep to him to guard, with the condition that if he lost any one of them, his soul would be required for that sheep’s soul. Should he not be very afraid?

But if he entrusted the others to any one of those sheep—perhaps the weaker and more foolish one—and said: ‘Sheep, take care of these sheep, and know that if you lose any one of them, I shall require its blood from your hand, and your soul shall be required for its soul,’ should not that sheep be afraid? What security could it have?

So it is with me. I,” he said, “I am the little boy; I am the weak and feeble sheep; I am as easy to snatch away as anyone else. God has entrusted me with the care of his sheep, so that I may govern, guard, and feed them, on the condition that, if any of them perishes through my negligence, my soul shall be required for its soul, and God shall require its blood from my hand. Therefore I fear; therefore I am troubled, because I know that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God.” [Col. 1051C]

And the kindly brother said:

“Lord, may God be with you. Why do you think and say such things? No one thinks what you think; look, the other abbots rejoice and are cheerful.”

He replied:

“Perhaps God has given them security; therefore they are joyful and cheerful. But he has not given it to me. For this reason I rightly fear, because I know that he exacts his money with interest from those to whom he has entrusted it.”

## SAYINGS OF ANSELM

Royal judgment is judgment sought voluntarily; a monk’s judgment is imposed. The abstinence of any secular ruler proceeds from his own will. A monk’s abstinence depends upon the judgment of his superior. The sadness of a king or any powerful person is proud. A monk’s sadness is sweet and full of compunction. Three things make a person live honorably among human beings: modesty, silence, and moderation.

A certain monk of Bec was being sought for the episcopate of the Church of Beauvais. Since St. Anselm, the abbot, was unwilling to give his assent to this election and would not grant his monk to those who requested him, the petitioners said:

“Lord, we are choosing him; he is not putting himself forward. Why do you not grant what we ask?”

“If God himself were choosing me,” he replied, “I would still be afraid, because he chose Saul through the prophet and Judas the traitor by himself, and both were rejected.” [Col. 1052C]

[Col. 1051C]

309–310. SOME USEFUL SAYINGS (G)*

### COLLECTED FROM THE SAYINGS OF ST. ANSELM, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Note: [Col. 1051D] The last editor of St. Anselm published in the appendix (pp. 545–547) a small collection of several sentences drawn from his writings, entitled *Some Useful Sayings*, etc. In all appearance, this is the same collection which, in a manuscript of Thomas Digby (*Bib. Angl.*, MS. par. I, no. 1759), bears the title *Sentences of Anselm*. In what has been printed, it is stated that a copyist collected it from the discourses Anselm delivered orally. This copyist, moreover, could very well have been [Col. 1052D] Alexander, first a monk of Bec and later of Canterbury, to whom Wion and Possevin attribute a similar collection. In any case, the latter part of what is found in the appendix is nothing other than, word for word, the last of St. Anselm’s homilies on a passage of the Epistle to the Hebrews; thus this little collection could be joined to the genuine works of our saint, since it contains only his own words.]

(From the Vatican Library.)

O human being, who consist of a rational soul and human flesh, of miserable condition, filled with many miseries, wretched and pitiable; poor, blind, naked, subject to very many necessities—return to your heart. Why do you wander outside? What do you seek outside? Why do you devote yourself to carnal things? Why do you entangle yourself in worldly affairs? Why do you wrap yourself in vanities? You delight in lower things and withdraw from everything inward and higher; through outward things you are scattered, and in the things within you are confused.

The more you approach the world, the farther you withdraw from God. The wiser you are outwardly, the more foolish you become inwardly. The more you gain outside, the more you lose within. The more you wander among outward things, the more you are emptied within. The more anxious you are about temporal things, the more destitute you are in spiritual things.

Why is it that you arrange everything but do not wish to arrange yourself? Why are you prudent in everything yet foolish concerning yourself? Why are you careful to make all outward things good, yet allow yourself always to be evil and useless? Does the Spirit of God sleep in you while the spirit of the world keeps watch in you? Is reason idle in you while sensation is vigorous? Is the Spirit of God extinguished in you while the flesh of the world rules you? Does love of earthly things burn in your heart while love of eternal goods dies in you? You love the world and abandon God? You remember everyone and forget yourself? You desire and love the things that are upon the earth, but do not care about heavenly things? You draw near to destruction and become far from salvation? You run toward the devil and distance yourself from God?

Return, return, transgressing human being, to your heart, because almighty God speaks peace to the one who turns back to his heart. God gave you everything in this world, and you abandon God because of everything? God made everything for you, and you abandon yourself because of everything? Because of everything that comes before you, you abandon God, and therefore everything will abandon you. Because of creatures you leave the Creator, and therefore all creatures will rise up against you, because by offending the Creator you have offended every creature.

And therefore all creatures, which were made for your service and benefit, will be turned toward your vengeance and punishment; and there will be woe for you without end, because you did not wish to possess the good that has no end.

Recognize yourself, then, human being; recognize yourself. Consider that you accomplish nothing. Pay attention to the fact that you are vile and evil. Weep, wretched human being, weep continually for your sins. Wipe away your wickedness and misery with tears, because you sinned by your own will. Let it displease you above all things. Let it displease you with your whole heart, and let it continually displease you that you dared to offend the Lord of immeasurable majesty, who has power over all flesh and can cast body and soul into Gehenna. [Col. 1053D]

Let your heart become bitter toward yourself with the bitterest bitterness, because you offended the supreme God and Father of incomprehensible majesty and ineffable mercy—he who is kind and merciful toward the ungrateful and evil—easily, willingly, gladly, and with delight.

Displease yourself entirely, so that you may entirely please him who is the highest, true, and only God; no one pleases him except the one who displeases himself, and no one displeases him except the one who pleases himself. For God scatters the bones of those who please human beings, and what is lofty and beautiful among human beings is abominable before God.

It is astonishing in your case, wretched human being: toward evils you are wholly eager, wholly ready, wholly pliable, wholly clever and mobile, and wholly anxious; but toward good things you are wholly hard, wholly lazy, wholly unbelieving, and rebellious toward what is good.

From where do you have this, except from the flesh, which you love and follow so greatly? Because you follow the flesh, you love the flesh; and because you follow the flesh, you do the works of the flesh, and with it you will be punished.

The fruit of your flesh is lust, desire, weakness, frailty, and pain. A worm and corruption, a rotting and fetid stench. You yourself are so blinded by the darkness of ignorance that you do not know what you are. You do not consider where you are going, nor notice what you have done, nor understand the enemy’s ambushes and deceitful temptations; wholly negligent, you do not think where you ought to be heading.

You do not know the way, and you do not seek it, for a great road remains before you. You diligently seek food, clothing, and rest, and all the needs of the flesh whenever you lack them; but concerning the life and salvation of your soul, you are always lukewarm and do not care, although you are always in need, full of wickedness and evil.

Wretched human being, for the sake of feeding and clothing your wretched body, and satisfying the pleasures of the flesh—which after a few days will be devoured by worms—you labor anxiously, run and hurry about, keep watch, and do not let your eyes sleep, so that you may fill your belly. But why do you not labor anxiously for your soul, which must be presented to God in heaven, so that you may feed it with good works and clothe it with virtues, lest the shame of its nakedness appear?

Sad human being, you always seek to fill your belly; why do you not feed your hungry soul? You are always concerned about a vessel of dung; why are you not concerned about the image of God? You feed what is sterile and does not bear fruit, but do not satisfy your hungry soul with good things?

Woe to you, because your soul fails within you from hunger. Woe to you, and woe will be to you, because you render to Caesar what is Caesar’s but do not render to God what is God’s; therefore you are accursed by God and will be put to shame by him.

See, wretched human being, see: everything is vanity, everything is foolishness, everything is madness—whatever you think, whatever you desire, whatever you say, whatever you do in this world—except only what you do in God, for God, and to the honor of God. Whatever you do without God is entirely wickedness and vanity, because nothing is good without the supreme good.

Certainly, the greater misery of a human being is to be without him without whom he cannot exist.

[Col. 1054D]

See, wretched human being, that you were created in the image and likeness of God; that, because of the immense love of our Lord Jesus Christ, you were redeemed and liberated by a most shameful death; that, solely through his immeasurable mercy, you were called to see the glory of the supreme God; and that, from the moment you began to exist, you were invited by the Most High Father of all truth, through his only Son, to have eternal life with him.

Wretched human being, recognize this honor. Understand your dignity and honor, by which you have been honored by so great a majesty. For the eternal and immeasurable God created you, formed you, and invited you. The greatest honor, and the broadest love.

Know your honor, human being, and run, giving thanks, to the one who invited you, lest, if in your ingratitude you refuse to go and allow yourself to be hindered by a farm, oxen, or a wife, the angry Lord command you to be burned and the door of eternal life be closed to you forever.

Know, then, human being, your honor, and honor your Creator. But alas! Today it can rightly be said of you, human being:

“Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”

It is certainly fitting and just that the one who did not wish to be a companion of the angels should become like the beasts; and that the one who destroyed in himself the image and likeness of God should have the image and likeness of beasts cling to him.

Know yourself, then, wretched human being; know that you are better than birds and more worthy than all living creatures. Do not be like senseless beasts, which think only about the present life, desire only carnal and bodily things, love earthly and temporal things, because they know nothing else.

[Col. 1055B]

Human being, do not subject yourself to the flesh; do not be a lover of the world. Do not allow yourself to be a son of the devil, for the honor of your most powerful, wisest, and incomprehensible Father, the Most High God.

For the sake of the wondrous name of the eternal God, do not make yourself your own adversary and murderer. For the love of the kindest God, do not make yourself the enemy and opponent of almighty God. For the sake of the majesty of Christ the Lord, the beloved Son of God, do not make yourself the companion of demons and of the burning of eternal fire—you who were redeemed by the most precious blood of the immaculate Lamb.

Do not despise so great a price, which the Son of God deigned to pay for you, lest you be enveloped in everlasting fires. Then you will have the greatest repentance, but without remedy. Then you will suffer unimaginable pain, but without end; you will be full of torments, yet will never be relieved.

For whoever does not weep while he has time to weep will mourn with eternal mourning, but without fruit.

Return, then, to yourself; return, and do not delay in turning to him who made you by his power, redeemed you by his wisdom, called you to himself by his unspeakable goodness, still awaits you every day, and will crown you. [Col. 1056B]

What do you seek outside him? What? What do you desire besides him? What pleases you without him? He made all things, he possesses all things, he is all things.

Whatever good you desire, whatever beautiful thing you seek, whatever sweet and delightful thing you pursue—you will find it all in him and enjoy it in him. If you wish to rejoice, he is joy, etc.

As Master Anselm expounded these things, N., the amanuensis, collected them.

(From the Corbie manuscripts, MS 596.)

God fashioned man by word or will alone, not through an angel, as some maintain. And note that in the other works Genesis says: “God said, and they were made.” But when it speaks of the creation of man, it says: “The hands of God made man,” or: “Let us make man [Col. 1055C] in our image and likeness.” This does not mean that he was made more substantially than the others, but that the dignity of man is shown: he was made by God himself, the supreme craftsman, not by his craftsmen, and was made with such great deliberation.

He is said to be “in the image of God” because he is rational and wise like God. “According to the likeness” means likewise. God is one—not as we are, in whom different things, such as substances or accidents, are joined into one—but in an ineffable manner he is in all things and completes all things, yet is changed in relation to things. When they are cut, he is not cut; when they are mutilated, he is not mutilated; when they are increased, he is not increased; when they are diminished, he is not diminished; when they are defiled, he is not defiled.

If it is asked how this can be known, the soul provides the likeness: the soul is in the body, yet when the body is cut, the soul is not cut; when it is increased, the soul is not increased; when it is diminished, the soul is not diminished. And thus, as regards the likeness of God, one must understand that Scripture rarely calls man “the image of God,” since that designation belongs properly to the Son of God alone, but says that he is “according to the image.”

Augustine: “Every Adam, when he perversely wishes to be like [God], falls into captivity; whence let him cry out to the one from whom he fell: ‘Who is like you?’” The just man who loves his enemies and does good to them is like God, in whose image he was made, and who makes his sun rise upon the just and unjust and sends rain upon the just and unjust. But this is obedience, not pride.

He is therefore rightly like God who believes that the supreme God is in need of nothing, while he himself exists not through himself but with God. But whoever wishes to exist through himself, like God, exists through no one. He perversely wishes to be like God, as the devil did, who refused to be subject to him; and the man who . . . did not wish to be held as a servant under a command, wished to have no one ruling over him and to be like God.

## Master Anselm on the verse: “For it was fitting that he, through whom are all things and from whom are all things” (Hebrews 2:10).

[Col. 1055D]

If almighty God had made no creature at all, he could have been fully blessed in himself, since he needed nothing and was entirely sufficient for himself. Yet, wishing in his supreme goodness to make a creature blessed—for this was to come about solely through knowledge and love of him—he made angelic creatures by whom he would be praised, not so that anything might be added to him from their praise, but to them.

Moreover, by that same goodness, so that praise might not be imperfect, he created corporeal creatures and wished to make them blessed. For this reason he placed a rational spirit in a body, so that by governing it well he might be blessed in God together with the body; and thus the praise of God might be complete from every creature.

Hence all things are said to praise God, since rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—strive to recognize and praise God’s marvelous power and goodness both in themselves and in the other creatures. Thus the Apostle says: “For him are all things,” that is, for his praise and glorification; “and through him are all things,” that is, nothing exists superfluously.

If this is true—or rather, because it is true—it is necessary that man be led to glory [Col. 1057A]. Since this necessity proceeds from the greatest goodness of God, as we have said, man, having been lost through his sin, is not led to glory; therefore he himself does not praise God. Consequently, corporeal creation does not praise him either; and so it was made in vain.

If this is so, then even the angels do not praise him fully, since their number has been diminished. But in order that all these absurd consequences might be suppressed at the very source from which they arise, let us establish that lost man is led to glory, and, with its author assisting us, let us consider the order of his glorious salvation.

God created man in the middle condition, so that, if he remained obedient to him, once his obedience had been completed he would pass from mortal to immortal without the intervention of death; but if not, he would fall from mortality into death. Persuaded, therefore, by the devil, and in accordance with God’s terrible threat, he passed from being mortal to being dead and was justly possessed by the devil, to whom he had willingly consented.

Nevertheless, God wished to seek him out, because, although he had fallen willingly, he had fallen through another’s persuasion. The devil, however, ought not to have been sought out, because he fell from the firmness of his own nature through himself, without any external persuasion.

It was therefore necessary that man have an author of salvation through whom, by a just order, he might return to God. Let us therefore see who this author could have been.

If he were simply God, he could indeed conquer the devil and rescue man. But if he took man away from the devil—who, as the Apostle says, held the power of death—even though he had unjustly invaded what belonged to another, nevertheless, because he held a man who had willingly consented to him, this would be mere power, not the reason of justice.

If he were simply man, how could he resist in a corrupted nature, when, placed in a better condition, he had fallen so easily? Here it must be noted that God’s grace does not force free choice.

Again, if an angel undertook this struggle, why should the devil thereby be defeated and lose man? There would be no reason for it. Nor could an angel accomplish this in man, because, if he were found weak in his own simple and strong nature, he would be found even weaker when joined to this weak nature—namely, the human nature.

It was therefore necessary that the author of salvation be God in man: as God, he could; as man, he ought, in a fitting and fully ordered manner. Thus, just as the devil by evil fraud first seized what belonged to another, so God, by a good—so to speak—fraud, would make the possession his own through grace. And just as that man fell through his own freedom, so this man would resist the devil through the freedom of his will.

He also had to suffer, so that the devil might sin against one in whom he found no guilt, by punishing him. For the devil attacked him, as he did the others, with every kind of temptation: first with flatteries, like a dragon, then with harshness, like a lion; finally, he killed him. Thus the devil most justly lost all his dominion over men when he extended himself beyond what was permitted.

Hence the common law still holds that one loses what is owed when he demands more than what is owed. Therefore, just as the devil lost his right over the one who did not consent to him, so he lost it over all that man’s descendants who imitate his innocence.

But this man ought not to remain in death, because in that case he would have benefited neither himself nor anyone else. He therefore had to be perfected through suffering, so that he might likewise perfect his followers. This is what the Apostle says: “It was fitting,” and so forth.

Mark each step separately. It was fitting that he should lead many sons into glory: that is, the Father, for whose praise and glorification all things were made; and this was accomplished by giving them an author of salvation, namely [Col. 1058C] Christ, and by giving him over to suffering, and thus bringing him to perfection.

If you carefully attend to this order, you will see that man ought to have been saved even if no angel had fallen.

---

# THE WORKS OF SAINT ANSELM, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, PART THREE: FOUR BOOKS OF LETTERS

[Col. 1057C]

## 311. NOTICE

Saint Anselm himself testifies, in Letter 7 of Book III, that he had lived as a monk for thirty-three years when he wrote to Prior Baldric of Bec, already Archbishop of Canterbury: three years without office, fifteen as prior, and the same number as abbot, from which office he was taken to the see of Canterbury.

Accordingly, you have his letters arranged separately in four books. The first book contains those he wrote while not yet abbot; the second, those he sent as abbot; the third and fourth, those he sent as archbishop. This fourth book, which we have added, is filled with letters that had until now remained unpublished and that we have drawn from various manuscripts.

[Col. 1059]

## LETTERS

## BOOK ONE, CONTAINING THE LETTERS ANSELM WROTE WHILE NOT YET ABBOT
