[Col. 1059A]

### LETTER ONE, TO LANFRANC

He congratulates him on his election as archbishop and courteously returns to him a cup given as a friendly gift.

[Note: [Col. 1059A] Compared with manuscript Vict. Ef. 20 and the Louvain manuscript, which, more than the others, contains thirteen letters of Anselm: Books I, 1, 5, 8, 11, 29, 33, 37, and 56, and Book IV, 104. From the same manuscript the little work *On Peace and Concord* was also transcribed. The very distinguished lord of Nonancourt, notable for both nobility and learning, sent these materials to us.]

To his lord and father, greatly to be revered with love by Catholics and to be loved with reverence, the Archbishop LANFRANC, brother ANSELM, wholly his own.

Glory to God in the highest, who has placed the lamp of your faith and wisdom [Col. 1060A] upon a prominent lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in his house.

[Note: [Col. 1059B] “Who has placed the lamp of your faith.” This alludes to the Gospel parable in Matthew 5:15 and Luke 11:33, namely, that a lit lamp is to be placed upon a lampstand. By “the lamp of faith,” Anselm understands Lanfranc himself, a faithful and prudent servant of God, shining everywhere with the light of his teaching and devotion. Having been raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury, he shone as the star of England in the sky, as William of Malmesbury says in Book III of *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*:

> Like Lucifer, dispersing the fleeing stars,  
> he brings forth the bright day with rosy face.

Since we encountered him already at the very threshold, adorned with pontifical insignia, so that it might be known what sort of man he had formerly been, we were pleased to narrate what we found in notes to the old tables of the Archbishops of Canterbury, preserved in manuscript in our library, in these words:

“Lanfranc was educated from the years of his childhood in the schools of the liberal arts and secular laws, in accordance with the custom of his homeland, with a secular purpose. Born of noble ancestry among the citizens of the city of Pavia [Col. 1059C] in Italy, while still a young man he often overthrew veteran advocates opposing him in legal actions by the torrent of his eloquence, speaking appropriately. Even at that age he knew how to produce judgments that jurists, judges, and city magistrates gladly accepted. Pavia remembers these things.

“But when he was in exile, and, like the philosopher Plato once did, he began to philosophize, an eternal fire kindled his mind, and the love of true wisdom illumined his heart. He perceived, with Ecclesiastes—whose ecclesiastical reading he had not yet learned through use—that the goods of the world are vanity (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Thus, suddenly despising the world and renouncing both it and himself, he embraced the religious profession and submitted himself to the regular yoke.

“He chose a monastery in Normandy, frightening in its location and poverty. By his prudence and vigilant care he enriched it and advanced it into a state of the most excellent order, governing the brotherhood with strict yet gentle discipline and serving as a holy abbot with humble and useful counsel.

“For although he wished to devote himself solely to his own mortification, God, the examiner of thoughts, discovered and revealed him, so that a lamp gathering itself together might spread both into the valley and toward the heights. Under that master, through obedience, the library of philosophical and divine literature shone forth, and he was most powerful at solving the knots of questions in both fields.

“Herodian in grammar, Aristotle in dialectic, Cicero in rhetoric, and the interpreters of law and Scripture in sacred learning would recognize in Lanfranc an intellect and diligence worthy of admiration. All Athens, when it flourished unharmed and sat in the highest seats of instruction, would rise before Lanfranc in every kind of eloquence and discipline.

“So Hilarion of Palestine and many other despisers of temporal glory, although they constantly fled, never remained hidden. So Augustine, the keenest investigator of the omnipotent and indivisible Trinity; Jerome, the most faithful interpreter of Hebrew truth; Gregory of Rome; Nazianzenus; and many other blessed teachers first shone in philosophy and then in the Church through their books.

“This same monk was zealous to slay with the sword of the word any sects that attacked the Catholic faith. Indeed, at the Roman and Vercelli synods he pierced Berengar of Tours, the heresiarch—or of Angers, whose doctrine, more harmful than poisoned weapons, offered death to souls from the saving Host—with the blade of spiritual eloquence, most holily explaining and most truthfully proving that the bread and wine placed upon the Lord’s table are, after consecration, the true flesh and true blood of the Lord Redeemer.”

[Note: [Col. 1059D] Lanfranc places these matters before Berengar in the introductory letter to his treatise *On the Holy Eucharist*.]

“After being overcome, Berengar swore once at Rome and again at Tours to observe this judgment, at the same time declaring that anyone who thought otherwise should be struck with excommunication. For he anathematized every heresy, especially the one by which he had been disgraced when, while seeking the brilliance of empty praise, he had become stained.

“But the thoroughly deceived and obstinate man did not faithfully remain in his wholesome purpose of overturning that doctrine, adding the crime of schism to the violation of an oath repeated twice. Since fear of punishment prevented him from publicly preaching what he had publicly condemned, he whispered the same things in private disputations at home and, through disciples corrupted by money and deceit, disseminated them abroad [Col. 1060D].”

[Note: [Col. 1059D] William of Malmesbury writes the same in Book III of *On the Kings of England*, p. 63 of the London edition. Lanfranc above and Guitmund of Aversa in Book I of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* say the same.]

“The blasphemer regretted having lost the booklets of his perverse doctrine, which he himself had thrown into the fire at Rome lest he be burned. Accordingly, he composed a new writing in order to support the old error more securely and extend it more durably into future years [Col. 1061B]. To destroy this work, the aforementioned defender of truth issued a letter, or little book, written in lucid and elegant style, weighty with sacred authorities and unshakably consistent in the consequences of its arguments.

“For, rich in the fullness of charity, he strove to bring back to life through right faith those dead in heresy, leaving to every baptized brother of his a sufficient, clear, and not tediously lengthy exposition of the true understanding of the Eucharist.

“Wise and devout abbots, as well as metropolitan bishops, both revered Lanfranc’s wisdom and devotion and rejoiced to be subject to his authority and correction. How many churches sought him as abbot or bishop with incredible longing! Rome, the head of the Christian world, pressed him with letters and tried to retain him by entreaty and by force.

“For they knew him to be most skilled at distinguishing whatever was honorable from whatever was contrary to it, most diligent at assigning each person his due according to the measure of reason, most ready to undertake and endure difficult and arduous things for the sake of the true good, and likewise most cautious in governing hand [Col. 1061C] and tongue with consideration and courtesy.

“They knew—if I may speak briefly and plainly—that this life of his was rightly called a very straight and safest road to the harbor of eternal life.

“But he considered it too great a thing to preside over brothers in second place, never abandoning in his heart the lowest position. He would gladly have left the abbey of Caen, which he had accepted under compulsion, and fled to anchorites or monasteries far away, had not many difficulties stood in the way—difficulties which he could not overcome by any means without grave injury to his soul.

“Yet consolation for the holy man in his sorrow over that laborious office was provided by the fact that the building of the place was then just beginning. We insert here this memorial of the knowledge and virtue of that Father. Therefore, let us not repeat it at greater length elsewhere.

“Invited to the height of the archbishopric, he crossed the sea sorrowfully, excusing himself and hoping for joy in returning. The king, however, received with joy a helper in the cultivation of Christianity, overcame his reluctant refusal, and sent the priors of the Church of Canterbury with cheerful and festive orders. Much dignity of the secular kingdom and of religion was also present.

“The aforementioned abbot and archbishop was enthroned after the most honorable election, to be adorned with the pallium of honor, though he had already been marked by both a spiritual and a rational pallium. Many bishops and abbots attended the ordination, together with the greatest multitude of clergy and people. It was celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of December.”

Thus far the old tables, from which an obscure and veiled script—announcing the imminent end of the work unless the salutary remedies of printing came to its aid—forced me to extract these passages.]

Lanfranc was consecrated Bishop of Canterbury by Bishops Giso of Wells and Walter of Hereford in the year 1070, on the sacred day of the beheading of Saint John the Baptist.

And lest anyone think that what was said above about Rome’s soliciting Lanfranc with letters is rhetorical exaggeration, let him read Pope Alexander II writing to William the Conqueror, king of the English, as follows:

“To receive an increase of virtues, we exhort Your Glory to heed the counsels of our brother Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury. We grieve that, as our dearest member and one of the foremost sons of the Roman Church, he is not continually joined to our side; but from the fruit that he bestows upon the Church in your kingdom, we derive consolation for his absence.”

Thus far Alexander.

That several other churches also sought him as bishop is confirmed by the Chronicle of Bec in his Life:

“At that time (in the year 1066), the city of Rouen was deprived of its holy and venerable archbishop Maurilius. Then all the clergy and people gathered and wished to choose Lanfranc as his successor. But he avoided undertaking such a burden with all his strength, humbly desiring rather to be subject than to preside.

“When the king observed this, he arranged to substitute John, whom he had appointed bishop of Avranches. But in order that this might be done canonically, he sent the same abbot of Caen, Lanfranc, to Rome to seek permission. Bearing the burden of this embassy—for he wished to provide for the churches—he obtained from Pope Alexander the sacred pallium together with permission for this promotion, and brought it back with him. Hence there was joy throughout all Normandy.”

Perhaps I shall be accused of ἐξ ὀρθολογίας—“from right reasoning”—and not without cause, because, in transcribing the notes on Lanfranc, from a monk of Bec to Archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 1062C], I have not begun with his monastic life. Perhaps I am weaving a disorderly commentary; but it is not too late, if the matter is serious.

Lanfranc was therefore born at Ticinum, commonly called Pavia, a town of Insubria in Cisalpine Gaul, to parents who were likewise native citizens of Ticinum and members of its leading families. His father was a man highly skilled in law and of senatorial rank, whom blind death, all the more unjustly, took from Lanfranc while he was still a young man.

When Lanfranc was required to take his deceased father’s place, he left his native land, carried elsewhere by an insane love of learning.

After this, during the reign of Henry I, king of France of that name, and William, surnamed the Conqueror, duke of the Normans, he came to Avranches, a city of Lower Normandy, where it is unnecessary for me to recount what he did and what happened after he departed, since Vincent of Beauvais has anticipated me in Book XXVI of the *Historical Mirror*, chapter 36—especially since I acknowledge that he has drawn even the little he reports from a fuller account of the same man’s deeds [Col. 1062D] in the manuscript Chronicle of Bec.

At last, after being rescued from the danger related above by Vincent, Lanfranc came to Bec, a monastery then obscure in the estimation of that time and people, such as travelers had told him it was and as he had learned.

“Then perhaps,” says the Bec manuscript, “the abbot was occupied in building a furnace and was working with his own hands. Approaching him, Lanfranc said: ‘God save you.’ The abbot replied: ‘God bless you. Are you a Lombard?’ He answered: ‘I am.’ ‘What do you want?’ ‘I wish to become a monk.’

“Then the abbot ordered a certain monk named Roger to show him the book of the Rule. After reading it, Lanfranc replied that, with God’s help, he would observe everything. Hearing this and knowing who he was and where he came from, the abbot gladly granted what he requested. Lanfranc fell on his face and kissed his feet.

“Greatly venerating and loving in the abbot the humility of his spirit and the dignity of his speech, Lanfranc became a monk there. It was the year 1042, as the letter of the Chronicle of Bec records.

“After he had put on the cowl and, though reluctantly, opened a school of letters, his name very quickly began to fly through the mouths of learned men, as I shall reveal by the testimony of contemporary writers in Letter 16 of this book.”

Around the year 1063, William the Conqueror founded at Caen [Col. 1063C] a monastery in memory of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and placed Lanfranc over it, though Lanfranc resisted and was finally overcome by the persistence of the nobles and Normans. A note to Letter 13 of this book will explain the reasons for founding this monastery.

Scarcely three years had passed—that is, the year 1067—when death came to Saint Maurilius, bishop of Rouen. The Normans sought to have Lanfranc appointed in his place, but he wearied them with a firm refusal despite their firm insistence.

Finally, the year 1070 placed upon his shoulders the honor and burden that he had previously rejected, although, as was his custom, he firmly declined it. For this reason William, king of the English, had sent envoys to Normandy. Hermenfrodus, bishop of Sion, also returned from England—where he had sailed with two cardinals of the Holy Roman Church sent by Pope Alexander to crown William the Conqueror with the diadem of the English kingdom, as William had requested—and announced to Lanfranc, at a council of the bishops and abbots of Normandy, the king’s petition, together with his own will and that of the other legates of the Apostolic See [Col. 1063D].

Lanfranc asked for a delay. For he clearly and certainly understood that the business of an archbishop and the leisure of a monk could not proceed together.

The queen pleaded with him, together with her son. Abbot Herluin ordered him, though unwilling, to obey, since Lanfranc was accustomed to obey him as Christ. The assembled nobles also earnestly urged him to do so. The king’s command had dictated this pressure from every side, for he knew the worth of his most beloved Father when he invited him to higher things.

Lanfranc did not reject obedience in a hasty decision—for he governed every action and word by the rule of discretion—but avoided offending so many who asked, supported, and urged him. Thus he crossed the sea sorrowfully, excusing himself and hoping for joy in returning.

But who can resist the divine ordering, and by what counsel? The king received him with joy and due reverence as a helper of the Christian religion, beautifully overcoming his resistance through humility and majesty.

Since William of Malmesbury, Matthew Parker in *The Ecclesiastical Antiquities of Britain*, and after them Cardinal Baronius in the *Annals* have recounted in detail what he did as bishop, I shall not repeat it [Col. 1064C]. I shall merely combine one or two matters drawn from his deeds as narrated in the Chronicle of Bec, as follows:

“When the glorious King William was staying in Normandy, Lanfranc was the prince and guardian of England, with all the princes subject to him and assisting in matters concerning the defense, administration, or peace of the kingdom, according to the laws of the country.

“He was devoted to reading both before and after becoming bishop, as far as he was able. Since the books of Scripture had been excessively corrupted through the fault of scribes, he diligently corrected all the books of both the Old and New Testaments, as well as the writings of the holy Fathers, according to orthodox faith. He also corrected meticulously many of the texts that we use night and day in the service of the Church, doing this not only himself but also through his disciples.

“As far as he could, he retained poverty in the plainness of his dress, maintaining frugality amid many kinds of luxury. Many great and valuable gifts were offered to him, and he cheerfully gave them to those who asked him or were in need.”

The second matter I promised was sent to us by Lanfranc’s biographer in these exact words:

“On a certain feast of the Three Magi, on which a crowned king was accustomed to hold court, on the day of the feast of Saint Martin, while the king sat at table wearing his crown and royal garments and Lanfranc sat beside him, a certain jester, seeing the king radiant with gold and jewels, exclaimed in the great hall in a voice of flattering admiration: ‘Behold, I see God!’

“Lanfranc, turning to the king, said: ‘Do not allow such things to be attributed to you. These are not the things of man but of God. Order him to be severely beaten, so that he may never dare to repeat such words.’

“The king ordered this to be done at once.”

What remains concerning Lanfranc will be added in Book II.]

He has established the lamp of your faith and wisdom [Col. 1060A] upon a prominent lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in his house.

We therefore pray almighty God that it may burn in such a way that it is not consumed [Note: [Col. 1059A] `Ut non consummatur` (“so that it is not consumed”) is the reading of the Victorine and Picard manuscripts: `ut non consumatur` (“so that it is not consumed”).]; that it may shine for others in such a way that it is never extinguished for him; and that, after imparting his light to the English for a long time, he may be transferred with the angels to participation in the eternal divine light [Note: [Col. 1059A] The readings are `cum Anglia` (“with England”), manuscript Vict.; `cum Anglis` (“with the English”), manuscript Louvain; and `cum angeli` (“with angels”).].

For just as we desire whatever good things we possess, if any there are, to be yours, so we by no means consider whatever things are yours to be ours [Col. 1061A]. Although many unexpected changes often strive to take you away from me, they can in no way separate our souls, which are joined together—not, at least, detach my soul, which clings to you, from you.

Therefore, to pass over what you know and what I do not doubt, because you cannot escape the one whom you do not carry within you, you cannot entirely abandon the one who follows you wherever you go and embraces you wherever he remains.

You said, as Lord Hernostus reported to me, that with cheerful generosity and friendly confidence you desired the dear cup which you, most dear, had given to one dearer. I therefore do not return your gift to you, lest I somehow become less indebted to you; rather, I most gladly give you what I possess as dearer than the whole world [Col. 1063A].

Let our most beloved brothers who are with you read, after the letter addressed to Your Sublimity, this very brief and sufficient letter sent by me: my longing for you always increases, and the love of which you were once aware in me never decreases.

---

## 312. LETTER II

[Note: [Col. 1063B] Compared with two manuscript copies in the same Victorine manuscript mentioned above, and with the Louvain manuscript, and with manuscript Vict. Bd. 18, also called EE. 13.]

### TO ODO AND LANZO

At Lanzo’s request, he prescribes a rule for a holier life.

To my lords, friends, and most beloved brothers, ODO [Note: [Col. 1063B] The Victorine and Louvain manuscripts read `Sooni` (“to Sooni”) ] and LANZO, brother ANSELM, of Bec: a sinner in life, a monk in habit; to despise temporal things for the sake of eternal things, and to receive eternal things in exchange for temporal things.

Since true love, just as it is laudably bestowed, is likewise demanded without reproach from the one who loves, I do not think myself shameless if I reveal to you to some degree the love I bear you, so that I may either acquire your love for myself or make the love already acquired more perfect.

But because, on account of our greatly separated way of life, you cannot perceive my heart’s goodness either through services or at least through conversation, let this epistolary greeting be a sign to you that the memory of your affection remains alive in me.

When your reverend brotherhood first made itself known to my lowliness through its presence, my soul impressed and bound it deeply to itself in the embrace of charity, so that, by loving, it clearly expressed your image within itself. Through that image you remain always present to me, even while absent. Thus, although our sight of one another is rare, the affection is not rare but continuous.

Thus far this spontaneous greeting of charity has been directed to both of you. From this point onward a due exhortation will be addressed to one: to one of you because it was requested by one; but I shall rejoice in the double benefit of my labor if it is received by both as though spoken to each individually.

Indeed, I remember, my lord and friend Lanzo, that you asked many times for my lukewarmness to be applied to your fervor for holy living, so that through letters of admonition it might kindle you to spiritual love.

Because I considered it improper for a cold man to attempt to warm a hot one, I certainly wished to refuse. But then, considering that a burning fire is increased by a cold breath, I could not entirely refuse what you asked.

Therefore, since you can find much better in the sacred pages whatever you request from me, and since, out of reverence for your gentle gravity, I wish to obey you willingly as far as I am able, I shall proceed between the two in this way: first I shall enjoin upon you the care of studying Holy Scripture; then, in my own person, I shall add a few things not from my own judgment but from the judgment of that same Scripture [Col. 1065A].

[Note: [Col. 1065D] The same material appears in Letter 43.]

I therefore admonish and entreat you, dearest brother, that, as it is written, “Keep your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23), and let nothing draw your mind away from guarding it.

Let it carefully examine what it acquires each day by advancing, lest—God forbid—it lose something by falling back. For just as in the virtues it is more difficult to attain by striving to something one has not possessed than to lack it through laziness, so it is more burdensome to recover what is lost through negligence than to attain what no one is known to have possessed before.

[Note: [Col. 1065C] The Victorine manuscripts read `difficillima est` (“it is most difficult”); the printed reading is `difficilius est` (“it is more difficult”).]

Therefore, dearest one, always reckon the past as almost nothing, so that you neither disdain to hold on to what you have attained [Note: [Col. 1065C] The Victorine manuscripts read `temere non` (“not rashly”) for `tenere non` (“not to hold”).], nor, even if through weakness you are unable to add anything to it, cease striving through persistence [Col. 1065B].

Since among the many who are called only a few are chosen, we are all certain of this, because Truth has said it; but, since Truth has not said how few they are, we are all uncertain of their number.

Therefore, whoever does not yet live as one of the few should either gather himself among the few by correcting his life or fear with certainty that he is rejected. But whoever already judges himself to be among the few should not immediately trust in the security of election.

For none of us knows to how small a number the elect will be reduced. No one therefore knows whether he is already among the few elect, even though he may already resemble the few among the many who are called.

Let no one, looking backward, consider how many he has passed on the road to the heavenly homeland. Rather, with unwavering attention directed toward what lies ahead [Note: [Col. 1065C] The manuscripts read `in anteriora interitus` (“toward the things ahead of destruction”) for `in anteriora intentus` (“intent upon the things ahead”).], let him carefully consider whether he is already walking together with those whose election no faithful person doubts [Col. 1065C].

See, therefore, dearest one, that the fear of God which you have conceived does not grow lukewarm through any circumstance [Note: [Col. 1065C] The Victorine manuscripts and the Picard edition read `qualiter occasione` (“through whatever circumstance”) for `qualibet occasione` (“through any circumstance”).]; rather, let it be fanned by an unfailing zeal and grow hotter day by day, until it shines for you, transformed into eternal security.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] The same material appears in Letter 27.]

For it must be carefully avoided, dearest brother, that which many do—or rather, many not so much in number as in foolishness—who, the longer they live, nourish in themselves a greater hope of continuing to live. Casting aside fear of approaching death, they fall away from their purpose of holy living.

It is truly the case that the longer someone has lived, the less time he has left to live; and the farther he advances from the day of his birth, the nearer he comes to the day of his death and to the reckoning for his entire life.

Therefore, just as you see your life increase day by day in the past, so be certain that the time allotted to live well decreases for you each day.

Be watchful, then, my friend, to spend the time of life that remains to you—for you do not know how brief it is—in such a way that from day to day you extend your holy purpose of mind [Note: [Col. 1065C] Some manuscripts read `meritis propositum` (“purpose of merits”) for `mentis propositum` (“purpose of mind”), and so forth.] toward better things.

Thus, if anything weighs upon you in living well, the more you consider that your labor is hastening toward its end and that you are drawing near to rest and the crown [Note: [Col. 1065C] In one copy of manuscript 28, `appropinquare desideras` (“you desire to draw near”) replaces `appropinquare consideras` (“you consider that you are drawing near”).], the more strongly you will advance, strengthened manfully by pressing onward and persevering more joyfully.

Therefore, do not grow weary of what you have begun [Col. 1066B], but rather, in hope of heavenly help and for love of the blessed reward, begin those things that are advantageous to you and that you have not yet undertaken, so that, with Christ as your guide, you may reach the blessed fellowship of the saints.

Our letter has now exceeded all bounds; but so that it may likewise end with those with which it commonly began, attend, my two friends; listen, both of you, my beloved ones; I beg you, retain in your memory, for the sake of our mutual affection, the conclusion of my foolish address. I call the wording foolish because it is mine, but not the meaning, because it is God’s. Listen, therefore, and do not, because of what is mine, despise what is God’s [Note: [Col. 1065C] “Because of what is God’s”: MSS. Vict. and Ed. Pic. read, “because of what is mine, despise what is his, and, while he mourns, laugh; despise his mockery”; MS. Lovan. reads, “because of what is mine, despise what is God’s.”].

Whenever the world smiles at you with some favor of its own kind, do not smile back at it. Certainly, it does not smile for this purpose—that in the end you may laugh—but so that, under its mocking prince, you may mourn with him while he mourns [Col. 1066C]. Rather, therefore, whenever it smiles upon you, shudder at its laughter; by shuddering, mock the laugher, so that afterward you may mock its mocker and laugh while he mourns.

My friends [Note: [Col. 1065C] “Mock its mocker and laugh while he mourns. My friends”: one MS. reads, “laugh at its mocker. My friends”; MS. 18 reads, “mock its mockery, laugh at it, and laugh while he mourns.”], do not love the world or the things that are in the world (1 John 2:15); for it is truly written, “The world is passing away, and its desire” (ibid., 17), and “whoever is made a friend of this age is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4).

It has no hay on its horn [Note: [Col. 1065D] “It has no hay on its horn.” Anselm says this cleverly, to show that the world is a certain harmful and deceitful animal. He says that it does not have hay on its horn, as once did unruly oxen, from whose horns something was hung by which those who might happen upon them could protect themselves; rather, it has gold on its horn, so that, by the glitter of the shining metal, it may blind those who look at it and seize those fleeing from it more cautiously and gently. Gold tied to its horns also plainly represents pride, which is accustomed to flow from an abundance of possessions. For everyone knows that “to take up horns” and “to lift up horns” means to be proud. The following saying of the Greeks supports this: γενναῖος εἷ ἐκβαλαντίου, “You are noble from your purse” [the Greek is printed in this form], indicating that riches give birth to pride as to a daughter. Thus the world has gold on its horn, because it displays nothing but what is splendid to its lovers; but it carries hay tied to its tail, which, by the tail—the animal’s hindmost part—signifies that at the end of this life it will boil away the sordid and muddy desire of human beings. Moreover, this verse of Anselm’s is artfully composed from two half-verses of Horace and Virgil, altered. For Horace says in *Satires* I.4.34:

> He has hay on his horn.

But Virgil says in *Eclogues* IX.24:

> Beware of confronting the he-goat; he strikes with his horn.

] It has gold on its horn, but look at its hindquarters: it has hay [Note: [Col. 1065C] “Hay on … it has hay”: MS. 18 reads, “poison on … it has poison.”] on its tail; “the tail strikes—beware!” Beware, I say, and farewell [Note: [Col. 1065C] “I say, and farewell”: MS. 18 reads, “he says, and farewell.”].

[Col. 1067A]

## LETTER III [Note: [Col. 1067D] Compared with one manuscript copy, Cod. Vict. Ef. 20, and Lovan.]

### TO ROBERT THE MONK

He requests Robert’s prayers and the friendship of Anastasius, his fellow monk.

To the most beloved and reverend lord Robert, monk, brother Anselm of Bec, the least among those living holy lives, wishing in temporal matters to will eternity, and in eternal matters not to will temporality.

When I consider, vigorous soldier of God and dearest to me—when I consider the advancement of your vigor [Note: [Col. 1067D] “Dearest, the advancement of your vigor”: one MS. reads, “dearest, the advancement of your vigor”; MS. Lovan. reads, “dearest, when I consider the advancement of your vigor”—] and the barrenness of my sluggishness, I scarcely dare suggest to your holiness any mention of our mutual friendship. For, since in all the actions of my lukewarm life there is nothing that can compensate for the benefits of your affection, I blush either to demand from you what is owed by a friend or even to be called your friend.

But again, when I see others running easily toward the return to our heavenly homeland, while I, weighed down by sins and lukewarmness [Note: [Col. 1067D] “Weighed down by sins and lukewarmness”: one MS. reads, “weighed down by time”; MS. Lovan. reads, “weighed down by the body”; another reads, “weighed down by time”—], can scarcely move along the same road, great necessity compels me to cry out from the depths of my heart to those who run ahead of me—not so that their awaited speed may be made slower, but so that my tardiness, snatched along by those who run, may become swifter.

Therefore, since my prayers are such that they either do me no good or little good, I do not dare offer you prayers that I have proposed should be yours; but I beg that they may be kindled by the fervor of your prayers, so that they may effectively benefit both me [Note: [Col. 1067D] “Benefit me”: one MS. reads, “benefit me”] and you. For this is what my heart wills before God, and this is how my mouth prays to God: that whatever ought to benefit me may benefit you no less than me [Note: [Col. 1067D] “And whatever”: one MS. reads, “and whatever”; another, “whatever.”].

Come, then, venerably lovable and lovably more venerable man; be certain, while I live, of this intention of ours, and be solicitous to perfect in me the charity that will be yours. For if you pray for your neighbor, I know that what will be repaid to you is true; and if you obtain something, know that whatever is granted to me belongs to you.

To make this more effective, I beg and beseech you to make that holy man Anastasius, whose desirable companionship you enjoy, acquainted with me, commending me to him as much as you can in my absence [Note: [Col. 1067D] “As much as you can, make him acquainted”: one MS. reads, “afterward make him acquainted”; another, “as much as you can, make him acquainted, etc.”], so that you may share that friend of yours with me, and share me, your servant, with him. Thus, from this day onward, while we live, through you and with you, may I revere him as another friend Robert, and may he possess the same servant, Anselm.

For since I am unworthy, I do not dare ask what nevertheless I presume to desire: that I, as it were another Robert, may use the same Anastasius, and that he may enjoy me as another Robert. His good fragrance has already been sweetly diffused through many people of this homeland; how much more delightfully it breathes upon my soul, and with how much greater ardor that soul burns toward his friendship and acquaintance [Col. 1068A].

From the time I heard of his life, I have already held and embraced this friendship and acquaintance as much as I can; and I pray that he too may pray with me, so that they may grow for us as much as they can grow in God.

Both of you, my dearest, farewell. I beg you: while in Babylon, feel the same thing, so that in Jerusalem you may share the same thing. I do not say this as though I feared that discord would ever come upon you, but because I truly desire that concord may never depart from you.

## LETTER IV. TO GONDULPH

Although he writes less frequently, he has not forgotten the one to whom he ought to write more frequently.

To the reverend lord, dearest brother, most steadfast friend, Lord Gondulph, brother Anselm sends greetings.

[Col. 1068B]

When I resolve to write to you, beloved soul of my soul, when I resolve to write to you, I am uncertain where I should most appropriately begin my address. For whatever I think about you is sweet and pleasing to my heart; whatever I wish for you is what my mind conceives as best.

I have seen you to be such that you know how I love you; I hear you to be such that God knows how I desire you. Hence, wherever you go, my love follows you; and wherever I remain, my desire embraces you.

And when you ask me through your messengers, exhort me through your letters, and press me through your gifts to remember you:

> Let my tongue cleave to my jaws if I do not remember you (Psalm 136:6),

if I have not placed Gondulph among the chief objects of my friendship. Here I do not mean Gondulph, my lay father, but Gondulph the monk, our brother.

How, then, could I forget you? He who is impressed upon my heart like a seal upon wax—how could he be withdrawn from my memory? Moreover, why, as I hear, do you complain with such grief that you never see my letters, and seek with such love to receive them often, when you always have my conscience with you? When you are silent, I know that you love me; and when I am silent, you know that I love you (John 21:16).

You are conscious with me, since I have no doubt about you; and I am your witness, since you are certain about me. Since, therefore, we are each conscious of the other’s consciousness, all that remains is for us to communicate to one another those things that concern us, so that together we may either rejoice or be anxious for one another [Col. 1068D].

What concerns me, and for what I would have you rejoice or be anxious with me, you will learn better from the bearer of this little note than from the writer of the letter [Col. 1069A].

Greet Lord Lanfranc the younger, nephew of our reverend lord and father, Archbishop Lanfranc, and offer them the willingness of our faithful service. Since he is so close and dear to the one whom I both love and revere with such affection that I love what he loves—and since I hear that his character is lovable—if he deigns to receive it, I offer him our fidelity and ask for his friendship.

Greet Lord Osbern, who is with you, as our beloved brother, in place of Osbern, my most beloved deceased friend. I ask you and all my friends, in words less ample than I know how and with affection as great as I can, that wherever Osbern is, his soul is my soul. Let me therefore receive in him, while he lives, whatever I might have hoped for from friendship after he has died, so that they may be at ease when I am dead [Col. 1069B].

Farewell, farewell, my dearest. And, in order that I may repay you according to your importunity, I beg, and beg, and beg: remember me, and do not forget the soul of my beloved Osbern. But if I seem to burden you too much, forget me and remember him.

I sent another letter to Lord Henry; but with your names exchanged throughout: let yours be his, and his yours.

## LETTER V [Note: [Col. 1069D] Compared with two manuscript copies of one Codex Vict., noted above.]

### TO HENRY

He loves Henry more intensely because of his good character and religious way of life; and the absence of a friend must be endured through obedience.

To the lord and dearest brother Henry, revered for his merits and character, brother Anselm sends greetings.

[Col. 1069C]

The more, dearest, report testifies to me that your way of life toward all people grows daily in moral integrity together with religious holiness [Note: [Col. 1069D] “Toward all”: the MSS. read, “toward all women”;]—the more surely the heart of your friend is inflamed with the desire to see what he hears while loving it, and to enjoy what he loves while hearing of it [Note: [Col. 1069D] “And to enjoy”: the MSS. read, “and to finish”; another reading is “and to enjoy.”].

Since I do not doubt that we love one another in like manner, I also do not doubt that we desire one another in like manner. For those whose minds the fire of love has fused into one [Note: [Col. 1069D] “The fire of love”: one copy of MS. 20 reads, “the force of love”], are reasonably distressed if the place of their way of life separates their bodies.

But since, whether we live or die, we belong not to ourselves but to the Lord (Romans 14:8), we must pay greater attention to what the Lord, whose we are, does with us than to what we, who are not our own, desire. Let us therefore preserve the desire of brotherly love in such a way that we serve the command of the heavenly will; and let us display the obedience of subjection demanded by the almighty arrangement in such a way that we retain the affection of love bestowed by the divine distribution.

For we shall not be able to adapt God’s ordering to our advantage better than by desiring, in our own arrangements, to obey his will [Note: [Col. 1069D] “To our advantage”: one copy of MS. 20 reads, “to your advantage”; “in our arrangement”: one copy of MS. 20 reads, “in your arrangement”] [Col. 1070A] [Note: [Col. 1069D] “Desiring to obey.” Here the letter ends in one copy of MS. 20; in the other copy of the same codex the letter is complete, as in the printed editions.].

Finally, since each of us has several people present whom we love equally because they are loved by those whom we love, let us enjoy them with reasonable delight, and let us prepare to enjoy those same people not with delightful reason. And let us pray earnestly that one day, with our present and absent friends present together, we may enjoy the presence of God together.

For when, under the guidance of heavenly mercy, we reach the homeland for which we long, although we may arrive by different paths, we shall be happier insofar as, as though recalled from different exiles, we shall meet together.

I do not exhort your serenity, dearest, because I fear that you do not act in this way, but because I desire that you may advance without failing in what you do well.

I commend to you Lord Herluin, our beloved and loving friend, as you will learn from his way of life [Col. 1070B]. He will be able to tell you better than I can in the brevity of a letter what concerns me and for what things I ask your affection.

Consider the letter I sent to Lord Gondulph, with the name changed, to be yours and his; for whatever our affection writes either to you or to him, whether by revealing itself or by asking something, it says the same thing both to you and to him.

But since, on behalf of the most beloved soul of our deceased brother Osbern, I can neither pray to God nor ask people for enough, I repeat to you that whatever I write to Lord Gondulph concerning him, I say to you.

The lord abbot and the whole congregation of our brothers greet you and Lord Gondulph, giving great thanks for your gifts, but much greater thanks for your character and good pursuits.

Farewell, and hold the soul of Osbern, my other self [Col. 1070C], not as his, but as my own.

## LETTER VI [Note: [Col. 1069D] Compared with two manuscript copies of Vict. in the same codex.]

### TO HUGH

He instructs Hugh to bear the burden of his superior, even if that superior is undisciplined, and not to depart from him.

To the lord Hugh, deservedly revered for holiness and to be loved as a brother because of the duty of charity, brother Anselm wishes to live holily with prosperity in this life and happily with eternity in the future.

I briefly reply to the letters of your blessedness, because at present I do not have the opportunity to dictate much. If you cannot bear in concord the burden of your dealings with the man with whom you have business, it is healthier for both of you that, after humbly requesting and receiving permission from him, you rest from the anxiety of that burden than that, while quarrelling under the same weight, you grievously harm one another.

But if he does not grant you permission, it is better for you to bear the burden, even uselessly, through obedience than to cast it off impatiently through disobedience.

And if you have discovered that he is not corrected by your counsel but is harmed by it, it is better to become silent and, with the Prophet (Psalm 28:10), to keep silence from good things, and, according to the Apostle, insofar as it depends on you, to have peace with all people (Romans 12:18), than by speaking uselessly about good things to provide an occasion for the evil one.

Since the care of the office of leadership has been entrusted not to you but to him, it is not demanded of you that you be responsible if, because your counsel is neglected, the flock is not well governed through the fault of the shepherd.

Nevertheless, so long as he does not compel you to turn from good to evil, you should not take counsel to despise by departing—unless he grants permission—the submission and stability that you have professed, if you see that under him every means and opportunity for living well is still available to you.

But if in some respect his administration hinders your endeavors, though it does not block the way of salvation, it is better for you, secretly judging yourselves unworthy of greater grace by God’s judgment and because of your sins [Col. 1071B] [Note: [Col. 1071D] “By God’s judgment, unworthy”: the MSS. read, “by God’s judgment, your being unworthy”;], to live humbly and without sin in lesser goods than to strive for greater things through the sin of death.

For no one ought voluntarily to incur death unless he cannot otherwise escape a worse death.

May almighty God, and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Wonderful Counselor (Isaiah 9:6) and Angel of Great Counsel, teach you to do his will in such a way that he may grant you to see his glory, holy lord and dearest brother.

## LETTER VII [Note: [Col. 1071D] Compared with one manuscript copy, Vict. Ef. 20.]

### TO GONDULPH

He thanks Gondulph for the benefits he has bestowed upon the men of Bec.

Anselm to Gondulph.

[Col. 1071C]

For this reason I wished, as a friend to so great a friend, to preface my greeting so briefly: because I could not thereby disclose my affection to my beloved more abundantly. Whoever knows Gondulph and Anselm well, when he reads “Anselm to Gondulph,” does not fail to understand what is implied, or how great an affection is understood beneath it.

I think I should leave it to you, who are another self to me, to understand this as you wish, and turn my pen to the execution of the letter.

Lord Robert presses and compels the lord abbot and me, together with our whole congregation, to return thanks to you for the many benefits of your affection [Note: [Col. 1071D] “Lord Robert … the lord abbot”: one MS. reads, “Lord Robert … Lord Abbot”; another reads, “Lord Robert … the lord abbot.”]. But we do this unwillingly, because with the mouth of the mind we continually and most willingly murmur thanks to you for your whole life.

Indeed, it seems to be an insult to you if, among so many of your good qualities, this one is singled out and proclaimed with the giving of thanks while the greater ones are kept silent, or if your purpose of charity is judged still to need the nourishment of praise and encouragement.

Finally, we desire by loving, pray by desiring, and hope by praying that you may live through heavenly grace in such a way that, if something worthy of thanks is sought in the works of your charity, nothing unworthy of praise may be found in the actions of your will.

Thus may your life loosen the tongues of those who love you not so much by displaying certain things worthy of praise [Col. 1072A] as it may weary the voices of those who admire you by presenting itself wholly as worthy of approval.

And while the mouths of those who praise search for parts in which their proclamation may be opened, may they encounter the whole, whose fullness closes them; and may the familiar practice of the virtues and their habitual love so affect your mind, as though by making it drunk, that not only may whatever you bring forth in action taste of your inward affection, but your mind may marvel that anyone could fail to perceive that same charity in you.

For when someone is known to have such a purpose in life, the more his progress advances in that purpose, the more willingly he not only pursues the favor of those who admire him, but marvels at the error of those who follow him—

in order, then, that we may finally declare our view, and, I believe, yours, concerning the acceptance of your actions: whatever you laudably do toward us or anyone else, we hold most gratefully; but we think that its praises should be reserved for that day when all the upright in heart will be praised (Psalm 63:11), and when each person’s praise will come from God.

Greet, on our behalf, the reverend and beloved lord and our father, Archbishop Lanfranc, his nephew, and our beloved brothers who are with him, as you see fit.

Moreover, since all those who cling to me cling to you, to whom I cling, and since I instructed you through Lord Herluin that I desire them to be bound wholly to our friendship, place them with me in the inner chamber of your memory, there where I sit continually, and where they too pray with me; place them around me together with me.

But the soul of my Osbern, I beg you, my dear one [Col. 1072C], place nowhere but in my bosom.

Farewell, farewell, friend—therefore sweetest because most genuine. Farewell; and if you cannot forget me, certainly your servant, certainly your friend, certainly your beloved, remember me.

When I speak to you, I speak to Lord Henry. Farewell, then, both of you.

## LETTER VIII [Note: [Col. 1071D] Compared with the two aforementioned manuscript copies and Lovan.]

### TO HERLUIN

An exhortation powerfully inflaming hatred of the age.

To Lord and beloved brother Herluin, brother Anselm sends greetings.

You have begun, my dearest, to taste that the Lord is sweet (Psalm 33:9). Take care, therefore, lest you so fill yourself with the taste of the age, which flows abundantly toward you, that you empty yourself of the taste of God, which quickly and secretly flows away from the unwary.

Consider it carefully, my brother, again and again, and know with complete certainty [Col. 1072D] that those whom the sweetness of the age attracts are seized by eternal bitterness, while those whom God’s sweetness draws are satisfied by perpetual blessedness.

Certainly it is true, it is not false—truly, I say, it is what the Spirit of God says [Note: [Col. 1071D] “The Spirit of God says”: the MSS. read, “the Scripture of God says.”] through the mouth of God’s friend: “The friend of this age is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4) [Note: [Col. 1071D] “Is constituted”: MS. 1 reads, “will be constituted.”]. It is indeed so; it is altogether immutable [Note: [Col. 1071D] “Indeed it is so; altogether”: the MSS. read, “Indeed it is so altogether”; another reading is, “Indeed it is so. Altogether.”].

These are not merely words to be heard; the reality itself must be feared with terror. If, therefore, you do not love being constituted an enemy of God, shudder with abhorrence at being a friend of this age [Col. 1073A].

A friend of this age is anyone who is a friend of worldly pleasures. I beg you, friend, do not love worldly delights. When they are absent, do not extend your heart toward them; when they are present, do not set your heart upon them (Psalm 61:44); but whether they are absent or present, always desire to hide yourself from them.

If the world, or anything belonging to the world, smiles upon you, do not smile back at it. Certainly, brother, it does not smile at you so that you may laugh in the end; it pretends to smile so that it may mock you.

Be ever cautious, therefore, dearest, so that you may anticipate it and turn its fraud back upon it. When it deceitfully smiles at you, mock it truthfully. And certainly you will never mock it more truly than if, when it laughs against you, you weep against it.

You must devote yourself to these tears with all the greater diligence because it is better to weep for a short time by choice against a false laugh than, under a true mockery, to mourn forever and by necessity [Note: [Col. 1073D] “Under a true mockery, to mourn forever and by necessity”: the MSS. read, “under mockery, to mourn forever through necessity.”].

Let Lord Gondulph read this letter [Note: [Col. 1073D] “Lord Gondulph”: the MSS. read, “Lord Gundulph.”], not so that he may do what he reads, but so that he may read what he does. If the fervor of his devotion wishes this letter to be his, let him put his own name in place of yours, and let it be his.

Farewell, both of you.

## LETTER IX [Note: [Col. 1073D] Compared with the aforementioned two copies of Vict.]

### TO ABBOT GERBERT

He congratulates the abbot because, at his request, he came to the aid of an afflicted widow.

To the venerable lord and father, Abbot Gerbert, brother Anselm, his servant.

Just as we must believe that where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20), so we must act so that where misery abounds, mercy may abound all the more [Note: [Col. 1073D] “Where misery abounds”: the MSS. read, “where misery may abound.”]. For if grace is enlarged where the offense is greater, how will mercy contract where greater compassion is owed?

Since “whatever one sows, that one will also reap” (Galatians 6:7), and “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7), trusting in your kindness because of this consideration, I prostrate myself in spirit at the feet of your holiness, interceding for that poor widow whose soul, in the tribulation of widowhood and poverty, you mercifully refreshed for God’s sake when, through my intervention, you released her from that very small service which the poor woman was paying to your greatness [Note: [Col. 1073D] “When you released her from that”: MS. 1 reads, “when you released that.”].

I therefore beg you with all the supplications of which I am capable [Col. 1073D] not to withdraw now the hand of consolation that you extended to her when she was so heavily pressed by widowhood and poverty, now that her multiplied troubles—including grief over her deceased son—torment her soul miserably.

I certainly know that it may be considered presumptuous for a little man—who is owed nothing and can repay nothing—to seek that something be granted through his intercession. But the immensity of mutual affection so joined me and the aforementioned brother, the son of this widow—his life itself requiring it—the two of us, namely, being joined together, that, when he died, I wished to substitute myself for him as a son to his mother, so that I would no longer be ashamed to be solicitous, even importunately, on behalf of my mother.

Let it be, however, that anyone judges this shamelessness of my importunity as excessive. So long as the merciful kindness of your goodness is praised by widows and orphans, and approved by Christ, who will receive in them and repay on their behalf [Note: [Col. 1073D] “Approved.” MS. 1 adds the following, which belongs to Letter 7: “In order, then, that we may finally declare our view, and, I believe, yours, concerning the acceptance of your actions: whatever you laudably do toward us or anyone else, we hold most gratefully; but we think that its praises should be reserved for that day when all the upright in heart will be praised, and when each person’s praise will come from God.”]—

## LETTER X [Note: [Col. 1073D] Compared with one manuscript copy of Vict.]

### TO RODULPH

He says that he never stated that he would no longer lend Rodulph his books; rather, he is sincerely ready to lend him everything.

To the lord Rodulph, reverend for his merits and character, and to the sweetest brother in charity and purpose, brother Anselm.

I formerly received your letter—your letter, I say, from one truly beloved and truly loving. Its inner face bore things that pierced me with pious compassion; but what it carried outwardly on its back wounded me with intolerable grief.

Unless I first wipe away the pain of this bruise through an apology, our spirit, languid from grief and mute from shame, will fail to respond to those things which friendly compassion desires, and our mind will despise, as though rightly, the words of our sincerity as fictitious pretenses.

For my mind—wholly devoted to you and to our other most beloved lords, and, if you deign to permit me so to say, to the brothers of your, or rather our, congregation [Note: [Col. 1073D] “Devoted”: one MS. reads, “most devoted.”]—cannot endure at all that you should even suspect that the following words came from my mouth: “We shall no longer lend you our books.” If I could ever have said this, believe me, and I will confess it myself: I was never a true friend to you, but a deceitful pretender.

For, as far as I am concerned, how could I deny anything to those for whom I would not hesitate to give my life?

Yet if some lack of kindness—not of the stomach but of the mind—had vomited such words from me, you reported them back with such humility, such admirable patience, such submissive apology, and such submission as satisfied the matter, that I was more deeply ashamed and more profoundly repentant that I had ever said anything similar.

Nor did I order the letter that was sent to you concerning the return of the books to be written in that way; nor did I know that it had been composed in that form before the recitation of those who brought the books.

Therefore, with the abbot’s permission, with my consent, and with none of the brothers objecting, and with our advantage and yours mutually balanced, we will gladly send you whatever books you request—or rather, whatever we possess [Col. 1075A]. As for those of ours that you have, we will let you keep them for as long as you need them.

I would more gladly have written to my dearest friend, panting in spiritual combat and calling forth his friend’s compassion through pious sighs—not because he is in need, but because he desires it—a consolation of whatever kind I could offer, than an apology for myself, lest a friend believe something hostile of me.

But since the former could be recovered later, while it was intolerable for a friend to endure the latter, and since the narrowness of a letter could not contain the breadth of both affections [Note: [Col. 1075D] “The narrowness of a letter”: one MS. reads, “lest the narrowness of a letter”; another, “nor could the narrowness of a letter”—], I postponed what delighted me in order to exclude what wounded me.

For I am so completely certain, dearest brother, of the purity of your affection that, if you have believed that anything in my affection toward you has diminished, I am in no way certain that you could even think of it without sadness [Col. 1075B].

How, then, could I fail to transfer that grief into my own heart? Or rather, how could I not say that the grieving heart is my own, since it grieves because of my love?

I therefore beg you, dearest, that if you should henceforth hear anything about me that seems contrary to the rule of charity toward you, let your heart—my other self—not believe it without investigation, lest my heart—your other self—be wounded.

Greet on my behalf all my lords, your brothers. Among them I can find no one who is not beloved; from among them I can choose no one as beloved above the others. Yet through longer experience they have greater confidence, together with you, in my fidelity; and neither your sincerity nor theirs is hidden from you or from them.

Farewell, and may they fare well.

## LETTER XI [Note: [Col. 1075D] Compared with the same manuscript copy.]

### TO THE SAME

He encourages Rodulph, whose duties as provost were calling him back from the work of more frequent reading and prayer, and who judged himself unequal to those duties.

To Rodulph, truly beloved brother, brother Anselm.

So that I may not, prompted by the feeling of my heart, remain silent about what I do not dare say because your letter forbade it—I who feared to call you “my lord” in the greeting—I will at least dare to show myself his servant in the continuation of the letter.

For I love Lord Rodulph with such charity as a brother not of my flesh but of my soul that in this very relationship I am ready to serve him as a servant. Therefore, if you order me to keep silent about what you are to me—as indeed, to speak from conscience, you are by the quality of your character—at least let me be permitted to confess what I am to you by my first intention.

Let brother Anselm, then, be silent to his lord Rodulph, and let Anselm, his servant, speak to brother Rodulph [Note: [Col. 1075D] “Anselm, his servant”: the MS. reads, “servant Anselm.”].

I received your letter, dearest brother, from your affection, and in it I read my own desire. For what your charity kindles in you with such longing—that wherever I remain, you may be with me—is the same as what sets my heart aflame, so that wherever I am, I may live with you.

And just as you ask my counsel so that this may be possible, so I pray God for help that it may not be otherwise [Col. 1076A]. If he deigns to hear us, may our dwelling together, with his help, be such that our whole life may be an act of thanksgiving to him.

But since neither you nor I belong to ourselves—for whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord (Romans 14:8)—if he who knows better than we do what pleases him or benefits us arranges us otherwise than we wish, let us patiently endure whatever we understand him to desire concerning us, if we do not wish to displease him ourselves.

For as brief as our life is, so near is the time when they will rejoice over the mutual presence of him and us, never again to be separated. Let us take care, if he grants it, to pass through this very brief life by acquiescing in him in all things.

Meanwhile, whatever proximity of place contains us or distance separates us [Col. 1076B], may charity always make one soul out of the two of us.

As for what you so earnestly ask me to obtain from Archbishop Lanfranc—when he returns from England, if you cannot be with me—I reply that, just as I desire for you what I understand to be more pleasing to God and more useful to you, so I will endeavor, if I can, to make it happen.

Meanwhile, carry out cheerfully what you are doing; perform cheerfully what you are undertaking. For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).

But since you complain that, because of what you are doing, the urgency of the task hinders you from reading or praying, let this be no small consolation to you: “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). In what you are held back, another is drawn forward; in what you bend down, another is raised up; in what burdens you, another is carried.

And remember that a servant who returns home empty runs more quickly; but when he is burdened, the whole household comes out to meet him more joyfully [Col. 1076C]. Nor is he rebuked by anyone because he comes more slowly [Note: [Col. 1075D] “Because he comes more slowly”: the MS. reads, “because he is slow in coming.”]; rather, because he has been usefully wearied, he is ordered to rest.

But if you say that your vigor or skill is not sufficient for the duty imposed upon you, I reply according to your judgment of yourself, not according to mine: even a diseased eye, alone in the head, is not sufficient to carry out the office of seeing, and yet it does not fail in what it can do, since it alone can do that within its body.

Since the letter has now exceeded its proper bounds, and the other matters you have written about require conversation more than writing—since the sacred books abound in writing—let us meanwhile entrust these matters confidently to God and pursue them with constant prayers; let us await our conversation with a common desire and bring the letter to an end by mutual agreement [Col. 1076D].

## LETTER XII. TO LANFRANC

He gives thanks for gifts.

To the reverend lord, beloved father, venerable Archbishop Lanfranc, brother Anselm, his servant.

Our letter gives you great thanks for the great gifts that we have received from your generosity; but we keep far greater thanks for you in the treasury of our heart, because of the greater gifts that we know are ready in your good will. For since such abundance flows to your servant from the mere spontaneous overflow of your kindness, it is sufficiently clear with what wealth your kindly affection would pour itself forth from within, if the need of one you love—which I say neither immodestly nor without experience—should demand it. Nor do I say this as though the gifts mentioned above were now teaching me for the first time to understand your paternal affection toward me; rather, since I have been ignorant of how much I ought to trust in it, from this I can gather something of it. For you by no means fully display your benevolence through cloak and gold, concerning one whom you love closely, beyond cloak and gold. Although you know well that you do this without offending me, nevertheless I am not reluctant to write it, because I desire this, pray for it in my desire, and propose it in my prayer: that you may never do so without justification.

[Col. 1077B] Concerning Girard, who is held back from our way of life because of his many debts, and concerning whom you gave instructions about what was ready in your mercy, Lord Robert will tell you what I think and what I have done, so far as was possible for you, in order that your almsgiving might be brought to completion. If he comes to you, and no agreement is reached between you and him concerning the full amount of money, I, your servant, ask your merciful kindness that, on account of the journey he undertakes in reliance upon you and on our advice, neither his debts should increase nor what he possesses diminish, and that pain and sorrow should not increase as a result of his labor.

[Col. 1078A]

## LETTER XIII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript copy]

### TO GIRARD. He advises one desirous of abandoning the world to go to Lanfranc, from whom he will receive what will release him from his debts.

To Girard, moneyer of Arras, brother Ainert, brother Anselm sends greeting.

The venerable Lanfranc, archbishop of the English—who was formerly prior in our monastery and abbot [Note: Of Caen. It would be more correct and more explicit to say *Campidomum*, as Cenalis shows in book II of *De re Gallica*, in a summary of considerable extent. Nevertheless, usage, and also the authority of the common people, has prevailed: “The right and rule of speech rests with him who has the power to decide” (Horace, *The Art of Poetry*, 72). Thus one should say *Cadomum*, not *Cadonum*, as in the printed edition of Gemmeticensis, book VII of *History of the Norman Dukes*, chapter 2. Caen is in fact a town of Normandy subject to the bishop of Bayeux, and is famous for an academy of no little distinction; in common speech, Caen. But here Anselm uses the name for the monastery founded in memory of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, still inhabited by Benedictine brethren. He took great care to have it magnificently built.

“That noble bastard, whom fate long ago carried away,

Was Augustus’s equal; that majesty subdued

The English, so the duke clothed himself as king; the tree sent

Its roots high into the air . . . .”

[Col. 1077D] These are lines from an eulogy or epigram written about four hundred years ago by an English monk of Rienall, and preserved among us in a manuscript concerning William the Conqueror. The suburban land on which the abbey stands was for that reason called Abbots’ Borough. The biographer of Lanfranc gives the following account of the building’s origin. Lanfranc opposed the marriage of the daughter of the count of Flanders, whom the duke himself had married, because they were joined by close blood relationship. Consequently, by authority of the Roman pope, all Neustria had been suspended from and placed under interdict with respect to the duties of Christianity. For this reason Lanfranc went again to the Roman pope—for he had already gone to Rome on account of a certain cleric named [Col. 1078C] Berengar, who taught a doctrine about the sacraments of the altar different from that held by the Church. Lanfranc, speaking with Pope Nicholas, demonstrated that the pope’s decision burdened only those who had neither joined the couple together nor were able to separate them. For the duke was unwilling under any circumstances to dismiss the girl whom he had taken. When the supreme pontiff heard this and recognized it as true, after obtaining a dispensation he permitted the marriage, but on condition that the duke and his wife build two monasteries, in which they would gather separate communities of men and women, who would serve God there day and night under the rule of holy religion and pray for their salvation. The duke obeyed the apostolic dispensation, and they built two monasteries on the estate that antiquity called Caen: the duke built one for monks in the name of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, and his wife built the other for nuns in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.]

of Caen, whom you yourself, I think, have seen—recently heard of your intention and your difficulty. Therefore, moved by compassion for you, his holiness instructed us that, if he were certain that you would come to our way of life, he would give you, for God’s sake, one hundred solidi [Note: “Certain solidi” in the manuscript; “one hundred solidi” in the corrected text] of English coinage as assistance toward paying your debts. He also added that, if necessary, he would add something more.

Therefore we advise you to go to him as soon as you can [Note: “As soon as you can, etc.” in the manuscript; “as soon as you will ever be able, etc.” in the manuscript]. If he asks you for any security, or your pledge, or an oath, then, by that security—or however he orders you—explain to him how much you owe, how much you trust yourself to possess from your own resources, and set before him a deadline that you can safely keep. Within that time, come to our monastery with the intention of becoming a monk there [Note: “So that you may be a monk, etc.” in the manuscript; “so that you may there be a monk, etc.”], if he will have taken pity on you to such an extent that you are able to repay the money you owe.

Do not hesitate to do what we advise, because [Note: “The same most merciful and most reverend archbishop. William of Malmesbury commends Lanfranc above all for this one virtue, in these words, in book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*: ‘Meanwhile, when Father Lanfranc was strengthening his character with every virtue and composing his spirit, they say that almsgiving was especially his distinguishing mark. The Bec Chronicle notes the same *prognosticon* (foretoken): that true saying of Christ, “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” [Luke 11:41]. Having received this saying from those who applauded him, he said to the Lord with a cheerful face: “Let us therefore strive in mutual exchange: you by giving, I by distributing.” Heavenly and praiseworthy mercy answered the wish of the man, and such abundance flowed to him that it could fill and surpass every extent. Nor was he sluggish in distributing, driving away and shaking off from his own person the vice of avarice, familiar to the Lombards [Col. 1079D]. He was not an inconsiderate teacher, nor did his generosity waste away, since discretion and cheerful courage seasoned it. The brightness of his face did not fall to the ground, but was most pleasing to the recipient, like the newly rising morning sun, which, dispersing the clouds, stills the winds and clears the air. Thus bread, shoes, and everything pertaining to food and clothing were expended for the poor. Coins were not given without mature consideration and deeper counsel, because the common people of this age, even with a stuffed purse, would digest hunger with a dry mouth.’ (Petronius, *Satyricon*, 82.) He avoided giving money for food as though it were sacred, lest he diminish his supply. To needy clerics and monasteries he amassed an immense quantity of money, often inviting those who were more ashamed to ask. Nor was the archbishop ashamed, with his robe gathered high, to serve food to the poor and to set scholars of slender means against one another in debate. After the words, both went away happy, while the victor received the prize of knowledge and the defeated the consolation of modesty. And again: ‘His common love toward all and his individual love toward each person will never be blotted out. He never allowed anyone to remain sad; but if he saw anyone under a cloud, he immediately asked the cause and sought it out, and, once he knew it, promptly remedied it. He freely offered young men coins with which they might meet the needs arising from their own poverty. If a gift happened to be lost, he doubled it, and ordered that this be done secretly from the others.’ These are William’s accounts of Lanfranc’s truly Christian and perfect mercy toward the needy. Although they may perhaps be too lengthy, I was not sorry to copy them out, so that a reader who loves virtue might possess something of the holiness of so great a man and Catholic teacher, beyond what most closely agrees with Anselm’s words.”]

the same most merciful and reverend [Col. 1079A] archbishop is extremely merciful, especially with regard to the salvation of souls; he is very devoted to almsgiving and has sufficient abundance of gold and silver. And if you owe so much that he is unwilling to give you enough to repay it, we are confident that, first for God’s sake and then for love of us—who, trusting in his great mercy, give you this advice [Note: “Confidently” in the manuscript; “trusting” in the corrected text]—he will give you so much that, in going to him, you will not regret either your labor or any money you have spent.

Also carry him this letter, so that it may serve as testimony that we are sending you to him. If you are able to free yourself from your debts, arrange that Lord Engelardus know this; and when he comes to us, let him give you some sign by which we may recognize him as your witness that you have been released from debt. Do not delay doing what we advise. [Col. 1079B] For we have instructed the same archbishop concerning this very matter, which we are writing to you [Note: “What we are writing, etc.” in the manuscript; “what we are writing to you, etc.” in the corrected text]. Farewell.

## LETTER XIV [Note: Compared with two manuscript copies of one Victorine codex]

### TO GONDULF. He testifies to his exceptional love for Gondulf, as above in letters 4 and 7.

To his beloved lover, the beloved lover Lord Gondulf, brother Anselm sends what Anselm sends to Gondulf.

Another who is conscious of his own conscience—that is, of mine [Note: “That is, of mine” in Manuscript Copy 1; “the same as mine” in another copy]—keeps urging me and urging me to let my letters fly across the sea to him, and to let them fly more often, as though he wished to learn the state of my friendship. But what will my letter teach you that you do not know, O you who are another soul? Enter the chamber [Note: “Enter the chamber” in the manuscript; “enter the chamber” without *in* in Copy 1] of your heart, and consider the affection of your true love; and you will recognize the love of your true friend.

Although we are not equal in the likeness of our conduct, I nevertheless do not dare to say that we are unequal; but certainly we are not unlike in the quality of our mutual love. For I confess—though with shame, I confess, I say—that my lukewarm charity is surpassed by your ardent charity; but it is not unlike yours [Note: The manuscripts read “not in a dissimilar way”; the corrected text reads “not unlike”], because it is formed according to the same rule. For just as you strive to love me with no less ardor [Col. 1080A] than yourself, so I endeavor not to love you with greater lukewarmness than I love myself [Note: The manuscripts and the Picard edition read “so therefore”; the corrected text reads “so I”]. If you demand more, I certainly neither wish for less nor can do more. Finally, may your love obtain for me by prayer that I love myself as much as is fitting; and your lover will love you, so that you yourself may now say, “It is enough” [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “It is not enough”].

Remember—not, I say, me, because I affirm that you do this yourself for your own sake—but those whom I once took care to commend to you. Greet those whom you customarily greet on our behalf. Know that the gifts you give are very pleasing to the lord abbot and to us, your brothers, but it is much more pleasing to us to hear [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “that you help”; the other manuscripts read “what we have heard”; another reads “what we hear”] about your life. We therefore desire and pray that almighty God may preserve by increasing and increase by preserving the good things that he works in you, so that the same blessed Lord may have something with which to repay you with an eternal kingdom forever. Let it be so, let it be so. [Col. 1080B] Amen.

## LETTER XV [Note: Compared with the same manuscript copies in one codex]

### TO HENRY. That it is not expedient for him to hurry to Italy to free his sister from the yoke of servitude.

To the most beloved lord and brother Henry, brother Anselm sends greeting.

Since, as my conscience bears witness, I do not wish to love you less than I love myself, I strongly resist giving you advice in a manner different from that in which I would advise myself. I find no counsel more useful or more universally applicable than the one by which wisdom advises us that, so that repentance may not follow our actions, we should do everything with counsel. Since this counsel has been given with the greatest wisdom and is true in the fullest sense, to the extent that anyone neglects it, to that extent he chooses not to rejoice in his actions but to repent of them. Therefore, whoever advises you to use this counsel must be heard no less attentively than the one whom everyone must obey in everything.

For this reason your friend speaks these words to you about counsel, most beloved, because I hear that in a certain matter you are preparing to act against the counsel of your friends [Col. 1081A]. For, as I have been told, you wish to go from England to Italy to defend your sister, whom you hear that a certain rich man is deceitfully subjecting to unjust servitude. I beg you, dearest, by whatever mutual friendship exists in you, and by whatever joy concerning you you wish me to have: do not do it.

For what difference does it make to monks and to those who profess that they wish to flee the world, whom or by what name they serve in the world? Finally, is not every human being born for labor, and a bird for flying? (Job 5:7.) Is not every human being, or nearly every human being, a servant either under the name of one who provides [Note: The manuscripts read “either under the name of providing”] or under the name of serving? Is not the servant who has been called in the Lord the Lord’s freedman, and the free person who has been called in the Lord Christ’s servant? Therefore, if everyone labors and serves in this way, and the servant is thus the Lord’s freedman while the free person is Christ’s servant [Col. 1081B], what difference does it make—apart from pride—with respect either to the world or to God, whether someone is called servant or free?

The Apostle says: “If you were called as a servant, do not let it trouble you” (1 Cor. 7:21). And shall we take such great care for others concerning what we are either forbidden [Note: The manuscripts read “either forbid”] or do not need to take care of for ourselves?
