Even if it is good to wish to free a person who has been assigned to a violent condition, what you intend is not so good that it is worth holding the plow of Christ and looking so far backward (Luke 9:62); worth a monk interrupting his way of life after so long an interval; worth exposing himself with so singular a will to so many bodily and spiritual dangers, and to dangers involving so many labors; worth resisting, as one intimate friend reproves another according to charity, the counsel of all his friends—lesser, equal, greater, and superiors [Note: The manuscripts and the Picard edition read “lesser and superiors”; another manuscript reads “greater and superiors”].

Since, then, these many and great things are certain disadvantages, or rather evils [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “so many as well as such great things”], if that one good—which is so inopportune, so uncertain, and so harmful—is set against them, what intelligent person would call it a good, rather than not a good, or even an evil?

Believe, therefore, dearest, in the counsel of your friends more than in your own deliberation, unless you consider yourself wiser than all of them. For because your mind weighs its great affection together with that small good, it deceives itself and does not examine with an equal scale the things that must be weighed by themselves. If you persist in your own will—which, with God protecting you, will not happen [Col. 1082A]—then, just as you will be acting against the judgment of all your friends, so you will have the consent of none of them [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “the consent of no one of them”] in a matter harmful to you.

The lord abbot greets you as his most beloved son; he wishes everything written here by me to be regarded as his own beloved words [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “he wishes his own words”; another reads “he wishes them to be his”]. Submit, therefore, to his admonitions and ours, so that by obeying a kindly father and agreeing with a brotherly friend, you may bring joy if you love father and brother.

Greet on our behalf our beloved brothers, Lord Herluin and Lord Osbert. Farewell, and if I can do anything for you, tell me as soon as you can how you incline yourself toward the will of one who loves another carnally—I mean your own will—or yield to the judgment of those who love you spiritually.

## LETTER XVI [Col. 1082B]

### TO AVESGOT. He gives the reasons that prevent him from undertaking responsibility for the studies of the young man commended to him.

To his most beloved lord and friend Avesgot, brother Anselm sends greeting.

At the beginning of my reply I state that our conscience bears witness to what this letter says. I therefore give thanks—since for the present I can do nothing else—to your charity, which makes itself ready to serve our needs in the manner revealed by your letter. I certainly respond to a similar willingness; but I am deeply sorry that I cannot prove it by my actions in response to your first request. For I now have neither the permission, nor the intention, nor the opportunity for that sort of study in which your beloved protégé, about whom you wrote, might make progress, as I once did or as your holiness supposes [Col. 1082C]. I therefore ask that your love toward me not be disturbed in any way, since my intention is always to serve your friendship, although ability does not accompany it equally. For true friendship can exist wherever good will always remains strong, even if there is never an urgent need to ask, nor an ability ready to provide.

Finally, concerning what is said to me in your letter:

“Your knowledge is nothing unless another knows that you know this.”

Although Persius said this not to restrain display but to express it, I reply:

“My knowledge is nothing if another knows what sort it is.”

But as for what you ask [Note: On Lanfranc’s fame. William of Malmesbury writes on this subject in the passage recently cited: “His fame [Lanfranc’s] went out to the remotest regions of Latinity, and Bec was a great and famous school of learning.” And again, in book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, he calls him “a man comparable to the ancients in knowledge and religion; concerning whom it may seriously be said:

‘A third Cato has fallen from heaven . . .’

(Juvenal, *Satires* II, line 40.) [Col. 1082D] So deeply had a heavenly flavor imbued his heart and palate, and so greatly did all Latinity, through his teaching, stir itself toward knowledge of the liberal arts.” Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1080, writes: “Lanfranc, distinguished for learning and piety, shines in England; formerly abbot of Caen, he was ordained archbishop of Canterbury.” Abbot Ingulf writes in his *History*: “The most reverend patriarch Lanfranc succeeded Stigand as archbishop of Canterbury; formerly abbot of Caen, he was the most praised and brilliant teacher of all the liberal arts.” But almost one illustrious proof of such great renown escaped me, which William of Malmesbury reports in book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English* in these words: “At that time Lanfranc was most famous in learning and worldly wisdom. That Alexander the Apostolic received him with reverence was shown most honorably when, as Lanfranc came to Rome, he set aside the haughtiness of the Roman brow and graciously rose to meet him, declaring that he was paying this reverence not to his archbishopric but to his mastery of letters. Therefore, he said, he had done what belonged to honor, while Lanfranc ought to do what belonged to justice, so that, as was the custom of all archbishops, he should prostrate himself at the feet of the vicar of Saint Peter. Lanfranc returned what was owed,” and so forth. He repeats this also near the end of book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*. I shall not go further, except to add another passage of William of Jumièges from book VI, chapter 8, of his *History of the Norman Dukes*, in these words: “There was a certain man born in Italy, Lanfranc by name, whom all Latinity—restored by him to its ancient state of learning—acknowledges with due love and honor. Greece itself, the teacher of nations in liberal studies, gladly listened to and admired his students.” A little later, concerning this same man after he had become a monk of Bec, he says: “When rumor revealed this deed, it spread it far and wide, and the man’s most celebrated fame soon raised Bec and Abbot Herluin throughout the world. Clerics came running, the most renowned sons of dukes, teachers of Latin schools, powerful laymen, and men of high nobility; many, for love of him, presented lands to that same Church.” Thus far William, reproducing the very words of Gilbert of Bec in the manuscript life of Herluin, first abbot of Bec, in the Bec Chronicle.]

why the fame of Lanfranc and Guitmund flies farther through the world than mine: surely it is because not every flower gives off the fragrance of a rose with equal scent, even if it does not deceive with a different color. Farewell.

## LETTER XVII [Note: Compared with the same two manuscript copies, Ef. 20]

### TO WILLIAM AND ROGER. He promises them a share in his prayers.

To his lords and brothers, willingly loving and deservedly beloved, William and Roger, brother Anselm sends greeting.

After our lord and friend Ermerus [Note: The manuscripts read “Ermerna”; the corrected text reads “Ermerus”] returned from Rome, he reported your request to me—that I should remember you in my prayers—with such earnest entreaty that shame compelled me to grant what was so insistently requested, while conscience forbade me, since I did not possess what was hoped for [Note: The manuscripts read *quo sperabatur* (“that in which hope was placed”); the corrected text reads *quod sperabatur* (“what was hoped for”)]. Since I had already willingly and modestly granted more fully what I had previously done, having learned through others the sincerity of your devotion toward God and your affection toward me, after not much time the same friend of ours and yours asked with equal insistence that our letter should testify this to you.

With heavenly mercy consenting, therefore, I promise that I will pray for you; and if divine regard works any good in me, I promise that you will share equally with me in it through true charity. But whether this will benefit you I entrust to him from whom every good comes.

In carrying out for you the gift of charity that lies within our power, we humbly ask that you in turn render us that same service that lies within yours. Having granted these things—which, if they are to benefit you, I do not know as one conscious of my own merits—I admonish you as beloved friends and brothers concerning matters that, just as I do not doubt they are harmful if neglected, so I do not doubt they are salutary if observed. Learn only this, most beloved: learn so that you may be capable of the truth, which is Christ; and live so that you may prove that you wish to be followers of Christ, who is the truth [Col. 1083C].

Lord Lambert, your teacher—whom I have learned from the reports of many to be lovable to all both for the sincerity of his intellect and for the uprightness of his conduct—was kind enough to greet me and ask me to pray for him through a cleric coming from those regions and bringing me a message from your affection. I wish you to greet him on our behalf and bind him to you by the bond of love that he has with me [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “and that you may bind him”; the corrected text reads “and bind him”].

## LETTER XVIII [Note: Compared with the same manuscripts]

### TO HIS UNCLES LAMBERT AND FOLCERAD. He asks to be informed of his uncles’ well-being.

To his revered lords, sweetest nurturers, and most beloved uncles, Lambert and Folcerad, brother Anselm sends this wish: that they may pass through temporal goods by despising them, so that they may remain in eternal goods by enjoying them.

Would that, when reading my letter, my uncles might feel the affection that my eyes testify while I dictate it. At the very beginning my spirit was quicker to draw out tears [Note: The manuscripts read “with tears”; the corrected text reads “tears”] than my stylus to impress letters. For neither the long passage of time [Col. 1084B] nor the distance of places has been able to take from my body what began at my birth from your stock [Note: The manuscripts read “from your stock”; another reading is “from our stock”] and what I received as I grew from your nurture; likewise, no anxiety and no occupation can diminish in my soul the love of you that it conceived both by nature and by your kindness [Note: The manuscripts read “my soul was able”; the corrected text reads “in my soul is able”].

Therefore, since my heart burns unceasingly with love for you, it always ardently thirsts for your happiness. I ask you, then, to have your son informed of the state of your well-being through the bearer of this letter, by whom, if you wish, you may learn what concerns me. Although this lord, who deigns to be our messenger, is very rich and belongs to one of the noblest families of the Normans, he himself, together with his mother, brothers, and sister, has joined himself to me in so intimate a familiarity of affection that his mother calls me son and her children call me brother—except that, by equal agreement, they have granted me the dignity of firstborn.

## LETTER XIX [Note: Compared with the manuscripts mentioned above]

### TO LANFRANC. He congratulates Lanfranc on having sent his nephew to Bec rather than elsewhere, and excuses Girard’s delay.

To his own lord, whom he loves reverently as his own father and reveres with affection, the archbishop Lanfranc, whom he embraces as the mother of the Catholic Church, his brother Anselm sends this message: that he is his.

We have always had, and certainly always ought to have, thanks for your paternal affection, by which you keep us ever present to you; but since we cannot always express them, we certainly must not now remain silent. For you overflow with such an abundance of that same affection that you recently proved it to be entirely complete by an essential sign—something that we too knew—and affirmed it to be inviolable by a most beloved pledge, as we likewise hoped. For you sent us your most beloved nephew, Lord Lanfranc, and wished him to become a monk in our monastery rather than in any other. Therefore, just as it is not credible that someone would wish to entrust what is most beloved to him to people he does not love [Col. 1085B], so it is not ordinarily possible that someone would fail to love the place where the person he greatly loves dwells. In this action of yours you showed not only that the constancy of your affection toward us remains, but also—and we regard this as no less pleasing—that you possessed certainty concerning our affection toward you.

We therefore give thanks first to him from whom every good comes, and then to your paternal greatness: thanks because you love us in this way; thanks because you trust us in this way; thanks because you entrust such a pledge to us. Let these words be spoken not only for me but for our entire community.

For myself, I shall say briefly, as one who understands: you have recently lightened considerably, by increasing it, the unequal burden of the priorship with which you once burdened me not lightly. And while my weak spirit groaned beneath the weight, you have made it so that now it does not wish—I do not say “it wishes,” but almost does not wish—to lay down what weighs upon it [Note: Manuscript 1 ends the letter here; Manuscript 2, like the printed editions, continues].

Through the generosity of your piety you redeemed your Girard from Flanders, from the world for God, at our suggestion. Thus, if I were not yours, I would confess myself a servant bought by you. Let your holiness know that, on the day appointed by you, he could not have been released from his creditors without serious loss. Nevertheless, on the first Sunday of Lent he came, magnificently proclaiming your mercy toward him, and explaining how your dignity favored not so much our petition as our slight expression of willingness in his case, and declared that it wished always to favor it.

He said that he wished, and that insofar as he possessed the ability he could, to repay what he owed in such a way that he would have something to bring back with him; but because of certain obstacles he had been unable to do so according to the agreement, as was necessary. He therefore returned, promising that, God willing, he would come to Bec at Easter and remain there [Col. 1086A], if not in the way he wished, then in the way he could [Note: The manuscript reads “if it is not in the way he wishes, then in the way he can”; the corrected text reads “then in the way he can”].

If he has therefore done wrong because he did not fully carry out the promise made to you, since malice does not seem to have committed this offense [Note: The manuscript reads “sees”; the corrected text reads “seems”], I confidently ask, as I am accustomed to do, for your kindness to permit your son, in the place of his father, to absolve him from this guilt when he begins to live with us. In this matter I shall confidently presume this concession if I read no prohibition.

## LETTER XX [Note: Compared with the aforesaid manuscripts, with Manuscript Corb. 160, Manuscript Flor., and Manuscript 267]

### TO GONDULF. Concerning three prayers to the Mother of God.

To Lord Gondulf [Note: “To Lord Gondulf” in the manuscripts. Manuscripts 160 and 167 read: “To his own lord, his own; to his friend, a friend; to his brother, a brother; to Gondulf, Anselm—perseverance in holiness for the love of happiness, and for the reward of holiness eternity in blessedness”], brother Anselm sends this message: that Anselm sends it to Gondulf.

[Col. 1086B]

There is no need for my mouth to speak at length about the former friendship’s well-being to one whom I know to be my other heart in mutual affection. To say briefly, then, what you know: just as my love for you has never changed by diminishing since it began, so I am concerned that it may always be changed by increasing [Note: The manuscript reads “may never be changed in me”; another reads “may never be changed”].

A certain brother asked me not once but often to compose some substantial prayer concerning Saint Mary. While he was making this request outwardly in person, you, though absent, were persuading me inwardly. For since I foresaw that, if it were composed, it would eventually be yours, I accepted more willingly what he wanted. I therefore made one prayer, as I had been asked; but, recognizing that I had not satisfied the petitioner in it, I was moved to make a second [Note: Some manuscripts read “I was imitated”; others, “I was invited”; the corrected text reads “I was moved”]. Since I likewise had not satisfied him in that one, I completed a third, which would finally suffice [Note: The manuscripts read “which finally sufficed”; the corrected text reads “which would finally suffice”].

Receive, then, these prayers, which were made with your intention in mind; and do not criticize their length, which was caused by another’s request [Note: Manuscript 267 reads “length”; the other reading is “greatness”]. Would that they were so long [Note: Manuscripts 160, 267, and Flor. read “may they be so long”; another reads “may they be that long”] that, before one reaches the end of any of them by reading—or rather by meditating—what they were made for might be found within them through heavenly regard: namely, the compunction of contrition or love [Note: The manuscripts read “to that which”; another reads “that to which”].

Finally, for this reason I wished to divide these very prayers into sentences by paragraphs [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “these very prayers”; another reads simply “the prayers”], so that, forestalling the tedium of their length, you may, whenever you wish, interrupt your reading of them [Note: The manuscripts and the Picard edition read “begin”; Manuscript 267 reads “interrupt”; another reads “break off”].

## LETTER XXI [Note: Compared with Manuscript Victor. Ef. 20]

### TO RODULPH. He urges Rodulph to write out the Antiphonary in musical notation.

To his most beloved lord and brother Rodulph, brother Anselm sends blessed eternity and eternal blessedness.

The venerable lord Prior Helgotus, our beloved and lover—and yours as well—desires to exhort you by his prayers to notate the Antiphoner, but he considers that no slight burden of labor is involved in the undertaking itself [Note: [Col. 1087C] *Nonnullis in re*, “in some matters,” in one manuscript; *non-nullius in re*, “of no small weight in the matter,” in another]. Since, therefore, in venerable humility he does not wish his prayers, although he could, to weigh so heavily that they might suspend the burden impending, he earnestly begs that we take care to weigh our prayers together with his against the labor mentioned above.

But since neither he nor we attempt to lighten the burden of the desired work for our friends by our requests in such a way as to try to burden you with indiscriminate entreaties, we contemplate and set before you the benefit of your neighbors and the reward of your charity and obedience. Thus we ask your brotherhood, thus we advise your affection: that you not be reluctant to devote to this work, to which you are being urged, the time which you willingly do not hesitate to spend on any other writings.

If you say that this is nothing, or very little, then just as you are certain that this nothing or very little is wholly insufficient, so we are not doubtful that it will advance the matter to some degree. But so that the breadth of your generosity may add something beyond what our request presumes, we accept your good will with thanksgiving in such a way that we entirely reject its burdensome inconvenience.

That man who recently, while dying, received the monastic habit from you—if he also received the blessing, send us his name and the day of his death [Note: [Col. 1087D] “So that it may be entered in the Calendar.” *Calendarium* properly signifies the tables of the Almanac-makers arranged according to the order of the days, and especially those which we have placed before books of the canonical hours, where feast days and ordinary days may be seen distinguished by their rubrics and titles. Here Anselm takes it for the book in which individual religious churches record the day on which each of the brothers or benefactors died. Hence some call this daily record an *obituary*; others, using a Latin-Greek expression, a *mortilogium*; and some, more aptly, a *necrology*, that is, a book of the dead or deceased. Thus Bede, in Book IV, chapter 14 of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, calls books in which the deposition of the dead was recorded *codices*. These funeral registers originated from other twofold tablets—which the Greeks called δίπτυχα (*diptycha*)—from whose individual pages the deacon, in a loud voice during the solemn rites of Mass, recited in their proper place the names of the living and the offerings of the dead, as the most learned John Stephen Durand explains more fully in Book II, chapters 34 and 43, *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*. In that work, as he observes, *dipteriis* is corruptly read in Alcuin instead of *diptychis*. I have likewise observed that in most printed manuscripts of Gratian, including those published by Antonius Contius, *dictitis* is wrongly printed. Cajetan, indeed, in 24, question 2; Stephen, bishop of Tournai, the first commentator on these decrees—not John Seneca, as Genebrard writes in his *Chronicle*—a man of more polished learning; and John Flaventinus, the scholiast of Gratian, both saw manuscript copies in our library, although they did not yet state this point. Elsewhere *diptycis* is read; our two manuscript copies of Gratian likewise read it.], so that he may be entered in our Calendar.

## LETTER XXII [Note: [Col. 1087C] Compared with the two aforementioned Victorine manuscripts].

### LANFRANC TO ANSELM

He earnestly requests the prayers of Anselm and others, and commends his nephew to him.

To his lord, father, brother, and friend ANSELM, LANFRANC, a sinner [Note: [Col. 1087C] “Lanfrancus prays,” in the manuscripts and Picard’s edition; “Lanfrancus, a sinner,” in another], perpetual salvation from God.

Your blessedness knows very well what is advantageous for me, and so forth. See the entry on Lanfranc in volume CL of the *Patrologia*.

[Col. 1088A]

## 320 LETTER XXIII [Note: [Col. 1087C] Compared with the aforementioned manuscripts and with the Cottonian manuscript].

### LANFRANC TO LANFRANC AND GUIDO

The archbishop Lanfranc writes to his nephew and his companion, who are undergoing their novitiate as monks at Bec.

To his most beloved brothers LANFRANC and GUIDO, brother LANFRANC sends perpetual blessing from God.

Since, as I believe, by divine providence, and so forth. See the entry on Lanfranc, under the year 1089, in volume CL of the *Patrologia*.

## LETTER XXIV [Note: [Col. 1087C] Compared with one manuscript from the aforementioned two Victorine manuscripts].

### ANSELM TO LANFRANC

To Lanfranc concerning his nephew, who was received at Bec for his novitiate, about whom Letters 19 and 22 above speak. He also commends Mauritius, who is suffering from a disorder of the head.

To the reverend lord, father truly to be loved and beloved, Archbishop LANFRANC, to be embraced as a Catholic mother, his brother ANSELM, wholly his in whatever worthier way he can be.

Whenever it pleases you that something pleases me, this too certainly pleases me; and that which was already pleasing becomes more pleasing. You indicated that you were joyful because I, to say nothing of other matters, received our most beloved man, your nephew, with great rejoicing [Note: [Col. 1087C] One manuscript reads *inde laetos*, “joyful on that account,” with *laetos* inserted].

I have therefore been made joyful by this joy of yours also; and the joy which I had concerning our aforementioned dear one, although it always remains vigorous, has been renewed by being increased, since I learned that what I had—something I do not blush to confess—intended to accomplish in large part by receiving him in this way, had come to pass according to my desire, through the merits of my lord in every respect: your faithful brother and son Mauritius, whom you separate from yourselves for us, from the one who loved him more than anyone else, and whom he loved more than anyone else [Note: [Col. 1087C] One manuscript has *amabat*, “he loved,” instead of *amabatur*, “he was loved.”] You yourselves should judge what you owe him. For however insignificant the one whom he loves in this way, and by whom he is loved in this way, may be, you certainly owe him this: that he should love no less, and be loved no less, by that person.

Since, therefore, I know the uprightness of your justice, and you know our mutual affection, we shall dispense with commending him further. Concerning his illness of the head, I especially beg your piety, insofar as I have influence with you, that, for God’s sake and for the reward of eternal salvation, while you press the matter, his condition may be investigated and treated as far as possible by our beloved friend, Lord Albert the physician.

## LETTER XXV [Note: [Col. 1089D] Compared with the same manuscript].

### TO HENRY

He commends to him the monk Mauritius, who is suffering from a disorder of the head.

To his lord and most beloved brother HENRY, brother ANSELM sends enduring well-being in the present life and eternal happiness in the future.

I believe that you are aware how I have loved our lord, brother, and son Mauritius, whom we are sending to you. Since, therefore, we do not doubt that our beloved ones are loved by our beloved friend and lover [Note: [Col. 1089D] One manuscript reads *dilectiore*, “by the more beloved,” instead of *dilectore*, “by the lover”], we confidently commend him to you as one beloved to one beloved.

May he find me in you, whom I am, as it were, leaving in your place. For this reason we sent him, and no other, to your fatherly affection: because we heard that he specifically sought it from you. Be, then, an Anselm to our Mauritius, and I shall be a Lord Henry to your Holward. Concerning his disorder of the head, I especially beg you that, through your insistence, our beloved friend Lord Albert may investigate it and, insofar as God grants him the ability, come to his aid.

## 321 LETTER XXVI

### TO GONDULF

He says that thanks need not be offered to a friend for gifts sent; he remains concerned about the monk Mauritius.

To Lord GONDULF, brother ANSELM.

[Col. 1089C]

If I did not know that I am wholly yours and that you are wholly mine, I would return thanks for your gifts. But since what is yours is mine, and what is mine is yours, when you give me what is yours, why should I bow before you, when I am not receiving another’s possessions but what is mine?

If you recognize that you are another Anselm—not because of merits by which you surpass me, but through mutual affection—let my beloved brother and son, Lord Mauritius, perceive this. I beg you, in all things showing concern for him for the sake of the love of God and neighbor, to act toward him in my place.

Concerning his disorder of the head, I beg you, insofar as I can, that, through your prayers and assistance, he may be treated as far as possible by our lord and friend Albert the physician.

## LETTER XXVII [Col. 1089D]

### TO HERLUIN

He says that he pours out a prayer to God daily on Herluin’s behalf, although Herluin scarcely reads his admonitions; and he asks him to show himself a brother toward Mauritius.

To his lord and most beloved brother HERLUIN, brother ANSELM sends greetings.

Although you scarcely ever read our admonition, nevertheless let it be known to you, dearest one, that, caring for you every day, I pour out before God whatever prayer I can on your behalf. Remember, my friend, what I often told you in person by admonishing you, and what I later wrote while absent.

[Note: [Col. 1089D] The same matter appears in Letter 2 above.]

Beware, most loving brother, of what many fools do: the longer they live, the greater the hope of living they foster for themselves; and, casting away fear of death as it hastens, they fall away from their purpose of holy life. For it is truly the case that the longer someone has lived, the shorter is the time he will live; and the farther he becomes from the day of his birth, the nearer he becomes to the day of his death and to the reckoning for his entire life.

Just as, therefore, you see your life increasing into the past with each passing day, so you must be certain that the time available for living well decreases for you daily. Be concerned, then, dearest one, to spend the time that remains—for you do not know how short it is—in such a way that from day to day you extend your holy purpose toward better things. Thus, the more you consider your labor hastening toward its end, and yourself drawing near to rest and the crown, the more strongly you will advance, strengthened manfully by perseverance, pressing forward with greater vigor and continuing with greater joy.

Therefore, do not fall away from what you have begun through weariness; rather, in hope of heavenly assistance and for love of the blessed reward, begin those things which are advantageous to you and which you have not yet undertaken, so that, with Christ as your guide, you may reach the blessed fellowship of the saints.

I commend Lord Mauritius to you—you know that he is my beloved and my lover—in such a way that he may rejoice to have found a brother among foreigners, and that you may prove that, although far away, you have remained steadfast in our friendship.

## LETTER XXVIII [Note: [Col. 1089D] Compared with the same manuscripts].

### TO ALBERT

He urges him to turn from the world and commends Mauritius to him, so that he may treat him by his medical skill.

To his lord, brother, and most beloved friend ALBERT, brother ANSELM sends this wish: that you may pass through temporal goods by despising them, so as to remain in eternal goods by enjoying them.

Your dignity sought, through its letter, the affection of my love with such exalted humility. Your letters did not recently persuade me of it by reverently entreating me; rather, your character had long ago impressed itself upon my mind by commending itself in a lovable way. For, from the time when I happened to attain full knowledge of you, my heart was certainly not without desire and affection for you. You ought not to have doubted this if you remembered that journey which we once made together from Bec to Rouen. There we clung together in such great familiarity through conversation that our mutual love, conceived in our minds long before, from the time when we first knew one another, was displayed more fully; and something which I still desire, pray for in desiring, and await in praying, was promised to me by you.

It is this: if ever the desire for heavenly happiness were kindled in your mind by heavenly grace to such an extent that it entirely burned up the longing for earthly falsehood, your affection would entrust itself to no way of life except that of either the monastery of Caen or the monastery of Bec.

But since the matter which chiefly called you there has now been removed from Caen, now only Bec awaits you with greater certainty.

[Note: [Col. 1091A] Since the name and place occur and will occur very frequently, it is useful to explain them, and it will be useful to have explained them. Moreover, concerning its founder, Herluin, a man adorned with splendid ornaments of virtue, both order and reason, as well as no small benefit to the reader, urge—or rather compel—us to say something. For, as Gilbert Crispin says in the preface to his *Life*, Herluin rejected the world, which smiled upon him and suited his desires, at precisely the age when others more vehemently thrust themselves into what rejects them; and he rejected it in a homeland where, at that time, for an armed soldier in good health to become a monk was regarded as a portent. Let us now continue briefly, in Gilbert’s own words, the explanation we have begun.

His father traced his origin to the Danes, who first occupied Normandy. His mother was closely related to the dukes of Flanders. His father was named Ansgot, his mother Heloye.

Count Gilbert of Brionne, grandson of Richard, the first duke of Normandy, had Herluin—who had been raised by the count Godefrid, his son—at his side and held him in the highest esteem among all the leading men of his court. Herluin was exceedingly skilled in arms and bore them with no lesser courage. All the families throughout Normandy regarded him as outstanding in arms, and they exalted him through every military accomplishment and through the cultivation of his body.

He turned his mind away from dishonorable things; toward the honorable things that courtiers value, he devoted all his effort. He had already passed thirty-seven years in the most pleasant condition of this life when at last his mind began to be inflamed by fear of God and love of him, and to grow cold toward love of the world. Turning the eye of his heart from outward things toward himself, he went more frequently to church, prayed devoutly, often burst into tears, and often transformed the whole day by fasting.

His former zeal was no longer evident in arms or bodily adornment; this sufficiently indicated the alteration in his mind, which he still concealed under serious dissimulation. The renunciation of military service and every other secular occupation was the sum of his desire; yet he did not know where to turn or what manner of life to adopt. At that time there was scarcely any guide or leader along the straight path in Normandy.

But just as “the Spirit blows where he wills” (John 3:8), so “his anointing teaches the one whom it inspires about all things” (1 John 2:27). Therefore, renouncing military service, dressed in a shabby covering, with beard and hair uncut, he long continued to serve among the courtiers, so that, when he departed from Egypt, that true Hebrew might gain his estates for God together with himself.

Although he sat at his lord’s table, amid many kinds of food he ate only coarse bread and drank water. Everyone laughed at him, and everything he did was considered madness. By threats, promises, insults, and favors, his lord and all his attendants could not turn him from his purpose. Nevertheless, he did not wish to depart without the lord whom he served.

Meanwhile, Count Gilbert, because of a ruinous loss which one of his countrymen was plotting against him, sent Herluin to Robert, prince of Normandy. But the man of peace utterly refused to undertake schemes that would bring harm to anyone. His lord persisted in his decision, urging and threatening him to carry his message to Robert and bring back his answer. Herluin was now placed in a position where he had to show whether he preferred to serve a heavenly or an earthly lord.

Therefore, completely renouncing the mission, he departed from the court. When the count learned this, he immediately ordered all Herluin’s goods and his poor dependents to be seized. Herluin returned to the count on their behalf, intending to plead the cause of the innocent. Among other things he said:

“Let everything that belongs to me be sold, provided that the poor, who have deserved your anger by no crime, are restored what is theirs.”

Gilbert, who was greatly possessed by the pride of worldly eminence, was moved to pity. Having taken Herluin aside, he inquired into the cause of such a change of mind and the end he intended. Herluin replied in a few words and with many tears:

“By loving the world and serving you, I have until now neglected God and myself too greatly. Entirely intent on the cultivation of the body, I have received no instruction for my soul. Therefore I beg you: if I have ever deserved anything good from you, let me spend what remains of my life in a monastery, while your affection toward me remains intact; and give to God with me the possessions that I have had.”

His heart stirred to tears, Gilbert could not bear to let him continue speaking, and he granted his dependent the freedom he desired for himself and all his possessions [f. addition: “he granted it”].

Immediately Herluin undertook the work of constructing a place of God’s service at Burneville (they call it Bonneville). He not only presided over the work but also performed it himself, digging the earth, carrying out the trench, transporting stones, sand, and lime on his shoulders, and placing them in the wall. While others were away during the appointed hours, he gathered whatever the work required, excluding idleness from every part of the day. As much as he had formerly been more delicate through swollen vanity, so much more patient was he now, through true humility, in enduring every labor for God.

Except on the days when it was not permitted, he took food that was neither elaborate nor plentiful, after completing his day’s work. Since he could not study during the day, he spent almost the whole night memorizing the psalter. Through these exercises the new soldier of Christ trained himself with great joy.

He learned the first elements of letters when he was already nearly forty years old, and, by divine grace assisting him, he progressed so far that he was considered not only highly learned but also truly remarkable in explaining and understanding the meanings of Holy Scripture. This must be attributed solely to divine grace, for he devoted himself to this study only during the night, since he never interrupted the execution of his daytime work on account of reading.

Again the ancient enemy found a way to oppose him.

Herluin had visited a certain monastery to inquire about the life of monks. After praying, he approached the cloister door with every reverence and great trembling, as though it were the gate of paradise, greatly desiring to learn what the monastic habit was, what the monks’ conduct was, and what discipline of sitting in the cloister was practiced. But he saw that an entirely different gravity was maintained from that which the cenobitic order requires. He was troubled and became uncertain which manner of life he should approve.

When the custodian of the monastery saw him standing there and looking attentively inward, he suspected him of being a thief. He struck him with his fist on the neck and, pulling him by the hair with all the force he could, thrust him outside as far as the door. But the most patient man did not answer the monk with a single impatient word for the injury inflicted upon him. Nor was the enemy defeated only once; wherever he was overcome, he fell, God being victorious.

[Col. 1093B]

At last, after the church which he had built had been consecrated [f. addition: “the church”] by Hebert, bishop of Lisieux, Herluin had his hair tonsured, was clothed by the same bishop in the habit of sacred religion, and shortly afterward was ordained priest. He was appointed abbot over many brothers who had already devoted themselves to that rule.

He was set before the others as one to be imitated, for three years patiently enduring before secular people the reproach of spiritual life. Those whom he had received to govern he ruled with the greatest strictness, but according to the custom of the earlier Fathers.

It was a sight to see: after completing the office in church, the abbot sowing with seed slung about his neck, carrying a rake or hoe in his hand, leading the way to the agricultural work, while all the monks persisted in labor until the end of the day. Their daily food was rye bread and a herb with salt and water. The water was nothing but muddy, because there was no spring anywhere nearer than two miles.

They proclaimed it a heavenly benefaction whenever better bread, cheese, or some other food was available from any source. The example of their master and their own efforts closed every avenue to murmuring. The abbot was first to the work and last to leave it.

His noble mother likewise devoted herself there to such service for God. After granting to God the estates she possessed, she performed the office of a servant, washing the clothing of those who served God and carrying out with the greatest care whatever external work was assigned.

One day, while she was roasting grain for the work of the servants of God, the house somehow caught fire on every side. Someone ran up, announcing with lamentation that the houses had burned and that Herluin’s mother had been burned there. Although he was covered with tears, he raised his hands to God:

“Thanks be to you, God,” he said, “because the fire has taken my mother while she was serving you.”

What steadfastness in the love of God—that, struck by so many battering rams of the devil, could not be shaken! Yet the aforementioned lady suffered no harm in that conflagration.

After some time, Herluin was divinely warned in a vision to leave the solitary rural place, which entirely lacked suitable advantages, and transfer his dwelling to a place under his jurisdiction. This place was called Bec from the stream flowing there, and lay a mile from Brionne Castle. It is located in the Brionne forest itself, in a deep valley enclosed on either side by wooded hills, convenient for every human use. Because of the density of the forest and the refreshment provided by the stream, many wild animals gathered there. There were only three houses belonging to three mills, and that alone was habitable.

Although the aforementioned forest belonged to Count Gilbert as his private delight, and various portions of the soil belonged by right to various people, nevertheless, with God’s help and Herluin’s firm hope, the entire forest of Brionne came to belong to the men of Bec [f. addition: “belonged”].

Thus far we have told the story of Herluin in the very words of his biographer Gilbert Crispin, interrupting them occasionally insofar as I observed that this would contribute something to illustrating the establishment of the monastery of Bec and the glory of its founder.

For in his own age Herluin was no obscure star of our Gaul, and especially of Normandy. We shall scatter some of his rays elsewhere, where the occasion is more suitable, and especially when we speak of his death.

The account recorded by the author of the *History of the Norman Dukes*, Book VI, chapter 9, is so narrow and brief that it constricts the man’s extensive glory with undue severity. But so that our descendants may by no means be unaware how much external wealth he left for love of Christ, we shall enumerate it from his charter, where he says:

“Let it be known to all cultivators of the Christian religion that I, Abbot Herluin, son of Ausgot, with my brothers Odo and Roger standing by and praising the act, at the command of Count Gilbert, and with Albert and Ranulf consenting, together with Count Robert and Archbishop Robert, have given to Saint Mary the third part of the land of Burneville and whatever belongs to it; and Taville and Surcey, with whatever belongs to them; and the land of Sarnay, with whatever belongs to it, which my father Ausgot possessed during his life; and also the full dowry of my mother, given to me at my father’s command, before the witnesses Fulbert the priest, Vital, Rainald, and many others.”

Bec awaits you more surely than Caen, about which you had previously been uncertain. Therefore, since I desire your way of life especially for your sake, so that you may more surely await and more abundantly receive heavenly things in place of earthly things, eternal things in place of things that perish, true things in place of false things, and blessed incorruptibility in place of miserable mortality, I await it with greater ardor insofar as, if it should come to pass, I hope through it to share your life with me.

We are sending Lord Mauritius, our lord by his merits, our brother in religious life, and our most beloved son in care, to England at the command of our reverend lord and father, the archbishop. To the extent that our friendship can influence you, his illness requires, and your medicine, with God’s help, suffices, we entrust him to your hands to be treated for God’s sake.

Thus may temporal health be granted to him through your treatment [Note: [Col. 1091A] One manuscript reads “temporally safe” instead of “temporal health”], eternal health be repaid to you through divine mercy, and brother Anselm—whom you already possess as a friend—be purchased by you as a servant.

## LETTER XXIX [Note: [Col. 1093A] Compared with three Victorine manuscript copies in Codices Ef. 20 and Bd. 18, and with the Louvain manuscript].

### TO LANZO

He warns Lanzo to beware of the devil’s temptations.

To his beloved, beloved; to his friend, friend; to his brother, brother, LANZO [Col. 1094A] [Note: [Col. 1094C] *Lanzoni*: thus five of our manuscript copies, Eadmerus in the Antwerp edition of 1551, and William of Malmesbury in Book V of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English* and Book III of *The Deeds of the Bishops*. The printed copies therefore previously had *Lautonem* incorrectly. It is clear how many fruits of piety he gathered from the seed sown by Anselm, since the monastery of Saint Pancras at Lewes in England—which he governed, in the diocese of Selsey—became so renowned for its religious reputation that it easily took the palm from the other monasteries.

This Lanzo had first undergone his monastic novitiate at Cluny, a monastery in the diocese of Mâcon in Gaul, which William the Pious, duke of Aquitaine, built so magnificently that Paradin, in the book *On the Ancient State of Burgundy*, chapter 12, testifies that he stopped in astonishment when viewing it from afar. To show how tenacious he was of his religious discipline, although in his final illness he was tortured so severely that he was never tranquil even for a moment—whether sitting, walking, lying down, or standing—he nevertheless never spoke at night, as the librarian of Malmesbury says in Book V of *On the English Kings*. When the brothers asked him to break his silence, he did not consent, lest they taste the impropriety of his monastic state, since after receiving the monastic habit he had never spoken after leaving Compline until Prime of the following day.

To this man, who, as the same librarian observes shortly afterward, observed the rule of Saint Benedict more than the other men of his age and venerated the blessed Mother of God and her solemnities with singular devotion, it was granted, according to his accustomed practice, to celebrate the principal Mass in the community both on the passing of Saint Benedict and on the feast of Saint Mary, called the Annunciation of the Lord. On the eighth day after the aforementioned passing of Saint Benedict, he was overtaken by illness, and nevertheless on the eighth day after the Annunciation of the Lord he departed to Christ.

Anselm expressly mentions this letter in Letter 104 to Guarnerus, Book III. Eadmerus included a substantial part of it in Book I, chapter 15 of his *Life of Anselm*.]

ANSELM wishes him holiness in temporal life and happiness in eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] See Letter 2 above.]

When I consider, dearest one, the desire with which you and I desire one another, there is one thing that consoles me concerning our separation: I hope, through divine mercy, for our eternal union in the future life. For I am certain of my own conscience and have no doubt about yours, since, however much geographical distance may separate us [Note: [Col. 1095C] One manuscript reads *detineat*, “may hold us back”; another *destineat*, “may set us apart”; the Louvain manuscript reads *distinguat*, “may distinguish us”], charity makes one thing of our two souls.

Hence it comes about that our souls, present to one another in affection [Note: [Col. 1095C] One manuscript reads *et dilectione*, “and in love,” and the Louvain manuscript *in dilectione*, “in love”], embrace one another, while absent in bodily life they desire one another [Note: [Col. 1095C] The manuscripts read *amplectentur*, “will embrace,” instead of *amplectantur*, “embrace”]. But when, with God’s help, the pilgrimage of this life has been completed, we shall meet, by different roads, in the homeland toward which we sigh, approaching him to whom we strive and in whom we hope [Note: [Col. 1095C] The manuscripts and Picard’s edition read *Deo adjuvante*, “with God helping”; another reading is *illo adjuvante*, “with him helping”]. There, with God’s approval, we shall rejoice in one another all the more intensely the more patiently we now endure the divine ordering concerning us.

Meanwhile, however, since doing what renews and enkindles charity is not to resist God’s ordering but to obey it, we ought, whenever possible, to visit one another at least through mutual greetings. Although it may be enough that I have done this in the present letter, I am nevertheless compelled to add some admonition of ours, which your affection—not my foolishness—has always made sweet to you [Note: [Col. 1095C] One manuscript reads *tua charitas*, “your affection,” instead of *tui charitas*, “your affection for you,” as in the received text], at the urging of the Lord and our mutual friend Ursus [Note: [Col. 1095C] One manuscript reads *Ursone*; two others and the Louvain manuscript read *Urso* or *Ursione*].

For even if I can say nothing to you that you do not know, what you receive as spoken by one beloved and loving will nevertheless cling more firmly to your memory [Note: [Col. 1095C] The manuscripts, Picard’s edition, and the 1573 column read *suspiciens*, “looking upon” or “regarding”; the Louvain manuscript reads *suscipies*, “you will receive”].

You entered upon and professed the warfare of Christ, dearest one. In it, not only must the violence of an openly resisting enemy be driven back, but the cunning of one who seems to offer counsel must also be avoided. Often, when the openly malicious enemy cannot destroy Christ’s novice by wounding him with evil will, the crafty adversary malevolently attempts to extinguish him with the cup of poisonous reasoning [Note: [Col. 1095C] The manuscripts and Picard’s edition read *populo*, “with the people”; the Louvain manuscript reads *poculo*, “with a cup”].

When he cannot overwhelm a monk with hatred of the life he has professed, he strives to undermine him through disdain for the way of life in which he is living. And although he seems to grant that the monk’s purpose should be maintained, nevertheless, because he began it under such circumstances, among such people, or in such a place, he does not cease to accuse him, through countless deceits, of being exceedingly foolish and imprudent. Thus, while persuading him that he is ungrateful for the benefit of God by which he began, he ensures that, by a just judgment, he neither advances toward better things nor maintains what he received, or else persists in it uselessly.

For while he is incessantly occupied with laborious thoughts about changing his place—or, if it cannot be changed, at least about condemning his beginning—he never strives toward the perfection of the end. Since he dislikes the foundation he laid, he is in no way willing to build the structure of a good life upon it.

Hence it happens that, just as a little tree, if it is often transplanted or, newly planted in the same place, is disturbed by repeated uprooting, cannot take root and quickly becomes dry, never reaching any fertility of fruit [Note: [Col. 1095D] “Thus the unfortunate monk.” This seems to refer not inaptly to the following passage of the lyric poet:

“Whoever delights in another’s lot  
necessarily hates his own.

Each fool unjustly blames an undeserving place.

The mind is at fault, for it never escapes itself.”

Horace, Book I, verses 11 and 13],

so the unfortunate monk, if he is frequently moved by his own desire from place to place, or, while remaining in one place, is often shaken by hatred of it, never established by the roots of love, grows weak for every useful exercise and is enriched by no abundance of good works. And when he perceives, if he happens to reflect upon it, that he is in no way progressing toward good but toward evil, he unjustly directs the entire cause of his misery not toward his own character but toward that of others [Note: [Col. 1095C] MS 18 and the Louvain manuscript read *sed in suis, sed* (“but in his own, but”)], and from this he unhappily kindles himself all the more toward hatred of those among whom he lives [Note: [Col. 1095C] The manuscripts read “hatred, among whom”; the Louvain manuscript reads “kindles hatred of those among whom.”]

Therefore, whoever undertakes the cenobitic way of life [Note: [Col. 1095D] “Whoever undertakes the cenobitic purpose ought to strive to take root in whatever monastery he has professed, unless it is such that he is compelled to do evil there. This is a very clear passage for strengthening the resolve of many cenobites who, carried away by a desire for a stricter life, often transfer to another monastery, only to be compelled shortly afterward to leave because they are unequal to the burden—not without great sorrow and the grave danger of temptation to which those who depart are exposed.

Master Adam of Saint Victor, a man of the same age as Hugh, Richard, and several other most religious Fathers of our monastery, in the dialogue *On the Instruction of a Disciple*—which he dedicated to our canonical Fathers of the archiepiscopal church of Saint Andrew in Scotland—asks the same man, already bound by the oath of a professed religious life, and hears him answer:

‘What if, inflamed by a desire for greater perfection and a stricter order, I should wish to amend my life and improve my way of living? Do you advise me to migrate to a place where I can do this?’

Teacher: “Certainly, I do not advise it.”

Disciple: “Why?”

Teacher: “First, because I suspect your weakness: you may be able to endure this order, but perhaps you cannot endure that one. Second, because I fear that by your departure some loss and scandal may be inflicted upon those who remain after you leave.”

Disciple: “And why should that happen?”

Teacher: “Are you not one of the ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride? (Matthew 25:1.)”

Disciple: “I desire, indeed, to be one of the five wise virgins.”

Teacher: “You are either a wise virgin or a foolish one.”

Disciple: “Certainly I am.”

Teacher: “If you are foolish, I do not advise you to depart anywhere, lest the departure of a fool prove itself foolish. But if you are wise, I nevertheless advise you to remain, so that your wisdom may come to the aid, before all others, of the mother who conceived and carried you—that is, your own household.”’

A little later, when the disciple objects that the brothers’ well-known conduct makes him hated because he is greatly opposed to it, he says: “Do you then wish me to remain while hated?”

[Col. 1097B]

“Teacher: Not at all, but with affection. For I want you to dwell as Abel with Cain, as Isaac with Ishmael, and as Jacob with Esau. Their wickedness may benefit you, provided that your patience does not fail you. But if they are such as to drag you into sin, then I advise you to depart elsewhere, where you can please God.”

D. Bernard—whose epitaph the aforementioned Adam of our community also composed—untangles in the following manner this question also, which arose among several questions of the abbot of Colombes in his book *On Precept and Dispensation*:

“From the good which one has once vowed, it is not permissible to descend. I wholly advise against changing the place which each person has chosen for himself and to which he has bound himself by his own will and spoken commitment.”

Nor does Saint Pope Gregory advise otherwise. For he says:

“All the perfect carefully observe themselves with great subtlety of discernment, lest they should ever slip into worse things, whether in deed or in thought.”

And after adding a few words he says:

“Let the pact of stability therefore prescribe every subsequent descent into laxity, every contentious departure, every wandering and curious roaming, and, finally, every frivolity of inconstancy—not, however, in those matters which follow in the sequence of one’s profession, namely, conversion of conduct and obedience according to the rule. For if these things cannot perhaps be obtained there because of the wickedness and irreligion of those who live together there, I unhesitatingly advise, under the guidance of the spirit of freedom, that one pass to another place where a person will not be hindered from fulfilling the vows which his lips have uttered.”

A little later he explains his meaning more fully, saying:

“Perhaps someone wishes to pass from the institutions of the Cluniacs to bind himself to the poverty of the Cistercians, choosing the purity of the rule rather than those customs. If he consults me, I do not advise it, unless he has first secured the assent of his own abbot. Why? First, because of the scandal to those whom he abandons; next, because it is not safe to leave certainties for uncertainties. Perhaps he can bear one way of life but not the other; third, I suspect the fickleness by which we often reject, once we have tested it, what we previously desired because it seemed easy—almost in a single moment both desiring and rejecting the same thing, as lightly as irrationally.”

Thus far Bernard there. I have passed over much that a more eager reader will not pass over, although I do not think I have omitted anything that necessarily had to be written. If it pleases, let the following also serve as a conclusion, since it appears at the end of the *Apology to Abbot William*, in these words:

“Just as those who have perhaps vowed something greater are not permitted to descend to what is lesser, lest they apostatize, so it is not expedient for everyone to pass from lesser goods to greater ones, lest they become accomplices. For I know that some have hastened from other congregations and institutions to our order, knocked at its door, and entered. By doing so they both left scandals behind among their own people and brought them to us as well: just as their rash departure disturbed them, so their wretched conduct disturbed us, because they contemptuously rejected what they had held and rashly presumed upon what they could not sustain.”

Bernard concludes by adding:

“Although, therefore, we know some of them who, with God as their helper, have begun courageously and, with him as their protector, persevere still more courageously, it is nevertheless safer for us to persevere in the good which we have begun than to begin something in which we shall not persevere. And let all of us strive equally that, according to the Apostle’s counsel, ‘all our affairs may be done in charity’ (I Cor. XVI, 2).”

Consult him a third time in Letter 7 to the monk Adam, beginning after the middle with the words, “For, to say nothing of the rest,” etc., and in Letter 115 to a nun of Saint Mary of Troyes.

The divine Thomas goes along with Bernard’s opinion in Part II, Question 189, Article 8, saying:

“To pass from one religious order to another, unless because of great benefit or necessity, is not praiseworthy, both because those who are left behind are thereby greatly scandalized, and also because, other things being equal, a person makes progress more easily in the religious order to which he is accustomed than in one to which he is not accustomed.”

So he speaks, and immediately afterward adds the distinguished opinion of Abbot Nestorius on this matter. Most compilers of summaries follow D. Thomas. The reasons for changing monasteries which D. Thomas sets out there can be derived from what has already been said.

Joannes Gerson, a man whom even Luther, in his judgment after abandoning monastic life, regarded as no ordinary figure, does not depart from D. Thomas in the fourth *Consideration* of his letter to a certain Carthusian. He warns that:

“A religious ought to observe that in the house of the heavenly Father there are many dwelling places (John XIV, 2), and many roads by which one may reach them; and, according to Augustine’s saying, in the way of God one person goes in one manner and another in another. For this reason each person ought to walk in the vocation in which he was called.”

Again, in the fifth *Consideration* he says:

“The devil has no more effective device for doing harm than persuading a religious to become dissatisfied with the state which he has already assumed and professed. He attempts this now under the guise of contemplative quiet, now under the shadow of the claim that everything he does in his vocation is useless.”

These are extracts from Gerson.

Joannes Ketelius, or Cacabus, proposes the following meditation in Thomas à Kempis:

“It is useful for me to regard the exercises of this house as surpassing those of other houses, and to have the firm resolve to die in this state, and not to wish to separate myself from it for any reason, while always preserving obedience.”

Thomas à Kempis, a man of most enlightened mind and well aware of these storms by which the hearts of candidates and of those recently enrolled in Christ’s army are shaken, makes his novices cautious in Part II of the *Sermons to Novices*, Sermon 5, as follows:

“Any religious can save his soul and make virtuous progress in his own order and in the place provided for him by God, if he diligently observes what the order has established and what the superior commands and advises. Therefore let no unstable person deceive himself, nor think foolishly and vainly about another place, prophesying more pleasant things to himself about uncertain futures: ‘O God, if only I were in such a place and order, how well and devoutly I would conduct myself, and never again complain or be disturbed about anything.’”

These are a few of the many admonitions Thomas gives his followers. He then adds the example of a certain regular canon:

“He was finally overcome and exhausted by the long struggle of this hidden temptation and went over to the Augustinian hermits. As soon as he arrived there, he was clothed in the monastic habit, and with such fervor in his burning heart that, if the Fathers had judged it appropriate, he would have given his name that very day. Scarcely eight days had passed when he was struck by the gravest sorrow and longing for his former monastery, so much so that he could take neither food nor sleep. Compelled by this, he disclosed his inward distress. The Fathers were astonished, severely rebuked his childish fickleness, returned his canonical habit to him, and he went back to his father’s house, where he was disciplined. Later, through the harm caused by his inconstancy, he became better and more steadfast.”

Joannes Gerson, in the eleventh *Consideration* of the letter cited above, tells a somewhat similar story, but a more dreadful one, about Joannes Borbonius, a Celestine:

“He, having been received by the Franciscans known as the Observants under the appearance of a stricter order, departed shortly afterward and took a wife; he was killed by her relatives when he was returning from Rome, in the year 1598.

“Our revered Father Joannes Hurtaldus of Paris, a bishop’s deputy in sacred matters, while returning from Fontevrault after completing a visitation and passing through Angers, encountered a certain Franciscan from Bammet. This monastery lies not far from the city. Seized by misguided zeal, the man had sought the Capuchins; but soon, attacked by the noonday demon, he abandoned both his cowl and the Catholic faith, and at Saumur, a town in the archdiocese of Tours, professed Calvinism.

“Once, when I was visiting the monks of the Fuliens who live in a suburb of Paris and was conversing with the venerable superior of that monastery about these matters, he asserted that he had seen twelve external monks as novices, of whom only one had remained in their order.

“I know a certain young regular canon, a man of remarkable simplicity, who frankly confessed during a conversation that he had been struck so violently by this insane storm that he had thought nothing of all the institutions of his monastery, until, coming to his senses and having gained a more favorable breeze, he exclaimed: ‘Good heavens, what am I doing? I am thinking of moving elsewhere in order to live better. When shall I become more diligent outside in observing canonical discipline, when I observe it more negligently at home?’ After this correction he became more courageous and thereafter laughed steadfastly at the demon who attacked him.”

While I was working out these matters, I asked a certain most religious man—whose name I discreetly omit—what he thought about them. He said that such a move is permitted when someone has completed the full cycle of his own order, but that even then the powers of mind and body must be examined with the greatest exactness. Indeed, even if they seem extremely strong, the dangers to salvation accompanying such changes are so great that the matter must be undertaken with mature deliberation. Thomas à Kempis above, and the other spiritual Fathers, teach how those who are weaker may evade the assaults of the devil who recommends these changes of religious life, expose his snares, and endure unharmed the daily skirmishes arising either from relaxing the observance of the monastic institution or from the perversity of certain undisciplined brothers.

To this may be added Lanfranc’s answer when questioned about these monastic doubts, which our Anselm copied near the end of his poem *On Contempt of the World*. In the manner of a notary, I shall also append the very wise decree of D. Stephen of Muret, founder of the Grandmontine brethren, which I read in the rule written in his own hand preserved among us. He prescribes as follows under the heading “On Not Receiving Men from Another Religion”:

“We altogether prohibit men of another religion from being received into this religion. For your customs differ greatly from theirs. You are accustomed to carry dung and wood, to heat the oven, and to make bread and many other things, since you have no servants of your own. When you were doing such things, they would often reproach you, saying: ‘We never dealt with such lowly matters in our religion.’ Moreover, a person who has never been in a discipline can more easily be kept within it when he has only recently left the world than a person who, having once departed from it, must be recalled to it.

“Furthermore, if, after a long period of examining your customs, they should wish to return to the habit of their former religion, then the very person to whose obedience they had previously submitted might receive them as his own sheep. Without permission, they could bring accusations against your community, and some disgrace could thereby befall both you and them. They must therefore in no way be received.

“Hence Solomon says: ‘A heart entering upon two paths will have no rest’ (Eccli. III, 28). Hence James says: ‘A man double-minded is unstable in all his ways’ (James I, 8).”

Thus far the decree of that most holy man. By forbidding external monks to be received among his own, he very clearly warned that such men ought not to migrate either to their own monasteries or to those of another sect.

Relevant here also is chapter 15 of Julius Faciaeus’s *On Mortification*, published at Paris in 1598.

The venerable Father Nicolaus Grenierius, thirty-six years ago prior of our monastery—and a prior distinguished by integrity, inferior to none of his brethren in learning—examines, in Lecture 4 on the Rule of Saint Augustine, how a religious person may live in an irreligious monastery and yet be unwilling to leave it, compelled by brotherly charity, fear of future scandal, or personal weakness and a trembling conscience:

“Then,” says our Grenierius, “one may hope that he can remain in his unreformed monastery without sin, provided that he lives there soberly, devoutly, and justly, observing these conditions: namely, that he grieve over the unreformed state of his monastery and desire its reform in essentials, especially in the common ownership of goods. Likewise, he must do what lies within him to introduce reform, and he must not distribute the goods entrusted to him without the express permission of his superior. Nor must he conduct himself as a secular person, but, as has been said, live devoutly, soberly, and justly (Titus II, 12).

“Devoutly toward God, so that he thinks rightly and catholically and, as far as he can, performs the divine office carefully and reverently; soberly toward himself, so that, following the Apostle’s exhortation, he abstains from bodily desires, which wage war against the soul (I Peter II, 11); justly toward others, so that in everything he shows himself to be a minister of God, taking care not to give anyone, by word or deed, as far as he reasonably can, a harmful example, and especially not to offend any of those with whom he lives.”

Thus Grenierius.

If someone undertakes such a proposal, it is advantageous for him, in whatever monastery he has professed, unless it is such that he is compelled there to do evil against his will, to strive with all the intention of his mind to take root there in the roots of love, and to refrain from judging the customs of others or of the place, provided they are not contrary to the divine commandments, even if they seem useless.

Let him rejoice that at last he has found a place where he may decide to remain throughout his life, not unwillingly but voluntarily, having driven away every anxiety about moving elsewhere; so that, at peace, he may devote himself diligently only to seeking the exercises of a devout and approved life.

[Note: Two manuscripts and the edition read “And, at peace, he may devote himself only to the exercises of a devout and approved life” (*et quietus ad sola piae probataeque vitae*); the Lovaniensis manuscript reads “that, at peace, he may devote himself only to the exercises of a devout life” (*ut quietus ad sola piae vitae*).]

[Note: Some manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “may seem uselessly” (*inutiliter videantur*), rather than “may seem useless” (*inutiles videantur*).]

But if, in spiritual fervor, he seems to desire certain greater and more useful things than the institutions of his present monastery permit, let him judge either that he is deceiving himself—by preferring things equal to equals or greater things to greater—or that he is presuming to be able to do what he cannot; or else let him believe that he has not deserved what he desires.

[Note: Manuscript 18 and Lov. read “lesser things to greater” (*minora majoribus*) instead of “greater things to greater” (*majora majoribus*).]

If he is deceived, let him give thanks to divine mercy, because he is being protected from his error, lest, by changing his place or manner of life without advantage—or even with loss—he needlessly incur the charge of inconstancy and fickleness, or, exhausted by attempting things greater than his strength, fail in what he previously undertook, or even fall away into things worse than those former ones.

[Note: Manuscript 18 and the Cologne edition read “for by which he is protected from his error” (*qua ab errore*) instead of “because he is protected from his error” (*quia ab errore*).]

But if he desires, without yet having deserved them, things truly better than those presently at hand, let him patiently endure the divine judgment, which unjustly denies nothing to anyone. Otherwise, by provoking the just Judge through impatience, he may deserve not to receive what he does not have and to lose what he has received, or uselessly to retain what he does not love.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads “what he does not love” (*quod non amat*) with *quia*, “because he does not love it.”]

But whether he perceives toward himself mercy or judgment in the things which he does not have and desires, let him rejoice in what he has received and render worthy thanks to the generosity of heaven.

[Note: Two manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “the mercy of God” (*Dei*) instead of “whether mercy” (*seu misericordiam*); manuscript 18 reads *si vero*, “but if indeed.”]

And because he has been able to reach whatever harbor from the stormy whirlwinds of the world, let him beware of introducing into the tranquility of the harbor the storm of fickleness and impatience, so that his mind, kept safe by constancy and gentleness, may be devoted to the vigilant concern of the fear of God and to the delight of love.

[Note: Manuscript 18 and Lov. read “may be devoted to anxious concern and to the delight of love” (*sollicitudini et amoris delectationi sit vacua*); the Cologne edition reads “may not be devoid of the concern and delight of love” (*sollicitudinis et amoris delectationis non sit vacua*); another reading has “may be devoted by concern and by the delight of love” (*sollicitudine et amoris delectatione sit vacua*).]

For fear guards through anxious concern, while love perfects through delight.

[Note: Manuscript 18 reads “makes progress” (*proficit*) instead of “perfects” (*perficit*).]

I know that these matters require greater breadth either of writing or of conversation if it is to be understood more fully by what deceits the ancient serpent ensnares the inexperienced monk in this kind of temptation, and conversely by what arguments the prudent monk may dissolve and destroy his crafty persuasions. But since I have already exceeded the brevity which a letter requires, and since everything I have said—or had to say—concerns the preservation of peace of mind, let this brief exhortation bring our letter to an end.

Nor should you think, dearest friend, that I say these things because I suspect you of suffering from any disturbance of mind. But since the aforesaid lord Ursus compels me to write you some admonition, I do not know what I should urge more than that you beware of what, under the appearance of a right intention, I know sometimes steals upon certain novices.

[Note: Manuscript 18, the Cologne edition, and the Lov. manuscript read *Ursio* rather than *Ursus*. Manuscript 18 and Lov. read *subripere*, “to steal upon,” instead of *subrepere*, “to creep in.”]

Therefore, my friend and dearest brother, your beloved lover advises, admonishes, and entreats you with all the inward affection of his heart to strive with all your strength for a peaceful mind. Without it, no one can discern the snares of the crafty enemy or perceive the exceedingly narrow paths of virtue.

[Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read *augustissimas*, “most narrow,” rather than *angustissimas*, “narrow.”]

A monk living in a monastery cannot attain this peace at all without constancy and gentleness; and he cannot attain it unless he strives to observe as religiously the institutions of his monastery which are not forbidden by the divine commandments, even if he does not understand their rationale.

Farewell, and may the almighty Lord perfect your steps in his paths, so that your footprints may not be moved (Ps. XVI, 5); so that you may appear in God’s sight in righteousness and be satisfied when his glory appears (ibid., 15). Pray that I may do so with you, for I too pray that you may do so with me.

[Note: Manuscript 18 adds “Amen.”]

[Col. 1102A]

## LETTER XXX

[Note: Compared with two manuscripts, Vict. in Cod. Ef. 20.]

### TO ARNULF

He advises him not to choose a place where he may teach, but one where he may more readily be taught.

To his lord and dearest brother Arnulf, brother Anselm, greetings.

Your fraternal affection has asked that we might converse together in person. I too have desired and continue to desire this ever since you assumed the habit of holy living. But because I am not my own man, nor do I wish to be, I have not yet been able to attain the fulfillment of this common desire, and I do not know whether I shall be able to do so.

Briefly, then, because of the limited time, I answer in writing the matters which you entrusted to me. Concerning the young brother about whom you ask, neither the lord abbot nor our congregation would grant your request unless they had first learned, through the experience of prolonged conduct, what kind of life he lived.

As for your proposal to go somewhere where you can live according to your purpose, I approve and encourage it. I nevertheless give you this preliminary warning: do it with the permission of your abbot; and wherever God directs your journey, if you wish to obtain the reward of monks, live according to the rule under the obedience of an abbot, not according to your own will.

Do not choose a place where you may benefit others and instruct them, but one where you may advance through others and be instructed by others for spiritual warfare. For you will make orderly progress if you desire first to be taught rather than to teach.

Moreover, if you consider both the end of your purpose and the exercise by which it is reached, you will realize that devoting your life to the study of the schools, since you renounced the world, is in no way expedient for you.

[Note: The manuscripts read *proponitur*, “it is proposed,” instead of *proponitis*, “you propose”; they read *impendistis*, “you devoted,” instead of *impenditis*, “you devote.”]

May your beloved affection be a source of joy to me. Although in this pilgrimage we are separated and travel toward our homeland as though by different roads, let us nevertheless pray for one another, so that in our homeland we may rejoice together in God eternally.

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: Compared with one of the manuscripts mentioned above.]

### TO LANFRANC

On the holy progress of Lanfranc’s nephew and the headache from which he suffered.

To his most desired lord and father, Lanfranc, archbishop—revered with love and loved with reverence as a Catholic mother—brother Anselm sends his greeting: may he shine long in the holiness of the present life and rejoice eternally in the happiness of the life to come.

If I could dictate and write as easily as I can speak, there would never be a shortage of my letters for the one to whom my heart so often speaks, except when I was faced with a shortage of messengers. But since there are so many things that prevent me from dictating that even meditation now prevents me from recounting how many they are, I beg that your paternal eminence not be angry because the letters of your little servant rarely reach you.

[Note: One manuscript reads “your patient eminence” (*patiens vestra*) instead of “your paternal eminence” (*paterna vestra*).]

Although the pen grows rusty when the hand lies idle, yet far be it that the mind should grow dull while the tongue is silent.

But leaving these matters aside, concerning my most sweet beloved, your nephew, whose conduct I know you always wish to know about, I report to you what my conscience attests. He is so careful to avoid the things which must be avoided that none of us can rightly find him blameworthy. He applies himself to humble kindness and kindly humility; to quiet, silence, and prayer, so that he is deservedly loved by all.

Thus each day he makes me, already happy about him, still happier; and I, to say nothing of the common affection of those near him, regard him as a beloved lover, both for your sake and for his own merits.
