There is, however, something which, although I truly believe that divine providence deals mercifully with him, I cannot see without the distress of compassionate affection. For the paternal discipline of God afflicts him daily with such a headache for many months now that sometimes his cheerful way of life is separated from the common gathering, and his attention is altogether prevented from reading or from any serious meditation.

I report this to you so that I may not be answerable before you for keeping silent about it, and so that you may, if you can, provide some help to my dearest brother through Lord Albert.

[Note: One manuscript reads *charitativa*, “compassionate,” instead of *charitativae*, “of compassionate affection”; another reads *dum affligit*, “while he afflicts,” instead of *divina quotidie affligit*, “divine [discipline] daily afflicts.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “the lord abbot” (*D. Abbatem*) instead of “Lord Albert” (*Dominum Albertum*).]

So that the physician may recognize the kind of illness from some of its signs: his temples are almost always as though beaten; his forehead is always heavy, especially when he bends forward. The brighter the light or the louder the sound, the more troublesome it is. Often, especially after eating, his entire face becomes very red; at the same time, not only his face but his whole head seems to burn.

Lord Guido, whom we assigned to the instruction of the boys, commends himself through gentle obedience and humility in diligence, so that we can alike take pride in you, through whom we have him, and in ourselves, who have such a man.

Your Lord Osbern, enriched by an affection made cheerful by piety, grows venerably fatter day by day; and through his progress in knowledge, his assiduous study, the clarity of his intelligence, and his tenacious memory, he increases daily in a praiseworthy manner.

It is not only because your paternal affection joins us together—a bond of which we boast fraternally—but also because his merits require it, that we rejoice in and are bound together by so pleasant a union of mutual affection that we can no longer be separated without some rending of both souls and wounding of both hearts.

But whenever this occurs, when your command recalls him, my own rift remaining open in its gap, he himself will be consoled by the healing of the greater rift which he now suffers.

There is, however, something which compels me, in sympathy with him, to grieve. As a certain illness which he says is known to you increases, he is often so severely afflicted that at times he is brought to the danger of his life. First, a sudden chill affects his entire head, then his heart and whole body violently; immediately afterward his heart, suffering from excessive pulsation, fails together with all the senses and powers of his body, as happens when the blood has been drained.

After this collapse, once he seems to revive, he immediately burns as though feverish with the heat of his whole body. Headache follows, together with severe disturbance, as though he were about to vomit. Often, especially when he is singing, he is so tormented by confusion in his head that the place where he is seems to rotate around him.

Since I neither know nor can love him better than by loving him as you do, I refrain from asking your fatherhood to care for him.

I have heard that Saint Dunstan established a rule of monastic life. If this is so, I would gladly see the famous Life and institutions of so great a Father.

[Col. 1104B]

## LETTER XXXII

[Note: Compared with the manuscript mentioned above.]

### TO HENRY

He gives thanks for the monk Mauritius, who was carefully cared for.

To his lord and brother, his friend Henry, brother Anselm sends wishes for persevering holiness in this life and eternal happiness in the future life.

You have laudably discharged what you charitably owe when, as he himself wrote to me, you have shown yourselves kind and beneficent toward our common brother Mauritius in everything.

[Note: One manuscript reads *Mavortio* instead of *Mauricio*.]

Yet you make me no small debtor to you in gratitude because you bestow the benefits of your charity upon him more generously out of love for me.

But since I and you have not only now begun to learn what we may trust one another to do for each other, I thought it more fitting to keep these same thanks locked in the treasury of my mind than to write them on a sheet of paper to someone who already knows them.

[Note: One manuscript reads *dicimus*, “we say,” instead of *discimus*, “we learn.”] For I never doubt that a person’s good will is always ready—not only when it acts upon an opportunity presented to it, but always do I consider it worthy of thanks.

Since at present I cannot respond to your merits by deeds more suitably, I repay to the monks of yours who are with me, as far as I can, what you bestow.

Because you recently promised your presence, desired by me and by your other brothers, if the revered lord archbishop were not crossing the sea at this time, we hope—since the date you gave us has passed—that this same venerable Father will come to us before Easter.

May this happen with his prosperous cheerfulness and cheerful prosperity! But if, as we expect, we do not see him, know that we shall not release you from the obligation of your promise unless we see you.

For you wrote that you hoped our arrival would take place; we hold to this as though you had promised that it would occur. Farewell.

[Col. 1105A]

## LETTER XXXIII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript and the Leuven codex. The Leuven manuscript reads: “To Lord Gondulf, brother Anselm.”]

### TO GONDULF

That one need not write to a friend whose memory is perpetually in one’s heart.

His own to his own, friend to friend, brother to brother: Anselm sends Gondulf perseverance in holiness for the love of happiness, and, as the reward of holiness, eternity in happiness.

[Note: One manuscript reads “eternity and happiness” (*aeternitatem et foelicitatem*) instead of “eternity in happiness” (*aeternitatem in foelicitate*).]

Gondulf himself and Anselm are witnesses that you and I have no need to indicate our mutual affection to one another through letters. For your soul and mine do not permit themselves to be absent from one another; rather, they continually embrace each other. Nothing is lacking to us of one another except that we are not bodily present to each other.

Why should I describe my love for you on paper when you constantly preserve its true image in the treasury of your heart? For what else is your love toward me than the image of my love toward you?

Your will, which is known to me, therefore invites me to write you something because of our bodily absence. But since we are known to one another through the presence of our souls, I do not know what to say to you except that the Lord may do for you what he knows to be pleasing to him and beneficial to you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO MAURITIUS

He congratulates Mauritius on recovering his health and requests Saint Dunstan’s rule and Bede’s book *On Times*.

To his dearest brother and son Mauritius, brother Anselm sends the integrity of his affection and, with God’s protection, its perpetual endurance.

I have placed this kind of salutation at the head of the letter addressed to your affection, not because I think myself worthy of the paternal reverence due to anyone, nor because I consider my love to be of any importance; rather, ever since I have known you, I have always tried—whether or not I have been able—to show you both a brother’s love and a father’s care.

Because I know that you regard this intention of mine as familiar and welcome, I do not doubt that you will be pleased if I entrust to you the elevation of myself and my affection to some position of honor in your regard.

Since, then, what may seem like an arrogant salutation has been excused, let the execution of a brotherly address now follow.

Just as I do not doubt that your love for me burns and that you rejoice in my love for you, so I am certain that each day, desiring, you await—and awaiting, desire—the consolation of hearing or reading some message from me, because you suffer separation from your beloved lover.

When I received your letter of affection, a greater joy expanded the heart of your friend than the sadness which, I confess, I felt when you departed from us. When you departed, I grieved less because I had awaited, in desiring it, what you now report to have happened; but now I rejoice more truly because you report that what I awaited in hope has happened.

Because it seemed to reach my knowledge much too slowly, I had intended, before receiving your letter, to send one to your affection precisely to investigate this matter.

First, then, I give thanks to God, from whom every good comes, for the good things you have written about yourself. Next, I thank all those who, because of their love for me, show you the good of charity.

But I admonish you, my dearest, to ensure that you deserve to retain, through the display of your conduct, the favor and benefits of those with whom you live—benefits which you were able to obtain before they knew your manner of life.

As for your return, which you indicate that you desire, I have decided for now to suppress the matter in silence, until at a more suitable time we can reasonably bring our desire before the revered lord and father, Archbishop Lanfranc, whose will we ought to obey.

[Note: A manuscript reads “what you prefer to hear” (*magis audire*) instead of “what you desire more to hear” (*majus audire*).]

Concerning Saint Dunstan’s rule, I have written to the lord archbishop. Nevertheless, urge Lords Henry and Gondulf on our behalf to seek out that same rule and Bede’s *On Times* in those regions, as good as they may be but, in any event, the best copies they can find, because you know that certain matters in our copies need correction. They should lend the books to me promptly, and I shall return them.

May the almighty Lord always and everywhere keep you for himself, brother—and, since this is what you prefer to hear, dearest son, farewell. Do not wait rarely for our letters because of the barren obstacles that hinder me; rather, I beg you, often make me happy through yours. I say again what I always wish: farewell.

[Note: On the Rule of Saint Dunstan. “The most holy Dunstan, abbot of Glastonbury, afterwards bishop of Worcester, then archbishop of Canterbury, held his see for twenty-seven years; he lies in the metropolitan church of the Most Holy Trinity, above the altar dedicated in his name, beside the high altar of that same Most Holy Trinity, whose feast falls on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.” Thus reads the manuscript *Table of the Archbishops of Canterbury* in our library concerning Dunstan. This removes the error of Peter Equilinus, who writes in Book VIII, chapter 49, of his *Catalogue of Saints* that Dunstan passed to heaven on the Ides of September. More concerning that most holy man was left in writing by Osbern, cantor of the Church of Canterbury; William of Malmesbury, Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English* and Book II of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, chapters 7, 8, 9, and 10; more particularly, in two books composed on his life (as Bale testifies in Century 2 of *British Writers*); Henry of Huntingdon, archdeacon, Book V of his *History*; Roger Hoveden, in the first part of his *Annals*, from 919 (the year in which he reports that Dunstan was born) to 988; and Guido, abbot of Saint-Denis, manuscript in our library, chapter 5 of his *Sanctilogy*, for the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June. Anselm mentions Saint Dunstan’s Rule above, in Letter 31, and Bale expressly mentions it in Century 2, calling it the *Rule of Monastic Life*. Bale also assigns to him the *Archiepiscopal Benedictionary*, Book I of *Ordinations of the Clergy*, *On the Rule of Saint Benedict*, *On Occult Philosophy*, laws concerning tithes against priests addressed to the pope, solutions of doubts about the Eucharist, and letters to various persons. But in Letter 19 of Book III, with Christ’s help, we shall vindicate him from the impious buffoonery of Matthew Parker, pseudo-archbishop of Canterbury.]

[Col. 1107A]

## LETTER XXXV

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO MAURITIUS

That he does not write because of the scarcity of messengers to carry letters; he requests aphorisms with glosses.

To his dearest brother and son Mauritius, brother Anselm sends divine protection in prosperity and a fortress in adversity.

[Note: One manuscript and the Picard edition read “to his dearest father and son” (*patri et filio suo charissimo*) instead of “to his dearest brother and son” (*fratri et filio suo charissimo*). Another manuscript reads “a fortress in adverse circumstances” (*in adversa munitionem*) instead of “a fortress in adversity” (*in adversis munitionem*).]

If this were true—that your beloved affection complained in the second letter sent me, namely, that after you crossed the sea I had neglected you by visiting you with none of my letters—then, if anyone asserted that I had acted most improperly, I would not defend myself; and even if everyone else remained silent, I would myself rebuke myself quite severely. [Col. 1107B] For far be it from me now to neglect one whom, from childhood and from our first acquaintance, I loved with such devotion, to the measure of my ability, as you yourself can testify—especially now that you have advanced in moral goodness and love of God as far as heavenly clemency has deigned to grant, and are striving to advance day by day. This is what my heart has always desired for you, and what my devotion has earnestly pursued.

Indeed, before you sent me your earlier letter, I had prepared a letter to send you through the first person who might present himself as a suitable messenger. But since I considered the bearer of your letter an appropriate person to bring back my reply, it happened—contrary to both his own expectation and desire—that he was delayed so long that my letter, answering your first, was kept from your sight until your second letter was delivered to me. [Col. 1107C] Although many Normans cross over to the English, very few, so far as I know, do so; and among those few there is scarcely anyone whom I can trust to carry our mission without delay and without negligence.

But so that the matter itself may excuse me before my accuser [Note: The manuscript reads “but also the matter” (*sed et res*) for “but so that the matter” (*sed ut res*),] I am sending two letters of mine, answering your two, by the bearers of yours. And since the matter is troublesome for me, because I was unable to do separately and at the proper times what I should have done, I have at least resolved to do it all at once, both to persuade the unbelieving and to satisfy the suspicious.

As for the matter concerning which you so insistently asked me to press the reverend lord and our father, the archbishop, I tried to do so as diligently as I could and according to your wishes in a certain letter I sent him. [Col. 1107D] If, therefore, with his grace—which we must always embrace—it should happen that you return to us, as both you and I desire, insofar as it is expedient for you, bring with you what has been written concerning the aphorism. Meanwhile, however, do what you can without inconvenience to yourself: first obtain the text; then, if you are able, the glosses. Above all, take care that whatever you bring from it is corrected with the greatest diligence. If anything remains unfinished when you return, and if Lord Gondulf can complete it through someone at a suitable opportunity, leave the task assigned to his care. It will be much better, however, if Lord Gondulf can obtain the actual exemplar so that it may be lent to me. Greet Lord Herluin, reminding him to remember both himself and me. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI

[Note: Collated with two of the previously mentioned manuscripts, manuscript 20.]

### TO ALBERT

He gives thanks for care shown to Mauritius of Bec and recommends flight from the world.

To ALBERT, his lord, brother, beloved friend in Christ, and one desired for Christ, brother ANSELM, that he may despise earthly things for heavenly ones and receive heavenly things in place of earthly ones.

I confess that I am unable to repay your piety, according to your merit and my desire, even with thanks alone, let alone with a reward, for the mercy that you have deigned to show my beloved brother Mauritius in his illness. Since, however, I am in some way capable of the one but wholly unequal to the other, I would seem unjust to myself if I failed in what I can do. I therefore offer you as much thanks as my ability permits; but I reserve for you a far richer reward to be repaid by Christ, for it is Christ himself, as he bears witness, whom you are tending in his sick servant Mauritius.

I also ask that, just as you will not be wearied of receiving the full reward, so you may not be reluctant, insofar as it lies within you, to bring the healing you have begun to completion. But after these preliminary remarks concerning what I owe in thanksgiving, what follows will concern a certain reply that I still owe you. Formerly, when I replied to your letter of affection, I did not set down everything I had conceived in my mind, so that your prudence might receive less wearisomely what it saw written with fewer words. [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *studiose* (“eagerly”) for *fastidiose* (“wearisomely”).] [Col. 1108C] The present letter, therefore, belongs to that same reply.

When I observe that your truly beloved uprightness pursues with such devotion the love of a worthless little man—I mean my own love—I confess that it deserves by such earnest pleading something greater than my love can provide. But since I have nothing greater than love that I can give you, I offer love itself as greatly as I can according to my measure. I consider that no one can demand from me a greater love than that I should wish to love him as myself. Therefore, if I advise you to do what you know that, when I was as you now are, I singularly advised myself to do—if, by counselling it, I held to it; by holding to it, loved it; by loving it, profess it in my habit; and throughout my life strive for it—judge for yourselves whether you ought to reject it, when I faithfully offer you what you earnestly ask of me.

Finally, let the very authority of the reverend lord and our father, the archbishop—whose judgment neither his own prudence will allow to be deceived nor his justice to deceive—decide whether it is fitting for you, or whether it is injurious to me, for you to assert by seeking our affection that it pleases you, while proving by despising the practice of that very affection, in which it is more genuine, that it displeases you.

Although you are not unaware of where I wish to lead, I am nevertheless not reluctant to disclose my advice more clearly—indeed, not my advice but God’s. If, then, you have already learned that everything in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world; if you already know that the world will pass away, and its desire with it (1 John 2:16–17); if you have read that whoever is a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God (James 4:4); if you believe that everyone who has left his house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life (Matthew 19:29; Mark 10:25; Luke 18:20): I exhort you, do not love the world or the things that are in the world (1 John 2:15), but leave them and follow the poverty of Christ, so that in their place you may receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life. Amen; let it be so.

## LETTER XXXVII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscripts and with the Leuven manuscript.]

### TO FRODELINA

He arranges a mutual sharing of merits with her.

To the distinguished lady FRODELINA, worthy of reverence with love on account of the merit of her holiness, and worthy of love with reverence, brother ANSELM of Bec, a sinner in life, a monk in habit, servant of the servants and maidservants of God: steadily increasing holiness in the present life and eternal happiness in the life to come.

After I perceived the fragrance of your good reputation, which, sweetly scented, flies far and wide, I always desired to reach your acquaintance by some favorable opportunity, so that through acquaintance I might in some measure deserve to attain friendship; and, since I see that I greatly need good merits of my own, that I might mingle myself somewhat with yours through the communion of charity.

But I give thanks to God because, while I cherished this desire and eagerly awaited its fulfillment [Note: The manuscripts read *voluntatis affectum* (“the desire’s affection”); the Leuven manuscript reads *voluntatis effectum* (“the desire’s fulfillment”).], I was informed by our common brother and friend in Christ, Lord Hugh, the recluse of Caen [Note: The manuscripts read *dominum Hugonem*; the printed text has *domnum Hugonem*.], that your holiness was awaiting from me a similar outcome with a like affection. Therefore, since I discover—and rejoice in discovering—that Christ has answered, without our knowledge, your desires, which he knows to arise from his own love, and has joined us, even while we were unaware, in equal prayers and similar affection, I now send you this letter without fear of the charge of presumption, trusting in our mutual love.

Indeed, most beloved lady—and therefore both lady and most beloved, because you are greatly superior in the merits of your life—I know that there is little or nothing in me that deserves to be expected for the increase of your holiness. Yet because I desire to share in your greater goods, I do not know with what face I could deny you participation in my goods, whatever they may be, when you desire it.

If, then, our Lord Jesus Christ has worked or will work any good in me, I pray—and may he himself grant it according to the true love of God and neighbor—that it may be reckoned to you no differently than to me. I also ask that, although my merits can in no way equal yours, your blessedness may deign, according to that same charity, to admit me in some measure to a share in your merits. [Note: The manuscripts read “into the same charity”; the Leuven manuscript reads “according to the same charity.”]

Although your mind, fervently inspired by the divine Spirit, does not need admonition [Note: The manuscripts omit “I ought” (*deberem*).], I ought nevertheless, in accordance with the obligation of my profession, to write some exhortation to your holiness, were I not afraid of making the letter too long. May God grant that I may one day discharge this obligation, either by speaking with you or by writing.

May the almighty Lord so guard you in this temporal life from every evil that after this life he may establish you in eternal blessings, lady greatly to be loved and revered in Christ. May he so make us mutually mindful of one another in his love—me of you and you of me—that it may please him and profit us unto eternal life. Amen.

## 326 LETTER XXXVIII

[Note: Collated with one of the aforementioned manuscripts.]

### TO GUILLELMUS

He rejoices in having received Guillelmus’s added letter and turns him away from the vanity of the world.

To the reverend Lord GUILLELMUS, to be loved and beloved with the whole affection of the heart, brother ANSELMUS, his own [Note: The manuscripts read “his brother Anselmus”; “brother Anselmus his own”]: for the love of happiness, perseverance in advancing holiness; for the reward of holiness, eternity in sufficient happiness.

The letter of your sweet kindness that I received rejoiced my heart through the heading of your beloved name; refreshed it with the fragrance of sublime humility; satisfied it with the savor of profound charity; and pierced it with the affection of pious lamentation. Although I never wish to fail in answering its request, I confess that I am wholly unable to answer it adequately.

For, since I am conscious throughout my whole self and in everything that is in me that there is nothing worthy of so great a request, and since your benefits—and, what is much greater and dearer to me, your love toward me—deserve more from me than my very self, no devotion of words is sufficient for my affection by which I might offer myself to you, since I can offer nothing more. Thus your holiness may not doubt that the constant remembrance of you exists in me as in what belongs to you; and if anything divine is in me, may you be certain that, as something belonging to you, it is yours.

Since, then, I know that I am a debtor not only of prayer but also of admonition and every kind of solicitude for the salvation of one whose own I profess myself to be, your faithful beloved asks and admonishes you: do not let the seed of good will, which by divine regard has begun to germinate in you, wither through love of the world; do not let the feet of you who have begun to walk on the eternal road—not only through works of mercy but also through the intention of a higher path—be caught in the snares of the world.

But carefully turn away the eyes of your mind, lest they see vanity (Psalm 118:37); and by unfailing intention keep them always turned toward the truth.

## LETTER XXXIX

### TO MAURITIUS

That he has received the gifts sent.

To his most beloved friend and brother—and, since this is heard more clearly, his most beloved son—MAURITIUS, brother ANSELMUS, greetings.

I received the precious gift of your precious affection with the same charity with which it was sent; and I have decided to retain it for the purpose you request, so that it may preserve a fuller remembrance of you—not so much in expectation of receiving another, as because I know that this pleases you and you signify as much by your words.

For this I would give you thanks in writing, were it not that you know I was always prepared to give you something more before there was anything that I could repay. For I have always been, and remain, ready to expend myself and whatever I can, for you and on your behalf. The bearer is in haste, and I am forced to restrain the words of my heart that are trying to burst forth. Nevertheless, I add this: I remain what I have been to you. Farewell.

## LETTER XL

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO HELGOTUS

He commends to him the brother of Abbot Roger.

To the reverend Lord and Father, sweetest friend, HELGOTUS, brother ANSELMUS: lasting prosperity in the present life and eternal happiness in the future.

Lord Abbot Roger [Note: The manuscript reads “Rogerius”; “Rogerus”]—certain of you and of me, because the fire of charity has fused us into one heart and one soul, so that what one of us would not wish the other to know [Note: The manuscript reads *scire noverit* (“knows [it] to know”) for *scire noluerit* (“would not wish [him] to know”).], the other cannot fail to wish—asked me to commend to your holiness through me his brother Gonfridus, who resides at Caen.

He did not ask that you ever favor him in any matter of injustice [Note: The manuscript has plural *faveantur* (“they may be favored”) for singular *faveatur*.], or that through you anything be relaxed of the service he owes to the lord abbot and your monastery; but that, because of your love, you might deign to show him more familiarly the charity that you know you owe to every neighbor whenever reason seems to require it.

If, therefore, your prudence judges that what so great a friend asks of me is not improper, I can in no way decently refuse it [Note: The manuscript reads “I can decently refuse”; “I may decently refuse.”] Nothing remains, then, except that you should willingly grant what is honorable for all friends. Greet the duke and our venerable Father and lord, Lord Abbot [Note: The manuscripts read “our Lord Abbot”; “our Lord, Lord Abbot”], and all our beloved lords and brothers who are with you. May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds (Philippians 4:7).

## LETTER XLI

[Note: Collated with two manuscripts in the aforesaid codex and with the Gothic Edition and the Cologne edition of 1573.]

### TO LANFRANC

He praises Lanfranc’s modesty concerning the smallness of the gifts and gives his opinion concerning the monks’ abstinence.

To his lord and Father, the archbishop LANFRANC, most worthy of reverence, devotion [Note: The manuscripts read “reverence, devotion”; “of reverence and devotion”], and affection of love, his servant and son, brother ANSELMUS, subject to him in submission and love, who is his own.

Just as your paternal love knows how it is not absent from me and, when it does not give, is generous, and, when secure, is solicitous, so know—or rather, you know—that our fidelity, even when silent, is never ungrateful.

For when you do not send your beloved friend precious gifts as usual, you gently satisfy me with an excuse more precious than gifts; and although you are certain that I think nothing contrary to the Christian faith, you nevertheless take care lest anyone form either an opinion of perversity or a false opinion concerning me [Note: The manuscripts read “when I sent” (*cum enim misi*) for “when you do not send” (*cum enim mihi non mittitis*); manuscript 1 has singular *satagit* (“takes care”) for plural *satagitis*.] Indeed, when such an explanation of your gifts as the one you gave me comes from so great a person concerning so small a gift, it is much more precious than purple and gold.

You certainly did not send this gift because you thought I needed it, since you are by no means unaware that it is always stored for me in the treasury of your heart; but because your kindness could not permit a messenger from you to pass empty-handed to me.

For when I receive your gifts, I do not need their commendation, since I have no doubt that they are produced by a genuine love for me; nor, when they do not flow in abundance, do I need an explanation, because I am certain that they cease for some just reason which, if I understood it together with you, I would choose together with you. [Note: The manuscripts read “that they cease for some reason”; “that they cease for some just reason.”]

As for your command that, concerning certain assertions that are neither mine nor those of any Christian, I should simply express the judgment of truth that you know me to hold, I receive it with the greatest gratitude and obey it most willingly.

I learned in the Christian school what I hold; by holding it I affirm it; by affirming it I love it: for if someone among those who possess the world’s goods gives to one in need even a cup of cold water, out of true love of God and neighbor, he performs almsgiving and will not lose his reward (1 John 3:17).

Concerning the abstinence of monks, this is my opinion: the greater the love of God or neighbor with which a monk abstains from the foods set before him, the greater the almsgiving he performs and the greater the reward he acquires.

[Col. 1113A]

## LETTER XLII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscripts.]

### TO HENRY

He laments that he scarcely has leisure for writing, reading, and prayer.

To the most beloved lord, friend, and brother HENRY, brother ANSELMUS: prosperous longevity in the present life and happy eternity in the future [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “the happiness of the future”; “happy eternity in the future.”]

Although true love, once kindled, always burns without the need for constant fanning, friends nevertheless receive no small pleasure from it, whether those present receive it through mutual conversation or those absent through the frequent exchange of reminders.

Since, then, by the arrangement of heavenly providence we cannot rejoice in one another’s presence, we ought at least to gladden one another through alternating greetings sent by letter—not as much as we wish, but as much as we can. Therefore, if I were permitted to do so as often as I wished, I would certainly send you my note very frequently, and would ask for yours in return.

For, through the action of my sins, I see that I have been deprived not only of the opportunity to dictate but also of that of reading, meditating, or praying, so much so that I believe God’s mercy has been removed from me. Hence, although this is not enough to restore that divine mercy, I nevertheless grieve inconsolably, because, while I have so great an impediment to quiet, no benefit of my restlessness consoles me.

In this matter, although I do not seem justified in accusing occupations—which are nevertheless lowly and barren, and which I dare not neglect—I cannot, when I examine the matter more deeply, excuse my own slothfulness. For my mind is so constrained by a kind of natural narrowness, and languishes in weakness of good will, that it is wholly unequal to even one small concern when everything else is excluded, and collapses, overcome by the weight of any burden or temptation.

Therefore, my dearest brother and lord, since through charity I would that my merits, if I had any, were yours, and I trust that what is yours is mine, despairing of my own slothfulness, I beg and exhort your energy: since I feel myself rejected because of my inadequate progress arising from my own defect, may I deserve to be recalled through your unfailing progress. May your fraternity, now and forever beloved by me, prosper and prosper.

## LETTER XLIII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscripts.]

### TO HERLUIN, GONDULF, AND MAURITIUS

He exhorts the monks of Bec, then residing at the Church of Canterbury, always to advance toward better things.

To the lords, brothers, and most beloved friends HERLUIN, GONDULF, and MAURITIUS, brother ANSELMUS: by ascending from virtue to virtue, to reach Christ, the supreme virtue of God.

Since you are united by one purpose in which you all equally persevere, and since what I commonly desire for you is not different, I join you together in the address of a single letter.

If your affection remembers well what sort of people I have always wished to see you when present, it knows sufficiently what sort of people I continually desire to hear you are when absent. For, as your conscience bears witness, I did not merely give but wished to give from my heart to all of you the love of a brother, and to one of you in addition the care of a father. No intervening distance of land or sea has been able to break my affection for you.

Although the present counsel and admonition of our reverend lord and father, the archbishop [Note: The manuscripts read “lord and father” (*domini patris*) for “lord and our father” (*domini et patris nostri*).], together with the continual meditation of each of you upon what your habit professes, and the frequent kindling of mutual conversation in holy fervor, should be sufficient to make your well-begun efforts advance daily toward better things, unfailing love nevertheless requires that our exhortations, whatever they may be, should not fail you even though you are absent and have no need of them.

I therefore admonish and beg you, my beloved, to let nothing draw your minds away from their own guardianship. Carefully examine what they acquire each day by progressing, lest—God forbid—they lose something by failing. For just as in the virtues it is more difficult to attain something not yet possessed through effort than to avoid sloth, so it is more grievous to recover what is lost through negligence than to acquire what no one is known previously to have possessed.

Therefore, most beloved, always reckon the past as almost nothing, so that you neither disdain to retain what you have attained nor cease always to strive to add something to it, even if through weakness you cannot do so [Note: The manuscripts read “you do not rashly disdain”; “you do not disdain to retain.”]

For since among the many who are called few are chosen (Matthew 20:16), we are all certain, because Truth says so; but how few they are, we are all uncertain, because Truth is silent. Therefore, whoever does not yet live as one of the few should either correct his life or gather himself among the few; otherwise let him fear with certainty that he is rejected. But whoever already seems to himself to be among the few should not immediately rely upon the security of election.

For none of us knows to how small a number the elect will be reduced. Certainly no one knows whether he is already among the few elect [Note: The manuscripts read *nullus itaque* (“therefore no one”) for *nullus utique* (“certainly no one”).], even if he is already like one of the few among the many who are called. Therefore, let no one look backward and calculate how many he is ahead of on the road to the heavenly homeland; rather, with unwavering attention fixed on what lies ahead, let him carefully consider whether he is already walking together with those whose election no one doubts.

See, then, my beloved, that the fear of God which you have conceived does not grow lukewarm through any circumstance; but, as though fanned by unfailing devotion, let it grow hotter day by day until, transformed into eternal security, it shines upon you.

Farewell, my most beloved friends; and I ask you, by the fraternal charity that you owe me, to pray more earnestly than usual, lest I, who exhort you to advance, bring to completion the pitiable decline that I truly began long ago and have now almost completed.

## LETTER XLIV

[Note: Collated with the two aforementioned exemplars in the same manuscript.]

### TO HERNOSTUS

He rouses one crushed by the sharpest pains to patience.

To HERNOSTUS, formerly a companion and brother loved with equal intimacy, now the lord and Father reverently loved, bishop of Rochester [Note: *Hernostus*, elsewhere *Arnostus* or *Hernostus*, as it is read in these words in the lists of the bishops of Rochester in the Victorian manuscript: “After the restoration by Archbishop Lanfranc, the monk Hernostus of Bec became bishop.” That is all they contain. At the consecration of this Hernostus, however, when the following verse was found upon the altar:

“Quickly bring forth the first robe,” etc.,

Lanfranc foretold that he would soon die. Nor did the event disappoint the holy archbishop’s prophecy. Accordingly, he died that same year, after the sharpest and longest bodily sufferings, toward the steadfast endurance of which Anselmus here rouses and consoles him.

Moreover, “Ronestrensis,” “Rocestrensis,” and “Ronecestrensis” are now obsolete forms derived from “Rocestria” or “Ronecestria,” as Henry of Huntingdon also reads them in Book I of his *History*, in this verse:

“Witness Ely, beautiful in situation; Ronecestra, beautiful to behold.”

Today it is called Roffa, a city of the county of Canterbury, situated on elevated ground; from it the bishops of Rochester take their name. The biographer of Lanfranc, in the Bec manuscript Chronicle, also records the information given above concerning Arnostus.] Brother ANSELMUS: complete health in this life and perfect happiness in the future.

When I hear that your flesh is worn down by frequent and severe afflictions almost to the point of death, my affection is saddened with human sorrow. [328] But when I consider that through these things your soul is nourished for eternity, your progress consoles me with spiritual joy.

It is known to your holiness that in the tribulation of the flesh the rust of sins is burned away by burning, and through patience the life of the just is brought to completion [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “life arises”; “life is brought to completion.”] For it is written that God chastises every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12:6); and that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope, while hope does not disappoint (Romans 5:3); and that patience has its perfect work (James 1:4).

From this it is doubtless understood that one ought to rejoice in tribulation with as much affection as one must strive through hope and the perfection of works toward the inheritance of the sons. For although it is always pleasing to God if we never dissent from his ordering, we please him especially when, even in our adversity, we cheerfully consent to his will.

And although he is most just, nevertheless, since he is also most merciful, he will by no means compel those to pay the repeated penalty for their sins in the future age whom he sees here gladly advancing to meet punishment. Therefore, the more patiently we now endure him as severe, the more lenient we may be able to expect the strict Judge to be [Note: The manuscripts read “more lenient”; “milder.”]

By these and other such meditations, then, my reverend lord, as your paternal holiness knows, may you draw from the weakness of the flesh a consideration of the soul’s progress; from bodily illness, the soul’s salvation; from punishment, pardon; from tribulation itself, consolation; and from sorrow, joy [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “by considering the mind”; “by considering the soul’s progress.”]

May almighty and most merciful God so make you agree in all things with his will in this world that in the future he himself may agree in all things with your happiness. My sweetest Father and reverend lord, I beg that your paternal holiness not forget his faithful servant [Note: The manuscripts read “his servant”; “his faithful servant”], absent in body but cleaving to you in mind. May your body and soul always prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER XLV

### TO LAMBERT AND FOLCERALD

That they may not be seized by the lethargic sleep of the world.

To his reverend lords, most beloved uncles, and sweetest nurturers, LAMBERT and FOLCERALD, brother ANSELMUS: to despise temporal goods for eternal ones, and to receive eternal things in place of temporal ones.

Although, by the ordering of heavenly providence, distances of place and time separate us, no circumstance can or will diminish for me the affection of your love, with divine grace protecting me. And since it is certain that a similar affection for me clings no less similarly to your hearts, I have no doubt that, just as I always desire to know what concerns you, so you desire always to know what concerns me.

You will be able to learn and communicate these things more fully through the bearer of this note than the brevity of a letter would suffice to explain. May he from whom, to whom, and for whom alone this same desire is known make clear to you and persuade you of the desire my heart holds for you in the way he himself knows to be expedient for you.

Nevertheless, to say something from the abundance of my heart, I fear nothing more concerning you than that you may persist in love of the world and in worldly life, sleeping until the end, and that when you awaken after the end you may find little or nothing in your hands together with the men of wealth.

## LETTER XLVI

[Note: Collated with one manuscript from the two aforementioned ones.]

### TO FOLCERALD

He is held by an extraordinary desire to see him, but is prevented because soldiers in France allowed no one free passage.

To FOLCERALD, his kinsman according to the flesh and most beloved brother in Christ, brother ANSELMUS: to go from virtue to virtue in such a way as to see the God of gods in Zion.

[Col. 1117A]

I myself considered coming to you and, prostrating myself at the feet of your reverend abbot, asking with all the humility I could muster that he not separate the souls—by “me and you” I mean souls so closely joined by the bond of flesh and spirit [Note: The manuscript reads *ne animae* (“lest the souls”) for *ne animas* (“lest [he] separate the souls”).]—through the violent separation of our way of life, not merely dividing but tearing them apart.

But such a cruel and unrestrained savagery of malicious men [Note: The manuscript reads *saevitas* for *saevitia* (“savagery”).] is raging in France that I dare not expose either myself, any monk, or any knight to so great a danger. Indeed, when Lord Rodulfus was returning after bringing you back, he was captured in the archbishopric of Rheims together with his servants, all their horses having been taken, although he protested that he was traveling under the protection of the archbishop of Rheims. They were detained for some time and were finally released, barely retaining one horse.

Finally, even if I could visit you without any danger, the king and our lord abbot, in whose power I am, do not wish to give me permission to go. Yet I receive from them neither help nor advice by which I might have you; nor do they consider it a matter of honor that, after asking twice in vain, with such devotion, from so far away, and in letters so humble and friendly, they should perhaps ask a third time in vain.

I have written these things to you, my beloved, so that you might have someone through whom you could send me word, since I desire so greatly to know what concerns you. At the same time, you should know that I now expect no human assistance by which I might attain the companionship I desire so greatly, so that we may pray and await the favor of God alone toward our desire, according to his good pleasure, and meanwhile obediently and patiently endure his disposition concerning us.

For he will fulfill our desire more quickly and kindly if he sees that we desire not what we want but what he himself wills [Note: The manuscript reads “you will fulfill”; “he will fulfill.”] Although you derive great and sufficient consolation from the holy and paternal kindness of your abbot, which you used often to praise joyfully to me when you were present, I nevertheless will not cease desiring from you what I desire concerning you [Note: The manuscript reads “I desire from you”; “I desire concerning you.”]

I do not know through whom I can send you the prayers that, when you were with me, I had arranged to have written. The bearer of this letter did not dare to carry them to you, fearing that they might be taken from him. For when I sent him to you the first time, he says that he was captured and stripped, and that his clothes were searched in case anything that could be taken might be found in them [Note: The manuscript reads *discusas*, a spelling of *discussas* (“rummaged through” or “searched”).]

I ask you to tell me by letter what concerns you. May the Lord who guards Israel guard you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul (Psalm 120:7).

## LETTER XLVII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO PETER

He rejoices in his honorable studies and exhorts him to a purer life.

To his most beloved cousin PETER, brother ANSELMUS: willingly to abandon the good things that must necessarily be lost, so that he may be able to receive those that are held eternally.

I cannot say, my most beloved, with how great a joy my heart exulted when I heard from our beloved brother and cousin, Lord Folcerald, that you had not only reached the age you now possess but had also made progress, and were advancing day by day, in good and honorable studies.

My joy was greatly increased when he told me that you desired to see me. Remembering and preserving the great friendship that formerly existed between me and your grandfather, father, and mother, and the immense affection I had for you when you were still a very small boy, I always desire for you things better than which I cannot desire; and when I hear good things about you, I rejoice in a way beyond which I cannot rejoice [Note: The manuscript reads “and thus I always desire”; “I always desire.”]

Therefore, kindled by a desire for you in God, I pray God to grant that we may live together in this life for as long as we are to live, and rejoice together in glory in the future. Hence I exhort, beg, and entreat you, my most beloved: believe that what Truth said is true, and love what he promised to those who leave the world for his sake.

Begin preparing so great a gain; hasten toward so great a profit, so that, leaving what belongs to the world, you may receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life (Matthew 19:29). If God inspires this in you, I ask you, my beloved, not to hesitate, because of the hardship of the journey, to come to your friend and kinsman who longs for you.

For if we live together, our mutual joy in one another will be present to us in such fullness, and whatever seems burdensome will be so much lighter.

[Col. 1118C]

## LETTER XLVIII

[Note: It is clear that this was written by Anselmus when he was already abbot; for Lanfranc had greeted him as abbot, with Anselmus marking the first letter.] [Note: Collated with the aforesaid exemplar.]

### TO LANFRANC

He protests against the honorific form of address.

To his reverend lord and Father, the archbishop LANFRANCUS, brother ANSELMUS, his own, insofar as he is his own.

[The supplied source ends here, mid-letter.]

Just as the prophet Zechariah, in order to commend the authority of his prophecy, repeats at almost every verse, “Thus says the Lord,” so I would like the letters that I address to your paternal eminence to bear so frequently at their head, as though painted there, the words: “To the Lord and Father—and his, because I am his own,” so as to impress upon you who is speaking, to whom, and with what disposition. For I have engraved this in my mind as something impressed there—not, I say, that I know how to feign it, but rather that I have engraved it—in such a way that whatever I set forth at the beginning of our greeting may appear expressed at its conclusion. Since, then, I write to you so often under this title, I complain as I ask, and ask as I complain, why you never write back to me, but to some lord and father of yours, marked at the beginning of the letter. But if you write to your servant and son, why do you attempt, by a relative opposition, to overturn what you cannot destroy by an opposite negation? [Note: “Submerge”: manuscript; “overturn”: printed reading.] I therefore beg that whenever I receive a letter from your graciousness, I may either see to whom you are writing, or at least see to whom you are not writing.

## LETTER XLIX

### TO HENRY

He gives thanks for the gold, though the giver’s intention is praised more highly than the gift; and he asks pardon for Osbern.

To his reverend lord and friend, Lord Prior HENRY, Brother ANSELM sends greetings.

I write to give you great thanks for the gold that you sent; but in my heart I hold much greater thanks for the good will toward me that you have preserved. Each day I experience that good will much better and more clearly in my beloved, our common brother Maurice, than in thousands of pieces of gold and silver. For from those who come from him I hear that you treat him with such honor and affection that it is clear that you love me, who love him, by no means slightly.

I have read the letter that you sent to your dearest son, our brother Salvino. In it you expressed so kindly both your affection for him and a mention of me greater than I deserve, that I perceived there a certain great petition—wisely concealed and concealing wisdom—namely, that I, whom you describe as kind toward others, should extend my care and affection to him whom you love so dearly. And so let it be, since that is what you wish. For I love him both for God’s sake and for his own; and because he professes himself a friend of Lord Gondulf, my love increases still further, since he is the beloved of Lord Prior Henry.

In the same letter I found that, through spontaneous kindness, you had granted your beloved and mine pardon for a certain fault. And because your little servant, our brother Osbern, recognizes that he too sinned together with him—not through pride, but through thoughtlessness—and does not feel that pardon has been granted to him, I have learned that he is saddened by his fault and anxious about receiving forgiveness.

I therefore beg you to display toward me what you praise in me: so that, together with me, you may carry compassionate concern for his affliction; and just as, through your own goodness alone, you forgave Salvino, so may you, through your kindness and our affection, forgive Osbern if he has sinned against you.

## LETTER L

[Note: Compared with the two manuscripts mentioned above.]

### TO GONDULF

This is a familiar letter.

To his brother, a brother; to his beloved, the beloved—GONDULF—to have lasting holiness in this life, increasing day by day; in the future, eternal life and happiness that is always complete: ANSELM.

All who come from Lord Gondulf report that Lord Gondulf desires a letter from me. In it, I know well, you expect nothing other than to read about the mutual affection of our love. I am certain that you do not do this so that your love may be roused by letters lest it fall asleep, or so that my love may be made known in its vigilance. For just as you are certain of your affection for me, so you do not doubt mine for you.

You therefore ask for my writings so insistently that you may see on paper what we bear together, formed in the innermost mind; seeing it, read it; reading it, rejoice with me. But what [can be said], if no eye has seen, no ear has heard, but it has entered only into the heart of man, what affection diligent hearts prepare for those who love them? (1 Cor. 2:9.)

Your experienced conscience is my witness: neither by sight [Note: “Conscience; because”: manuscript 1; “your conscience, because”: another reading] nor by hearing [Note: “Neither by use”: the manuscripts and edition; Picard’s edition has “neither by sight”] can anyone perceive the flavor of this affection, except insofar as it is conceived in the mind by each person. Since you know, then, that the flavor of love [Note: “Because of love”: the manuscripts; “because the flavor of love”: another reading] is recognized neither by the eyes nor by the ears, but is delightfully tasted only by the mouth of the heart, by what words or letters can your love and mine be described?

And yet you press me importunately [Note: “You press me unjustly”: manuscripts; “you press me”: printed reading] to do what cannot be done. Let our consciences suffice—those consciences by which we are mutually aware of how much we love one another. May almighty God love you and, by loving you, protect you, so that nothing may be done by you, in you, or concerning you except what pleases him and benefits you.

## LETTER LI

[Note: Compared with the same manuscripts.]

### TO MAURICE

Concerning the letters received from Maurice and his approaching return to Normandy. He asks him to bring the *Aphorisms* with their glosses.

To his beloved friend, brother, and dearest son MAURICE, Brother ANSELM wishes such progress from virtue to virtue that he may cling to the virtue of virtues.

Having read through the letter that your affection recently sent to your beloved, I was delighted by the expression of your feelings and made glad by your promise to return. For just as I rejoice when you answer me, who love you, by loving me in return, so I always desire to enjoy the presence of my beloved beloved. Concerning your return, neither the archbishop whom I reverence sent me any instructions, as you once indicated in one of your letters that you supposed; nor will the lord abbot be displeased if you return, although you indicated in that same writing that you feared he would be; and it will give me great pleasure, something about which, I think, you have never doubted.

If you can write all the glosses of the *Aphorisms*, I shall be glad; but if not, I advise you not to omit those dealing with Greek or unusual names [Note: “But if not, do not omit those ...”: the manuscripts; “but if not; those ... do not omit”: another arrangement]. As for the time that you have decided to spend on the little book concerning pulses, I would rather that you devote it to completing whatever there is in the *Aphorisms*. For the knowledge contained in that little book is useful only to those who occupy themselves with it through very frequent and diligent practice. Nevertheless, if you can do anything concerning it after the *Aphorisms*, I shall gladly receive it.

I especially urge this concerning both works: whatever you do, corrected through the most diligent investigation, should deserve to be called complete. For in an unfamiliar and unusual text I would rather have one part intact in truth than the whole corrupted by falsehood.

Above all, I give you as much thanks as I can, because wherever you live in such a way that, although it was not I but the Holy Spirit who taught you to live well, it is nevertheless an honor to me, even among strangers and foreigners, to have raised such a disciple. You will be dearer to God and to God’s friends in proportion as you are found more proven in a dangerous way of life.

Farewell, and take care lest, by promising to return and not returning, you deceive your friend. Greet our beloved brother, Lord Herluin [Note: “Our brother Lord”: manuscript 1; “your brother Lord”: another reading].

## LETTER LII

[Note: Compared with the two manuscripts mentioned above.]

### TO FULCO

That he should accept the dignity offered to him, which he cannot refuse without disobedience.

To his reverend lord and father [Note: “And reverend brother”: the manuscripts], his dearest friend FULCO, Brother ANSELM wishes that, in the present life, he may be so disposed through divine grace that in the future he may deserve to be numbered among the saints.

Your holiness, which is dear to me, compels me by your prayers to promise what my service, always ready insofar as it can be without making promises, is prepared to accomplish. For I know that my prayers are so weighed down by worthlessness in God’s sight that I am ashamed to promise them to anyone; yet I have devoted myself to you so completely that my ability strives each day to pray for you.

Therefore, both in this matter about which your affection recently wrote to me, and in everything concerning you, know that our prayers, whatever they may be, will not be lacking for you.

Although your prudence does not need our advice, since you command it, let this present note offer it briefly. We know that it is safer for a person, always fearing his weakness, to refuse, insofar as he can, so great a burden than, trusting in his strength, readily to place it upon his shoulders [Note: “That it is safer”: the manuscripts].

But since it is written, “None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself; for whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s,” we must walk by the way of discretion between fear of our own weakness and obedience to the Lord’s will, so that we may seem to reject neither.

First, therefore, commend yourself to divine mercy with a pure disposition of mind, asking that he order your life according to his good pleasure. Then, with a simple mind and humble effort, refuse to undertake the burden in whatever ways you can—except for sin alone. But if you cannot avoid it except through sin, undertake it obediently and carry it carefully.

May almighty God permit nothing to be done by you or concerning you except what pleases him and benefits you.

## LETTER LIII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscripts.]

### TO WALTER

That he should not abandon care of the flock entrusted to him because of slander.

To his venerable lord and father, Abbot WALTER, Brother ANSELM of Bec, a sinner in life, a monk in habit, wishes, through the holiness of the present life [Note: “Of the present”: manuscript 1], to merit the happiness of the future.

Since it is written, “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Ecclus. 32:24), and elsewhere, “For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 25:3), we must take great care not to follow our own will too much against everyone’s counsel, even if it appears right to us.

For not everything that seems right to individuals is right, since it is written, “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Prov. 12:13), and, “There are ways that seem right to human beings, whose end descends even to the depths of hell” (Prov. 14:12).

Therefore, lest, like fools, we judge error to be rectitude and hold to ways whose end descends even to the depths of hell, no one ought to entrust the ordering of his life to his own unexamined judgment. Rather, he must carefully consider whether it conflicts with the judgment of the many—and especially of the wise—or with obedience, mercy, or finally charity.

It is therefore all the more astonishing why your holiness and prudence, almost against everyone’s counsel, against the obedience imposed upon you by divine disposition through your archbishop and through a regular election, and against mercy and charity, expose the sheep entrusted to you by abandoning them, deprived of pastoral care, to be torn apart by attacking wolves, so long as you consider that even one of them can be advanced toward salvation through your care.

Let your charity therefore comply—yes, let it comply—and, bound by so many prayers [Note: “Charity, and so many”: the manuscripts; “let your charity comply, and, bound by so many”: another reading], return to your monastery and mercifully resume the care you abandoned. By consoling and helping the desolate, you will deserve a recompense of divine consolation and assistance.

For the slander that usually terrifies you most has been extinguished by the common consent of the abbot of Saint Arnulf and the brothers of your monastery, so that it can no longer impede you in any way.

## LETTER LIV

[Note: Compared with the manuscripts mentioned above.]

### TO HENRY

That he should patiently endure the envy and slanders of malevolent people.

To his dearest lord and father, Lord Prior HENRY, Brother ANSELM wishes complete prosperity in the present life and eternal happiness in the future.

If I had learned through your messenger with what disgrace your charity was being defamed, with what grief and misery [331] you were being afflicted; and if you had consequently sought my counsel and assistance, as you say; and if I had given no answer, I confess that you would rightly have been astonished and would have said that I had done what I ought not to have done.

But let your holiness believe me: I do not remember ever having heard such a message from you. I did hear from certain people—not from those who admitted that they were your messengers—that you were not in good standing with the lord archbishop. But when I asked why, they indicated certain inconveniences indirectly without stating anything definite.

While I was therefore awaiting more certain information about the matter, I heard that a complete reconciliation had taken place between you. As for the desire for which you indicate that you wish to have permission from the lord abbot and from me, I once heard about it—I no longer know from whom—in such a way that I understood that my assistance was desired for this purpose, but that no answer was being sought. Since I was absolutely certain that the lord abbot would never grant it, I thought, and still think, that the matter should be covered by complete silence rather than revealed in words to no purpose.

As for what you write—that, through God’s mercy, the truth has become clear, while falsehood and its inventors have been confounded and obscured—know that I rejoice more truly over the solidity of the truth, which I believed, than I grieved over the fiction of falsehood, which I never believed.

Concerning the envious people whom you still endure as they bark and lie in wait, I say what you know: vice always envies virtue. If, then, you wish to be free from the persecution of envy, either find a place where you can hide from the vicious, or renounce virtue. You will do neither, because one is impossible and the other detestable.

What remains, then, except that, armed with the weapons of justice, you pass on your right and on your left, with the Apostle, “through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute” (2 Cor. 6:8); and that, whatever they themselves may plot, you direct your strong and tranquil mind not toward them but toward your own steps?

For if your eyes are always toward the Lord, he will draw your feet out of the snare (Ps. 24:15); while they themselves will fall into the pit that they made (Ps. 7:16), and the trap that they concealed will seize them (Ps. 34:8). Then, as it has already begun to do, free truth will stand forth in glory, while confused falsehood will be overwhelmed in disgrace.

Yet in this matter you must carefully observe, as befits a perfect servant of God, that you do not rejoice in the confusion of your enemies and then reproach them for it; by reproaching them, proclaim it; by proclaiming it, spread it abroad; and by spreading it abroad, increase it—lest you be judged in God’s sight to delight in the punishment of your enemies.

Rejoice, then, in your liberation in the secrecy of your mind and in God’s presence, giving him thanks; but as for their sin or its outcome, disregard it with a gentle mind while praying for them.

As for the fact that you show yourself afflicted by the frequent agitation of the man whom you love more than almost all others, I see no other counsel than the best one: you need only complete the virtue of patience, which you have maintained courageously for so long.

In no way will you more effectively, or more honorably and profitably for yourself, flee toward peace of mind, appease him, or overcome the hidden enemy who attacks you through this very tribulation, so that you may receive the crown of victory. “No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:3); nor does anyone compete lawfully who has not persevered to the end, whether in his own struggle or in resisting the attack.

For it is written, “Let patience have its perfect work” (Jas. 1:4), and, “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 24:19). But if you embrace patience in your mind while striving to avoid tribulation, know—or rather, you know—that patience exists only in tribulation.

Rejoice, therefore, in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint (Jas. 1:3; Rom. 5:4).

You say that you cannot in any way be with yourself without the full favor of the archbishop. To your prudence I reply: you can nowhere be well if, insofar as it depends on you, you do not have that favor. But if you have not disdained to possess it, yet cannot possess it, so that you must be elsewhere rather than with him, you can nowhere be better—and nowhere more rightly—than with us [Note: “Because it is more rightly to be ... with you”: the manuscripts; “because nowhere more rightly to be ... with us”: another reading]. For no reason would the lord abbot and your brothers grant anything else.

The vigor of your holiness is not valued so little or loved so little that those who can justly retain it would willingly or easily wish to be without it. May almighty God protect and order your life so that you may prevail over every attack and adversity and receive the everlasting crown. Pray for me.

## LETTER LV

[Note: Compared with one of the manuscripts mentioned above.]

### TO MAURICE

He rejoices to hear that Maurice is studying under Arnulf the Grammarian.

To his beloved brother and son MAURICE, Brother ANSELM.

I have heard that you are studying under Lord Arnulf. If this is true, it pleases me, since I have always desired your progress, as you yourself have partly experienced—and certainly never more than now.

I have also heard that he is very capable in declension; and you know that I have always found it burdensome for boys to decline, which is why you have progressed far less than would have been beneficial for you. I know that you have made progress with me in the knowledge of declension.

I therefore urge you, beg you, and command you as my dearest son to make every effort to decline with the greatest diligence whatever you read from him, and whatever else you can. Do not be ashamed to study this even in matters in which you think you have no need [Note: “Even in matters in which”: the manuscript; “even in matters”: another reading], as though you were only now beginning it anew. In this way, what you know, confirmed by hearing him, you will retain more securely; if you make a mistake in anything, you will correct it under his instruction; and you will learn what you do not know.

But if he reads nothing to you and this is due to your negligence, I am displeased; and I want you to strive to make it happen insofar as you can, especially with Virgil and the other authors whom you have not read with me, except those in which something indecent is heard.

If, because some obstacle prevents you, you cannot read from him, at least make this effort: decline, from beginning to end, as diligently as I advised above, as many whole books as you can of those you have read, whenever you can.

Also show this letter to that dearest friend of ours. In it, so that I may briefly and earnestly plead with him on your behalf [Note: “So that I may briefly”: the manuscript; “so that”: another reading], I ask him to show you how much I can rely upon his true friendship. And I declare [Note: “And I judge”: the manuscript] that whatever he does for you, he will do for no one other than my own heart.

For it is a long time since he and I have been certain of our mutual friendship—if he deigns to remember what I shall never forget.

Greet him most respectfully on our behalf, as well as the lord prior, my lord Gondulf, and the other lords and brothers of ours who are with you. Farewell, my sweetest son, and do not despise the counsel of one who loves you with a father’s affection. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI

[Note: Compared with the two manuscripts mentioned above, bound together in one codex, and with the Leuven manuscript; also with the Gothic edition, the 1575 edition, and the manuscript of Saint-Evroul. In the latter, the treatise on incontinent priests is found from the words “Concerning priests,” through “compels confession.”]

### TO WILLIAM

Concerning an excommunicated count who took part in sacred rites. [Col. 1125B] Concerning incontinent priests and those who, having fallen, hold sacred orders.

To his reverend lord and father, Abbot WILLIAM, Brother ANSELM wishes lasting prosperity in this life and eternal happiness in the future.

From the time your probity deigned to make itself known to me, I conceived such affection for it that its memory is always sweet to me. I have found that this was not without reason, since I recognized both that your life exists as one worthy of love and reverence, and that your fatherhood is not without affection toward my littleness. [Note: [Col. 1125C] The manuscripts read “my fatherhood”; the Editio reads “my littleness” or “my depravity.”] For brothers coming from you have often edified me not only by their account of your holiness, but also honored me by conveying your greetings.

[Col. 1125C] Therefore, although whatever there is in me is wholly unable to correspond to such merits, it is nevertheless my task to offer as much love and reverence as I can. But entrusting to God the preservation and increase of these things in us, I shall answer—not presumptuously, but obediently—the matters on which your wisdom has deigned to consult my littleness: perhaps not what is sufficient, but what seems right to me.

Your count, who, though excommunicated, mingles with you while you celebrate the divine offices, seems to me to require humble admonition, lest, by despising the sentence of those in whom God affirms that he is heard when they are heard and despised when they are despised, and that he binds when they bind and looses when they loose, [Note: [Col. 1125C] The manuscripts and the Editio read “when they bind,” not the alternate grammatical form.] he aggravate God’s judgment against himself—God, from whom no human being can flee anywhere.

It would therefore be better for him, through salutary humility, to abstain from those things from which the apostolic sentence separates him, than through presumptuous contempt to thrust himself into those things which, sought only through humility, are beneficial, but always harmful when presumptuously undertaken in disorder. Nor should he, without any advantage to himself and indeed to his serious harm, compel you—because you do not wish to offend him—to provoke God and the authority of the apostolic see gravely, whom you could not have as an ally in appeasing. The apostolic authority would also accept his explanations more readily and kindly if it learned that he had revered its sentence. [Note: [Col. 1125C] The manuscripts read *pacandos*, “to be appeased,” rather than *placandos*, “to appease.”]

But if that count rejects this admonition, you know that God must be feared more than man. [Note: [Col. 1125C] The manuscripts and the Editio read “you know,” rather than “you know” in the singular.] I therefore think that either he must be dealt with according to the apostolic sentence already issued, or that the apostolic authority itself, or someone acting in its place, must again be consulted about this matter.

As for priests who openly display themselves as rejected by God through a way of life involving condemned lust, it must be held absolutely that which apostolic foresight has established by ecclesiastical and just judgment and severity. [Note: [Col. 1125C] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “open lust”; the printed text reads “openly condemned lust.” The same manuscript reads “with just severity,” rather than “by just judgment and severity.”]

[Col. 1126C] It is wholly unfitting that one should stand reverently where men who stink with persistent, open, and shameless lust serve at the holy altars while despising the prohibition of God and the saints—or rather, they do not serve, but, so far as they are concerned, defile them. [Note: [Col. 1125C] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “they should stand,” rather than “one should stand.”] [Note: [Col. 1125D] “Not that anyone should consider the things they administer contemptible,” and so forth. Anselm has published the truest explanation of the papal prohibition; since most have not devised anything similar, some contend that Gregory VII’s prohibition was holy and pious, while others call it impious and opposed to the Gospel. Sigebert, otherwise extremely hostile to Gregory, as appears from the works written against him, says that it was enacted as a new example and, “as it seemed to many, through an inconsiderate prejudice, against the judgment of the Fathers, who asserted that ecclesiastical sacraments operate equally through good and wicked ministers.” Later writers repeat Sigebert’s words and indiscriminately mix all sorts of borrowed material with their own, namely Matthew Paris; Thomas Walsingham in the *Hypodigma Neustriae*; Vincent of Beauvais; Nauclerus; John Frasquetius, whose manuscript is in our library; and Achilles Gassarus in his *Epitome of Chronicles*, where, on the basis of the example of the Henrician bishops assembled at Worms in 1077, he calls Gregory a necromancer. But all historians speak very differently about him, including the Germans, as the learned Genebrard carefully observed in Book IV of his *Chronicles*, and Papirius Masson in Book V of *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*. It is also clear from what Gratian reported, distinction 32, canon “No one [shall celebrate] Mass,” and the canon beginning “Moreover,” in which Urban, Gregory’s successor, resolves the argument drawn from the Fathers, that Gregory did not institute this as a new practice or contrary to the mind of the holy Fathers. Gregory did not prohibit the sacrifices of married priests as worthless, but wished those priests, moved by this shame, to return to themselves. Any other disadvantages and scandals that some claim arose from this measure, every sensible person will acknowledge should be attributed not to the law but to human wickedness. For, as Saint Jerome rightly writes in his letter to Amandus: “Putrid flesh requires the sword and the cautery; the fault lies not with the medicine but with the wound, when the physician does not spare with merciful cruelty, so that he may spare; he rages so that he may show mercy.” Thus Gassarus impiously called Gregory a necromancer, strongly disagreeing in this with Volaterranus, whom he promises in his prefatory letter to follow in his enumeration of the popes. For in Book XXII of his *Anthropology* Volaterranus writes of Gregory: “This man, because he was pious and an exceptionally ardent defender of the Christian religion, endured great labors.” Hartmann Schedel, in the sixth age of his *Register of Chronicles*, calls Gregory a man most pleasing to God and human beings, prudent, just, merciful, and a patron of the poor, orphans, and widows; the one and most ardent defender of the Roman Church against the wickedness of heretics and the power of evil princes who forcibly sought to seize ecclesiastical possessions. He says that Gregory died holily and piously. Schedel was a German writer, older than Gassarus. I have brought forward both him and Volaterranus, whom Genebrard omitted, so that no witness to Gregory’s innocence might be lacking.]

It is not that anyone should think the things they administer contemptible, [Col. 1127A] but that they should consider the administrators accursed, so that those who do not reverence the presence of God and the angels, or who, driven away by human abhorrence, [Note: [Col. 1127D] The manuscripts and the Gothic and Cologne editions read “driven away,” rather than “repelled,”] may cease to defile sacred things. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “may not dare,” rather than “may cease.”]

Nor is it at all fitting that those who by their impurity make themselves strangers to the ministers serving at the altar should be companions of those who partake of the altar. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript omits the passage beginning “Nor is it at all fitting” and continuing through “of those who have fallen.”]

Concerning those who have fallen while possessing sacred orders, and who, through spontaneous humility, confess secretly to those to whom they ought to confess, it must by no means be asserted that they can never again use those same orders, if, by the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart, appeasing God (Psalm 50 [51]:19), they earnestly strive to advance in virtue. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “spontaneously,” rather than “through spontaneous humility”; “a contrite heart,” rather than “a contrite and humbled heart”; and “turn back,” rather than “strive.”]

For neither is anyone’s ministry rejected before God on account of a fault which God himself forgives; nor is the dignity of the sacred order discolored among human beings on account of a person whose sin they themselves do not know. For these two reasons, a carnal fall prohibits access to and return to sacred orders. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “to the sacred Order,” in the singular, rather than “to sacred orders,” and “access or return,” rather than “access to and return.”]
