But since it is almost always hidden whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered (Psalm 31 [32]:1), and whose have not, it is always safer for one conscious of a crime to abstain, through praiseworthy humility, from those offices which require a person pleasing to God than to presume upon them through blameworthy security. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The manuscripts and the Gothic and Cologne editions read “always safe,” rather than “always safer”; the Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “humility pleasing to God,” rather than simply “praiseworthy humility.”] The former he can always do without God’s disapproval; the latter he ought not do unless God approves.

But whoever wishes to support the opinion that permits a return to the ministry of sacred order after a fall by no other basis than authority—namely, that of the Scriptures—[Col. 1127C] [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “is supported by the Scriptures,” rather than “is supported, namely, by the authority of the Scriptures.”] should read the letter of blessed Pope Calixtus addressed to all the bishops established throughout Gaul, [Note: [Col. 1127D] The manuscripts of Saint-Evroult and Louvain read “the decree addressed to all the bishops established throughout Gaul,” rather than “the letter addressed to all the bishops established throughout Gaul,”] and the letter of blessed Pope Gregory addressed to Secundinus. There they confirm this opinion with such firm and almost identical reasons and authorities that it needs no proof from anyone else.

But since the same blessed Gregory carefully prohibits this very thing in certain other letters, so that he may not contradict himself, [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads: “But since the same blessed Gregory carefully prohibits this very thing in certain other letters, so that he may not be contradictory to himself: concerning …” Another manuscript reads: “But since the holy Gregory and other holy Fathers seem elsewhere carefully to prohibit this very thing: concerning …”] it is understood that he prohibited it in the case of public sins, but granted it, after fitting penance, in the case of hidden sins. For a crime which is not charged by God is neither rejected nor discredited by human beings, as I have already said; nevertheless, in such a matter it is safer for each person to fear more before God than to trust himself. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “to fear more before God himself,” rather than “to fear more before God.”]

I do not at all think that a person should be unwillingly prohibited when he voluntarily and secretly discloses a hidden crime through humble confession, lest the salutary path of confession be closed to many who would prefer to conceal themselves utterly in death rather than, on this account, be brought into certainty or suspicion regarding some crime. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “they would choose utterly to conceal themselves in death,” rather than “would prefer to be utterly concealed in death.”]

Nor is the one to whom he confesses condemned for sin if he does not compel the person confessing to cease from the ministry of his order without that person’s consent. Rather, he seems guilty of a grave crime if he does compel him, because in this way he forces both the person confessing to repent of his confession and many who have not yet confessed to dread confession. [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Saint-Evroult manuscript reads “the one confessing,” rather than “the person confessing,” and “by confessing,” rather than “the person confessing.” The note adds: “Here the treatise ends in the Saint-Evroult manuscript.”]

For it is sufficiently clear how much less evil it is for any sinner to approach the altar with love for the confession he has completed and with hope of mercy, in a humbled mind, than to thrust himself into it with hatred of confession and despair of pardon, with a hardened heart, whether in desire or even in action.

Thus the person who hears the confession must not be judged a participant in the lesser guilt, when he permits another to remain in the ministry—not by consenting, but by prudently preventing the greater evil. He does, however, seem to be the author of a greater crime when he drives many toward it, even if not intentionally, by fearing in a disorderly way what is lesser more than what is greater.

It is manifest, however, that those who, in humble contrition, trample down proud shame and judge themselves, voluntarily consent to an imposed cessation: they minister much more safely when permitted—or even commanded—than those who, because of human shame, refuse to allow God to judge justly between himself and them. Nevertheless, as stated above, the person to whom they confess acts much more dangerously if he prohibits the former against their will than if he prohibits the latter, who abstain voluntarily.

And since it is necessary for both groups to abstain, at least for a time, I think that those who do not willingly cease, and who do not readily hasten toward it, should merely be released from the prohibition; but those who abstain voluntarily should even be recalled from it, so that they do not presume. For in the former, if they are recalled, presumption is covered by the cloak of obedience; in the latter, humility is strengthened by the power of obedience.

This recall must not be undertaken indiscriminately, but with the great discernment of a superior who carefully considers the confession. For it often happens that someone does not overcome human shame through the immense horror of his crime and the force of humility, but through the darkness of folly and the hardness of shamelessness fails to perceive the foulness of his wickedness and his shame, and through negligence does not desire his office. Such a person must never be called or recalled to his sacred ministry.

But when humility pleads on behalf of the penitent, contrition prompts him, and a change of life intercedes for him, then, if the superior, comforting him not so much by reference to any merits as by reference to God’s great mercy and the abundance of his compassion, invites him to resume the use of his office, I think he may appear to have acted prudently rather than rashly.

For in such a case it is often necessary to anticipate faintheartedness, to exclude suspicion of contempt, to display goodwill, and to show compassion. In this way, those who are such are summoned to perfection all the more effectively the more kindly they are treated, and are bound all the more firmly to their good resolve.

I could have woven into this many more passages from the writings of the Fathers; but the brevity proper to a letter, which already protests that it has extended itself too far, does not permit it. I have therefore simply explained to your fatherhood, as commanded, what I think about the matters on which you asked.

May the almighty Lord direct you in these matters and in all those which you must undertake in such uprightness of truth that he may repay you with himself for them.

If I were present before you and before your holy congregation—about which I hear many good things from many people in agreement—I would prostrate my whole body before you with a suppliant mind, and ask that you grant me, in fraternal charity, perpetual participation in the good things which God works in your monastery. But since I cannot do this, I presume—not on the basis of my merits, but of your holiness—to ask you to request this for me from those same sons of yours, not with a humbled body but through a kindly death, and to grant it together with them.

Farewell.

## EPISTLE LVII [Note: [Col. 1129D] Collated with one Victorine manuscript in Codex Ef. 20.] TO LANFRANC. [Col. 1129D] He replies favorably concerning Lanfranc’s nephew, and also concerning Osbern. He sends the Epistles of blessed Paul.

To his lord and father, Archbishop LANFRANC, to be revered with the honour due to reverence and cherished with the affection due to the Catholic mother, his brother ANSELM, his own, wishes what belongs to his own.

Although your fatherly holiness receives the letters of my humility less often than it ought, my heart nevertheless keeps intact the fidelity owed to you, written nowhere but in itself. Your messenger, who saw what concerns my most beloved nephew, your nephew, and heard it from him, can tell those who inquire more fully than my letter can describe. As far as concerns me, both for your sake and for his own, to say nothing of brotherly charity, he has bound me to himself, not against my will, in such a way that I should not wish to withhold myself from any advantage of his which I can promote. [Note: [Col. 1129D] The manuscript reads “I should wish to withhold myself”; the printed text, “I should wish to withhold myself from him.”]

I confess that Lord Osbern, whom your authority orders to be brought back to you, had so adhered to my mind with the glue of affection that my heart can bear his separation only with a certain tearing of itself. For my conscience, rather than my pen, bears him witness that he has lived among us in such a manner that, from all who sincerely love a good purpose of will, he deserves more the affection of charity than the harshness of any severity. [Note: [Col. 1129D] The manuscript reads “than any severity.”]

Although, therefore, your holy kindness, which is always accustomed to stand by the good, has no need of admonition, the affection inspired by the merits of the aforesaid brother nevertheless compels me to pray with all my effort that, not only because he has deserved it but also because your faithful servant desires it and asks for it in desiring, you may receive him kindly and treat him kindly, unless you judge that his life deserves otherwise. Moreover, since I do not dare to say that you should ever send him back to us, I think I may freely say this: that while I live I should never wish to be separated from him.

We gladly obey your command in sending you the Epistles of blessed Paul; but, since we do not have elsewhere what in the same codex belongs to your work, you can readily know what we should sometimes wish you to do.

[Col. 1130C]

## EPISTLE LVIII [Note: [Col. 1129D] Collated with the same manuscript.] TO HENRY.

To Lord HENRY, his most beloved friend and reverend prior, brother ANSELM: may you sow holiness on earth and reap blessedness in heaven.

He commends Osbern to him. My beloved Lord Osbern, who is yours and is returning to you [Note: [Col. 1129D] The manuscript reads “is being brought back.”], freely accuses and execrates the perversity of his former life. So far as I have been able openly and secretly to learn from the life which he shared with us, he is so inflamed with love for a praiseworthy life that his inward person may deservedly be judged either already changed for the better, or beyond doubt easily changeable.

Your prudence indeed knows [Col. 1130D] that never is so great an exercise of kindness needed as in a new and inexperienced conversion from reprobate to approved morals, lest good beginnings, which may be nourished and brought to progress by the encouragements of kindness, be impeded or indeed broken by the harshness of severity. I therefore beseech your beloved holiness that, as befits the discernment of your government and benefits the aforesaid brother, you may, setting aside every remembrance of his past perversity, nourish with the milk of clear affection the infancy of his better purpose, unless perhaps—which I do not think—he should show that he has returned to his former wickedness not from weakness but from will. [Note: [Col. 1129D] The manuscript reads “setting aside” in the singular; the printed text, “setting aside” in the plural.]

For you will in no way demonstrate to him more aptly that love lay concealed beneath the severity which he experienced in error than if it is then made manifest in the correction of his error. Finally, as it seems to me, no one ought to be driven to the path of a right life unless he cannot be drawn to it. I also beseech—or rather, as a debt which friends owe one another, demand—that, just as I wish to love all whom I know beloved by your beloved brotherhood, so Lord Osbern may greatly rejoice that, in gaining my affection, he has increased yours.

Farewell.

## EPISTLE LIX [Note: [Col. 1131D] Collated with the same manuscript.] TO GUNDULF. [Col. 1131B] He gives thanks, in his own name and those of Hugh and Basilia, for presents sent by him.

To his lord, brother, and most beloved friend Lord GUNDULF, brother ANSELM, his own, wishes what belongs to his own.

Since you cannot admonish my laziness by prayers to send you letters of greeting, you turn to another plan and knock upon me with your gifts, so that I may at least send back thanks; and so that he whom endearments cannot draw to writing may at least be driven by shame to give thanks. I therefore give thanks to your affection, which is sweet to my heart, not in proportion to the dearness of your gifts, but in proportion to the greater dearness of your charity, by which they are made and seasoned and through which your gifts taste sweet to me.

For your charity is dearer to me than anything you can give me, by as much as you can send far away from yourself the things you give, but cannot dismiss charity from yourself. Those things can cross the sea without you; but this cannot leave your heart. Whether you give this to me or do not give it, I know that something always burns in you. Whether I speak to it [Note: [Col. 1131D] The manuscript reads “whether I speak,” rather than “whether I may speak.”] or am silent, know that my heart always responds with like affection.

Lord Hugh and Lady Basilia, his wife, give you warm thanks for the kindnesses which you send them, the gifts which you dispatch, and the prayers which you make and promise for them. I myself presented your gifts to them, read your letter, and conveyed your words; all of which they received with the greatest gratitude and joy.

334

## EPISTLE LX [Note: [Col. 1131D] Collated with the same manuscript.] [Col. 1131D] TO MAURICE. He asks letters from him and praises him because he is loved by everyone everywhere.

To Lord MAURICE, his most beloved brother and son, brother ANSELM: may you advance in wisdom and grace before God and human beings.

It is a long time since we visited one another by our letters, because we did not doubt the firmness of our mutual affection and because, when occasion offered, we greeted one another through the speech of messengers. But lest by any occasion love itself be thought to grow cold, I think it expedient that it should sometimes seem to burn through little letters, as though sparks flashing forth from each of us to the other.

For precisely because I cannot have you with me while I desire you who desire me, I do not love you less but more. Since I see that you are loved by persons greater and better than I [Note: [Col. 1131D] The manuscript reads “I love [you] by persons greater than I”; the printed text, “you are loved by persons greater and better than I.”] in such a way that they do not wish to let you go, I understand that you ought to be loved the more. Hence it is almost doubtful to me whether I rejoice more because you make yourself so lovable, or grieve more because I cannot enjoy one so lovable.

But since I know that you ought to be loved by me not only for my sake but also for yours, the question is settled: it is certain that I ought to rejoice more over the presence of the good things that are with you than to be saddened over the absence of your body from me. Finally, I have always desired that you might be lovable to God and to good people, and, as you know, have worked according to my ability while you were with me. Nor has that desire grown cold because, when you were absent, my effort could not do more than it did while you were with me. You cannot, however, be wherever you are loved; but wherever you are, you can be loved and be good.

Therefore may God be entreated that you may be there and such as God wishes you to be, and as benefits you—while our mutual desire, which mutual love requires, remains unharmed. And since the blessed God has already made you, wherever you may be, lovable to the good, greet our beloved brothers and friends Lord Herluin and Lord Guy [Note: [Col. 1131D] The manuscript reads “Herluin and Lord Gundulf”; the printed text, “Herluin and Lord Guy.”], Lord Elmer, and Lord Hulward, cousin of Lord Osbern.

## EPISTLE LXI [Note: [Col. 1131D] Collated with the same manuscript.] OF DURAND TO ANSELM. Praise of Anselm’s *Meditations*; he asks him for the Epistles of blessed Paul.

DURAND, abbot of the House of God by God’s favour alone, wishes eternal salvation to Lord ANSELM.

Two Bayeux men, educated in letters, young men of distinguished bearing in every manner of comportment—the younger is named Roger, the other William—these two, and besides them several others, but especially they, have distilled into our ears the oil and sweetness of both your name and your religious life. Then: “My life terrifies me”; for that writing, carefully considered [Note: [Col. 1131D] The manuscript and the Picard edition read “carefully and considered”; the printed text, “carefully considered.”], together with what follows it, and, besides this, other things most devoutly published and written concerning your contrite spirit and the compassion of your contrite heart, cause us, while we read your pious tears, to shed our own. [Col. 1132D] [Note: [Col. 1131D] *Meditation* 2, above, p. 207.]

Thus we marvel at both things: that so great a dew of blessing overflows in your heart, and that from there a stream descends silently into our hearts. For it is truly so: the devotion of your written prayer awakens in us the devotion of sleeping compunction, so that, as if leaping forth in mind, we rejoice with you, loving those things in you—or rather in them, you—on account of them [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript reads “always on account of them”; the printed text, “on account of them.”], and through them, God and you.

Intercede, therefore, because you can intercede, for us who intercede for you as we can; and send us, if you have any, other things written by you which we do not possess, as one known and asked in a love which is continuous on both sides. We also ask for the unity of fellowship in the body itself of the congregation, and we send you to exercise an embassy for us in that matter; for, abounding in charity, you will be able faithfully to request this and yourself to grant what has been requested.

Ready to give a pledge of our love, we ask a pledge from you. Choose what you can receive from us; we choose [Col. 1133B] [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript more correctly reads “ask … we ask,” rather than “choose … we choose.”] the Epistles of Paul from you. Nor do we pretend deception in this, as though we were first ready to receive but not first ready to give—something most remote from the sacrament of charity, which is God. Rather, burning with charity, however we may ask, we are ready not to refuse ourselves and what is ours when suitably asked by any of this holy profession. Therefore let these two brothers of yours, inflamed with desire, have you as their helper [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript reads “with you helping,” rather than “having you as helper.”] in all things, because the will of all in all things depends on you.

## EPISTLE LXII [Note: [Col. 1133D] Collated with the same manuscript.] TO DURAND. He answers the preceding letter.

To Lord and Father DURAND, abbot [Col. 1133C] of the monastery called the House of God, worthy by merit of holiness to be revered with love and loved with reverence, brother ANSELM of Bec, a sinner in life and a monk in habit: may you so persevere in advancing holiness in this life that in the life to come you may rejoice in sufficient blessedness.

When I received the letter of your fatherhood, it poured great joy into my heart; but when I considered my life, not only did the same joy pour itself back almost wholly out of my heart, but worthy sorrow besides poured heavily over my mind. For, because I learned that your holiness had loved me, an unknown little man, so much as to deign to visit and greet me by letters from so far away, my humility was not without reason seen to owe itself exultation. [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript reads “exaltation,” rather than “exultation.”]

But when I consider that you do not love me at all unless you suppose me to be something, while I am nothing, I understand that you do not love a person vile and contemptible before God and human beings—which I am—but a vigorous man of some virtue, which I certainly am not. Therefore, fearing not only that your love may benefit me little or nothing, because I am not what you love, but also that my lukewarmness, which you do not recognize in me, may harm me greatly, I pray and beseech you: regard me or love me as if I were already of some spiritual advancement; but love me to this end: that, in loving me, you may pray that I may become so. [Col. 1134A]

Thus both your estimation of me will be true, your affection toward me true, and my exultation in your love secure. I ask, therefore, with all the humility I can, your reverend fatherhood to act by your holy prayers, so that both what I am as yet to my harm may be taken away from me, what I am not yet to my benefit may be bestowed on me, and what you mercifully bestow on your needy neighbour may be repaid to you. [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript reads “bestowing,” rather than “you bestow.”]

I do not dare promise our prayers for you to your reverend blessedness, because they are very worthless; but, because you deign to request them, I ought not to refuse them. Therefore, if they are anything, or will become anything through the support of your merits, let them belong in true charity [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript reads “in the life of charity,” rather than “in true charity.”] to you and to the saints who either are or will be of the monastery divinely entrusted to you.

Although what I grant you from myself is either too much or nothing, I nevertheless presume to ask something great from you. My mind therefore prostrates itself before your reverend fatherhood and before all the brothers of your holy congregation, humbly beseeching that you may grant me, your servant and a brother of your monastery, to be as one of you forever, and cause my name to be subscribed last where your names are written. The matters which are answered to your commands and which are commanded, our reverend lords and brothers, your sons who came to us, will relate better by speaking than we can by writing.

May almighty God grant that you live in the House of God in this age in such a way that, among the blessed who dwell in God’s house for ages of ages, you may praise God: lord Father, and lords brothers in Christ. Amen.

## EPISTLE LXIII [Note: [Col. 1133D] Collated with the same manuscript.] TO LANFRANC. That he may examine Anselm’s *Monologion*.

To his lord as servant, to his father as son, to the reverend Archbishop LANFRANC, brother ANSELM.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] See Epistle 74 below.] I would more gladly have read in person before you, if it had been convenient, that little work which I sent for examination by your fatherly judgment. Since this cannot now be, I should very much wish to ask that your fatherly prudence, sweet to me, would not disdain either to hear it read by someone else or to direct what ought to be done with it—unless I feared that I might be indiscreetly troublesome to your dignity, which I do not doubt is unceasingly occupied with many great deliberations on weightier affairs. [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript reads “to be examined,” rather than “for examination.”]

Therefore, since I wish nothing to please me in such a way as to displease you, as it belongs solely to your experience to judge how far it is permissible for you to do what I indicate that I greatly desire, so it belongs to your choice to decide whether you wish it. Yet even importunately I shall not cease to ask your authority that, concerning the same little work, whether heard or unheard, your authority may determine what ought to be done. [Col. 1135A]

I placed no title before it, since I did not judge it of such worth that I should deem it worthy of its own name. If, therefore, it should please your judgment that what I have written should stand as written, let it receive both firmness and a name from him from whom it will receive authority; and through you let it be given to your servant, my beloved brother and fellow servant Lord Maurice, who is one of those at whose strongest urging it was made. But if your examination should decide otherwise, let the copy which I send you be returned neither to me nor to the aforesaid brother, but be removed from the world, buried, sunk, consumed, or scattered by some element. Whatever your judgment decides concerning it, I urgently ask that you order it made known to me in some way, so that the copy which I retained may not receive a different sentence from that which I sent.

Concerning my most beloved one, your nephew, I beseech you with heart, mouth, and letter, as far as I can, that as soon as you learn that he has recovered health, you do not allow me to lack any longer his lovable companionship. For I tell you truly that he showed himself to me, while present, and to all of ours who love good morals, in such a way that, if he can be brought back without any disadvantage to himself—which we do not wish in any way—we must desire him while absent. [Note: [Col. 1135D] The manuscript reads “his disadvantage,” rather than “any disadvantage to himself.”]

## EPISTLE LXIV [Note: [Col. 1135D] Collated with the same manuscript.] TO HENRY. He counsels obedience and patience.

To Lord HENRY, his most beloved brother and prior, brother ANSELM: through a long good life may you deserve eternal blessed life.

The lord abbot and the congregation of your brothers received, praised, and loved the gifts of your charity with joy; but certainly much more they loved charity itself, which never fails to wish as much as it can and always wishes more than it can. The lord abbot also received with gratitude, and my littleness received, read, and heard with gratitude, that your prudence sought the counsel of him as father and of me as brother, and promised to act wholly in accordance with it. Thus, indeed, it becomes a wise person to use wise counsel. For wise counsel is, as you know, counsel which advises that all things be done with counsel.

Since, therefore, the whole counsel in the matter on which you ask advice consists in obedience and patience, [Note: [Col. 1135D] The manuscript reads “you asked advice,” rather than “you ask advice,”] and it is written that God prefers obedience to sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22), and that patience has a perfect work (James 1:4), you seek and receive the counsel of none more justly than of him to whom you owe obedience; and you observe none more perfectly than when you hold patience steadfastly.

This, therefore, is what the lord abbot advises and asks; and, so that your zeal may not only acquiesce in the adviser and petitioner—which is praiseworthy—but also obey the commander—which is to be crowned—this he commands. Therefore I, your brother and lover, advise and urge this: that the condition of your whole life may rest on these two columns, namely obedience and patience.

Concerning patience, your belovedness knows well that it must be demanded with resolve not only when one who deserves it is punished, but also willingly shown when one who does not deserve it is afflicted. There impatience is to be detested, lest the guilty person be condemned more unhappily; here patience must be preserved, so that the innocent person may be crowned more happily.

Concerning obedience, the lord abbot gives this command, which I do not think you doubt: whatever you obey for the reverend lord and our father Archbishop Lanfranc, he receives it as though obedience were rendered to himself. Indeed, he receives it more gratefully than if you obeyed himself, by as much as he desires through himself to obey Lanfranc; and by as much as, in what you obey, you obey not only him but another for his sake, he judges your obedience itself to be greater. [Col. 1136B]

Although, if we consider ourselves [Note: [Col. 1135D] The manuscript reads “if we advised ourselves,” rather than “if we consider ourselves”] and him to whom we invite you to render obedience, there are beyond doubt many things in us and in him for which we ought of our own accord and diligently to obey him.

Farewell.

## EPISTLE LXV [Note: [Col. 1135D] Collated with the same manuscript.] TO MAURICE. Concerning Maurice’s return from England to Bec, and the correction of the *Monologion*.

[The supplied source ends here.]

To the lord and brother, dearest son, MAURITIUS, brother ANSELM sends a servant’s reverence, a brother’s affection, and a father’s care.

I always desire you, dearest son, and I do not doubt that you always desire me. But since neither of us belongs to himself, and we are not mutually one another’s except through the affection of charity, I advise and exhort you that, as long as those whom divine providence has placed over us command us to remain separated, we should not seek to hasten our cohabitation against their will; and if they kindly consent to our desire, we should introduce no delay.

Therefore, concerning what we heard through Lord Robert—that our lord the archbishop has promised to send your affection back to us shortly—if he kindly favors your wish, and if it does not displease the lord abbot, it pleases me very much. But if he does not kindly favor the petitioner, but permits it to be extorted with some resentment [Note: [Col. 1135D] The manuscript reads *eum aliquo*; *cum aliquo* is more correct.], it pleases neither the lord abbot nor me that you should return in this way.

I am sending through Lord Robert the writing which I produced at your insistence and that of certain other brothers, and which you request should be transmitted to you, so that our lord and father the archbishop may examine it. By letter [Note: [Col. 1135D] Epist. 63 above.] I ask him that, unless he orders it to be destroyed, he return to you the copy he receives.

Ask him, therefore, if you are going to return shortly, to give his order concerning that writing before you return, so that you may either bring it with you confirmed, or report to me that it has been destroyed. But if, after it has been received, you delay returning, send me that copy as soon as you can through a trustworthy messenger [Note: [Col. 1137D] The manuscript reads *mitte exemplar*; *mitte mihi exemplar* is correct.], so that, if our lord the archbishop has corrected anything in it, the copy which I have retained with me may also be corrected accordingly, and I may quickly send one of these two copies back to you.

If, however, the same little work should be accepted with such a sentence of confirmation that it is judged to require no correction, keep the copy that was sent for as long as you wish. Only, whether this is so or otherwise, inform me by letter as soon as you can of whatever our lord the archbishop has judged concerning it, or by what title he has ordered it to be designated.

Greet our beloved brother, Lord Herluin, and exhort him on my behalf not to fall away from the good beginning which I have seen in him, through love of any passing pleasure; but, just as he approaches the final day from day to day, so may he advance daily toward contempt for temporal things and love of eternal ones.

Greet Lord Arnulf of Beauvais, Lord Hulvard the Englishman, cousin of Lord Osbern, and Lords Vitalis and Roger, Brother Samuel, and the men of Caen. Farewell, and always advance in the Lord, dearest son.

## LETTER LXVI [Note: [Col. 1137D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO LANFRANC. He desires the return to Normandy of Guido, a neophyte of Bec.

To his dearest friend and most faithful lover, LANFRANC, brother ANSELM sends perfect health of body and soul. [Col. 1137C] [Note: [Col. 1137D] The manuscript has *profectam*; *perfectam* is correct.]

Whenever I recall your sweet affection, I am certainly wearied by your prolonged delay. Although until now the hope of recovering your health has greatly consoled the anguish of my heart over your absence, I can no longer avoid grieving, because both the perfection of health for you and your beloved presence for me are delayed so long. For—not as the common saying goes, that what is far from the eyes is far from the heart—not, I say, does your kindly gentleness grow colder in me the farther it is removed from me in place and time; rather, the less I can enjoy it according to my desire, the more fervently its longing burns in the mind of one who truly loves you. [Note: [Col. 1137D] The manuscript has *voto possum*; *pro voto possum* is correct.]

Therefore, although you are with him—of whom I would not dare say that I love you as much as he does, nor ought I to demand that you love me as much as him—I nevertheless presume to ask that, whenever you can do so with his kindly permission and without inconvenience to yourself, you gladden your friend by your return.

I greet with you my dearest lord and brother, Lord Guido. To open my heart’s conscience plainly, I desire unceasingly to have him with me through love, and through obedience I endure his absence from me only impatiently. As a beloved person addressing one beloved, I advise and beg him diligently to examine his life amid his very occupations; to advance daily in the good qualities which I hear from everyone coming from there that he possesses; and, if any traces of the old man still remain in him, to withdraw from them continually.

Farewell, both of you.

## LETTER LXVII [Note: [Col. 1137D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO ROGER. He awaits Roger’s arrival.

To his beloved in Christ, desired, hoped-for, and awaited ROGER, brother ANSELM, his beloved: wisely to choose what is more pleasing to God and more salutary for himself, steadfastly to hold it, and happily to bring it to completion.

What we have entrusted to the counsel of God alone, I do not dare determine by my own judgment. Yet I may express my desire: certainly your delay troubles me; certainly the length of my waiting for you torments me. For my heart neither wishes nor is able to forget that—you did not merely promise this to me, but foretold it—you said that I could expect you to return and remain. And certainly you spoke seriously.

Therefore my eyes are fixed upon your word, saying: “When will you comfort me?” (Ps. 118:82). May I not be deceived, because I have hoped in you; may I not be put to shame, because I have awaited you; may those whom you sent ahead as the first fruits of your fruit [Note: [Col. 1137D] The manuscript has “those whom you sent ahead, the first fruits of the journey”; “those whom you sent ahead, the first fruits of your fruit” is correct.] and as the pledge of your arrival not be astonished, nor say why you have placed them there, where you have disdained either to precede or to follow them—especially since they entered among us most willingly and were received by us in hope of your following.

May the Lord direct your way in his sight (Ps. 5:9); and with your heart directed, may the Lord grant you according to your heart and confirm all your counsel (Ps. 19:5).

## LETTER LXVIII [Note: [Col. 1137D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO LANFRANC. Concerning several matters which Lanfranc noticed in Anselm’s little work, which Anselm himself defends by the authority of Saint Augustine.

To his lord and father, LANFRANC, worthy archbishop of the Catholic Church, with a son’s love and reverence, brother ANSELM, his servant in submission, his son in affection, his disciple in instruction, offers what he can best offer.

My heart gives immense thanks to your eminence, who amid so many and such great occupations of your dignity [Col. 1138D] [Note: [Col. 1137D] The manuscript has the singular *occupationem*; the plural *occupationes* is correct.] neither finds it burdensome nor considers it beneath you, in fatherly kindness, to attend to the verbosity of my leisure and, with kindly wisdom, to correct it.

For you ask that my affection toward you not grow cold on account of these things, since, with God and his saints as witnesses, you do this out of affection; and I too am certainly a witness of this in my conscience. Far be it from me, therefore, to be displeased at receiving counsel which I too, from across the sea, earnestly seek [Note: [Col. 1137D] The manuscript reads *gero*; *peto* is correct.], and which you send out of sincere affection.

I therefore gratefully receive your fatherly admonition [Col. 1139A] and humbly offer my reply. Concerning those things said in that little work which you wisely and salutarily advise should be weighed more carefully on the scale of the mind, compared with those learned in the sacred books [Note: [Col. 1139D] The manuscript reads *breviora*; *breviori* is correct.], and, where reason fails, supported by divine authorities: both after your fatherly and loving admonition and before it, I have done this as far as I could.

For throughout that entire, whatever its quality, discussion, my intention was that I should assert absolutely nothing there unless I saw that it could be defended without hesitation either by the canonical writings or by the sayings of blessed Augustine. And now, whenever I review what I said, I can perceive that I asserted nothing else. [Note: [Col. 1139D] The manuscript has *asseverem*; *assererem* is correct.]

Indeed, neither my own reasoning, however necessary it might have seemed, nor anything else would have persuaded me to presume to state first those things which you incorporated into your letter from that work, and certain others which you did not incorporate. For blessed Augustine himself proves those very things in the book *On the Trinity* through his great arguments, so that, discovering them as if they were my own through a shorter argument, I stated them in reliance upon his authority. I say this not by defending any of the things I said before you, but by showing that I did not presume upon them from myself, but took them from another.

However these matters may stand, the writing itself awaits your authoritative order either to be preserved or destroyed. There are nevertheless certain things which I said there that could have been expressed better in another way, and which I expressed in such a manner that they can more easily be understood wrongly than rightly. I do not deny this, distrustful as I am of my own foolishness; and I hope that they can be corrected, confident as I am in your wisdom.

Therefore, concerning what you say about discussing that same little work with you—would that it might happen according to the kindly will of God, so that I might be permitted to confer with you both about it and about anything else I wished.

## LETTER LXIX [Note: [Col. 1139D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO GONDULF. He offers congratulations on his episcopal dignity.

To his once most beloved brother, now his sweetest father, formerly and now his reverend lord, the venerable bishop GONDULF, brother ANSELM, always his, offers this wish: that he may fulfill the episcopal office in such a way as to obtain an eternal reward.

Before I was permitted to send your sweet holiness a letter of rejoicing over your exaltation, I heard that your episcopal election had come to you not for governance but for labor, not for joy but for tribulation. On the one hand, therefore, I wish to rejoice with your fatherhood, as with one whose former life divine grace has shown to be pleasing to God, in that he deigns to number you among the princes of his Church. On the other hand, I am compelled to grieve with your fraternity, as with one who, by the very fact that he has been more exalted, is burdened with greater tribulation.

Yet when I also consider that, according to the testimony of divine Scripture, from tribulation is born patience, which possesses perfect work (James 1:4), and testing, which produces hope, and hope does not disappoint (Rom. 5:4), I certainly understand that your holiness should not so much be commiserated in tribulation on account of the labor you undergo from it, as congratulated on account of the perfection and hope toward which you advance through it.

Glory, therefore, in the highest to God, whose sight found your life so pleasing that he exalted it as an example; and glory in the highest to God, who loved you so greatly that he placed you in the fire of tribulation, so that he might refine your works to perfection and your hope to its proper strength.

For if all things work together for good for those who love God (Rom. 8:28), why should those who love him not give thanks for the good while rejoicing in all things? Yet they must do this while, since no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred (Eccles. 9:1), they serve the Lord in fear and rejoice before him with trembling. [Note: [Col. 1139D] The manuscript has “and because”; “so that because” is correct.]

Every servant of God must observe this, however: that he should not consider something a tribulation which is not one. For when he counts as tribulation something that he ought not even to feel, he may be judged there by the very fact that he grieves over what he ought not to grieve over, having succumbed through the tenderness of weakness [Note: [Col. 1139D] The manuscript has *temeritudine*; *teneritudine* is correct.] where he thinks he has overcome through the strength of patience. For by judging himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.

I therefore exhort your holiness not to consider in any way a tribulation what harms neither body nor soul. Nor, if adversity in those things which a servant of God ought to despise makes you sad, should you prove that you love transitory things more than is fitting and eternal things less than is proper. For each person plainly shows that he loves those things whose injury he cannot endure without sadness. No one considers himself troubled except when he suffers adversity in what he loves.

I commend our beloved brother Richard to your fatherly care with all the charitable concern we can offer, so that it may not harm him that he is separated from our way of life, but may rather benefit him that he is joined to your familiar companionship.

## LETTER LXX. TO MAURITIUS

He urges him to endure his absence patiently for as long as God has so ordained concerning them.

To the lord, dearest brother, Lord MAURITIUS, brother ANSELM sends the wish to please God and human beings.

Although the more I love you, the more I would like to have you with me, I love you even more for the reason that I cannot have you. For since I love you not so much for myself as for God and for yourself, I love you more because you conduct yourself in such a way that those who have you do not easily wish to send you away, than if they were ready to dismiss you easily because you had been neglected.

Therefore I beg you as a brother, and admonish you as a dearest son, with that care and diligence which you well know I have always had toward you, [Col. 1141A] to advance more and more in good conduct, and, as long as our lord and venerable father, the archbishop Lanfranc, commands it, to endure our separation patiently with me as a divine arrangement, and not through impatience to diminish in any way that which causes me to love you more.

For although I greatly love and desire you, so that you may remain joined to me by living with me, I desire even more that you remain indissolubly attached to good conduct. Let your entire concern, therefore, be to live wherever you are in a manner befitting a good man and a servant of God; and be certain that God will provide you with what will benefit you.

## LETTER LXXI [Note: [Col. 1141D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO PAUL. He rejoices at his promotion to the abbacy of Saint Alban’s and prescribes how he ought to conduct himself in it.

To his lord and father, the reverend and beloved abbot PAUL, brother ANSELM sends the wish that he may live holily in temporal prosperity, so that he may live blessedly in eternal happiness.

Glory in the highest to God, before whose sight your hidden life was so pleasing that he exalted it publicly as an example and established it as a path for those striving from earth toward heaven by the way of virtue, so that in the heavenly kingdom he may rejoice not only in the recompense of his own holiness, but that his joy of eternal happiness may be multiplied on account of the many whom he will win for God.

Although your holiness has been set over barbarians whom, because of the diversity of languages, you cannot teach with words, you nevertheless cannot entirely excuse yourself before the strict Judge if you neglect to win others for God. What you cannot say to them in speech, you can show them by your life. For a good example persuades more effectively than words, to the extent that good conduct is loved in one who is silent, while eloquence is despised in one who is sluggish.

Therefore strive more to be loved by everyone through gentleness and mercy than to be feared through excessively severe justice that spares no one. Let people of every order entrusted to you rejoice that they have been commended to a father and shepherd; let them not shudder that they have been handed over to a tyrant and exactor. Let those close to you rejoice that God has sent them a counselor and helper; let them not complain that an invader of others’ property or a persecutor has attacked them from the left.

For there are many prelates of our order who, as if concerned that God’s property not be destroyed in their hands, act so that God’s law may be scattered in their hearts. They strive so hard to be prudent, lest they be deceived by others, that they become crafty in deceiving others. They are so cautious not to become spendthrifts and irrationally lose what they have that they become avaricious, and what they preserve rots uselessly. Thus they diligently strive always to acquire something for the servants and poor of God and for the holy [Note: [Col. 1141D] The manuscript has “of God, holy”; “of God and for the holy” is correct.] place, while always deceitfully attempting to take something away from someone. They are animated by zeal to correct fools in such a way that they are inflamed by cruelty or by the desire to collect money.

Let your prudence carefully guard against these things. Arrange the external matters entrusted to you in such a way that God’s commandments govern your interior life, and let your mind always say to God: “From your presence let my judgment proceed” (Ps. 16:1).

Defend yourselves through prudence from those who do harm, in such a way that through simplicity you do not wish to harm anyone, as it is written: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

Guard the possessions of your monastery in such a way that you do not forget what is written: “If anyone who possesses the substance of the world sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17). And elsewhere: “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:38).

Take care to increase those same possessions in such a way that this does not slip from your mind: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20:17).

Reprove sinners in such a way that neither cruelty nor avarice is present, because it is written: “If a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1); and again: “Nor will the avaricious possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

I do not write these things to your fatherhood, dearest to me, because I think that you act otherwise, but because you commanded it and I wished our letter to follow you; and for that to happen, it was necessary to say something.

## LETTER LXXII [Note: [Col. 1141D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO HUMFRID. He asks him to devote himself to the instruction of the man who delivers Anselm’s letters to him.

To his lord and brother in Christ, dearest HUMFRID, brother ANSELM of Bec— a sinner in life, a monk in habit—sends the wish to despise earthly things for heavenly ones and to receive heavenly things in place of earthly ones.

First I give thanks and return the affection owed for your gratuitous benevolence, which the bearer of this little letter affirms that he has recognized in you toward me. Because he has considerable confidence in this, he earnestly asks me to assist him with your affection, so that, invited by my prayers, you may bestow upon him more attentively the benefits of your teaching which you mercifully impart to him.

If this were harmful or useless to you, I would scarcely presume to ask it—not for another, but certainly for myself—or perhaps would not dare ask it at all. But now, since it is neither harmful nor useless, and since the divine recompense will be incomparably more useful to you than your generosity will be to this man, I beg and beseech you, as I think, neither boldly nor shamelessly but as a friend, to remember what is written: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10:8).

Even if you perhaps bought your learning from a human teacher so that he might teach you, he could indeed sound words into your ears, but he could not open your heart to understanding; only God could do that, for no one has given to God first so that God might repay him. If we are commanded to make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity (Luke 16:9), who will receive us into eternal dwellings, how much more should we do so from the understanding of truth?

But if you are unwilling to do anything for me because you owe me nothing, then do something by which you may make me your debtor.

I have spoken on behalf of another; but I will add a few words on behalf of your beloved fraternity, for which I would wish to say more. Remember, dearest, and ponder continually in your mind what is written: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because the world and its desire will pass away” (1 John 2:16–17). And because the friends of this age will be constituted enemies of God (James 4:4).

I beg and beseech you: do not trust the world, even when it favors you, because it does not favor you in order to cherish you, but in order to suffocate you. For the world is in darkness, and its glory is not glory but a consuming fire.

Therefore, dearest [Note: [Col. 1143D] The manuscript has the singular “dearest”; the plural is correct.] do not run into it, like a moth flying into the nocturnal fire; for it first charms by its brightness [Note: [Col. 1143D] The manuscript reads *charitate*; *claritate* is correct.] the one whom it later torments with burning. O how much more wisely and happily you would abandon the world and follow Christ, so that when Christ comes in his majesty, you may judge the world with Christ (Matt. 25:31), and, receiving a hundredfold, may possess eternal life (Matt. 19:29). May this come to pass. Amen.

## LETTER LXXIII [Note: [Col. 1143D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO IDA. He commends her for her charity toward the men of Bec and toward everyone.

To his reverend and dearest lady, most distinguished in nobility both of lineage and of life [Note: [Col. 1143D] The manuscript has “dearest in nobility”; “most distinguished in nobility” is correct.], the countess IDA, brother ANSELM sends the wish to advance from virtue to virtue and to ascend from earthly dignity to the heavenly kingdom.

To say nothing of your other good works, through which the name of your nobility spreads far and wide all around with the fragrant scent of holiness, you certainly bestow so many and such great benefits upon people of every order who go to your monastery or come from our monastery that we have now grown accustomed to them, and they have become so familiar to us, that it might be burdensome for you if we were to express our thanks to you individually in words or letters, while we possess nothing with which to repay you according to your merits.

Therefore we send you to God and place him between us and you, so that, just as you do what you do for his sake, he may repay you on behalf of us for whom you do it. [Note: [Col. 1143D] The manuscript has “on behalf of you for whom”; “on behalf of us for whom” is correct.]

At the insistence, however, of that brother whom you sent to us after he had been lost to his own people, and to whom you showed the kindest consolation in his great desolation, I have written this letter to your reverend holiness, so that you might know that what you did for him is no less pleasing to me than if it had been done to me personally; that everything he said concerning his situation is true; that he kept your command in everything which you commanded us through him; and that your man, serving him faithfully and kindly according to your instruction, brought him to them.

May God repay you for these and your other good works with everlasting blessedness. But in doing good, do not grow weary, for in due time you will reap without failing (Gal. 6:9).

## LETTER LXXIV [Note: [Col. 1143D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO RAINALD. Concerning not disseminating the *Monologion* indiscriminately.

To his lord and father, the reverend abbot RAINALD, brother ANSELM sends greetings.

I would by no means send you that little work, which you request from me with such earnestness and from so far away, if I could have refused to obey your wishes. For I fear that, when it comes into the hands of certain people who are more intent on criticizing what they hear than on understanding it, if they happen to read there something they have not previously heard or noticed, they may immediately shout [Note: [Col. 1143D] The manuscript reads *audiverint nec animadverterint ... clamant*; *audierunt nec animadverterunt ... clament* is correct.] that I have written things unheard-of and contrary to the truth. Since, being far away, I shall not be able to answer them, they will not only think that by denying the truth they are supporting it, but will also persuade others who rashly believe them, before hearing what exactly they are criticizing, that I am an advocate of falsehood.

I have already suffered the excessively hasty criticism of such people because, following blessed Augustine, I spoke about the persons and substance of God. They now recognize, however, that they criticized without due consideration, and on this occasion they rejoice that they have come to understand what they had not previously noticed.

For they did not know that “three persons” is not properly said of God in the same way as “three substances”; nevertheless, because of the lack of a name properly signifying that plurality which is understood in the supreme Trinity, Latins say that three persons are to be believed in one substance, while Greeks, no less faithfully, confess three substances in one person.

I therefore earnestly beseech your holiness to show this little work not to verbose and contentious people, but to reasonable and peaceful ones. If it should happen that someone criticizes something in it in such a way that his reasoning seems worthy to you of a reply, I ask that you communicate to me by his letter or your own what he criticizes and for what reason [Note: [Col. 1143D] The manuscript has *quare*; *quave* is correct.], so that, with the peace of charity and love of truth preserved on both sides, either his criticism may correct me or my reply may correct him.

[Col. 1144D]

## LETTER LXXV. TO GILBERT

He bears his friend’s absence with the greatest difficulty.

To his lord, brother, friend, beloved and loving GILBERT, brother ANSELM sends what he cannot write.

Your sweet gifts are sweet to me, dearest friend; but they can in no way console my heart, desolate because of you, from longing for your affection. Certainly, if you were to send every fragrance of spices, every brilliance of metals, every preciousness of stones, every variety of woven fabric, my heart would refuse them; indeed, it could not be consoled in its division until my soul, torn apart, had received its other half.

The anguish of my heart is witness to this as I think upon it; the tears that darken my eyes and wet my face and fingers as they write these words bear witness as well. You knew, as I myself did, my affection toward you; but I myself did not know it. He who separated us from one another taught me how much I loved you. Truly, a person has no knowledge of good or evil who has not experienced both.

For, without having experienced your absence, I did not know how sweet it was for me to be with you, nor how bitter it was to be without you. But through this very separation of ours you have another person present with you, whom you love no less—or certainly more; whereas you, you, I say, have been taken away from me, and no one has been offered in your place.

While you rejoice in your consolation, only a wound remains in my mind. Perhaps those who rejoice over you are offended that I say these things to you. But if they rejoice because they possess what they desired, why do they prevent the one who has always loved you from grieving over his loss? Let them excuse me from themselves, if they see me in them.

Otherwise, you yourself should understand how sympathetically and consolingly they act toward me in this matter, and from what source my pain might be soothed—when no one who can console me wishes to do so, and no one who wishes to can do so. But may he who can do everything he wishes console me in such a way that no one is saddened, and may he sadden no one in such a way that the fullness of love for you is preserved everywhere. Amen.

[Col. 1145C]

## LETTER LXXVI [Note: [Col. 1145D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO WALTER. He gives thanks and excuses himself from solving the question proposed.

To the lord who willingly loves him, deservedly beloved, not as an unknown man but as a familiar friend, GUALTER, brother ANSELM sends what is his own.

If my heart were harder than stone and colder than ice, it ought certainly to grow warm at the fire of your affection and soften under the oil of your sweet address. For the letters by which your sweet affection and beloved wisdom have deigned to make themselves known to my smallness blaze with such a fervor of charity, breathe forth such a fragrance of kindness, and are so delightful in their sweetness and so fruitful in salutary admonition [Note: [Col. 1145D] The manuscript has *facundae*; *foecundae* is correct.] that my mind does not wish to rest until my eyes see its face, my ears hear its voice, and my soul enjoys the presence of the one who, though he was so unknown to me, freely anticipated me with such great love; who took such useful pains to exhort me, absent as I am, toward advancement through his letters; and who so wisely warned me to preserve whatever good qualities there may be in me.

Would that the opinion which the rash talk of people who speak about what they do not know has taught you concerning me were true! Then your admonition, which arose from an abundance of good will and a prudent consideration of human frailty, would be necessary for me.

Blessed in all things be God, who has enriched you with such great charity and stirred you with such charitable concern. May he himself see my desire, so that one day I may deserve to rejoice in your companionship through a way of life pleasing to God, in such a way that, while we live, no change may separate us. [Note: [Col. 1145D] The manuscript reads *aliquanto merear*; *aliquando merear* is correct.]

Concerning the solution of the question which you ask me to write, know that I have neither the leisure nor the ability to believe myself equal to the task. You have with you our reverend lord and father, Abbot Gerbert, who can satisfy you in person through conversation concerning the question you have written about, and concerning the others for which you have indicated that you wish to approach my smallness, better than I can satisfy you either by speaking or writing.

Nevertheless, I beg you not to despise our charity by looking down upon my foolishness. Charity ought to be loved more than knowledge. “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1). Indeed, since every useful kind of knowledge depends upon charity, “on these two,” charity and love, “the whole law and the prophets depend” (Matt. 22:40).

And since, where two or three are gathered in the name of truth (Matt. 18:20), truth itself says, in the counsel and promise of truth, that it is in their midst: if we come together in that name with the affection of charity, the knowledge of truth will be present to us.

If I knew that it was your wish to come to us, I would send you a definite time when this could suitably happen, lest perhaps, if you came at a time when I was not at home, you should undergo vain labor and cause me sadness.

## LETTER LXXVII [Note: [Col. 1145D] Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO ADALA. That she may obtain from her son a discharge from military service for a veteran soldier.

To his reverend lady, the countess [Note: [Col. 1145D] *Adala*. Thus it is read in William of Malmesbury, Book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, and in the history of Matthew Paris. But because this name closely resembles the English word *Adeling*, that is, “noble” or “magnate,” and because this Adala may likewise have been the daughter of William the Conqueror, surnamed the Bastard, king of the English, I think it more correct to read *Adela*, as also in letters 5, 82, 138, 145, 150, 161, and 203 of Ivo of Chartres, and in Book VIII, chapters 34 and 39, of William of Jumièges, *History of the Dukes of Normandy*. For the sake of this Adela, Hugh of Fleury, a monk at Fleury on the Loire, wrote a history in six books, from Abraham to the grandsons of Charlemagne; he sent its autograph to Ivo of Chartres in 1110, as is noted in a handwritten copy in the Victorine Library, not yet printed. Finally, having trampled underfoot the pomp of the world, after Stephen, count of Blois and her husband, had died, and seeing that her son had reached lawful age for conducting affairs, she married God in the convent at Marcigny, when Peter the Venerable presided over Cluny. That convent recognizes his authority, and Adela, after living there religiously, died in 1137. William of Jumièges, in the passage cited immediately above, notes that she was the mother of Stephen, her second son, king of the English; William of Malmesbury and Matthew Paris record her religious profession.] ADALA, brother ANSELM of Bec, a sinner in life, a monk in habit, sends the wish that through lasting prosperity in the present life she may pass to eternal happiness in the life to come.

Although I recognize that I have merited nothing before your eminence by which you ought to grant our prayers, except that, from the time when you deigned to make yourself known to my smallness, I have always wished before God that you might share in our prayers, whatever they may be—if indeed this is worthy either of being said or remembered—the lord Engelhard of the castle commonly called Lenis, our friend, presses me to assist him before your piety [Note: [Col. 1147B] The manuscript reads *illum adjuvem apud*, etc.], so that he may have you as his helper before your son.

Now an old and broken man, he wishes to leave military service—or rather, the wickedness which until now, as long as he could, he vigorously practiced—and to pass the little life that remains in such a way that, if he cannot accomplish good, at least he may cease from evil, lest by sinning to the end he be punished without end.

Therefore he hopes, desires, and beseeches that through me he may have your assistance, and through your assistance obtain from your son peaceable possession of his estates. [Note: [Col. 1147B] The manuscript and the Picard edition read: “that he may have your assistance, and through your assistance obtain peace,” etc.]

But your prudence knows well that all people ought to be helpers of good pursuits and, as partners cooperating in good works, sharers in their rewards. Therefore, although I have deserved nothing from you, I, your servant, do not nevertheless ask your holiness shamelessly to help the man mentioned above, for God’s sake, to obtain what he desires; because it will benefit you, and you ought to do this even without being asked.

## BOOK TWO [Note: [Col. 1147C] “The second book of the letters of Blessed Anselm, which he wrote after he became abbot of Bec,” manuscript 1. “Here begin the letters of the venerable Anselm after he was ordained abbot at Bec,” written in Codex Ef. 20.]

CONTAINING THE LETTERS WHICH ANSELM WROTE WHILE HE WAS ABBOT OF BEC

[Col. 1147C]

### 341 LETTER ONE [Note: [Col. 1147C] This letter, like the following ones, was compared with the aforementioned Victorine manuscript Codex Ef. 20.]

#### TO LANFRANC. He gives thanks for Lanfranc’s almsgiving to the men of Bec and explains the poverty of the monastery of Bec.

To the revered lord and father, Archbishop Lanfranc, Brother Anselm, servant and fellow servant of his brothers of Bec, with those same brothers as his lords, wishes lasting prosperity in this life and eternal happiness in the life to come.

We continually give thanks for the many benefits of your paternal eminence. For although we do not always say this, we nevertheless always keep it in our hearts. And certainly, as it is written, “A helper in times of need, in tribulation” (Psalm 9:10), the blessing of your generosity—namely, the twenty pounds which Lord Abbot Herbert recently brought us—came at such a time of need, that is, when we were placed in such great poverty, like the early and latter rain falling upon us (Hosea 6:3). Yet, although it was consumed most swiftly and completely, it left behind no trace of satiety; just as, in Pharaoh’s dream, the fertile ears of grain and the fat cows were devoured by the barren and seemingly famine-wasted ones (Genesis 41:18). Nevertheless, it sustained us, and scarcely even until now, so that we might not utterly perish.

Indeed, the costly purchases of vegetables and oats almost throughout the entire period [Note: After the death of Lord Herluin, abbot of Bec, and founder of the monastery. Here I add the account of his death which I promised in Book I, Letter 28, without fearing that I shall later find a more suitable place for it. In the year 1077, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, Lanfranc came to Bec in order to consecrate the larger basilica, whose foundation stone he himself had laid second. On the third day after its consecration he departed; as he was leaving, Herluin accompanied him for two miles. “He loved him above all others, and was loved by him,” says the Chronicle of Bec. When he returned to the monastery and withdrew into his cell, giving free rein to his tears, he said: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen” (Luke 2:29–30) “what I greatly desired and prayed continually to see before I died. You have fulfilled what I wished; now your servant will gladly go to you, at whatever hour it pleases you.” Thus he ended his speech, though not his weeping. It was the year of Christ 1077, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November. From that time he seemed to proceed slowly toward the threshold of death, for he became seized by weakness and infirmity in all his limbs. He remained so until the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September of the following year, on which day he took to his bed in his final illness. When the monks heard this, their grief itself became more grievous.

Meanwhile dawned the third—and penultimate—day of Herluin’s life, on which he asked to be fortified with the final and most trusted aids of the Church. Then, as the manuscript Chronicle of Bec says, “the sons came to bid farewell to their most loving father, interrupting the psalms and other prayers with tears and sobs. At last the time came for confession. He began to confess; but overcome by the devotion of his remaining sons, and himself breaking into tears, he could say nothing. Nevertheless, struggling to find his voice, he absolved his sons, and, giving blessing and peace to all, absent and present alike, commended them to the immortal Father; and, as he could do no more, he asked those departing to pray for him. Their grief and tears became their prayers, for scarcely could the psalm be continued while each looked at the other, as though he already saw the father bereft of his brother, and burst into tears. They dared not weep openly before him, because, rejoicing in good hope, he wished to see them all not weeping but rejoicing. If he sensed that anyone was being stirred to sob among the tears, he immediately restrained him with his customary gravity.”

At last, around midnight on Saturday, the seventh day before the Kalends of September, he breathed forth his most holy soul, in the year 1078 of the incarnate Christ, in the eighty-fourth year of his age and the forty-fourth of his monastic profession. His body was buried in the middle of the monastic apse and covered with a black stone carved with various figures, which I saw with my own eyes.

The manuscript of Bec had three inscriptions composed for him. I omit two of them, since they may be seen in Book VI, chapter 9, of the *History of the Dukes of the Northmen* by Gemmeticus; I include the third, which reads as follows:

You underwent, Father Herluin, in accordance with your condition,  
the human fall which you could not overcome.

At first a soldier, you held what belongs to the world;  
but, with God showing mercy, afterward you abandoned the world.

You often bore patiently the burden of poverty,  
for you wisely distributed your possessions to the poor.

You deserved to become the first founder of Bec,  
and you were its monk and ruler.

You wished all who lived with you to live as a holy flock;  
if anything oppressed it, you grieved in the manner of a father.

You taught those entrusted to you by divine commission.  
Behold, beneath this tomb you are ash, to which you gave limbs.

Therefore let the people of Bec venerate you with pious praises,  
and let them pray that the Lord grant you the heavenly kingdom.

The necrology of Bec records his death in these few words: “On the seventh day before the Kalends of September died Lord Abbot Herluin, of venerable memory, shepherd and founder of this monastery.”]

after the death of Lord Herluin, the abbot, and the lands which we likewise purchased after his death—to say nothing of the great bell, which we imprudently began when one was broken and another discordant, but completed only with great difficulty, adding and spending far more than we had anticipated—and many other matters, on which we expended much besides what has been mentioned. Indeed, the year from which we have somehow emerged came very close to overwhelming us [Note: The manuscript reads “came very close”; the edited text reads “came very close to overwhelming us”]; but the year into which we have entered threatens us much more closely with scarcity of many things.

But may God, who from heaven looked down upon the sons of men (Psalm 52:3), look upon us from the hearts of those who abound. Moreover, since we always need your counsel and assistance, we now greatly need the support of yourself and your clergy in the affairs of our church, which we have found it necessary to make known to you through the living voice of the bearer of this letter. Once you know of them, if you know anything that might help us in these matters, we beg that your holiness promptly take care to send us word [Note: The manuscript reads “we beg that you promptly”; the edited text reads “we beg that your holiness promptly send us word”]. For we are compelled to plead all these matters before the king on the Sunday after the feast of the holy apostle Andrew.

## Epistle II

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

To Lanfranc. Thanks are returned for his generosity, especially for the gold he had sent for making a chalice.

To his revered lord and most kindly father, Archbishop Lanfranc, Brother Anselm, together with his fellow servants and lords, the brothers of the monastery of Bec, which is his—

We send great thanks in writing for your great and frequent generosity, and we preserve immense thanks in our hearts for your immense and continual goodwill. Since, by God’s generosity, your abundance is so great that, though you so often supply our poverty, it can in no way diminish, so great is your goodwill that your abundance could sooner be exhausted than your goodwill diminished.

And may God, who gave you both the will and the action [Note: The manuscript reads “according to his will”; the edited text reads “according to your goodwill”] (Philippians 2:13), preserve both in you. To your holiness, who grants us so many benefits, we wish him to be their recompense; indeed, on our behalf we appoint him your debtor and guarantor, as though lending at interest. Therefore, spend securely and cheerfully, as you have begun so well, expecting to receive a thousandfold return; for neither you nor we wish to deceive, nor can our guarantor do so.

We send your servants and sons, our brothers, to your footsteps. Just as they go at your command, so let them remain, return, or do whatever else they may do, according to your arrangement and whatever we shall direct. Your son, the abbot of Bec, as they say, borrowed from your servant, Brother Anselm, the gold which you sent for the chalice [Note: The manuscript reads “changed”; the edited text reads “borrowed”]. The man who was to make the chalice did not have the gold, while the other meanwhile needed it. But, according to the agreement, the gold will be returned fashioned into a chalice, and in whatever form you prefer for the chalice.

In the meantime, your servant will use the chalice which you, as prior at Bec, previously possessed [Note: The manuscript reads “you possessed”; the edited text reads “you previously possessed”] and gave to the succeeding prior. But know that he would never have entrusted the gold to anyone unless under your surety; for you stood surety because you ordered it. It is sufficiently clear whom one must trust, lest, under the surety of a father and lord, the son deceive the servant [Note: The manuscript reads “lest he be seen”; the edited text reads “lest he be trusted”].

## Epistle III

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

To Gondulf. He declares his intimate friendship with him, however much an episcopal dignity may separate them, and commends to him the monks of Bec whom he is sending to England.

To the lord and friend, father and brother, revered and beloved Bishop Gondulf, Brother Anselm, who formerly, and from the time when we loved one another more deeply—

Although episcopal dignity and the reverence due to holiness so exalt your person above me that they leave me far below, nevertheless—what I say not out of pride but out of love—the former familiarity and familiar friendship always raise me to equality with you. Thus, however far a vigorous bishop and an insignificant monk may be separated in dignity and merit, Gondulf and Anselm are always joined by familiar affection.

Therefore I will never presume less upon you because of your episcopate, nor trust you less because of your holiness, since we have always been one heart because of the equal familiarity of our affection. Indeed, I shall presume and trust you all the more whenever reason requires it, since you possess greater earthly resources through your dignity and greater spiritual opportunity through your holiness.

Since in both of us the will is equal—that each wishes the other to benefit as much as possible—it is necessary that the one who can do more should benefit the other more. You ought therefore to take care that your great devotion benefits me before God more than you expect my devotion—which is certainly either wholly nonexistent or almost so—to benefit you [Note: The manuscript reads “either truly nonexistent, or either”; the edited text reads “either truly nonexistent or almost nonexistent”].

I do not say this so that I should not pray for my true friend as I am able, but to show that what I can do is exceedingly little. Thus the one who can do more should help the one who can do less, so that the latter may be able to do more for the work of the former and for his own. Nor should your prayer for me grow cold because mine for you cannot burn with equal intensity.

For whoever loves someone benefits that person through love: know that he benefits himself more than the other [Note: The manuscript reads “than others”; the edited text reads “than the other”]. The possession of love itself is far greater than what one person bestows upon another through love. To the latter is granted only what love can do for a time [Note: The manuscript reads “love grants”; the edited text reads “love is granted”]; but to the former love itself is granted here, and in the future it is repaid in the measure of its own worth.

I commend to your fatherly love and loving fatherhood our brothers and your own, whom we are sending to England, so that, wherever need arises, they may be supported by your assistance, governed by your counsel, their lives examined by your diligence, and approved or corrected by your judgment.

## Epistle IV

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

To Baldwin. He entrusts the highly commended monks of Bec, sailing to England, to his care and governance.

To the lord and revered father, Abbot Baldwin, Brother Anselm, that he may live holily in this age and blessedly in the age to come.

Although I know that I have deserved nothing from your holiness except goodwill alone [Note: The manuscript reads “they know”; the edited text reads “I know”], your well-known kindness toward many makes me presume upon you, so that, when need arises, I do not hesitate to ask what would not disgrace you.

For I also confess that my willingness to obey is ready, should your fatherhood require something of my insignificance. Indeed, the love which we have always owed one another both makes us ready to serve and gives us confidence to ask. Therefore, trusting in the commandment of love, in the experience of your kindness, and in the awareness of our own willingness, I commend to your fatherly love and loving fatherhood our brothers and your own, whom we are sending to England, so that, wherever need arises, they may be supported by your assistance, governed by your counsel, their lives examined by your diligence, and approved or corrected by your judgment.

## Epistle V

To Henry. He commends the same monks of Bec to him.

To the lord and dearest brother Henry, Brother Anselm sends greetings.

Although our brotherhood addresses your charity less often in letters, love nevertheless does not grow cold in our conscience. For once love arises between rational beings according to a true reason, it is never extinguished so long as its root lives.
