Therefore neither you nor I ought to doubt our mutual affection, since we cannot enjoy one another’s physical presence; rather, we ought always to persevere in certainty of that affection so long as we preserve the immutable cause of its origin. I commend to your fraternal love and loving fraternity our brothers and your own, whom we are sending to England, so that, wherever need arises, they may be supported by your assistance, governed by your counsel, their lives examined by your diligence, and approved or corrected by your judgment.

## Epistle VI

Anselm and Richard to Richard and Rohais. He gives thanks for their benefits and entrusts to their care the men of Bec whom, at their urging, he is sending to England.

To his dearest lord Richard and his dearest lady Rohais [Note: “To his dearest lord Richard and his dearest lady Rohais.” It is clear not only from this heading but also from the words that follow in Anselm’s letter—“For the more good things you do and promise us”—that these are the people of whom Herluin, first abbot of Bec, speaks near the end of his charter, where he lists both the alms bestowed upon his monastery and their donors. Concerning these people he writes: “Richard, son of Count Gilbert, gave to the same monastery two estates, Totine and Estrahan, with his wife and sons, Roger and Gilbert witnessing and consenting; and two parts of the tithe of Hondemeresto, Cypestedehe, Gnentum, Blacingeleth, Beccesurdum, and Tornecrusto, and of Vualenterona. And Rohais, the wife of that Richard, with his consent, gave to the same monastery what she possessed in her own domain at Hamecelessan, both in lands and in other possessions.” Thus it stands in the signed charter.

Furthermore, I think that the little Richard whom Anselm names at the beginning of the letter is that same man who was later abbot of the monastery of Ely, mentioned below in Book III, Letter 126. That he and his parents were English is also clear from the English names of the donated properties just listed, and from Anselm’s words near the end of the letter: “We therefore commend them to you, so that, just as they are going to England,” and so forth. Moreover, the name Rohais plainly sounds English when pronounced fully.]

Brother Anselm and Brother Richard, the little monk, together with the whole congregation of Bec, send greetings and faithful prayers.

We first return great thanks to God, from whom every good will comes and for whose love all good things are done for us; then to you, for all the good things which you do and promise us. In this you clearly show that your love, which you have always had for our monastery, never diminishes but grows more and more. For the more good things you do and promise us, the surer a love you demonstrate.

May almighty God and his holy mother Mary, whom we pray for you every day and for whose love you do everything for us, repay you in the kingdom of heaven. We send our brothers to you, as you commanded. We therefore commend them to you, so that, just as they go to England at your command and in your hope, so everything they do, and how or from what means they live, may be entirely in your care and under your providence.

## Epistle VII

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

To Richard and the monks of Bec. That the men of Bec who have been brought to England may live religiously, and that Henry the chamberlain may be restrained from drunkenness.

Brother Anselm, called abbot of Bec, sends greetings and a fatherly blessing in love to his dearest brothers and sons, Richard and the others of the congregation of Bec living in England.

If you live safely, prosperously, and finally in concord and according to God, my soul rejoices with your charity in brotherly and fatherly affection. My conscience is witness that nothing makes me so glad as the prosperity and uprightness of those who, by some divine judgment, have been entrusted to my insignificance; nothing makes me so sad as their adversity and strength.

Therefore I beg you as brothers and admonish you as dearest sons always to preserve an abiding remembrance of monastic religion, and to display in life and conduct what the habit of your religion professes. For neither place nor any time excuses anyone from living well, since no one can ever exclude good will from the hearts of human beings against their will, and the ordering of conduct, arranged according to the circumstances of things, can remain firm amid every disturbance.

God never demands works beyond one’s ability when he sees the integrity of good will and good conduct. I therefore desire that in all things you present yourselves without any excuse, showing yourselves to be lovers not of the world or of the things that are in the world, but of God and of the things that belong to God (1 John 2:15). Thus, when others praise God for your good conduct, may you be able to rejoice in God in the present life and the life to come, and may I truly rejoice with my brothers and sons.

[Note: Concerning Lord Henry, who was chamberlain. I have found that this title does not signify only one thing. First, Abbot Joachim, explaining chapter 1 of the Apocalypse, used it for a secretary: “Nor is it surprising,” he says, “if he is called the chamberlain of heaven”—he means John the Evangelist—“who reclined above the Lord’s breast,” and so forth.

If neither of these meanings applies, the word may designate a kind of gourd, which, because it covers chambers and galleries with creeping shoots and tendrils, is thought by Marius Grapaldus to have received this name. Onuphrius, in his explanation of obscure ecclesiastical terms, agrees with this etymology, but looks elsewhere as well: he teaches that the chamberlain—after the title of archdeacon of the Roman Church had disappeared—was so called because he cared for the ecclesiastical monies kept in chambers; and he says that this title existed in the time of Gregory VII.

This interpretation is supported by the title “chamberlain” in Epistle 152 of Book III, where I noted in the margin that the Peter mentioned there had been a Cluniac monk and chamberlain to Urban II and Paschal. In the ancient statutes of the monastery of Fleury on the Loire I read that on the Thursday of Holy Week: “When the sermon has ended, at the abbot’s command the chamberlain rises, together with his assistant, and through them new footwear is distributed to the brothers.”

In Book I, chapter 10, of our statutes, the duties of the person bearing this title are explained more fully in these words: “It belongs to the office of the chamberlain to seek out and receive at the appointed time all the monastery’s rents and revenues, whether from villages, lands, mills, or any other possessions. From the money received he must, every week and insofar as possible, discharge his responsibility to the abbot and the aforementioned depositaries. The granaries, ploughs, arable lands, and other cultivated parts of the monastery, as well as the livestock and all common animal husbandry, also belong to his care, so that he may provide whatever is necessary for restoring, managing, or preserving everything. In the monastery, all care of external affairs and the administration of the entire estate belong to him: the stable and all its equipment, everything belonging to the stable and the horses, and the servants working there are under his supervision.”

And shortly afterward: “The grain store, cellar, and barn belong to the chamberlain’s care and supervision.” In the preceding chapter: “The cellarer shall provide for the monastery’s expenses, just as the chamberlain gathers its receipts.”

Thus far the Victorian Statutes, from which the chamberlain’s ministry is explained in greater detail and corresponds most exactly to Anselm’s usage here. In chapter 31 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, the cellarer appears to perform the office which the Victorian chamberlain performs, but all his duties are not set out with such particularity and precision.

From Eadmer it is clear that the duties of the chamberlain and cellarer were different. I also see that some people gave this name to household servants, although formerly it belonged above all to the chief and highest official of the royal chamber, as I read in Letter 190 of Ivo of Chartres, where Galeran is called the king’s chamberlain.

In charters of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, and of his son Louis VII, the earlier one, issued at Châlons in 1103, is subscribed in this manner: “The sign of Guy the chamberlain.” The later one, issued at Paris by Louis VII, son of Louis the Fat, to affirm his father’s magnificence, was granted in 1117 at Paris in the basilica and bears this subscription: “The sign of Hugh the chamberlain.”

I omit other places from which I could have brought forward similar evidence, lest I appear to the reader more fastidious than scholarly in a matter so slight. I shall add only one example: the man whom in most monasteries they call the procurator or steward is here called the chamberlain, among us *Chambrier*, just as our Frenchmen commonly call the pope’s chamberlain.

Formerly, however, the royal chamberlain was also called by this name, as is plainly shown by the following heading of a letter by Laurence Primfactius prefixed to his French translation of Cicero’s *On Old Age*, made in 1405: “To the most excellent, glorious, and noble prince Louis, uncle of the king of France, Duke of Bourbon, Count of Clermont and Forez, Lord of Beaujeu, grand chamberlain and first peer of France.”

Two manuscript copies of this translation are preserved in our library. What Laurence Primfactius, clerk of that same Louis of Bourbon, called the *grand chambrier*, people today call the *grand chambellan*, or first chamberlain.]

Concerning Lord Henry, who was chamberlain, I hear that he behaves disorderly in many respects, especially in drinking, so that he drinks with drunkards in the guild and becomes drunk with them [Note: The manuscript reads “that he may make drunk”; the edited text reads “that he may become drunk”]. If this is true, I cannot say how much my heart grieves over such great ruin of a brother. For this misery will not remain solitary for long; unless, with God looking upon him, he quickly corrects himself, it will draw him on to other precipices of death.

Therefore, just as an abbot ought to prohibit a monk, so I, whatever sort of sinner I may be, by the authority of God, his saints, and ourselves, prohibit him from daring, once he has learned of this prohibition of ours, to drink any longer in the guild or in the company of those who gather solely to become drunk [Note: The manuscript reads “to live”; the edited text reads “to drink”].

I also command that, if he cannot deny his former disorder, he not neglect to repent of it according to the judgment of our lord Archbishop Lanfranc, or of Lord Bishop Gondulf, or of yourselves; and that thereafter, with God’s help, he take care to guard himself from drunkenness and malicious words.

But if he refuses altogether to correct himself, I prefer—disregarding every advantage which we ought to gain through him in England—that he return to us to be governed under discipline rather than remain far from discipline and be ruined.

I kindly ask Lord Henry of Gournay to bear patiently and calmly what he so earnestly requests in his letters, until Lord Richard comes—who, as I heard from the king, will shortly come to us—and until what shall then be arranged concerning him and all of you who were sent on account of that same Lord Richard, by the counsel of ourselves and our brothers, can be endured with kind patience and patient kindness.

## Epistle VIII

To Mauritius.

[Compared with the same manuscript and with the manuscript of Saint-Evroul.]

Concerning a monk who has remained too long at court. And concerning evil: whether it is something.

Brother Anselm, called abbot of Bec, sends greetings and God’s blessing to his beloved brother and son Mauritius.

Concerning that brother about whom you wrote to me, as the matter required—that, neglecting the life of the cloister, he remains at the king’s court according to the inclination of his own will—I wish you and the other brothers who are with you to conduct yourselves as follows.

If he comes to you, I permit you to receive him and to offer him the service of brotherly love. Nevertheless, show him on your part that you fear this may displease me [Note: The manuscripts read “that you may seem”; the edited text reads “that you fear”]. Rebuke him, though with due moderation, for such great presumption and disobedience. For he is now remaining neither by our command nor by our permission; indeed, he is not afraid openly to oppose our command.

I neither order him to return nor permit him to remain. For I perceive certain reasons which still compel me to tolerate his presumption by pretending not to notice it. But unless he corrects himself quickly, setting aside all the reasons for which I still await him, I shall necessarily have to exercise the severity of the rule against him.

I would rather have his spontaneous correction than inflict upon him any chastisement of harsher discipline [Note: The manuscript reads “the name, however”; the edited text reads “his spontaneous correction”].

Moreover, the short work which I recently composed at the request of certain brothers who frequently question me, as you know, about such matters—namely, how, when evil is said to be nothing, its name can signify something—I have now sent enclosed with this letter to you by the bearer, as you requested.

If evil is nothing, how does its name signify something? Again, if, upon hearing the name “evil,” we understand something which we dread and judge ought to be avoided, how can either evil be nothing or the name of evil signify nothing? And what is “nothing” itself?

Yet since “to be nothing” and “not to be something” are in no way different, how can one say what that is which is not something? Nevertheless, the very name which we call “nothing” [Note: The manuscripts read “the name of nothing”], if it signifies nothing—that is, if it does not signify something—is not a name; but it is a name.

Although, therefore, no one says that nothing is something, and we are always compelled to confess that nothing is nothing, no one can deny that the name “nothing” is significant. But conversely, if this very name does not signify nothing but something, what is signified seems unable to be nothing and rather to be something.

If, then, what is signified is not nothing but something, how can it be true that it is signified by this name, namely “nothing”? For what is truly called nothing is truly nothing and therefore is not something. Thus, if what is signified by this name is not nothing but something, as consequence seems to show, it is falsely and incongruously called by this name.

But conversely, if, according to everyone’s judgment, that which is called “nothing” is truly nothing and in no way something, does anything seem more consistent than that this very name “nothing” should signify nothing—that is, should not signify something [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Evroul reads “that is not”; the edited text reads “that is, should not”]?

What, then, is the case? This name, namely “nothing,” does not signify nothing but something; and it does not signify something but nothing. Perhaps signifying nothing and something are not contradictory? But if they are not contradictory, either some thing must be found which is both something and nothing—which cannot be understood—or this word signifies nothing and something according to different considerations.

For it is clear that this word, “nothing,” differs in no way in meaning from what I say, “not something.” Nothing is clearer than that this word—namely “not something”—removes entirely from the understanding every thing and everything that is something; and by its utterance signifies that no thing at all, nor anything that is something, is to be posited.

But since the removal of something cannot be signified except together with the signification of that very thing whose removal is signified, it is necessary that this word “not something,” by destroying what is something, signify something. Yet because, by taking away everything that is something, it signifies no essence which the understanding of the hearer might retain as though existing, the word “not something” signifies no thing and nothing that is something.

Therefore, the expression “not something,” by these different modes, in some respect signifies a thing and something, and in no respect signifies a thing or something. It signifies by denying, and does not signify by establishing.

For this reason the name “nothing,” which destroys everything that is something, by destroying does not signify nothing but something; and by establishing does not signify something but nothing. Consequently, it is not necessary that nothing be something because its name signifies something in some manner; rather, it is necessary that nothing be nothing because its name signifies something in this manner.

In this way there is no contradiction between evil being nothing and the name “evil” being significant, if it signifies something by destroying in such a way that it establishes no thing. Yet although in this manner “evil” and “nothing” truly signify something, what is thus signified is neither evil nor nothing; nevertheless, in another respect in which they signify something, what is signified is something—but not truly something, only something according to appearance.

For many things are spoken of according to the form of expression which are not so according to reality. For example, “to fear” is called active in the form of the word, although in reality it is passive. Likewise, blindness is called something according to the form of speech, although in reality it is not something.

Just as we say of someone that he has sight and that sight is in him, so we say that he has blindness and that blindness is in him, although blindness is not something but rather “not something”; and to have it is not to have something, but rather to lack that which is something.

For blindness is nothing other than lack of sight, or the absence of sight where sight ought to be. But lack of sight, or absence of sight, is no more something where sight ought to be than where it ought not to be. Therefore blindness is no more something in the eye, because sight ought to be there, than lack or absence of sight is something in a stone, where sight ought not to be [Note: The manuscripts read “sight as in a stone”; the edited text reads “sight in a stone”].

Many other things likewise are called something according to the form of speech although they are not something, because we speak of them as we speak of things that exist [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Evroul reads “we speak in this way”]. In this way, then, evil and nothing signify something, and what is signified is something not according to reality but according to the form of speech.

For “nothing” signifies nothing other than “not something,” or the absence of those things which are something; and evil is nothing other than “not good,” or the absence of good where good ought or ought reasonably to be. But what is nothing other than the absence of that which is something is itself not something.

Evil, therefore, is truly nothing, and nothing is not something; yet in a certain manner they are something, because we speak of them as though they were something when we say, “He did nothing,” or “What he did is nothing or evil,” just as we say, “He did something or something good,” or “What he did is something or good.”

## Epistle IX

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

To the monks of Bec.

Concerning his prosperous arrival in England, which he also wishes announced to Lady Eve.

To the lords and dearest brothers serving God in the monastery of Bec, Brother Anselm, their servant and fellow servant, wishes always to live holily and to receive the reward of a holy life.

Knowing—and certainly knowing—that you most eagerly desire news of my safety and prosperity, I could not weary you by any delay. Therefore, on the very day on which Lord Girard departed from me at the hour called prime, after I had entered the sea, divine protection brought me by prosperous navigation to English soil at the ninth hour, without the hardship that many voyagers commonly endure [Note: [Col. 1157D] *Solent* (“they commonly endure”)—the manuscript reads *perduxit* (“he brought”): “he brought me at the ninth hour”]. It also granted that I should reach our lord and father, Archbishop Lanfranc, in the evening and be received with joy at his estate called Limingis [Note: [Col. 1157D] The manuscript reads *Limingia*]. The following day I wrote this letter, both to fulfill your aforementioned desire and to remind you that your holy purpose should always burn more ardently and advance toward better things [Note: [Col. 1157D] The manuscript reads *commoverem* (“I would stir”) rather than *commonerem* (“I would remind”)]. I therefore entreat you as a brother and exhort you as a father to strive to conduct yourselves in peace and in monastic religion, so that you may be blessed through the reward of your diligence and I may one day rejoice in your blessedness. May the almighty Lord defend you by his protection from every adversity and show you his mercy through continual prosperity of body and soul. Tell our mother and lady Eva—who awaits with equal eagerness, together with you, news of her firstborn son—that she should pray that, just as through her prayers she obtained, together with you who feared for me, that I might depart from you prosperously, so she may obtain that I can return joyfully to you.

## LETTER X [Note: [Col. 1157D] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO RODULF. He rejoices that Rodulf has turned to the religious life.

Brother ANSELMUS, called abbot of Bec, to his once most dearly desired friend, now lord, brother, and dearest son, the new soldier of Christ, RODULF [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads *Rudolpho* rather than *Rodulpho]: may, through contempt for earthly and false riches, he attain heavenly and true riches [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads “heavenly riches” rather than “heavenly and true riches”].

Glory to God in the highest, who gives human beings good will on earth (Luke 2:14): his exalted right hand, according to my desire, has changed the will of my beloved and longed-for friend from the vanity of the world—which benefits no one in the end and harms all who love it—to the truth, which has never harmed anyone and benefits all who seek it.

I speak briefly to you, sweetest to my heart, in writing, although, as my conscience bears witness, I long to see you above all people and to speak with you face to face, more than with anyone living on earth. For I know the devil’s malicious envy: gnashing his teeth, he wastes away because you are escaping from his hands—indeed, from his mouth. Hence I am certain that he will try to deceive you in many ways: either by the burden of God’s service that you have chosen, or by the attraction of serving him through love of the world, which you have abandoned [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads *quam reliquisti* (“which you abandoned”) rather than *quem reliquisti* (“which you abandoned,” agreeing with *amorem*]. For this reason, since by God’s grace I hope to be able to advise you against all his wiles—for they consist in falsehood and weakness, if firm hope in God is not lacking—and since I know for certain that no counsel at present will suffice for your desire more than mine [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads *sufficeret* (“would suffice”) rather than *sufficere* (“suffices”), my soul will have no rest within me until my eyes see my longed-for friend, my mouth addresses my most beloved son, and my heart instructs my new fellow soldier against the devil’s darts [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads “my fellow soldier” rather than “my new fellow soldier”].

I therefore pray almighty God, who has separated you from love of worldly vanity, and his most holy mother, who received you fleeing to her under her protection, to preserve you from every disturbance of the purpose you have begun. And I beg you, by him whose grace inspired you to begin this, not to let any ambushes or suggestions of the enemy frighten you. For the enemy strives to trouble you for this purpose: that he may rejoice in your defeat. But God permits him to do so for this purpose: that he may give you the means by which he himself will grant you the crown of victory. For, as the Apostle says, “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy 2:5).

Wait, therefore, until I come; for, God granting it, you will receive consolation for all that now troubles you [Note: The manuscript reads “because you will receive consolation” rather than “because, God granting it, you will receive consolation]. May the Lord guard you from every evil. Amen.

## LETTER XI [Note: [Col. 1159D] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO HUGH. Concerning certain little works requested by the archbishop, and explaining why he prefixed the title “abbot” to his works in order to exclude ambiguity of name.

To the lord and father, the venerable archbishop of Lyon, HUGH—revered with affection and loved with reverence—brother ANSELMUS, called abbot of Bec: toward his beloved father, a faithful son.

If I wished to write how great and how welcome to me are the honor and sweetness of your friendship, which I trust from your promise that I possess, and how much I desire, even though I have not deserved to receive it, not to lose it through faithful willingness, if I cannot otherwise deserve it, perhaps I would have to subtract something, lest I seem to add beyond the truth. But what in a letter I do not dare sufficiently to praise [Note: [Col. 1159D] See Letter 17 below; the manuscript reads “but in a letter” rather than “but what in a letter”], I shall take care, God granting it, faithfully to preserve in the shrine of my heart.

By the brothers who bear this letter, whom I have learned to be lovers of your holiness and devoted to your eminence, I send you, as you ordered, what you requested from our writings. In this matter I know that I am serving not so much someone else’s usefulness as your will. Therefore, if you regret having spent your time reading it in vain because you will not find what you think you will find [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads “what you do not think you will find”], you should blame not the sender but the one who demanded it.

As for the questions about which I said I wished to write, and concerning which your reverence admonished me, if I were to say how much I am hindered from dictating [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads *impediat* (“hinders”) rather than *impediar* (“I am hindered”)], no one who does not know my manner of life could believe it [Note: [Col. 1159D] The manuscript reads “cannot be believed” rather than “could not be believed]. Yet if at some time, by God’s grace, I am able to accomplish what I wish in this matter, your prudence will know it, if I can make it known.

The aforementioned brothers, lamentably complaining about the inner destruction of their monastery, humbly entreated me with affection to ask that in their tribulation they might be relieved by the consolation of your paternal counsel. But just as your wisdom does not need our counsel, so neither does your goodwill need our prayers. Nevertheless, if you wish me to say what I think would presently benefit them, until the religion of monastic life is restored in their church through the presence of a regular abbot by the visitation of heavenly grace, I judge that it would be better for them, with your permission, to choose meanwhile a place where they may live usefully according to their purpose than to be forced to remain where, through lack of bodily and spiritual goods, they live sadly and uselessly—or, unbearably oppressed by that same deprivation, depart disobediently.

As for the fact that I added the name “abbot” to my own name in the titles of my little works, I did not do so to display a more honored person, but to exclude ambiguity of name.

## LETTER XII TO HELINAND [Col. 1160D]  
He exhorts him to persevere and to resist steadfastly the devil’s various temptations, which he describes.

[Note: [Col. 1159D] Compared with the same manuscript and with the Gothic and Cologne editions of 1573.]

The servant of the servants of God dwelling in the monastery of Bec, brother ANSELMUS, to his beloved brother and longed-for son HELINAND: may he happily complete what he has begun well.

Blessed is God, from whom every good and perfect gift descends (James 1:17) [Note: The manuscript and edition read “every good gift” rather than “every gift”], who has turned your eyes away so that they do not see vanity (Psalm 118:37), and has raised your soul to follow truth.

It remains, therefore, my longed-for son, that you carefully consider that “no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62). For the ancient enemy will not cease attacking you with cunning devices of many kinds, all the more vigorously as he sees you more earnestly wishing to escape his snares.

Often he will bring before your mind’s eyes how delightful are the things in which you were accustomed to live, so that he may immediately add how difficult it is to lack accustomed pleasure, how impossible it is to persevere throughout one’s whole life in a certain austere rigor and rigid austerity; with the result that, because of the memory of accustomed delight, your soul will dread the sobriety of the higher life all the more.

Sometimes, under the appearance of discretion, he will pretend to advise you more beneficially than you have resolved—to be precise, that, while abandoning depravity, you should wish to remain in your clerical calling by living religiously [Note: The manuscript and edition read “or that you may remain” rather than “that you should wish to remain”], so that by correcting your life you may save your soul and not, through indiscretion, undertake a burden that you cannot bear.

But if he realizes that he cannot turn you away in any way from your intention of the more perfect life, he will pretend, as though going with you, to approve your purpose; yet he will never cease placing many snares beside the road.

At one time, taking advantage here of an opportunity for sin and there of a temptation urging you, the crafty enemy will add a persuasion of this sort: “What you have resolved to do is so good that it could destroy any enormity of crimes. Why, then, do you hesitate meanwhile to satisfy your desire, since, whether your sins are many or few, you do not doubt that you will soon wipe them all away by grieving equally over them?” [Note: The manuscript and edition read “not to be wiped away” rather than “not wipe them all away.”]

At another time he will try to deceive you in this way: “What you wish to do is indeed good, but it is not undertaken at the proper time unless, when youthful wantonness has grown cold—youthful wantonness that cannot bear the weight of that regular discipline—maturity of age itself has adapted itself to the gravity of religious life.”

If he sees that you are so weak that your intention could be impeded if it became known, he will strive by every means to have it disclosed on any pretext to those by whom you could be held back, whether by force, affection, or some persuasion.

He will also promise that, if you are willing to defer for a while the good you intend, you will be able to do it much more fruitfully and advantageously: through the salvation of many whom you will draw with you, and through the financial benefit that will accrue to the monastery from the money you will gather from every side.

What more? He will try to accuse you of levity and inconsiderate haste because you wished to bind yourself not only by a promise but also by promising a pledge, with an indissoluble vow—when you could nevertheless, and perhaps better, accomplish the same thing with a free will [Note: The manuscript reads “What more is there?” rather than “What more?”].

I would like to write somewhat more extensively about what should be answered to all these arguments, if the convention of a letter did not compel me to keep within brevity. Receive, then, briefly and truly, the counsel of your friend against these things.

The person who thinks it too austere [Note: [Col. 1161D] The manuscript and edition read “an austere task” (*munus austerum*) rather than “too austere”]. and impossible to lack worldly pleasure and persevere in the practice of the virtues has never tasted how great, through love and hope of the heavenly kingdom, is the pleasure of not serving but ruling over vices—a pleasure worthy of praise and delight.

The person who thinks it better for him to live religiously in clerical dress [Note: The manuscript and edition read “to live religiously for himself” rather than “to live religiously in clerical dress”] than to undertake the unbearable burden of monastic life should consider throughout the whole world with what joy that burden—singable, that is, worthy of being sung—is borne by both sexes, every age, and every kind of human being.

Let him also know that it is much more difficult to preserve the holiness of life among secular people by free will than within the cloister of monks under discipline.

I do not now say that the purpose of this life reaches a higher degree of humility than all other ways of life, which higher exaltation follows—except that no one abandons the monastic purpose in order to live better, and every kind of human being hastens toward the monastic life in order to draw nearer to God.

The person who adds sins to sins [Note: [Col. 1161D] The manuscript and edition read “adds sin to sins”] because he awaits the remission of all sins, while loving sin, proves that he does not love forgiveness and therefore does not deserve absolution from sins [Note: The manuscript reads “remission” rather than “absolution”].

The person who postpones correcting his life until a future age, perhaps an age that will never come, abandons a certain good for an uncertain one; and by despising what he loses, he proves that he does not love what he expects and deserves not to receive it.

The person who is not certain that he possesses such constancy that he cannot in any way be turned from his good purpose should conceal his good intention altogether, so that it may become public only when it passes into action.

The person who postpones a good he wishes to do so that it may be done better does well, if it is certain that it will be better. But if the better good is uncertain, and losing the lesser good is excessively harmful and irrecoverable, the advice is that he should hasten to do the lesser good, lest by waiting too long for the greater he do neither the greater nor the lesser.

The person who judges it levity to wish by a vow to bind oneself to doing what is good, so that one is no longer free not to do it, should judge that teacher frivolous who says, “Vow and repay” (Psalm 75:12). For the one who vows what is good is in no way to be blamed [Note: The manuscript and edition read “who knows” rather than “who vows”]; rather, the one who does not fulfill what he vowed is to be blamed.

For it is certain that the person who makes a good vow pleases God by the vow itself. Therefore, whoever has vowed something good should not regret that he has done something pleasing to God; rather, he should hasten to fulfill what he vowed, so that he may please him more.

These counsels and consolations, dearest son, I have judged especially necessary for you at present. I, whom you chose as father and counselor—not because of my dignity but because of your will—have dictated them with paternal concern. Do not cease meanwhile to remember them, until, with God’s inspiration and his help, you complete what you have vowed.

Farewell, longed-for one, dear to my heart, and hasten to satisfy my desire concerning you—may it please almighty God that you do so! Amen.

## LETTER XIII [Note: [Col. 1163C] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO LANFRANC. He sends him Gislebert and asks that he return him shortly.

To the lord and revered father, Archbishop LANFRANC, brother ANSELMUS, servant of the servants of God dwelling at Bec, together with those same lords of his: faithful servants to their lord, reverent sons to their revered father.

Concerning Lord Gislebert, we have fulfilled your order that we should send him to you. But the fact that he was sent later than you ordered was not due to negligence [Col. 1163B] but to many hindrances, which it would now take too long to recount.

Know, however, that if anyone causes him to remain in England, he will inflict upon our church a loss—both now and in the future, inwardly and outwardly—so grave and so great that it cannot be expressed briefly, and he will cause sorrow as well.

Therefore, as far as we may, subject to justice and reverence for your holiness, we beg and implore you, by the compassion and charity that we have always known your fatherhood to possess toward us, that, if you see it can be done without opposing God’s will, he be returned through your insistence to brothers and friends who desire him for their certain salvation and the benefit of others, rather than being handed over to strangers, to the danger of his own loss and their uncertain benefit.

In brief, we implore what we greatly desire and believe expedient, knowing that a few words suffice for your wisdom. But if your prudence should recognize that the divine disposition so resists our petition that it must necessarily be otherwise [Note: The manuscript reads “would necessarily be” rather than “must necessarily be”], I entrust to your authority what your prudence would advise me, if I were present, to grant or do in the matter itself [Note: The manuscript reads “would consider” rather than “would advise”].

## LETTER XIV [Note: [Col. 1163C] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO THE MONKS OF BEC. That the monk who, against his abbot’s will, was staying at the monastery of Saint Magloire in Paris for study should return to his own monastery.

Brother ANSELMUS, abbot of Bec, sends greetings to the brothers of Bec [Col. 1164A] [Note: [Col. 1163D] “To those dwelling at Conflans.” From the ambiguity of this expression, I confess, an error had entered my mind: I supposed it to be the town of Cis-Rhenish Germany called Confluent, as Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book 8, chapter 13, puts it: “where the notable river Moselle and the Rhine meet.” I saw nothing that could be objected to this conjecture, except that later I came across the small manuscript chronicle of Bec, specifically under the year 1080: “Count Ivo of Beaumont on the Oise, and his wife Adelaida, wishing Saint Honorina to be served by monks devoted to God at Conflans, gave it, together with everything belonging to it, to the monastery of Bec, under the free authority and governance of the abbots of that monastery. To this donation the revered bishop of Paris, Goffridus, consented, together with the canons of the church of Saint Mary of Paris, concerning the parish and benefice—for it is always the custom of good men to favor good deeds.” And shortly afterward: “In the year 1081 the house of Conflans was founded under the lordship of the abbot of Bec; in the year 1083 the monks of Bec dwelling at Conflans were transferred from the old church, which is called the Chapel, to the new church, together with the body of Saint Honorina.” Conflans, therefore, of which there is now discussion, is Comopolis, six miles west of Paris, where the Oise and Seine meet; hence its name, Conflans, perhaps more correctly Confluent. There is also a village of the same name one thousand paces east of Paris, so called because the Marne and Seine meet nearby.]

Send our letter to Benedict, a monk of Saint Peter above the Dive, who is staying at Paris for study and living in the monastery of Saint Magloire. For I command and advise him to return to his own monastery, from which he is absent against the will of his abbot [Note: The manuscript reads “outside the will” rather than “against the will”]. His abbot has promised me that, if he returns, he will show him mercy and gentleness for love of us [Note: The manuscript reads “mercy for our sake” rather than “mercy and gentleness for love of us”].

If he wishes to do this, help him in every way with charitable concern and kindness, as you would a monk of our monastery, so that he may travel either by horse as far as our monastery or by boat as far as Fraisnos. Do what Lord Rodulf commanded you concerning his horse and the monk of Saint Germain; but do not say that this order came from me—say that it came from Lord Rodulf.

Farewell, and know that, by God’s mercy, I am recovering well from the illness I recently had. Make this known to our friend, Lord Ursio [Note: The manuscript reads “to Lord Ursio” rather than simply “to Ursio.”] We are still awaiting the letters that Lord Mauritius was supposed to send us. Farewell again.

## LETTER XV [Note: [Col. 1163C] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO FULCO. He begs that a repentant apostate monk be treated more mildly.

To the revered lord and father, Abbot FULCO, brother ANSELMUS: fidelity in prayer and service.

Your son, who had departed improperly from your fatherhood, has returned humbly, repentant and prepared for every satisfaction according to your judgment. He does not so much ask that you remit the punishment he deserved as that, through your mercy, you place him at least as the last member within the flock that by his fault he had left.

I therefore beg your holiness not so much to let your strictness consider what he did in sinning [Note: [Col. 1163C] The manuscript reads: “what your severity does through sinning, etc.”] as to let your piety weigh what he does in humble repentance.

Again and again I beg the brothers and our lords, your other sons, to show that they rejoice while entreating your fatherhood’s mercy for him, because “their brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:24).

By what measure you should show this same brother your judgment or your mercy, as it is written, “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Psalm 100:1) [Note: The manuscript reads “I will sing to the Lord” rather than “I will sing to you, Lord”], belongs to your authority and your prudence—only let mercy exalt itself above judgment [Note: The manuscript reads “mercy above judgment” rather than “mercy exalt itself above judgment”].

## LETTER XVI [Note: [Col. 1165B] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO GISLEBERT. He congratulates him on having assumed the governance of the abbey of Westminster.

To his most beloved one, formerly his son by divine disposition, now by God’s grace his fellow abbot, GISLEBERT [Note: [Col. 1165C] Gemmeticensis and the manuscript Chronicle of Bec read *Gisleberto*; Trithemius, followed by Sixtus Senensis, reads *Gislebertus*. In these forms, however, one observes only a transposition of the vowel *e*. Gislebert’s byname was Crispin, and I found the reason for it in the Chronicle of Bec, narrated in these words:

“Before the Northmen, under Duke William, conquered England, there was in Neustria, now called Normandy, an outstanding man named Gislebert, distinguished by birth and nobility. Because of the appearance of his hair, he is said to have first been given the name Crispin. For in the springtime of his youth he had curly and stiff hair, standing erect upward and, so to speak, bristling backward, like the branches of a pine, always tending upward; therefore he was surnamed Crispin, as though *crispus pinus*, ‘curly pine.’ We still see this backward bristling of the hair in those descended from Gislebert’s family. Thus they too are distinguished from the other sons of the Northmen by the same surname.”

This Gislebert, therefore, marked by the surname Crispin, had by his wife Gemoret three sons: Gislebert Crispin of Tillieres, a castle founded in the region of Évreux by William the Bastard, duke of the Northmen, and commonly called Tillieres or Tullieres; Robert, who, because of his military valor and the honor bestowed upon him by the emperor, eventually died after envious Greeks gave him poison; and William, the father of our Gislebert. As we noted above in Letter 10, William married a woman named Eva, who gave birth to Gislebert—the man presently under discussion—who bore both his grandfather’s name and surname.

“His father William,” says the Chronicle of Bec, “offered him in his tender years to the fathers of Bec to be nurtured for God under regular discipline, and with the boy provided much support from his temporal possessions. Instructed by their teaching and the examples of holy conduct, he progressed with divine assistance in divine and philosophical studies, so that he learned all the arts they call liberal down to the last detail, and, himself placed over many, dispensed their streams within religion. His perfection in active and contemplative life was so great that, when God placed Lanfranc over the Church of Canterbury in the highest pontificate, Lanfranc, at God’s call, appointed him to govern Westminster. And he pleased God and human beings, as we believe, by the grace of such holiness that he displayed humility more conspicuously than all the prelates of his time and praised it more especially and more highly. For thirty-two years he benefited the place more than he ruled it; and in a good old age, full of days and holiness, he was gathered to his fathers and brought the end of this life to a close.”

Thus the Chronicle of Bec speaks of Gislebert, the son, monk, and abbot of Westminster. Anyone who reads not only the subject of the letter but also Anselm’s words will see that this passage is especially appropriate here. Florence of Worcester assigns the year 1117 to Gislebert’s death; comparison of this calculation with the number of years for which he presided yields the year of his election, namely 1084. William of Jumièges praises [the word is omitted] his secular and divine learning—for he records that he excelled in both—in book 7, chapter 22, §5 of the *History of the Dukes of Normandy*. The manuscript Life of Herluin, founder of Bec, book 1, and the manuscript Chronicle of Bec—again mentioned in the manuscript Life of Lanfranc and above in Gemmeticensis—also attest him. Besides these are Homily 47 on the *Song of Songs*, said by an addition to Trithemius’s *Commentary on Isaiah*, book 1, to survive at Eberbach; *The Fall of the Devil*, book 1; *On the Soul*, book 1; a book addressed to the cantor of Sées; and book 1, *A Disputation with a Certain Jew*, issued against the Jews, which Trithemius alone mentions and which a manuscript in our library preserves.]

Brother ANSELMUS to GISLEBERT: may you live long in holiness and prosperity in this present life, and happily with eternity in the future.

Although late, because illness hindered me, I write to my beloved friend about the new grace divinely given to him. Yet, as far as benevolent intention is concerned, I speak not coldly: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth joy to people of good will” (Luke 2:14) [Note: The manuscript reads “joy and peace to people” rather than “joy to people”], who has manifested his judgment concerning you—a judgment that he had until now kept hidden with himself, although we had always believed good things about you according to human estimation.

For in that purpose of life in which his grace has always instructed you through wisdom and nurtured you in holiness, he has appointed you father, teacher, and shepherd of souls. Much more should be hoped for you and for those like you, whose life was nourished in holy conduct, than for me and those like me, whose life was formerly worn down by worldly conduct.

For you, when you are promoted to the care of others, one may hope that, while instructing others to resemble you, your righteousness will be perfected. But concerning you one must fear, when we are burdened with so great a weight, lest our injustice be increased by God’s hidden judgment [Note: The manuscript reads “our injustice” rather than “lest our injustice”].

Therefore, the more rightly one should hope for your holiness in the office you have undertaken, the more gladly and securely one should rejoice in the grace granted to you. May almighty God, who has appointed you guardian of others, himself so assist and guard you by his grace that, for your righteousness and theirs, he may repay you with eternal blessedness.

## LETTER XVII [Note: [Col. 1165B] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO HUGH [Col. 1166B]. He wishes the titles of two little works to be changed, one to be called *Monologion* and the other *Proslogion*.

To the lord and venerable father, Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, brother ANSELMUS: in the present age, to live holily; in the future, blessedly.

The weight of your authority makes me give weight to my trifles. Since your eminence values our little works so highly as to deem them worthy of requesting and reading, it seems to me that there is something in them pleasing to so great a man. Therefore I do not think I will be laughed at by your prudence if I consider how these same works ought more suitably to be titled.

I therefore ask that, if you can recover the little books I sent to your holiness at your command [Note: The manuscript reads “at the command of your holiness” rather than “to your holiness at your command”], you cut from their titles what is written there—namely, “On the Reason of Faith”—as superfluous; that you call the work which I named *Monoloquium* *Monologion*; and that you title the other not *Alloquium* but *Proslogion*. In accordance with the correction of the titles, please amend the end of the preface to the shorter book, which speaks of those same titles.

Why I ask that this change be made, if it is made, is neither so necessary to explain nor suitable to the epistolary brevity I have adopted. But if you act according to my request, I wish to repay your fatherhood in this way: if God grants me the opportunity to write what I desire, I will not, I think, withhold from your sight works that will please you no less than the earlier ones.

Your fidelity, which I once commended to my heart, preserves and will preserve it, God protecting; nor does it hope, or will it hope, otherwise concerning the favor of your holiness.

## LETTER XVIII TO THE MONKS OF BEC  
Concerning his prosperous voyage to England.

To his most dear and longed-for lords, the servants of God dwelling at Bec, their servant, brother ANSELMUS: may they advance from virtue to virtue, so that they may deserve to behold the God of gods in Zion.

As soon as I came out of the sea onto English soil, on the Sunday in the middle of Lent, at the third hour, I dictated this letter to make your affection rejoice at the prosperity of our journey. For, by God’s grace favoring your prayers, everything has gone prosperously and honorably—beyond my hope—for me and for those who are with me, on land and sea, since I departed from you.

I therefore ask you, just as you have done until now, to help our pilgrimage by your prayers in the future as well. But I ask much more that you gladden our return by living well.

## LETTER XIX [Note: [Col. 1167D] Compared with the same manuscript.]  
### TO WILLIAM. He persuades a soldier of the world to enlist in the army of Christ.

To his desired one in God, his beloved—and, I hope, his desiring—friend WILLIAM, brother ANSELMUS, called abbot of Bec: may he despise dangerous and wretched vanity and seek the secure and blessed truth.

The Almighty Lord has so occupied my soul with love for you, my beloved and longed-for friend [Col. 1167D]—by his grace, not by my merits—that, caught between the desire for your salvation and fear for your danger, my soul cannot rest from the day-and-night anxieties that spur it on your behalf [Col. 1168A]. Blessed be God in his gifts; would that he had taken from you hatred of your soul as he gave me love for your salvation.

Bear with me, dear friend, and tolerate your lover if I seem importunate to you [Note: [Col. 1167D] The manuscript reads *importunius tibi*, “more importunate to you,” instead of *importunus tibi*, “importunate to you”], and if I speak with you more harshly than you wish. For love of your soul compels my soul and does not allow it to endure your hating the soul whose love it always carries within itself. Receive, therefore, dearest friend, with love the words of your lover, which I ask God to grant you.

You are, beloved, you are what love with sorrow and sorrow with love declares:—may God remove it from you—you hate the soul beloved by my soul; for “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6). Certainly the things in which you take such pleasure, my beloved [Col. 1168B], are iniquity and iniquities. The force of the torrent of worldly ruin that carries you along, my longed-for friend, is iniquity and iniquities.

Iniquity is the bloody confusion of wars. Iniquity is ambition for worldly vanity. Iniquity is an insatiable greed for false goods and false riches [Note: [Col. 1167D] The manuscript reads: “Confusion. Iniquity is an insatiable …” instead of “Iniquity is the worldly vanity’s ambition. Iniquity is an insatiable …”]. Alas for me! I see the one whom I desire to retain by loving him so greatly being dragged along by a cunning enemy deceiving his heart. God, friend of humanity and liberator, do not let the enemy drag away your servant.

You say to me, my longed-for brother: “I do not love these things, but my brother, who is entangled in them; and therefore I hasten to become entangled in them with him, so that I may help and protect him.” Woe—the grievous sorrow arising from the grievous error of Adam’s children! Why, O man, do you not rather say: “I do not love these things, but Christ my God; and therefore, fleeing these things, I hasten to him, so that through him I may be helped and protected”?

When you hear the crash of the collapsing world over your brother, do you despise Christ, who calls you [Note: [Col. 1167D] The manuscript reads *vocante Christo*, “with Christ calling,” instead of *vocantem Christum*, “Christ calling you,”] and run beneath the very ruin, so that a little man may help and protect a little man, a tiny worm a tiny worm, beneath so confused a burden and so burdensome a confusion? Answer, brother: who will help and protect you, the one helping and protecting him? God, whom you strive less to follow than that very brother of yours [Note: [Col. 1167D] The manuscript reads: “Protecting? God … your brother?” instead of “Who will help and protect you, the one helping and protecting him? God, whom you strive less to follow than that very brother of yours.”].

You despise following Christ, who calls you, in peace, in your homeland, and among relatives and friends, so that, as God’s heir and his co-heir (Romans 8:17), you may possess the kingdom of heaven. Yet through so many and such difficult hardships of travel, through the turbulence of seas [Col. 1168D] and stormy tempests, you run into the confusion of war to your brother, so that you may see him—if I may put it so—holding the kingdom of the Greeks. And you think [Note: [Col. 1167D] The manuscript reads *et ut putas*, “and as you think,” instead of *et tu putas*, “and you think”] that God would help and protect him more through you than without you, or you yourself on his account [Col. 1169A] more than for his own sake—or rather, that he would do this much less? For he is angered if he sees anyone loved by anyone more than he is loved [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads: “For he is angered if he wishes …” instead of “or you yourself on his account … For he is angered if he sees …”].

But perhaps you say: “If I begin to follow Christ, I fear that through my weakness I may fail.” Once again and again we must grieve and mourn over the error of the children of humanity. They do not fear failure when they run with all their desire toward things that are always failing—indeed, toward failure itself [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads simply “things that fail,” instead of “things that always fail”]—but they do not dare advance toward God, who never fails and promises his help, because they fear failure. They rejoice in failing so that they may fail, and fear advancing lest they fail.

Believe, I beg you, in God’s counsel, and commit yourself entirely to God’s help; you will not experience failure in God’s service. “Cast, beloved and longed-for friend”—and, dear friend, “cast your burden upon the Lord, and be confident,” since the Holy Spirit promises that “he himself will nourish you” (Psalm 55:23).

Do not delay your great good any longer, and fulfill my desire concerning you, so that I may have you, following after Christ, as my companion; and let us strive together, so that you may see me as yours and I may see you as my companion [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads *possem videre*, “I might be able to see,” instead of *possim videre*, “I may be able to see,”] in Christ’s inheritance, by his gift.

Do not be ashamed to break the chains of the vanity you have chosen; for it is not disgrace but honor to pass into the freedom of truth. Be ashamed to love God less than the treasurer of Beauvais, who, a youth of your age or younger [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads “a younger young man” instead of “a young man of lesser age”], delicate and exceedingly handsome, very rich and noble, and an immoderate lover of the world, once—when I was in England as I am now—came to Bec for some reason. He had intended to depart immediately, but, suddenly changed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he promised that he would remain there as a monk, immediately taking our tonsure and habit, and affirming that he was then happier than he had ever been in his life.

Do not blush to profess yourself Christ’s poor man, because the kingdom of heaven will be yours. Do not fear making yourself the soldier of so great a king, because the king himself will be with you in every danger [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads “in danger” instead of “in every danger]. Do not delay any longer in this life to begin the better way that you have resolved upon, lest perhaps in another life you delay receiving the blessed crown.

I advise, counsel, beg, entreat, and command you, as one most beloved, to leave that Jerusalem which is now not a vision of peace but of tribulation, and to abandon the treasures of Constantinople and Babylon, to be plundered with bloodstained hands; and begin the way to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the vision of peace, where you will find treasures received only by those who despise these worldly ones.

[Col. 1169D] I finish this long letter unwillingly, because my mouth, from the abundance of my heart, desires to speak much to you. May the Almighty God, who causes my heart to rejoice over the man I mentioned above—though with a similar but unequal desire, since I desired him with less hope than I desire you—to rejoice beyond what it hoped [Col. 1170A], not disappoint my greater hope and greater desire concerning you. And if God would deign to inspire this in your heart before my return, know that God is at Bec with our brothers, in my absence as in my presence. May the Lord direct your heart according to his will, and, according to his mercy, satisfy my will concerning you. Amen.

## LETTER XX [Note: [Col. 1169D] Compared with the same manuscript]. TO HENRY. Concerning sending Folcerald to Bec, so that he may live there under Anselm’s direction; he requests a letter secured with that abbot’s seal.

To the reverend lord and father, Abbot HENRY, Brother ANSELM, called Abbot of Bec: lasting prosperity in this life and eternal happiness in the life to come.

[Col. 1170B]

The bearer of this letter reported to me that your holiness was prepared, concerning your son Lord Folcerald [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads “Lord Folcerald”], to fulfill our wish. Since I see neither your letter nor your seal as reliable testimony to the letter, I am not entirely credulous; yet when I remember that, when a friend asks another friend for three loaves, even if he does not rise because he is his friend, nevertheless because of his persistence he rises and gives him as many as he needs (Luke 11:8) [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads “as many as are necessary,” omitting “he has”], I am not wholly incredulous.

For if the laziness of a sleepy friend is overcome at midnight by persistence [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads “the persistence of the night” instead of “at midnight by persistence], how much more will the persistence of so many friends obtain something from your charity?

Therefore, if God has placed it in your heart to grant your aforesaid son entirely to our Church under the governance of its abbot, I do not ask that he return, nor is it expedient that he come back because of the dangerous hardship of the long journey [Col. 1170C] [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscript reads “I ask [for] difficulty” instead of “I do not ask; nor is it expedient that he return because of the dangerous hardship of the long journey”]. I beg, by that same persistence, that a letter bearing your seal show me your unquestionable will. Once we are certain, it will be our concern to determine how we shall receive him.

## LETTER XXI [Note: [Col. 1169D] Compared with the same manuscript]. TO FOLCERALD. That it is not expedient for him to come to Bec in order to return; nor should he be received without letters from his abbot bearing the abbot’s seal.

To his dearest brother in Christ, his kinsman according to the flesh, FOLCERALD, Brother ANSELM sends greetings.

If Lord Abbot Henry is prepared to grant you permanently to our Church—for otherwise I do not advise you to come, since it is not expedient—nor is it easy for a monk to travel such a long journey there and back. You ought to have insisted that he inform me of this by his letter and seal, as I instructed, lest you needlessly force a poor man to labor through so long a journey.

For it is not fitting that I begin so important a matter on the mere word of such a little man [Col. 1170D–1171A]. I therefore advise you either to send, as I said, letters bearing the seal of the aforesaid lord abbot, or to abandon entirely what cannot in any way be done, and commit the whole ordering of your life to divine mercy.

## LETTER XXII [Note: [Col. 1171D] Compared with the same manuscript, the edition, and column 1573]. TO HUGH. He suggests instructions by which Hugh may educate secular people who come to him.

To the most beloved lord and friend HUGH, enclosed, Brother ANSELM, called Abbot of Bec: to be excluded from evils and enclosed in good things.

Two laymen recently came to me, saying that they had been sent by your affection to take something from our instruction, by which they might be inflamed to love their heavenly homeland [Col. 1171B] [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript and edition read “the heavenly Father … they might approach” instead of “their heavenly homeland … they might be inflamed”]. They also reported that you had asked to receive from me something briefly written by which you might incite the minds of secular people who come to you to despise this age and desire the eternal kingdom.

You can accomplish this much better yourselves, insofar as you drink more freely from the sweetness of heavenly life. For what I observe, as it were, from afar, you experience by tasting; what I chew with my fasting mouth in my mind, you swallow with the affection of your heart. What I understand, however imperfectly, about the rightness of holy life, you practice in your works; and what I can speak, however imperfectly, you taste by doing.

Therefore, just as a person who is full belches more sweetly than one who is fasting, so your exhortation, in what it seeks to persuade, will imprint itself more sweetly. Yet because I cannot refuse anything to your will, although you would find what you ask of me expressed much better in the breadth of Sacred Scripture, I shall nevertheless say something according to your request, lest you accuse me of despising it.

Thus I think that someone there who is of limited understanding and unable to grasp higher matters can be invited to desire eternal blessedness in the following way.

Dearest brother, God cries out that he has the kingdom of heaven for sale. This kingdom of heaven is such that no mortal human eye can see its blessedness and glory, no ear hear it, and no heart conceive it (1 Corinthians 2:9)—yet you may conceive it in some manner.

Whoever has deserved to reign there will have in heaven and on earth whatever he himself wills; but whatever he does not will will not exist in heaven or on earth [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript reads “Whatever he wills will not exist” instead of “whatever he does not will will not exist]. For there will be such love between God and those who are there, and among those people themselves, that everyone will love everyone else as himself, but all will love God more than themselves.

For this reason, no one there will will anything except what God wills; and what one wills, all will will; and what one or all will, God himself will will. Therefore, whatever each person wills will be so concerning himself, all others, the whole creation, and God himself.

[Col. 1172A] Thus each person will be a perfect king, because whatever each individually wills will exist; and all together with God will be one king, and, as it were, one person, because all will one thing, and what they will will exist.

God cries out from heaven that he has this reward for sale. If someone asks at what price, the answer is: He who wishes to give the kingdom in heaven has no need of an earthly price; nor can anyone give God something he does not possess, since everything that exists belongs to him.

Yet God does not give so great a thing without any price, because he does not give it to one who does not love it. No one gives what he holds dear to someone for whom it is not dear. Therefore, since God does not need your possessions, and should not give so great a thing to one who despises it, he asks only for love, without which he should not give it. Give love, then, and receive the kingdom; love, and possess it.

Finally [Col. 1172B], since reigning in heaven [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript and edition read “since in heaven,” instead of “since reigning in heaven”] means nothing other than being joined by love with God and with all the holy angels and human beings into one will, so that all may exercise one power together: love God more than yourself, and you are already beginning to possess what you wish to have perfectly with him.

Be in harmony with God and with human beings [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript reads “with God and human beings,” omitting the second “with”], provided that they themselves are not in discord with God; and you are already beginning to reign with God and with all the saints. For to the extent that you now agree with God and with human beings, your God and all the saints will agree with you in your will.

If, then, you wish to be a king in heaven, love God and human beings as you ought, and you will deserve to be what you desire.

But you will not be able to have this love perfectly unless you have emptied your heart of every other love [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript reads “unless you empty it,” instead of “unless you have emptied it”] [Col. 1172C]. The human heart and this love are like a vessel and oil. For just as a vessel takes less oil the more water or another similar liquid it contains, so the heart excludes this love to the extent that it is occupied by another love.

There is also this difference: just as stench is contrary to fragrance and darkness to light, so every other love is contrary to this love. Therefore, just as contraries can never be completely present together, so this love cannot coexist with any other love in one heart.

Hence those who fill their hearts with love of God and neighbor want nothing except what God wills, or what another human being wills, provided that it is not against God [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript and edition read “concerning God” instead of “against God”].

Hence they persist in prayers, heavenly conversations, and reflections; for it is sweet to desire God, to speak and hear about him, and to think about the one whom they love greatly [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript and edition read “whom they love” instead of “whom they love greatly”].

Hence they rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), show mercy to the miserable, and give to those in need, because they love other human beings as themselves.

Hence they despise riches, powers, pleasures, and being honored or praised. For one who loves these things often does something against God and against [Note: [Col. 1171D] The manuscript and edition read “concerning God and concerning” instead of “against God and against”] his neighbor. Thus the whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments (Matthew 22:40).

Therefore, whoever wishes to have perfectly that love by which the kingdom of heaven is purchased should love contempt, poverty, labor, and submission, as holy men do. For “whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14) [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript and edition read “Thus whoever …” instead of “For whoever …”].

I have said these things briefly to you, dearest friend [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript and edition read “these things, dearest friends,” instead of “these things to you, dearest friend”], as you requested; but in explaining them your prudence will be able to produce much more than I have said.

If, nevertheless, your holiness wishes to read something more extensively stated by me about the fullness of eternal blessedness, you can find it at the end of my little book called the *Proslogion*, where I discussed complete joy. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER XXIII [Note: [Col. 1173D] Compared with the same manuscript]. [Col. 1173B] TO PETER. That a cleric cannot be detained unwillingly by an abbot before he has freely promised stability; and that he must remain in the monastery where he first made his petition and vow to become a monk.

To the reverend lord and father, Abbot PETER, Brother ANSELM, called Abbot of Bec: through holiness in the present life to attain happiness in the life to come.

I acknowledge myself to be a brother of your holiness, and that I wish to preserve this brotherhood, as you request. Since you wish this to be made known concerning Lord Ursio the cleric [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “because of the cleric Lord Ursio”], who made his petition and vow to become a monk among you and now remains with us, we shall certainly do nothing less for him than we would ask your charity to do for us.

Know, moreover [Col. 1173C], that he made his petition and vow to become a monk among us before he did so among you. If, therefore, you think that you can justly recall him because of this petition and vow, which he made later, overcome by the persistence of those who pleaded with him, we can much more justly retain him, since he made this earlier promise to us, coming from far away of his own free will and compelled by none of your persuasion [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “not him” instead of “we can retain him”; and “and far away” instead of “coming from far away”]. For he is much more bound to keep the truth in his first free promise than in violating that same first promise.

If you have witnesses and his confession concerning the aforesaid petition and vow, we have more, because we possess his intention together with witnesses and his confession, and we received his promise first [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “confession, not more,” instead of “we have more”].

Finally, your prudence is not unaware that, for however long a novice remains in the monastery in the safety of his own person, voluntarily requesting conversion to the monastic life, before profession, the period is deferred according to our rule in order to test his stability. Meanwhile no one can compel him to remain [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “no one can compel,” instead of “no one can compel him”]; rather, free power to depart is granted to him.

I do not say that he does not sin [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “it is not pleasing,” instead of “I do not say that he does not sin”] if he abandons the good will he has accepted, and if, deceived by the devil’s persuasion, he shudders at what he so often promised with his mouth in a good spirit. But I say that, although he is accused before God of falsehood [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “they are accused,” instead of “he is accused”], it is nevertheless not the abbot’s role to force him to fulfill what he promised.

You recognize that this principle must be observed equally by us and by you [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “since you know this principle,” instead of “you recognize that this principle”]. Therefore, if you wish to bring the aforesaid cleric back to you, send for him. If he wishes, he has free power to depart from us; but if he does not wish to do so, he ought not to suffer accusation from your discretion while remaining with us, nor ought we have any wish to expel him.

In this way I think that I am treating you with the fraternal affection you request: if I were to ask that you do something for me in an orderly manner, I would not refuse to do the same for your brotherhood.

We have explained, in response to your accusation, the reason for our defense [Col. 1174B]; but since this matter is being dealt with between us and you, we do not dare give you advice. Nevertheless, we are not forbidden to say what advice we ourselves would use in a similar matter [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “advice to be given in the matter,” instead of “what advice we ourselves would use in a similar matter].

Our advice would always be that we should not retain any novice against his will if he wished to go to another monastery before that surrender of himself which he makes through the spontaneous acceptance of the cowl. Rather, insofar as we can, we absolve him and, if he asks, offer him our advice and assistance at the same time [Note: [Col. 1173D] The manuscript reads “together, if he asks,” instead of “offer him our advice and assistance at the same time”].

If, abandoning his good will, the monk no longer wishes to be a monk, we do not release him from the vow by which he made himself a debtor; but, inflicting no force upon him, we leave him to God’s reckoning, to whom he made himself a debtor.

If the aforesaid cleric remains with us, and you wish to retain his possessions, which he gave to us as he gave himself, before he made his petition and vow to become a monk among you [Col. 1174C], you will suffer no accusation from us. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV. TO IDA. He gives her great thanks for the benefits conferred upon him and others on his account.

To her most beloved lady, the illustrious Countess IDA, most renowned for the nobility of her lineage and character, Brother ANSELM, servant of the servants of God dwelling at Bec, together with those same lords, wishes to remain until the end in ardent desire for God and to rejoice without end in the desired vision of God.

We would wish with all our heart to give thanks to your revered highness, but we cannot give thanks worthy of the greatness of the goodwill and benefits that you bestow upon us and upon many on our account [Col. 1174D]. We therefore pray that he for whose sake you do so much good to us and to all whom you can may repay you according to the multitude of his riches, as we desire.

Nevertheless, out of the abundance of our love, we urge you not to grow weary in doing good, so that in due time you may reap without weariness. Lord Richard [Col. 1175A], the bearer of this letter, has promised us that, if God grants it to him, he will return to us and remain with us thereafter. We therefore ask your reverence to encourage him according to the wisdom you possess, and, in everything in which he needs your help, to assist him for the love of God and of us.

Greet our lord the count, your husband, and your sons on our behalf, since we have no more faithful messenger to them concerning us than you yourself, just as you would greet your own faithful friends.

## LETTER XXV [Note: [Col. 1175D] Compared with the same manuscript]. TO WILLIAM. That if he loves Anselm, he should come to Bec and flee the world.

To his beloved, his lover, his longed-for friend WILLIAM [Col. 1175B] [Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads “Guillenco” instead of “Guillelmo”], Brother ANSELM, called Abbot of Bec: not to love the world or the things that are in the world, but to be loved by God and to love God.

What should I say first in my letter to my beloved lover, except what my love most demands? The beloved soul of my soul, by sending me a letter blazing with love and fragrant with love, asks me for signs of love and letters of consolation.

What, then, is sweeter, what more delightful, what greater consolation to love, than love? What can I write, therefore, that would console you, my lover [Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads “my love” instead of “my lover”], more than this: my soul loves you so greatly that, unless it holds you, my heart is not consoled concerning you, nor is my desire satisfied.

For when, with such great love and such great insistence, you ask me to love you, you make me love you not only by will but also desire you by necessity. Certainly, nothing consoles one who desires except what satisfies the desire, and nothing torments more than delay.

Your love wishes to be consoled by a letter of my love; my love longs to be delighted by the presence of your love. If, then, you do not wish to torment my soul, satisfy the desire that you have kindled so earnestly and so intensely [Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads “enough” instead of “satisfy”]. How can you tell me that you love me, and, beloved soul of mine, allow my heart to be tormented so that I may love you?

Finally, if your inmost feelings burn with the same love as mine, your soul must melt with the same desire as mine. But how could it be possible for you to wish me to love you while you do not likewise love me?

Do not, then, be cruel [Col. 1175D] to your soul and mine; come and console yours and mine. But when you leave your city, be Lot: do not look back [Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads “do not look back,” without “be”]. Keep your eyes before you, so that you may learn the road by which to come; do not keep them behind you, so that you may forget the road by which to return. Thus, with the Apostle, forget what lies behind and stretch yourself toward what lies ahead (Philippians 3:13).

I say openly: come in such a way that we may live together, if you wish us to console one another. [Col. 1176A]
