I could urge your love, my dearest friend, from many sayings of Sacred Scripture, to despise the world and its desire, if you did not already know the things I would say to you. Remember, dearest friend, that through vanity we pass to truth. Do not love vanity if you wish to obtain truth.

Know that I am setting out for England before this midpoint of Lent and, God willing, will return to our monastery around Pentecost. If, however, God should inspire in you what I desire and what would be beneficial for you, you know that it has always harmed those who are ready to delay [Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads “he knows how to delay,” instead of “it has always harmed those who are ready to delay”]; and there would be people who would receive you with joy, just as, long ago, in my absence, they similarly received Lord Ralph, the son of Lancelin.

May the Almighty Lord go before all your intentions and actions with his counsel, and follow after them with his help, my sweetest friend, dear to my heart.

351

## LETTER XXVI [Note: [Col. 1175D] Compared with the same manuscript]. TO THE MONKS OF BEC. He exhorts them, while the head of the monastery is absent, to live with complete integrity, and explains to them the reasons for his stay in England.

To the dearest lords and brothers, the servants of God dwelling at Bec, Brother ANSELM, their servant: always to advance humbly toward better things and never to fail.

You have done well, because you informed me about the affairs of the late lord Hugh and about those that concern you; and because you made known that God’s grace protects you and yours, you have greatly gladdened me, who have always desired this. Since I know that you likewise desire to know what is happening around me, know that, ever since I departed from you—with your prayers accompanying me—everything has prospered for me, through God’s mercy (1 Esdras 8:23), and for those who are with me. Wherever I am, whether traveling or staying, I am, by God’s gift, no otherwise situated than I would be in our own affairs.

Since the king was unwilling to confirm our charter concerning the possessions we have in England except in the presence of the donors, who had not all been present at the Easter court, he ordered me to wait until Pentecost for his court, where all have now assembled together. When this confirmation has been completed, with God favoring your prayers, I desire to return to those whom I long for and who long for me.

[Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads *et gratia* (“and the grace”) instead of *et quia gratia* (“and because the grace”).]

[Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads *desiderante* (“desiring”) instead of *desiderantem* (“who have desired”).]

It is known to your sweetness, my beloved, that your religion—“pure and undefiled before God and the Father” (James 1:27)—is my desire, and that your good life is my joy in this world.

[Note: [Col. 1175D] The manuscript reads *dilecti mihi* (“beloved to me”) instead of *dilecti mei* (“my beloved”).]

If, therefore, I have earned anything from your charity for the sake of this wish—apart from saying anything about living well—I first ask and beseech you, as the greater matter, that by living well you may gladden my heart, whether I am absent or present, and fill my desire and joy with your goodness. May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds (Philippians 4:7), so that you may be increasingly diligent—for such is what you are by God’s grace—in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3).

Give our most beloved lord Hugh of Gournay and lord Odo, our old friend and our new fellow-soldier, as well as the most dear ladies and our mothers, lady Eve and lady Basilia, our warmest greetings on our behalf, as sweetly as you can; and, by serving and honoring them, comfort them as befits you and them and as you know to be our wish. If I remain longer than I have said, bear with me; for I hope in God that it will not be without some benefit.

[Note: [Col. 1177A] The manuscript reads *de Gornago* (“of Gournay”) instead of *de Gornaco* (“of Gornaco”).]

[Note: [Col. 1177A–B] The editor writes: “Lord Hugh of Gournay,” elsewhere more correctly *Gornaco*. Thus it occurs in Letter 7 of Book II, in Gemmeticensis, Book VIII, chapter 8 of the *History of the Norman Dukes*, and in the charter of Herluin, where it reads: “Hugh of Gournay gave the same monastery the tithe from three holdings which he possessed in England.” Again, in another clause: “Hugh of Gournay gave the same monastery half the mill of the village called Boscis Girardi, which afterward his wife and son granted.” Witnesses: Aufridus the monk, Ralph son of Toraldus, Roger Cochelin, and many others.

“Gournay,” however, is the town in Normandy which still exists, bordering Beauvais and lying westward opposite Beauvais. I have not considered it irrelevant to point this out, since there is also a castle of the same name four miles from Paris, beside the Marne, in sight of the monastery of Chelles.”]

[Note: [Col. 1177B–1180D] The editor adds a lengthy account of Eve and Basilia, whom Anselm calls “mothers.” Both women, he says, showed a mother’s affection toward the monks of Bec.

Eve, a Frank by birth and of noble family, married the equally distinguished William, surnamed Crispin, lord of Neaufles and count and viscount of the Norman Vexin. “Eve,” says the manuscript Chronicle of Bec, “adapting herself to her husband’s character, began above all to love the Church of Bec, embracing the abbot and monks with all her heart as though they were born from her, and venerating them with great devotion. Whatever garments and precious objects she possessed for adornment, she spent for the use of the church and the brothers, and she loved the Mother of the Lord and her Church of Bec with all her heart.

“After her husband William died, she devoted herself entirely to God’s service, living in holy widowhood, intent on fasting and prayers, abstaining from meat and rich food until the end of her life, as far as her sex and age permitted, and giving many alms to the needy. After some years she was veiled by William, archbishop of Rouen, and remained subject to the monastery of Bec until her death. When she died, she was buried beside her husband.”

Thus far the Chronicle speaks of Eve in its account of her husband William, who toward the end of his life put on the monastic cowl at Bec and, after his death there, received burial beside the cloister where the church was to be built.

One page later the Chronicle resumes its account of Eve, Basilia, and Aufrida, Basilia’s niece. I append it here so that it may again be clear why Anselm calls the first two women “mothers.” The Chronicle says:

“In the time of Saint Anselm, abbot of Bec, three noble ladies placed themselves under the authority of that house: Basilia, the wife of Hugh of Gournay; Aufrida, Basilia’s niece; and Eve, the wife of William Crispin. Since these three lived together at Bec, they made an agreement among themselves that they would be taken from this world one after another, and they chose three Sundays on which they would end their lives.

“First came Aufrida, Basilia’s niece, who was advanced in age but, as was said, a virgin in body and consecrated to God. As she awaited the hour of her death, she said to the priors Baldric and Roger and to the others who had gathered for her passing: ‘When I close my eyes, this house seems full of people dressed in white and black.’ They answered: ‘Lady, you will go to the Lord with those dressed in white.’ Not long afterward she died in the deep night, on Sunday, the fourth day before the Nones of January.

“After she had been buried, her lady Basilia began to fall ill. When she had been troubled for several days by severe bodily illness, she was veiled by William, archbishop of Rouen, and then died on another Sunday, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, and was buried as was fitting for such a person.

“The third did not survive her long, for weakened by age and fasting, she suddenly began to lose her bodily strength. After the death of her husband William Crispin, she had devoted herself to complete continence and had persevered at Bec in God’s service until the end of her life. Many years earlier she had received the sacred veil from the aforementioned William of Rouen.

“As her illness increased day by day, and she continued to go daily to the church, on the feast of Vincent she had herself carried into the church in the morning. There she was visited by the whole community and anointed; everything else customarily provided for dying Christians was performed for her. When the community was departing, she raised her hand, blessed them, and said: ‘I commend you to God, my sons.’ For she loved them so tenderly as though she had given birth to them all.

“After she had been carried back home, while she was sitting by the fire, she said: ‘It seems to me that I and this fire are in the church.’ She spent that day and the following night in this state. When she was already nearing death, the brothers were present to assist her with psalms and prayers whenever necessary. Among them was a certain Ralph, son of Lancelin, who asked her, if possible, to appear to him after her death and tell him what she had found.

“She promised that she would, if God allowed it. Thus she died on the third Sunday, the tenth day before the Kalends of February, and was committed to the earth and laid among her own people. A few days after her death she appeared to the sleeping monk who had asked her to tell him what she had found. When he saw her, he said: ‘What is it, lady? How are you?’ She answered that she had received sixty years of penance.

“When he was astonished and asked the reason, she said: ‘Because I loved little dogs and other things of that kind, and took excessive delight in them; therefore I received such a long penance.’

“Thus these three ladies departed from the world on three Sundays. The first, as we have said, died in the first part of the night; the second died at midnight while Matins was being sung; the third breathed out her final spirit in the morning while Prime was being sung.”

Thus far the Chronicle of Bec.

Moreover, how great were the benefits which William Crispin and his wife Eve bestowed upon the monks of Bec is openly declared by this clause of the charter of Herluin: “With the consent of the count of Normandy, William Crispin and his wife gave the aforementioned monastery a son to become a monk, and with him the benefice held by Osbern son of Valo from their household, together with the church situated in the borough called Blangei and everything belonging to it.” Witnesses: Arnulf the priest and Ralph Dastin.

Again, not far from the exact wording of the charter: “William Crispin gave the same monastery the tithe of the mill and of all his lordship which he possessed at Maisnil-Fulbert.” Witnesses: Pagan of Moritania and Gilbert Dastin.

Thirdly: “To the aforementioned monastery William Crispin gave, for the lights of the altar in the borough of Passy, twenty shillings from the toll; and in the borough of Estrepagny, twenty shillings from the toll for the same purpose; and a thirteenth part of all the grain which he possesses in that village, and one hospes. He also gave four pounds of deniers, in addition to the twenty shillings already mentioned, given for the lights in the aforementioned village of Passy, and his entire share in the mills of that village—that is, a sixth part of the mills—and half of all the woodland belonging to him in that village. He also gave forty shillings from the toll of the borough of Linarolt, in addition to the gifts mentioned above. He gave forty shillings from the toll of Blangei. He also gave half of the enclosure called Blancart outright at present, and the remaining half after the death of his wife Eve, with her permission and consent.”

As for the count of the Normans mentioned above, you may think him someone other than William surnamed the Bastard. For in Herluin’s charter he is repeatedly so called, and the following words openly and plainly state that he was the very man who conquered the English: “William, king of the English, confirmed this donation when he was count of the Normans.” Although many noblemen are listed there, and the count is mentioned only by that bare title, he alone is called “count of the Normans,” that is, duke of the Normans.]

## Letter XXVII. To Robert

That he should return to his monastery, from which he had departed without cause and while the abbot was absent.

To his most beloved lord and brother Robert, Anselm sends greetings and the attainment of everlasting life.

I have been told that, after I went to England, you did not wish to remain in your monastery. If this happened with a good intention and for a reasonable cause, it can in some way be tolerated; but if it happened out of resentment, know that I am greatly surprised. For even if you had some reason which seemed right to you for withdrawing from your monastery, you ought, out of love for me, to have waited until you had informed me of the matter which offended you; and afterward, in accordance with our counsel, you ought, as befitted a servant of God, to have calmed your heart.

I therefore ask that, if you love me and my counsel, just as I have always loved and do love you, you come to your monastery and there serve God with the others in a peaceful and kindly way of life. But if you refuse to listen to me, know that this is not beneficial for your soul, and that you grieve me. If it is burdensome for you to keep the things I commended to you, I would rather that you abandon them than that you do anything which harms your soul or reputation. I say nothing now of the unsuitable words spoken about you in England on this account.

May your sweet charity be of benefit to me, and may it do nothing that grieves me, for your kindness is pleasing to me.

## Letter XXVIII. To Haymo and Rainald, Monks

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

That they should put on the cowl at Bec. They had come there from far away in order to visit Anselm, who earnestly exhorts them to do so.

To his most beloved and most longed-for kinsmen, Haymo and Rainald, brother Anselm, servant of the servants of God who dwell at Bec, sends the strength to despise vanity with all their power and to strive toward truth with all their affection.

When I heard, souls most dear to my soul—whom my soul loves as it loves itself, and concerning whom it desires what it desires concerning itself—that you had sought my face from so great a distance, I cannot express how great a joy flooded my heart, how greatly my hope in you expanded, and how my desire for you, already burning, blazed more intensely.

Already, my most beloved, my eyes long for the sight of your faces; my arms reach out for your embraces. My mouth longs for your kisses, and whatever remains of my life desires your companionship, so that my soul may rejoice with you in the complete joy of the life to come.

This is what my burning innermost being wishes and prays for concerning you, my dearest; this it now hopes more confidently and for this it yearns more ardently, because the will of the Most High has brought you to Normandy. For I hope while praying, and pray while hoping, in him who by his grace has accomplished so much, that according to my desire he will complete what he has begun.

But since, until I see what I desire, my longing continues to spur me on, “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). Taste, my most beloved, how sweet the Lord is (Psalm 33:9); but you cannot know this at all so long as the world is sweet to you. You know, my most beloved, that the world and its desire will pass away (1 John 2:17), but God will remain (Psalm 101:13), and all his glory.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] The manuscript reads “the world will pass away, and all its glory” instead of “the world and its desire will pass away; but God will remain, and all his glory.”]

Whoever therefore loves the world pursues vanity and will attain miserable want; but whoever, having despised the world, chooses God follows truth and will find blessed sufficiency.

But why should I delay speaking openly of the desire of my heart? I shall say it: may God persuade you.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] The manuscript reads “I shall say: may God persuade” without the colon.]

My desired ones, you can do nothing better than take up the way of monastic life; and nowhere can you do this better than with the one who desires and is able, God granting it, to serve and counsel you in this matter.

I surely do not deceive you, because I am your friend; and certainly I am not deceived, because I have experience. Let us therefore be monks together, let us serve God together, so that now and in the future we may rejoice together in one another; let us be one flesh, one blood, one soul, one spirit.

In the end, you approached; by approaching you kindled; by kindling you fanned into flame; by fanning into flame you consolidated my soul with your souls.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] The manuscript reads “approaching, kindling” instead of “approaching, you have kindled; by kindling.”]

It can be split apart, but it can no longer be separated. You cannot drag it with you into the world. Either, then, you will remain with it, or you will tear it apart.

But if you cling to it, you are not only kinsmen but also kindred in spirit. If you tear it apart, however, you are not kinsmen but truly blood-related and carnal. If this is why you came, judge for yourselves what kind of men you must be called.

But far be it from you, dearest ones; may God avert it, my beloved, that you should so irreparably wound the soul loving you and innocent toward you, and that you should so intolerably disappoint the good hope I have placed in you.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] The manuscript reads *vos diligentem* instead of *animam vos diligentem* (“a soul loving you”).]

Oh, how my love burns within my heart! How my entire affection struggles to burst forth all at once! How it seeks to express itself in words—yet no words suffice! How much it wishes to bring forth—yet neither time nor paper can contain it!

Speak, O good Jesus, to their hearts, without whom no voice has power over their ears. Tell them to leave everything and follow you. Promise them that, when you come to judge, they will sit with you and judge with you. Do not separate from me those whom you have joined to me with so great an affection of flesh and spirit; but gather them with those whom, while serving you, you commanded to serve me.

Lord, you are the inner witness; and the tears which flow as I write this are the outward witnesses. If they do with me what I desire, how joyful my heart will be! If they do this elsewhere than where I know better than they do what is expedient for such men, how fearful and anxious my mind will be! If they cling to the world, how sorrowful and sad my soul will be!

I speak too much, but immense love compels me. Beloved and longed-for ones, farewell and remain. Remain, I say, and remain steadfast. Would that I might hear before I come that this has begun, and find it so when I arrive!

## Letter XXIX. To Henry

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript and with the Gothic edition and Col. 1575.]

[Note: The edition reads *Anselmus dictus abbas* (“Anselm called abbot”) instead of “Anselm, abbot.”]

[Note: The manuscript and edition read *voluntatis profectionem* (“the advancement of good will”) instead of *voluntatis perfectionem* (“the perfection of good will”).]

[Note: The manuscript and edition read *quod ivistis concessit* instead of *propter quod ivistis, concessit efficere*.]

[Note: The manuscript and edition read *et qua* instead of *de qua*.]

[Note: The manuscript and edition read *et nominis* instead of *et nomina*.]

That he should leave the world as soon as possible.

To his lord, brother, and friend Henry, brother Anselm, abbot of Bec, sends the perfection and fulfillment of good will.

Blessed is God in his gifts and holy in all his works (Psalm 144:17), who has granted your affection the power to accomplish so much of what we desired and for which you went. We pray that he may deign to complete what is still lacking both from our vow and from your reward.

Concerning this matter I am sending you our counsel through our brothers. I greatly rejoice in the duke’s favor and affection, about which you wrote to me; and for this I give thanks to God, to him, and to you. I also intend to do so by letter, when your messengers, as I hear has been arranged, return to him.

Since I do not know whether this will need to happen before I return, send me, as soon as you can, his first name and the names of his wife and sons. I retain only his own name, for he is called Vitalis.

But since your sweet affection has so bound me to itself by its goodness that my heart desires the same for you as for myself, and since I have already conceived great hope from your words, my mind cannot rest until my desire concerning you has been satisfied. Although no speech will suffice for me until God completes what I desire, I shall nevertheless recall a few things in friendly familiarity, since I am not speaking to one who does not know them.

Consider, therefore, dear friend, whatever worldly glory you may possess: what its end is, and at the end what fruit and what reward. And, on the other hand, consider what awaits those who trample worldly glory underfoot.

If you say that not monks alone attain salvation, that is true. But who attain it more securely and more fully: those who strive to love God alone, or those who wish to combine the love of God and the love of the world?

Perhaps someone will say that there is danger even in the monastic order. O man who says this, why do you not consider what you are saying? O rational nature, is this rational counsel: because danger exists everywhere, should you choose to remain where the danger is greater?

In the end, if the one who strives to love God alone preserves his commitment to the end, his salvation is certain. But if the one who wishes to love the world does not abandon his chosen way before the end, his salvation is either nonexistent, doubtful, or lesser. And certainly the one who does not choose what he knows to be more certain and better proves that he loves that good either not at all or very little.

But many say: “God is more greatly angered with a sinful monk than with another person, because he falls from a higher commitment.” This is true so long as he remains in sin. But certainly God receives a repentant monk more kindly and familiarly, if he returns to his commitment, than a non-monk who has not come to that commitment.

For even after a grave sin, the one whose commitment is both before and after the sin—a commitment greater than which he cannot have—is more pleasing to God than the one who neither before nor after a similar sin wishes to make a commitment, though he cannot have a better one.

If, therefore, it is better for both the innocent and the penitent to come to, or return to, the monastic life than to remain away from it, why do you delay? If you are taken from this life first, the loss is irreparable.

I could say much, dearest one, about the greatness and certainty of the monastic life, and about its peace and joy, if the letter did not exceed its proper limits. Hurry, therefore, toward so great a good, for you will come to the highest good by no good means more effectively.

I have seen many people promise this and postpone it; death carried them away in such a way that they neither completed the undertaking by which they were hindering themselves nor began the one they were promising. I greatly fear this for you; but may God avert it from you, dearest one. Farewell, and do not delay.

[Note: [Col. 1181D] The manuscript reads *ne hoc inciperent* instead of *nec hoc inciperent*.]

## Letter XXX. To Walchelm

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

That a monk given for a limited period cannot be retained against the will of the abbot who demands his return. He also intercedes for Gilbert.

To the lord and revered father Walchelm, bishop of Winchester, brother Anselm sends the fidelity of prayer and service.

[Note: [Col. 1181D] The manuscript more correctly reads *Walchelinum* instead of *Walchelmum*.]

In accordance with what I knew to be your wish, I spoke with the lord abbot of Mount Saint Trinity. He entirely denies that his predecessor, lord abbot Rainer, made you any grant concerning lord Stephen, a monk of his monastery. He thinks thus to assert this denial, because he says that he granted the same brother to you at your request on the condition that, whenever he was recalled by that abbot, or afterward by the prior of his monastery, he would return without excuse; and that your reverence received him without compulsion.

[Note: [Col. 1183D] The manuscript reads “he thinks thus” instead of “he thinks he can support this.”]

Nevertheless, I persuaded him as much as I could not to hasten anything against your will. Whatever he now wishes, he has either already written to you or will write to you; meanwhile, let all offense concerning the delay of the brother’s return be removed.

[Note: [Col. 1183D] The manuscript reads: “What he finally wishes to write to you, he has either already written or will write.”]

In the meantime, if I can accomplish anything more with him, I shall try, according to what I know to be your desire in this matter.

Lord Robert, our brother and fellow-servant under your holiness—whom I would like to call one devoted to you, because I know it to be so, but I do not dare, since perhaps not everyone who hears believes—placing I know not what confidence in me, presses me insistently to intercede with your piety on behalf of my brother Gilbert.

But it is always very difficult for me to ask anything of anyone against that person’s will, especially of one whose kindness I never wish to offend. Thus I am hemmed in on every side. If I am not moved by appeals to your piety, I shall be excessively hard; but if I extort something by entreaties from one who is unwilling, I fear that I may appear importunate even in asking for something which ought to be granted voluntarily.

Since, therefore, I dare neither remain silent nor ask, at least let your servant humbly question your kindly wisdom in order to learn. For “the lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Matthew 2:7).

I therefore desire to be taught by your wisdom: if before God a father does not bear the iniquity of his son, nor a son that of his father, does a brother bear the iniquity of his brother before a kinsman?

For we see this happen not only among many strangers but also among certain relatives whose authority is not easily to be criticized. In the end, just as it is true that “every soul is mine: the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son” (Ezekiel 18:4), so it seems plausible that, just as a brother’s flesh is his own, so is the flesh of his blood-relative brother; and if anyone’s guilt passes to a kinsman, a son is nearer to his father than a brother is to his brother.

If, therefore, this question seems capable of solution to your piety, let it teach the aforementioned Gilbert, since he is nearby, its solution; and let him entrust the answer he has received to me, who am in doubt about it.

Farewell.

## Letter XXXI. Pope Gregory to Anselm

He commends himself and the Church to Anselm’s prayers and commands him to do justice to one of his converts.

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Anselm, venerable abbot of Bec: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Since the good fragrance of your fruits has wafted all the way to us,” and so forth. See the text above under Gregory VII, volume 148 of the *Patrologia*.

## Letter XXXII. Urban II to Anselm

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

That he should assist a bishop inexperienced in ecclesiastical affairs; that he should not delay visiting the Apostolic See; and that he should send to it what Hubert, his legate and subdeacon, had collected from the revenues of Saint Peter.

Urban, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Anselm, venerable and most beloved abbot: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Knowing the distinction of your religion and learning,” and so forth. The text appears above under Urban II, volume 151 of the *Patrologia*.

## Letter XXXIII. Anselm to Urban

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

He explains the severe persecution which the bishop of Beauvais suffers from both clergy and laity, and asks for an Apostolic See privilege for his monastery against episcopal domination.

To the revered lord Urban, supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church, brother Anselm, with due submission, sends the faithful service of the servants of God who dwell at Bec.

I give thanks with mouth and heart, as much as I can, to your highness, because your kindness has deigned to honor my littleness with a letter and to gladden me with apostolic blessing. For the tribulation of you and the Roman Church, which is the tribulation of us and of all truly faithful people, we do not cease to pray constantly to God, asking that he may give you relief from evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner (Psalm 93:13).

We are also certain—even if it seems to us that he is still delaying—that he will not allow the rod of sinners to rest upon the lot of the righteous (Psalm 124:3), because he will not abandon his inheritance (Psalm 93:14), and the gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).

Concerning our most beloved bishop of Beauvais, whom I compelled to undertake the episcopal burden after carefully investigating his character and entry into office, with all the diligence I knew and could exercise: I was compelled in many ways by the religious—for so far as I could understand it—insistence of the king of the Franks, the clergy of Beauvais, and many others, with the consent of the archbishop of Reims, and with no one resisting, lest I fear offending God if I failed to do so.

Your holiness knows with what intention, after he had undertaken the episcopate, he once sought it [the Apostolic See], what he did, and how he returned. Why he now presents himself once more before your majesty will become known more fully through his own speech than through our letters. For I know that he detests falsehood, especially in this matter before you, and hopes, because of the purity of his conscience, that truth is not opposed to him in this case.

But when the matter itself has been carefully examined, neither will your prudence need our counsel nor will justice need entreaties. I shall therefore say only this now: whether the matter has already come to your knowledge through someone else, or whether it is about to do so, I do not know; but the fact is that this same bishop suffers no small persecution for the sake of justice (Matthew 5:10), which he strives to preserve in obedience to your command.

For the canons and priests of his bishopric—apart from very few—and certain laymen are inflamed with such hatred against him, and kindle outsiders, whoever they are and by whatever means they can, so that they immoderately detest not only him but also those who offer him any assistance, and try to portray them as detestable, that he may be able to say with the Prophet:

“All day long they curse my words; all their thoughts against me are for evil. They inhabit and hide themselves; they watch my heel” (Psalm 55:6).

The canons and priests do this to him because he wishes to prohibit them from wicked customs, especially improper relations with women; and because he tries to prevent their sons, or those whom they choose as heirs according to their own pleasure, from succeeding hereditarily to prebends and from advancement to sacred orders.

The laymen act thus because he does not wish to support their disorderly invasions of ecclesiastical property.

I therefore consider it very necessary, and humbly ask you as my lord, to send him back strongly strengthened by your letters. Thus, by commending him to the archbishop of Reims and to the other neighboring bishops, to the clergy and citizens of Beauvais, and to the nobles of that bishopric, may your authority protect him against malevolent schemes, so that in carrying out your commands he may find them not so much adversaries as allies.

I venture to ask some favor from the generosity of your kindness for the Church of Bec. But this boldness rises not so much from my own presumption as it descends from the reverent and most dear kindness which you have deigned to show toward my littleness in letters sent through the aforementioned bishop of Beauvais and in words conveyed to me by him and by certain others.

It is indeed a new circumstance that our monastery has not yet been confirmed by any antiquity, by any apostolic authority, or by any privilege, but has been divinely preserved in your time and by the command of your clemency. Therefore, so that it may rejoice to be honored and confirmed by some gift of your authority, according as your religious discretion judges best, we put forward no merits of our own; rather, we entrust the matter to the will of God and to your kindness.

For I do not think it is unknown to your excellence that many bishops take not so much pleasure in nourishing monasteries with fatherly kindness and instructing them through episcopal care as in burdening them with a certain harsh domination and according to their own will.

Nevertheless, under the fatherly sanctity of our revered archbishop William, our faithful and beloved friend, we have no fear.

[Note: [Col. 1185C–1186D] The editor supplies a lengthy historical note on Archbishop William of Rouen. He was William, archbishop of Rouen, to whom Letter 68 of Book III is addressed and whom the manuscript Chronicle of Bec frequently mentions. According to William of Jumièges, he succeeded John, who died in 1079. He was a nephew of Rathbodus—or, according to the manuscript table of the bishops of Sées preserved at Saint-Victor, a nephew of Bishop Rathbandus—and a monk of Saint-Étienne at Caen, eventually becoming abbot after Lanfranc.

The Caen monks later replaced him, when he was appointed archbishop of Rouen, with Gilbert of Coutances, as William of Jumièges records. In 1081 he held a synod at Lisieux, attended by many bishops and by William the Bastard, king of the English, according to Matthew Paris in his *Greater History*.

That archbishop alone, as though he regarded the thunderous bolts of papal anathemas everywhere as nothing, arranged the incestuous marriage of Philip, king of the Franks, with Bertrada, wife of Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou, as all the Frankish annals recount. I do not, however, find this Bertrada among Fulk’s wives in the *Treatise on the Counts of Anjou* preserved in manuscript at the Victorine Library.

Because of these marriages, wrongly and improperly joined by William, Pope Urban was so enraged against him that the interdict remained for many years; Anselm, otherwise a close friend of Urban, could scarcely reconcile them. This is noted by William of Malmesbury in Book V of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*. Indeed, he did not reconcile them. For in Letter 140 of Book III of our Anselm’s letters, near the end, he says: “We have entrusted to your deliberation the case of the archbishop of Rouen and the interdict pronounced by justice. Whatever you shall grant, I grant,” and so forth.

This was the year of William’s election mentioned above; the manuscript table of the archbishops of Rouen and the notices of Anthony Du Chevalier confirm this. To the same William there is also extant Letter 80 of Ivo of Chartres. He died in 1110, and was succeeded by Geoffrey, dean of Le Mans, according to the same table and to William of Jumièges, Book VIII, chapter 14 of his history.]

Your servants, our fellow-servants and my lords, the brothers of our community, who do not cease to pray with me each day for your fatherhood, desire to commend themselves with me to your prayer and blessing.

[Note: [Col. 1185C] The manuscript reads “to be commended” instead of “to commend themselves.”]

## Letter XXXIV. To Urban

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

He fears that the bishop may be overwhelmed by such severe trials and wishes him to be released from the episcopate.

To his revered lord, the universal pontiff of Christians, Urban, brother Anselm sends what belongs to him.

Concerning the bishop of Beauvais, what I think I shall say briefly, but with great feeling, and I desire it to be known to your piety. He is accomplishing nothing in the episcopate; indeed, he is himself prevented from exercising proper care. He benefits neither the affairs of the Church nor, in the future, do I—or any of those who know the matter and wish to consider it according to God—expect anything better, but rather something worse. This is not because there is any fault of ill will in his innocent life, but because he is not the sort of man who can bear so great a burden or beware of such wickedness rushing upon him and so many surrounding snares.

Therefore I greatly fear that he may be swallowed up by an excessive sorrow, in which his heart is deeply afflicted and by which he is bound by no other bond than your sole command. For this reason, I and his other friends according to God prostrate ourselves with him at the feet of your mercy, asking that it open its innermost compassion to him and mercifully rescue him from so great an evil and danger, in which he feels himself to be without benefit. Do not prevent a gentle lamb from fleeing from the midst of wolves and lions surrounding and rushing upon it; nor prevent an innocent boy from coming out of the furnace of the Chaldaeans. Your Excellency will be able to hear from that very man how, in my humble judgment, this might most suitably be done, if you are willing.

For in that way, unless your prudence judges otherwise, wickedness will in no way boast that it has prevailed through falsehood; rather, innocence will rejoice that it has escaped through freedom of mind. Perhaps your wisdom may wonder why I seem to be so inconsistent with myself [Note: The manuscript reads “since thus”; the edited text reads “why thus”]: I compelled him to become a bishop, yet now I wish him to leave the episcopate. But I confess to the one before whom I must not conceal my conscience that I perceived and foretold the evils he now suffers when he was being sought for the episcopate. Yet those who sought him with great insistence and, in agreement, pressed upon me overwhelmed my judgment with their own.

I feared to assert in my heart that God was more present in my solitary perception and will than in the unanimity of many who loudly declared that they were seeking him simply for God’s sake. This also presented itself to my mind: God often works more through the life of the unlearned who seek what belongs to God than through the cleverness of the learned who seek what belongs to themselves [Note: MS: “through the life of those seeking what belongs to God, rather than through the cleverness of those seeking what belongs to themselves”; edited text: “through the life of the unlearned seeking what belongs to God, rather than through the cleverness of the learned seeking what belongs to themselves”].

Behold, before you is the reason why I consented to his becoming a bishop, and why I now desire to change what I consented to under compulsion. It is subject to your judgment whether what I am doing and what I did ought to be punished, corrected, or accepted.

May almighty God long preserve your fatherly holiness for us in complete prosperity. Amen. I desire and earnestly request that this letter be known only to you, if it pleases you, whatever your judgment of it may be.

## Letter XXXV

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript. See Letter 41 and Letter 51 below.]

### To John

[Col. 1187D]

Concerning the false and impious assertion of a certain man who said that the three Persons in God are three things.

To his lord and beloved brother JOHN, brother ANSELM, may he always advance toward better things.

As for the letter your affection sent me concerning the man who says that the three Persons in God are three things, or that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate together with the Son, I delayed answering for so long because I wished to speak more fully about the matter. But since, with many occupations hindering me, I have not been able to do so after receiving your letter [Note: The manuscript reads “after receiving the letter”; the edited text reads “after receiving your letter”], I shall meanwhile answer briefly. In the future, if God deigns to grant the opportunity, I intend to discuss it more extensively.

When, therefore, he says that the three Persons are three things, he either wishes this to be understood according to the three relations—that is, according to the fact that God is called Father, Son, and the Spirit proceeding from the Father and from the Son [Note: MS: “and the Son” (*et filio*); edited text: “and from the Son” (*et a filio*)]—or according to that which is called God [Note: The manuscript reads “according to which”]. But if he says that those three relations are three things, he says this superfluously. For no one denies that, in this sense, the three Persons are three things. Nevertheless, it must be carefully understood in what way the relations themselves are called things, and what sort of things they are; and whether those same relations do anything with respect to the substance, as many accidents do, or not.

Although he does not seem to understand the three things he mentions in this way, since he adds that the three Persons have one will or power. For those three Persons do not have will or power according to their relations, but according to the fact that each Person is God [Note: MS: *persona Deus*; edited text: *persona Deus est* (“each Person is God”)]. If, then, he says that the three Persons are three things according to the fact that each Person is God, he either wishes to establish three gods, or he does not understand what he is saying.

To show what I think of the opinion stated above, let these remarks suffice for the present to your affection. As for your request that I remain with you before you depart for Rome, know that, insofar as concerns your honorable affection, I would gladly wish to do so. But insofar as I understand the matter, it would be of little use to you because of my many occupations and would be an impediment to you. For I have clearly perceived that, unless you remain with the bishop until you depart, he himself will help you little or not at all in what you must do; nor can I do anything for you that would be of value in undertaking the journey.

## Letter XXXVI

### To Gislebert

He praises the manner of life established by the abbot. He leaves to him a brother whom he had brought back to the cloister.

To his friend, brother, lord, father, beloved and revered beloved, the abbot GISLEBERT, brother ANSELM: holiness persevering in a long life with prosperity, and unfailing happiness in eternity [Col. 1188D].

If I wished to write about the affection of our mutual love, I fear that I would either seem, to those who do not know, to exceed the truth, or would have to subtract something from the truth. Although I knew how great and genuine that affection was when it displayed itself eye to eye, kiss to kiss, embrace to embrace, I now experience it much more deeply when I see him irrecoverably absent—the one in whom I delighted with such great joy.

For just as the prosperous person does not know what need is, and one who abounds in delicacies does not know what hunger is, so one who enjoys a friend does not feel the soul’s languor when deprived of him. Since, therefore, what we are to one another can neither be adequately written nor am I speaking to one who does not know, let these matters meanwhile be set aside. I pray with you that, when at some time we see each other again eye to eye, kiss to kiss, embrace to embrace, we may recall our love, not having forgotten it.

Regarding what your charity has deigned to explain to me about your manner of life, I give thanks to God, because I can see nothing there that is not praiseworthy. Concerning that brother whom you brought back to the cloister, I grant what you wish until it appears otherwise to you or to us; but let your prudence examine his hidden matters and counsel him as it judges appropriate.

I am astonished and grieve over the loss you reported. As for the fact that your charity deigns to excuse itself because you cannot now do what you would wish, I give thanks for your graciousness and good will. Concerning lord Lanfranc, I have known or been able to do nothing better than what I did and said in England. Farewell.

## Letter XXXVII

### To Ida

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

What one who wishes to avoid falling short ought to strive toward: progress.

To his revered and most beloved lady, the countess IDA, brother ANSELM: may she reach eternal things through temporal goods.

[Col. 1189C]

Just as the true love I have for your reverence according to God cannot fail in its integrity, so it ought never to fail in wholesome exhortation. Although, therefore, I always hope that your prudence looks out for itself in every way, lest the crafty enemy be able by some deception to violate your resolve to live well, nevertheless it must not be judged superfluous if I merely urge you to practice more earnestly what you practice well.

For no one is sufficient to preserve the joy of the good life he has already ascended to if he does not always desire to advance to something higher. Therefore the person who always wishes to avoid falling short must always strive toward progress. Thus may your reverence—or rather, may God—always and everywhere guard your heart, mouth, and actions, so that your life may never and nowhere fall into great or small guilt [Note: The manuscript reads “into great or small guilt”; the edited text reads “in great or small guilt”].

I reported to the king of the English the matter of the monastery you had requested from me, but he certainly did not approve my doing it. Send us lord Richard’s silver by the bearer of this letter [Note: The manuscript reads “by the present bearer”]. Farewell.

## Letter XXXVIII

### To Robert

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

One who intended to sin but was divinely prevented, and afterward rejoices that he did not sin, is not guilty as though he had committed the crime after being abandoned by God.

To his lord and father, the revered abbot ROBERT, father ANSELM, called abbot of Bec: prosperity in this life and happiness in the future life.

In answering your reverence about the matter concerning which, through your son William, you deign to seek the advice of my humble self, I would like to set forth examples and authorities. But because his haste and my occupations hinder me—as he himself bears witness—I am scarcely permitted to explain the truth of the matter simply.

No Catholic’s prudence is unaware that, just as the person who wishes to do a good work but is prevented, and afterward rejoices that he was unable to do what he rightly wished, is not to be praised for failing to do the good he had resolved upon, so the person who plans to perform an evil work but is not permitted to do so, and afterward rejoices that he was not handed over to his desire, must by no means be judged to have committed the crime he intended.

For although, as long as someone remains in the will to commit a crime, he is to be judged guilty of that crime if he ends his life in that state, there is nevertheless a great difference between the person whom the anger of the heavenly Judge abandons even to a rejected action and the person whom grace, rescuing him from the precipice of the deed, restores to a good will.

The one who tries to attribute the same guilt equally to these persons is therefore greatly blameworthy, since divine wisdom has willed to order their evil wills so differently. The person who either falls into the act or is abandoned in a malicious intention is to be marked with the name of criminality—not the person who is neither plunged into the work of evil nor drawn out of a perverse intention.

The latter has been preserved from that for which he can joyfully give thanks; the former has been abandoned to that for which he must sorrowfully seek pardon. It is certain that the latter will receive a reward for such joy; for the former it is much if, through sorrow for sin, he escapes punishment.

I would have liked to write more, but since, as I said, I am not permitted to do so, accept these remarks as testimony to what your aforementioned son will report to you from our living voice, even if interrupted [Note: The manuscript reads “testimonies to what”; the edited text reads “as testimony to what”]. Receive them without criticism. Farewell.

## Letter XXXIX

### To Lambert

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

He exhorts this noble man to the monastic life.

To his beloved and desired in Christ, LAMBERT, brother ANSELM, abbot of Bec: with all his heart may he despise the vanity of this world and strive toward eternal truth.

[Col. 1190D]

My most beloved brother and son, lord Rodulf of Beauvais, formerly your companion and now your true friend and one who longs for you, has told me so much about your nobility and the uprightness of your character [Note: The manuscript reads “and of your character”; the edited text reads “about your nobility and the uprightness of your character”], which adorns the nobility of your birth, that my heart is compelled by no small affection both to love you while longing for you and to long for you while loving you.

Therefore, since my soul wishes to love your soul neither less nor more than itself, it cannot desire anything for it other than what it desires for itself. This, then, is my desire for you: that, leaving the world, you follow Christ, and through temporal humility and poverty attain eternal exaltation and riches.

Let no carnal occasion hold you back or delay you, my beloved. For certainly it is neither wise nor expedient to lose, diminish, or even postpone eternal good for the sake of temporal good. If heavenly grace deigns to inspire you with this—would that my eyes might see it—and if, according to my desire, you deign to choose my companionship and counsel for this, my soul, already opening wide its arms to meet you, sings to you:

> “My heart is ready, my beloved; my heart is ready” (Psalm 56:8).

Farewell, most sweet one, farewell. Remember continually how uncertain and brief human life is, and how infinite are the goods or evils that follow.

## Letter XL

### To Ermengarda

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

She had vowed continence with her husband’s consent; but when her husband wished to become a monk, she was unwilling. Therefore Anselm begs her to consent.

To the lady ERMENGARDA, beloved in God, brother ANSELM, abbot of Bec: greetings and faithful prayers [Note: The manuscript reads “and faithful prayer”; the edited text reads “and faithful prayers”].

Although I do not know you by sight, I belong to that order which ought to wish well and give salutary counsel to all people. No one, therefore, ought to find it surprising if I admonish your reverence according to what I hear to be expedient.

I have heard, most beloved lady, what the situation is between your husband and you, since your nobility does not permit this to remain hidden but causes it to be proclaimed far and wide. In this matter I first give thanks to God, from whom every good comes: he has given your husband such constancy that he despises temporal glory, and has granted you to endure so manfully so many tribulations in defense of chastity. Yet this must be so understood that, in despising the world, he does not love himself more than you, nor should anything in this world be dearer to you than he.

Certainly, in this both of you are beloved by God and good people; both are praiseworthy. Indeed, in such great and genuine mutual love, you should be understood to love not so much your bodies as your souls. For by no care or mutual love can you rescue your bodies from temporal death; but, if you know how to govern your love rightly, you can acquire eternal life for your souls.

What is it, then, revered woman, woman of proven chastity, what is it that compels you to hinder your husband from seeking the salvation of his soul perfectly, which you love no less than your own? You must not even think that you do this for the sake of the vile pleasure of the flesh, which you despised so thoroughly after he had departed from you that, when you could not have him, you endured many tribulations and rejected many persuasions rather than take another husband.

But if you hold back his soul from advancing toward its salvation for the sake of temporal glory and advantages, which you love and which you hope to retain through him, how do you love that soul when you place your uncertain, worthless, and transitory advantages before its sure and eternal good [Note: The manuscript reads “you propose”; the edited text reads “you place before”]? Or how can you demand that he put the eternal goods of his soul after the temporal goods of your body, if you place the goods of your body before the goods of his soul?

See, therefore, most beloved lady; see, strong and prudent woman; see whether, if you do this, you are not governing your love well and loving your husband, who loves you, rightly. What if you compel him to abandon concern for his soul in deference to your will, and then, when your death or his occurs—or when some other circumstance, as often happens, strikes—he is of no benefit to you and you do him harm? Indeed, if you harm his soul, you harm your own.

Oh, how much better, revered lady, how much more praiseworthy, you show that you love your husband if you not only permit but also advise and help him to strive, with God’s inspiration and assistance, to complete what he has begun! If, by loving his good, you make it your own; if you believe with complete certainty that the more firmly you abandon human assistance for the love of God and neighbor, the more familiarly and securely you entrust yourselves to divine protection.

Let your prudent strength and strong prudence therefore trust in God. Just as, if that husband were dead, you would endure his absence unwillingly, without benefit to either him or you, so, while he lives, willingly endure that absence for the sake of his great reward and yours. Grant him the freedom to do what he desires, so that you may share his reward.

For if God cares for widows who are widows not for his sake, he will cherish much more the woman whom he sees willingly widowed for love of him. If it should happen—which perhaps it will not—that you lose earthly honor, do not grieve, because you will receive a better one in heaven. And certainly, when something is greatly despised by better and wiser people, it is not a matter for great grief if it is lost.

I would have liked to offer further counsel, but I do not dare; yet I am not afraid to pray. May almighty and merciful God grant you contempt for the world, just as he granted it to your husband, so that in the heavenly kingdom you may be your husband’s equal, a sister and a lady beloved in God.

## Letter XLI

### To Falcon

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

Concerning Roscelin, who claimed that Lanfranc and Anselm agreed with him that there are three things in God and that they could truly be called three gods if usage permitted it.

[Col. 1192D]

To his most beloved lord and friend, the revered bishop of Beauvais, FULCO, brother ANSELM, called abbot of Bec: greetings.

I hear—although I cannot believe it without reservation—that the cleric Roscelin says that the three Persons in God are three things separated from one another, as three angels are, yet in such a way that there is one will and power; or that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate, and that they could truly be called three gods if usage permitted it. In this opinion he asserts that Lanfranc, of venerable memory, held the same position, and that I do as well.

Therefore, it has been said that a council is to be convened shortly by the venerable archbishop of Reims, Rainald [Note: This council is mentioned again by Anselm in chapter 1 of *On the Incarnation of the Word*. The archbishop to whom Ivo of Chartres’s Letter 13 is extant is also mentioned; there he is called Rainaldus—as in the preface to Anselm’s book *On the Incarnation of the Word*—though Rainoldus would be the more exact form. Thus I read it in the Tables of the archbishops of Reims apud Democnar. and in the privilege which he himself, in the third year of his pontificate, granted to Theodoric, the second abbot of Saint-Hubert in the Ardennes.] Therefore, since I think your reverence will be present there, I want you to be instructed about what you ought to answer on my behalf if reason requires it.

As for Archbishop Lanfranc, his life was known to many religious and wise men [Note: “Archbishop Lanfranc, whose life was known to many religious men, etc.” I do not know with what audacity this scoundrel—Roscelin—dared to accuse Lanfranc, an otherwise wholly upright man, not even slightly suspected of heresy, indeed its most vehement enemy, of so serious an error. Yet what would he not dare against the holiest men, if he does not hesitate to wage war against God himself like the giants of old? Although Anselm’s faith and authority are sufficient among all Catholics to clear his teacher of the charge, a defense drawn from Lanfranc’s own words would nevertheless be more welcome and more powerful. We shall provide it after first stating Roscelin’s conclusion, which Anselm reports as follows:

> “The cleric Roscelin says that the three Persons in God are three things separated from one another, as three angels are, yet in such a way that there is one will and power; or that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate, and that they could truly be called three gods if usage permitted it.”

This impious conclusion of Roscelin can be overthrown by these words of Lanfranc, written to Rainald, bishop of Poitiers:

> “The Lord Jesus Christ, in the same Person, is true man and true God. According to his humanity, he hungered, thirsted, and, by assuming the other weaknesses of human nature, assumed a man apart from sin; according to his divinity, by which he is in all things equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, he endured none of these things.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Only-Begotten of the Father came into the world in such a way that he nevertheless never departed from the Father’s bosom.”

And shortly afterward:

> “This manner of speaking was stated above because blows and wounds inflicted on the man assumed by the Son of God brought upon him the force of suffering.”

And a third time:

> “Otherwise, if that aforesaid teacher”—he means Saint Hilary of Poitiers, whom he clears of Gaianism, while Berengar the sacramentarian had heaped that charge upon Hilary—“had wished the flesh to be understood as insensible and incapable of suffering, he would certainly not have referred, in the statement mentioned above, to the man assumed by the Son of God as a man like us.”]

Lanfranc, when he says in these passages that Christ, in the same Person, is true man and true God, and attributes the assumption of human nature to him alone, plainly professes that Christ alone was incarnate. Moreover, when he says that Christ was true God in the same Person and, according to his divinity, was in all things equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, he clearly teaches that three gods cannot be said to exist.

For numbers were instituted to signify the multiplicity of things; therefore, where you find something that is unique, multiplication is entirely pointless. But according to Lanfranc, Christ is, in his divinity, in all things equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit—that is, he is altogether the same, according to the Athanasian Creed:

> “As the Father is, so is the Son; and so is the Holy Spirit.”

Roscelin has therefore divided one and the same nature with his impious and wicked calculations.

Lanfranc’s final statement also plainly demonstrates the unseparated and inseparable connection of the divine natures: he says that the Only-Begotten of the Father came into the world in such a way that he nevertheless never departed from the Father’s bosom. For who, when something is never separated from another, would weaken the statement by saying that it was separated?

Would that the diligence of our predecessors had consulted Lanfranc’s commentaries on the letters of Saint Paul, listed by Peter of Christiavilla, a monk of Bec, in the catalogue of the Library of Bec in 1483, as I read in the Library of Bec. From these I would have produced many more testimonies, by which we might rightly accuse Roscelin of *stellionatus*—fraudulent sophistry.

“This charge is sufficiently disproved both by his absence and by his death.” Not every death provides an excuse, but especially a death unaccompanied by any sinister rumor of heresy, as Anselm testified shortly above concerning Lanfranc.

His death occurred in the year of Christ 1089, the nineteenth year of his pontificate and the third year of William surnamed Rufus, king of the English, according to Henry of Huntingdon, book II; Matthew of Westminster in the *Flores Historiarum*; Roger of Howden in the *Annals*; and the archiepiscopal records of Canterbury [Col. 1197B] in our manuscript library, in these words:

> “In the third year of William Rufus, king of the English, Lanfranc, metropolitan archbishop of Canterbury, died and was buried in the basilica of the Holy Trinity—which he himself had built with magnificent workmanship—before the Crucifix. He sat for nine years, and the see was vacant for five years. Lanfranc, jewel of priests and flower of monks, archbishop of Canterbury, died in England on the fifth day before the Kalends of June.”

Concerning this venerable Father, many things are related—written by Gilbert Crispin, a contemporary of Herluin and Lanfranc and a monk of Bec—“in the *Deeds of Herluin, abbot of holy memory, and of Anselm, his successor, and in the *Deeds of the Normans*.” Thus reads the manuscript account concerning Lanfranc.

The writers, however, agree neither about the month of his death nor about the day. Roger of Howden; the earlier part of the *Annals of Florence*; and the Worcester writer in the *Chronicle* reckon the ninth day before the Kalends of June; Matthew of Westminster the ninth day before the Kalends of April; Matthew Parker, in *The Ancient British Church*, the fourth day of June; Peter of Equilinus, book VI of the *Catalogue*, chapter 47, the fifth day before the Nones of July; Bale, *British Writers*, century 13, the fifth day before the Kalends of July; and the Canterbury Tables and the manuscript *Chronicle of Bec*, the fifth day before the Kalends of June.

If anyone should accuse me of being too scrupulous or overly concerned with an almanac, he should know that I have made ample provision for myself and have anticipated his scruples, should he press any of them. For from these differing calendars he can nevertheless derive a calculation more consistent with the evidence: namely, that June witnessed Lanfranc’s death.

The authors also disagree substantially about the year. Of those mentioned above, the more accurate judgment is held and written by those whose view is supported by the date of his anointing, namely the year 1070: William of Malmesbury, book I of *On the Deeds of the English Bishops*; Roger of Howden on the same subject; Matthew Paris in the *Greater History*; and the account of Lanfranc’s election and anointing recorded at the beginning of his letters.

The others who report his death place it in 1090, such as the Worcester writer [Col. 1197D] and George Lily in the *Chronicle of the Kings of England*. They record his ordination in 1071, as do the Canterbury Tables, and agree with Lily in saying that the archbishopric was vacant for five years.

Finally, all agree on this: that Lanfranc sat for nineteen years, although, as I have warned, Malmesbury’s opinion is much more credible, since he was flourishing while Lanfranc was declining. He preserves both the time during which the Church of Canterbury was governed and the period of its vacancy, counting more than four years and leaving the year of Lanfranc’s death and of Anselm’s succession to him begun by several months. He takes *excessit*—“he passed away”—in the sense signified by three of his words as four, although one can truly count this year, since Anselm, elected in March of the year 1093, took up the administration on the day before the Nones of December, when he had been anointed with sacred oil and adorned with pontifical insignia.

If, then, someone says that the year 1070, begun during most of its course—having extended to September, when Lanfranc was consecrated—should be counted, he may say that Lanfranc died in 1089, or alternatively in 1090. Neubrigensis, book I of *English Affairs*, chapter 2, thinks that Lanfranc died on a day in 1087. On the other hand, the author of the *Memorial of Histories*, otherwise a most diligent man, places it in 1096.

But when the earlier matters, which are connected, are necessary, the matters that follow also become necessary. I shall spare Volaterranus; religion will bear with it. For in book III of his *Commentaries*, under the title “On Narbonese Gaul,” near the end, he says that Lanfranc acted as schoolmaster under Pope Honorius III. Yet afterward, in book XXII, he notes that Honorius III was succeeded by Innocent III, that is, in the year 1216. Nor will he deny that our Anselm heard Lanfranc; nevertheless, in book XIII of the same *Commentaries*, he observes that Lanfranc flourished in the year 1058.

Now that the historical disagreement has been adjudicated, let us continue with what remains recorded in the Canterbury Tables concerning Lanfranc’s death:

> “Many things,” they say, “were produced about him at Canterbury in verse or prose; and many things were also published by the men of Bec, whom he himself had taught, as well as by other sophists, concerning the spiritual gifts divinely given to him.”

Archbishop, etc. See above, column 1049.

“The Anselm of Bec, however, inserted the aforesaid memory of his compatriot tearfully into a volume in heroic verse.”

Thus far the Victorian codex and the manuscript of Bec. If anyone desires more, let him consult William of Malmesbury, the writer of Jumièges, Roger of Howden, Matthew Paris, Thomas Walsingham in the *Hippodigma of Neustria* under the year 1071; Florence of Worcester in the *Chronicle*; Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book XXV, chapters 36, 37, and 43.

To these funeral collections I have added the latest item. Although it occurred while Lanfranc was still alive, because it was covered in such a way that only his death revealed it, we uncover it here alone. The manuscript *Chronicle of Bec* supplied it in these words:

> “To the most reverend Father WILLIAM, and to the entire congregation of Saint Mary of Bec, brother WILLIAM, abbot of Cormeliensis, a foster-son of your piety.

[The supplied source ends here.]

“Dear lords and brothers, I relate to you something concerning the venerable Father Herluin and his prior Lanfranc which, as I believe, was known to no mortal except myself. Lanfranc himself related it to me with his own lips and strictly forbade me to tell anyone so long as he lived. Having observed his prohibition until now, I at last disclose it with confidence, since no prohibition restrains me any longer. I call upon God himself as the witness to the truth of this disclosure—God whom I know to be the destroyer of all liars—for the Psalm says: ‘You will destroy all who speak falsehood’ (Psalm 5:7).

“This Lanfranc, during Father Herluin’s leadership, humbly entered Becc for the sake of conversion; and, once received, he persevered there most steadfastly until the end of his life, divine grace protecting him. At that time Becc was small in its buildings, poor in worldly fortune, and poorer still in its religious discipline. The aforesaid father indeed possessed strength through the love of God, but lacked the consolation of useful brothers. Yet, in accordance with what is written, ‘Entrust your concern to the Lord, and he himself will sustain you’ (Psalm 54:23), he continually entreated God’s mercy with prayers, asking that he send him such a man by whose consolation he might be comforted, by whose counsel encouraged, and by whose assistance supported.

“God therefore sent him Lanfranc, learned in the liberal arts, distinguished for the uprightness of his conduct, fortified by divine reason, and supported by the virtue of discernment. He proved useful to him in all things and suited to everything he piously desired. Indeed, through his goodness and industry, his teaching and effectiveness, divine mercy ordered this monastery, as all know, according to the discipline of sacred religion; enlarged it with many honors, lands, and estates; and elevated it, through numerous noble and honorable persons, to the praise and glory of his name.

“But I shall come to the account that occasioned these preliminary remarks. Seeing the brothers’ indolence, the depravity of their conduct, and their transgression of discipline, and also suspecting that certain men envied him because they feared he would become influential, Lanfranc did not know what to do or where to turn. He was wearied by their dishonorable way of life and ardently longed for the sweetness of a solitary existence.

“Accordingly, pretending to be ill, he asked Fulcrannus the gardener to bring him every day the roots of certain thistles, which he claimed would provide a remedy for his digestive disorder. He did this in order to accustom his body to such food, as though he were preparing to live in the wilderness. When, therefore, he was already preparing body and mind for flight by a nocturnal escape, and Lord Herluin the abbot suspected nothing of the matter, an exceptionally gifted boy, Hugo, who had recently died—the son of Baldrich of Auverville and nephew of the same abbot—appeared to him as he rested in bed, clothed in white.

“Not at all disturbed by the sight, the abbot addressed him affectionately: ‘What is it, my son? How are you?’ And the boy replied cheerfully: ‘I am well, Father, because through God’s mercy and your intercession I have been freed from every torment. But God has sent me to you to tell you this: if you do not look after yourself, you will not have Master Lanfranc.’

“The astonished abbot asked: ‘How so, my son?’ The boy answered: ‘Because he desires a solitary life and has resolved to leave the monastery. He does not approve of the brothers’ conduct and way of life. Consider, therefore, what you should do, since it is not in your interest.’ Having said this, the boy disappeared.

“Struck with astonishment at what he had heard, the abbot passed the remainder of the night awake in vigils and prayers. At first light, as soon as he was able to speak, he summoned Lanfranc and had him sit alone with him. The abbot’s heart was tormented by inward grief; his voice was constricted in his throat; and the tears that burst forth abundantly revealed the pain of his heart.

“Seeing this, Lanfranc threw himself upon the ground and humbly begged the abbot to tell him why he was weeping so bitterly. At last the abbot broke out in these words:

“‘Alas for me, whom God threatens with such a loss! Woe is me, who have lost my counsel and forfeited my help! Many times, with great sighs, I have asked God, and with abundant tears I have entreated divine mercy, to grant me such a man that, through his counsel and assistance, I might reform this place and restore to the monks whatever was pleasing to God. When God brought you here, Brother Lanfranc, I believed that the prayers of my humility had been heard. I intended to transfer my burden to you. I hoped that you would bear the whole weight of my responsibility. Yet now—for I do not know why—you are striving to leave this place, abandoning me, and you desire to go into the wilderness.’

“Lanfranc, realizing that his intention had been exposed, and that the purpose of his heart, which he had thought hidden, had been clearly revealed, immediately fell at the abbot’s feet and humbly asked how such things had become known to him. The abbot then disclosed the vision to him in a gentle voice and explained what had been divinely revealed to him through the boy, as we have related above.

“Lanfranc was struck with wonder and greatly admired God’s grace in the abbot. Prostrate upon the ground, he immediately confessed to the Father everything he had intended, with a contrite heart. Having accepted his penance and obtained absolution, he promised that he would never leave him and would obey his commands in all things.

“The abbot gave immense thanks to almighty God and, as soon as he could, appointed Lanfranc prior, entrusting to his care everything within and outside the monastery that lay under its jurisdiction. Divine protection made them so united in mind that no occasion for disagreement ever arose between them.

“Lanfranc, neither wishing to disclose the vision publicly nor to conceal it entirely, told it to a certain monk named William, whom he had raised and taught from childhood and loved dearly, commanding him not to tell anyone so long as he lived in the body. William kept this command until extreme old age. After Lanfranc’s death, when no prohibition any longer bound him, he wrote down what he had heard and related it to the abbot and monks of Becc, as we have digressed above.”

Thus far William’s letter, whose summary the Becc biographer incorporated into his Life of the same Lanfranc. From it I shall report one thing only, and that the final one: when the Canterbury church, first begun by Lanfranc himself and eventually brought to its summit by William of Gurbol, the third archbishop after him, was to be consecrated, the ashes of all those buried there were raised according to custom. At that time a certain monk cut off a piece of Lanfranc’s chasuble, which filled everyone who smelled it with an exceedingly fragrant odor.

because nothing of that kind was ever heard concerning him, both his absence sufficiently exonerates him from this charge, and his death rules out any new accusation against him. As for me, I want all people to hold this opinion of me as true. Thus I hold what we confess in the Creed when we say: “I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.” And: “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth.” And: “Whoever wishes to be saved, it is necessary above all that he hold the catholic faith,” and what follows.

These three principles of Christian confession [Note: “of Christian religion” in the manuscript], which I have set forth here [Note: “proposed” in the manuscript], I both believe in my heart and confess with my mouth; and I am certain that whoever wishes to deny any one of them—and specifically whoever asserts as truth the blasphemy which I stated above that I heard Roscelin utter—whether human being or angel, is anathema. And to make the matter certain, I say that so long as he persists in this obstinacy, let him be anathema. For he is altogether not a Christian.

But if he has been baptized and raised among Christians, he is in no way to be heard; nor should any account of his error be demanded from him, nor our truth presented to him. Once his perfidy has become indisputably known, he must either anathematize the poison which he spewed forth in uttering it, or be anathematized by all Catholics unless he repents.

For it is utterly foolish and unbridled [Note: “endless” in the manuscript] to recall to the uncertainty of wavering questions what has been most solidly founded upon the firm rock [Note: the manuscript reads: “founded, questions”]. Our faith must be defended by reason against the impious, not against those who profess to rejoice in the honor of the Christian name. From the latter it is justly to be demanded that they hold unshaken the pledge made at baptism; to the former it should reasonably be shown how unreasonably they despise us.

For a Christian ought to advance through faith toward understanding, not approach faith through understanding—or abandon faith if he is unable to understand. When he is able to reach understanding, he rejoices; but when he cannot, he venerates what he is unable to grasp.

I ask that these letters of ours be carried to the aforesaid council by your holiness; or, if you should not go, that they be sent through one of your learned men [Note: “through one of your letters” in the manuscript]. If the circumstances of my name require it, let them be read in the hearing of the entire assembly; otherwise, there will be no need for them to be read [Note: the manuscript reads: “there will be no need for them to be displayed.”] Farewell.

## LETTER XLII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO LANFRANC

That he ought never to consent to be appointed abbot against the will and counsel of his superior; and that, since he did not enter through obedience, he should in no way be blessed by him.

Brother ANSELM, although unworthy, nevertheless abbot of the monastery of Becc, to Brother LANFRANC, a monk of the same monastery: to turn away from evil and do good.

I, Brother Anselm, your lover in God, your faithful counselor, your abbot by divine arrangement and your election, admonish, advise, and command you, Brother Lanfranc, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to read this faithful letter of mine attentively more than twice or three times, and, standing with your heart before the strict Judge, in whose presence you always are, to consider my words and counsel.

If it should happen in any way that someone else reads it—because you are unwilling or unable to read it—I adjure him by almighty God not to withhold from your soul this salutary counsel, but to disclose to you this command of mine, whether you are hearing or reading it, and to present the entire letter to you for reading. If he refuses to do this, may God demand your sin from him, so that there may be no excuse on the day when God’s just judgment is revealed.

Before you accepted the gift of the abbacy [Note: “the gift of the abbot” in the manuscript], I told you and others, privately and publicly, in heart and by mouth, that I did not want you to accept it; that I would neither approve nor advise it; and that I would never command it. If you accepted it without my command, I also said that you would never receive the abbatial blessing from any bishop with my consent.

Yet, by some hidden judgment from above, I did not know what I would feel when you accepted that same office. But after it had happened, a heavy burden of the matter suddenly entered my heart, and God’s terrible judgment disclosed itself: “I heard, and my belly trembled; I considered, and I was afraid” (Habakkuk 3:16). “My heart was broken within me; all my bones trembled” (Jeremiah 23:9).

I perceived that the matter was detestable before God and before all who had been enlightened by him.
