Therefore, as I sorrowfully say, you first, and through you our entire order, and above all I, your grieving and shame-filled father, together with your mother, our Church, have become “a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us” (Psalm 78:4). To all who hear of it, it has become an example of dishonoring and destroying the Church of God, of which you have made yourself the beginning and leader in our time and in this region.

Bear with me, son, for speaking so harshly. I am not driven by anger arising from hatred; pain arising from love compels me. Your sorrowful brother desires to help his brother who is perishing; the trembling shepherd hastens to rescue from the jaws of the lion the sheep of his formidable lord. The grieving father strives to recall his wretched son, who is hastening into hell.

Return, then; return to your heart. Examine your deed and shake your mind awake. You rejected the eternal counsel and held to a rejected counsel. For “the Lord rejects the counsels of princes, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 32:10).

Christ, the truth, did not make you abbot, but your greed and the rashness of those who do not perceive the things that are God’s. Remember that “whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber. The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy” (John 10:1). My son, you did not enter by the door, because you did not enter through Christ. You did not enter through Christ, because you did not enter through the truth. You did not enter through the truth, because you did not enter through uprightness.

A monk does not enter an abbacy through uprightness if he does not enter through a regular election and through obedience. Do not excuse yourself. You will say to me: “I did not enter through obedience because you did not forbid me.” That is sufficient to remove uprightness, because you did not enter through obedience.

It is true that I did not say, “I forbid it,” or “I command you not to do it.” I saw that this was sufficient for an intelligent man, because I kept saying without interruption: “My heart does not want it; it does not approve it; my mouth does not advise or command it, nor will it command it. If you accept the abbacy without my command, you will never receive the blessing from the archbishop.”

A monk ought not to wait for an order from his superior’s mouth if he knows his abbot’s will or counsel. Since, then, you did not enter through the door, it is painful for me to say it; but consider and understand what the truth calls you and what it testifies that you have come to do.

## LETTER XLIII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO WANDREGISILUS

He consoles those afflicted in tribulation and states that he never consented to Lanfranc’s becoming their abbot.

To the lords and dearest brothers, Lord Walter, prior of the monastery of Saint Wandregisilus [Note: Saint Wandregisilus. This monastery is still called by the name of its founder; in common usage, Saint-Wandrille, approximately ten miles from Rouen. It is elsewhere called Fontanella in the Life of Saint Audoenus, or Fontonilla in Gemmeticus, Book VII of the Dukes of Normandy, chapter 23, on account of the spring flowing nearby. It was destroyed by the Normans and rebuilt by Richard II, duke of Normandy. The monastery was constructed by Wandregisilus himself, ten miles from Rouen], and to the other monks of the same monastery who are with him, Brother ANSELM: after present tribulation, temporal and eternal consolation.

Lord Northmannus asked me on your behalf to write some consolation to your affection and to show you our position concerning Lanfranc. As for consolation, because of the shortness of time it is enough for me to write what Holy Scripture says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience; and patience has a perfect work” (James 1:2). And elsewhere: “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations” (Acts 14:21). And: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear; but with the testing he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Since so many good things are truly promised to us through tribulation, we must neither be broken nor despair nor in any way abandon our good purpose because of any tribulation. Rather, the more we are worn down by the adversity of tribulation, the more fervently we must persevere in our good resolve, after the likeness of the mustard seed [Note: “the multitude of the grain” in the manuscript] (Matthew 13:51).

Therefore be confident that, with God’s assent, joy will follow tribulation. If anyone among you should fail in this tribulation, say: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19), because he was not rooted with us.

As for our will, our mind and tongue declare that if I had once wished and commanded Lanfranc to be your abbot—which certainly I did not do—he has shown himself so cruel toward you that now I could not even wish it. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO GISLEBERT

That he was seized by a most troublesome fever while returning from Caen to Becc, but that it fled when he considered asking them for the assistance of their prayers.

[Col. 1199B]

To the reverend Lord and Father, Abbot GISLEBERT, and to the lords and brothers entrusted to his holiness who reside in the monastery at Caen, Brother ANSELM: that he may be a faithful servant and brother.

After I recently departed, having been taken away from your longed-for presence—as you know—I was unable to visit Becc before the feast of Saint Benedict because of many impediments. During that interval, while I was afflicted with many cares and bodily pains, a fever suddenly attacked me in France, fiercely threatening that I would never again see you or our other lords at Becc, and greatly frightening me. Twice it dared to touch your servant.

But when it saw me intently considering sending to you and to as many others as I could for the aid and assistance of your prayers, it fled in terror from the man whom it had terrified. Yet it eagerly seized and carried away with it the small amount of appetite for eating and sleeping, and of bodily strength, that I possessed. Thus I have not yet been able to drive from me these slaves of its—namely, disgust and sleeplessness, together with the weakness associated with them, which are accustomed always to follow in its tracks.

I report this to your affection because I always wish the condition of my littleness to be known to you, and I do not doubt that you wish the same. Know that until I see you, I always acknowledge myself your debtor and bound to come to you. Help me, therefore, with your prayers, so that according to my desire I may discharge my debt. Farewell, now and always.

## LETTER XLV

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO HENRY

He pleads on behalf of a runaway monk who wishes to return to the fold and repay borrowed money.

To the lords and friends, and dearest brothers, Lord Prior HENRY and the others residing with him in the Canterbury monastery, servants of God in Christ’s Church, Brother ANSELM: always to advance toward better things in the purpose of a holy life and never to fail.

[Col. 1201A]

Our dearest brother Moses, who through youthful levity and another’s deceit abandoned your cloister of holy conduct—like the son of our mother Eve, who was deceived in paradise and thereby lost the delights of paradise—has, under the protection of heavenly providence, neither squandered his substance with prostitutes nor, compelled by hunger, fed another’s pigs, nor desired to be filled with the pods that pigs eat [Note: “to be filled with the pods” in the manuscript]. Rather, with the satiety of his mind, which he had received from your spiritual table, not yet exhausted, he has at last arrived at our monastery, as at a familiar harbor after many voyages across the sea of the world.

Although, because of consciousness of his guilt, he fears the severity of justice, since the Apostle says, “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 5:29), he nevertheless desires by every means to be gathered again into the flock in which he was suckled and nourished. And because he now judges himself unworthy to be called either son or brother, he wishes at least to deserve to be among you as one of your hired servants.

He fears even more for his servant, whom he himself drew into consenting to and serving his own offense, than for his own flesh, since he sees that, if the servant were punished by a just judgment with some penalty, an account would be demanded from his own soul.

He is also so anxious about money borrowed from another under an agreement of repayment, which he recklessly spent through another’s deceit, that unless, through the help of your generosity and with permission to seek assistance wherever he can, he happens to be relieved of that debt, he never hopes that his heart can be comforted of this shame.

But because he realizes that his own prayers can neither suffice nor ought to suffice for so many and such great matters, he asks me, your servant, since he presently has no one more faithful to you or more confident that he can obtain something from you, to intercede on his behalf.

Yet since there is no greater intercession than skin for skin, the placing of one soul in exchange for another, as the Lord says, “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his soul for his friends” (John 15:13), let your affection know that Lord Moses is clothed from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, all around, in the skin of your servant Brother Anselm, and that his mouth is my mouth.

If anyone among you is one against whom I have voluntarily sinned at some time, let him first strike my skin for the aforesaid fault and forbid my mouth food. After this fault, however, I most earnestly commend my skin to Brother Moses to guard, as he loves his own; but I do not commend it to you so as to spare him. For if my skin is wounded or more severely stripped because of his fault, I shall demand it from him; but if anyone spares him, I shall thank that person.

As for his servant, know that I have no other skin, because his salvation is my salvation and his soul is my soul.

Since what he requests concerning the money is easy to provide, I think it will not be difficult to obtain it from your mercy. Before he begins to return, we wish to hear your will concerning all these matters through your letters. This is not because he would refuse, if you commanded it, even to hasten to torments, but because he wishes to return with good hope and joy to those whom he longs for. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO GONDULF

He pleads on behalf of the same runaway.

To the lord and Father, truest friend, reverend Bishop GONDULF, Brother ANSELM: to persevere in holiness in this life and remain in happiness in the future [Note: “to remain in happiness” in the manuscript].

If we knew that repayment of your benevolence and benefits consisted in giving thanks, we would certainly fill many sheep skins with thanksgivings. But because we know that your reward rests not in an irrevocable voice or perishable writing, but in the fullness of eternal happiness, we therefore refrain from returning thanks for each of your benefits individually.

Just as we know that your mutual affection remains unchanging in you, so we take care to preserve it inviolate in ourselves.

Concerning Brother Moses, a young man from Canterbury who is now in our monastery and wishes to return to his monastery in England, we ask your holiness to grant him, for love of us, forgiveness of his offense, as we trust you will; and to ensure that he be kindly received by Lord Henry the prior and the entire congregation.

May it please your holiness to read the letter which we sent concerning this matter to the aforesaid prior and congregation [Note: “that he be received; may it please your holiness to ensure this by the letter” in the manuscript]. According to what we request in it, before Brother Moses departs from us, may we deserve to receive the common will of your benevolence in letters marked with your seal. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO GISLEBERT

Concerning the fever by which he was afflicted and from which he recovered, as he writes above in Letter 44.

To the lord, servant; to the friend, friend; to the beloved, beloved; to Lord Abbot GISLEBERT, Brother ANSELM: everlasting joy.

If all is well, sound, and prosperous with the beloved Lord Abbot Gislebert, my beloved lover, my heart truly rejoices in it, because that is certainly my desire. If a stranger had bestowed upon us and our affairs the affection and benefits which you bestow, we would certainly have expressed great thanksgiving in writing and speech, lest we should fail in it [Note: the manuscript reads: “If you bestow them, certainly a stranger would bestow them upon strangers, we would…”]. But since this is done by one in whom we can never despair, we believe that it is enough always to offer greater thanks with a ready will, especially since you yourselves know that we keep this same gratitude continually in the treasury of our hearts.

I know that your affection desires to learn how our condition stands. By God’s protection, according to our circumstances and the changing character of this time, all would be well and prosperous, except that when I was recently in France, while I was already afflicted by certain other labors, a slight fever suddenly attacked me and frightened me more than it harmed me.

But when it saw my mind intensely turned toward sending to our friends for the assistance of their prayers, it fled in terror after having twice touched the terrified man. As a result, for some time afterward I suffered loss of appetite, difficulty sleeping, and greater weakness of my limbs.

I greet with all the devotion I can our most beloved lords and brothers, your sons, concerning whose sweet affection toward me, known to me by experience, I rejoice whenever I reflect upon it.

Concerning Richard, your servant, who followed you into England at your command, I should like, if it does not displease you, to ask your benevolence on his behalf. Since God has acquitted him by his judgment of the charge brought against him, and since he has not abandoned the faithful service he began, there is now nothing that ought to oppose the good will you initially showed toward him.

He is a just man, and it is more fitting for the authority of your honor that your constancy repel every assault of perversity directed against him than that another’s unworthy obstinacy should turn aside the praiseworthy intention of your benevolence. May your affection, ever sweet to me, remain well.

## LETTER XLVIII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO WALTER

A layman recently converted is to be instructed in the spirit of gentleness.

To the most beloved lord and brother WALTER, Brother ANSELM, abbot of Becc: greetings.

Lord Robert of Briodua gives you great thanks for the kindness which you show him beyond anything he could ever have hoped, and, with his thanksgiving, he testifies to you that you have suffered many unpleasant things both from him and from others on his account.

Therefore I give you thanks with affection, praise you with thanksgiving, and, in praising you, ask your discernment to remember that “a bruised reed is not to be broken” (Matthew 12:20; Isaiah 42:3), and that “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke 5:31), so that he may persevere in what he has begun.

For it is to be hoped that he who, through your patience and by God’s mercy, has already advanced to some degree will progress through that same mercy to greater things if you persevere in what you have begun. This itself is a great sign of his progress: he wishes, through me, your friend, to be highly commended to the one through whom he recognizes that he has advanced—not so that you should consent to his vices, but so that you may accommodate his weakness and gradually raise him from them as a sick man is raised.

He does not yet dare promise that he will soon wholly abandon the conduct in which he was brought up in a manner contrary to what is expedient. But with willingness and desire he promises that whenever he falls, he will, with God’s help, rise through your assistance and counsel and through your prayers, and that eventually he will stand steadfastly in good conduct [Note: “rise again” in the manuscript].

Greet on our behalf the lords and brothers, the monks of your congregation. As a faithful friend, I ask them to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3), if they wish to be the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), who, just as he cannot be divided, cannot dwell in discord. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO GIRARD

That a certain monk of Becc may be excused from governing the church of Saint Vulmar, lest wolves devour the lamb and lions the sheep.

To the lord and Father, reverend Bishop GIRARD of the Morini, Brother ANSELM, called abbot of Becc: that he may be yours.

It would be useful to say much because of the necessity of the matter, but because of many considerations I may not. In a brief address, therefore, and with great affection, I beg your paternal compassion both to act yourselves and to persuade our lord the archbishop of Reims, on your part and mine, to do what belongs to your prudent discernment: namely, that this brother of ours not be vexed fruitlessly any longer, nor, because of him, be deprived of suitable counsel and arrangement concerning the church of Saint Vulmar.

It is impossible for him to remain peacefully any longer in that same church because of many matters which would take too long to recount, or to make progress toward any useful end except with excessive labor. Therefore, again and again I beg you not to attend so exclusively to the rigor of your authority that, through your severity, you needlessly break the soul of your neighbor beyond repair.

I beg you, do not continue returning the fleeing lamb to the wolves; do not entrust the sheep to lion cubs who must be subdued; do not drive an innocent man who protests into the furnace of the Chaldeans without any beneficial result.

Permit another to be appointed in his place, whose mind is more prepared to endure the inward and outward struggles associated with evil conduct, and who may attempt what he has proved himself unable to do—namely, to bring those living together into useful concord, if in any way, with God’s help, this can be achieved.

But if your judgment should immovably decide something contrary to our wish, first build peace and good will in the aforesaid church, and then recall him, pacified and benevolent, into a peaceful household among benevolent people. Farewell.

## LETTER L

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO JOHN AND BOSO

He consoles him in his grief over the loss of his notebooks and promises to send him the musical composition.

To the friends, beloved ones, Lord JOHN and Lord BOSO, Brother ANSELM: inviolable joy in this life and the future.

Although wisdom and affection are delightful and sweet, in the uncertainty of this life they sometimes produce pain and bitterness. The truer and greater they are, the more rarely and the more severely they do so. For the wiser are deceived less often; but when this happens, they are hurt more deeply. And those who love more truly offend those whom they love less often. Yet when this happens, they afflict themselves more severely.

Therefore, when you sent word that you were taking so heavily the fact that you had done something slightly carelessly—if indeed what you did concerning our notebooks should be judged careless [Note: “what concerning” in the manuscript]—you demonstrated that this did not arise from habit or negligence, but from that necessity which follows from the fact that there is no human being who does not sin.

Thus you prove yourselves certainly more prudent in caution and more fervent in affection. The more truly I perceive this, the more rightly I must confess that the injury to your hearts ought to injure my heart.

When you wrote to me about the wound inflicted on your hearts because of your affection for me, since you feared that you had offended me, you inflicted a similar wound upon my heart. Insofar as I learned that you loved me through the pain of your concern, and insofar as you grieved, I rightly grieved as well.

Heal your wound, therefore, so that it may cease to ache, just as you wish to heal mine so that it may not suffer with you. What you feared was lost is safe, and we possess what you left in safety.

Greet the reverend and most beloved Lord Abbot Rodulf and our beloved brothers entrusted to him. We shall reclaim the musical composition you request from the prior of Caen, to whom we entrusted it, and we shall send it to you as soon as we can [Note: “as quickly as possible” in the manuscript].

## LETTER LI

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO BALDRICH AND THE OTHER MONKS

Concerning his prolonged stay in England, his prayer to Saint Nicholas, and his letter against Roscelin.

To his longed-for ones, Lord Prior BALDRICH and the other brothers who are with him, Brother ANSELM, theirs: always to be well within and without.

I cannot yet entrust you with any information about the benefit of our journey to England, insofar as it concerns our Church. For the king still delays replying to our petition, although he himself and the other princes of England show me love and honor far beyond my due. Concerning my safety, the monk of Lord Abbot Gislebert, who is the bearer of this letter, will be able to inform you better than our letter; I want you to welcome him with great kindness [Note: Col. 1205D: the manuscript reads suscipiatis, “receive,” for excipiatis, “welcome.”]. I do not expect our return before Lent. Write to me about the things taking place around you—whatever you know that I ought to know. Send me the prayer to Saint Nicholas that I composed [Col. 1206C], and the letter that I began to write against the statements of Roscelin; and send whatever other letters of mine Lord Mauritius has which he has not sent [Note: Col. 1205D: the manuscript reads “your other letters” instead of “my other letters”]. Greet our mothers, Lady Eva and Lady Basilia. Farewell.

## LETTER LII [Note: Col. 1205D: compared with two Victorine manuscripts]. TO ERNULF

That a profession made and kept by a monk is not to be demanded from him again when he is blessed as abbot.

To the lord and friend, Abbot Ernulf [Note: Col. 1205D: the manuscripts read “To the lord and father, Abbot” instead of “To the lord and friend, Abbot”], Brother Anselm sends greetings for the present and future life.

Your brother, Lord Nicholas, told me on your behalf that I should send you our advice concerning this matter, because the Bishop of Bayeux is inviting you to the blessing [Col. 1206D] that is owed to your election.

But whatever I think about it, I have already told your affection in person. For we know that we must always show, in word and deed, regular obedience to our superiors. To repeat that obedience in writing, so long as we are known not to have renounced it, is certainly superfluous [Note: Col. 1205D: the manuscripts read est, quod (“is, that/which”) for est, ad quod (“is; for which”)]; and if anyone wishes to compel us to do so when we are promoted to the leadership of an abbey, this appears to be done without any reason.

For when we professed the conversion of our way of life and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 1207A; Note: the manuscripts read “the profession of our morals,” for “the conversion of our way of life unto obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict”], we certainly promised obedience—not only to abbots, nor only for as long as we should remain under an abbot, but to all our superiors, and for as long as we should live. For the same Rule teaches that a monk must submit himself with complete obedience to his superior, and that, following the example of the Lord, we must preserve obedience unto death (Philippians 2:8).

Therefore, if someone has once written and read a monastic profession, and has never renounced it, it is pointless for anyone to demand another from him. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. TO LANFRANC AND ALL THE MONKS OF BEC

Brother Anselm and the whole congregation of the monastery of Bec send to the lord and revered father, Archbishop Lanfranc, that which is his.

[Col. 1208A]

Grieving deeply over the illness of your fatherly holiness, we do not cease praying to God for your health. For we regard your illness as our tribulation and your health as our safety; and we understand that your life is necessary not only for us but also for Holy Mother Church, to the extent that your name reaches.

By God’s favor, your instruction concerning the employment of Lombards will henceforth be observed. We earnestly ask you to assist Lord Baldwin, whom we are sending to England on our affairs—affairs that he will be able to explain to you himself, insofar as you come to know them and they find favor with your fatherly kindness—as is your custom.

May almighty God preserve your life for us and for his Church for a long time, in health and prosperity, and also in holiness pleasing to him. Amen.

[Col. 1207A]

## PART THREE OF THE WORKS.—THE FOUR BOOKS OF LETTERS

1057 **Admonition**

1059 **Book One**, containing the letters Anselm wrote before he became abbot.

1059 **Letter I.** To Lanfranc. He congratulates him on his election as archbishop and amicably returns a cup that had been given to him as a friendly gift.

1063 **Letter II.** To Odo and Lanzo. At Lanzo’s request, he prescribes a rule for a holier life.

1067 **Letter III.** To the monk Robert. He asks for his prayers and for the friendship of Anastasius, his fellow monk.

1068 **Letter IV.** To Gondulf. Although he writes less frequently, he has not forgotten him, to whom he ought to write more frequently.

1069 **Letter V.** To Henry. He says that he loves Henry more deeply because of his good morals and religious way of life; and that the absence of a friend must be endured through obedience [Col. 1221].

1070 **Letter VI.** To Hugh. He instructs Hugh to bear the burden of his prelate, even though the latter is undisciplined, and not to leave him.

1071 **Letter VII.** To Gondulf. He gives Gondulf thanks for the benefits he had bestowed upon the men of Bec.

1072 **Letter VIII.** To Herluin. An exhortation kindling hatred of the world.

1073 **Letter IX.** To Abbot Gerbert. He congratulates the abbot because, at his request, he came to the aid of an afflicted widow.

1074 **Letter X.** To Rodulf. He says that he never stated that he would no longer lend him his books; indeed, he is sincerely prepared to lend him everything.

1075 **Letter XI.** To the same. He encourages Rodulf, whom the business of the provostship was calling away from frequent reading and the work of prayer, and who judged himself unequal to those duties.

1076 **Letter XII.** To Lanfranc. He gives thanks for gifts.

1078 **Letter XIII.** To Girard. He advises Girard, who desires to leave the world, to go to Lanfranc, from whom he will receive what will enable him to settle his debt.

1079 **Letter XIV.** To Gondulf. He attests his singular love for Gondulf, as in Letters 4 and 7 above.

1080 **Letter XV.** To Henry. That it is not expedient to hasten to Italy to free his sister from the yoke of servitude.

1082 **Letter XVI.** To Avesgot. He cites the obstacles on account of which he advises him to undertake responsibility for the studies of the young man commended to him.

1083 **Letter XVII.** To William and Roger. He promises them a share in his prayers.

1084 **Letter XVIII.** To his uncles Lambert and Folcerad. He asks to be informed of his uncles’ safety.

1084 **Letter XIX.** To Lanfranc. He congratulates Lanfranc on having sent his nephew to Bec rather than elsewhere, and excuses Girard’s delay.

1086 **Letter XX.** To Gondulf. Concerning three prayers to the Mother of God.

1086 **Letter XXI.** To Rodulf. He urgently asks Rodulf to transcribe an antiphoner in musical notation.

1087 **Letter XXII.** From Lanfranc to Anselm. He earnestly requests Anselm’s prayers and those of others, and commends his nephew to him.

1088 **Letter XXIII.** From Lanfranc to Lanfranc and Guido. From Archbishop Lanfranc to his nephew and the latter’s companion, monks undergoing their novitiate at Bec.

1088 **Letter XXIV.** To Lanfranc, concerning the nephew received at Bec for his novitiate, mentioned above in Letters 19 and 22. He also commends to him Maurice, who is suffering from a head ailment.

1089 **Letter XXV.** To Henry. He commends to him the monk Maurice, who is suffering from a head ailment.

1089 **Letter XXVI.** To Gondulf. He says that a friend should not be thanked for gifts sent by him; he is still concerned about the monk Maurice.

1089 **Letter XXVII.** To Herluin. He says that day by day he pours out a prayer to God in Herluin’s name, although Herluin scarcely reads his admonitions. He asks him to show himself a brother toward Maurice.

1090 **Letter XXVIII.** To Albert. He suggests conversion from the world; he also commends Maurice, asking Albert to treat him by his medical art.

1093 **Letter XXIX.** To Lanzo. He warns Lanzo to beware of the devil’s temptations.

1102 **Letter XXX.** To Arnulf. He advises him not to choose a place where he will teach, but one where he will be taught more.

1102 **Letter XXXI.** To Lanfranc. Concerning the holy progress of Lanfranc’s nephew and the head pain from which he was suffering.

1104 **Letter XXXII.** To Henry. He gives thanks for the careful treatment of the monk Maurice.

1105 **Letter XXXIII.** To Gondulf. One need not write to a friend whose memory is perpetually in one’s heart.

1105 **Letter XXXIV.** To Maurice. He congratulates Maurice on his restored health; he asks for the Rule of Saint Dunstan and Bede’s book *On Times*.

1107 **Letter XXXV.** To Maurice. He does not write because of the lack of messengers to carry letters; he asks for aphorisms with glosses.

1108 **Letter XXXVI.** To Albert. He reports his thanks for Maurice of Bec’s care [Col. 1222], and advises flight from the world.

1109 **Letter XXXVII.** To Frodelina. He arranges a mutual sharing with her of merits.

1110 **Letter XXXVIII.** To William. He rejoices at William’s letters brought to him, and turns him away from the vanity of the world.

1111 **Letter XXXIX.** To Maurice. He says that he has received the gifts sent.

1111 **Letter XL.** To Helgot. He commends to him the brother of Abbot Roger.

1112 **Letter XLI.** To Lanfranc. He praises Lanfranc’s modesty concerning the smallness of the gifts, and gives his opinion concerning the monks’ abstinence.

1113 **Letter XLII.** To Henry. He is grieved that they scarcely have leisure for writing and scarcely any leisure for reading and prayer.

1113 **Letter XLIII.** To Herluin, Gondulf, and Maurice. He exhorts the monks of Bec, then residing in the Church of Canterbury, always to advance toward better things.

1115 **Letter XLIV.** To Hernostus. He rouses one oppressed by the sharpest pains to patience.

1116 **Letter XLV.** To Lambert and Folcerad. He warns them not to be seized by the lethargic sleep of the world.

1116 **Letter XLVI.** To Folcerad. He says that he is held by an extraordinary desire to see him, but is detained because in France the soldiers allowed no one free passage.

1117 **Letter XLVII.** To Peter. He congratulates him on his honorable studies and exhorts him to a purer life.

1118 **Letter XLVIII.** To Lanfranc. He protests against being addressed with an honorific title.

1119 **Letter XLIX.** To Henry. He gives thanks for the gold, although in it the giver’s disposition is praised more than the gift; and he asks pardon for Osbern.

1119 **Letter L.** To Gondulf. A familiar letter.

1120 **Letter LI.** To Maurice. Concerning the letters received from Maurice and his imminent return to Normandy. He asks him to bring with him aphorisms with glosses.

1121 **Letter LII.** To Fulk. That he should accept the dignity offered to him, which he cannot refuse without disobedience.

1121 **Letter LIII.** To Walter. That he should not abandon responsibility for the flock entrusted to him on account of slander.

1122 **Letter LIV.** To Henry. That he should patiently endure the envy and slanders of ill-wishers.

1124 **Letter LV.** To Maurice. He congratulates him on hearing Arnulf the Grammarian.

1125 **Letter LVI.** To William. Concerning an excommunicated count who was involving himself in sacred matters. Concerning incontinent priests and lapsed persons holding sacred orders.

1129 **Letter LVII.** To Lanfranc. He writes favorably about Lanfranc’s nephew, and also about Osbern. He sends the Epistles of Blessed Paul.

1130 **Letter LVIII.** To Henry. He commends Osbern to him.

1131 **Letter LIX.** To Gondulf. He gives thanks, in his own name and in the names of Hugh and Basilia, for the gifts sent by Gondulf.

1131 **Letter LX.** To Maurice. He demands letters from him and praises him because he is loved by everyone everywhere.

1132 **Letter LXI.** From Durand to Anselm. Praise of Anselm’s meditations; he asks Anselm for the Epistles of Blessed Paul.

1133 **Letter LXII.** To Durand. A response to the preceding letter.

1134 **Letter LXIII.** To Lanfranc. He asks him to examine the *Monologion* he had published.

1135 **Letter LXIV.** To Henry. He advises obedience and patience.

1136 **Letter LXV.** To Maurice. Concerning Maurice’s return from England to Bec and the correction of the *Monologion*.

1137 **Letter LXVI.** To Lanfranc. He desires the return to Normandy of Guido, a novice of Bec.

1138 **Letter LXVII.** To Roger. He awaits Roger’s arrival.

1138 **Letter LXVIII.** To Lanfranc. Concerning several matters Lanfranc had noticed in Anselm’s little work, which Anselm himself defends by the authority of Saint Augustine.

1139 **Letter LXIX.** To Gondulf. He congratulates him on his pontifical dignity.

1140 **Letter LXX.** To Maurice. He admonishes him to endure Anselm’s absence patiently, for as long as God has so disposed concerning them.

1141 **Letter LXXI.** To Paul. He rejoices in his advancement to the abbacy of Saint Albans and prescribes how he ought to conduct himself there.

1142 **Letter LXXII.** To Humfrid. He asks him to devote himself to the instruction of the man who delivers his letters to him.

1143 **Letter LXXIII.** To Ida. He commends her for her charity toward the men of Bec and toward everyone [Col. 1223].

1144 **Letter LXXIV.** To Rainald. Concerning not making the *Monologion* widely public.

1144 **Letter LXXV.** To Gilbert. He says that he bears his friend’s absence with the greatest difficulty.

1145 **Letter LXXVI.** To Walter. He returns thanks and excuses himself concerning the solution of the proposed question.

1146 **Letter LXXVII.** To Adala. That she should obtain from her son leave from military service for a veteran soldier.

1147 **Book Two**, containing the letters Anselm wrote while he was abbot of Bec.

1147 **Letter I.** To Lanfranc. He gives thanks for his alms to the men of Bec and explains the poverty of the monastery of Bec.

1149 **Letter II.** To Lanfranc. Thanks are given for his generosity, especially for the gold he had sent for making a chalice.

1150 **Letter III.** To Gondulf. Although he is a bishop, Anselm professes a familiar friendship with him; and he commends to him the monks of Bec whom he is sending to England.

1151 **Letter IV.** To Baldwin. He entrusts to his care and governance the highly esteemed monks of Bec who are sailing to England.

1152 **Letter V.** To Henry. He commends the same men of Bec to him.

1152 **Letter VI.** From Anselm and Richard to Richard and Rohaid. They give thanks for benefits and entrust to Richard’s care the men of Bec whom they are sending to England at his urging.

1153 **Letter VII.** To Richard and the monks of Bec. That the men of Bec who have been brought to England should live religiously, and that Henry the chamberlain should be restrained from drunkenness.

1155 **Letter VIII.** To Maurice. Concerning a monk remaining too long at court, and concerning the evil—whether it is something.

1158 **Letter IX.** To the monks of Bec. Concerning his successful arrival in England, which he also wishes to have announced to Lady Eve.

1158 **Letter X.** To Rodulf. He rejoices that Rodulf has converted to the religious life.

1159 **Letter XI.** To Hugh. Concerning certain of Anselm’s little works requested by the archbishop, and the fact that he prefixed the title “abbot” to the titles of his works in order to exclude ambiguity.

1160 **Letter XII.** To Helinand. He exhorts him to persevere and to resist steadfastly the devil’s various temptations, which he describes.

1163 **Letter XIII.** To Lanfranc. He sends Gislebert to him and asks that he return him soon.

1163 **Letter XIV.** To the monks of Bec. That the monk who, against the abbot’s will, was staying in the monastery of Saint Magloire at Paris for the sake of study should return to his own monastery.

1164 **Letter XV.** To Fulk. He begs that the penitent apostate monk be treated more gently.

1165 **Letter XVI.** To Gislebert. He congratulates him on being appointed to govern the abbey of Westminster.

1166 **Letter XVII.** To Hugh. He wishes the titles of two little works to be changed, one to be called *Monologion*, the other *Proslogion*.

1167 **Letter XVIII.** To the monks of Bec. Concerning his prosperous voyage to England.

1167 **Letter XIX.** To William. He urges the soldier of the world to enlist in the service of Christ.

1170 **Letter XX.** To Henry. Concerning sending Folcerad to Bec: he asks that Folcerad live there under Anselm’s governance and requests a letter secured with the abbot’s seal.

1170 **Letter XXI.** To Folcerad. It is not expedient for him to come to Bec and then return; nor should he be received without letters bearing the seal of his abbot.

1171 **Letter XXII.** To Hugh. He offers him counsels with which he may instruct laypeople who visit him.

1173 **Letter XXIII.** To Peter. Before a cleric has freely promised stability, he cannot be detained unwillingly by an abbot. He must remain in the monastery in which he first made his petition and vow to become a monk.

1174 **Letter XXIV.** To Ida. He gives her great thanks for the benefits she has bestowed upon him and the others for his sake.

1175 **Letter XXV.** To William. If he loves Anselm, he should come to Bec and flee the world.

1176 **Letter XXVI.** To the monks of Bec. He exhorts them to live with complete integrity while the head of the monastery is absent, and gives them the reasons for his stay in England.

1179 **Letter XXVII.** To Robert. He asks that the man who had left his monastery without cause, while the abbot was absent, return to it [Col. 1224].

1179 **Letter XXVIII.** To the monks Haymo and Raynald. He earnestly exhorts them—who had come there from a distant place to visit Anselm—to put on the cowl at Bec.

1181 **Letter XXIX.** To Henry. That he should leave the world as soon as possible.

1182 **Letter XXX.** To Walchelm. A monk lent for a time cannot be retained against the will of the abbot who demands him back. He also intercedes for Gislebert.

1183 **Letter XXXI.** From Pope Gregory to Anselm. He commends himself and the Church to Anselm’s prayers and commands him to do justice to one of his converts.

1184 **Letter XXXII.** From Urban II to Anselm. That he should assist a bishop who is less knowledgeable in ecclesiastical affairs. That he should not delay visiting the Apostolic See, and should send to it what Hubert, his subdeacon and legate, had collected from the census of Saint Peter.

1184 **Letter XXXIII.** From Anselm to Urban. He explains the harsh persecution suffered by the bishop of Beauvais from both clergy and laity. He asks for an apostolic privilege for his monastery against episcopal domination.

1186 **Letter XXXIV.** To Urban. He fears that the bishop may be overwhelmed by such grave hardships and wishes him to be released from the episcopate.

1187 **Letter XXXV.** To John. Concerning the false and impious assertion of someone who said that the three persons in God were three things.

1188 **Letter XXXVI.** To Gislebert. He praises the manner of life established by the abbot. He leaves with Gislebert a brother whom he had brought back into the cloister.

1188 **Letter XXXVII.** To Ida. Whoever wishes to avoid failure must strive toward progress.

1189 **Letter XXXVIII.** To Robert. Someone who had resolved to sin but was divinely prevented from doing so, and who afterward rejoices that he did not sin, is not guilty as though he had committed the crime itself after being abandoned by God.

1190 **Letter XXXIX.** To Lambert. He exhorts this noble man to the monastic life.

1191 **Letter XL.** To Ermengard. With her husband’s consent, she had vowed continence; but when her husband wished to become a monk, she did not wish it. Anselm therefore begs her to consent.

1192 **Letter XLI.** To Fulk. Concerning Roscelin, who said that Lanfranc and Anselm agreed with him that there were three things in God and that one could truly say that there were three gods.

1194 **Letter XLII.** To Lanfranc. He ought never to have consented to being made abbot against the will and advice of his prelate; and since he did not enter through obedience, he must in no way be blessed by that prelate.

1196 **Letter XLIII.** To Wandregisil. He consoles those afflicted in tribulation. He also says that he never consented to Lanfranc’s becoming their abbot.

1199 **Letter XLIV.** To Gislebert. He says that he was seized by a most troublesome fever while returning from Caen to Bec; nevertheless, it departed when he began considering asking them for the aid of their prayers.

1200 **Letter XLV.** To Henry. He pleads for a runaway monk who desires to return to the fold and repay borrowed money.

1202 **Letter XLVI.** To Gondulf. He pleads for the same runaway monk.

1203 **Letter XLVII.** To Gislebert. Concerning the fever by which he was seized and about which he writes above in Letter 44.

1204 **Letter XLVIII.** To Walter. A layman recently converted should be instructed in a spirit of gentleness.

1204 **Letter XLIX.** To Girard. He asks that a certain monk of Bec be excused from governing the church of Saint Ulmar, lest wolves devour the lamb and lions the sheep.

1205 **Letter L.** To John and Boso. He consoles him in his grief over the loss of his quires. He promises to send him music.

1206 **Letter LI.** To Baldric and the other monks. Concerning his prolonged stay in England; his prayer at Saint Nicholas; and his letter against Roscelin.

1206 **Letter LII.** To Ernulf. A profession once made and kept by a monk must not be demanded from him again when the abbot is blessed.

1207 **Letter LIII.** To Lanfranc and all the monks of Bec. He sympathizes with Lanfranc, who is suffering from illness.

**END OF VOLUME ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-EIGHT.**
